rel.note: The second heading names Solomon again, this time over the collection of short sayings.
The purpose statement returns to "a proverb," the kind of saying this title introduces.
Here the book names "the wise" as another source of its sayings beside Solomon.
This heading shows that Hezekiah's men later copied more of Solomon's proverbs, so the book was gathered over time.
Agur's heading shows that the words of men other than Solomon also stand in the book.

units.notes:
• *Proverbs* translates mashal, a word wide enough to cover a brief maxim, a byword, a parable, a poem, and even a prophet's mocking song, which Isaiah calls a "proverb against the king of Babylon" (Isaiah 14:4). That range explains why the title stands over the long poems of chapters 1–9 as well as the short sayings from chapter 10 on.
• Where the word mashal comes from is uncertain. Some connect it with a verb meaning "to rule," others with one meaning "to be like" or "to compare." Because neither origin is settled, the meaning of "proverb" is best learned from how Scripture uses the word, not from either derivation.
• Solomon's name returns in the headings at 10:1 and 25:1. The second adds that "the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied" more of his proverbs, so the book reached its final form no earlier than Hezekiah's reign, long after Solomon's death.
• Bridges: "Solomon is recorded as the wisest of men; a man of wisdom, because a man of prayer." Compare 1 Kings 3:5–12, where Solomon asks for wisdom and God grants it.
• Compare 1 Kings 4:29–34, where Solomon's wisdom excels "the wisdom of all the men of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt," and people come from all nations to hear him.
units.summary: Solomon's name heads the book, but even Israel's wisest king needed to walk in the wisdom he wrote down.
units.principle: Wisdom is a gift God gives, not a possession anyone owns; even the wisest must keep walking in what they have received.
units.insight: Solomon's story holds both the glory and the warning of this book. God gave him "a wise and understanding heart" (1 Kings 3:12), yet in old age "his wives turned his heart after other gods" (1 Kings 11:4). His proverbs remain true, because their wisdom came from God. But his life shows that possessing wisdom and walking in it are not the same thing. That should sober every reader who knows the right answers. The title also points beyond Solomon. As son of David, king of peace and builder of the temple, he foreshadows a greater King. Jesus said of Himself, "indeed a greater than Solomon is here" (Matthew 12:42). In Him wisdom was not only possessed but perfectly lived. Whoever has failed to walk in what he knows finds in Christ both forgiveness and a new beginning.
units.application: If you teach, preach or lead a Bible study, pray this week for grace to live what you explain, not only to explain it. Parents, let your children see you obey a proverb, not just quote one. Young people, read one proverb each day this week and write down one decision it should shape. When someone uses a proverb as a guarantee against a person in pain, gently remind them that proverbs describe how life generally works.

rel.note: The motto names the same pair, wisdom and instruction, as what fools despise.
Truth, wisdom, instruction and understanding are to be bought and never sold, the same treasures this verse names.
The same word for instruction is used of the LORD's chastening, showing that this training includes correction.
Wisdom is called the principal thing, the goal this purpose statement sets first.

units.notes:
• *Wisdom* translates chokmah, a word Scripture also uses for a craftsman's skill. When the LORD filled Bezalel "with the Spirit of God, in wisdom" to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), the word described skilled hands. In Proverbs it is that kind of practiced skill, applied to the whole of life.
• Ironside defines this wisdom as "the ability to use knowledge aright," that is, the ability to put what one knows to right use.
• *Instruction* translates musar, which means training and discipline and includes correction. Proverbs uses the same word for "the chastening of the LORD" in 3:11, so the instruction this book offers corrects as well as informs.
• *Perceive* means to discern, to see the difference between things. Paul prays for the same gift, "that you may approve the things that are excellent" (Philippians 1:10).
• Wisdom and instruction return as a pair in 1:7, where they are what fools despise, and in 23:23: "Buy the truth, and do not sell it, Also wisdom and instruction and understanding."
units.summary: Proverbs was written to make you skilled at living, not just informed about life.
units.principle: Wisdom is a skill learned under instruction and correction, and it shows itself in the ability to tell true voices from false ones.
units.insight: Many of us want information more than formation. We would rather know about wisdom than submit to the training that makes us wise. Eve heard two voices in the garden, God's word and the serpent's question, and failed to tell them apart (Genesis 3:1–6). The serpent's words sounded like insight; they led to death. The same contest runs through this chapter and through every life. Jesus Himself "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men" (Luke 2:52). He grew in the skill of living as the true Son. In Him we find both the wisdom we lack and the patience that trains us in it. James puts the test plainly: "be doers of the word, and not hearers only" (James 1:22). The question is not how much we know but whether what we know has become skill.
units.application: Pick one area this week where you know more than you practice, such as your tongue, your spending or your temper. Ask God to train you there, and invite a trusted friend to tell you when you slip. Parents, explain the reason behind a rule, not just the rule. Before you share or act on something you read online, stop and ask whether it is true and wise, not only whether it is persuasive.

rel.note: The gang's plan to ambush the innocent without cause is the opposite of justice, judgment and equity.
Doing righteousness and justice pleases the LORD more than sacrifice, which is why wisdom's fruit is moral.
The same three nouns return as what the son who seeks wisdom will come to understand.
Wisdom herself walks in the way of righteousness and the paths of justice.

units.notes:
• The word translated *wisdom* here is not the same as in 1:2. It comes from a verb meaning to act prudently or with insight, and it describes the good sense that knows how to act well and succeed. The ESV renders the phrase instruction in "wise dealing," the NASB instruction in "wise behavior."
• *Justice* translates the Hebrew word usually rendered "righteousness," and the ESV and NASB begin the list with "righteousness."
• The same three Hebrew nouns return together in 2:9, where the NKJV has "righteousness and justice, Equity." There they describe what the son who seeks wisdom will come to understand, so the purpose stated here is the result promised there.
• *Equity* pictures what is level and straight. Ironside: equity "is uprightness, or moral integrity."
• Compare Micah 6:8, "to do justly, To love mercy, And to walk humbly with your God," and 21:3, where doing righteousness and justice pleases the LORD more than sacrifice.
units.summary: You cannot be wise in God's sense and crooked at the same time.
units.principle: God's wisdom always bends a life toward what is right and fair; skill without integrity is not wisdom.
units.insight: When Zacchaeus received Jesus into his house, his money changed before anyone told it to. "If I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Received grace became justice, judgment and equity at once. That is how this book expects wisdom to work. It refuses to separate private devotion from public fairness. Many of us keep a quiet corner of crookedness: a padded expense, a shaded answer, a rule bent for friends. The wisdom Proverbs offers will not live beside it. Jesus is the "Branch of righteousness" who "shall execute judgment and righteousness in the earth" (Jeremiah 33:15). To receive His instruction is to let Him straighten what is crooked in us.
units.application: Look this week for one place where you have tolerated a little crookedness: an expense report, a tax form, a promise to a customer, the way you tell the story of a conflict. Make it straight, and make restitution if you owe it. If you supervise others, decide one case this week on what is right rather than on who is easier to please. Young people, ask a parent or mentor what fairness would look like in a situation you face.

rel.note: The simple believes every word, which is why he needs the prudence this book gives.
The sinners' enticement uses the same verb from which "simple" comes, showing who is most at risk.
The simple for whom this book was written are the ones whose turning away finally slays them.
The prudent foresee danger and hide while the simple walk into it, the very prudence this verse offers.
The young man devoid of understanding shows what becomes of the simple who never receive this instruction.
Wisdom calls the simple to understand prudence, the same gift promised here.

units.notes:
• *Simple* translates peti, from a verb meaning to be open or easily persuaded. The same verb is translated "entice" in 1:10, so the simple are, by their very name, the people sinners set out to entice.
• Phillips, quoted by Guzik: "The word indicates the person whose mind is dangerously open."
• *Prudence* comes from a root meaning to be shrewd. A related word describes the serpent in Genesis 3:1, where the NKJV has "cunning." Proverbs uses the word in its good sense: the practical shrewdness that sees danger coming. Jesus asks the same of His disciples: "be wise as serpents and harmless as doves" (Matthew 10:16).
• Plato's school was said to bar anyone who was not trained in geometry. Bridges, drawing on Cartwright, contrasts the invitation over Solomon's doors: "Let the ignorant, simple, foolish, young enter."
• The NKJV ends the verse with a dash, treating 1:5 as an aside before the list of purposes resumes in 1:6.
units.summary: Proverbs gives the easily led the foresight that hard experience would otherwise have to teach them.
units.principle: Wisdom is offered first to the inexperienced and uncommitted, so that foresight can teach them what painful mistakes would otherwise have to.
units.insight: The simple person's danger is not wickedness but openness. He "believes every word" (14:15) and follows whoever reaches him first. The young man of 7:7, "devoid of understanding," walks toward the adulteress's house for exactly that reason. Daniel, a young man taken to a foreign court, shows the other way. He "purposed in his heart" that he would not defile himself with the king's food (Daniel 1:8). His settled conviction decided the matter before the pressure could wear him down. Most of us carry simple places, areas where we have never settled what we believe or what we will refuse. The good news is that God does not despise the simple. "The LORD preserves the simple" (Psalm 116:6), and His word is "making wise the simple" (Psalm 19:7). Christ the Good Shepherd goes after the one sheep that has wandered off (Luke 15:4).
units.application: Name one area where you are still undecided and therefore easy to sway: what you watch, how you spend, how far you will go in a relationship. Settle it this week, before the moment comes, as Daniel did. Parents, talk with your teenagers about specific pressures before they face them, not after. If you mentor a new believer, give him clear convictions and the reasons behind them, not only encouragement.

rel.note: Where there is no counsel people fall, which is why the man of understanding seeks it.
The fool is right in his own eyes, while the wise man heeds counsel.
The ear of the wise seeks knowledge, the same hunger to keep learning.
Fools despise the instruction that the wise man gladly hears.
Instruction makes a wise man still wiser, the same growth this verse describes.

units.notes:
• *Learning* translates leqach, a word related to the verb behind "To receive" in 1:3. It describes teaching that a person takes in and makes his own. The wise man keeps receiving more of what he has already begun to receive.
• *Wise counsel* translates a word for guidance in making plans. It always appears in the plural and only in the wisdom books, and it is used for the planning needed to wage war (20:18; 24:6). It has often been connected with ropes and the steering of a ship, which would picture counsel as the skill of steering a course, though that origin is not certain.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Proverbs is not simply for the naive and the gullible; everyone can grow by its teachings."
• Compare 12:15, "he who heeds counsel is wise," and 18:15, where "the ear of the wise seeks knowledge."
units.summary: The mark of a wise person is not how much he knows but how readily he still listens.
units.principle: Wisdom grows by listening; the wiser a person becomes, the more he seeks instruction and counsel from others.
units.insight: Moses had met God at the burning bush and led Israel out of Egypt, yet he listened when his father-in-law told him he was wearing himself out. "So Moses heeded the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said" (Exodus 18:24). Apollos was eloquent and "mighty in the Scriptures." Still he let Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain "the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:24–26). Pride stops listening once it thinks it has arrived. Humility keeps learning, because it knows how much it has not yet seen. Even the boy Jesus was found in the temple "both listening to them and asking them questions" (Luke 2:46). If the Son of God listened and asked, no believer outgrows the need to learn. Who still has permission to correct you?
units.application: Before your next major decision at work, in ministry or with money, ask two people with more experience for counsel, and listen without defending yourself. If you lead a team, make a habit of asking, "What am I missing?" Seasoned believers, keep a learner's seat: join a class or read a book that stretches you. Young leaders, find an older mentor and meet with him or her regularly.

rel.note: The title introduced the proverb; this verse trains the reader to understand it.
A later heading introduces "the words of the wise," the very phrase this verse uses.
God conceals a matter and kings search it out, the kind of searching this verse trains.
Searching for wisdom as for hidden treasure leads to understanding the fear of the LORD.

units.notes:
• *Enigma* translates a word paired with "proverb" again in Habakkuk 2:6, where the NKJV renders it "taunting riddle." The KJV has "the interpretation."
• *Riddles* is the word used of Samson's riddle (Judges 14:12) and of the "hard questions" with which the queen of Sheba came to test Solomon (1 Kings 10:1). In both stories the meaning had to be worked out by someone with insight.
• Henry on why interpretation matters: without it "the proverb is a nut uncracked."
• The psalmist uses the same vocabulary: "I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old" (Psalm 78:2). Matthew 13:35 applies that verse to Jesus' parables.
units.summary: Some truths lie on the surface; others reward only the reader who stops, digs and asks.
units.principle: God hides some treasure beneath the surface of His word so that those who search may find it, but the deeper meaning always stands on the plain one.
units.insight: Jesus taught in parables that hid truth from the indifferent and opened it to those who asked. To His disciples He said, "it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 13:11). On the Emmaus road He explained "in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself" (Luke 24:27). Later "He opened their understanding, that they might comprehend the Scriptures" (Luke 24:45). The deepest things hidden in the Scriptures are made plain in Him. Our problem is often not that Scripture is too hard but that we are in too much of a hurry. We skim and move on. This verse invites patience: read a saying slowly, ask what it compares and why, and pray for light. The Lord who opened Scripture on that road still opens it to those who ask.
units.application: This week take a single proverb and stay with it for several days. Read it aloud, ask what image it uses, look up one cross-reference, and pray, "Open my eyes" (Psalm 119:18). Small-group leaders, ask one open question that makes the group search the text instead of handing them the answer. Preachers and teachers, give the plain meaning first, before any deeper application.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, joining the motto to the training this verse names.
The fool despises the same wisdom and instruction the book was written to give.
Those who perish "did not choose the fear of the LORD," the refusal this motto warns against.
The wise man gladly hears the instruction that fools despise.
The book closes by praising a woman who fears the LORD, framing the whole book with this motto.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, the motto repeated at the close of the prologue.

units.notes:
• *Beginning* translates re'shit, the word used for "firstfruits" in 3:9, the first and best portion of the harvest. That use supports the sense of foremost as well as first. The parallel saying in 9:10 uses a different word that stresses the starting point.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, calls the fear of the LORD "the first and controlling principle, rather than a stage which one leaves behind."
• Bridges defines it as "that affectionate reverence, by which the child of God bends himself humbly and carefully to his Father's law."
• *Fools* here and in 1:22 translates two different Hebrew words, a difference English cannot show. In both verses the fool is known by his attitude to truth: here he despises wisdom and instruction; in 1:22 he hates knowledge.
• The same conviction appears in Psalm 111:10 and Job 28:28 ("Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom"). In Proverbs the motto returns at 9:10 and 15:33, and the book closes by praising "a woman who fears the LORD" (31:30).
units.summary: See God rightly, and everything else can begin to be seen rightly.
units.principle: True knowledge starts with a right view of God and keeps Him at its center; refusing correction is folly, however bright a person is.
units.insight: When Isaiah saw the LORD high and lifted up, he cried, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" (Isaiah 6:5). When Peter saw Jesus' power over the fish, he fell at His knees: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord!" (Luke 5:8). That is the fear of the LORD, a true sight of God that exposes us. Yet Jesus answered Peter, "Do not be afraid" (Luke 5:10), and drew him closer. The psalmist holds both together: "there is forgiveness with You, That You may be feared" (Psalm 130:4). The fool keeps God at a distance and calls it independence. The humble draw near trembling and find mercy. Ask yourself where your view of God has shrunk to fit your comfort. Much of the confusion in our lives starts there.
units.application: Begin each day this week with a passage that shows God's greatness, such as Isaiah 6, Isaiah 40 or Psalm 145, before you check your phone. Students and professionals, ask how your field looks when God is put at its center. Parents, teach your children awe as well as rules by pointing out creation, answered prayer and God's holiness. When you catch yourself brushing off correction, stop and ask what it reveals about your view of God.

rel.note: The next verse gives the reason to listen: the parents' teaching becomes the son's honor.
The son is to listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old.
A king's mother teaches her son, showing again that a mother's voice carries wisdom.
The father's address becomes the LORD's own fatherly correction, which Hebrews 12:5-6 quotes.
The father calls his children to hear and recalls being taught by his own father.
The son is again told to keep his father's command and not forsake his mother's law.

units.notes:
• *Law* translates torah, the word Israel used for the Law of Moses, but its basic sense is instruction or direction. Proverbs uses it of the mother's teaching here and in 6:20, and of the speech of the woman of valor in 31:26, "the law of kindness." Calling a mother's teaching torah gives it real weight.
• Bridges: "No ancient system, so fully as the Bible, recognises the Mother's just and equal claims." Compare 6:20; 23:22; and Leviticus 19:3, which names the mother first: "Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father."
• Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the parallel address of 3:11–12, "My son, do not despise the chastening of the LORD," as God's word to believers. That is why the father's "my son" can also be heard as the voice of God.
• Other ancient wisdom writings were framed the same way. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope is presented as a father's teaching to his son, so this form would have been familiar to the first hearers.
• Henry on teaching that persuades rather than merely commands: "when we tell them what they must do we must tell them why."
units.summary: Wisdom's first classroom is the home, and both a father's voice and a mother's count.
units.principle: God places His first lessons of wisdom in the hands of parents, and a wise child listens to both father and mother.
units.insight: Timothy's faith "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5), and from childhood he had known the Holy Scriptures (3:15). A mother's and grandmother's teaching shaped a pastor. Jesus Himself, the eternal Son, went home to Nazareth and "was subject to them" (Luke 2:51). Listening to parents is not childish; it is the humility in which wisdom grows. Some readers had no father or mother who taught them God's ways. For them the verse's deeper meaning is a comfort: "When my father and my mother forsake me, Then the LORD will take care of me" (Psalm 27:10). God Himself says "My son" to all who trust Him (Hebrews 12:5–6). Whatever your upbringing, the question now is whether you are listening, and whether those who come after you hear anything from you.
units.application: Parents, set aside one unhurried conversation this week to pass on a lesson God has taught you, and explain the reason behind it. Fathers, back up the mother's teaching in front of the children. Adult children, call a parent or grandparent and ask what they have learned about walking with God. If you grew up without godly parents, ask an older believer in your church to speak into your life.

rel.note: The gang promises houses full of spoil, but the son's true adornment is his parents' wisdom.
The previous verse gives the command that this verse supports with a reason.
Keeping sound wisdom and discretion becomes life to the soul and grace to the neck.
Wisdom places the same ornament of grace on the head of the one who embraces her.
The son is told to bind his parents' teaching on his heart and tie it around his neck.

units.notes:
• *Graceful ornament* is literally a garland or wreath of grace. The same phrase returns in 4:9, where Wisdom "will place on your head an ornament of grace; A crown of glory she will deliver to you."
• *Chains* are necklaces worn as marks of honor or favor. Proverbs also speaks of binding wise teaching around the neck (3:3; 6:21), and 3:22 says sound wisdom will be "grace to your neck."
• Henry: "Those are truly valuable, and shall be valued, who value themselves more by their virtue and piety than by their worldly wealth and dignity."
• Compare 1 Peter 3:4, where the lasting adornment is "the incorruptible beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit," and Titus 2:10, "adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things."
units.summary: The teaching a young man feels as a fence turns out to be his crown.
units.principle: A life shaped by godly instruction carries a beauty and honor that no wealth can buy.
units.insight: Joseph wore Pharaoh's gold chain, but his honor began long before the palace. As a slave in Potiphar's house he refused sin because he feared God: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). The character formed in him while he was a slave was later seen by all Egypt. The world tells the young to find honor in what they can grab, show or own. Proverbs says the lasting ornament is character. The gang's spoil will be stripped away, but wisdom worn in the heart cannot be taken. Christ wore a crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29) so that we could be clothed with "the garments of salvation" and "the robe of righteousness" (Isaiah 61:10). Every grace we wear is finally His gift. What are you most proud to be known for: what you own, or who you are becoming?
units.application: Parents, when you see your child act with wisdom, honesty or kindness, name it and praise it so they feel its honor. Young people, think of the people you most admire and ask whether it is their possessions or their character you admire. This week, choose one piece of instruction you once resented from a parent or mentor, and thank that person for it.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, which is why the son must refuse.
A violent man entices his neighbor into a way that is not good, the same kind of enticement.
The command to keep off the gang's path puts this refusal into action.
The same verb for being willing describes those who would have none of Wisdom's rebuke.
The simple, named from the same root as "entice," are the ones sinners target.
The son is told not to enter the path of the wicked but to avoid it and turn away.

units.notes:
• *Entice* comes from the same root as *simple* in 1:4, a root meaning to be open or easily persuaded. Sinners aim at the open, uncommitted heart.
• *Consent* translates a verb meaning to be willing. It returns in 1:25 and 1:30, where those who refuse Wisdom "would have none" of her counsel and rebuke. The son is told not to be willing toward sinners; the scoffers are not willing toward Wisdom.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "They can do thee no harm unless thy will join in with them." In other words, the gang has no power over the son unless his own will agrees.
• Compare 16:29, "A violent man entices his neighbor, And leads him in a way that is not good," and James 1:14, where each one is tempted "when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed."
• Paul gives the same warning about companions in 1 Corinthians 15:33: "Evil company corrupts good habits."
units.summary: Temptation can knock, plead and flatter, but it cannot come in without your yes.
units.principle: Sinful pressure has no power without the heart's consent, so the safest answer to enticement is an early, settled no.
units.insight: Potiphar's wife spoke to Joseph "day by day," yet "he did not heed her" (Genesis 39:10). He had settled the matter before the pressure came: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (39:9). Eve, by contrast, kept the conversation going until desire did the rest (Genesis 3:1–6). Jesus met every enticement in the wilderness with a short, settled word: "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). We often lose these battles because we keep negotiating. We tell ourselves we are only listening. The father's counsel is wiser: refuse early, and refuse simply. The One who refused every temptation now stands beside those who are tempted. "He Himself has suffered, being tempted," and "He is able to aid those who are being tempted" (Hebrews 2:18).
units.application: Decide now what you will say when the pressure comes: the invitation to cut a corner at work, the party where the plan changes, the group chat that turns cruel. Keep the answer short, and leave early. Parents, rehearse with your children a simple line they can use to refuse their friends. Youth leaders, teach that saying no to a group takes courage and is not rudeness.

rel.note: The words of the wicked are "Lie in wait for blood," the same speech the gang uses.
The same verbs return, showing that the ambush is really set for the gang's own blood.
Wisdom's open public call stands against the gang's secret invitation.
The book aims to teach justice, judgment and equity, the very things this ambush violates.
The wicked are warned not to lie in wait against the dwelling of the righteous.
Hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• *Without cause* translates chinnam, "for nothing." It can go with the ambush (attacking for no reason) or with the victims (people who gave no reason to be attacked); the sense is much the same either way. The same word is translated "in vain" in 1:17.
• The same Hebrew word describes those who hate the psalmist "without a cause" (Psalm 69:4), words Jesus applied to Himself: "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25).
• Judges 9:25 shows this crime in Israel's history: the men of Shechem "set men in ambush against him on the tops of the mountains, and they robbed all who passed by them."
• Bridges traces how the pitch grows: "The invitation at first was seemingly harmless--Only come with us. Soon the demand rises--Cast in thy lot with us."
• Compare 12:6, "The words of the wicked are, 'Lie in wait for blood,'" and Psalm 10:8, where the wicked "sits in the lurking places of the villages" and murders the innocent in secret.
units.summary: Sin rarely opens with the crime; it opens with "Come with us."
units.principle: The pull of belonging can draw a person into wrongs he would never choose alone, so every invitation must be judged by where the group is going.
units.insight: The gang's pitch has not changed. It begins with "Come with us" and only later reveals the cost. Judas went to the chief priests and was welcomed. Within days he was saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" (Matthew 27:4). Jesus was the true Innocent ambushed without cause. His enemies "plotted to take Jesus by trickery and kill Him" (Matthew 26:4), and He said, "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25). The hunger to belong is not evil; God made us for fellowship. But a heart starved for acceptance will pay almost any price for it. Christ offers a belonging that never requires us to harm anyone. He calls us into His own family, where the price of belonging was paid by Him. Whose "Come with us" has been pulling at you?
units.application: Before you join a group, team, deal or circle of friends, ask where it is going and what it will require of you later. Parents, ask your teenagers not only who their friends are but what those friends invite them to do. If you are lonely, do not let that pain choose your companions; ask God and your church for godly friends. Leaders, make sure your group's welcome never comes with a hidden price.

rel.note: The death the gang boasts of dealing out lies in wait for their own lives.
Those who refuse Wisdom are swept away by a whirlwind, a reversal of the gang's boast of swallowing others whole.
Hell and Destruction are never full, the endless appetite the gang claims for itself.
The grave is named among the things that are never satisfied.

units.notes:
• *Whole* translates tamim, "complete." The NKJV renders the same word "blameless" in 2:21. Here it describes victims swallowed entire, and it may also hint that they are blameless people, like "the innocent" of 1:11.
• In Numbers 16:30 and 16:33, the word the NKJV renders "pit" is Sheol, the same word used here for the grave.
• Sheol's endless appetite is a recurring picture: "Hell and Destruction are never full" (27:20). Compare 30:15–16 and Isaiah 5:14, "Sheol has enlarged itself And opened its mouth beyond measure."
• Henry: "Who could imagine that human nature should degenerate so far that it should ever be a pleasure to one man to destroy another!"
units.summary: The gang boasts it can swallow people like the grave, but only God can swallow up death.
units.principle: Violence dresses itself in boasts of power, but those who make themselves masters of death only hasten their own.
units.insight: Korah and his company stood in proud rebellion, and the ground opened and swallowed them (Numbers 16:31–33). The gang borrows that terror for their boast, not knowing they are describing their own end. Human beings were never meant to hold the power of death; only God does. In the gospel God turns the gang's picture around. He "will swallow up death forever" (Isaiah 25:8), and "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54). Christ went down into death and rose again, so that "through death He might destroy him who had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14). The verse also searches us. The urge to crush, to win completely, to leave an opponent with nothing, lives in more hearts than gangs. It shows up in arguments, in business and online. Christ's victory frees us from needing to swallow anyone.
units.application: Watch your words in conflict this week. When you want to win completely, to humiliate rather than resolve, stop and choose words that leave the other person whole. Parents, be alert to music, games or talk that makes cruelty sound strong and exciting to your children. If you have been crushed by someone else's power, take your fear to the One who has defeated death itself.

rel.note: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing.
Greed for gain troubles the very household it is supposed to enrich.
Those who refuse Wisdom are also filled, but with the bitter fruit of their own way.
The son's true adornment is his parents' wisdom, not the gang's spoil.
Treasures gained by lying are the fleeting fantasy of those who seek death.
By knowledge rooms are filled with all precious riches, the honest way to the wealth the gang promises.

units.notes:
• *Precious possessions* is literally "all precious wealth." The same Hebrew phrase returns in 24:4, "By knowledge the rooms are filled With all precious and pleasant riches." Wisdom offers the very thing the gang promises, but gained the right way.
• *Spoil* is plunder, the goods stripped from victims or carried off in war.
• Henry: "They call it precious substance; whereas it is neither substance nor precious; it is a shadow." ("Substance" is the KJV's word for possessions.)
• Compare 10:2, "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing," and 21:6, where treasures gained by a lying tongue are "the fleeting fantasy of those who seek death."
units.summary: Sin always advertises the treasure and hides the price tag.
units.principle: Wealth gained by harming others is never as precious as it looks; wisdom offers lasting riches gained by right means.
units.insight: Achan saw among the spoils "a beautiful Babylonian garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold." He confessed, "I coveted them and took them" (Joshua 7:21). He hid them in his tent, and they brought death on his house. Sin always shows the garment and hides the grave. Jesus asked the question this verse forces on us: "what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?" (Matthew 16:26). Few readers will rob a traveler. Many will be tempted to fill their houses by shortcuts: cheating, exploiting or squeezing others. The heart that wants more, fast, is the soil where the gang's offer grows. Christ shows the opposite road to true riches: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9).
units.application: When an offer promises fast money, ask who pays for it. Business owners, check whether any profit depends on someone else being deceived or squeezed. Employees, refuse the shortcut even when "everyone does it." Young people, be wary of friends whose money seems to come from nowhere. Parents, model contentment by talking at the table about what you are thankful for rather than what you want next.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, the end of those who share the gang's purse.
The same word for bag holds honest weights that are the LORD's work.
The gang casts its lot by its own scheme, but every decision of the lot belongs to the LORD.
The father's conclusion shows what unjust gain finally costs those who share it.
Whoever is a partner with a thief hates his own life.

units.notes:
• *Purse* translates kis, the word used for the merchant's bag of weights in 16:11: "All the weights in the bag are His work." There the bag holds honest weights that belong to the LORD; here it holds the takings of robbery.
• *Lot* appears again in 16:33: "The lot is cast into the lap, But its every decision is from the LORD." The gang stakes its future on its own scheme; the wise know the LORD decides.
• Henry describes the escalation from "Come with us" (1:11) to "Cast in your lot": "At first they pretend to ask no more; but the courtship rises higher."
• Compare Jacob's words about the violence of two of his sons: "Let not my soul enter their council; Let not my honor be united to their assembly" (Genesis 49:6).
units.summary: The gang offers a shared purse, but whoever shares its purse shares its end.
units.principle: Partnership in wrongdoing always costs more than it pays; whoever shares the takings shares the guilt and the outcome.
units.insight: Judas kept the money box for Jesus and the Twelve. John records that "he was a thief, and had the money box; and he used to take what was put in it" (John 12:6). Even in the company of Jesus, a shared purse became a snare to a greedy heart. The early church shows the opposite picture. Believers "had all things in common" (Acts 2:44), not by robbing others but by giving to them. That is the one purse the gospel creates. The gang's offer appeals to two deep longings, belonging and fairness. Both are good desires that only God can rightly satisfy. In Christ we are brought into a family and given "an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and that does not fade away" (1 Peter 1:4). We do not need a gang's share when we have His.
units.application: Before you go into business, invest, or sign on with anyone, look hard at their character, because you will share their reputation and their risk. Young people, if a group's "fair share" comes from cheating or stealing, walk away now. Church leaders, build a fellowship where people find real belonging and practical sharing, so the lonely are not left to look for it among the wrong crowd.

rel.note: The command to refuse consent is now put into action by keeping the foot off the path.
The next verse gives the reason: their feet run to evil.
The son is told not to enter the path of the wicked but to avoid it and pass on.
The path of the just grows brighter, while the way of the wicked is darkness.
He is to ponder the path of his feet and remove his foot from evil.

units.notes:
• *Way* and *path* are the book's chief pictures for a course of life. The image runs through Proverbs: "the path of the just is like the shining sun," while "The way of the wicked is like darkness" (4:18–19).
• Ironside: "The only safe course is to part company at once."
• Psalm 1:1 traces the same slide in three steps: the blessed man does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of the scornful.
• Jesus used the same picture of two ways: the narrow gate and difficult way that lead to life, and the broad way that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13–14). Compare 4:14–15 and 4:26–27.
units.summary: The surest way to avoid a destination is never to start down its road.
units.principle: Avoiding sin's end requires refusing sin's road, and the first step is the easiest one to refuse.
units.insight: Lot "pitched his tent even as far as Sodom" (Genesis 13:12). Soon he "dwelt in Sodom" (14:12), and later he was "sitting in the gate of Sodom" (19:1). No one forced him; each step felt small. Peter "followed Him at a distance," then "sat with the servants and warmed himself at the fire" (Mark 14:54). Within hours he was denying Jesus with curses (14:71). The road always goes further than we planned. Yet the risen Jesus met Peter on the shore and restored him (John 21:15–17). There is a way back for anyone who has walked too far. But the father's counsel is better still: do not start. Where are your feet drifting this week, and toward what?
units.application: Identify one first step that has led you into sin before: a website, a certain friend's apartment, a late-night conversation, a second drink. Remove that step this week. Parents, help your children name places and situations they should simply not go. Leaders, if you see a team member drifting toward a compromising group, speak early and kindly, before the habit sets.

rel.note: He sins who hastens with his feet, showing the danger of haste itself.
Their running feet are the reason the son must hold his own foot back.
The wicked cannot sleep until they have done evil, the same eagerness.
Feet swift in running to evil and hands that shed innocent blood are among what the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• Isaiah 59:7 has nearly the same words: "Their feet run to evil, And they make haste to shed innocent blood." Paul quotes the Isaiah wording in Romans 3:15, in his description of all humanity apart from grace (Romans 3:10–18).
• The verse is missing from Codex Vaticanus, an important manuscript of the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament), and from the Coptic and Arabic versions. The NET Bible's textual note judges that it fits its context well enough to be original. It stands in the Hebrew text, and the NKJV and other major English versions include it.
• Henry: "The way of sin is down-hill; men not only cannot stop themselves, but, the longer they continue in it, the faster they run."
• Compare 6:17–18 and 4:16, where the wicked "do not sleep unless they have done evil."
units.summary: Walk with people who run toward evil, and you will soon be running too.
units.principle: Sin gathers speed, and those who walk beside eager evildoers will be swept along at their pace.
units.insight: Paul borrows these words, in Isaiah's form, to describe not just gangs but all of us: "Their feet are swift to shed blood" (Romans 3:15). Left to ourselves, our feet run the wrong way. That is humbling. It means the difference between the son and the gang is grace, not native goodness. Saul of Tarsus once hurried toward Damascus "breathing threats and murder" until Christ stopped him on the road (Acts 9:1–6). Jesus set His own feet on a different road. "He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), hurrying not to shed blood but to give His own. Now He sends out people whose feet carry good news: "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace" (Romans 10:15).
units.application: Notice who in your life is always in a hurry toward trouble: the coworker eager for gossip, the friend who pushes every boundary. Slow down your involvement with them. When you feel rushed toward a decision that troubles your conscience, wait a day before you act. Parents, teach your children that pressure to "do it now" is often a sign that something is wrong.

rel.note: The next verse shows the gang caught in the very ambush they set.
The prudent man sees evil and hides himself, unlike those who walk into a trap they can see.
The son is told to free himself like a bird from the hand of the fowler.
The young man hastens like a bird to the snare, not knowing it will cost his life.

units.notes:
• The saying is read three ways. Many take it as above: a bird avoids a net it sees, but the gang does not. Others read it of a bird that sees the net and still flies in for the bait, so that even plain warning does not stop the greedy. A third view applies it to the son, who has been warned and should not be caught. The NLT expresses the first: "If a bird sees a trap being set, it knows to stay away."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, takes the second view: "The bird does not see any connection between the net and what is scattered on it; he just sees food that is free for the taking."
• *In vain* translates the same word as "without cause" in 1:11. The gang attacks the innocent for nothing, and their own net is spread for nothing.
• Bridges, contrasting the bird with man: "She shuns the net spread in her sight; man rushes into it."
• Compare 7:23, "As a bird hastens to the snare, He did not know it would cost his life," and 6:5.
units.summary: A bird has sense enough to avoid a net it sees; the greedy walk into theirs.
units.principle: A warning seen and ignored leaves a person more foolish than a bird; God exposes the trap so that we need not walk into it.
units.insight: Samson watched Delilah set the trap three times. Each time she cried, "The Philistines are upon you," and each time he saw what she was doing (Judges 16:6–15). Yet he stayed, told her his secret, and was taken (16:17–21). He had more warning than any bird and less sense. That is the strange blindness of desire. We can see the net clearly and still convince ourselves the bait is worth it. The father does for his son what God does for us in His word: he lets his son watch the net being spread. Scripture names the trap before we reach it. With every temptation God also promises to "make the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The question is not whether we have been warned, but whether we will use the sense He has given.
units.application: Write down one trap you have already been warned about by Scripture, a friend or your own past: a relationship, a habit, an investment that looks too easy. Look at it plainly and decide now not to go near it. Parents, explain to your children how scams, predators and peer pressure actually work, so the net is spread in their sight. Mentors and counselors, name the trap clearly, because vague warnings rarely protect anyone.

rel.note: The wicked will fall by his own wickedness.
The words of the gang's plan return here, now aimed at their own lives.
The gang boasted of swallowing others alive, but the lives at risk are their own.
The bird-and-net saying prepares for this verse's reversal.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, the same reversal in another image.
Whoever leads the upright astray falls into his own pit.

units.notes:
• The verse repeats the two verbs of 1:11 word for word, *lie in wait* and *lurk secretly*, but changes their object from "the innocent" to "their own blood" and "their own lives." The repetition makes the reversal unmistakable.
• Proverbs states the same principle in 26:27: "Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, And he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him." Compare 28:10 and Psalm 7:15–16; 9:15.
• Dr. Jermin, quoted by Bridges, says wickedness "ensnareth the ensnarers, and murders the murderers." That is, it traps those who set traps.
• Judges 9 shows the pattern in Israel's history. The men of Shechem set ambushes on the mountains (9:25), and in the end "all the evil of the men of Shechem God returned on their own heads" (9:57).
units.summary: The ambush you set for someone else is really set for you.
units.principle: Evil planned against others turns back on the planner; in God's world violence comes home, though not always quickly or visibly.
units.insight: Ahab and Jezebel arranged the death of innocent Naboth to take his vineyard. Elijah met Ahab in that very vineyard: "In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, dogs shall lick your blood, even yours" (1 Kings 21:19). The pattern holds even when it takes years. Asaph nearly stumbled watching the wicked prosper, until he went into the sanctuary and "understood their end" (Psalm 73:17). This truth comforts the one who has been wronged. You do not need to set your own ambush, because God has not stopped governing His world. It also searches the heart. Every scheme to bring someone down is a trap laid on our own road. At the cross the powers of evil set their greatest ambush, and it became their own defeat (Colossians 2:15).
units.application: If you are tempted to scheme against a rival at work, a neighbor or a former friend, stop: you are digging on your own road. If someone is scheming against you, do not answer with a counter-plot. Keep doing right, document what you must, and leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19). Parents, when a child plots revenge on a sibling or classmate, use this verse to show where plots lead.

rel.note: The same expression, greedy for gain, describes one who troubles his own house.
The shared purse the gang offered is the gain that takes their lives.
Wisdom widens the principle: every chosen way bears its own fruit.
Riches pursued by overwork make themselves wings and fly away.
He who hates covetousness will prolong his days.

units.notes:
• *Greedy for gain* pairs a verb and a noun built from the same Hebrew root, roughly "gaining gain." The noun refers to profit gotten unjustly, not honest earnings. The same expression recurs in 15:27.
• *Owners* translates the plural of ba'al, a word for a lord or master. Those who think of themselves as masters of their gain lose their lives to it.
• Henry: "They have little reason to be proud of their property in that which takes away the life of the owners and then passes to other masters."
• Compare 1 Timothy 6:9, where those who desire to be rich fall into "many foolish and harmful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition," and Luke 12:15.
units.summary: Greedy people think they own their gain until their gain owns them and takes their life.
units.principle: Gain pursued by wrong means becomes a master that destroys the one who thought he owned it.
units.insight: Gehazi ran after Naaman for silver and garments, and went out from Elisha's presence a leper (2 Kings 5:20–27). Judas took thirty pieces of silver and soon could not bear to keep them (Matthew 27:3–5). Jesus told of a rich man who planned bigger barns and heard God say, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). Greed promises life and takes it. Often it works slowly, hardening the heart, souring friendships and crowding out God. Before we point at the gang, we should ask what we are greedy for: money, recognition, comfort or control. Jesus said that "one's life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses" (Luke 12:15). He gave His life so that we could find ours in Him, not in what we own.
units.application: Review your budget and calendar this week, and ask what gain is costing you in sleep, family time or integrity. If you run a business, ask whether any practice profits from someone else's loss. Give away something this week that you would rather keep, as a sign that it does not own you. Parents, talk with your children about the difference between working hard and wanting more at any cost.

rel.note: The gang lurks in secret, while Wisdom speaks openly.
Wisdom again raises her voice publicly beside the paths and at the gates.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, which is why she calls so loudly.
Folly also calls in public, so the personification alone does not identify the speaker.
Wisdom cries out from the highest places of the city.

units.notes:
• *Wisdom* here is plural in form in Hebrew, but the verb with it is singular, so one speaker is in view. The plural probably expresses the fullness of wisdom. The same form appears in 9:1, and the KJV margin explains it as "Excellent wisdom."
• *Calls aloud* translates a verb that usually describes a ringing shout, often of joy. Here it is a loud public cry that summons people to listen.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, says the scene shows "that the offer of wisdom is to the man in the street, and for the business of living, not to an élite for the pursuit of scholarship."
• Jesus spoke of "the wisdom of God" sending prophets (Luke 11:49) and said "wisdom is justified by her children" (Matthew 11:19). Paul says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).
• Wisdom's public call returns in 8:1–3 and 9:3; Folly imitates it in 9:13–16.
units.summary: While sin whispers in the shadows, Wisdom shouts in the street.
units.principle: God's wisdom is not hidden or reserved for a few; it calls openly to everyone in the middle of ordinary life.
units.insight: On the last day of the feast, "Jesus stood and cried out, saying, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink'" (John 7:37). Before the high priest He said, "I spoke openly to the world… and in secret I have said nothing" (John 18:20). Wisdom's cry in the street became a Man's voice in the temple courts and on the hillsides of Galilee. That removes the excuse that God is silent. The gang whispers; Wisdom shouts. Our problem is rarely that God has not spoken. Other voices are simply closer, quieter and more flattering. The same Christ still calls through His word, through preaching, and through the conscience He awakens. Today, in the noise of your ordinary day, which voice are you leaning toward?
units.application: Build a daily habit of listening: ten minutes in Scripture before the news, the feed or the inbox. Turn off one source of background noise this week and use the time to pray. Preachers and teachers, take God's word where people actually are, in plain language and in public places. Parents, let your children hear you speak of God naturally in ordinary moments, not only at church.

rel.note: The afflicted are not to be oppressed at the gate, the very place where Wisdom calls for justice.
The fool has nothing to say in the gate, where Wisdom speaks.
The husband known in the gates shows the gate as the place of public honor and judgment.
Wisdom again cries out by the gates and at the entrance of the doors.

units.notes:
• *Chief concourses*: the Hebrew word means noisy or bustling, and the noun "streets" is understood. The ESV and the 1984 NIV render it the head of the "noisy streets," and the NASB has "noisy [streets]," bracketing the supplied word.
• *Gates*: the gate served as a town's courtroom, market and meeting place. Boaz settled Ruth's case before ten elders at the gate (Ruth 4:1–2), and the husband of 31:23 is "known in the gates."
• Henry: "Truth seeks not corners, nor is virtue ashamed of itself."
• Wisdom's public call is repeated in 8:1–3, where she stands where the paths meet and cries out by the gates. Contrast 24:7: the fool "does not open his mouth in the gate."
units.summary: Wisdom speaks loudest where life is busiest: the marketplace, the courtroom, the gate.
units.principle: God's wisdom belongs in public life, in trade, law and daily decisions, not only in places of worship.
units.insight: In Athens Paul "reasoned in the synagogue… and in the marketplace daily with those who happened to be there" (Acts 17:17). Jeremiah was told to "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word" (Jeremiah 7:2). God's voice has always gone to the busy places. That confronts our habit of keeping faith in a Sunday compartment. Wisdom has a word for the contract, the hiring decision, the vote, the courtroom and the checkout line. If her voice is missing from our working hours, it is not because she stopped calling there. Christ is Lord of Monday as much as Sunday. Where in your public life have you quietly told Wisdom she is not welcome?
units.application: Before your next work decision, ask what Scripture says about honesty, fairness or speech, and let it shape the choice. Business owners and managers, review one policy this week for justice and kindness. If you serve on a board, jury or committee, pray before you decide. Believers in public roles, look for respectful ways to let wisdom from God's word be heard.

rel.note: A wise son heeds his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.
The scorners' delight in mockery is turned back on them when calamity comes.
Hatred of knowledge returns as the reason for the end Wisdom describes.
The simple who love their drifting are finally slain by their turning away.
The scoffer is proud and haughty and acts with arrogant pride.
The scoffer resents correction, the problem of the will named here.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew "How long" is asked once but carries through all three lines, and the ESV repeats it before the scoffers. Where the NKJV begins the second line with "For," the Hebrew has only the ordinary word for "and."
• *Scorners* translates letsim. The NKJV renders the same word "scoffer" in 9:7–8 and 13:1; the two English words describe the same person, the proud mocker who will not be corrected (21:24).
• *Fools* here translates a different Hebrew word from the "fools" of 1:7, though English cannot show the difference. Both are known by their attitude toward truth.
• Bridges: "In other cases man delights, not in his ignorance, but in its removal." The simple are strange because they enjoy their ignorance instead of wanting it cured.
• Compare Elijah's question to Israel: "How long will you falter between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21).
units.summary: The real danger for the uncommitted is not rebellion but loving to stay undecided.
units.principle: Indecision about God is not neutral; loved and indulged, it hardens into mockery and hatred of the truth.
units.insight: Felix listened to Paul speak of righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and he trembled. Then he said, "Go away for now; when I have a convenient time I will call for you" (Acts 24:25). Two years passed, and Scripture records no turning (24:27). That is loving simplicity: not saying no, only saying not yet. Jesus looked over Jerusalem and spoke His own "how long": "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37). His lament is grief, not contempt. It is also a warning, because drifting hardens into scorn when it is loved long enough. Where have you been keeping God waiting? Today the call is still open.
units.application: Name one matter on which you know God's will but keep postponing obedience: forgiveness, a habit, baptism, giving, a hard conversation. Set a date this week and act. Notice whether you have started joking about things you once took seriously, because that is the scorner's road. Parents and youth leaders, gently press the undecided toward a real decision rather than leaving them comfortable on the fence.

rel.note: Whoever heeds rebuke gets understanding, the promise given here.
Those who refused to turn will one day call and not be answered.
The simple are called to turn, yet their turning away slays them.
The LORD gives wisdom, and from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.
A wise man loves the one who rebukes him and grows wiser by instruction.

units.notes:
• *Pour out* translates a verb that pictures water bubbling up from a spring. Proverbs uses it of speech: the mouth of fools "pours forth foolishness" (15:2), and a related form describes the wellspring of wisdom as "a flowing brook" (18:4).
• *Turn* comes from the same root as the "turning away" of 1:32. Wisdom calls the simple to turn; in the end they turn away instead.
• Peter quoted Joel 2:28 at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and Jesus promised that whoever believes in Him would have "rivers of living water" flowing from within, speaking "concerning the Spirit" (John 7:38–39).
• Bridges, who reads the promise of the Holy Spirit here, says of the Bible reader: "We do not want a new revelation, we only want a Divine Teacher."
• Compare 15:31–32: "The ear that hears the rebukes of life Will abide among the wise… he who heeds rebuke gets understanding."
units.summary: Turn when Wisdom corrects you, and correction becomes the doorway to a flood of understanding.
units.principle: God gives more of His wisdom to those who turn when they are corrected; receiving rebuke opens the way to understanding.
units.insight: At Pentecost Peter told the crowd that God had made the Jesus they crucified "both Lord and Christ." They were "cut to the heart" and asked what to do. Peter answered, "Repent… and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:36–38). Rebuke, then turning, then outpouring: this verse's order, carried into the New Testament. Peter also said the exalted Christ had "poured out this which you now see and hear" (Acts 2:33). In that light, the One whose voice calls through Wisdom is also the One who gives His Spirit to all who come. Our instinct under correction is to defend ourselves. Wisdom offers a better way: turn, and receive. What rebuke have you been resisting that might be the door to fresh understanding?
units.application: The next time a spouse, boss, pastor or friend corrects you, resist the urge to explain yourself. Say, "Thank you; let me think and pray about that," and then do it. Ask the Holy Spirit each day this week to open Scripture to you as you read. Leaders and parents, when you correct someone, also point them to the hope of change, not only to the fault.

rel.note: The next verse completes the charge by naming the counsel and rebuke they rejected.
The often rebuked who harden their neck are suddenly destroyed.
Blessed is the man who listens to Wisdom, watching daily at her gates.

units.notes:
• Wisdom's words closely resemble the LORD's indictment in Isaiah 65:12: "Because, when I called, you did not answer; When I spoke, you did not hear." Compare Isaiah 66:4 and Jeremiah 7:13.
• Paul quotes Isaiah 65:2 in Romans 10:21: "All day long I have stretched out My hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
• *Regarded* means paid attention or listened closely. No one even took notice of the offered hand.
• Henry says the hearers "regarded the operations of his hand no more than the declarations of his mouth." In plain terms, they ignored both what Wisdom did and what she said. (Henry writes "his" because he hears Christ speaking in Wisdom's words.)
• Compare 29:1: "He who is often rebuked, and hardens his neck, Will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."
units.summary: Wisdom held out her hand, and no one took it; that is the tragedy.
units.principle: God's call is earnest and personal, and those who persistently refuse it bear the responsibility for what follows.
units.insight: Jesus told of a king who prepared a wedding feast and sent servants to call the guests, "and they were not willing to come." He sent again, "But they made light of it and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his business" (Matthew 22:3, 5). The refusal was not dramatic; it was busy. That is how many outstretched hands are refused. Yet the parable also shows the King's heart, because He sent again. When Peter began to sink, "Jesus stretched out His hand and caught him" (Matthew 14:31). On the cross His arms were stretched out for the very people who had refused Him. The warning in this verse is real, but love speaks it. Is there a hand you have been too busy to take?
units.application: Think of the ways God has been reaching for you: a sermon that stung, a friend's concern, a nudge in your conscience. Respond to one of them this week instead of postponing it. Parents, if a child keeps ignoring your appeals, keep your hand out, but also explain plainly what refusing will cost. Pastors and mentors, keep calling people patiently, as the King in the parable did.

rel.note: He who hates correction is stupid.
He who hates correction will die.
The same verb for being willing marks the son's refusal of sinners and these hearers' refusal of Wisdom.
The previous verse begins the indictment that this verse completes.
Wisdom repeats this charge almost word for word before announcing the outcome.

units.notes:
• *Would have none* translates the same verb as "Do not consent" in 1:10, a verb meaning to be willing. The son is told not to be willing toward sinners; these hearers were not willing toward Wisdom.
• *Disdained* translates a verb meaning to let go or let loose. The KJV says they "set at nought" all Wisdom's counsel.
• Henry says they refused rebuke "as if they had never done any thing that deserved reproof."
• Compare Luke 7:30, where "the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the will of God for themselves," and 12:1, "he who hates correction is stupid."
units.summary: People who will neither be led nor corrected have closed both doors that wisdom uses.
units.principle: Refusing both guidance and correction leaves a person with no way to be helped; teachability is the hinge of wisdom.
units.insight: When Rehoboam became king, the old men who had served Solomon gave him wise counsel. "But he rejected the advice which the elders had given him" and followed the harsh advice of his young friends (1 Kings 12:8). Ten tribes broke away that very day. He did not lack counsel; he lacked willingness. The same verb marks the son who must not be willing toward sinners (1:10). The heart is always unwilling toward someone: either we refuse the gang or we refuse Wisdom. The question is not whether we have heard good counsel but whether we have let any of it change us. Christ, though He was the Son, "learned obedience by the things which He suffered" (Hebrews 5:8). Through Him God gives His people a willing, teachable heart.
units.application: Ask yourself which counsel you have set aside in the last year, from a parent, pastor, doctor, financial adviser or Scripture itself. Pick one piece and act on it this week. Young leaders, before a major decision, seek the input of people older than your peers and weigh it seriously. Parents, model receiving correction from your spouse or even your children with grace.

rel.note: The fear of the wicked will come upon him.
The scorners' delight in scorning explains the reversal in Wisdom's words.
Those who listen live without the terror that falls on mockers.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble.

units.notes:
• *Terror* translates pachad, dread. The same noun returns in 1:27 and again in 1:33, where whoever listens lives "without fear of evil." The terror that comes on those who refuse is set against the security of those who listen.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Wisdom does not laugh at disaster, but at the triumph of what is right over what is wrong when your disaster happens."
• Compare 3:34, "Surely He scorns the scornful, But gives grace to the humble," and Psalm 2:4.
• Israel's history records the same reversal. "They mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against His people, till there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16). The verse before says God kept warning them "because He had compassion on His people" (36:15).
units.summary: Those who laughed at Wisdom's warning will find the laughter turned back on them.
units.principle: Mockery of God's wisdom will finally be exposed and reversed, yet the warning is given in mercy so that mockers may turn first.
units.insight: Psalm 2 shows the nations raging against the LORD and His Anointed, and God laughing at their plots (2:1–4). Yet the same psalm ends with an invitation: "Kiss the Son… Blessed are all those who put their trust in Him" (2:12). The laughter is not the last word; the welcome is. Judah's leaders mocked God's messengers for years, though He kept sending them out of compassion (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Only when mockery hardened past every warning did judgment fall. This verse should sober anyone who makes faith a joke or has stopped taking God's warnings seriously. But no one should hear in it a God who enjoys suffering. Jesus wept over the city He warned (Luke 19:41). Listen while His voice is still calling.
units.application: If you have joked about faith, sin or judgment to fit in, stop, and where needed apologize to those who heard you. Parents, do not let mockery of God go unaddressed at home; respond calmly but seriously. Preachers and teachers, speak this warning with tears, as Jesus did, never with relish. If you fear you have scorned too long, turn to Christ today, because the warning exists so that it will not be too late.

rel.note: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous stands.
The gang boasted of swallowing others whole; those who refuse Wisdom are swept away themselves.
The listener dwells safely while the storm sweeps others away.
Calamity comes suddenly and without remedy.

units.notes:
• *Storm*: the KJV has "desolation" and Ironside "tempest." The NKJV, ESV and NASB read "storm." Either way the picture is sudden, overwhelming ruin.
• *Distress and anguish* translate two Hebrew nouns that sound alike, tsarah and tsuqah. The matching sounds add force to the line, much as "trouble and turmoil" would in English.
• Compare 10:25, where the wicked vanish in the whirlwind while "the righteous has an everlasting foundation," and 6:15: "Suddenly he shall be broken without remedy."
• Compare Matthew 7:24–27, where the same storm beats on two houses, and only the one built on hearing and doing Jesus' words stands.
units.summary: Refused wisdom does not leave quietly; its consequences arrive like a storm.
units.principle: The consequences of refusing wisdom often arrive suddenly and overwhelmingly, while a life built on God's word stands in the storm.
units.insight: Belshazzar feasted with the vessels taken from God's temple and praised his idols. That night a hand wrote on the wall, his knees knocked together, and before morning he was dead (Daniel 5:5–6, 30). Jesus said people in Noah's day "did not know until the flood came and took them all away" (Matthew 24:39). Storms come to every life, wise and foolish. The difference is the foundation. Jesus described two houses struck by the same rain, floods and wind (Matthew 7:24–27). The one that stood belonged to the man who heard His words and did them. Henry: "Those that will not admit the fear of God lay themselves open to all other fears." What is your life built on before the storm arrives?
units.application: Do a foundation check this week: where are you hearing Jesus' words without doing them? Put one into practice. If you sense a storm building in your marriage, finances or health because counsel was ignored, act now while there is time. Parents, prepare your children for life's storms by building habits of prayer and obedience before trouble comes. Church leaders, teach the whole counsel of God, including its warnings.

rel.note: The earlier call to turn, refused, is the reason these later cries go unanswered.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry himself and not be heard.
One who turns his ear from the law finds even his prayer an abomination.
Those who seek Wisdom diligently while she calls will find her.

units.notes:
• *Seek me diligently* translates a verb built from the noun for dawn. Its older sense was probably looking for the dawn or rising early, which is why the KJV has "seek me early." Modern versions take it as earnest seeking.
• The same verb appears in 8:17, where Wisdom promises, "those who seek me diligently will find me." The difference is timing and heart: one seeks Wisdom herself while she calls; the other seeks escape after refusing her.
• The shift from "you" in 1:22–27 to "they" in 1:28–32 marks the change from direct appeal to a description of what will happen to those who refuse.
• Henry guards the verse from misuse: "ordinarily, while there is life there is room for prayer and hope of speeding." ("Speeding" here means succeeding.)
• Compare Hebrews 12:17, where Esau sought the lost blessing "diligently with tears," and Matthew 25:10–12, where "the door was shut."
units.summary: The time to seek Wisdom is while she is calling, not after the storm has come.
units.principle: There comes a time when refused wisdom can no longer spare a person from the harvest he has sown, so the time to seek God is now.
units.insight: King Saul set God's word aside for years. When the Philistines gathered against him, he inquired of the LORD, but "the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams or by Urim or by the prophets" (1 Samuel 28:6). Saul's unanswered prayer is a sobering picture. Yet a thief dying on a cross turned in his last hours and heard, "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). The door is open to anyone who turns. H. A. Ironside learned this passage as a boy, and at fourteen it brought him to Christ. He recalled, "I fell down before Him confessing myself a lost, undone sinner." The warning did its work in him. Let it do its work in you today, while He may be found.
units.application: If you know God is calling you to turn from something, turn today rather than waiting for consequences to force the issue. If you are already reaping a hard harvest, do not despair; call on the Lord with a repentant heart, not only for relief. Pastors and friends, never use this verse to tell a repentant person it is too late. Parents, teach your children that obeying early is easier than repairing later.

rel.note: Fools hate knowledge, the charge repeated here.
The motto names the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, the very thing these refused.
Those who seek wisdom come to understand the fear of the LORD.
Wisdom urges her hearers to choose her instruction rather than silver.

units.notes:
• "The fear of the LORD" appears in 1:7 and again here, so the chapter's argument is framed by the beginning of knowledge and the refusal that ends in ruin.
• *Choose* names a deliberate act of preference. Proverbs urges the opposite choice in 8:10, "Receive my instruction, and not silver," and warns in 3:31, "choose none of his ways."
• Henry: "They hated to be told that which they could not bear to know."
• Compare John 3:19, "men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil," and Joshua 24:15, "choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve."
units.summary: Ruin rarely begins with a lack of facts; it begins with refusing to see God rightly.
units.principle: The fear of the LORD is a choice every person must make, and refusing it, not lack of knowledge, is the root of ruin.
units.insight: Moses set the choice before Israel: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Mary of Bethany sat at Jesus' feet while Martha hurried, and Jesus said, "Mary has chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:42). The fear of the LORD is not an accident of temperament. It is chosen, and chosen again, in daily moments of attention and surrender. Many of us do not hate God openly; we simply choose other things first. Yet the choice to see Him rightly is always welcomed: "The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear Him, In those who hope in His mercy" (Psalm 147:11). What will you choose first tomorrow morning?
units.application: Choose the fear of the LORD in concrete ways this week. Begin each morning with Scripture before screens, make one decision based on what pleases God rather than what is easiest, and confess one area where you have preferred your own way. Parents, explain your family's choices by pointing to God, not just to rules. Teachers and students, ask what difference it makes to see your subject in God's light.

rel.note: A fool despises his father's instruction, but he who receives correction is prudent.
The earlier charge pairs the rejection of counsel with the refusal of rebuke.
The next verse pronounces the sentence that follows this repeated refusal.
The often rebuked who harden their neck are suddenly destroyed without remedy.
The ruined young man regrets having hated instruction and despised correction.

units.notes:
• *Would have none* translates the verb meaning to be willing, the same verb used in 1:10 ("consent") and 1:25. *Despised* is stronger than the "disdained" of 1:25: it means to treat with contempt or spurn.
• Henry on how they heard correction: "they called reproofs reproaches, and took them as an insult." In other words, they treated every correction as an attack.
• Compare 5:12–13, the late regret of the young man who says, "How I have hated instruction, And my heart despised correction!" and 15:5, "he who receives correction is prudent."
• Compare 29:1: "He who is often rebuked, and hardens his neck, Will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."
units.summary: No one who despised every warning can claim he was never warned.
units.principle: Repeated correction that is repeatedly despised leaves a person without excuse; humility receives rebuke as a gift.
units.insight: Pharaoh heard warning after warning through Moses. Each time relief came, "he hardened his heart and did not heed them" (Exodus 8:15). Plague after plague came, and the word was despised every time. Peter, by contrast, was sharply rebuked by Jesus: "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23). Years later Paul rebuked him publicly (Galatians 2:11). Yet Peter wrote of "our beloved brother Paul" (2 Peter 3:15). The difference between the two men was not the strength of the rebuke but the response of the heart. Every rebuke is either despised or received. The same Spirit who humbled Peter can give us a heart that welcomes correction instead of resenting it.
units.application: Keep a short list this month of the corrections you receive and how you respond. Where you bristled, go back and thank the person. Supervisors, when you must correct someone, do it privately and clearly. Parents, when a child despises correction, address the attitude as well as the action. Ask God to soften any place where you have heard the same warning many times.

rel.note: The backslider in heart will be filled with his own ways.
The gang hoped to fill their houses with spoil; those who refuse Wisdom are filled with their own devices.
Greed taking the lives of its owners is an earlier example of a choice turning on those who made it.
The repeated refusal of the previous verse is the reason for this sentence.
He who sows iniquity will reap sorrow.

units.notes:
• *Fancies* translates a word meaning plans or schemes; the KJV and ESV have "devices." It comes from the same root as the word for "counsel" in 1:25 and 1:30. Those who rejected Wisdom's counsel are filled with counsels of their own.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, says that when the fool and the scorner seem fixed in their ways, "it is their fault, not their fate: they are eating of the fruit of their own way."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik, puts it in an everyday proverb: "Eat as they baked, drink as they brewed."
• Compare 14:14, "The backslider in heart will be filled with his own ways."
• Compare Romans 1:24, where God "gave them up" to the desires they insisted on.
units.summary: God need not invent a punishment for the stubborn; He lets them eat what they planted.
units.principle: God's judgment often consists in giving people what they chose; every way bears its own fruit.
units.insight: In the wilderness Israel despised the manna and craved meat. God gave them quail "until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you" (Numbers 11:20). The psalmist sums it up: "He gave them their request, But sent leanness into their soul" (Psalm 106:15). Sometimes the hardest judgment is getting exactly what we wanted. This verse should make us careful about what we insist on. It also points to the gospel. On the cross Christ took the bitter fruit of a way that was not His own: "the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Those who come to Him are not left to be filled with their own devices. They are filled with His life. Are you insisting on your own way, or receiving His?
units.application: Look at one area of your life where you are reaping something hard. Ask what you sowed there, without self-pity or blaming others.
