Then sow differently: a new habit, a restored relationship, a confessed sin. Parents, let children experience reasonable consequences instead of always rescuing them. Leaders, when a plan you insisted on fails, own it openly and learn from it.

rel.note: The backslider in heart is filled with his own ways.
The simple who love simplicity are the ones whose drifting finally slays them.
Wisdom's call to turn is answered by the simple turning away.
The false ease of fools destroys them, while the listener's security is real.
The book was written to give prudence to the very simple who are here in danger.

units.notes:
• *Turning away* comes from the verb translated "Turn" in 1:23. Jeremiah uses the same noun for Israel's backsliding, joined to a promise: "Return, you backsliding children, And I will heal your backslidings" (Jeremiah 3:22).
• *Complacency* describes ease or quiet; the KJV renders it "prosperity." Here the context shows a careless ease that ignores danger.
• Bridges: "The word gradually becomes a burden, then a scorn." He means God's word: neglected little by little, it first feels heavy and is finally mocked. He adds, "To desire ease, therefore, is to embrace a deadly enemy."
• Compare Amos 6:1, "Woe to you who are at ease in Zion," Luke 12:19–20, and Hebrews 2:1, "lest we drift away."
units.summary: Most people are not lost through dramatic rebellion but through slow drift and comfortable ease.
units.principle: Drift and complacency destroy as surely as open rebellion, because they do not feel dangerous to the one caught in them.
units.insight: Paul wrote with grief, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Scripture records no dramatic fall, only a slow turning of the heart. The rich farmer told his soul, "take your ease; eat, drink, and be merry," on the very night his soul was required of him (Luke 12:19–20). The church at Laodicea said, "I am rich… and have need of nothing," not knowing it was "wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). Drift and ease rarely feel like danger, and that is what makes them deadly. But the Lord who warned Laodicea also stood at its door and knocked (Revelation 3:20). To those who drift He still says, "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely" (Hosea 14:4). Where have you been drifting?
units.application: Check for drift this week. Is your prayer thinner than a year ago? Your church attendance, your giving, your hunger for Scripture? Name one area and take a concrete step back. If life is comfortable right now, use the season to go deeper rather than coast. Small-group leaders, reach out to members who have quietly faded instead of waiting for them to return.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence and a place of refuge.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous run and are safe.
The terror that sweeps over mockers like a storm is the fear from which the listener is kept.
The false ease of fools destroys them, unlike the true security of the listener.
The son who keeps wisdom walks safely and need not fear sudden terror.

units.notes:
• *Fear of evil* uses the same noun as "terror" in 1:26–27. The terror that comes on those who refuse is set against the quiet of those who listen.
• *Secure* describes being at ease and undisturbed; the KJV has "quiet from fear of evil."
• Henry: the one who listens "shall not only be safe from evil, but quiet from the fear of it."
• The promise is developed in 3:23–26, where the son who keeps wisdom is told, "Do not be afraid of sudden terror" (3:25). Compare Psalm 112:7: "He will not be afraid of evil tidings; His heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD."
• Compare 14:26, "In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence," and 18:10.
units.summary: The listener is not promised a life without storms, but a heart without terror in them.
units.principle: Those who listen to God's wisdom find a security deeper than their circumstances, though not a life free from suffering.
units.insight: Paul sailed through a storm so violent that "all hope that we would be saved was finally given up." Yet he stood among the crew and said, "take heart, men, for I believe God that it will be just as it was told me" (Acts 27:20, 25). He was not spared the shipwreck; he was spared the terror. Jesus slept in the boat while His disciples panicked, then asked them, "Why are you so fearful?" (Mark 4:40). That is the security of the listener. It is not the absence of trouble but the presence of a trusted voice. Christ promises, "My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me. And I give them eternal life" (John 10:27–28). The safest place in any storm is within hearing of the Shepherd's voice.
units.application: When anxiety rises this week, open Scripture before you open the news, and let God's word speak first. Memorize 3:25–26 or Psalm 112:7. If you are walking through suffering, do not read this verse as a broken promise; read it as an invitation to peace within the trouble. Parents, model calm trust in front of your children when hard news comes. Pastors, offer the anxious both comfort and the habit of listening.

rel.note: Wisdom's hearers refused her call and counsel, the opposite of the son who receives and treasures what he is told.
The same verb for storing up returns there: the son stores his father's words, and the LORD stores up sound wisdom for the upright.
The son is again told to let his heart keep the father's commands rather than forget them.
Commands bound on the heart go with the son and guide him when the parent is absent, which is why they must be kept within.
The father repeats almost the same command to keep his words and treasure his commands within.

units.notes:
• The word translated "treasure," tsaphan, means to hide or store up. The father uses the same verb in 2:7, where the LORD "stores up sound wisdom for the upright." The son who stores up his father's words finds that God has been storing up wisdom for him.
• The KJV reads "hide my commandments with thee"; the ESV has "treasure up my commandments with you."
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, calls storing up "a figure that implies that most teaching cannot be used immediately but that some time will pass before education's effects are felt." Instruction is kept now for the day it will be needed.
• Proverbs 7:1 repeats almost the same line: "My son, keep my words, And treasure my commands within you."
• Compare Psalm 119:11, "Your word I have hidden in my heart, That I might not sin against You," and Luke 2:19, where Mary "kept all these things and pondered them in her heart."
units.summary: What you store in your heart today will guide you tomorrow, when no one is there to remind you.
units.principle: Wisdom begins when instruction is welcomed and kept in the heart, not merely heard and forgotten.
units.insight: Many people hear good counsel; few keep it. Jesus described the good ground as those who, "having heard the word with a noble and good heart, keep it and bear fruit with patience" (Luke 8:15). Joseph, alone in a foreign house, answered temptation with a conviction he carried inside: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). That is what a treasured word does when the moment comes. Bridges puts it simply: "Let the heart be the hiding-place for the treasure." So ask yourself what God has said to you that you received gladly and then let slip. In the light of the New Testament, the father's "My son" also carries the voice of our heavenly Father, whose word still "speaks to you as to sons" (Hebrews 12:5).
units.application: Choose one word of Scripture or one piece of godly counsel you received this month, and write it where you will see it every day. Parents, do more than correct; give your children a few clear sayings worth keeping, and repeat them often. Young people, when a parent or mentor tells you something true, write it down instead of shrugging it off. Before a hard decision this week, ask what you have already been told.

rel.note: The prudent heart and the wise ear actively seek knowledge, the posture this verse calls for.
The simple love their simplicity and scorners delight in scorning, the opposite of a son who leans in to understand.
The words of the wise open with the same call to incline the ear and apply the heart.
Heart and ears are again joined in receiving instruction and knowledge.
The father again asks his son to give attention and incline his ear to his sayings.

units.notes:
• The ESV reads "making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding." In Hebrew, the verb behind the NKJV's "incline your ear" means to make attentive, while the verb for bending or turning stands behind "apply your heart" in the second line. The ESV follows that order; the NKJV moves the bending picture to the ear. Either way, ear and heart are both turned toward wisdom.
• The same pairing of ear and heart returns in 22:17 and 23:12: "Apply your heart to instruction, And your ears to words of knowledge." In 4:20 the father says again, "Incline your ear to my sayings."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Attention of body, intention of mind, and retention of memory, are indispensably desired of all wisdom's scholars." In other words, every student of wisdom must give it body, mind and memory, the whole person and not the ear alone.
• Henry: "We must apply our hearts to them, else inclining the ear to them will stand us in no stead." In plain English, listening without the heart will do us no good.
• Compare Isaiah 50:4, "He awakens My ear To hear as the learned," and James 1:22.
units.summary: Wisdom is not overheard in passing; it is caught by people who lean in and care.
units.principle: Real learning takes both an attentive ear and a willing heart; hearing without caring changes nothing.
units.insight: Mary of Bethany "sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word," while Martha was distracted with much serving (Luke 10:39–40). Jesus said Mary had "chosen that good part" (Luke 10:42). The boy Samuel learned to say, "Speak, for Your servant hears" (1 Samuel 3:10). Our problem is seldom that we cannot hear; it is that we half-listen. We sit through sermons planning the afternoon and nod at counsel while composing our reply. The heart decides what the ear will catch. Jesus Himself lived with an inclined ear. He said, "As I hear, I judge" (John 5:30), and He did nothing on His own apart from the Father. He is both the model of a listening Son and the One who can open our dull ears to hear.
units.application: The next time you open the Bible or sit under preaching, put the phone away and ask one question: "What is God saying to me here?" Parents, when your child speaks, turn and look at them; you teach listening by doing it. Employees and students, when a supervisor or teacher corrects you, hear them to the end before you defend yourself, then ask one question that shows you want to understand.

rel.note: Wisdom raises her voice to call the simple, and here the son raises his voice in answer.
Those who refused Wisdom will call when it is too late; the son is urged to cry out now, while she is calling.
The son's cry is answered because the LORD Himself gives wisdom.
Wisdom promises that those who seek her diligently will find her, the same hope behind the son's cry.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, "lift up your voice" is the same expression used of Wisdom in 1:20, "She raises her voice in the open squares," though the NKJV words the two places differently. The repeated wording ties the son's cry to Wisdom's call.
• The ESV reads "if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding."
• Bridges: "Earthly wisdom is gained by study; heavenly wisdom by prayer." He adds that prayer must not stand in place of hard work but should "give energy to it."
• Compare James 1:5; Psalm 119:18; Ephesians 1:17–18.
units.summary: Wisdom answers people who cry out for it, not those who assume they already have enough.
units.principle: Wisdom is given to the humble who know their need and ask for it; self-sufficiency never cries out.
units.insight: When Solomon was newly crowned, he did not pretend to be ready. He prayed, "I am a little child; I do not know how to go out or come in," and asked for an understanding heart (1 Kings 3:7, 9). The request pleased the LORD, and He gave him wisdom (1 Kings 3:10–12). Blind Bartimaeus cried out all the more when the crowd told him to be quiet, and Jesus stood still and called him (Mark 10:47–49). God is moved by need that is honest enough to ask. Our trouble is often not that God is silent but that we never really ask. We read, plan and decide, then pray as an afterthought. A prayer for wisdom is a confession that we do not have it. Jesus promised that the Father gives good gifts, even the Holy Spirit, to those who ask Him (Luke 11:13).
units.application: Before your next big decision, about a job, a relationship or a move, stop and ask God for wisdom out loud, specifically, and more than once. Leaders, open planning meetings by asking for discernment, not only for a blessing on what you have already decided. Young people, keep a short list of the questions you are bringing to God, and watch how He answers through Scripture, counsel and circumstances.

rel.note: Getting wisdom and understanding is better than gold and silver.
The next verse names what the search finds: the fear of the LORD and the knowledge of God.
The seeker digs, but the LORD is the One who gives the wisdom that is found.
Wisdom's gain is better than silver and more precious than rubies, the value that makes the search worth it.
Wisdom herself tells the hearer to choose her instruction rather than silver.

units.notes:
• The silver in view is silver that has been mined and smelted, not metal found lying pure in the ground. The picture is the miner's long labor, not a lucky find.
• Job 28:1–11 describes ancient miners tunneling for silver, gold and gems, then asks, "But where can wisdom be found?" (Job 28:12). This verse draws the same comparison in brief.
• Jesus used the same picture of buried wealth: the kingdom of heaven is "like treasure hidden in a field," for which a man gladly sells all that he has (Matthew 13:44).
• Ironside: "reading books about the Bible is a very different thing to searching the Word for oneself." Helps have their place, but the digging must be our own.
• Compare 3:14–15; 8:10–11, 19; 16:16.
units.summary: People will tunnel through rock for silver; wisdom is worth far more of our digging.
units.principle: Wisdom is found by people who value it above wealth and search for it with patient, persevering effort.
units.insight: Our effort shows what we treasure. People rise early and work late for money, yet many give God's word a hurried glance. The man in Jesus' parable found treasure in a field, and "for joy over it" he sold all he had to buy that field (Matthew 13:44). Paul counted his former gains as loss "for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). That is the search this verse describes, and it ends in a Person: Christ, in whom every treasure of wisdom is hidden (Colossians 2:3). Bridges gives a miner's rule for reading Scripture: "Dig up and down the field; and if the search be discouraging, dig again." Ask yourself where your best energy goes, and whether Christ is worth more to you than silver.
units.application: Choose one book of the Bible and stay in it for a month, reading slowly and writing down questions. Trade a little screen time each day for searching Scripture. Parents, let your children see you dig: talk at the table about something you found in the Word. Small-group leaders, push past quick answers; ask what a verse means, then where else Scripture says the same thing.

rel.note: The book's motto places the fear of the LORD at the beginning of knowledge, the very thing the seeker comes to understand here.
The digging for hidden treasure in the previous verse is the search that ends here in finding God.
The second "Then" adds the next result: after knowing God, the son understands how to live.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life and favor from the LORD, the same discovery at the end of the search.
The fear of the LORD and the knowledge of the Holy One are again joined as the heart of wisdom.

units.notes:
• "God" in the second line translates Elohim, the ordinary Hebrew word for God, while "the LORD" in the first line translates God's personal name. Setting the two side by side shows that knowing the LORD and knowing God are one and the same knowledge.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "In short, 'knowledge of God' refers to personal intimacy with him through obedience to his word."
• "Then" marks the turn from the conditions (2:1–4) to the results. A second "Then" follows in 2:9, so the son gains two things: knowing God (2:5) and knowing how to live (2:9).
• The fear of the LORD is "the beginning of knowledge" (1:7) and "the beginning of wisdom," and "the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding" (9:10).
• Compare Jeremiah 29:13; John 17:3; 2 Corinthians 4:6.
units.summary: The search for wisdom was always, underneath, a search for God Himself.
units.principle: The goal of seeking wisdom is not cleverness but God Himself: a right view of Him and a personal knowledge of Him.
units.insight: Moses had seen God's mighty works, yet he still prayed, "Please, show me Your glory" (Exodus 33:18). The deepest seekers are never satisfied with information about God. Jesus defined eternal life this way: "that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). In Christ the search of this verse reaches its end, for God "has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). It is possible to study the Bible for years and remain a stranger to its Author. Jesus told the scholars of His day that they searched the Scriptures yet were unwilling to come to Him (John 5:39–40). Is your study leading you to worship, or only to more knowledge?
units.application: When you finish reading Scripture, ask two questions: "What did I learn about God?" and "How should I respond to Him?" Then respond, in praise, confession or obedience, before you close the Bible. Teachers and small-group leaders, end each lesson by turning the group toward God, not only toward the lesson's points. Parents, talk with your children about who God is, not only about what He expects.

rel.note: Wisdom promises to make her words known to those who turn, wisdom given by speech.
Because knowledge comes from God's mouth, the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins.
The son's cry for discernment is answered here: the LORD is the One who gives it.
The search for hidden treasure describes the effort with which the son seeks what the LORD gives.
Every word of God is pure, which is why wisdom that comes from His mouth can be trusted.

units.notes:
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, on the whole search of 2:1–6: "The search, strenuous as it must be, is not unguided." The seeker is led by the God he seeks.
• "From His mouth" ties wisdom to God's spoken word. Compare Deuteronomy 8:3, "man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD," which Jesus quoted against the tempter (Matthew 4:4).
• Henry: "The Lord not only is wise himself, but he gives wisdom, and that is more than the wisest men in the world can do."
• The semicolon at the end of the verse in the NKJV shows that the sentence continues into 2:7–8.
• Compare Job 32:8; Daniel 2:21, "He gives wisdom to the wise"; James 1:5, 17.
units.summary: We dig, but God gives; wisdom is never self-made, it comes from the mouth of the LORD.
units.principle: Wisdom is both sought and given: God gives it through His word to those who seek it with all their heart.
units.insight: Daniel and his friends studied hard in Babylon, yet Scripture says, "God gave them knowledge and skill in all literature and wisdom" (Daniel 1:17). When the king's dream threatened their lives, they prayed together, and Daniel blessed the God who "gives wisdom to the wise" (Daniel 2:21). Hard work and humble dependence went together. Two errors lie on either side of this verse. Some treat Bible study as self-improvement, as if diligence earns insight. Others wait for God to drop wisdom on them without ever opening His word. Both miss the God who speaks. In these last days He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), who "became for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30). Every true insight you have received was His gift, and that should make you both grateful and humble.
units.application: Before you read Scripture, ask God to speak, then read expecting Him to. When you gain an insight, thank Him instead of congratulating yourself. Preachers and teachers, prepare diligently and pray as though everything depends on God, because it does. If you have been waiting for guidance without opening the Bible, start reading; if you have been studying without praying, stop and ask.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, the protection this verse describes.
The same verb for storing up appears there: the son treasures his father's commands, and here the LORD stores wisdom for him.
The next verse continues the LORD's care, guarding the paths of justice and preserving His saints.
The LORD is again called a shield, there to those who put their trust in Him.
The son is told to keep the same sound wisdom that the LORD stores up for the upright.

units.notes:
• The word translated "sound wisdom," tushiyyah, describes wisdom that works and can also mean the lasting success such wisdom produces. It returns in 3:21, "Keep sound wisdom and discretion," and in 8:14, where Wisdom says, "Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom."
• "Stores up" is the same verb as "treasure" in 2:1. The son stores his father's words; the LORD stores wisdom for the upright.
• The ESV and NASB render "walk uprightly" as walk "in integrity." The Hebrew word behind it means completeness, a life that is whole and sound.
• Henry: "Even those who walk uprightly may be brought into danger for the trial of their faith, but God is, and will be, a buckler to them." A buckler is a small shield.
• Compare Genesis 15:1; Psalm 84:11; Proverbs 30:5.
units.summary: God not only supplies wisdom for the upright life; He guards the people who live it.
units.principle: God prepares wisdom for those who walk with integrity and shields them on the way, though not always from hardship.
units.insight: The LORD told Abram, "Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward" (Genesis 15:1). Abram still faced famine, long delay and hard tests, but he never walked unshielded. Daniel was not spared the lions' den, yet God "sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22). Some believers assume that walking uprightly guarantees an easy road, and they are shaken when trouble comes. Others quietly trust their own cleverness to protect them. This verse corrects both. The shield is God Himself, not our skill and not our circumstances. In the light of the New Testament, those who belong to Christ are "kept by the power of God through faith for salvation" (1 Peter 1:5). Where are you trusting your own defenses instead of His?
units.application: If a decision this week tempts you to cut a corner, choose integrity and trust God to cover you. If you are suffering even though you have walked uprightly, do not conclude that God has dropped His shield; bring the trouble to Him. Business owners and employees, keep your dealings straight when no one is checking. Parents, teach your children that God's protection is real but is not a promise of an easy life.

rel.note: The upright keep to the highway that departs from evil, the road God guards here.
The same guarding verbs return there, showing that the LORD keeps His people partly through the discretion He gives them.
The previous verse begins the LORD's care, storing wisdom for the upright and shielding them.
The son who keeps wisdom will walk safely in his way, the human side of God's keeping.

units.notes:
• The word translated "saints," chasidim, comes from the same root as chesed, God's steadfast, loyal love. It describes people who are faithful and devoted to the LORD.
• "Guards" and "preserves" are watchman words. The same two Hebrew verbs return in reverse order in 2:11: "Discretion will preserve you" uses the verb behind "preserves" here, and "Understanding will keep you" uses the verb behind "guards." The LORD's guarding is carried out in part through the wisdom He gives.
• The KJV reads "He keepeth the paths of judgment." In older English "judgment" here means justice.
• Guzik: "God not only gives wisdom in His word; He actively works to defend, guard and preserve those who walk in His ways."
• Compare 1 Samuel 2:9; Psalm 37:28; Jude 24.
units.summary: God watches over the road itself, and over everyone who walks it as His own.
units.principle: The LORD keeps watch over the way of justice and over the people who belong to Him, so the faithful never walk alone.
units.insight: Hannah sang, "He will guard the feet of His saints" (1 Samuel 2:9), after years of tears, not before them. God's keeping does not mean an easy road; it means a kept traveler. David was hunted by Saul for years, yet he wrote that the LORD "does not forsake His saints; They are preserved forever" (Psalm 37:28). On the night before the cross, Jesus prayed for His disciples, "Holy Father, keep through Your name those whom You have given Me" (John 17:11). He also promised that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand (John 10:28). Our hearts often doubt that God is watching the road we are on. Yet the One who calls us to the path of justice has already taken responsibility for it. You are not walking unwatched.
units.application: If you feel alone in doing what is right at work or school, remember who guards that path, and keep walking it. This week, pray by name for a believer who is under pressure, asking God to keep their feet. Pastors and parents, remind those in your care that faithfulness is not a solo effort: God keeps His people, and His people should watch over one another.

rel.note: The book's purpose statement names the same three qualities the son now comes to understand.
Those who seek the LORD understand justice, while evil men do not.
The crooked, devious paths of evil men stand against the equity and good path the wise son understands.
The first "Then" gave the first result, knowing God, which comes before knowing how to live.

units.notes:
• The three Hebrew nouns behind "righteousness," "justice" and "equity" are the same three named in the book's purpose statement, where the NKJV translates them "Justice, judgment, and equity" (1:3). The son receives exactly what the book set out to give.
• "Equity" means straightness or evenness, fair dealing with nothing bent. It stands against the "crooked" ways of the evil men in 2:15.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the word for "path" here "refers to 'cart tracks,' 'wagon ruts.'" The good path is a well-worn road others have walked before.
• Righteousness, justice and equity are learned by living them. A person who knows them only from books seldom practices them or profits from them.
• Compare 28:5; Psalm 25:9; Micah 6:8.
units.summary: A heart that knows God carries a compass for every crossroads.
units.principle: Right living grows out of knowing God; moral clarity is the fruit of a right view of Him, not a substitute for it.
units.insight: Solomon asked God for a heart to "discern between good and evil" (1 Kings 3:9). Soon two harlots came before him with one living child and one dead (1 Kings 3:16–27). His judgment made all Israel see "that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice" (1 Kings 3:28). Wisdom from God showed itself in fairness to two women of no standing. That is the fruit this verse describes. Many of us want a rule for every situation. God offers something better: a heart that knows Him and therefore recognizes the good path. Ironside: "It is not so much 'holding the truth,' as being held by that truth." If your knowledge of God has not yet made you fairer at home, at work and in the church, ask Him to let it reach that far.
units.application: When you face a choice with no clear rule, ask first what you know of God's character, then ask which option fits it. Managers, check whether your decisions are fair to the person with the least power in the room. Parents, settle sibling disputes by hearing both sides before you judge. Church leaders weighing a hard situation, pray for discernment before you settle on a policy.

rel.note: It is a pleasant thing to keep wise words within, the same pleasure this verse describes.
Wisdom is again pictured as sweet to the taste and good for the soul.
Wisdom that has entered the heart becomes the discretion and understanding that guard the son.
The evil men delight in doing evil, the opposite appetite from the son who finds knowledge pleasant.
The heart is the spring of life, which is why wisdom must enter it to protect the whole person.

units.notes:
• The small word that opens the verse can mean "when" or "for." The NKJV and KJV read "When," so 2:10 sets the scene for the guarding in 2:11. The ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV read "For," so 2:10 gives the reason the son will understand every good path (2:9). Either way, the key is wisdom inside the heart.
• Bridges: "Clear knowledge floating in the head is deep ignorance." Knowledge that never reaches the heart does not protect anyone.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The more wisdom one learns, the more one desires and enjoys it."
• Proverbs later uses taste to describe the same pleasure: "My son, eat honey because it is good," and "So shall the knowledge of wisdom be to your soul" (24:13–14). Compare Psalm 119:103, "How sweet are Your words to my taste," and Jeremiah 15:16.
• Compare Psalm 1:1–2; Proverbs 4:23.
units.summary: Wisdom guards you best when it is no longer a rule you keep but a delight you love.
units.principle: Truth protects best when it has moved from the head to the heart and become a delight, not just a duty.
units.insight: Jeremiah was mocked and threatened for the message he carried, yet he wrote, "Your words were found, and I ate them, And Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart" (Jeremiah 15:16). That delight kept him going. Lot's wife left Sodom with her feet, but her heart looked back (Genesis 19:26), and Jesus said, "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). We fight temptation with willpower and lists of don'ts, but the deeper cure is a new love. Jesus said, "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me" (John 4:34); obedience was His delight, not His burden. Only God can change what we enjoy, for it is God "who works in you both to will and to do for His good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13). Do you obey God's word like a prisoner, or like someone who has found treasure?
units.application: This week, read a psalm of delight such as Psalm 19 or Psalm 119:97–104, and ask God to make His word sweet to you. Notice what you look forward to most, and whether God's word is anywhere on that list. Parents, aim at your children's hearts, not only their behavior; let them see the joy of knowing God. If you are fighting a besetting sin, pray for a new love, not only more willpower.

rel.note: The book promised discretion to the young man; here that discretion stands guard over him.
Wisdom must first enter the heart and become pleasant before it can stand guard.
The next verse names the first danger the guards of discretion and understanding deliver him from.
The LORD's guarding of His saints, told with the same verbs, is the source of the guarding wisdom does here.
Wisdom, loved and not forsaken, will preserve and keep the son, the same two guarding words.

units.notes:
• The word translated "discretion" is the same one used in the book's purpose statement, "To the young man knowledge and discretion" (1:4). It means the capacity to think things through and plan with purpose.
• The verb for "preserve" here is the same verb rendered "preserves" in 2:8, and "keep" is the same verb rendered "guards" in 2:8. The two guarding words appear in reverse order, so the LORD's guarding of His saints is carried out in part through the discretion and understanding He gives them.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, says wisdom "keeps its follower from making decisions that will later bring only regret."
• Bridges says wisdom in the heart works as a keeper, "like the military guard for the safety of the royal person." He means the bodyguard posted around a king.
• Compare 4:6; 6:22; Philippians 4:7, where the peace of God "will guard your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."
units.summary: Let wisdom in, and it stands guard at the door, spotting danger before you reach it.
units.principle: Wisdom welcomed into the heart becomes an inner guard, helping a person see danger early and refuse it.
units.insight: Abigail saw what David could not see in his anger. She met him on the road, and her discretion kept him from shedding blood. David answered, "blessed is your advice and blessed are you, because you have kept me this day from coming to bloodshed" (1 Samuel 25:33). That is discretion at work: seeing where a road leads before taking it. Most falls do not begin with a dramatic choice but with small steps nobody thought through. The wise person has learned to ask, "Where does this lead?" before saying yes. We cannot post this guard by willpower; God gives it as His word settles into our hearts. Jesus said of His disciples, "I kept them in Your name" (John 17:12), and He still keeps His own. Ask Him to make you discerning before the moment of temptation, not only during it.
units.application: Before you agree to a plan, an invitation or a purchase this week, ask, "Where does this lead in a month, a year, ten years?" Young people, decide ahead of time where you will not go and what you will not do, so the decision is made before the pressure comes. Leaders, slow your team down long enough to think through the consequences. When a trusted friend raises a caution, listen the way David listened to Abigail.

rel.note: The gang of chapter 1 also works by talk, enticing the son with words before drawing him into evil.
Discretion and understanding are the guards that carry out this rescue.
Wisdom's second rescue is from the flattering woman, so both dangers in the chapter work through words.
The worthless man walks with a perverse mouth and devises evil, the same figure described more fully.
Wisdom hates the perverse mouth, which shows why the speech in this verse is so dangerous.

units.notes:
• The word translated "perverse things," tahpukot, comes from a verb meaning to turn over. It describes speech that turns the truth upside down. The same word returns in 2:14, "the perversity of the wicked." Wisdom names the same danger in 8:13: "the perverse mouth I hate."
• The KJV reads "the man that speaketh froward things." "Froward" is an older English word for contrary or perverse.
• Ironside: "Two enemies are seen besetting the feet of the young man." To beset is to surround and attack. The perverse man of 2:12–15 is the first; the immoral woman of 2:16–19 is the second.
• Bridges: "The tempter bears his character upon his lips." What a man really is shows in what he says.
• Compare Isaiah 5:20; 1 Corinthians 15:33; 2 Timothy 3:13.
units.summary: Evil often arrives not as a weapon but as a voice that makes wrong sound right.
units.principle: Evil usually reaches us first through words that twist the truth, so wisdom must teach us to recognize the voice before it moves our feet.
units.insight: The first temptation in the Bible came as a twisted question: "Has God indeed said...?" (Genesis 3:1). The serpent turned God's generous permission into a stingy rule and His warning into a lie. Every perverse voice since has worked the same way. Absalom stole the hearts of Israel with smooth complaints against his father's government long before he raised an army (2 Samuel 15:3–6). Today the voice may come through a friend, a show or a podcast that slowly makes sin sound sensible and obedience sound naive. Isaiah pronounced woe on those "who call evil good, and good evil" (Isaiah 5:20). The answer is not to stop listening but to listen to the right Voice. Jesus met every twisted word of the tempter with "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Whose words are shaping how you see right and wrong?
units.application: Pay attention this week to the voices that make wrong seem normal: a coworker's jokes, a series you are watching, a friend's advice. Ask whether they are turning good and evil upside down. Parents, talk with your teenagers about the persuasive voices in their lives, and teach them to ask, "What is this trying to make me believe?" Young people, if a friend's talk keeps pulling you toward what you once knew was wrong, step back.

rel.note: The road these men chose turns out crooked and devious, the end of leaving the upright path.
The same verb for leaving describes the immoral woman forsaking her husband, so both dangers begin by abandoning what is good.
The son is called to keep to the paths of righteousness, the very paths these men have left.
The path of the just shines ever brighter, the opposite of the ways of darkness.
The way of the wicked is like darkness, where they do not know what makes them stumble.

units.notes:
• "Leave" is the same Hebrew verb translated "forsakes" in 2:17. The perverse men forsake the paths of uprightness, and the immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth. Both dangers begin by abandoning something good.
• The shift from "the man" in 2:12 to "those who leave" here shows a company, not a lone man: a gang joined together in evil.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The promised protection is first defined as deliverance from apostate men who have opted for dark and crooked paths". "Apostate" means people who have turned away from what they once held.
• Compare 4:18–19; John 3:19–20; Ephesians 5:8–11; 1 John 1:6–7.
units.summary: No one wanders into darkness by accident; first he walks away from the light.
units.principle: Walking in darkness begins with leaving the light; drifting from the right way is a choice before it becomes a condition.
units.insight: Demas once worked beside Paul, but Paul later wrote, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). He did not start in darkness; he walked into it. Judas spent three years with Jesus, then took the bread and "went out immediately. And it was night" (John 13:30). Few people abandon the faith in a single moment. They leave the straight path one compromise at a time, and the darkness grows easier as their eyes adjust. Bridges: "Readily do they leave the paths, which they never heartily loved." That is the deeper problem: a path walked without love is easy to leave. Jesus is the light of the world, and whoever follows Him "shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life" (John 8:12). Where have you been drifting from the light?
units.application: If you notice yourself hiding something from a spouse, a parent or a pastor, treat it as a sign that you are drifting toward darkness, and bring it into the light by telling someone you trust. Parents, keep conversation open and calm so your children do not feel they must hide. If a friend who once walked with God is drifting, reach out this week, gently and without scolding.

rel.note: To do evil is like sport to a fool, the same pleasure in wrongdoing.
Companions shape character, which is why time with people who delight in evil is so dangerous.
The son is warned not to desire the company of evil men whose lips talk of trouble.
The son learns to take pleasure in knowledge, setting his appetite against the delight in evil described here.
The wicked cannot sleep unless they have done evil, an appetite for wrongdoing like the one pictured here.

units.notes:
• "Perversity" is the same word as "perverse things" in 2:12: speech and conduct that turn the truth upside down.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the word for "delight" "expresses exuberant, enthusiastic, spontaneous shouts of joy". These men do not sin quietly; they celebrate it.
• Compare 10:23, "To do evil is like sport to a fool." Such men treat wrongdoing as entertainment.
• Paul describes the same hardening in people who not only practice evil "but also approve of those who practice them" (Romans 1:32).
• Compare 4:16–17; Psalm 1:1; 1 Corinthians 13:6.
units.summary: When sin becomes a pleasure instead of a regret, the heart has turned a dangerous corner.
units.principle: What a person enjoys shows where his heart has gone; delight in evil, whether one's own or another's, marks a heart far from God.
units.insight: Herod and his soldiers mocked Jesus and sent Him back to Pilate, and "That very day Pilate and Herod became friends with each other" (Luke 23:11–12). Shared delight in wrongdoing can bind people more tightly than shared virtue. Bridges: "Poisoned themselves, they would poison all around them." Most of us would never cheer outright evil, but the same appetite shows up in smaller forms: laughing at cruelty, enjoying a scandal, savoring someone else's fall. Love, Paul says, "does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6). The cure is a new set of delights. In Christ we become new creations (2 Corinthians 5:17), and sin slowly loses its taste. What makes you laugh, and what do you enjoy watching? Those answers reveal more about your heart than the beliefs you state.
units.application: Notice this week what you laugh at and what you choose to watch. If it celebrates what God calls evil, turn it off. Young people, if your friends enjoy getting someone in trouble or mocking the weak, do not join in, and look for friends who rejoice in what is good. Parents, notice what your children find funny and talk about it gently. If you catch yourself enjoying another's downfall, confess it and pray for that person.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, while the one who perverts his ways will be found out.
The one who is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall, the end the crooked road hides.
Leaving the paths of uprightness explains how the crooked course begins.
The wise son understands equity and every good path, the straight road these men have abandoned.
The son is told to ponder the path of his feet and not turn to the right or the left, the opposite of devious paths.

units.notes:
• The ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV have "paths" in the first line and "ways" in the second, the reverse of the NKJV and KJV. The Hebrew uses two different words for a road or track, and the meaning is the same either way.
• "Crooked" is the opposite of the "equity," or straightness, that the wise son comes to understand in 2:9.
• "Devious" describes people who turn aside and slip away from the road, so their course is hard to follow or trust.
• Bridges: "But the crookedness of their ways hides the end from view." The winding road keeps its travelers from seeing where it finishes.
• Compare 10:9; 28:18; Isaiah 59:8, "They have made themselves crooked paths"; Luke 3:5.
units.summary: A crooked road hides where it ends; only a straight path lets you see where you are going.
units.principle: Crooked living cannot be trusted or followed safely; the straight path of integrity lets a person see where he is going.
units.insight: Jacob spent his early years on a crooked road. He grasped, schemed and deceived his father and his brother (Genesis 27). Deceit came back to him through Laban (Genesis 29:25) and later through his own sons (Genesis 37:31–33). Yet God met him at Peniel, wrestled him to a limp and gave him a new name (Genesis 32:24–28). The crooked man was not beyond God's reach. We all know the pull of the crooked path: the half-truth that avoids trouble, the clever excuse, the story told to look better. Each twist makes the next one easier and the end harder to see. John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus with Isaiah's promise that "The crooked places shall be made straight" (Luke 3:5). Christ still straightens what sin has bent. What crooked habit would you bring to Him?
units.application: If you have been telling half-truths at work or at home, straighten one this week by telling the whole truth, even if it costs you. Leaders, make your decisions and finances open enough that others can follow your path. Young people, be wary of friends whose stories keep changing; a crooked road is hard to leave once you are on it. Parents, praise your children for honesty that cost them something.

rel.note: Wisdom's first rescue was from the man of perverse speech, so both dangers in the chapter work through words.
The next verse shows who she is: a wife who has forsaken her husband and forgotten the covenant of her God.
The immoral woman's lips drip honey and her mouth is smoother than oil, the same smooth speech.
The father's command is to keep the son from the flattering tongue of a seductress.
The same line about the seductress who flatters with her words recurs there, word for word.

units.notes:
• The two Hebrew words behind "immoral woman" and "seductress" both describe an outsider. The first, zarah, describes a woman who is a stranger; the KJV and NASB render it "strange woman" and the ESV "forbidden woman." The second, nokriyah, is the word for a foreigner; the ESV and NASB render it "adulteress." Here the words mark her as outside the young man's home and God's ways; the verse does not settle her nationality.
• "Flatters" translates a verb meaning to make smooth. Her flattery is speech made smooth and easy to swallow; compare 5:3, "her mouth is smoother than oil."
• Proverbs 7:5 repeats the second line word for word: "From the seductress who flatters with her words."
• Ironside: "Unquestionably the primary meaning is clear on the face of the passages that concern her." The warning is first of all about real sexual sin.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The subtlety of the appeal comes from flattering speech—the adulteress talks smoothly".
units.summary: The seductress wins with words before anything else: smooth flattery aimed at a young man's pride.
units.principle: Sexual temptation usually works through flattering words that feed pride and desire; wisdom listens past the words to where they lead.
units.insight: Delilah pressed Samson with her words "daily" until he told her all his heart, and he lost his strength, his sight and his freedom (Judges 16:16–21). Joseph faced daily invitations from his master's wife and refused, and when she seized him, he ran (Genesis 39:10–12). The difference was not the strength of the temptation but the state of the heart. Flattery works because part of us wants to believe it. A lonely or unappreciated heart is most open to the voice that says, "You deserve this." That is why the father aims at the son's heart first (2:10), and why the warning places responsibility on the young man, not on women in general. In Christ we have a better word than flattery: we are loved and "accepted in the Beloved" (Ephesians 1:6). Where are you most hungry to be admired?
units.application: Men, notice when someone's attention and praise make you feel more appreciated than your wife does, and treat that feeling as a warning, not a gift; bring it into the open with a trusted friend. Married couples, speak sincere praise to each other so flattery finds less room. Young men, decide now where you will not go. Parents, talk openly with your sons and daughters about flattering words and where they lead.

rel.note: The same verb for forsaking describes the perverse men leaving the paths of uprightness.
Her flattering words to the young man are built on the unfaithfulness described here.
The unfaithful, who break faith as she has, are the ones uprooted at the chapter's end.
The call to rejoice with the wife of one's youth pictures the faithfulness this woman has abandoned.
The man who joins in adultery lacks understanding and destroys his own soul.

units.notes:
• The word for "companion," alluph, describes a close friend or intimate partner, here her husband. The KJV renders it "guide." The same word appears in Jeremiah 3:4, where Israel calls God "the guide of my youth."
• Malachi describes a wife in similar terms, using a different Hebrew word for "companion": "she is your companion And your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14).
• Another reading takes "the covenant of her God" as the LORD's covenant with Israel, whose commandments forbid adultery (Exodus 20:14). The two readings overlap, since a marriage vow broken in adultery also breaks God's commandment.
• Henry says of the marriage covenant that God is "not only a witness, but a party" to it: the vows are made to Him as well as to the spouse.
• Compare 5:18; Matthew 19:4–6; Hebrews 13:4.
units.summary: A vow broken to a husband is a vow broken before God.
units.principle: Marriage is a covenant made before God, so unfaithfulness wrongs both a spouse and the LORD who witnessed the vow.
units.insight: David's adultery with Bathsheba wronged Uriah, yet David confessed, "Against You, You only, have I sinned, And done this evil in Your sight" (Psalm 51:4). He saw that his sin reached past the people he hurt to the God who had witnessed every vow. That is what this verse teaches. We often treat promises as private agreements we may revise when feelings change; God treats them as sacred. Jesus said of marriage, "what God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6). Yet the God who keeps covenant also forgives covenant-breakers who return to Him, as David found (2 Samuel 12:13). Christ "loved the church and gave Himself for her" (Ephesians 5:25), the faithful Husband who never forsakes His own. What promises have you quietly begun to forget?
units.application: Married couples, read your vows together this week and thank God for each year kept. If your marriage has grown cold, take one concrete step toward your spouse instead of away. If someone is drawing you away from your spouse, end the contact. Pastors and mentors, teach young couples that the wedding vow is spoken before God. If you have broken a vow, confess it to God and seek wise counsel.

rel.note: The next verse adds how hard it is to come back once a person has gone down that road.
Her feet go down to death and her steps lay hold of hell, the same downward road.
Her house is again pictured as the way to hell, descending to the chambers of death.
Wisdom has built her own house, which leads to life rather than death.
Folly's guests are found among the dead, the same end as the immoral woman's house.

units.notes:
• The word translated "the dead," rephaim, refers to the departed, those who have passed into the realm of the dead; the ESV renders it "departed." It recurs in 9:18, "the dead are there," and 21:16, "the assembly of the dead."
• The verb behind "leads down" means to sink. The ESV and NASB say her house "sinks down to death."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Not only does she sink down to death, but her paths lead to the 'shades'". "Shades" is an older word for the spirits of the dead.
• The two houses run through Proverbs 1–9. The immoral woman's house leads to death (2:18; 7:27), while Wisdom builds her house and invites the simple to life (9:1–6). Folly's house ends the same way as hers: "the dead are there" (9:18).
• Compare 5:5; 14:12; Romans 6:23; James 1:15.
units.summary: Sexual sin has an inviting door, but the floor behind it slopes down to death.
units.principle: Sin advertises pleasure but leads downward to death; where a road ends matters more than how its entrance looks.
units.insight: Amnon's lust for his half-sister ended in disgrace for Tamar and, two years later, in his own death (2 Samuel 13:14–15, 23, 28–29). The pleasure lasted an evening; the ruin spread through David's house. Sin always hides its price. The serpent spoke of opened eyes, never of a closed garden (Genesis 3:5, 23–24). Every temptation presents itself as a way to life and is really a slope toward death. At a deeper, layered level, the two houses picture two ways of life: the immoral woman, like Folly, stands for sin, the world and idolatry, while Wisdom's house pictures the true Church. Christ went down into death Himself to free those who were held by the fear of it (Hebrews 2:14–15). Which house is your life walking toward?
units.application: Before you click, text, flirt or open a door you should not, picture where it ends, not just how it starts. If you are battling sexual temptation, ask a trusted friend to hold you accountable this week. Parents, teach your teens to think past the moment: "Where does this road go?" Pastors, preach the cost of sin plainly, and the cross more plainly still.

rel.note: The way of life winds upward for the wise, the path those who go to her do not regain.
Mercy is promised to whoever confesses and forsakes sin, which keeps this warning from being read as a bar to repentance.
Her house leads down to death, the road from which this verse says few return.
The sentence continues there with wisdom's purpose: to keep the son on the way of goodness.
The wicked man is caught in the cords of his own sin, the grip that makes return so hard.

units.notes:
• "None who go to her return" is a strong general statement about the power of the path, not a ruling that restoration is impossible. Henry's paraphrase, "None, or next to none," shows he heard it the same way: return is rare, not impossible.
• The phrase "the paths of life" stands opposite "her paths to the dead" (2:18). Compare 15:24, "The way of life winds upward for the wise, That he may turn away from hell below."
• The dash at the end of the NKJV verse shows that 2:20 completes the thought, returning to the purpose of wisdom's rescue.
• The KJV reads "neither take they hold of the paths of life." The picture is of a grip that sin has loosened, so that the road back is hard to take hold of.
• Compare 5:22; 28:13; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11; John 8:10–11.
units.summary: The road of sexual sin is built for going in, not coming back; only grace makes a way home.
units.principle: The way of sexual sin pulls hard and rarely lets go, so flee it early; yet no one who confesses and forsakes sin is beyond God's mercy.
units.insight: Hold this verse with two hands. With one it warns: sexual sin grips and hardens the heart, and the way back is hard. Samson never recovered his eyes. With the other, Scripture shows the way home. David fell, confessed and heard, "The LORD also has put away your sin" (2 Samuel 12:13). Jesus told a woman caught in adultery, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:11). Paul wrote to believers who had lived in sexual sin, "And such were some of you. But you were washed" (1 Corinthians 6:11). Bridges calls such returns proof of "how far the 'arm of the Lord' can reach," meaning God's saving power. If you have fallen, do not let this verse tell you there is no way back. Let it show you how deep the pit was, and how great the Savior who lifts you out.
units.application: If you are standing near this road, turn back today; the earlier you turn, the easier it is. If you have fallen into sexual sin, confess it to God and to a pastor or mature believer this week, and take concrete steps to cut off the path. Friends and church leaders, when someone confesses, meet them with truth and grace, not shock or contempt. Parents, make sure your children know there is always a way home.

rel.note: In the way of righteousness is life, the reason to keep to it.
Walking with wise people makes a person wise, which is how the way of good people is learned.
The perverse men left the paths of uprightness, the opposite of keeping to the paths of righteousness.
Those who go to the immoral woman do not regain the paths of life, while the son is kept on them.
The path of the just shines brighter and brighter, the continuing walk this verse calls for.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "the way of good men" and "the paths of the righteous." The way of goodness is also the road that good people have walked before.
• Henry: "we must cease to do evil, in order that we may learn to do well." Compare Isaiah 1:16–17, "Cease to do evil, Learn to do good."
• Bridges: "Not only does it deliver from evil men; but it guides us into the way of good men."
• Proverbs pictures the same continuing walk in 4:18: "the path of the just is like the shining sun, That shines ever brighter unto the perfect day."
• Compare Psalm 23:3; Jeremiah 6:16; Hebrews 12:1–2.
units.summary: Wisdom does not only pull you off the wrong road; it keeps you walking the right one.
units.principle: God rescues us from evil not only to keep us safe but to set us walking, step by step, in what is good.
units.insight: Caleb did more than refuse to side with the frightened spies (Numbers 14:6–9). Forty-five years later he could still say, "I wholly followed the LORD my God" (Joshua 14:8, 10). Enoch "walked with God three hundred years" (Genesis 5:22). A faith that is only about avoiding sin wears thin. There must be a road to walk, not only a ditch to avoid. David sang of the Shepherd who "leads me in the paths of righteousness For His name's sake" (Psalm 23:3). The One who rescues also leads. In Christ the way of goodness has a face, for He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Is your Christian life mostly a list of things you do not do, or a road you are walking with Him?
units.application: Pick one good habit to replace one bad one this week: Scripture in place of the late-night scroll, a call to an older believer in place of an hour of idle talk. Find someone further down the road and walk with them. Parents, give your children good things to do, not only rules about what to avoid. Leaders, celebrate faithfulness over time, not only dramatic moments.

rel.note: When the whirlwind passes, the righteous still stand on an everlasting foundation.
The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not inhabit the earth, the same two ends in one line.
The root of the righteous cannot be moved, the same security pictured as remaining in the land.
The blameless will inherit good, the same hope for those whose lives are whole before God.
The next verse gives the opposite end: the wicked cut off and the unfaithful uprooted.

units.notes:
• The word translated "blameless," temimim, describes what is whole, complete and sound. It is the same word rendered "whole" in 1:12, where the gang plans to swallow its victims "whole."
• Jesus' words in Matthew 5:5 come from Psalm 37:11, "But the meek shall inherit the earth," a psalm that again and again contrasts the righteous who inherit the land with the wicked who are cut off.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Here the wise man speaks after the manner of Moses' law, under which he lived". The promise is framed in the covenant language of Deuteronomy.
• Ironside reads the verse in its first setting: "It is not the heavenly but the earthly hope that here comes before us." The New Testament carries that hope forward to the meek and to a new earth (Matthew 5:5; 2 Peter 3:13).
• Compare 10:30; Psalm 37:9, 29; Deuteronomy 4:1.
units.summary: Those who walk God's way have a place with Him that no one can take away.
units.principle: God gives the upright a lasting place with Him, first pictured in Israel's land and fulfilled in the inheritance Christ gives His people.
units.insight: Abraham lived in the land of promise as a stranger, dwelling in tents, yet "he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:9–10). He was secure under God's care, and his true inheritance was larger than the ground under his feet. Many believers today feel unsettled, moving between jobs and homes, unsure where they belong. This verse speaks to that ache. God gives His people a place: a secure standing with Him now, and at the end "new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells" (2 Peter 3:13). The meek, not the grasping, inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). In Christ we already hold an inheritance "reserved in heaven" for us (1 Peter 1:4). Where are you trying to secure your place by grasping instead of trusting?
units.application: If you feel uprooted by a move, a job loss or a season of instability, bring that fear to God and remember that your place with Him is secure. Resist the urge to grab security through shortcuts or compromise. Parents, build a home where God's ways are lived, so your children learn what it means to belong. Church members, welcome newcomers this week and help them find a place among God's people.

rel.note: The wicked will not inhabit the earth, while the righteous will never be removed.
The perversity of the unfaithful destroys them, the same people who are uprooted here.
The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous stands.
The woman who broke faith with her husband and her God shows what the unfaithful are like.
The previous verse describes the upright who remain, the opposite of those uprooted.

units.notes:
• The word the NKJV renders "earth" here is the same word it renders "land" in 2:21. The ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV render it "land" in both verses, keeping the contrast between those who remain in the land and those cut off from it.
• "Unfaithful" describes the treacherous, those who betray a trust. The description fits both the woman who betrayed her husband (2:17) and the men who left the right paths (2:13).
• The KJV reads "the transgressors shall be rooted out of it," and its margin offers "plucked up" for "rooted out."
• Wiersbe, quoted by Guzik: "There's a price to pay if we would gain spiritual wisdom, but there's an even greater price to pay if we don't gain it."
• Compare 10:30; 12:3, 7; Psalm 1:4–6; Psalm 37:9–10; Matthew 15:13.
units.summary: The wicked think they are planted forever, but God uproots what He did not plant.
units.principle: The way of the wicked ends in removal under God's judgment; what is not rooted in Him cannot last.
units.insight: Asaph nearly lost his footing when he saw the wicked prosper. Then he went into the sanctuary of God: "Then I understood their end" (Psalm 73:17). Psalm 37 tells the believer not to fret over evildoers, "For they shall soon be cut down like the grass" (Psalm 37:2). God's timing is not ours, and the wicked sometimes flourish for years, but their end is certain. Jesus said, "Every plant which My heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted" (Matthew 15:13). This truth sobers us, because apart from grace we were all among the unfaithful. It also comforts us. Christ "was cut off from the land of the living" (Isaiah 53:8) so that we might be "rooted and grounded in love" (Ephesians 3:17). Where are your roots really planted?
units.application: When you are tempted to envy someone who prospers by cutting corners, read Psalm 73 and remember where that road ends. If you have been wronged by a faithless person, leave the uprooting to God instead of taking revenge. Parents, show your children both ends of the road, gently but plainly. If you are walking a crooked path yourself, turn now while there is time.

rel.note: The heart that keeps the father's commands is the tablet on which mercy and truth must be written.
The father repeats his own father's charge to let the heart retain his words and keep his commands.
Parental commands are to be bound on the heart continually, the same inward keeping urged here.
The son is again told to keep the father's commands and write them on the tablet of his heart.

units.notes:
• *Law* is *torah*, teaching or instruction, the same word used of the mother's "law" in 1:8.
• *Keep* (natsar) means to guard or preserve. The same verb returns in 4:23, "Keep your heart with all diligence."
• Forgetting here is willful neglect, not weak memory; compare Deuteronomy 4:23 and Psalm 119:93, "I will never forget Your precepts."
• Bridges: "The heart is the first thing that wanders from God: the first also that returns."
• Compare 4:4; 7:1–3; Deuteronomy 6:6; Psalm 119:11; Jeremiah 31:33; John 14:15.
units.summary: God is not after a son who remembers the rules but a son who treasures them.
units.principle: Lasting obedience grows from a heart that treasures God's word, not from rules kept only under supervision.
units.insight: Joash "did what was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest" (2 Chronicles 24:2). When his old mentor died, Joash listened to new voices and Judah drifted into idolatry (24:17–18). His obedience had lived in another man's presence, not in his own heart. Many of us know that pattern: faithful under a parent's roof, a pastor's eye or a spouse's watch, and careless when alone. The father wants more than compliance. Ironside: "Love is the spring of true service to the Lord." That is why Jesus tied obedience to love: "If you love Me, keep My commandments" (John 14:15). And it is why the new covenant promises what no parent can give, God's law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). Ask yourself who you are when no one is checking.
units.application: Parents: aim past behavior to the heart. Explain the why behind your rules, and pray for your children to love God, not only to comply. Young people leaving home: decide now which of your parents' convictions you will keep as your own, and write them down. All of us: choose one passage this week, such as Psalm 119:11, and memorize it so it goes with you where no one is watching.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD prolongs days, stated as the same general pattern rather than a guarantee.
The length of days promised for keeping the father's commands is the gift Wisdom holds in her right hand.
The peace added here is the character of every path Wisdom walks.
Receiving the father's sayings is again tied to many years of life.
Wisdom herself says that by her days are multiplied and years of life added.

units.notes:
• *Long life* is literally "years of life" (shenot chayyim). The ESV and NASB keep that wording, and the KJV notes it in the margin.
• *Peace* (shalom) is wholeness and well-being in every part of life, not only the end of hostility.
• Bridges leaves the length of life in God's hands: "length of days is the promise to the righteous; whether for earth or for heaven, as their Father deems fittest for them."
• Long life and peace return together in 3:16–17, where length of days is in Wisdom's right hand and "all her paths are peace."
• Compare 4:10; 9:11; 10:27; Psalm 34:12–14; Ephesians 6:2–3.
units.summary: Long life is a gift only when peace comes with it, and wisdom tends to bring both.
units.principle: Living God's way generally preserves life and brings wholeness, though God alone sets the length of any life.
units.insight: We tend to measure blessing by length; God measures it by fullness. Methuselah lived 969 years, and Scripture records almost nothing else about him (Genesis 5:27). John the Baptist died young in Herod's prison, yet Jesus said no one born of women was greater (Matthew 11:11). The wise way usually adds years, and we should thank God when it does. The deeper gift is peace. Jesus, whose earthly life was short, left His disciples that very gift: "Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you" (John 14:27). So if you are anxious about how long you will live, there is a better question to ask. Are you at peace with God through Christ (Romans 5:1)? That peace does not end when your years do.
units.application: Young people: count the cost of the shortcuts that shorten lives, such as reckless driving, drunkenness, sexual sin and uncontrolled rage, and choose the slower, wiser way. If you are grieving a faithful believer who died young, do not read this verse as a verdict on that person; their times were in God's hand (Psalm 31:15). If your days are full but your heart is restless, seek peace where Jesus offers it, not in more time.

rel.note: The same pair, mercy and truth, stands at the center of how iniquity is atoned for and evil is left behind.
Mercy and truth that sustain a private life also preserve a king and his throne.
The heart on which mercy and truth are written is the same heart that must keep the father's commands.
Sound wisdom, like mercy and truth, becomes an ornament of grace to the neck.
The next verse gives the fruit of keeping mercy and truth: favor with God and man.
The father's words are again to be bound on and written on the tablet of the heart.

units.notes:
• *Mercy and truth* are *chesed* and *emet*, steadfast love and faithfulness, the pair used of the LORD in Exodus 34:6. The ESV has "steadfast love and faithfulness," the NLT "loyalty and kindness."
• *Tablet* (luach) is the word used for the stone tablets of the law (Exodus 31:18).
• Bridges, quoting F. Taylor, on keeping the two together: "The want of one buries the commendation of the other."
• Some older interpreters also read the pair as God's own mercy in making promises and His truth in keeping them. The next verse, with its favor "in the sight of God and man," shows that the father mainly means qualities the son himself practices.
• Compare 6:21; 7:3; 16:6; 20:28; 2 Corinthians 3:3.
units.summary: Wear faithful love where everyone can see it, and write it where only God can.
units.principle: Faithful love must be both visible in conduct and written on the heart; either one alone falls short.
units.insight: Ruth gave Naomi this kind of love. She could have gone home to Moab, but she bound herself to her mother-in-law: "wherever you go, I will go" (Ruth 1:16). Boaz saw it and called it kindness (Ruth 3:10). Most of us lean one way. Some are truthful but hard, quick to be right and slow to be kind. Others are warm but unreliable, kind in the moment and careless with their word. The father will not let us choose. Only the gospel joins the two perfectly: "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Ironside: "The law was truth, but it was truth without grace." In Christ we receive both, and His Spirit writes them on hearts of flesh (2 Corinthians 3:3). Which of the two has slipped off your neck?
units.application: In a conflict at home or at work, check both questions: Am I being truthful? Am I being kind? If you tend to be blunt, add mercy before you speak. If you tend to smooth things over, add truth, even when it costs you. Parents and leaders: keep your promises, small ones included, because faithfulness is love people can count on. Choose one relationship this week where loyalty has slipped and begin to restore it.

rel.note: Good understanding gains favor, while the way of the unfaithful is hard.
When a man's ways please the LORD, even his enemies are brought to peace with him.
A good name and loving favor are worth more than riches.
This verse gives the result of keeping the mercy and truth commanded in the verse before.
The esteem faithful love earns now is completed in the glory the wise inherit.

units.notes:
• *Favor* (chen) is goodwill, the grace one finds in another's eyes, as Noah "found grace in the eyes of the LORD" (Genesis 6:8).
• *High esteem* is *sekel tov*, "good sense" or "good insight." The KJV has "good understanding" with "good success" in the margin; the ESV reads "good success," the NASB "good repute."
• Joseph shows the pattern: the LORD was with him and gave him favor with his master and with the keeper of the prison (Genesis 39:2–4, 21).
• Bridges: "What is more lovely than thus to live down reproach by consistent godliness?" To "live down reproach" is to outlast criticism by living faithfully over time.
• Compare 13:15; 16:7; 22:1; Romans 14:18.
units.summary: Mercy and truth win two audiences at once: God above and the people watching you.
units.principle: Faithful love tends to win the trust of God and people alike, though faithfulness never depends on applause.
units.insight: Daniel served kings so faithfully that his rivals "could find no charge or fault, because he was faithful" (Daniel 6:4). The king himself labored until sundown to rescue him (6:14). Yet that same faithfulness put him in the lions' den. Favor with God and favor with people usually travel together, but when they part, the wise choose God's. Our hearts often reverse the order. We chase a reputation and hope character catches up. The father points the other way: hold to mercy and truth, and let esteem follow. Jesus grew in favor with God and men (Luke 2:52), and later was "despised and rejected by men" (Isaiah 53:3). He never traded faithfulness for approval. Whose approval are you working hardest to win?
units.application: Employees and students: build your reputation the slow way, by keeping your word and treating people kindly when there is nothing to gain. Leaders: ask whether people trust you because of your title or because of your faithfulness. If you have lost someone's respect, do not argue for it; rebuild it with steady mercy and truth. If you are mistreated for doing right, remember that God's favor does not wait on public opinion.

rel.note: Whoever trusts in the LORD is called happy, the blessing of the whole-hearted trust commanded here.
The man who trusts in his own heart is called a fool, the very self-reliance this verse forbids.
The trust commanded at the start of the chapter returns as the LORD Himself becoming the son's confidence.
Trust with all the heart is carried into every path by acknowledging the LORD in all one's ways.
Refusing to lean on one's own understanding is the same humility as refusing to be wise in one's own eyes.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "lean" pictures resting the body's weight on something, as Saul leaned on his spear (2 Samuel 1:6) and a king leaned on an officer's hand (2 Kings 5:18; 7:2). Self-reliance is pictured as leaning on a support that will give way.
• The verb translated "trust," *batach*, means to rely on someone and feel secure in him. It is the same command as Psalm 37:3, "Trust in the LORD, and do good."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Do not rely, or lean as on a broken crutch, depicts what is meant by ‘trust.’" The second line defines trust by showing its opposite.
• Trust does not switch off the mind. Bridges: "practical faith strengthens, not destroys, its power; invigorates, not supersedes, exertion." In plain words, faith makes thinking and effort stronger; it does not replace them.
• Compare 28:26, "He who trusts in his own heart is a fool"; 16:20; 22:19, where the sayings are given "So that your trust may be in the LORD"; Psalm 62:8; Philippians 3:3.
units.summary: Lean your whole weight on God; your own understanding was never built to carry it.
units.principle: Whole-hearted reliance on God, not confidence in our own judgment, is the foundation of a wise life; the mind serves trust and does not replace it.
units.insight: King Asa shows both sides of this verse. Facing a vast Ethiopian army, he prayed, "help us, O LORD our God, for we rest on You" (2 Chronicles 14:11), and God gave the victory. Years later, threatened by the king of Israel, he paid the king of Syria for help instead. The prophet Hanani told him, "you have relied on the king of Syria, and have not relied on the LORD your God" (16:7). "Rest on" and "relied on" translate the same verb this verse uses for "lean." Asa did not stop thinking; he stopped trusting. Many of us drift the same way. We pray hard in the crisis, then quietly lean on our plans, savings and contacts once life settles. Jesus trusted His Father fully, even in death: "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit" (Luke 23:46). Where are you leaning your weight right now?
units.application: If you face a decision this week, such as a job offer, a move or a hard conversation, do your homework, then bring the whole matter to God before you settle it. Ask yourself where you have already decided without Him. Young adults: seek the counsel of older believers, not only your own reasoning. Leaders: tell your team you are praying over a decision. If you are anxious, name one thing you are gripping tightly and hand it to the LORD in prayer.

rel.note: The righteousness of the blameless makes his way straight, using the same picture of a level path.
Committing one's works to the LORD brings established plans, the same promise of guidance for those who acknowledge Him.
A man plans his way but the LORD directs his steps, showing that human planning and divine guidance work together.
The straight paths God gives are the paths on which the wise walk safely without stumbling.
Acknowledging God in all one's ways is how whole-hearted trust in the LORD is lived out.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "acknowledge," *yada*, is the common Hebrew word for "know." To acknowledge God in all your ways is more than mentioning Him; it is living with Him in view.
• The verb translated "direct," *yashar*, means to make straight or level. The ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV promise that He will "make straight" your paths; the KJV and NKJV have "direct." The same verb describes the highway made straight for God in Isaiah 40:3.
• Bridges: "He loves to be consulted." No matter is too small to bring to Him.
• Israel's leaders show the cost of skipping this step. They made a treaty with the Gibeonites on the evidence of their eyes, "but they did not ask counsel of the LORD" (Joshua 9:14).
• Compare 16:3, 9; 11:5; Psalm 37:5; James 4:13–15.
units.summary: Do not keep God for emergencies; bring Him into every road you take, and He will level it.
units.principle: God guides the person who invites Him into every decision, and His guidance leads where it should even when the road is hard.
units.insight: Wherever Abraham pitched his tent, he built an altar to the LORD (Genesis 12:7–8; 13:18). His moving life was marked by worship at every stop. David asked the LORD before he went to Keilah and before he went up to Hebron (1 Samuel 23:2; 2 Samuel 2:1). Our hearts tend to divide life into God's part and our part. We pray about the surgery and the move, but we run our spending, our schedules and our speech on our own. Jesus lived the other way. He said, "the Son can do nothing of Himself, but what He sees the Father do" (John 5:19), and He prayed all night before choosing His apostles (Luke 6:12–13). The straight path is not first a better plan. It is a closer walk with the One who knows the way.
units.application: Start each day this week by naming its main tasks before God and asking Him to direct them. Before a purchase, a commitment or a reply you might regret, pause for one sincere prayer. Parents: let your children hear you pray over ordinary decisions, not only emergencies. If you stand at a crossroads, such as a career change or a serious relationship, search Scripture, seek godly counsel and pray. Then take the next faithful step and trust God to straighten the road.

rel.note: The fool's way is right in his own eyes, but the wise listen to counsel.
The wise man fears and departs from evil, while the fool rages and is self-confident.
By the fear of the LORD one departs from evil, joining the same two commands found here.
The man wise in his own eyes is said to have less hope than a fool, showing why this warning matters.
Refusing to be wise in one's own eyes is the humble side of refusing to lean on one's own understanding.
The next verse names the blessing that follows the humble fear of the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Wise in your own eyes" means rating yourself wise by your own standard. Isaiah pronounces a woe on those "who are wise in their own eyes, And prudent in their own sight" (Isaiah 5:21).
• Paul echoes this verse in Romans 12:16: "Do not be wise in your own opinion."
