• Fearing the LORD and turning from evil belong together throughout Scripture: "by the fear of the LORD one departs from evil" (16:6). Compare 8:13, "The fear of the LORD is to hate evil," and Job 28:28.
• Seneca, quoted by Bridges: "I suppose that many might have attained to wisdom, had they not thought they had already attained it."
• Compare 12:15; 14:16; 26:12; 1 Corinthians 3:18.
units.summary: The surest sign you are not wise is being sure you are.
units.principle: Self-confidence closes the door to wisdom; a right view of God humbles the mind and turns the feet away from evil.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar walked on his palace roof and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built… by my mighty power and in the honor of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30). He was wise in his own eyes, and God humbled him until he lived like an animal. Then, he says, "I… lifted my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me" (4:34). His right mind came back when he looked up. Self-made wisdom is hard to see in ourselves. It sounds like "I already know that," "I don't need advice," or "my case is different." Jesus thanked His Father for hiding these things "from the wise and prudent" and revealing them "to babes" (Matthew 11:25). The door into God's wisdom is low; only those who bow can enter it. Where have you stopped being teachable?
units.application: This week, ask someone who knows you well, such as a spouse, friend or elder, "Where do you see me being stubborn?" Listen without defending yourself. Leaders: invite disagreement before you decide, and thank the person who gives it. Students and young adults: when a parent or mentor warns you, take a day to weigh the warning before you dismiss it. If there is a sin you keep returning to, take one concrete step away from it today.

rel.note: A sound heart is life to the body while envy rots the bones, the same link between inner life and body.
Pleasant words bring health to the bones, another inward good that strengthens the body.
A broken spirit dries the bones, the opposite of the refreshment promised here.
This verse names the blessing of the humble fear of the LORD commanded in the verse before.
The father's words are again called health to all the flesh of those who find them.

units.notes:
• The word translated "flesh" normally means the navel, which the KJV keeps ("health to thy navel"). The ESV and NASB, like the NKJV, take it to stand for the whole body.
• The KJV margin explains the word behind "health" as medicine and the word behind "strength" as a watering or moistening. The ESV and NASB use "refreshment." The picture is of bones kept moist and alive.
• Dried-up bones picture a person worn down within: "a broken spirit dries the bones" (17:22). Compare 15:30 and 16:24, where good news and pleasant words bring health to the bones.
• Henry: "Envy is the rottenness of the bones; the sorrow of the world dries them; but hope and joy in God are marrow to them." Marrow, the living center of the bone, is the KJV's word in this verse.
• Compare 4:22; Psalm 32:3–5; 3 John 2.
units.summary: Pride and sin wear down the whole person; humble fear of God works like medicine to the bones.
units.principle: Humble reverence for God and turning from sin tend to bring wholeness to body as well as soul, though sickness is never proof of spiritual failure.
units.insight: David knew what hidden sin does to a body: "When I kept silent, my bones grew old Through my groaning all the day long" (Psalm 32:3). When he confessed, the weight lifted (32:5). Guilt, resentment and pride are heavy loads, and many of us carry them in our sleep, our stomachs and our tempers. The fear of the LORD sets them down. Yet Scripture refuses to make health a scorecard. Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and told Timothy to take a little wine for his frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5:23). The deepest healing this verse points toward is the one Christ gives: "by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). If you are ill, do not hear this verse as an accusation. If you are carrying unconfessed sin, hear it as an invitation.
units.application: If bitterness or guilt is wearing you down, confess it to God this week, and to a trusted believer if that helps (James 5:16). Make amends where you can. Caregivers and friends of the sick: never suggest that someone's illness proves a lack of faith; pray with them and help carry the load. Busy workers and parents: notice whether pride, worry or overwork is costing your body, and practice rest as an act of trust.

rel.note: The one who scatters and the generous soul are enriched, the same pattern of giving that is not a loss.
The same verb of honoring describes the person who shows mercy to the needy, another way to honor God with possessions.
The word for firstfruits is the word for the beginning of knowledge, so both verses speak of what comes first and best.
The next verse gives the result of honoring the LORD with the firstfruits: God's generous provision.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "honor," *kabed*, comes from a root meaning heavy. To honor the LORD is to give Him weight in your life and treat Him as weighty.
• The word translated "firstfruits," *reshit*, is the word translated "beginning" in 1:7: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." The fear of the LORD is the first and chief part of knowledge; the firstfruits are the first and best part of the harvest.
• Israel brought its firstfruits in a basket and confessed that the LORD had brought them into the land He gave them (Deuteronomy 26:1–11). The gift was a statement of who owned the land and its crops.
• Firstfruits were offerings brought to God at His sanctuary. Garrett, quoted by Guzik, says of this verse that "this is the only place where Proverbs alludes to the ceremonial worship," and he adds that its real concern is gratitude toward God and confidence in Him rather than in wealth.
• Henry: "God, who is the first and best, must have the first and best of every thing".
• Compare 11:24–25; 14:31; Exodus 23:19; 1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7.
units.summary: Give God the first and best, not the leftovers, and you confess that all of it is His.
units.principle: Giving God the first and best of what we receive confesses that all we have comes from Him and belongs to Him.
units.insight: Cain and Abel both brought offerings, but Abel brought "of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat" (Genesis 4:4), the first and the best. The widow at the temple gave two small coins, "all that she had" (Mark 12:44), and Jesus said she gave more than all the rich. The question this verse asks is not mainly "How much?" but "Which part?" Many of us give God what is left after everything else is paid, and our giving shows where our trust really rests. The gospel answers our grudging hearts with God's own generosity. He did not give us leftovers; He "did not spare His own Son" (Romans 8:32). "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). Hearts that have received that gift learn to give first.
units.application: When you are paid this week, set aside your gift to God first, before the bills and the spending, and decide the amount prayerfully. Households: talk together about what giving the first and best looks like in your budget. Business owners and farmers: honor God from the first of a new contract, harvest or sale. If money is very tight, start small, but start first; God looks at the willing heart behind the gift (2 Corinthians 8:12).

rel.note: The blessing of the LORD makes one rich and adds no sorrow, naming God as the source of the plenty.
The generous soul is made rich and the one who waters is watered, the same pattern of God's provision for givers.
The one who trusts in riches will fall, a warning against turning this promise into trust in wealth.
The son is told not to wear himself out to get rich, which keeps this verse from becoming a formula for wealth.
The plenty pictured here follows from honoring the LORD with the firstfruits commanded in the verse before.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "overflow" means to break out or burst through. The KJV has "thy presses shall burst out with new wine," a picture of juice spilling over the sides.
• Henry: "He does not say thy bags, but thy barns, not thy wardrobe replenished, but thy presses". The promise is barns and winepresses, not money bags and fine clothes: plenty for living and giving, not for display.
• Malachi 3:10 uses similar language of God opening "the windows of heaven" to those who bring the tithe. That passage may be connected as an application, but this verse speaks of firstfruits.
• Ironside: "None shall find Him in their debt."
• Compare 10:22; 11:28; 23:4–5; Philippians 4:19; 2 Corinthians 9:8; 1 Timothy 6:9–10.
units.summary: You can never out-give God, but you cannot buy riches from Him either.
units.principle: God faithfully provides for those who honor Him first, yet His provision meets needs and funds good works; it is not a formula for wealth.
units.insight: The widow of Zarephath had one handful of flour left when Elijah asked her to make him a small cake first (1 Kings 17:12–13). She did, and "The bin of flour was not used up, nor did the jar of oil run dry" (17:16). She never became rich, but she and her son did not go hungry. That is the shape of this promise. Our hearts twist it in two directions. Fear says, "If I give first, I will not have enough." Greed says, "If I give, God will make me rich." Jesus answers both: "seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matthew 6:33). "These things" are food and clothing. Is it fear or greed that shapes your giving?
units.application: If fear keeps you from giving, take one step of trust this week: give first, then watch how God provides for your needs. If someone has told you that giving guarantees riches, set that teaching beside 23:4–5 and 1 Timothy 6:9–10. Pastors and teachers: present this verse as God's faithfulness, never as a sales pitch. If your barns are already full, ask whether they are for storing up or for doing good (Luke 12:16–21; 2 Corinthians 9:8).

rel.note: Whoever loves instruction loves knowledge, but the one who hates correction is called stupid.
Disdaining instruction is despising one's own soul, while heeding rebuke brings understanding.
Fools despise wisdom and instruction, the very attitude the son is warned against here.
The next verse gives the reason not to despise the LORD's correction: it comes from His love.
The reproofs of instruction are called the way of life, showing why correction must not be despised.

units.notes:
• The word translated "chastening," *musar*, is the word for discipline and instruction found throughout Proverbs, as in "the instruction of your father" (1:8). Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "‘Discipline’ primarily involves teaching or training rather than punishment for wrongdoing."
• The verb translated "detest" means to loathe something or be sick of it. The KJV has "neither be weary of his correction."
• Hebrews 12:5 quotes this verse from the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament: "My son, do not despise the chastening of the LORD, Nor be discouraged when you are rebuked by Him." Its second line differs from the Hebrew, which the NKJV follows here.
• Job 5:17 gives the same command: "do not despise the chastening of the Almighty."
• Bridges calls for "the just mean between hardness and despondency": the balanced middle between shrugging off God's correction and collapsing under it.
units.summary: God's discipline is training, not a sentence; do not shrug it off, and do not sink beneath it.
units.principle: God's correction should be received neither with contempt nor with despair, but as training from a Father who means our good.
units.insight: Ahaz shows the hardened response: "in the time of his distress King Ahaz became increasingly unfaithful to the LORD" (2 Chronicles 28:22). Manasseh shows the humble one: "when he was in affliction, he implored the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly" (33:12), and God restored him. Most of us lean toward one error. Some shrug off every hard providence as bad luck and never ask what God might be teaching. Others sink under it and conclude God has given up on them. Not every trial is correction; Jesus said of the man born blind that neither he nor his parents had sinned (John 9:3). But when God does correct, Hebrews points us to Jesus, who endured the cross, so that we do not "become weary and discouraged" (Hebrews 12:3). Which way does your heart lean?
units.application: When something you did wrong brings painful consequences this week, ask God what He is teaching you instead of blaming circumstances. If you feel crushed by a past failure, read Hebrews 12:5–11 slowly and remember that you are being trained, not discarded. Parents and mentors: correct with patience and explain the purpose, so your children learn what God's discipline is like. Friends of the suffering: do not tell them that their pain must be God's punishment.

rel.note: The father who loves his son disciplines him promptly, the human picture of the LORD's loving correction.
Correcting a son brings rest and delight, showing the good end that loving discipline seeks.
This verse gives the loving reason behind the command not to despise the LORD's chastening.
Reproofs of instruction are the way of life, the purpose behind the correction a loving father gives.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "corrects" means to set someone right by rebuke or reproof. It comes from the same root as "correction" in 3:11.
• Hebrews 12:6 follows the Septuagint: "For whom the LORD loves He chastens, And scourges every son whom He receives." The Greek translators read the Hebrew letters for "as a father" as a verb meaning "makes suffer"; the two readings differ only slightly in the Hebrew letters. The NKJV follows the standard Hebrew text.
• Bridges: "His discipline is that of the family; not of the school; much less of the prison."
• The verse cannot be turned around. Suffering by itself does not prove that someone is God's child, and it does not prove that someone is being punished.
• Compare 13:24; 29:17; Deuteronomy 8:5, "as a man chastens his son, so the LORD your God chastens you"; Psalm 94:12; 119:67, 71.
units.summary: God corrects His children because He delights in them, not because He has given up on them.
units.principle: God's correction flows from His love and delight and aims at our growth; it never gives people license to be harsh.
units.insight: Peter boasted that he would never deny Jesus, and he denied Him three times. After the resurrection Jesus did not pretend it had not happened. Three times He asked, "Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?" and "Peter was grieved" (John 21:17). The questions hurt, but they were not rejection. Each question came with a fresh commission to feed and tend His flock (John 21:15–17). That is how the Lord corrects those He loves. Many of us hear every rebuke as a verdict on our worth, because human correction so often came with anger or contempt. Our Father is different. Ironside: "Our God and Father never so deals with us." Christ the Bridegroom corrects His church in the same love, because He wants His bride whole (Revelation 3:19). Can you receive His correction as proof of His delight?
units.application: Parents: correct your children the way God corrects you, for their good, with delight in them and never in rage (Ephesians 6:4). Apologize when you have disciplined in anger. Leaders and employers: when you must correct someone, make your commitment to that person clear. If you are under correction from God, a pastor or a friend, thank Him that He has not left you to yourself. If anyone uses this verse to excuse abuse, name it as wrong and get help.

rel.note: The search for wisdom as for hidden treasure, described in chapter 2, is the search whose finding is celebrated here.
The poem that opens with happiness for the one who finds wisdom closes with happiness for those who retain her.
Wisdom is called the principal thing, and the son is urged to get understanding with all his getting.
Wisdom herself calls the man who listens to her blessed and says that whoever finds her finds life.

units.notes:
• "Happy" translates *ashre*, the word that opens Psalm 1:1, "Blessed is the man." Ross, quoted by Guzik: "‘Blessed’ describes heavenly bliss stemming from being right with God".
• The word for "Happy" here and the word for "happy" in 3:18 come from the same root, so the praise of wisdom in 3:13–18 begins and ends on the same note.
• The verb translated "gains" means to bring out or draw out; the KJV margin has "draweth out." Henry pictures the seeker drawing wisdom from God: "he draws it with the bucket of prayer from the fountain of all wisdom".
• The verse follows the LORD's correction in 3:11–12. Hardship received in the right spirit is one of the places where wisdom is found (Psalm 119:71).
• Compare 8:34–35; 2:1–6; 4:7; James 1:5.
units.summary: The happiest discovery a person can make is not buried treasure but wisdom.
units.principle: True happiness belongs to those who find and take hold of God's wisdom, and it is worth every effort spent in the search.
units.insight: Jesus told of a man who found treasure hidden in a field, "and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field" (Matthew 13:44). That joy is the happiness of this verse. Mary of Bethany found it sitting at Jesus' feet while her sister hurried about, and Jesus said she had "chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:42). We look for happiness in many places: a raise, a relationship, a quiet weekend. Most of them are good gifts, and none of them can bear the weight of our joy. In the light of the New Testament, the wisdom this verse praises has a name. Christ is the One "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). Have you found Him, or only heard about Him?
units.application: Make room this week for the search that leads to finding: a set time each day in Proverbs or the Gospels, with a notebook for what you learn. Young people: ask an older believer how they gained wisdom and what it cost them. If you are going through a season of correction, ask what wisdom God is offering you in it. Parents: talk at the table about what makes a person truly happy, and let your children hear you name wisdom, not only success.

rel.note: Getting wisdom is said to be much better than getting gold, and understanding better than silver.
The son is told to buy truth and wisdom and never sell them, using the same language of trade.
The comparison climbs from silver and gold to rubies and to everything a person could desire.
Wisdom says her fruit is better than gold and her revenue than choice silver.

units.notes:
• The word behind "proceeds" and "profits" means the gain made from trade. The KJV renders it "merchandise," keeping the picture of a merchant's business.
• Solomon, whose name heads the book, traded on a grand scale; his ships brought gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:26–28). Yet the book ranks wisdom above the gold that filled his treasury.
• Henry: "It is not only a surer, but a more gainful merchandise to trade for wisdom". In plain words, wisdom is both the safer and the more profitable trade.
• Compare 8:10–11, 18–19; 16:16; 23:23; Job 28:12–19.
units.summary: Measured as an investment, wisdom outperforms silver and gold every time.
units.principle: Wisdom yields a return no money can match, so it must be ranked above wealth in every choice.
units.insight: When God offered Solomon whatever he asked, Solomon asked for "an understanding heart," not riches, and the request pleased the Lord (1 Kings 3:9–10). The rich young ruler faced the opposite choice. Jesus offered him treasure in heaven, and "he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:22). Each of us makes that trade more often than we notice: overtime instead of worship, a promotion that costs our integrity, a purchase instead of time with our children. Paul had weighed everything he once valued and said, "I also count all things loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). Our calendars and bank statements quietly reveal what we rank highest. What would yours say?
units.application: Before your next major financial decision, such as a job change, a large purchase or an investment, ask, "Will this make me wiser or only richer?" Parents: when you praise your children, praise good judgment and character as much as grades and earnings. Employees tempted to cut ethical corners for a bonus: count what you would lose in wisdom. Set aside time this week to invest in wisdom as deliberately as you invest money.

rel.note: Gold and rubies are plentiful, but lips of knowledge are the truly precious jewel.
The virtuous wife is valued far above rubies, the same measure given to wisdom here.
The ranking that began with silver and gold now rises to rubies and everything a person could want.
Wisdom repeats this verse almost word for word, calling herself better than rubies and beyond every desire.

units.notes:
• The precise stone named by the word behind "rubies," *peninim*, is uncertain; red coral is one suggestion. The ESV and NASB have "jewels." The point is the highest value, whatever the exact gem.
• Proverbs 8:11 repeats this verse almost word for word: "For wisdom is better than rubies, And all the things one may desire cannot be compared with her."
• Bridges: "This inestimable blessing must have the throne." Wisdom is beyond price, so it must rule over every other desire.
• Jesus' parable of the merchant who sold everything for one pearl of great price pictures the same ranking (Matthew 13:45–46).
• Compare 20:15; 31:10; Job 28:18, "the price of wisdom is above rubies."
units.summary: Line up everything you have ever wanted; wisdom still stands at the front of the line.
units.principle: Nothing a person can desire is worth more than wisdom, and every other good is safe only when wisdom rules it.
units.insight: Esau came in hungry and sold his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34). In that moment the thing he desired outranked the thing that was precious, and Hebrews calls him a "profane person" for it (Hebrews 12:16). Demas served beside Paul, then left him, "having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Desire is rarely evil in itself, but it is a poor judge of value. The verse asks you to set your desires side by side and see which one you would trade wisdom for. Asaph learned to say, "there is none upon earth that I desire besides You" (Psalm 73:25). That is where the ranking finally leads: wisdom draws us to God Himself. In Christ, the treasure worth more than everything has a name.
units.application: Write down the three things you most want this year. Next to each, ask whether pursuing it would make you wiser or cost you wisdom. Young people choosing schools, careers or a spouse: let wisdom and godliness weigh more than prestige or appearance. Parents: notice which desires your home celebrates most. When a strong desire pulls at you this week, pause and ask whether it is worth more than walking wisely with God.

rel.note: Riches, honor and life come by humility and the fear of the LORD, the same gifts wisdom holds here.
The one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished, the danger of chasing wisdom's gifts without wisdom.
The length of days that wisdom holds in her right hand is the gift promised for keeping the father's commands.
Wisdom herself says riches and honor are with her, enduring riches and righteousness.

units.notes:
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "Wisdom is here represented as a great and generous princess distributing gifts to her subjects."
• Solomon is the Old Testament picture of this verse. He asked for wisdom, and God added what he had not asked: "both riches and honor" (1 Kings 3:13).
• Bridges limits the gifts to what truly helps: riches and honor "so far as may be for her children's good". God gives these as a wise Father, not as wages owed.
• The book keeps these gifts under its warnings against greed and trust in riches (11:28; 23:4–5; 28:20).
• Compare 3:2; 8:18; 22:4, "By humility and the fear of the LORD Are riches and honor and life"; 1 Timothy 6:17–19.
units.summary: Wisdom arrives with both hands full; chase her gifts instead of her, and you may lose both.
units.principle: Life, provision and honor tend to come with wisdom, but they must be received as her gifts, never pursued in her place.
units.insight: Solomon shows this verse in both directions. He asked for wisdom, and God added riches and honor he had not asked for (1 Kings 3:13). Later, surrounded by those gifts, he let his wives turn his heart after other gods (11:4). He kept the gifts for a while and lost his grip on the wisdom that brought them. Our hearts are tempted the same way. We want what wisdom brings, such as security, respect and a long, comfortable life, more than we want wisdom itself. Then we take shortcuts to the gifts. Jesus reorders our desires with a different promise of honor: "If anyone serves Me, him My Father will honor" (John 12:26). The honor that matters most comes from the Father, and no one can take it away. Are you seeking wisdom, or only her gifts?
units.application: When you set goals for health, money or career, add a goal for growing in wisdom, such as a book of Scripture to study or a mentor to meet. Young adults: refuse shortcuts to wealth or status that require compromise. Those who have prospered: hold riches and honor loosely and use them for others (1 Timothy 6:17–19). If you are struggling financially or facing illness while walking wisely, do not conclude that God has failed you; these gifts are general fruits, not wages.

rel.note: Those who counsel peace have joy, joining the pleasantness and peace of this verse.
The peace that marks all of wisdom's paths is the peace added to those who keep the father's commands.
The path of the just shines brighter and brighter, another picture of wisdom's good road.
The immoral woman's way begins sweet and ends bitter, the opposite of wisdom's pleasant paths.

units.notes:
• The word translated "pleasantness," *no'am*, means delight, beauty or sweetness. The same word describes "the beauty of the LORD" in Psalm 27:4 and 90:17.
• "Peace" is *shalom*, wholeness and well-being in every part of life, as in 3:2.
• Bridges asks whether Wisdom is "a sullen matron, who entertains her followers only on sighs and tears". He answers that this picture of a grim, joyless guide is a lie meant to keep people from wisdom.
• Henry: "There is not only peace in the end, but peace in the way".
• Compare 5:3–4; 4:18; Psalm 16:11; 119:165, "Great peace have those who love Your law"; Romans 8:6.
units.summary: The way of wisdom is not a joyless march; it is the most pleasant road a person can walk.
units.principle: God's ways are not a burden that steals joy but the road on which true pleasure and peace are found.
units.insight: The younger son in Jesus' parable thought pleasure lay in the far country. He found it there for a while, and then he found himself feeding pigs and longing for their food (Luke 15:13–16). Paul and Silas, beaten and chained in a Philippian jail, were "praying and singing hymns to God" at midnight (Acts 16:25). The world's road starts sweet and ends bitter; wisdom's road can be hard and still be pleasant. Many believers secretly think of obedience as the price they pay rather than the shape of their joy. Jesus calls weary people to Himself with these words: "My yoke is easy and My burden is light" (Matthew 11:30). Is your obedience a burden you resent or a road you walk with Him?
units.application: Parents: let your children see joy in your faith, not only rules. Tell them what obedience has spared you and what it has given you. Young people who fear that following Christ will make life dull: talk with a mature believer about the joys of the wise road. If your Christian life feels like a grim march, ask whether you are walking with Him or only working for Him, and make room this week for worship, rest and gratitude.

rel.note: The fruit of the righteous is called a tree of life, the same image of life-giving wisdom.
A desire fulfilled is a tree of life, another use of the Eden image for what refreshes the soul.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life, showing wisdom's life reaching into speech.
The happiness promised to those who retain wisdom completes the happiness of those who first find her.
The son is told to take firm hold of instruction and keep her, for she is his life.

units.notes:
• "Take hold of" translates a verb meaning to seize or grasp firmly; "retain" means to hold fast. The ESV and NASB speak of those who "hold her fast," stressing a continuing grip.
• Proverbs uses the tree of life image three more times: for the fruit of the righteous (11:30), a desire fulfilled (13:12) and a wholesome tongue (15:4).
• Henry: "True grace is that to the soul which the tree of life would have been, from which our first parents were shut out for eating of the forbidden tree."
• Bridges: "God honours perseverance in the weakest saint." The promise rests on continuing to hold on, not on the strength of the one holding.
• Compare Genesis 2:9; 3:22–24; Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14.
units.summary: What Adam lost at the gate of Eden, wisdom holds out again to everyone who will grasp it.
units.principle: Wisdom gives true life to those who grasp it and keep holding on, and in Christ the way to the tree of life is opened again.
units.insight: Jacob wrestled through the night and would not let go: "I will not let You go unless You bless me!" (Genesis 32:26). That is the grip this verse describes. Jesus warned of another kind of hearer, who receives the word "with joy" yet "endures only for a while" (Matthew 13:20–21). Many of us took hold of wisdom once, at a retreat, a conversion or a crisis, and have slowly loosened our grip since. The happiness of this verse belongs to those who keep holding. The tree that Adam lost is offered again in Christ: "To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the midst of the Paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7). At the end, the tree of life stands beside the river of the city of God (22:2). Hold on to the One who holds it out.
units.application: Think back to a time when God's wisdom first gripped you, and ask what has loosened your hold since. Choose one habit this week that keeps you holding on, such as daily Scripture, weekly worship or a standing meeting with a believing friend. Mentors and small-group leaders: reach out to those who started strong and have drifted. Parents: help your children not only begin with God but continue with Him.

rel.note: A house is built by wisdom and established by understanding, the same pairing God used in building the world.
Agur asks who has established all the ends of the earth, a question this verse answers.
The next verse carries the same wisdom from the founding of the world to its daily watering.
Wisdom speaks as one present when God set the heavens and the foundations of the earth, developing this verse's truth.

units.notes:
• "Founded" is a builder's word for laying a foundation. "Established" means to set firmly in place; the KJV margin has "prepared." The same pair of ideas appears in 24:3: "Through wisdom a house is built, And by understanding it is established."
• Jeremiah uses similar language of the LORD: "He has established the world by His wisdom" (Jeremiah 10:12).
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "This section shows that the wisdom that directs life is the same wisdom that created the universe".
• The New Testament names the Son as the One through whom God made all things (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:16–17; Hebrews 1:2). Proverbs 8:22–31 is where that connection is most fully developed.
• Compare Psalm 104:24; 136:5, "To Him who by wisdom made the heavens"; Job 38:4–7.
units.summary: The wisdom that built the universe is the same wisdom God offers you for Monday morning.
units.principle: The wisdom God offers for daily life is the same wisdom by which He made the world, so living wisely is living with the grain of creation.
units.insight: When Job demanded answers, God asked him, "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job 38:4). Job had no answer but worship (42:5–6). This verse gives the same perspective in a single line. God's commands are not arbitrary rules laid on top of life. They are the Maker's instructions for the world He built. When we resist them, we are not only breaking rules; we are working against the grain of reality, and we get splinters. In the light of the New Testament, the wisdom that founded the earth has a face. "All things were created through Him and for Him. And He is before all things, and in Him all things consist" (Colossians 1:16–17). The One who holds the universe together invites you to learn from Him (Matthew 11:29).
units.application: The next time a command of Scripture seems inconvenient, such as rest, sexual faithfulness or generosity, ask how it fits the way God made people to flourish. Scientists, engineers and students: let the order you study lead you to worship the One who designed it. Parents: on a walk or under the night sky, show your children that the God who made it all also gives the wisdom they need for school, friendships and choices.

rel.note: A king's favor is compared to dew on the grass, using the same image of refreshing blessing.
Agur asks who has bound the waters in a garment, pointing to the same Creator who governs the waters here.
The wisdom that founded the earth and established the heavens is the knowledge that still waters the world.
Wisdom was present when God strengthened the fountains of the deep and set the sea its limit.

units.notes:
• "Broken up" translates *baqa*, to split or cleave open, the verb used in Genesis 7:11 for the flood. Interpreters differ on whether 3:20 refers to creation, to the flood or to God's ongoing provision of springs and rain; the setting of creation and provision favors the first or the third.
• "Depths" is the plural of the word for "the deep" in Genesis 1:2, the waters God ordered at creation.
• Dew was the summer lifeline of Israel's farms. God withheld it as a judgment (1 Kings 17:1; Haggai 1:10) and promised it as a blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5).
• Bridges sees God's knowledge in every drop of dew: "each of these countless drops falling from this Fountain of life."
• Compare 8:24, 28; Job 38:28, "who has begotten the drops of dew?"; Psalm 104:10–13.
units.summary: God's wisdom did not just build the world once; it waters it every morning.
units.principle: God's wisdom both made the world and keeps sustaining it, so the One who offers us wisdom can be trusted with our daily needs.
units.insight: When Gideon asked for a sign, God soaked a fleece with dew while the ground stayed dry, and the next night did the reverse (Judges 6:36–40). The dew did exactly what God said. Elijah announced that there would be no dew or rain except at his word, and for years there was none (1 Kings 17:1). Then rain came at God's command (18:41–45). We rarely think about the water that reaches our taps or the rain on the fields that feed us. This verse asks us to notice. The God who opened the deep and sends the dew is not distant from ordinary needs. Jesus pointed to the same care: our Father "sends rain on the just and on the unjust" (Matthew 5:45). If He waters the world each morning, He can be trusted with your tomorrow.
units.application: Begin tomorrow by thanking God for one ordinary provision, such as water, food or rain, that you usually take for granted. Farmers, gardeners and anyone whose work depends on the weather: pray over your work and receive good seasons as His gifts. If you are anxious about provision this week, read Psalm 104:10–15 and Matthew 6:25–33, then name your need to the God who waters the earth.

rel.note: Discretion, once kept, becomes the son's protector and preserves him.
The sound wisdom the son must keep is what the LORD stores up for the upright.
The next verse names what sound wisdom and discretion give when they are kept close.
The perverse person, described with a form of the same verb as "depart," is the one who has turned aside from wisdom.
The father again tells his son not to let his words depart from his eyes but to keep them in his heart.

units.notes:
• The first line does not say what must not depart; the second line names it. The ESV renders the first line as a command not to lose sight of "these," and the 1984 NIV puts the two lines in reverse order.
• The verb behind "depart" means to turn aside. Another form of the same verb describes the "devious" in 2:15 and the "perverse person" in 3:32. Letting wisdom slip out of view is the first step toward a crooked life.
• Henry: "He who learns to write must always have his eye upon his copy". A child learning handwriting keeps looking at the model page; so must the son with wisdom.
• Ironside quotes an unnamed writer: "It is not enough that one hold the truth, if the truth hold not him."
• Compare 4:21; 7:1–3; Deuteronomy 4:9; Hebrews 2:1.
units.summary: Wisdom is not found once and filed away; it has to be kept in sight every day.
units.principle: Wisdom must be kept in view and guarded daily, or it slowly slips away.
units.insight: Peter walked on the water while his eyes were on Jesus. "But when he saw that the wind was boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink he cried out, saying, 'Lord, save me!'" (Matthew 14:30). He did not jump; he looked away. Most spiritual decline happens the same way. No one decides to abandon wisdom. We simply stop looking at it. Busyness, screens, worries and small compromises fill our field of vision until God's word is out of sight. Hebrews warns that we must pay close attention to what we have heard, "lest we drift away" (Hebrews 2:1). Its cure is to keep "looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith" (12:2). What has crowded wisdom out of your view this month?
units.application: Put wisdom where you will see it this week: a verse on your phone's lock screen, a proverb on the refrigerator, a reading plan by your bed. Students and young workers: before a big decision, review what you already know from Scripture instead of starting from zero. Parents: repeat the same core truths often, because children keep what they hear again and again. If you notice you have drifted, do not wait; return today.

rel.note: Parental instruction is called an ornament of grace and chains about the neck, the same image used here.
The life and grace promised here belong to the son who keeps sound wisdom and discretion in view.
Mercy and truth are bound around the neck just as wisdom becomes grace to the neck.
The father's words are life to those who find them, the inner life promised here.
Wisdom places an ornament of grace on the head of the one who embraces her.

units.notes:
• "Soul" is *nefesh*, the whole living self, not only the spiritual part of a person.
• "Grace," *chen*, means charm, beauty or favor; the ESV and NASB render it "adornment." The same word is "favor" in 3:4 and "grace" in 3:34, so the chapter ties together wisdom's beauty, favor with people and God's grace to the humble.
• Henry: "Life to the soul is life indeed."
• Compare 1:9; 4:9, "She will place on your head an ornament of grace"; 4:22; Deuteronomy 32:47.
units.summary: Wisdom is both the life inside you and the beauty others see on you.
units.principle: Wisdom kept close enlivens a person within and adorns him without, so its benefits are both private and public.
units.insight: Stephen's opponents "were not able to resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke" (Acts 6:10). As they accused him, they "saw his face as the face of an angel" (6:15). His inner life showed on the outside. That is the two-sided gift of this verse. We are tempted to work on only one side. Some polish the outside, a good image and a likable manner, while the soul runs dry. Others cultivate private devotion that never becomes visible kindness. Wisdom joins the two. Jesus is the perfect picture: people "marveled at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth" (Luke 4:22), because His words came from a life wholly given to the Father. What would people see if your inner life became visible?
units.application: If you feel dry inside, do not just work harder on the outside; spend unhurried time with God this week and let Him renew you. Young people who care about how others see them: build character before image. Leaders: let your public decisions come out of private prayer. Parents: praise the wisdom you see in your children's choices, so they learn that wisdom is beautiful.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, using the same word for safety.
The steady foot of the wise is finally kept by the LORD, who guards it from the snare.
The safety the wise enjoy is the same safety a trusting neighbor should be able to find beside them.
The safe walk described here is on the straight paths the LORD directs for those who acknowledge Him.
The son who holds to instruction will walk unhindered and run without stumbling.
The way of the wicked is like darkness, and they do not know what makes them stumble.

units.notes:
• "Safely" translates *betach*, security or confidence. The same word appears in 1:33 ("will dwell safely"), in 10:9 ("walks securely") and, as "for safety's sake," in 3:29.
• Compare 4:12, "When you walk, your steps will not be hindered, And when you run, you will not stumble."
• Henry: "The way of duty is the way of safety."
• Asaph confessed how close he came to falling when he envied the wicked: "my feet had almost stumbled; My steps had nearly slipped" (Psalm 73:2).
• Compare Psalm 37:23–24; 91:11–12; 121:3; Jude 24.
units.summary: Wisdom will not clear every rock from the road, but it teaches your feet where to step.
units.principle: Wisdom gives steady footing for daily life, though it does not exempt the wise from every hardship.
units.insight: Joseph saw the trap Potiphar's wife set for him and refused: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). When she grabbed him, he ran (39:12). Wisdom gave him steady feet. Peter was told to "Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation" (Matthew 26:41), but he slept, and within hours he stumbled badly. Most falls are not sudden. They come from walking without looking, assuming we will be fine. Yet even Joseph, who did not stumble, ended up in prison for a time. Wisdom keeps us from many falls, not from all suffering. Our final safety rests on Christ, "Him who is able to keep you from stumbling" (Jude 24). Where are you walking this week without watching your step?
units.application: Identify one place where you tend to stumble, such as a website, a friendship or a certain time of night, and plan a different route before you reach it. Young people: decide your limits on dating, drinking and online life before the moment comes. Business travelers and anyone away from home: set boundaries ahead of time. Parents: teach your children to see the obstacles in the road, not only to obey rules.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD leads to life, and the one who has it rests satisfied and untouched by evil.
The wicked flee when no one pursues, while the righteous are bold, the opposite of fearless rest.
The fearless rest of night is followed by freedom from dread of sudden terror.
The father's commands keep the son when he sleeps, the same night-time protection promised here.

units.notes:
• "Sweet" translates a word for what is pleasant or agreeable. The same word describes bread gained by deceit, "sweet to a man" at first, that later fills the mouth with gravel (20:17). The sleep of the wise is a sweetness that does not turn sour.
• The ESV begins the first line with "If." The NASB and 1984 NIV repeat the opening words of the first line in the second, where the NKJV has "Yes."
• Henry: "The way to have a good night is to keep a good conscience".
• Peter slept between two soldiers on the night before his expected execution, so soundly that an angel had to strike him to wake him (Acts 12:6–7).
• Compare 6:22; 19:23; Psalm 3:5; 127:2; Leviticus 26:6.
units.summary: A clear conscience and a trusted Father make the softest pillow.
units.principle: The rest that comes from a clear conscience and trust in the LORD reaches even into the night, though it is no promise against every sleepless hour.
units.insight: David wrote Psalm 3 while fleeing from his own son Absalom. With enemies on every side he could still say, "I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the LORD sustained me" (Psalm 3:5). Jesus slept in the stern of the boat while the storm terrified His disciples (Mark 4:38). Yet the same Jesus spent a night of anguish in Gethsemane while His friends slept (Luke 22:44–45). Sleeplessness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith. But it is worth asking what keeps us awake. Some of us lie awake because of guilt we have not confessed. Others lie awake rehearsing fears we have not handed to God. The verse invites both to lay their burdens down before they lay their heads down. "He gives His beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2).
units.application: Tonight, before you sleep, confess any known sin and name your worries to God one by one (Philippians 4:6–7). Parents of anxious children: pray Psalm 4:8 with them at bedtime. Those who carry work home: set a time to put it down. If grief, pain or illness keeps you awake, do not add guilt to the burden. Ask God for His presence, and tell a friend or doctor if sleeplessness continues.

rel.note: Terror comes like a storm on those who refuse wisdom, while the one who keeps wisdom need not fear it.
Whoever listens to Wisdom will dwell safely and be secure, without fear of evil.
The fear of man brings a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD will be safe.
Freedom from sudden terror follows the fearless rest of the night.
The next verse gives the reason the son need not fear: the LORD will be his confidence.

units.notes:
• "Sudden terror" is fear that strikes without warning, the terror that comes "like a storm" on those who refuse wisdom (1:27).
• The word translated "trouble" is the word the NKJV renders "storm" in 1:27 (where the written Hebrew text has a slightly different spelling). The ESV has "ruin," the KJV "desolation" and the NASB "onslaught." These show the two possible senses: ruin that falls on the wicked, or an attack the wicked make.
• Henry weighs both readings and favors the ruin that overtakes the wicked, taking comfort that "God knows who are his and how to separate between the precious and the vile."
• Noah in the flood and Lot at Sodom show God sparing the righteous when judgment falls on the wicked (2 Peter 2:5–9).
• Compare Psalm 46:1–3; 91:5–7; 112:7, "He will not be afraid of evil tidings"; Isaiah 43:2.
units.summary: Trouble may come suddenly, but it does not have to rule your heart.
units.principle: Those who keep wisdom and trust the LORD need not be ruled by dread, though they are not promised freedom from trouble.
units.insight: Elisha's servant woke to find the city surrounded by an enemy army. "Alas, my master! What shall we do?" Elisha answered, "Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them" (2 Kings 6:15–16). Then God opened the servant's eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. The danger was real; so was the protection. Many believers live braced for the next bad phone call. That dread is not proof that you lack wisdom; it is a burden Jesus wants to carry with you. He did not promise a life without trouble: "In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). The settled heart rests on what it cannot yet see.
units.application: If a sudden crisis comes this week, such as a diagnosis, a layoff or an accident, pause and pray before you react, then take the next wise step. If you live with constant dread, write down your fears and pray through Psalm 46. If you have been harmed by others, bring your fear to God and to trusted people, and take wise steps to be safe. Church members: come alongside anxious believers with presence, not lectures.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence and a place of refuge for His children.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous run and are safe.
Whoever trusts in the LORD will be safe, while the fear of man brings a snare.
The foot that does not stumble is the foot the LORD keeps from the snare.
This verse gives the reason behind the command not to fear sudden terror.
The LORD as the son's confidence completes the call to trust Him with all the heart.

units.notes:
• The word for "confidence," *kesel*, can also mean the side or flank of the body. The line could then picture the LORD at the son's side; the main sense of trust and security is the same.
• Being "caught" pictures an animal taken in a hunter's trap. Compare 1:17, where the net is spread in vain in the sight of the bird.
• Henry: "God has engaged to keep the feet of his saints." "Engaged" here means pledged or promised.
• Hannah sang the same truth: "He will guard the feet of His saints" (1 Samuel 2:9).
• Compare 14:26, "In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence"; 18:10; 29:25; Psalm 91:3; 121:3.
units.summary: Your safety does not rest on how clever you are but on whose you are.
units.principle: The security of the wise rests on the LORD Himself, who guards those who trust Him, not on human skill or favorable circumstances.
units.insight: Saul hunted David for years with spies, spears and armies. When the LORD delivered him, David sang, "The LORD lives! Blessed be my Rock!" (Psalm 18:46). Psalm 124 celebrates the same rescue: "Our soul has escaped as a bird from the snare of the fowlers; The snare is broken, and we have escaped" (124:7). Notice who broke the snare. We are tempted to trust our own alertness: the right security system, the right investments, the right contacts. Those can be wise precautions, but they make poor gods. Jesus speaks of His sheep in the strongest terms: "neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand" (John 10:28). That is the confidence this verse offers. Who or what are you really counting on to keep you safe?
units.application: When fear rises this week, say the truth of this verse aloud: "The LORD will be my confidence." Take sensible precautions, but notice when they become your real hope. If someone is setting a trap for you, such as a hostile coworker or a false accusation, act wisely, keep honest records and commit the outcome to God. Parents: teach your children both to be careful and to trust the One who keeps them.

rel.note: Despising a neighbor is sin, but showing mercy to the poor brings happiness.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry himself and not be heard.
The person with a generous eye shares his bread with the poor and is blessed, the positive side of this command.
The next verse forbids putting off until tomorrow the good that is due and already in hand.

units.notes:
• "Those to whom it is due" is literally "its owners" in Hebrew, as the KJV margin notes. It is the same word rendered "owners" in 1:19. The good being withheld already belongs, in a sense, to the person who is owed it.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The Hebrew of Proverbs 3:27a (‘…from its owners’) brings out the injustice, not merely inconsiderateness, of delay." ("3:27a" is the verse's first line.)
• Bridges widens the duty beyond legal debts: "Kindness is therefore a matter, not of option, but of obligation; an act of justice no less than of mercy."
• James warns employers that the wages they kept back "cry out" and that the cries of the workers have reached the ears of the Lord (James 5:4).
• Compare Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Romans 13:7–8; Galatians 6:10.
units.summary: When good is owed and in your hand, keeping it back is not caution; it is injustice.
units.principle: When good is owed and we are able to give it, the ability itself creates the duty; withholding it is injustice, not prudence.
units.insight: A priest and a Levite saw a wounded man on the Jericho road. Both had the power to help, and both "passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31–32). A Samaritan stopped, paid for the man's care and promised to return (10:33–35). Jesus ended the story, "Go and do likewise" (10:37). Our withholding is rarely dramatic. It is the invoice we pay late because the money is useful to us, the reference we never write, the help we could give but do not want to be bothered with. We find reasons. Zacchaeus stopped finding them when he met Jesus: "if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Jesus Himself "went about doing good" (Acts 10:38). Whose good is sitting in your hand right now?
units.application: Employers and managers: pay wages, invoices and promised bonuses on time, and do not use delay as free credit. Anyone who owes a debt: contact the lender this week with a plan, even if you cannot pay it all. Church members: when you see a need you are able to meet, such as a meal, a ride or a bill, meet it now instead of waiting for someone else. If you have authority to approve something another person needs, do not sit on it.

rel.note: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, the hidden cost of making a neighbor wait for what is due.
Pity shown to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who will repay it.
No one knows what tomorrow will bring, so promising tomorrow what can be given today is unwise.
Delay is the polite form of withholding the good that the previous verse forbids.

units.notes:
• "Neighbor" translates *rea*, anyone close at hand: a fellow townsman, coworker or friend. Jesus widened the word to anyone in need whom we are able to help (Luke 10:29–37).
• Henry quotes a Latin proverb: "Bis dat, qui cito dat -- He gives twice who gives speedily."
• Bridges: "A little given in time of need is more than a larger sum when the time is gone by."
• Delay can hide a hope that the need will be forgotten or that someone else will meet it. Paul urged the Corinthians to finish the gift they had eagerly promised a year earlier (2 Corinthians 8:10–11).
• Compare 13:12; 27:1, "Do not boast about tomorrow"; Leviticus 19:13; Galatians 6:10.
units.summary: "Tomorrow" is the politest way to say no; if you have it today, give it today.
units.principle: Delaying good we are able to give today is a hidden refusal; love acts promptly.
units.insight: Joseph asked Pharaoh's chief butler, the royal cupbearer, one favor: remember me when you are restored. "Yet the chief butler did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (Genesis 40:23). Two full years passed before he spoke up (41:1, 9). The delay cost the cupbearer nothing and cost Joseph two more years in prison. Our "tomorrow" often works the same way. It feels harmless to us because we are not the one waiting. Behind it may be convenience, mild resentment, or a hope that the need will go away. Jesus never answered need that way. When a leper begged for healing, Jesus said, "I am willing; be cleansed," and "immediately the leprosy left him" (Mark 1:41–42). What have you promised someone "tomorrow" that you could do today?
units.application: Look at your list of promises: the returned call, the repaid loan, the reference letter, the help with a move. Keep one today. Business owners: pay small suppliers and contractors promptly; for them a late payment can be a crisis. Parents: keep promises to your children quickly, because waiting teaches them that your word is soft. When someone in need asks and you are able to help, give now, not "next week."

rel.note: Deceit fills the heart of those who devise evil, while counselors of peace have joy.
Those who devise evil go astray, but mercy and truth belong to those who devise good.
The neighbor's sense of safety uses the same word as the safe walk of the wise, a trust the son must protect.
Quarreling with a harmless man and plotting against a trusting neighbor are twin wrongs against peace.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "devise" can mean to plow or to engrave. In settings like this it means to plot, working out a plan the way a farmer works a field. It returns in 6:14, "He devises evil continually."
• "For safety's sake" uses the same word as "safely" in 3:23 and 1:33. The neighbor feels as secure beside the son as the wise feel walking in wisdom's way.
• Henry: "It is against the laws both of honour and friendship to do a man an ill-turn and give him no warning." An "ill-turn" is a harmful act.
• Bridges on betrayal by someone trusted: "No trial cuts so keenly." David knew it well (Psalm 55:12–14).
• Compare 6:16–19; 12:20; 14:22; Deuteronomy 27:24, "Cursed is the one who attacks his neighbor secretly."
units.summary: The neighbor who sleeps easy because he trusts you must never become your target.
units.principle: Plotting harm against someone who trusts us is a double evil, because it turns trust itself into a weapon.
units.insight: When Abner came to Hebron in peace, Joab "took him aside in the gate to speak with him privately, and there stabbed him" (2 Samuel 3:27). Abner was off guard because he felt safe. Jesus knew this wound from the inside. Quoting Psalm 41:9, He said of Judas, "He who eats bread with Me has lifted up his heel against Me" (John 13:18). Most of us will never plot violence, but the same seed grows in smaller forms. We quietly build a case against a coworker, take advantage of a neighbor's good faith, or use what a friend told us in confidence. The person beside us trusted us, and we treated that trust as an opening. Christ, who was betrayed, can forgive betrayers and heal the betrayed. Would the people who trust you be right to feel safe?
units.application: Examine any plan you are making that involves another person: would you be comfortable if that person knew every detail? Coworkers: refuse to join quiet campaigns against a colleague. Neighbors: settle disputes openly and kindly instead of scheming. Friends: never use what someone told you in confidence as leverage. If you have betrayed someone's trust, confess it and seek to make it right.

rel.note: Strife is like releasing water, so contention should be stopped before a quarrel starts.
The gang attacks the innocent without cause, the extreme of the causeless hostility this verse forbids.
It is honorable to stop striving, since any fool can start a quarrel.
Meddling in a quarrel that is not one's own is like grabbing a dog by the ears, another form of needless strife.
Plotting against a trusting neighbor and quarreling with a harmless one are twin wrongs against peace.

units.notes:
• "Strive" translates *riv*, a word for a quarrel or a lawsuit. The 1984 NIV renders it "accuse," reflecting its possible legal sense.
• "Without cause" is the same Hebrew word used in 1:11 for the gang's attack on the innocent "without cause."
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Do not be of a litigious, quarrelsome spirit." "Litigious" means quick to sue.
• Henry: "When accounts are balanced, it will be found there is little got by striving."
• Compare 17:14; 20:3, "It is honorable for a man to stop striving"; 26:17, 21; Romans 12:18; 2 Timothy 2:24.
units.summary: Do not pick a fight with someone who has given you no reason; peace is worth more than winning.
units.principle: Wisdom refuses pointless conflict and keeps peace with those who have done no harm, while still confronting real wrong when it must.
units.insight: Saul hunted David though David had done him no harm. David pleaded, "What have I done? What is my iniquity?" (1 Samuel 20:1). Saul's jealousy turned a loyal servant into an enemy, and his kingdom never recovered. Abraham chose the other way. When his herdsmen quarreled with Lot's, he said, "Please let there be no strife between you and me" (Genesis 13:8), and he let Lot choose first. Many of our fights begin in irritability rather than injustice: a tone we resent, a slight we imagine, a need to be right. Jesus knew causeless hostility better than anyone: "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25). Yet He, "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). Which of your current conflicts would end if you let go of being right?
units.application: Before you send a sharp email, file a complaint or start an argument this week, ask, "Has this person actually harmed me?" Spouses and roommates: let small irritations go. Church members: do not turn differences of taste into battles. If you have been truly wronged, this verse does not forbid you to seek justice; seek it calmly and through proper channels (Matthew 18:15–17).

rel.note: The gang's offer of easy wealth through violence is the oppressor's way the son must not choose.
The heart must not envy sinners but stay in the fear of the LORD, because there is a future hope.
The son is told not to envy evil men, whose hearts devise violence.
Envy of the wicked is needless, for the evil man has no future.
The next verse gives the reason: the crooked are an abomination to the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Oppressor" is literally "a man of violence" (*ish chamas*), as the KJV margin notes; the ESV and NASB put "man of violence" in the text.
• Proverbs returns to this theme: "Do not be envious of evil men, Nor desire to be with them" (24:1). Compare 23:17 and 24:19.
• Henry: "do not think him a happy man, nor wish thyself in his condition."
• Psalm 37 develops the same counsel at length: "Do not fret because of evildoers, Nor be envious of the workers of iniquity" (37:1).
• Compare 1:10–19; 16:29; Psalm 73:16–17.
units.summary: The violent man's success is worth neither your envy nor your imitation.
units.principle: The apparent success of those who prosper by force is no reason to envy them or copy their methods.
units.insight: Asaph nearly lost his footing watching violent men prosper. They seemed healthy, proud and untroubled (Psalm 73:3–12). Then, he says, "I went into the sanctuary of God; Then I understood their end" (73:17). Envy rarely announces itself. It sounds like "They cut corners and got ahead," or "Maybe being kind is for losers." Before long, envy starts copying. Jesus faced the ultimate shortcut when the devil showed Him "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" and offered them for one act of worship (Matthew 4:8–9). He refused, choosing the cross over a crown gained the wrong way. Whose success do you secretly envy, and which of their methods have you begun to borrow?
units.application: Young people: do not admire the classmate, online personality or relative who gets ahead by intimidation or cheating; watch where that road ends. Employees and business owners: refuse methods that crush competitors or workers, even when they seem to work. If you are suffering under an oppressor, bring your anger and envy to God in prayer, as Asaph did. Parents: talk with your children about the bullies and power players they see.

rel.note: The perverse in heart are an abomination to the LORD, but the blameless in their ways are His delight.
The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, while He loves the one who follows righteousness.
The LORD stores up sound wisdom for the upright, part of the confidence He shares with them.
The son must not let wisdom turn aside from his eyes; the perverse person, named with a form of the same verb, is one whose way has turned aside.
This verse gives the reason the son must not envy the oppressor or choose his ways.

units.notes:
• "Perverse" is a form of the verb rendered "devious" in 2:15 and "depart" in 3:21, a verb meaning to turn aside. The perverse person has turned aside from the straight way.
• "Abomination," *to'evah*, names what the LORD finds detestable. Proverbs often sets it against His delight (11:1, 20; 12:22; 15:8).
• "Secret counsel," *sod*, is the inner circle of trusted friends and the confidences they share. The 1984 NIV uses "confidence," and the NASB says the LORD is "intimate" with the upright.
• Poole, quoted by Bridges: "They are God's friends, to whom he familiarly imparts, as men used to do to their friends, his mind and counsels". "Familiarly" means as close friends do.
• Compare 11:20; 15:8–9; Genesis 18:17; Amos 3:7; John 15:15.
units.summary: The crooked may get the world's inside track, but the upright are taken into God's confidence.
units.principle: God detests crooked ways but draws the upright into close friendship and confidence with Himself.
units.insight: Before judging Sodom, the LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am doing?" (Genesis 18:17). Abraham is called "the friend of God" (James 2:23), and God brought him into His counsel. "The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11). We live in a world that prizes access: the inside track, the private meeting, the right contacts. Crooked people often get there first. This verse offers something better than any inner circle on earth. Jesus said to His disciples, "I have called you friends, for all things that I heard from My Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). Friendship with God is not won by cleverness; it is enjoyed by the upright, made upright by grace. Is anything crooked in your life keeping you at a distance?
units.application: If you have been tempted to cut a corner to gain an advantage, choose the straight way this week, even if it costs you. Leaders: refuse back-room deals and make your decisions in the open. Believers who feel far from God: ask Him to show you anything crooked, confess it, and make time to listen to Him in His word. Parents: let your children see that honesty matters more to you than getting ahead.

rel.note: The wicked are overthrown, but the house of the righteous will stand.
The house of the wicked is overthrown while the tent of the upright flourishes.
The LORD destroys the house of the proud and protects the widow's boundary, His judgment and care at work in households.
The gang plans to fill their houses with spoil, but such houses end under the LORD's curse.

units.notes:
• "Home" translates *naveh*, a poetic word for a dwelling. It can mean the abode of shepherds and their flocks, but in poetry it often means simply a habitation, and that is its sense here.
• The contrast between the house of the wicked and the dwelling of the upright appears again in 14:11: "The house of the wicked will be overthrown, But the tent of the upright will flourish."
• Henry: "a blessed family, though poor, has no reason to envy a cursed family, though rich."
• Bridges: "Many a homely cottage, tenanted by a child of Abraham, shines more splendidly than the princely palace of the ungodly." "Homely" here means plain and simple.
• Compare 12:7; 15:6, 25; Deuteronomy 28:1–6, 15–19; Malachi 2:2.
units.summary: A mansion can stand under God's curse and a shepherd's hut under His blessing.
units.principle: God's curse and blessing reach into households according to the character of those who live there, not the size of the dwelling.
units.insight: When the ark of God stayed in the house of Obed-Edom, "the LORD blessed Obed-Edom and all his household" (2 Samuel 6:11). Ahab built a powerful dynasty on idolatry and murder, and his house was swept away (2 Kings 10:11). What fills our homes is more than furniture. It is either God's blessing or His opposition. This verse is not a tool for judging other families; Job's household suffered terribly though Job was blameless. It is a question for our own. When Jesus entered Zacchaeus's home, He said, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). Christ can bring blessing into any home, however humble and however troubled its past. What kind of house are you building?
units.application: Parents: pray over your home and family this week, and read Scripture together, even briefly. If your household carries a pattern of sin, such as anger, addiction or dishonesty, take one concrete step to break it, with help if needed. Those living in small or humble homes: do not envy bigger houses; God blesses the home of the just. Hosts: open your home to others as a place where God is honored.

rel.note: When pride comes, shame follows, but wisdom is with the humble.
Pride goes before destruction, and it is better to be humble with the lowly than to share spoil with the proud.
A man's pride brings him low, but the humble in spirit retain honor.
The grace given to the humble now leads to the glory the wise inherit in the next verse.
Correcting a scoffer brings shame on the corrector, showing the scorner's contempt that God turns back on him.

units.notes:
• The scorner is the mocker who sneers at correction (1:22; 9:7–8; 21:24). The book describes him more fully elsewhere; here he stands for pride in its most defiant form.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The verse uses a strong anthropomorphic idea: ‘He mocks the proud mockers.’" An "anthropomorphic" idea describes God in human terms; the point is that He turns the scorner's contempt back on him.
• The Hebrew text has two forms of the last word. The letters written in the text spell the word for "afflicted," which the NASB follows. The traditional reading marked by the scribes gives the word for "humble," which the NKJV, ESV and 1984 NIV follow. The two words are close in form and meaning.
• "Grace" is the same word as "favor" in 3:4 and "grace" in 3:22; the ESV has "favor" here.
• Leighton, quoted by Bridges: "His sweet dews and showers of grace slide off the mountains of pride, and fall on the low valleys of humble hearts, and make them pleasant and fertile."
• Compare 11:2; 15:33; 16:18–19; 29:23; Luke 1:51–53; 18:14.
units.summary: God scorns the mocker's pride but pours out His grace on the lowly.
units.principle: God opposes the proud and pours His undeserved favor on those who humble themselves before Him.
units.insight: Jesus told of two men praying in the temple. The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men. The tax collector would not even lift his eyes and prayed, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" Jesus said the second man went home justified (Luke 18:11–14). The scorner is not always loud. He can sit in church, rolling his eyes at correction and quietly ranking himself above others. Grace runs downhill, to the low places. The supreme picture is Christ Himself: "He humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also has highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:8–9). In God's kingdom the way up is always down. Where is God inviting you to take the lower place?
units.application: This week, receive one correction without arguing or explaining yourself. Notice sarcasm and mockery in your speech, especially toward people who disagree with you, and replace it with respect. Leaders: model humility by admitting mistakes openly. If you feel you have nothing to offer God, take heart; He gives grace to the humble. Parents: praise humility in your children as much as achievement.

rel.note: Shame comes to the one who disdains correction, while the one who heeds rebuke is honored.
The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
The glory of the wise follows the grace God gives the humble, and the shame of fools follows His scorn of the scornful.
The favor and high esteem promised early in the chapter are completed in the glory the wise inherit.
Wisdom promises to bring honor and a crown of glory to the one who embraces her.

units.notes:
• "Glory," *kavod*, comes from a root meaning heavy, the same root as "honor" in 3:9. Those who give the LORD weight receive lasting weight themselves.
• The Hebrew of the second line is difficult. Its verb can mean to lift up or to carry off, so the line may mean that fools carry off shame or that shame lifts fools up for all to see. The KJV margin gives the literal sense as shame exalting fools, and the ESV has "disgrace."
• Bridges pictures the second sense: fools lifted up "like Haman upon his elevated gallows," raised high only to be exposed (Esther 7:9–10).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "By contrast, fools are those who acquire or earn, not inherit, by their intractability, public shame." "Intractability" means stubborn refusal to be taught.
• Compare 3:4; 4:8–9; 13:18; 14:18; Daniel 12:2–3; Romans 8:17.
units.summary: Every life leaves an inheritance; the only question is whether it is glory or shame.
units.principle: Each way of life leaves its own inheritance: lasting honor for those who walk in wisdom and shame for those who refuse it.
units.insight: Haman thought, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?" (Esther 6:6). Instead he led Mordecai through the city in royal robes, and before long he was hanged on the gallows he had built (7:10). Mordecai, who had quietly refused to bow to Haman, received the honor Haman craved. Glory and shame often arrive late, but they arrive. Each of us is writing a legacy now, in choices no one applauds: a promise kept, a temptation refused, a correction received. The gospel makes the inheritance a gift, not a wage. In Christ we are "heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together" (Romans 8:17). What will your life leave behind?
units.application: Imagine what your family and church will say about you at your funeral, then choose one habit this week that moves your life toward that legacy. Young people: weigh today's choices by where they lead in twenty years. Parents and grandparents: the faith you live out is the inheritance your children will keep. If shame from past folly weighs on you, bring it to Christ, who endured the cross, "despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2), to give you a new name.

rel.note: The book’s first appeal also calls a child to hear a father’s instruction.
The father renews this call to listen as he opens his second appeal.
The call to listen returns a third time to open the chapter’s final appeal.
The father again addresses “my children” and asks them to pay attention to his words.

units.notes:
• “Children” is the plural of the Hebrew word for “son,” so the ESV and NASB have “sons.” The father returns to the singular “my son” in 4:10 and 4:20.
• “Instruction” is the word Proverbs uses for training that includes correction and discipline (1:2, 8; 13:1). It is teaching that shapes a person, not only information.
• Henry draws the lesson for learners of every age: “Let all that would receive instruction come with the disposition of children, though they be grown persons.”
• Compare 7:24, where the father again says, “listen to me, my children,” and Deuteronomy 6:6–7, where Israel’s parents are told to teach God’s words diligently to their children.
units.summary: Wisdom is not overheard in passing; it comes to those who lean in and listen.
units.principle: Understanding comes to those who listen on purpose; deliberate attention is the first step of every learner, at any age.
units.insight: The boy Samuel heard the LORD call him three times before he knew whose voice it was. Then he answered, “Speak, for Your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10). That is the posture this verse asks for. Many of us hear a great deal of teaching and listen to very little of it. Our ears are open while our minds are elsewhere. In the light of the New Testament, the father’s appeal carries the voice of our heavenly Father, who trains and corrects His children because He loves them (Hebrews 12:5–6). On the mountain of the Transfiguration the Father said of Jesus, “This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!” (Luke 9:35). So the question is not whether wise words are being spoken to us. It is whether we are leaning in to hear them.
units.application: Parents: gather your children for teaching when you have their attention, not while screens and chores compete, and ask them to tell you what they heard. Students and young adults: when a parent, pastor or mentor offers counsel, put the phone away and listen to the end before you answer. Anyone sitting under teaching this week: write down one thing you heard and act on it before the next Sunday.

rel.note: The word translated “doctrine” here is the “learning” a wise man hears and increases.
The father again asks his son not to forget his law but to keep his commands.
The call not to forsake teaching becomes a call to take firm hold of instruction and not let go.
A son is told not to forsake the law of his mother, the same charge to hold on to parental teaching.

units.notes:
• “Doctrine” translates leqach, the word rendered “learning” in 1:5: “A wise man will hear and increase learning.” It means what is received and taken in. The ESV has “precepts” and the NASB “sound teaching.”
• “Law” is torah, which means teaching or instruction. Elsewhere the same word names the Law of Moses, but in Proverbs 1–9 it is a parent’s instruction (1:8; 3:1; 6:20). That is why the father can call it “my law.”
• Bridges describes the teaching that deserves the name “good doctrine” as “that which humbles the soul before God; that which exhibits the free grace of the Gospel.”
• Compare 2 Timothy 4:3–4, which warns of people who will not endure sound doctrine and turn aside to fables, and 6:20, “do not forsake the law of your mother.”
units.summary: The best teaching in the world does you no good once you let go of it.
units.principle: Sound teaching blesses only those who keep holding it; what is received once must be kept for life.
units.insight: King Joash did what was right all the days of Jehoiada the priest (2 Chronicles 24:2). When his teacher died, Joash listened to new voices, and Judah left the house of the LORD to serve idols (24:17–18). He had received good doctrine; he did not keep it. Drift rarely looks like rebellion at first. It looks like a little less prayer, a few new opinions, a quiet loosening of the grip. Jesus described seed that sprang up quickly and withered because it had no root (Matthew 13:5–6, 20–21). Paul’s charge to Timothy fits this verse: “continue in the things which you have learned and been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them” (2 Timothy 3:14). What good teaching once took root in you, and are you still holding it?
units.application: If you were raised on sound teaching and have drifted, name one truth you have let go and return to it this week. Parents of teenagers: explain why your teaching is good, not only what it says, so your children can hold it when you are not there. Church members: test new ideas against Scripture before adopting them, and talk with an older believer before abandoning what you were taught.

rel.note: The mother’s law is honored beside the father’s instruction, as the mother’s love is remembered here.
Training in youth shapes the whole of life, stated as a general principle rather than a guarantee.
King Lemuel’s words are “the utterance which his mother taught him,” another son shaped by a parent’s teaching.
The next verse gives the words this loved son was taught by his father.

units.notes:
• The phrase “the only one” translates yachid, the word used of Isaac as Abraham’s “only son” in Genesis 22:2, though Abraham also had Ishmael. The word marks a child as unique or especially beloved. The KJV has “only beloved,” and the NASB “the only son.”
• “Tender” describes someone young and soft, easily shaped. Henry, on why childhood is the time to teach: “the branch is easily bent when it is young and tender.”
• Bridges: “The more dearly he was loved, the more carefully was he taught.”
