• Compare 1:8, where the mother’s teaching is honored beside the father’s, and 2 Timothy 3:15, where Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures “from childhood.”
units.summary: Every good teacher was once a child someone loved enough to teach.
units.principle: Love shows itself in teaching; children who are cherished should also be carefully instructed.
units.insight: This father remembers being loved and being taught, and the two belong together. Training is one of love’s truest forms. Yet many readers did not grow up as anyone’s “only one.” Their homes held neglect, absence or worse. Scripture does not shut them out. Timothy’s father is described only as a Greek (Acts 16:1), yet Paul became his father in the faith and called him “a true son in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2). God gives spiritual fathers and mothers to those who lacked them, and He Himself is “a father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5). Jesus spoke as a Son taught by His Father: “as My Father taught Me, I speak these things” (John 8:28). Whatever your story, you can become a learner now and one day pass on what you received.
units.application: Parents: let your affection show up as instruction. Tell your children why you live as you do, and share what your own parents or mentors taught you. If you grew up without a godly home, look for an older believer at church who can mentor you, and ask. Grandparents: tell your grandchildren how God taught you and kept you; your story may become the one they pass on.

rel.note: Keeping the father’s commands in the heart is joined to length of days and long life.
The heart that must retain the grandfather’s words is the spring of life the father later charges his son to guard.
The previous verse describes the loving home in which these words were first taught.
The same words, “Keep my commands and live,” tie obedience to life again.

units.notes:
• Where the grandfather’s words end is debated; some end them at 4:4 or 4:5, and others carry them further. The NKJV’s quotation marks give 4:4–9 to him. Older commentators assumed the grandfather was David and the father Solomon, but the point does not depend on it. Geier, quoted by Bridges: “provided that we pay due obedience to the instruction, it matters little, whether we have it in the words of David or Solomon.”
• “Keep my commands and live” returns word for word in 7:2, where the father adds, “And my law as the apple of your eye.”
• Bridges offers comfort to the forgetful: “Often (and this is a comfort to a weak memory) words may be lost to the memory, yet practically retained in the heart.” (“Practically” here means in practice: the lesson still shapes how we live.)
• Compare 2 Timothy 1:5, Deuteronomy 6:6–7 and Matthew 19:17, where Jesus says, “if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
units.summary: The best lesson parents pass on is often the one they first received: hold God’s words, and live.
units.principle: Truth proven across generations is worth keeping, and it gives life only when it is held in the heart and obeyed.
units.insight: Paul traced Timothy’s faith back two generations. It “dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Faith is personal, but it is rarely solitary; most of us believe because someone carried the truth to us. The grandfather’s concern is the heart. A child can memorize every rule and keep none of them, because the words never reached the place where choices are made. Jesus lived this verse perfectly. He said, “I have kept My Father’s commandments and abide in His love” (John 15:10), and by His obedience many are made righteous (Romans 5:19). Where we have failed to keep God’s words, He kept them for us. Ask yourself whether the truths you were taught are living in your heart or only in your memory.
units.application: Parents and grandparents: pass on not only rules but the reasons behind them, and tell how God’s ways proved true in your family. Young adults: ask an older relative or church member what they learned from their parents about following God, and write it down. If you came to faith without a Christian heritage, you can begin one; every godly family line starts with one person who listened.

rel.note: Getting wisdom and understanding is worth more than getting gold and silver.
The same verb commands the reader to buy truth, wisdom and understanding and never sell them.
Wisdom is to be sought like silver and hidden treasure, the effort that “get” calls for.
The command to get wisdom is repeated and grounded in wisdom being the principal thing.

units.notes:
• “Get” translates qanah (also spelled qana), the ordinary verb for acquiring or buying. It returns in 4:7 and 23:23. Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “Qana means to acquire moveable goods through a financial transaction.” Wisdom costs something, and it is worth the price.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: “What it takes is not brains or opportunity, but decision. Do you want it? Come and get it.”
• “Turn away” pictures bending aside from the road; the KJV has “decline,” which in older English meant to turn aside. The danger is not only forgetting the words but leaving the road they mark out.
• Compare 2:4–5, where wisdom is sought “as silver”; 1 Kings 3:9, where the young Solomon asks God for “an understanding heart”; and James 1:5.
units.summary: Wisdom is never picked up by accident; it is bought on purpose and kept for life.
units.principle: Wisdom must be pursued deliberately and kept faithfully; neither the first choice nor the long obedience can be skipped.
units.insight: Solomon began this way. As a young king he asked God for an understanding heart, and God gave him wisdom beyond any man of his day (1 Kings 3:9–12). Yet when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). He got wisdom, but he did not keep it; he turned away. His story is the sharpest warning this verse could have. No one is beyond drifting, however gifted or well taught. Wisdom is God’s gift, yet we are told to get it, because He gives it to those who ask and seek (James 1:5). In the light of the New Testament, getting wisdom means coming to Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), and then remaining in Him (John 15:4).
units.application: Young people: decide this week what you will give up to get wisdom, perhaps an hour of screen time traded for Scripture or a conversation with a wise mentor. New believers: begin a simple habit of reading one chapter of Proverbs a day. Believers of many years: watch for the slow swerve, and ask a trusted friend whether they see you drifting anywhere.

rel.note: The same two verbs promise that discretion will preserve and understanding will keep.
Not forsaking wisdom becomes taking firm hold of instruction and keeping her as life.
The son is told to treat wisdom as a sister, the close loyalty that guards him from the seductress.
Wisdom herself promises to love those who love her.

units.notes:
• “Preserve” and “keep” are two words for guarding. Compare 2:11, where discretion and understanding make the same promise: “Discretion will preserve you; Understanding will keep you.”
• The Hebrew word for wisdom is feminine, so the poem pictures her as a woman. Ross, quoted by Guzik: “The teacher uses feminine verbs to promise protection and safety.” The feminine comes from the grammar and the poetry; it does not make wisdom a goddess or a literal woman.
• Wisdom speaks of the same mutual love in 8:17: “I love those who love me, And those who seek me diligently will find me.”
• Henry adapts the shopkeeper’s proverb “Keep thy shop, and thy shop will keep thee” to this verse: “Keep thy wisdom, and thy wisdom will keep thee.”
• Compare 7:4 and John 14:21, where Jesus says the one who has His commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Him.
units.summary: Wisdom guards those who will not leave her; love her, and you will find yourself kept.
units.principle: What we love, we hold on to, and the person who holds on to wisdom in love is guarded by it.
units.insight: Ruth would not leave Naomi. “Entreat me not to leave you,” she said, and she held to Naomi and to Naomi’s God when going home would have been easier (Ruth 1:16). Her loyalty led her into blessing she could not have imagined. Wisdom asks for that kind of devotion. Many people want wisdom’s protection without wisdom’s company. They consult her in a crisis and ignore her the rest of the time. But protection follows love. In Christ the picture becomes personal. He is the Wisdom we are called to love, and He promises that no one will snatch His sheep out of His hand (John 10:28). Our safety rests finally on His keeping of us, not on our grip on Him. Is your relationship with Him love, or occasional consultation?
units.application: If you turn to God’s wisdom only in emergencies, set a daily time this week simply to read and pray, not to fix a problem. Husbands and wives: make loyalty to Christ the shared center of your home, and tell each other one way His word guarded you this week. Young people pressured to drop your convictions to fit in: stay loyal; the wisdom you keep will keep you.

rel.note: Getting wisdom is better than gold, the same ranking of wisdom above every other acquisition.
The word for “principal” is the “beginning” of knowledge, which is the fear of the LORD.
Wisdom’s gain is better than silver and fine gold, and nothing a person desires compares with her.
The urgent command to get wisdom is first given here and then grounded in this verse.

units.notes:
• “Principal” translates reshit, the word for “beginning” in 1:7: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” The ESV and NASB take it as “beginning” here too, so in those versions the line says that the first step toward wisdom is to decide to get it.
• The phrase “all your getting” uses a noun formed from the same verb as “get” (4:5). It means acquisitions or possessions, which is why the line can mean either “with all you acquire” or “at the cost of all you own.”
• Bridges, speaking of wisdom: “It can have no place, if it has not the first place. If it be anything, it will be everything.”
• Ironside: “It is not knowledge merely which the soul needs, but the wisdom and intelligence to use knowledge aright.” (“Aright” means rightly.)
• Compare 3:13–15; 16:16; Matthew 13:45–46; Philippians 3:7–8.
units.summary: Put wisdom first and pay what it costs, because every other gain depends on it.
units.principle: Wisdom is life’s first priority, worth more than anything it costs, because every other good is used well or badly depending on it.
units.insight: Jesus told of a merchant who found “one pearl of great price” and “sold all that he had and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). Paul lived that parable. Everything he once counted as gain, his pedigree, learning and zeal, he counted as loss “for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). That is what “principal” means: first, with everything else arranged around it. Most of us say wisdom matters most, but our calendars and bank statements show what we actually treat as first. The heart quietly puts career, comfort or approval first and fits God in around them. Christ, who “became for us wisdom from God” (1 Corinthians 1:30), is not one priority among many. He asks to be first.
units.application: Look at last week’s calendar and spending and ask what they say is “the principal thing.” Students choosing a school or career: weigh where you will grow in wisdom and character, not only in income. Parents: let your children see you choose wisdom over gain, such as refusing a profitable shortcut that would compromise your integrity. Then put one concrete step toward wisdom first in your week.

rel.note: Before honor is humility, the qualification on how wisdom lifts a person up.
Wisdom holds riches and honor in her hand, the honor she brings to those who embrace her.
The wise inherit glory while shame is the legacy of fools.
The honor Wisdom gives is pictured next as an ornament of grace and a crown of glory.

units.notes:
• “Exalt” translates a verb that appears in this form only here. Elsewhere the same verb describes heaping up a raised road, as in “Build up, build up the highway!” (Isaiah 62:10). Here it means to lift wisdom high and prize her; the ESV and NASB have “Prize.”
• The opposite outcome is stated in 3:35: “The wise shall inherit glory, But shame shall be the legacy of fools.”
• Ironside: “Mere knowledge may puff up and render the possessor thereof contemptible; but the word of wisdom is always in season.”
• Compare 1 Samuel 2:30, “those who honor Me I will honor,” and James 4:10.
units.summary: Honor wisdom and she lifts you up, with a dignity that does not depend on rank.
units.principle: Those who prize wisdom receive a lasting dignity: not always rank or fame, but the honor of a life well lived before God.
units.insight: Joseph honored God’s ways in Potiphar’s house and was thrown into prison for it (Genesis 39). Daniel kept praying at his open window and was thrown to the lions (Daniel 6:10, 16). Embracing wisdom does not always bring quick promotion. God did later raise both men, but the honor that mattered was already theirs in the prison and the den: they walked with Him. The heart wants honor on its own terms and schedule, and it often exalts its reputation instead of wisdom. Jesus is the pattern of this verse. He humbled Himself to the death of the cross, and “Therefore God also has highly exalted Him” (Philippians 2:8–9). In God’s kingdom the way up runs through humility (15:33). What are you exalting, wisdom or your own image?
units.application: Employees: when a shortcut would advance you but compromise your integrity, choose wisdom and leave the promotion to God. Leaders: honor the wise people on your team, not only the impressive ones. Young people: notice who your heroes are, and prize people for character more than following. If you are overlooked for doing right, take heart; the honor wisdom gives does not depend on anyone noticing.

rel.note: Gray hair is a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness, honor that grows from a righteous life.
Parental instruction is called a graceful ornament on the head, the same image used here of wisdom.
Sound wisdom becomes life to the soul and grace to the neck, another picture of wisdom adorning the one who keeps it.
The previous verse promises the honor that this crown pictures.

units.notes:
• The “ornament of grace” recalls 1:9, where parental instruction is “a graceful ornament on your head,” a garland of beauty. The ESV renders the two images “graceful garland” and “beautiful crown.”
• The KJV margin offers an alternative for the second line: “she shall compass thee with a crown of glory,” that is, surround you with it.
• Henry: “a crown that shall never totter, a crown of glory that shall never wither.” (“Totter” means to wobble or fall.)
• Compare 16:31, “The silver-haired head is a crown of glory, If it is found in the way of righteousness,” and 1 Peter 5:4, “the crown of glory that does not fade away.”
units.summary: The world’s crowns fade; the crown wisdom gives a faithful life does not.
units.principle: Wisdom adorns a life with grace and honor that outlast any earthly position.
units.insight: Near the end of his life Paul sat in a Roman prison with no title and no wealth. Yet he wrote, “there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4:8). The world saw a condemned prisoner; heaven saw a crowned man. This verse corrects our sense of what makes a life beautiful. We admire the visible crowns of money, platform and applause, and we overlook the quiet grace of an older believer whose life has been faithful. Jesus wore a crown of thorns before He was “crowned with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:9), and those who belong to Him share His path: grace now, glory later. The crowns we chase fade. The one wisdom gives does not.
units.application: Honor the faithful older believers in your church this week with a note or a visit; they wear the crown this verse describes. Parents: when you praise your children, praise kindness and wise choices more than trophies. If you are aging and feel overlooked, remember that a life lived God’s way carries a beauty that does not fade. Leaders: measure success by faithfulness, not only by visible results.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD prolongs days, while the years of the wicked are shortened.
Keeping the father’s commands adds length of days and long life, the same general pattern.
The call to hear first opened the chapter’s first appeal.
The call to listen returns to open the chapter’s final appeal.
Wisdom says that by her days will be multiplied and years of life added.

units.notes:
• “Receive” means to take hold of and accept, more than letting sound reach the ear. The father wants his sayings welcomed, not merely heard.
• Henry places the promise under God’s rule: the years will be “as many in this world as Infinite Wisdom sees fit.” (“Infinite Wisdom” here means God.)
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik, gives the common-sense side of the pattern: “Vice and intemperance impair the health and shorten the days of the wicked,” as anyone can observe.
• Long life appears as the general fruit of wisdom in 3:2, 3:16, 9:11 and 10:27, always as a pattern, not a guarantee. Compare Ephesians 6:2–3 and Psalm 34:12–14.
units.summary: Wisdom tends toward long life, but the length of a life is not the measure of its faithfulness.
units.principle: Receiving wise instruction tends toward a longer, fuller life, though God alone sets the number of anyone’s days.
units.insight: Jesus had all wisdom and kept every word of His Father, yet He died while still a young man. Stephen, “full of faith and the Holy Spirit,” was among the first to die for Him (Acts 6:5; 7:59–60). Their short lives were not failures of wisdom. So this verse must never be used to wound a grieving family or to suggest that someone who died young did not listen to God. At the same time, the pattern is real. Many lives are shortened by folly: addiction, violence, recklessness. The heart can hear this verse selfishly, as a bargain for more years. Its deeper meaning is that wisdom is the way of life, and in Christ that life does not end (John 11:25–26). Our times are in God’s hand (Psalm 31:15).
units.application: Young people: the choices that most often cut lives short, such as drunk driving, drugs and violence, are choices you can refuse now. Parents and pastors: when a believer dies young, do not use this verse to explain it; grieve with the family and point them to Christ’s promise of life. All of us: act this week on one piece of wise counsel about health, rest or habits that you have been brushing aside.

rel.note: Training a child in the way he should go is the work this father describes, stated as a general principle.
Some leave the paths of uprightness to walk in ways of darkness, the opposite of the right paths the father has shown.
The father’s teaching aims to keep his son on the paths of righteousness, the same right paths he says he has led him in.
The next verse describes the freedom of walking the right paths the father has shown.
The path of the wicked is the road the father warns his son never to enter.
The right paths the father has shown become the path of the just that shines ever brighter.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind “right” means straightness or uprightness. It comes from the same root, the basic Hebrew word-stem, as “the upright” in 2:7 and 2:21, so “right paths” are the roads upright people walk.
• Henry: the father “not only taught his son by good instructions, but led him both by a good example and by applying general instructions to particular cases.”
• The road image runs through the chapter: “way” or “path” appears in 4:11, 14, 18, 19 and 26.
• Compare Psalm 23:3, “He leads me in the paths of righteousness,” and 1 Corinthians 11:1.
units.summary: A good guide does not just point out the road; he walks it first and leads you along it.
units.principle: Faithful teachers lead by example as well as by instruction, and those they lead are still responsible to keep walking the road.
units.insight: Paul could write, “Imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). He did not only explain the way; he walked it in front of the churches. That is what this father has done. His example sobers every parent and leader, because children follow our steps more than our words. Yet the verse also frees the faithful parent whose grown child has wandered. The father did his part; the son must still choose. A parent is responsible for teaching and leading, not for every choice a child later makes. Christ is the perfect Guide. As the Good Shepherd He “goes before” His sheep, and they follow Him (John 10:4). He never asks us to walk a road He has not walked Himself.
units.application: Parents: let your children see you pray, apologize, give and tell the truth; walk the path before you point to it. If your grown child has strayed despite your teaching, lay down guilt that is not yours and keep praying. Mentors and small-group leaders: share your own road openly, including where you stumbled. New employees: notice who leads by example, and learn from them.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely.
Keeping wisdom means walking safely without your foot stumbling.
The right paths of the previous verse are the road on which the son walks freely.
The wicked stumble in darkness and do not know what trips them.

units.notes:
• The KJV has “straitened,” an older word for narrowed or squeezed; the ESV has “hampered” and the NASB “impeded.”
• Henry: “Those that make God’s word their rule shall walk at liberty, and be at ease in themselves.”
• Compare Psalm 18:36, “You enlarged my path under me, So my feet did not slip,” and Psalm 119:45, “I will walk at liberty, For I seek Your precepts.”
• The verse is answered by 4:19: the wise run without stumbling, while the wicked stumble and do not even know why.
units.summary: Wisdom gives you room to move; folly hems you in until every step is a trap.
units.principle: Living God’s way frees a person from many of the traps folly sets, so that he can move with confidence even under pressure.
units.insight: David praised the God who “enlarged my path under me” (Psalm 18:36). He also knew the other kind of road. After his sin with Bathsheba, his own choices hemmed him in: deceit, a murder to hide a pregnancy, and the sword that would not depart from his house (2 Samuel 11–12). Sin promises freedom and delivers a cage. Many people feel trapped and do not see that the walls went up one foolish choice at a time. Jesus said, “if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed” (John 8:36). He forgives the past and opens a wider road ahead. Where do you feel hemmed in today, and which choices built those walls?
units.application: If you are tangled in debt, a lie or a broken relationship, take one step toward untangling it this week: make the budget, tell the truth or ask forgiveness. Young adults: build habits now that keep the road clear later, such as living within your means and keeping your word. Leaders under pressure: decide ahead of time what you will not do, so you can move fast without stumbling.

rel.note: Wisdom is a tree of life to those who take hold of her and retain her.
The charge not to forsake the father’s teaching is renewed as a call to grip it.
The father’s words are life to those who find them, the same life this verse promises.
Not forsaking Wisdom and loving her is the loyalty this firm grip expresses.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, the reason given here for holding on.

units.notes:
• Hebrew nouns are either masculine or feminine in form. The noun for “instruction” is masculine, yet the pronoun “her” that points back to it is feminine. That is a matter of grammar, not of instruction having a sex; the feminine probably continues the portrait of Wisdom as a woman from 4:5–9.
• The ESV and NASB have “guard” for the NKJV’s “Keep.”
• Bridges: “the animated exhortation to take fast hold, shows the struggle necessary to retain our principles.” In other words, the father urges so earnestly because holding on is hard.
• Compare 3:18, where Wisdom is “a tree of life to those who take hold of her,” and Revelation 3:11, “Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown.”
units.summary: Instruction is not a childhood lesson to outgrow but a lifeline to grip with both hands.
units.principle: Wisdom must be held with a firm and lasting grip, because letting go of it is letting go of life.
units.insight: Jacob wrestled through the night and would not let go: “I will not let You go unless You bless me!” (Genesis 32:26). That is the grip this verse asks for. Many people hold God’s instruction loosely, as long as nothing pulls against it. Then a crisis, a relationship or a disappointment tugs, and they find their hold was only habit. When many disciples turned back from Jesus, He asked the Twelve whether they would leave too. Peter answered, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). That is the reason to hold on: Christ is our life (Colossians 3:4). And He holds us more firmly than we hold Him. What is pulling at your grip right now?
units.application: If a hard season has loosened your hold on God’s word, choose one passage this week and memorize it. Parents of teenagers and college students: do not assume early teaching will hold on its own; keep the conversation going by call, text and visit. Anyone tempted to drop a conviction to keep a relationship or a job: talk it through with a mature believer before you let go.

rel.note: The companion of fools is destroyed, the reason the wicked path must not be entered.
The father’s first warning also tells his son not to walk in the way with sinners.
The right paths the father has shown stand opposite the path of the wicked.
Four quick commands drive home the same warning to keep away from the wicked path.
The next verses describe the people whose path the son must not enter.

units.notes:
• Psalm 1:1 traces a similar slide into sin, from walking to standing to sitting: the blessed man “walks not in the counsel of the ungodly, Nor stands in the path of sinners, Nor sits in the seat of the scornful.”
• Ironside: “The true pilot may not know every rock or reef, but his wisdom consists in taking the safe channel.” A ship’s pilot does not need to study every hazard; he keeps to the safe channel. So the son does not need to explore the wicked path; he stays off it.
• Bridges: “It is far more easy to shun the occasion of sin, than the sin when the occasion presents it.” (“Occasion” means the situation that invites the sin.)
• Compare 13:20, “the companion of fools will be destroyed,” and 1 Corinthians 15:33, “Evil company corrupts good habits.”
units.summary: The surest way to avoid where the wrong road ends is never to take its first step.
units.principle: Sin is best resisted at its first step, before a path becomes a habit.
units.insight: Lot “pitched his tent even as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12). Later he was living in Sodom (14:12), and in the end he sat in its gate (19:1). He never planned to become part of that city; he only moved a little closer each time. Most falls happen that way. The heart tells itself it can stand near the edge without slipping, and it is wrong more often than it admits. The father’s warning is a kindness. He would rather his son miss some excitement than lose his soul. Christ taught us to pray, “do not lead us into temptation, But deliver us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13). We cannot pray that sincerely while walking toward the very path we ask Him to keep us from.
units.application: Young people: if a group of friends is drawing you toward drinking, cruelty or sexual sin, step away before the first party, not after it. Parents: know your children’s companions and talk openly about where certain friendships lead. Adults: identify the first step in your most common temptation, such as a website, an app or a private lunch with a coworker, and refuse that step this week.

rel.note: The prudent man sees evil coming and hides himself, while the simple walk on into it.
The warning not to enter the wicked path is pressed home by these four commands.
The chapter closes with the same call to remove the foot from evil.
The son is told to keep his way far from the immoral woman’s door, the same rule of distance.

units.notes:
• Bridges: “Not only avoid it when near, but avoid nearness to it.”
• Henry, on the father’s warning: “he does not say, Keep at a due distance, but at a great distance, the further the better.”
• The same counsel is given about the immoral woman in 5:8: “Remove your way far from her, And do not go near the door of her house.”
• Compare 1 Thessalonians 5:22, “Abstain from every form of evil,” and 2 Timothy 2:22, “Flee also youthful lusts.”
units.summary: Wisdom does not test how close it can walk to sin; it keeps as far away as it can.
units.principle: Safety from sin lies in distance, not in self-confidence; the wise turn away early and keep moving.
units.insight: When Potiphar’s wife grabbed Joseph’s garment, he did not stay to reason with her. He “fled and ran outside” (Genesis 39:12). Peter took the opposite course. He followed Jesus “at a distance” into the high priest’s courtyard and sat with the servants to see how it would end (Matthew 26:58). Within hours he had denied his Lord three times. The heart loves to ask, “How close can I get without sinning?” That question is already a step onto the path. Jesus, tempted in every way, never toyed with temptation. He answered each one with God’s word and sent the tempter away (Matthew 4:10). By His Spirit we can learn the same quick refusal.
units.application: Decide in advance which places, websites and situations are off-limits for you, and do not reopen the question when temptation comes. Young adults: if a friend’s plan for the evening heads somewhere wrong, leave early instead of waiting to see. Married people: keep clear boundaries with coworkers and old flames, even when nothing has happened. Parents: teach your children that walking away is strength, not weakness.

rel.note: The enticers’ feet run to evil and hurry to shed blood, the same eagerness for harm.
The wise lie down and sleep sweetly, while the wicked cannot sleep until they have done harm.
This portrait gives the reason for the warning not to enter the path of the wicked.
The next verse completes the portrait with the food and drink of the wicked.
The worthless man devises evil continually, never resting from mischief.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB use “stumble” where the NKJV and KJV have “fall”: the wicked lie awake until they make someone stumble.
• Psalm 36:4 describes a wicked man who plots harm at night: “He devises wickedness on his bed.” Compare Micah 2:1.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: “The Bible does not hide the fact that one can become as zealous for evil as for good.”
• Compare 1:16, “their feet run to evil”; 6:14; and Acts 23:12, where some of Paul’s enemies bound themselves not to eat or drink until they had killed him.
units.summary: Some people cannot rest until they have done harm; do not learn their restlessness.
units.principle: Evil indulged long enough becomes a compulsion, and those ruled by it spread ruin to others.
units.insight: Haman had wealth, honor and the king’s favor, yet he told his wife and friends, “all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” (Esther 5:13). Hatred robbed him of every pleasure until he could do harm. That is the inner life this verse describes. Sin promises satisfaction and delivers restlessness. Isaiah said, “the wicked are like the troubled sea, When it cannot rest” (Isaiah 57:20). Before we point at others, we should ask what keeps us awake: a grudge we rehearse, a plan to get even, a habit we cannot quit. Jesus invites the restless, “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
units.application: If you lie awake rehearsing how to get back at someone, write the grievance down, give it to God in prayer and refuse to act on it. Parents: notice whether your child’s friends enjoy hurting others through mocking or bullying, and step in early. If you are being targeted by someone like this, keep a record of what happens, get help from those in authority and do not try to match their schemes.

rel.note: The soul of the unfaithful feeds on violence, the same diet pictured here.
Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet but turns to gravel, the end of the bread of wickedness.
The previous verse shows the restless compulsion behind this diet of evil.
Folly’s stolen water and secret bread show how wrongdoing is made to taste pleasant.

units.notes:
• Henry holds both senses together: “Mischief is meat and drink to them; they feed and feast upon it,” and “All they eat and drink is got by rapine and oppression.” (“Mischief” means harm; “meat” means food; “rapine” means plunder.)
• Psalm 14:4 uses the same picture of evildoers “Who eat up my people as they eat bread”: they consume others as casually as a meal.
• Compare 13:2, “the soul of the unfaithful feeds on violence,” and Job 15:16, which speaks of man “Who drinks iniquity like water!”
units.summary: What you feed on, you become; the wicked have made harm their daily bread.
units.principle: What a person habitually takes in shapes what he craves, and evil indulged becomes the very thing he lives on.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth’s vineyard. Jezebel arranged false witnesses, Naboth was stoned, and Ahab went down to take possession (1 Kings 21:13–16). That is bread of wickedness, a meal bought with someone else’s ruin. Few of us will go that far, but the same appetite can grow in smaller ways: enjoying gossip that wounds, profiting from another’s loss, relishing someone’s humiliation. Jesus spoke of a different food: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me” (John 4:34). He also offers Himself as the bread of life (John 6:35). The question is what you have been feeding on, because over time what we feed on becomes what we crave.
units.application: Examine where your income comes from; if any of it depends on deceiving or exploiting people, make it right this week. Notice what entertainment you enjoy; if violence or cruelty has become a pleasure, change what you watch and play. Parents: talk with your teenagers about media that makes harm look like fun. Business owners: refuse profits that come from someone else’s ruin.

rel.note: The light of the righteous rejoices while the lamp of the wicked is put out.
Some leave the paths of uprightness to walk in ways of darkness, abandoning the light this verse describes.
The right paths the father has taught are the path of the just that grows brighter.
The way of the wicked is like darkness, the other half of this pair.

units.notes:
• “Shining sun” translates nogah, a word for bright radiance; the word itself means brightness rather than naming the sun. Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says nogah “refers to the light’s bright gleam or radiance, as from the moon.” The KJV has “shining light,” and the ESV and NASB “the light of dawn.”
• The phrase “the perfect day” is literally “the established day,” commonly understood as the full light of noon.
• Bridges, on the path of the just: “It is a rising and advancing, not a declining, sun.”
• Compare Matthew 13:43, “Then the righteous will shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” Philippians 1:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.
units.summary: The road of the righteous is a sunrise: it keeps getting brighter until full day.
units.principle: The life lived God’s way grows in light, understanding and goodness, even through dark seasons, toward the full light of day.
units.insight: The disciples understood little at first. They argued about who was greatest, misread Jesus’ words and fled at His arrest. Yet after the resurrection and Pentecost they preached with clarity and courage (Acts 2; 4:13). Their path grew brighter. Peter’s light went into eclipse on the night he denied Jesus, but his Lord restored him (John 21:15–19). This verse comforts the believer who feels slow, because growth is measured in years, not days. It also challenges the believer who has stopped growing, for the sunrise does not stall at dawn. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life” (John 8:12). Is your path brighter than it was a year ago?
units.application: New believers discouraged by slow progress: compare where you are with where you were a year ago, not with a mature saint. Believers of many years: name one area where your light has dimmed or stalled, and take one step forward this week. Parents and mentors: point out the growth you see in those you lead, because it encourages them to keep walking toward the light.

rel.note: A way can seem right to a man while its end is death, the blindness of the dark road.
Those who leave the paths of uprightness walk in the ways of darkness.
The wise run without stumbling, while the wicked stumble without knowing why.
The path of the just shines ever brighter, the other half of this pair.

units.notes:
• “Darkness” here translates a Hebrew word for thick gloom, the dark of night when nothing can be seen; the ESV has “deep darkness.”
• Bridges: “The darkness is wilful, and therefore accountable.” (“Wilful” means chosen: the wicked are responsible for the dark they walk in.)
• Henry: “They fall into sin, but are not aware which way the temptation came by which they were overthrown, and therefore know not how to avoid it the next time.”
• Compare John 3:19, “men loved darkness rather than light,” and 1 John 2:11.
units.summary: The wicked keep falling in the dark and never see what tripped them.
units.principle: Persisting in sin darkens a person’s understanding, so that he keeps stumbling without seeing the cause.
units.insight: When Judas left the Last Supper to betray Jesus, John records simply, “And it was night” (John 13:30). He walked out of the presence of the Light of the world into a darkness that grew until it destroyed him. Saul’s story moves the same way: from disobedience, to jealousy, to attempts on David’s life, to a medium’s house the night before his death (1 Samuel 28). Neither man saw clearly what was tripping him. The frightening thing about this darkness is that it feels normal from inside. That is why we need light from outside ourselves: God’s word and honest friends. Yet the darkness is not final for anyone who turns. Jesus said, “I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in Me should not abide in darkness” (John 12:46).
units.application: If you keep falling into the same trouble, such as the same argument, the same debt or the same relapse, ask a wise friend or pastor to help you see what is tripping you. Parents: help your children trace consequences back to choices, gently and specifically. Pray for a friend walking in darkness, and offer light without condemnation when the door opens.

rel.note: The words of the wise also open with “Incline your ear and hear.”
The son is asked to incline his ear to wisdom, the same posture of attention.
The first call to give attention opened the chapter’s first appeal.
The second call to hear opened the appeal about the two paths.
The father again asks his son to pay attention and lend his ear before a serious warning.

units.notes:
• “Give attention” repeats the father’s words in 4:1. It means listening closely, with the intent to respond.
• Calls to listen open each of the father’s three appeals in this chapter (4:1, 10, 20). Compare 5:1 and 7:24, where the same kind of call introduces a serious warning.
• Henry: “The attentive hearing of the word of God is a good sign of a work of grace begun in the heart and a good means of carrying it on.”
• Compare 22:17, “Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise”; Hebrews 2:1; James 1:19.
units.summary: Even a well-taught heart needs to be called back to listen, again and again.
units.principle: Life-shaping truth must be received with deliberate attention, and the call to listen must be renewed often.
units.insight: When Jesus visited Bethany, Mary “sat at Jesus’ feet and heard His word,” while Martha was “distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:39–40). Jesus said Mary had chosen “that good part” (10:42). Martha was not wicked; she was busy. Busyness is often why we do not incline our ears. We hear sermons while planning lunch and read Scripture while thinking about email. The father’s patience is striking: he calls his son to listen for the third time in one chapter. God is like that. He keeps speaking, and in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The question is whether we will stop long enough to lean in. Without that earnest attention, Hebrews warns, we drift (Hebrews 2:1).
units.application: This week, give one block of time to Scripture and prayer with your phone in another room. Parents: when your child speaks, turn from the screen and look at them; you are teaching them how to listen to you. Church members: before the sermon begins, pray, “Speak, Lord,” and note one thing to apply. Teachers and parents: repeat key lessons patiently; even a well-taught son needed the call three times.

rel.note: The same command tells the son not to let sound wisdom and discretion depart from his eyes.
The heart where these words are kept is the spring the father next charges his son to guard.
Parental teaching is to be bound continually upon the heart.
The father’s commands are to be bound on the fingers and written on the tablet of the heart.

units.notes:
• “Depart” is the same verb as in 3:21, “let them not depart from your eyes.” It means to turn aside or slip away, the way a thing drifts out of view when no one is watching it.
• Bridges: “Let the word be kept in the midst of the heart. Here only can it be operative.” (“Operative” means effective, at work.)
• Ironside: “It is the heart controlled by Scripture that assures a walk in the truth.”
• Compare Deuteronomy 6:6–8; Psalm 119:11, “Your word I have hidden in my heart, That I might not sin against You”; Jeremiah 31:33.
units.summary: Truth kept out of sight soon slips out of mind; truth kept in the heart guides from within.
units.principle: God’s word guides a life only when it is kept both in steady view and deep in the heart.
units.insight: When Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness, He answered each time, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). The word was in the midst of His heart, ready when He needed it. The psalm that Hebrews applies to Christ says it plainly: “I delight to do Your will, O my God, And Your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8; Hebrews 10:5–7). Many believers own several Bibles but carry very little of Scripture inside them. This verse exposes the gap between having the word nearby and having it within. Under the new covenant God promises to write His law on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). We cooperate by reading, memorizing and pondering, as Mary “kept all these things and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).
units.application: Put one verse where you will see it daily, on a phone lock screen, a mirror or a dashboard, and learn it by heart by Sunday. Parents: memorize a short passage together as a family at dinner. Anyone facing a recurring temptation: find a Scripture that speaks to it and keep it ready, as Jesus did in the wilderness. Small-group leaders: open each meeting by reciting a verse together.

rel.note: The tongue of the wise promotes health, another picture of wise words bringing healing.
Fearing the LORD and departing from evil are health to the flesh and strength to the bones.
Instruction is to be held fast because she is the son’s life.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, as whoever finds these words finds life.

units.notes:
• The word translated “health” can mean health, healing or cure. The KJV margin explains the word as “medicine,” and the ESV has “healing.”
• Henry: the words of wisdom “will be both food and physic to us.” (“Physic” is an older word for medicine.)
• Cartwright, quoted by Bridges, on God’s word: “Some medicines are good for one part of the body; some for another. This is good for all the body, and all the soul.”
• Compare 3:8; 12:18; Psalm 107:20, “He sent His word and healed them”; John 6:63.
units.summary: God’s words are not a burden that drains life but medicine that gives it.
units.principle: God’s wisdom nourishes the whole person, body and soul, as a general blessing, while faithful people may still suffer illness.
units.insight: Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5:23), and he left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Faithful people get sick. So this verse must never be used to blame the ill for their illness or to promise healing to everyone who reads the Bible. Yet many of us carry burdens God’s words were meant to lift: worry, resentment, shame, sleepless striving. The heart often treats Scripture as a duty to tick off rather than medicine to take. Jesus said, “The words that I speak to you are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63). His word also promises a coming day when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, receive His words as daily bread and daily medicine.
units.application: If anxiety or bitterness is wearing you down, take a passage such as Philippians 4:6–7 or Psalm 23 as a daily “dose” this week. Caregivers and pastors: when someone is ill, bring Scripture as comfort, never as an accusation. Anyone neglecting their health: wisdom includes rest, food and exercise, so treat your body as part of what God’s word cares for.

rel.note: The son is told to be wise and guide his heart in the way.
As water reflects a face, the heart reveals the person, which is why it must be guarded.
The father’s words are to be kept in the midst of the heart that this verse charges the son to guard.
Guarding the heart moves outward at once to guarding the mouth.
The grandfather’s first command was for the heart to retain his words.

units.notes:
• The phrase “with all diligence” is literally “above all keeping,” as the KJV margin gives it. The Hebrew can mean “with every kind of guarding” or “more than anything else you guard”; either way, nothing deserves more care.
• “Issues” means outflows or sources; the ESV and NASB have “springs.” The heart is pictured as the spring from which the streams of a life flow.
• Bridges: “If the citadel be taken, the whole town must surrender.” (A citadel is the fortress at the center of a city.)
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: “The corrupt heart draws one down to the grave, but Wisdom protects the heart from that corruption.”
• Compare Matthew 15:19, “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts”; Luke 6:45; Jeremiah 17:9; and 23:26, “My son, give me your heart.”
units.summary: Guard the spring and the whole stream runs clean; neglect it, and everything downstream is polluted.
units.principle: The inner life is the source of the outer life, so guarding what we think, desire and love must come before every other kind of protection.
units.insight: Before Cain killed his brother, God warned him: “sin lies at the door. And its desire is for you, but you should rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). The murder in the field began as unguarded anger in the heart. That is the pattern this verse addresses. We tend to guard our image and neglect our inner life, and then wonder where our words and actions came from. Yet the heart cannot simply be scrubbed clean by effort; Jeremiah asked of its deceit, “Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). God’s answer is a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), given through Christ. Then God Himself posts a guard: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). We keep our hearts by staying close to Him.
units.application: Ask what most often enters your heart: the shows you watch, the voices you follow, the thoughts you rehearse at night. This week remove one source of poison and add one source of life. Parents: talk with your children about what they let into their minds, not only how they behave. Leaders under pressure: build time with God into the start of your day, before the busy hours begin.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, while the perverse tongue is cut out.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, and those who deal truthfully are His delight.
The guarded heart of the previous verse shows itself first in the mouth.
The worthless man walks with a perverse mouth, a portrait of what the son must not become.
Wisdom hates the perverse mouth, the speech the son is told to put away.

units.notes:
• “Deceitful” comes from the same root, the basic Hebrew word-stem, as “crooked” in 2:15. “Perverse” is a noun meaning deviation or turning aside, built on the same root letters as “devious” in 2:15 and “perverse” in 3:32. Both words picture speech that bends away from what is straight.
• The KJV margin renders the line “frowardness of mouth and perverseness of lips.” “Froward” is an older word for stubbornly contrary.
• Ironside: “Where His Word has its place in the soul, the lips manifest it.”
• Compare 6:12, where the worthless man “Walks with a perverse mouth”; 8:13; Ephesians 4:25, 29; 1 Peter 2:22.
units.summary: A guarded heart speaks straight; crooked words show where the guard has slipped.
units.principle: Guarding the heart includes refusing every form of twisted speech, because words both reveal the heart and shape it.
units.insight: Isaiah saw the LORD high and lifted up and cried, “Woe is me, for I am undone! Because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). The first sin he named was in his mouth. Then a seraph touched his lips with a coal from the altar, and his iniquity was taken away (6:6–7). That is the gospel order: confession, then cleansing. Most of us excuse crooked speech as small: a half-truth to avoid conflict, an exaggeration to look good, a sarcastic jab. Yet these are the heart showing through. Jesus, “Who committed no sin, Nor was deceit found in His mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), bore the guilt of our words. Through Him our lips can be cleansed and retrained.
units.application: For one week, notice every time you shade the truth in excuses, sales pitches or social media posts, and correct it on the spot. Employees and managers: refuse to spin reports or performance reviews. Parents: own up in front of your children when you exaggerate. Friends: if sarcasm has become a habit, ask someone close to you how your words land.

rel.note: The person of understanding keeps wisdom in sight, while the fool’s eyes roam to the ends of the earth.
The eyes of man are never satisfied, which is why they must be kept fixed.
The steady gaze is joined to weighing the path of the feet.
The son is warned not to let the seductress capture him with her eyelids, a concrete case of the wandering gaze.

units.notes:
• “Eyelids” stands for the gaze, what a person looks at; the ESV and NASB render it “gaze.”
• Bridges: “The pleasure of sin, and the seductions of a tempting world, do not lie in the road.” They lie off to the side, so a gaze fixed ahead does not find them.
• Ironside: “As the plowman cuts a straight furrow when the eye is on a distant point directly before him,” so a believer walks straight when his eyes are fixed on Christ.
• Compare Job 31:1, “I have made a covenant with my eyes”; 6:25; Luke 9:62; Hebrews 12:2.
units.summary: Where your eyes wander, your feet will soon follow.
units.principle: Focused attention keeps a life on course; whatever captures our gaze will soon direct our steps.
units.insight: Achan confessed the order of his sin: “When I saw… I coveted them and took them” (Joshua 7:21). The eye led the way. Peter walked on the water while his eyes were on Jesus, but “when he saw that the wind was boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink he cried out” (Matthew 14:30). Screens make wandering eyes easier than ever, and the heart rarely notices the drift until the feet have followed. The remedy is not only looking away from sin but looking toward Someone: “looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2). Eyes fixed on Him have less room for what would pull us off the road. Where has your gaze been resting this week?
units.application: Set up filters and screen-time limits on the devices where your eyes most often wander, and tell a trusted friend you have done it. Men and women alike: decide ahead of time where you will not let your gaze linger, such as certain accounts, shows or people. Students: close every tab you do not need while you study. Parents: help your children notice how ads and feeds are designed to capture their eyes.

rel.note: The prudent considers well his steps, while the simple believes every word.
A man plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps, the balance to careful human pondering.
The steady gaze of the previous verse goes with weighing each step.
Pondering the path leads into the final command not to swerve to either side.
The immoral woman’s ways are unstable, the opposite of the established ways that come from pondering one’s path.

units.notes:
• The verb behind “Ponder” can mean to weigh or consider, or to make level or smooth. The current NIV gives “Make level” as a footnote reading, and the KJV margin offers “ordered aright” for the second line.
• Hebrews 12:13, “make straight paths for your feet,” draws on the wording of this verse.
• Henry: “put the word of God in one scale, and what thou hast done, or art about to do, in the other, and see how they agree.”
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “The son must take care that every step conforms with that way; one false step could prove fatal.” (“That way” is the straight path of wisdom.)
• Compare 14:15, “the prudent considers well his steps,” and Haggai 1:5, “Consider your ways!”
units.summary: Most people drift into trouble because they never stop to ask where their road leads.
units.principle: Choices weighed against God’s word produce a steady life; thoughtless steps produce a drifting one.
units.insight: When the Gibeonites arrived with moldy bread and worn-out sandals, the men of Israel sampled their provisions, “but they did not ask counsel of the LORD” (Joshua 9:14). They made a treaty they could not undo. They had not pondered the path. The prodigal son, by contrast, stopped in the pig field and “came to himself” (Luke 15:17). He weighed where his road had taken him and turned toward home. Many of us move fast and think later. The heart prefers momentum to reflection, because reflection might require change. Jesus never drifted. When the time came, “He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), choosing the road to the cross for us. Take time this week to weigh your own road.
units.application: Before a major decision this month, such as a move, a job, a purchase or a relationship, write down where this path is likely to lead in five years and weigh it against Scripture. Young adults: talk the decision through with a mature believer before you commit. Leaders: put a weekly pause on your calendar to review direction, not only tasks. Couples: ask together where your current pace is taking your family.

rel.note: The highway of the upright is to depart from evil, and keeping that way preserves the soul.
Fearing the LORD and departing from evil is the same call to remove the foot from evil.
The four commands to avoid the wicked path are summed up in this final call.
The pondered, established path of the previous verse is the road the son must not leave.
The next chapter applies this command to the immoral woman’s door.

units.notes:
• Henry: “there are errors on both hands, and Satan gains his point if he prevails to draw us aside either way.” (“On both hands” means on both sides.)
• Bridges: “Never forsake a plain for a doubtful command.” In other words, do not leave a clear duty for an uncertain one.
• The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, adds two lines after this verse that are not in the Hebrew text. English versions translated from the Hebrew leave them out.
• Compare Deuteronomy 5:32; Joshua 1:7; Isaiah 30:21; 2 Kings 22:2.
units.summary: Stay on the straight road; sin waits in the ditches on both sides.
units.principle: Faithfulness is steady obedience that refuses both the obvious sin and the subtle detour, keeping the whole person on God’s road.
units.insight: Josiah became king of Judah at eight years old, the son of a wicked father. Scripture’s verdict on his life is this verse in action: “he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (2 Kings 22:2). He also shows that a faithful life does not depend on a godly upbringing. Swerves come from both sides. Some drift into open sin; others swerve into harshness or pride in their own goodness. Both leave the road. Jesus walked the straight path perfectly. In the wilderness He refused every detour Satan offered, even shortcuts dressed in Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11). He kept to the road all the way to the cross, so that those who swerve could be forgiven and set back on the path. Which way are you most tempted to swerve?
units.application: Name the direction you most often swerve: toward compromise and indulgence, or toward harshness and self-righteousness. Ask a trusted friend which one they see in you. Parents: teach both obedience and grace, so your children do not swerve into rebellion or legalism. Young men and women: decide now, before the warnings of chapters 5–7, that your feet will stay off roads that lead to sexual sin.

rel.note: The father's earlier appeal also asks the son to incline his ear to wisdom as the first step toward safety.
The father makes the same request in nearly the same words, asking his son to incline his ear to his sayings.
The ruined man confesses he never inclined his ear, the exact opposite of the listening asked for here.
Keeping the father's words is named there as the very thing that guards the son from the immoral woman.

units.notes:
• "Lend your ear" here and "inclined my ear" in 5:13 translate the same Hebrew verb, natah, to stretch out or bend toward. The warning section opens with an ear the father asks for and closes with an ear the ruined man refused to give.
• The KJV has "bow thine ear"; the ESV has "incline your ear." Each pictures a listener leaning in, not overhearing from across the room.
• Ironside: "To hear with no thought of heeding, is not what is contemplated." The father wants listening that leads to obedience.
• The father's appeals run through chapters 1–7. Compare 2:1–2, 4:20 and 7:1–5, where keeping his words is what keeps the son from the immoral woman.
• Compare Deuteronomy 6:6–7, where parents teach God's words in the ordinary moments of the day, and Luke 8:18, "take heed how you hear."
units.summary: The father claims his son's ear before temptation starts whispering into it.
units.principle: The best defense against temptation is a heart already listening to wisdom before temptation speaks.
units.insight: Every young person will hear a voice on this subject; the only question is which voice gets there first. Israel was told to talk of God's words "when you sit in your house, when you walk by the way" (Deuteronomy 6:7), and this father is doing exactly that. Many of us learned about sex from silence or shame, and some of us are passing that silence on to our children. The father's openness is a form of love. Bridges warns that self-discipline on its own "is powerless, as the green withs to bind the giant," like the fresh bowstrings Samson snapped (Judges 16:7–9). Only wisdom received into the heart holds. Jesus, the Wisdom of God, still says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!" (Matthew 11:15). The question is whether my ear is bent toward Him, or only somewhere near Him.
units.application: Parents: do not wait for the culture, the school or a phone to teach your children about sex. Start the conversation early, in plain and modest words, and keep it going as they grow. Young people: decide now whose voice you will lean toward, and take your questions to a godly parent, pastor or mentor instead of the internet. Anyone: before you scroll tonight, open God's word and give it the first hearing.

rel.note: The words of the wise are to be kept within and fixed upon the lips, the same picture of knowledge ready for use.
There discretion guards the son; here the son is told to guard discretion, so each keeps the other.
The son's lips are to keep knowledge, while the immoral woman's lips drip honey; two kinds of speech compete for him.

units.notes:
• "Discretion" translates mezimmah, careful forethought or planning. Elsewhere the word can describe scheming (12:2), but here it means thinking ahead for good. In 2:11 discretion guards the son; here the son guards discretion.
• The KJV reads "regard discretion"; the ESV reads "keep discretion."
• Henry pictures knowledge kept on the lips as wisdom "ready at thy tongue's end," available the moment it is needed.
• The same phrase describes the priest in Malachi 2:7: "the lips of a priest should keep knowledge."
• Compare 22:17–18; Psalm 119:9, 11; and Matthew 4:4, where Jesus answers temptation with "It is written."
units.summary: Two sets of lips compete for a young man: his own, stocked with truth, and the seductress's, dripping honey.
units.principle: Truth stored up in advance becomes clear judgment and ready words when temptation arrives.
units.insight: When the serpent spoke to Eve, she repeated God's command but added to it (Genesis 3:3), and the smooth voice won. When Satan spoke to Jesus in the wilderness, He answered each temptation with Scripture He knew exactly: "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). That is the difference between lips that keep knowledge and lips that have let it slip. Jesus was "in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15), and He met temptation with God's word on His lips. Many of us know right from wrong in general but have no ready words when desire argues its case. The heart that has hidden God's word has something to say back, and the Spirit brings that word to mind when it is needed.
units.application: Young people: memorize a few short verses on purity, such as 1 Corinthians 6:18 and Psalm 119:9, so that you have words ready in the moment. Decide ahead of time what you will say if someone flirts with you, sends a suggestive message, or invites you somewhere you should not go. Husbands and wives: talk through your boundaries together before a situation tests them. Discretion is planning, not improvising.

rel.note: The father first described the same woman as the seductress who flatters with her words.
Against her honeyed lips the father sets the son's own lips, which are to keep knowledge.
The next verse sets her sweet beginning beside her bitter, wounding end.
His teaching is meant to keep the son from the flattering tongue of a seductress, the same danger in speech.
The story of chapter 7 shows her enticing speech and flattering lips actually causing a young man to yield.

units.notes:
• "Immoral woman" translates zarah, a stranger or outsider; "seductress" in 5:20 translates nokriyah, a foreigner or outsider. In chapters 2, 5 and 7 these words mark her as outside the son's marriage and outside God's ways. They do not by themselves settle whether she was an Israelite.
• The KJV has "strange woman," the ESV "forbidden woman," and the NASB "adulteress."
• The Hebrew behind "drip honey" closely matches the bridegroom's praise of his bride: "Your lips, O my spouse, Drip as the honeycomb" (Song of Songs 4:11). The sweetness celebrated within marriage there is the bait of adultery here.
• Henry says her words are smooth "that the poisonous pill may go down glibly and there may be no suspicion of harm in it."
• Compare 2:16; 6:24; 7:21; and Psalm 55:21, "His words were softer than oil, Yet they were drawn swords."
units.summary: Temptation never arrives tasting bitter; it comes sweet as honey and smooth as oil.
units.principle: Sin's most dangerous approach is pleasant words that make wrong feel safe and right feel unnecessary.
units.insight: The first temptation came as smooth words: "You will not surely die" (Genesis 3:4). Ever since, sin has preferred to talk its way in. An affair rarely begins with an open invitation to sin. It begins with attention, sympathy and flattery: "No one understands you the way I do." Potiphar's wife spoke to Joseph "day by day," and he did not heed her, nor would he even be with her (Genesis 39:10). The honey works because something in us wants to be admired and wanted, which is why the father deals with the ear and the lips first. When men flattered Jesus to trap Him, "He perceived their craftiness" (Luke 20:23). By His Spirit He gives His people the same discernment, to taste words before we swallow them.
units.application: Husbands and wives: be wary of anyone outside your marriage who makes you feel more understood than your spouse does; that warmth is the honey. Notice when a coworker's or online friend's compliments start to feel like something you need. Young men and women: when someone's words make crossing a line feel easy and safe, treat that ease as the warning. Weigh the words; do not just enjoy them.

rel.note: A way can seem right at first while its end is death, the same gap between beginning and end.
"At last" in 5:11 returns to the "end" named here and shows the bitterness in the man's own groaning.
The honey and oil of her first approach stand against the wormwood and sword of her end.
Folly also promises sweetness in secret while hiding that her guests end in the depths of the grave.

units.notes:
• "Two-edged sword" is literally a sword "of mouths." Hebrew called the edge of a blade its "mouth," so a sword with mouths is a sword with edges. Ross, quoted by Guzik, says the image "signifies that a liaison with this woman brings pain and destruction."
• The "mouth" that is "smoother than oil" in 5:3 translates a different Hebrew word, literally her palate, from the "mouths" of the sword in 5:4. So the link between 5:3 and 5:4 lies in the picture rather than in a repeated word: speech that felt smooth turns out to cut.
• Wormwood (la'anah) also stands for bitterness in Deuteronomy 29:18, Lamentations 3:19 and Amos 5:7, where Israel turns "justice to wormwood."
• Henry: "What was luscious in the mouth rises in the stomach and turns sour there."
• Compare 9:17–18; 14:12; Psalm 55:21; and Hebrews 11:25, "the passing pleasures of sin."
units.summary: Sin shows you the first taste and hides the aftertaste; wisdom judges a road by where it ends.
units.principle: Every temptation must be judged by its end, not its beginning; the sweetest sins often leave the deepest wounds.
units.insight: Amnon was so consumed with desire for his half-sister Tamar that he made himself sick (2 Samuel 13:2). Yet once he had forced her, "the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her" (2 Samuel 13:15). Honey turned to wormwood at once, and the sword cut through David's whole house. Sin advertises the first chapter and tears out the last. Our hearts are easily fooled because desire lives in the present moment. Moses looked further ahead, "choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin" (Hebrews 11:25). There is another two-edged sword, the word of God (Hebrews 4:12). It also cuts, but it cuts to heal, exposing sin so that Christ can forgive and cleanse it.
units.application: Before you take a first step toward an inappropriate relationship, play the story forward: picture telling your spouse, your children and your church. Young people: when a relationship pushes you toward sexual sin, ask where it will leave you in five years, not how it feels tonight. If you are already tasting the wormwood, do not hide it. Bring it to God and to a trusted believer; the word that cuts is also the word that heals.

rel.note: Her house leads down to death and those who go to her do not regain the paths of life, the same downward road.
The son is to keep his own feet on a level, established path, while her feet go down to death.
Her house is the way to the grave, descending to the chambers of death, the end this verse already sees.

units.notes:
• "Hell" translates Sheol, the realm of the dead. The ESV reads, "her steps follow the path to Sheol"; the KJV, "her steps take hold on hell."
• "Lay hold of" translates tamak, to grasp and hold firmly. The father used the same verb at 4:4, "Let your heart retain my words." The son is to hold fast to his father's words; her steps hold fast to the grave.
• Ironside: "dark and terrible the ending of association with her."
• Compare 2:18–19; 7:27; 9:18; James 1:14–15; Romans 6:23.
units.summary: Every step with the adulteress is a step downhill, and the hill ends in the grave.
units.principle: Sin is not a level detour from life but a downward road whose end is built into its beginning.
units.insight: James traces the same slope: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, "and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death" (James 1:15). No one sets out to reach the bottom of the hill; people only plan the next step. That is why the father shows his son the destination now. Our hearts like to think we can walk a little way down and climb back whenever we choose. Samson thought so, until the day he woke expecting to shake himself free as before, and "he did not know that the LORD had departed from him" (Judges 16:20). Another road exists, and another Person walks it. "The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). Christ went down into death Himself so that those on the downward road could be brought up into life.
units.application: Take stock of your direction, not only your last decision. Are your habits online, at work or in your friendships sloping toward someone who is not your spouse? Change direction now, while turning back is still easy. Parents: help your teenagers see where a relationship or habit leads, not only whether it is "that bad" yet. Leaders: when someone confides that they are drifting, help them turn around before the slope steepens.

rel.note: Those who go to her do not regain the paths of life, which is why her road must never be weighed as that path.
The same verb tells the son to ponder the path of his own feet instead of weighing hers.
The son must not weigh her road as a way of life, but the LORD weighs every road and knows where each one ends.

units.notes:
• "Ponder" translates palas, to weigh or to level a path. It appears at 4:26, "Ponder the path of your feet," and at 5:21, where the LORD "ponders all his paths." The son is to weigh his own path, not hers.
• In Hebrew, the verb form for "you" (spoken to a man) and the form for "she" are spelled the same way, so the verbs of this verse can be read either way. The NKJV and KJV address the son. The ESV, NASB and NLT make the woman the subject; the NLT reads, "For she cares nothing about the path to life. She staggers down a crooked trail and doesn't realize it."
• "Unstable" pictures wandering or staggering, the walk of someone with no fixed direction. The KJV has "moveable."
• The KJV reads, "Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable." Older commentators took this to mean she keeps her victim from serious thought; Henry says "she often changes her disguise," so she is never seen for what she is.
• Compare 2:19; 4:26; 14:12.
units.summary: The moment you start weighing temptation as a real option, you have begun walking toward it.
units.principle: Wisdom refuses to treat sin as a live option; whoever keeps measuring a forbidden road will soon be walking it.
units.insight: Eve looked at the forbidden tree and "saw that the tree was good for food, that it was pleasant to the eyes" (Genesis 3:6). She began weighing what God had already ruled out. David did the same on his rooftop. He "sent and inquired about the woman" (2 Samuel 11:3) before he ever sent for her. Sin rarely asks for a decision at first; it asks only for consideration. Our hearts are skilled at reopening questions God has closed: "Maybe this would be different. Maybe I deserve this." Jesus called Himself "the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). He is the road worth weighing, and His way does not shift under our feet.
units.application: When you catch yourself imagining a relationship with someone other than your spouse, or rehearsing how an affair might work, stop the calculation and call it temptation. Single adults: do not entertain arrangements you already know God forbids, even in your head. Pastors and counselors: when someone says "I'm just thinking about it," recognize that the thinking is already a step, and help them close the question.

rel.note: The father there also calls his children to hear the instruction of a father.
The son is told not to turn away from the words of the father's mouth, the same call not to depart.
After telling the story of the young man's fall, the father makes this same appeal to his children to listen to the words of his mouth.

units.notes:
• "Children" is literally "sons"; the ESV has "O sons." The same plural address opens 4:1 and returns in 7:24, where the father repeats this appeal almost word for word: "Now therefore, listen to me, my children."
• "Depart" means to turn aside from a road. The picture is not open rebellion but drifting off the line the father's words have drawn.
• Bridges: "Can we wonder then at parental earnestness, forcing back the children playing on the brink of a precipice?"
• Compare 4:5 ("Do not forget, nor turn away from the words of my mouth") and Hebrews 2:1, "we must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away."
units.summary: Every generation meets the same honeyed voice, so every generation needs a father who says, "Listen now."
units.principle: Drift, more often than open defiance, is how people leave the path of wisdom, so the time to hold on is now.
units.insight: The father's urgency is that of a parent pulling children back from the edge of a cliff; it is love, not harshness. Lot's wife did not run back to Sodom. She only looked back (Genesis 19:26). Departing from God's word usually starts that small: a glance, a doubt, a slow change in what we laugh at. Hebrews warns believers to give earnest heed "lest we drift away" (Hebrews 2:1). The heart drifts most easily when it assumes it is in no danger. The Good Shepherd goes after the one sheep that has wandered (Luke 15:4), and His voice still calls His own back to the path (John 10:27). The question for each of us is whether, this week, we are listening more to God's word or to the smooth voices around us.
units.application: Parents and grandparents: say the hard things now, with urgency and warmth, instead of waiting for a crisis. Youth leaders: speak plainly to your group about sexual temptation; they are already hearing other voices. Each of us: notice where you are quietly drifting, such as entertainment you once avoided, private messages you would not want read, or a Bible you have stopped opening. Turn back at the first step, not the fiftieth.

rel.note: The son is told to avoid the way of evil, not travel on it, turn from it and pass on, the same counsel of distance.
The sentence continues into the costs that lie beyond her door, which give the command its urgency.
No one can carry fire in his bosom or walk on hot coals unharmed, which is why distance is the only safe course.
The young man of chapter 7 takes the very path to her house that the father tells his son to avoid.

units.notes:
• "Remove your way far from her" stresses distance: the son is to take his whole route away from hers, not merely say no at her threshold. The KJV has "come not nigh the door of her house."
• Henry: "Those that would be kept from harm must keep out of harm's way." In practice that can mean taking a different street altogether, even if it is the long way round.
• Bridges: "The snare as it approaches becomes more enticing."
• Compare 4:14–15; 6:27–28; Romans 13:14; 1 Corinthians 6:18, "Flee sexual immorality"; and 2 Timothy 2:22, "Flee also youthful lusts."
units.summary: The man who never goes near the adulteress's door never has to fight the battle inside her house.
units.principle: Wise people do not test their strength against temptation at close range; they choose routes that keep them far from it.
units.insight: Joseph is the picture. Day after day he refused even "to be with her" (Genesis 39:10), and when Potiphar's wife finally seized him, "he left his garment in her hand, and fled and ran outside" (Genesis 39:12). He lost his coat and his position, but he kept his integrity. David, by contrast, stayed in Jerusalem when kings went out to battle and walked his rooftop at evening (2 Samuel 11:1–2). Pride says, "I'm strong enough to handle this." Wisdom says, "I'm not, so I won't go." Jesus taught us to pray, "do not lead us into temptation" (Matthew 6:13), and we cannot pray that sincerely while walking toward the door. Fleeing is not cowardice. It is faith acting on what God has said.
units.application: Name your doors and stay away from them. For one person that is a certain app or website; for another it is late-night texting with a coworker, traveling alone with a colleague, or a place where an old flame shows up. Husbands and wives: agree on boundaries together, such as no private meetings behind closed doors and open access to each other's phones. Pastors and counselors: guard your own settings as carefully as you urge others to.

rel.note: Lemuel's mother also warns her son not to give his strength to women who will destroy him.
This verse begins the list of costs that explain why the son must stay away from her door.
The adulterer there also loses honor, getting wounds and dishonor and a reproach that will not be wiped away.
The jealous fury of the wronged husband, who will not spare, is one likely meaning of "the cruel one."

units.notes:
• "Honor" translates hod, a word used elsewhere for splendor and majesty. The NASB renders it "your vigor," which brings out the sense of personal strength.
• Suggestions for "the cruel one" include the injured husband (6:34–35), the woman herself, and those who exploit the man once he is exposed. The ESV's "the merciless" keeps the description general, as the Hebrew does.
• Henry reads "the cruel" as the sin itself: "Those years that should be given to the honour of a gracious God are spent in the service of a cruel sin."
• Compare 6:32–33; 31:3, "Do not give your strength to women"; and Genesis 49:3–4, where Reuben loses the honor of the firstborn through sexual sin.
units.summary: The adulterer thinks he is getting something; in fact he is giving himself away.
units.principle: Sexual sin persuades a person to hand over his own dignity and best years to those who will not care for them.
units.insight: Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, "the excellency of dignity," yet he lost his place because he "went up to your father's bed" (Genesis 49:3–4). Esau sold his birthright "for one morsel of food" (Hebrews 12:16). We rarely feel the trade in the moment; the bill comes later. The verse asks a searching question: to whom am I giving my best years? Moses prayed, "So teach us to number our days, That we may gain a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12).
