For anyone who has already given years away, there is hope. God promised His repentant people, "I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten" (Joel 2:25). In Christ, God does not always remove every consequence, but He redeems the life that turns to Him and gives it a future.
units.application: If you are drifting toward an affair, count the cost in specific terms: your children's trust, your ministry or career, the years of rebuilding. Write it down if that helps you see it. Young men and women: your youth is not a season to spend on what you will regret; give it to God and to the person you may one day marry. If you have lost years to sexual sin, bring them to God and let Him begin the restoration.

rel.note: A companion of harlots wastes his wealth, the same drain on resources.
The son is told to drink from his own cistern; the man who ignores this ends with strangers filling themselves on what is his.
The same Hebrew word for strangers appears there: what should be his alone ends up shared with strangers.
By means of a harlot a man is reduced to a crust of bread, and the adulteress preys on his life.

units.notes:
• "Wealth" translates koach, which basically means strength or power. The ESV and NASB render it "strength," and the KJV margin notes "thy strength." The word covers the vigor and working capacity of a man's life, not only his money.
• "Labors" translates a word for painful toil; the same Hebrew word describes the pain of childbirth in Genesis 3:16. What cost him so much effort goes to someone else.
• Henry: his labor goes to "the house of a stranger, that neither has right to it nor will ever thank thee for it."
• Compare 6:26, "by means of a harlot A man is reduced to a crust of bread"; 29:3; and Luke 15:13, 30.
units.summary: The man who went after the strange woman ends with strangers feeding on everything he worked for.
units.principle: What is spent on sin is taken from the people God entrusted to us; unfaithfulness robs a household.
units.insight: The prodigal son "wasted his possessions with prodigal living" (Luke 15:13), and his brother summed it up bitterly: he "devoured your livelihood with harlots" (Luke 15:30). He ended up feeding another man's pigs and longing to eat what they ate (Luke 15:15–16). Strangers fed on his inheritance, and he labored in a stranger's field. Today the drain takes other forms: secret spending, legal costs, two households where there was one. But Jesus did not end the story in the pig pen. When the son "came to himself" and went home, the father ran to meet him (Luke 15:17, 20). That is the heart of God toward every prodigal who returns, and Christ told the story so that we would know it.
units.application: Husbands and wives: keep your finances open to each other; secret accounts and hidden spending are often the first sign of a hidden life. Fathers and mothers: remember that your time and energy are your family's provision, not only your paycheck. If you are tempted, think concretely about what an affair would take from your children. If you are already in the far country, go home: tell the truth and start rebuilding.

rel.note: The end of mirth may be grief, which is exactly what this man discovers.
"At last" here returns to the bitter "end" of 5:4 and lets the son hear it in the man's own groaning.
The young man of chapter 7 goes like an ox to the slaughter, not knowing it will cost his life, the same ruin of the whole person.

units.notes:
• "Mourn" translates naham, to groan. A noun from the same Hebrew root describes "the roaring of a lion" at 19:12 and 20:2, which shows how deep a cry the word describes. The ESV has "groan."
• "Flesh and body" together describe the whole physical person. Compare 1 Corinthians 6:18: "he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body."
• Ironside: "To learn by painful experience, if the word of God is not bowed to, is a bitter and solemn thing."
• Compare 5:4; 7:22–23; 14:13, "the end of mirth may be grief"; and Psalm 32:3.
units.summary: At the end of the road of adultery regret arrives, but too late to save what it mourns.
units.principle: Sin borrows against the future, and the body and heart eventually pay what the moment spent.
units.insight: David knew this groaning. Of a season when he hid his sin, he wrote, "When I kept silent, my bones grew old Through my groaning all the day long" (Psalm 32:3). Hidden sin wears a person down from the inside. Yet David's groaning was not the last word: "I acknowledged my sin to You... And You forgave the iniquity of my sin" (Psalm 32:5). There is a groaning of regret that only looks back, and a groaning of repentance that turns to God. Paul calls them worldly sorrow, which produces death, and godly sorrow, which produces repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). If your body or heart bears the marks of sexual sin, bring that groaning to Christ, who "has borne our griefs And carried our sorrows" (Isaiah 53:4).
units.application: Young people: count the physical and emotional cost of sexual sin while you are young and healthy, not afterward. Anyone carrying a secret: do not wait for your body or your marriage to break down before you confess. Talk to God and to a trusted pastor or counselor this week. Those who have lived with regret for years: let godly sorrow do its work, then receive forgiveness instead of punishing yourself with endless replays.

rel.note: Whoever hates correction is called stupid, the verdict this man finally passes on himself.
Disdaining instruction is despising one's own soul, the self-harm this lament confesses.
Those who hated knowledge and despised Wisdom's rebuke eat the fruit of their own way, as this man does.
The instruction he says he hated is the very thing he dies for lack of at the chapter's close.

units.notes:
• "Instruction" translates musar, discipline or training. It returns at 5:23, where the man dies "for lack of instruction," so the chapter closes on the very thing he says he hated.
• "Correction" is a reproof that exposes a wrong course. The KJV has "my heart despised reproof."
• Henry: "because he hated to be reformed he therefore hated to be informed." The man did not want to change, so he did not want to be told.
• Compare 1:7; 1:29–31; 12:1, "he who hates correction is stupid"; 15:32; and Hebrews 12:11.
units.summary: The adulterer's ruin began long before the affair, on the day he started resenting correction.
units.principle: Moral collapse usually begins in a heart that resents correction, long before it shows in conduct.
units.insight: King Saul is a sad picture of this man. When Samuel confronted him, he made excuses and blamed the people (1 Samuel 15:20–21), and his kingdom was torn from him. David, confronted by Nathan after his adultery, said simply, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). The difference between them was not the size of the sin but the response to correction. Our hearts bristle when someone points out a fault. We call it being misunderstood; the father calls it hating instruction. "For whom the LORD loves He chastens" (Hebrews 12:6). Correction from God, through His word or His people, is the love of a Father who will not let His children walk into ruin without warning.
units.application: This week, notice how you respond when someone corrects you, whether a spouse, a boss, a pastor or a friend. Do you explain, defend or deflect? Try simply saying, "You may be right; let me think about that." Parents: let your children see you receive correction well. Leaders: keep people around you who are free to tell you hard things, and thank them when they do.

rel.note: A wise son heeds his father's instruction, the very response this man failed to give.
The book's first call to hear a father's instruction shows the teaching he had and refused.
The father asks his son to lend his ear; this man confesses he never inclined his.

units.notes:
• "Obeyed" translates shama, the ordinary verb "to hear." In Hebrew, to hear someone's voice often means to heed it; the same verb opens "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4).
• "Inclined my ear" repeats the verb natah from 5:1, "Lend your ear." The father asks for a bent ear; the ruined man confesses he never gave one.
• Henry: "Those who have had a good education and do not live up to it will have a great deal to answer for another day."
• Compare 1:8; 13:1; Matthew 7:24–27; and James 1:22, "be doers of the word, and not hearers only."
units.summary: The ruined man was never short of teachers; he was short of an ear that would bend.
units.principle: Exposure to good teaching protects no one; only a heart that leans toward it and obeys is safe.
units.insight: Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. Both heard His words, but only one did them, and only his house stood when the storm came (Matthew 7:24–27). The ruined man of this verse had heard plenty. Judas walked with Jesus for three years and still betrayed Him. Many church-raised young people can quote the right verses and still walk into ruin, because hearing was never the same as heeding. The searching question is not "Have I been taught?" but "Have I bent toward what I was taught?" Christ is a patient Teacher who still says, "Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me" (Matthew 11:29). The ear that turns to Him now will not have to speak this lament later.
units.application: Take one piece of counsel you have heard more than once, from a parent, pastor or friend, and act on it this week. Students and church-raised young adults: your Bible knowledge is a gift, but it will not protect you unless you obey it. Parents and teachers: measure success not by how much your children know but by whether they are learning to heed. Pray for hearts that bend, theirs and yours.

rel.note: The one who perverts his ways will become known, as this man's hidden sin did.
Hidden wickedness is revealed before the assembly, the same movement from secrecy to public exposure.
Before his sin was exposed to the congregation it already lay open before the eyes of the LORD.
The adulterer gets wounds and dishonor, and his reproach is not wiped away, the same public shame.

units.notes:
• "Assembly" (qahal) and "congregation" (edah) are two Hebrew words both used of Israel gathered as a community. Placed side by side, they stress that his disgrace took place before the whole people.
• The NLT brings out the public shame: "I have come to the brink of utter ruin, and now I must face public disgrace." The KJV has "I was almost in all evil."
• Older commentators read the KJV's "almost in all evil" in more than one way. Some took it to mean the man went on sinning in heart even while he sat in worship; others took it to mean he was made a public example of judgment. The verse itself leaves the form of his ruin unstated.
• Compare 6:33; 10:9; 26:26; and Numbers 32:23, "be sure your sin will find you out."
units.summary: Sin that began in whispers ended in front of the whole congregation.
units.principle: Secret sin seldom stays secret, and a place among God's people cannot shelter a heart that refuses correction.
units.insight: David sinned in secret and tried to cover it with a murder. Nathan's message from the LORD was blunt: "For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, before the sun" (2 Samuel 12:12). His family's shame played out in public for years. Many who have fallen sat in church every week while their hearts drifted, and attendance did not keep them. Church is a gift, but it is not a vaccine. Yet the place of public shame can also become a place of public grace. Jesus did not condemn the woman brought to Him in adultery before the crowd. He sent her accusers away and told her, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:11).
units.application: If you are living a double life, do not count on it staying hidden. Bring it into the light yourself, first to God and then to a trusted leader, before it comes out on its own. Church leaders: build a culture where people can confess struggles early, not only after a public fall. When a brother's or sister's sin becomes public, respond with grief and a path to restoration, not gossip (Galatians 6:1).

rel.note: The man who will not drink from his own cistern ends with strangers filled with his wealth.
The next verse continues the water picture, asking whether these springs should be poured out in the streets.
The call to rejoice with the wife of your youth shows plainly what the cistern and well stand for.
Folly offers stolen water that seems sweet, the counterfeit of the water from one's own well.

units.notes:
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "'Water' in Proverbs 5:15, as in Song of Solomon 5:1, stands for quenching one's sexual thirst."
• The Song of Songs uses the same images for the bride: "A garden enclosed Is my sister, my spouse, A spring shut up, A fountain sealed" (Song of Songs 4:12), and "A well of living waters" (Song of Songs 4:15).
• Households kept their own cisterns. The Assyrian envoy tempted Jerusalem's defenders with the promise that each would "drink the waters of his own cistern" (2 Kings 18:31).
• The water images run without a break from 5:15 to 5:18: cistern, well, fountains, streams and fountain. "The wife of your youth" in 5:18 makes their meaning plain.
• Compare 9:17, "Stolen water is sweet," where Folly offers the counterfeit.
units.summary: The father does not tell his son to stop being thirsty; he tells him where to drink.
units.principle: God does not answer forbidden desire by condemning desire but by giving it a good and lawful home in marriage.
units.insight: Speaking of the one wife God allows a man, Henry puts it sharply: "nature will be content with that, but lust with nothing." Desire within God's design can be satisfied; desire outside it never is. Jesus met a woman at a well who had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband (John 4:16–18). Her thirst was real, and no relationship had quenched it. Jesus offered her water that would become "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). Marriage is a good cistern, but no spouse can be the fountain of life; only Christ is. That is good news for single, widowed and divorced readers as much as for married ones. A heart satisfied in Christ is the heart best able to enjoy His other gifts, or to wait for them.
units.application: Husbands and wives: invest in your physical and emotional relationship on purpose. Plan time alone, speak kindly, and pursue each other as you once did (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). When your marriage feels dry, the answer is to dig deeper into your own well, through open conversation, prayer and, if needed, counsel, not to look over the fence. Single believers: bring your longing to Christ without shame; He does not despise it, and He meets you in it.

rel.note: The father has just told his son to drink from his own well, so the answer to this question is plainly no.
The next verse states outright what the question implies: these waters are to be his alone.
The streets and open squares where the waters would be wasted are where the immoral woman lurks.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew has no word that marks the verse as a question, so translators must decide from context. The NKJV, ESV and NASB read a question expecting "no." The KJV reads a statement: "Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad." The context favors the question, because 5:15 says to drink from your own well and 5:17 says "only your own."
• Some older commentators, reading the KJV, took the streams as children going out from a faithful home, and the AMP adds "children" in parentheses.
• Wiersbe, quoted by Guzik: "To commit sexual sin is to pour this beautiful river into the streets and the public squares. What waste!"
• Compare 5:17; 7:12; and 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5.
units.summary: Love poured out everywhere is not multiplied; it is wasted in the street.
units.principle: Sexual love is precious because it is kept; spreading it around does not enlarge it but spends it.
units.insight: Our culture says that freedom means spreading ourselves around and that commitment means loss. The father says the opposite: love poured into the street is simply wasted. Solomon's own life shows it. He "loved many foreign women," and "his wives turned away his heart" (1 Kings 11:1, 3). More did not bring more joy; it brought a divided heart. The same is true of the eyes and the imagination. Jesus said that whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5:28). A heart scattered across screens and fantasies has little left for the one person God gave. The psalmist prayed, "Unite my heart to fear Your name" (Psalm 86:11), and God still gathers scattered hearts and makes them whole.
units.application: Men and women alike: be clear about where your desire is leaking out, whether through pornography, flirtation, an emotional affair or constant fantasy. Each is water running in the street. Choose one concrete step this week to stop the leak, such as filtering software, an accountability partner, or deleting an app or a contact. Parents: teach your children that purity is not fear of sex but keeping a precious gift for the right person.

rel.note: The immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth, breaking the exclusive bond this verse commands.
The same word for strangers shows where unfaithfulness leads: strangers filled with what was his.
The question of 5:16 expects no; this verse states the positive command behind it.

units.notes:
• "Strangers" here is the same Hebrew word rendered "aliens" in 5:10, and its feminine form is the word behind "immoral woman" in 5:3 and 5:20. The man who goes after the stranger ends up sharing what is his with strangers.
• The ESV reads, "Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, sums up the water picture of 5:16–17: "What is at issue is private versus common property."
• Compare 2:17; 6:29; Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4; and Song of Songs 2:16, "My beloved is mine, and I am his."
units.summary: A well shared with strangers is no longer your own; married love stays full by staying exclusive.
units.principle: Exclusivity is not a limit on married love but the soil in which its trust and joy grow.
units.insight: Exclusive love reflects God Himself. He calls Himself "a jealous God" (Exodus 34:14), not because He is insecure but because covenant love is undivided by nature. The prophets describe Israel's idolatry as adultery, giving to strangers what belonged to God alone (Jeremiah 3:20; Hosea 2:2). Paul applies the same exclusiveness to the Church: "I have betrothed you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:2). So the question reaches beyond marriage. Who else is drinking from the well of my heart? Christ gave Himself wholly for His people, and He asks for the whole heart in return. A faithful marriage and a faithful single life both bear witness to that undivided love.
units.application: Husbands and wives: guard the private things of your marriage. Do not share intimate details or complaints about your spouse with a coworker or friend of the opposite sex; that is often how a stranger first comes to the well. Keep no secret relationships, accounts or conversations. If someone outside your marriage is becoming your main confidant, redirect that closeness back home now.

rel.note: He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD, the blessing this verse celebrates.
A prudent wife is from the LORD, which is why she is to be received with joy.
The immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth; the son is to rejoice in the wife of his.
The cistern and well of 5:15 are named here for what they are: the wife of your youth.
The next verse develops this gladness with tender and frank delight in the wife.

units.notes:
• "The wife of your youth" appears again in Malachi 2:14, where the LORD is witness between a man and the wife of his youth whom he has betrayed.
• Scripture repeats the call to married joy: Ecclesiastes 9:9, "Live joyfully with the wife whom you love all the days of your vain life," and Deuteronomy 24:5, which kept a newly married man home for a year to "bring happiness to his wife."
• Henry: "Mutual delight is the bond of mutual fidelity."
• Bridges: "Tender, well-regulated, domestic affection is the best defence against the vagrant desires of unlawful passion." ("Vagrant" here means wandering.)
• Compare 12:4; 18:22; 19:14; 31:10–12.
units.summary: God wants more than a faithful marriage; He wants a glad one.
units.principle: Delight in one's own spouse is both God's command and one of His strongest protections against unfaithfulness.
units.insight: Isaac brought Rebekah into his mother's tent, "and she became his wife, and he loved her" (Genesis 24:67). Years later he was seen "showing endearment to Rebekah his wife" (Genesis 26:8). Delight did not have to fade with time. Many marriages drift not into hatred but into dull coexistence, and that dullness is where a stranger's honey tastes sweetest. In the light of the New Testament, marriage points beyond itself: husbands are to love their wives "just as Christ also loved the church" (Ephesians 5:25), and God rejoices over His people "as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride" (Isaiah 62:5). Not everyone reading this has a glad marriage; some are single, widowed or hurting. All may know the Bridegroom whose delight in His people never fades.
units.application: Husbands: tell your wife this week, in specific words, what you still delight in about her, and plan something for her joy, not just around your schedule. Wives: the call to rejoice is yours as well. Do not save your best humor and energy for people outside the home and bring only leftovers to your spouse. Couples in a dry season: do not settle for coexistence; pray together, talk openly, and seek a counselor if needed.

rel.note: The heart of a husband safely trusts his wife, who does him good all her days, the security of the love celebrated here.
The command to rejoice with the wife of your youth is filled out here in tender and physical terms.
The same verb for being enraptured is turned into a question about delight wasted on a seductress.
The verb for being enraptured with a wife becomes "go astray" for the fool who would not be.

units.notes:
• "Doe" translates the feminine form of the word for the wild mountain goat, or ibex, a sure-footed climber of rocky slopes.
• "Satisfy" translates ravah, to drink one's fill. The KJV margin renders it literally "water thee," which ties the line to the water images of 5:15–18.
• "Be enraptured" translates shagah, whose basic sense is to wander, stray or reel; the KJV margin gives "err thou," and the ESV has "be intoxicated." The same verb returns in 5:20 ("be enraptured") and 5:23 ("go astray"), linking delight in a wife, infatuation with a seductress, and the fool's final straying.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "It is highly important to see sexual delight in marriage as God-given…"
• Compare Song of Songs 4:5; 1 Corinthians 7:3–5; and Hebrews 13:4, "Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled."
units.summary: Scripture is not embarrassed by married delight, and the people of God need not be either.
units.principle: Within marriage, sexual delight is God's good gift, meant to be enjoyed for a lifetime and not merely tolerated.
units.insight: Some believers grew up hearing that sex was dirty, and they carried that shame into marriage. Others grew up hearing that sex was everything, and they carried that hunger into everything. Scripture corrects both. The God who made the body gave us the Song of Songs and moved this father to speak of married love without embarrassment. Paul tells husbands and wives not to deprive one another (1 Corinthians 7:5). Bishop Davenant, quoted by Bridges, pictures a man tossing on the waves out in the world but at home with his wife "in repose, as in a desired haven." Married love is meant to be that haven. For those whose marriage is painful, or who are single or widowed, this verse is not a reproach. It shows the gift as God made it and points to the Giver, who is good.
units.application: Married couples: talk with each other about your intimacy, kindly and without shame; delight is something you cultivate together. If past shame or hurt stands in the way, seek help from a wise Christian counselor. Parents: when you teach your children about sex, teach that it is good within marriage, not only dangerous outside it. Single, widowed or hurting readers: this verse describes God's gift, not a verdict on your life.

rel.note: The delight the son is to find in his wife is the same delight this question refuses to waste on a seductress.
The same word for bosom appears there: taking fire to one's bosom is what this embrace really is.
Whoever commits adultery lacks understanding and destroys himself, the plain answer to the father's question.

units.notes:
• "Enraptured" translates shagah, the verb of 5:19 and of "go astray" in 5:23: delight in the right place, infatuation in the wrong place, and finally straying into ruin.
• "Arms" translates a word for the bosom or lap; the ESV, NASB and KJV have "bosom." The same word appears in 6:27, "Can a man take fire to his bosom."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "In view of the better way of conjugal bliss with the blessed wife, involvement with the unchaste wife is absurd." ("Conjugal" means married.)
• Bridges: "none but the infatuated would leave the wholesome fountain for the poisoned and forbidden spring."
• Compare 6:32, "Whoever commits adultery with a woman lacks understanding"; 9:17–18; and Jeremiah 2:13.
units.summary: Why trade the blessed delight of your own marriage for a stranger's bitter cup?
units.principle: Sin is foolish as well as wrong, because it trades a real and blessed gift for a counterfeit that cannot satisfy.
units.insight: God once put a similar charge to Israel: "For My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, And hewn themselves cisterns—broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Every sin is a bad trade. Esau traded his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:34); Judas traded his Lord for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). The father does not shout at his son; he asks him to think. God often deals with us the same way: "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18). If you are drawn toward someone who is not your spouse, let the question land gently: why? What do I imagine I will find there that God has not already offered me in Christ and in the gifts He has given?
units.application: When attraction to someone outside your marriage pulls at you, stop and answer the father's question out loud or on paper: "Why?" Name what you are really looking for, whether attention, escape or affirmation. Then take that need to God and, where fitting, to your spouse. Young singles: ask the same question of any relationship that is pulling you away from Christ. Mentors: ask questions as this father does, rather than only handing out rules.

rel.note: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, watching the evil and the good, the same truth that no path is hidden.
He who weighs the hearts knows what we claim not to know and renders to each according to his deeds.
Sin that the LORD already sees is later exposed before the congregation as well.
The son must not weigh her road as a way of life, but the LORD weighs every road and judges where it leads.
The seductress counts on secrecy because her husband is away, but no one is away from the eyes of the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Ponders" translates palas, the verb of 4:26 and 5:6. At 4:26 the son was told to weigh his own path; at 5:6 he was warned not to weigh her road as if it were the path of life; here the LORD weighs every path. Translations vary: the 1984 NIV has "examines," the NASB "watches."
• The word translated "paths" describes tracks worn by wheels. Kidner, quoted by Guzik, calls them "the (waggon-) tracks made by constant use; a better everyday term would be 'habits'." God sees not only single acts but the ruts our lives wear.
• Bridges: "Practical atheism is the root of human depravity." Practical atheism means living as if God did not see, even while believing He exists.
• Compare 15:3; 24:12; Psalm 139:1–4; and Hebrews 4:13, "all things are naked and open to the eyes of Him to whom we must give account."
units.summary: The road to an affair is never as private as it feels; the LORD sees every step.
units.principle: Nothing we do is hidden from the LORD, who sees every path and weighs where it leads; living in that knowledge is the root of purity.
units.insight: Joseph's defense against temptation was not mainly the fear of being caught but his awareness of God: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). Hagar, alone and mistreated in the wilderness, found comfort in the same truth and called the LORD "You-Are-the-God-Who-Sees" (Genesis 16:13). God's sight is a warning to the one plotting in secret and a comfort to the one being faithful in secret. Our hearts easily act as if the screen, the hotel room or the private conversation were beyond His notice. But "The eyes of the LORD are in every place" (15:3). In Christ, the God who sees everything is also the Father who forgives and cleanses the one who comes into the light (1 John 1:9).
units.application: Before you open an app, send a message or take a detour you would hide from your spouse, pause and say, "The LORD sees this." Parents: teach your children that God's eyes are both a warning and a comfort, not a threat to frighten them. Anyone being faithful when no one notices, such as a spouse keeping vows in a hard marriage or a single person staying pure, take heart: the LORD sees that too.

rel.note: The unfaithful are caught by their own lust, the same self-made trap.
Whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, the way out of the cords this verse describes.
By transgression an evil man is snared, as the wicked man here is caught by his own iniquities.
The young man of chapter 7 goes like an ox to slaughter and a bird to the snare, the trap closing in story form.

units.notes:
• "Entrap" translates lakad, a word used for catching prey in a trap and for capturing a city. The ESV reads, "The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin."
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "The lifelong occupation of the ungodly man is to twist ropes of sin."
• Ironside: "The very sins in which he now delights are the links he is forging to make the chain that shall bind him forever."
• Compare 11:6, "the unfaithful will be caught by their lust"; 29:6; John 8:34, "whoever commits sin is a slave of sin"; and Judges 16:21.
units.summary: Sin needs no jailer: every repeated choice adds another strand to the rope that binds the sinner.
units.principle: Sin enslaves through repetition and holds its servant by his own choices, but God's mercy can loosen what sin has bound.
units.insight: Samson treated Delilah's ropes as a game. He snapped them again and again (Judges 16:9, 12), until the day the Philistines put out his eyes and bound him with bronze fetters (Judges 16:21). His own appetites had done the binding long before the enemy did. Many who struggle with pornography or a secret relationship know the feeling: "I can stop whenever I want," until they cannot. Jesus said that whoever commits sin is a slave of sin, and then He gave the promise: "Therefore if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed" (John 8:36). He came "To proclaim liberty to the captives" (Luke 4:18). Confessing and forsaking sin, the way of 28:13, is how those cords begin to come loose.
units.application: If you are caught in a habit of sexual sin, stop telling yourself you can quit alone. This week, tell one trusted, mature believer and ask that person to check in with you regularly (James 5:16). Put accountability in place and remove the easy access. Pastors and small-group leaders: create safe places where people can confess without being crushed. Parents: if your child is caught in this, respond with firmness and hope, not only anger.

rel.note: Fools die for lack of wisdom, the same end for the same refusal.
The instruction he said he hated is the very thing he dies for lack of.
The verb for being enraptured with one's wife becomes the verb for going astray in folly.
The immoral woman has cast down many, and her house is the way to the chambers of death, the end of this road.

units.notes:
• "Instruction" is musar, the word the ruined man said he hated in 5:12. The chapter closes on the very thing he refused.
• "Go astray" translates shagah, the verb rendered "enraptured" in 5:19 and 5:20. The ESV reads, "because of his great folly he is led astray."
• Ironside: "Having refused instruction in life, he shall die without it; left to go astray in the folly his soul loved."
• Compare 7:26–27; 10:21, "fools die for lack of wisdom"; 28:13; and 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
units.summary: The man who hated instruction ends by dying for lack of it.
units.principle: Refusing wisdom leads at last to death, but no one who turns to Christ is beyond His cleansing.
units.insight: The chapter closes in darkness so that the son will run toward the light. Bridges asks whether there is any remedy and answers, "Thanks be to God! cleansing is provided for the impure." Paul wrote to believers in Corinth who had once been sexually immoral and adulterers: "And such were some of you. But you were washed" (1 Corinthians 6:11). David, after his great fall, prayed, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10), and God heard him. The same Jesus who told a woman caught in adultery to "go and sin no more" (John 8:11) shed His blood so that "the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). The warning is real, and so is the welcome. No one who has strayed is too far to be found.
units.application: If you are on the wrong road, the most urgent thing you can do is receive instruction now: talk to a pastor, open Scripture, confess to God. Do not wait for the end of the road. Parents: make sure your children know there is always a way home, even after failure. Church leaders: let every warning you give about sexual sin end with the gospel's offer of mercy (28:13; 1 John 1:9).

rel.note: Shaking hands to become surety for a friend is called the act of a man devoid of understanding.
Pity on the poor is lending to the LORD, which keeps the warning against rash pledges from becoming a ban on generosity.
The father forbids shaking hands in pledge and shows the cost plainly: a guarantor who cannot pay may lose the bed from under him.
The next verse shows what the pledge has done: the son is trapped by the words of his own mouth.
The chapter opens with a debt the son can still escape and closes with a wrong no payment can settle.

units.notes:
• Surety means standing as guarantor for another person's debt. Proverbs returns to it again and again (11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27; 27:13), which shows how common and how costly the practice was.
• "Shaken hands in pledge" renders a Hebrew phrase meaning to strike the palms, the public gesture that sealed an agreement. The KJV keeps the picture: "if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger."
• Whether the "friend" and the "stranger" are the same person, or the friend is the borrower and the stranger the lender, is debated. The ESV and NASB have "neighbor" for "friend," which shows the word's general sense.
• Scripture also shows a weighed, loving pledge. Writing to Philemon about the runaway slave Onesimus, Paul took the debt on himself freely and knowingly: "put that on my account" (Philemon 18).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Even to the recipient, an unconditional pledge may be an unintended disservice by exposing him to temptation." A borrower who knows someone else will pay may grow careless.
units.summary: A handshake takes a moment, but a guarantee for someone else's debt can bind you for years.
units.principle: Goodwill is not reason enough to promise what you cannot control; generosity gives freely, but wisdom refuses rash guarantees.
units.insight: Rash pledges usually grow from good motives tangled with weaker ones: the wish to be liked, the fear of saying no, the pride of seeming able. Judah's pledge for Benjamin shows that standing surety can be noble when it is weighed, costly love (Genesis 43:9; 44:32–33). The father's warning targets the quick, unweighed promise. The question for us is not only "Can I afford this?" but "Why am I saying yes?" In the light of the New Testament, the word "surety" gains a deeper meaning: "Jesus has become a surety of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). He did not pledge rashly. He counted the full cost of our debt and paid it with His own blood. Bridges: "Our God, while he warns us against suretyship, has taken it upon himself." Because Christ has stood surety for us, we need not prove our worth by promising more than we can give.
units.application: If a friend, adult child or coworker asks you to cosign a loan, slow down. The safest counsel is not to cosign. If you choose to help, give only what you are able and willing to lose, and consider a gift you can afford instead of a guarantee you cannot. Parents, talk with your young adults about cosigning before the first car loan or apartment lease. Pastors, teach this plainly; many church families carry debts they signed for someone else.

rel.note: The one who guards his mouth preserves his life, while the son here opened his mouth too quickly and was caught.
A fool's lips become the snare of his soul, the same picture of a person trapped by his own speech.
Rashly devoting something to God and then reconsidering is called a snare, another promise spoken too quickly.
The previous verse names the pledge that has now become the trap.
Because his own words have caught him, the son must now act to be released.

units.notes:
• "Snared" and "taken" are hunting words. The first pictures an animal caught in a trap, the second the moment the hunter seizes it. The picture returns in 6:5, where the son must escape "like a bird from the hand of the fowler."
• The KJV reads "the words of thy mouth" in both lines, and Ironside's version has "the sayings of thy mouth." Every version names the son's own speech as the cause of his trouble.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Becoming surety is folly because the surety makes promises for the future that he cannot control." Compare 27:1: "you do not know what a day may bring forth."
• Jephthah's rash vow shows how a quick promise can bind a person to grief: "I have given my word to the LORD, and I cannot go back on it" (Judges 11:35).
• Compare 18:7; 20:25; Ecclesiastes 5:2, 5.
units.summary: No enemy sets this trap; a hasty pledge from your own mouth springs it.
units.principle: A promise is easy to make and hard to escape, so words that bind the future must be weighed before they are spoken.
units.insight: Scripture shows how quickly words can bind. Herod, pleased by a dance and eager to look generous before his guests, promised Herodias's daughter whatever she asked. When she asked for John the Baptist's head, Herod gave it, "because of the oaths and because of those who sat with him" (Mark 6:26). We are rarely trapped by what we carefully planned. We are trapped by what we said to look kind, capable or important. Jesus calls His people to plain speech: "let your 'Yes' be 'Yes,' and your 'No,' 'No'" (Matthew 5:37). Speaking that way takes a heart secure enough to disappoint people. The gospel gives that security. God's word to us is never rash and never broken, for "all the promises of God in Him are Yes, and in Him Amen" (2 Corinthians 1:20). His faithfulness frees us to make fewer promises and keep them.
units.application: Before you say yes to anything that binds your money, time or name, give yourself a pause: "Let me pray about it and answer you tomorrow." Young adults, practice this with roommates, leases and business partners. Leaders, do not make promises in a public moment that you have not counted privately. If your words have already trapped you, do not pretend they were never spoken. Own them, and begin the honest steps the next verses describe.

rel.note: The borrower is servant to the lender, which explains why a guarantor finds himself in another person's hand.
Pride brings a man low while the humble in spirit retain honor, so humbling himself is the son's path to recovery.
The trap of the son's own words is the reason he must now go and plead.
The next verse adds urgency: he must not sleep until the pleading succeeds.
The pleading this verse calls for is the all-out escape pictured by the gazelle and the bird.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "humble yourself" is rare. Its basic sense is to stamp or trample, so it pictures a man lowering himself before another. It appears elsewhere only in Psalm 68:30, where the NKJV has "submits himself."
• The verb translated "plead" means to press or urge hard. The ESV has "hasten" and "plead urgently," and the NASB "importune," an older word for asking again and again. Every version stresses humble, persistent pressing.
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, gives the force of the first verb: "offer thyself to be trodden upon, or throw thyself down at his feet."
• Ironside: "pride is generally the incentive to suretyship." In plain words, the wish to look generous or well off is often what leads a man to guarantee another's debt.
• Compare Matthew 5:25: "Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him."
units.summary: Pride would rather stay trapped than admit a mistake; wisdom swallows its pride and gets free.
units.principle: When pride has led us into a trap, humility is usually the way out, and the sooner we humble ourselves the less it costs.
units.insight: Underneath many pledges lies the desire to look generous, capable or well off. The same pride then keeps people stuck. It is easier to keep paying for a bad promise than to go and say, "I was wrong; please release me." Jacob, who had cheated his brother, went to meet Esau and "bowed himself to the ground seven times" (Genesis 33:3). His humility opened a door that twenty years of distance had closed. The prodigal son rehearsed his humble words and went home (Luke 15:18–21). Ask where pride is keeping you in a situation you could leave by asking. The gospel goes deeper still. We owe God a debt no pleading can clear, and Christ, who "humbled Himself" (Philippians 2:8), paid it in full. Those who have received such grace can afford to humble themselves before people.
units.application: If you have cosigned a debt you cannot carry, do not wait for the crisis. Go to the borrower this week and ask him to refinance or release you, and if needed ask the lender what a release would take. Be humble and persistent, not angry. If you are the borrower, work to free your friend from the risk you asked him to take. Church leaders, make it safe for members to talk about debt without shame, so they ask for help early.

rel.note: A guarantor who cannot pay may lose his bed, which shows why he should give up sleep now to get free.
The one who keeps wisdom lies down unafraid and sleeps sweetly, the rest this son can enjoy once he is free.
Later in the chapter sleep is pictured as safe under the guard of wise teaching.
The son must go and plead for release, and this verse says he must not rest until he has done it.
The same words, sleep and slumber, describe the sluggard who rests when he should act.

units.notes:
• Proverbs 6 uses sleep three ways. Here it must be refused because danger is growing; in 6:9–10 the sluggard loves it too much; in 6:22 the sleeping son is kept safe by his parents' teaching.
• David used the same words in a vow of devotion: "I will not give sleep to my eyes Or slumber to my eyelids, Until I find a place for the LORD" (Psalm 132:4–5).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, explains why delay was dangerous in that world: "seizure of assets and home and even the selling of the debtor into slavery were common penalties" for unpaid debt.
• Compare 22:27, where the guarantor who cannot pay has his bed taken "from under you." The son who will not give up sleep now may lose his bed later.
units.summary: Some problems should cost you a night's sleep, because sleeping on them only makes them worse.
units.principle: Delay strengthens a trap; when danger is real and growing, wisdom acts before it rests.
units.insight: Procrastination about money, conflict and sin usually wears a calm face: "It can wait until tomorrow." Lot lingered in Sodom even after the angels warned him, until "the men took hold of his hand" and brought him out (Genesis 19:16). His delay nearly cost him everything. Paul applies the same urgency to anger: "do not let the sun go down on your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26). Some matters must be settled before we sleep. Where are you resting comfortably on something God has told you to deal with? The deepest form of this urgency is the gospel itself: "now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). God's patience is real, but His goodness is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), not to lull us into drift.
units.application: List the obligations that are quietly growing: a cosigned loan, an unpaid bill, a promise you cannot keep. Choose one and take the first step before you go to bed tonight: a phone call, an email, a meeting request. Married couples, talk openly about any debt either of you has guaranteed. Small-business owners, review the personal guarantees on your leases and loans this month and ask how to be released from them.

rel.note: The one who is surety for a stranger will suffer, which is why the son must escape quickly.
The prudent man sees danger and hides himself, while the simple go on and suffer.
The son has come into his friend's hand, and now he must get out of that hand like a gazelle.
The young man flies into the snare like a bird, while the son here is told to escape like a bird from the fowler.

units.notes:
• "Gazelle" is the NKJV word; the KJV has "roe," a small deer. Both name a swift, alert animal of the hills that is hard to hold once it starts to run.
• The word "hand" ties these verses together. The son has come "into the hand" of his friend (6:3), and now he must escape "from the hand" of the hunter and the fowler.
• Scripture uses the fowler's snare as a picture of deadly danger from which God rescues: "Surely He shall deliver you from the snare of the fowler" (Psalm 91:3).
• The bird and the snare return in 7:23, where the young man goes to the adulteress "As a bird hastens to the snare." Here the bird flees the trap; there it flies into one.
• Compare 22:3, "A prudent man foresees evil and hides himself."
units.summary: A handshake can get you into the trap; only a gazelle's all-out run will get you out.
units.principle: Getting out of a trap takes far more effort than getting into it, so wisdom escapes with all its strength and does not linger.
units.insight: A snared animal does not debate; it fights to get free. We often do the opposite. We stay in bad debts, compromising partnerships and sinful habits because getting out feels embarrassing or costly. David shows a better way. When Saul's spear struck the wall beside him, "David fled and escaped that night" (1 Samuel 19:10). He did not stay to prove a point. Where do you feel a snare tightening while you flutter half-heartedly? Psalm 124 uses the same picture of a bird and a snare and adds something more: "The snare is broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the LORD" (Psalm 124:7–8). The bird does not break the snare; God does. In Christ He breaks the snares we cannot, for "if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed" (John 8:36). Our part is to run when He opens the way.
units.application: Name one trap you have stayed in too long: a cosigned note, a business partnership pulling you into wrong, a cycle of credit card debt, a friendship that keeps drawing you into sin. Take a decisive step this week, not a half-step. Get help from a wise believer or a financial counselor if you need a plan. Parents, when an adult child is caught, help him see the urgency, but do not rescue him from every consequence.

rel.note: The lazy man desires and has nothing, while the diligent is made rich, the outcome the ant's ways point toward.
The teacher looks at the lazy man's field, considers it well and receives instruction, the same learning by observation the sluggard is told to practice.
Agur also holds up the ant as small but exceedingly wise because she prepares her food in summer.
The next lines spell out the ant's ways that the sluggard is told to consider.
The father turns from the ant to address the sluggard directly and ask how long he will sleep.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word translated "sluggard" is the same word the NKJV renders "lazy man" elsewhere in Proverbs (for example 13:4; 26:13–16). The NKJV uses "sluggard" only here and in 6:9.
• The ant returns in 30:24–25 among the "four things which are little on the earth, But they are exceedingly wise": "The ants are a people not strong, Yet they prepare their food in the summer."
• Bridges cites a Roman moralist: "It is a shame … not to learn morals from the small animals." His footnote names Seneca.
• The ant is an example to imitate, not a symbol with a hidden meaning. Her lesson is plain: steady, self-driven work and preparation for what is coming.
• Jesus also taught from creation: "Look at the birds of the air" (Matthew 6:26). Compare Job 12:7: "But now ask the beasts, and they will teach you."
units.summary: God sends the man who will not work to a classroom the size of an anthill.
units.principle: God has written lessons of diligence into His creation, and the person who will not work must humble himself to learn them.
units.insight: Sending a grown man to learn from an ant is humbling, and it is meant to be. Laziness rarely calls itself by name. It says "I'm resting," "I'll get to it," or "That's not my job." But Paul told the church plainly, "If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Refusing work quietly refuses God's design for us. Yet this verse is a call, not a sentence: "be wise." The sluggard can still learn. Jesus said, "My Father has been working until now, and I have been working" (John 5:17). In Him our work stops being a way to earn God's favor and becomes service offered to Him. Before you look for the sluggard around you, ask where the label fits you.
units.application: Pick one task you have avoided, such as the garage, the job application or the Bible study you promised to prepare, and give it a set time this week. Young people, if you want something to happen, do not wait to be pushed. Parents, give children real responsibilities and let them see you work cheerfully. But be careful never to call someone lazy who is sick, grieving, depressed or carrying burdens you cannot see; ask and help before you judge.

rel.note: The son who gathers in summer is wise, and the son who sleeps in harvest brings shame.
The diligent will rule while the lazy end up under forced labor; the ant needs no ruler, but the sluggard ends up under one.
The lazy man will not plow in the cold season and so has nothing at harvest, the reverse of the ant.
The ants are not strong, yet they prepare their food in summer, the same foresight described here.
The ant's busy gathering stands against the sluggard's folded hands.
These lines describe the ways the sluggard was told to go and consider.

units.notes:
• The word translated "Overseer" is the word used for the Israelite foremen in Egypt, who were beaten when the brick quota was not met (Exodus 5:14, where the NKJV has "officers"). The ant needs no one standing over her like that.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Aristotle also asserted that ants labor without rulers to direct them." Ancient observers saw what Proverbs describes.
• Some later critics mocked the idea of ants storing grain. Ironside answers: "In Palestine there is a species of ant which is not carnivorous, but feeds on grain and does indeed store its food in harvest time."
• Compare 30:27, where the locusts "have no king, Yet they all advance in ranks," another creature that keeps order without a ruler.
• Compare 10:5: "He who gathers in summer is a wise son; He who sleeps in harvest is a son who causes shame."
units.summary: The ant has no boss and no reminder, yet she is ready before winter comes.
units.principle: Faithful work does not wait to be watched or pushed, and wise people use seasons of opportunity to prepare for seasons of need.
units.insight: Joseph is Scripture's great picture of the ant's foresight. During seven years of plenty he "gathered very much grain, as the sand of the sea" (Genesis 41:49), so that when famine came there was bread for Egypt and for his own family. The ant's first lesson searches the heart: Do I work the same way when no one is watching? Paul calls servants to work "not with eyeservice, as men-pleasers," but "heartily, as to the Lord and not to men" (Ephesians 6:6; Colossians 3:23). The believer works before a Lord who sees everything. That is not a threat but a freedom, because He notices what no one else does. Jesus said, "I must work the works of Him who sent Me while it is day; the night is coming when no one can work" (John 9:4). Every season of opportunity is a gift that will not last forever.
units.application: Employees, do the job well when the manager is out of the office. Students, start the paper before the deadline forces you to. Young adults, use your strong earning years to save and to get out of debt before family costs or a downturn arrive. Families, build a small emergency fund in the good months. Believers, store up God's word in the easy seasons; you will need it in the hard ones.

rel.note: Laziness casts a person into deep sleep, and the idle go hungry.
Loving sleep leads to poverty, while opening your eyes leads to bread.
The lazy man turns on his bed like a door on its hinges, moving without ever rising.
The same words for sleep and slumber mark the urgency of the trapped son, who must refuse the rest the sluggard loves.
The father who sent the sluggard to the ant now confronts him directly.

units.notes:
• "Slumber" and "sleep" are the same pair of words the father used in 6:4. There the son was to give up sleep to escape danger; here the sluggard's sleep is the danger.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Sleep is the defining characteristic of the sluggard (cf. Proverbs 20:13)." That verse reads, "Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty."
• Compare 26:14: "As a door turns on its hinges, So does the lazy man on his bed." He moves, but he never gets up.
• Bridges applies the question to the soul: "Every day's slumber makes it more improbable, whether thou wilt ever awaken at all." In plain words, each day of delay makes waking up less likely.
• Compare Romans 13:11: "now it is high time to awake out of sleep."
units.summary: The sluggard never refuses to get up; he just never decides when.
units.principle: Delay is the sluggard's favorite way of saying no; the time to begin a duty is now, not a later moment that never arrives.
units.insight: Jonah ran from God and slept in the bottom of the ship while the storm raged, until the captain shook him: "What do you mean, sleeper? Arise, call on your God" (Jonah 1:6). In Gethsemane Jesus found His disciples sleeping and asked, "What! Could you not watch with Me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40). God still asks "How long?" of people who mean to obey later. The question exposes our own hearts. What has God told you to do that you plan to do "soon"? The call also carries hope. A question that asks "When will you rise?" assumes that rising is still possible. "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14). The One who calls us to get up also gives the power to do it.
units.application: Name the thing you keep saying you will start "soon": the hard conversation, the exercise plan, the Bible reading, the job search. Put a date and time on it today, and tell someone who will ask you about it. Parents, when a teenager procrastinates, ask "When?" and help him set a concrete start. Managers, replace vague assignments with clear deadlines. Pastors, invite hearers to respond to God's call now, not someday.

rel.note: The lesson of the lazy man's field repeats these words almost exactly.
The lazy man is too weary even to bring his hand from the bowl to his mouth, the same love of ease pictured by folded hands.
The sluggard's small delays run straight into the poverty that comes on him in the next verse.
The son in danger must refuse sleep and slumber, the very things the sluggard keeps asking for.
The ant gathers in summer while the sluggard folds his hands.

units.notes:
• Verses 10–11 return almost word for word in 24:33–34, as the lesson drawn from the overgrown field of the lazy man (24:30–34). The NKJV reads "to sleep" here and "to rest" in 24:33.
• The KJV begins, "Yet a little sleep." The "yet" shows that the sluggard has already slept and is asking for more.
• Henry says of sluggards that "they are cheated of all their time by being cheated of the present moments." Lost lives are usually lost a few minutes at a time.
• Folded hands appear again in Ecclesiastes 4:5: "The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh."
• Compare 19:24 and 26:15, where the lazy man will not even lift food from the bowl to his mouth.
units.summary: Nobody chooses ruin all at once; the sluggard just asks for a few more minutes, again and again.
units.principle: Small delays repeated become a way of life; what we postpone a little at a time we can lose all at once.
units.insight: Scripture shows how much can turn on a small delay. In the Song of Solomon the bride hears her beloved knocking at night and answers, "I have taken off my robe; How can I put it on again?" By the time she opens the door, "my beloved had turned away and was gone" (Song of Solomon 5:3, 6). Her excuse was small, and her loss was real. Our hearts work the same way with prayer, repentance and obedience: "Not tonight; tomorrow." Hebrews urges believers "that you do not become sluggish, but imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises" (Hebrews 6:12). The cure is not a burst of guilty effort. It is a daily yes to Christ, who said, "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me, and to finish His work" (John 4:34). Small faithful steps, repeated, build a life too.
units.application: Notice your "a little" phrases this week: "just one more episode," "five more minutes," "I'll answer that later." Choose one and replace it with a small action done now. Students, start assignments the day they are given, even for fifteen minutes. Workers, do the unpleasant task first. Parents, help children build the habit of finishing chores before play. Leaders, praise steady small progress, not only big results.

rel.note: A slack hand makes a person poor, while the hand of the diligent makes rich.
Pity on the poor is lending to the LORD, which keeps this warning from becoming contempt for those in need.
The same images of the prowler and the armed man close the lesson of the overgrown field.
The little delays of the previous verse are what open the door to this poverty.
The troublemaker's ruin also comes suddenly, so both figures meet consequences they did not see coming.

units.notes:
• "Prowler" renders a Hebrew expression for one who walks about or travels. The KJV has "one that travelleth," the NASB "vagabond," the ESV "robber" and the current NIV "thief."
• "Armed man" is literally "a man of the shield," a soldier equipped for battle. Ironside's version reads "a man with a shield."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "It is not riches the lazy person lacks; it is food, the necessity of life." The poverty in view is real want, not merely a smaller income.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik, on the armed man: "That is, with irresistible fury; and thou art not prepared to oppose it."
• The same two lines close the lesson of the lazy man's field in 24:34. Compare 10:4 and 20:13.
units.summary: Poverty creeps in quietly while the sluggard sleeps, then overpowers him like an armed man.
units.principle: Persistent idleness tends to bring a want that grows unseen and then arrives with force, though not all poverty comes from laziness.
units.insight: Jesus told of a servant who buried his master's money instead of putting it to work. The master called him "You wicked and lazy servant" and took away even what he had (Matthew 25:26–28). The loss came suddenly, at the day of reckoning, but it was built over a long season of doing nothing. The same pattern reaches beyond money. A marriage, a friendship or a prayer life can be robbed slowly by neglect, until one day the loss is undeniable. That is a sobering mirror for our own hearts. Yet this verse must never become a stick to beat the poor. Proverbs also says, "He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD" (19:17). The warning is for the capable who will not work, and it comes while there is still time to change.
units.application: Look at one area where neglect has been quietly building: unpaid bills, a job search you keep postponing, a home repair, a strained relationship. Take one concrete step this week, before the "armed man" arrives. Parents of adult children living at home, set clear and loving expectations about work. Friends and churches, when someone is in need, ask before you judge. Help the struggling generously, and challenge the able-bodied idle with patience and truth.

rel.note: The ungodly man digs up evil with burning words, and the perverse man sows strife, the same destructive figure.
The one with a deceitful heart and a perverse tongue falls into evil.
The son is told to put away the deceitful mouth and perverse lips that mark this man.
The portrait that begins with his mouth reaches its source in his perverse heart.
God's list of what He hates names the lying tongue that this man uses as a way of life.

units.notes:
• "A worthless person" is literally "a man of belial." Here belial is not a personal name but the Hebrew word for worthlessness, describing someone good for nothing and destructive. The KJV and older versions often left the word untranslated, which is why it can sound like a name.
• The same word describes Eli's sons, whom the NKJV calls "corrupt" (1 Samuel 2:12), and the two "scoundrels" hired to testify falsely against Naboth (1 Kings 21:10, 13).
• By New Testament times the word had become a name for Satan: "And what accord has Christ with Belial?" (2 Corinthians 6:15). That later use shows how dark the term was.
• Bridges: "What a contrast between the inactivity of the sluggard and the unwearied diligence of the naughty person!" In older English "naughty" meant wicked, not merely mischievous.
• Compare 4:24: "Put away from you a deceitful mouth, And put perverse lips far from you."
units.summary: The sluggard wastes his life doing nothing; the troublemaker spends his doing harm.
units.principle: A crooked mouth reveals a crooked life; the person who habitually twists the truth endangers everyone around him.
units.insight: Eli's sons served at the tabernacle, yet Scripture says they "did not know the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:12). They used holy things to feed their own appetites, and their corruption spread through Israel's worship. Worthlessness can wear religious clothes. James warns that "the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity" (James 3:6), and Jesus taught that "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). So this portrait is not only a warning about others; it is a question for us. Do we bend the truth to get our way, shade a story to look better, or speak one way to a person's face and another behind his back? The cure for a crooked mouth is not better technique but a new heart. Jesus said, "You must be born again" (John 3:7), and God still makes crooked people straight.
units.application: Leaders, watch for the person whose words consistently twist situations and set people against each other, and address it early. Young people, be careful whom you let close; a friend with a crooked mouth will eventually turn it on you. In your own speech this week, catch yourself when you exaggerate, shade the truth or say something you would not say in the person's presence, and correct it on the spot.

rel.note: The one who winks with the eye causes trouble, the same secret signal described here.
A man winks his eye to devise perverse things, joining the gesture to a scheming mind.
The hater who disguises himself with kind words is another portrait of an outward show that hides a wicked heart.
The secret signals of eyes, feet and fingers flow from the perverse heart named in the next verse.
God's list of hated things moves through the same body parts, the eyes and the feet.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "shuffles his feet" is usually understood as scraping or rubbing the feet to make a secret sign. Some scholars connect it with a verb meaning to speak, which explains the KJV's "he speaketh with his feet." The ESV and NASB read "signals."
• Winking is linked with trouble elsewhere in Proverbs: "He who winks with the eye causes trouble" (10:10); "He winks his eye to devise perverse things" (16:30). Compare Psalm 35:19: "Nor let them wink with the eye who hate me without a cause."
• Isaiah names "The pointing of the finger, and speaking wickedness" among the things God's people must put away (Isaiah 58:9).
• Bridges says the troublemaker "makes every member—eyes, feet, and fingers—vocal and significant." In plain words, every part of his body speaks for his scheme.
units.summary: A deceiver's body can tell a lie his lips never speak.
units.principle: Deceit is not limited to words; a crooked heart can turn any gesture into a tool, but nothing is hidden from God.
units.insight: The most infamous signal in Scripture was a kiss. Judas told the soldiers, "Whomever I kiss, He is the One; seize Him" (Matthew 26:48). A sign of affection became a signal for betrayal. That is the troublemaker's art: ordinary gestures carrying a hidden meaning shared with accomplices. Most of us will never plot like this man, but we know smaller versions. There is the knowing glance at someone's expense, the eye-roll that undercuts a coworker, the nudge that turns a joke into a wound. Each says, "We're in on something you're not." Jesus stands in contrast: "I spoke openly to the world… and in secret I have said nothing" (John 18:20). Following Him means letting our faces and hands say what our words say.
units.application: In meetings, at the dinner table or in a small group, refuse to join the eye-rolls and side-glances that mock someone present. Parents, teach children that a smirk or a whispered signal can wound as much as words. Leaders, if you see signals passed behind someone's back, name it kindly and invite open conversation instead. If you have been the target, take comfort that God sees what others hide.

rel.note: Deceit fills the hearts of those who devise evil, while counselors of peace have joy.
A perverse man sows strife and a whisperer separates close friends, the same harvest of division.
The whole course of life springs from the heart, which is why this man's perverse heart produces a life of trouble.
The perverse mouth and secret signals described there flow from the perverse heart named here.
God hates a heart that devises wicked plans, the same plotting heart described here.
Sowing discord closes both the troublemaker's portrait and the list of things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• The word translated "Perversity" is plural in Hebrew, suggesting many kinds of crookedness in one heart. Bridges, citing Poole: "not one but many; the heart so filled with them, that the vessel cannot hold more."
• The verb translated "devises" is the same verb translated "plow" in 20:4 ("The lazy man will not plow"). With "sows" in the next line, the picture is of a farmer at work, but the field he works is trouble.
• Ironside says this man scatters "evil words as one might scatter thistledown, to bring forth a harvest of sorrow that can never be fully destroyed." Thistledown is the light, fluffy seed of the thistle, which drifts everywhere.
• Compare 16:28: "A perverse man sows strife, And a whisperer separates the best of friends."
• Compare Matthew 15:19: "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts."
units.summary: The troublemaker's heart is a seedbed, and the crop he plants is division.
units.principle: Discord is planted on purpose by a corrupt heart, so the cure for a divisive life begins inside, not with better tactics.
units.insight: Absalom shows how discord is sown. He stood by the city gate and told every man with a complaint, "your case is good and right; but there is no deputy of the king to hear you" (2 Samuel 15:3). Day after day he planted distrust between Israel and David, until "Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6). The harvest was civil war. Sowing discord often looks like sympathy: "I'm only saying what everyone's thinking." This verse asks what we are planting in our homes, workplaces and churches. Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9). The troublemaker's heart cannot fix itself, but Christ "Himself is our peace," who "has broken down the middle wall of separation" (Ephesians 2:14). He makes divided people one, and He turns sowers of discord into sowers of peace.
units.application: Before you pass along a concern about someone, ask whether you are speaking to the person who can fix it or only spreading it. Employees unhappy with a decision, take it to your manager, not to the break room. Church members, refuse to be recruited into a faction. Leaders, deal quickly and fairly with legitimate complaints, so no one can use them to divide. In your family, be the one who plants trust.

rel.note: The calamity of the rebellious rises suddenly, and no one knows the ruin it brings.
The one who hardens himself against rebuke will suddenly be destroyed without remedy, the same sudden and final end.
The father's words are health to all who find them, the healing this man is left without.
Ruin also comes on the sluggard without warning, so both figures of the chapter meet consequences they did not see coming.
The next verse explains his end: the LORD hates the ways this man has practiced.

units.notes:
• "Without remedy" is literally "and there is no healing." The noun is the word rendered "health" in 4:22, where the father's words are "health to all their flesh." The schemer is left without the healing that wisdom gives.
• The same ending appears in 29:1: "He who is often rebuked, and hardens his neck, Will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy."
• Henry: "he that devised mischief shall fall into mischief." In older English "mischief" meant serious harm, not mere naughtiness.
• The verse does not name who breaks him, but the next verse names the LORD as the One who hates his ways (6:16).
• Compare Psalm 73:18–19: "Oh, how they are brought to desolation, as in a moment!"
units.summary: The schemer who spends years arranging trouble for others never sees his own coming.
units.principle: Delayed judgment is not cancelled judgment; those who keep sowing harm often meet a sudden end they never saw coming.
units.insight: Absalom's long campaign against his father seemed to succeed for a while. Then in a single afternoon his head caught in a terebinth tree, and Joab and his young men ended his life (2 Samuel 18:9–15). Psalm 73 records the struggle of watching the wicked prosper, until the writer "went into the sanctuary of God" and "understood their end" (Psalm 73:17). This verse comforts those wounded by a schemer: God has not overlooked what was done. It also warns us. The longer we get away with something, the more we assume we always will. Peter explains the delay: the Lord "is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). God's patience is an open door, and whoever turns now finds the healing the schemer refused.
units.application: If someone's scheming has hurt you, resist the urge to engineer their downfall yourself; leave judgment to God and protect yourself wisely. If you are a leader, do not mistake a troublemaker's long run of success for safety; address the pattern. If you recognize yourself in this portrait, do not count on time. Confess the damage to God, go to the people you have divided, and begin repairing it this week.

rel.note: What is an abomination to the LORD is set against those who are His delight, showing the other side of His hatred.
Agur uses the same rising-number form, three and then four, to build toward the last item.
The troublemaker's sudden ruin is explained here: he practiced what the LORD hates.
The numerical form points ahead to the seventh item, the one who sows discord among brethren.
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil, and Wisdom names pride and the perverse mouth among the things she hates.

units.notes:
• The same rising-number pattern appears in the prophets, "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four" (Amos 1:3), and repeatedly in Proverbs 30:15–31.
• In Proverbs "abomination" often stands opposite what is "His delight": "Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, But those who deal truthfully are His delight" (12:22; compare 11:1, 20).
• The Hebrew reads literally "an abomination of his soul," as the KJV margin notes, and Ironside's version has "an abomination of His soul." The phrase shows that God's hatred of these things is deep and personal, not casual.
• Henry: "God hates sin; he hates every sin; he can never be reconciled to it."
• Other abominations in Proverbs can be gathered beside this list, among them dishonest scales (11:1), the proud in heart (16:5), and worship offered by the wicked (15:8; 28:9).
units.summary: God is not neutral about sin; He hates what destroys the people He loves.
units.principle: God's hatred of sin flows from His holiness and His love; what He hates is what ruins people and denies His character.
units.insight: Many people picture God as mildly disappointed with sin, much as we are. Scripture corrects us: "You are of purer eyes than to behold evil" (Habakkuk 1:13). When Isaiah saw the LORD's holiness, he cried, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" (Isaiah 6:5). A right view of God begins there. Yet God's hatred is not like our spite. It is the fierce opposition of a good Father to what destroys His children, and nearly every item on this list wounds a neighbor. Of the Son, Scripture says, "You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness" (Hebrews 1:9). Jesus hated sin so completely that He bore it on the cross to break its power over us. So this list is not a door slammed shut but a mirror held up. Ask which of these seven you have excused, and bring it to the One who forgives.
units.application: Read 6:16–19 slowly this week and pray through each line, asking God to show you where any of these has taken root. Parents, teach children this list as a picture of what love refuses to do, not only as a set of rules. Pastors and small-group leaders, use it to name sins plainly, then point people to Christ's forgiveness. When you are tempted to shrug at a "small" lie or a proud glance, remember how God sees it.

rel.note: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, while truthful dealing is His delight.
Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD, the inward root of the proud look.
The violent gang plans to lie in wait to shed blood and ambush the innocent, the hands this verse condemns.
The troublemaker's perverse mouth and signaling eyes are judged here as a lying tongue and a proud look.
Wisdom hates pride, arrogance and the perverse mouth, the same sins that open God's list.

units.notes:
• "A proud look" is literally "eyes raised high." The ESV and NASB have "haughty eyes," and the KJV margin gives the same literal sense. Compare 21:4: "A haughty look, a proud heart, And the plowing of the wicked are sin."
• Henry: "pride is the first, because it is at the bottom of much sin and gives rise to it."
• Ironside: "For he is of one ilk who would with his tongue destroy the good name of another with him who would with wicked hands take his brother's life." In plain words, the slanderer and the murderer belong to the same family.
• Jesus joins the second and third items when He calls the devil "a murderer from the beginning" and "a liar and the father of it" (John 8:44).
• The opposite posture appears in Psalm 131:1: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, Nor my eyes lofty." Compare 12:22; 16:5, 18.
units.summary: The list God hates starts with the eyes, because pride looks down before it lies or strikes.
units.principle: Pride is the root that feeds deceit and violence, and God hates all three because they despise both Him and the people made in His image.
units.insight: Scripture shows each of these in action. Nebuchadnezzar looked over Babylon and boasted of what he had built "by my mighty power," and he was humbled that very hour (Daniel 4:30–33). Ananias and Sapphira lied to look generous and fell dead (Acts 5:1–10). Innocent blood was shed most terribly at the cross, where even Judas confessed, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood" (Matthew 27:4). Yet that same blood "cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). Jesus is the opposite of all three: He "humbled Himself" (Philippians 2:8), "nor was deceit found in His mouth" (1 Peter 2:22), and He laid down His life instead of taking one. Before you hold this list up to others, start with your own eyes. Where do you look down on someone? Pride is easy to see in everyone but ourselves.
units.application: Notice this week when you mentally rank people beneath you: the server, the struggling coworker, the church member with less education. Confess it to God and serve that person. Tell the truth even when a small lie would save face. Parents, model apologizing when you exaggerate. Leaders, do not let anger at someone grow into wishing him harm (Matthew 5:21–22). If you have harmed someone, own it fully and seek to make it right.

rel.note: The violent gang's feet run to evil and make haste to shed blood.
The one who plots to do evil earns the name of schemer.
The call to keep the heart with all diligence is the remedy for a heart that devises wicked plans.
The son is told to ponder the path of his feet and remove his foot from evil, the opposite of feet that run to it.
The troublemaker's feet already serve his schemes with secret signals; here God names feet swift in running to evil.
The troublemaker devises evil continually, the same plotting heart God names here.

units.notes:
• "Wicked plans" (KJV "wicked imaginations") are schemes worked out ahead of time. God saw the same thing before the flood: "every intent of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5).
• Isaiah uses the same picture: "Their feet run to evil, And they make haste to shed innocent blood" (Isaiah 59:7). Paul echoes it in Romans 3:15: "Their feet are swift to shed blood."
• Ironside: "'A heart that deviseth wicked imaginations' is the spring of all the rest." In plain words, the planning heart is the source of every other sin on the list.
• Henry says the eagerness of sinners "may shame us who go about that which is good so awkwardly and so coldly." People often chase wrong with more energy than believers give to doing right.
• Compare 24:8: "He who plots to do evil Will be called a schemer."
