units.summary: Sin is planned in the heart before the feet ever start running.
units.principle: Evil is usually planned before it is done, so guarding the heart is the first defense against running toward sin.
units.insight: When Joseph's brothers "saw him afar off, even before he came near them, they conspired against him to kill him" (Genesis 37:18). The plot formed in resentful hearts before their hands ever acted. Yet Joseph later told them, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). God's hatred of wicked plans stands beside His power to overrule them. The verse also searches us. How quickly do our feet move toward what we want, and how slowly toward what God asks? The gospel gives us new feet. Isaiah sang, "How beautiful upon the mountains Are the feet of him who brings good news" (Isaiah 52:7), and Paul applied the words to those who preach the gospel of peace (Romans 10:15). Christ redirects the whole person, heart and feet together.
units.application: When you catch yourself rehearsing a plan to get even, embarrass someone or get your way by deception, stop at the planning stage and bring it to God. Young people, notice where your feet go quickly, whether to certain websites, friends or places, and set up guardrails before you need them. Parents, talk with teenagers about how temptations are planned before they are acted on. This week, put the energy you give your own goals into serving someone else.

rel.note: A faithful witness does not lie, while a false witness pours out lies.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and the one who speaks lies will not escape.
False witness against a neighbor is pictured as a club, a sword and a sharp arrow.
The troublemaker's steady work is the same sowing of discord that closes this list.
The rising count of six and then seven places this item in the position of emphasis.

units.notes:
• Five of the seven items echo the portrait of 6:12–15: the eyes (6:13, 17), the mouth and tongue (6:12, 17), the feet (6:13, 18), the heart that devises evil (6:14, 18) and the sowing of discord, which ends both passages (6:14, 19). The list gives God's verdict on the kind of man described just before it.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Seventh, the one who unleashes conflicts (see Proverbs 6:14) again climactically brings the catalogue to its conclusion." That is, the list reaches its high point with the troublemaker.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "None love a mischief-maker, and yet we are apt to think of the sin with something less than the Divine intolerance for it."
• Lying appears twice in the list, as "A lying tongue" (6:17) and "A false witness who speaks lies" (6:19). Proverbs warns that "A false witness will not go unpunished" (19:5).
• Compare 25:18: "A man who bears false witness against his neighbor Is like a club, a sword, and a sharp arrow."
units.summary: God saves His strongest emphasis for the person who turns brothers against each other.
units.principle: God hates lies that pervert justice and words that divide His people, because truth and unity are precious to Him.
units.insight: Jezebel had two scoundrels accuse Naboth falsely, and an innocent man was stoned so a king could have a vineyard (1 Kings 21:10–13). At Jesus' trial "many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree" (Mark 14:56). The Truth Himself was condemned by lies. The night before He died, Jesus prayed for His people "that they all may be one" (John 17:21). Sowing discord among believers works against that prayer. Many of us would never lie in court, yet we repeat a story we have not checked, or stir up a faction at church and call it concern. Paul's charge is to keep "the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3). Christ, falsely accused, answered with silence and love, and He makes peacemakers of those He forgives.
units.application: Before you repeat anything negative about someone, ask whether it is true, whether you know it firsthand, and whether repeating it will heal or divide. If you are asked to give testimony at work, in a church matter or in court, say only what you know. Church members and staff, when you sense a split forming, go to the people involved and seek peace instead of choosing sides. Parents, never recruit one child against another.

rel.note: The father's first appeal sets his instruction beside the mother's law in almost the same words.
The son is told to listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old, keeping honor for both parents through life.
The eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother's guidance meets a grim end, the opposite of keeping their teaching.
The wise woman has the law of kindness on her tongue, a picture of the mother's teaching this verse honors.
The command and law named here are what the son must bind continually on his heart.

units.notes:
• The verse closely echoes 1:8. There the son is to "hear the instruction of your father"; here he is to "keep your father's command." The second line is the same in both verses.
• The word translated "law" is torah, which means instruction or teaching. It is the word used for God's law, and here it names a mother's teaching. The wise woman of 31:26 has "the law of kindness" on her tongue.
• Henry warns grown children never to "think it a mighty achievement (as some do) to get clear of the restraints of a good education." In plain words, escaping a godly upbringing is nothing to boast about.
• The teaching in view is the godly instruction of a faithful home, which passes on God's ways. The verse does not ask a child to follow a parent into sin.
• Compare Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:1–3.
units.summary: What a godly home teaches is not a childhood stage to outgrow but a guide for life.
units.principle: Godly instruction received at home is meant to be kept for life, and drifting from it is usually slow before it is final.
units.insight: Timothy's faith "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice," and "from childhood you have known the Holy Scriptures" (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). A mother's patient teaching shaped a pastor. Many of us carry words a parent or grandparent planted long ago, and some of us have drifted from them without ever deciding to. The verse calls us back. It also speaks to those whose parents never taught them God's ways. God is "A father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5), and He gives His children a family of faith, older believers who can be fathers and mothers in the Lord (1 Timothy 5:1–2). In the light of the New Testament, the father's "my son" also echoes the voice of our heavenly Father, who instructs and corrects those He loves (Hebrews 12:5–6).
units.application: Young adults, write down three things your parents taught you that were true and godly, and thank them if you can. If you have drifted from that teaching, ask where the drift began. Parents, teach together; let children hear both of you speak of God's ways. Single parents, do not lose heart, because your faithful teaching matters. Older believers, take an interest in a young person who lacks godly parents and pass on what you have learned.

rel.note: Mercy and truth are bound around the neck and written on the tablet of the heart, the same twin picture.
The son is to keep his father's words in the midst of his heart.
The parents' command and law named there are what the son must now bind on his heart.
Teaching bound to the heart becomes the guide, guard and counselor the next verse describes.
The father's commands are bound on the fingers and written on the heart before the next warning about the seductress.

units.notes:
• The same picture runs through the father's speeches: bind mercy and truth around the neck (3:3), keep his words "in the midst of your heart" (4:21), and "Bind them on your fingers" (7:3).
• Moses told Israel, "these words which I command you today shall be in your heart," and "You shall bind them as a sign on your hand" (Deuteronomy 6:6, 8). The father brings that pattern into the home.
• Henry: "Phylacteries upon the hand were of no value at all, any further than they occasioned pious thoughts and affections in the heart." Phylacteries were small boxes holding Scripture passages, later worn by Jewish men on the arm and forehead (compare Matthew 23:5). In plain words, the boxes were worth something only if they turned the heart toward God.
• Compare Colossians 3:16: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly."
units.summary: Truth tied to the heart is ready the moment temptation knocks.
units.principle: Truth guards us only when it is held close and constant, written on the heart and worn openly in daily life.
units.insight: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered each time, "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). The word He had carried since childhood was ready the moment it was needed. That is what this verse pictures: truth held so close that temptation meets it before it meets us. Much of our failure comes not from never having heard the truth but from keeping it at a distance, filed away for Sunday. The psalmist hid God's word in his heart "That I might not sin against You" (Psalm 119:11). The New Covenant promise goes further: God Himself writes His law on His people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10). What we cannot bind there by effort alone, His Spirit engraves. Ask yourself which truth you would reach for first if temptation came tonight.
units.application: Choose one verse of Scripture, or one piece of godly counsel your parents gave you, and memorize it this week. Write it where you will see it every morning. Parents, put Scripture where children will meet it: on the refrigerator, in the car, at bedtime. Teenagers and college students, carry memorized verses into the places where you know temptation waits. Small groups, recite a verse together each week until it sticks.

rel.note: When wisdom enters the heart, discretion preserves and understanding keeps the son from the way of evil.
Kept wisdom brings safe walking by day and sweet sleep by night.
Unhindered steps belong to the one who takes firm hold of instruction and does not let go.
Teaching bound on the heart is what leads, keeps and speaks in this verse.
The son caught in a pledge must give up sleep, while the son who keeps this teaching sleeps under its guard.

units.notes:
• The three lines follow Moses' pattern for teaching God's words "when you walk by the way, when you lie down, and when you rise up" (Deuteronomy 6:7).
• "They will speak with you" is "it shall talk with thee" in the KJV, and Ironside's version has "it shall be thy meditation." The teaching becomes an inner conversation, not just a memory.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, applies "they will speak with you" to Scripture itself: "This Bible is a wonderful talking book; there is a great mass of blessed talk in this precious volume."
• Compare 3:22–24, where wisdom brings safety on the road and sweet sleep at night, and 4:12: "When you walk, your steps will not be hindered."
• Compare Psalm 63:6: "When I remember You on my bed, I meditate on You in the night watches."
units.summary: Teaching kept in the heart walks with you by day, guards you by night, and greets you at dawn.
units.principle: Instruction treasured in the heart becomes a constant companion that guides, guards and counsels through every part of life.
units.insight: Joshua was told to meditate on God's law "day and night" (Joshua 1:8), and David wrote, "I will both lie down in peace, and sleep; For You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). Many people go through the day with other voices in their heads: worry, criticism, advertising, the last argument. This verse asks whose voice speaks to you first when you wake and last before you sleep. The father's teaching can lead, keep and speak because it carries God's own ways. In the light of the New Testament, Jesus promised the Holy Spirit, who would "bring to your remembrance all things that I said to you" (John 14:26). The word we store, the Spirit brings back at the very moment we need it.
units.application: This week, begin and end each day with a few minutes in Scripture before you check your phone. Parents, make bedtime and breakfast natural times to speak of God, as Moses described. Commuters, use the drive to listen to Scripture read aloud. If you wake at night with anxiety, recite a verse you know by heart. Grandparents, write to a grandchild about one verse that has walked with you through life.

rel.note: The one who keeps instruction is in the way of life, while the one who refuses correction goes astray.
The ear that hears life-giving rebukes abides among the wise and gains understanding.
The path of the just shines brighter while the way of the wicked is like darkness, the contrast that the lamp addresses.
The ruined man confesses that he hated instruction and despised correction, and so came to the verge of total ruin.
The sentence continues there, naming what this lamp protects the son from.

units.notes:
• A psalm uses the same pairing for God's word: "Your word is a lamp to my feet And a light to my path" (Psalm 119:105). The father's teaching shares that light because it passes on God's ways, though his first subject is the instruction of the home.
• "Reproofs of instruction" are corrections that teach. Henry describes them as reproofs that "not only show us our faults, but instruct us how to do better."
• Bridges: "A lamp, so full of light, in this dark world is an inestimable gift." "Inestimable" means too valuable to measure.
• Proverbs repeatedly ties correction to life: "He who keeps instruction is in the way of life, But he who refuses correction goes astray" (10:17); compare 15:31–32.
• Compare 2 Timothy 3:16: Scripture is "profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness."
units.summary: Wise instruction is a lamp for the next step, and even its corrections light the way to life.
units.principle: God's instruction lights the next step of the path, and correction received humbly is part of the road to life, not an obstacle on it.
units.insight: David was on his way to kill Nabal and his household when Abigail met him with a humble rebuke. David answered, "Blessed is the LORD God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! And blessed is your advice" (1 Samuel 25:32–33). One reproof kept him from shedding blood. Most of us do not resist God's word in general; we resist the part that corrects us. Yet "no chastening seems to be joyful for the present, but painful; nevertheless, afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness" (Hebrews 12:11). Think of the last time someone corrected you. Did you thank God or defend yourself? Jesus said, "I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life" (John 8:12). His correction is never rejection; it is light for the way home.
units.application: This week, when someone corrects you, whether a spouse, a boss, a friend or a pastor, say "Thank you; let me think about that" before you defend yourself. Parents, explain the reasons behind your correction so it teaches as well as stops. Leaders, build a culture where truthful feedback is welcome. When you face a decision in the dark, do not wait for the whole road to light up; take the next step Scripture makes clear.

rel.note: A flatterer spreads a net for his neighbor's feet, showing what flattery is for.
Wisdom delivers the son from the immoral woman, the seductress who flatters with her words.
Her lips drip honey and her mouth is smoother than oil, the same smooth speech.
The sentence begins there: the commandment is a lamp, and this verse names what that lamp protects him from.
The father's commands are kept so they may guard the son from the seductress who flatters with her words.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew wording behind "the evil woman" is unusual. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads "married woman," and some modern versions, the NRSV among them, follow it here. The NKJV follows the standard Hebrew reading.
• The KJV calls her "a strange woman," older English for a woman who is an outsider, one who does not belong to the man she pursues. The NKJV's "seductress" names what she does without deciding where she comes from.
• The KJV has "the flattery of the tongue"; the Hebrew pictures smoothness, as in 5:3: "her mouth is smoother than oil."
• Each warning about the adulteress in chapters 5–7 is introduced by a call to hold on to the father's words (5:1–2; 6:20–23; 7:1–5). The teaching comes first, then the warning.
• Compare 2:16; 7:5, 21.
units.summary: Flattery works best in the dark, which is why wise teaching is given as a lamp.
units.principle: God's word, held close, protects us from voices that flatter us toward sin.
units.insight: Samson fell not to the Philistines' strength but to Delilah's persistent words: "she pestered him daily with her words and pressed him" until he told her everything (Judges 16:16–17). Flattery and pressure are powerful because they speak to what we already want to hear. That is why the father does not only warn; he gives his son something better to listen to. "How can a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed according to Your word" (Psalm 119:9). The question for each of us is which voice is louder in our lives: the one that flatters our desires or the one that tells us the truth. Jesus, the Good Shepherd, says, "My sheep hear My voice" (John 10:27), and His sheep "do not know the voice of strangers" (John 10:5). Those who know His voice learn to recognize a stranger's.
units.application: Young men and women, notice who tells you only what you want to hear, whether in person, in messages or online, and treat that flattery as a warning sign. Married people, be cautious of a coworker or friend whose compliments make you feel more understood than your spouse does; that is the moment to step back and tell someone you trust. Parents, talk with teenagers about flattery as a tool of manipulation, and keep Scripture before them.

rel.note: The eyes of man are never satisfied, which is why a welcomed glance never stays a glance.
The call to keep the heart with all diligence explains why the battle against lust begins inside.
The son is told to let his eyes look straight ahead, the general rule this verse applies to sexual temptation.
The son is told to rejoice in the wife of his youth and be satisfied with her love, the right home for desire.
The father asks why his son should be enraptured by an immoral woman, the same desire this verse forbids.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "lust after" is chamad, the same verb used in the commandment "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife" (Exodus 20:17). The father's warning speaks in the language of the Tenth Commandment.
• "Allure" translates the common verb for taking; the KJV has "neither let her take thee with her eyelids." The glance is pictured as a hunter's grip.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "'Eyes' are singled out here because the painted eyes and the luring glances are symptoms of seduction (see 2 Kings 9:30)." In that verse Jezebel "put paint on her eyes."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "It is a small praise to have a good face and a naughty nature – a beautiful countenance and a base life." In older English "naughty" meant wicked.
• Compare James 1:14–15, where desire conceives and gives birth to sin.
units.summary: Adultery begins long before the act, in a desire welcomed and a glance returned.
units.principle: Sexual sin is fought first in the heart and the eyes; whatever desire we welcome there will soon look for a way to act.
units.insight: David saw from his roof "a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to behold" (2 Samuel 11:2). The look became a question, the question became a summons, and a king fell. Job, by contrast, said, "I have made a covenant with my eyes; Why then should I look upon a young woman?" (Job 31:1). Jesus took this verse's teaching to its root: "whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). That standard leaves none of us innocent, and it is meant to. It drives us to the One who gives new hearts. Christ does not only forbid the lustful look; He forgives it and, by His Spirit, gives a heart that delights in what is pure. The battle is fought daily, but it is fought with grace.
units.application: Make Job's covenant concrete this week. Men and women alike, decide in advance what you will not look at: certain websites, shows or social media accounts. Install accountability tools if you need them. When an attractive person catches your eye, look away before the second look. Married people, turn your desire toward your own spouse (5:18–19). Parents, teach children early that the eyes are a door that must be guarded.

rel.note: The harlot is a deep pit and the seductress lies in wait as for a victim, the same hunting picture.
A companion of harlots wastes his wealth, the first cost named here.
The man who goes to the immoral woman gives away his honor, his years and his wealth to others.
The precious life she hunts is the soul the adulterer destroys by his own choice.
The young man follows her like an ox to the slaughter and does not know it will cost his life.

units.notes:
• The first two lines are read differently in the versions. The NKJV, the NASB and the 1984 NIV take them as a man brought down to a loaf or crust of bread. The ESV and the 2011 NIV read them as a statement about price (ESV: "the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread"). Either way, a lesser cost is set beside the deadly cost of adultery.
• Neither reading approves of prostitution, which Proverbs condemns elsewhere (23:27; 29:3). The comparison only shows how much worse the adulteress's cost is.
• "Adulteress" is literally "a man's wife," a woman married to another man, as the KJV margin notes.
• "Prey upon" is a hunting verb; the KJV has "will hunt for the precious life." Bridges: "Like the insatiable huntsman, who never loses sight of his prey, till he has pursued it to death." In plain words, she does not stop until the ruin is complete.
• Compare 7:22–23, where the young man goes "as an ox goes to the slaughter" and "did not know it would cost his life."
units.summary: The harlot costs a man his bread; another man's wife can cost him his life.
units.principle: Sexual sin always costs more than it promises, and adultery puts a person's whole life at stake.
units.insight: The prodigal son wasted his inheritance until he "would gladly have filled his stomach with the pods that the swine ate" (Luke 15:16). His older brother later told their father where it went: "devoured your livelihood with harlots" (Luke 15:30). That is the first line of this verse lived out: a man reduced to a crust. Samson's story shows the hunting picture of the second line. Hunted by a woman paid to find his weakness, he lost his strength, his eyes and his freedom, and ended as "a grinder in the prison" (Judges 16:21). Where in your life is something promising pleasure while it quietly drains your money, energy or soul? The prodigal's story does not end in the pigpen. His father saw him a long way off and ran to him (Luke 15:20). Whatever sexual sin has cost you, the Father still runs toward the one who comes home.
units.application: Count the cost before temptation arrives. If you are drawn to pornography or paid sexual content, look at what it is already taking from you: money, time, sleep, intimacy, self-respect. Talk to a pastor or counselor this week. Married people, refuse emotional or physical closeness with someone else's spouse, however innocent it seems at first. Parents, speak plainly with your children about the real costs of sexual sin and the real joys of faithfulness.

rel.note: The father asks why his son would be embraced in the arms of a seductress, the same embrace pictured here as fire.
Keeping far from her door is the practical response to a danger pictured as fire.
A second question repeats the point with hot coals underfoot.
Two verses later the father applies the picture of fire to the man who goes in to his neighbor's wife.
The fire taken into the bosom is answered by the burning fury of the wronged husband.
The son is told not to stray into her paths, because her house is the way to death.

units.notes:
• "Bosom" here is the same Hebrew word rendered "arms" in 5:20: "be embraced in the arms of a seductress." The embrace she offers is the fire he must not hold.
• Bridges: "the temptation acts upon a congenial nature like fuel, not water, on the fire." In plain words, our own desires feed temptation instead of putting it out.
• Bridges also gives the voice of self-confidence that this question answers: "I can look to myself; I need not go too far, and I shall get no harm."
• Compare 5:8: "Remove your way far from her, And do not go near the door of her house."
• Compare Romans 13:14: "make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts."
units.summary: No one carries fire against his chest and walks away unburned.
units.principle: Some sins cannot be handled safely at close range; the only wise distance from adultery is far away.
units.insight: Joseph did not stay to argue with Potiphar's wife or to test his own strength. "He left his garment in her hand, and fled and ran outside" (Genesis 39:12). He lost a coat and kept his integrity. Paul gives the same counsel: "Flee sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18) and "Flee also youthful lusts" (2 Timothy 2:22). Fleeing is not weakness; it is wisdom that knows what fire does. The hardest part is admitting that we are not the exception. "Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). Yet the same passage promises that with every temptation God "will also make the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The way of escape is real, and it usually looks like running.
units.application: Identify the fire you are tempted to hold close: a flirtatious friendship, late-night messaging, a private browser, a closeness at work that has no witnesses. Put distance there this week. Leaders and pastors, set boundaries for meetings, travel and counseling before you need them. Married couples, share passwords and schedules freely with each other. Young singles, decide your physical boundaries in daylight, not in the moment.

rel.note: The son is told not to enter or travel the path of the wicked but to turn away and pass on.
The first question pictures fire held close; this one pictures fire walked on.
The next verse applies the two pictures of fire to the man who goes in to his neighbor's wife.
The young man's route near her corner and onto the path to her house shows the steps this verse warns against.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?" Ironside's version has "scorched." The NKJV "seared" means burned on the surface.
• Henry: "The way of this sin is down-hill, and those that venture upon the temptations to it hardly escape the sin itself." Here "hardly" means scarcely.
• Proverbs 7 shows these steps in slow motion: the young man passes "near her corner," takes "the path to her house," and goes "In the twilight, in the evening" (7:8–9).
• Compare 4:14–15: "Do not enter the path of the wicked… Avoid it, do not travel on it."
units.summary: Every step toward adultery is a step on hot coals, however careful you think you are.
units.principle: Sin is a path as well as an act, and each step taken toward it makes the burns deeper.
units.insight: Peter did not plan to deny Jesus. He "followed at a distance" (Luke 22:54), then stood among the servants warming himself at "a fire of coals" (John 18:18), and before the night ended he had denied his Lord three times. His fall came one step at a time. Adultery usually comes the same way: a lingering conversation, a private message, a meeting no one knows about, each step seeming survivable until the feet are blistered. Where are your steps taking you? Are you moving closer to a person, a place or a habit you know is dangerous? The path can be left at any step. After His resurrection Jesus met Peter beside another "fire of coals" and restored him with three questions of love (John 21:9, 15–17). Christ still meets people who have been burned.
units.application: Trace your own path backward from a recent temptation and name the first step that led there. Remove that step this week. Managers and pastors, avoid closed-door meetings and car rides alone with someone of the opposite sex where there is no accountability. Dating couples, plan time together in places that help you keep your boundaries. If you are already on the coals, tell a trusted believer today and get off the path.

rel.note: The immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God, the other side of the betrayal.
The son must not devise evil against a neighbor who lives near him in trust, the very trust adultery betrays.
A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, so no secrecy makes the adulterer innocent.
The two pictures of fire are what this verse now applies to adultery.
The same warning goes on to show that the adulterer destroys his own soul.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb behind "shall not be innocent" can mean either to be free of guilt or to be free from punishment. The NKJV and KJV keep the first sense; the ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV the second ("go unpunished"). On either reading the adulterer does not escape.
• "Neighbor" is the same ordinary word translated "friend" in 6:1. The adulterer wrongs someone near him, someone he knows.
• Bridges answers the man who later blames the strength of the temptation: "He cannot afterwards plead the strength of the temptation. Why did he not avoid it?"
• The commandments name both the act and the desire: "You shall not commit adultery" and "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife" (Exodus 20:14, 17).
• Compare Hebrews 13:4: "Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled; but fornicators and adulterers God will judge."
units.summary: Adultery is never a private matter; it breaks into a neighbor's home.
units.principle: Adultery always wrongs a neighbor as well as God, and no one who commits it escapes its guilt and consequences.
units.insight: Uriah was one of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39), so loyal that he refused to sleep in his own house while the army camped in the field (2 Samuel 11:11). David took that loyal neighbor's wife and then arranged his death. Paul calls Christians to holiness "that no one should take advantage of and defraud his brother in this matter" (1 Thessalonians 4:6). Adultery is a theft from a brother as well as a sin of the body. Before temptation goes further, think of the spouse at home, the children, the friend whose trust would be broken. Yet "shall not be innocent" is not the last word for a guilty person who turns to God. Christ, the truly innocent One, was made sin for us so that we might be made righteous in Him (2 Corinthians 5:21). Forgiveness is real, though it does not erase every consequence.
units.application: If you are drawn toward someone who is married, picture that person's spouse and children, and step back now. Husbands and wives, build friendships with other couples that protect each other's marriages. Pastors and counselors, never meet someone of the opposite sex in a way that invites private closeness. If you have crossed the line, stop, confess to God, and seek pastoral help about how to tell the truth to those you have wronged.

rel.note: A hungry mouth drives a person on, the same pressure of need behind this thief.
Agur knows that poverty can tempt a person to steal, so he asks for neither poverty nor riches.
The next verse completes the thought: even the hungry thief must repay in full.
The adulterer has no hunger to plead; he lacks understanding and destroys his own soul.

units.notes:
• "To satisfy himself" is literally "to fill his soul." Here "soul" means his appetite and, more broadly, his life; the KJV keeps "to satisfy his soul." The same Hebrew word ends 6:32, where the adulterer "destroys his own soul."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "The thief steals out of want; the adulterer of wantonness." "Want" means need; "wantonness" means unrestrained desire.
• Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches, "Lest I be poor and steal, And profane the name of my God" (30:9). Need can tempt a person toward theft, but it does not make theft right.
• Compare Ephesians 4:28: "Let him who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor."
units.summary: People understand a starving thief, but no one can plead hunger for taking another man's wife.
units.principle: Need can explain a wrong without excusing it, and a sin committed without any need at all has no defense.
units.insight: When Nathan confronted David, he told of a rich man who "had exceedingly many flocks and herds" yet took a poor man's only lamb. David burned with anger: "the man who has done this shall surely die!" (2 Samuel 12:2, 5). David saw at once how wicked a theft without need was. Then Nathan turned the story on him: "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). It is easy to see the inexcusable in others. This verse also teaches compassion. People do not despise a starving thief, and Scripture calls God's people to make sure no one has to steal to eat (Ephesians 4:28; James 2:15–16). Our own sins rarely come from desperate need. More often they come from wanting more than God has given. The gospel meets both the hungry and the greedy at the same table of grace.
units.application: When you hear of someone who stole out of desperation, respond with compassion and practical help, not only judgment. Churches, make it easy for families in crisis to ask for help with food and rent. In your own life, ask what excuses you give for the sins you repeat, and whether any of them are real needs. Employers, pay fairly and on time. Parents, teach children that being hungry or wronged never makes stealing right.

rel.note: A debtor who cannot pay may lose even his bed, the same loss of all the substance of one's house.
The hungry thief whom people pity is the one who must still repay in full.
The thief's debt can be paid off, but the adulterer's reproach will not be wiped away.
The thief can make restitution, while the wronged husband refuses every payment.

units.notes:
• In Exodus 22 the Law of Moses required double restitution in several cases (Exodus 22:4, 7, 9) and fourfold or fivefold for a sheep or an ox that had been slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1). None of these names a sevenfold payment, so "sevenfold" here is best taken as full repayment rather than a fixed legal penalty.
• Seven often signals completeness in Scripture. Compare Psalm 79:12, where the psalmist asks God to repay the enemies "sevenfold," that is, in full measure.
• Ironside sets the thief beside the adulterer: "at least it is possible to make amends, though it take all one has."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "But what restitution can the adulterer make, should he make him amends with as much more?" In plain words, no amount of payment can undo adultery.
• Compare 6:35, where the wronged husband refuses every payment.
units.summary: Even a theft driven by hunger can cost everything a man owns; adultery costs far more.
units.principle: Wrongs against property can be repaid, even at great cost, but some wrongs against people cannot be bought back.
units.insight: Zacchaeus met Jesus and said, "if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Grace made him eager to repay. Restitution is a mark of true repentance; where we can make things right, we should. Yet this verse also shows something money cannot fix. A thief can return what he took. A betrayer cannot hand back trust, innocence or lost years. That is a sobering word to anyone weighing a sin he thinks he can "make up for" later. It is also why the gospel is such good news. The debt we could never repay, Christ paid: "you were not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold… but with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18–19). Those He forgives become people who make right what they can.
units.application: If you have taken something, whether money, credit, time or property, make it right this week, adding something extra if you can. Employees who padded hours or took supplies, confess and repay. Parents, when a child steals, require restitution as well as an apology. Before you do something you think you can make up for later, remember that some things cannot be returned. Church leaders, help repentant people work out fair plans for restitution.

rel.note: The adulteress hunts for his precious life, yet the man who yields is the one who destroys his own soul.
Whoever touches his neighbor's wife shall not be innocent, and this verse shows that the guilty man destroys himself.
The thief steals to fill his soul because he is starving, while the adulterer destroys his soul with no such need.
The young man devoid of understanding is the same kind of man, heading toward the seductress's house.
Whoever sins against Wisdom wrongs his own soul, the same self-inflicted harm.
Wisdom invites the very person who lacks understanding to turn in and learn, so the lack need not be final.

units.notes:
• "Lacks understanding" is literally "lacks heart," as the KJV margin notes. In Proverbs the heart is the seat of thought and judgment, so a man who "lacks heart" lacks sense. The same expression appears in 7:7 and 9:4.
• "Soul" is the same Hebrew word used in 6:30, where the thief steals "to satisfy himself," literally "to fill his soul." The thief fills his soul; the adulterer destroys his.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The vixen hunts for his life, but he is responsible for his self-destruction." A "vixen" here is a cunning, predatory woman; the blame for the man's ruin still rests on him.
• Paul makes a similar point: "he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body" (1 Corinthians 6:18).
• Compare 5:22–23 and 8:36: "he who sins against me wrongs his own soul."
units.summary: The adulterer cannot blame hunger, the woman or anyone else; he wrecks himself.
units.principle: Adultery is self-destruction dressed up as satisfaction, and the one who chooses it bears the responsibility for his own ruin.
units.insight: David was a man of great wisdom and courage, yet in the matter of Bathsheba he acted like a man without sense. Afterward he described what hidden sin did to him: "When I kept silent, my bones grew old Through my groaning all the day long" (Psalm 32:3). Sin had begun destroying him from the inside. The adulterer often tells himself he is finally getting what he needs. This verse says he is losing himself. That truth sobers anyone who imagines he is the exception. It also opens a door. David's prayer, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10), was answered. When a woman caught in adultery was brought to Jesus, He said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:11). The One who forgives also restores what sin destroys.
units.application: If you are entertaining an affair, emotional or physical, stop and count what you are already losing: sleep, peace, prayer, truthfulness with your spouse. Talk to a pastor or Christian counselor this week. Men's and women's groups, make it normal to confess temptation before it becomes sin. If you have fallen, do not hide as David did for a season; confess to God, and get help to bring the truth into the light.

rel.note: A good name is worth more than great riches, which is why the reproach of adultery is so costly.
The one who confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, so lasting reproach among people is not the limit of God's forgiveness.
The ruined man's shame is public, in the midst of the assembly and congregation.
The man who goes to the immoral woman gives his honor to others and mourns at last.
The thief's debt can be repaid, but the adulterer's reproach is not wiped away.

units.notes:
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "His reproach shall not be wiped away; although it be forgiven by God, yet the reproach and scandal of it remains."
• Bridges: "He gets a wound—not like the soldier or the martyr for Christ—full of honour; but rankling on his conscience." "Rankling" means festering, still painful long after the injury.
• Reuben's sin with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22) followed him for decades. At Jacob's deathbed it cost him the firstborn's place: "Unstable as water, you shall not excel, Because you went up to your father's bed" (Genesis 49:4).
• Compare 5:9–14, where the man who ignored instruction ends in shame "In the midst of the assembly and congregation."
units.summary: God can wipe away the guilt of adultery, but people may remember the reproach for years.
units.principle: God's forgiveness is complete for those who confess, but sin's consequences among people can last long after the guilt is gone.
units.insight: Nathan told David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die." In the same breath he said the child would die, and trouble followed David's house for years (2 Samuel 12:13–14). David was fully forgiven and still lived with consequences. That is a hard truth and a merciful one. It is hard, because no one should imagine adultery can be undone with an apology. It is merciful, because the verse never says God's mercy runs out. "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). People may remember a past sin, but God casts confessed sins "Into the depths of the sea" (Micah 7:19). If a repentant believer carries such a reproach, do not keep reopening the wound.
units.application: If you are considering an affair, weigh the reproach: your children's trust, your ministry, your name in your town. If you have confessed and repented, receive God's forgiveness fully and be patient while trust is rebuilt with your spouse, family and church. Pastors and elders, guide restored believers wisely: forgiveness is immediate, but restoring trust and leadership takes time. Church members, treat the repentant with grace, not gossip.

rel.note: The wronged are told not to repay evil but to wait for the LORD, guidance for a betrayed spouse.
Wrath and anger are fierce, but no one can stand before jealousy.
The fire the adulterer took into his bosom is now met by the fire of the husband's fury.
The husband's unsparing anger explains why he will accept no payment.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew root behind "jealousy" is also used for God's jealousy over His people, a protective zeal for a covenant relationship: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God" (Exodus 34:14).
• "Fury" translates a word for hot anger; the KJV has "the rage of a man." Compare 27:4: "Wrath is cruel and anger a torrent, But who is able to stand before jealousy?"
• Song of Solomon 8:6 joins love and jealousy: "For love is as strong as death, Jealousy as cruel as the grave."
• Henry: "If thou art not afraid of the wrath of God, yet be afraid of the rage of a man."
• The proverb describes what a wronged husband does, not what he should do. Proverbs elsewhere tells the wronged to wait for the LORD instead of repaying evil (20:22).
units.summary: A wronged husband's fury is a fire the adulterer lit himself.
units.principle: Adultery provokes the deepest anger a person can feel, because it violates the most intimate covenant between two people.
units.insight: When Potiphar heard his wife's false accusation against Joseph, "his anger was aroused," and he threw Joseph into prison (Genesis 39:19–20). If a lie about adultery could provoke such fury, the truth of it provokes far more. This verse asks the tempted to look past the moment to the face of the husband or wife who will be wounded. It also speaks to those who have been betrayed. The anger you feel is not strange; jealousy for a covenant reflects God's own heart, and Paul could speak of "godly jealousy" (2 Corinthians 11:2). Yet God's word to the wounded is, "Beloved, do not avenge yourselves" (Romans 12:19). Bring your fury to the One who judges justly. He has been betrayed by His own people, and He knows how to heal.
units.application: If you are tempted toward someone else's spouse, picture the day the husband or wife finds out, and let that picture stop you now. If you have been betrayed, find a pastor or Christian counselor and a trusted friend to walk with you; do not carry the anger alone, and do not act on it in revenge. Churches, protect and care for betrayed spouses instead of rushing them toward a quick reconciliation.

rel.note: Riches can ransom a man's life in some troubles, but this verse names a wrong no ransom can settle.
An offended brother is harder to win than a strong city, the same hardness of a deeply wronged heart.
The chapter opened with a debt the son could escape by humbling himself; it closes with a debt no payment can settle.
The thief can restore what he took, while the wronged husband accepts no payment at all.
The husband's unsparing fury is the reason no gift will appease him.

units.notes:
• The NASB renders "recompense" as "ransom." The Hebrew line reads literally that he will not "lift the face" of any ransom, and the KJV margin gives "He will not accept the face of any ransom." He will not even look with favor on the payment held out to him.
• The word for "recompense" is kopher, the price that could redeem a life (Exodus 21:30; 30:12). Compare 13:8: "The ransom of a man's life is his riches."
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "This is an injury that admits of no compensation."
• Henry: "If a man would give all the substance of his house, it would atone for a theft … but not for adultery." "Atone" here means make amends.
• Compare 6:31, where the thief's restitution is possible, and 18:19.
units.summary: Money can repay a theft, but no gift can buy back a betrayed marriage.
units.principle: Some sins create debts no human payment can settle, so the wise avoid them instead of planning to pay for them later.
units.insight: The husband in this verse refuses every ransom. Scripture tells of another wronged Husband. Through Hosea, God pictured His unfaithful people as an adulterous wife, then told the prophet to buy her back: "So I bought her for myself for fifteen shekels of silver" (Hosea 3:2). The One who had every right to refuse payment paid it Himself. In the light of the New Testament, the Son of Man came "to give His life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). This does not make adultery small. It shows how great the debt is that only God could pay. If you are weighing a sin you plan to fix later, hear this verse: some debts no gift can settle. If you are already in that debt, look to the cross, where the wronged One paid the ransom for the guilty.
units.application: Do not plan to sin now and apologize later; some damage cannot be bought back. If an affair has come to light in your marriage, do not try to fix it with gifts. Pursue repentance, truthfulness, counseling and time. If you are the wounded spouse, you need not pretend that gifts heal betrayal. Pastors, walk patiently with couples through restoration. Parents, teach your children that faithfulness now prevents debts no one can pay.

rel.note: The father uses the identical line, "And treasure my commands within you," in his first appeal to receive his words.
The son is again told to let his heart keep the father's commands rather than forget them.
Kept commands are pictured as a guide and a lamp that keep the son from the evil woman, the same purpose this chapter pursues.
The father opens the chapter by asking his son to keep his words and closes it by asking his children to listen to them.

units.notes:
• The word translated "treasure," tsaphan, means to hide or store away something precious. The psalmist uses the same verb: "Your word I have hidden in my heart, That I might not sin against You" (Psalm 119:11).
• The second line repeats 2:1 word for word, "And treasure my commands within you," so the father's final warning reaches back to his first appeal to receive his words.
• The KJV has "lay up my commandments with thee." Bridges urges that God's word be laid up "carefully, not on our shelves, but on our hearts."
• Guzik, Enduring Word: "The implication is not that Bible reading provides a magical protection against sexual immorality." What protects is a heart that loves and obeys what it has stored.
• Compare Deuteronomy 11:18 and Luke 2:19, where Mary "kept all these things and pondered them in her heart."
units.summary: Win the contest of voices early: get God's word inside you before temptation starts talking.
units.principle: Instruction protects as it is treasured; the heart that values God's word stores it up before the hour of testing comes.
units.insight: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered each lie with "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). The words He had stored were ready when the tempter spoke. The psalmist asked the question every young person faces: "How can a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed according to Your word" (Psalm 119:9). The issue is not whether we own a Bible or have heard sermons, but whether we treasure what we have heard. Many people know the right verses and still fall, because the words were filed away, not loved. Behind the father's "My son" we can hear our heavenly Father's voice (Hebrews 12:5–6). He speaks early, because He loves us before temptation ever arrives.
units.application: Choose one passage on purity or faithfulness, such as 7:24–27 or 1 Corinthians 10:13, and carry it this week until you can say it from memory. Parents, do more than set rules: tell your teenagers why you treasure God's word, and let them hear you pray it. If you are single and lonely, or married and drifting, store up God's promises now, while things are quiet. Each evening, ask whether you obeyed what you read, not only whether you read it.

rel.note: Keeping the father's commands is joined to length of days, long life and peace.
The father passes on his own father's words, "Keep my commands, and live," the same promise of life through kept instruction.
The commandment is called a lamp and the way of life that keeps the son from the evil woman, which explains why it must be guarded so carefully.
The chapter that opens with "Keep my commands and live" ends at the chambers of death, the end of the young man who did not keep them.

units.notes:
• "Apple of your eye" translates 'ishon, literally "little man," commonly explained as the tiny image of oneself seen in another person's pupil. The English "apple" is an old way of naming the round pupil.
• The same expression describes God's care for His people: "He kept him as the apple of His eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10). Compare Psalm 17:8 and Zechariah 2:8. The God who guards His people this way asks them to guard His word the same way.
• Henry hears a second sense in "Keep my commands and live": "Keep them as you would your life, as those that cannot live without them."
• Bridges warns against softening God's law: "To explain it away, or to lower its requirements, breaks down the barrier, and gives an easy entrance to temptation."
• Compare 4:4, "Keep my commands, and live," and 3:1–2, which joins kept commands to length of days and peace.
units.summary: Guard God's word the way your eyelid guards your eye: instantly, instinctively, without debate.
units.principle: God's word is the way to life, not a restriction on it, and it deserves the most careful protection we can give.
units.insight: We guard our eyes without thinking, yet we often guard God's word only after thinking it over, and by then the moment has passed. Daniel settled the question early. Before the king's food ever reached him, he "purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself" (Daniel 1:8). Because the decision was already made, the pressure of the moment did not move him. Notice the love inside the command. God first kept Israel "as the apple of His eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10); He asks us to treasure His word because He has first treasured us. Jesus put it in the language of love: "If you love Me, keep My commandments" (John 14:15). Obedience is not the price of His love but the way we guard a relationship we cannot live without.
units.application: Decide in advance where your eyelid closes: the app you will not open when alone, the conversation you will not continue, the late-night message you will not answer. Young people, settle these lines with a parent or mentor before you need them. Leaders and pastors, watch for the slow habit of explaining a command away because it is inconvenient; that is how the barrier comes down. When your conscience flinches, treat it like dust in the eye and respond at once.

rel.note: The father uses the same two images, binding around the neck and writing on the tablet of the heart, for mercy and truth.
What is written on the heart matters because "out of it spring the issues of life."
The son is told to bind his parents' teaching continually on his heart, the same inward keeping.
The young man "devoid of understanding," literally lacking heart, shows what happens when nothing has been written within.

units.notes:
• "Tablet" translates luach, the word used for the stone tablets on which God wrote the Ten Commandments (Exodus 31:18; 34:1). The father wants his words written within as lastingly as God's law was carved in stone.
• Compare Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18, where Israel is told to bind God's words on the hand, and Proverbs 3:3, where the father uses the same pair of binding and writing, and Proverbs 6:21, where he again says to bind his teaching on the heart.
• God promises to do this writing Himself: "I will put My law in their minds, and write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33; compare Hebrews 8:10 and 2 Corinthians 3:3).
• Ironside: "It is the making it one's own, the daily feeding upon it, that preserves the soul."
• Henry pictures the commands worn on the finger "as thy wedding-ring, the badge of thy espousals to God," that is, the sign that a person belongs to God as a bride belongs to her husband. The image fits a chapter about faithfulness.
units.summary: God's word belongs on the hand that acts and in the heart that wants.
units.principle: Truth that stays outside us will not hold us; God's word must shape both the deeds of our hands and the desires of our hearts.
units.insight: Some in Jesus' day took Moses' command literally, binding small boxes of Scripture to their arms and foreheads, and Jesus noticed how broad they made them (Matthew 23:5). The words were on their hands but not on their hearts. Something is always being written on the heart: the images we linger on, the lyrics we repeat, the grudges we rehearse. The question is which writing will go deepest. The good news is that this is not left to our effort alone. God promised a new covenant in which He writes His law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Paul says the Spirit writes Christ there, "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of flesh, that is, of the heart" (2 Corinthians 3:3). Ask Him to do what you cannot.
units.application: Put a verse where your hand goes: your phone's lock screen, the dashboard, the laptop you use late at night. Then work on the heart: read that verse slowly each morning and ask God to write it deeper. Fathers and mothers, let your children see Scripture in your daily routine, not only on Sundays. If you mentor a young believer, ask what is being written on their heart through what they watch and hear, not only what they read.

rel.note: When wisdom enters the heart and is pleasant to the soul, it delivers the son from the seductress who flatters with her words.
The son is told to love wisdom and embrace her, the same affectionate closeness pictured here as family.
The closeness with wisdom urged here has its purpose stated in the next verse: to keep the son from the immoral woman.
Wisdom promises to love those who love her, so the closeness the father urges is returned.

units.notes:
• "Nearest kin" translates moda', a rare word for a close relative or intimate acquaintance; a closely related form describes Boaz as a "relative" of Naomi's husband (Ruth 2:1). The ESV and NASB have "intimate friend."
• "My sister" is a term of tender love in the Song of Songs: "You have ravished my heart, My sister, my spouse" (Song of Songs 4:9). The son is to speak to wisdom with that warmth.
• Bridges: "Man must have his object of delight. If wisdom is not loved, lust will be indulged."
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "Thousands of men are kept from evil courses by the love and friendship of sisters, and women friends."
• Compare 4:6–8, where the son is told to love wisdom and embrace her, and 2:10–16, where wisdom entering the heart delivers him from the seductress.
units.summary: The best protection against a false intimacy is a true one, so make wisdom family.
units.principle: A heart is guarded less by prohibitions than by a stronger love; the one who delights in wisdom is not hungry for counterfeit intimacy.
units.insight: This verse diagnoses something we often miss: sin feeds on emptiness. Paul's coworker Demas left him, "having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). His heart had found another love. Mary of Bethany chose to sit at Jesus' feet and listen, and Jesus said she had chosen "that good part, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:42). Ask yourself what you turn to when you are lonely, bored or tired. For the Christian, the deepest form of this closeness is friendship with Christ, who "became for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30). Friendship with Him is the closeness that crowds out counterfeit closeness.
units.application: Build real closeness with wisdom: a daily time in Scripture you look forward to, not one you merely endure. Young men and women, cultivate friendships with godly peers and older believers who can see what you cannot. Parents, aim for your children to love wisdom, not only obey rules; talk about why God's ways are good. If you are lonely, name it to God and to a trusted friend instead of letting a screen or a flirtation fill the gap.

rel.note: The father first described the seductress who flatters with her words in the same wording this verse repeats.
The seductress's mouth is "smoother than oil," the same smooth speech named here.
The father's commands are said to keep the son from the evil woman and the flattering tongue of a seductress.
The flattering lips warned of here are the very lips that seduce the young man at the climax of the story.
The wisdom and understanding the son embraces as family are what keep him from her.

units.notes:
• "Immoral woman" and "seductress" translate words meaning a woman who is a stranger or outsider (zarah and nokriyah). The KJV keeps the older "strange woman" and "stranger"; the ESV has "forbidden woman" and "adulteress." In context the words mark her as outside the young man's home and outside God's ways; the text does not settle her nationality.
• "Flatters" translates chalaq, to make smooth. The same idea describes her mouth as "smoother than oil" in 5:3. Smooth words slide past a person's defenses.
• Ironside: "Satan has no more powerful weapon for the overthrow of the young than flattery."
• Compare 2:16; 5:3; 6:24, three earlier warnings against the same smooth tongue, and 29:5, "A man who flatters his neighbor Spreads a net for his feet."
units.summary: Wisdom kept close is the guard at the door when the flatterer comes calling.
units.principle: The defense against flattering words is not suspicion of everyone but a heart already filled with wisdom's voice.
units.insight: Herod Agrippa sat on his throne in royal robes while the crowd shouted, "The voice of a god and not of a man!" He accepted the praise, and he was struck down (Acts 12:21–23). Flattery works because it tells us what we already want to believe about ourselves. That is why the father does not simply say, "Avoid her." He fills his son with a better voice first. Ask yourself whose words have the most room in your mind: the voice that says you deserve this and no one will know, or the voice of God's word. In the light of the New Testament, the strongest defense is a Person. Jesus is the Word made flesh (John 1:14), and He promised those who abide in His word, "you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (John 8:32).
units.application: Notice the voices that tell you what you want to hear: the coworker who praises you just before suggesting a late drink, the online stranger who says no one understands you like they do. Name flattery when you hear it. Parents, teach your teenagers how manipulation sounds, using real examples. Married people, if someone outside your marriage starts making you feel uniquely seen, treat that as a warning light, and tell your spouse or a trusted friend.

rel.note: Another observer looks at a scene of ruin and turns what he sees into instruction for the reader.
The father watching from his window is a small picture of the LORD, before whose eyes every path lies open.
The father tells what he saw from the window so that he can call his children to listen when the story ends.

units.notes:
• A "lattice" was a screen of crossed slats over a window. The same Hebrew word appears in Judges 5:28, where Sisera's mother "cried out through the lattice" for a son who would never come home. The KJV has "casement," an older word for a hinged window.
• Henry describes the writer as one who writes "as a minister, a prophet, who is by office a watchman, to give warning of the approach of the enemies." Compare Ezekiel 33:7, where God sets a watchman to warn His people.
• Ironside: the scene "has been duplicated not only by the thousands, but millions of times, and is as true to-day as in the days of Solomon."
• Compare 24:30–32, where another observer looks at the field of the lazy man and says, "I looked on it and received instruction."
units.summary: The father watched one young man's ruin so that his own son would not have to live it.
units.principle: The wise learn from watching where other people's paths end, so that they do not have to learn by walking there themselves.
units.insight: Paul said the failures of Israel in the wilderness "were written for our admonition" (1 Corinthians 10:11), and among the first he named was sexual immorality (10:8). God does not tell these stories to shame the people in them but to spare us. Yet we tend to watch someone else's fall and think, "My situation is different." The father at the window sees the whole road; the young man sees only the next step. Temptation always works this way: it narrows our view to the next step. There is One who watches with more than a father's care. Jesus wept over Jerusalem because He saw where its path would end (Luke 19:41–44). His warnings are love, not control.
units.application: Learn from others' falls without gossiping about them. When a leader or friend falls into sin, ask, "What steps did they take, and am I taking any of them?" Parents and mentors, tell young people true stories of where compromise led, including your own when that is wise. Pastors, preach this chapter plainly; the father did. And if someone older warns you about a path you are on, thank them before you argue.

rel.note: Whoever walks with wise men becomes wise, while the companion of fools is destroyed, which explains the danger of drifting among the simple.
The book was written to give prudence to the simple, the uncommitted group this young man belongs to.
The same expression, lacking heart or understanding, describes the man who commits adultery and destroys his own soul.
The son is told to write the commands on his heart; this young man lacks heart, with nothing written within.
Wisdom calls to the very person described here, the one who lacks understanding, and invites him to her house.

units.notes:
• "Devoid of understanding" is literally "lacking heart." In Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of understanding and judgment, so the phrase describes a person with no settled inner convictions. The same expression describes the adulterer in 6:32 and the people both Wisdom and Folly call in 9:4 and 9:16.
• "The simple" are the open and inexperienced, easily swayed either way. Proverbs was written "To give prudence to the simple" (1:4). The ESV has "a young man lacking sense."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Young, inexperienced, featherbrained, he is the very sort to need arming with borrowed wisdom."
• Henry notes the company the young man keeps: "if those that are simple choose such for their companions as are like themselves, simple they will still be." Compare 13:20.
• Compare Matthew 12:43–45, where a house left "empty, swept, and put in order" is soon filled with worse.
units.summary: The young man was not wicked, only empty, and an empty heart does not stay empty for long.
units.principle: Sin seldom begins with open rebellion; it begins with an uncommitted heart that has not yet given itself to what is right.
units.insight: Lot did not move into Sodom in a day. He looked toward the well-watered plain, "pitched his tent even as far as Sodom" (Genesis 13:10–12), and later sat in its gate (19:1). Like the young man here, he was marked less by open rebellion than by a heart that was never settled. Jesus warned that a house left "empty, swept, and put in order" does not stay empty (Matthew 12:44–45). A neutral heart is not a safe heart. Many people in church are like this young man: not hostile to God, just uncommitted, drifting with friends who are drifting too. The cure is not mere willpower but a heart that is filled and owned. In Christ "you are complete" (Colossians 2:10), and a full heart has no room to rent.
units.application: Ask yourself plainly whether your heart is committed or merely undecided in the areas where you are tempted. Young people, choose friends who are going somewhere with God, not only friends who are fun; you will become like your company (13:20). Youth leaders and parents, look past outward behavior to the quiet, drifting kid who seems ordinary. This week, write down one area where you have been "neutral" and make a clear decision before God.

rel.note: The son is told to avoid the path of the wicked and pass it by, the opposite of taking the path to her house.
The father commanded his son not to go near the door of her house, the very distance this young man fails to keep.
The questions about carrying fire and walking on hot coals expose the folly of thinking a person can come close to adultery unharmed.
The father's closing command not to stray into her paths reverses the step this young man takes.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "took the path" pictures stepping or marching along, a deliberate walk rather than a stumble. The KJV has "he went the way to her house."
• Bridges, quoting Geier: "Who would avoid sin must avoid temptation to sin."
• Henry: "when we have nothing to do the devil will quickly find us something to do."
• Compare 4:14–15: "Do not enter the path of the wicked… Avoid it, do not travel on it; Turn away from it and pass on."
• Compare Psalm 1:1, where walking, standing and sitting trace the same gradual drift toward sin.
units.summary: Nobody falls into sin from across town; the fall begins with a walk toward temptation's corner.
units.principle: Distance from temptation is a choice made before temptation speaks, and whoever walks toward sin's corner is responsible for where he ends up.
units.insight: Job made a decision long before any temptation arrived: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; Why then should I look upon a young woman?" (Job 31:1). He chose his distance in advance. Peter shows how coming close works in other sins too. He "followed at a distance" and sat down among the enemies at their fire (Luke 22:54–55), and before morning he had denied his Lord three times. Most of us do not plan to sin; we just keep walking past the corner. Jesus told His disciples, "Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation" (Matthew 26:41), and He taught us to pray, "do not lead us into temptation" (Matthew 6:13). It makes no sense to pray that prayer and then walk toward her house.
units.application: Identify your "corner": the website, the coworker's office after hours, an old flame's social media page, the bar after a fight at home. Then change your route. Married couples, agree on simple boundaries together, such as no private messaging or meals alone with someone you find attractive. Students, plan your evenings so that boredom does not plan them for you. If you are already on the path to her house, turn around now; the next step will be harder.

rel.note: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good, so no hour is truly hidden.
The way of the wicked is like darkness, and those who walk it do not know what makes them stumble.
The young man walks into the dark, but the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, who ponders all his paths.
The seductress's assurance that her husband is away appeals to the same hope that no one will see.

units.notes:
• "Black" translates 'ishon, the same word rendered "apple" (the pupil of the eye) in 7:2. Used of the night, it means the middle, darkest point of the night; the NASB has "the middle of the night." The son was told to guard his father's law like the pupil of his eye; this young man walks into the darkest part of the night.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Foolish men think to hide themselves from God, by hiding God from themselves."
• Henry: "We must take heed, not only of idle days, but of idle evenings, lest they prove inlets to temptation."
• Compare Job 24:15, "The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight, Saying, 'No eye will see me,'" and John 3:19–20, where people love darkness "because their deeds were evil."
units.summary: The dark feels safe only because we forget Who is watching.
units.principle: Sin seeks the cover of darkness, but nothing done in the dark is hidden from the LORD, who sees every path.
units.insight: Achan buried stolen silver under his tent and thought it was hidden, but God brought it into the open (Joshua 7:21–22). The dark always feels safer than it is. Notice what darkness offers: not pleasure itself, but the feeling that no one will know. That feeling is a lie, for "the darkness and the light are both alike to You" (Psalm 139:12). Yet the light is not only a threat. Jesus said, "I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life" (John 8:12). He does not expose us in order to shame us but to bring us home. "If we walk in the light as He is in the light," the blood of Jesus Christ His Son "cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7).
units.application: Notice your dark hours: late at night, alone on a screen, on a business trip, when your spouse is asleep. Put safeguards in those hours, such as devices out of the bedroom or a friend who checks in when you travel. Teenagers, agree with your parents on a reasonable curfew and keep it. If you are hiding something, bring it into the light with one trusted believer this week; secrets grow in the dark and shrink when spoken.

rel.note: The harlot is a deep pit who lies in wait as for a victim, the same planned hunt described here.
The adulterous woman who wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wickedness," shows the same concealed and hardened heart.
The son is told to keep his heart with all diligence for life, while this woman guards her heart to conceal her purpose.
The father warns against lusting after her beauty and notes that an adulteress preys upon a man's precious life.

units.notes:
• "Crafty heart" is literally "guarded of heart." The verb is the one translated "Keep" in "Keep your heart with all diligence" (4:23). The son is to guard his heart for life; she guards hers to hide her purpose. The KJV has "subtil of heart," the ESV "wily of heart."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Outwardly, she keeps nothing back; she is dressed, as we say, to kill; inwardly, she gives nothing away…"
• Henry observes that she is "not a common prostitute, for she was a married wife." Her clothing is both a disguise and a signal (compare 6:26, which distinguishes a harlot from an adulteress).
• Compare Genesis 38:14–15, where Judah took a veiled woman sitting by the road for a harlot.
units.summary: Temptation does not ambush the man who walks to its corner; it simply keeps the appointment.
units.principle: Opportunity for sin meets those who put themselves in its path, and what attracts on the outside usually hides a plan on the inside.
units.insight: Judas came to Jesus with a greeting and a kiss, and the kiss was the signal for His arrest (Matthew 26:48–49). Outward affection hid an inward plan. That is what a crafty heart looks like, and temptation always wears its best face. But this verse also turns the question toward us. The son is to guard his heart for life; this woman guarded hers to hide what she intended. It is possible to keep a heart guarded for the wrong reasons, hiding motives even from ourselves, for "The heart is deceitful above all things" (Jeremiah 17:9). Jesus "knew what was in man" (John 2:25). He saw through Judas's kiss and still called him "Friend" (Matthew 26:50). He invites us to stop hiding our hearts and open them to Him.
units.application: Expect temptation to look attractive and to hide its cost. If you find yourself near your own "corner," a place you know you should avoid, an available opportunity is not a sign from God but a test of where you have been walking. Single adults, be wary of relationships that look exciting but come with hidden agendas. Parents, teach your sons and daughters that a person's real intentions show over time, not in the first impression. Ask a trusted friend to help you see what you might be missing.

rel.note: The immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God, the commitments this woman's feet abandon.
The virtuous wife watches over the ways of her household, while this woman's feet will not stay at home.
The son is told to ponder the path of his feet and not turn aside, the opposite of her wandering feet.
Folly is called clamorous with the same word used here for loud, linking the two women's portraits.

units.notes:
• "Loud" and "clamorous" (9:13) translate the same Hebrew word, which the NASB renders "boisterous" in both verses. It is one of several details that link this woman with Folly's portrait in 9:13–18.
• "Rebellious" comes from the verb translated "stubborn" in Deuteronomy 21:18, "a stubborn and rebellious son," someone who refuses correction and goes his own way. The KJV has "loud and stubborn."
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "She is continually exposing herself, and showing by her gait and gestures what she is, and what she wants."
• Henry: "Virtue is a penance to those to whom home is a prison." In plain words, goodness feels like a punishment to someone who treats home as a prison.
• Compare 2:17, the immoral woman "who forsakes the companion of her youth," and 31:27, the wise wife who "watches over the ways of her household."
units.summary: The adulteress would not stay where her marriage vows had placed her, so she went looking for someone else.
units.principle: Restlessness that refuses the boundaries of our commitments will go looking for something to fill it.
units.insight: Hosea's wife Gomer had the same restless feet. "I will go after my lovers," she said (Hosea 2:5), and she left her home for other men. Yet God told Hosea, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by a lover and is committing adultery" (Hosea 3:1), and Hosea bought her back (3:2). Restlessness is not only her problem. Many of us carry a low-grade discontent with the life God has given us, the marriage, the job, the season, and that discontent keeps our feet moving. The answer is not a new place but rest in God. Jesus invites the restless, "Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). A heart at rest in Him does not need the street.
units.application: Pay attention to restlessness in your marriage or calling before it takes you somewhere. Husbands and wives, when you notice you would rather be anywhere but home, talk about it with each other or a counselor instead of filling the gap elsewhere. Single adults, bring loneliness to God and to your church family instead of letting it drive you. Leaders, watch for a pattern of resisting every boundary and accountability; stubbornness about small limits often grows into bigger ones.

rel.note: The violent gang says, "Let us lie in wait," using the same hunter's verb for their ambush.
Wisdom raises her voice openly in the same streets and squares where the seductress lies in wait.
The harlot lies in wait as for a victim and increases the unfaithful among men.
Because she lurks at every corner, her claim to have sought this young man alone is flattery she would have offered anyone.
Folly sits by the highest places of the city to call to those who pass by, the same public hunting ground.

units.notes:
• "Lurking" translates 'arab, to lie in ambush. It is the verb of 1:11 and 1:18, where the violent gang lies in wait for others and in the end lies "in wait for their own blood."
• The KJV prints verses 11–12 in parentheses, "Now is she without, now in the streets," marking them as a description set off from the story.
• Bridges quotes the traveler Dr. Richardson, who saw such women in Egypt "sitting at the doors of their houses, and calling on the passengers as they went by" (that is, the passersby), "in the same manner as we read in the Book of Proverbs."
• Compare 1:20–21 and 8:1–3, where Wisdom cries in the same streets, squares and gates, and 23:28: "She also lies in wait as for a victim."
• Compare 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil "walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour."
units.summary: Wisdom calls out in the open square; the seductress lies in wait on the very same streets.
units.principle: Temptation is not confined to one corner we can easily avoid; it lies in wait along ordinary paths, so the heart must be guarded everywhere.
units.insight: God warned Cain, "sin lies at the door. And its desire is for you, but you should rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). Sin is pictured as something crouching, waiting. The woman at every corner gives the same picture in a city street. We like to imagine temptation lives in one bad neighborhood we can avoid. In reality it waits along ordinary routes: the office, the phone, the gym, even church. That is why distance alone is not enough; the heart has to be guarded too. Yet we are not alone on these streets. Christ "Himself has suffered, being tempted," and so "He is able to aid those who are being tempted" (Hebrews 2:18). The One who walked our streets without sin walks them with us now.
units.application: Map where temptation lurks in your ordinary week, not only the obvious places: the commute, the lunch break, the late scroll. Plan a response for each. Parents, talk with your kids about how online spaces are public squares where predators and pornographers lie in wait. Workers who travel, decide before you leave how you will spend evenings in the hotel. When you notice a pattern of temptation at one place or time, tell someone who will pray and ask you about it.

rel.note: The wicked man "hardens his face," the same bold, shameless look she puts on here.
The adulterous woman eats, wipes her mouth and says she has done no wickedness, the same shamelessness.
The father asks why his son would be enraptured by an immoral woman and embrace a seductress, the embrace this verse begins to depict.

units.notes:
