• "With an impudent face" is literally "she made her face strong," or firm; the KJV margin gives "she strengthened her face." To make the face strong was to put on a bold look that refuses to show shame, which is why the NASB has "a brazen face" and the ESV "with bold face."
• The same Hebrew expression, making the face strong, lies behind 21:29, where the NKJV has "A wicked man hardens his face."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Her bold attire matches her bold approach, for a harlot knows no shame (Proverbs 30:20)."
• Compare Jeremiah 3:3, "You have had a harlot's forehead; You refuse to be ashamed," and Jeremiah 6:15, "Nor did they know how to blush."
units.summary: The seductress touched the young man before she reasoned with him, because temptation works on body and imagination together.
units.principle: Temptation works on the senses before it argues, and a conscience hardened against shame has already traveled far from God.
units.insight: Potiphar's wife pressed Joseph day after day, and at last "she caught him by his garment, saying, 'Lie with me'" (Genesis 39:10–12). Joseph left the garment in her hand and ran. When temptation touches, the time for debate is over. This verse also warns about what happens to a conscience over time. Paul describes people who, "being past feeling, have given themselves over to lewdness" (Ephesians 4:19). Shamelessness does not arrive in a day; it grows each time we silence the blush. If your conscience still stings, thank God, for it is a mercy. And if shame weighs on you for what you have done, bring it to Christ, who "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2), so that you could be free of it.
units.application: Decide now what you will do if someone makes a physical advance: leave, not linger. Young couples, set physical boundaries before the date, not in the moment. Coworkers, treat a lingering touch or a hug that feels charged as a signal to create distance. If you notice that something that once made you blush no longer does, whether jokes, shows or habits, take it as a warning and ask God to restore a tender conscience.

rel.note: The LORD detests the sacrifice of the wicked but delights in the prayer of the upright, so her offerings gain her nothing.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, all the more when it is brought with wicked intent, as hers is.
Even prayer becomes an abomination when the ear is turned away from God's law, which shows why her worship cannot excuse her sin.
The adulterous woman says, "I have done no wickedness," the same self-justification dressed here in religious words.

units.notes:
• Peace offerings were fellowship sacrifices; the worshiper ate much of the meat with family and friends. A thanksgiving offering had to be eaten the same day, and a vow or freewill offering by the next day (Leviticus 7:15–16).
• Gurnall, quoted by Bridges: "She durst not play the harlot with man till she had played the hypocrite with God." ("Durst not" means "dared not.")
• Henry: "it is sad that a show of piety should become the shelter of iniquity."
• Compare 15:8 and 21:27, "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; How much more when he brings it with wicked intent!"
• Compare 1 Samuel 2:22, where Eli's sons lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting.
units.summary: The seductress checked the religious box by day and planned adultery for the night.
units.principle: Religious activity cannot cover deliberate sin; when worship is used to quiet the conscience, it becomes part of the sin.
units.insight: Absalom asked his father's permission to go to Hebron and pay a vow to the LORD, and he used the trip to launch his rebellion (2 Samuel 15:7–10). Jesus spoke of men who "for a pretense make long prayers" (Mark 12:40). Religious cover is one of sin's oldest tricks. It works on us too. We can let church attendance, giving or ministry feel like credit in an account, as if obedience in one area pays for disobedience in another. God is not bargained with. After his own adultery David learned what God desires: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, A broken and a contrite heart" (Psalm 51:17). The way back is not more religious activity but confession, and Christ's one sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12) cleanses what no vow can cover.
units.application: Watch for religious reasoning that makes room for sin: "God wants me to be happy," "I prayed about it and feel peace," "I serve so much, I deserve this." Pastors and church leaders, be alert when ministry activity increases while private integrity decreases; that pattern often comes before a fall. Spouses and friends, do not let someone's church involvement silence your concern. Before Sunday, confess one area where you have been using devotion as cover.

rel.note: A flattering mouth works ruin, the end toward which her praise is leading the young man.
A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet, exactly what her words are doing.
She was lurking at every corner, so her claim to have sought him in particular is false.
Wisdom promises that those who seek her diligently will find her; the seductress borrows the same words for a counterfeit pursuit.

units.notes:
• "Diligently to seek" here and "seek me diligently" in 8:17 translate the same Hebrew verb, shachar. The seductress's words echo Wisdom's promise, but she offers a counterfeit of what Wisdom truly gives.
• Wiersbe, quoted by Guzik: "She appeals to the young man's male ego as she flatters him and makes him think he's very special to her."
• She even treats the meeting as God's arrangement. Bridges says she acts "as if her meeting was a happy providence, the reward of her religious services."
• Compare 29:5, "A man who flatters his neighbor Spreads a net for his feet," and 26:28, "a flattering mouth works ruin."
units.summary: Flattery says, "I was looking for you," to every man who walks by.
units.principle: Flattery that makes us feel uniquely chosen is often the bait of a trap set for anyone who passes by.
units.insight: Behind this line is a hunger we all share: to be sought, wanted and chosen. The seductress exploits it, and so does every temptation that whispers, "This was meant for you." The answer is not to deny the hunger but to bring it to the One who truly seeks. Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus stopped, called him by name and said, "today I must stay at your house" (Luke 19:5). Unlike the seductress, Jesus meant it for this one man, and He told why He had come: "the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). Those who know they have been sought and found by Christ are much harder to flatter, because their deepest longing has already been met.
units.application: When someone outside your marriage tells you that you are the one they have been looking for, recognize the line for what it is. Married people, keep meeting your spouse's need to feel wanted; neglect makes flattery sound like water in a desert. Teenagers, be wary of anyone online who makes you feel uniquely special very quickly; that is a common grooming tactic. Parents, affirm your children often and specifically, so that a stranger's praise does not land in an empty place.

rel.note: The virtuous wife also makes tapestry coverings, but to honor her household, not to lure a man into sin.
Her lips drip honey but her end is bitter as wormwood, the hidden cost behind this luxurious picture.
The father warns against lusting after her beauty in the heart, the inward response her description seeks to stir.
Her description moves from what the young man can picture to what he can smell, engaging every sense.

units.notes:
• "Tapestry" translates marbaddim, decorated coverings. The same word appears in 31:22, where the virtuous wife "makes tapestry for herself." The book sets the two women side by side: one prepares coverings to lure a man into adultery, the other to honor her household.
• The KJV reads, "I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt."
• Egypt was famous for fine linen. Pharaoh clothed Joseph "in garments of fine linen" (Genesis 41:42), and Ezekiel lists "Fine embroidered linen from Egypt" among the luxuries of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:7).
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "She designs to inflame his lust by the mention of the bed, and by its ornaments and perfumes."
• Compare James 1:14, "each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed."
units.summary: Temptation furnishes a room in your imagination before it ever opens the door.
units.principle: Sin works first through a picture in the imagination; whoever lets temptation furnish his thoughts has already begun to walk toward the act.
units.insight: Eve "saw that the tree was good for food, that it was pleasant to the eyes" (Genesis 3:6) before she took the fruit. The order is the same every time: see, imagine, desire, take. Jesus went to the root when He said that looking at a woman to lust for her is adultery already committed in the heart (Matthew 5:28). Today screens supply the imagination endlessly, and adultery often begins as a scene rehearsed in the mind. We cannot always stop an image from appearing, but we can refuse to decorate it. Paul calls us to bring "every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5). Christ, who calls us to this, gives the power to do it.
units.application: Notice the moment your imagination starts building a scene it should not, and change the subject of your thoughts on purpose: pray, get up, call someone. If you struggle with pornography, install filters and set up accountability, but also feed your mind with good things (Philippians 4:8). Married couples, invest imagination and creativity in your own marriage. Parents, talk with older children about how advertising and entertainment try to build scenes in their minds.

rel.note: The father commends delight in the wife of one's youth, the rightful setting for the pleasures she misuses.
Her sweet start hides a bitter end, as the perfume here hides the price.
The appeal to the eyes in her description of the bed now extends to the sense of smell.
Folly calls stolen water sweet, but her guests do not know that the dead are there.

units.notes:
• Myrrh, aloes and cinnamon appear together in Song of Songs 4:14 among the bride's spices, and myrrh and aloes scent the royal bridegroom's garments in Psalm 45:8.
• Myrrh and aloes were also burial spices: Nicodemus brought "a mixture of myrrh and aloes" for the body of Jesus (John 19:39). Trapp, quoted by Guzik, saw a warning here: "This might have minded the young man that he was going to his grave…" ("minded" means reminded).
• Bridges imagines what memory will later make of these scents: "the fragrance of exciting perfume … changed into the bitterness of wormwood and gall."
• Compare 5:3–4, where the immoral woman's lips drip honey but "in the end she is bitter as wormwood."
units.summary: Temptation names every pleasure it offers and never once mentions the price.
units.principle: Sin borrows the good gifts God made for marriage and uses them as bait, but stolen pleasure always hides its cost.
units.insight: Every gift in this verse is good. God made fragrance, and the Song of Songs celebrates these very spices in the love of a bride and bridegroom. Sin cannot create anything; it can only steal and twist what God made. That is why temptation so often feels beautiful. The question to ask is not "Is this pleasant?" but "Is this mine to take?" The same myrrh and aloes appear once more in Scripture, carried by Nicodemus to the tomb of Jesus (John 19:39). Christ died for every person who has taken what was not theirs. He did not come to rob us of pleasure but to restore it to its proper place: "I have come that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly" (John 10:10).
units.application: When something good is offered in the wrong setting, ask whose it is: Is this mine to enjoy? Husbands and wives, put effort into making your own home and bedroom a place of delight; neglect leaves a vacuum. Single adults, enjoy God's good gifts of beauty and friendship without letting them become bait. If you struggle with a specific temptation, write down its real cost, to God, your family and yourself, and read it when the pleasant version comes to mind.

rel.note: The same language of being satisfied celebrates a husband's delight in his own wife, the love she counterfeits.
The immoral woman's lips drip honey, the sweet speech that dresses up what she offers.
Folly says stolen water is sweet, giving the same pleasant name to forbidden pleasure.

units.notes:
• "Take our fill" translates rawah, to drink one's fill or be saturated, the same verb as "satisfy" in 5:19.
• The word for "love" in the first line, dodim, is the plural used in the Song of Songs for the delights of love between bride and bridegroom: "your love is better than wine" (Song of Songs 1:2). Here the same word dresses up an adulterous night.
• The KJV has "let us solace ourselves with loves." To "solace" is to comfort or delight.
• Henry: "Of love, does she say? Of lust she means… True love is from heaven; this is from hell."
• Compare Isaiah 5:20, "Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil."
units.summary: Sin rarely introduces itself by its real name.
units.principle: Renaming sin does not change its nature; whatever we will not call by its true name already has a hold on us.
units.insight: Amnon told his friend, "I love Tamar" (2 Samuel 13:4). After he forced her, "the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her" (13:15). Lust wearing love's name always shows its true face in the end. Our age is full of soft names for sin: an affair becomes "finding myself," pornography becomes "harmless," betrayal becomes "following my heart." Ask yourself what words you use for your own sins. Scripture defines love by a cross, not a feeling: "By this we know love, because He laid down His life for us" (1 John 3:16). Love gives itself for another's good; lust takes another for its own pleasure. Calling sin by its right name is the first step of confession, and confession is where cleansing begins (1 John 1:9).
units.application: Practice plain speech about sin. When you catch yourself saying "slip," "mistake" or "connection," ask what God would call it. Parents, teach your children the biblical words for sexual sin and why they matter, so the culture's euphemisms do not shape them. Pastors and counselors, speak tenderly but truthfully. And if you have been calling an affair or an addiction by a softer name, name it plainly to God this week and to one trusted person.

rel.note: The immoral woman forsakes the companion of her youth, as this wife speaks of her husband without calling him hers.
She plans around her husband's eyes, but the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.
A wronged husband's fury will not spare in the day of vengeance, a consequence her assurance ignores.
Her reassurance continues in the next verse with the details of her husband's trip and return.
The young man's choice of the dark night rests on the same hope that no one will see.

units.notes:
• "My husband" is literally "the man." She speaks of her own husband without calling him hers, a detached way of referring to him; the KJV's "the goodman" (the master of the house) keeps that impersonal wording. Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "she represents my husband by 'the man', not by 'my husband.'"
• Bridges suggests why she avoids the word: "perhaps the name of husband might have awakened conscience."
• Her words show that she is an adulteress, not a professional prostitute. Compare 6:34–35, where a wronged husband's jealousy "will not spare in the day of vengeance."
• Compare Hebrews 4:13: "all things are naked and open to the eyes of Him to whom we must give account."
units.summary: Temptation rarely says, "This is right"; it says, "No one will know."
units.principle: When the only question we ask is whether we will be caught, we have already forgotten the God who sees.
units.insight: David also reasoned that no one would know. While Bathsheba's husband was away at war, David took her, and when she conceived he tried to cover it up (2 Samuel 11:4–15). But "the thing that David had done displeased the LORD" (11:27), and Nathan told him, "you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel" (12:12). Many people's purity rests on the fear of being caught; take away the risk and their resolve disappears. That is only caution, not purity. God wants a heart that stays faithful when no one is watching, because He is watching. And for those who have already sinned in secret, David's story does not end with exposure. "I have sinned against the LORD," he said, and Nathan answered, "The LORD also has put away your sin" (12:13).
units.application: Test your integrity by asking what you would do if you were certain no one would ever find out. If you travel for work, or your spouse does, set up accountability for those seasons: regular calls, shared locations, a friend who asks. Married couples, speak warmly of your spouse to others; refusing to name or honor a spouse, as she does, is often a sign of a heart drifting away. If you are hiding something, remember that secrecy is not safety.

rel.note: A man's heart plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps, so her careful plan leaves out the One who rules outcomes.
She calculates her husband's return but forgets the LORD, who ponders all of a person's paths.
This verse completes the assurance begun there that her husband is far away.
Folly promises secret pleasure while hiding that the dead are there, the same concealed destination.

units.notes:
• "The appointed day" is literally "the day of the full moon," and the ESV and NASB read "full moon." The Hebrew word occurs elsewhere only in Psalm 81:3, "At the full moon." The KJV margin offers "the new moon," and Ironside's rendering reads "at the day of the new moon."
• Henry suggests she may be painting her husband as careless with money to excuse herself: "Whether justly or not, she insinuates that he was a bad husband… it is often groundlessly suggested, but is never a sufficient excuse."
• Compare Numbers 32:23, "be sure your sin will find you out," and Galatians 6:7, "God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."
units.summary: The seductress planned around her husband's schedule but not around God's eyes.
units.principle: Sin plans carefully for human consequences and forgets the God who sees and the day of reckoning that surely comes.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man who planned carefully for years ahead and forgot God. "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). The seductress's planning is detailed: the trip, the money, the date of return. Sin is often well organized. We clear the browser history, choose the time, arrange the excuse. What we leave out of the calculation is God. Yet the day of reckoning is not only a warning. For those who have run to Christ, the day He returns is a day of hope, because "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). The person who lives ready for that day has no need to plan around it.
units.application: Notice when you are doing the logistics of sin: planning times, hiding records, preparing excuses in advance. That planning is itself a warning sign; stop and tell someone. If your work takes you away from home, guard your marriage by staying in touch daily and deciding where you will be in the evenings. If you are the one at home, guard your evenings too. Anyone who has made a careful plan to sin, put God into the calculation before you take the next step.

rel.note: The immoral woman's mouth is smoother than oil, the persuasive smoothness that wins here.
The father's commands were meant to keep the son from the flattering tongue of a seductress, the tongue that prevails over this young man.
Against her enticing speech, the father calls his children to pay attention to the words of his mouth.
The father warned at the start that her danger lay in her flattering words, and here that warning comes true.

units.notes:
• "Enticing speech" translates leqach, the word rendered "learning" in 1:5 and "doctrine" in 4:2. The father's teaching and her persuasion are described with the same word, two teachers competing for one student. The ESV has "seductive speech" and the NASB "many persuasions."
• "Seduced" translates a verb meaning to drive or push along; the KJV reads, "with the flattering of her lips she forced him."
• Bridges, quoting South: "Man cannot be ruined till he has been made confident to the contrary." In other words, a man must first be persuaded that he is safe.
• Henry: "His corruptions at length triumphed over his convictions."
• Compare 5:3 and 6:24, the father's earlier warnings about her smooth tongue.
units.summary: Temptation rarely wins the argument; it wins by being given the floor.
units.principle: Whoever keeps listening to temptation will eventually be carried by it; resistance must be settled before the persuasion begins.
units.insight: A man of God received a clear command not to eat or drink in Bethel. Then an old prophet met him and claimed, "an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD," but the old prophet was lying (1 Kings 13:18). The man of God listened, went back, and a lion killed him on the road (13:24). He knew God's word, but he let a persuasive voice override it. That is the danger of this verse. We rarely fall at the first word; we fall after we have listened long enough. Ask yourself whose arguments you keep entertaining. James gives the answer: "Resist the devil and he will flee from you. Draw near to God and He will draw near to you" (James 4:7–8).
units.application: Stop negotiating with temptation. When an inner voice or an outside one starts building a case for sin, end the conversation instead of answering every argument: close the chat, leave the room, hang up. Married people, do not keep up flirtatious banter "just for fun." Young people, notice how long you let a persuasive friend talk before you say no. Counselors and pastors, help people see that the fall usually comes after the listening, not before it.

rel.note: The prudent man foresees evil and hides himself, while the simple pass on and are punished, as this young man does.
The wicked are caught in the cords of their own sin and die for lack of instruction, the same self-made trap.
Calamity comes suddenly on the wicked man, the same suddenness that marks this fall.
The pictures of the ox and the fool continue into the arrow and the snare of the next verse.

units.notes:
• "Immediately" translates pit'om, "suddenly," the word used of sudden calamity in 3:25 and 6:15. Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Suddenly (Proverbs 3:25; 6:15) fixes the moment of decision…"
• The second image is read in different ways. The NKJV and KJV have "as a fool to the correction of the stocks," and the NASB "as one in fetters to the discipline of a fool." The ESV, the NLT and the 1984 NIV picture a stag or deer caught in a trap, reading the difficult Hebrew differently. The word the NKJV renders "stocks" refers to an ankle chain, which explains "fetters." All the readings describe a creature walking unaware into restraint or death.
• Bridges: "As the ox goeth to the slaughter, unconscious of his fate, perhaps dreaming of rich pasture."
• Compare Jeremiah 11:19, "I was like a docile lamb brought to the slaughter," and Isaiah 53:7.
units.summary: Sudden falls are slow decisions finally coming due.
units.principle: Small compromises left unchecked end in a moment of yielding, and the one who takes them walks toward ruin without seeing it.
units.insight: Esau traded his birthright for one bowl of stew in a single moment, but Genesis names the deeper problem: "Thus Esau despised his birthright" (Genesis 25:32–34). Hebrews holds him up as a warning against being "a fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright" (Hebrews 12:16). Many people say of their fall, "It just happened." This verse says otherwise. Look back at your own small steps; they are leading somewhere. Scripture gives one more picture of a lamb led to slaughter. Of Christ, Isaiah wrote, "He was led as a lamb to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7). The young man walked blindly to death for his own sin. Jesus, "knowing all things that would come upon Him" (John 18:4), walked to death for ours, so that those who have gone the young man's way can be forgiven and set free.
units.application: Trace your own patterns backward. If you have fallen before, write down the steps that came first, such as tiredness, loneliness, a certain place or time, a first click, and put a guard at the earliest one. Recovery groups and accountability partners, focus on early steps, not just the final act. Parents, teach teenagers that big decisions are usually made in small moments long before the crisis. When you feel the "suddenly" coming, call someone before, not after.

rel.note: Whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, the hope offered to anyone who has fallen into this snare.
The cords of a man's own sin hold him, and he dies for lack of instruction.
An adulteress preys upon a man's precious life, the cost named here.
This verse completes the pictures of the ox and the fool begun there.
Folly's guest does not know that the dead are there, just as this young man did not know it would cost his life.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads, "Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The arrow piercing the liver may refer to the pangs of a guilty conscience…" Even so, the image is first of a fatal wound.
• Bridges sums up the exchange: "for a cup of pleasure drinking an ocean of wrath!"
• Compare 1:17–19, where the violent "lie in wait for their own blood," and Ecclesiastes 9:12, "Like birds caught in a snare, So the sons of men are snared in an evil time."
• Compare 9:18, "But he does not know that the dead are there," and James 1:15, "sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death."
units.summary: The seductress promised a night of love; it lasted only until the arrow struck.
units.principle: Sin hides its price until the bill comes due, and its wages are death; only Christ's gift of life answers that cost.
units.insight: Every sin hides its price. The bird sees only the bait, and the young man sees only the night. Paul names the price plainly: "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23). That death is more than a funeral. It is a marriage broken, a conscience defiled, a walk with God grown cold. But Paul's sentence does not end there: "the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The prodigal son also went after pleasure and found it cost him everything (Luke 15:13–16). When he came to himself and turned home, his father "ran and fell on his neck and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). If you have already paid some of this price, do not stay in the snare. "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).
units.application: Count the cost before temptation does the counting for you. Write down who would be hurt if you went ahead: your spouse, your children, your church, your own walk with God. Parents, talk with your teenagers about consequences without scare tactics; show both the real cost and the real hope. If you are in the snare now, reach out today to a pastor, counselor or trusted friend. Confession breaks the trap's hold; secrecy tightens it.

rel.note: The father makes the same appeal to his children to hear him in the middle of his earlier warning about the immoral woman.
The father who opened by asking his son to keep his words closes by asking all his children to listen to them.
The father's words are set against the enticing speech and flattering lips that carried the young man away.
What the father saw from his window is the ground of the appeal he now makes.
Wisdom opens her closing appeal with the identical words, "Now therefore, listen to me, my children."

units.notes:
• "My children" is literally "sons," the same address as in 4:1 and 5:7; Ironside's rendering reads "O ye sons." Wisdom opens her own closing appeal with the identical words, "Now therefore, listen to me, my children" (8:32).
• Bridges calls the chapter "God's solemn warning to children, whether in years, understanding, or experience."
• Henry: "give ear to a father, and not to an enemy."
• Compare Hebrews 12:5, where the Father's instruction in Proverbs speaks to believers "as to sons."
units.summary: The father told the story for one reason: so his children would not become its sequel.
units.principle: Every life is shaped by the voices it listens to; the wise learn from another's ruin by giving their attention to the voice that tells the truth.
units.insight: Eli warned his sons about their sin, including their immorality with the women at the tabernacle door. "Nevertheless they did not heed the voice of their father" (1 Samuel 2:22–25). The warnings were given; they were not received. The difference between the young man in the story and the son who survives is not information but attention. Both heard voices; only one listened to the right one. Whose words have most of your attention right now: Scripture, or the steady stream of voices on your phone? On the mount of transfiguration the Father spoke from the cloud: "This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!" (Mark 9:7). Christ's voice is the last word over every other, and He says, "My sheep hear My voice" (John 10:27).
units.application: Give the father's voice more time than the tempter's: set a daily window for Scripture before you pick up your phone. Parents, do not stop at one talk about sexual purity; this father warned in chapters 2, 5, 6 and 7. Keep the conversation open through the teen years. Young adults, seek out an older believer whose words you will invite into your decisions. Pastors, preach the warnings of Proverbs plainly; your people are hearing other voices every day.

rel.note: The son is told not to enter the path of the wicked but to turn away from it and pass on.
The father joins keeping the heart with pondering the path of the feet, the same two guards commanded here.
The son is told to remove his way far from her and not go near the door of her house.
The young man took the path to her house, the very step this command forbids.

units.notes:
• "Turn aside" translates satah, the verb used in Numbers 5:12 for a wife who "goes astray" from her husband, and in 4:15, "Turn away from it and pass on." So the word carries a hint of unfaithfulness even in the heart's first leaning.
• Bridges: "Familiarity with sin weakens abhorrence." He adds, "Dread the first step, and dream not that you can stop yourself at pleasure in her course" ("at pleasure" means whenever you choose).
• Compare 4:23–27, where guarding the heart is joined to watching where the feet go, and 5:8, "Remove your way far from her."
• Compare 1 Corinthians 6:18, "Flee sexual immorality."
units.summary: Guard the heart before it leans, and the feet will not need rescuing later.
units.principle: Sin is best resisted at its beginning: guard the heart's first leaning and refuse the first step onto the wrong road.
units.insight: The man who wrote these warnings did not keep them. When Solomon was old, "his wives turned his heart after other gods; and his heart was not loyal to the LORD his God" (1 Kings 11:4). Wisdom known is not the same as wisdom kept. Your heart leans somewhere every day, so ask where it is leaning. Notice whether your thoughts drift toward a person, a website or a fantasy when you are tired or bored. Paul gives both sides of the escape. Our part: "Flee also youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace" (2 Timothy 2:22). God's part: "God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The way out is real, and it usually comes early.
units.application: Build your way of escape before you need it. Name the "paths" that lead toward sexual sin for you, such as certain apps, late-night hours or private conversations, and close one this week. Married couples, keep your hearts turned toward each other with regular, unhurried time together. Youth leaders, teach students to decide their boundaries in advance. When your heart starts to lean, pray at once and change your setting; do not wait to see how far it goes.

rel.note: Pride goes before destruction, which is why strong men who trust their strength are the ones she casts down.
No one can carry fire against his chest without being burned, however strong he is.
Whoever commits adultery destroys his own soul and gets wounds and dishonor that are not wiped away.

units.notes:
• Translations take the word rendered "strong men" ('atsumim) in two ways. The NKJV and KJV understand it as strength; the ESV and 1984 NIV read "a mighty throng" and the NASB "numerous," understanding it as great number.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The language of Proverbs 7:26 is military in tone. The lady who was so desirable has slain whole armies."
• Scripture names strong men who fell to sexual sin: Samson (Judges 16), David (2 Samuel 11) and Solomon. Nehemiah said of Solomon, "Nevertheless pagan women caused even him to sin" (Nehemiah 13:26).
• Compare 1 Corinthians 10:12, "let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall."
units.summary: The seductress's victims were not weaklings; they were strong men who trusted their strength.
units.principle: No one is too strong, gifted or experienced to fall into sexual sin, and self-confidence is itself a step toward ruin.
units.insight: Samson tore apart a lion with his bare hands, yet he could not stand against Delilah (Judges 14:6; 16:15–17). David killed Goliath, yet he fell after one look from a rooftop (2 Samuel 11:2–4). Their stories warn that gifts, victories and spiritual experiences do not make anyone safe. Bridges: "Self-confidence has ruined many a promising profession," that is, many who once professed faith with great promise. The most dangerous thought is "That could never be me," and it comes easily to people in ministry and leadership. Yet even this verse leaves room for grace. David, among the wounded, cried, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10), and God restored him. Christ's strength is made perfect in the weakness we finally admit (2 Corinthians 12:9).
units.application: Leaders, pastors and anyone with influence: do not trust your track record. Put guardrails in place that assume you could fall, such as openness with your spouse, accountability with peers and care with one-on-one meetings. Older believers, do not assume temptation is only for the young. If you see a respected friend drifting, speak up gently and early. And if you have fallen, remember that the road back runs through confession, not concealment.

rel.note: The immoral woman's house leads down to death, and none who go to her return.
Her feet go down to death and her steps lay hold of hell, the same destination.
The chapter that opens with "Keep my commands and live" closes at the chambers of death.
Wisdom has built her house and spread her table, offering life to the simple who turn in, the opposite of this house.
Folly calls the simple into her house with the same lie, and her guests are in the depths of hell.

units.notes:
• "Hell" translates Sheol, the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead; the ESV and NASB keep "Sheol." "Chambers" are inner rooms, the word used when the bride says, "The king has brought me into his chambers" (Song of Songs 1:4).
• Gemser, quoted by Waltke and Guzik: "Her bedroom is no ballroom, but a battlefield where corpses lie about…"
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "In the hour of sin's glamor it is good for the soul to look through to the end…"
• Compare 2:18–19, "For her house leads down to death," and 5:5, "Her feet go down to death, Her steps lay hold of hell."
• In the light of the New Testament the image reaches into a person's relationship with God: James calls friendship with the world spiritual adultery (James 4:4), and Revelation sets the harlot (Revelation 17) against the Bride of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7). This deeper application does not replace the literal warning about adultery.
units.summary: The seductress's bedroom was furnished for pleasure and built as a stairway down to death.
units.principle: Every path of sin, however pleasant its entrance, leads downward to death, while Wisdom's house leads to life.
units.insight: This is the father's last word, and it is meant to frighten us off a deadly path. But Scripture never leaves the warning without a way. Her house is "the way to hell"; Jesus says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). In the light of the New Testament, the One who calls from Wisdom's house is Christ Himself, and His table gives life. Some readers are already inside her house. Remember the thief who was dying beside Jesus. With almost nothing left, he said, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom," and he heard, "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:42–43). It is never too late to walk out of her house and into His.
units.application: Look past the doorway of any temptation to where the stairway leads, and say the destination out loud. Parents, finish conversations about purity with both the warning and the gospel: there is a way out and a way back. If you are caught in an affair or an addiction, take one step out this week: end the contact, tell your pastor or a trusted friend, and seek counsel. Churches, be a place where people can admit they are in her house and find help to leave.

rel.note: Wisdom first raises her voice in the open squares and at the city gates, the same public call that opens this chapter.
The seductress works in the twilight and the dark, while Wisdom calls aloud in the open.
The open call described here becomes Wisdom's own first-person address to all people.
Wisdom again cries out from the highest places of the city as she invites the simple to her table.

units.notes:
• The question expects agreement: "Of course she does." Verses 1–3 describe Wisdom in the third person; from verse 4 to the end of the chapter she speaks as "I."
• The word translated "wisdom," chokmah, is a feminine noun, and it is the same word throughout Proverbs. That grammar explains why Wisdom is pictured as a woman, but it proves nothing about who she is. The identification with Christ rests on the New Testament (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30; Colossians 2:3), not on Hebrew grammar.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "A chapter which is to soar beyond time and space, opens at street-level…" The poem that will reach back before creation (8:22–31) begins in the public places of an ordinary town.
• Jesus also called out in public: on the last day of the feast He "stood and cried out" (John 7:37).
• Compare 1:20–21, where Wisdom first raises her voice in the open squares, and 9:3, where she "cries out from the highest places of the city."
units.summary: Sin whispered in the dark; Wisdom shouts in the daylight, so no one can say they never heard her.
units.principle: God's wisdom does not hide; it calls openly to everyone, so no one misses it for lack of a voice.
units.insight: Chapter 7 left a young man walking into the dark. Chapter 8 opens with a voice that has been calling the whole time. That is how God deals with people. After Adam hid among the trees, the LORD God came calling, "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). At the feast in Jerusalem Jesus "stood and cried out," inviting the thirsty to come to Him and drink (John 7:37). Wisdom's voice is the voice of Christ, and He still calls loudly enough to be heard over our noise. The question is not whether He is speaking but whether we are listening. Many people say God has gone silent when they have simply stopped listening, or have listened only to the whisper at the corner. The answer is not to strain for some new voice but to turn toward the One who has never stopped calling.
units.application: If you have drifted, stop telling yourself God has been silent. This week, read one of the Gospels and listen again to Christ's public voice. Parents, do not leave your children to hear only the world's whispers; speak about wisdom openly at the table and in the car. Preachers and teachers, call as Wisdom does, plainly and in public, and not only to people who already agree.

rel.note: A way that seems right can end in death, which is why Wisdom stands where roads divide.
The father tells his son to ponder the path of his feet and not turn aside, the choice Wisdom calls for where the paths meet.
The young man turns down the path to the seductress's house at the very kind of crossroads where Wisdom takes her stand.
The chapter that opens at the fork in the road closes there, with life for those who find Wisdom and death for those who hate her.

units.notes:
• "Where the paths meet" renders a Hebrew phrase that reads literally "a house of paths," a place where roads come together. The KJV has "in the places of the paths."
• Henry contrasts the adulterous woman, who "spoke in secret," with Wisdom, who "speaks openly; truth seeks no corners, but gladly appeals to the light."
• The crossroads image runs through Scripture: "Stand in the ways and see, And ask for the old paths, where the good way is, And walk in it" (Jeremiah 6:16). Compare Isaiah 30:21, "This is the way, walk in it."
• Jesus set the same two ways before His hearers: the narrow gate that leads to life and the broad way that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13–14).
units.summary: Wisdom waits at the crossroads, not at the crash site.
units.principle: God's wisdom meets us at the point of decision, so the time to listen is before the turn, not after the fall.
units.insight: Every life has crossroads: a first drink, a second look, a shortcut at work, a relationship that should never begin. Most ruin is decided there, in a moment that felt small. Lot looked out over the well-watered plain, chose by sight, and "pitched his tent even as far as Sodom" (Genesis 13:10–12). The rest of his sad story flowed from that fork. Joseph met his crossroads in Potiphar's house and refused: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). Christ stands where our paths meet. He does not wait only at the end of the road to pick up the pieces, though He does that too; He speaks before we turn. The question for the heart is whether we stop at the crossroads long enough to hear Him, or keep walking because the turn feels familiar.
units.application: Before a decision that sets your direction, such as a job offer, a dating relationship or a large purchase, stop at the fork and ask what Wisdom says before you take a step. Young people, learn to recognize the crossroads: the moment you feel the pull toward the seductress's "corner" (7:8), the place of temptation, is the place to turn. Parents and mentors, talk with your children before their big decisions, not only after the damage is done.

rel.note: Wisdom's first speech is also delivered at the openings of the city gates.
The fool has nothing to say in the gate, the very place where Wisdom raises her voice.
Wisdom comes to the doors of the city to call; the blessed person answers by waiting at the posts of her doors.
Wisdom again calls from the public heights of the city when she invites the simple to her house.

units.notes:
• The gate was the center of public life. Boaz settled the matter of Ruth before the elders at the gate (Ruth 4:1–2), and Absalom stood "beside the way to the gate" to win the hearts of Israel (2 Samuel 15:2–6). Wisdom goes to the same place to win hearts for good.
• The KJV reads "at the coming in at the doors." Henry takes the doors as people's homes: "she follows men to their own houses."
• Ironside: "Anywhere and everywhere that men are to be found, there is she—her cry and entreaty sounding above all the bustle of life."
• Jesus taught the same way: "I spoke openly to the world. I always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where the Jews always meet, and in secret I have said nothing" (John 18:20).
units.summary: Wisdom does not wait in a quiet corner; she calls from the hilltop, the crossroads and the busy city gate.
units.principle: God's wisdom is not confined to sacred places; it speaks into the public and ordinary places where life is lived.
units.insight: We tend to think of God's voice as belonging to church buildings and quiet times. Wisdom stands at the gate, where court cases were settled and deals were made. Jesus did the same. He called Matthew from his tax booth (Matthew 9:9), taught on the seashore and in the villages, and could say, "in secret I have said nothing" (John 18:20). The Wisdom of God walks into the places where we buy, sell, argue and decide. That is both a comfort and a challenge. It is a comfort, because there is no place where His voice cannot reach us. It is a challenge, because there is no place where we can claim His word does not apply. The heart's quiet evasion is to keep Christ for Sunday and handle Monday's gate by other rules.
units.application: Name your "gates": the office, the job site, the group chat, the school board meeting. Listen for Wisdom's word there, not only in church. Business owners and employees, bring Scripture's standards into contracts, deadlines and sales calls. Believers in public roles, speak wisdom where decisions are made, with grace and clarity, instead of saving it for private conversations.

rel.note: Wisdom's first speech also calls the simple and promises to make her words known to all who turn.
The public cry described in the opening verse becomes Wisdom's direct address here.
Wisdom calls the sons of men because, as the creation poem reveals, her delight was with the sons of men.
Wisdom's open invitation, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here," carries the same wide welcome.

units.notes:
• "Sons of men" is a Hebrew way of saying "human beings." The same phrase frames Wisdom's speech: she calls the sons of men here and delights in them in 8:31.
• Henry stresses how wide the call is: Wisdom speaks "not to you, O scholars! but to you, O men! O sons of men! even the meanest." In his English, "the meanest" means the lowliest.
• Bridges hears the gospel's open offer in this verse: "It is the proclamation of the Gospel 'to every creature.'" He is quoting Mark 16:15.
• Compare Isaiah 55:1 ("Ho! Everyone who thirsts, Come to the waters") and Matthew 11:28 ("Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest").
units.summary: Wisdom's invitation is addressed to the whole human race, and your name is on the envelope.
units.principle: God's call to wisdom is addressed to every human being, before any of us has made ourselves worthy of it.
units.insight: Wisdom does not send out a select invitation. Jesus called fishermen and a tax collector, and He spoke with a Samaritan woman whom others avoided (John 4:7–9). At Cornelius's house Peter learned, "In truth I perceive that God shows no partiality" (Acts 10:34). The phrase "sons of men" ties Wisdom's call to her delight: Christ calls us because He delights in us (8:31), not because we have impressed Him. Some hearts hear the call and think, "Not me; I am too far gone." Others think, "Not them; they are too far gone." This verse answers both. Wisdom's voice is "to the sons of men." Your name is in that address, and so is the name of the person you have written off.
units.application: If you have felt shut out from God's wisdom because of your past or your background, read this verse as spoken to you by name. Church leaders, look at who your ministry actually reaches and ask whom you have quietly left out. Believers, invite the coworker or neighbor you assumed would not be interested; Wisdom's call is addressed to them too.

rel.note: Wisdom's first speech also addresses the simple and fools and promises her words to those who turn.
The book was written to give prudence to the simple, the very gift Wisdom offers here.
The simple young man devoid of understanding shows where the simple end up if they refuse the understanding heart Wisdom offers.
The prudence Wisdom offers the simple here is the companion she says she lives with.
Wisdom again calls the simple and the one who lacks understanding to forsake foolishness and live.

units.notes:
• The simple (peti) are uncommitted: not set against wisdom, but not committed to it, and so easily led; "The simple believes every word" (14:15). The fool (kesil) is morally deficient and despises instruction (1:7). Wisdom calls both.
• "Prudence" ('ormah) is shrewd, practical good sense. A related word, used of the "prudent" man in 14:15, describes the serpent as "cunning" in Genesis 3:1. The same sharpness can serve evil or good; Wisdom puts it to good use.
• "Be of an understanding heart" reads literally "understand heart," with the same verb as "understand prudence" in the first line. "Heart" here means inner sense and judgment, which is why the ESV has "learn sense" and the NASB "understand wisdom."
• Henry: "Though you are ever so simple, Wisdom will take you for her scholars."
• Compare 1:4, 1:22 and 9:4–6, where Wisdom tells the simple, "Forsake foolishness and live."
units.summary: Wisdom begins with her least promising students and offers each of them exactly what he lacks.
units.principle: No one is too simple or too foolish to be invited to wisdom, but the invitation must be answered.
units.insight: Jesus did the same thing: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance" (Luke 5:32). He chose Peter, who spoke before he thought, and Thomas, who doubted. Paul reminded the Corinthians that "not many wise according to the flesh" were called, yet Christ became for them "wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:26, 30). That is hope for anyone who knows his own record of foolish choices. The verse also searches the heart. The simple person's danger is drift, and the fool's danger is refusing to be taught. Wisdom offers an understanding heart, but she offers it to people who will stop and listen. Which describes you more today: drifting, or resisting?
units.application: If you have been drifting, name one area where you need prudence, such as money, a relationship or your phone habits, and ask a wise friend for counsel this week. Parents and youth leaders, do not give up on the teenager who seems not to care; Wisdom starts with the simple. If you mentor someone who keeps repeating the same mistake, keep offering wisdom with patience and hope.

rel.note: The book's purpose includes receiving equity, the same uprightness that marks Wisdom's words.
The wise teacher also offers "excellent things" so that the hearer may know the certainty of the words of truth.
The seductress wins the young man with flattering lips, the opposite of Wisdom's right and upright words.
Wisdom's promise of right things is filled out: every word is righteous and none is crooked.

units.notes:
• "Excellent things" translates negidim, the plural of a word for a leader or prince, so Wisdom promises princely, noble words. The ESV and NASB have "noble things." Henry: "princely things, so the word is."
• "Right things" translates a word for what is level and upright. The same word appears as "equity" in the book's purpose statement (1:3).
• The seductress "flatters with her words" (7:5), and "With her flattering lips she seduced him" (7:21). Wisdom's speech is the opposite: it is level, not slippery.
• Compare Psalm 19:8, "The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart," and John 7:46, where the officers sent to arrest Jesus said, "No man ever spoke like this Man!"
units.summary: Smooth words slide down easily and lead astray; straight words may sting, but they lead home.
units.principle: Words worth hearing are measured by whether they are true and right, not by whether they are pleasant.
units.insight: The officers sent to arrest Jesus came back empty-handed, saying, "No man ever spoke like this Man!" (John 7:46). His words were princely and straight at the same time. He told the woman at the well the truth about her five husbands, and in the same conversation He offered her living water (John 4:10–18). Our hearts, though, are drawn to smooth words. We follow the voices that flatter us and avoid the friend, preacher or passage that cuts straight. The seductress succeeded because her words were easy to swallow. Wisdom asks for a hearing because her words are worth more, even when they cost us something. Whose voice do you go to when you want to feel better, and whose when you need the truth?
units.application: This week, notice which voices you seek out: podcasts, friends, feeds. Add one that tells you the truth plainly. If you counsel, teach or parent, speak straight words with grace rather than smooth words that avoid the issue. Pastors and small-group leaders, offer your best teaching to new believers and strugglers, not only to the mature.

rel.note: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, the same revulsion Wisdom's lips feel toward wickedness.
Every word of God is pure, as every word from Wisdom's mouth is true.
A lying tongue stands among the things the LORD hates, which Wisdom hates with Him.
Wisdom names the perverse mouth among the things she hates, the same hatred of false speech.

units.notes:
• "Truth" ('emet) comes from a root meaning firm or reliable, the same root behind the word "amen." True words are words you can stand on.
• "Abomination" (to'evah) is what the LORD detests: 3:32; 6:16; 11:1, 20; 12:22. Here Wisdom's lips share that revulsion.
• Set against "truth," the "wickedness" in view is above all false speech. Henry draws the lesson for believers: "His word to us is yea, and amen; never then let ours be yea and nay." In plain terms, God's word is settled and sure, so ours should not waver between yes and no.
• Compare John 14:6 ("I am the way, the truth, and the life"), Titus 1:2 (God "who cannot lie") and Revelation 3:14, where Christ is "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness."
units.summary: Wisdom does not merely avoid lies; she finds them as revolting as the LORD does.
units.principle: Truth is not only a rule to keep but a character to share; the wise come to hate falsehood as God does.
units.insight: Jesus did not only tell the truth; He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Revelation calls Him "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness" (Revelation 3:14). Wisdom's lips find wickedness detestable because truth is her nature. Our trouble is that we tolerate falsehoods we would never call lies: the padded résumé, the excuse to the boss, the half-story that makes us look better. Ananias and Sapphira's lie concerned only the price of a field, yet Peter said Ananias had lied "to the Holy Spirit" (Acts 5:1–4). The goal is not only fewer lies but a new taste, a heart that, like Christ's, finds deceit distasteful. That taste grows as we spend time with the One who is the truth.
units.application: Watch for the small falsehoods you have stopped noticing: inflated numbers, convenient excuses, "I'm almost there" when you have not left. Correct one this week. Employees and business owners, refuse to shade reports or sales claims even when everyone else does. Parents, let your children hear you tell the truth when it costs you, such as admitting a mistake or returning extra change.

rel.note: Evil men speak perverse things and walk crooked ways, the twisting that has no place in Wisdom's words.
Every word of God is pure, as every word of Wisdom is righteous.
The father tells his son to put away a deceitful mouth and perverse lips, so that his speech matches Wisdom's.
Wisdom promised right things from her lips; here she shows there is no exception to that promise.

units.notes:
• "Crooked" comes from a verb meaning to twist, and "perverse" means bent or distorted. Words from the same two roots describe Israel as "A perverse and crooked generation" in Deuteronomy 32:5, a phrase Paul echoes in Philippians 2:15.
• The KJV has "nothing froward or perverse." "Froward" is older English for stubbornly contrary.
• Even true words can be bent into error, as when Satan quoted Psalm 91:11 to Jesus with a twist (Matthew 4:6–7). Of Wisdom's words Bridges says, "But here all is unchangeable righteousness."
• Compare 2:15, where evil men are those "Whose ways are crooked"; 4:24; and Psalm 12:6, "The words of the LORD are pure words."
units.summary: With Wisdom there is no fine print: every word runs straight, and none of them hides a trap.
units.principle: God's word can be trusted whole, because none of it is bent to serve a hidden purpose.
units.insight: In the wilderness Satan quoted Scripture to Jesus, but he bent the promise of Psalm 91 into a dare (Matthew 4:6). Jesus answered with straight words: "It is written again, 'You shall not tempt the LORD your God'" (Matthew 4:7). The serpent's oldest method is the same twist: "Has God indeed said...?" (Genesis 3:1). Twisting is how deception works, whether in the seductress's religious excuse or in our own self-justifications. We rarely tell ourselves outright lies; we bend the truth until it points where we want to go. Christ's words have nothing crooked in them, and they can bear the full weight of a life. The heart question is whether we come to His word to be straightened or to find a verse that will bend our way.
units.application: When you read Scripture, ask what it says before asking how it supports you. Watch for twisted reasoning in your own decisions, such as calling greed "providing" or gossip "sharing a concern." Leaders and teachers, refuse to bend a text to support a point you had already decided to make. Friends, if someone is twisting God's word to excuse sin, say so gently and plainly.

rel.note: Knowledge is easy to him who understands, while the scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it.
The book admits enigmas and riddles, so the plainness of Wisdom's words belongs to the willing learner rather than to every saying alike.
The LORD Himself gives wisdom and understanding, which is why the willing find her words clear.

units.notes:
• "Plain" describes what lies straight ahead in full view; the ESV has "straight." The point is not that wisdom is shallow but that it is open to anyone who wants it.
• Proverbs admits that some sayings are hard: it was written "To understand a proverb and an enigma, The words of the wise and their riddles" (1:6).
• Bridges: "Scripture difficulties belong not to the Book itself, but to man's blind and corrupt heart."
• Bishop Reynolds, quoted by Bridges, says that in God's word "the wisest Solomon may fetch jewels for ornament, and the poorest Lazarus bread for life."
• Compare Psalm 119:130 ("The entrance of Your words gives light; It gives understanding to the simple"), John 7:17 and Luke 24:45.
units.summary: Wisdom's words are plain to the willing; the hardest part of God's word is often obeying it.
units.principle: Understanding God's wisdom depends more on a willing heart than on a brilliant mind, and it grows as it is put into practice.
units.insight: Jesus said, "If anyone wills to do His will, he shall know concerning the doctrine" (John 7:17). Willingness comes before clarity. The disciples had heard the Scriptures all their lives, yet they missed their meaning until the risen Christ "opened their understanding" (Luke 24:45). Our confusion is not always a matter of the mind. Often a passage feels unclear because it is unwelcome; we understand enough to know it will cost us. The scribes could quote Micah's prophecy of Bethlehem to Herod, yet Scripture gives no sign that they went to see the Child (Matthew 2:4–6). Christ still opens minds and hearts. Ask Him first to make you willing, and clarity will follow.
units.application: When a passage seems confusing, first obey what is already plain in it, then ask about the rest. New believers, do not let anyone convince you the Bible is only for experts; read it with a willing heart and a simple prayer. Teachers, admit the hard texts openly while showing that the main paths of wisdom are clear enough to walk today.

rel.note: It is much better to get wisdom than gold and understanding rather than silver.
Wisdom's proceeds are better than silver and her gain than fine gold.
The next verse gives the reason for this choice: wisdom is better than rubies.
Wisdom returns to the same comparison: her fruit is better than fine gold and her revenue than choice silver.
The instruction Wisdom ranks above silver is the instruction she later urges her children to hear and not disdain.

units.notes:
• "Instruction" (musar) is discipline that trains, including correction. The same word returns in 8:33, "Hear instruction and be wise."
• "Not silver" means "rather than silver," a common Hebrew way of ranking two things. Hosea 6:6 speaks the same way: "For I desire mercy and not sacrifice."
• "Choice gold" is a poetic term for the finest gold the market could offer.
• Solomon made this choice at Gibeon, asking for "an understanding heart" rather than riches (1 Kings 3:9–13).
• Compare 3:14; 16:16; Psalm 19:10 ("More to be desired are they than gold, Yea, than much fine gold") and Psalm 119:72.
units.summary: The correction you would rather avoid is worth more than the paycheck you would rather have.
units.principle: Whenever what trains us and what enriches us compete, wisdom chooses what trains us.
units.insight: At Gibeon God said to young Solomon, "Ask! What shall I give you?" Solomon asked for an understanding heart rather than riches, and God was pleased (1 Kings 3:5–11). Yet in later years Solomon made silver as common as stones and let his heart turn after other gods (1 Kings 10:27; 11:4). Choosing wisdom over wealth is not a single decision but a daily one. Judas made the opposite choice. He walked beside Wisdom in person and sold Him for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). The heart that loves money will always find correction too expensive. Christ offers instruction worth more than anything we could be paid, and He Himself is the treasure (Colossians 2:3).
units.application: Before taking a job, promotion or deal, ask whether it will cost you the teaching, church life or accountability that keeps you wise. When correction comes from a boss, a spouse or an elder, receive it as something worth more than a bonus. Young adults, choose mentors and settings that will train you, even if another path pays more at first.

rel.note: Getting wisdom is much better than getting gold.
The book closes by measuring the virtuous wife with the same comparison, wisdom lived out in a life.
The father had already said that wisdom is more precious than rubies and that nothing desired compares with her.
This verse gives the reason for Wisdom's call to choose instruction over silver and gold.

units.notes:
• "Rubies" (peninim) names a precious stone or jewel that cannot be identified with certainty. Lexicons suggest coral or pearls, and the ESV and NASB have "jewels."
• The verse nearly repeats 3:15, and 31:10 uses the same measure for the virtuous wife: "her worth is far above rubies."
• Job's poem on wisdom makes the same point: no gold or gem can buy it, "For the price of wisdom is above rubies" (Job 28:18).
• Ironside applies the verse to God's written word: "The best writings of the best men are not to be compared with it."
• Compare Matthew 13:45–46, the merchant who sold all he had to buy one pearl of great price.
units.summary: List everything you have ever wanted, and Wisdom still outweighs the whole list.
units.principle: Nothing a person can desire is worth trading for wisdom, because wisdom shapes how every other good is used.
units.insight: Jesus told of a merchant who found "one pearl of great price" and "went and sold all that he had and bought it" (Matthew 13:46). Paul, who once had every credential, counted it all loss "for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). In Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). Most of us agree that wisdom is precious, but our calendars and bank statements reveal what we actually treasure. Moses weighed the same choice and chose well, "esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt" (Hebrews 11:26). What do the hours of your week say you believe is beyond compare?
units.application: Write down the three things you want most this year, then ask yourself whether you would trade any of them for wisdom. Look at where your money and time went last week, and move one thing toward getting wisdom: a book, a mentor, an hour in Scripture. Parents, praise character in your children more than trophies, grades or looks.

rel.note: The prudent show their wisdom by understanding their own way, practical wisdom at work.
The book was written to give prudence, knowledge and discretion, the very companions Wisdom names here.
When wisdom enters the heart, discretion and understanding come with her to guard a person.
The prudence Wisdom offers the simple is the companion she lives with.

units.notes:
• "Prudence" ('ormah) is the same practical good sense Wisdom offered the simple in 8:5. There she held it out; here she says she lives with it.
• "Discretion" (mezimmot) means plans or purposes. The word can be used in a bad sense, as in "a man of wicked intentions" (12:2), but here it is wise planning that thinks ahead. The KJV's "knowledge of witty inventions" reflects the same idea; in older English "witty" meant skillful or ingenious.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Prudence is defined, wisdom applied to practice; so wherever true wisdom is, it will lead to action."
• Compare 1:4; 2:10–11; 14:8 ("The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way"); and Ephesians 1:8, where God's grace "He made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence."
units.summary: Wisdom is not a theory shut up in a library; she lives under the same roof as practical good sense.
units.principle: True wisdom always comes down to earth; it shows itself in sound practical judgment and careful planning.
units.insight: Scripture shows wisdom living with prudence in ordinary skill. Bezalel was filled "with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exodus 31:3). Abigail's quick, sensible planning kept David from shedding blood in anger (1 Samuel 25:18–33). Henry applies the verse to the greatest plan of all, our salvation: "We had found out many inventions for our ruin; he found out one for our recovery." Christ, the Wisdom of God, did not merely know what was right; He planned and carried out our rescue. Many believers keep faith in one compartment and practical decisions in another. Wisdom refuses that split. If Christ dwells in you, His wisdom should show up in your budget, your calendar and the way you handle conflict.
units.application: Pick one practical area your faith has not yet reached, such as your budget, your schedule or how you will approach a hard family conversation, and apply wisdom there this week. Planners and managers, pray over your plans and then plan carefully; prudence is not unspiritual. Young adults, learn practical skills like budgeting, cooking and showing up on time as part of following Christ.

rel.note: Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD, the same pride Wisdom hates.
By the fear of the LORD one departs from evil, the practical side of hating it.
The father joins fearing the LORD with departing from evil and refusing to be wise in one's own eyes.
The LORD's list of what He hates also begins with pride and includes lying speech.
Wisdom's lips find wickedness an abomination, the same hatred of evil she names here.

units.notes:
• "Pride and arrogance" translates two Hebrew words that come from the same root and sound alike (ge'ah and ga'on). Naming pride twice, with two forms of the same word, stresses pride in every form it takes.
• Proverbs 16:6 shows the practical side of this definition: "by the fear of the LORD one departs from evil." Hating evil is not only a feeling; it turns a person away from evil in what he actually does.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "God's people partake of the Divine nature, and so have God-like both sympathies and antipathies." In plain terms, they come to love what God loves and hate what He hates.
• Bridges: "A proud disciple of a lowly Saviour! how offensive is this contradiction to our Master!"
• Compare 3:7; 6:16–19; 16:5, 18; Psalm 97:10 ("You who love the LORD, hate evil!"); and Romans 12:9 ("Abhor what is evil. Cling to what is good.").
units.summary: To see God rightly is to hate what He hates, and pride is the first thing to go.
units.principle: Reverence for God shows itself in hatred of evil, above all hatred of the pride that puts self in God's place.
units.insight: Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, and his first words were, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" (Isaiah 6:1, 5). Seeing God rightly exposed the sin of his own lips. That is the fear of the LORD: a right view of God that changes what we love and what we hate. King Uzziah went the other way. When he was strong, "his heart was lifted up, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16). Christ, the Wisdom of God, showed His hatred of pride by living its opposite: He "did not come to be served, but to serve" (Matthew 20:28). Most of us find it easy to hate pride in others. Wisdom asks whether we hate it in ourselves: in the need to be right, to be noticed, to be thanked.
units.application: Ask God to show you one place where pride is running your choices, such as refusing to apologize, needing credit or talking down to someone, and deal with it this week. Leaders, invite correction openly and thank the person who gives it. Parents, model repentance by saying "I was wrong" to your children. When you catch yourself excusing your own sharp tongue, call it what Wisdom calls it.

rel.note: No wisdom or counsel succeeds against the LORD, because true counsel belongs to Him.
A wise man is strong, and wise counsel wins the battle: counsel and strength together.
The father urges his son to keep the same sound wisdom, which becomes life to his soul.
Wisdom's counsel and strength are what enable kings to reign and rulers to decree justice.

units.notes:
• "Sound wisdom" (tushiyyah) means practical success, wisdom that works. The father used the same word in 3:21, "Keep sound wisdom and discretion," and said the LORD "stores up sound wisdom for the upright" (2:7).
• "Strength" (gevurah) is might, the power to act. Isaiah 11:2 pairs the same two ideas in describing the Messiah: "The Spirit of counsel and might."
• Henry, applying the verse to Christ: "He is understanding itself."
• Bridges: "His self-existent power is ever ready to execute the purpose of his counsel." In other words, Christ's strength always stands ready to carry out what His counsel has planned.
• Compare 21:30; 24:5–6 ("A wise man is strong"); Isaiah 9:6, where the Child is called "Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God"; and 1 Corinthians 1:24.
units.summary: Good advice without strength stalls, and strength without good advice wrecks; Wisdom brings both.
units.principle: Real wisdom joins sound counsel with the strength to carry it out; knowing what is right is only half of it.
units.insight: Isaiah named the coming Child "Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6): counsel and might in one Person. Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). That matters exactly where most of us fail. Peter knew he should stand by Jesus and promised boldly that he would, yet he denied Him that same night (Matthew 26:33–35, 69–75). He had the counsel without the strength. After Pentecost the same Peter stood before the council and would not be silenced (Acts 4:13, 19–20). Christ does not only tell us what to do; He gives the strength to do it: "I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13). Where are you trying to obey with knowledge alone?
units.application: When you face a hard decision, seek counsel from Scripture and from wise people, then pray for strength to follow through; do not stop at knowing. If you lead a team or a family, pair clear direction with real support so people can carry it out. When you feel too weak for a known duty, such as an apology, breaking a habit or speaking up, ask Christ for strength and take one step today.

rel.note: A throne is established by righteousness, the justice Wisdom enables rulers to decree.
The king's heart is in the LORD's hand, so even the highest ruler is under God's governance.
Kings reign by the counsel and strength Wisdom claims as her own in the previous verse.
The next verse extends Wisdom's authority from kings to every prince, noble and judge.
The verb for decreeing justice is the verb for God marking out the earth's foundations, so just laws should echo creation's order.

units.notes:
• "Decree" translates a verb meaning to cut in or engrave, and so to fix a rule. The same verb describes God drawing the horizon and marking out the earth's foundations (8:27, 29). Just laws are meant to echo the order God engraved in creation.
• "Rulers" translates a word for high officials or dignitaries; the KJV has "princes."
• Henry: "They reign by him, and therefore ought to reign for him."
• Ironside adds a needed qualification: "It is not that rulers always act according to understanding, but that none rule at all save by the appointment of infinite wisdom."
• Compare Daniel 2:21 ("He removes kings and raises up kings; He gives wisdom to the wise") and Romans 13:1.
units.summary: Every throne that rules well is borrowing its wisdom from a higher throne.
units.principle: All rightful authority depends on God's wisdom and answers to it, whether or not rulers acknowledge it.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar learned this the hard way. He boasted over "great Babylon, that I have built," and was driven out until he knew "that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men" (Daniel 4:30–32). Solomon began his reign by asking for "an understanding heart to judge Your people" (1 Kings 3:9), and Israel saw "that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice" (1 Kings 3:28). Christ is the King by whom kings reign, and every throne answers to His. That steadies believers when politics shakes us. It also humbles anyone with a little authority, whether a manager, a pastor or a parent. Your authority is borrowed, and it is given to serve justice, not yourself.
units.application: If you hold authority at work, in church or at home, ask for wisdom before you make rules, and check those rules against God's justice. Pray by name for those who govern, including leaders you did not vote for (1 Timothy 2:1–2). When political news unsettles you, remember who reigns above every throne, and let that steady your words and your posts.

rel.note: Judges who justify the wicked and condemn the just are an abomination to the LORD, the opposite of rule by wisdom.
The ruler who judges the poor with truth has his throne established, wisdom's justice at work.
Lemuel's mother shows what wise judging looks like: opening the mouth for the poor and judging righteously.
The previous verse begins the list with kings and rulers; this one carries it down to every prince and judge.

units.notes:
• Some Hebrew manuscripts end the verse with the word for "righteousness" instead of "earth," which lies behind the ESV's "all who govern justly" and the NASB's "All who judge rightly." The NKJV and KJV read "earth." The sense of just rule is the same on either reading.
• "Nobles" translates a word that can also mean the generous or willing-hearted, as in Isaiah 32:8, "a generous man devises generous things." True nobility is meant to be generous.
• Bridges: "Every kingdom is a province of the universal empire of the 'King of kings.'"
• Abraham asked the question every judge must face: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" (Genesis 18:25). Compare Psalm 2:10, "Be instructed, you judges of the earth," and Psalm 82:1–4.
units.summary: No judge sits so high that he is not sitting under a wisdom higher still.
units.principle: Every human authority, high or low, is accountable to God's wisdom and exists to carry out His justice.
units.insight: Jehoshaphat set judges in the cities of Judah and charged them, "you do not judge for man but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment" (2 Chronicles 19:5–6). That is this verse put into practice. Pilate thought he held final power, but Jesus answered, "You could have no power at all against Me unless it had been given you from above" (John 19:10–11). Every judge, official and supervisor will one day give account to the Judge of all the earth, the Man God has appointed, Christ Himself (Acts 17:31). That is a sobering word for those who hold power. It is a comforting word for those who have been wronged by power: unjust rulers do not have the last word.
units.application: Officials, supervisors, school administrators and elders: make your next decision as if you will explain it to God, because you will. If someone in authority has treated you unjustly, take it to God in prayer, use proper channels of appeal, and trust that the final Judge sees. Citizens, support leaders who govern justly, not merely those who favor your side.

rel.note: Those who search for wisdom as for hidden treasure will find the knowledge of God.
The father promises that wisdom will keep the one who loves her.
The seductress seeks the young man diligently with the same verb, but her seeking leads to death.
Wisdom's love for those who love her shows itself in the inheritance she gives them.
The diligent seeker of this verse is the one who watches daily at Wisdom's gates.

units.notes:
• "Seek me diligently" here and "Diligently to seek" in 7:15 translate the same Hebrew verb. The KJV has "seek me early," a rendering older preachers used to urge the young to seek God in the morning of life.
• Jesus spoke in the same terms: "He who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and manifest Myself to him" (John 14:21).
• Ironside guards against misreading the verse: "it would be very faulty to limit His love alone to those who return that love." God's love comes first (1 John 4:19); the verse describes the friendship that grows when that love is returned.
• Compare 4:6 ("Love her, and she will keep you"); Jeremiah 29:13 ("And you will seek Me and find Me, when you search for Me with all your heart"); Matthew 7:7–8; and Colossians 2:3.
units.summary: Wisdom returns love for love, and no one who seeks her with all his heart comes away empty.
units.principle: God's love comes first, and those who answer it with love and wholehearted seeking come to know Him more and more.
units.insight: Bridges: "The first kindling of the flame is of him." We love because He first loved us (1 John 4:19). Yet love that is returned grows into closeness. Mary of Bethany sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word, and He said she had chosen "that good part, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:39–42). Zacchaeus "sought to see who Jesus was" and climbed a tree to do it, only to find that Jesus had come "to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:3–10). Seeking Christ is never one-sided. Many of us seek Him casually, when it is convenient, and then wonder why He feels distant. The promise is for those who seek diligently.
