What would it look like for you to seek Him this week the way you would search for buried treasure?
units.application: Set a regular, unhurried time to seek Christ in His word and in prayer, and guard it as you would an important appointment. Young people, do not wait until life settles down; seek Him now. If you feel far from God, do not conclude that He has stopped loving you, because His love came first. Start seeking again, diligently, and expect to find Him.

rel.note: A little with righteousness is better than great revenue without justice, which keeps wisdom's riches in their right order.
Riches, honor and life come by humility and the fear of the LORD, not apart from them.
Riches chased for their own sake fly away like an eagle, unlike the enduring riches joined to righteousness.
The father says wisdom holds riches and honor in her left hand.
Wisdom's riches are found along the paths of righteousness and justice, where she gives her inheritance.

units.notes:
• "Enduring" describes wealth that lasts; the KJV has "durable riches." The pairing with "righteousness" is the key: lasting wealth and right living belong together.
• Henry gives the needed balance: the wise "shall have as much riches and honour as Infinite Wisdom sees good for them."
• Compare 3:16; 10:22; 22:4 ("By humility and the fear of the LORD Are riches and honor and life"); and 23:4–5.
• Jesus spoke of treasure laid up "in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys" (Matthew 6:20), and Paul of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8).
units.summary: Wisdom's riches last because they come joined to righteousness; money without righteousness grows wings.
units.principle: Lasting wealth is wealth joined to righteousness; whatever God gives through wisdom is measured first by right living and His favor.
units.insight: Abraham was rich, yet he refused even "a thread to a sandal strap" from the king of Sodom, so no one could say a pagan king had made him rich (Genesis 14:22–23). His riches and his righteousness went together. Gehazi chased Naaman's silver and came home with leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27). The difference was not the money but the heart. Christ, the Wisdom of God, "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). The enduring riches He gives are first His righteousness and His presence. So the question for us is whether we want what Wisdom gives, or only what we hope she will help us buy.
units.application: Review how you earned and spent money this month; if any income depends on cutting corners, change it. Business owners, build wealth in ways you would gladly explain to God and to your employees. If you are struggling financially while trying to live rightly, do not read this verse as an accusation. God promises to meet needs, and He gives riches that money cannot measure.

rel.note: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, the living fruit that gold cannot match.
A little with righteousness outweighs vast revenues without justice, the same comparison of yield.
Wisdom's proceeds are better than silver and her gain than fine gold.
Wisdom already set her instruction above silver and choice gold.

units.notes:
• "Revenue" translates a word for yield or produce, often the harvest of the land. The same word is "her gain" in 3:14 and "revenues" in 16:8: "Better is a little with righteousness, Than vast revenues without justice."
• "Fine gold" is refined, pure gold, the best grade the market knew.
• Henry Martyn, the missionary, quoted by Bridges, found in God what no wealth gives: "With thee there is no disappointment."
• Compare 3:14; 8:10; 16:16; and Galatians 5:22–23, the fruit of the Spirit.
units.summary: The best return on a life is not what it earns but what wisdom grows in it.
units.principle: What wisdom produces in a person outweighs and outlasts any income, so it deserves first place in what we pursue.
units.insight: Jesus warned that "one's life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses," and told of a rich fool who built bigger barns and died that night (Luke 12:15–21). He had a harvest but no fruit. Compare Paul in a Roman prison, poor in goods, yet able to say, "I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). That contentment was wisdom's fruit. Christ is the vine, and fruit comes from abiding in Him (John 15:5). Our hearts measure success by the balance sheet. Wisdom asks a different question: what is growing in you, such as love, patience and self-control, that no market could buy and no downturn can take away?
units.application: At the end of this week, review it by fruit as well as by income: where did you grow in patience, kindness or self-control? Parents, celebrate character in your children as loudly as you celebrate achievements. If your work pays well but is shrinking your soul, talk with a wise friend about what needs to change. If it pays little but grows good fruit, give thanks.

rel.note: Riches, which 23:5 calls "that which is not," fly away, while Wisdom gives substance, what truly exists.
The father's teaching leads his son to keep to the paths of righteousness, the road Wisdom walks.
The wise inherit glory, the same language of inheritance Wisdom uses for those who love her.
Wisdom's love for those who love her is expressed in the inheritance she gives them.
The enduring riches joined to righteousness are the treasuries Wisdom fills along her road.
The way of righteousness Wisdom walks is the way she later calls her children to keep.

units.notes:
• v20 "Traverse" means to walk about or walk along; the KJV has "I lead." Either way, Wisdom is on the road, not beside it.
• v20 Henry: "In medio virtus--Virtue lies in the midst." Wisdom keeps to the center of the path and keeps her followers from veering to either side (4:27).
• v21 "Wealth" translates yesh, the ordinary Hebrew word for "there is." This is the only place in the Old Testament where it serves as a noun meaning substance, what really exists; the KJV has "substance." Wisdom's gift is what is real, unlike the riches that 23:5 calls "that which is not," wealth that disappears.
• v21 Henry: "All their happiness they have as heirs; it is grounded upon their sonship."
• Compare 2:20; 3:35 ("The wise shall inherit glory"); Psalm 23:3 ("He leads me in the paths of righteousness"); and 1 Peter 1:4, "an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and that does not fade away."
units.summary: The inheritance is found along Wisdom's road, never by a shortcut around it.
units.principle: God's richest gifts are inherited by those who love Him and walk His way; they are received as a child's inheritance, not earned as a wage.
units.insight: "He leads me in the paths of righteousness For His name's sake" (Psalm 23:3). The Shepherd walks the road ahead of His sheep. Abraham walked with God for decades as a stranger in the land he had been promised, for "he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:9–10). His treasury was filled, but not all of it in this life. Christ, the Wisdom of God, makes us heirs: "if children, then heirs—heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:17). Our hearts want the inheritance without the road, the treasury without the righteousness. Wisdom will not divide them. The question is whether we love her, and the Lord she reveals, for who He is, or only for what we hope He will give.
units.application: When a shortcut promises gain, such as a padded expense report or a deal that skirts the law, stay in the middle of the road; the inheritance is found there. Parents, teach your children to work and give as heirs of God, not as people afraid there will never be enough. If you have walked rightly and still struggle financially, take heart: your treasury is not measured by your bank balance.

rel.note: Agur's question about the Creator and "His Son's name" points toward the same eternal Son.
The LORD founded the earth by wisdom, so wisdom was His before the first of His works.
The next verse states plainly what "at the beginning of His way" means: Wisdom was established from everlasting.
The Wisdom who belonged to the LORD before creation is the one who stood beside Him as the world was made.

units.notes:
• The verb rendered "possessed" (qanah) usually means to get or acquire. In a few poetic passages it is used of God as the One who brings something into being, as when Genesis 14:19 calls Him "Possessor of heaven and earth." Translations therefore differ: the NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV have "possessed"; the 1984 NIV "brought me forth"; the NLT "formed me."
• The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, rendered the verb "created." In the fourth century Arius and his followers used that rendering to argue that the Son was a created being. The church rejected the teaching at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325, confessing the Son as "begotten, not made."
• Bridges calls the Greek rendering "most unwarrantable—one of the main pillars of the Arian heresy." "Unwarrantable" means without any justification.
• Ironside: "He was begotten, not in the sense of having beginning of life, but as being of one nature and substance with the Father."
• Compare 3:19 ("The LORD by wisdom founded the earth"); John 1:1–3; John 17:5; and Colossians 1:16–17.
units.summary: God was never without His Wisdom, and the Son was never one of God's creatures.
units.principle: Poetic language about God's Wisdom must be read in the light of Scripture's plain teaching: the Son is the Maker of all things, not one of the things made.
units.insight: The Son we trust is not a creature who rose to greatness but the eternal Word who "was in the beginning with God" (John 1:2). That changes everything about our salvation. Only One who is God could show us the Father fully: "He who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). When Thomas saw the risen Christ, he did not call Him the first of God's works; he said, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Jesus Himself said, "before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58). Our hearts are prone to shrink Christ to a size we can manage, a helpful teacher or a good example. This verse lifts our eyes. The One who calls us at the crossroads (8:2) belonged to the Father before the first star was made, and He never had a beginning. Worship Him as that.
units.application: When someone tells you Jesus was only a great teacher or a created spirit, be ready to open John 1:1–3 and Colossians 1:16–17 with them, patiently and kindly. Parents and Sunday school teachers, teach children early that Jesus did not begin at Bethlehem; He came from the Father. In your own prayers this week, worship Christ as eternal God, not only as your helper.

rel.note: Agur asks who established the ends of the earth and what is His Son's name, the question this eternal Wisdom answers.
The LORD founded the earth and broke up the depths by wisdom, which was with Him before the earth existed.
Wisdom belonged to the LORD at the beginning of His way, which this verse explains as from everlasting.
Wisdom was brought forth before the mountains and hills, another way of placing her before all creation.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "established" is used of installing a king: "Yet I have set My King On My holy hill of Zion" (Psalm 2:6). Here it means Wisdom was set in place. The ESV and KJV have "set up," the NLT and 1984 NIV "appointed," and the current NIV "formed."
• "From everlasting" is the language of God's own eternity: "Even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God" (Psalm 90:2). Micah says the Ruler to come from Bethlehem has goings forth "from of old, From everlasting" (Micah 5:2).
• Holden, quoted by Bridges, says it is scarcely possible to find Hebrew terms "more expressive of the eternity of Wisdom than those which Solomon employs from this verse to the thirtieth."
• Ironside: the verse carries us "Far back of the beginning of Gen. 1:1, to that 'unbeginning beginning' of John 1:1". In plain terms, the verse reaches back past the "beginning" of Genesis 1:1, when creation started, to the "beginning" of John 1:1, when the Word already was.
• Compare John 1:1–2; 17:5; Colossians 1:17; and Revelation 22:13.
units.summary: Wisdom is older than the oldest thing on earth, because she was there before there was an earth.
units.principle: Christ is eternal; before time, matter or history began, the Wisdom of God already was.
units.insight: Jesus told His critics, "before Abraham was, I AM," and they picked up stones, because they understood He was claiming God's own eternity (John 8:58–59). On the night before the cross He prayed for the glory He had with the Father "before the world was" (John 17:5). The One who knelt to wash His disciples' feet (John 13:3–5) was older than the ground He knelt on. That should both humble and steady us. Our troubles are recent; He is from everlasting. Our plans began yesterday; His purposes were settled before the mountains. When life feels unstable, the heart needs something older than the crisis. Christ is.
units.application: When anxiety rises, read John 17:5 and Colossians 1:17 aloud and remind yourself who holds all things together. If you teach or disciple new believers, explain that Jesus is eternal God, not a being who began at Bethlehem. Older saints facing the end of life, take comfort: the One who was there before the world began is the One who will receive you.

rel.note: By His knowledge the LORD broke up the depths, the very waters Wisdom preceded.
The same words "I was brought forth" place Wisdom before the mountains and hills.
The fountains of the deep that did not yet exist here are later made strong while Wisdom watches.

units.notes:
• "Depths" is the plural of the word for "the deep" in Genesis 1:2 (tehom), the waters that covered the earth before God ordered it.
• The 1984 NIV ("I was given birth") and the AMP ("I was born") make the birth language of "brought forth" explicit. The picture is poetic. It speaks of Wisdom coming from God, not of a time when she did not exist.
• Bridges calls "the only-begotten Son" "a term which it is much safer to adore than to expound." He means that the Son's eternal relation to the Father is a truth to worship, not one to take apart.
• Compare John 1:18 ("The only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him") and Colossians 1:15.
units.summary: Before the first ocean or the first spring, God's Wisdom was already with Him.
units.principle: The Son's relation to the Father is eternal; He comes from the Father without ever having had a beginning.
units.insight: The disciples once watched Jesus walk on the dark waters of Galilee in the night (Matthew 14:25–33). The waters that frightened them were younger than the One walking on them. Peter began to sink when he looked at the wind and the waves. Our fears rise the same way, when the depths around us seem older and stronger than the One beside us. They are not. The deep waters came later; the Son was already with the Father. "Brought forth" also speaks of closeness. The Son is "in the bosom of the Father" (John 1:18), and the One who comes to us in the storm comes from the Father's heart.
units.application: When you feel in over your head, remember that the depths are younger than the Christ who holds you, and pray through Psalm 46:1–3. Teachers and parents, use the language of Father and Son carefully, explaining that it describes eternal closeness, not a beginning. Worship leaders, choose songs that honor Christ as the eternal Son, not merely as a helper or friend.

rel.note: The name of the LORD is the true strong tower, the security that outlasts every earthly mountain.
Wisdom was established from everlasting, so she is older than the mountains and hills.
The same "I was brought forth" places Wisdom before the depths and springs.
The list of what came after Wisdom moves on from the hills to the fields and the first dust.

units.notes:
• "Settled" pictures the mountains sunk into their bases, like pillars set in place. Compare God's question to Job: "To what were its foundations fastened?" (Job 38:6).
• Eliphaz asked Job, "Are you the first man who was born? Or were you made before the hills?" (Job 15:7). No human being could say yes; Wisdom can.
• Ironside: "Christ is eternally the Son, yet truly the Begotten." That is, He has always been the Father's own Son.
• Compare Psalm 90:2; Micah 5:2; and John 8:58.
units.summary: The mountains look ancient, but they are younger than the Wisdom who calls you.
units.principle: The eternal Son is older than the most lasting things in creation, so He alone is a foundation that cannot be moved.
units.insight: Henry, recalling Eliphaz's question to Job, answers it: "But before the hills was the eternal Word brought forth." Mountains seem permanent, which is why people have always looked to them for security. Psalm 121 lifts its eyes to the hills and then past them: "My help comes from the LORD, Who made heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:1–2). Christ is older than the hills and stronger than them. He said that heaven and earth would pass away, but His words would not (Matthew 24:35). We build our lives on things that feel like mountains: a career, a reputation, a marriage, a church. They are good gifts, but they are not eternal. What in your life have you treated as a mountain that cannot move? Rest your weight on the One who was there before it.
units.application: Name one "mountain" you lean on for security, such as savings, health, a job or a relationship. Thank God for it, and consciously place your trust in Christ instead. When a long-standing support gives way, through a church split or the loss of a parent, remind yourself who was there before the hills. Mentors, help younger believers build on Christ rather than on circumstances.

rel.note: The LORD founded the earth by wisdom, the earth that did not yet exist when Wisdom was with Him.
The poem's list of what came after Wisdom moves from the hills there to the fields and dust here.
The inhabited world Wisdom preceded is the same world she later rejoiced in.

units.notes:
• "Primal dust" reads literally "the head of the dusts," meaning the first or chief part of the dust; the KJV has "the highest part of the dust of the world." Henry mentions a reading that takes the chief part of the dust to mean man himself, made from the dust yet the finest part of it: "dust enlivened, dust refined."
• "World" here and "inhabited world" in 8:31 translate the same Hebrew word (tevel), a poetic word for the world as the home of people and creatures. The world Wisdom preceded is the world she would delight in.
• Compare Genesis 2:7; Psalm 103:14 ("He remembers that we are dust"); and 1 Corinthians 15:47, "The first man was of the earth, made of dust; the second Man is the Lord from heaven."
units.summary: Wisdom was with God before the first speck of the dust from which Adam would be made.
units.principle: Christ existed before the very dust from which humanity was made, so He stands outside creation as its Lord.
units.insight: Henry draws out the contrast: "the first Adam was made of the earth, the second had a being before the earth." Paul says the same: "The first man was of the earth, made of dust; the second Man is the Lord from heaven" (1 Corinthians 15:47). We are dust, and God does not forget it: "He remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). That is humbling, but it is also tender. The Son who was before the dust took on our nature in order to save us (John 1:14; Hebrews 2:14). Our pride forgets that we are dust. Our despair forgets that the Lord from heaven has joined Himself to dust like ours. Both need this verse.
units.application: When you are tempted to think too highly of yourself, remember Genesis 2:7. When you feel worthless, remember that the eternal Son took on our nature. Gardeners and farmers, let your work in the soil remind you who was there before the first field. Those caring for the dying, speak gently of the One who was before the dust and has promised to raise it again.

rel.note: Agur asks who ascended to heaven and established the ends of the earth, questions answered by the Wisdom who was there.
By understanding the LORD established the heavens, the same work Wisdom witnessed here.
The boundary drawn on the deep is completed when God assigns the sea its limit.

units.notes:
• "Drew a circle" uses the same verb as "decree" in 8:15 and "marked out" in 8:29, a word meaning to cut in or engrave. The noun "circle" (chug) appears in Isaiah 40:22: "It is He who sits above the circle of the earth."
• The KJV has "when he set a compass upon the face of the depth," a compass being a drawing instrument. Henry pictures God working "as the workman marks out his work with his line and compasses."
• Henry also insists that Wisdom was present "not as a spectator, but as the architect, when the world was made."
• Compare Genesis 1:1–8; Job 26:10; Psalm 104:2 ("Who stretch out the heavens like a curtain"); and Colossians 1:16.
units.summary: The voice that calls at the crossroads belongs to an eyewitness of creation.
units.principle: Creation is God's ordered work, and the wisdom that calls us to live rightly is the same wisdom that set the boundaries of the world.
units.insight: God humbled Job with a question: "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job 38:4). Job had no answer, because he had not been there. Wisdom can say, "I was there." That is why her counsel can be trusted: she speaks as an eyewitness who saw how the world was put together. In Christ "all things were created that are in heaven and that are on earth" (Colossians 1:16). We often live as though God's ways were arbitrary rules laid over a world that really works some other way. They are not. The One who drew the horizon knows where the lines of life belong. Do you trust His boundaries, or do you treat them as suggestions?
units.application: The next time you see a horizon, at the sea or across open country, let it remind you that God sets boundaries and keeps them. When a command of Scripture feels restrictive, whether about sex, money or speech, remember who drew the lines and why. Parents, explain your household rules as boundaries that protect, the way God's limits order creation.

rel.note: Agur asks who has bound the waters in a garment, the work this verse describes.
By understanding the LORD established the heavens, the work Wisdom watched.
By the LORD's knowledge the depths were broken up and the clouds drop dew, the same waters above and below.
The springs that did not exist before Wisdom was brought forth are here made strong.

units.notes:
• "Clouds" translates a word that can mean either the skies or the clouds; Ironside's translation reads "the skies above."
• "The fountains of the deep" appear again at the flood, when "all the fountains of the great deep were broken up" (Genesis 7:11). The springs God made firm at creation He also opened in judgment.
• Cowper's hymn, quoted by Ironside, sings of this scene: "He wrought by weight and measure; And Thou wast with Him then." ("Wrought" means worked.)
• Compare 3:19–20; Job 26:8 ("He binds up the water in His thick clouds, Yet the clouds are not broken under it"); and Psalm 33:7.
units.summary: God made even the clouds firm; nothing is too light or too deep for His ordering.
units.principle: God's wisdom governs both what seems flimsy and what seems bottomless; nothing in His world lies outside His ordering.
units.insight: When Jesus "rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, 'Peace, be still!'" the wind ceased and there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). The One who had made the clouds firm and the deep springs strong was speaking to His own handiwork. Elijah prayed, and the heavens held back rain; "he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain" (James 5:17–18). Our lives have their clouds, things that feel insubstantial and uncertain, and their depths, fears that seem to have no bottom. Wisdom was present when God made both firm. Whatever feels shapeless in your life is not beyond the reach of the One who established the clouds.
units.application: When the future feels as shapeless as a cloud, such as an uncertain diagnosis, a long job search or a wandering child, pray to the God who makes clouds firm. Farmers, gardeners and everyone who depends on the weather, thank Him for rain as a gift of His ordering. Teachers of children, use the water cycle to show that God's wisdom holds the world together.

rel.note: The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and ordered its waters, the same work described here.
The verb for marking out the earth's foundations is the verb for rulers decreeing justice.
The circle drawn on the face of the deep is the first boundary set on the waters.
The sea keeps God's command; Wisdom then calls her children to keep her ways.

units.notes:
• "Marked out" here, "drew a circle" in 8:27 and "decree" in 8:15 all translate the same Hebrew verb, which means to cut in or engrave, and so to mark out or decree. The order God fixed in creation and the justice rulers are to decree are described with the same word.
• "Limit" translates a word for a fixed boundary or statute; the KJV has "When he gave to the sea his decree."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The chaotic energy of the sea operates within strict limits."
• Compare Job 38:8–11 ("This far you may come, but no farther, And here your proud waves must stop!"); Psalm 104:9; and Jeremiah 5:22.
units.summary: The sea keeps the line God drew for it; we are the ones who keep crossing ours.
units.principle: All creation keeps the boundaries God has set except the rebellious human heart, and wisdom calls us back within His lines.
units.insight: Henry exclaims, "How able, how fit, is the Son of God to be the Saviour of the world, who was the Creator of it!" The disciples saw it on Galilee when the waves obeyed His word, and they asked, "Who can this be, that even the wind and the sea obey Him!" (Mark 4:41). The sea keeps its boundary. Adam and Eve crossed theirs, and so have we (Romans 3:23). Jonah ran from God's command and found that the sea obeyed God better than the prophet did (Jonah 1:4, 15). The same Lord who sets the sea's limit can set new limits in a heart that has run wild. What line has God drawn for you that you keep testing?
units.application: Identify one boundary God has set that you keep pushing against, whether in your thought life, your spending or your speech, and confess it plainly. Parents, when you set limits for your children, explain that boundaries are part of God's good order, not just your preference. Leaders, keep your own rules before you enforce them on others.

rel.note: The LORD founded the earth by wisdom, the Wisdom who worked beside Him as a master craftsman.
The Wisdom who belonged to the LORD before His works is the one at His side as they were made.
God's delight in Wisdom flows on into Wisdom's delight in the sons of men.
As Wisdom was daily God's delight, the blessed person watches daily at Wisdom's gates.

units.notes:
• The word rendered "master craftsman" ('amon) is very rare and has been understood in two main ways. The NKJV, ESV and NASB take it as a skilled worker (ESV and NASB "master workman"; NLT "the architect"). The KJV reads "as one brought up with him," taking it as a child being raised, a reading found in some medieval Jewish interpreters. Others suggest "faithful one." Each reading fits the scene of closeness and delight.
• "Rejoicing" translates a verb that can also mean to laugh or to play; the same verb describes children "Playing in its streets" (Zechariah 8:5). Wisdom's joy before God is free and glad.
• "His delight" here and "my delight" in 8:31 translate the same Hebrew noun: God delighted in Wisdom, and Wisdom delighted in humanity.
• Compare Isaiah 42:1 ("My Elect One in whom My soul delights!"); Matthew 3:17; John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:16; and Hebrews 1:2.
units.summary: Before there was a world, there was joy: the Father delighting in the Son, the Son rejoicing before Him.
units.principle: Creation flows from the joy shared between the Father and the Son, so the world and our life in it were made for delight, not out of need.
units.insight: At the Jordan the heavens opened and the Father said, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). That delight did not begin at the baptism; it is as old as eternity. Before there was a world, there was love and joy within God. So God did not make us because He was lonely or needed servants. He made the world out of overflowing gladness, and He saves us so that we may share it. Jesus prayed that His disciples might have "My joy fulfilled in themselves" (John 17:13). Many believers picture God as permanently disappointed in them. Yet those who are in Christ are "accepted in the Beloved" (Ephesians 1:6), held within the Father's delight in His Son.
units.application: If you serve God out of fear of disappointing Him, read Matthew 3:17 and Ephesians 1:6 this week, and thank Him that in Christ you share the Son's welcome. Workers and craftsmen, do your work with gladness, reflecting the joy in which the world was made. Parents, let your children see that you delight in them, not only that you correct them.

rel.note: The inhabited world Wisdom rejoices in is the world she existed before.
God's delight in Wisdom is the source of Wisdom's delight in humanity.
Because Wisdom delights in people, she offers them life and the LORD's favor.
Wisdom calls the sons of men because, as this verse shows, she delights in them.

units.notes:
• "Inhabited world" translates tevel, the same poetic word as "world" in 8:26. The world Wisdom was before is the world she delights in.
• The noun for "delight" is used in Jeremiah 31:20, where God asks of Ephraim, His people, "Is he a pleasant child?" (literally, "a child of delights"). It describes cherished, affectionate joy.
• Ironside: "It is not of Adam unfallen He speaks, but of his sons—therefore sinners lost and guilty." In other words, the "sons of men" Wisdom delights in are Adam's fallen children, not Adam before his sin.
• Cowper's hymn, quoted by Ironside: "And couldst Thou be delighted / With creatures such as we, / Who, when we saw Thee, slighted / And nailed Thee to a tree?"
• Compare Genesis 1:26–31; Luke 2:14; John 1:14; and Hebrews 2:14–16.
units.summary: Of everything God made, Wisdom's favorite was people, and the Son proved it by becoming one.
units.principle: God's wisdom delights in people, and that delight is why He calls them and why the Son came to save them.
units.insight: The angels at Bethlehem sang, "on earth peace, goodwill toward men!" (Luke 2:14). That goodwill was not new; Wisdom's delight was with the sons of men before the world began. Jesus showed it wherever He went. He took little children in His arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), ate with tax collectors, and wept at the grave of His friend Lazarus (John 11:35). He set His delight on people who were not delightful, and He did it knowing what it would cost: "for the joy that was set before Him" He "endured the cross" (Hebrews 12:2). Many of us believe God puts up with us but cannot imagine that He enjoys us. This verse says otherwise. Let His delight be the ground on which you come to Him.
units.application: This week, begin your prayers by thanking God that He delights in His people, and then bring Him your needs. Church members, delight in people the way Christ does, including the awkward newcomer and the difficult neighbor, not only the easy ones. Parents and grandparents, tell your children often that you enjoy them, reflecting the Savior's delight in the sons of men.

rel.note: Happy is the man who finds wisdom, the blessing Wisdom promises to those who keep her ways.
The father used the same words to call his children to listen before he warned them about the seductress.
Wisdom's ways are the way of righteousness and the paths of justice she walks herself.
The sea keeps God's command; Wisdom's children are called to keep her ways.

units.notes:
• "Blessed" ('ashre) is the word that opens Psalm 1: "Blessed is the man Who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly." It describes a flourishing life under God's favor, and it appears twice in this closing appeal (8:32, 34).
• "Now therefore, listen to me, my children" repeats the father's words in 7:24 almost exactly; Wisdom takes up the parent's voice. The KJV has "O ye children."
• Bridges: "It is no mean and undeserving person that calls. It is none other than the Wisdom of God." ("Mean" here means lowly.)
• Compare Luke 11:28 ("blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it!"); John 13:17; and James 1:25.
units.summary: The One who stood beside the Creator now leans down and calls you "my children."
units.principle: Who is speaking determines how we should listen; the One who made the world calls us to keep His ways, and in keeping them we are blessed.
units.insight: On the mountain of transfiguration the Father pointed to His Son and said, "Hear Him!" (Matthew 17:5). Wisdom's "Now therefore" carries the same weight: after all she has revealed about herself, the only fitting response is to listen. Yet Jesus warned that hearing is not enough. The wise man is the one who "hears these sayings of Mine, and does them" (Matthew 7:24). The blessing belongs to those who keep His ways. Notice too the tenderness of "my children." The eternal Son does not shout orders at strangers; He is "not ashamed to call them brethren" (Hebrews 2:11). Our hearts often hear God's commands as burdens. Here they come in the voice of One who loves us and wants us blessed.
units.application: After you read Scripture each day this week, write down one specific way you will keep what you read, and do it before the day ends. Parents, speak to your children in Wisdom's tone: firm about the way and warm in the address. Young believers, connect obedience with blessing; walking Christ's way is not a loss of happiness but the road to it.

rel.note: Poverty and shame come to the one who disdains correction, while the one who heeds rebuke is honored.
The one who disdains instruction despises his own soul, the same verb and the same warning.
The ruined man looks back and confesses that he hated instruction and would not obey his teachers.
The instruction Wisdom urges her children to hear is the instruction she ranked above silver.

units.notes:
• "Disdain" translates a verb meaning to let go, let loose or neglect. The same verb appears in 13:18 ("him who disdains correction") and 15:32 ("He who disdains instruction despises his own soul").
• "Instruction" (musar) is training that includes correction, the same word Wisdom ranked above silver in 8:10.
• Ironside: "To refuse instruction and spurn the ways of understanding is to trample on divine affection and to harden the heart against divine grace."
• Henry: "What we know is known in vain if it do not make us wise."
• Compare 5:12–13; 12:1; Hebrews 2:1 ("lest we drift away"); and Hebrews 12:5.
units.summary: Most people do not reject wisdom by slamming the door; they simply let it slip quietly away.
units.principle: Wisdom comes by receiving instruction, and it is lost less often by open rebellion than by quiet neglect.
units.insight: Hebrews warns that we must give earnest heed to what we have heard, "lest we drift away" (Hebrews 2:1). Drift is quieter than rebellion, and far more common. King Saul did not begin by defying God outright. He kept back part of what God told him to destroy and explained it away, until Samuel said, "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). The rich young ruler did not argue with Jesus; he simply "went away sorrowful" (Matthew 19:22). Christ, the Wisdom of God, still instructs His people through His word, His Spirit and His church, and sometimes through hard providences. The question is not whether we have ever rejected Him outright, but what instruction we are quietly letting slip.
units.application: Think of a correction you received recently, from a spouse, a supervisor, a pastor or a sermon, that you have let slide. Act on it this week. Employees and students, ask for feedback and receive it without defending yourself. Parents, help your children learn not only to obey but to welcome correction, and thank them when they take it well.

rel.note: Happy is the man who finds wisdom, the same blessing promised to the one who listens to her.
Those who seek Wisdom diligently find her, and daily watching at her gates is what that seeking looks like.
Wisdom came to the doors of the city to call; now the blessed person comes to wait at her doors.
Wisdom was daily God's delight; the blessed person makes Wisdom a daily pursuit.

units.notes:
• "Posts" are doorposts (mezuzot), the word used in Deuteronomy 6:9, "You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates." The gates and doorposts where God's words were written are the places where the blessed person waits.
• "Watching" translates a verb for staying awake and alert, the way a watchman keeps his post.
• Henry: "See here what a good house Wisdom keeps, for every day is dole-day; what a good school, for every day is lecture-day." A "dole-day" was a day when gifts were handed out to the poor.
• Bridges: "Wisdom's child will ever be familiar with Wisdom's gates."
• Compare Psalm 84:10 ("I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God"); Psalm 130:6; and Revelation 3:20.
units.summary: Wisdom's blessing goes to the one who keeps showing up at her door, not to the occasional visitor.
units.principle: The blessing of wisdom belongs to those who seek it daily and expectantly, as an ongoing relationship rather than an occasional visit.
units.insight: Young Samuel slept in the house of the LORD, and when God called, he answered, "Speak, for Your servant hears" (1 Samuel 3:10). Anna "did not depart from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day," and she was there when the infant Christ was brought in (Luke 2:37–38). Mary of Bethany sat at Jesus' feet. None of them was following a technique; they loved to be near Him. Christ now stands at our door and knocks (Revelation 3:20), and He invites us to wait at His. Many of us come to God's door only in emergencies. Wisdom describes a different life: daily, expectant, glad to wait. Where is your doorpost, the place and time where you wait for Him?
units.application: Choose a daily time and place to wait on Christ in Scripture and prayer, in whatever form suits your season of life, and keep it this week. Parents of young children, short daily moments count; the point is expectancy, not length. Busy professionals, guard the first minutes of the day from your phone. Church members, treat gathered worship as a door you are eager to reach, not an obligation.

rel.note: The same words, "obtains favor from the LORD," describe the man who finds a wife, linking Wisdom with the wife of worth.
The book's closing question, "Who can find a virtuous wife?", takes up the language of finding first used of Wisdom.
Happy is the man who finds wisdom; she is a tree of life to those who take hold of her.
Wisdom offers life because her delight was with the sons of men.
Finding Wisdom brings life, while missing or hating her is loving death.

units.notes:
• The words "obtains favor from the LORD" return in 18:22, "He who finds a wife finds a good thing, And obtains favor from the LORD," and the book closes with the question "Who can find a virtuous wife?" (31:10). The language of finding links Wisdom at the start of the book with the wife of worth at its end.
• Henry: "nor can we obtain God's favour, unless we find Christ and be found in him."
• Lawson, quoted by Bridges: "The smiles of God make heaven; and they that obtain favour of the Lord, have a heaven upon earth."
• Compare 3:13–18; John 17:3 ("And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent"); and 1 John 5:12 ("He who has the Son has life").
units.summary: The life Wisdom promised now has a name, and the name is Jesus.
units.principle: Life and God's favor are found in a Person; whoever finds Christ, the Wisdom of God, finds both.
units.insight: Andrew ran to his brother with the news, "We have found the Messiah" (John 1:41). Philip told Nathanael, "We have found Him of whom Moses in the law, and also the prophets, wrote" (John 1:45). That is this verse fulfilled: Wisdom found, and life with Him. Paul's highest hope was to "be found in Him, not having my own righteousness" (Philippians 3:9). We look for life in many places: success, relationships, pleasure, even religion. They can give good things, but they cannot give life. Only Christ can, and with Him comes the favor of the Father, who delights in the Son. Have you found Him, or are you still searching among good things for what only He gives?
units.application: If you have been looking for life in achievement, a relationship or a substance, name it, and bring that search to Christ in prayer this week. Believers, tell one friend how you found Him, as Andrew did. Young people, test every promise of "life" around you, from popularity to pleasure, against this verse. Pastors, keep pointing people to the Person, not merely to principles.

rel.note: A way may seem right, but its end is death, the end chosen by those who hate Wisdom.
The one who disdains instruction despises his own soul, just as the one who sins against Wisdom wrongs it.
The turning away of the simple slays them, the same self-destruction that comes from refusing Wisdom.
The chapter ends at the same fork in the road where Wisdom first took her stand.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life and the LORD's favor; whoever misses her wrongs his own soul.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "sins against me" is the common verb for sinning, and it can also mean to miss. It describes the slingers of Judges 20:16, who could "sling a stone at a hair's breadth and not miss." The ESV and 1984 NIV read "fails to find me," and the NLT "those who miss me injure themselves," which brings out the contrast with "finds me" in 8:35.
• "Wrongs" translates a verb related to the Hebrew word for violence (chamas). The one who misses Wisdom does violence to his own soul.
• Henry: those who hate Wisdom "love that which will be their death, and put that from them which would be their life."
• Compare 1:32; 9:12; 14:12; 15:32; and Ezekiel 18:31–32: "For why should you die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of one who dies."
units.summary: Refusing Wisdom does not hurt her; it is a slow way of choosing death.
units.principle: Rejecting God's wisdom harms no one so much as the one who rejects it; to refuse Christ is to choose death over life.
units.insight: Jesus lamented over Jerusalem: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37). That is the heart behind this warning. The Wisdom who delights in the sons of men does not want them to die. Esau traded his birthright for a bowl of stew and later found no way to undo it (Genesis 25:29–34; Hebrews 12:16–17). He did not set out to love death; he simply wanted the stew more than the blessing. Most people who refuse Christ are not shaking a fist at Him; they want something else more. Yet "the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). The door of verse 34 is still open. Turn and live.
units.application: If you have been putting off a response to Christ, do not wait for a better moment; turn to Him today. Believers, identify one "bowl of stew" like Esau's, something small you keep choosing over God's blessing, and give it up. Parents, warn your children with love and tears, not only rules, as Wisdom does. Friends who share the gospel, speak of judgment the way Wisdom does, from a heart that wants people to live.

rel.note: The wise woman who builds her house is the everyday picture of what Wisdom does here on a grand scale.
Through wisdom a house is built and established, the same truth this verse pictures in Wisdom's finished house.
The immoral woman's house leads down to death, while Wisdom's house is built to receive guests into life.
Folly sits at the door of her house but is never said to have built it, while Wisdom has built and hewn.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "Wisdom" here, chokmot, is plural in form, as in 1:20, yet the verbs "has built" and "has hewn" and the word "her" are singular. Hebrew sometimes uses a plural to stress fullness. The wording presents one Wisdom who possesses wisdom in full measure, not many wisdoms.
• "Hewn" means cut out of stone. Wisdom has not pitched a tent; she has quarried pillars meant to stand. Compare 24:3, "Through wisdom a house is built," and 14:1, "The wise woman builds her house."
• Henry: "Wisdom, not finding a house capacious enough for all her guests, has built one on purpose." Capacious means roomy: Wisdom's house is built to hold everyone she invites.
• The New Testament speaks of the Church as "the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15). Compare Ephesians 2:20–22 and Hebrews 3:3–4.
• Compare 9:14, where Folly "sits at the door of her house," but is never said to have built it.
units.summary: Wisdom finishes building the house before she sends out a single invitation.
units.principle: Wisdom offers a life that is already built and ready, solid enough to stand and roomy enough for every guest she calls.
units.insight: Before the simple hear a word, the house stands finished. This is the order of grace throughout Scripture. God planted a garden in Eden and made it ready, "and there He put the man whom He had formed" (Genesis 2:8). Jesus told His disciples, "I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). At the deeper level, Christ is the Wisdom who builds, and "He who built the house has more honor than the house" (Hebrews 3:3). Our hearts tend to treat wisdom as a project we must finish before God will receive us. This verse turns that around. We do not build the house and then invite God in; He builds it and invites us. Folly also has a house in this chapter, but nothing is said of her building it (9:14), and every life is living in one house or the other.
units.application: If you are a new believer, or still standing outside, stop trying to get your life in order before you come to Christ; the house is ready now. If you are a parent, build habits of Scripture, prayer and shared meals before a crisis comes, so your children have somewhere solid to turn in. If you lead in a church, ask whether your ministry is built to receive guests or only to keep regulars comfortable.

rel.note: Wisdom's enduring riches and fruit better than gold match the richness of the table she sets.
Wisdom prepares her own meat and wine at her own cost, while Folly offers only stolen water and secret bread.
The feast prepared here is the one Wisdom invites her guests to eat and drink.

units.notes:
• "Slaughtered her meat" is literally "slaughtered her slaughter": the verb and its object come from the same Hebrew root. The 1611 KJV printed "her beastes" but noted in the margin that the Hebrew reads "her killing." The repetition underlines that this is a costly feast with meat, not a plain meal.
• Wine was often mixed before it was served. In some ancient settings it was mixed with water; older commentators such as Bridges took it as wine made richer with spices. Either way, the hostess has prepared it with care.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Slaughtering, like the difficult and responsible activity of building a house, was normally a man’s job…" Wisdom, pictured as a woman, does even this heavy work herself, so nothing is left for her guests to do.
• The NLT renders the line "She has prepared a great banquet," which keeps the sense but loses the picture of meat, wine and table.
• Compare Isaiah 25:6, where the LORD makes "for all people A feast of choice pieces"; and Luke 14:16–17, "Come, for all things are now ready."
units.summary: Wisdom's feast costs the hostess everything and asks nothing of the guest but an appetite.
units.principle: Wisdom's blessings are prepared at the host's own cost and offered freely; the guest's part is to come hungry and receive.
units.insight: Wisdom does the slaughtering, the mixing and the setting. Abraham did the same for his three visitors, hurrying to the herd for a tender calf and setting food before them himself (Genesis 18:6–8). Generous hospitality costs the host. In the light of the New Testament, the cost of this table is plain: "Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us" (1 Corinthians 5:7), and at His table He says, "this is My body which is broken for you" (1 Corinthians 11:24). The father of the prodigal did not ask his son to cook the calf; he said, "let us eat and be merry" (Luke 15:23). Many of us still come to God as if we must bring something to the table: a better record, stronger feelings, more effort. The table is already furnished. Henry: "It is all Wisdom's own doing." Our part is to come hungry.
units.application: When you come to the Lord's Table this month, come as a guest, not as someone paying the bill: confess your sin, then receive. If you host a small group or a family meal, prepare with care, so people know they were expected. If you teach, do the hard work of study beforehand, so those you serve receive a table already set rather than your unfinished thoughts.

rel.note: Wisdom's first appearance shows her raising her voice in the streets and squares, as she does from the city's heights here.
Wisdom cries out from the heights and at the city gates, the same public calling she does here.
Folly takes her seat by the same highest places of the city, so the two rival calls sound over the same town.

units.notes:
• "City" here translates qeret, a rare poetic Hebrew word rather than the common one. It occurs only five times in the Old Testament, and three of them come in these scenes: 8:3, 9:3 and 9:14. Verses 3 and 14 also share the same Hebrew wording for "the highest places," so the reader hears Wisdom and Folly calling from the same heights.
• "Maidens" are young women servants. A noble lady sending her maids fits Wisdom's portrait as a woman; compare Pharaoh's daughter and her maidens (Exodus 2:5) and Esther's maids (Esther 4:4).
• Ironside: "Nor does Wisdom wait for men to seek her out."
• Compare 1:20–21 and 8:1–3, where Wisdom also calls in public places, and Luke 14:21–23, where the master sends his servant into the streets and lanes, then the highways and hedges.
units.summary: Wisdom does not wait to be found; she sends her servants out and raises her own voice.
units.principle: Wisdom takes the initiative: God's call goes out openly and actively to people who would never come on their own.
units.insight: In Proverbs, Wisdom pursues people, and that is the heart of the gospel. After the first sin, the LORD God came calling Adam: "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). Jesus sent out the Twelve and then the seventy (Luke 9:1–2; 10:1), yet He also preached Himself. Read at the deeper level, Jesus preaching in person is Wisdom crying out herself. Henry: "Our Lord Jesus was himself the publisher of his own gospel," that is, its first preacher. The maidens only carry the invitation; the feast and the call belong to Wisdom. Paul called himself and his companions "ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us" (2 Corinthians 5:20). If you came to Christ, someone was sent to you, and behind that person stood the Lord who called you Himself. Do we see ourselves only as guests at the table, or also as maidens sent out with the invitation?
units.application: This week, carry one invitation. Ask a coworker, neighbor or relative to a meal, a service or a conversation about Christ, instead of waiting for them to show interest. If you preach or teach, speak plainly and publicly, as Wisdom does from the heights. If you lead a ministry team, remind volunteers that they are servants carrying someone else's invitation, so the results rest with the Host.

rel.note: The simple believe every word, which explains why Wisdom must reach them before another voice does.
The same Hebrew phrase for lacking heart describes the young man who walked toward the immoral woman's house, the person Wisdom now calls first.
Wisdom's earlier address to the simple ones calls the same uncommitted hearers to understand prudence.
Folly repeats this call to the same hearers almost word for word, but leads them to a different table and a different end.

units.notes:
• "Simple" translates peti, a word for someone open and inexperienced, easily persuaded either way. The same word marks the young man seen "among the simple" in 7:7 and the hearers Wisdom addresses in 1:22 and 8:5.
• "Lacks understanding" is literally "lacking heart." The same Hebrew phrase is rendered "devoid of understanding" at 7:7 and "lacks understanding" here and at 9:16. The NKJV's varied English hides that all three verses describe the same kind of person.
• Henry: "he that wants a heart (so the word is) let him come hither, and he shall have one." In older English "wants" means lacks: the one who lacks a heart is invited so that he may receive one.
• Folly repeats this call almost word for word in 9:16, so the same invitation will come from two different houses.
• Compare Matthew 9:13, "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance," and 1 Corinthians 1:26–29.
units.summary: Wisdom's guest list begins with the people who know the least and need her the most.
units.principle: God's wisdom is offered first to those who know they lack it, and admitting our need is the door into her house.
units.insight: If we were giving a banquet, we would invite the impressive. Wisdom invites the simple. Jesus did the same. He ate with tax collectors and sinners, and when He was criticized He said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick" (Matthew 9:12). Peter and John were "uneducated and untrained men," yet people "realized that they had been with Jesus" (Acts 4:13). Bridges puts the invitation plainly: "Here, sinner, is thy warrant—not thy worthiness, but thy need." A warrant is the right to come in. The heart's danger is not being simple; it is refusing to admit it. The simple who know their emptiness turn in, and those who think they are full walk past. Which are you this week: someone who knows he lacks heart, or someone who assumes he has enough?
units.application: If you feel out of your depth spiritually, take that as your invitation, not your disqualification: join the class, open Proverbs, ask the question. If you mentor young people, go after the drifting ones before other voices reach them; a text, a coffee or a ride to church can carry Wisdom's call. Church leaders, build entry points for people who know nothing yet, and do not assume a basic level of Bible knowledge.

rel.note: Eating good honey pictures taking in the knowledge of wisdom, the same image behind Wisdom's invitation to eat her bread.
The father's words are life and health to those who find them, which is what Wisdom's food gives those who eat.
Wisdom freely gives bread and wine from her own table, while Folly offers stolen water and bread eaten in secret.
The bread and mixed wine offered here are the feast Wisdom prepared with her own hands.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "bread" often means food in general, which is why the NLT renders the line "Come, eat my food." The invitation is to the whole meal, not a crust.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Just as food and drink give physical life, Solomon’s teachings give spiritual life."
• Henry: "What we eat and drink we make our own." Food that is eaten becomes part of the body, and instruction that is received becomes part of the person.
• Compare Isaiah 55:1–2, "Come, buy and eat… Without money and without price"; Jeremiah 15:16, "Your words were found, and I ate them"; and Matthew 4:4.
• Compare John 6:35, 51 and 1 Corinthians 11:24–25, where Christ gives Himself as the bread and the cup of His table.
units.summary: Wisdom is not a dish to admire; it is food to eat until it becomes part of you.
units.principle: Truth helps only when it is received and taken in, and God offers it freely to all who will come and feed on it.
units.insight: The prophet Ezekiel was told to eat the scroll before he spoke God's word, and it was "in my mouth like honey in sweetness" (Ezekiel 3:3). God's word is meant to be digested, not only admired. Many believers stand at Wisdom's table reading the menu. They know verses, own study Bibles and enjoy good sermons, yet remain hungry. Jesus said, "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). When the crowds turned away from His hard words, Peter answered, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:68). The invitation is personal: "my bread," "the wine I have mixed." Christ does not send us to a buffet of ideas; He offers Himself. The question is not whether we have seen the table, but whether we have eaten.
units.application: Choose one passage this week and feed on it: read it slowly each morning, memorize a line, and ask at night where it shaped your day. Parents, read Scripture at the dinner table, so your children connect God's word with nourishment and not only with rules. If you lead a Bible study, move past information to the question "What will we do with this?" so the group takes the food in rather than only discussing it.

rel.note: Walking with the wise rather than with fools shows what it means in practice to forsake the foolish.
The turning away of the simple slays them, the end Wisdom's guests escape by forsaking simpleness.
The brightening path of the just and the dark way of the wicked are the two roads behind Wisdom's call to go in the way of understanding.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, the same promise held out in her command to forsake foolishness and live.
Wisdom's guests are told to live, while Folly's guests are found among the dead.

units.notes:
• "Foolishness" translates the plural of the word for "simple" in 9:4, and its plain sense is "simple ones." The KJV takes it that way, "Forsake the foolish," meaning leave the company of the simple. The NKJV and most modern versions translate it as the condition itself; the NLT has "Leave your simple ways behind." Either way, the command ties back to the invitation of 9:4.
• "Go" translates a verb meaning to walk straight ahead or keep advancing. In other forms the same Hebrew root means to call someone happy or blessed, and Young's Literal Translation reads "be happy" here. Most versions take it as walking, which fits the picture of a road.
• Bridges, reading with the KJV's "forsake the foolish": "Thou must forsake either them or Christ." He means the company of the foolish; no one can keep both.
• Compare 13:20, "He who walks with wise men will be wise, But the companion of fools will be destroyed"; and Isaiah 55:7.
units.summary: You cannot sit at Wisdom's table and keep your old seat at Folly's.
units.principle: Receiving wisdom always means leaving something behind; life comes by turning from folly and walking a new road, not by adding wisdom to an unchanged life.
units.insight: When Jesus called Levi from the tax office, "he left all, rose up, and followed Him" (Luke 5:28). Zacchaeus did not just host Jesus for dinner; he gave half his goods to the poor and restored fourfold what he had taken (Luke 19:8). A meal with Christ changed the direction of their lives. Our hearts want the feast without the forsaking: Christ's comfort, but our own road. Jesus is the way and the life together (John 14:6), so we cannot have His life while refusing His way. Yet the command comes wrapped in promise. "Live" is not a threat. The same Lord who says "forsake" also says, "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14). What He asks us to leave is what was killing us.
units.application: Name one foolish habit or relationship that keeps pulling you back, and take one concrete step away from it this week: delete the app, end the late-night conversation, change the route home. Young people, choose friends who walk the way of understanding (13:20). Parents, when your children make a fresh start, help them build new routines, not only drop old ones. Mentors, ask not only what someone is leaving but where they will walk next.

rel.note: A scoffer does not listen to rebuke, which is why correcting him only brings shame on the one who tries.
The scoffer does not love the one who corrects him, the attitude that turns rebuke into harm for the rebuker.
Speaking to a fool only invites contempt for wise words, the same wasted effort described here.
The scoffer who answers correction with contempt here is the one Wisdom warns will bear the cost of his scorn alone.
The observation about the scoffer becomes counsel in the next verse, set beside the wise man who loves correction.

units.notes:
• "Harms himself" is literally "his blemish." The Hebrew word, mum, means a blemish or defect, whether physical or moral. The KJV has "getteth himself a blot," and Young's Literal Translation "his blemish." The one who rebukes walks away with a stain on his name, which matches the "shame" of the first line.
• "Scoffer" translates lets, the mocker. He is the most dangerous of the fools in Proverbs, because his problem is his will: the fool cannot be wise, but the scoffer will not be. Compare 1:22 and 13:1; in 21:24 "Scoffer" is the proud man's name.
• Verses 7–12 sit between the two banquets like a small collection of sayings. The NKJV punctuation keeps them inside Wisdom's speech, which closes at the end of 9:12.
• Ironside: "Reproof will only be wasted on the scorner."
units.summary: Correct a scoffer and he will not change; he will make you pay for trying.
units.principle: A heart that has decided not to learn turns correction into an occasion for contempt, and the one who corrects it often bears the cost.
units.insight: Scripture shows the scoffer's response again and again. When Hezekiah's runners carried the king's invitation to keep the Passover, many "laughed at them and mocked them" (2 Chronicles 30:10). When a prophet rebuked King Amaziah, the king cut him off: "Cease! Why should you be killed?" (2 Chronicles 25:16). Jesus Himself was mocked by the people He came to save, and He bore it (Luke 23:35–36). So the verse comforts those who were scorned for speaking the truth: the failure was not necessarily theirs. It also searches us. Do I make the people who correct me pay for it, with sarcasm, coldness or a quick comeback? Whenever we answer correction with contempt, we are taking the first steps on the scoffer's road.
units.application: If you have tried again and again to correct someone who only mocks, you are free to stop arguing; pray, keep loving, and wait for a better moment. Parents of adult children and leaders facing a hostile critic especially need this permission. Then turn the verse on yourself. The next time a spouse, boss or friend corrects you, notice your first reaction. If it is sarcasm or a counterattack, stop and ask them to tell you more.

rel.note: Striking a scoffer still makes the simple who watch more careful, so dealing with a scoffer is never wholly wasted and this verse is no rule of silence.
The faithful wounds of a friend explain why a wise person loves the one who rebukes him.
The one who rebukes finds more favor in the end than the flatterer, the same love this verse says a wise man gives the one who rebukes him.
The preceding verse describes the shame and harm that make this counsel against correcting a scoffer necessary.
The wise man who loves rebuke here is the one who grows still wiser when instructed in the next verse.

units.notes:
• Both lines use the same Hebrew verb, which the NKJV renders first "correct" and then "rebuke." The identical action draws opposite responses, which sharpens the contrast between the scoffer and the wise.
• A person's response to correction shows the direction of his life. The deeper someone goes into folly, the less correction he can bear; the further he goes in wisdom, the more he welcomes it.
• Bridges: "Yet this prudence must not degenerate into cowardice." In other words, holding back with a scoffer never cancels the duty to speak truth to those who can still hear it.
• Compare 19:25, where punishing a scoffer still makes the simple who watch more careful, even though the scoffer himself does not change.
• Compare Matthew 7:6, "nor cast your pearls before swine"; Psalm 141:5, "let him rebuke me; It shall be as excellent oil"; and 28:23.
units.summary: One rebuke can make an enemy or a friend; the difference is the heart that hears it.
units.principle: How a person receives correction reveals the heart, and wisdom both welcomes rebuke and discerns when and to whom to give it.
units.insight: Two kings show the two responses. Ahab said of the prophet Micaiah, "I hate him, because he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil" (1 Kings 22:8). David, confronted by Nathan's "You are the man!" answered, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). Paul withstood Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11), and Peter later wrote of "our beloved brother Paul" (2 Peter 3:15). Henry: "It is as great an instance of wisdom to take a reproof well as to give it well." So the verse asks which king lives in us. Do the people who correct us end up closer to us or further away? Christ's own correction is love, not rejection: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19). A heart that knows it is loved can afford to be corrected.
units.application: Before you correct someone, ask whether he has shown any willingness to hear. With a mocking coworker or an adult child who scorns every word, use fewer words, wait for a better moment and pray more. With a teachable friend or team member, speak plainly and lovingly; silence would fail them. And when you are rebuked this week, thank the person before you defend yourself. That habit marks the wise man of this verse.

rel.note: The prudent heart acquires knowledge and the wise ear seeks it, the same hunger to learn shown here.
The prologue opens with the same words: a wise man will hear and increase learning.
The verb for adding learning returns when years of life are added, tying growth in learning to the blessing of life.
The wise man who loves the one who rebukes him is the same man who grows wiser when instructed.

units.notes:
• The first line in Hebrew says only, "Give to a wise man"; the word "instruction" is supplied by translators. The second line shows what kind of gift is meant, because its verb means to make known, which the NKJV renders "Teach." Whether the gift is correction, counsel or teaching, the wise man turns it into growth.
• "Increase in learning" uses the same Hebrew words as 1:5. The verb means to add, and it returns two verses later, where years of life "will be added" (9:11). The one who keeps adding learning is also the one promised added years.
• Ironside: "The less a man knows, as a rule, the more he thinks he knows."
• Compare 18:15, "the ear of the wise seeks knowledge"; Matthew 13:12, "For whoever has, to him more will be given"; and 2 Peter 3:18.
units.summary: The wise are not the people who have stopped learning but the ones who learn the most.
units.principle: Teachability is both the mark and the engine of wisdom: the wiser a person truly is, the more eager he remains to learn.
units.insight: Moses had met God at the burning bush and led Israel out of Egypt, yet when his father-in-law Jethro told him he was wearing himself out, "Moses heeded the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said" (Exodus 18:24). Apollos was "mighty in the Scriptures," yet he let Priscilla and Aquila explain "the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:24, 26). Great servants of God stay students. Writing from prison, Paul still said, "Not that I have already attained" (Philippians 3:12). Our pride whispers that experience exempts us from instruction. The wise person can receive teaching from anyone, even a spouse, a new believer or a child. Jesus Himself, as a boy in the temple, sat among the teachers, "both listening to them and asking them questions" (Luke 2:46).
units.application: Put yourself under teaching this week, whatever your experience: read a solid book, ask an older believer a real question, or invite feedback on your work. Pastors and teachers, ask someone you trust to review a sermon or lesson and name one thing to improve. Parents, let your children see you learn, admit mistakes and change your mind when shown a better way. Employees, ask your supervisor what would make your work better.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, restating that wisdom is learned in reverence before God.
The book's opening motto calls the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge, framing chapters 1–9 with this verse.
The fear of the LORD and the knowledge of God are joined there as they are here.
Agur confesses he lacks the knowledge of the Holy One, the same title and plural form used here.
When Folly copies Wisdom's words, only the fear of the LORD enables the simple to tell the two calls apart.

units.notes:
• "The Holy One" translates qedoshim, which is plural in form, here and at 30:3. Hebrew sometimes uses a plural to stress greatness. The word refers to the one God and stresses His holiness; it does not count holy beings. Joshua 24:19 offers a parallel: in "He is a holy God," both "God" and "holy" are plural in form. The KJV has "the holy."
• Two different Hebrew words stand behind "beginning" in 1:7 and here. The word in 1:7, reshit, means the first part, and can also mean the chief or choicest part; the word here, techillah, means a beginning or starting point. Both verses make the fear of the LORD the place where wisdom starts; the change of word varies the expression, not the idea.
• The first line matches Psalm 111:10 word for word in the NKJV; compare also Job 28:28 and 15:33.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "This title for the Lord underscores his ‘otherness,’ the sphere of his sacredness, separated from the mundane, the common…" Waltke means that God is set apart from everything ordinary.
• Some older commentators read the second line as "the knowledge of holy things." The parallel with "the fear of the LORD" favors reading it as God Himself, the Holy One.
units.summary: Every road to wisdom starts at the same place: seeing God as He really is.
units.principle: A right view of God is the starting point of all true wisdom, and whoever starts anywhere else will misjudge everything else.
units.insight: Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, heard the seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy," and said, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" (Isaiah 6:3, 5). His pride was exposed, and then God cleansed and sent him. That is the fear of the LORD for a child of God: not cringing dread but a right view of Him that puts everything else in its place. Bridges: "The child of God has only one dread—to offend his Father; only one desire—to please and delight in him." Christ Himself delighted in the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:3), and in Him "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). Many of our anxieties come from a small view of God and a large view of everything else. The cure is not more technique but a clearer sight of Him.
units.application: Begin each decision this week, at work, with money or in a conflict, by asking, "What is true about God here?" before asking what will work. Parents, teach your children who God is, His holiness, goodness and power, and not only His rules. If you lead worship or teach, give people a large view of God, not only advice for living. Spend five minutes daily in a passage on God's holiness, such as Isaiah 6 or Revelation 4.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD prolongs days, the general blessing Wisdom ties to her motto.
The father promises length of days and years of life in the same Hebrew words Wisdom uses here.
Receiving the father's sayings makes the years of life many, the same promise in his voice.
The verb for adding learning to the wise returns here for adding years, so growth in wisdom and fullness of life go together.

units.notes:
• "Years of life will be added" uses the same Hebrew words as 3:2, "For length of days and long life And peace they will add to you." The NKJV's "long life" there and "years of life" here translate the same phrase, so Wisdom repeats in her own voice the promise the father gave at the start of the prologue.
• The verb "added" is the same Hebrew verb as "increase" in 9:9. The one who keeps adding learning is the one to whom years are added.
• Bridges, on what makes the years worth having: "And truly the value of life is only realized in the knowledge and service of God."
• Compare 3:16; 4:10; 10:27; Psalm 90:12. On the limits of the general rule, compare Isaiah 57:1, "The righteous perishes, And no man takes it to heart."
units.summary: The wise way tends to lengthen life, but length of days is a blessing, not a bargain.
units.principle: Living God's way generally preserves and lengthens life, yet the number of our days stays in God's hands, and their true worth lies in knowing Him.
units.insight: When King Hezekiah was sick, the LORD said, "I will add to your days fifteen years" (2 Kings 20:6). Yet Josiah, one of Judah's most faithful kings, died in battle at thirty-nine (2 Kings 22:1; 23:29), and Stephen, "full of faith and the Holy Spirit," was stoned (Acts 6:5; 7:58–60). Jesus, in whom all wisdom is found, laid down His life in His early thirties. So the verse gives us no formula for a long life and no ground for judging a grieving family. It does tell us which way life runs: Folly empties and shortens life, and Wisdom fills and lengthens it. Ask where your own habits are pointing. In the light of the New Testament, the final answer to this promise is Christ's word: "He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live" (John 11:25). The years Wisdom adds reach into eternity.
units.application: Choose one wise habit this week that guards your life and health: drive carefully, rest, refuse the extra drink, break the reckless pattern. Young people, remember that most choices that shorten lives are made in youth. If you are comforting a family who lost a godly person early, do not use this verse to explain the loss; grieve with them and point them to the resurrection. If you are older, ask God to make your remaining years count (Psalm 90:12).

rel.note: A foolish son grieves his mother, a reminder that folly also hurts others even though its outcome lands on the fool.
The backslider is filled with his own ways while the good man is satisfied, each receiving the fruit of his own path.
Judgments are prepared for scoffers, describing the load the scoffer will carry himself.
Whoever sins against Wisdom wrongs his own soul, the same personal cost the scoffer bears alone.
The scoffer who shames and harms the one who corrects him is the one who must carry the cost of his scorn himself.

units.notes:
• "Bear" means to lift and carry a load. Paul uses the same picture of personal responsibility in Galatians 6:5, "each one shall bear his own load."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "This is perhaps the strongest expression of individualism in the Bible." The verse stresses that each person answers for his own response to Wisdom.
• The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, adds three lines after this verse that are not in the Hebrew. They describe a man who leans on falsehoods, tries to rule the winds, and gathers barrenness in a dry land. The NKJV and other English versions follow the Hebrew and leave them out.
• Compare 8:36, "he who sins against me wrongs his own soul"; and Ezekiel 18:20.
units.summary: No one can be wise for you, and no one can carry your scorn for you.
units.principle: Each person reaps the fruit of his own response to God's wisdom: its gain cannot be borrowed, and its loss cannot be handed to someone else.
units.insight: Esau traded his birthright for a single meal, and afterward "he found no place for repentance, though he sought it diligently with tears" (Hebrews 12:17). No one else could carry that loss for him. The Pharisees "rejected the will of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30). Yet the gospel answers this verse in a surprising way. The weight the scoffer must bear alone is the very weight Christ came to carry: He "Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree" (1 Peter 2:24). Bridges: "A surety indeed there is. But his scorning rejects him." A surety is one who takes another person's debt on himself. The only one who must carry his scorn alone is the one who scorns the Savior who would carry it. Is there any place where you are still scoffing, hoping the cost will fall on someone else?
units.application: Parents, you cannot be wise for your teenager; teach, pray, and then let consequences teach too, rather than absorbing every cost yourself. Young adults, stop leaning on your parents' faith and make Wisdom's choice your own. If you are carrying the fallout of someone else's foolish choices, you can love them without taking on the weight that belongs to them. And if you have been scoffing at correction, bring it to Christ today.

rel.note: The wise woman builds her house while the foolish woman pulls hers down, the same contrast drawn between Wisdom and Folly.
The seductress is called loud with the same Hebrew word used for Folly's clamor.
Folly knows nothing, and her guest does not know that the dead are in her house.

units.notes:
• "Foolish woman" is literally "woman of folly." The second word, kesilut, is an abstract noun meaning folly or stupidity, found only here in the Old Testament. Because she is named by the quality itself, the NLT can render the phrase "The woman named Folly."
• "Clamorous" is the same Hebrew word rendered "loud" in 7:11, so the link between Folly and the seductress of chapter 7 rests on the wording itself.
• "Simple" here translates a rare noun related to the word for "simple" in 9:4; it means silliness, being easily enticed. The ESV reads "seductive," following a scholarly proposal to read a slightly different form meaning one who entices. The NKJV, KJV and NASB ("naive") keep the sense of simpleness.
• Bridges: "the tempter, from the very habit of deceiving, becomes the victim of her own delusion!" The one who deceives others ends up deceived herself.
• Ironside: "Folly, too, has her temple, and, alas, many are her devotees!" He means that Folly's house, like Wisdom's, draws people who give themselves to her.
units.summary: Folly is loud because she has nothing to say.
units.principle: Volume and confidence are not wisdom; the voice that pushes hardest often knows least about where it leads.
units.insight: Delilah wore Samson down: she "pestered him daily with her words and pressed him, so that his soul was vexed to death" (Judges 16:16). She did not win him by argument but by noise and pressure, and he gave in. Folly works the same way. She rarely persuades; she wears people down. The noise of our age, with its endless feeds, ads and voices telling us what we deserve, is clamorous in just this way, and none of it knows where it is taking us. Our hearts are drawn to whatever is loudest and nearest. By contrast, the LORD came to Elijah not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12).
