Wisdom's voice is worth turning down the noise to hear. Which voice has had the most of your attention this week?
units.application: Notice which voices are loudest in your week: a screen, a pushy friend, a craving that will not let up. Loudness is not a reason to obey. Young people, when someone pressures you hard and fast, slow down and ask what they really know about where this leads. Parents, explain to your children that the pushiest voice is often the emptiest. Set a daily time of quiet with Scripture, so Wisdom's voice is not drowned out.

rel.note: The seductress lurks at every corner, waiting for her victim just as Folly waits at her door.
Wisdom built her house and hewed its pillars, but Folly is only said to sit at the door of hers.
Wisdom calls from the same highest places after preparing her feast and sending her maidens, while Folly only sits.

units.notes:
• "Seat" translates kisse, which is usually rendered "throne" in the Old Testament and means a seat of honor. Young's Literal Translation reads "throne" here. The word hints that Folly claims a seat of honor she has not earned.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Probably chairs were so rare that only the highest nobleman owned one." A seat signaled rank, which shows how much Folly claims for herself.
• "The highest places of the city" uses the same Hebrew wording as 9:3, so Wisdom and Folly call from the same heights.
• Ironside: "so ready are men to give heed to Folly, that she needs none to go about entreating them to enter her house." Wisdom sends her maidens out; Folly only has to wait.
• Compare 23:28, where the seductress "lies in wait as for a victim," and 7:10–12, where she waits at the corners for the young man.
units.summary: Folly never built her house; she only took the best seat in town.
units.principle: Temptation does not need to earn its place or work hard; it claims prominence and waits, so position and visibility are no proof of worth.
units.insight: God warned Cain before he killed his brother: "sin lies at the door. And its desire is for you, but you should rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). Sin sat at Cain's door the way Folly sits at hers, waiting. Abraham also sat at his tent door, but he was watching for strangers to serve, and he ran to meet them (Genesis 18:1–2). Folly sits watching for someone to take. Our hearts easily assume that whatever sits in the high places must be safe: the popular, the fashionable, the thing everyone important seems to do. Folly's throne is borrowed. In the light of the New Testament, only One has earned the seat of honor: Christ, who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high after He had purged our sins (Hebrews 1:3). Let His throne, not the world's high seats, decide what is worth entering.
units.application: This week, ask of every prominent offer, whether a trend, a popular show or a deal everyone seems to be taking, what is actually inside the house. Young people, do not mistake popularity for approval. If you have a platform as a leader or influencer, remember that a high seat does not make your message true; examine what you offer. Parents, talk with your children about the people and platforms they admire, and how to test them.

rel.note: The straight paths the LORD directs are the very paths Folly tries to pull people away from, described in the same Hebrew words.
The father's counsel not to turn to the right or the left is the answer to Folly's call to turn aside.
Those Folly calls here become her called ones, her guests found in the depths of Sheol.

units.notes:
• "Go straight on their way" is literally "make their paths straight," as the NASB reflects. It uses the same Hebrew verb and noun as 3:6, "He shall direct your paths." The people Folly targets are already walking the kind of straight path that 3:6 describes.
• The verb "call" is the same verb used for Wisdom's crying out in 9:3. It also lies behind "her guests" in 9:18, literally "her called ones," the people who answered the call Folly gives here.
• Bridges: "Satan is so angry with none as with those, who are going right on."
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, describes them as people "going innocently and directly about their business without any unchaste design," that is, with no thought of sin.
• Compare 4:25–27, "Do not turn to the right or the left," and Matthew 26:41, "Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation."
units.summary: Temptation does not only hunt the lost; it calls loudest to people walking the right way.
units.principle: Being on the right road is no immunity from temptation; those who walk straight must keep watch, because enticement aims at the faithful.
units.insight: Joseph was simply doing his job. He "went into the house to do his work," and Potiphar's wife, who had spoken to him "day by day," was waiting (Genesis 39:10–11). He fled. Israel had just promised, "All that the LORD has said we will do" (Exodus 24:7), and soon they were dancing around a golden calf (Exodus 32). Even Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted right after His baptism (Matthew 4:1). He was tempted "in all points" as we are, "yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15), and so He can help us when we are tempted. The heart that says, "I'm doing well; this won't touch me," is the heart Folly calls to most. "Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). Yet God "will also make the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13).
units.application: If this season is going well, spiritually, in marriage or in ministry, put guardrails up now: an accountability friend, filters on your devices, no private meetings that invite compromise. Pastors and leaders, expect temptation after victories, not only in dry times. Young people heading to college or a first job, decide beforehand where you will not turn aside. Like Joseph, plan your exit before you need it.

rel.note: A way can seem right and still end in death, which is why a pleasant-sounding call must be judged by its end.
The young man lacking heart who followed the seductress shows what happens to the hearer Folly addresses here.
The fear of the LORD is where the discernment begins that lets the simple tell Wisdom's call from Folly's.
Wisdom speaks the same words to the same hearers, but calls them to a feast that leads to life.

units.notes:
• Folly's words repeat Wisdom's in 9:4 almost exactly. In the NKJV the two calls differ only in an exclamation mark and the added "And."
• "Lacks understanding" is literally "lacking heart," the same Hebrew phrase used at 9:4 and at 7:7 for the young man who walked into the seductress's house.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "To obey the call of wisdom is to live. To yield to the clamor of folly is to die."
• Compare 2 Corinthians 2:11, where Paul says of Satan, "we are not ignorant of his devices," and Hebrews 5:14, on senses "exercised to discern both good and evil."
units.summary: Two houses, one invitation: the words sound the same, but the tables and the endings do not.
units.principle: Similar words can lead to opposite ends, so an invitation must be judged by its table and its destination, not by how it sounds.
units.insight: The serpent did not open by denying God; he opened with God's own words: "Has God indeed said…?" (Genesis 3:1). In the wilderness the devil quoted Psalm 91 to Jesus (Matthew 4:6). Evil learns Wisdom's vocabulary. That is why simpleness is so dangerous: the person who cannot tell the voices apart will follow whichever is nearer or sweeter. Jesus answered with Scripture rightly understood: "It is written again" (Matthew 4:7). He said His sheep know His voice and will not follow a stranger (John 10:4–5). So the question is not whether an invitation sounds good, but whose voice is speaking. Do I know my Shepherd's voice well enough to recognize an imitation?
units.application: When an offer uses Wisdom's language, such as freedom, fulfillment or "you deserve this," ask where it leads and what it asks you to take that is not yours. Parents, teach children that bad choices often come wrapped in good words, and practice spotting them together in ads and shows. If you counsel others, help them test an appeal by its fruit and its end, not its slogans. Daily time in Scripture trains your ear for the true voice.

rel.note: Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet at first and later fills the mouth with gravel, the hidden end of Folly's sweet bread.
Drinking water from one's own cistern pictures the faithful marriage that stolen water betrays.
The seductress promises secret pleasure because her husband is not at home, the same appeal Folly makes.
Wisdom slaughtered, mixed and furnished her own feast, while Folly has prepared nothing.
Wisdom freely gives the bread and wine she prepared, while Folly offers what is stolen and hidden.

units.notes:
• "Eaten" is supplied in translation; the Hebrew reads literally "bread of secrecies." The 1611 KJV noted this in its margin: "of secrecies."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "If Proverbs 9:10 is the motto of the wise, here is that of the sophisticated." Folly's slogan stands opposite Wisdom's motto.
• Bridges: "Ah! sinner—there is no such thing as secret sin." Compare 5:21, "For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD."
• Compare 20:17, "Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, But afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel"; Romans 7:8; and Hebrews 11:25, "the passing pleasures of sin."
• Compare Jeremiah 2:13, where God's people forsake "the fountain of living waters" for "broken cisterns that can hold no water."
units.summary: Everything on Folly's table is stolen or hidden, and she sells the theft as the flavor.
units.principle: Forbidden pleasure draws its sweetness from the theft and the secrecy, and that sweetness is a lie that hides its cost.
units.insight: Eve saw that the fruit was "pleasant to the eyes" (Genesis 3:6), and the one forbidden tree became the one she wanted. Augustine confessed that as a youth he stole pears and threw most of them away; he wanted the forbidden act, not the fruit. David took another man's wife in secret, and God answered, "For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel" (2 Samuel 12:12). Achan hid stolen goods in his tent, and they were found (Joshua 7:21–22). Folly's lie is that the stolen is sweeter than the given. Where is secrecy making something feel sweeter to you? The gospel answers with a better offer. Jesus told a woman who had had five husbands, "whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst" (John 4:14, 18). What we steal leaves us thirsty; what He gives satisfies.
units.application: If you are hiding a relationship, a browsing habit or a "harmless" secret, bring it into the light this week by telling God and one trusted person. Married couples, invest in your own well: time, affection and honest conversation (5:15–19). Young people, when the thrill of something comes mainly from its being forbidden, treat that as a warning sign. Leaders, refuse any private arrangement you would be ashamed to have known.

rel.note: The one who wanders from understanding rests in the assembly of the dead, where Folly's guests are found.
The immoral woman's paths lead to the dead, using the same Hebrew word for the shades of the departed.
The seductress's house is the way to hell, descending to the chambers of death, the same end as Folly's guests.
Folly knows nothing, and so her guest does not know what waits inside her house.
Her guests are literally her called ones, the passersby she called from her seat.
Wisdom's guests are told to forsake foolishness and live, while Folly's guests end among the dead.

units.notes:
• "The dead" translates rephaim, the shades of the departed in Sheol. Proverbs also uses the word at 2:18 and 21:16, where the man who wanders from understanding "Will rest in the assembly of the dead."
• "Hell" translates Sheol, the Old Testament word for the realm of the dead. The NKJV and KJV read "hell," the ESV and NASB keep "Sheol," and the NLT has "the grave." The verse does not describe that realm beyond placing Folly's guests in its depths.
• Henry: "Thus does Solomon show the hook; those that believe him will not meddle with the bait."
• Bridges: "Satan shows only the sparkling cup, and the glaring light. Ask to look into the inner chamber."
• The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, adds four lines after this verse that are not in the Hebrew, urging the reader to hurry away from Folly's place and not to drink from a stranger's fountain.
• Compare 7:27; 14:12; Romans 6:23; James 1:15.
units.summary: Folly's door promises a party, but the rooms behind it are full of the dead.
units.principle: Sin hides its end from those it invites, so every invitation must be judged by where it leads, not by how it looks at the door.
units.insight: The young man of chapter 7 went after the seductress "as an ox goes to the slaughter," and "He did not know it would cost his life" (7:22–23). Samson woke from sleep on Delilah's knees and "did not know that the LORD had departed from him" (Judges 16:20). Folly's guests always find out too late. The prodigal son went to the far country to live as he pleased and ended up longing for the pigs' food (Luke 15:13–16). He came home, and his father said, "this my son was dead and is alive again" (Luke 15:24). That is the gospel's answer to this verse. Christ shared our flesh and went through death to free those held by the fear of it (Hebrews 2:14–15). If you have been sitting at Folly's table, the door to Wisdom's house is still open. Get up and go home.
units.application: Before you say yes to a pleasure you know is wrong, follow it to the end: picture your marriage, your reputation and your conscience a year from now. Young people, ask someone older who has walked that road what they found inside. Parents, tell your children plainly about consequences, not only rules. If you are already inside Folly's house, do not wait to hit bottom; call a pastor or trusted believer today and walk out.

rel.note: The wise son who gathers in summer and the son who causes shame close the section that this verse opens.
The same first line, a wise son who makes a father glad, is set against a foolish man who despises his mother.
The foolish son again brings grief to his father and bitterness to his mother, showing both parents share the sorrow.
The father's first appeal honors both father and mother, the same two parents whose joy and grief this verse describes.
The father of the righteous rejoices, and both father and mother are called to be glad over a wise child.

units.notes:
• "The proverbs of Solomon" is the first new heading since 1:1. The collection it opens runs from 10:1 to 22:16 and holds 375 verses in the NKJV numbering.
• "Grief" is a heavy sorrow that weighs a person down; the KJV has "heaviness." Esau's marriages were "a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35), one grief shared by both parents.
• Some older interpreters thought the verse meant that fathers rejoice and mothers grieve. Bridges answers that the inspired writer "interchangeably ascribes these exercises of feeling to both parents." In plain words, Proverbs speaks of either parent feeling the joy or the sorrow (17:25; 23:24–25).
• The first line returns word for word in Hebrew at 15:20, "A wise son makes a father glad." Proverbs 17:25 returns to the foolish son, who is "a grief to his father, And bitterness to her who bore him."
units.summary: A child's choices never stay private; they come home as a father's joy or a mother's tears.
units.principle: Wisdom and folly are never private; the way a child walks becomes joy or sorrow for everyone who loves him.
units.insight: Scripture knows both sides of this verse. David, old and bedridden, blessed God when Solomon was made king (1 Kings 1:47–48), but earlier he had wept "O my son Absalom" over a rebel son (2 Samuel 18:33). Yet a grieving parent is not always a failed parent. God Himself says He raised children who rebelled against Him (Isaiah 1:2). Matthew Henry comforts parents who taught faithfully: they "will have for their support under their heaviness that they have done their duty." That is, they may rest in their faithfulness. The verse also asks every son and daughter, of any age: what are you carrying home to those who love you? Only one Son made His Father wholly glad: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). In Him the prodigal is welcomed home, and a father's grief turns into a feast (Luke 15:24).
units.application: Young people and adult children: before a major decision, ask how it will land at home, and if you have caused grief, go back and say so. Parents: tell your children specifically when their wise choices make you glad, not only when they disappoint you. Parents grieving a wayward child: keep praying and keep the door open, and refuse the lie that your child's choice is the final verdict on your faithfulness.

rel.note: The next verse names the reason wicked treasure fails: the LORD Himself casts away the desire of the wicked.
The same second line, "righteousness delivers from death," answers riches that cannot help in the day of wrath.
The gang that grabs for treasure lies in wait for its own blood; greed takes away the life of its owners.
Treasure gained by a lying tongue is a fleeting fantasy pursued by those who seek death.

units.notes:
• The second line returns word for word in 11:4, where it answers a different first line: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath."
• Matthew Henry explains what kind of deliverance is meant: righteousness delivers "though not from the stroke of death, yet from the sting of it." The righteous still die, but death cannot destroy them (1 Corinthians 15:55–57).
• Jeremiah pictures dishonest gain as a partridge sitting on eggs that never hatch: the man who gets riches unjustly loses them, "And at his end he will be a fool" (Jeremiah 17:11).
• Compare Mark 8:36: "For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?" Compare also the rich fool of Luke 12:16–21.
units.summary: Stolen money can buy almost anything except the one thing that matters at the end: life.
units.principle: Wealth gained by wrong cannot buy what matters most, but a righteous life keeps a person on the road that leads away from death.
units.insight: Achan hid stolen silver and gold under his tent, and it cost him his life (Joshua 7:20–26). Judas took thirty pieces of silver and could not bear to keep them (Matthew 27:3–5). Bridges asks the verse's question directly: "What was the profit of the thirty pieces of silver to Judas?" The pull of dishonest gain rarely starts with a robbery. It starts with a padded expense, a hidden fee, a small lie on a form. The verse asks what we are trusting to keep us safe. In the end, the righteousness that delivers from death is not one we produce. God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Those who receive that gift then live righteously, not to earn life but because they have been given it.
units.application: If you run a business or handle money at work, refuse the padded invoice, the hidden charge and the unreported cash, even when "everyone does it." If you have gained something dishonestly, make it right, as Zacchaeus did when he met Jesus (Luke 19:8). Parents: talk with your children about how money is earned, not only how much of it there is.

rel.note: Wicked treasure profits nothing because, as this verse explains, the LORD casts away what the wicked crave.
The desire of the righteous is granted while the wicked meet what they fear, the other side of the LORD pushing away their craving.
The righteous eat until satisfied while the stomach of the wicked is in want, the same contrast of appetite.
Agur asks God for the food allotted to him, trusting God for daily provision without riches or poverty.

units.notes:
• The word translated "soul," nephesh, can mean the appetite as well as the whole living person. Both fit here: God cares for the hungry body and for the person who lives in it.
• The word translated "desire" has two quite different meanings: a craving, usually a bad one, or ruin. The NKJV's "desire" and the ESV's "craving" take the first sense: the LORD pushes aside what the wicked long for. The KJV has "substance," the wicked man's goods.
• Bridges keeps both truths together: God "may for the exercise of faith suffer us to hunger," but "not to famish." In other words, God may allow His people to go hungry for a time to train their faith, but He does not abandon them.
• Compare 13:25; Psalm 33:18–19, where the LORD's eye is on those who fear Him, "to keep them alive in famine"; and Matthew 6:31–33.
units.summary: The LORD is not neutral: He keeps the righteous from starving and sweeps aside what the wicked crave.
units.principle: God sustains those who walk with Him and resists the cravings of those who defy Him, though He may let His people know hunger for a season.
units.insight: When David fled from Absalom, exhausted and hungry in the wilderness, God fed him through unlikely hands, including Shobi, an Ammonite, the brother of a king who had humiliated David's messengers (2 Samuel 17:27–29; 10:1–4). Elijah was fed by ravens and then by a poor widow (1 Kings 17:4–16). Yet Jesus Himself went hungry for forty days. When the devil urged Him to make bread, He answered, "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). The soul God will not let starve is fed first by Him. The verse also searches us. Is there a craving God keeps pushing aside, and we keep reaching for? His refusal may be mercy. The rich fool got everything he grasped and lost his soul the same night (Luke 12:16–21).
units.application: If you are in a lean season, such as a lost job or a hard month, tell God your need plainly and accept help from His people; that is often how He feeds the righteous. If you have plenty, quietly supply a family in need this week. If something you crave keeps slipping away, ask whether God is resisting it before you push harder.

rel.note: The same words, "makes rich," name the blessing of the LORD as the source behind diligent hands.
The hand of the diligent rules while the lazy man ends in forced labor, the same contrast of hands.
Poverty can come from injustice rather than neglect, which keeps this verse from blaming every poor person.
The soul of the diligent is made rich while the lazy man desires and has nothing.
The plans of the diligent lead to plenty while haste leads to poverty, adding planning to steady work.

units.notes:
• The word translated "slack" can also mean deceitful, and the margin of the KJV offers "deceitful hand." Matthew Henry says it "may be read" that way. The idea fits: the careless worker takes the place and the wages of a worker without doing the work.
• The word for "the diligent" returns in 12:24, 13:4 and 21:5, each time set against the lazy or the hasty, so this verse begins a thread the collection keeps following.
• Ironside: "Faith and laziness do not mingle." He adds that what idle people call faith "is really presumption," that is, expecting God to do what He has given us hands to do.
• Compare 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12, "If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat," and Ecclesiastes 9:10.
units.summary: Careless hands slowly empty a house; steady hands slowly fill it.
units.principle: Steady, careful work generally builds a household up and neglect tears it down, though God, not effort alone, is the giver of every good gift.
units.insight: Ruth was poor, widowed and a foreigner, but her poverty was not laziness. She asked to glean and worked "from morning until now" in the fields of Boaz (Ruth 2:7), and God raised her up to become an ancestor of David and of Christ. God's callings often found people at work: Gideon was threshing wheat when the Angel of the LORD appeared (Judges 6:11), and the shepherds were keeping watch when the angels came (Luke 2:8). Our hearts are quick to dress up laziness in spiritual language, calling it waiting on God when it is really avoidance. Jesus spent years at a carpenter's bench (Mark 6:3), and He said, "My Father has been working until now, and I have been working" (John 5:17). Diligent hands are not a way to earn God's favor; they are one way to share His character.
units.application: Employees: give a full day's attention to the work you are paid for, especially when no one is checking (Colossians 3:23). Students: start the assignment early, not the night before. Church leaders and members: learn the difference between a brother who will not work and one who cannot. The first needs exhortation and accountability; the second needs practical help and patience.

rel.note: The wise son and the foolish son of the opening verse return here, framing the section.
The lazy man appears again, now seen from the side of those who depend on him.
The same "son who causes shame" loses his place to a wise servant, showing where the shame leads.
The lazy man will not plow in season and begs at harvest, another picture of a missed season.
The ant gathers in summer and harvest while the sluggard sleeps, the full portrait behind this verse.

units.notes:
• "A son who causes shame" translates the same Hebrew wording in 17:2, where such a son loses his place to a wise servant, and in 19:26, where he mistreats his father and mother.
• Joseph gathered grain through seven years of plenty to meet the famine that followed (Genesis 41:46–49). He shows the wise son's sense of timing on a national scale.
• Bridges applies the verse to youth: "It is as much the will of God, that the young should gather knowledge, as that the farmer should gather his harvest."
• Matthew Henry warns that whoever "idles away the days of his youth will bear the shame of his indolence when he is old." Indolence means laziness.
• Compare Jeremiah 8:20, "The harvest is past, The summer is ended, And we are not saved!" and 2 Corinthians 6:2, "now is the day of salvation."
units.summary: The harvest waits for no one; wisdom works while the season is open.
units.principle: Opportunities come in seasons, and wisdom acts while the door is open instead of waiting until it closes.
units.insight: Paul worked through every season God gave him, but he had to write, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Demas slept through the harvest. Jesus lived with the opposite urgency: "I must work the works of Him who sent Me while it is day; the night is coming when no one can work" (John 9:4). He told His disciples the fields were already "white for harvest" (John 4:35). Some seasons do not return: a child's early years, a friend's openness to the gospel, our own youth. The heart's favorite word is "later." Yet the gospel holds hope for those who have slept too long. In Jesus' parable, workers hired at the eleventh hour still received a full day's wage (Matthew 20:6–9). The Lord of the harvest still calls, and it is not too late to wake up.
units.application: Young people: the habits, skills and knowledge of Scripture you gather now are your harvest, so do not sleep through it. Parents of small children: these years will not come back; spend them on what lasts. Believers: if a friend is open to talking about God right now, do not wait for a better moment. Name one open opportunity this week and act on it before it closes.

rel.note: The same second line returns, now set against the life-giving mouth of the righteous, closing the section this verse opens.
The blessing that rests on the head of the righteous in life carries on in how they are remembered after death.
The man who disguises hatred with his lips shows what it looks like when speech covers harm.
A faithful man abounds with blessings, the same picture of blessing gathering on the righteous.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB read that the mouth of the wicked "conceals violence," and the NLT has "the words of the wicked conceal violent intentions." The 1984 NIV takes the other sense, "violence overwhelms."
• Matthew Henry takes the second sense: "Their mouths shall be stopped with shame for the violence which they have done." In that reading the wicked are finally left with nothing to say for themselves.
• "Covers" is a catchword, a repeated word that links neighboring sayings. The Hebrew verb, kasah, recurs in 10:11, in "love covers all sins" (10:12) and in "Whoever hides hatred" (10:18). The wicked cover violence, love covers sins, and the liar covers hatred.
• Compare 28:20, "A faithful man will abound with blessings"; Psalm 3:8, "Your blessing is upon Your people"; and Numbers 6:24–27.
units.summary: The righteous wear their blessings in the open; the wicked hide violence behind their words.
units.principle: A righteous life gathers blessing in the open, while a wicked heart must keep hiding behind its words.
units.insight: Blessing rests on the head because it comes from above. God gave Aaron the words "The LORD bless you and keep you," and said, "So they shall put My name on the children of Israel, and I will bless them" (Numbers 6:24, 27). The wicked work the other way, hiding harm under pleasant words. The spies sent to trap Jesus opened with flattery: "Teacher, we know that You say and teach rightly" (Luke 20:21). All the while they were looking for words to use against Him (Luke 20:20). The verse asks what lies behind our own words, at home, at work and online. Christ is the righteous One on whose head every blessing rests. He wore a crown of thorns for us, and He is now "crowned with glory and honor" (Hebrews 2:9). In Him God has "blessed us with every spiritual blessing" (Ephesians 1:3).
units.application: Before a hard conversation, ask what your words are covering: a desire to help, or a desire to win or wound. If you lead others, make your praise and your correction the same in private and in public. If someone's smooth words keep arriving with hidden demands, name what you see, kindly and plainly. Parents: speak a blessing over your children by name, so they hear it and remember it.

rel.note: The blessings that rest on the head of the righteous in life become the blessed memory of this verse.
The same picture of rottenness in the bones describes slow, inward decay, the image used here for a wicked name.
A good name is worth more than great riches, which explains why a blessed memory is so valuable.
The wise inherit glory while shame is the legacy of fools, the same contrast in what a life leaves behind.

units.notes:
• The first line reads literally "the memory of the righteous is for a blessing," and the ESV has "is a blessing." The wording suggests that their memory becomes a blessing to others, not only that people speak well of them.
• Jewish readers took the line as a duty. Matthew Henry describes the custom of "not naming an eminently just man that is dead without adding, Let his memory be blessed." The custom lives on in the phrase "of blessed memory."
• The verb "rot" is related to the noun translated "rottenness" in 12:4 and 14:30, where it describes decay in the bones. The same picture of slow decay lies behind what happens to the name of the wicked.
• Compare 22:1, "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches"; Psalm 112:6, "The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance"; and Hebrews 11:4, where Abel "being dead still speaks."
units.summary: Every life leaves something behind it: the fragrance of blessing or the smell of decay.
units.principle: What a person is outlasts what a person has; a righteous life goes on blessing others after it ends, and a wicked one spoils.
units.insight: When Mary of Bethany poured costly oil on Jesus, He said that wherever the gospel is preached, "what this woman has done will also be told as a memorial to her" (Mark 14:9). Two thousand years later, it still is. Jeroboam the son of Nebat built a kingdom, yet Scripture remembers him again and again as the man "who made Israel sin" (1 Kings 14:16). The verse asks what will remain of us: not titles or possessions, but the fragrance or stench of how we lived. That question can frighten us, because we know what our names deserve. The dying thief knew it too. He prayed, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom," and Jesus answered, "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:42–43). The One whose name is above every name chooses to remember sinners who come to Him.
units.application: Write down how you hope your family, church and coworkers will remember you, then compare it with your last month, and change one thing. At funerals and anniversaries, give specific thanks for the righteous who have gone before. Parents and grandparents: tell your children the stories of faithful people in your family and church, so that their memory keeps doing good.

rel.note: The same second line, "a prating fool will fall," returns beside the man who winks with the eye.
Keeping instruction places a person in the way of life, the result of the teachable heart described here.
The fool is right in his own eyes while the wise man heeds counsel, the same contrast between receiving and refusing.
The fool delights not in understanding but in expressing his own heart, a portrait of the prating fool.
Instruction given to a wise man makes him wiser, because the wise in heart receive it.

units.notes:
• "Prating" means chattering. The margin of the 1611 King James Version gives the Hebrew literally as "a fool of lips," and the ESV calls him "babbling."
• The verb "fall" means to be thrown or thrust down. The KJV margin offers "be beaten" only as an alternative rendering.
• Matthew Henry: "Those that are full of tongue seldom look well to their feet, and therefore stumble and fall." A person busy talking is not watching where he walks.
• Compare 12:15; 18:2, "A fool has no delight in understanding, But in expressing his own heart"; and James 1:19, "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak."
units.summary: Wise people listen their way to safety; fools talk their way into a fall.
units.principle: A teachable heart keeps a person standing, while a mouth that will not stop to listen leads to a fall.
units.insight: Young Samuel said, "Speak, for Your servant hears" (1 Samuel 3:10), and the LORD let none of his words fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19). Belshazzar knew all that had happened to his father Nebuchadnezzar, yet Daniel told him, "you ... have not humbled your heart, although you knew all this" (Daniel 5:22). He fell that same night. Even the Son of God received before He spoke: "as My Father taught Me, I speak these things" (John 8:28). Mary of Bethany chose the better part when she "sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word" (Luke 10:39). The verse exposes a common habit: we listen only long enough to prepare our answer. A teachable heart is not weak. It is the kind of heart God builds on, and the kind that does not fall.
units.application: In your next meeting or family argument, let the other person finish, then repeat back what you heard before you answer. When a boss, parent or elder gives you an instruction, ask a clarifying question instead of explaining why it will not work. Young people: find one older believer whose counsel you will actually take this month. Leaders: ask whether you are known for listening or only for talking.

rel.note: Hatred covered by deceit is revealed before the assembly, the same exposure that comes to the crooked.
The blameless walker is saved while the one perverse in his ways falls, the same pair of walks.
The LORD is a shield to those who walk uprightly, the source of the security this verse describes.
The one who keeps wisdom walks safely in his way without stumbling, another picture of the secure walk.

units.notes:
• A later saying sets the same pair side by side: "Whoever walks blamelessly will be saved, But he who is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall" (28:18).
• "Perverts" means to twist or make crooked. Matthew Henry pictures such a man as one who "looks one way and rows another," a picture of someone who pretends to be heading one way while he is really going another.
• The upright man's security has a source: the LORD "is a shield to those who walk uprightly" (2:7).
• Compare Psalm 26:1, "I have walked in my integrity"; Luke 12:2, "For there is nothing covered that will not be revealed"; and 1 Timothy 5:24–25.
units.summary: A life with no hidden side has nothing to fear from the light.
units.principle: A life with nothing to hide can walk without fear, but crooked ways are eventually brought into the light.
units.insight: Ziba lied to David about his master Mephibosheth and was handed Mephibosheth's land as a reward (2 Samuel 16:1–4). For a while the lie worked. But when the king returned, Mephibosheth's unwashed feet and untrimmed beard showed he had mourned for David all along (2 Samuel 19:24–27). Joseph walked the other road. He refused Potiphar's wife, lost his position and went to prison, yet God brought his integrity into the light (Genesis 39–41). A double life is exhausting. It means remembering which story was told to whom and dreading every knock at the door. Jesus could ask His enemies, "Which of you convicts Me of sin?" (John 8:46), and no one could answer. We cannot ask that. But David's prayer is open to us: "I will walk in my integrity; Redeem me and be merciful to me" (Psalm 26:11). Integrity begins by bringing hidden things to the One who redeems.
units.application: If you are keeping something that would shame you if it came out, such as a hidden account, a private habit or a padded report, bring it into the light now, with God and with someone you trust. Managers: make it safe for employees to admit mistakes early. Parents: let your children see you admit when you were wrong, so they learn that truth is safer than hiding.

rel.note: The second line first appears there, set against the teachable heart instead of the sly signaler.
A perverse man sows strife and a whisperer separates friends, the kind of trouble hidden signals cause.
The one who winks his eye devises perverse things, the same secret signal of malice.
The worthless man winks with his eyes and sows discord, the fuller portrait of the troublemaker here.

units.notes:
• The second line in the Hebrew text repeats 10:8, and the NKJV, ESV and NASB follow it. The NLT's "but a bold reproof promotes peace" follows the ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, which calls the one who reproves boldly a peacemaker.
• Where the NKJV has "But," the ESV reads "and," because the Hebrew connecting word can mean either. On that reading both lines describe people who bring trouble.
• Matthew Henry compares the two men. The chatterer's case "is less dangerous of the two," because he mainly harms himself, and "The dog that bites is not always the dog that barks." In other words, the quiet signaler often does more harm than the noisy talker.
• Compare 6:13; 16:30, "He winks his eye to devise perverse things"; and Psalm 35:19.
units.summary: A sly wink can wound others without a word, and a loose mouth wounds its owner.
units.principle: Hidden signals of malice wound others as surely as open words, and every misuse of communication ends in harm.
units.insight: The most famous signal in Scripture was a kiss. Judas told the soldiers, "Whomever I kiss, He is the One; seize Him" (Matthew 26:48). A sign that should mean love became a sign of betrayal. David's prayer against those who "wink with the eye" also complains that they "hate me without a cause" (Psalm 35:19), and Jesus took those words for Himself: "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25). He knew what it was to be the target of glances and whispers. The verse reaches into ordinary life: rolled eyes across a meeting table, a look exchanged when someone leaves the room, a message forwarded with a knowing comment. None of these can be quoted back, yet they wound. The cure is not better manners but a heart made new, so that our eyes, lips and hands all tell the same truth.
units.application: In meetings, group chats and at the dinner table, refuse to join the silent signals: the knowing look, the eye roll, the side message about someone in the room. If you have a concern, say it openly and kindly to the person. Leaders: watch for groups that communicate in code, and bring the conversation into the open. If you tend to talk too much, practice stopping halfway through your next opinion.

rel.note: The lips of the righteous feed many, a second picture of speech that sustains others.
The same second line first appears there, set against blessings on the head of the righteous.
The law of the wise is a fountain of life, the same image applied to wise teaching.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, showing where life-giving speech comes from.
The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook, another picture of words as running water.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew phrase behind "a well of life" is the one the NKJV renders "a fountain of life" in 13:14 and 14:27.
• Matthew Henry calls the righteous man's mouth "a constant spring, whence issues good discourse for the edification of others." In other words, it keeps flowing with talk that builds people up.
• On the second line Henry gives two examples of a mouth that covers violence: "Joab kissed and killed, Judas kissed and betrayed" (2 Samuel 20:9–10; Matthew 26:49).
• Compare 18:4, "The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook"; Psalm 36:9; John 4:14; 7:38.
units.summary: A mouth can be a spring in the desert or a cover for harm; the heart behind it decides which.
units.principle: Words from a righteous heart give life to others, while words that cover harm are a danger however pleasant they sound.
units.insight: Jesus sat by a well in Samaria and offered a weary woman "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). She left her water jar, went back to her town, and her words drew many people to Him (John 4:28–30, 39). One conversation with Christ turned her mouth into a well of life for others. Jesus promised the same to all who believe: "out of his heart will flow rivers of living water," which He said of the Spirit (John 7:38–39). The verse asks whether people come away from our words refreshed or drained. A well can give only what flows into it. Words that give life cannot be produced by technique. They come from a heart that keeps drinking from God.
units.application: Before you visit someone who is sick or grieving, pray that your words will refresh rather than lecture. Parents: end the day with a word of blessing or encouragement for each child. Friends and coworkers: when someone is discouraged, offer one specific, true encouragement instead of quick advice. If your speech keeps turning sharp, look at what you are taking in, and spend more time in Scripture and prayer.

rel.note: The same verb describes hatred hidden behind lying lips, the opposite use of covering.
The same word for sin appears there: many words multiply the offenses that love must cover.
A wrathful man stirs up strife while the patient man calms it, another picture of what keeps conflict alive.
Covering a transgression seeks love while repeating it separates friends, the same choice between covering and stirring.
Open rebuke is better than hidden love, which keeps covering from becoming silence about real wrong.
Covering one's own sins brings no prosperity, so the covering love gives is for others' offenses, not one's own.

units.notes:
• "Covers" is the same Hebrew verb used in 10:6 and 10:11, where the wicked cover violence, and in 10:18, where the liar hides hatred. Here the same act of covering is put to good use.
• For "all sins" the ESV reads "all offenses." The Hebrew word, pesha, is often translated "transgression," a wrong that breaks faith with another person or rebels against God. It is the same word translated "sin" in 10:19.
• Peter quotes the line: "And above all things have fervent love for one another, for 'love will cover a multitude of sins'" (1 Peter 4:8). Compare James 5:20, where turning a sinner back from his error will "cover a multitude of sins."
• Ironside guards the verse against misuse: "Other's faults, not my own, I am called upon to cover." Love covers a brother's sin not by ignoring it but by lovingly showing him his sin, so that he can confess it and it can be put away.
units.summary: Hatred keeps the old wound open; love lets it heal.
units.principle: Love refuses to keep offenses alive and chooses to forgive, without ever hiding wrongdoing that must be confronted or stopped.
units.insight: When Noah lay uncovered in his tent, Ham went out and told his brothers. Shem and Japheth took a garment, walked in backward and covered their father without looking (Genesis 9:22–23). That is the difference between hatred and love. Joseph did the same for the brothers who sold him: "do not therefore be grieved or angry with yourselves" (Genesis 45:5). Yet love is not silence about danger; Nathan's love for David made him say, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). The verse searches our hearts. Which old injury do we keep retelling? Bridges asks, "What is our brother's all against us, compared with our all against God?" The answer is the gospel: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered" (Psalm 32:1). Those whose sins Christ has covered learn to cover the sins of others.
units.application: When an old offense comes to mind, refuse to retell it to a third person; take it to God instead. Spouses: stop bringing past failures into present arguments. Church members: when you hear a damaging story, ask whether repeating it serves anyone's good. But if someone is being abused, harmed or endangered, love speaks up and reports it. Covering never means hiding a crime or leaving the vulnerable unprotected.

rel.note: The same Hebrew expression, lack of heart, lies behind "lack of wisdom" where fools die.
Beatings are prepared for the backs of fools, the same result for those who will not learn by words.
A rod for the fool's back repeats the second line's warning about correction that comes by force.
The young man "devoid of understanding" shows what lacking heart looks like in a life.

units.notes:
• "Devoid of understanding" is literally "lacking heart," the phrase used in 7:7 and 9:4. In Proverbs the heart stands for inner sense and judgment, so this man lacks the very faculty that would let him learn. The same expression lies behind "lack of wisdom" in 10:21.
• The 1611 King James Version reads "void of understanding" and notes in its margin that the Hebrew word is "heart."
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "He that can learn, and will not learn, should be made to learn."
• Compare 19:29; 26:3; and Psalm 32:9: "Do not be like the horse or like the mule, Which have no understanding, Which must be harnessed with bit and bridle."
units.summary: Learn through your ears, or you will learn the hard way.
units.principle: Correction comes to everyone; the wise receive it through words, and those who refuse words receive it through pain.
units.insight: Solomon asked God for "an understanding heart" (1 Kings 3:9), and people came from all nations to hear the wisdom of his lips (1 Kings 4:34). His son Rehoboam would not listen. He rejected the counsel of the elders and told the people, "my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scourges!" (1 Kings 12:14). He lost ten tribes almost at once (1 Kings 12:16–19). God usually speaks first in words: Scripture, a friend's counsel, a pricked conscience. When we will not hear, He loves us too much to leave us alone, and the lesson comes harder (Hebrews 12:6). Yet the gospel holds a greater wonder. Isaiah says of the Servant, "The chastisement for our peace was upon Him, And by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). The One who had all understanding bore the stripes meant for us.
units.application: When a parent, pastor, doctor or friend warns you, take it the first time, while correction is still only words. Parents: explain and warn patiently before you discipline, so your children learn to listen. Leaders: seek out people who give wise counsel and give them room to speak. If you are living under painful consequences now, ask what God was saying earlier that you did not hear.

rel.note: The prudent man conceals knowledge while the heart of fools proclaims foolishness, the same contrast of storing and spending.
Guarding the mouth preserves life while opening wide the lips brings destruction.
A fool's mouth is his destruction, the danger this verse says is near.
The LORD stores up sound wisdom for the upright, the same verb used here for the wise storing knowledge.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "store up" is the one used in 2:7, where the LORD "stores up sound wisdom for the upright." It means to hide something away as a treasure. The wise do with knowledge what the LORD does with wisdom.
• The word "destruction" links three sayings: here, 10:15 ("The destruction of the poor") and 10:29 ("destruction will come to the workers of iniquity").
• Matthew Henry: "We must continue laying up as long as we live; and be sure to lay it up safely, that it may not be to seek when we want it." In plain words, store knowledge so that it is not missing when you need it.
• Compare 12:23; 13:3; 18:7; and Matthew 13:52, the householder "who brings out of his treasure things new and old."
units.summary: The wise keep knowledge in the storehouse; the fool spends every thought the moment it arrives.
units.principle: Wisdom stores knowledge until it is needed, while a mouth that spends every thought invites its own ruin.
units.insight: Mary heard the shepherds' report and "kept all these things and pondered them in her heart" (Luke 2:19). She stored up what God was doing long before she understood it. Nabal did the opposite. When David's men asked for help, he answered with insults, "Who is David?" (1 Samuel 25:10), and within days he was dead (1 Samuel 25:38). Even the boy Jesus sat in the temple "both listening to them and asking them questions" (Luke 2:46). Our age invites us to publish every thought as soon as we have it. The verse calls us to fill the storehouse before we open the door. The psalmist shows the way: "Your word I have hidden in my heart, That I might not sin against You" (Psalm 119:11).
units.application: Before you post, reply to everyone or vent, wait a day and ask whether the words need to be said, by you, now. Students and young believers: memorize one passage of Scripture this month and keep a notebook of what you learn. Teachers and leaders: prepare more than you will say, so that your words come from a full store and not an empty one.

rel.note: The next saying turns from what money does to where each person's earnings go.
Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, the limit of wealth's protection.
Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, so the exposure of the poor calls for mercy, not contempt.
The name of the LORD is the strong tower where the righteous are truly safe, unlike the fortress of wealth.
The same first line adds that the strong city is a high wall only in the rich man's own esteem.

units.notes:
• "Destruction" is the same word used in 10:14 and 10:29. Here it is the ruin that poverty can bring when there is nothing to fall back on.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "This is a plain recognition of the power of wealth, and the paralysis of poverty."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, keeps money in its place: "You may be called to forgo wealth; you must certainly rate it below honesty."
• Compare Ecclesiastes 7:12, "wisdom is a defense as money is a defense"; 1 Timothy 6:17; and James 2:5.
units.summary: Money builds walls and poverty leaves people exposed, but no wall of wealth is as strong as it looks.
units.principle: Money gives real but limited protection in this world; the only refuge that cannot fail is the LORD Himself.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man whose wealth was a strong city. He dressed in purple and feasted every day, while Lazarus lay at his gate, exposed to hunger and to the dogs (Luke 16:19–21). The walls held for a lifetime, then failed in a moment, and the poor man was carried by the angels to Abraham's side (Luke 16:22). The verse tells the truth about money without worshiping it. The rich are tempted to trust their walls, and the poor are tempted to think poverty must be the end of them. Both need the strong tower of the LORD's name (18:10). Christ entered our exposure: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). In Him the poor have a fortress, and the rich have a reason to open their gates.
units.application: If you have savings, be thankful and prudent, but ask whether your peace depends on the balance. Use your walls to shelter someone exposed, such as covering a single parent's car repair or a widow's utility bill this month. If you are struggling financially, do not hide it from your church family; ask for help and counsel. Employers: remember how small a setback can ruin a low-wage worker.

rel.note: The previous saying shows what money does; this one asks where each person's gain goes.
The wicked man's work is deceptive while sowing righteousness brings a sure reward.
Righteousness leads to life and pursuing evil leads to death, the same two directions.

units.notes:
• The two lines use different Hebrew nouns. The first means work or the wages that work earns; the second means produce or yield, a word often used of crops and income. The ESV distinguishes them as "wage" and "gain," the KJV as "labour" and "fruit."
• Matthew Henry: "The things of this world are good or evil, life or death, as they are used, and as those are that have them." In other words, money does good or harm depending on how it is used and on the character of the one who has it.
• Cain and Abel each brought an offering from his own work to God (Genesis 4:3–8). Abel offered in faith (Hebrews 11:4); Cain's offering came from a heart that soon turned to murder. What each did with the fruit of his work showed which way he was walking.
• Compare 11:18–19; Ephesians 4:28, where the former thief works so "that he may have something to give him who has need"; and Galatians 6:7–8.
units.summary: Everyone gets paid; what matters is whether your earnings serve life or feed sin.
units.principle: The direction of a person's gain matters more than its size; earnings either serve life or feed sin.
units.insight: Zacchaeus had grown rich by cheating. When Jesus came to his house, the direction of his money changed in a day: "I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold" (Luke 19:8). In the same Gospel, women whose lives Jesus had touched "provided for Him from their substance" (Luke 8:3). Their earnings served life. The verse asks what our earnings are feeding. Jesus said, "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21), and a bank statement can be a searching spiritual document. Grace does not only forgive what we did with money; it turns our gain toward life. And labor given to Christ is never wasted: "your labor is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 15:58).
units.application: Look at last month's spending and ask where your earnings went: toward life, or toward habits that harm you or others. Choose one regular gift to your church or to someone in need. Young workers: decide now, before the next raise, what portion will go to giving and saving. Business owners: ask whether your profits strengthen your employees and community or only your own comfort.

rel.note: The wise in heart receive commands, the teachable spirit that keeps instruction.
Loving instruction is set against hating correction, the same two responses.
Whoever disdains instruction despises his own soul, while whoever heeds rebuke gets understanding.
The man who dies for lack of instruction goes astray in his folly, the end of refusing correction.
Reproofs of instruction are the way of life, the same road this verse describes.

units.notes:
• The final verb has a form that usually means to make someone else wander. The ESV takes it that way, "leads others astray," while the NKJV and NASB read "goes astray." The 1611 KJV reads "erreth," meaning goes wrong, and gives "causeth to err" in its margin.
• Matthew Henry: "The traveller that has missed his way, and cannot bear to be told of it and shown the right way, must needs err still." "Must needs" means he is bound to keep wandering.
• "The way of life" recalls the father's lesson in 6:23 and the two ways of chapters 1–9: correction is part of the road, not an interruption of it.
• Compare 12:1; 15:32; Hebrews 12:11; and Revelation 3:19.
units.summary: How you take correction decides which road you walk, and who follows you down it.
units.principle: A person's response to correction sets the direction of his life, and often of the lives of those who follow him.
units.insight: When Samuel confronted Saul, the king insisted, "But I have obeyed the voice of the LORD" (1 Samuel 15:20), and he lost his kingdom (1 Samuel 15:23). When Nathan confronted David, the king said, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13), and he was restored. Both sinned badly; the difference was what each did with correction. A leader who will not be corrected rarely goes astray alone. Our hearts are quick to defend, explain and shift blame. David learned to pray, "Let the righteous strike me; It shall be a kindness" (Psalm 141:5). Behind faithful correction stands the love of Christ Himself: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. Therefore be zealous and repent" (Revelation 3:19). His rebuke is not rejection but the affection of One who wants us near.
units.application: The next time someone corrects you, say "thank you" before anything else, and wait a day before defending yourself. Parents: correct in a way that keeps your child on the road, explaining the reason. Leaders: your refusal to be corrected will mislead those who follow you, so invite feedback from people under your authority. Young believers: ask a mature Christian to tell you where you are drifting.

rel.note: The same verb describes love covering sins, the opposite of hatred covered so it can work in secret.
The talebearer reveals secrets while the faithful spirit conceals a matter, the slanderer's opposite.
The words of a talebearer go down into the inmost body, showing why slander does such damage.
The man who disguises hatred with his lips and stores up deceit is the full portrait of the first line.

units.notes:
• "Hides" is the same Hebrew verb translated "covers" in 10:12. Love covers sins and makes peace; here hatred is covered so that it can work in secret.
• Bridges asks of the hypocrite's mask, "Is there not an Eye that looks through, and a Hand that will tear off, the flimsy cover?" The Eye and the Hand are God's.
• Leviticus 19:16–17 forbids both sins and gives a third way: "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people... You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor."
• Compare 26:24–26; 11:13; and Psalm 55:21, "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, But war was in his heart."
units.summary: Hatred either hides behind a smile or travels as a rumor; the first makes a liar, the second a fool.
units.principle: Hatred has no safe outlet in speech; hidden, it makes us liars, and spread, it makes us fools.
units.insight: Joab met Abner at the gate and took him aside "to speak with him privately," then stabbed him (2 Samuel 3:27). That is hatred hidden. Jeremiah's enemies took the other route. They accused him, "You are defecting to the Chaldeans!" and he was beaten and imprisoned on a lie (Jeremiah 37:13–15). That is hatred spread. Jesus suffered both. He was betrayed with a kiss and slandered as "a glutton and a winebibber" (Matthew 11:19), yet "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). Few of us will ever stab a rival. But polite words over private resentment, and a story passed on "just so you know," are the same sins in smaller form. Christ offers a third way: bring the resentment to God and, where needed, to the person (Matthew 18:15).
units.application: If you notice yourself smiling at someone you resent, name the resentment to God today and ask Him to deal with it. Before you pass on a story about someone, ask: Is it true? Is it mine to tell? Will it help them? Church members and coworkers: when someone brings you gossip, ask whether they have spoken to the person directly. Leaders: refuse to act on unverified reports.

rel.note: The same word for sin appears there, the offenses that love covers.
The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, which keeps restraint from becoming mere silence.
Guarding the mouth preserves life, the reward of restrained lips.
The one with knowledge spares his words, and even a fool seems wise when he holds his peace.
There is more hope for a fool than for a man hasty in his words.

units.notes:
• The word translated "sin" is the same word translated "sins" in 10:12, a wrong that breaks faith with others. Many words multiply the very offenses that love has to cover.
• The verb behind "restrains" is the one translated "spares" in 17:27, "He who has knowledge spares his words."
• Bridges: "a talent for conversation is valueless both to the possessor and to the auditors, except it be connected with a talent for silence." Auditors are listeners.
• Compare 17:27–28; 29:20; James 1:19; and Matthew 12:36, where Jesus warns that people will give account for "every idle word."
units.summary: The more words you spend, the more likely some of them are sin.
units.principle: Self-control in speech is wisdom: say what should be said, and leave unsaid what should not.
units.insight: Job's friends did their best work in the first week. They sat with him seven days, "and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:13). Then they began to talk, and their many words ended in God's verdict, "you have not spoken of Me what is right" (Job 42:7). On the mountain of transfiguration Peter filled the silence, "not knowing what he said" (Luke 9:33). Jesus stood before Pilate and "answered him not one word" (Matthew 27:14), yet at the right time His words were life. James admits, "we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man" (James 3:2). Only One was. The rest of us need His forgiveness for careless words and His Spirit to guard our lips.
units.application: In your next meeting or class, make your point once and then stop. When you visit someone who is grieving, plan to listen more than you speak; presence often says more than explanations. Spouses: in an argument, hold back the extra sentence you know will wound. As Matthew Henry puts it, "Little said is soon amended." But when someone needs truth or comfort from you, do not hide behind silence.

rel.note: The next saying shows what such valuable speech does: it feeds many.
A word fitly spoken is pictured as gold in settings of silver, the same value placed on good speech.
Silver dross only coats a clay pot, while the tongue of the righteous is refined silver throughout.
Out of the heart spring the issues of life, which explains why a worthless heart makes worthless words.
Wisdom's revenue is better than choice silver, the same measure of worth.

units.notes:
• "Worth little" is literally "like a little," meaning next to nothing.
• Choice silver has had its dross removed. Compare 26:23, where "silver dross" only coats a cheap clay pot. There the shine is a surface; here the silver is pure throughout.
• God's own words are described the same way: "The words of the LORD are pure words, Like silver tried in a furnace of earth, Purified seven times" (Psalm 12:6).
• Wisdom uses the same comparison for her gifts: "My fruit is better than gold, yes, than fine gold, And my revenue than choice silver" (8:19). Compare 25:11 and Luke 6:45.
units.summary: The words of the righteous are worth more than the wicked man's whole heart.
units.principle: The worth of words is settled in the heart; a purified life gives speech its value.
units.insight: Peter had no money. At the temple gate he told a lame man, "Silver and gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk" (Acts 3:6). His tongue was choice silver. Later Simon the sorcerer offered money for the power of the Spirit, and Peter answered, "your heart is not right in the sight of God" (Acts 8:21). The man with silver in his hand had a heart worth little. The verse humbles us, for no heart is pure silver by nature. But God does not leave it there: "I will give you a new heart" (Ezekiel 36:26). Those who heard Jesus "marveled at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth" (Luke 4:22). He makes His people's hearts new, and their words begin to carry His worth.
units.application: Value the words of godly people around you: write down one piece of counsel from an older believer this week and act on it. Before you speak into a hard situation, ask God to search your heart first (Psalm 139:23). Parents and teachers: praise the character behind a child's kind words, not only the words. When choosing whom to listen to, weigh their life, not just their eloquence.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, a second picture of words that sustain others.
The same Hebrew expression, lack of heart, describes the one who needs the rod.
The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, the worth behind words that feed many.
The lips of the wise disperse knowledge, the same picture of speech that spreads good to others.
The man who dies for lack of instruction shows the same end as fools who die for lack of wisdom.

units.notes:
• "Feed" translates ra'ah, the same verb behind "shepherd" in Psalm 23:1, "The LORD is my shepherd." The righteous do with words what a shepherd does with pasture.
• "Lack of wisdom" is literally "lack of heart," the same expression behind "devoid of understanding" in 10:13. The 1611 King James Version reads "for want of wisdom" and marks "of heart" in its margin as the Hebrew wording.
• Matthew Henry: "While the righteous feed others fools starve themselves."
• Compare 15:7; 5:23; John 21:15–17; and Amos 8:11, which warns of a famine "Not a famine of bread, Nor a thirst for water, But of hearing the words of the LORD."
units.summary: The righteous feed others with their words, while fools starve beside a full table.
units.principle: Words from a righteous heart nourish many people, while those who refuse wisdom starve themselves.
units.insight: Jesus fed five thousand with a boy's lunch, and the next day told the crowd, "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). After His resurrection He asked Peter three times about his love and gave him one work: "Feed My sheep" (John 21:17). Peter, who had failed so loudly with his lips, would now use them to feed others. Samuel promised Israel, "I will teach you the good and the right way" (1 Samuel 12:23), while King Saul, who heard the same words, did not profit from them. The verse asks two questions. Whom are my words feeding? And am I eating, or starving beside a full table? No one can feed others for long without being fed by the Good Shepherd Himself.
units.application: Choose one person you will intentionally encourage from Scripture this week: a new believer, a struggling friend or a child. Parents: read and talk about a short passage at one meal each week. Small-group leaders and teachers: feed on the passage yourself before you prepare to teach it. If you feel spiritually starved, put yourself where the Word is taught and ask a mature believer to read the Bible with you.

rel.note: The same words, "makes rich," describe the diligent hand, the means God's blessing uses.
Trusting in riches leads to a fall, which keeps this verse from becoming a promise of wealth.
A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, the sorrow God does not add.
Greed takes away the life of its owners, the sorrow that comes with wealth not given by the LORD.
Wearing oneself out to get rich is futile because riches fly away, the toil that adds nothing to God's blessing.

units.notes:
• The word translated "sorrow," 'etseb, is the word used in Genesis 3:16, "In pain you shall bring forth children," and it is closely related to "toil" in Genesis 3:17. It covers both pain and painful labor. That is why the line can mean either that the LORD adds no sorrow to His blessing or that toil adds nothing to it. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and NLT take the first reading.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "God giveth to his, wealth without woe, store without sore, gold without guilt." "His" means His people.
• 10:4 and 10:22 belong together. The LORD's blessing is the first cause of riches, and diligence is the means He uses; the sluggard expects plenty without work, and the self-reliant expect it from work alone.
• Compare 15:16; Psalm 127:2, "It is vain for you to rise up early, To sit up late, To eat the bread of sorrows; For so He gives His beloved sleep"; and 1 Timothy 6:6–10.
units.summary: God's riches come without the hidden bill that greed always sends later.
units.principle: Every good gift comes from the LORD, and what He gives does not carry the hidden sorrows of wealth gained by greed.
units.insight: Abraham refused even a thread from the king of Sodom, "lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich'" (Genesis 14:23). He wanted no riches that did not come from God's hand. Gehazi went the other way. He ran after Naaman's silver, got it, and carried leprosy home with it (2 Kings 5:20–27). Ahab had a palace and still lay on his bed sulking over a neighbor's vineyard (1 Kings 21:4). Our hearts are prone to measure God's blessing by a bank balance. Ironside corrects that: "It is not that the blessing of the Lord insures freedom from tribulation in a world like this." Paul, who knew both hunger and plenty, could still write, "my God shall supply all your need according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:19). The richest blessing is Christ Himself, and He adds no sorrow with Himself.
units.application: Before you chase a raise, a deal or a purchase, ask whether it will come with sorrow attached: debt, strained relationships, compromised honesty or lost time with family. Thank God aloud for specific provision this week. Pastors and teachers: never present this verse as a promise of wealth; point people to God's care for their needs. If you are struggling financially, your lack is not a sign that God's blessing has left you.

rel.note: Fools mock at sin, the same light treatment of evil.
Folly is joy to the one without discernment while the man of understanding walks uprightly.
The man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I was only joking," shows evil treated as play.
The wicked rejoice in doing evil and delight in perversity, the fool's sport in fuller form.
Wisdom rejoices before the LORD with the same kind of delight the fool finds in evil.

units.notes:
• The noun behind "sport" means laughter or play. It belongs to the same Hebrew word family as the verb translated "Rejoicing" in 8:30–31, where Wisdom delights before the LORD. The fool finds that kind of delight in doing evil.
• Several versions fill out the short second line. The ESV makes wisdom the man of understanding's "pleasure," the NASB supplies words so that wisdom is his "sport" as evil is the fool's, and the NLT has "living wisely brings pleasure to the sensible."
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "A man of understanding finds sport in wisdom."
• Compare 2:14, those "Who rejoice in doing evil"; 15:21, "Folly is joy to him who is destitute of discernment"; and 26:18–19.
units.summary: What you laugh at shows what you love.
units.principle: What a person enjoys reveals his heart; the fool delights in evil, and the wise delight in wisdom.
units.insight: Belshazzar threw a party and called for the gold cups taken from God's temple. His guests drank from them and praised their idols (Daniel 5:2–4). Holy things became entertainment, and that night the king was slain (Daniel 5:30). The soldiers in Pilate's headquarters turned the suffering of the Son of God into a game, with a robe, a reed and a crown of thorns (Matthew 27:27–31). The verse asks what amuses us. Much of our entertainment invites us to laugh at what grieves God: cruelty, betrayal, adultery and contempt. A heart that laughs at sin is drifting toward the fool's sport. The cure is not grimness but a better delight. The Son could say, "I delight to do Your will, O my God" (Psalm 40:8), and He gives His people a share in that joy.
units.application: Notice what you laughed at this week, in shows, online and in conversation, and drop one source of entertainment that makes sin look like fun. Bridges asks whether we should not "guard against mischievous jokes, tending to wound a neighbour's character." Parents: teach children the difference between having fun and making fun of someone. Coworkers: refuse to join the joke at someone's expense, and find your delight in doing good.

rel.note: The whirlwind that sweeps away the wicked shows how the feared disaster arrives.
The hope of the righteous ends in gladness while the expectation of the wicked perishes, the same two endings.
The LORD casts away the desire of the wicked, while here He grants the desire of the righteous.
The desire of the righteous is only good while the expectation of the wicked is wrath.
Wisdom warns that terror will come like a storm on those who refuse her, the dread of the first line.

units.notes:
• The word for "fear" here is a different Hebrew word from the one in "the fear of the LORD" (10:27). It means dread, and the ESV renders it with the verb "dreads."
• The builders of Babel said, "let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered," and the LORD scattered them (Genesis 11:4, 8). What they feared came upon them.
• Bridges explains how God grants the desires of the righteous: He answers "not according to our wishes, but our wants." In other words, He gives what His people truly need, not every request.
• Compare 10:28; 11:23, "The desire of the righteous is only good"; 1 John 5:14–15; and Hebrews 2:15.
units.summary: In the end the wicked meet what they dread, and the righteous receive what they long for.
units.principle: Each person finally meets what his heart has been facing: the wicked their dread, and the righteous their longing for God.
units.insight: Felix listened as Paul reasoned about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and he "was afraid" (Acts 24:25). Instead of turning, he sent Paul away until a more convenient time. The dread was a mercy he refused. Hannah carried a different burden, a longing for a child, poured out before the LORD. Later she said, "For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition" (1 Samuel 1:27). The verse asks what lives in our hearts when we think about the future. Hidden dread is often God's warning; holy longing is His invitation. Christ came to "release those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage" (Hebrews 2:15). In Him the believer's deepest desire, to see God, will be granted in full (1 John 3:2).
units.application: If a fear of being found out keeps nagging you, treat it as a warning: confess and make things right while there is time. Write down what you most desire, and ask whether those desires are set on God or only on comfort. When a prayer seems unanswered, keep praying, and trust Him to give what you need. If you comfort anxious friends, point them to Christ, not only to coping techniques.

rel.note: The dread of the wicked comes upon them, and this verse shows it arriving like a whirlwind.
The righteous will never be removed, the final security this verse pictures as a foundation.
The root of the righteous cannot be moved, another picture of the lasting foundation.
The wicked are overthrown and are no more while the house of the righteous stands.
Wisdom warns that destruction comes like a whirlwind on those who refuse her.

units.notes:
• The second line has no verb in Hebrew; it reads literally "and a righteous one, a foundation forever." The KJV takes it to mean that the righteous person himself "is an everlasting foundation." The NKJV says what he has, while the ESV says he "is established forever."
• Matthew Henry: the righteous "lie hid, like a foundation, which is low and out of sight, but they are fixed." A foundation is not admired, but it holds when everything above it is shaken.
• The flood in Noah's day swept away a whole generation that seemed secure (Luke 17:26–27). Compare Psalm 1:4, where the ungodly are "like the chaff which the wind drives away."
• Compare 12:3, 7; Isaiah 28:16; Matthew 7:24–27; and 1 Corinthians 3:11.
units.summary: The storm does not decide who is left standing; the foundation does.
units.principle: Storms come to everyone; what decides the outcome is not the storm but what a person stands on.
units.insight: A great wind struck the house where Job's children were feasting, and they all died (Job 1:19). The righteous are not spared every storm. Yet Job was not swept away. Out of the ruins he said, "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). Daniel's enemies seemed secure in the king's court, but when the storm turned, they were gone and Daniel stood (Daniel 6:24–28). The verse asks what we are standing on, and storms reveal the answer. A career, a reputation and a healthy body are good gifts but poor foundations. Paul names the only one that lasts: "For no other foundation can anyone lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:11). Those built on Him may lose much, but they cannot be blown away.
units.application: Before the next crisis comes, check your foundation: is your peace tied to your health, job or savings, or to Christ? Parents: build your children's faith now, through Scripture and prayer at home, not only in emergencies. If you are in a storm today, such as a diagnosis, a layoff or a loss, remember that losing things is not the same as being swept away. Friends: stand with those in the storm.

rel.note: The son who sleeps in harvest is the same lazy man, seen from his family's side.
A wicked messenger falls into trouble, while a faithful ambassador brings health, the two kinds of servant this verse sets before the sender.
A faithful messenger refreshes those who send him, the opposite of the irritation described here.
Sending a message by a fool cuts off one's own feet, another picture of the cost of an unreliable messenger.
The sluggard's full portrait stands behind the lazy man of this verse.

units.notes:
• A later saying gives the opposite picture: a faithful messenger refreshes his masters "Like the cold of snow in time of harvest" (25:13).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The drinker expected sweet wine but instead received sour vinegar." The sting is the gap between what was expected and what arrived.
• Matthew Henry: the slothful servant "occasions him grief to see his business neglected and undone, as smoke sets the eyes a weeping." That is, the master is pained to see his work left undone, as smoke makes the eyes water.
• Compare 13:17, "A wicked messenger falls into trouble, But a faithful ambassador brings health"; 26:6; and Matthew 25:26.
units.summary: A lazy worker is a small, constant sting to everyone who counts on him.
units.principle: Laziness is never only private; the one who will not do his part burdens everyone who depends on him.
