units.insight: In Jesus' parable, a servant was given money to put to work. He kept it wrapped in a handkerchief and brought it back with excuses (Luke 19:20–23). His master was not merely disappointed; he was provoked. Jesus is the opposite of the lazy man. He said, "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me, and to finish His work" (John 4:34). On the night before the cross He could tell the Father, "I have finished the work which You have given Me to do" (John 17:4). The verse asks who is waiting on us: an employer, a spouse, a ministry team, an aging parent. Do we refresh them or sting them? Christ's finished work is our rest when we have failed, and His Spirit makes us faithful messengers in turn.
units.application: If someone is waiting on you for a reply, a report or a promised repair, do it today or tell them plainly when you will. Employees and volunteers: finish the small errand as carefully as the big project. Supervisors: before you label someone lazy, ask whether illness, overload or unclear instructions are the real problem. Parents: give children small errands and praise them when the errands are done well.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life that turns a person from the snares of death.
The fear of the LORD leads to life, the same truth stated as a direction.
Keeping the father's commands adds length of days and long life.
Wisdom says days will be multiplied and years added, the same verb used here for prolonging days.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "prolongs" means "adds." The margin of the 1611 King James Version gives the Hebrew as "addeth," and it is the same verb used when Wisdom says years of life "will be added" (9:11).
• The fear in this verse is not the dread of the wicked in 10:24, which is a different Hebrew word. One is awe toward God; the other is terror of what is coming.
• The LORD is named four times in this chapter (10:3, 22, 27, 29), each time in a saying about outcomes.
• Bridges: whether the life of one who fears God "be shortened or prolonged, he lives long in a little time." A short life lived for God is not a short life in God's sight.
• Compare 3:1–2; 14:27; 19:23; and Psalm 90:12, "So teach us to number our days."
units.summary: Fearing God adds days to a life, but God's purposes, not a formula, number them.
units.principle: The fear of the LORD tends to preserve life and wickedness tends to shorten it, though God alone sets the length of any life.
units.insight: King Hezekiah, sick to the point of death, wept before the LORD, and God said, "I will add to your days fifteen years" (2 Kings 20:6). Yet Stephen, full of faith and the Holy Spirit, was stoned in the first days of the church (Acts 7:59–60), and John the Baptist was beheaded in prison (Mark 6:27). We cannot read God's verdict from the length of anyone's life. Jesus Himself was "cut off from the land of the living" (Isaiah 53:8). Yet Isaiah also said of Him, "He shall see His seed, He shall prolong His days" (Isaiah 53:10). Through the resurrection the One who died young now lives forever, and He shares that endless life with all who fear God. The real question is not how long we will live but whether we are living in the fear of the LORD now.
units.application: If you are grieving someone who died young, refuse any voice that reads their death as God's judgment; God's purposes are not a formula. If you are drifting toward reckless habits, such as heavy drinking, rage or dangerous risks, remember that the fear of the LORD protects life. Parents: model awe and obedience before God at home. Friends of the grieving: bring presence and prayer, not explanations.

rel.note: The desire of the righteous is granted while the wicked meet their dread, the same two endings.
The desire of the righteous is only good while the expectation of the wicked is wrath.
When a wicked man dies his expectation perishes, the same end stated at the moment of death.
There is a hereafter, and the hope of the one who fears the LORD will not be cut off.

units.notes:
• Because the first line has no verb, it can be read as a promise ("will be gladness") or as a present fact ("is gladness"). Both are true: hope in God is joyful now and ends in joy.
• Bridges: "For none have a stronger hope than those, who have no ground for hope." The wicked often feel most confident when they have least reason to be.
• False expectation can last right up to the end. In Jesus' warning, many will say "Lord, Lord" on that day and still be turned away (Matthew 7:21–23).
• Compare 11:7; 23:18, "your hope will not be cut off"; Romans 5:5; and Hebrews 6:19, hope as "an anchor of the soul."
units.summary: Hope anchored in God ends in joy; hope anchored anywhere else comes to nothing.
units.principle: Hope is only as good as what it rests on; hope in God ends in gladness, and every other expectation perishes.
units.insight: Haman went home from the queen's banquet sure of his future. When the king asked what should be done for the man he delighted to honor, Haman thought, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?" (Esther 6:6). Before long his expectation had perished with him (Esther 7:10). Simeon spent years "waiting for the Consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25). When he held the infant Jesus, he said, "Lord, now You are letting Your servant depart in peace" (Luke 2:29). His hope ended in gladness. The verse asks what we are counting on: a promotion, a retirement, a relationship, our own goodness? Peter names the hope that cannot perish. God "has begotten us again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). A hope anchored in a risen Savior cannot be buried.
units.application: Write down the three things you are most counting on for the next five years, and ask which of them would survive your death. If you are facing disappointment, let it drive your hope deeper into God rather than into bitterness. Parents: talk with your children about Christ's return, not only about careers. Believers in hard seasons: let your steady gladness show; it speaks to others more than arguments.

rel.note: The upright who find strength in the LORD's way are the righteous who will never be removed.
In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence and a place of refuge.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous are safe, the same stronghold.
The same words, "destruction will come to the workers of iniquity," are set against the joy of doing justice.

units.notes:
• The word translated "strength" means a place or means of safety, a refuge or stronghold. The ESV, NASB and NLT render it "stronghold."
• "Destruction" is the catchword already heard in 10:14 and 10:15; here it is the end of those who work iniquity.
• Matthew Henry: "the same providence, like the same sun, softens the one and hardens the other." The same dealings of God have opposite effects, depending on the heart that meets them.
• Compare 18:10; 21:15, which repeats "destruction will come to the workers of iniquity"; Nehemiah 8:10; and 2 Corinthians 2:15–16.
units.summary: The same road that strengthens the upright breaks those who fight against it.
units.principle: God's way does not bend; it is a stronghold for those who walk in it and ruin for those who set themselves against it.
units.insight: Nicodemus first came to Jesus by night, afraid to be seen (John 3:2). Later he spoke up for Jesus before the council (John 7:50–51). At the end he came openly with spices to bury Him (John 19:39). Walking in the way of the LORD made a timid man strong. Jesus said, "I am the way" (John 14:6), and He has the same double effect the verse describes. To those who believe He is precious, but to the disobedient He is "A stone of stumbling And a rock of offense" (1 Peter 2:7–8). The question is not whether we will meet God's way, but whether we will walk in it or crash against it. Weak believers need not wait to feel strong before they obey. Strength is found on the road, one step at a time.
units.application: If you feel too weak to keep obeying, take the next small step anyway; strength comes on the road. If you keep running into the same wall, ask whether you are fighting God's way. Leaders: shape your habits and decisions by God's ways, and you will find them holding you up. Parents: show your children that God's commands are a shelter, not a cage.

rel.note: The righteous have an everlasting foundation, the same security pictured as a building.
The way of the LORD is strength for the upright, the source of the stability promised here.
The root of the righteous cannot be moved, the same truth in a picture of a tree.
The upright dwell in the land while the wicked are cut off from the earth, the same two endings.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "earth" is also the ordinary word for "land," and the ESV renders it "the land." The NKJV of 2:21–22 uses both English words for it.
• Bridges explains that the verse is not about the troubles everyone shares but about "the state of the two classes as in the purpose and mind of God." It speaks of how God finally deals with each, not of every day's circumstances.
• Psalm 125:1 gives the same picture: "Those who trust in the LORD Are like Mount Zion, Which cannot be moved, but abides forever."
• Compare 12:3; Psalm 37:9–11, 29; and Matthew 5:5, "Blessed are the meek, For they shall inherit the earth."
units.summary: The righteous may lose a house, but they will never lose their place.
units.principle: Those who belong to God will never be uprooted from the place He gives them, while the wicked have no lasting place.
units.insight: Abraham was promised the land, yet God "gave him no inheritance in it, not even enough to set his foot on" (Acts 7:5). The only ground he owned was a cave where he buried Sarah (Genesis 23:17–20). Still he was not removed. He lived in tents because "he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:10). Many believers today lose homes, jobs and even countries. The verse does not deny their loss; it promises them a place no one can take. Jesus said of His sheep, "neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand" (John 10:28), and He promised that the meek "shall inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). Those who grasp at the earth will not keep it. Those who belong to Christ will inherit it.
units.application: If you have lost a home, a job or a country, take this verse as God's promise of a place He will not take away, and let your church family help you now. If you are settled and secure, hold your property loosely and use it to give others a place: host a student, house a family in crisis or help a refugee. Young adults: build on what cannot be removed before you build a career.

rel.note: Restraining the lips is wise, and this verse balances it: the righteous mouth also brings forth wisdom.
The same word for perverse links this verse to the next, and together they close the chapter on speech.
A man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth, the same picture of speech as fruit.
The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly while the mouth of fools pours out foolishness.
Wisdom hates the perverse mouth, which explains why the perverse tongue is cut out.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "brings forth" is a poetic word meaning to bear fruit. It is used of the righteous as fruitful trees in Psalm 92:14, "They shall still bear fruit in old age." The NASB renders it "flows."
• The word translated "perverse" means twisted or turned upside down. The same word appears in 10:32, linking the two verses that close the chapter.
• Matthew Henry: "the froward tongue shall be cut out, as surely as the flattering one," pointing to Psalm 12:3, where the LORD cuts off flattering lips. "Froward" is an older word for perverse.
• Compare 8:13, where Wisdom says she hates "the perverse mouth"; 15:2; and Matthew 12:33–35.
units.summary: A righteous mouth bears wisdom the way a healthy tree bears fruit; a twisted tongue gets cut away.
units.principle: Wise speech grows naturally from a righteous life, and speech that twists the truth will not last.
units.insight: Jezebel wrote letters full of lies to have Naboth stoned so that Ahab could take his vineyard (1 Kings 21:8–14). Her twisted words worked for a moment, but her end was swift and terrible (2 Kings 9:30–37). Elijah, whom she hated, spoke the word of the LORD, and his words still bear fruit. Jesus used this verse's picture: "a tree is known by its fruit" (Matthew 12:33). He also said, "Every branch in Me that does not bear fruit He takes away; and every branch that bears fruit He prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:2). Fruitful speech is not produced by trying harder to say the right thing. It grows from abiding in Christ. The verse asks whether our words are fruit or thorns, and the answer usually lies in how close we are staying to the Vine.
units.application: Before giving advice, ask whether it comes from time in God's Word or only from your own opinion. If you have a habit of twisting facts to win arguments, confess it and ask someone close to hold you accountable. Teachers and parents: let your instruction be the fruit of your own walk with God. Older believers: do not go quiet; your mouths can still bear fruit in old age (Psalm 92:14).

rel.note: The same word for perverse pairs the two closing sayings on the mouth of the righteous and the wicked.
A word spoken in due season is good, the fitting speech the righteous know.
Righteous lips are the delight of kings, words that are acceptable to those who hear them.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
Wisdom delivers from the man who speaks perverse things, the mouth described in the second line.

units.notes:
• The word for "acceptable," ratson, means goodwill, favor or what pleases. In 11:1 the same word is translated "His delight," where a just weight pleases the LORD. Acceptable words please God as well as the people who hear them.
• "Perverse" is the same word as in 10:31, so the chapter closes with a matched pair of sayings.
• Bridges insists that acceptable speech "must involve no compromise of principle," and that the preacher "must discriminate his statements, without diluting them." In plain words: choose the fitting way to say the truth, but never water it down.
• Compare 15:23; 16:13, "Righteous lips are the delight of kings"; 25:11; and Colossians 4:6, "Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt."
units.summary: Righteous lips know the fitting word; wicked mouths know only how to twist one.
units.principle: Righteous speech has learned what is fitting and pleasing to God, while wicked speech becomes skilled only in twisting.
units.insight: When David rode out to destroy Nabal's household, Abigail met him on the road. Her words were humble, wise and fitting, and David answered, "blessed is your advice and blessed are you, because you have kept me this day from coming to bloodshed" (1 Samuel 25:33). Gideon calmed the angry men of Ephraim with a few well-chosen words, and "their anger toward him subsided" (Judges 8:1–3). The Servant of the LORD says, "The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary" (Isaiah 50:4). Jesus knew what to say to a grieving widow, a proud Pharisee and a disciple who denied Him. The verse asks whether our skill with words serves life or harm. The Lord who knew the fitting word teaches it to all who learn from Him.
units.application: Before a hard conversation, with a teenager, an employee or a grieving friend, ask God for the fitting word and the right moment. Leaders: deliver hard news with truth and kindness together, never one without the other. If you are known for a sharp, clever tongue, use that skill to build people up instead of cutting them down. Write one encouraging note this week to someone who needs it.

rel.note: The abomination-and-delight pairing returns, moving from the dishonest scale to the twisted heart behind it.
Honest dealing extends to how goods are sold when neighbors are in need.
Honest weights and scales belong to the LORD, which explains why cheating with them offends Him.
Diverse weights and measures are again called an abomination to the LORD.
The same pairing of diverse weights and dishonest scales is condemned as an abomination.

units.notes:
• "A just weight" is literally "a perfect stone," as the 1611 King James margin notes: a whole, full-weight stone. The Hebrew word for a weight is the ordinary word for a stone, because merchants carried their weights as stones in a bag (Deuteronomy 25:13, "differing weights, a heavy and a light").
• For "Dishonest scales" the 1611 King James margin gives the Hebrew as "balances of deceit": the scale itself is made to lie. Henry: "A balance cheats, under pretence of doing right most exactly, and therefore is the greater abomination to God."
• Proverbs sets "abomination" and "delight" against each other here, in 11:20, and again in 12:22 and 15:8. It returns to honest weights in 16:11, 20:10 and 20:23.
• The prophets condemned the same fraud. Amos 8:5 exposes merchants who shrank the measure, raised the price and falsified their scales; compare Micah 6:11.
• Compare Matthew 7:12 and Luke 19:8, where Zacchaeus promises to restore fourfold anything he has taken by false accusation.
units.summary: The God of the altar is also the God of the marketplace, and He loves an honest scale.
units.principle: God watches ordinary business as closely as worship; every dishonest measure offends Him and every honest one pleases Him.
units.insight: This verse will not let anyone keep God for Sunday and the scale for Monday. Ironside says that small cheats, such as a yardstick slightly short or a pound weight under standard, "are the things that indicate character, and tell of a good conscience put away." The cheater has silenced his conscience. The thumb on the scale is rarely the first sin. It grows from a heart that has stopped fearing God where no one checks. Zacchaeus shows the cure. When Jesus came to his house, this longtime cheat promised to give half his goods to the poor and to repay fourfold anything he had taken by fraud (Luke 19:8). Grace did not make him careless about money; it made him honest. Christ, who "committed no sin, Nor was deceit found in His mouth" (1 Peter 2:22), turns cheats into people whose dealings God delights in.
units.application: If you run a business, check your prices, invoices and product claims this week as if God were the auditor, because He is. Employees: give the full hour you are paid for and report expenses exactly. Sellers and contractors: describe what you sell truthfully, defects included. If you find you have shortchanged someone, make it right, as Zacchaeus did, even if no one would ever have known.

rel.note: Seeking many counselors is humility in practice, the opposite of the pride that brings shame.
Pride produces strife, while wisdom is with the well-advised, the humble who take counsel.
Pride goes before destruction, the fullest statement of the truth this verse introduces.
Pride brings a man low while the humble in spirit retain honor.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble, the reason humility receives wisdom.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew words for "pride" (zadon) and "shame" (qalon) sound alike. The ear hears shame arriving with pride, just as the line says, and the matching sound makes the saying easy to remember.
• The word translated "humble" appears only here in the Old Testament and means modest; the KJV has "lowly." A verb from the same root appears in Micah 6:8, "to walk humbly with your God," which describes a lowly, modest walk before God.
• Ironside: "Nothing is more detestable in God's sight than pride on the part of creatures who have absolutely nothing to be proud of."
• Scripture's gallery of pride followed by shame includes Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:16–21), Haman (Esther 6:6–12; 7:10), Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:30–33) and Herod (Acts 12:21–23).
• Compare 13:10; 16:18; 29:23; Luke 14:11; James 4:6.
units.summary: Pride walks in the front door with shame right behind it; humility opens the door to wisdom.
units.principle: Pride sets a person up for disgrace, while humility keeps a person teachable, and the teachable are the ones who grow wise.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar shows both halves of this verse in one life. Walking on his palace roof, he boasted, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…?" Within the hour he was driven out to live like an animal (Daniel 4:30–33). When his reason returned, he praised the God who is "able to put down" those who walk in pride (Daniel 4:37). Pride is easy to see in others and hard to see in ourselves. It can even hide in the mind, as a refusal to trust God beyond what we can work out for ourselves. Bridges: "There is no greater proof of proud folly, than believing only what we understand." The deepest picture of humility is Christ, who "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death" (Philippians 2:8). Those who follow Him down that low road find that the way down is the way to understanding.
units.application: Notice where you resist correction: from a spouse, a supervisor, an elder or even a child. That resistance is pride at the door. Leaders: ask someone who reports to you what you are missing, and thank them when they tell you. Students and young workers: ask the question you are embarrassed to ask. If you were embarrassed recently, ask what God may be teaching you before you defend yourself.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, while the one who perverts his ways is exposed.
Righteousness straightens the path of the blameless, while the wicked fall by their own wickedness, the same pattern in new images.
Walking blamelessly brings safety, while the perverse in his ways will suddenly fall.
The upright remain in the land while the unfaithful are uprooted, the long outcome of the two characters.

units.notes:
• "Integrity" (tummah) comes from a root meaning complete or whole: a life with no hidden compartments. The same word describes Job, who "holds fast to his integrity" under testing (Job 2:3).
• The Hebrew word for "perversity" means crookedness or crooked dealing and appears in the Old Testament only here and in 15:4. It stands against "upright," whose basic sense is straight. The ESV has "crookedness," the KJV "perverseness."
• Henry pictures integrity as a steady course at sea: "he needs not tack about every time the wind turns." To "tack about" is to change direction; the honest man does not have to reset his course every time circumstances shift.
• Ironside: "It is not so much intelligence that is lacking among the mass of saints as real integrity of heart."
• Compare 10:9; 28:18; Psalm 25:21, "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me."
units.summary: Integrity is a compass carried inside; crookedness is a road that leads its traveler to ruin.
units.principle: A person's settled character steers his life; integrity keeps him on course, while crooked dealing ends by destroying the one who practices it.
units.insight: Ahab's palace held two kinds of men. Obadiah ran the king's household, yet he "feared the LORD greatly" and hid a hundred prophets from Jezebel (1 Kings 18:3–4). Ahab "sold himself to do wickedness" (1 Kings 21:25), and his crooked dealing over Naboth's vineyard brought his house to ruin. Integrity guided Obadiah through a dangerous court; perversity destroyed his master. Joseph shows the same guide at work in private. Alone with Potiphar's wife, he did not need to weigh his options: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). The question for each of us is what steers us when no one is watching. Jesus, whose food was to do the will of the One who sent Him (John 4:34), walked a straight road to the cross, and He makes crooked people whole.
units.application: Decide now what you will not do, before the pressure comes. A salesperson can settle in advance that he will not shade the truth to close a deal. A student can decide she will not cheat, even when classmates do. A manager can refuse to adjust a report before the numbers come in. Write down one line you will not cross this week, and ask a trusted friend to hold you to it.

rel.note: The same second line, righteousness delivers from death, set against treasures gained by wickedness.
The chapter returns to riches: whoever trusts in them will fall.
The rich man imagines his wealth is a strong city, the very confidence that fails on the day of wrath.
Riches make themselves wings and fly away, so they cannot be leaned on.

units.notes:
• The second line is identical to 10:2b in the NKJV. The first line of 10:2, "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing," speaks of ill-gotten money; here it speaks of the day of wrath, so the point widens to any money at all.
• Deliverance links the sayings of this section: "delivers" (11:4), "deliver" (11:6), "is delivered" (11:8) and "will be delivered" (11:9). The Hebrew uses one verb in 11:4 and 11:6 and a different one in 11:8 and 11:9, so the link is a thread of thought carried by related words.
• Henry: "In the day of public judgments riches often expose men rather than protect them."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik, recalls the wealthy English churchman Cardinal Henry Beaufort asking, as he faced death, "Wherefore should I die, being so rich?" ("Wherefore" means "why.")
• Compare Psalm 49:6–9; Ezekiel 7:19; Luke 12:16–21; 1 Peter 1:18–19.
units.summary: Money can buy almost anything except a way out of God's judgment.
units.principle: Wealth has real uses but no saving power; only righteousness before God holds when judgment comes.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man whose fields produced so much that he planned bigger barns and said to his soul, "take your ease; eat, drink, and be merry." God answered, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:19–20). His wealth was real, and on that night it was useless. The heart quietly trusts money for things only God can give: security, significance, safety against the future. This verse asks what we are counting on for the day when nothing can be bought. In the light of the New Testament, the righteousness that delivers from death is finally the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). We were "not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold," but "with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18–19).
units.application: Look at what you are trusting for security. If your savings, pension or business is what lets you sleep at night, thank God for it, and then tell Him plainly that it cannot save you. Parents: talk with your children about what money can and cannot do. If someone near you is facing death, do not let every conversation stay on wills and accounts; gently ask where their hope rests.

rel.note: Integrity guides the upright while perversity destroys the unfaithful, the same truth in different images.
The next saying repeats the pattern: righteousness rescues the upright, and the unfaithful are caught by their own lust.
The same verb: the LORD directs, or makes straight, the paths of those who acknowledge Him.
The wicked man is entrapped by his own iniquities, as he falls here by his own wickedness.

units.notes:
• "Direct his way aright" translates a verb meaning to make straight or level. It is the same verb used in 3:6, "He shall direct your paths." The 1611 King James margin gives the sense as "rectifie," to make right or straight; the ESV says righteousness "keeps" his way straight.
• "Blameless" describes a person who is whole and sincere before God, not one who has never sinned.
• Compare Isaiah 26:7, "The way of the just is uprightness; O Most Upright, You weigh the path of the just," and Hebrews 12:13, "make straight paths for your feet."
• Compare 5:22, "His own iniquities entrap the wicked man," and 11:3.
units.summary: Righteousness clears the road ahead; wickedness digs the hole its own owner falls into.
units.principle: Right living tends to keep the road ahead clear, while wickedness lays the obstacles that bring the wicked down.
units.insight: Ahithophel was David's trusted counselor, so respected that his advice was "as if one had inquired at the oracle of God" (2 Samuel 16:23). He betrayed David to join Absalom. When his counsel was set aside, he went home, put his household in order and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23). No soldier struck him; he fell by his own wickedness. Daniel shows the other road. His enemies "could find no charge or fault" in him (Daniel 6:4), and his straight life became his protection. Most pits we fall into we dig ourselves: the lie that needs another lie, the shortcut that needs covering. Christ calls Himself "the way" (John 14:6). Walking with Him is not always an easy road, but it is a straight one, and He walks it with us.
units.application: Before you make a decision this week, ask a simple question: what is the straight road here? A worker tempted to cover a mistake can admit it today, before the cover-up becomes the bigger problem. A teenager tempted to lie to parents about where she was can tell the truth now. If you are already tangled in a lie, stop digging. Confess it to God and to the person you deceived.

rel.note: The LORD casts away the desire of the wicked, the same word translated lust here.
The preceding saying makes the same point: the wicked fall by their own wickedness.
By transgression an evil man is snared, while the righteous sing.
His own iniquities entrap the wicked man, and he is caught in the cords of his sin.

units.notes:
• The word for "lust" is the same word translated "desire" in 10:3, "He casts away the desire of the wicked." It means a craving, usually an evil one, though it can also mean ruin. Both senses fit the verse: the craving becomes the ruin.
• "Caught" is the language of capture. The ESV says the treacherous are "taken captive" by their lust. The KJV has "taken in their own naughtiness," using "naughtiness" in its older, stronger sense of wickedness.
• Henry: "Their sin will be their punishment; that very thing by which they contrived to shelter themselves will make against them."
• Compare 5:22; 29:6 ("By transgression an evil man is snared"); James 1:14–15; 1 Timothy 6:9.
units.summary: We are rescued by the life we choose and caught by the cravings we chase.
units.principle: Righteousness protects those who live by it, while evil desire becomes the trap that captures those who serve it.
units.insight: Achan saw a beautiful garment, silver and a wedge of gold among the spoils of Jericho. "I coveted them and took them," he confessed (Joshua 7:21). The desire that promised to enrich him destroyed him and troubled all Israel. James traces the same path: each one is tempted "when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed," and desire gives birth to sin, and sin "brings forth death" (James 1:14–15). The snare is rarely forced on us; we walk toward it because we want what is in it. The good news is that the trap can be broken. Jesus said, "whoever commits sin is a slave of sin," and also, "if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed" (John 8:34, 36).
units.application: Name the craving that keeps pulling at you: money, approval, a screen, a person who is not yours. Then cut off its supply this week. A man fighting pornography can install accountability software and tell a friend. Someone drawn into overspending can delete the shopping apps. A leader hungry for recognition can do one good thing in secret. Do not wait for the snare to close; walk the other way while you can.

rel.note: The expectation of the wicked will perish, while the hope of the righteous ends in gladness.
The chapter sharpens the point: the expectation of the wicked is not only lost but replaced by wrath.
The wicked is banished in his wickedness, but the righteous has a refuge even in death.
For the one who fears the LORD there is a hereafter, and his hope will not be cut off.

units.notes:
• "The unjust" translates a plural Hebrew word that can come from a noun meaning strength or wealth, or from a similar-looking word meaning wickedness. The NKJV and KJV take the second sense. The ESV reads "the expectation of wealth," and the 1984 NIV what he expected from his "power." Either way, the line restates the loss of everything the wicked man leaned on.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "the expectation or hope of the wicked lies wholly on this side of the grave, and perishes at death."
• Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress gives a picture of this hope: Ignorance crosses the river of death with a ferryman named Vain-hope, but at the gate of the Celestial City he has no certificate and is carried away.
• Compare 10:28; 14:32; Job 8:13 ("the hope of the hypocrite shall perish"); Psalm 49:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:19.
units.summary: A hope built on this life alone is buried with the man who built it.
units.principle: Any hope that rests on this life alone dies with the one who holds it; only hope anchored in God outlasts death.
units.insight: Many hopes feel confident right up to the end. The rich fool had plans for many years and one night to live (Luke 12:19–20). Saul consulted a medium the night before his last battle, looking for a word that would rescue his plans, and found only the news of his death (1 Samuel 28:19). The question is not how strongly we hope but what our hope rests on. Robert Leighton, in a comment on 1 Peter 1:3 quoted by Bridges, calls such hopes "not living, but lying hopes, and dying hopes." Against them stands the "living hope" God gives "through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). Christ has gone through death and come out the other side. Hope that rests on Him is anchored "behind the veil" (Hebrews 6:19), and it does not perish.
units.application: Ask what you are really hoping in: retirement, a relationship, your children's success, your health. These are good gifts, but none of them can carry you through death. If you are grieving someone, this verse is not a tool for judging the one you lost; leave that with God. If a friend seems to hope in nothing beyond this life, look for a gentle opening to speak of the hope you have in Christ.

rel.note: The thread of deliverance continues: the righteous escape the hypocrite's destructive mouth through knowledge.
The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, the same exchange of places.
Whoever digs a pit falls into it, the trouble planned for another returning on the planner.
The one who leads the upright astray falls into his own pit, while the blameless inherit good.

units.notes:
• The KJV says the wicked "cometh in his stead," and the ESV that the wicked "walks into" the trouble. Both bring out the idea of one taking the other's place.
• 21:18 states the same exchange: "The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous, And the unfaithful for the upright."
• Scripture's reversals include Israel delivered through the Red Sea while the Egyptians drowned in it (Exodus 14:21–28), the men who threw Daniel's friends into the furnace killed by its flames (Daniel 3:22), and Daniel's accusers thrown to the lions (Daniel 6:24).
• Ironside: "He who seeks to ensnare the upright will fall into the meshes of his own gin." A "gin" is a snare or trap.
• Compare 26:27; 28:10; Psalm 7:15–16.
units.summary: God often turns trouble around, so the trap set for the righteous closes on the wicked.
units.principle: God does not always spare His people from trouble, but He brings them through it, and He often turns the harm meant for them back on those who meant it.
units.insight: The gospel turns this proverb inside out. At the cross the righteous One was not delivered from trouble. He stepped into the trouble that belonged to the wicked. Barabbas, a guilty man, walked free while Jesus took his place (Mark 15:15). Peter puts it plainly: "Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God" (1 Peter 3:18). That is why believers can trust God when trouble comes. Mordecai's rescue was dramatic, but ours cost far more. If you are in trouble now and see no way out, hold on to Psalm 34:19: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, But the LORD delivers him out of them all." The verse speaks of an exchange, and the deepest exchange has already been made for you.
units.application: If someone is scheming against you at work, in the family or at church, resist the urge to fight fire with fire. Do right, keep honest records if you must, and leave the reversal to God. If you have been brought through a hard season, tell someone the story this week; it strengthens faith. And if you are the one setting a trap for someone, stop now. Traps have a way of closing on the people who set them.

rel.note: What the wicked mouth does to one neighbor here, it does to a whole city there.
The thread of deliverance runs on: the righteous are delivered from trouble, and here from a destructive mouth.
The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them.
The man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet, the hypocrite's method in another image.
Knowledge and discretion keep a person from the man who speaks perverse things, the deliverance this verse promises.

units.notes:
• The word translated "hypocrite," chaneph, is rendered "the godless" in the ESV and the 1984 NIV. It describes a person estranged from God, not only someone who pretends; his false front grows out of a godless heart.
• Henry: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, but no tongue more fatal than the flattering tongue."
• Scripture shows the hypocrite's mouth at work. Ziba slandered Mephibosheth to win his master's land (2 Samuel 16:1–4; 19:24–27), and Potiphar's wife destroyed Joseph's good name with a lie (Genesis 39:13–20).
• Bridges: "Knowledge supplies principle and steadfastness." Feelings can be swayed by smooth talk; settled knowledge of the truth holds a person steady.
• Compare 2:10–12; 12:6; 29:5; Romans 16:18–19.
units.summary: A hypocrite's tongue can ruin a neighbor without lifting a hand, but truth gives the righteous a way out.
units.principle: Words can ruin a person as surely as weapons, and the best defense against deceit is a mind formed by truth.
units.insight: Nehemiah was rebuilding Jerusalem's wall when his enemies sent a friendly invitation: "Come, let us meet together." He saw the trap and answered, "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" (Nehemiah 6:2–3). Later a hired prophet urged him to hide in the temple, and Nehemiah "perceived that God had not sent him" (Nehemiah 6:12). Knowledge delivered him. Jesus met smooth words the same way. When the Pharisees flattered Him before their trap question about taxes, He "perceived their wickedness" and said, "Why do you test Me, you hypocrites?" (Matthew 22:18). We are more easily flattered than we think. The cure is not suspicion of everyone but a heart so full of God's truth that falsehood sounds wrong.
units.application: Before you repeat something about a neighbor, coworker or church member, ask whether it is true, whether it is yours to tell, and whether it will build them up. If someone flatters you in order to steer you, slow down and test the advice against Scripture and wise friends. Parents: teach your children to recognize the friend who praises them only when he wants something. Read Scripture daily; truth you know is protection you carry.

rel.note: The next saying explains the city's joy: the blessing of the upright exalts it, and the mouth of the wicked overthrows it.
A balancing word: do not gloat when an enemy falls, so that relief at justice never becomes delight in ruin.
When the righteous rejoice there is great glory, but when the wicked rise people hide themselves.
When the righteous rule the people rejoice, and when the wicked rule they groan.

units.notes:
• "Jubilation" translates a Hebrew word for a ringing shout of joy; the ESV renders it with "shouts."
• Scripture records such cities. When Mordecai went out in royal robes, "the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad" (Esther 8:15). When the murderous queen Athaliah was removed, "all the people of the land rejoiced; and the city was quiet" (2 Kings 11:20).
• Bridges: "The people of God unite in the shouting; not from any selfish feeling of revenge; much less from unfeeling hardness towards their fellow-sinners."
• Compare 28:12, 28; 29:2; Ezekiel 33:11; Revelation 19:1–2.
units.summary: A city cheers when good people prosper and breathes easier when oppressors fall.
units.principle: No life is purely private: the righteous bless their community and the wicked burden it, so their rise and fall are felt by all.
units.insight: God says, "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). That keeps our hearts honest when we read this verse. A community may rightly feel relief when an abuser is removed or a corrupt official falls, yet believers rejoice in God's justice, not in a person's ruin. The verse also asks a searching question. If my influence were removed, would my workplace, my street or my church feel loss or relief? Joseph's rise blessed all Egypt, and the people told him, "You have saved our lives" (Genesis 47:25). Christ calls His people the salt of the earth and the light of the world (Matthew 5:13–14), the kind of people whose good a city has reason to celebrate.
units.application: Ask how your presence affects the places where you live and work. A business owner can pay fairly and on time, so employees' families are better off. A neighbor can be the one who clears the elderly widow's walk. A public servant can refuse the favor that would cost the town. When someone who harmed your community falls, give thanks for justice, pray for the person, and refuse to gloat.

rel.note: The preceding saying describes the city's joy, and this one gives its reason.
The hypocrite's mouth destroys one neighbor; here the wicked mouth overthrows a whole city.
Righteousness exalts a nation, the same truth on a larger scale.
Scoffers set a city aflame while wise men turn away wrath, words that destroy or protect a community.

units.notes:
• Henry describes "the blessing of the upright" as "their advice, their example, their prayers, and all the instances of their serviceableness to the public interest."
• One chapter of 2 Samuel shows both lines. Sheba son of Bichri blew a trumpet and with a few words drew Israel away from David (2 Samuel 20:1–2). Then a wise woman of Abel spoke with Joab and saved her city from destruction (2 Samuel 20:16–22).
• Abraham's plea for Sodom shows how much a few righteous people can matter to a city: the LORD said He would spare it for the sake of ten (Genesis 18:32).
• Compare 14:34; 29:8 ("Scoffers set a city aflame, But wise men turn away wrath"); Jeremiah 29:7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2.
units.summary: It takes a lifetime of blessing to build a city up and only a mouth to tear it down.
units.principle: A community rises on the blessing of upright lives and can be torn down by reckless, wicked words.
units.insight: Absalom did not begin with a sword. He stood at the city gate and told every man with a complaint, "Look, your case is good and right; but there is no deputy of the king to hear you." So "Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:3, 6), and his words split a kingdom. By contrast, God told the exiles in Babylon to "seek the peace of the city" and pray for it, "for in its peace you will have peace" (Jeremiah 29:7). Our words are building or demolishing something every day: a family, a congregation, a town. Jesus calls His followers "a city that is set on a hill" (Matthew 5:14), a people meant to bless the place where God has put them. Is my mouth adding to the walls or loosening the stones?
units.application: Pray by name for your mayor, school board and local leaders this week (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Before posting about local politics or church decisions, ask whether your words will build up or stir up. A church member can refuse to join the parking-lot complaint and take concerns to the right person instead. A business owner can support something good in the neighborhood. Small, steady blessings build a city.

rel.note: Many words invite sin, but restraining the lips is wise.
The next saying names a second sin of the tongue: betraying a neighbor's confidence behind his back.
Despising a neighbor is called sin, while mercy toward the poor brings happiness.
The person of understanding spares his words and keeps a calm spirit, and even a fool seems wise when silent.

units.notes:
• "Devoid of wisdom" is literally "lacking heart," as the KJV margin notes ("destitute of heart"). The same expression appears at 9:4 and 10:13. In Proverbs the heart is the center of thinking and choosing, so to lack heart is to lack sense.
• "Holds his peace" means keeps silent. Compare 17:28, "Even a fool is counted wise when he holds his peace."
• Bridges: "A man of understanding may see much in his neighbour to excite his pity, and stir up his prayers, but nothing to despise."
• Compare 14:21 ("He who despises his neighbor sins"); Matthew 5:22; 7:3–5; Galatians 6:1.
units.summary: It takes no wisdom to belittle a neighbor and a great deal of it to keep quiet.
units.principle: Contempt for others exposes a lack of wisdom, while understanding shows itself in the restraint that refuses to belittle.
units.insight: When Shimei followed David along the road, cursing him and throwing stones, Abishai offered to take off his head. David held his peace: "let him alone, and let him curse" (2 Samuel 16:11). He saw God's hand even in an insult. Contempt usually grows from a quiet sense that we are better than others. Paul punctures it: "what do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). Jesus is the deepest example. Peter describes Him as the One "who, when He was reviled, did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). The One with every right to despise us held His peace and went to the cross for us. Those who know that grace lose their taste for belittling others.
units.application: This week, catch the eye-roll and the sarcastic remark before they leave you. Spouses: refuse to mock each other in front of others, even as a joke. Coworkers: when the team starts belittling an absent colleague, change the subject or say something good about that person. If a neighbor annoys you, pray for them before you talk about them. When correction is needed, give it privately and gently (Galatians 6:1).

rel.note: The preceding saying condemns open contempt for a neighbor; this one condemns betraying him in secret.
Covering a transgression seeks love, while repeating a matter separates friends.
The same first line: the one who goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets, so keep away from him.
Settle a dispute directly and do not disclose another's secret, or your own reputation will suffer.
Without a talebearer strife dies out, as a fire goes out without wood.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew of "A talebearer" as "one who walks about, being a talebearer," a picture of someone going from place to place with his stories. Proverbs repeats the first line in 20:19.
• Ironside: "Talebearing, even though the tales be true, is most mischievous." A story does not become fit to spread just because it is accurate.
• Bridges sets a limit on the duty of silence: a faithful friend's "bosom is a cover of concealment, except when the honour of God and the interests of society plainly forbid." Confidentiality does not shelter crimes or danger to others.
• Doeg the Edomite shows the talebearer's harm: he reported to Saul that the priest Ahimelech had helped David, and eighty-five priests were killed (1 Samuel 22:9–18).
• Compare 16:28; 17:9; 18:8; 26:20; 1 Timothy 5:13.
units.summary: A gossip carries your secrets around town; a faithful friend lets them rest.
units.principle: Trustworthiness is proven by what a person refuses to repeat; faithful people keep confidences, while gossips break the bonds that hold people together.
units.insight: When Joseph finally revealed himself to the brothers who had sold him, he first cried, "Make everyone go out from me!" No one else was present while he made himself known to his brothers (Genesis 45:1). He kept their shame private even in the moment of truth. That is a faithful spirit. Gossip feeds something in us: the pleasure of knowing, the small power of being the one who tells. Proverbs calls a talebearer's words "tasty trifles" (18:8). The gospel moves the other way. Love "will cover a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8), and Jesus taught us to go first to the one who wronged us, "between you and him alone" (Matthew 18:15). He knows every secret about us. He does not broadcast them; He bore them on the cross (1 Peter 2:24).
units.application: When someone begins, "I probably shouldn't tell you this, but…," answer kindly, "Then let's not." If a friend confides in you, do not pass it on, even as a prayer request, without permission. Families: keep household matters in the household. Pastors and small-group leaders: guard what you hear in counseling. But if someone is being abused or endangered, faithfulness means telling the proper authorities.

rel.note: Seeking counsel is the humility that receives wisdom, the opposite of the pride that brings shame.
The fool trusts his own eyes, but the one who heeds counsel is wise.
Plans fail without counsel but are established by many counselors.
Wise counsel guides even war, ending with the same words, in a multitude of counselors there is safety.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "counsel" means direction or guidance, and it is the same word translated "wise counsel" in 1:5; the ESV has "guidance." A people without that guidance has no one to set its course, and so it falls.
• Proverbs repeats the thought in 15:22 and 24:6, which ends with the same phrase, "in a multitude of counselors there is safety."
• Bridges: "The nation, therefore, without counselors is like a ship in the midst of the rocks without a pilot."
• Henry: "two eyes see more than one."
• Compare Exodus 18:13–24, where Moses takes Jethro's advice to share the work of judging, and Acts 15:6–29, where the church settles a hard question in council.
units.summary: No one sees the whole road alone; a people with many wise advisers walks safely.
units.principle: Wise decisions are rarely made alone; seeking many sound counselors guards a people, a family or a person from avoidable falls.
units.insight: Rehoboam had two sets of advisers. The elders who had served Solomon urged him to lighten the people's load; the young men he grew up with told him to be harsher. He took the second advice, and ten tribes broke away (1 Kings 12:6–16). He had counsel, but he chose the counselors who told him what he wanted to hear. Ahab had four hundred prophets agreeing with him, and that crowd led him to his death (1 Kings 22:6, 34–37). A multitude of counselors helps only when they are wise and free to disagree. Pride resists advice; humility asks for it. Christ is called "Wonderful, Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), and the wisest counsel begins by bringing our plans to Him.
units.application: Before a major decision this month, such as a job change, a move, a large purchase or a ministry plan, ask at least two mature believers for their honest view, including someone likely to disagree. Leaders: build a team that is free to tell you no. Young people: talk with your parents or a mentor before you commit. Couples: make large financial decisions together, not alone.

rel.note: The same chapter commends open-handed generosity, showing the surety warning is not a ban on helping others.
Only a man devoid of understanding shakes hands in a pledge for another.
Do not guarantee debts you cannot pay, or you may lose your own bed.
The father's fuller warning about pledging for a stranger and how to get free.

units.notes:
• The KJV says the surety "shall smart for it." The 1611 margin gives the Hebrew as "shall be sore broken," and renders the Hebrew behind "suretiship" literally as "those that strike hands," the handshake that sealed a pledge.
• Proverbs repeats the warning in 6:1–5; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27; 27:13.
• Judah shows what a surety may cost. He pledged himself to his father for Benjamin's safety, and later offered to remain a slave in Egypt in the boy's place (Genesis 43:9; 44:32–33).
• Ironside, speaking of Christ: "He was the stranger's Surety." In the NKJV, Hebrews 7:22 gives Jesus the same title: "Jesus has become a surety of a better covenant."
units.summary: Signing for a stranger's debt hands your future to someone you have no reason to trust.
units.principle: Rash guarantees for people we do not know put our households at risk; wise generosity gives freely but does not pledge what it cannot afford to lose.
units.insight: This verse protects families, and it also prepares us for the most surprising surety in Scripture. Hebrews calls Jesus "a surety of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). He did the very thing this proverb warns against. He pledged Himself for strangers, people who were "alienated and enemies" in mind (Colossians 1:21), and He suffered for it to the full. Bridges: "Had he hated suretyship, he would have been sure." In other words, He could have stayed safe, and we would have perished. The proverb's caution still stands for us; we cannot carry other people's debts without limit. But we can marvel that Christ did. Because He was willing to suffer for strangers, strangers like us are now secure.
units.application: If a friend or relative asks you to cosign a loan, ask two questions: could you pay the whole debt without harming your family, and are you willing to lose it? If not, say no kindly. If you can help, consider giving a smaller amount outright instead of guaranteeing a larger one. Young adults: never sign for someone you barely know, however urgent the story. If you already have, follow 6:3–5 and seek release quickly.

rel.note: A lovely woman without discretion wastes her beauty, the opposite of the gracious woman who keeps her honor.
Greedy gain takes away the life of its owners, the end of riches seized by force.
A good name and loving favor are worth more than great riches.
The woman who fears the LORD is the one to be praised, the root of the gracious woman's honor.

units.notes:
• "A gracious woman" is literally "a woman of grace," someone marked by favor and charm of character, not only of appearance.
• For "ruthless men" the ESV has "violent men" and the KJV "strong men." Older commentators who followed the KJV read the verse as a comparison: as strong men hold on to riches, so a gracious woman holds on to honor. The NKJV and ESV set the two possessions against each other.
• The Greek Septuagint expands this verse with extra lines that are not in the Hebrew; the NKJV follows the Hebrew.
• Ruth shows this honor: Boaz tells her, "all the people of my town know that you are a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:11).
• Compare 22:1; 31:30; 1 Peter 3:3–4.
units.summary: Grace holds on to honor; ruthlessness can only hold on to money.
units.principle: What we gain by kindness lasts longer and is worth more than what we take by force.
units.insight: Abigail was married to Nabal, a harsh man rich in sheep and goats. When Nabal insulted David's men, David set out to destroy his household. Abigail met him on the road with gifts and gracious words, and David answered, "Blessed is the LORD God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!" (1 Samuel 25:32). Nabal kept his riches about ten more days and then died (1 Samuel 25:38). Abigail kept her honor and later became David's wife. Ironside: "Nothing is so truly lovely and admirable as a gracious, conciliatory spirit." We are tempted to think toughness protects what matters most. Christ, "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14), received the name above every name not by seizing but by giving Himself (Philippians 2:7–9).
units.application: Women and men alike: choose kindness when you could win by force, whether in a family argument, a business deal or a church meeting. Mothers and grandmothers: your gracious character will shape your family's memory more than anything you own. Young women: do not trade your character for attention or advantage. Leaders: refuse to treat people roughly to protect profits; the honor you lose is worth more than the money you keep.

rel.note: The one who waters others is watered himself, the same return of kindness to the kind.
The same verb, trouble: the man who troubles his own house inherits only wind.
The righteous care even for an animal, while the so-called mercies of the wicked are cruel.
Whoever follows righteousness and mercy finds life, righteousness and honor.

units.notes:
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The kindness spoken of is hesed, steadfast love, like God's." The merciful man is literally "a man of hesed," the loyal love God shows His people.
• "Troubles" is the verb used of Achan, who "troubled" Israel (Joshua 7:25). Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The word 'trouble' may recall Joshua 7:25-26—Achan troubled Israel." The same verb returns in 11:29, "He who troubles his own house."
• The ESV reads the verse more simply: the merciful man "benefits himself," and the cruel man "hurts himself."
• Compare 11:25; 12:10; 21:21; Matthew 5:7; James 2:13.
units.summary: Mercy refreshes the one who shows it; cruelty wounds the one who deals it.
units.principle: Kindness tends to bless the one who gives it and cruelty to wound the one who practices it, because we cannot harm others without harming ourselves.
units.insight: Jesus told of a servant forgiven a debt he could never pay, who then seized a fellow servant by the throat over a small sum. His master "delivered him to the torturers" (Matthew 18:34). His cruelty became his own prison. Bitterness works the same way in the heart: the grudge we hold ends up holding us. The widow of Zarephath shared her last meal with Elijah, and her own household was kept alive through the famine (1 Kings 17:13–16), though most mercy is repaid less visibly. Jesus said, "Blessed are the merciful, For they shall obtain mercy" (Matthew 5:7). Mercy flows from people who know they have received it. At the cross God showed us mercy beyond measure, and those who have tasted it begin to pass it on.
units.application: Show one deliberate kindness this week to someone who cannot repay you: a lonely neighbor, a struggling coworker, a difficult relative. If you are nursing a grudge, name it before God and release it; it is hurting you more than the other person. Parents: when a child is harsh with a sibling, help them see how cruelty spoils their own joy. Supervisors: correct firmly, but without contempt.

rel.note: The labor of the righteous leads to life, while the wages of the wicked lead to sin.
The next saying follows the two roads to their ends: righteousness to life, the pursuit of evil to death.
Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet but turns to gravel, the deceptive wage in another image.
The one who sows iniquity reaps sorrow, the opposite harvest to the one who sows righteousness.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew words for "deceptive" (sheqer) and "reward" (seker) sound alike. Sheqer means a lie; seker means wages or hire. The first line speaks literally of wages of deception and the second of a true wage, so the wordplay sets false pay beside real pay. The ESV has "deceptive wages."
• Gehazi shows deceptive wages. He lied to get silver and garments from Naaman, and he received Naaman's leprosy with them (2 Kings 5:20–27).
• Bridges: "nor will he, as the world has done, reward us with ciphers instead of gold." A "cipher" is a zero; the world pays in empty numbers, but God does not.
• Compare 10:16; 20:17; 22:8; Hosea 10:12; James 3:18.
units.summary: Sin pays its workers in counterfeit coin; righteousness sows a seed whose harvest is sure.
units.principle: Gain built on deceit proves false in the end, while a life sown in righteousness yields a lasting reward from God.
units.insight: Jacob deceived his father to get the blessing, then spent twenty years being deceived by Laban, who "changed my wages ten times" (Genesis 31:7). Deceptive work tends to pay in its own currency. The tempter offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship (Matthew 4:8–9), a payment he had no right to make. Sowing righteousness is slower and less dramatic. Bridges reminds us that the reward is "not of debt, but of grace." God does not owe us; He delights to give. So Paul urges, "let us not grow weary while doing good, for in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart" (Galatians 6:9). Every faithful day is seed in the ground, and the Lord of the harvest does not forget it.
units.application: If you are tempted to get ahead at work by padding numbers or taking credit for others' work, count what that "pay" will cost you. Keep sowing instead: the student who studies faithfully while others cheat, the employee who does quality work no one checks, the parent who keeps teaching when children seem not to listen. Name one righteous seed you will sow this week, and leave the harvest to God.

rel.note: The labor of the righteous leads to life, while the wages of the wicked lead to sin.
The preceding saying contrasts deceptive wages with the sure reward of sowing righteousness.
In the way of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
The chase runs both ways: here a man pursues evil, there evil pursues sinners.
A way can seem right and still end in death, which is why the direction of a life matters.

units.notes:
• The first Hebrew word of the verse can be read as "so" or "thus," as in the NKJV and KJV, or as a word meaning right, true or firm. The ESV takes the second sense and speaks of one who is "steadfast in righteousness." Either reading sets life against death.
• "Pursues" is the language of the chase. Pharaoh's army "pursued" Israel into the sea and drowned there (Exodus 14:23–28).
• Henry: "The more violent a man is in sinful pursuits the more eagerly bent he is upon his own destruction."
• Compare 10:16; 12:28; 13:21 ("Evil pursues sinners"); 14:12; Romans 6:23.
units.summary: Every life is headed somewhere: righteousness walks toward life, and the chase after evil runs toward death.
units.principle: The direction of a life determines its destination: righteousness tends toward life, and the pursuit of evil toward death.
units.insight: Balaam wanted the reward Balak offered so badly that he kept looking for a way around God's word. The New Testament speaks of those who "have run greedily in the error of Balaam for profit" (Jude 11), and Balaam himself died among Israel's enemies (Numbers 31:8). He pursued evil to his own death. Many people are running hard in a direction they never chose on purpose; they drifted into it one decision at a time. Moses set the choice before Israel: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Jesus came "that they may have life, and that they may have it more abundantly" (John 10:10). It is never too late to turn around, for "the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23).
units.application: Take a hard look at where your habits will lead in five years if nothing changes: your spending, your screen time, your temper, your secret indulgences. Young people: the friends you run with set your direction. Parents: talk with your teenager about where small choices lead. If you see that you are chasing something that leads to death, turn today. Repentance is a change of direction, not just a change of speed.

rel.note: The same abomination-and-delight pairing, first applied to dishonest and honest scales.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who deal truthfully are His delight.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, but the prayer of the upright is His delight.
The one with a deceitful heart finds no good, showing where the twisted heart leads.
The perverse person is an abomination to the LORD, but His secret counsel is with the upright.

units.notes:
• "Perverse" means twisted or crooked. The KJV has "froward," an older word for stubbornly contrary.
• The same two Hebrew words, "abomination" and "delight," are set against each other in 11:1, in this verse, and again in 12:22 and 15:8.
• Bridges: "They themselves are his delight." God delights not only in the right things the upright do but in the people themselves.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The proverb calls for a transformation of human affections to correspond with God's affections." We are meant to come to love what God loves and hate what He hates.
• Compare 3:32; 17:20; Psalm 51:10; Ezekiel 36:26.
units.summary: The God who hates a crooked scale hates a crooked heart, and He delights in people who walk straight.
units.principle: God looks past conduct to the heart; He detests inward crookedness and delights in people whose hearts and ways are whole.
units.insight: God said to Satan, "Have you considered My servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man" (Job 1:8). Jesus saw Nathanael coming and said, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!" (John 1:47). God notices the straight-hearted with joy. But who has such a heart? David knew his heart fell short and prayed, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10). God promised exactly that: "I will give you a new heart" (Ezekiel 36:26). At the Jordan the Father said of Jesus, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17), and in Him believers are "accepted in the Beloved" (Ephesians 1:6). A twisted heart can become God's delight, but only as He makes it new.
units.application: Ask God to search the places in your heart no one else can see: a private resentment, a hidden double standard, a secret you manage carefully. Pastors and ministry leaders: guard against public faithfulness that hides a crooked private life. Parents: aim at your children's hearts, not only their behavior. When you see integrity in a coworker or friend, tell them; you are echoing God's delight.

rel.note: The chapter's closing saying argues that if even the righteous are repaid on earth, the wicked surely will be.
In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, and His children have a refuge.
The same phrase: though the proud join forces, none will go unpunished.
The father warns his son against the sinners' invitation to join their band, whose schemes end in their own ruin.
The righteous man walks in integrity and his children are blessed after him.

units.notes:
• "Though they join forces" is literally "hand to hand," as the KJV has it: "Though hand join in hand." Other versions take the phrase as a statement of certainty: the ESV has "Be assured," the NASB "Assuredly."
• 16:5 uses the same phrase: "Though they join forces, none will go unpunished."
• Henry: "Though justice may come slowly to punish the wicked, and mercy may come slowly to save the righteous, yet both will come surely."
• Scripture shows such alliances failing: the builders of Babel (Genesis 11:4–9), Korah's company (Numbers 16:1–33), and the rulers gathered "against the LORD and against His Anointed" (Psalm 2:2).
• Compare 14:26; 20:7; Ezekiel 18:20; 2 Timothy 1:5.
units.summary: The wicked may link arms, but no alliance can stop God's justice, and godly lives bless the next generation.
units.principle: Numbers cannot shelter the wicked from God's justice, and the blessing of a godly life commonly reaches beyond one generation.
units.insight: The rulers of Jesus' day joined forces against Him. Herod and Pilate, enemies before, became friends the day they handled His case (Luke 23:12), and the early church saw Psalm 2 fulfilled in their alliance. Yet they could do only "whatever Your hand and Your purpose determined before to be done" (Acts 4:28), and the One they crucified rose. No coalition outlasts God. The second line speaks to anxious parents. Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). John Dodd and Robert Cleaver, whose 1614 exposition of Proverbs Bridges quotes, put it simply: "The best way for any man to do his children good, is to be godly himself." Parents cannot save their children, but they can live so that their children see what grace looks like.
units.application: Parents and grandparents: pray for your children by name, and let them see your faith on ordinary days, not only on Sundays. If your grown child has wandered, this verse is not a verdict on your parenting; keep praying and leave the outcome with God. Young people: do not join a group's wrongdoing because everyone is in it; numbers never excuse sin. Leaders: refuse to cover for a colleague's misconduct out of loyalty.

rel.note: The gracious woman keeps her honor, the opposite of the lovely woman who wastes her beauty.
Honor does not fit a fool, the same principle of something fine placed where it does not belong, applied to men.
Discretion preserves the one who receives wisdom, the quality this woman has turned away from.
Beauty is passing, but a woman who fears the LORD will be praised, the answer to beauty without discretion.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "discretion," ta'am, means taste, and by extension judgment, a sense of what is fitting. The line says literally that the woman turns aside from taste; the 1611 King James margin gives "departeth from." She has the beauty but has turned away from the judgment that would make it fitting.
• The same word, ta'am, appears when David thanks Abigail: "blessed is your advice" (1 Samuel 25:33). Abigail was a woman "of good understanding and beautiful appearance" (1 Samuel 25:3); she had both the gold and the judgment.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Instead of gaining honor by her natural gift, she wins ridicule."
• Absalom shows the same mismatch in a man. No one in Israel was praised as much for his good looks (2 Samuel 14:25), yet he used his charm to steal a kingdom and died with his head caught in a tree (2 Samuel 18:9–15).
• Compare 2:10–11; 26:1; 31:30; 1 Samuel 16:7.
units.summary: Beauty without good judgment is a gold ring on a pig: real treasure in the wrong place.
units.principle: Outward beauty or gifting without moral judgment is wasted and out of place; character, not appearance, gives a life its worth.
units.insight: Our culture spends great effort on the gold ring and little on the judgment that makes it fit. Scripture is honest that beauty is a real gift; Sarah, Rachel, Esther and David were all beautiful. But when Samuel admired Eliab's appearance, God told him, "the LORD looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Bridges: "Many a lovely form enshrines a revolting mind." The same is true of talent and charisma in men and women alike. Of the coming Servant the prophet said, "He has no form or comeliness" (Isaiah 53:2), yet no life was ever more beautiful than Christ's. Peter urges believers to cultivate "the hidden person of the heart," with "a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God" (1 Peter 3:4). That beauty does not fade, and it never ends up in the mud.
units.application: Parents: praise your children's choices and character more than their looks or talents. Young women and young men: ask whether you are investing more in your appearance or your online image than in wisdom and self-control. If you are dating, look for discretion, not only attraction. Gifted leaders and performers: talent without judgment will be wasted, so seek people who will hold you accountable for how you use it.

rel.note: The desire of the righteous will be granted, while what the wicked fear comes upon them.
The hope of the righteous ends in gladness, but the expectation of the wicked perishes.
The one who seeks good finds favor and the one who seeks evil finds trouble, the same outcomes of longing.
Earlier in the chapter the expectation of the wicked perishes at death; here it is replaced by wrath.

units.notes:
• The ESV says the desire of the righteous "ends only in good," taking the verse as a statement about outcomes.
• When desires are submitted to God's will, Bridges writes, "I shall be equally happy, whether they be granted or withheld."
• Israel's craving in the wilderness shows the second line. God gave them the meat they demanded, "But sent leanness into their soul" (Psalm 106:15; compare Numbers 11:31–33).
• Compare 10:24; 10:28; 11:7; Psalm 37:4; Romans 2:5.
units.summary: What we long for shows where we are headed: the righteous toward good, the wicked toward wrath.
units.principle: Desires shaped by God lead to good, while the hopes of the wicked lead only to judgment; what we long for shows where we are headed.
units.insight: In Gethsemane Jesus told His Father what He desired, and then added, "nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39). That is the shape of a righteous desire: honest about what it wants, yet surrendered to God. His desire ended in good beyond measure, the joy set before Him (Hebrews 12:2). Our desires are often mixed with selfishness and fear. The answer is not to stop desiring but to bring our desires to God until He reshapes them: "Delight yourself also in the LORD, And He shall give you the desires of your heart" (Psalm 37:4). The question is not only what I want but whom I want most. Asaph answered, "there is none upon earth that I desire besides You" (Psalm 73:25).
units.application: Write down what you most want right now: a job, a spouse, a child, healing, success. Pray over the list, asking God to purify the desires that are good and remove the ones that are not. Parents: help your children name what they want and bring it to God. If a longing has gone unanswered for years, keep bringing it to Him; the righteous do not get every wish, but their road ends in good.

rel.note: The warning against rash surety balances this verse: generosity gives freely but does not sign away what it cannot afford to lose.
The generous soul is made rich and the one who waters is watered, the same paradox restated.
Withholding grain in a time of need shows what withholding more than is right looks like in business.
The one with a generous eye who shares his bread with the poor will be blessed.
The one who gives to the poor will not lack, while the one who hides his eyes gathers curses.

units.notes:
• This verse has three lines in the NKJV rather than the usual two. The ESV says the one who withholds "suffers want."
• "Scatters" is the verb used of the righteous man in Psalm 112:9: "He has dispersed abroad, He has given to the poor."
• Bunyan's riddle, quoted by Ironside: "A man there was, though some did count him mad, The more he cast away, the more he had."
• Paul builds on the same principle in 2 Corinthians 9:6–11. God enriches givers "for all liberality" (9:11), that is, so that they can keep giving, not so that they can live in luxury.
• Compare 11:25; 19:17; 21:26; 22:9; 28:27.
units.summary: The open hand that scatters tends to gather more; the clenched fist that hoards ends up empty.
units.principle: Generosity tends to enlarge a life and stinginess to shrink it, though God's answer to giving is not a financial formula.
units.insight: Jesus watched a poor widow drop two small coins into the temple treasury and said she had given more than all the rich, because "she out of her poverty put in all that she had" (Mark 12:44). She did not leave richer in money. She left richer in a way Jesus valued more. Nabal, by contrast, refused to share bread and water with David's men and lost everything within days (1 Samuel 25:10–11, 38). The heart that withholds is usually afraid: afraid there will not be enough, afraid of losing control. The gospel answers that fear. "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). Christ scattered everything, and His giving is what makes us rich.
units.application: Look at your budget this week and ask where fear is making you hold back more than is right: from your church, from a struggling relative, from a fair wage you owe. Give something that stretches you, and do it cheerfully, not as an investment. Business owners: pay workers and suppliers promptly. Parents: let your children see you give. Do not expect a check in the mail in return; expect God's care.

rel.note: The warning against guaranteeing a stranger's debt keeps generosity wise, giving freely without pledging what one cannot afford to lose.
The merciful man does good for his own soul, kindness returning to the kind.
The one who scatters increases, the same paradox of generosity in the image of sowing.
Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who repays it, the ground of the giver's refreshment.
The one with a generous eye who shares his bread will be blessed.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads, "The liberal soul shall be made fat," and its margin gives the Hebrew of "liberal soul" as "soul of blessing." To be "made fat" was a picture of plenty and health.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "If I want to get water I must give water."
• Bridges: "The Minister is refreshed by his own message of salvation to his people." Teachers and helpers often find themselves fed by what they give.
• Compare 11:17; 11:24; 19:17; 22:9; Isaiah 58:10–11 ("You shall be like a watered garden"); Acts 20:35; 2 Corinthians 9:6–8.
units.summary: Pour yourself out to refresh others, and you will find your own soul refreshed.
units.principle: Those who refresh others are refreshed themselves; generosity enriches the giver's own life under God's care, though not as a promised financial return.
units.insight: Tired and thirsty, Jesus sat by a well in Samaria and offered a woman "living water" (John 4:10). When His disciples came back with food and urged Him to eat, He said, "I have food to eat of which you do not know" (John 4:32). Giving life to her had fed Him. Many believers know this from experience. The visit you did not feel like making, the hour teaching children, the meal carried to a grieving home left you more alive than before. Paul remembered Onesiphorus, who "often refreshed me" (2 Timothy 1:16), and told Philemon that "the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you" (Philemon 7). A dry, inward-turned soul is often one that has stopped watering anyone else.
units.application: If you feel spiritually dry, look for someone to water this week: write to a missionary, take a meal to a new mother, sit with a widow after church, encourage a weary pastor. Small-group leaders and Sunday school teachers: your preparation feeds you before it feeds them. Parents: serve alongside your children, so they learn that giving refreshes. Give without keeping score; God sees.

rel.note: Blessings rest on the head of the righteous, the same image used for the fair seller.
God's delight in honest dealing in the marketplace, which includes how goods are sold in a time of need.
Withholding more than is right leads to poverty, the principle behind this picture of the grain hoarder.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard.
The one who hides his eyes from the poor will have many curses.

units.notes:
• The NLT spells out the setting: "but they bless the one who sells in time of need."
• Joseph is the commended seller. He stored grain in the years of plenty, then opened the storehouses and sold to Egypt and the nations during the famine (Genesis 41:56–57).
