• Nehemiah confronted nobles who exploited a famine by lending at interest and taking fields and children as pledges (Nehemiah 5:1–13). Amos condemned merchants impatient to sell grain with false measures (Amos 8:4–6).
• Henry says those who hold stores should be "content with moderate profit, and not aim to make a gain of God's judgments," that is, not profit from a disaster.
• Compare 3:27; 10:6; 21:13; 28:27.
units.summary: Hoarding bread while neighbors go hungry earns curses; selling it fairly brings blessing.
units.principle: Profiting from other people's desperation brings a community's curse, while meeting needs fairly in business brings blessing.
units.insight: Joseph held the grain of Egypt during the famine, and the whole world came to buy from him (Genesis 41:57). He did not use the crisis to ruin people but to keep them alive. Years later he told his brothers, "God sent me before you to preserve life" (Genesis 45:5). Modern versions of the grain hoarder include price gouging after a disaster, cornering scarce supplies, or a landlord squeezing tenants who have nowhere else to go. The heart behind them is the same: my gain matters more than your need. Christ shows the opposite heart. He is "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and He gives Himself freely to all who come. Those who have received Him cannot be indifferent to a neighbor's hunger, of body or of soul.
units.application: Business owners: when a crisis raises demand, price fairly instead of squeezing customers who have no choice. Landlords: weigh a struggling tenant's situation, not only the market rate. If you have more than you need in a shortage, whether food, supplies or time, share it or sell it at a fair price. Believers: do not hoard the gospel; look for one person this week who is hungry for hope, and offer it.

rel.note: The desire of the righteous ends in good and the expectation of the wicked in wrath, the same two outcomes of what people seek.
A good man obtains favor from the LORD, while a man of wicked intentions is condemned.
The one who digs a pit for others falls into it, as trouble comes to the one who seeks evil.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, the deepest source of the favor found here.

units.notes:
• Henry takes the verb behind "earnestly seeks" in the sense of rising early to look for something: "He that rises early to that which is good (so the word is)."
• The word translated "favor" is the same word translated "His delight" in 11:1 and 11:20. The favor found by the one who seeks good includes God's own pleasure in him.
• The NLT puts the second line vividly: "but if you search for evil, it will find you!"
• Bridges: "The ceaseless energy of Satan's servants in seeking mischief … puts to shame our indifference!" People who seek harm often work harder at it than believers work at doing good.
• Compare 8:35; 12:2; 26:27; Matthew 7:7.
units.summary: Go looking for good and you will find favor; go looking for trouble and it will find you.
units.principle: People generally find what they set themselves to seek: those who pursue good find favor, and those who plot evil bring it on themselves.
units.insight: Ruth went out to glean and spent herself caring for her mother-in-law. Boaz noticed, and she asked him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes?" (Ruth 2:10). She had sought good, and favor found her. Haman spent his energy seeking evil for Mordecai and the Jews, and it came back on him (Esther 7:10). Adoni-Bezek, who had cut off the thumbs and big toes of seventy kings, suffered the same and confessed, "as I have done, so God has repaid me" (Judges 1:7). Jesus "went about doing good" (Acts 10:38). Those who follow Him do not wait for good to come to them; they go looking for good to do. What are you looking for when you wake up each morning?
units.application: Start each day this week by asking, "What good can I do today, and for whom?" Then look for it: the coworker who needs help meeting a deadline, the neighbor whose yard is overgrown, the teenager who needs an adult to listen. If you catch yourself looking for a way to get even with someone, stop; that search ends badly. Leaders: reward people who seek the good of others, not those who seek advantage.

rel.note: The flourishing righteous of this verse bear the fruit that is a tree of life.
Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, the reason trust in them ends in a fall.
The righteous run to the name of the LORD as a strong tower, while the rich man imagines his wealth is his strong city.
Riches make themselves wings and fly away, so they cannot hold the weight of trust.

units.notes:
• The ESV compares the righteous to a green "leaf," while the KJV has "branch."
• Jeremiah draws the same contrast between trusting in man and trusting in the LORD. The one who trusts the LORD is "like a tree planted by the waters," and "its leaf will be green" (Jeremiah 17:7–8).
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Riches were never true to any that trusted to them."
• Henry: the one who trusts in riches falls "as a man who lays his weight on a broken reed, which will not only disappoint him, but run into his hand and pierce him."
• Compare 11:4; 18:10–11; 23:4–5; Mark 10:24; 1 Timothy 6:17.
units.summary: Lean on money and you will fall with it; root your life in God and you will stay green.
units.principle: Wealth is a gift to be used, never a foundation to be trusted; lives rooted in God flourish when trust placed in riches fails.
units.insight: A rich young ruler came running to Jesus, eager for eternal life. Jesus looked at him, loved him, and told him to sell what he had and follow Him. The young man "went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:22). His riches did not only fail him later; they held him back from life that very day. Jesus added, "how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God!" (Mark 10:24). Money quietly offers what only God can give: safety, worth, a future. Paul tells the rich not "to trust in uncertain riches but in the living God, who gives us richly all things to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17). Jesus said, "I am the vine, you are the branches" (John 15:5). Branches joined to Him stay green.
units.application: Ask what would happen to your peace if your savings or income disappeared tomorrow. If the answer frightens you, that is where your trust has shifted. Give something away this week as a declaration that God, not money, is your security. Those who are wealthy: be rich in good works and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:18). Those who are struggling: if your life is rooted in God, you are not less secure than the rich.

rel.note: The same verb, trouble: the cruel man troubles his own flesh as this man troubles his own house.
The wise woman builds her house while the foolish pulls it down with her own hands.
The one who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, naming one way a man ruins his household.
A wise servant rules over a son who causes shame, the same reversal of fool and wise.

units.notes:
• "Inherit the wind" means to be left with nothing, since wind cannot be held, stored or passed on. Compare Hosea 8:7, "They sow the wind, And reap the whirlwind," and Ecclesiastes 1:14, "grasping for the wind."
• "Troubles" is the verb used of Achan, whose sin brought trouble on Israel and destruction on his own family (Joshua 7:24–26).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, names Nabal, who "by selfishly hoarding his food and water for his own men, hung disaster over his household" (1 Samuel 25:17).
• Compare 14:1; 15:27; 17:2; Luke 15:13–16.
units.summary: Whoever wrecks his own household inherits nothing but wind.
units.principle: Those who harm their own households through greed, cruelty or folly are left with nothing they can keep, while wisdom builds a house that lasts.
units.insight: The younger son in Jesus' parable took his inheritance, wasted it in a far country, and ended up hired out to feed pigs, longing to eat what they ate (Luke 15:13–16). He had troubled his father's house and inherited the wind; the fool became a servant. Eli honored his sons above God, and his household fell (1 Samuel 2:29–34). Many people today are trading their families for careers, addictions or anger, and they will find their hands empty at the end. But Jesus' story does not end at the pigpen. The son came home, and while he was still far off, his father ran to meet him (Luke 15:20). It is not too late to stop troubling your house and come home.
units.application: Fathers and mothers: ask your spouse and children, "Is there anything I do that makes our home harder to live in?" and listen without defending yourself. If anger, drinking, gambling or overwork is troubling your house, get help this week from a pastor, counselor or recovery group. Young adults: learn to manage money now, so folly does not make you a servant later. Build your house with patience and kindness.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, another picture of a life that nourishes others.
The righteous flourish like green foliage, and here that living tree bears life-giving fruit.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life, one form the fruit of the righteous takes.
Greed takes away life, the deadly use of the expression that the wise use here to win people.
Wisdom herself is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, the fuller treatment of this image.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew of "winneth" as "taketh." The ESV says the wise man "captures" souls, and the NLT that "a wise person wins friends." In 1:19 the same kind of expression is deadly: greed "takes away the life of its owners."
• The Greek Septuagint reads the second line very differently, as a statement that the lives of the lawless are taken away before their time. The NKJV follows the Hebrew.
• The tree of life appears in Proverbs at 3:18; 11:30; 13:12 and 15:4, and returns in Revelation 22:2, where its leaves are "for the healing of the nations."
• Daniel 12:3 speaks of "those who turn many to righteousness," and James 5:20 of the one who "turns a sinner from the error of his way."
• Bridges: "For wise indeed we must be to win souls; so hard are they to be won!"
units.summary: A righteous life becomes a tree others can eat from, and the truly wise draw people toward life.
units.principle: A righteous life nourishes others like a tree of life, and true wisdom shows itself in drawing people toward life and toward God.
units.insight: Andrew met Jesus and "first found his own brother Simon," telling him, "We have found the Messiah," and he brought him to Jesus (John 1:41–42). The Samaritan woman left her water pot and told her town, "Come, see a Man" (John 4:28–29). Neither had training; both bore fruit. Paul became "all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22), which took patience and wisdom. Before people are won by our words, they are usually drawn by our lives: kindness, steadiness, joy in hardship. That fruit grows only from union with Christ, who said, "He who abides in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit" (John 15:5). In Him the tree of life is restored, and every life joined to Him feeds others.
units.application: Think of one person who does not yet know Christ, and pray for them by name every day this week. Ask what fruit of your life they can see: patience at work, kindness to your family, fairness in business. Look for a natural opening to share your hope, as Andrew did with his brother. Parents: the fruit of your life is your children's first nourishment. Churches: train believers to share their faith wisely and gently.

rel.note: The wicked will not go unpunished even when they join forces, the certainty this verse argues from the lesser to the greater.
Evil pursues sinners while good is repaid to the righteous, the same principle of repayment.
The LORD corrects those He loves as a father corrects his son, the repayment the righteous receive on the earth.

units.notes:
• The KJV begins the verse with "Behold," rendering a Hebrew particle that presents the first line as a given.
• Peter's quotation follows the Greek translation, which reads "scarcely saved" where the Hebrew has "recompensed on the earth." The NKJV of each passage translates its own text, so the two wordings should not be forced to match.
• Bridges: "We are recompensed in the earth; not, as we deserve to be, in hell." For believers, God's discipline is correction, not condemnation.
• Scripture shows God repaying His own servants in this life. Moses was barred from entering Canaan (Numbers 20:12), and the sword did not depart from David's house after he had Uriah killed (2 Samuel 12:9–10).
• Compare 3:11–12; 11:21; Luke 23:31; Hebrews 12:6–11.
units.summary: If God corrects His own children in this life, the defiant should not imagine they will escape Him.
units.principle: God's justice reaches everyone: if He corrects His own people in this life, those who defy Him will surely answer to Him.
units.insight: On the road to the cross Jesus told the weeping women, "if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?" (Luke 23:31). If the innocent Son suffered so, what awaits those who reject Him? This verse humbles everyone who reads it. Believers should not be surprised when God corrects them; Moses and David both felt His hand. Yet "we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world" (1 Corinthians 11:32). Our discipline is a Father's love, because the judgment we deserved fell on Christ. The unbeliever should not mistake God's patience for indifference. The verse that sobers the righteous warns the sinner to run to the only refuge, the Savior who bore God's judgment for all who come to Him.
units.application: If you are a believer under God's discipline, do not despair or resent it; ask what He is correcting, and turn (Hebrews 12:11). Parents: discipline your children in love, as the Father does, never in rage. If you have been presuming on God's patience in some hidden sin, take this verse as a warning and repent now. Pastors and teachers: preach both God's fatherly correction and His final judgment.

rel.note: Keeping instruction leads in the way of life, while refusing correction leads a person astray.
The fool who is right in his own eyes shows why someone hates correction, and the wise man who heeds counsel shows what loving instruction looks like.
Despising instruction harms one’s own soul, while heeding rebuke gains understanding.
The LORD’s own correction is an act of love, which is why His children should not despise it.
The scoffer hates the one who corrects him, while the wise man loves him and grows wiser.

units.notes:
• The word translated “instruction,” *musar*, means discipline, training that includes correction; the ESV has “discipline.” It is the word behind “chastening” in 3:11, “Do not despise the chastening of the LORD.”
• The word translated “correction,” *tokachat*, is a reproof that shows a person where he is wrong. Proverbs often pairs the two words, as in 10:17 and 15:5.
• The word translated “stupid,” *ba’ar*, means brutish, like a beast; the KJV has “brutish.” Asaph uses the same idea of himself: “I was so foolish and ignorant; I was like a beast before You” (Psalm 73:22).
• Bridges explains why correction is hard to love: “the submission of the will is our only road to Christian attainment.”
• Compare Psalm 32:9 (the horse and mule, “Which have no understanding”) and Hebrews 12:5–11.
units.summary: The road to knowing more runs straight through being told you are wrong.
units.principle: Willingness to be corrected is the doorway to every kind of growth; whoever shuts that door chooses to stay as he is.
units.insight: Hating correction is rarely about the facts. It is pride protecting itself. When the Book of the Law was read to King Josiah, he tore his clothes, and God noted that his heart was tender (2 Kings 22:11, 19). King Asa had served the LORD for years, yet when the seer Hanani rebuked him, Asa was enraged and put him in prison (2 Chronicles 16:7–10). A person can be teachable in youth and hard in later years. The real test is what we do with correction we think is unfair or badly delivered; that is where the heart shows. The gospel makes correction bearable. The Father disciplines the children He loves (Hebrews 12:5–6), and because Christ has borne our condemnation, a rebuke can no longer destroy us. It can only train us: “afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:11).
units.application: When someone corrects you this week, whether a spouse, a boss or a small-group leader, say “thank you” and ask one clarifying question before you explain yourself. If you lead or parent, invite correction out loud: ask your team or your teenager, “What is one thing I could do better?” and do not argue with the answer. Then recall one rebuke from the past year that you brushed aside, and weigh it again before the Lord.

rel.note: The LORD detests a perverse heart and delights in the blameless, just as He favors the good and condemns the schemer.
The LORD’s favor toward the good man reappears as His delight in those who deal truthfully.
The same “man of wicked intentions” is hated by people, as here he is condemned by God.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates.
Wisdom promises the same favor from the LORD to whoever finds her.

units.notes:
• “Favor,” *ratson*, is goodwill, acceptance and pleasure. The same word returns in 12:22, where those who deal truthfully are the LORD’s “delight.” The phrase “obtains favor from the LORD” appears also in 8:35 and 18:22.
• “A man of wicked intentions” is literally a man of schemes, someone whose plans are his way of life. The same expression appears in 14:17: “a man of wicked intentions is hated.”
• The verse describes a man who lives by schemes, not every believer who falls. David fell into a wicked plan against Uriah (2 Samuel 11:14–15) and was brought to repentance (Psalm 51).
• Henry: “We are really as we are with God.”
• Compare 1 Samuel 16:7 (“the LORD looks at the heart”), Psalm 5:12 and Hebrews 4:12–13.
units.summary: God’s smile rests on goodness, and His verdict reaches plans no one else can see.
units.principle: God’s verdict on a life rests on its character and its hidden intentions, not on how it appears to others.
units.insight: Scripture shows both men. Cornelius was a devout man who gave generously, and the angel told him that his prayers and alms had “come up for a memorial before God” (Acts 10:4). Ahithophel gave brilliant counsel aimed at destroying David, but “the LORD had purposed to defeat the good advice of Ahithophel” (2 Samuel 17:14). Only God saw both hearts fully. That is sobering, because our private plans lie open to Him: the grudge we rehearse, the angle we are quietly working. It is also hopeful. Jesus grew “in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52), and in Him the Father has made us “accepted in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). The favor this verse describes is finally a gift received in Christ, and that gift produces the goodness the verse commends.
units.application: Before a hard meeting or conversation this week, ask what you actually intend: to help, or to win, to get even, to look good. Name the answer to God. If you lead, judge your decisions by their motive as well as their outcome, and invite someone to question your reasons. If someone has been scheming against you, take comfort that God sees what others miss; you do not have to expose it yourself.

rel.note: The wicked vanish like a passing whirlwind, while the righteous have an everlasting foundation.
The righteous will never be removed, which is the same stability pictured here as an unmoved root.
The root that cannot be moved also yields fruit, and the two root sayings frame verses 1–12.
What wickedness cannot establish, truthful speech establishes forever.
The house of the righteous standing after the wicked are overthrown is the same stability seen in a household.

units.notes:
• “Established” translates a verb meaning made firm, fixed and lasting. Proverbs uses it again in 12:19, “The truthful lip shall be established forever,” and in 16:12, “a throne is established by righteousness.”
• The Hebrew verb behind “cannot be moved” is the one the Psalms use for the person God holds steady: “I shall not be moved” (Psalm 62:6); “Surely he will never be shaken” (Psalm 112:6).
• Henry: “That prosperity which is raised by sin is built on the sand, and so it will soon appear.”
• Psalm 73:18 describes the prosperous wicked as set “in slippery places”: high for a time, but with nothing firm under their feet.
• Compare Psalm 1:3–4 and Jeremiah 17:7–8, where the one who trusts the LORD is a tree planted by water.
units.summary: Wickedness can lift a man up, but only righteousness can root him down.
units.principle: Security gained by wrongdoing never lasts, but a life rooted in God holds firm through every storm.
units.insight: Abimelech murdered seventy brothers to seize a throne and was dead within three years, fatally struck by a millstone a woman dropped from a tower (Judges 9:5, 22, 53–54). Wickedness lifted him up; it could not hold him there. The righteous, by contrast, may lose leaves and branches. Henry: “The root of the righteous shall not be moved, though their branches may be shaken.” Job lost his children, his wealth and his health, yet he said, “I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). Where is your root? Security built on reputation, a bank balance or a clever arrangement can be blown over in an afternoon. Paul urges believers to be “rooted and built up in Him and established in the faith” (Colossians 2:7). The root that cannot be moved is a life grounded in Christ. It holds because He holds it, not because our grip is strong.
units.application: If you are tempted to get ahead by a shortcut, such as padding a résumé, shading a report or cutting a corner on your taxes, remember that what wickedness builds will not hold. If you are in a storm, losing a job or carrying grief, do not judge your footing by the shaking branches. Put your roots down this week through daily time in the Word, honest prayer and faithful worship with God’s people.

rel.note: The wise woman builds her house, while the foolish tears it down, the same contrast of honor and decay.
A contentious wife is a constant drip, while a prudent wife is a gift from the LORD.
The same “woman of strength” is praised at length, the wife whose husband safely trusts her.
Her husband known in the gates shows what it means for a wife to be his crown.
The husband is called to rejoice in and be faithful to his wife, so the responsibility for the marriage runs both ways.

units.notes:
• “Excellent wife” translates *eshet chayil*, literally “a woman of strength.” *Chayil* means strength, ability and worth; it is the word in “mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). The same phrase is “virtuous wife” in 31:10 and “virtuous woman” of Ruth in Ruth 3:11. The KJV has “virtuous woman” here too, but the strength in view is far wider than chastity.
• “Rottenness” translates a Hebrew word for decay that the Old Testament always uses in a figurative sense. A related verb appears in 10:7, “the name of the wicked will rot,” and the noun returns in 14:30, “envy is rottenness to the bones.”
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “The ignoble wife invisibly saps his strength and vitality and deconstructs him from within.”
• Compare 14:1; 19:13–14; 31:10–31; Ephesians 5:25–33; 1 Peter 3:1–7.
units.summary: No one wears a crown alone: a wife of strength puts her honor on her husband’s head.
units.principle: A spouse’s character either adds honor to the marriage or quietly eats away at it from within, and both partners carry that responsibility.
units.insight: Abigail was married to a fool, yet her wisdom protected her household and kept David from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–33). Jezebel, by contrast, “stirred up” Ahab to the worst evil of his reign (1 Kings 21:25). A spouse’s character reaches into everything. Bridges: “She is not the ring on her husband’s finger, or the chain of gold around his neck.” She is his crown. Yet the verse does not hand women a scorecard. Husbands are called to the same faithfulness and delight (5:15–19), and to love their wives “just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Shame in a home rarely arrives all at once; it grows through small contempt, secrecy and neglect. Ask whether your presence at home is building honor or causing quiet decay. Christ’s self-giving love is the pattern and the power for both husband and wife.
units.application: Husbands, name one specific way your wife has brought honor to your home, and tell her, then tell others in her hearing (31:28). Wives, ask the Lord whether any habit, such as a sharp tongue in public, secret spending or steady criticism, is wearing your husband down from within. Both of you: deal with small contempt early, before it becomes rot. Young men and women considering marriage: look for strength of character, not only charm (31:30).

rel.note: Trustworthy counsel brings safety, while the counsel of the wicked brings deceit.
Deceit lives in the heart of those who devise evil, while counselors of peace have joy, the same contrast of thoughts and counsel.
The deceitful thoughts of this verse become the ambushing words of the next.
Because the issues of life spring from the heart, the heart must be kept with all diligence.

units.notes:
• “Thoughts” means plans and intentions as well as ideas. “Right” translates *mishpat*, the common word for justice: the plans of the righteous are just.
• “Counsels” translates the word Proverbs uses for skilled guidance, the “wise counsel” a person needs in 1:5 and the counsel without which “the people fall” in 11:14. Here that same skill is put to the service of deceit.
• Henry: “We mistake if we imagine that thoughts are free.” He means that thoughts are not beyond God’s sight or His commands.
• Deceitful counsel in Scripture: Jonadab’s plan for Amnon (2 Samuel 13:3–5) and Haman’s advice to the king under a show of loyalty (Esther 3:8–9).
• Compare Psalm 1:1 (“Blessed is the man Who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly”), Romans 12:2 and Philippians 4:8.
units.summary: Advice is only as straight as the mind that gives it.
units.principle: Conduct flows from thought, so the character of a counselor matters as much as the sound of his counsel.
units.insight: Herod spoke like a fellow seeker when he told the wise men to find the Child and “bring back word to me, that I may come and worship Him also” (Matthew 2:8). His counsel was murder dressed up as devotion. The verse also searches us, because every deed begins as a thought. Henry draws a wise line: “A good man may have in his mind bad suggestions, but he does not indulge them and harbour them till they are ripened into bad projects.” By “suggestions” he means tempting thoughts that come unbidden, and by “projects” settled plans. A passing thought is not yet a plan; the danger lies in keeping it and feeding it. Paul calls believers to bring “every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). A renewed mind is God’s work in us (Romans 12:2), and from it comes counsel others can trust.
units.application: Before you follow advice about money, marriage or a career move, ask not only “Does this sound right?” but “What kind of person is giving it, and what does he gain?” If you counsel others as a manager, mentor or friend, check your own motive first: are you steering them toward their good or toward your convenience? When an ugly thought comes, refuse to rehearse it; turn it into prayer.

rel.note: The hypocrite destroys his neighbor with his mouth, while knowledge delivers the righteous.
The deceitful counsels of the wicked in verse 5 become the murderous words of verse 6.
A true witness delivers souls, the rescuing speech of the upright.
The enticers’ invitation to “lie in wait to shed blood” is the speech this verse exposes.
The call to deliver those drawn toward death shows what the mouth of the upright is for.

units.notes:
• “Lie in wait” is the language of ambush. It is the same verb the enticers use in 1:11, “Let us lie in wait to shed blood.”
• The NLT renders the second line “but the words of the godly save lives,” taking “them” as the intended victims.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: “The vivid picture of ‘lying in wait for blood’ conveys that the wicked make a trap by their false accusations.”
• Henry: “A man may sometimes do a very good work with one good word.”
• Compare 11:9; 14:25 (“A true witness delivers souls”); 24:11–12; 31:8–9.
units.summary: The same mouth that can set an ambush can open an escape.
units.principle: Words can be weapons or rescues, and the upright choose to use theirs to protect those in danger.
units.insight: Naboth died because of words. Jezebel wrote letters, two scoundrels gave false testimony, and an innocent man was stoned (1 Kings 21:8–13). Words had lain in wait for blood. Jonathan used words the other way. He “spoke well of David” to his angry father and, for a time, turned Saul back from killing him (1 Samuel 19:4–6). Most of us would never plot harm. But we often stay silent when one word from us would rescue someone. The enemies of Jesus sent spies to catch Him in His words, and His answers left them silent (Luke 20:20–26). Now He speaks for us: “we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Those He has defended are called to open their mouths for others.
units.application: When you hear talk that could ruin someone, such as a rumor at the office, a pile-on in a group chat or an unfair charge in a church meeting, do not simply stay out of it. Speak the true word that protects the person. If you supervise people, make sure anyone accused has a fair chance to answer. If a friend is walking into a trap, warn them plainly this week.

rel.note: The wicked vanish like a passing whirlwind, while the righteous have an everlasting foundation.
The unmoved root of the righteous is the same stability seen here in a standing house.
The house of the wicked is overthrown, while the tent of the upright flourishes.
A house is built and established by wisdom and understanding, which is why the righteous house stands.

units.notes:
• “Overthrown” translates *haphak*, to turn over or overturn. It is the verb used when God “overthrew” Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25).
• “Are no more” is a single Hebrew word meaning “and they are not” (KJV “are not”). The line ends as abruptly as the life it describes.
• The NLT renders the second line “but the family of the godly stands firm,” bringing out the sense of “house” as household.
• Henry likens the wicked to “the apples of Sodom, which look fair, but touch them and they go to dust.” The phrase comes from an old account of fruit near the Dead Sea that looked ripe but crumbled when touched.
• Compare 10:25; 14:11; Psalm 37:35–36.
units.summary: When the storm has passed, what is still standing tells you what it was built on.
units.principle: What is built on wickedness collapses without a trace, but a household built on righteousness outlasts the storm.
units.insight: Haman looked unstoppable, yet within a year of his plot against the Jews he was hanged and his ten sons were killed (Esther 3:7; 7:10; 9:10). Noah looked foolish building an ark on dry land, but by faith he “prepared an ark for the saving of his household” (Hebrews 11:7). Standing is not measured on a sunny day. The verse asks what our house is built on. A family can look strong in reputation, income and activity and still be standing on sand. Righteous families still suffer storms, illness and loss. The point is not that the wind stays away, but that a house on the right foundation holds. “For no other foundation can anyone lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Build there, and what you build will outlast the storm.
units.application: Parents, take a clear look at what your household is built on this week. Compare the hours given to screens, sports and work with the minutes given to Scripture and prayer together. Choose one practice to add, such as a short family reading at dinner. If you are tempted to envy a family that seems to have everything without God, read Psalm 37:35–36 and remember how quickly such houses fall.

rel.note: The perverse in heart are an abomination to the LORD, so the contempt of people matches God’s own judgment.
After true honor comes counterfeit honor: the man who honors himself but lacks bread.
Skill in one’s work brings a person before kings, one way wisdom is commended.
The wise inherit glory while fools inherit shame, the same contrast of commendation and contempt.

units.notes:
• “Of a perverse heart” is literally “perverse of heart,” as the 1611 KJV margin notes; the ESV has “a twisted mind.” In Proverbs the heart is the whole inner person: thinking, will and desire.
• Ironside: “The world can appreciate sobriety and spiritual intelligence, though it may refuse or even persecute it.” By “sobriety” he means sound, serious judgment.
• Wisdom commended and perverseness despised: Pharaoh raised Joseph over Egypt because he saw “a man in whom is the Spirit of God” (Genesis 41:38–40). Nabal’s own servant called him “such a scoundrel that one cannot speak to him” (1 Samuel 25:17).
• Compare 3:35; 22:29; 2 Corinthians 10:18, where the commendation that counts is the Lord’s.
units.summary: Wisdom earns respect slowly, and a twisted heart eventually shows on the surface.
units.principle: Over time a life’s true character comes into view, so lasting respect must be built on wisdom rather than image.
units.insight: Stephen’s opponents “were not able to resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6:10), and they stoned him anyway. Wisdom is often recognized even by people who reject it. Temple officers sent to arrest Jesus came back saying, “No man ever spoke like this Man!” (John 7:46), yet He was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). So this verse does not promise applause. It describes the usual weight of a life over time, and it directs us to the commendation that matters most: the Master’s “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). Ask what you are cultivating. You can grow wisdom that others may one day recognize, or a reputation that covers a crooked heart. The first lasts; the second is found out.
units.application: If you are building a career or a ministry, work on judgment and character rather than image; respect earned slowly lasts. If you supervise people, praise good judgment specifically when you see it. If you are overlooked or mocked for doing what is wise, keep going and leave the commendation to the Lord. And ask a trusted friend whether anything in your attitude has become twisted.

rel.note: True honor is earned by wisdom, while the self-honoring man of this verse has only a show.
One man makes himself rich yet has nothing, the same gap between appearance and reality.
Another “better than” saying values a little with the fear of the LORD over great treasure with trouble.
A humble spirit among the lowly is better than sharing spoil with the proud.

units.notes:
• “Slighted” means lightly esteemed, thought little of; the KJV has “despised.”
• Some translations read “has a servant” as “works for himself.” The Douay version, quoted by Ironside, has “Better is the poor that provideth for himself,” and the RSV is similar. On either reading the modest man has what he needs.
• Bridges: “Nothing is so despicable as to be proud, where there is nothing to be proud of.”
• Compare 13:7 (“There is one who makes himself rich, yet has nothing”); 15:16; Luke 14:11; 1 Timothy 6:6–8.
units.summary: Plain bread at a quiet table beats a grand title over an empty plate.
units.principle: Real provision and an honest station are worth more than an image of importance with nothing behind it.
units.insight: The church at Laodicea said, “I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing,” while Jesus saw them as “wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). That is this verse in spiritual form: honoring ourselves while we lack bread. Pride is expensive. It spends on image what should go to substance, whether money on appearances or energy on seeming spiritual. Christ went the other way. Though He was rich, He became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9) and “made Himself of no reputation” (Philippians 2:7). He was slighted by the world, yet He lacked nothing of the Father’s love. In Him we can stop performing. There is freedom in being thought little of while God Himself provides our bread.
units.application: If you are stretching to keep up appearances with a car payment, a house, a wardrobe or a lifestyle you cannot afford, make one decision this week to live within your means, even if someone thinks less of you. Young adults: a modest start without debt is better than a showy one on credit. Leaders: stop guarding your image, and admit one limitation to your team.

rel.note: The merciful man does good for his own soul, while the cruel man troubles his own flesh.
Knowing the state of one’s flocks is the same attentive care the righteous man gives his animal.
The righteous “considers” (knows) the cause of the poor, the same attentive care extended to people who cannot defend themselves.

units.notes:
• “Regards the life” is literally “knows the soul of his animal,” using *nephesh*, the common Hebrew word for life or soul. To know the animal’s life is to pay attention to what it needs. Compare 27:23, “Be diligent to know the state of your flocks.”
• “Tender mercies,” *rachamim*, means compassion and is related to the word for womb, the inward parts seen as the seat of tender feeling. The 1611 KJV margin offers “bowels,” the older English way of speaking about deep compassion.
• Care and cruelty toward animals: Jacob refused to drive his flocks too hard because the nursing animals would die (Genesis 33:13–14). Balaam beat his donkey three times (Numbers 22:23–28).
• Bridges, quoting John Locke: “they who delight in the sufferings and destruction of inferior creatures, will not be apt to be very compassionate and benign to those of their own kind.” (“Benign” means kind.)
• Compare Exodus 23:12 and Deuteronomy 22:6–7.
units.summary: Watch how someone treats a creature that cannot speak, and you learn who they are.
units.principle: True righteousness shows itself in care for the weak and dependent, while a hard heart turns even its kindness into cruelty.
units.insight: Pilate offered what he thought was mercy: “I will therefore chastise Him and release Him” (Luke 23:16). He would have a scourge laid across an innocent man’s back to calm a crowd. That is what the tender mercies of the wicked look like. God is the opposite. “The LORD is good to all, And His tender mercies are over all His works” (Psalm 145:9). He spared Nineveh with its “much livestock” in view (Jonah 4:11), and not one sparrow falls apart from the Father’s will (Matthew 10:29). To be righteous is to reflect that care. The test is often a creature or person who cannot repay us: the animal, the small child, the aging parent, the worker who cannot complain. Our patience with the dependent shows what is really in us.
units.application: Parents, if a child is rough with a pet or a smaller sibling, take it seriously and teach gentleness; it shapes the heart. If you keep animals, whether pets, livestock or a working dog, give them proper food, rest and care, even when it costs you time. Employers: notice whether your “kindness” to staff actually helps them or only makes you look generous. Mercy is measured by what it does for the one who receives it.

rel.note: The hands that till the land are repaid, and so is the mouth: both work and words bring their own harvest.
Diligent hands that bring bread here also bring responsibility and rule.
Waking up to work brings the same reward: being satisfied with bread.
The neglected field of the man devoid of understanding is the opposite of the tilled land.
The same first line returns, with the result spelled out: frivolity ends in poverty.

units.notes:
• “Frivolity” translates *reqim*, empty or worthless things. The KJV reads “vain persons,” taking the word as worthless people rather than worthless things; the ESV has “worthless pursuits.”
• “Devoid of understanding” is literally “lacking heart.” The same phrase describes the young man led astray in 7:7, “A young man devoid of understanding.”
• Ironside applies the verse to Scripture: “God’s word is a field well worth our tilling.”
• Henry: “Keep thy shop and thy shop will keep thee.” It is an old saying: tend your business, and it will support you.
• Compare 24:30–34; 28:19; 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12.
units.summary: Steady work on what is yours feeds a household; chasing what is empty feeds nobody.
units.principle: Faithful, ordinary work on what God has entrusted to us normally brings provision, while chasing empty things reveals a lack of sense.
units.insight: Before sin entered the world, God placed Adam in the garden “to tend and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Ordinary work is part of God’s good design, and Jesus Himself was known in Nazareth as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). The pull of frivolity is the hope of a harvest without plowing. It shows up in lottery dreams, endless entertainment and friends who never build anything. The same is true of the soul. Timothy had known the Scriptures from childhood and was urged to continue in them (2 Timothy 3:14–15). King Jehoiakim cut God’s word apart with a knife and burned it (Jeremiah 36:22–23). One tilled the field; the other burned the seed. What are you tilling, and what are you chasing?
units.application: List the empty pursuits that take your best hours, whether endless scrolling, a scheme that promises easy money or a crowd that never builds anything. Replace one of them this week with steady work on what God has given you: your job, your home, your studies. Young people: be wary of anyone selling a shortcut to wealth. Believers: till God’s word daily, even one chapter read slowly.

rel.note: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, the fruitfulness that grows from their root.
The root that cannot be moved is the root that here yields fruit; together the two sayings frame verses 1–12.
The enticers’ hunger for spoil is the same coveting of evil men’s gain.
The greedy covet all day long, while the righteous give and do not hold back.

units.notes:
• The word the NKJV renders “catch,” *metsod*, is spelled like Hebrew words for a hunting net and for a stronghold. The 1611 KJV reads “the net,” with “the fortresse” in its margin; the ESV has “the spoil.”
• Henry: “The wicked desires only a net wherewith to fish for himself; the righteous desires to yield fruit for the benefit of others and God’s glory.” (“Wherewith” means “with which.”)
• The enticers of chapter 1 promised to “fill our houses with spoil” (1:13), the same appetite for other people’s goods.
• Compare Exodus 20:17; Psalm 1:3; Galatians 5:22–23.
units.summary: The wicked keep eyeing someone else’s net; the righteous grow fruit of their own.
units.principle: Envy of what others have gained by wrong is a restless hunger, while a life rooted in God bears fruit of its own.
units.insight: Achan saw a fine garment, silver and gold among the spoils of Jericho, and he confessed, “I coveted them and took them” (Joshua 7:21). He wanted a catch that was not his, and it cost him everything. Coveting rarely begins with theft. It begins with looking: comparing salaries, homes, followers, even another church’s growth, until our own field seems worthless. The righteous are freed from that restless looking because their life has a root. Jesus said, “He who abides in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for without Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Fruit is not grabbed from someone else’s net; it grows from union with Christ. The question is not what others have caught, but where your roots are.
units.application: Notice this week when you feel a stab of envy at someone’s success, whether a coworker’s promotion, a friend’s house or another ministry’s numbers. Name it before God, then thank Him for one specific thing He is growing in your own life. If you run a business or lead a ministry, refuse to copy a rival’s shady methods because they seem to work. Invest instead in the slow work of prayer and Scripture.

rel.note: The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the trouble falls on the wicked instead.
The righteous come through trouble, and no grave trouble finally overtakes them.
Guarding the mouth preserves life, while opening the lips wide brings destruction.
A fool’s lips are the snare of his soul, the same trap set by one’s own mouth.
An evil man is snared by transgression, while the righteous sings and rejoices.

units.notes:
• “Transgression,” *pesha‘*, is a strong word for rebellion, a deliberate crossing of a line. The 1611 KJV margin gives the first line as “the snare of the wicked is in the transgression of lips”; the Hebrew word order puts the sin of the lips first, so the emphasis falls on the lips as the place where the trap is set.
• The ESV says the righteous “escapes from trouble.”
• Henry: “Many a man has paid dearly in this world for the transgression of his lips, and has felt the lash on his back for want of a bridle upon his tongue.” (“For want of” means “for lack of.”)
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik, repeats the old saying “A liar had need of a good memory”.
• Compare 18:7 (“his lips are the snare of his soul”); 29:6 (“By transgression an evil man is snared”); Psalm 64:8.
units.summary: A liar builds his own trap one sentence at a time.
units.principle: Sinful speech eventually traps the one who uses it, while truthful speech leaves a person free to face trouble with nothing to hide.
units.insight: The Amalekite who brought David news of Saul’s death claimed to have killed the king himself, expecting a reward. David answered, “your own mouth has testified against you” (2 Samuel 1:16). Gehazi told one lie to Naaman and another to Elisha, and he went out a leper (2 Kings 5:22–27). Lies feel like an escape in the moment, but they keep demanding more lies, and each one adds a strand to the snare. The righteous are not spared trouble. Jesus said, “In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Those who belong to Him do not have to manage a web of stories. They can face trouble with an open face, trusting the One who brings them through.
units.application: If you have told a lie at work or at home that you are now maintaining, end it this week. Tell the truth and accept the cost before the snare tightens. Parents: help children see that a lie never stays small, and be gentle with the child who confesses. If you are in trouble for doing right, whether a false accusation or a hard season at work, keep your words clean. You will have nothing to take back.

rel.note: Tilling the land brings bread, the recompense of the hands that this verse sets beside the fruit of the mouth.
A man eats well by the fruit of his mouth, the same harvest of speech.
A man is filled from the fruit of his mouth, because death and life are in the power of the tongue.
The LORD will render to each man according to his deeds, which is why the work of the hands returns to him.

units.notes:
• Proverbs returns to “the fruit of his mouth” in 13:2 (“A man shall eat well by the fruit of his mouth”) and 18:20 (“A man’s stomach shall be satisfied from the fruit of his mouth”). The next verse there adds, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (18:21).
• “Recompense” means what is paid back, a person’s due return for what he has done.
• Henry, on what this means for those who teach: “While we are teaching others we may ourselves learn, and feed on the bread of life we break to others.”
• The parable of the unmerciful servant shows a man’s own dealings coming back on him (Matthew 18:23–35).
• Compare Isaiah 3:10; Galatians 6:7–9.
units.summary: Your words are seeds, and sooner or later you eat the harvest.
units.principle: Both words and deeds are a kind of sowing, and under God each brings a harvest back to the one who sowed it.
units.insight: Mordecai once reported a plot against King Ahasuerus, and the deed was written down and forgotten (Esther 2:21–23). Years later, on a sleepless night, the king had the record read, and Haman himself had to lead Mordecai through the city square in honor (Esther 6:1–11). The fruit of his mouth came back to him. Words do not vanish when they leave us. Jesus said, “For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). That should sober us about careless speech. It should also encourage us about faithful words no one seems to notice: the note of thanks, the prayer, the patient explanation to a child. None is wasted. “Let us not grow weary while doing good, for in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart” (Galatians 6:9).
units.application: Think of one person who needs a good word from you this week, such as a discouraged coworker, a tired spouse or a teenager who rarely hears praise, and give it. If you teach or lead, remember that faithful words often bear fruit long after you see results. Before you send a sharp email or post, ask what harvest it will bring back. Then work with your hands as carefully as you speak.

rel.note: Loving instruction and hating correction show the same divide as heeding counsel and trusting only one’s own eyes.
A way that seems right can end in death, which is why a person’s own sense of rightness is not enough.
Listening to counsel and receiving instruction is the path to being wise in later days.
There is more hope for a fool than for the man wise in his own eyes.
The father warns his son not to be wise in his own eyes but to fear the LORD.

units.notes:
• “Right” means straight or upright: the fool sees his own road as straight. The same word appears in 14:12, “There is a way that seems right to a man, But its end is the way of death.”
• Similar sayings about being right “in his own eyes” appear in 16:2, 21:2 and 26:12.
• Bridges: “His chief danger is his security.” He means the fool’s feeling of being safe and sure of himself.
• Moses listened to his father-in-law Jethro and shared the work of judging the people (Exodus 18:13–24).
• Compare 1:5; 11:14; 19:20; James 1:19.
units.summary: The fool’s problem is not that he is often wrong, but that he never suspects it.
units.principle: The person who cannot imagine being wrong cannot be taught, while the one who seeks and heeds counsel keeps growing wiser.
units.insight: Rehoboam asked for counsel, but only to confirm what he already wanted. He rejected the elders who urged him to serve the people, took the harsh advice of the young men he had grown up with, and lost ten tribes (1 Kings 12:6–16). A fool can sit through a meeting of wise counselors and walk out unchanged. Our blind spots are, by definition, invisible to us. That is why the humble ask, keep asking, and give real weight to the answer. Above every human adviser stands the One whose name is “Wonderful, Counselor” (Isaiah 9:6). He does not scold the one who asks: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach” (James 1:5). Being teachable before Him is the root of being teachable before others.
units.application: Before a major decision this week, whether a purchase, a job change or a hard conversation, ask two people you trust what they see that you might be missing. Ask before you have decided. Leaders: build a team that can disagree with you, and thank the person who does. Parents of teenagers: let your children hear you ask for advice, so they learn that wise people listen.

rel.note: The same prudent man who covers shame also conceals knowledge, while the fool displays both anger and folly.
The one slow to wrath has great understanding, while the impulsive man exalts folly.
Covering a transgression seeks love, while repeating a matter separates friends.
Discretion makes a man slow to anger, and his glory is to overlook a transgression.
A fool vents all his feelings, while a wise man holds them back.

units.notes:
• “At once” is literally “in the day,” meaning on the same day. The 1611 KJV reads “presently,” with “in that day” in its margin. The fool’s anger shows on the very day he is provoked.
• “Prudent,” *‘arum*, describes someone shrewd and careful. The same word returns in 12:23, “A prudent man conceals knowledge.” In both verses the prudent man covers what the fool puts on display. The ESV says the prudent “ignores an insult.”
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: “It is not so much that the wise man represses anger or feelings but that he is more shrewd in dealing with it.”
• Compare 14:29; 17:9; 19:11; 29:11; James 1:19–20.
units.summary: Anyone can show his anger on the spot; it takes wisdom to let an insult go.
units.principle: Self-control in the moment of insult marks the wise, while anger that must be shown at once marks the fool.
units.insight: When Saul was first made king, some rebels sneered, “How can this man save us?” and brought him no presents. “But he held his peace” (1 Samuel 10:27). Years later the same Saul hurled a spear at David in a jealous rage (1 Samuel 18:10–11). The same heart can do both. A quick temper feels like strength, but it shows that our feelings are in charge. Jesus was mocked, spat on and falsely accused, and “when He was reviled, did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). He could cover shame because He entrusted Himself to the Father who judges righteously. Ask what you do with the first hot moment after an insult. The fruit of the Spirit includes self-control (Galatians 5:23), and He can give what temperament cannot.
units.application: When someone insults you this week, in traffic, in a meeting or online, wait a day before you respond, and ask whether it needs a response at all. Parents: when a child provokes you, lower your voice instead of raising it. Leaders: do not air a staff member’s slight in public. If an offense is real and serious, deal with it privately and calmly (Matthew 18:15).

rel.note: Truthful speech is established forever, while the lying tongue lasts only a moment.
The LORD detests lying lips and delights in those who deal truthfully.
A true witness delivers souls, while a deceitful witness speaks lies.
A faithful witness does not lie, while a false witness pours out lies.
A false witness who speaks lies is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• “Speaks” translates a verb meaning to breathe out or utter. It is the verb behind the false witness who “speaks lies” in 6:19 and 19:5 and “will utter lies” in 14:5. “Truth” here means faithfulness, speech that can be relied on, so every witness breathes out either what can be trusted or a lie.
• The ESV renders “declares righteousness” as “gives honest evidence,” which brings out the courtroom setting.
• Bridges: “A false witness does not always deal with open lying, but with deceit—truth misrepresented, concealed, and thus turned into falsehood.”
• Doeg reported a true fact to Saul but left out what would have cleared the priests, and eighty-five priests were killed (1 Samuel 22:9–18).
• Compare 14:5, 25; 19:5, 9; 25:18; Deuteronomy 19:16–19.
units.summary: Whether in a courtroom or a kitchen, every witness serves either justice or a lie.
units.principle: Truthful testimony serves justice, while a false witness, even one who shades or hides the truth, serves only deceit.
units.insight: At Jesus’ trial “many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree” (Mark 14:56). False witnesses helped send the only truly innocent Man to the cross. Against them stands Christ Himself, “the Faithful and True Witness” (Revelation 3:14), who told the truth about God and about us and died for it. Most of us will never testify in court, but we bear witness every day. We retell a conflict, describe a coworker to the boss, write a review, or report what a child did. It is easy to stay technically accurate while leaving the wrong impression. The Spirit of truth (John 16:13) forms in believers a love for the whole truth. Those who belong to the true Witness are called to speak as He does.
units.application: When you retell a conflict this week, tell it the way the other person would agree it happened. If you supervise people, write evaluations you could defend face to face. If you are called to testify, whether at work, in court or in a church matter, tell the whole truth even when it costs a friend. Parents: praise a child who gives an accurate report against his own interest.

rel.note: A good word that gladdens an anxious heart is one way the tongue of the wise brings health.
A wholesome, healing tongue is a tree of life, while perverse speech breaks the spirit.
Pleasant words bring sweetness to the soul and health to the bones.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, which is why it can both pierce and heal.
A false witness is like a sword and a sharp arrow, one form of the piercing speech warned against here.

units.notes:
• “Speaks” here translates a verb for rash, thoughtless speech. It is used of Moses, who “spoke rashly with his lips” at Meribah (Psalm 106:33), and of careless oaths in Leviticus 5:4. The ESV has “rash words.”
• “Health,” *marpe’*, means healing or remedy. The same word stands behind “A wholesome tongue is a tree of life” (15:4). The KJV says simply that the tongue of the wise “is health.”
• Bridges: “Many will speak daggers without compunction, who would be afraid to use them.” (“Without compunction” means without a pang of conscience.)
• Henry: “The tongue is death or life, poison or medicine, as it is used.”
• Compare 15:4; 16:24; 18:21; Ephesians 4:29; James 3:5–10.
units.summary: Some words leave scars long after they are forgotten; wise words help wounds close.
units.principle: Words have real power to wound or to heal, and wisdom chooses speech that restores.
units.insight: Hannah knew both kinds of speech. Her rival Peninnah provoked her year after year until she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:6–7). Eli first wrongly accused her of drunkenness, but when he heard her story he said, “Go in peace,” and “her face was no longer sad” (1 Samuel 1:14–18). The same mouth can wound and heal, sometimes in one conversation. Most sword thrusts are not planned; they come from haste, sarcasm or the need to win. The Servant of the LORD, fulfilled in Jesus, says, “The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary” (Isaiah 50:4). Bring Him the wounds others’ words have caused, and the wounds your own words have caused, and ask for a tongue like His.
units.application: This week, catch one sharp or sarcastic remark before it leaves your mouth, especially at home, where we are least guarded. If you know you wounded someone with words, go back, name what you said, and ask forgiveness. Managers and parents: when you must correct, say what is true and helpful, and leave out the sting. Write a note of encouragement to someone who is hurting.

rel.note: The truthful witness serves righteousness, and here truthful speech is shown to last.
Truthful dealing is the LORD’s delight, which is why it endures while lies pass away.
What wickedness cannot establish, truthful speech establishes forever.
The one who speaks lies shall perish, the end of the lying tongue.
Treasures gained by a lying tongue are a fleeting fantasy, the same short life of a lie.

units.notes:
• “Established” is the same verb used in 12:3: wickedness cannot establish a man, but the truthful lip will be established forever.
• “For a moment” uses a Hebrew expression that lexicons explain as the time it takes to blink an eye. The lie lasts about that long. The NLT renders the line “but lies are soon exposed.”
• Henry: “Those therefore that make a lie their refuge will find it a refuge of lies.” He echoes Isaiah 28:15, 17.
• At the stake in Oxford in 1555, Hugh Latimer told Nicholas Ridley that by God’s grace they would that day light such a candle in England as, he trusted, would never be put out. The truth they died for outlasted the fire.
• Compare 19:9; 21:6; Psalm 52:4–5; 2 Corinthians 13:8.
units.summary: A lie can win the moment; only the truth is still standing at the end.
units.principle: Truth endures because it rests on what is real, while every lie is a short-term loan against future exposure.
units.insight: Jacob’s lie won his father’s blessing in an afternoon (Genesis 27:18–29). It also cost him twenty years away from home, and he was deceived in turn by Laban and later by his own sons (Genesis 29:25; 37:31–35). The lie lasted a moment; its fruit lasted decades. Every liar is betting that the moment will last. It never does, because God has made a world in which truth outlives falsehood. Jesus said, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away” (Matthew 24:35). His word is the truthful lip established forever, and those who speak in line with it share in its permanence. Ask where you are trading tomorrow’s trust for today’s convenience.
units.application: If you are tempted this week to shade a story so you look better to a spouse, a boss or a customer, remember how short the payoff is. Tell it straight. If you are under a false accusation, do not answer a lie with a lie; keep telling the truth calmly and leave your vindication to God. Parents: show your children that you value a truthful confession more than a perfect record.

rel.note: The deceitful counsels of the wicked stand against the right thoughts of the righteous, as deceit here stands against counsel for peace.
Those who devise evil go astray, while mercy and truth belong to those who devise good.
The father forbids devising evil against a neighbor who lives trustingly nearby.
The worthless person devises evil continually and sows discord, the opposite of the counselor of peace.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb translated “devise” is the same verb translated “plow” in 20:4. Proverbs uses it for plotting evil in 3:29 and 6:14, 18. The picture is of a man working out his evil plan the way a farmer works his field, carefully and ahead of time.
• The ESV speaks of those who “plan peace,” which makes the parallel with “devise” in the first line clearer.
• Henry: “Let them imagine it ever so artfully, deceivers will be deceived.” By “imagine” he means plot or plan.
• Compare 12:5; 14:22 (“mercy and truth belong to those who devise good”); Matthew 5:9; James 3:17–18.
units.summary: Plotters carry a hidden darkness; peacemakers carry a joy no scheme can give.
units.principle: Plotting evil requires a deceitful heart and robs it of peace, while seeking peace for others brings joy to the one who seeks it.
units.insight: Absalom stood at the city gate winning the hearts of Israel with friendly words while he plotted against his father (2 Samuel 15:1–12). Deceit filled his heart, and it ended in his death (2 Samuel 18:9–15). Barnabas did the opposite. When the church feared the newly converted Saul, “Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” and vouched for him (Acts 9:26–27). Peace followed, and the gospel spread. Peacemaking is costly, but it is joyful work, because it shares in God’s own work. Christ made “peace through the blood of His cross” (Colossians 1:20), and He calls peacemakers “sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). Ask whether your counsel tends to widen conflicts or to heal them.
units.application: When friends or family members are at odds this week, ask whether your words are feeding the conflict or calming it, and refuse to carry tales between them. If you lead a team or a church group, look for one quarrel you can help resolve, and talk with each person privately first. If you catch yourself planning a hidden move against someone, stop; it will cost you your joy.

rel.note: The righteous come through trouble, which shows that this verse does not mean they never face it.
Those who reject wisdom are filled to the full with their own way, as the wicked here are filled with evil.
A righteous man may fall seven times and rise again, the balance this saying needs.
The LORD is the confidence of His people when trouble from the wicked comes.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV has “grave trouble,” the ESV has “No ill” and the KJV “no evil.” The NKJV’s wording narrows the sense to serious harm.
• “Filled” pictures the wicked having their fill of the evil they chose, as in 1:31, where those who reject wisdom “shall eat the fruit of their own way, And be filled to the full with their own fancies.”
• Henry: “though they may come into trouble, into many troubles, yet to them those troubles shall have no evil in them.”
• God sets limits on what His people face: He does not allow them to be tested beyond what they can bear, and with the testing He makes a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).
• Compare 24:16; Psalm 34:19 (“Many are the afflictions of the righteous, But the LORD delivers him out of them all”); Romans 8:28.
units.summary: Trouble may come to the righteous, but it never gets the last word.
units.principle: God does not exempt the righteous from trouble, but He keeps it from having the final word, while the wicked end up filled with the evil they chose.
units.insight: Job’s friends read this kind of proverb backward. Eliphaz asked, “Who ever perished being innocent?” (Job 4:7), and concluded that Job’s suffering proved his sin. God said they had not spoken of Him what was right (Job 42:7). The verse does not teach that the suffering are guilty. It teaches that the righteous are never abandoned to harm. Joseph was sold, slandered and imprisoned, yet he could say, “you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Paul was “hard-pressed on every side, yet not crushed” (2 Corinthians 4:8). In Christ, nothing “shall be able to separate us from the love of God” (Romans 8:39). Trouble may come to your door, but in Him it does not have the final word.
units.application: If you are walking with someone through illness, loss or hardship this week, never hint that their suffering must be their fault; sit with them and pray. If you are the one suffering, read Psalm 34 and tell God plainly what you fear, trusting that He has set limits to this trouble. Young believers: do not envy the wicked when they seem to escape; they are filling up on what will harm them.

rel.note: The same abomination-and-delight pairing applied to the merchant’s scales.
The same abomination-and-delight pairing applied to the heart.
The truthful witness and the false witness open the run of sayings that this verse brings to its high point.
Truthful speech endures while lies pass, because the LORD delights in truth and detests lies.
The LORD’s favor rests on the good man, as His delight rests here on those who deal truthfully.
A lying tongue and a false witness are among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• “Abomination,” *to‘evah*, means something detestable, utterly abhorrent to God.
• “Deal truthfully” is literally “do faithfulness”: acting reliably as well as speaking accurately. The ESV has “act faithfully.” “His delight” is the same word translated “favor” in 12:2.
• Ironside draws a careful line: “It is well to remember that it is intentional deceit that is here in question.” An honest mistake is not a lie.
• Ananias and Sapphira lied about their gift, and Peter told Ananias, “You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:4).
• Compare 6:16–19; 11:1, 20; 13:5; Psalm 15:1–2; Ephesians 4:25.
units.summary: God does not merely dislike lies; He detests them, and He delights in people who keep faith.
units.principle: God detests deliberate deception because He is the God of truth, and He takes pleasure in people whose words and dealings can be trusted.
units.insight: Lying shows whose family we resemble. Jesus said the devil “is a liar and the father of it” (John 8:44), while He Himself is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). That is why lying lips are an abomination: they copy the enemy and contradict the character of God, “who cannot lie” (Titus 1:2). Most of our lies are small and social. We say we are busy when we are not, or ask someone else to say we are out. They still train the heart to treat truth as negotiable. Yet the God who detests lies forgives liars. Peter denied Jesus three times, once with an oath, and the risen Lord restored him three times by the sea (John 21:15–17). His delight rests on those He is making truthful.
units.application: Take inventory this week of your small lies: the excuse to get off the phone, the inflated number, the “I never got your email.” Choose one and stop it completely. Parents: never ask a child to lie for you, even to say you are not home. Employees and business owners: deal truthfully in what you do as well as what you say, from timesheets to product claims.

rel.note: Wise people store up knowledge, while the mouth of the foolish is near destruction.
The same prudent man covers shame there and conceals knowledge here.
The prudent act with knowledge, while a fool lays open his folly.
The wise use knowledge rightly, while fools pour out foolishness.
The one with knowledge spares his words, and even a fool seems wise when silent.

units.notes:
• “Conceals” translates the same verb as “covers” in 12:16, and the same word for “prudent” appears in both verses. The prudent man covers an insult there and his knowledge here, while the fool puts both his anger and his folly on display.
• Bridges: “Nothing can justify speaking contrary to the truth. But we are not always obliged to tell the whole truth.”
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: “Someone who is careful in what he says will be equally careful about whom he confides in.”
• Young Elihu held back until the older men had finished speaking, though he was “full of words” (Job 32:4–7, 18).
• Compare 10:14; 13:16; 15:2 (“the mouth of fools pours forth foolishness”); 17:27–28.
units.summary: The wise do not say everything they know; fools tell everyone everything they think.
units.principle: Wisdom shares knowledge at the right time and for the good of others, while folly cannot stop putting itself on display.
units.insight: Samson “told her all his heart” (Judges 16:17), and the secret of his strength went straight to the Philistines. Jesus, by contrast, knew what His disciples could bear: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). Love decides what to say and when. The urge to say everything we know is often pride dressed up as helpfulness. We want to be the one who knew first, who corrected the error, who had the inside story. Discretion is a form of humility and of care. It keeps confidences, waits for the right moment, and lets someone else have the last word. Ask whether your speaking serves others or serves your image.
units.application: Before you speak up in a meeting, a Bible study or a family argument this week, ask: Does this need to be said, by me, now? If not, wait. Keep a confidence someone shared with you, even when telling it would make you look informed. Teachers and leaders: give people what they can use today, not everything you know. Young people: you do not have to post every opinion.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent makes rich, while the slack hand brings poverty; here diligence brings rule.
The one who tills his land is satisfied with bread, the everyday fruit of the same diligence.
The lazy man who will not finish his work and the diligent man’s precious possession close the section this verse opens.
The man who excels in his work stands before kings, the advancement diligence earns.
The full portrait of the sluggard explains how the lazy man ends up in want and bondage.

units.notes:
• “Lazy man” translates *remiyah*. Two Hebrew words share this spelling, one meaning slackness and the other deceit. The KJV has “slothful,” and its 1611 margin offers “deceitful.” Set against the diligent, the word means slackness here; it is the word behind the “slack hand” of 10:4.
• “Forced labor” is the word used for the labor gangs Solomon raised (1 Kings 9:21); the KJV says the slothful shall be “under tribute.”
• Ironside: “It is not ability only that causes one to succeed, and secures advancement.”
• Solomon promoted Jeroboam, “seeing that the young man was industrious” (1 Kings 11:28).
• Compare 10:4; 13:4; 22:29; Romans 12:11 (“not lagging in diligence”).
units.summary: Those who will not discipline themselves to work usually end up working on someone else’s terms.
units.principle: Faithful effort generally leads to trust and responsibility, while unwillingness to work leads to being ruled by others.
units.insight: Joseph was a slave and then a prisoner, yet in both places his faithful work led to his being put in charge (Genesis 39:4, 22). Diligence in small places prepared him to govern Egypt (Genesis 41:41). Jesus told of servants entrusted with their master’s money. To the faithful the master said, “you were faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things,” while the buried talent drew the words “You wicked and lazy servant” (Matthew 25:21, 26). Laziness promises freedom but ends in bondage: to debts, to others’ demands, to our own appetites. This verse is not a word against the sick, the disabled or the unemployed who cannot find work. It is a word to the heart that will not work. Christ’s grace frees us from serving ourselves so that we can serve Him gladly.
units.application: Employees: do this week’s ordinary tasks with care and on time, especially the ones no one checks; trust is built there. Students: start the assignment before you feel like it. Parents: give children real responsibility and let them taste the reward of finishing. If you are out of work through no fault of your own, take heart; this verse is not aimed at you. Keep doing what you can, and let your church help.

rel.note: The tongue of the wise promotes health, and a good word to the anxious is one form of that healing.
Sorrow of heart breaks the spirit, the inner heaviness this verse describes.
A word spoken in due season is good, the timely word that gladdens the anxious heart.
Pleasant words bring sweetness to the soul and health to the bones.
A merry heart does good like medicine, while a broken spirit dries the bones.

units.notes:
• “Anxiety,” *de’agah*, is worry or fearful care. The KJV says that heaviness in the heart “maketh it stoop,” keeping the picture of a heart bent low under its weight. The ESV says anxiety “weighs him down.”
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, describes the good word as including “encouragement, kindness, and insight.”
• King Artaxerxes noticed Nehemiah’s sad face and asked what he needed; the king’s favorable answer opened the way to rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1–8).
• Compare 15:13, 23; 17:22; Isaiah 35:3–4; Philippians 4:6–7.
units.summary: Worry bends the heart toward the ground; a kind word can help it look up.
units.principle: Worry weighs heavily on the inner life, and a timely, kind word is real help to a burdened heart, though not a substitute for every other kind of care.
units.insight: When Elijah lay under a broom tree asking to die, God did not lecture him. He let him sleep, fed him twice, and only later spoke to him (1 Kings 19:4–8). God cares for the whole person, and a good word often comes alongside rest, food, time and, when needed, a doctor’s care. Still, words matter. Jesus spoke them constantly: “Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2); “Be of good cheer! It is I; do not be afraid” (Matthew 14:27). His best word is an invitation: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Bring Him what weighs on you, “casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Then carry that good word to someone else.
units.application: Think of one person carrying a visible weight this week, such as a coworker facing layoffs, a parent with a sick child or a student under pressure. Send a specific, sincere word of encouragement, and follow it with practical help if you can. If someone you love is struggling with depression, keep speaking kindly, and also help them find pastoral and medical care. If you are anxious, name the worry to God in prayer (Philippians 4:6).

rel.note: Walking with the wise makes a person wise, while the companion of fools is destroyed.
The father’s first warning is not to consent when sinners entice.
Friendship with an angry man teaches his ways and sets a snare for the soul.
A good friend sharpens a person as iron sharpens iron, the opposite of being led astray.

units.notes:
• The first line (“The righteous should choose his friends carefully”) is difficult in Hebrew because its first word can be read in two ways. Read as a form of a verb meaning to search out or explore, it gives the NKJV’s “choose his friends carefully,” the 1984 NIV’s rendering about being cautious in friendship, or the ESV and NASB’s “guide” to his neighbor. Read as a form of a verb meaning to excel, it gives the KJV’s “more excellent than his neighbour,” with “abundant” in the 1611 margin.
• On the “guide” reading, the righteous man helps his neighbor find the way, as Nathan did when he confronted David (2 Samuel 12:1–14).
• Henry on the way of the wicked: “It seems to them to be not only a pleasant way, but the right way.”
• Compare 1:10–19; 13:20; 22:24–25; 1 Corinthians 15:33 (“Evil company corrupts good habits”).
units.summary: Friendship is never neutral: every companion is walking somewhere and inviting you along.
units.principle: Companions shape the direction of a life, so the wise choose their closest friends with care.
units.insight: Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, “a very crafty man,” whose advice set off rape, murder and a family torn apart (2 Samuel 13:3–5, 28–29). Jehoshaphat was a godly king, yet his alliance with Ahab nearly cost him his life, and a prophet asked him, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 18:31; 19:2). Good people are often led astray not by enemies but by friends. Jesus was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19), so this verse is not a call to avoid the lost. It is a call to choose carefully whose counsel shapes us. The best Friend is the One who laid down His life and says, “You are My friends if you do whatever I command you” (John 15:14). Walk closest with Him, and with those who walk with Him.
units.application: Parents: know your children’s closest friends by name, and make your home a place those friends want to be. Young people: ask of each close friend, “Am I more like Christ or less after time with this person?” Adults: notice who shapes your decisions about money, marriage and work, and add one wise, older believer to that circle this month. Keep loving those who do not know Christ, but do not let them steer.

rel.note: Diligence that leads to rule and laziness that ends in forced labor open the section this verse closes.
The lazy man desires and has nothing, while the diligent is made rich.
The lazy man buries his hand in the bowl and will not bring it to his mouth, the same failure to finish.
It wearies the lazy man even to bring food back to his mouth.

units.notes:
• The verb rendered “roast” occurs only here in the Old Testament, so its meaning cannot be checked against other passages. The NKJV, KJV, ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV all take it as roasting.
