Lexicons also give the sense “set in motion,” which would mean the lazy man does not even stir up his game. Either way he gains nothing from the hunt.
• The second line’s Hebrew word order is unusual, so translations word it differently. The ESV speaks of the “precious wealth” the diligent man gains, and the KJV of the “substance” of a diligent man as precious.
• The Hebrew word for “lazy man” is the same as in 12:24; set against diligence, it means slackness, not deceit.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: “Just as one who might hunt but never cook what he finds, so the lazy person never completes a project.”
• Compare 13:4; 19:24; 26:15; Ruth 2:17.
units.summary: The lazy man loves the thrill of the chase but will not do the work that makes dinner.
units.principle: Beginning is not enough; diligence that carries work through to completion is what turns effort into lasting good.
units.insight: Jesus described seed on stony ground that sprang up quickly and was received “with joy,” yet withered because the hearer had “no root in himself” (Matthew 13:20–21). Many of us start well: a Bible reading plan in January, a ministry with enthusiasm, a promise to pray for someone. The hunt is exciting; the roasting is dull. Ruth gleaned all day and then, at evening, “beat out what she had gleaned” (Ruth 2:17). She finished. So did our Lord. He said to the Father, “I have finished the work which You have given Me to do” (John 17:4), and from the cross, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). Because He finished, we can trust that “He who has begun a good work in you will complete it” (Philippians 1:6). We can ask Him for grace to finish what He has given us.
units.application: Look at what you have started and not finished: a project at work, a repair at home, a course of study, a commitment at church. Choose one and finish it this week, or release it openly. Parents: teach children to complete chores, not just begin them. Leaders: reward follow-through, not only bright ideas. If illness or exhaustion is what keeps you from finishing, that is not laziness; ask for help and rest.

rel.note: The labor of the righteous leads to life.
Righteousness leads to life, while pursuing evil leads to death.
The righteous has a refuge in his death, a further glimpse of the hope this verse may hold.
The path of the just shines ever brighter, the same road seen from another angle.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, the life found on the righteous way.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew of the second line is very compact; it reads literally, “and the way of a path, not death.” The NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV read it as “no death,” and the NLT as “that path does not lead to death.” The 1984 NIV goes further, rendering the line as a path of immortality by taking “not death” as a single idea.
• Henry: “There is not only life at the end, but there is life in the way.”
• Reading the verse in the light of the New Testament, Ironside says that for the righteous, death “is but the end of the way opening into the gladness and glory of the Father’s house.”
• Compare 4:18; 10:16; 11:19; Psalm 16:10–11; John 11:25–26.
units.summary: Righteousness is not only the road to life; it is the road where life is already found.
units.principle: The way of righteousness is where true life is found now, and in Christ that life reaches beyond death.
units.insight: Enoch “walked with God; and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). His road ran straight into God’s presence. Most believers will pass through death, yet when Stephen was stoned, Scripture says simply that “he fell asleep” (Acts 7:60). Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live” (John 11:25). This verse invites every reader to ask which road he is on. The way of righteousness is not earned by our own goodness. Christ is the righteous One who walked it perfectly and opened it to all who trust Him. On that road there is life now, and in Him even the last step is not the end.
units.application: Ask this week which road your daily choices are building, in how you spend money, speak at home and treat people at work. If you are grieving a believer who has died, read John 11:25–26 and 2 Timothy 1:10 aloud, and let them comfort you. If you are facing your own mortality, talk with your pastor about the hope of the gospel. Young people: choose the righteous way early; life is found on it now.

rel.note: The chapter returns to the same contrast: refusing correction leads to poverty and shame, while regarding a rebuke brings honor.
The father's instruction that opens the chapter is the same training a loving parent gives in the discipline saying that nearly closes it.
A fool despises his father's instruction, while the one who receives correction is prudent, the same two sons seen from another angle.
Wisdom calls even the scornful to turn at her rebuke, which keeps hope open for the scoffer of this verse.
The fullest portrait of the scoffer, who repays correction with shame and hatred, set beside the wise man who loves the one who rebukes him.

units.notes:
• The word translated "instruction," musar, is a broad word for a father's training, discipline and correction. It returns in 13:18 as "correction" and stands behind "disciplines" in 13:24, so the chapter begins and ends with a father training his son.
• The first line in Hebrew has no verb. It simply sets "a wise son" beside "his father's instruction," and translators supply the link: the NKJV has "heeds," the ESV "hears," the KJV "heareth," and the NASB adds "accepts."
• The saying moves from "instruction" in the first line to the sharper word "rebuke" in the second. Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, says the change shows that the scoffer "does not respond to any level of discipline."
• Compare 9:7–9; 12:1; 15:5, 12; Hebrews 12:5–11.
units.summary: The wise son is not the one who never needs correcting, but the one who listens when it comes.
units.principle: A person's wisdom shows less in what he knows than in how he receives correction.
units.insight: Eli's sons show the scoffer's road. Their father warned them, but "they did not heed the voice of their father" (1 Samuel 2:25), and both died on the same day (1 Samuel 4:11). David shows the other road. When Nathan said, "You are the man!" David answered, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). The perfect wise Son is Christ Himself. "Though He was a Son, yet He learned obedience by the things which He suffered" (Hebrews 5:8), and His ear was open to His Father morning by morning (Isaiah 50:4–5). The verse searches us. Bridges: "If I am reluctant to hear the faithful rebuke of men, I am prepared to resist the rebuke of God." Scoffing rarely begins with open contempt. It begins with a defensive answer, a rolled eye or a change of subject. Yet no one is too far gone to start listening.
units.application: Parents: correct in a way that can be heard, and praise a child for listening, not only for performing. Young people: when a parent or teacher points out a fault, try saying, "You may be right; tell me more," before you defend yourself. Employees and leaders: the next time feedback stings, write it down and act on one part of it this week. If you have refused correction for years, start with one conversation; Wisdom's door is still open.

rel.note: A man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth, nearly the same saying a chapter earlier.
The same treacherous people reappear, and their way proves hard.
The chapter begins and ends with eating: the righteous is satisfied, while the stomach of the wicked goes wanting.
The next saying adds that the guarded mouth preserves life, while unguarded words bring destruction on the speaker.
A man's stomach is satisfied from the fruit of his mouth, and death and life are in the power of the tongue.
The violent men of the father's warning eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence, the same appetite named here.

units.notes:
• The words "feeds on" are supplied by the NKJV. The second line in Hebrew has no verb; it simply sets "violence" beside "the soul of the unfaithful" and leaves the reader to make the link. The KJV has "shall eat violence," and the ESV and NASB render "soul" here as "desire."
• "Soul" translates nephesh, the inner self with its appetites and desires. The same word stands behind "life" in 13:3 and "soul" twice in 13:4, tying the opening sayings together around appetite, speech and life.
• "Unfaithful" describes people who act treacherously, breaking faith with those who trust them. The same word returns in 13:15: "the way of the unfaithful is hard."
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, says the treacherous "Shall have that violence and injury returned upon themselves, which they have offered to others in word or deed."
• Compare 12:14; 18:20–21; Matthew 12:34–37.
units.summary: Your words are seed, and one day you will sit down to eat the harvest.
units.principle: Speech is never only spoken; it is sown, and the speaker eventually lives on what it grows.
units.insight: This verse asks two questions: what are my words growing, and what is my soul hungry for? Doeg the Edomite had the wrong appetite. He informed on the priests of Nob to King Saul, then killed them himself (1 Samuel 22:9–18). David wrote of such a man, "You love all devouring words, You deceitful tongue" (Psalm 52:4). Jesus shows the other harvest. In Nazareth the people "marveled at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth" (Luke 4:22). He taught that "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). So appetite shows the heart. Jesus also said, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, For they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6). If our cravings are wrong, the answer is not only to guard our words. We must bring our appetites to Christ, who can give us a new hunger.
units.application: Before a hard conversation this week, ask what your words will grow: trust or suspicion, peace or resentment. Parents: notice what your children are learning from the way you speak about others at the dinner table. Managers and team leaders: speak in ways that build trust, because you will live inside the culture your words create. And if you catch yourself enjoying someone else's harm, even in a comment or a post, confess that appetite to God.

rel.note: In the multitude of words sin is not lacking, but the one who restrains his lips is wise.
The previous saying shows words feeding the speaker; this one shows unguarded words bringing him down.
The same verb for guarding returns when righteousness guards the blameless, closing the section that this saying helps open.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, which explains why guarding the mouth guards the life.
Whoever guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from troubles, the same truth in nearly the same words.

units.notes:
• The 1984 NIV renders the second line "speaks rashly," which captures the sense of the picture. The KJV, ESV and NASB keep the image of lips opened wide.
• The verb behind "guards" here returns in 13:6, "Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless." The man who guards his mouth is matched, at the close of the opening sayings (13:1–6), by righteousness that guards the blameless.
• "Life" translates nephesh, the same word rendered "soul" in 13:2 and 13:4. What a person lets out of his mouth reaches the very center of his life.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The old Arab proverb is appropriate: 'Take heed that your tongue does not cut your throat'."
• Compare 10:19; 18:21; 21:23; Psalm 141:3; James 3:2–6.
units.summary: Guard the gate of your mouth and you guard your life; leave it open, and ruin walks in.
units.principle: The person who rules his tongue protects his own life, and the person who lets it run free arms it against himself.
units.insight: Jephthah opened his mouth wide with a rash vow before battle, and it cost him his only daughter (Judges 11:30–35). Shimei poured out curses on David as he fled (2 Samuel 16:5–8), and those words were remembered against him years later (1 Kings 2:8–9, 44–46). Henry: "A guard upon the lips is a guard to the soul." Our Lord shows the guarded mouth perfectly. When He was reviled, He "did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23), yet when truth needed speaking He spoke it plainly. Most of us regret far more of what we said than of what we left unsaid. An unguarded tongue is not a personality type but a heart not yet under God's rule. So we ask God for the watchman we cannot keep alone: "Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; Keep watch over the door of my lips" (Psalm 141:3).
units.application: Before you post, send or reply in anger, wait an hour and ask whether the words need to be said, by you, now. Leaders: do not make promises in a meeting that you have not thought through. Friends trusted with a confidence: let it stop at your gate. Parents in a heated moment: lower your voice and shorten your sentences. Pray Psalm 141:3 each morning this week before the day's conversations begin.

rel.note: A slack hand makes poor, but the hand of the diligent makes rich, the outward side of this inward contrast.
Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, the satisfaction the lazy man wants but never reaches.
Injustice can leave hardworking people in want, so this saying about laziness must never be turned against the poor.
The chapter closes with the righteous eating to the satisfying of his soul, the same satisfied soul this verse describes in the diligent.
The desire of the lazy man kills him because his hands refuse to labor, the same craving without work.
The fuller portrait of the sluggard who needs the ant to teach him and sleeps his way into poverty.

units.notes:
• "Made rich" translates a Hebrew verb that means to be made fat, the picture of a well-fed body. In Proverbs it describes a person who is satisfied and prospering. The KJV, NASB and YLT keep "made fat," and the ESV has "richly supplied." The same verb appears in 11:25, "The generous soul will be made rich."
• The verb "desires" belongs to the same word family as the noun "desire" in 13:12 and 13:19. The lazy man's empty craving is set against the two later sayings about desire fulfilled.
• The NKJV uses "sluggard" only in 6:6 and 6:9 and "lazy man" elsewhere, though the Hebrew word is the same.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Affection without endeavour is like Rachel – beautiful, but barren." By "affection" he means desire, and by "endeavour" effort. Rachel was beautiful but for years had no children (Genesis 29:17, 31).
• Compare 21:25–26; 2 Thessalonians 3:10.
units.summary: Wanting is not the same as working; the lazy soul starves on its own wishes.
units.principle: Desire without effort leaves a person empty, while desire joined to faithful work tends to be satisfied.
units.insight: The exiles who returned from Babylon wanted God's house rebuilt, but they kept saying, "The time has not come." So they sowed much and brought in little (Haggai 1:2–6). Ezra, by contrast, "had prepared his heart to seek the Law of the LORD, and to do it" (Ezra 7:10). The sharpest application is spiritual. Bridges: "He would gladly be a Christian, if it cost him no trouble." Many of us want to pray more, know Scripture better or break an old habit, yet the wish never becomes a step. Jesus called the servant who buried his talent "wicked and lazy" (Matthew 25:26). Grace does not make us idle. Paul said he labored more abundantly than all the others, "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10). The cure for empty wishing is not guilt but grace that puts our hands to work.
units.application: Pick one desire you have carried for months, such as a habit of prayer, a course to finish or a debt to pay down, and turn it into a first step with a day and a time this week. Students and young workers: show up early and finish what you start. Parents: help a child connect wanting with working, through chores or saving toward something. And do not judge a struggling neighbor as lazy; ask what is keeping them from work.

rel.note: The one who perverts his ways will become known, the exposure that brings the wicked man to shame.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, which is why the righteous man shares His hatred of lying.
Agur prays, 'Remove falsehood and lies far from me,' the prayer of a heart that has learned to hate lying.
A lying tongue and a false witness stand among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Is loathsome" comes from a Hebrew root meaning to smell bad, and figuratively to become offensive. The same root describes the leftover manna that "bred worms and stank" (Exodus 16:20). The picture explains the NKJV's word: falseness becomes as offensive as a bad smell.
• In Hebrew the two verbs of the second line describe the wicked man causing something, not only suffering it. Read that way, he spreads offense and brings shame and disgrace on others, which is how the ESV takes the line. The NKJV and KJV describe what he becomes: loathsome, and brought to shame.
• Ironside: "Truth in the inward parts is the secret of practical righteousness."
• Compare 6:16–19; 12:22; Psalm 119:163; Ephesians 4:25.
units.summary: A righteous heart hates lies; a heart that tolerates them eventually smells of them.
units.principle: Truthfulness is rooted in what the heart hates; whoever makes peace with lying will in time be exposed and shamed by it.
units.insight: Gehazi lied to Naaman for silver, then lied to Elisha's face, and he went out a leper, his hidden falseness made visible to everyone (2 Kings 5:20–27). Yet the verse does not say the righteous never lie. Peter denied his Lord with oaths (Matthew 26:69–74). Later, restored, he urged believers to lay aside "all deceit" (1 Peter 2:1). The difference is not a spotless record but what the heart has come to hate. Bridges asks a searching question: "Is not strict truth often sacrificed to courtesy?" The excuse to avoid a meeting, the padded report, the story improved in the retelling: these are where hatred of lying is tested. Jesus is the truth (John 14:6), and "Nor was deceit found in His mouth" (1 Peter 2:22). To love Him is to come to hate what He hates.
units.application: This week, notice the small lies: the excuse that is not quite true, the exaggerated story, the "I'm fine" that hides something you should say. Correct one, even when it is awkward. Employees: refuse to pad a report or a timesheet. Parents: let your children hear you correct yourself when you have overstated something. If you have been caught in a lie, do not cover it with another; confess it plainly to the person and to God.

rel.note: He who walks with integrity walks securely, the same protection pictured here as a guard.
The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perversity of the unfaithful destroys them.
The righteousness of the blameless directs his way, while the wicked fall by their own wickedness.
Evil pursues sinners while good is repaid to the righteous, the same two outcomes in another picture.
The one who guards his mouth in the earlier saying is himself guarded here, using the same verb.

units.notes:
• "Guards" is the same Hebrew verb used in 13:3, "He who guards his mouth." The repetition links the two sayings: the one who keeps watch over his mouth is himself kept by righteousness.
• "The sinner" is literally "sin" in Hebrew, as the margin of the original 1611 KJV notes. The word can also mean a sin offering, which is how Young's Literal Translation renders it, but the setting of moral ruin supports the NKJV's reading.
• The ESV reverses the subjects of the second line, making sin the force that overthrows the wicked; the sense is much the same.
• Henry heads his two points on this verse "Saints secured from ruin" and "Sinners secured for ruin": a person's own way either keeps him from ruin or holds him fast for it.
• Compare 10:9; 11:3, 5–6; Psalm 25:21.
units.summary: Integrity stands guard over the one who keeps it; wickedness turns on the one who uses it.
units.principle: A life of integrity becomes its own protection, and a life of wickedness becomes its own undoing.
units.insight: Daniel's enemies searched his life and "could find no charge or fault" (Daniel 6:4). His integrity did not keep him out of the lions' den, but God kept him safe inside it. Joseph's integrity first sent him to prison (Genesis 39:20), yet God used that road to raise him. So the guard of righteousness is not a promise of an easy road. It is protection from the deeper ruin a double life brings. Saul shows that ruin. Jealousy, disobedience and half-truths wore him down until he fell on his own sword on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:1–4). No enemy needed to defeat him; his own way already had. For the believer, the "breastplate of righteousness" (Ephesians 6:14) rests finally on Christ's righteousness given to us, worked out in a life that is the same in private and in public. Where is my life still divided?
units.application: Look for one area where your private life does not match your public one, such as what you watch, how you speak about your spouse or how you handle expenses, and bring it into line this week. Leaders: make decisions you would be content to see reported. Young adults starting a career: settle your boundaries on honesty now, before the first pressure comes. If you are suffering for doing right, keep doing it; integrity is guarding you in ways you cannot yet see.

rel.note: The one who scatters yet increases supplies the generosity reading some older writers find in the second line.
The slighted man who has a servant is better off than the one who honors himself but lacks bread, the same gap between show and reality.
The next saying keeps weighing riches and poverty realistically: wealth can ransom a life but also exposes it to threats.
The rich man is wise in his own eyes, but the discerning poor man sees through him, another warning against judging by outward standing.

units.notes:
• Both verbs, "makes himself rich" and "makes himself poor," describe a person doing something to himself: he makes himself out to be rich or poor. That is why the ESV, NASB and AMP render both with "pretends."
• Some older commentators also allow a reading of the second line in terms of generosity: a person becomes poor by giving freely and yet is truly rich, in the spirit of 11:24. The parallel with pretended wealth in the first line favors the reading of pretense that most translations adopt.
• G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "Our own age abounds with men who have made themselves rich, and yet have nothing."
• Compare 12:9; Luke 12:15–21; 2 Corinthians 6:10.
units.summary: The size of a person's display tells you nothing about the size of his treasure.
units.principle: Appearances are an unreliable measure of wealth or worth, so wisdom looks past the display to the reality.
units.insight: The church at Laodicea dressed itself in its own success: "I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing." Christ's verdict was that it was "wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). The opposite error is real too. Some believers think so little of what God has given them that they bury their gifts and live as if they had nothing. Both measure by the wrong scale. Bridges: "riches are more justly estimated by their use than by their possession." The question is not how rich I look, or how humble, but what I have before God and how I use it. The gospel goes beyond this proverb. Christ did not pretend anything: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). In Him the poorest believer holds treasure no display can match.
units.application: Before a purchase meant to impress, ask whom you are trying to convince and what it will cost you later. Couples: agree to live within your means, even when friends do not. Church leaders: do not judge a newcomer's worth, or a giver's faithfulness, by clothes or car. If you have been pleading poverty while sitting on resources others need, open your hand. And ask Christ to show you what you already have in Him.

rel.note: The rich man's wealth is his strong city, the protective use of money this verse admits.
Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, the ransom money cannot pay.
The previous saying warns against judging wealth by appearances; this one weighs its real benefits and costs.
The rich man imagines his wealth as a high wall, a reminder that money's protection has limits.

units.notes:
• The second line repeats the exact Hebrew words that 13:1 uses for the scoffer who "does not listen to rebuke," but in a new sense. In 13:1 the scoffer refuses correction; here the poor man is simply never threatened. The ESV renders the word for rebuke here as "threat."
• The line is brief, and its exact sense is debated. Ironside: "The verse is confessedly ambiguous" (that is, admittedly unclear). The reading that the poor are spared threats fits the parallel with ransom best and is followed by most modern translations.
• Scripture shows a ransom at work. After Jerusalem fell, ten men about to be killed by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah saved their lives by telling him of stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey hidden in a field (Jeremiah 41:8).
• It also shows the poor passed over. When Babylon carried Judah's leading people into exile, the captain of the guard "left some of the poor of the land as vinedressers and farmers" (2 Kings 25:12).
• Compare 10:15; 11:4; 18:11; Ecclesiastes 5:12.
units.summary: Money can buy back a life, but it also makes that life worth threatening.
units.principle: Wealth brings both protection and exposure, so neither riches nor poverty should be envied or despised.
units.insight: Money can ransom a body from a kidnapper, but it cannot ransom a soul. "None of them can by any means redeem his brother, Nor give to God a ransom for him" (Psalm 49:7). Jesus asked, "what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" (Matthew 16:26). The rich fool of His parable had goods for many years but could not buy one more night (Luke 12:20). Bridges: "when all the treasures of earth would have been beggared in the ransom, the riches of heaven were freely poured out." That is, all earth's treasure could not have paid that ransom. We were redeemed "not with corruptible things, like silver or gold," but "with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18–19). That frees us from envying the rich and from fearing for our own possessions. Whatever we have or lack, our true life has already been bought back.
units.application: If you have wealth, thank God for the protection it can buy, and hold it loosely; it also draws envy, lawsuits and false friends. If you have little, notice the freedoms that come with it: fewer things to guard and fewer people wanting something from you. Parents: teach children that money is a tool, not a measure of anyone's worth. And when you lie awake anxious about losing what you own, remember the ransom already paid for you.

rel.note: The hope of the righteous will be gladness, but the expectation of the wicked will perish.
The one who curses his parents has his lamp put out in deep darkness, the same image of a life and household ending.
The second line is repeated word for word: the lamp of the wicked will be put out.
The path of the just shines ever brighter while the way of the wicked is like darkness.

units.notes:
• The 1984 NIV renders "rejoices" as "shines brightly," taking it as a picture of a bright, lively flame. The ESV and NASB keep "rejoices," and the KJV "rejoiceth."
• The second line is repeated word for word in 24:20, where it follows "there will be no prospect for the evil man."
• The righteous have "light," the wicked only a "lamp." Henry draws out the difference: the light of the righteous is like the sun, while the wicked have "a lamp of their own kindling, which will presently go out and is easily put out." ("Presently" means soon.)
• Compare 4:18–19; 20:20; Job 18:5–6; Matthew 25:1–13.
units.summary: The light of the righteous grows glad and bright; the lamp of the wicked flickers toward darkness.
units.principle: A life lived in God's way grows in joy and endures, while a life without Him burns down and goes out.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable, the foolish virgins carried lamps that looked like everyone else's until the night grew long. Then they cried, "our lamps are going out" (Matthew 25:8). An outward show of faith cannot keep burning without the oil of a living relationship with God. Jesus said, "I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life" (John 8:12). The light of the righteous is borrowed light, and that is why it lasts. Believers do pass through dark seasons. Micah said, "When I sit in darkness, The LORD will be a light to me" (Micah 7:8). Bridges: "Sometimes it may be obscured, but only that it may break out more gloriously." So ask: is my faith a light that rejoices, or a lamp I keep lit by my own effort?
units.application: If your faith has become grim duty, spend time this week simply enjoying God: read a psalm of praise aloud, sing, or thank Him for ten specific gifts. If you are walking through a dark season, tell a trusted believer and let them carry light to you. Parents: let your children see joy in your faith, not only rules. And if you have kept up appearances while your heart has gone cold, return to the Lord before the night grows long.

rel.note: When pride comes, then comes shame, but with the humble is wisdom; the humble stand where the well-advised stand here.
The fool is right in his own eyes, but he who heeds counsel is wise.
Plans go awry without counsel and are established by many counselors, the practical fruit of being well-advised.
He who is of a proud heart stirs up strife, tracing quarrels to the same root.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word translated "pride," zadon, describes insolence or presumption, a self-assertion that will not yield. The same word stands behind "When pride comes" in 11:2, and in Deuteronomy 18:22 a false prophet is said to have spoken "presumptuously" using the same word. The ESV and NASB have "insolence," and the AMP adds "presumption" beside pride.
• "Nothing but" renders a Hebrew word meaning "only," which the KJV places at the start of the line: "Only by pride cometh contention."
• Henry: "Foolish pride is the great make-bate." A "make-bate" is an old word for a troublemaker who stirs up quarrels.
• Compare 11:2; 28:25; James 4:1; Philippians 2:3.
units.summary: Pride grows only one crop, strife; the humble ask for advice and harvest wisdom.
units.principle: Pride turns disagreements into quarrels, while humility seeks counsel and so finds both wisdom and peace.
units.insight: When the herdsmen of Abram and Lot quarreled, Abram refused to fight for his rights. "Please let there be no strife between you and me," he said, and he gave the younger man first choice of the land (Genesis 13:8–9). At the Last Supper the disciples argued over which of them was greatest (Luke 22:24), while Jesus took a towel and washed their feet (John 13:4–5). He who had every right to assert Himself "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death" (Philippians 2:8). Pride is hard to see in ourselves. Bridges, borrowing from Bishop Hall, calls it "the inmost coat, which we put on first, and put off last." In my present conflict, what am I presuming: that I am right, that I am owed, or that God is on my side? The quarrel may end the day I ask for counsel instead of agreement.
units.application: In your next disagreement at home, church or work, ask yourself before you speak, "What if I am wrong here?" Then ask one wise person outside the conflict for counsel, and listen. Husbands and wives: let the first sentence of a hard conversation be a question, not a verdict. Leaders: invite pushback before a decision, not after it. If a quarrel has dragged on for months, look for the pride beneath it, starting with your own.

rel.note: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, the same truth about wealth gained wrongly.
Wealth gathered by honest work can last into a second generation, while the sinner's hoard passes to others.
An inheritance gained hastily at the beginning will not be blessed at the end.
The plans of the diligent lead to plenty, but haste leads to poverty, showing the steady way of gathering by labor.
The one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished, while the faithful man abounds with blessings.

units.notes:
• The first line speaks literally of wealth "from vapor." The word is hebel, familiar from Ecclesiastes as "vanity," something empty and without substance. The KJV reads "by vanity" and YLT "from vanity." The NKJV and NASB take that emptiness as dishonesty or fraud, while the ESV's "gained hastily" reflects a slightly different reading of the Hebrew word.
• "By labor" is literally "by the hand," as the margin of the original 1611 KJV notes. The phrase pictures wealth gathered by hand, little by little.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The metaphor of getting money from a vapor suggests what English speakers call 'easy money,'" a phrase he goes on to fill out with tyranny, injustice, extortion, lies and windfalls gained at others' expense.
• Henry: "That which is won ill will never wear well."
• Compare 10:2; 20:21; 21:5–6; 28:20; Ephesians 4:28.
units.summary: Easy money leaks away; money earned a handful at a time tends to stay and grow.
units.principle: The way wealth is gained shapes whether it lasts; honest, patient work builds what shortcuts cannot keep.
units.insight: Judas took thirty pieces of silver to betray Jesus, and within days he threw the money down in the temple; it bought only a field to bury strangers in (Matthew 27:3–7). Zacchaeus had grown rich by cheating, but when Jesus came to his house he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). Grace changed the way he handled money. The Son of God Himself spent most of His earthly life as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). Paul turns the thief toward the same road: "let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give him who has need" (Ephesians 4:28). So the verse searches more than criminals. Where am I hoping for money without work, or cutting corners to get it faster?
units.application: If you are tempted by a get-rich-quick scheme, a gambling app or a shortcut on your taxes, walk away this week. Young workers: set up a small, steady savings habit from every paycheck, even if the amount feels too small to matter. Business owners: price fairly and pay what you owe on time. If you have gained something dishonestly, make it right, as Zacchaeus did. And whoever you are, give from what you earn.

rel.note: The hope of the righteous will be gladness, the joy that comes when long-held hope is fulfilled.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, another of the four uses of the image.
A desire accomplished is sweet to the soul, the second saying about fulfilled longing that frames this part of the chapter.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life, applying the same picture of renewal to healing speech.
Wisdom is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, the fullest use of the image in Proverbs.

units.notes:
• "Deferred" translates a Hebrew word meaning drawn out or prolonged, a hope stretched over a long time. YLT renders it "prolonged."
• The word "desire" returns in 13:19, "A desire accomplished is sweet to the soul," so the two sayings about fulfilled longing frame verses 12–19.
• "Tree of life" appears four times in the NKJV of Proverbs: 3:18; 11:30; 13:12; and 15:4. Its fullest treatment is at 3:18, where Wisdom "is a tree of life to those who take hold of her."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "How many see we lie languishing at hope's hospital, as he at the pool of Bethesda!" In plain English: how many people we see lying ill in hope's hospital, like the man lying at the pool of Bethesda, ill for thirty-eight years (John 5:2–9).
• Compare Psalm 13:1–2; 119:82; Revelation 22:1–2.
units.summary: Long waiting can make the heart sick, and the long-awaited answer can bring it back to life.
units.principle: Prolonged waiting wounds the heart and fulfilled longing renews it, and God gives words for both the ache and the joy.
units.insight: Hannah knew this sickness. Year after year "she wept and did not eat" (1 Samuel 1:7), and God did not rebuke her tears; He heard her prayer and gave her Samuel. Sarah waited until laughter seemed impossible, then laughed for joy at Isaac's birth (Genesis 21:6). Old Simeon waited his whole life for "the Consolation of Israel," and at last he held the Child in his arms (Luke 2:25–30). If your heart is sick from waiting, God is not disappointed in you. The psalmists prayed, "How long, O LORD?" (Psalm 13:1), and He kept their prayers in Scripture for us. Not every longing is met in this life. Yet in Christ the deepest desire is secured: the tree of life, whose leaves are "for the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:2). That hope will not be deferred forever.
units.application: If you are waiting on a wayward child, a diagnosis, a spouse or a job, tell God plainly how it feels; lament is prayer, not failure. Friends and pastors: when someone is heartsick from waiting, sit with them before you offer advice, and never treat their sorrow as weak faith. When a long prayer is answered, mark it: tell the story, write it down, celebrate it together as a church. And read Revelation 22 when the waiting feels endless.

rel.note: The next saying shows why the word should be feared: the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life.
He who heeds the word wisely will find good, the reward of fearing the commandment.
He who keeps the commandment keeps his soul, while the careless will die.
Those who hated knowledge and despised Wisdom's reproof eat the fruit of their own way, the destruction named here.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "will be destroyed" can also mean to be held in pledge, like property held as security for a debt; the Brown-Driver-Briggs lexicon lists this verse under both meanings. The NASB follows the pledge sense with "in debt": the one who despises the word becomes bound to pay the penalty of what he ignored.
• "Will be rewarded" comes from the same Hebrew root as shalom, "peace," which is why the margin of the original 1611 KJV offers "in peace" as an alternative. The setting of repayment favors the NKJV's rendering.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, on the pair "word" and "commandment": "The use of these two terms has religious significance: they most often refer to Scripture."
• Compare 16:20; 19:16; Isaiah 66:2; Hebrews 12:25.
units.summary: How you treat God's word now decides where you will stand at the end.
units.principle: A person's response to God's word, whether contempt or reverence, sets the course of his life and its end.
units.insight: King Jehoiakim listened to Jeremiah's scroll being read, cut it piece by piece with a scribe's knife and threw it into the fire (Jeremiah 36:23). His contempt did not destroy the word; it destroyed him. His father Josiah heard the Book of the Law and tore his clothes, and God said, "your heart was tender" (2 Kings 22:19). Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. Both heard His words; only one did them, and only his house stood (Matthew 7:24–27). Most of us will never burn a Bible. We despise the word more quietly, by hearing it without heeding it. Bridges marks the right kind of fear: "The slave fears the penalty; the child the commandment." God's children tremble at His word because they love the One who speaks it (Isaiah 66:2).
units.application: Choose one command of Scripture you have been treating as optional, such as forgiving someone, keeping your word or giving generously, and obey it this week. When you hear a sermon, write down one thing to do and do it before the next Sunday. Parents: let your children see you open the Bible and change your plans because of it. Small-group leaders: end each study by asking, "What will we do with this?" and not only "What did we learn?"

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, the same Hebrew phrase applied to good speech.
The previous saying warns against despising the word; this one shows the life that word gives.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life to turn one from the snares of death, nearly the same words said of reverence for God.
Understanding is a wellspring of life to him who has it, another use of the same phrase.
The parents' commandment and teaching are a lamp and a light that keep the son from danger, the protective work of instruction.

units.notes:
• The word behind "law" is torah, which means instruction or teaching. It is the same word used for the father's and mother's teaching in 1:8 and 3:1, which is why the ESV and NASB translate it "teaching" here. It need not refer to the Law of Moses in this saying, though the wise teach in harmony with it.
• The phrase "fountain of life" appears four times in Proverbs: in 10:11, where the NKJV renders it "a well of life"; here; in 14:27; and in 16:22, where it becomes "a wellspring of life."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "There is only one fountain of life, but there are many snares of death (cf. 2 Tim. 2:24-26)."
• Compare Psalm 36:9; Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:14.
units.summary: Wise teaching is a spring that keeps flowing and a hand that pulls you back from hidden traps.
units.principle: Wise, God-shaped teaching keeps giving life to those who drink from it and turns them from dangers they cannot yet see.
units.insight: Israel's tragedy was leaving the spring for a cistern. God said, "they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, And hewn themselves cisterns—broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Every generation repeats that choice when it trades sound teaching for whatever voices are loudest. Paul warned Timothy of the snare that comes with the desire to be rich, and his counsel was the fountain at work: "But you, O man of God, flee these things" (1 Timothy 6:9–11). At a Samaritan well Jesus offered water that would become "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). All wise teaching finally flows from Him. So ask yourself: what teaching am I drinking from most days, and is it turning me away from snares or walking me toward them?
units.application: Name the main voices shaping you right now: podcasts, feeds, friends, books. Replace one hour of noise this week with Scripture or sound teaching. Young people: find an older believer and ask what snares they wish someone had warned them about. Pastors and teachers: aim your teaching at the real traps your people face. Parents: do not only warn children about danger; give them a steady spring of God's word at home.

rel.note: The same treacherous people appear earlier with an appetite for violence; here their road turns hard.
Thorns and snares lie in the way of the perverse, another picture of the hard road.
The one who keeps mercy and truth finds favor and high esteem in the sight of God and man.
The way of the wicked is like darkness, and they do not know what makes them stumble.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "unfaithful," which describes people who act treacherously, is the same word used in 13:2. The repetition links the two descriptions of the treacherous.
• The adjective behind "hard" usually means ever-flowing or lasting, like a stream that never dries up, which makes the line difficult to render. The Brown-Driver-Briggs lexicon calls its meaning here very uncertain and mentions "firm" or "rugged" as possibilities. The NKJV, NASB and KJV read "hard," the ESV "their ruin," and the NLT speaks of destruction.
• Bridges: "They dream of a flowery path; but they make to themselves a hard way."
• Compare 3:3–4; 1 Samuel 2:26; Luke 2:52.
units.summary: Good sense wins goodwill, but treachery wears out the road under its own feet.
units.principle: Wisdom tends to win the goodwill of others, while treachery makes life harder for the one who practices it.
units.insight: Jacob's early life shows how hard the treacherous road is. He deceived his brother and his father, then spent twenty years with an uncle who deceived him in return (Genesis 27; 29:25; 31:41). Late in life he said, "few and evil have been the days of the years of my life" (Genesis 47:9). Joseph walked the other road. In Potiphar's house, in prison and before Pharaoh, his good sense won favor (Genesis 39:4, 21; 41:38–40). Jesus Himself "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men" (Luke 2:52). To all who are worn out by sin's hard road He says, "Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). Is my road getting harder because I keep choosing my own way?
units.application: At work, build favor the slow way: keep your word, do careful work and treat people fairly instead of maneuvering for advantage. Students: be the classmate others trust with a group project. If you have been cutting corners or playing people against each other, notice how tired it has made you, and come clean with the person you have wronged. Parents and mentors: praise good judgment in young people, not only results.

rel.note: A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims foolishness.
The prudent considers his steps, which is what acting with knowledge looks like.
The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, but the folly of fools is deceit.
The mouth of fools pours forth foolishness, the same display of folly.
The fool delights not in understanding but in expressing his own heart, the reason he lays his folly open.

units.notes:
• The margin of the original 1611 KJV gives "spreadeth" as the literal sense of the Hebrew behind "layeth open," and YLT reads "spreadeth out." The picture is of folly spread out on display; the ESV renders it "flaunts."
• "Every prudent man" makes the saying a rule of character: prudence always shows itself in the way a person acts, just as folly always shows itself in the fool.
• Henry: "It is wisdom to be cautious." He adds that the prudent man will not "launch out into business which he has not acquainted himself with."
• Compare 12:23; 14:8, 15; 15:2; 18:2; Ecclesiastes 10:3.
units.summary: Prudence thinks before it moves; folly sets out its foolishness like goods on a market table.
units.principle: Wise people let knowledge govern their actions, while foolish people reveal their folly by acting and speaking without it.
units.insight: Abigail's husband Nabal answered David's messengers with insults, and his own wife said of him, "Nabal is his name, and folly is with him!" (1 Samuel 25:25). Abigail heard the facts, weighed the danger and acted quickly, and her prudence saved her household (1 Samuel 25:18–35). Isaiah foretold of the Messiah, "Behold, My Servant shall deal prudently" (Isaiah 52:13). Jesus showed it when His enemies tried to trap Him over paying taxes to Caesar. He asked for a coin, looked at it and gave an answer that left them marveling (Matthew 22:15–22). Folly rarely sees itself. We notice the folly others display long before we see our own. Where do I speak or act before I know enough?
units.application: Before a major decision this week, whether a purchase, a job change or a reply to a hard email, write down the facts you know and the facts you still need, and ask someone who knows more. Social media users: do not post opinions on matters you have not studied. Leaders: gather the facts before you respond to a complaint. Parents: teach teenagers to ask, "Where does this lead?" before saying yes to a plan.

rel.note: The lazy man is like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes to those who send him.
The tongue of the wise promotes health, using the same word for the healing a faithful ambassador brings.
A faithful messenger is like the cold of snow in time of harvest, refreshing the one who sent him.
Good news from a far country is like cold water to a weary soul, the healing a faithful messenger carries.
Sending a message by a fool is like cutting off one's own feet, the damage a wicked messenger does.

units.notes:
• The phrase behind "a faithful ambassador" reads literally "an envoy of faithfulness," that is, a messenger whose defining mark is trustworthiness.
• The word behind "health," marpe, means healing or cure; the ESV and NASB have "healing." It is the same word used in 12:18, "the tongue of the wise promotes health."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, explains how much was entrusted to envoys: "They were authorized to speak in the 'I' style of the client." In other words, the envoy spoke his master's words as if the master himself were speaking.
• Compare 10:26; 25:13; 26:6; 2 Corinthians 5:20.
units.summary: The same message can wound or heal, depending on who carries it.
units.principle: Those entrusted with another's message carry a weighty responsibility; faithfulness brings healing, and unfaithfulness brings trouble.
units.insight: Ten of the twelve spies sent into Canaan came back with a distorted report, and it spread fear through the whole camp. Those men died by the plague, and a generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 13:32; 14:36–37). Abraham's servant shows the faithful envoy. Sent to find a wife for Isaac, he refused to eat until he had told his errand (Genesis 24:33). Jesus is "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5). He said, "I have not spoken on My own authority; but the Father who sent Me gave Me a command, what I should say" (John 12:49). Now He sends us: "we are ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:20). Every believer carries a message that heals. Am I adding to it, softening it, or delivering it faithfully?
units.application: When you pass on a message for a boss, a parent or a friend, deliver it accurately, without adding your own spin or leaving out the hard part. Employees: report bad news promptly and plainly. Parents carrying news between a child and an ex-spouse: be a healer, not a carrier of blame. Pastors and teachers: preach what the text says, not what will please. And look for one person this week who needs to hear the good news of Christ from you.

rel.note: Whoever loves instruction loves knowledge, but the one who hates correction is stupid.
The chapter opens with the same contrast between the son who heeds instruction and the scoffer who will not hear rebuke.
Some poverty comes from injustice, so this saying must never be used to blame every poor person.
He who disdains instruction despises his own soul, using the same verb and object.
A wise rebuker to an obedient ear is like an ornament of gold, the honor that comes from receiving correction.
The scoffer answers correction with hatred while the wise man loves the one who rebukes him and grows wiser, the same two responses that lead here to shame or honor.

units.notes:
• The word behind "correction" here is musar, the same word translated "instruction" in 13:1 and "disciplines" in 13:24, a broad word for training and discipline. The ESV renders it "instruction" here.
• The verb behind "disdains" means to let go or neglect. Wisdom uses the same verb of those who refused her call: "Because you disdained all my counsel" (1:25). It appears with the same object in 15:32, "He who disdains instruction despises his own soul."
• Bridges: "Man's pride deems it a degradation to receive reproof. God counts it 'brutish to hate it.'" (He is quoting 12:1, where the NKJV calls the one who hates correction "stupid.")
• Compare 12:1; 15:5, 31; 25:12; Hebrews 12:11.
units.summary: Correction costs a moment of pride; refusing it can cost a great deal more.
units.principle: Refusing correction tends to bring loss and disgrace, while receiving it with humility leads to honor.
units.insight: After Jerusalem fell, Johanan and the army captains begged Jeremiah to ask God what they should do and promised to obey. When the answer came, "Do not go to Egypt!" they refused it and went anyway, and the disaster they feared followed them there (Jeremiah 42:1–22; 43:1–7). Apollos was already an eloquent preacher when Priscilla and Aquila took him aside and "explained to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26). He received it, and God used him greatly in Achaia (Acts 18:27–28). The prodigal son ignored his father's ways until poverty and shame brought him "to himself" (Luke 15:17), and even then the father ran to meet him. The way back is always open. What correction am I letting slip past right now? "Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you in due time" (1 Peter 5:6).
units.application: Think of the last correction you received, from a spouse, a supervisor, a doctor or a friend, and ask whether you acted on it or let it go. Do one thing about it this week. Employees: after a review, thank the reviewer and set one goal from it. Students: rework the assignment the teacher marked. Parents: let your children see you accept correction when they are right. And when you correct others, do it privately and kindly so it can be heard.

rel.note: The desire of the righteous will be granted, showing whose longings tend to be fulfilled.
When the desire comes it is a tree of life, the same sweetness of fulfilled longing.
The lazy man's desire comes to nothing, the empty craving set against the sweetness of desire fulfilled.
The highway of the upright is to depart from evil, the very turning fools detest.
Another saying where 'abomination' describes human revulsion rather than the LORD's.
The father's call to fear the LORD and depart from evil is the path the fool refuses.

units.notes:
• The NLT makes the implied link explicit: "fools refuse to turn from evil to attain them."
• Proverbs usually speaks of what is an abomination to the LORD. Here, as in 29:27, the word describes human revulsion, and the irony is that fools detest the very turning that would bring them good.
• The word "desire" links this saying with 13:12, "when the desire comes, it is a tree of life." The two sayings frame verses 12–19.
• G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "Men will not pay the price of departing from evil, and so fail of the sweetness of fulfilled desire." ("Fail of" means fall short of.)
• Compare 3:7; 16:17; Psalm 37:4; John 3:19–20.
units.summary: Fools want the sweetness of answered desire but will not leave the road that keeps it from them.
units.principle: The good that people long for is often kept from them by the evil they refuse to leave.
units.insight: Herod Antipas liked listening to John the Baptist. He knew John was "a just and holy man," and he "heard him gladly" (Mark 6:20). But he would not give up Herodias, and in the end he had John beheaded rather than turn from his sin (Mark 6:17–28). That is this verse in one life: a man drawn toward good who detested leaving evil. Jesus said, "men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil" (John 3:19). The gospel does more than call us to turn. It changes what we love. Bridges marvels at the "mighty change" that can make it "an abomination to commit evil, as it now is to depart from it." Then Psalm 37:4 opens before us: "Delight yourself also in the LORD, And He shall give you the desires of your heart." What sin am I holding while I pray for good things?
units.application: Write down a good desire you are praying about, such as a healed marriage, freedom from debt or a closer walk with God. Then ask what you are unwilling to give up that stands in its way: a habit, a grudge, a secret. Take one step away from it this week. Recovery groups and accountability partners know this verse well; find one. Parents: when a teenager wants more freedom, show them how leaving foolish choices is the road to it.

rel.note: The father's first warning is not to walk in the way with sinners who entice.
Making friends with an angry man teaches his ways and sets a snare for the soul, the same influence in one case.
As iron sharpens iron, a man sharpens his friend, the good side of companionship.
A companion of gluttons shames his father, another warning about the company a son keeps.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, the word for "companion" (roʿeh) and the verb behind "will be destroyed" (yeroaʿ) sound alike, so the line plays on their sound: the one who keeps company with fools comes to harm. Kidner, quoted by Guzik, cites Knox's translation of the Latin Vulgate, which imitates the sound-play with an English rhyme: "Fool he ends that fool befriends."
• The margin of the original 1611 KJV gives the literal sense of the verb behind "will be destroyed" as "broken," and the ESV and NASB speak of suffering "harm."
• "Walks with" pictures sharing a road day by day, the language of the father's first warning: "My son, do not walk in the way with them" (1:15).
• Compare 1:10–19; 22:24–25; Psalm 1:1; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10; 15:33.
units.summary: Show me your companions, and I will show you who you are becoming.
units.principle: People tend to become like the companions they choose, so choosing companions is choosing a direction.
units.insight: King Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders and "consulted the young men who had grown up with him" (1 Kings 12:8). Their counsel split his kingdom. Joash did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest, but after Jehoiada died he listened to the leaders of Judah and turned to idols (2 Chronicles 24:2, 17–18). Companions shape us more than we admit. Yet Jesus was called "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19). He sat with them to lead them home, not to follow them. And when the council saw the boldness of Peter and John, ordinary men, "they realized that they had been with Jesus" (Acts 4:13). The best companionship of all is His. Who is shaping my road right now, and am I leading or being led?
units.application: List the five people you spend the most time with, including online voices, and ask where each one is taking you. Young people: choose at least one friend who is a step ahead of you in following Christ, and spend regular time with them. Parents: know your children's friends by name and open your home to them. Keep loving unbelieving friends and coworkers, but make sure you are the one setting the direction.

rel.note: What the wicked fear comes upon them, and the desire of the righteous is granted.
Whoever earnestly seeks good finds favor, but trouble comes to the one who seeks evil, the same two outcomes for two ways of life.
The righteous are recompensed on the earth, and much more the wicked and the sinner.
The next saying gives one example of good repaid: an inheritance that reaches the grandchildren.
Righteousness guards the blameless while wickedness overthrows the sinner, the same outcomes in another picture.

units.notes:
• The ESV renders "evil" in the first line as "disaster," and the NASB renders the "good" of the second line as "prosperity." The Hebrew word for good is broader than material wealth.
• The picture of pursuit recalls the avenger of blood in Israel's law, who hunted down a manslayer (Numbers 35:19; Deuteronomy 19:6). A psalm uses the same idea: "Let evil hunt the violent man to overthrow him" (Psalm 140:11).
• Bridges, on judgment that comes late but still comes: "The delay even of centuries does not weaken the certainty."
• Compare 11:31; Psalm 23:6, where "goodness and mercy" follow the one who belongs to the LORD; Galatians 6:7–9.
units.summary: Sin sends trouble after the sinner like a pursuer, but good is waiting to repay the righteous.
units.principle: Under God's rule, wrongdoing sets trouble on the sinner's trail, and righteousness is not forgotten but repaid.
units.insight: Joseph's brothers sold him and covered it with a lie. More than twenty years later, in a strange land, their own words caught up with them: "We are truly guilty concerning our brother" (Genesis 42:21). Their sin had followed them all that time. Boaz blessed Ruth for her kindness to Naomi, "The LORD repay your work" (Ruth 2:12), and God did, in ways she could not have imagined. The gospel adds what no proverb could. The evil that pursues sinners was allowed to overtake Another: "the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Those who run to Christ find that what follows them now is "goodness and mercy" (Psalm 23:6). Is there something I am still running from that I could bring to the cross instead?
units.application: If an old wrong keeps following you, stop running: confess it to God, and where possible make it right with the person you hurt. If you are suffering though you have done right, do not conclude that God has forgotten you; keep sowing good (Galatians 6:9). Parents: help children see that consequences are not bad luck but a pattern God built into His world. Leaders: do not cover up a problem; it will follow you.

rel.note: Wealth gathered by honest labor increases, which is how a good man has something to pass on.
The previous saying states the general rule that good is repaid to the righteous; this one gives an example.
The righteous man walks in his integrity, and his children are blessed after him.
A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, the most valuable part of any inheritance.
Wealth gained by extortion is gathered for one who will pity the poor, the same reversal of the sinner's hoard.

units.notes:
• "Children's children" is literally "sons of sons," which YLT reflects with "sons' sons." The good man's influence reaches two generations past his own.
• Job makes a similar observation about the wicked man who heaps up silver: "the just will wear it, And the innocent will divide the silver" (Job 27:17).
• Bridges, on the first line's picture of an inheritance: "It cannot however be meant as an universal statement. Many good men have no inheritance to leave."
• Ironside: the good man "bequeaths to his descendants an honored name and a holy example—an inheritance of incalculable value."
• Compare 20:7; 28:8; Ecclesiastes 2:26; Psalm 103:17.
units.summary: A good life leaves something for the grandchildren; a sinner's hoard ends up in other hands.
units.principle: Faithfulness builds a legacy that can outlive the faithful, while under God's rule the sinner's hoard does not stay with the one who gathered it.
units.insight: Paul traced Timothy's faith back two generations: it "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). Lois may have left little money, but she left her grandson faith. Haman spent his life gathering power and wealth, and on the day he fell the king gave Haman's house to Esther, who set Mordecai over it (Esther 8:1–2). Yet the righteous are not meant to wait for windfalls. Our best inheritance is not on earth at all. In Christ we have "an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and that does not fade away, reserved in heaven" (1 Peter 1:4). That frees us to give our grandchildren what lasts: prayer, example, a good name and the gospel. What will my grandchildren receive from the way I am living today?
units.application: Parents and grandparents: make a will, and avoid leaving debt as your legacy where you can. Even more, tell your grandchildren the stories of God's faithfulness in your family, and pray for them by name. Young couples: start small, steady habits of saving and giving now that can outlast you. If you envy someone who got rich by cutting corners, remember that such wealth does not stay with them, and keep your eyes on what lasts.

rel.note: Refusing correction leads to poverty, but this verse shows that not every poor person has refused correction.
The chapter's closing contrast between the satisfied righteous and the hungry wicked is a general pattern, which this verse keeps from being turned into blame of the poor.
The earlier saying links diligence with plenty; this one keeps it from being read as if all poverty came from laziness.
He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker, naming the wrong behind the waste in this verse.
Do not rob the poor or crush the afflicted, for the LORD will plead their cause.
A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food, another picture of a harvest swept away.

units.notes:
• The word behind "fallow ground," nir, refers to farmland, but dictionaries describe it differently. The Brown-Driver-Briggs lexicon defines it as tillable ground not yet tilled, while Strong's dictionary connects it with plowing and freshly plowed land. In the LORD's call through Jeremiah, "Break up your fallow ground" (Jeremiah 4:3), the ground has not yet been broken. Either way, the verse describes land able to produce a real harvest.
• The Hebrew of the second line is compressed and difficult. The KJV speaks of what "is destroyed for want of judgment," while the ESV and NASB say the harvest is swept away by injustice. The NKJV's "waste" conveys the same loss.
• Some older commentators read the line as a lesson in careful management of a small plot. The words "lack of justice" point instead to wrongs done to the poor.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "According to this proverb, the lack of food for the hard-working poor is due to tyranny, not the environment."
• Compare 14:31; 22:22–23; Isaiah 5:8; James 5:4.
units.summary: Some poverty grows from idle hands, but some is stolen from hardworking ones by injustice.
units.principle: Poverty is not always the fault of the poor; injustice can strip hardworking people of what their labor produced.
units.insight: Naboth had a good vineyard, his family's inheritance. He lost it, and his life, not through laziness but through a rigged trial arranged by Queen Jezebel for King Ahab (1 Kings 21:1–16). In Nehemiah's day, families who worked their fields had to mortgage them to wealthy fellow Jews, and Nehemiah rebuked the nobles: "What you are doing is not good" (Nehemiah 5:9). Jesus warned against those "who devour widows' houses" (Mark 12:40), and He announced that He had come "To preach the gospel to the poor" (Luke 4:18). This verse searches our assumptions. When we see someone in need, is our first thought, "What did they do wrong?" Scripture asks us to consider first what may have been done to them, and whether we can help.
units.application: Before you judge a family in need, learn their story. Employers and managers: pay fair wages on time, and check whether your policies quietly cost the poorest workers most. Voters, jurors and church boards: weigh how decisions affect people who have no lawyer or lobbyist. Churches: support ministries that help the poor keep what they earn, such as legal aid, debt counseling and fair lending. If you have been wronged this way, bring it to God; He sees what was taken.

rel.note: The chapter opens with the son who heeds his father's instruction, the fruit of the training described here.
Chasten your son while there is hope, the same urgency as disciplining promptly.
Foolishness is bound up in a child's heart, and the rod of correction drives it far away.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.
The LORD corrects the one He loves, as a father the son in whom he delights, the pattern for a parent's discipline.

units.notes:
• "Promptly" translates a Hebrew verb formed from the word for dawn. It carries the sense of seeking early or earnestly, like someone who rises at dawn to attend to a task. The KJV has "betimes" (early), the ESV "diligent," and the NASB "diligently." The same verb describes seeking Wisdom: "those who seek me diligently will find me" (8:17).
• "Disciplines" is musar again, the chapter's word for a father's training (13:1, 18). The chapter begins and ends with a father forming his son.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Ephesians 6:4 warns against undue severity; but the obligation remains."
• The discipline this verse calls for is far broader than punishment. The verse speaks of the rod in its historical setting and of a parent's duty to train; it does not prescribe a technique, settle questions of child development or guarantee a child's response. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends nonphysical forms of discipline.
• Compare 3:11–12; 19:18; 22:15; 29:15, 17; Colossians 3:21; Hebrews 12:5–11.
units.summary: Love does not leave a child to himself; it takes the trouble to train him early and patiently.
units.principle: Loving parents take the trouble to train and correct their children, patiently and early, as God trains His own, and never in a way that crushes them.
units.insight: Adonijah grew up uncorrected: "his father had not rebuked him at any time by saying, 'Why have you done so?'" (1 Kings 1:6). The unchecked son grew into a man who grabbed for King David's throne. God is the Father who never neglects His children: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19). His correction is never rejection. It is love at work, training us "that we may be partakers of His holiness" (Hebrews 12:10). Bridges names the hidden root of neglect: "The indulgence of our children has its root in self-indulgence." It is easier to look away than to do the patient work. Yet harshness is no better, for anger and humiliation misrepresent the Father. Which way do I lean: avoidance, or correction driven by frustration instead of love?
units.application: Parents: teach before you correct. Set clear expectations, explain the reasons, and deal with deliberate wrongdoing early, while it is small, and never in anger. Tell honest mistakes, tiredness and immaturity apart from defiance. After correcting, reassure your child of your love and restore the relationship. If you have been harsh, ask your child's forgiveness. Grandparents and church leaders: support parents who are trying to train patiently, and come alongside single parents carrying this work alone.

rel.note: The LORD will not let the righteous soul famish but casts away the desire of the wicked, the same contrast as His own doing.
The chapter opens with a man eating well by the fruit of his mouth and closes with the righteous eating to satisfaction.
Injustice can bring want even to the hardworking poor, so this pattern must not be turned into blame.
The diligent soul is made rich, an earlier picture of the satisfied soul this verse completes.
Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with trouble, the contentment of the righteous at his table.

units.notes:
• The chapter begins and ends with eating. In 13:2 a man "shall eat well by the fruit of his mouth," and here the righteous "eats to the satisfying of his soul," while the stomach of the wicked is left wanting.
• "Soul" translates nephesh, the inner self with its appetites, the word that runs through the chapter's sayings on desire (13:2, 4, 19).
• Henry: "Nature is content with a little and grace with less; enough is as good as a feast."
• Compare 10:3; 15:16; Psalm 37:16–19; Philippians 4:11–13; John 6:35.
units.summary: The righteous sit down to enough and are satisfied; the wicked can have plenty and still go hungry.
units.principle: Contentment is the portion of those who walk with God, while those who live without Him find that no amount satisfies.
units.insight: Daniel and his friends asked for vegetables and water instead of the king's rich food, and after ten days they looked healthier than all the rest (Daniel 1:12–15). The rich man in Jesus' parable "fared sumptuously every day" (Luke 16:19), yet in the end he begged for a drop of water. Satisfaction is not measured by the size of the meal. Paul had "learned in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). Jesus offers the deepest satisfaction of all: "I am the bread of life. He who comes to Me shall never hunger" (John 6:35). Bridges: "Christ is a substitute for everything; nothing for Him." He can fill the place of anything we lack, and nothing can fill His place. What am I feeding on, hoping it will finally satisfy?
units.application: At your next family meal, thank God aloud for specific things on the table, and let children name what they are grateful for. If you always want more, whether food, gadgets or upgrades, try a week of "enough," buying nothing beyond what you need. Those living on little: you are not forgotten, and contentment is real wealth. Those with plenty: share a meal with someone who has less. And feed daily on Christ, the bread of life.

rel.note: The chapter returns to houses, showing that the dwelling built on wickedness falls while the upright flourish.
A house is built and established through wisdom and understanding, the same truth stated without the picture of a woman.
The woman of valor watches over the ways of her household, the wise builder of this verse drawn in full.
Wisdom herself builds a house, the grand pattern the wise woman follows in a single home.
Folly also sits at the door of her house, but her guests end in the depths of hell, the full picture of the house folly tears down.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew opens with a plural, literally "the wise ones of women." That is why the KJV reads "Every wise woman" and the ESV "The wisest of women." The NKJV's singular gives the same sense: this is the kind of woman who builds her house.
• The second line in Hebrew begins with the ordinary word for folly, not a word for a foolish woman. So the ESV reads that folly "with her own hands tears it down." That reading strengthens the echo of chapter 9, where Wisdom and Folly each have a house (9:1, 14).
• Bridges on the foolish woman's ruin: "it is the doing, or rather the undoing, of her own hands."
• Two mothers show the contrast. Moses' mother hid him, made him an ark of bulrushes and nursed him (Exodus 2:1–10). Ahaziah's mother "advised him to do wickedly" (2 Chronicles 22:3), and she later set out to destroy the royal family (2 Kings 11:1).
• Compare 24:3–4 ("Through wisdom a house is built"); 31:10–31; Titus 2:3–5.
units.summary: No enemy has to break in when our own hands are pulling the house down.
units.principle: What wisdom builds tends to last, and what is torn down is most often torn down from the inside; every household bears the mark of the hands that shape it.
units.insight: Abigail was married to a man whose name meant fool, and his folly nearly brought David's sword on their whole household. She acted quickly and humbly, and her wisdom saved her house (1 Samuel 25:18–35). The verse is not first a measuring stick for someone else's home. It asks what my own hands are doing: the sharp word at dinner, the hidden spending, the prayerlessness that slowly loosens the walls. Yet no one builds alone. Wisdom built her house (9:1), and in the light of the New Testament Christ is the builder of His own house, "whose house we are" (Hebrews 3:3–6). Bring Him the cracks your own hands have made. He rebuilds what we have pulled down.
units.application: Take stock of one "house" you are responsible for this week: a marriage, children, a budget, a ministry. Ask what your hands added to it and what they pulled down. Parents: replace one habit that wears on the home, such as a phone at the table or a harsh tone, with one that builds. Husbands and wives: speak one building word to each other every day. If your home is hurting because of someone else's choices, refuse false guilt and keep building what is yours to build.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, while the one who perverts his ways will be exposed.
The wise man fears and departs from evil, showing again that right fear turns the feet.
The poor man who walks in integrity is set against the rich man perverse in his ways, the same two walks.
The fear of the LORD shows itself in departing from evil, the upright walk this verse describes.
The fear of the LORD hates the evil way and the perverse mouth, so the perverse walk cannot sit with true reverence.

units.notes:
• "Perverse" describes ways that bend away from what is straight; the ESV and NASB have "devious." The picture is a crooked road set beside the straight walk of the first line.
• Despising God does not require open blasphemy; disregarding His word in daily life is enough. When David took Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's death, Nathan asked him, "Why have you despised the commandment of the LORD?" (2 Samuel 12:9).
• Henry: "In this, more than in any thing, sin appears exceedingly sinful, that it despises God, whom angels adore."
• Ironside: "The testimony of the lips, if contradicted by the behavior, is of little worth."
• Compare 3:7; 8:13; 10:9; 28:6; Titus 1:16 ("They profess to know God, but in works they deny Him"); 1 John 2:6.
units.summary: Your feet tell the truth about what your lips say you believe about God.
units.principle: What we truly think of God shows less in what we say about Him than in how we walk when no one is watching.
units.insight: King Saul kept the forms of worship, yet he spared what God had told him to destroy. Samuel answered him, "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul never said aloud that God did not matter; his ways said it for him. That is the searching edge of this verse. We can sing with feeling on Sunday and cut corners on Monday, and the corners speak louder than the songs. A crooked habit we excuse as small is, at its root, a quiet verdict that God's word can be ignored. Yet the verse also holds out hope. Isaiah said of the coming King, "His delight is in the fear of the LORD" (Isaiah 11:3). Jesus walked that way perfectly and "committed no sin" (1 Peter 2:22). Those joined to Him receive a new heart, and reverence begins to reach the feet.
units.application: Pick one ordinary area where your walk and your words about God may not match: how you fill out a timesheet, how you speak about your spouse, what you watch when you are alone. Bring it into line this week. Parents: let children see your faith in how you handle money and mistakes, not only at church. Leaders: your team learns what you believe about God from how you treat people under pressure, so treat them as before Him.

rel.note: A rod is for the back of the one without understanding; here the fool's own proud mouth supplies that rod.
The mouth of the upright delivers them, as the lips of the wise preserve them here.
Guarding the mouth preserves life, the protection the lips of the wise give them.
Pride goes before destruction, the end toward which the fool's proud words are carrying him.
A fool's mouth is his destruction and his lips the snare of his soul, the same self-inflicted ruin.

units.notes:
• The word translated "rod" is not the word for the discipline rod of 13:24. It is a rarer word for a shoot or branch, so the fool's proud words are pictured as a stick growing out of his own mouth. The same word appears in Isaiah 11:1, where "a Rod" comes forth from the stem of Jesse.
• Several modern translations, following a slightly different understanding of the Hebrew, read the first line as a rod for the fool's "back" (ESV, NASB). The NKJV, with the KJV, reads "a rod of pride."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The fool's pride finds a rod in his mouth that lashes himself—he is his own worst enemy—and others."
• Bridges: "The rod in the mouth is often sharper than the rod in the hand."
• Compare 10:13; 12:6; 18:7 ("A fool's mouth is his destruction"); Psalm 64:8.
units.summary: The proud fool carries in his own mouth the stick that will beat him.
units.principle: Proud words are a weapon that turns on the one who wields them, while humble, guarded speech protects the speaker.
units.insight: Goliath walked into the valley cursing David by his gods and promising to give his flesh to the birds (1 Samuel 17:43–44). His proud mouth set the terms of his own fall. Nebuchadnezzar was still boasting, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built?" when the word of judgment fell from heaven (Daniel 4:30–31).
