Pride rarely stays in the heart; it climbs into the mouth. Before we look for the rod in someone else's mouth, we can listen to our own: the sarcasm, the boasting, the need to have the last word. Each of these is a stick we are handing to our own correction. Jesus had every right to speak proudly, yet "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). His Spirit can turn a proud tongue into one that protects and heals.
units.application: Before you post, reply or speak in a tense meeting this week, ask whether pride is putting a stick in your hand. Leaders: resist the cutting remark that proves you are right; it tends to come back on you. Young people: notice how often boasting or mocking gets a laugh and then gets you in trouble. When someone provokes you, let your lips protect you by answering briefly and calmly, or by saying nothing at all.

rel.note: The one who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, the harvest that the ox makes possible.
In all labor there is profit, the same truth that the strength of the ox brings increase.
The lazy man's field lies overgrown and broken down, the poverty that comes when no one will bear the cost of work.
Careful attention to flocks and herds supplies the household, the same farm wisdom that values the working animal.

units.notes:
• The word translated "clean" can also mean empty, and the 1984 NIV renders it "empty": without oxen the manger has no grain in it. Either way the picture is a farm that produces little. The ESV and NASB say "manger," the KJV "crib."
• In Israel the ox pulled the plow and trod out the grain. Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah called him (1 Kings 19:19), and the Law said, "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain" (Deuteronomy 25:4).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Orderliness can reach the point of sterility." In plain terms, too much love of order can leave a life or a church barren.
• Ironside applies the verse to churches that remove troublesome members too quickly: "It would be a drastic measure indeed to slay the oxen in order to have a clean stable."
• Compare 12:11; 14:23; 27:23–27; 1 Corinthians 9:9–10.
units.summary: A spotless stable usually means an empty barn; real fruitfulness is messy.
units.principle: Fruitfulness always costs something; wisdom accepts the mess and expense that real growth brings rather than settling for a tidy emptiness.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable, the servant who buried his talent kept everything clean and safe. He handed back exactly what he had been given, and his master called him "wicked and lazy" (Matthew 25:26). Fear of loss had made him barren. Many of us prefer the clean trough. We avoid the new ministry because people are messy, the child's questions because they take time, the new hire because training costs. Churches can do the same, putting difficult people out quickly to keep things tidy instead of laboring to restore them (Galatians 6:1). The Pharisees complained that Jesus "receives sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). He chose the mess of real people over the clean distance of the religious, and His harvest came through it. Ask where your love of order is costing fruit.
units.application: Parents: let the kitchen get messy while your children learn to cook; the mess is part of the increase. Pastors and ministry leaders: count the cost of a new outreach carefully, then accept it instead of protecting a tidy calendar. Business owners: invest in the tool or the person that will multiply the work, even if it complicates things for a season. If a difficult person is in your small group, labor for their growth before you look for a way to be rid of them.

rel.note: The one who speaks truth declares righteousness, while a false witness speaks deceit.
The true and deceitful witnesses return, now showing that true testimony delivers lives.
A false witness will not go unpunished, the end that awaits the liar of this verse.
The false witness who speaks lies stands among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Will utter lies" is literally "breathes out lies," as the ESV renders it. Lies come from the false witness as easily as breath. Proverbs uses the same expression in 6:19, 14:25, 19:5 and 19:9, where the NKJV has "speaks lies."
• Bridges: a faithful witness "is moved neither by entreaties nor bribes, neither by promises nor threats, to swerve from truth." In other words, neither pleading nor payment nor fear will bend his testimony.
• The ninth commandment stands behind the verse: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor" (Exodus 20:16). The Law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15) and gave a false witness the penalty he had tried to bring on another (Deuteronomy 19:16–19).
• Compare 12:17; 19:5, 9; Matthew 7:17 ("every good tree bears good fruit").
units.summary: Honesty on the witness stand is grown long before, in a thousand small truths.
units.principle: Truthfulness is a matter of character, not convenience; a faithful person tells the truth even when a lie would serve him.
units.insight: Jezebel hired two worthless men to swear that Naboth had blasphemed, and an innocent man was stoned so a king could have a vineyard (1 Kings 21:10–13). At Jesus' trial "many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree" (Mark 14:56). Simon Peter, warming himself in the courtyard that same night, denied he knew Him (Luke 22:55–62). Most of us would never lie under oath, yet we shade the truth to protect ourselves, as Peter did. The verse asks what our small answers reveal about the tree. The gospel meets us there. Christ is "the Faithful and True Witness" (Revelation 3:14), and He restored the man who denied Him. Weeks later Peter told the council, "we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20).
units.application: If you are asked to give a reference, report an incident or explain what happened at work, tell it straight, even when a softer version would protect a friend or yourself. Employees: refuse to sign or repeat what you know is false. Parents: admit the truth when you are at fault, so your children learn that honesty is safer than spin. If you have shaded the truth about someone, go back this week and correct it.

rel.note: The scoffer does not listen to rebuke, which explains why his search for wisdom fails.
The fool may hold the price of wisdom in his hand, yet he has no heart for it.
When the wise is instructed he receives knowledge, the ease of learning that belongs to the understanding.
Wisdom's words are plain to him who understands, just as knowledge is easy to him here.
The scoffer hates correction while the wise man grows wiser by it, the closed and open hearts of this verse.

units.notes:
• The words "find it" are supplied by the NKJV. The Hebrew says simply that the scoffer seeks wisdom and there is none, as Young's Literal Translation shows. The ESV says he seeks it "in vain."
• The scoffer in Proverbs is marked by contempt for correction (9:7–8; 13:1). His problem lies in his will, not in his intelligence.
• Bridges: "The failure lies at the scorner's own door."
• Pilate asked Jesus, "What is truth?" and went out before any answer came (John 18:38). He is a picture of a seeker with no intention of finding.
• Compare 8:9 ("They are all plain to him who understands"); 17:16; 21:11; Matthew 11:25; John 7:17.
units.summary: Wisdom is not hidden from the scoffer; he hides from it behind his scorn.
units.principle: Wisdom yields to humility, not to cleverness; a teachable heart learns easily, while a scornful one searches without end and finds nothing.
units.insight: Herod was glad to see Jesus because he hoped to watch a miracle, but Jesus gave him no answer at all (Luke 23:8–9). Herod had curiosity without humility. The Ethiopian official had both. Reading Isaiah, he admitted, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" and he went home rejoicing in Christ (Acts 8:31, 39). Jesus thanked His Father for hiding these things "from the wise and prudent" and revealing them "to babes" (Matthew 11:25). The question for us is not how much we know but whether we can still be taught. Cynicism about Scripture, the church or other believers can slowly close the door, even in people who have been in church for years. Humility opens it again. The Lord does not hide from the humble seeker.
units.application: When you read Scripture this week, come with a question you want God to answer, not an argument you want to win. Students and young adults: notice whether you mock the faith you were raised in more than you try to understand it. Small-group leaders: when someone asks questions only to score points, answer briefly and do not be drawn into endless debate. If you recognize scorn in yourself, ask God for a teachable heart and listen carefully to one person you have dismissed.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, the danger that makes leaving the fool's presence wise.
Speaking in a fool's hearing is wasted because he despises wise words, the reason not to stay and argue.
Answering a fool takes discernment, which this verse completes by showing when to stop and go.
Wisdom calls the simple to forsake foolishness and live, the turning away this verse commands.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew of the second line is compressed, and translations handle it differently. The NKJV and KJV make it a condition: leave when you see no knowledge in him. The ESV makes it the reason for leaving. The NASB makes it the result of staying: you will not find words of knowledge there.
• Bridges advises dealing with such a person briefly: "dispatch your business with him as in a shower of rain, and not to loiter in his society." In other words, do what you must, as you would in a downpour, and do not linger.
• Henry: "Sometimes the only way we have of reproving wicked discourse and witnessing against it is by leaving the company".
• Compare 13:20; 23:9 ("Do not speak in the hearing of a fool"); 26:4–5; Matthew 7:6; 1 Corinthians 15:33 ("Evil company corrupts good habits").
units.summary: Wisdom knows when to stop arguing and walk out the door.
units.principle: Love may seek a fool's good, but wisdom does not linger where nothing true is spoken, because the company we keep shapes who we become.
units.insight: Jesus practiced this verse. When the Pharisees and Sadducees demanded a sign to test Him, "He left them and departed" (Matthew 16:4). Of the blind guides who took offense at His teaching He said, "Let them alone" (Matthew 15:14). Paul reasoned in the synagogue at Corinth Sabbath after Sabbath, but when his hearers opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and turned to others (Acts 18:4–6). Neither stopped loving; both stopped feeding a conversation that was going nowhere. Many of us stay too long. We keep returning to the group chat that sours us, the friend who always pulls us back toward what we left, or the argument we will never win. Sometimes faithfulness looks like standing up, saying a kind goodbye and walking out the door.
units.application: Young people: if a friend's talk keeps pulling you toward what you know is wrong and never toward anything good, spend less time in that company. Online, leave the thread that has turned to mockery instead of posting one more reply. Parents: teach your children how to leave a conversation politely. Believers sharing their faith: keep loving and praying for the scoffer, but when talk turns to ridicule, end it graciously and leave room for God to work.

rel.note: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, the self-deceit set against understanding one's way.
The way that seems right but ends in death shows where the fool's self-deception leads.
The prudent considers well his steps, the same careful attention to one's own way that closes this section.
The prudent man foresees evil and hides himself, the practical fruit of understanding his way.
The father's command to ponder the path of your feet is the prudent man's practice here.

units.notes:
• The NLT draws out the self-deception the contrast implies: "fools deceive themselves." The ESV renders the last word "deceiving."
• The prudent man's concern is "his way," not his neighbor's. When Peter asked about John's future, Jesus answered, "what is that to you? You follow Me" (John 21:22).
• Henry: "we are travellers, whose concern it is, not to spy wonders, but to get forward towards their journey's end." In other words, a traveler's business is not sightseeing but making steady progress on his own road.
• Deceit that fools others ends by fooling the deceiver. Gehazi lied to Naaman and to Elisha and carried away leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27), and Ananias and Sapphira found they could not deceive God (Acts 5:1–10).
• Compare 4:26 ("Ponder the path of your feet"); 12:15; 14:15; Psalm 139:23–24; Galatians 6:4.
units.summary: The wise keep checking the map; the fool tells himself a comforting story about the road.
units.principle: True prudence begins with careful attention to one's own path, while folly deceives others and, worst of all, deceives itself.
units.insight: After his sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, David went on for months as if all were well. When Nathan told him of a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, David burned with anger at the injustice. He saw everything except himself, until Nathan said, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:1–7). That is the folly of fools at work: a heart that can read every road but its own. We are skilled at understanding other people's ways, their marriages, their parenting, their mistakes. The prudent turn the lamp on themselves first, and they pray as David learned to pray: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23). Self-examination before God is safe, because the One who exposes our way also forgives it (1 John 1:9).
units.application: Set aside twenty minutes this week to ask where your current road is heading: your spending, your use of time, a relationship you are drifting into. Write down the true answer. Parents and mentors: ask the young people you guide, "Where does this choice lead in five years?" Leaders: before you evaluate your team, evaluate your own decisions. When you catch yourself explaining away a warning sign, stop and look again.

rel.note: To do evil is like sport to a fool, the same laughter at wrongdoing.
Those who deal truthfully are the LORD's delight, part of the favor the upright enjoy.
The one who confesses and forsakes his sins finds mercy, the opposite of mocking at guilt.
Holding to mercy and truth brings favor in the sight of God and man, the favor found among the upright.

units.notes:
• The word translated "sin" here is the word for the guilt offering, the sacrifice brought to make amends for a wrong (Leviticus 5:14–19). The ESV reads "the guilt offering," and the 1984 NIV speaks of making amends for sin. Read that way, the fool mocks the very means of setting things right.
• The first line is grammatically unusual in Hebrew: "fools" is plural, but the verb "mock" is singular. Because of this, the translators' notes in the NET Bible discuss a proposal to reverse the line so that the guilt offering mocks fools. The NKJV, like the other major translations, keeps fools as the ones who mock.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Fools do wrong and scoff at making reparations, but they find no divine or mutual favor and acceptance." Reparations are amends made for harm done.
• Bridges: "Shall we make a mock at that, which was a crushing burden to the Son of God?"
• Compare 10:23 ("To do evil is like sport to a fool"); 28:13; 3:3–4.
units.summary: Laughing off guilt does not erase it; it only shuts the door on making things right.
units.principle: Those who make light of sin cut themselves off from repair, but those who face their wrongs and make amends find favor with God and with others.
units.insight: Zacchaeus did not laugh off his guilt. When Jesus came to his house, he stood and promised to give half his goods to the poor and to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus answered, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:8–9). That is favor among the upright. The fool's way is to joke about the padded expense report, the screen he should not be watching, the cutting remark: "Everyone does it." But sin is no joke to God. It cost the Son of God Gethsemane and the cross, where His soul was made "an offering for sin" (Isaiah 53:10). Is there a wrong you have laughed off instead of making it right? The cross is God's answer to that guilt, and confession and repair are the way back into favor.
units.application: If you have wronged a coworker, a spouse or a friend, do not wave it off with a joke. Name it, apologize and make it right, including repaying any loss. Parents: when a child laughs off a wrong, gently insist on an apology and a repair. Leaders: build a team where admitting a mistake is safe and mocking one is not. Friends: stop laughing along when sin is played for comedy.

rel.note: Laughter can hide a sorrowing heart, another reminder that the inner life is hidden from view.
Sorrow of the heart breaks the spirit, showing how deeply the inner life affects a person.
A broken spirit is a weight no one can bear, the kind of inner bitterness others cannot fully see.
Singing songs to a heavy heart is cruel, a warning to those who do not understand another's grief.

units.notes:
• "Its own bitterness" is literally "the bitterness of its soul," grief felt at the deepest level of a person.
• In the second line the KJV says a stranger does not "intermeddle" with the heart's joy, meaning he cannot step inside it and take part.
• Paul makes the same point: "what man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11).
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "We may not judge our brethren as though we understood them, and were competent to give a verdict upon them."
• Bridges, on David's wife Michal, who despised him for dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:16): "She knew him as a man of war, not as a man of God." She shared his victories but not his joy in the LORD.
• Compare 14:13; 18:14; 25:20; Romans 12:15; Hebrews 4:15.
units.summary: Every heart has rooms no one else can enter, except the God who made it.
units.principle: No one fully knows another person's sorrow or joy, so we owe one another humility in judging and tenderness in caring, and we can bring the whole heart to God, who knows it.
units.insight: Hannah prayed in such bitterness of soul that Eli the priest thought she was drunk and rebuked her (1 Samuel 1:10–14). The man who should have comforted her misread her completely. Job's friends did the same, and Job called them "miserable comforters" (Job 16:2). We do it too. We judge the widow for not moving on, or the quiet coworker for seeming cold, never knowing what they carry. Yet the verse also comforts. There is One who enters where no one else can. Jesus was "a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3), and He is a High Priest who can "sympathize with our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15). What you cannot explain to anyone, you can pour out to Him, and He will not misread you.
units.application: When someone you know is grieving, resist saying, "I know exactly how you feel." Say instead, "I can't fully know, but I'm here," and keep showing up. Pastors and small-group leaders: make room for people to share sorrow without rushing to fix it. Spouses and parents: ask questions before you judge a mood. When your own heart holds what no one understands, bring it to Christ in prayer, borrowing the Psalms when your own words fail.

rel.note: When the whirlwind passes the wicked are gone, but the righteous have an everlasting foundation.
The wicked are overthrown while the house of the righteous stands, the same reversal stated earlier.
The chapter's opening saying about building and tearing down a house is extended here to the righteous and the wicked.
The evil finally bow before the good, the same reversal of appearances over time.
The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked and His blessing on the home of the just.

units.notes:
• The KJV renders "tent" as "tabernacle," the older English word for a tent.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the word here "refers to a nomadic tent," the movable home of people on a journey, not a settled house.
• Bridges: "The feeblest state of the upright is more stable than the prosperity of the wicked."
• Abraham lived in tents with Isaac and Jacob in the land of promise, "for he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:9–10).
• Compare 3:33; 10:25; 12:7; Psalm 73:16–19; Matthew 7:24–27.
units.summary: A tent resting on God outlasts a mansion built on wickedness.
units.principle: What is built on wickedness will not last, however solid it looks, while the modest life of the upright, resting on God, flourishes in the end.
units.insight: Asaph nearly slipped when he saw the prosperity of the wicked. Their houses looked solid; his own life felt like a tent in the wind. Then he went into the sanctuary of God and understood their end: "Surely You set them in slippery places" (Psalm 73:2–3, 16–18). Many believers live in tents: small incomes, rented homes, ministries no one notices. Meanwhile people who cut corners seem to build mansions. The verse asks us to judge by the end, not by appearances. Jesus told of two builders; the house on sand looked fine until the storm came (Matthew 7:24–27). He Himself had "nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20), yet no life has ever flourished like His. Build on Him, and your tent will stand.
units.application: If you are comparing your modest life with someone who prospers by cutting corners, stop measuring by appearances and read Psalm 73 this week. Young couples starting with little: put integrity ahead of a bigger house. Business owners: refuse the profitable shortcut that would rot the foundation. Parents: tell your children why your family chooses honesty over advantage, so they learn which kind of house lasts.

rel.note: Considering one's steps with care is how the prudent avoid the road this verse warns about.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life that turns a person from the snares of death, the opposite end of the road.
Understanding one's own way is the prudence that guards against a way that only seems right.
The identical saying is repeated word for word, so the warning is given twice.
Trusting the LORD instead of leaning on one's own understanding is the way out of the road that only seems right.

units.notes:
• "Seems right" is literally "straight before a man," that is, straight in his own eyes. "Its end" translates a word for the latter end or outcome, the same word used in 14:13. The Hebrew has a plural, "ways of death," which the KJV keeps.
• Proverbs 16:25 repeats this verse word for word in the NKJV, so the two should be read together.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, sums up the danger of a road that looks straight: "The issue then is how deceptive evil is."
• Henry: "Self-deceivers will prove in the end self-destroyers."
• Compare 12:15 ("The way of a fool is right in his own eyes"); 16:2; 21:2; Judges 21:25; Jeremiah 17:9; Matthew 7:13–14; John 14:6.
units.summary: You can be sincere, confident and completely wrong all the way to the grave.
units.principle: Feeling right is not the same as being right; only a way tested by God's word can be trusted to end in life.
units.insight: Saul of Tarsus was sure he was serving God as he hunted down Christians. He said later, "I myself thought I must do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth" (Acts 26:9). His way seemed right, and it was heading toward death, until Christ stopped him on the Damascus road. Jesus warned that "wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction" (Matthew 7:13). The broad way does not feel evil; it feels normal. This verse humbles our confidence in our own sense of direction: the relationship we are sure is fine, the shortcut everyone takes, the religion that feels good. The answer is not to distrust every thought but to submit our sense of right to God. Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). His road ends in life.
units.application: Before a major decision this week, ask, "Does this only seem right to me, or have I tested it by Scripture and wise counsel?" Young adults choosing a relationship or career: invite an older believer to question you. Leaders: when everyone agrees too quickly, look again at where the plan ends. If you hold a belief about God mainly because it feels right, open the Bible and test it there.

rel.note: The heart knows its own bitterness, the hidden inner life that laughter can cover.
A merry heart makes a cheerful face, the good joy this verse does not despise.
A merry heart does good like medicine, showing the real worth of the joy this verse says cannot be relied on to last.
Singing to a heavy heart wounds it, so hidden sorrow calls for gentleness.

units.notes:
• "End" translates the same word for the latter end or outcome used in 14:12. The verbal link joins the way that ends in death and the mirth that ends in grief.
• The KJV reads, "the end of that mirth is heaviness."
• Haman went home from the queen's banquet "joyful and with a glad heart," but the sight of Mordecai at the king's gate soured it all (Esther 5:9–13). Solomon tested pleasure and called laughter madness (Ecclesiastes 2:1–2).
• Bridges: "Many a sigh is heaved amid the loud laughter of folly."
• Compare 14:10; 15:13; Ecclesiastes 7:2–4; Luke 6:25; John 16:22.
units.summary: A laughing face can hide an aching heart, and every earthly party ends.
units.principle: Outward cheer is no proof of inner peace, and earthly mirth is brief, so lasting joy must come from a deeper source than circumstances.
units.insight: The prodigal son's party in the far country ended among the pigs. Then he came home, and his father's house "began to be merry" with a joy that would last (Luke 15:13–24). There are two kinds of mirth, and only one has a good end. The verse is also a call to notice people. Some of the loudest laughter in a room comes from those who hurt most. The teenager who is always the joker, the colleague who never stops smiling, the church member who always says "I'm fine" may carry grief they cannot speak. We may be that person ourselves. Jesus promised His disciples sorrow and then joy: "your joy no one will take from you" (John 16:22). Joy rooted in Him survives when the laughter ends.
units.application: This week, look past the smile of one person who always seems fine: a friend, a teenager, a coworker. Ask a second question after "How are you?" Parents: notice when a child's jokes cover something deeper. If your own laughter has become a cover, tell one trusted person the truth. Before you reach for the next distraction to forget a heavy heart, bring that heaviness to God first.

rel.note: A man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth and hands, the reaping principle behind both lines.
Those who refuse Wisdom eat the fruit of their own way and are filled with their own fancies.
The turning away of the simple slays them, the deadly end of the drift this verse describes.
Keeping the heart with all diligence is the guard against backsliding in heart.
The one who is wise is wise for himself and the scoffer bears it alone, the same principle that each person is filled with what he has chosen.

units.notes:
• "Backslider" translates a word for one who turns back or turns away. "In heart" shows that the turning has happened inwardly, before anyone else can see it.
• The final phrase is brief in Hebrew, literally "from upon him." The KJV has "from himself," and the NASB and ESV take it to mean that the good man is filled with the fruit of his own good ways, matching the first line. The NKJV's "from above" is an interpretive rendering that names God as the source.
• Bridges guards against despair: "Every spot is not the leprosy." One sin does not prove that a believer has turned away in heart, just as one spot on the skin did not prove leprosy.
• Ironside: "Many a soul gives up in heart long before it is manifested in the life."
• Compare 1:31 ("Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their own way"); 4:23; 12:14; Jeremiah 2:19; Hosea 14:4; John 6:35.
units.summary: Turn away from God and you will get exactly what you chose, all of it.
units.principle: Whoever turns from God inwardly will be filled with his own choices and their bitter fruit, while the one who walks with God is satisfied by good that God supplies.
units.insight: Samson's turning began long before Delilah cut his hair, and in the end "he did not know that the LORD had departed from him" (Judges 16:20). He was filled with his own ways. Backsliding rarely begins with a dramatic sin. It begins with hurried prayer, Scripture read to quiet the conscience rather than to feed the soul, and small compromises excused. The heart drifts before the life does. Yet God's word to backsliders is not only warning. Through Hosea He promises, "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely" (Hosea 14:4). Peter, who denied Jesus three times, was restored by the risen Lord (John 21:15–17). Jesus offers what our own ways never can: "He who comes to Me shall never hunger, and he who believes in Me shall never thirst" (John 6:35). That is the good man's satisfaction from above.
units.application: Take a careful inventory: Is your prayer life cooler than it was a year ago? Is there a compromise you once resisted and now excuse? Name it to God this week. Small-group leaders: check on members who have quietly stopped coming, before the drift becomes a departure. Parents: watch for a child's heart turning before the behavior shows it, and keep the door home open. If you have wandered, come back now; God heals backsliding.

rel.note: Considering one's steps is how a person avoids the way that only seems right.
The simple inherit folly while the prudent are crowned with knowledge, the outcome of the habits described here.
The prudent understands his way, the same careful attention that opens this section.
Proverbs was written to give prudence to the simple, the hope held out to the credulous.
The prudent foresees evil and hides, while the simple pass on and are punished.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB render "every word" as "everything." The KJV says the prudent man "looketh well to his going."
• Bridges: "To believe every word of God is faith. To believe every word of man is credulity." Credulity is believing too easily.
• Eve believed the serpent's word over God's (Genesis 3:1–6). The Bereans, by contrast, "searched the Scriptures daily to find out whether these things were so," even when Paul was the speaker (Acts 17:11).
• Henry: "The prudent man will try before he trusts." To try is to test.
• Compare 1:4; 14:8; 22:3; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1.
units.summary: Believing everything is not open-mindedness; it is leaving the front door unlocked.
units.principle: Faith in God is not believing everything; wisdom tests every human word, and God gives that prudence to anyone willing to learn.
units.insight: A man of God came from Judah with a clear command from the LORD. Then an old prophet told him an angel had changed the instructions. He believed the lie, and it cost him his life (1 Kings 13:18–24). He was not wicked, only too ready to believe. Our age is full of such voices: the viral post, the investment that cannot fail, the teacher who flatters our desires. Paul warned of believers "tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine" (Ephesians 4:14). Credulity can pass for humility or openness, but it avoids the work of discernment. Yet no one has to stay simple. Christ has become our wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:30), and His Spirit guides into all truth (John 16:13). Ask Him for a settled, discerning heart.
units.application: Before you share a shocking story or post this week, check the source. Before you sign up for an offer that sounds too good, sleep on it and ask someone wise. Young people: test what influencers say about life and faith against Scripture. Parents: teach children to ask, "How do we know that's true?" Church members: weigh even popular teaching by the Bible, as the Bereans did, and be patient with friends who are easily swayed.

rel.note: The one who walks uprightly fears the LORD, showing again that right fear turns the feet.
By the fear of the LORD one departs from evil, the wise man's path in this verse.
The prudent sees danger and hides, while the simple go on and are punished, like the self-confident fool.
The man who is always reverent is happy, but the one who hardens his heart falls into calamity.
Fearing the LORD and departing from evil is the same pairing of fear and turning away.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "rages" can mean to be arrogant or to become furious. Here it stands opposite the wise man's caution: the fool pushes ahead in proud self-assurance. Young's Literal Translation has "transgressing," the NASB "arrogant" and the ESV "reckless."
• The 1984 NIV supplies "the LORD" as the object of the wise man's fear in the first line. The other translations leave the object unstated.
• Henry: "A wise man, for fear of harm, keeps out of harm's way."
• Joseph shows the wise man's fear. He refused Potiphar's wife, asking, "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" and when she seized him, he fled (Genesis 39:9, 12).
• Compare 3:7; 16:6 ("by the fear of the LORD one departs from evil"); 22:3; 28:14; 1 Corinthians 10:12.
units.summary: The wise are afraid of the right things; the fool fears nothing until it is too late.
units.principle: A healthy fear of evil and its consequences keeps the wise safe, while proud self-confidence carries the fool straight into the danger he refuses to see.
units.insight: Simon Peter was sure of himself. "Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble," he told Jesus (Matthew 26:33). Hours later he denied Him three times. Jesus had told him to "watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation" (Matthew 26:41), but Peter slept. Self-confidence is the fool's armor, and it is made of paper. Most of us say some version of "I can handle it" about the screen we keep to ourselves, the drink, or the friendship drifting toward something it should not be. The wise man is not braver than the fool; he is more realistic about his weakness. Jesus Himself prayed "with vehement cries and tears" and "was heard because of His godly fear" (Hebrews 5:7). Godly fear is not weakness. It is the way the Son walked, and He shares it with His people.
units.application: Name one place where you have been telling yourself, "I can handle it." Put a fence there this week: an accountability partner, a filter, a different route home. Young people: do not test how close you can get to sin without falling. Leaders: invite people who will warn you, and listen when they do. If you have been charging ahead against good advice, stop and ask what you are refusing to see.

rel.note: Those who devise evil go astray, the same deliberate planning of harm.
The one who is slow to wrath has great understanding, the opposite of the quick-tempered man here.
The wrathful man stirs up strife, but the one slow to anger calms it.
An angry, furious man stirs up strife and abounds in transgression, the folly of hot temper.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates, the sin of the schemer in the second line.

units.notes:
• "Quick-tempered" is literally "short of nostrils." The same Hebrew word means both nostrils and anger, so the phrase describes anger that flares quickly. The opposite phrase appears in 14:29, where "slow to wrath" is literally "long of nostrils."
• The word behind "wicked intentions" means schemes or plans. It can be used positively, as in 1:4, where the NKJV translates it "discretion," but here it describes plotting.
• Bridges names the two sins "the sudden passion, and the deliberate purpose; the gust and the continuance of the storm."
• Moses' sudden anger at Meribah kept him out of the promised land (Numbers 20:10–12). Absalom, by contrast, nursed his hatred of Amnon for two full years before he struck (2 Samuel 13:22–29).
• Compare 14:29; 15:18; 29:22; Ephesians 4:26 ("Be angry, and do not sin").
units.summary: Hot anger makes a man a fool; cold scheming makes him hated.
units.principle: Both the hot flare of temper and the cold plotting of malice are sins; the first makes a person foolish, the second makes him hateful.
units.insight: David shows how fast anger can carry even a godly man toward folly. When Nabal insulted him, David told his men, "Every man gird on his sword," and he swore to wipe out Nabal's household (1 Samuel 25:13, 21–22). Only Abigail's wisdom stopped him. Cain shows the colder sin. He nursed his anger, talked with his brother, and when they were in the field he rose up and killed him (Genesis 4:5–8). Most of us excuse one sin by pointing to the other. The hothead says, "At least I don't hold grudges." The cool schemer says, "At least I never lose my temper." This verse condemns both. Christ is the cure for each. He answered insults without insult (1 Peter 2:23), and He prayed for those who plotted His death (Luke 23:34).
units.application: If you have a quick temper, build in a pause this week: count to ten, leave the room, or wait a day before sending the email. Parents: apologize to your children when your anger outruns your judgment. If you are the calm one who keeps score, name the grudge you are nursing and lay it down before it becomes a plan. Leaders: watch for both the hothead and the quiet schemer on your team, and address each early.

rel.note: The simple believe every word while the prudent consider their steps, the habits that lead to these two outcomes.
The crown of the wise is their riches, while the foolishness of fools is only folly.
The wise inherit glory while shame is the legacy of fools, the same two inheritances.
Wisdom calls the simple to understand prudence, the hope that keeps folly from being final.

units.notes:
• The NLT says the simple are "clothed with foolishness." Set beside "crowned" in the second line, that rendering draws out the picture of folly and knowledge as things a person wears.
• The simple in Proverbs are the uncommitted: not set against wisdom, but not committed to it either, and so easily led (1:22, 32; 14:15).
• Bridges: "So long as he remains simple, he confirms his title." Every day of drifting strengthens his claim to folly.
• Ironside: "Wise and simple are relative terms, referring not so much to mental condition as to the fear of the Lord on the one hand, and indifferent self-sufficiency on the other."
• Compare 3:35 ("The wise shall inherit glory"); 4:9; 14:24; James 1:5.
units.summary: Folly is what you get by drifting; knowledge is a crown you have to reach for.
units.principle: Folly is the default inheritance of a drifting life, but knowledge crowns those who choose wisdom, and the call to choose remains open.
units.insight: Saul and David both wore Israel's crown, but they wore it differently. Saul drifted. He offered sacrifice in impatience, spared what God told him to destroy and blamed the people, and in the end he admitted, "I have played the fool" (1 Samuel 26:21). David, for all his sins, kept returning to God and was remembered as "a man after My own heart" (Acts 13:22). Folly rarely comes from one great decision. It is what piles up when we never decide. The phone, our default habits and the voices of the culture will gladly fill an uncommitted life. Yet God offers a better crown. Jesus invites the weary, "learn from Me" (Matthew 11:29), and God gives wisdom "liberally and without reproach" to anyone who asks (James 1:5).
units.application: Decide something this week instead of drifting: a daily time in Scripture, a mentor you will meet with, a habit you will end. Young adults: notice which voices are shaping you by default, and choose deliberately whom you will learn from. Parents: do not assume children will absorb wisdom just by being near it; teach it on purpose. If you feel stuck in old patterns, ask God for wisdom today and take one concrete step.

rel.note: The righteous is delivered from trouble and it comes on the wicked instead, the same reversal.
The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous, another picture of God's reversal over time.
The house of the wicked falls while the tent of the upright flourishes, the same overturning of appearances.
Do not fret over evildoers, for the evil man has no future, the patience this verse calls for.

units.notes:
• The verb "bow" is in the form normally used for a completed action, which Young's Literal Translation reflects with "have bowed." Most translations render it as a future or a general truth. The form presents the outcome vividly, as if already seen, but it does not by itself fix when or how the reversal happens.
• Bridges admits the limits: "This is not the general rule of the present dispensation. Righteous Lazarus bowed at the wicked man's gate." In this present age, as in Jesus' parable, the righteous poor man often lies at the rich man's gate (Luke 16:20).
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Ultimately the wicked will acknowledge and serve the righteous."
• Another picture of the reversal: the magistrates of Philippi, who had beaten and jailed Paul and Silas, came and pleaded with them (Acts 16:38–39).
• Compare 11:8; 13:22; 24:19–20; Psalm 37:34–36; Revelation 3:9.
units.summary: Those who strut past the righteous today may one day be knocking at their door.
units.principle: God's justice moves history toward the vindication of the righteous; the present order, in which evil often prevails, is not the final one.
units.insight: Mordecai sat at the king's gate and would not bow to Haman. Within days Haman was leading Mordecai through the city on the king's own horse, and soon after he was pleading with Queen Esther for his life (Esther 3:2; 6:11; 7:7). God can turn things that quickly, though often He does not. Many believers live long in the place of Lazarus at the rich man's gate. The verse does not deny that pain; it lifts our eyes to where history is going. Jesus Himself was mocked by soldiers who "bowed the knee before Him" in scorn (Matthew 27:29). Now God has exalted Him, "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Philippians 2:10). If you are the one being looked down on, take heart. If you are the one looking down, take warning.
units.application: If you are being sidelined at work or mocked for your faith, refuse to scheme for your own vindication; keep doing right and leave the timing to God. Parents: tell your children stories of how God has turned situations around, and be clear that He does not always do it quickly. If someone who once wronged you comes to you in need, receive them with the grace Joseph showed his brothers (Genesis 50:19–21).

rel.note: The next verse judges what this one observes: despising a neighbor is sin.
A true friend loves at all times and a brother is born for adversity, unlike the fair-weather friends of the rich.
Wealth makes many friends while the poor man is separated from his friend, the same observation.
All the brothers of the poor hate him and his friends go far from him, the isolation of poverty.

units.notes:
• The second line reads literally "many are those who love the rich," which the NASB and Young's Literal Translation follow. The wording suggests people who attach themselves to the rich for what they can gain.
• Verses 20 and 21 both use the same word for "neighbor," and the repetition binds this observation to the judgment that follows it.
• Henry: "This shows, not what should be, but what is the common way of the world." He calls such fair-weather company "swallow-friends, that are gone in winter," like birds that leave when the cold comes.
• Ruth clung to Naomi when she came home empty (Ruth 1:16–21), and Jonathan strengthened David when he had lost the king's favor (1 Samuel 23:16). These exceptions show what love looks like.
• Compare 17:17; 19:4, 6–7; Luke 15:13–16.
units.summary: Count the friends who come with the money, then count the ones who stay when it is gone.
units.principle: Wealth gathers friends and poverty scatters them, so true friendship is proved by who stays when there is nothing to gain.
units.insight: The prodigal son had company while his money lasted. When famine came, "no one gave him anything" (Luke 15:16). Job, stripped of everything, said, "My relatives have failed, And my close friends have forgotten me" (Job 19:14). That is the world this verse describes, and the question is which side of it we are on. We may not hate the poor, but we drift toward people who can help us and away from those who will cost us something. Jesus did the opposite. He chose fishermen, ate with outcasts and, "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is the friend who does not leave when we have nothing to offer. Those who know His friendship are free to befriend the people the world avoids.
units.application: Think of someone in your circle who has lost a job, a marriage or their health. Call them this week, not to fix anything, but to stay near. At church, notice who stands alone after the service, and go and sit with them. Leaders: ask whether the people closest to you are there because of what you can give. If you are the one going through loss, notice who stays, and thank them.

rel.note: The one devoid of wisdom despises his neighbor, the same contempt condemned here.
The previous verse shows how easily the poor are despised, the attitude this verse calls sin.
Mercy to the needy honors their Maker, using the same verb for showing mercy.
The one who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD, who repays, the blessing of mercy.
The generous eye that gives bread to the poor will be blessed.

units.notes:
• The ESV renders "happy" as "blessed." The NKJV keeps the Hebrew word order by placing "happy is he" at the end of the line.
• The same verb for showing mercy returns in 14:31 ("has mercy on the needy"), linking the two sayings about the poor in this chapter.
• Bridges: "Some men are so high, that they cannot see their lower brother."
• Boaz shows this mercy in action. He let Ruth glean among the sheaves and told his young men to leave grain for her on purpose (Ruth 2:15–16).
• Compare 11:12 ("He who is devoid of wisdom despises his neighbor"); 19:17; 22:9; Leviticus 19:18; James 2:1–9.
units.summary: God calls contempt for the poor sin, and He calls mercy toward them blessed.
units.principle: Contempt for those beneath us is sin against God, and mercy toward the needy carries its own deep blessing.
units.insight: James saw this verse broken in the church. A rich man with gold rings is given a good seat, while a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand or to sit on the floor. James names it: "if you show partiality, you commit sin" (James 2:1–9). In Jesus' parable, the priest and the Levite passed by the wounded man, but the Samaritan stopped, bandaged his wounds and paid for his care (Luke 10:30–35). Contempt usually looks like hurry, not hatred; we simply do not see. Christ saw. He touched the leper, noticed the widow's two mites and welcomed the children. Every act of mercy we show was first shown to us, for Christ did not despise us when we had nothing to offer Him (Romans 5:8).
units.application: Learn the name of someone your church or workplace tends to overlook, such as the custodian, the new immigrant family or the man who sleeps near the building. Greet them by name this week. Employers: pay fairly and on time, and treat the lowest-paid worker with respect. Parents: correct children who mock classmates for their clothes or homes. When you give, give face to face where you can, so mercy carries dignity as well as help.

rel.note: Deceit fills those who devise evil, while counselors of peace have joy.
The man of wicked intentions is hated, the same deliberate scheming set beside hot temper.
The command not to devise evil against a neighbor uses the same verb for planning harm.
The father urges his son to keep mercy and truth, the very qualities that belong to those who devise good.
The worthless man devises evil continually, the planner of harm this verse warns about.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "devise" has the basic sense of cutting in, as in engraving or plowing, and from that it comes to mean working out a plan. The same verb appears in "Do not devise evil against your neighbor" (3:29).
• The ESV renders "mercy and truth" as "steadfast love and faithfulness," a pair that runs through the Old Testament as a description of God's character. Compare Exodus 34:6, where the ESV has "abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" and the NKJV "abounding in goodness and truth."
• Bridges: "Wicked as it is to do evil, it is far more hateful to devise it."
• The builders of Babel planned a tower to make a name for themselves and ended scattered (Genesis 11:4–9). Haman's plot against the Jews ended on his own gallows (Esther 7:10).
• Compare 3:3, 29; 6:14, 18; 12:20; Isaiah 32:8 ("a generous man devises generous things").
units.summary: Everyone is planning something; the only question is whether it is good or evil.
units.principle: The heart's plans set the direction of a life; those who plan harm wander into ruin, while those who plan good walk in mercy and faithfulness.
units.insight: Joseph's brothers devised evil: "Come therefore, let us now kill him" (Genesis 37:20). Years later Joseph told them, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). God had been planning too. Our plans reveal our hearts. We rehearse revenge in the shower, script the cutting reply, map out how to get ahead of a rival. Few of us spend that much energy planning kindness. Yet the gospel itself is a plan of good. Before the foundation of the world God chose to show mercy in His Son (Ephesians 1:4–7), and "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Those who receive that grace begin to plan as He does: deliberately, generously, for the good of others.
units.application: Put good on your calendar this week the way you would a meeting: a visit to a lonely neighbor, a note to a discouraged coworker, a meal for a family in crisis. Parents: plan a family act of kindness together. Leaders: when you plan strategy, also plan how your decisions will treat the most vulnerable people they affect. If you catch yourself rehearsing revenge, stop and plan one act of good toward that person instead.

rel.note: The slack hand becomes poor while the diligent hand makes rich.
The one who tills his land has bread while the one who follows frivolity lacks sense, the same contrast between real work and empty pursuits.
The lazy man desires and has nothing, just as the talker talks and has nothing.
The crown of the wise is their riches, the honest profit of labor worn well.
Much increase comes by the strength of the ox, the same profit that comes from real labor.
The lazy man's desire kills him because his hands refuse to labor, the end of words without work.

units.notes:
• The KJV renders the second line "the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury," and the ESV has "mere talk tends only to poverty."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Great talkers are do-littles, for the most part."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "People should be more afraid of idle talk than of hard work."
• Jesus told of two sons. One said, "I go, sir," but did not go; the other refused, then regretted it and went. Only the second did his father's will (Matthew 21:28–31).
• Compare 10:4; 12:11; 13:4; 14:4; 21:25; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12.
units.summary: Talking about the work has never yet done the work.
units.principle: Real labor, however humble, bears fruit, while talk that never becomes action leaves a life empty.
units.insight: When famine struck Canaan, Jacob found his sons standing around. "Why do you look at one another?" he asked, and he sent them down to Egypt to buy grain (Genesis 42:1–2). Talk was not going to feed the family. Many of us live in that circle. We discuss the diet, the budget, the Bible-reading plan and the ministry idea, and the discussing feels like progress. Churches can hold meetings about outreach instead of reaching out. Faith itself can shrink into words. James asks, "What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works?" (James 2:14). Jesus did not merely speak of love. He worked it out to the end and could say, "It is finished!" (John 19:30). His finished work sets us free to work, not just to talk.
units.application: Pick one thing you have been talking about for months, such as a project, a hard conversation or a habit, and take the first concrete step this week. Employees: promise less and deliver more. Small-group leaders: end each meeting with one action people will take, not only ideas they discussed. Parents: when a teenager has big plans, help them name the first small task and do it together.

rel.note: The blessing of the LORD makes rich without adding sorrow, the source of wealth that becomes a crown.
The one who trusts in his riches will fall, the fool's misuse of wealth.
The prudent are crowned with knowledge, the same picture of the wise wearing a crown.
In all labor there is profit, the honest gain that becomes the crown of the wise.
Riches and honor are in Wisdom's left hand, wisdom's fitting gifts.

units.notes:
• The repetition in the second line is deliberate: folly yields only folly. The ESV says folly "brings folly."
• Henry: "Wisdom is good without an inheritance, but better with it." He echoes Ecclesiastes 7:11, "Wisdom is good with an inheritance."
• Riches crowned David's wisdom when he and the leaders gave willingly to build the temple (1 Chronicles 29:1–9), and Job used his wealth to be "eyes to the blind" and "a father to the poor" (Job 29:15–16).
• Ironside: "Whether poor or wealthy in this world's goods, the wise are always rich, because possessing treasure that can never fade away."
• Compare 3:16; 10:22; 11:28; 14:18; 1 Timothy 6:17–19.
units.summary: Wealth sits on the wise like a crown; on a fool it only puts more folly on display.
units.principle: Wealth reveals and enlarges what a person already is: in wise hands it becomes an honor and a means of good, in foolish hands only a bigger stage for folly.
units.insight: Nabal was very rich, with three thousand sheep, yet his wealth only made his folly louder. He insulted David's men, and while his household narrowly escaped destruction because of it, he held a feast "like the feast of a king" (1 Samuel 25:2–3, 10–11, 36). His own wife said, "Nabal is his name, and folly is with him" (1 Samuel 25:25). Money did not make him wise; it made his foolishness visible. The verse asks what our resources are revealing about us. A raise, an inheritance or a bonus is a test of the heart as much as a gift. Jesus told of a rich man who planned bigger barns and forgot his soul, and God called him "Fool!" (Luke 12:20). The true treasure is Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).
units.application: If God has given you more than you need, decide this week one way your money will do good beyond yourself: support a ministry, help a struggling family, fund a young person's training. Business owners: let generosity and fairness be the crown of your success. If you have little, remember that wisdom is the treasure that lasts, and do not envy the foolish rich. Parents: teach children that money shows character; it does not create it.

rel.note: The one who speaks truth declares righteousness, while a false witness speaks deceit.
The faithful and false witnesses appear earlier in the chapter, framing the sayings between.
The false witness will not go unpunished, and the one who speaks lies will perish.
The call to deliver those drawn toward death is what a true witness does in court.

units.notes:
• "Speaks lies" translates the same expression used in 14:5, literally "breathes out lies," so the two witness sayings bracket the sayings that lie between them.
• The ESV renders the first line "saves lives." In the NKJV, "souls" here means persons and their lives.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "A man who will trim the facts for you will trim them as easily against you; and a career or a life may hang on a word."
• Jonathan spoke truthfully to Saul on David's behalf, reminding him of David's loyalty, and Saul swore that David would not be killed (1 Samuel 19:4–6).
• Compare 6:19; 12:17; 14:5; 19:9; 24:11.
units.summary: At the right moment, one true sentence can save a life.
units.principle: Truth spoken at the moment it matters can rescue lives, while lies, however smooth, destroy; truthful testimony is a work of mercy.
units.insight: At Jesus' trial the council "sought false testimony against Jesus to put Him to death" (Matthew 26:59). False witnesses helped deliver the only innocent Man to the cross. Yet through that very death, "the Faithful and True Witness" (Revelation 3:14) delivers souls in the deepest sense. Every believer is now called to be His witness (Acts 1:8), telling the truth about Him so that others may be rescued. The verse also tests ordinary courage. Silence while a coworker is falsely blamed, a softened account to avoid trouble, a lie to protect our image: each can let harm fall on someone else. When the chief priests and Pharisees condemned Jesus without a hearing, Nicodemus asked, "Does our law judge a man before it hears him and knows what he is doing?" (John 7:51). Who needs you to tell the truth for them this week?
units.application: If you know the truth about a situation where someone is being blamed unfairly, speak up this week, even if it costs you. Managers: investigate before you discipline, and listen to the quiet witness. Students: do not join a false story about a classmate. Parents: praise children when they tell a hard truth. Believers: speak plainly of what you know of Christ; your testimony may be the word someone needs.

rel.note: The next verse pairs with this one: the fear of the LORD is life as well as security.
The righteous have a refuge even in death, the furthest reach of the refuge promised here.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous are safe, the refuge of this verse.
The fear of man brings a snare, while trust in the LORD keeps a person safe.
The LORD Himself will be the son's confidence and keep his foot, the strong confidence described here.

units.notes:
• The pronoun in the second line is simply "his" in Hebrew, so it can be read two ways. The NKJV capitalizes "His," meaning the LORD's children. The ESV and NASB read "his," meaning the children of the person who fears the LORD, so that a parent's reverence for God becomes a refuge for the next generation. Both readings are grammatically possible.
• Bridges: "We fear, yet we are not afraid." Reverence for God drives out the cringing dread that has no confidence in Him.
• Henry, on the second reading: "The children of religious parents often do the better for their parents' instructions and example and fare the better for their faith and prayers."
• Abraham feared God enough to offer Isaac, yet he was confident "that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19; compare Genesis 22:12).
• Compare 3:26; 18:10; 19:23; 29:25 ("The fear of man brings a snare"); Psalm 46:1; 1 John 4:18.
units.summary: Those who tremble before God are the ones who need not tremble before anything else.
units.principle: A right fear of God is not the enemy of confidence but its source; those who revere Him find in Him their surest refuge.
units.insight: Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-Nego stood before the king's blazing furnace. Because they feared God, they did not fear the king: "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us… But if not… we do not serve your gods" (Daniel 3:17–18). That is strong confidence born of the fear of the LORD. The fear of man works the other way. Peter, afraid of what certain men would think, drew back from eating with Gentile believers (Galatians 2:12). Many of us are anxious because we fear too many things and God too little. When God is seen rightly, the boss, the diagnosis and the critic shrink to their true size. In Christ this refuge is made sure. Through Him we cry, "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15), and His perfect love casts out tormenting fear (1 John 4:18), though never the reverence of His children.
units.application: When anxiety rises this week, name what you are afraid of, then spend a few minutes considering who God is, using Psalm 46 or Isaiah 40. Parents: let your children see you pray when you are afraid; your reverence can become their refuge. Employees under pressure to cut corners: let the fear of the LORD give you courage to say no. Leaders: make decisions as before God, not to please the loudest voice in the room.

rel.note: The same fountain and snares wording describes the teaching of the wise.
The way that seems right but ends in death is one of the snares the fear of the LORD turns a person from.
The previous verse shows the fear of the LORD as strong confidence and refuge, the security beside this life.
The fear of the LORD leads to life and keeps a person from evil.
The book's motto makes the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge, here also the wellspring of life.

units.notes:
• This verse repeats 13:14 except for its subject: there "The law of the wise is a fountain of life," here the fear of the LORD.
• A snare was a hunter's trap hidden on the path, sprung on the unwary, like the bird that "hastens to the snare" in 7:23. The fear of the LORD keeps a person alert to traps he would otherwise walk into.
• Henry: "It is a sovereign antidote against sin and temptation." Sovereign here means supremely effective.
• Bridges: "Not only is it a refuge from danger, but a fountain of life."
• Compare 1:7; 10:11; 13:14; 16:22; 19:23; Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:14.
units.summary: Reverence for God is not a dry duty; it is a spring that never runs dry.
units.principle: The fear of the LORD is a living, renewing source that both gives life and guards it, steering the reverent away from traps they could not otherwise see.
units.insight: Through Jeremiah, God grieved that His people had forsaken Him, "the fountain of living waters," and dug for themselves "broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Every sin is a trip to a broken cistern. Joseph turned from Potiphar's wife because he feared God (Genesis 39:9), and that reverence carried him past a deadly snare. Without it, temptations look harmless; with it, we see the trap under the leaves. Where are you drawing from: entertainment, approval, achievement? Jesus told the woman at the well that the water He gives becomes "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). A right view of God, renewed in His presence day by day, keeps that fountain flowing.
units.application: Start each day this week by reading a psalm that shows God's greatness, and ask Him to give you a right view of Himself. Young people: before you go where you know temptation waits, ask, "What does fearing God look like here?" Parents and teachers: present the fear of the LORD as a source of life and joy, not only of rules. When you sense a trap, such as a flattering offer or a secret invitation, step back and pray before you step in.

rel.note: Without counsel a people falls, another way a ruler's care for his people decides their welfare.
Righteousness exalts a nation, the condition under which a king's people truly flourish.
The other royal saying of this section shows the king's favor toward a wise servant, framing the section with this verse.
Mercy and truth preserve the king and uphold his throne, the kind of rule that draws a people.
When the righteous rule the people rejoice, the flourishing that is a ruler's honor.

units.notes:
• The sayings about the king in 14:28 and 14:35 frame the last section of the chapter.
• Bridges, quoting the commentator Geier: "He is not appointed for luxury or for pleasure; but that as a Head he may preside over his members; as a Shepherd, he may care for his flock."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "A prince's power varies with the size of his empire."
• Numbers alone are not the point. When David took pride in counting his fighting men, the census brought judgment on Israel (2 Samuel 24:1–15). A king's honor lies in a people who flourish under God, not in a headcount.
• Compare 11:14; 14:35; 20:28; 29:2; 29:4; Revelation 7:9.
units.summary: A ruler's real glory is the flourishing of the people he serves.
units.principle: Authority is honored by the flourishing of those it serves; leaders exist for their people, not people for their leaders.
units.insight: Rehoboam inherited a united kingdom. When the people asked him to lighten their load, the elders urged him to "be a servant to these people," but he answered harshly, and ten tribes walked away (1 Kings 12:7, 13–16). His honor shrank with his people. Every leader is tempted to measure success by the size of his own platform. Pastors count attendance, managers count output, parents count achievements. The verse asks a different question: are the people under your care flourishing? Jesus is the King whose honor is His people. He laid down His life for His sheep (John 10:11), and His glory will be "a great multitude which no one could number, of all nations" standing before His throne (Revelation 7:9). His crown is made of the people He has served.
units.application: Leaders at work, at church or at home: ask this week whether the people under you are growing, not just whether they are producing. Have one conversation that is only about their good. Pastors: measure health by discipleship, not only by numbers. Business owners: treat employee turnover as a mirror, not a nuisance. Parents: your household's honor is the flourishing of your children, not their image.

rel.note: The quick-tempered man acts foolishly, the opposite of the patient man's understanding.
The one slow to anger calms contention, while the wrathful man stirs up strife.
The one slow to anger is better than the mighty, the value of the restraint praised here.
Discretion makes a man slow to anger, tying patience to understanding as this verse does.
The man with no rule over his spirit is like a city without walls, the impulsive person exposed.

units.notes:
• "Slow to wrath" is literally "long of nostrils," a picture of anger that takes a long time to flare. The opposite phrase, "short of nostrils," describes the quick-tempered man of 14:17.
• For "impulsive" the KJV reads "hasty of spirit." The Hebrew is literally "short of spirit," the opposite of the patient man's long fuse.
• Henry: "A mild patient man is really to be accounted an intelligent man, one that learns of Christ, who is Wisdom itself."
• Even Moses, called "very humble" (Numbers 12:3), lost his temper at Meribah and "spoke rashly with his lips," and it cost him dearly (Psalm 106:32–33). Jonah's angry sulking over a withered plant put his folly on display (Jonah 4:1–9).
• Compare 15:18; 16:32 ("He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty"); 19:11; 25:28; James 1:19–20.
units.summary: A slow temper shows a large understanding; every outburst puts folly on a pedestal.
units.principle: Patience under provocation is understanding in action, while quick anger displays folly for all to see.
units.insight: When the false prophet Zedekiah struck Micaiah on the cheek before two kings, Micaiah did not strike back. He answered with calm truth and left the outcome to God (1 Kings 22:24–25). Zedekiah's slap exalted his folly; Micaiah's restraint showed understanding. God Himself is "Slow to anger, and abounding in mercy" (Psalm 103:8), and in Christ we see that patience in a human life. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that rejected Him, Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). Most of our outbursts happen at home, with the people we love most, over things we are later ashamed of. Ask the Spirit for the fruit of "longsuffering" (Galatians 5:22). It is His work in us, not merely a matter of personality.
units.application: Parents: when a child provokes you, lower your voice instead of raising it, and take a minute before you discipline. Spouses: agree on a signal that means, "Let's pause and come back to this." Employees and managers: never answer a heated email the same day. Drivers: let the person who cut you off go without a reaction. Each time you wait, you give understanding room to work.

rel.note: The wife who causes shame is like rottenness in the bones, the same picture of inner decay.
A merry heart does good like medicine while a broken spirit dries the bones, the same link of heart and body.
Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be zealous for the fear of the LORD, the cure for envy.
No one can stand before jealousy, showing how destructive the passion of this verse is.

units.notes:
• "Sound heart" is literally "a heart of healing"; Young's Literal Translation reads "healed heart." The same Hebrew word for healing is translated "health" in 13:17.
• The NASB renders "envy" as "passion." The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for jealousy; here it means the resentful wanting of what belongs to someone else.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "to nurse a resentment is bad for body as well as soul."
• Bridges, quoting Bishop Hall on envy: "this vice is executioner enough to itself!" Envy punishes the envious without anyone else's help.
• Haman had wealth, honor and the king's favor, yet he said, "all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (Esther 5:13).
• Compare 12:4; 17:22; 23:17; 27:4; James 3:16.
units.summary: Envy never touches the person you envy, but it slowly rots the one who carries it.
units.principle: A heart at peace tends toward wholeness of life, while envy corrodes the envious person from within.
units.insight: Saul eyed David with envy from the day the women sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, And David his ten thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7–9). From then on the king was tormented, hurling spears and hunting a loyal servant, until envy consumed his reign. Asaph confessed, "I was envious of the boastful," until he went into God's sanctuary (Psalm 73:3, 17). Envy hides behind respectable faces: the critique of a colleague's promotion, the scroll through other people's vacations, the faint pleasure when a rival stumbles. The cure is not simply trying harder to stop wanting. It is a heart healed by God's goodness. Paul learned to be content "in whatever state I am" through Christ who strengthened him (Philippians 4:11–13). A heart that has Christ has nothing left to envy.
units.application: Notice this week whose success stings you, and pray by name for that person's good. Cut back the scrolling that feeds comparison. Coworkers: congratulate the colleague who got the role you wanted, and mean it before God. Parents: help children celebrate a sibling's win instead of keeping score. If anxiety or bitterness is wearing on your body, bring it to God and, where needed, to a doctor or counselor; a sound heart and good care go together.

rel.note: Mercy to the poor brings blessing, using the same verb for showing mercy.
Sin is a reproach to any people, and oppression of the poor is one of the sins that disgrace a nation.
Mocking the poor reproaches his Maker, almost the same words as the first line.
The LORD is the maker of rich and poor alike, the ground of this verse's claim.
Do not rob or oppress the poor, for the LORD Himself will plead their cause.

units.notes:
• The first line is closely paralleled in 17:5, "He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker."
• The verb for showing mercy here is the same one used in 14:21 ("has mercy on the poor"), linking the two sayings about the poor in this chapter.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, places the verse in an old tradition of the ancient Near East: "warning rulers not to trample upon the rights of the poor." Read this way, the verse speaks to those who set wages, run courts and shape markets, not only to private giving.
• Job refused to deny justice to his own servants, asking, "Did not He who made me in the womb make them?" (Job 31:13–15).
• Compare 17:5; 19:17; 22:2, 22–23; Amos 2:6–7; James 5:4.
units.summary: The way we treat the poor is the way we treat the God who made them.
units.principle: Every human being bears the mark of the Creator, so injustice toward the poor insults God and mercy toward them honors Him.
units.insight: In Nehemiah's day the nobles of Jerusalem were charging their poorer brothers interest and taking their fields, and even their children, as security. Nehemiah confronted them: "Should you not walk in the fear of our God?" (Nehemiah 5:1–9). Their oppression was a failure to fear God. David shows the other side. He sought out Mephibosheth, lame and forgotten, so that he might "show him kindness," and gave him a place at the king's table (2 Samuel 9:1–13). This verse searches more than our giving. It reaches how we pay, price, hire and lend, and the systems we quietly benefit from. Jesus began His ministry announcing that He was anointed "to preach the gospel to the poor" (Luke 4:18). Those who honor Him will meet Him in the needy.
units.application: Employers: pay a fair wage on time, and do not take advantage of workers who cannot easily leave. Landlords and business owners: examine fees and practices that fall hardest on the poor. Citizens: support laws and ministries that protect the vulnerable, whatever your party. Families: serve together this month at a food pantry or with a refugee family, and learn names, not just needs.

rel.note: When the whirlwind passes the wicked is gone, but the righteous has an everlasting foundation.
When a wicked man dies his expectation perishes, unlike the refuge of the righteous.
In the way of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
The fear of the LORD gives strong confidence and a place of refuge, the refuge that holds even in death.

units.notes:
• The ancient Greek translation of Proverbs, the Septuagint, reads the second line differently, so the hope expressed in "in his death" rests on the Hebrew text. The NKJV and ESV follow the Hebrew, and the NASB also speaks of the righteous person's death.
• The KJV reads "hope" for "refuge": "the righteous hath hope in his death."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Job and the Psalms show occasional glimpses, such as this, of what lies normally beyond their view."
• Balaam prayed, "Let me die the death of the righteous" (Numbers 23:10), yet he was killed among Israel's enemies (Numbers 31:8). Stephen, stoned for Christ, asked the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and prayed for his killers (Acts 7:59–60).
• Compare 10:25; 11:7; 12:28; 14:26; Psalm 23:4; Philippians 1:21–23.
units.summary: Death strips the wicked of every shelter, but it cannot take God from the righteous.
units.principle: Wickedness leaves a person without shelter when the end comes, but the righteous have in God a refuge that death cannot take away.
units.insight: Paul, chained in prison and facing possible execution, could write, "For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Philippians 1:21). That is a refuge in death. Job, sitting in ashes with everything gone, still said, "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25). Many people spend their lives building shelters that death will knock down: savings, reputation, health, even family. These are good gifts, but none of them can go through death with us. Only God can. David wrote, "Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil; For You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). Christ went through death first and came out the other side. In Him the last enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26) has become the doorway home.
units.application: If you are facing serious illness, or sitting with someone who is dying, read Psalm 23 and John 14:1–3 aloud together. Pastors and chaplains: speak of the believer's hope plainly and gently at funerals and hospital beds. Everyone: ask whether you have a refuge that death cannot take, and settle that question with Christ now. Parents: talk with your children about death and hope before a crisis forces the conversation.

rel.note: The prudent conceals knowledge while the heart of fools proclaims foolishness, the same contrast.
The prudent acts with knowledge while a fool lays open his folly.
The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly while fools pour out foolishness, how each heart comes out in speech.
A fool vents all his feelings while a wise man holds them back.

units.notes:
• The second line is difficult, and translations differ. The ESV says that wisdom makes itself known even among fools, while the NLT adds a negative: "wisdom is not found among fools." The NKJV, with the KJV, reads it as a contrast in which fools reveal what is in them.
• Henry: "Many a foolish man takes more pains to show his folly than a wise man thinks it worth his while to take to show his wisdom."
• Bridges: "True wisdom, while it fixes its rest, sets up its throne, in the heart." Wisdom does not merely visit the heart; it settles there and rules.
• Compare 10:14; 12:23 ("A prudent man conceals knowledge, But the heart of fools proclaims foolishness"); 13:16; 15:2; 29:11; Matthew 12:34.
units.summary: Wisdom is at home in a quiet heart, while folly cannot stop announcing itself.
units.principle: True wisdom settles quietly in the heart and serves when needed, while folly cannot help displaying itself.
units.insight: At twelve years old Jesus sat among the teachers in the temple, listening and asking questions, and "all who heard Him were astonished at His understanding and answers" (Luke 2:46–47). Then He went home to Nazareth and was subject to His parents (Luke 2:51). Wisdom rested in Him; it did not need a stage. Nabal, by contrast, could not keep his folly in. When David's young men greeted him kindly, "he reviled them" (1 Samuel 25:14). Our age rewards display: the hot take, the instant opinion, the post that shows how much we know. The question is what our words reveal about our hearts. Jesus said, "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). Let Christ, "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), settle in your heart, and your words will follow.
units.application: In your next meeting or Bible study, listen longer before you speak, and ask one good question instead of offering an opinion. Students: you do not need to prove what you know in every conversation. Online, let some thoughts stay in your heart instead of your feed. Parents: praise the child who listens well, not only the one who talks most. When you must speak, let your words serve others, not impress them.

rel.note: The blessing of the upright exalts a city while the mouth of the wicked overthrows it.
The king's honor rests on a flourishing people, which righteousness makes possible.
Oppressing the poor reproaches God, one of the sins that bring reproach on a people.
A throne is established by righteousness, the same principle applied to rulers.
When the righteous are in authority the people rejoice, a nation lifted by righteousness.
A king establishes the land by justice while one who takes bribes overthrows it, righteousness lifting or ruining a whole people.

units.notes:
• The word translated "reproach" is spelled like the common Hebrew word for mercy or steadfast love, but here it is a rare word of the same spelling meaning shame or disgrace.
