Apart from this verse it occurs in Leviticus 20:17, where the NKJV has "it is a wicked thing." Young's Literal Translation reads it as "goodliness," which produces a very different sense.
• The Hebrew behind "any people" is a plural, peoples or nations, so the saying applies to every people, not to one nation only.
• Ironside: "History is but the perpetual illustration of what is here declared."
• Israel's own history shows both sides. Judah was established and honored when Jehoshaphat walked in God's ways (2 Chronicles 17:3–5, 10), and the northern kingdom was carried into exile when it forsook the LORD (2 Kings 17:7–18).
• Compare 11:11 ("By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted"); 16:12; 29:2; 29:4; Jeremiah 18:7–10.
units.summary: No nation is too great to be shamed by sin, or too small to be lifted by righteousness.
units.principle: God's moral order governs nations as well as individuals: righteousness raises a people, and sin brings disgrace on any people, however powerful.
units.insight: Nineveh was the capital of a cruel empire, yet when Jonah preached, the whole city from the king down repented, and God relented from the disaster He had announced (Jonah 3:5–10). Israel, the people God had chosen, went into exile because they "feared other gods" and rejected His statutes (2 Kings 17:7, 15). No people is too great to fall or too far gone to turn. It is easy to aim this verse at others: the other party, the other country. Daniel did the opposite. He prayed, "we have sinned and committed iniquity" (Daniel 9:5), counting himself among his people's sinners. The church is called to be salt and light within its nation (Matthew 5:13–16), and its first gift to a nation's righteousness is its own repentance and obedience.
units.application: Pray this week for your nation and its leaders by name, whatever their party (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Citizens: practice righteousness where you have influence: pay your taxes in full, tell the truth on forms, treat immigrants and the poor justly. Pastors: preach national righteousness without becoming a mouthpiece for a party. Parents: teach children that loving their country means wanting it to be good, not only great. Confess your people's sins as Daniel did, starting with your own.

rel.note: The son who sleeps in harvest causes shame, the kind of servant who draws the king's wrath.
The other royal saying of this section shows the king's honor in his people, framing the section with this verse.
Kings delight in righteous lips and love the one who speaks what is right, part of what makes a servant wise.
A wise servant will rule over a son who causes shame, the same two characters.
The man who excels in his work will stand before kings, the favor a wise servant receives.

units.notes:
• The word behind "wise" here describes a servant who acts with insight and prudence, the good sense that serves a master well. The ESV and NASB read "deals wisely" or "acts wisely."
• The royal sayings in 14:28 and 14:35 frame the last section of the chapter.
• Ironside: "Nothing causes one in authority to set value upon the services of a minister of state so much as the display of wisdom and discretion." A minister of state is a royal official.
• Daniel was distinguished above the other officials "because an excellent spirit was in him," and the king planned to set him over the whole realm (Daniel 6:3), while Haman, who brought shame, fell under the king's wrath (Esther 7:7–10).
• Compare 10:5; 16:13; 17:2; 22:29 ("Do you see a man who excels in his work? He will stand before kings"); Colossians 3:23–24.
units.summary: Wise, faithful work is noticed by earthly kings, and above all by the King of kings.
units.principle: Wise and faithful service brings honor under any good authority, while dishonest or foolish work brings shame on both the worker and the one he serves.
units.insight: Joseph served Potiphar so well that his master put everything in his hands, yet a lie sent him to prison. Even there he served wisely, and the keeper of the prison trusted him with everything (Genesis 39:4, 20–23). Earthly masters are not always fair, and wise servants are sometimes overlooked. Joseph's story shows that faithfulness is still never wasted. Paul told servants to work "as to the Lord and not to men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward" (Colossians 3:23–24). Our true Master sees the report no one reads and the classroom no one visits. The greatest Servant of all is Christ, who took "the form of a bondservant" and whom God has "highly exalted" (Philippians 2:7, 9). In Him our service is never in vain.
units.application: Employees: do your work this week as if Christ were your supervisor, especially the tasks no one will check. If you have been passed over, look first at your own work before blaming others, then keep serving faithfully. Managers: notice and reward the quiet, wise worker, not only the loud one. Church volunteers: serve with the same care on Tuesday as on Sunday. Young people starting jobs: build a reputation for good sense and reliability.

rel.note: The patient person who calms contention is the long-term form of the soft answer that turns away wrath.
The healing tongue that is a tree of life describes the same gentle speech from the side of the hearer.
A gentle tongue breaks a bone, showing the quiet strength that a soft answer carries.
The angry man who stirs up strife shows the harsh word of the second line at work in a whole personality.

units.notes:
• The words translated "harsh word" mean literally "a word of pain," a word that causes hurt. The same Hebrew word for pain is translated "labor" in 14:23 ("In all labor there is profit"). The KJV has "grievous words"; the NASB renders "soft" as "gentle."
• Scripture sets two answers side by side. Gideon calmed the angry men of Ephraim with a humble reply (Judges 8:1–3). Jephthah met the same tribe's complaint with a sharp reply, and the quarrel ended in bloodshed (Judges 12:1–6).
• Bridges: "Pride and passion on both sides strike together like two flints." ("Passion" here means hot temper; two flints struck together throw sparks.)
• Henry: "Rather than lose a jest some will lose a friend and make an enemy." (A jest is a joke.)
• Compare 15:18; 25:15; Ecclesiastes 10:4; James 1:19–20; 1 Peter 2:23.
units.summary: Anger needs fuel; a gentle answer refuses to supply it.
units.principle: We cannot control another person's anger, but we can refuse to feed it; gentleness generally calms conflict, though it never guarantees peace.
units.insight: Abigail met David on the road while he was riding to kill every man in Nabal's household. Her humble, gentle words turned him back from bloodshed, and David blessed God for her advice (1 Samuel 25:23–33). Rehoboam did the opposite. He "answered the people roughly," and the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:13–16). Our harsh words usually come from a heart that wants to win more than it wants peace. Jesus shows the better way: "when He was reviled, did not revile in return," but "committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). Gentleness becomes possible when we trust God with the outcome. Yet the cross also shows that the gentlest answer does not always stop the blows. If your gentleness was met with cruelty, the failure was not yours.
units.application: When a spouse, child or coworker comes at you hot this week, lower your voice before you answer, and respond to the issue, not the tone. Parents, model this when a teenager is angry; your calm teaches more than your rebuke. Leaders, take the sting out of a heated meeting by naming what is fair in the complaint. Gentleness does not mean staying in danger. If an exchange becomes threatening, step away and seek safety.

rel.note: The prudent man conceals knowledge until it is useful, while the heart of fools proclaims foolishness.
The mouth of fools feeds on foolishness, which is why foolishness pours out of it.
A word spoken in due season shows the timing that makes knowledge useful.
The same picture of a mouth pouring forth returns, set against the righteous heart that studies how to answer.
The lips of the wise disperse knowledge, the generous side of using knowledge rightly.

units.notes:
• "Uses knowledge rightly" is literally "makes knowledge good": the wise present what they know in a way that helps. The ESV has "commends knowledge," and the NLT "makes knowledge appealing."
• The verb behind "pours forth," naba', pictures water bubbling or gushing out of a spring. It returns in 15:28, "the mouth of the wicked pours forth evil." The ESV has "pour out," the NASB "spouts."
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Even wise counsel may be foolishly given."
• Bridges: "The wise commands his tongue. The fool—his tongue commands him."
• Compare 12:23; 15:28; Ecclesiastes 10:12–14; Colossians 4:6.
units.summary: Wise speech makes knowledge useful; foolish speech just gushes, with no filter and no aim.
units.principle: Knowledge becomes wisdom only when it is spoken with self-control, for the good of the one who hears.
units.insight: Jesus is the perfect picture of a tongue that uses knowledge rightly. He knew all things, yet He spoke to the crowds in parables "as they were able to hear it" (Mark 4:33). With the woman at the well He began by asking for a drink before He brought her life into the light (John 4:7–18). Paul stood among the idols of Athens and began from their own altar, "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD" (Acts 17:23). Many of us have the opposite problem. We know true things and say them carelessly, at the wrong time, to win rather than to help. A correct word poured out without love can close a heart that the truth was meant to open. Ask God to rule your tongue before it rules you (James 3:2–5).
units.application: Before you share what you know this week, ask three questions: Is it true? Will it help this person? Is this the time? Teachers and small-group leaders, answer the question that was asked instead of telling everything you know. Parents, give correction in a sentence, not a lecture. In online discussions, write your reply, wait an hour, and then decide whether it needs to be sent at all.

rel.note: If even the realm of the dead lies open before the LORD, the eyes that watch every place see every heart as well.
The LORD who sees every place is still far from the wicked in favor and near to hear the righteous.
The eyes of the LORD preserve knowledge and overthrow the words of the faithless, showing His watching as active care and judgment.
He who weighs the hearts knows what people claim not to know and will render to each according to his deeds.
All the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, who ponders every path.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "keeping watch," tsaphah, means to watch closely or to look out; the KJV has "beholding." The same root gives the Hebrew word for "watchman," used when God told Ezekiel, "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 3:17). The line pictures God's steady watchfulness, not a passing glance.
• Hagar, alone and mistreated in the wilderness, named the LORD "You-Are-the-God-Who-Sees" (Genesis 16:13).
• Henry: "this speaks as much comfort to saints as terror to sinners."
• G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "He is keeping watch upon the evil. It is never out of His sight."
• Compare 5:21; 15:11; 2 Chronicles 16:9; Psalm 139:1–12; Hebrews 4:13.
units.summary: No place is out of God's sight: a warning to the one who hides, a comfort to the one overlooked.
units.principle: Every life is lived in God's full view; His sight is a warning to those who hide evil and a comfort to those who do good unseen.
units.insight: Hagar ran from Sarai's harsh treatment and thought no one saw her. In the wilderness the Angel of the LORD found her, and she discovered that He is the God who sees (Genesis 16:6–13). Achan thought no one saw the silver and gold he buried under his tent, but it all came to light (Joshua 7:20–22). The same eyes saw both. Which do you feel when you remember that God is watching: dread or relief? Our answer shows what we are hiding. For the believer there is good news beyond the warning. The eyes before which "all things are naked and open" also look on our "great High Priest who has passed through the heavens," and so we may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:13–16).
units.application: If you serve where no one notices, such as caring for an aging parent, cleaning up after a church event, or praying for a wayward child, remember that God is keeping watch over your faithfulness. If you are tempted by something you would only do in secret, such as late-night browsing, padding an expense report or a private habit, picture God in the room, because He is there. Young people, integrity is who you are when only God is watching.

rel.note: The tongue of the wise promotes health, using the same word for healing, against words that pierce like a sword.
A soft answer turns away wrath, the gentle speech that this verse calls a healing tongue.
A broken spirit is harder to bear than sickness, which shows how serious the injury of perverse speech is.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, the same two outcomes this verse sets side by side.
Wisdom is first called a tree of life here, where the image and its Christ connection are treated in full.

units.notes:
• "Wholesome" translates marpe', the Hebrew word for healing; YLT has "healed tongue," and the KJV margin "the healing of the tongue." The same word is translated "health" in 12:18 and 13:17, so a wholesome tongue is one whose words heal.
• "Breaks the spirit" is literally "a breaking in the spirit." The KJV and YLT call it a "breach," the picture of a city wall broken through; the NASB says the spirit is crushed.
• Henry: "Hard words indeed break no bones, but many a heart has been broken by them."
• Ironside: "The healing tongue is the tongue of the peacemaker."
• Compare 3:18; 11:30; 12:18; 13:12; 18:21; Ephesians 4:29; James 3:5–10.
units.summary: Words can plant a tree of life in a person or knock a hole in the walls of his spirit.
units.principle: Speech is never neutral: healing words give life that keeps bearing fruit, and twisted words do damage that can last for years.
units.insight: Job's friends said many true-sounding things, but they broke a man who was already bruised, until he cried, "How long will you torment my soul, And break me in pieces with words?" (Job 19:2). Most of us can still recall a sentence spoken years ago that crushed something in us, and another that gave us life. This verse presses a harder question: which kind of sentences will others remember from us? A tongue becomes healing only when the heart behind it has been healed. Jesus spoke words of life to the broken, as to the woman dragged before Him: "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:11). In Him the tree of life is restored (Revelation 22:2), and those who feed on His words learn to speak like Him.
units.application: Think of someone whose spirit is low, such as a grieving widow, a discouraged pastor or a teenager who failed an exam, and send them a specific word of encouragement this week. Parents, notice the words you use when you are tired; sarcasm and labels like "lazy" or "stupid" break a child's spirit. If you know your words once crushed someone, go back, name what you said, and ask forgiveness. Healing words can reach old wounds.

rel.note: A wise son heeds his father’s instruction, while a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.
The one who regards a rebuke is honored, using the same verb as "receives correction" here.
The same word for instruction returns there as harsh discipline for the one who forsakes the way.
Disdaining instruction is despising one’s own soul, which shows what the fool of this verse is doing to himself.
The book’s motto says fools despise wisdom and instruction, and the father’s first appeal is to hear his instruction.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "receives," shamar, means to keep or guard. It is the same verb translated "regards" in 13:18. The prudent son holds on to correction instead of letting it go. The NASB reads "regards," the ESV "heeds."
• "Instruction," musar, is training that includes correction and discipline. The same word returns in 15:10 as "harsh discipline" and in 15:33 as "the instruction of wisdom."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "One's attitude toward parental teaching will determine one's lifelong attitude toward authority and instruction."
• A father's instruction at its best: David charged Solomon to know the God of his father and to serve Him "with a loyal heart and with a willing mind" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
• Compare 1:7–8; 12:1; 13:1, 18; 15:31–32; Hebrews 12:5–11.
units.summary: Everyone gets corrected; the difference between the fool and the wise is what they do with it.
units.principle: Correction comes to everyone; wisdom is shown not by escaping it but by receiving it.
units.insight: Eli rebuked his sons for their sins at the tabernacle, but "they did not heed the voice of their father" (1 Samuel 2:22–25), and their contempt ended in ruin. Even Jesus, who knew more than His parents, went home to Nazareth with them "and was subject to them" (Luke 2:51). Pride is the real obstacle. We despise instruction because it implies we were wrong. That pride does not stay pointed at earthly parents; a person who cannot hear a father's correction will find it hard to hear his Heavenly Father's (Hebrews 12:9). Yet the Father's correction is love, not rejection: "whom the LORD loves He corrects, Just as a father the son in whom he delights" (3:12). The prudent heart learns to hear correction as care.
units.application: Young people, the next time a parent corrects you, wait a day before deciding they are wrong, and look for what is true in what they said. Adult children, ask an older parent what they see in your life, and listen without defending yourself. Parents, keep instructing even when it seems ignored; a son may keep your words long after he resisted them. Employees, receive a supervisor's correction as training, not insult.

rel.note: The blessing of the LORD makes rich and adds no sorrow, the kind of treasure the righteous house holds.
A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, which keeps this verse from becoming a promise of wealth.
The greedy man troubles his own house, showing how wicked revenue brings trouble home.
The LORD curses the house of the wicked and blesses the home of the just, the same two houses seen here.

units.notes:
• YLT renders "much treasure" as "abundant strength," which draws out the sense of a household's stored-up resources, not money alone.
• In English the word "trouble" links 15:6, 15:16 and 15:27, three sayings about gain. The link is in the English and the theme, not in one Hebrew word; 15:16 uses a different word, one that describes turmoil.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Every righteous man is a rich man, whether he hath more or less of the things of this life." ("Hath" means "has.")
• Compare 3:33; 10:22; 15:16; Ecclesiastes 5:12; 1 Timothy 6:9–10.
units.summary: A righteous home holds treasure money cannot measure; a wicked income carries trouble money cannot cure.
units.principle: Wealth is only as good as what comes with it; God's blessing on an upright home outweighs any income gained by wrong.
units.insight: Achan saw a beautiful robe, silver and a wedge of gold, coveted them and hid them in his tent. The treasure brought trouble on his whole family (Joshua 7:20–26). By contrast, the widow of Zarephath had only a handful of flour and a little oil, yet her house did not run dry, because God was in it (1 Kings 17:12–16). The question for our hearts is not "How much do I have?" but "What comes with it?" Paul could describe himself "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Corinthians 6:10). In Christ the poorest believer's house holds treasure that the richest unbeliever cannot buy.
units.application: Before taking the extra deal, the shortcut or the questionable overtime claim, ask what it will bring home besides money. Business owners, refuse profit that depends on misleading customers, even if it costs a contract. Families with little, thank God together for the treasure in your house: peace, faith and one another. Parents, show your children that your home's real riches are not in the garage or the bank account.

rel.note: The lips of the righteous feed many, the same generous use of speech as dispersing knowledge.
The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, while the perverse tongue will be cut out.
The heart of the understanding seeks knowledge, which explains why the wise have knowledge to scatter and the fool has none.
The tongue of the wise makes knowledge good, the skill that lies behind spreading it well.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "disperse" means to scatter, as YLT renders it, so the wise spread knowledge widely.
• The second line ends with two short Hebrew words that the NKJV and ESV render "not so." YLT reads them "not right," which makes the line a judgment on the fool's heart itself rather than a statement that it does not spread knowledge.
• Henry: "it is not only a fault to pour out foolishness, but it is a shame not to disperse knowledge."
• Bridges, on those who keep what they know to themselves: "If not blots, they are blanks in the Church." (A blot does harm; a blank does nothing at all.)
• Compare 10:21; 10:31; Ecclesiastes 11:6; Matthew 13:3–9; 2 Timothy 2:2.
units.summary: The wise sow knowledge like seed in other lives; a foolish heart has nothing worth scattering.
units.principle: Knowledge is given to be shared; what a person spreads to others reveals what fills his heart.
units.insight: When persecution drove the believers out of Jerusalem, "those who were scattered went everywhere preaching the word" (Acts 8:4). Wise lips scatter seed wherever they are sent. Paul told Timothy to commit what he had heard "to faithful men who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). Knowledge that stops with us is wasted. Many believers have sat under good teaching for years and never passed a single truth to another person. That silence may say more about our hearts than about our knowledge. The servant who buried his one talent did no obvious harm, yet his master called him "wicked and lazy" (Matthew 25:26). Christ the Sower, the Son of Man who sows the good seed (Matthew 13:37), still scatters His word through ordinary lips.
units.application: Choose one truth God has taught you this year and pass it to someone younger in the faith this week, over coffee, in a text or at the dinner table. Grandparents, tell your grandchildren how God has been faithful to you. Small-group members, do not leave all the sharing to the leader. Experienced employees, take time to train the new hire instead of guarding what you know.

rel.note: The thoughts of the wicked complete the chapter’s three abominations, after their worship here and their way in 15:9.
The LORD hears the prayer of the righteous, restating the second line of this verse at the end of the chapter.
The next verse widens the view from the worship of the wicked to their whole way of life.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, and still more when it is brought with wicked intent.
Even the prayer of one who turns his ear from the law is an abomination, the same principle applied to prayer.

units.notes:
• "Abomination" appears three times in this chapter (15:8, 9, 26), each time set against what pleases the LORD: the worship, the way and the thoughts of the wicked.
• "His delight" translates ratson, a word for favor or acceptance, the same word translated "favor" in 14:9. The ESV reads "acceptable." The prayer of the upright is welcomed by God.
• Proverbs presses the point further: "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; How much more when he brings it with wicked intent!" (21:27). Compare 28:9, where even the prayer of one who refuses to hear the law is an abomination.
• Bridges: "Man judges by acts; God by principles." (By "principles" he means the motives and convictions behind the act.)
• Compare 1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 51:16–17; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24; Matthew 15:8.
units.summary: God weighs the worshiper before He receives the worship.
units.principle: God does not accept worship as a substitute for an upright heart, but He delights in the simplest prayer of one who walks with Him.
units.insight: Saul spared the best of Amalek's sheep and oxen, claiming they were "to sacrifice to the LORD," and Samuel answered, "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:21–22). Cain brought an offering, but God did not respect "Cain and his offering," because the problem lay in Cain himself (Genesis 4:5–7). We are not so different. It is easy to hope that church attendance, giving or serving will balance a sin we refuse to give up. God is not bought. Yet the second line is pure grace: the faintest prayer from an upright heart is His delight. The tax collector could only say, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" and he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). Through Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, the way into God's presence stands open to all who come with a true heart (Hebrews 10:19–22).
units.application: Before you give, sing or serve this Sunday, ask whether there is a sin you are refusing to forsake, or a wrong you have not made right; deal with it first (Matthew 5:23–24). Worship leaders and teachers, guard your private life more carefully than your public performance. If you feel too sinful to pray, pray anyway and tell God the truth; He delights in the prayer of a heart that turns to Him. Parents, teach children that God wants their hearts, not only their church manners.

rel.note: The LORD detests those of a perverse heart and delights in the blameless in their ways.
The thoughts of the wicked are the chapter’s third abomination, reaching beneath the way of life to the plans of the heart.
The verse before shows that the worship of the wicked is rejected because, as this verse explains, their way is rejected.
The one who follows righteousness and mercy finds life, righteousness and honor, the outcome of the pursuit God loves.
The path of the just grows brighter while the way of the wicked is darkness, showing what "way" means as the direction of a life.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "follows," radaph, means to pursue or chase. It is the same verb used in 13:21, where evil "pursues sinners." The ESV and NASB read "pursues."
• "The way" in Proverbs means the whole course of a life, the habits and direction a person keeps (compare 4:18–19).
• Henry: "he loves him who, though he have not yet attained, is following after righteousness, aiming at it and pressing towards it."
• Compare 11:20; 21:21; Psalm 1:6; Philippians 3:12–14; 1 Timothy 6:11.
units.summary: God does not only watch how we worship; He watches the road we walk all week.
units.principle: God judges the whole direction of a life, not isolated religious acts, and His love rests on those who keep pursuing what is right.
units.insight: Paul did not claim to have arrived: "Not that I have already attained, or am already perfected; but I press on" (Philippians 3:12). That is the person this verse says God loves, not the flawless but the one who keeps pursuing. David fell badly, yet he kept returning to the LORD, and God called him a man after His own heart (Acts 13:22). By contrast, the scribes and Pharisees kept careful religious forms while their way was full of greed and self-indulgence (Matthew 23:23–25). Where is your life running this week, toward righteousness or away from it? Christ Himself has become our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). Those who belong to Him are not yet perfect, but they are running after Him.
units.application: Look at your calendar and your bank statement from the past month; together they show the "way" you are walking. Name one area where you are coasting, and choose one concrete step of pursuit this week, such as a daily Scripture reading, a hard conversation or a generous gift. If you are discouraged by failure, remember that God loves the one who follows righteousness, not only the one who has finished. Mentors, praise direction, not only results.

rel.note: He who hates correction is called stupid, the same hatred of correction this verse warns against.
The scoffer who will not go to the wise shows how a person settles into hating correction.
Disdaining instruction is despising one’s own soul, the inner reason refusing correction ends in death.
The same word for instruction appears there as a father’s training, which here returns as harsh discipline.
The one who is often rebuked and hardens his neck is suddenly destroyed, the same road from refused correction to ruin.

units.notes:
• "Harsh discipline" is literally "bad discipline," using musar, the word for a father's instruction in 15:5; here it means painful correction. The KJV reads "Correction is grievous," and the ESV speaks of "severe discipline."
• "Forsakes the way" pictures someone who has left the right path he once knew, not merely someone who never found it.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "He that is embittered by rebukes, and not bettered by chastisements, shall die."
• King Amaziah silenced the prophet who rebuked him for turning to Edom's gods, and the prophet told him that God had determined to destroy him because he would not heed advice (2 Chronicles 25:14–16).
• Compare 5:11–13; 12:1; 13:18; 29:1; Hebrews 12:11.
units.summary: Correction refused gently comes back harshly, and the one who hates every warning is walking toward death.
units.principle: Correction refused does not disappear; it returns in harder forms, and the heart that hates every warning closes its own way back.
units.insight: Pharaoh heard warning after warning and hardened his heart each time, until the sea closed over his army (Exodus 14:26–28). Manasseh shows the other possibility. When he would not listen to the LORD's warnings, he was taken in chains to Babylon, and there he "humbled himself greatly" and prayed, and God brought him home (2 Chronicles 33:10–13). Harsh discipline can become the doorway back. The real danger is not being corrected but hating correction. Each of us has a place where we bristle when someone names our sin, and that reaction deserves attention before it hardens. For the Christian, even severe discipline comes from a Father who "scourges every son whom He receives" (Hebrews 12:6), so that we may share His holiness and live.
units.application: Think about the warnings you have heard more than once, from a spouse, a doctor, a pastor or your own conscience. Pick one and act on it this week, before it comes back harder. Parents of a rebellious teenager, keep warning and keep praying; Manasseh shows that hard consequences can still turn a heart. If you lead people, give correction early and gently, so that it does not need to become harsh later.

rel.note: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, the truth this verse carries down to the realm of the dead and the human heart.
A man’s ways seem pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirits.
Every way seems right to the one who walks it, but the LORD weighs the hearts.
The same pair, Hell and Destruction, appears as a picture of what is never satisfied.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew words are Sheol and Abaddon, as the ESV and NASB render them; the 1984 NIV reads "Death" for Sheol. The NKJV capitalizes "Destruction" here and in Job 26:6, treating it like a name.
• Abaddon appears again in Revelation 9:11 as the Hebrew name of the angel of the bottomless pit, whose Greek name is Apollyon.
• "How much more" is an argument from the greater to the lesser: if the harder thing is true, the easier thing must be true as well. If God sees the hidden world of the dead, He certainly sees a living heart.
• Henry: "God is greater than our hearts, and knows them better than we know them ourselves."
• Compare 15:3; 16:2; 21:2; 1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Hebrews 4:13.
units.summary: If God sees into the grave, no human heart can hide from Him.
units.principle: Nothing is hidden from God, not even the realm of the dead, so every human heart lies open before Him.
units.insight: Ananias and Sapphira sold land and kept back part of the price while pretending to give it all. The church saw a generous gift; God saw the heart, and Peter asked, "why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?" (Acts 5:3). Our hearts are skilled at hiding, even from ourselves (Jeremiah 17:9). That should sober us. Yet God's knowledge is also a mercy. When Peter had denied Jesus three times, he could only appeal to the Lord's knowledge of his heart: "Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You" (John 21:17). The One who sees everything forgives and covers the sin of those who trust Him (Psalm 32:1). So we can pray with David, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23).
units.application: Before you pray this week, take five minutes to ask God to show you a motive you have been hiding, perhaps the real reason behind a decision, or a resentment you have been calling "concern." If others misjudge your motives, rest in the fact that God knows your heart. Counselors, pastors and parents, remember that you see only the surface; leave final judgments of hearts to God (1 Corinthians 4:5).

rel.note: A scoffer does not listen to rebuke, while a wise son heeds his father’s instruction.
He who walks with wise men will be wise, which shows what the scoffer forfeits by refusing to go to them.
The one who hates correction will die, and this verse shows how the scoffer walks that road.
The ear that hears life-giving rebuke abides among the wise, the very company the scoffer avoids.
Correcting a scoffer earns his hatred, while rebuking a wise man earns his love.

units.notes:
• The scoffer is the person who mocks what is serious and refuses to be taught. The NKJV calls him both "scoffer" and "scorner," but they are one figure (compare 1:22; 9:7–8; 13:1).
• The ESV frames the first line around his dislike of being reproved. The Hebrew speaks of "one who corrects him," as the NKJV and NASB show, so the scoffer resents the person, not only the correction.
• Bridges: "The scorner has been his own flatterer so long, that he cannot bear to be brought down to his proper level."
• Henry: "We ought not only to bid the wise welcome when they come to us, but to go to them."
• Compare 9:7–8; 13:1, 20; 15:31; John 3:20.
units.summary: The scoffer stays a scoffer by avoiding the very people who could help him.
units.principle: Resenting correction leads a person to avoid the wise, and avoiding the wise locks folly in place.
units.insight: King Ahab had a prophet who told him the truth, and he said of Micaiah, "I hate him, because he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil" (1 Kings 22:8). He surrounded himself with agreeable voices and died in the battle Micaiah warned him against. Herod imprisoned John the Baptist for naming his sin, though he still liked to hear him (Mark 6:17–20). Scorn rarely announces itself. It shows up as quietly avoiding certain people: a certain friend, a certain sermon, a certain small group. Whom have you stopped calling because they tell you the truth? Jesus came to scoffers too. On the cross, while rulers sneered at Him, He prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34–35). The way back begins by going to the wise.
units.application: Name one person who has corrected you in the past year and whom you have quietly avoided since. Reach out this week and ask what else they see. Young adults, choose at least one older mentor who is free to tell you hard things. Leaders, check whether your inner circle contains anyone who disagrees with you. If you correct a scoffer and he turns on you, do not take it personally; Proverbs said he would.

rel.note: Anxiety weighs a heart down, while a good word makes it glad.
The merry heart returns two verses later as a continual feast, even when the days are hard.
The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, the outward side of the same link between face and heart.
A merry heart does good like medicine, while a broken spirit dries the bones.
A person’s spirit can sustain him in sickness, but no one can bear a broken spirit, which shows how deep this injury goes.

units.notes:
• "Merry" describes a glad, joyful heart, not empty frivolity. Bridges: "This merriment, however, widely differs from the noisy mirth of the ungodly."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, on the second line: "The words used here stress the pain and the depression with a note of despair."
• A related saying appears in 17:22: "A merry heart does good, like medicine, But a broken spirit dries the bones."
• Nehemiah could not hide his grief, and the king read it on his face: "This is nothing but sorrow of heart" (Nehemiah 2:2).
• Compare 12:25; 14:10, 13; 18:14; 2 Corinthians 7:10.
units.summary: The face shows the weather of the heart, and some storms reach deeper than the face.
units.principle: The state of the heart shapes the whole person; joy shows on the face, and deep sorrow can crush the spirit itself.
units.insight: Hannah wept and would not eat; she prayed "in bitterness of soul" (1 Samuel 1:7–10). After she poured out her heart to the LORD and received Eli's blessing, "her face was no longer sad" (1 Samuel 1:18). Her circumstances had not yet changed, but her heart had. Some people around us carry a broken spirit behind a smile, and others cannot smile at all. Neither needs a lecture. Jesus came "to heal the brokenhearted" (Luke 4:18), and He Himself was "a Man of sorrows and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3). He does not shame the sorrowful; He carries their sorrows (Isaiah 53:4). If your spirit is crushed today, you are not failing God. You are exactly the kind of person He came to bind up.
units.application: Watch faces this week: the coworker who has stopped smiling, the church member who slips out early, the child who has gone quiet. Ask a gentle question and listen without trying to fix things. If your own spirit feels crushed, do not hide it; tell a trusted friend or pastor, and consider seeing a doctor or counselor. Do not tell grieving people to cheer up. Sit with them, as Job's friends did before they spoke (Job 2:13).

rel.note: The mouth of fools pours out foolishness, the output of a mouth that has fed on it.
The lips of the wise disperse knowledge, which they have because their hearts sought it.
The heart of the prudent acquires knowledge and the ear of the wise seeks it.
A wise man will hear and increase learning, the same hunger that keeps the understanding heart seeking.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "feeds," ra'ah, is the one used for shepherding or grazing a flock; here it pictures fools steadily feeding on folly. The NLT renders the line "the fool feeds on trash."
• Ironside: "We become like that on which we feed; and we feed on what our hearts crave."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "As a hungry man seeks meat, or a covetous man gold, the more he hath, the more he desires." ("Meat" here means food, and "hath" means "has.")
• The Bereans "searched the Scriptures daily" to test what they heard, a picture of the understanding heart that keeps seeking (Acts 17:11).
• Compare 1:5; 9:9; 18:15; Psalm 119:103; Hebrews 5:14.
units.summary: You become what you feed on: the wise hunger for truth, while fools graze on trash.
units.principle: What we hunger for shapes who we become; understanding grows by seeking, and folly grows by feeding on what cannot nourish.
units.insight: Mary of Bethany "sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word," and Jesus said she had chosen "that good part" (Luke 10:39, 42). In the wilderness the mixed multitude lost their appetite for manna because they craved the food of Egypt (Numbers 11:4–6). Appetite is shaped by what we keep eating. Many believers wonder why they have no hunger for Scripture, while they graze for hours on news, feeds and gossip. The diet explains the appetite. Jesus is the bread of life (John 6:35), and Jeremiah could say, "Your words were found, and I ate them, And Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart" (Jeremiah 15:16). Hunger for God grows as we feed on Him.
units.application: Track for three days what you feed your mind on: screens, podcasts, conversations and reading. Then replace one hour of grazing with something that builds understanding, such as reading a book of the Bible straight through. Parents, notice what your children consume, and offer them better food instead of only banning the bad. Students, ask one more question in class; seeking is a habit before it is a gift.

rel.note: Even in laughter the heart may sorrow, a reminder that outward appearances do not settle a person’s inner state.
A merry heart and a broken spirit appear two verses earlier, describing the same inner life from another angle.
A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, which names the source of the continual feast.
A merry heart does good like medicine, the same strength of a glad heart in hard conditions.

units.notes:
• "Afflicted" translates 'ani, a word often used for the poor and oppressed; the 1984 NIV renders it "oppressed." The ESV calls the second man "cheerful," and YLT calls his feast a "perpetual banquet."
• Henry says the afflicted are "not to be censured or despised, but pitied and prayed for, succoured and comforted." ("Succoured" means helped.)
• Habakkuk shows the merry heart amid loss: "Though the fig tree may not blossom, Nor fruit be on the vines... Yet I will rejoice in the LORD" (Habakkuk 3:17–18).
• Compare 14:10; 15:13; 17:22; 2 Corinthians 6:10; Philippians 4:11–13.
units.summary: Hard days are real, but a heart at rest in God can make plain bread a feast.
units.principle: Outward hardship is real, but joy rooted in God can nourish a person in every circumstance; the afflicted deserve compassion, not blame.
units.insight: Paul and Silas sat in the inner prison with their feet in stocks after a severe beating, and at midnight they "were praying and singing hymns to God" (Acts 16:23–25). By every outward measure their day was evil, yet they had a feast. Paul later wrote from another prison, "I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). Notice the word "learned." The merry heart is not a personality type; it grows as we trust Christ in hard places. Yet this verse must never become a rod to beat the afflicted. Job's friends did that. If your days are hard, God does not scold you for it. He invites you to His table, where Christ Himself is the bread of life (John 6:35).
units.application: If you are in a hard season, begin each day this week by naming three gifts from God before you name the problems. It will not erase the pain, but it feeds the heart. Friends of the afflicted, do not tell them to be happy; bring a meal, sit with them and pray. Pastors and small-group leaders, check on members facing long illness, unemployment or caregiving, whose days run together.

rel.note: The continual feast of the merry heart is explained here: a little held with the fear of the LORD.
The next verse makes the same comparison with love at the table instead of the fear of the LORD.
The house of the righteous holds treasure while wicked revenue brings trouble, the same contrast seen from the side of gain.
A little with righteousness is better than vast revenues without justice.
A dry morsel with quietness is better than a house full of feasting with strife.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind "trouble," mehumah, describes turmoil or agitation. The NASB reads "turmoil," YLT "tumult," and the ESV keeps "trouble." It is a different word from the "trouble" of 15:6.
• A similar comparison appears in 16:8: "Better is a little with righteousness, Than vast revenues without justice." Compare also Psalm 37:16.
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "Riches and poverty are more in the heart than in the hand."
• Henry: "Those that have great treasure have often great trouble therewith." ("Therewith" means "with it.")
• Compare Ecclesiastes 4:6; 5:12; Luke 12:15; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5.
units.summary: Money can buy a bigger house, but not the peace the fear of the LORD brings into it.
units.principle: What we have matters less than whether we have it with God; contentment in the fear of the LORD outweighs wealth that comes with turmoil.
units.insight: Lot chose the well-watered plain near Sodom and gained wealth, but he lost almost everything else (Genesis 13:10–13; 19:15–26). Abram stayed in Canaan with God's promise (Genesis 13:14–17). The rich fool built bigger barns, and God said, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). Our culture measures life by accumulation, and so do our hearts. Paul answers that "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1 Timothy 6:6). The secret of contentment is not having less but having God. Jesus had nowhere to lay His head (Matthew 8:20), yet He is Himself the treasure. Whoever has Him has enough, and whoever lacks Him has nothing that lasts.
units.application: If you are weighing a promotion, a move or a second job this year, ask what it will do to your time with God and your peace at home, not only to your income. Young couples, do not let a bigger first house buy years of financial pressure. Those with little, thank God aloud this week for His provision. Those with much, give generously enough that money loosens its grip on you.

rel.note: Hatred stirs up strife but love covers all sins, which explains why love can make a plain meal rich.
The verse before makes the same comparison with the fear of the LORD, and together they rank God and people above wealth.
A dry morsel with quietness is better than a house full of feasting with strife.
The miser who says "Eat and drink!" while his heart is not with you shows a fine table spoiled by a grudging heart.

units.notes:
• The KJV renders "fatted calf" as a "stalled ox," an animal fattened in a stall rather than left to graze. The ESV and NASB read "fattened ox."
• A similar saying appears in 17:1: "Better is a dry morsel with quietness, Than a house full of feasting with strife."
• The finest meal can be a battlefield. Saul's new-moon feast ended with him hurling a spear at his own son (1 Samuel 20:24–34), and Absalom's sheep-shearing feast became the setting for murdering his brother (2 Samuel 13:23–29).
• Henry: "better have a slender dinner and be heartily welcome than a table richly spread with a grudging evil eye." (An "evil eye" here means a stingy, resentful host, not a curse.)
• Compare Psalm 133:1; Acts 2:46; 1 Corinthians 13:3.
units.summary: What is on the table matters less than the love around it.
units.principle: Love makes a modest table rich and hatred spoils the richest one; the quality of relationships outweighs the quality of provisions.
units.insight: After His resurrection, Jesus cooked breakfast on a beach, bread and fish over a charcoal fire, for disciples who had failed Him (John 21:9–13). It was a simple meal, full of restoring love. Compare the elder brother outside the feast for his returning brother. His father had killed the fatted calf, but the older son "was angry and would not go in" (Luke 15:27–28). The best meat in the house could not reach a heart full of resentment. Many homes have full tables and cold hearts, and the problem is rarely the menu. What would change if your family's meals carried more love and less tension? The gospel brings us to the Lord's own table, where forgiven people share one bread together (1 Corinthians 10:16–17).
units.application: Plan one simple family meal this week with phones put away and one question everyone answers. If there is tension at your table, settle it before the meal, not during it. Hosts, do not wait until you can afford to entertain well; soup and bread with a warm welcome are enough. Church leaders, keep fellowship meals simple enough that anyone can host and anyone can come.

rel.note: He who is slow to wrath has great understanding, while the impulsive exalts folly.
A soft answer turns away wrath, the single reply that a patient temperament gives again and again.
The one slow to anger is better than the mighty, which shows that patience is strength, not weakness.
A contentious man kindles strife as charcoal feeds burning coals and wood feeds fire.
An angry man stirs up strife and a furious man abounds in transgression.

units.notes:
• "Wrathful man" is literally "a man of heat." The word, chemah, means both heat and rage. The ESV and NASB read "hot-tempered"; the KJV says the patient man "appeaseth strife."
• "Slow to anger" translates the same Hebrew expression used of God Himself in Exodus 34:6, where the NKJV renders it "longsuffering."
• Ironside: "A wrathful man is of necessity a proud man; otherwise he would not be so easily stirred by what touches himself."
• Saul's jealous rage over a victory song drove him to hurl a spear at David (1 Samuel 18:6–11), while David twice refused to strike Saul when he had the chance (1 Samuel 24:4–12; 26:8–11).
• Compare 14:29; 16:32; 26:21; 29:22; James 1:19–20.
units.summary: A hot temper carries matches into every room; a patient spirit carries water.
units.principle: A short temper multiplies conflict and patience calms it, so temperament is a moral matter, not merely a personality trait.
units.insight: After Israel made the golden calf, the LORD passed before Moses and proclaimed His own name as "merciful and gracious, longsuffering" (Exodus 34:6), slow to anger, the very quality this verse praises. Peter says the Lord's patience is the reason people still have time to repent (2 Peter 3:9). Every believer is alive and forgiven because God is slow to anger. That changes how we treat the people who provoke us. Often a quick temper is pride defending itself: someone has touched what I think I deserve. The way out is not merely counting to ten but kneeling at the cross, where we see how patient God has been with us. Those who have received His patience learn to pass it on.
units.application: Notice where conflict follows you: the same arguments at home, the same tension at work. Ask a trusted friend whether you are the common factor. When you feel the heat rising this week, delay your response: leave the room, take a walk, or sleep on the email. Parents, model a calm apology after you lose your temper. Leaders, do not let a hot-tempered person set the tone of your meetings.

rel.note: The lazy man desires and has nothing while the diligent are made rich, the outcome of the blocked and open roads.
The lazy man’s claim that a lion is outside is one of the thorns he plants in his own way.
The lazy man’s field overgrown with thorns shows where his hedge of excuses finally leads.
The lazy man sees a lion in the road, the same imagined obstacle that blocks his path.

units.notes:
• "Is a highway" is literally "is raised up," the picture of a built-up road cleared for travel, as YLT renders it; the ESV reads "level highway."
• The NKJV uses "lazy man" here; the ESV reads "sluggard." The Hebrew word is the same as in 6:6, 6:9 and 13:4.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "Unthinking persons suppose that the sluggard lives a happy life, and travels an easy road."
• Bridges: "The difficulties are far more in the mind than in the path."
• Compare 6:6–11; 20:4; 22:13; 24:30–34; 26:13–16; Matthew 25:26.
units.summary: The lazy man plants his own thorns and then complains that the road is blocked.
units.principle: Laziness magnifies obstacles until they become excuses, while uprightness and honest diligence find the road open; laziness is a moral matter, distinct from inability or need.
units.insight: The ten spies and Caleb saw the same land. Ten saw only giants and walled cities and talked Israel into forty years of wandering; Caleb and Joshua saw God's promise (Numbers 13:30–14:9). Some of the thorns were real, but unbelief turned them into an impassable hedge. The servant who buried his talent blamed his master as "a hard man" (Matthew 25:24–26). Laziness always has a story about why the path is blocked. Where in your life, whether in work, prayer or a reconciliation you keep postponing, have you mistaken an excuse for a wall? Christ calls us to follow Him now, not when the road looks clear, and He gives strength for each step (Philippians 4:13).
units.application: Write down the task you have postponed longest and the reasons you have given. Cross out the excuses and do the first fifteen minutes today. Students, start the assignment the day it is given. Employees, finish one thing before starting the next. Parents, help a child break a big chore into small steps instead of letting them stall. If illness or limitation is the real barrier, seek help; that is not laziness.

rel.note: The first line repeats the opening saying of Solomon’s collection, where a foolish son is his mother’s grief.
The father’s first appeal is to hear a father’s instruction and not forsake a mother’s law.
The father of the righteous rejoices, and the son is urged to let his father and mother be glad.
The eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother comes to a terrible end.

units.notes:
• The first line uses the same Hebrew words in the same order as 10:1; "makes a father glad" here and "makes a glad father" there are only different English renderings. The second lines differ: in 10:1 a foolish son is "the grief of his mother," while here the foolish man actively despises her.
• Ironside: "A foolish man considers himself superior to his mother, and ignores her loving advice and helpful counsel."
• The command to honor father and mother is "the first commandment with promise" (Ephesians 6:2; Exodus 20:12).
• Compare 10:1; 17:25; 23:22–25; 30:17.
units.summary: A son's wisdom gladdens his father; a grown man's contempt for his mother exposes his folly.
units.principle: How grown children treat their parents reveals their character; wisdom brings joy to a home, and contempt for parents marks folly.
units.insight: Even from the cross, in agony, Jesus looked down and provided for His mother, entrusting her to John (John 19:26–27). He honored her when it cost Him most. Absalom shows the other path. He turned against his father and broke his heart, and David's cry, "O my son Absalom—my son, my son Absalom" (2 Samuel 18:33), shows how a son's folly wounds a parent. Adult children face quieter temptations: impatience with aging parents, embarrassment at their ways, the assumption that education or success has put us above them. That is the contempt this verse names. Honoring parents does not require agreeing with them on everything or excusing what was wrong, but it never looks down on them. Christ's care for Mary shows the heart of wisdom.
units.application: Adult children, call or visit a parent this week, ask for their advice on something real, and thank them. If a parent is aging, look for one practical way to lighten their load. Teenagers, notice your tone with your mother; contempt often begins as eye-rolling. Parents, the joy you want from your children grows best when you pray for their wisdom more than for their success.

rel.note: To do evil is like sport to a fool, but a man of understanding has wisdom.
Those who leave the paths of uprightness rejoice in doing evil, the same joy in folly.
The father urges a straight path that turns neither right nor left, the walk of the man of understanding.
The young man "devoid of understanding" is the one who wanders toward the immoral woman’s house, showing where joy in folly leads.

units.notes:
• "Destitute of discernment" is literally "lacking heart." In Hebrew the heart is the seat of understanding as well as feeling, so a person who lacks heart lacks sense. The same expression describes the young man led astray in 7:7, "A young man devoid of understanding."
• "Walks uprightly" is literally "makes his going straight"; the ESV reads "walks straight ahead."
• Henry, on the one who delights in folly: "He sins, not only without regret, but with delight."
• Compare 2:13–14; 10:23; 4:25–27; Ephesians 5:15–17; Hebrews 11:25.
units.summary: Show me what you enjoy, and I will show you the road you are walking.
units.principle: Delight in folly reveals a lack of understanding, while a wise person finds his satisfaction in walking a straight path.
units.insight: Samson treated his calling like a game. He enjoyed his riddles, his revenge and Delilah's company, until he woke up blind and bound (Judges 16:19–21). His folly was joy to him almost to the end. Moses chose the opposite, "choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin" (Hebrews 11:25). Our enjoyments are a mirror. What makes us laugh, what we scroll toward and what we look forward to all show what our hearts love. The cure is not a joyless life but a new delight. The person who has tasted Christ finds that "In Your presence is fullness of joy" (Psalm 16:11), and the straight path becomes the place of joy.
units.application: Look at what you laughed at or enjoyed last week: shows, jokes and conversations. Ask plainly whether any of it was folly you have learned to call fun. Parents, talk with your teenagers about the difference between harmless fun and pleasure that leads somewhere dark. Young adults, when friends call something "just fun," ask where it leads in five years. Replace one habit of empty amusement with something that delights you and builds you up.

rel.note: Where there is no counsel the people fall, but in the multitude of counselors there is safety.
The fool is right in his own eyes, while the one who heeds counsel is wise.
The same word for plans appears there, where God judges the schemes of the wicked before they are carried out.
Plans are established by counsel, using the same picture of plans made firm.
Wise counsel guides even a war, and many counselors bring safety.

units.notes:
• The word behind "counsel" in the first line, sod, means counsel taken together in close, confidential conversation; the NASB renders it "consultation." The second line uses a different word for the people who give counsel: "counselors" in the NKJV and KJV, "advisers" in the ESV.
• "Plans" translates the same Hebrew word that is rendered "thoughts" in 15:26, where the plans of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD.
• Henry gives a Latin proverb and its meaning: "Many eyes see more than one."
• The KJV reads "Without counsel purposes are disappointed," the picture of plans that come to nothing.
• Compare 11:14; 12:15; 13:10; 19:20; 20:18; 24:6.
units.summary: One mind sees part of the picture; many wise minds see the whole.
units.principle: Wise plans are tested in the company of wise counselors; refusing advice exposes plans to dangers one person cannot see.
units.insight: Rehoboam did ask for counsel. He heard the elders' wise advice and rejected it, then took the advice of the young men he had grown up with, who told him what he wanted to hear. The kingdom split (1 Kings 12:6–16). His problem was not a lack of counselors but a desire for agreement. In Acts 15 the early church faced its hardest question together, with apostles and elders listening to one another, and its decision "seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us" (Acts 15:28). Self-reliance often hides pride. Christ is called "Wonderful, Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), and He often guides through His word and His people together.
units.application: Before a major decision this month, such as a job change, a large purchase or a new ministry, list three wise people who will tell you the truth, and ask each of them. Include at least one who is likely to disagree. Couples, make big decisions together, not alone. Pastors and business leaders, build a team that can say no to you, and give them real permission to do it.

rel.note: A good word makes an anxious heart glad, showing what a well-timed word can do for the hearer.
The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly, and timing is part of using it rightly.
The righteous heart studies how to answer, the preparation that makes a timely word possible.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver, a picture of the timely word.

units.notes:
• "In due season" is literally "in its season," at its proper time; the ESV reads "in season."
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "This proverb sets forth the satisfaction of being able to say the right thing at the right moment."
• Ironside: "True words are not necessarily seasonable ones."
• Abigail shows the timing of a word: she waited until Nabal was sober the next morning before telling him what she had done (1 Samuel 25:36–37).
• Compare 12:25; 25:11; Ecclesiastes 3:7; Isaiah 50:4; Colossians 4:6.
units.summary: A true word becomes a good word when it arrives at the right moment.
units.principle: A word is good not only when it is true but when it is fitting and well-timed; the wise learn when to speak as well as what to say.
units.insight: Isaiah foretold the Servant of the LORD, who would say, "The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary" (Isaiah 50:4). Jesus fulfilled it. To a sinful woman weeping at a Pharisee's table He said, "Your faith has saved you. Go in peace" (Luke 7:50). To grieving Martha He spoke of resurrection before He wept with Mary (John 11:23–35). Most of us have spoken true words at the wrong time and watched them wound. Others have stayed silent when a word was needed. Ask the Lord for His timing as well as His words. The joy of a well-timed word is that it serves someone else, not ourselves.
units.application: Before you give hard news, correction or advice this week, ask whether this is the moment: is the person rested, calm and able to hear? Spouses, do not raise a serious issue at bedtime or in the middle of an argument. Friends of the grieving, offer presence first and explanations much later, if ever. Leaders, praise people promptly; encouragement loses much of its power when it comes late.

rel.note: The law of the wise turns one away from the snares of death, the same turning this verse describes.
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life that turns one away from the snares of death.
The path of the just shines brighter while the way of the wicked is darkness, another picture of two directions.
The immoral woman’s house is the way to hell, descending to the chambers of death, the downward road this verse turns from.
Folly’s guests are in the depths of hell, the opposite end of the upward way.

units.notes:
• The ESV, NASB and YLT read "Sheol" here, the same Hebrew word that stands behind "Hell" in 15:11; the 1984 NIV reads "the grave."
• The KJV reads "The way of life is above to the wise." The Hebrew is literally "on high," the same upward picture the NKJV gives with "winds upward."
• Ironside reads the verse in terms of a long life in this world, explaining that for the faithful Israelite "an early cutting off from this present life was a calamity to be dreaded."
• Some older commentators take the verse further. Henry calls it "the way that leads to eternal life." That reading fits the hope of the whole Bible, but this verse alone does not establish it.
• Compare 4:18–19; 13:14; 14:27; Matthew 7:13–14; Colossians 3:1–2.
units.summary: Every life is on a path that climbs or descends; wisdom climbs toward life.
units.principle: Wisdom sets a life on an upward course toward life and away from death, and every life is moving in one direction or the other.
units.insight: Hezekiah, told he would die, wept and prayed, and God added fifteen years to his life (Isaiah 38:1–5). For him, being turned away from Sheol meant more days on earth to walk with God. Jesus spoke of the same two directions: a broad way that leads to destruction and a narrow way that leads to life (Matthew 7:13–14). He did not leave the way as a mere direction; He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Few people drift upward. Paths that go down usually feel easy, and paths that climb take effort. Ask which way your habits, friendships and desires are taking you. Whoever follows Christ is walking uphill toward life.
units.application: Take an honest look at the direction of your life over the past year. Are your habits, friendships and use of time moving you up or down? Choose one downhill habit, such as an evening routine that crowds out God or a friendship that pulls you toward sin, and replace it this week. Parents, talk with your children about direction, not only single choices. Mentors, help younger believers see where small daily steps are leading them.

rel.note: The section that opens with the proud brought down closes with humility before honor.
Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD, the reason He tears down the proud man’s house.
The LORD pleads the cause of the poor and afflicted and plunders those who plunder them.
Moving the landmark of the fatherless brings their mighty Redeemer against the thief, the same defense God gives the widow.

units.notes:
• The "boundary" is the landmark or border stone that marked a family's property. The KJV reads "border," and the ESV speaks of the widow's "boundaries."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The story of Naboth (1 Kings 21) illuminates the saying; but it is relevant to all kinds of exploitation."
• Naomi and Ruth came home as widows with nothing, and through Boaz the family's land was redeemed and its name kept alive (Ruth 4:3–10).
• God calls Himself the defender of the widow throughout Scripture: Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 68:5; 146:9.
• Compare 16:5, 18; 22:22–23; 23:10–11; Luke 1:51–53.
units.summary: God tears down the proud man's house and stands guard over the widow's fence line.
units.principle: God opposes those who build on pride and defends those who cannot defend themselves; His justice brings down the proud and protects the vulnerable.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard, and Jezebel arranged false witnesses and a murder to get it. Ahab took the land, but God sent Elijah to pronounce judgment on Ahab's house (1 Kings 21:15–24). In the same book God fed a widow at Zarephath through a famine (1 Kings 17:8–16). Scripture calls Him "A father of the fatherless, a defender of widows" (Psalm 68:5). This verse is a warning to anyone who gains by pressing on the weak, and a comfort to those who have no one to defend them. God may not act on our timetable, but He is not neutral. Mary sang of the same pattern as Christ was coming: "He has put down the mighty from their thrones, And exalted the lowly" (Luke 1:52).
units.application: Churches, find out which widows in your congregation need help with repairs, paperwork, transportation or legal questions, and assign someone to each (James 1:27). If you handle estates, contracts or rentals, refuse any practice that takes advantage of someone who has no advocate. If you are a widow facing pressure, seek trusted counsel and remember that the LORD is on your side. Successful builders, examine what your success has cost others.

rel.note: The same word for plans appears there, where plans made with counsel are established.
The worship and the way of the wicked are the chapter’s first two abominations, and their thoughts complete the set.
Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the bones.
The devising of foolishness is sin, showing that schemes are judged before they are carried out.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Thoughts" translates machashavoth, a word for plans or devices, the same word translated "plans" in 15:22. The NASB and NLT read "evil plans."
• The second line reads literally "and pure are words of pleasantness." The ESV and NASB follow that order and make the gracious words the subject; the NKJV and KJV take "pure" as describing the speakers, whose words are pleasant.
• Bridges: "thoughts are the seminal principles of sin." He means that a thought is a seed: it contains "all the after fruit" of the act that follows.
• Compare 6:18 ("A heart that devises wicked plans"); 16:24; 23:7; Psalm 19:14; Matthew 15:19.
units.summary: Before a scheme becomes a deed, God has already judged the thought.
units.principle: God judges the heart's plans before they become actions, and He takes pleasure in words that flow from a pure heart.
units.insight: Joseph's brothers saw him coming from far off, and "even before he came near them, they conspired against him to kill him" (Genesis 37:18). The sin began in their thoughts before it reached the pit. Jesus said that "out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries" (Matthew 15:19), and He taught that hatred and lust are sins already in the heart (Matthew 5:21–28). That should humble us, because we are often proud that we did not act on what we privately rehearsed. Yet the second line holds out hope. A purified heart produces pleasant words, and God delights in them. David prayed for both: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart Be acceptable in Your sight, O LORD, my strength and my Redeemer" (Psalm 19:14).
units.application: Notice the private scenes you rehearse this week: the argument you win in your head, the revenge you imagine, the fantasy you replay. Bring them to God before they become words or actions. Parents, teach children that sin starts in thoughts, and help them name what they are thinking. Speakers and writers, review your words before you publish them, and ask whether they are pleasant because they are pure, not merely clever.

rel.note: He who troubles his own house will inherit the wind, the same self-inflicted ruin.
Trouble comes with the revenue of the wicked, the household cost that greed brings.
A wicked man takes a bribe in secret to pervert justice, the very gain this verse says to hate.
Greed for gain takes away the life of its owners, while this verse says the one who hates bribes will live.
He who hates covetousness will prolong his days, the same outcome of life attached to hating greed.

units.notes:
• "Greedy for gain" describes a person set on dishonest profit; YLT calls him a "dishonest gainer," and the NASB says he "profits illicitly." Where the NKJV has "bribes," the KJV and YLT read "gifts."
• A similar saying appears in 11:29: "He who troubles his own house will inherit the wind."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The 'greedy man' is the one who wants a big cut, who is in a hurry to get rich, and who is not particular how it happens."
• Ironside explains why a bribe must be hated, not merely declined: the "gift" "is really his price," the price at which a man is bought.
• Compare 1:19; 17:23; 28:16; Exodus 23:8; 1 Timothy 6:9–10.
units.summary: Greed promises to build up a house but ends up tearing it down.
units.principle: Dishonest gain brings trouble on the very household it was meant to enrich, while refusing to be bought preserves life.
units.insight: Gehazi ran after Naaman to collect the silver that Elisha had refused, and he brought leprosy on himself and his descendants (2 Kings 5:20–27). Greed rarely sees itself as greed. It calls itself provision, ambition or "taking care of my family." Yet families are often damaged not by poverty but by a parent's hunger for more. Samuel, by contrast, could stand before all Israel and ask, "from whose hand have I received any bribe?" (1 Samuel 12:3), and no one could answer. Judas sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver and lost everything (Matthew 26:14–16; 27:3–5). Jesus did the opposite: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). His generosity breaks greed's grip.
units.application: If you are tempted to cut a corner for money, such as padding hours, hiding income or accepting a gift that comes with expectations, refuse it this week and tell someone you trust. Buyers, officials and judges, set a clear personal rule about gifts and keep it. Parents, ask whether your work hours are costing your family more than your income gives them. Teach children that integrity is worth more than any deal.

rel.note: In many words sin is not lacking, but the one who restrains his lips is wise.
The same verb for pouring describes the mouth of fools, set against the tongue that uses knowledge rightly.
A word spoken in due season is good, the fruit of a heart that has studied how to answer.
The heart of the wise teaches his mouth, the same order of heart before speech.
There is more hope for a fool than for a man hasty in his words.

units.notes:
• "Studies" translates hagah, a verb meaning to meditate or ponder; YLT has "meditateth," and the ESV and NASB read "ponders." It is the verb used in Psalm 1:2 for meditating on God's law day and night.
• "Pours forth" translates the same Hebrew verb as in 15:2, where the mouth of fools pours forth foolishness: the picture of water gushing from a spring.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The advice is to say less but better things."
• Ironside: "Because a thing is true, it is not necessarily a fit subject to be discussed, and passed on from one to another."
• Compare 10:19; 16:23; 29:20; James 1:19; 1 Peter 3:15.
units.summary: The righteous think before they speak; the wicked speak before they think, if they think at all.
units.principle: Righteous speech is considered speech; the heart that ponders before answering protects both the truth and the hearer.
units.insight: When the king asked Nehemiah what he wanted, Nehemiah says, "So I prayed to the God of heaven," and then he answered (Nehemiah 2:4–5). His heart studied the answer in a breath of prayer. Peter, by contrast, blurted out a rebuke to Jesus about the cross and heard, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:22–23). Many of us pride ourselves on being frank and "just saying what we think." Often that is not honesty but a lack of restraint. Before His accusers Jesus kept silent when silence was wiser (Matthew 26:62–63; 27:12–14), and when He spoke, every word was weighed. God gives wisdom to all who ask (James 1:5), so we too can learn to pause, pray and then answer.
units.application: Practice a short pause before answering in every tense conversation this week: a breath, a silent prayer, then a reply. Parents, when a child asks a hard question, it is fine to say, "Let me think about that, and we will talk tonight." Managers, do not answer a heated email in the same hour. If you are known for being blunt, ask a friend whether your bluntness has wounded people you love.

rel.note: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, so His being "far" from the wicked means distance in favor, not in presence.
The prayer of the upright is the LORD’s delight, while the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination.
Those who refused Wisdom will call and not be answered, a picture of the distance this verse describes.
Whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, which keeps the way back open.
The prayer of one who turns his ear from the law is an abomination, the reason God is far from the wicked.

units.notes:
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "But this farness or nearness respects not God's essence, which is every where, but his gracious and helpful presence." ("Respects" here means "concerns.")
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Proverbs does not envision the wicked as repenting; if they did, they would be righteous."
• To "hear" prayer in Scripture often means to listen favorably and answer. Psalm 34:15 makes the same connection: "The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, And His ears are open to their cry."
• Compare 1:28; 15:8; 28:9; Psalm 66:18; Isaiah 59:1–2; James 5:16; 1 John 1:9.
units.summary: God is everywhere, yet He draws near to those who walk with Him and bends His ear to their prayers.
units.principle: God's favorable presence and listening ear belong to those who walk with Him, and the way back stays open to everyone who turns from sin.
units.insight: Saul had set himself against God's word for years, and at the end "the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams or by Urim or by the prophets" (1 Samuel 28:6). Elijah, "a man with a nature like ours," prayed, and God held back the rain and then sent it (James 5:17–18). The difference was not eloquence but the life behind the prayer. If your prayers feel as if they hit the ceiling, ask whether there is a sin you are holding on to (Psalm 66:18). Yet do not despair. The prodigal was "still a great way off" when his father ran to him (Luke 15:20). Through Christ, our Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1), those "who once were far off have been brought near" (Ephesians 2:13).
units.application: Before you pray this week, ask God to show you anything you are holding on to that He has told you to release, and confess it specifically (1 John 1:9). If you feel far from God, do not wait to clean yourself up first; turn and speak to Him today. Church prayer teams, pray by name for people who have drifted. Parents, let your children see you confess sin and pray, so they learn that God hears those who turn.

rel.note: A good word makes an anxious heart glad.
A merry heart makes a cheerful countenance, the bright face this verse sees from the other side.
Pleasant words are sweetness to the soul and health to the bones, the same effect on the body.
A merry heart does good like medicine, while a broken spirit dries the bones.
Good news from a far country is like cold water to a weary soul.

units.notes:
• "Makes the bones healthy" is literally "makes the bones fat," as the KJV, NASB and YLT render it, the picture of a well-nourished body. It is the same verb translated "made rich" in 13:4. The ESV reads "refreshes."
• The "light of the eyes" may mean a cheerful look from another person or the brightness of seeing something good; the 1984 NIV takes it as "A cheerful look."
• Ironside reads the good report in the light of the gospel: "The gospel of the glory of the blessed God is such a 'good report.'"
• Compare 12:25; 16:24; 17:22; 25:25; Isaiah 52:7.
units.summary: A bright face and good news can do for the soul what medicine does for the body.
units.principle: Encouragement cares for the whole person: a glad face and good news strengthen the heart and even the body.
units.insight: Old Jacob had grieved for Joseph for years. When his sons said, "Joseph is still alive," his heart stood still because he could not believe them; then "the spirit of Jacob their father revived" (Genesis 45:26–27). Good news reached his bones. The shepherds heard the best report ever given, "there is born to you this day in the city of David a Savior" (Luke 2:11), and they went to see it with their own eyes. The gospel is both a good report and a light that shines in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6). We forget how much our faces and our news affect others. A believer who carries the good news of Christ with a glad face is a gift to weary people.
units.application: This week, greet people at church, at work or at home with a face that shows you are glad to see them. Send a good report: tell parents something good about their child, or tell a pastor how a sermon helped you. Leaders, share good news with your team as quickly as you share problems. When you visit the sick, bring encouraging news and a bright face, not only sympathy.

rel.note: He who walks with wise men will be wise, the company this verse says the teachable ear will keep.
The scoffer will not go to the wise, while the teachable ear comes to live among them.
A wise rebuker to an obedient ear is like an ornament of fine gold.
Reproofs of instruction are the way of life, the same rebukes that lead to life.
A wise man loves the one who rebukes him and becomes wiser still.

units.notes:
