• The ESV and NASB render "the rebukes of life" as "life-giving reproof."
• YLT renders "abide" as "lodge," a word for staying the night, which pictures the teachable person settling in among the wise.
• Henry: "The ear that can take the reproof will love the reprover."
• Bridges: "Beautiful indeed is the sight of 'a wise reprover upon an obedient ear.'" He is quoting 25:12 in the KJV.
• Compare 6:23; 9:8–9; 25:12; 27:5–6; Psalm 141:5.
units.summary: The ear that welcomes correction earns a seat among the wise.
units.principle: Welcoming life-giving correction is the way into lasting fellowship with the wise; teachability is the door into wisdom.
units.insight: When Nathan told David the story of the stolen lamb and said, "You are the man!", David did not silence him. He said, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). Nathan remained a trusted counselor at David's court to the end of his reign (1 Kings 1:11–14, 32–34). Peter was publicly rebuked by Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14), yet later he called him "our beloved brother Paul" (2 Peter 3:15). A rebuke well received does not end a friendship; it can deepen it. Who in your life has earned the right to correct you? The Lord Himself says, "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19). His rebukes are always rebukes of life.
units.application: Ask one wise friend this week, "What is one thing you see in me that I may not see?" Then listen, thank them, and do not defend yourself. Young people, choose friends who are wiser than you and stay close to them. Small-group leaders, build a culture where loving correction is normal and welcome. If you have pulled away from someone who once rebuked you, go back and tell them you are ready to listen.

rel.note: Poverty and shame come to the one who disdains correction, while the one who regards rebuke is honored.
The one who hates correction will die, the end of despising one’s own soul.
The fool despises his father’s instruction, while the one who receives correction is prudent.
He who gets wisdom loves his own soul, the opposite of despising it.
The one who sins against Wisdom wrongs his own soul, the same self-harm this verse names.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "disdains," para', has the sense of letting go or neglecting. It is the same verb used in 13:18 and in 1:25, where Wisdom says, "you disdained all my counsel."
• "Gets understanding" is literally "acquires a heart." The heart is the seat of understanding, so the one who heeds rebuke gains the very sense he lacked. Compare 15:21, where the person without discernment is literally "lacking heart."
• Henry: "The fundamental error of sinners is undervaluing their own souls."
• Bridges: "Nothing teaches like experience; and no experience is more useful, because none so abasing, as rebuke." ("Abasing" means humbling.)
• Compare 8:36; 12:1; 13:18; 19:8; Matthew 16:26.
units.summary: Refusing correction is not self-respect; it is self-neglect.
units.principle: Rejecting correction harms the one who rejects it, while heeding rebuke is a true act of care for one's own soul.
units.insight: Dathan and Abiram, leaders in Korah's rebellion, refused even to come when Moses called them: "We will not come up!" The ground opened beneath them (Numbers 16:12–14, 31–33). They thought they were defending their dignity, but they were destroying themselves. Self-protection often looks like strength: no one will tell me what to do. That stance despises the very soul it claims to protect. The prodigal "came to himself" in the far country (Luke 15:17), accepted what his ruin was teaching him, and went home. Proverbs says, "He who gets wisdom loves his own soul" (19:8), and that love listens. Jesus asked, "what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?" (Matthew 16:26). Heeding His word is how we care for our souls.
units.application: Think of the correction you dismissed most recently, from a spouse, boss, doctor or pastor. Revisit it this week and ask what part of it was true. Students, read the comments on your graded work, not only the grade. Employees, ask your supervisor for one area to improve. Parents, explain to your children that correction is given for their good, and model receiving it yourself.

rel.note: The section opens with the LORD tearing down the house of the proud and closes with humility before honor.
The same line, "before honor is humility," follows a warning that a haughty heart comes before destruction.
The book’s motto, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, is restated here at the close of the collection.
Humility and the fear of the LORD bring riches, honor and life.
Pride brings a man low, but the humble in spirit will retain honor.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble, the source of the honor that follows humility.

units.notes:
• "Instruction" here is musar, the same word used throughout chapters 13–15 for a father's instruction, discipline and correction (13:1; 15:5). The fear of the LORD is pictured as the teacher who trains a person in wisdom; the ESV reads "instruction in wisdom."
• In the NKJV the second line is repeated exactly in 18:12, where it follows "Before destruction the heart of a man is haughty."
• Humility and the fear of the LORD are joined again in 22:4: "By humility and the fear of the LORD Are riches and honor and life."
• Bridges: "Indeed, without humility, honor would be our temptation, rather than our glory."
• Compare 1:7; 9:10; 29:23; Philippians 2:5–11; James 4:10; 1 Peter 5:5–6.
units.summary: The road to honor runs downhill first, through the low valley of humility.
units.principle: The fear of the LORD is the school of wisdom, and humility before Him is the path God honors, walked in surrender, not as a strategy.
units.insight: Joseph went down into a pit and a prison before he was raised to rule over Egypt (Genesis 41:14, 39–41). David tended sheep before he shepherded Israel (Psalm 78:70–72). The pattern is fulfilled in Christ. He "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross," and therefore God "highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:8–9). The cross came before the crown. Our hearts want honor without humility, the crown without the cross. Yet humility is not a strategy for getting ahead, and those who use it that way have missed it. True humility is the fear of the LORD at work: seeing God so clearly that we bow, and leaving our honor in His hands (1 Peter 5:6).
units.application: Look for one place this week to take the lower seat: let someone else get the credit, serve where no one will notice, or admit a mistake openly. Young leaders, accept the unglamorous assignments; they are training, not waste. If you have been passed over, leave the question of honor with God instead of campaigning for yourself. Begin each day by reading a psalm of praise, which puts God in His place and you in yours.

rel.note: The righteous heart studies how to answer, showing that careful preparation of words is commended, not dismissed.
The chapter closes as it opens, confessing that the final decision is "from the LORD."
The heart plans its way while the LORD directs the steps, the same pairing of human planning and divine rule that frames 16:1–9.
Many plans fill a man's heart, but the LORD's counsel is what stands.

units.notes:
• The word translated "preparations" comes from a verb meaning to set in order. It is used for drawing up troops for battle and for arranging words in an argument, as when Elihu says to Job, "Set your words in order before me" (Job 33:5). The ESV and NASB have "plans"; YLT has "arrangements."
• The KJV reads the verse differently: "The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD." On that reading even the heart's preparations come from God. The NKJV, ESV and NASB set the two lines against each other: man prepares, the LORD gives the answer.
• Balaam shows the verse at work. He came to curse Israel, yet each time he opened his mouth a blessing came out (Numbers 23–24). Henry: "It was a curse that was prepared in Balaam's heart, but the answer of the tongue was a blessing."
• Compare 16:9; 16:33; 19:21; Jeremiah 10:23; James 4:13–15.
units.summary: You can rehearse every word in advance, but the final answer belongs to God.
units.principle: People are responsible to plan and prepare, yet the final word and the final outcome rest with God.
units.insight: This verse corrects two opposite errors of the heart. The anxious person thinks everything depends on getting the words exactly right. The careless person thinks preparation does not matter because God is in control. Moses tried to excuse himself from speaking to Pharaoh because he was "slow of speech," and God answered, "I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall say" (Exodus 4:10–12). Jesus told His disciples not to worry in advance about what to say before rulers, "For it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak" (Matthew 10:19). Neither promise excused laziness; both freed God's servants from fear. Where do you rely on your own polish, and where do you avoid preparing at all? Bring both to God, do your part, and leave the outcome with Him.
units.application: Before a hard conversation this week, whether a talk with a teenager, a review with an employee or a word with a friend who has hurt you, think it through and write down what you need to say. Then pray over it and hold your script loosely. If the conversation turns in a way you did not plan, do not panic. If you preach or teach, prepare fully, then ask God to give the answer of the tongue.

rel.note: A way can seem right to a man and still end in death, the deadly result of trusting one's own verdict.
The human spirit is the lamp of the LORD, searching the inner depths of the heart, the hidden motives this verse says He weighs.
The same saying in nearly the same words: a man's way is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the hearts.
The One who weighs the hearts sees through every excuse of "we did not know."
Agur describes a generation pure in its own eyes yet not washed from its filthiness.

units.notes:
• The verb translated "weighs," *takan*, means to measure or weigh out. It returns in 21:2 ("the LORD weighs the hearts") and 24:12, which asks whether "He who weighs the hearts" will not see. The NASB has "weighs the motives."
• "Pure" means clean, free from stain; the KJV and NASB have "clean."
• Bridges: "If man were his own judge, who would be condemned? But man judges by acts; God by principles." By "principles" he means the motives that drive the acts.
• Belshazzar heard God's verdict in the same picture: he had been weighed in the balances and found lacking (Daniel 5:27).
• Compare 21:2; 30:12; 1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; 1 Corinthians 4:4–5.
units.summary: Every heart acquits itself, but God puts our motives on His scale.
units.principle: No one is a reliable judge of his own heart; the true measure of a life is God's weighing of its motives.
units.insight: Pilate washed his hands before the crowd and declared himself innocent of Jesus' blood (Matthew 27:24). The religious leaders would not enter the governor's hall, lest they be defiled, while they pressed for an innocent man's death (John 18:28). Both were clean in their own eyes. Self-justification feels like peace, but often it is only a quiet conscience that has stopped asking hard questions. Paul knew of nothing against himself, yet he wrote, "I am not justified by this; but He who judges me is the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:4). The gospel answers this verse. We cannot pass God's scale on our own, but Christ's perfect obedience stands in our place, and "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). So we can let God weigh us truthfully, without fear.
units.application: When you are sure you were completely in the right, in a marriage argument, a church disagreement or a decision at work, stop and ask what your motive was. Ask a trusted friend or your spouse, "What am I not seeing?" Leaders, invite honest feedback before you defend yourself. Parents, admit mixed motives to your children when you see them. End the day by praying Psalm 139:23–24 over one specific situation.

rel.note: The one who trusts in the LORD is called happy, the inner settledness that committed work brings.
The one who commits his works to the LORD is the one whose ways please Him, and God can bring even his enemies to peace.
The same verb for making firm stands behind the LORD directing the steps of the one who plans.
Whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe, set against the fear of man that unsettles the mind.
Trusting the LORD with all the heart and acknowledging Him in all one's ways is the same act as rolling one's works onto Him.

units.notes:
• "Commit" is literally "roll," as YLT renders it. The same verb stands behind Psalm 37:5, "Commit your way to the LORD," and behind Psalm 22:8, where mockers say of the sufferer, "He trusted in the LORD," literally that he rolled himself onto the LORD. Matthew 27:43 records the same taunt thrown at Jesus on the cross.
• "Established" translates *kun*, to make firm. The same verb stands behind "directs" in 16:9 and "established" in 16:12, so the chapter's sayings about plans and thrones share one word for God's steadying work.
• The NLT has "your plans will succeed," which can sound like a guarantee of success. The NKJV, ESV and NASB keep "established."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the verb "connotes a sense of finality; roll it unto the Lord and leave it there."
• Compare 3:5–6; Psalm 55:22; Philippians 4:6–7; 1 Peter 5:7.
units.summary: Roll the weight of your work onto God, and He will steady the one who works.
units.principle: Work done in trust is carried by God; the one who hands Him the outcome receives a steady mind, not a guaranteed result.
units.insight: Hannah carried a burden she could not fix. She poured out her soul before the LORD at Shiloh, and when she left, "her face was no longer sad" (1 Samuel 1:15, 18). Nothing in her situation had changed yet; she had rolled the weight onto God. Many of us pray about our work but keep gripping the result, and anxiety is often the sign that we have not let go. Ironside names the cost: "if I thus commit all to Him, I no longer choose for myself as to what the outcome should be." Jesus is the clearest picture. On the eve of the cross He prayed, "not My will, but Yours, be done" (Luke 22:42), and walked forward steady. His enemies mocked, "He trusted in God" (Matthew 27:43), and they spoke more truly than they knew.
units.application: Name one project that is keeping you awake: a business launch, an exam, a ministry plan, a child's future. Do the work it requires this week. Then, in prayer, hand over the outcome by name and stop rehearsing worst cases. Employees and students, give your best effort and leave the results with God. Leaders, open planning meetings by committing the work to the LORD, and then plan with care.

rel.note: The wicked will not go unpunished, the judgment this verse says they are headed for.
Even the lot is decided by the LORD, so nothing in His world, small or great, falls outside His rule.
No wisdom or counsel succeeds against the LORD, including the schemes of the wicked.
There is no future for the evil man, so the godly need not fret over the wicked who seem to prosper.

units.notes:
• "For Himself" translates a phrase that can mean "for its answer" or "for its purpose." Its noun, *ma'aneh*, is the word translated "answer" in 16:1, so the two verses echo each other: the tongue's answer comes from the LORD, and every created thing finds its answer, or end, in Him. The ESV and NASB read "purpose"; the KJV, like the NKJV, has "for himself."
• "The day of doom" is literally "the day of evil," meaning disaster; the KJV and NASB render it that way.
• Bridges guards God's goodness: "Wicked they are of themselves. He made them not so." God does not force anyone into wickedness, and He hates it.
• As Kidner puts it, quoted by Guzik, "there are ultimately no loose ends in God's world."
• Compare Genesis 50:20; Ezekiel 33:11; Acts 2:23; Psalm 73:17–19; 1 Timothy 2:4.
units.summary: God wastes nothing: even the wicked cannot escape His purpose or His judgment.
units.principle: God rules every part of His world, including the end of the wicked, yet He is never the author of evil and takes no pleasure in anyone's ruin.
units.insight: Joseph's brothers sold him for silver, and years later he told them, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Their sin remained theirs, yet it served a purpose they never planned. The cross is the greatest case. Jesus was delivered up "by the determined purpose and foreknowledge of God," and still the men who crucified Him did it "by lawless hands" (Acts 2:23). God ruled the evil without doing the evil. That truth steadies the believer who watches the wicked prosper: their day is coming. It also humbles us, since we were once among the wicked, and God's patience gave us time to turn (2 Peter 3:9). So the verse is never a reason to write anyone off. The God who appoints judgment still calls every sinner to turn and live.
units.application: When you see wicked people prosper, at work, in public life or in your own family's story, do not conclude that God has lost control. Read Psalm 73 slowly this week and pray it. When you are tempted to give up on someone as hopelessly wicked, remember that God calls the wicked to turn and live, and pray for that person by name. If you teach this verse, set Ezekiel 18:32 beside it.

rel.note: The same words, "Though they join forces," promise that the wicked will not escape punishment.
The chapter's central saying on pride shows the ruin toward which the proud heart is heading.
A proud look heads the list of seven things the LORD hates.
The fear of the LORD hates pride and arrogance, which is why it exposes the proud heart.

units.notes:
• "Abomination," *to'evah*, names what is detestable to God. Proverbs gathers a list of such things: dishonest scales (11:1), lying lips (12:22), the sacrifice of the wicked (15:8) and here the proud heart.
• "Though they join forces" is literally "hand to hand"; the KJV has "though hand join in hand." The NKJV uses the same wording in 11:21: "Though they join forces, the wicked will not go unpunished."
• "Will go unpunished" is literally "will be held innocent" or acquitted; YLT has "not acquitted." The proud will not be cleared at God's bar.
• Bridges on why God opposes pride: "When it thus strikes at God, what wonder that God strikes at it". Pride lifts the heart up against God, so God sets Himself against pride.
• Compare 6:16–17; Genesis 11:1–9; Psalm 2:1–4; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5.
units.summary: Pride can find allies, but no alliance can shield it from God.
units.principle: God sets Himself against the proud heart, and no number of allies can protect a person from His verdict on pride.
units.insight: At Babel people joined hands to build a tower and said, "let us make a name for ourselves" (Genesis 11:4). Their unity was real, and God scattered it in a moment. Pride loves company, because company feels like confirmation. A proud heart surrounds itself with people who agree and then calls the agreement wisdom. The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and His Anointed, and He who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:2–4). Yet the most dangerous pride is not in a crowd but in us, hidden under a humble look. "God resists the proud, But gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6). The way out is not to work harder at seeming modest. It is to come low before Jesus, who "humbled Himself" all the way to the cross (Philippians 2:8).
units.application: Notice where you draw confidence from numbers: the group chat that always agrees with you, the faction in a church dispute, the team that never questions the boss. Leaders, ask whether the people around you are partners in truth or only partners in pride. Young people, beware of the crowd that dares you to look down on others. This week, seek out one person likely to disagree with you, and listen.

rel.note: The verb for atonement returns there for appeasing a king's wrath, linking covering guilt with turning away anger.
Mercy and truth preserve the king, the same pair of covenant qualities named here.
Whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, the same union of forgiveness and turning from evil.
Mercy and truth, which here provide atonement, are to be bound around the neck and written on the heart.
"Fear the LORD and depart from evil" joins the same two things as this verse's second line.

units.notes:
• "Atonement is provided" translates *kaphar*, the verb used throughout Leviticus for making atonement. Here it is passive, so iniquity is atoned for, with no sacrifice mentioned. The KJV has "iniquity is purged." The same verb appears in 16:14, where a wise man will "appease" the king's wrath.
• "Mercy and truth," *hesed* and *emet*, are God's covenant love and His faithfulness. The ESV has "steadfast love and faithfulness," the NASB "lovingkindness and truth." The pair appears in 3:3 and 20:28, and the psalmist sings, "Mercy and truth have met together" (Psalm 85:10).
• Some read "mercy and truth" as a person's own kindness and faithfulness toward others. Even on that reading, the guilt of sin before God is covered only by His provision.
• Bridges on the second line: "The fear of the Lord is at once a bridle to sin, and a spur to holiness." It holds us back from evil and drives us toward good.
• Compare Exodus 34:6–7; Micah 7:18–20; Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
units.summary: God's mercy and truth cover the guilt of sin; the fear of the LORD breaks its hold.
units.principle: Sin is covered by God's own mercy and faithfulness, not by human merit, and true forgiveness produces a life that turns from evil.
units.insight: David knew both halves of this verse. After his sin with Bathsheba he did not offer God a better performance; he cried, "Have mercy upon me, O God, According to Your lovingkindness" (Psalm 51:1). And forgiveness did not leave him where it found him: "Then I will teach transgressors Your ways" (51:13). At the cross God's mercy and truth met fully. Mercy did not ignore sin, and truth did not cancel love. Bridges: "Mercy provides, truth accepts—the ransom." God's mercy supplied the payment, and His truth received it as meeting His justice, for God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Some of us still try to pay for our failures with good works; others enjoy forgiveness while keeping the sin. This verse closes both doors.
units.application: If you are carrying guilt over a sin already confessed, read Psalm 32 and thank God that the covering is His work, not yours. If you hope your good deeds will balance out a sin you have not confessed, stop and confess it. Parents, when you correct a child, pair forgiveness with a clear path forward. Anyone who has been forgiven: name one evil you will turn from this week, and ask a friend to hold you to it.

rel.note: The person whose ways please the LORD is the one who has committed his works to Him.
The king's heart is in the LORD's hand, the same power over hearts that can turn enemies to peace.
Kindness to an enemy is the godly person's part in the peace God may bring.
Holding to mercy and truth brings favor in the sight of God and man.

units.notes:
• "Makes … to be at peace" translates a verb from the same root as *shalom*, peace and wholeness. Its form means to cause: God brings the peace about. The NLT makes it sound as if the enemies simply become peaceful; the NKJV's capital "He" keeps the LORD as the one acting.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "A lifestyle pleasing to God disarms social hostility."
• Bridges sets this verse beside the persecution of the godly (2 Timothy 3:12): "Each statement limits the other." The saying about peace and the warning of persecution must be read together; neither cancels the other.
• Abimelech came to make a covenant with Isaac, saying, "We have certainly seen that the LORD is with you" (Genesis 26:28). Laban, pursuing Jacob in anger, was warned by God in a dream not to harm him (Genesis 31:24).
• Compare 3:3–4; 21:1; 2 Chronicles 17:10; Romans 12:18.
units.summary: The God you please is the God who can quiet your enemies.
units.principle: God holds the hearts of enemies in His hand, and a life that pleases Him often finds a peace it could never win by its own efforts, though faithfulness may still meet opposition.
units.insight: Jacob had cheated Esau, and twenty years later Esau came to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob wrestled with God through the night before he faced his brother, and the next morning Esau "ran to meet him, and embraced him" (Genesis 33:4). The decisive meeting was not with Esau but with God. Daniel's rivals searched his life for a charge and found none, "because he was faithful" (Daniel 6:4). Notice where we usually begin with an enemy: strategy, self-defense, rehearsed arguments. This verse begins with the question, "Do my ways please the LORD?" Even so, Jesus pleased the Father in everything and was still crucified. Peace with enemies is God's gift, not our wage. The deepest peace is the one He made with us "when we were enemies" (Romans 5:10).
units.application: If a coworker, relative or neighbor has set himself against you, examine your own conduct first and make right anything God shows you. Then pray for that person by name instead of rehearsing your defense. Do not compromise truth to buy peace. If you lead a church or team through conflict, put your energy into pleasing God and leave the softening of hearts to Him. If the opposition stays, keep doing right.

rel.note: A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, the same "better than" lesson.
The one greedy for gain troubles his own house, the cost of revenues without justice.
The next "better than" in the chapter also prefers a lowly portion with the right heart over gain shared with the proud.
The poor man who walks in integrity is better than the crooked rich man.

units.notes:
• "Without justice" uses *mishpat*, the ordinary word for justice or right judgment. The same word stands behind "judgment" in 16:10, "Honest" in 16:11 (literally scales of justice) and "decision" in 16:33. The KJV has "without right."
• "Revenues" translates a word for yield or produce, the harvest a field brings in. It is the word for "increase" in 3:9.
• Bridges draws a quiet lesson from the verse: "The fewer desires, the more quiet."
• Compare 15:16; 15:27; Psalm 37:16, "A little that a righteous man has Is better than the riches of many wicked"; Jeremiah 17:11; 1 Timothy 6:6–10.
units.summary: A small honest paycheck outweighs a fortune built on wrong.
units.principle: The way money is gained matters more to God than the amount; an honest little is richer than a dishonest much.
units.insight: Ahab had a palace and a kingdom, but he wanted Naboth's vineyard, and Jezebel got it for him through false witnesses and murder (1 Kings 21). Ahab gained the vineyard and lost everything. Elijah, meanwhile, lived on a widow's handful of flour and a little oil, and it did not run out (1 Kings 17:12–16). Zacchaeus shows the turn this verse calls for. When Jesus came to his house, he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). He chose the little with righteousness, and Jesus said, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). Our hearts are skilled at overlooking small injustices that pay well. Where in your finances is there a "without justice" you have learned not to see?
units.application: Look at one place where gain and honesty pull against each other: expense reports, taxes, a side deal, the price you quote a customer who does not know better. Choose the smaller, cleaner number this week. Business owners, pay workers fully and on time (James 5:4). Young people choosing a career, weigh the character of the work, not only the salary. If you have gained something wrongly, make it right, as Zacchaeus did.

rel.note: Plans succeed with many counselors, which shows that careful planning is commended within God's rule.
The heart prepares and the LORD gives the answer; the two verses frame 16:1–9 with the same truth.
The way a man plans for himself without the LORD may seem right and still end in death.
The same verb for making firm describes God establishing the thoughts of those who commit their works to Him.
Even the lot is decided by the LORD, the same rule over every human choice.
Many plans fill a man's heart, but the LORD's counsel will stand.

units.notes:
• "Plans," *chashab*, means to think, reckon or devise. "Directs" translates *kun*, to make firm, the verb behind "established" in 16:3 and 16:12. The ESV reads "establishes his steps."
• Bridges sums up both lines: "Thus man proposes; God disposes." People plan freely, and God governs how things turn out.
• Jeremiah prayed, "O LORD, I know the way of man is not in himself; It is not in man who walks to direct his own steps" (Jeremiah 10:23).
• Compare 19:21; 20:24; Psalm 37:23; James 4:13–15.
units.summary: Your heart may draw the map, but the LORD directs each step on the road.
units.principle: Wise people plan carefully and hold their plans humbly, because God governs the steps that carry them out.
units.insight: Saul went out looking for his father's lost donkeys and came home anointed king (1 Samuel 9–10). Saul of Tarsus set out for Damascus to arrest believers, and the Lord met him on the road (Acts 9:1–6). Paul later planned to preach in Asia and Bithynia, but the Spirit closed both doors and led him to Macedonia, where a church began in Lydia's home (Acts 16:6–15). Ironside: "People frequently think they are having their own way, when in reality the Lord is leading them." This truth frees the anxious planner and humbles the confident one. When God redirects your plans, nothing has been wasted. You are being led by One who sees the whole road, and His direction is kinder and wiser than your map.
units.application: Write down your plans for the coming season, at work, in your family or in ministry, and pray over each one. Say "If the Lord wills" in your heart, and mean it (James 4:15). When a door closes this week, ask what God may be opening before you push harder. Parents, help a teenager plan for college or work while teaching them to hold the plan open-handed. Leaders, leave room in your plans for God's redirection.

rel.note: The word for "judgment" here is the word behind "Honest" scales there, so courtroom and marketplace answer to one standard.
The throne is established by righteousness, the reason the king's verdicts must be just.
A king on the throne of judgment scatters evil with his eyes, the same weighty royal verdict.
The king who judges the poor with truth has a lasting throne, the reward of a mouth that does not transgress in judgment.
Lemuel's mother charges the king to judge righteously, the same duty laid on royal lips.

units.notes:
• The word translated "Divination," *qesem*, is the ordinary word for divination. Elsewhere in the Bible it names a forbidden practice (Deuteronomy 18:10; 1 Samuel 15:23). Here it pictures the decisive, almost oracle-like force of a king's verdict. The KJV softens it to "a divine sentence"; the ESV has "An oracle."
• The verb in the second line can state a fact or a duty. The ESV takes it as a statement, that his mouth does not sin in judgment; the NKJV's "must not" and the NASB's "should not" take it as a duty. The duty fits the sayings that follow, which assume kings can fail.
• Bridges calls 16:10–13 "a manual for kings; shewing, not what they are, but what God requires them to be".
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The Old Testament lends no support to the idea that the king can do no wrong".
• Compare 2 Samuel 23:3–4; 1 Kings 3:9, 28; Isaiah 9:7; 11:3–4.
units.summary: The more final a leader's word, the more it must be just.
units.principle: Authority magnifies the weight of every word, so those whose decisions are final carry the greatest duty to judge justly.
units.insight: Solomon asked God for "an understanding heart to judge Your people" (1 Kings 3:9). When he settled the case of two women claiming one baby, all Israel "saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice" (1 Kings 3:28). That is this verse at its best. Yet Solomon's later years show that a gifted mouth can still go astray (1 Kings 11:1–10). Most of us hold some small throne: a parent's verdict, a manager's review, an elder's decision. People treat our words as final, and that should make us tremble, not swagger. In the light of the New Testament, the judgments of one King, Jesus Christ, never fail. Isaiah saw His throne ordered "with judgment and justice" forever (Isaiah 9:7), and every human authority will answer to Him.
units.application: If your word settles matters for others, as a parent, supervisor, teacher, pastor or board member, slow down before your next verdict. Hear both sides fully, check the facts, and ask God for wisdom as Solomon did. When you realize you judged wrongly, say so and set it right. Employees and church members, pray for those in authority over you (1 Timothy 2:1–2) instead of only criticizing them.

rel.note: Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is His delight.
The king's just verdict and the merchant's just scale are named with the same word for justice.
Differing weights and measures are both an abomination to the LORD.
Diverse weights are an abomination, and dishonest scales are not good, the same standard restated.

units.notes:
• "The weights in the bag" is literally "the stones of the bag," because merchants carried stone weights in a pouch. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids having "in your bag differing weights, a heavy and a light."
• "Honest" translates *mishpat*, justice, so the line reads literally "a balance and scales of justice." The same word is "judgment" in 16:10, so the king's verdict and the merchant's scale answer to one standard. The ESV and NASB speak of a just balance and scales.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Equity is not a human invention, and thus kings do not have the authority to suspend or violate the laws of fairness."
• Ironside: "it is the same integrity that directs the decision of the upright king and the measures of the poorest of his subjects."
• Compare 11:1; 20:10, 23; Amos 8:4–6; Micah 6:11.
units.summary: Fair weights are not a human invention; they are the LORD's own standard.
units.principle: Fairness in buying, selling and measuring is God's own standard, binding on rulers and ordinary people alike.
units.insight: In Amos's day merchants could hardly wait for the Sabbath to end so they could get back to "Falsifying the scales by deceit" (Amos 8:5). They kept their religious calendar and cheated their neighbors in the same week. The LORD swore that He would never forget any of their works (Amos 8:7). Dishonest measuring rarely looks dramatic. It looks like a padded invoice, a shaved hour or an inflated résumé. This verse lifts those small matters into God's presence, because the weights are His work. It also humbles us. The God whose scales are perfectly just will weigh us too, and none of us measures up. At the cross He showed Himself both "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). Those He has dealt with so fairly should deal fairly with others.
units.application: Check your own scales this week. Business owners: are your prices, measurements and descriptions truthful? Employees: does your timesheet match your hours? Students: is the work you hand in your own? Anyone selling a car or a house: disclose what you know. Leaders and officials, apply one standard to friends and opponents alike. Teach children that fairness matters even in small trades and shared chores, because God owns the scales.

rel.note: Righteousness exalts a nation, the same principle applied to a whole people.
The king's weighty verdicts must be just, because his throne stands on righteousness.
Mercy and truth preserve the king, adding mercy to the righteousness that upholds a throne.
Removing the wicked from the king's presence establishes his throne in righteousness.
The king who judges the poor with truth has a throne established forever.

units.notes:
• The first line reads literally "an abomination to kings is doing wickedness." The 1984 NIV takes it of kings detesting wrongdoing in others; the NKJV, ESV and NASB speak of kings themselves doing evil.
• "Established" translates *kun*, to make firm, the verb behind "established" in 16:3 and "directs" in 16:9. The God who steadies the plans of those who trust Him also steadies a righteous throne.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, on how these sayings sounded in Solomon's day: "But coming from the golden age of Solomon, the ideal was still credible." In other words, while Solomon ruled well, a king who hated wickedness and ruled by righteousness did not sound like a dream.
• Compare 20:28; 25:5; 29:14; Psalm 45:6–7; Isaiah 16:5.
units.summary: Injustice saws through the legs of the very throne it sits on.
units.principle: Lasting authority stands on righteousness; leaders who practice or permit injustice are cutting away their own foundation.
units.insight: Rehoboam inherited Solomon's throne and chose to rule harshly, promising to make the people's yoke heavier. In a single day ten tribes walked away (1 Kings 12:12–19). Force could not hold what justice had not built. David, for all his failures, "administered judgment and justice to all his people" (2 Samuel 8:15). Everyone with influence is building on something, whether a family, a business or a congregation. The searching question is whether we excuse in ourselves what we would condemn in others. In the light of the New Testament, the Son's throne is the one this verse describes perfectly: "A scepter of righteousness is the scepter of Your kingdom" (Hebrews 1:8). His rule will never be shaken, because it never rests on anything but righteousness.
units.application: If you hold authority, ask where you have excused in yourself what you would discipline in others: a shortcut, a favor to a friend, a harsh word. Fix it this week. Parents, do not demand truthfulness from children while cutting corners yourself. Church leaders and managers, deal promptly with injustice in your organization, even when the offender is useful. Citizens, pray for leaders to rule justly, and hold them to it.

rel.note: The king's favor is toward a wise servant.
The king will be the friend of one who has grace on his lips and purity of heart.
The one who rebukes finds more favor afterward than the flatterer, the reward of righteous lips.
A ruler who listens to lies corrupts all his servants, the opposite of a king who loves right speech.

units.notes:
• The NASB renders the second line in the passive: the one who speaks what is right is loved.
• "Righteous lips" are lips that speak what is straight and true, the opposite of the "flattering mouth" that "works ruin" (26:28).
• Henry describes good kings as wanting their servants to "tell them that which is true, whether it be pleasing or displeasing".
• Compare 14:35; 22:11; 25:11–12; Psalm 101:6–7.
units.summary: Good leaders do not collect flatterers; they treasure the person who tells them the truth.
units.principle: Wise authority values truthful counsel above pleasant flattery, and those who serve should speak what is right.
units.insight: King Ahab had four hundred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear. When Jehoshaphat asked for another, Ahab said of Micaiah, "I hate him, because he does not prophesy good concerning me" (1 Kings 22:8). He went to battle on the flatterers' word and died. Eli is the opposite picture. When young Samuel brought him a hard word of judgment, Eli answered, "It is the LORD. Let Him do what seems good to Him" (1 Samuel 3:18). Most of us say we want honest feedback; few of us reward it. Watch how you treat the person who brings you an unwelcome truth. Jesus is the King whose lips were always right, and He calls His people to speak "the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15).
units.application: Leaders, name the people around you who never disagree, and invite one honest critic into your next decision. Thank, do not punish, the person who brings bad news. Employees and church members, when your boss or pastor needs to hear something hard, say it respectfully and plainly instead of going quiet or complaining elsewhere. Parents, reward a child who confesses or tells you an uncomfortable truth.

rel.note: A soft answer turns away wrath, the method the wise man uses to appease anger.
The king's wrath brings death; the light of his face brings life.
The verb for appeasing anger here is the verb for atonement there.
The king's wrath is like a lion's roar, while his favor is like dew on the grass.
Provoking a king to anger endangers one's own life.
Patience persuades a ruler, and a gentle tongue breaks a bone.

units.notes:
• "Appease" translates *kaphar*, the verb used for atonement in 16:6. Here it means to cover or pacify anger, which is why the KJV and YLT have "pacify."
• "Messengers of death" pictures officers sent to carry out a death sentence. Ahasuerus's anger sent Haman to the gallows that same day (Esther 7:7–10), and Herod's order sent the executioner to John the Baptist (Matthew 14:9–10).
• Bridges: "No common wisdom was needed to pacify his wrath."
• The Preacher gives similar counsel: if a ruler's anger rises against you, do not leave your post, because calmness can put great offenses to rest (Ecclesiastes 10:4).
• Compare 15:1; 19:12; 20:2; 25:15.
units.summary: A ruler's anger can kill, but wisdom knows how to calm it.
units.principle: Wisdom neither provokes nor flatters dangerous anger; it calms it with patience and fitting words.
units.insight: When Saul swore to kill David, Jonathan spoke well of David to his father and reminded him of David's loyalty, and Saul relented (1 Samuel 19:4–6). When Nebuchadnezzar ordered all the wise men killed, Daniel answered the captain "with counsel and wisdom," asked for time and sought God (Daniel 2:14–18). Neither man flattered; both spoke truth wisely. There is a greater wrath than any king's. In the light of the New Testament, God's wrath against sin is the true messenger of death, and no human wisdom can pacify it. Christ did what we could not. He is "the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 2:2), the covering that turns that wrath away. Those who know they are at peace with God can face lesser angers without panic.
units.application: When a boss, customer or family member is angry with you, resist both the urge to fight back and the urge to grovel. Lower your voice, listen fully, then speak a few true and fitting words (15:1). Employees, choose the right moment to raise a concern with an angry supervisor. Peacemakers in a church or family, follow Jonathan: speak up for the person under threat, and remind the angry person of what is true.

rel.note: The king's favor rests on a wise servant, showing who tends to receive it.
The king's wrath is like messengers of death, the opposite of the life his favor gives.
The king's favor is like dew on the grass, a second picture of refreshing royal favor.
Many seek the ruler's favor, but justice comes from the LORD, keeping royal favor in its place.

units.notes:
• "Latter rain" is the spring rain that fell before the grain harvest; the ESV and NASB have "spring rain." A cloud carrying it was a welcome sight to farmers waiting on their crop.
• The comparison returns in 19:12: "his favor is like dew on the grass."
• Esther shows verses 14 and 15 together. Coming before the king uninvited could mean death, but he held out the golden scepter and she lived (Esther 4:11; 5:2).
• Bridges carries the image up to God: "But think of the King of kings, before whom the mightiest Monarch is as dust." If an earthly king's favor is life, God's favor is far more (Psalm 30:5).
• Compare Job 29:23–24; Psalm 4:6; 30:5; 72:6.
units.summary: A ruler's smile can be like spring rain on a field waiting for harvest.
units.principle: Favor from those in authority can bring life and fruitfulness, and it points beyond itself to the far greater favor of God.
units.insight: Nehemiah was sad in the king's presence, which could have cost him dearly. Instead Artaxerxes asked, "What do you request?" and granted all he needed to rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:2–8). The king's face shone on him, and a city lived again. Most of us crave someone's approving look: a parent's, a boss's, a crowd's. The longing is real, but no human face can carry its full weight. The psalmist prayed, "LORD, lift up the light of Your countenance upon us" (Psalm 4:6). In Christ that prayer is answered. God's face shines on believers because Christ bore the wrath we deserved, and "we shall be saved from wrath through Him" (Romans 5:9). Seek His favor first, and you will not starve for anyone else's.
units.application: If you lead, remember how much your face and tone mean to the people under you. This week, give a specific word of approval to someone who works hard without notice. Parents, let your children see your face light up when they come into the room. If you are starved for a parent's or boss's approval, bring that hunger to God in prayer, and read Numbers 6:24–26 aloud over yourself.

rel.note: Buying the truth and refusing to sell it shows the same choice of understanding over silver.
Wisdom's gain is better than silver and gold and more precious than rubies.
The command to "get wisdom" at any cost uses the same verb.
Wisdom calls for her instruction to be chosen over silver and choice gold.
Wisdom's fruit is better than fine gold, in her own words.

units.notes:
• "Get" translates *qanah*, to acquire or buy. It is the verb of 4:5, "Get wisdom! Get understanding!" and of 23:23, "Buy the truth, and do not sell it." Wisdom is something a person must go after and pay for.
• The same comparison runs through the opening chapters: "For her proceeds are better than the profits of silver, And her gain than fine gold" (3:14), and "Receive my instruction, and not silver" (8:10).
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Wisdom and wealth are not incompatible; but this comparison is between wealth without wisdom and wisdom without wealth."
• Henry: "Grace will stand us in stead in a dying hour, when gold will do us no good." To "stand us in stead" means to serve us well.
• Compare 3:13–15; 8:10–11, 19; Job 28:15–19; Matthew 16:26.
units.summary: Gold can buy almost anything except the wisdom to use it well.
units.principle: Wisdom is worth more than any wealth, and a person must deliberately choose it over money.
units.insight: Solomon could have asked God for riches; he asked for an understanding heart, and God gave him wisdom and wealth besides (1 Kings 3:9–13). Later he let gold, wives and alliances draw his heart away (1 Kings 11:4). The verse is easy to agree with and hard to live. Our calendars and bank statements show what we are actually choosing. The rich young ruler "went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:22); he chose silver. Paul counted "all things loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). In Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). The surest way to grow in wisdom is to know Him.
units.application: Look at your calendar and budget for this week and ask what they say you value. Move one hour from screens or overtime to Scripture, a mentor or a class that grows wisdom. Young people choosing a college or job, weigh where you will grow in wisdom, not only what you will earn. Parents, praise your children's wise choices as warmly as their grades or trophies.

rel.note: Guarding the mouth preserves life, as guarding the way preserves the soul.
The way of the upright is a highway, the same image of a cleared and level road.
The gray head is a crown when it is found in the way of righteousness, the long end of the road kept here.
Keeping the commandment keeps the soul, the same guard-and-be-guarded pattern.
Pondering the path and removing the foot from evil describes how the highway is kept.

units.notes:
• "Highway" pictures a built-up road, cleared of stones and raised above the ground, unlike a rough track. Isaiah draws on the same picture of a raised road in "the Highway of Holiness," where "The unclean shall not pass over it" (Isaiah 35:8).
• "Keeps" and "preserves" translate two Hebrew verbs that both mean to guard or watch. The NASB has "watches his way." So the verse speaks of guarding twice: guard your road, and the road guards you.
• Bridges: "The real injury is not from our living in the world, but from the world living in us."
• Henry: "Keep thy way and God will keep thee."
• Compare 4:26–27; 19:16; Psalm 1:1–2; 1 John 5:18.
units.summary: For the upright, leaving evil is not an occasional detour; it is the road they live on.
units.principle: Turning from evil is not an occasional act but the direction of a godly life, and staying on that road guards the soul.
units.insight: Joseph stayed on the highway when Potiphar's wife pressed him day after day. He refused, and when she seized him, he ran (Genesis 39:10–12). He lost his coat and his freedom, but he kept his soul. David, years later, stepped off the road one evening, lingering on a rooftop, and the detour cost him dearly (2 Samuel 11:2–4). Most falls start with a small exit from the highway: a lingering look, a private compromise, a "just this once." Where have you begun treating departure from evil as an occasional effort instead of the road you live on? The road is not walked alone. Jesus called Himself "the way" (John 14:6), and He keeps those who walk with Him, so that no one can snatch them from His hand (John 10:28).
units.application: Identify one exit ramp that regularly takes you off the highway: a website, a late-night habit, a friendship that pulls you toward gossip or drinking. Close it this week. Young people, decide your boundaries before the party, not at it. Parents, talk with your children about the small first steps away from the right road. Accountability partners, ask each other about direction, not only about falls.

rel.note: When pride comes, shame follows, an earlier form of this warning.
Pride produces strife, another of the ruins pride leads to.
The next verse names the better way: a humble spirit with the lowly.
The LORD detests the proud in heart, which is why pride ends in ruin.
Before destruction the heart is haughty, and before honor comes humility.
A man's pride will bring him low, while the humble in spirit retain honor.

units.notes:
• "Destruction," *shever*, means a breaking or shattering, the word used of the spirit broken by a perverse tongue in 15:4. "Fall" means a stumbling; the NASB and YLT have "stumbling."
• "A haughty spirit" is literally a height of spirit: a person standing tall in his own eyes.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "A bulging wall is near a downfall." A wall that bulges outward is about to collapse; pride is the bulge.
• The thought returns in 18:12, "Before destruction the heart of a man is haughty, And before honor is humility," and in 29:23, "A man's pride will bring him low."
• Compare Isaiah 14:12–15; Daniel 4:30–37; Luke 18:14; 1 Corinthians 10:12; James 4:6.
units.summary: Pride walks a few steps ahead of every fall, and it never looks down.
units.principle: Pride blinds a person to his need before God and others, and that blindness leads to ruin; humility is the safe road.
units.insight: Scripture is crowded with this verse. Nebuchadnezzar looked over his city and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…?" and while the word was still in his mouth his kingdom was taken from him (Daniel 4:30–31). Haman boasted of his honors one day and was hanged on his own gallows soon after (Esther 5:11–12; 7:10). Peter declared, "I will never be made to stumble," and denied Jesus that night (Matthew 26:33–35, 69–75). Bridges pictures the haughty man with his head held high: "The man looks upward, instead of to his steps." We see pride easily in others and rarely in ourselves. Yet Peter's story does not end at the fall. Jesus restored him (John 21:15–17). Pride's road ends in ruin, but the humble who fall into His hands are lifted up.
units.application: Ask God this week to show you one area where you are presuming: on your health, your marriage, your spiritual strength or your standing at work. The next time someone challenges you, welcome the correction instead of defending yourself. Leaders, watch for the moment success makes you stop listening. Young people, beware the confidence that says "it could never happen to me" (1 Corinthians 10:12). Pray daily to stay low and teachable.

rel.note: Pride goes before destruction, which is why sharing the spoil of the proud is the worse choice.
An earlier "better than" in the chapter also prefers a lowly portion with righteousness to great gain without it.
Pride brings a man low, while the humble in spirit keep honor.
God scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble.

units.notes:
• "Lowly" translates a word for the poor and afflicted, people of low standing. The ESV and YLT read "the poor," the NASB "the lowly." The verse joins a humble spirit with a humble place.
• "Divide the spoil" pictures soldiers sharing plunder after a victory, a picture of worldly success won by force.
• Bridges: "Better is an humble spirit, than a high condition; to have our temper brought down, than our outward condition raised." By "temper" he means one's inner disposition.
• Compare 3:34; 15:33; 29:23; Isaiah 57:15; Matthew 5:3; Luke 1:51–53.
units.summary: Better to sit low with the humble than to stand tall with the proud on their way down.
units.principle: A humble heart among humble people is worth more than any success shared with the proud.
units.insight: Moses chose "rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin" in Pharaoh's court (Hebrews 11:25). He chose the lowly over the spoil. Ruth chose to go with poor, bitter Naomi rather than return to her own people (Ruth 1:16–17). Both choices looked like losses, and both were gains. We face smaller versions of this all the time: the clique that mocks others, the deal that requires looking the other way, the promotion that would cost us our humility. Henry calls this verse "a paradox which the children of this world cannot understand". Jesus lived it. Though He was rich, He became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He was "gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29), and He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
units.application: Look at the circles you are drawn to: the people you want to be seen with at work, at school or at church. This week, spend time on purpose with someone others overlook, such as an elderly shut-in, a newcomer or the coworker no one eats with. If success is offered on terms that require arrogance or cruelty, decline it. Parents, teach children to sit with the lonely child, not only the popular crowd.

rel.note: The one who fears the commandment is rewarded, while the one who despises the word is destroyed.
Committing one's works to the LORD is the trust that brings this happiness.
The one who trusts in the LORD will be prospered, set against the proud and greedy.
Whoever trusts in the LORD will be safe.
Trusting the LORD with all the heart is the trust this verse calls happy.

units.notes:
• "The word," *davar*, can also mean a matter or affair. The KJV reads, "He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good"; the ESV and NASB read "the word."
• "Happy is he" translates the declaration of blessing found in 3:13, "Happy is the man who finds wisdom," and 29:18, "happy is he who keeps the law." It is the word that opens Psalm 1, "Blessed is the man." The ESV and NASB read "blessed."
• Bridges: "Two things are needed for the success of a matter—wisdom and faith." In plain words, use the mind God gave you and trust the God who gave it.
• Compare 3:5–6; 13:13; 28:25; 29:25; Psalm 2:12; Jeremiah 17:7–8.
units.summary: Listen well and lean hard on God; that is where real happiness is found.
units.principle: True good and happiness come to those who attend wisely to God's word and rest their whole confidence in Him.
units.insight: When Esther faced a decree that could destroy her people, she did both halves of this verse. She handled the matter wisely, preparing a banquet and choosing her moment, and she trusted the LORD, calling a three-day fast before she went to the king (Esther 4:16; 5:4–8). Many of us lean to one side. Some trust God but will not think, and call it faith. Others think hard but will not trust, and call it responsibility. Luther, quoted by Bridges, said he had lost everything he held in his own hands, but "whatever I have been able to place in God's, I still possess." Jesus answered every temptation with the written word (Matthew 4:4) and "committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). He heeded and He trusted, perfectly.
units.application: Before a decision this week, such as a purchase, a job change or a hard conversation, do two things. First, search Scripture and seek wise counsel on the matter. Second, pray and deliberately hand the outcome to God. Students and young adults, do not mistake impulsiveness for faith. Planners and managers, do not mistake worry for responsibility. If you are anxious, read Jeremiah 17:7–8 and name what you are trusting instead of the LORD.

rel.note: The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly, while fools pour out folly.
The wise heart adds learning to the lips, the inner source of the sweet speech praised here.
Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, the same sweetness carried into healing.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver, showing how timing and grace serve truth.

units.notes:
• "Learning," *leqach*, can also mean persuasiveness, the power of teaching to win a hearing; the ESV and NASB have "persuasiveness." The same word describes the seductress's "enticing speech" (7:21), so persuasive speech can serve wisdom or folly.
• "Increases learning" repeats the wording of 1:5, "A wise man will hear and increase learning," and the same word returns in 16:23.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Wise teachers choose their words carefully and in so doing enhance the learning experience for their students."
• Augustine tells how the eloquence of Ambrose first drew him to listen and then slowly brought him to conviction (Confessions, Book 5).
• Compare 15:2; 25:11; Ecclesiastes 12:10; Colossians 4:6.
units.summary: Wisdom earns a name for itself, and kindness gives it a hearing.
units.principle: Real wisdom is recognized in time, and it teaches best when it speaks with grace.
units.insight: Abigail met David when he was on his way to kill every man in Nabal's household. She bowed, spoke humbly and wisely, and reminded him of the LORD's purposes for him. David answered, "blessed is your advice" (1 Samuel 25:33), and turned back. Her words were sweet, and they increased his understanding in the moment that mattered. Many of us have truth without sweetness. We are right, and we make sure everyone knows it. Others have sweetness without truth. The verse asks for both. Jesus spoke "gracious words" that left His hometown marveling (Luke 4:22), and the officers sent to arrest Him came back saying, "No man ever spoke like this Man!" (John 7:46).
units.application: Before you correct someone this week, whether a child, an employee, a spouse or a small-group member, think about how to say it as well as what to say. Begin with something true and kind. Teachers and preachers, prepare tone, illustrations and warmth, not only content. If you are known for being right but hard to listen to, ask a trusted friend how your words land, and change one habit.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, the same image applied to speech.
The law of the wise is a fountain of life, the same phrase as "wellspring of life."
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life that turns one from the snares of death.
Those who refuse wisdom eat the fruit of their own way, folly becoming its own punishment.

units.notes:
• "Wellspring of life" is the same Hebrew phrase rendered "fountain of life" in 13:14 and 14:27 and "well of life" in 10:11. The ESV and NASB have "fountain of life" here as well.
• "Correction," *musar*, is the book's word for discipline that trains. Translations take the line in different directions: the 1984 NIV says folly brings punishment to fools, the NLT says "discipline is wasted on fools," and the ESV speaks of the instruction of fools.
• Bridges on the fool's teaching: "Yet the stream cannot rise above its level." Words cannot rise higher than the heart they come from.
• Compare 1:31–32; 10:11; Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:14.
units.summary: Understanding keeps refreshing the one who has it, while folly keeps punishing its own.
units.principle: Understanding is a lasting source of life for its owner, while folly becomes its own harsh teacher.
units.insight: The prodigal son ignored his father's wisdom and learned from folly instead. Only when he was feeding pigs and longing for their food did he come to himself (Luke 15:15–17). Folly corrected him, painfully. Many of us learn this way: we refuse counsel and let consequences teach us. God in His mercy uses even that, but how much better to drink from the spring than to be dragged home by pain. Jesus offered the Samaritan woman water that would become "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). Understanding rooted in Him is not a reservoir that runs dry in a drought; it keeps flowing. Where are you still insisting on learning the hard way?
units.application: Name one area where you keep repeating the same painful mistake: money, anger, relationships or overcommitment. This week ask a wise person for counsel, and follow it. Parents, sometimes let a teenager feel the natural result of a foolish choice instead of rescuing every time, while staying close. Mentors and leaders, when someone refuses counsel again and again, keep praying for them and stay available for the day they are ready to listen.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, the fruit of a well-taught heart.
The heart of the righteous studies how to answer, the same heart-first pattern of speech.
Sweetness of the lips increases learning; this verse traces that learning back to the heart.
Keeping the heart with all diligence matters because the issues of life, speech included, flow from it.

units.notes:
• "Teaches" is literally "makes wise" or "makes prudent": the wise heart causes the mouth to act wisely. YLT renders it that way.
• "Learning," *leqach*, is the word used in 16:21; the ESV and NASB again have "persuasiveness." The two sayings belong together: 16:21 stresses the sweetness of the lips, and 16:23 the wise heart behind it.
• Bridges: "Who does not know the difference between one, who speaks of what he has read or heard, and one who speaks of what he has felt and tasted?"
• Compare 4:23; 10:31; 15:28; Luke 6:45.
units.summary: Good words are learned in the heart before they are spoken by the mouth.
units.principle: Speech is only as wise as the heart that trains it, so the way to better words is a better-taught heart.
units.insight: Jesus said, "out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks" (Luke 6:45). We often try to fix our speech at the level of the mouth: count to ten, choose better words, avoid certain topics. Those help, but the verse sends us deeper. A heart full of resentment will leak it; a heart full of God's word will overflow with it. Ezra "had prepared his heart to seek the Law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10): heart first, then life, then teaching. Isaiah heard the Servant say, "The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary" (Isaiah 50:4). Jesus is that Servant. He spoke such words because, as the same passage says, His ear was opened morning by morning to hear from the Father.
units.application: If your words have been sharp, careless or empty lately, do not only resolve to talk better; fill your heart. Memorize one verse this week and meditate on it before conversations. Teachers and preachers, pray over the text until it has taught you before you teach it. Parents, address a child's heart attitudes, not just their tone. Before an important conversation, spend ten quiet minutes asking God to teach your heart first.

rel.note: A good word makes an anxious heart glad.
The words of the pure are pleasant, the same "pleasant words" traced to a pure heart.
A wholesome, healing tongue is a tree of life.
Sweetness of the lips increases learning, the same sweetness here bringing healing.
The ungodly man's lips burn like fire, the opposite of words that heal.

units.notes:
• "Pleasant words" is literally "words of pleasantness," the same expression found in 15:26, where "the words of the pure are pleasant."
• "Health" translates a word for healing, used in 13:17, "a faithful ambassador brings health," and behind "wholesome" in 15:4. The NASB has "healing."
• "The bones" stand for the deep strength of the body. Compare 3:8, "It will be health to your flesh, And strength to your bones," and 17:22, "a broken spirit dries the bones."
• Bridges: "The sweets of pleasure are not always health." Honey is different: it both pleases and nourishes, and so do kind words.
• Compare 12:25; 15:23; Psalm 19:10; 119:103.
units.summary: Kind words are like honey: they taste good, and they heal.
units.principle: Gracious words both delight and heal, doing good to the whole person who receives them.
units.insight: When Paul was being led as a prisoner toward Rome, believers walked out to meet him at Appii Forum and Three Inns, and "he thanked God and took courage" (Acts 28:15). A few faces and words did what no physician could. Jonathan went to David in the wilderness and "strengthened his hand in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). Words like these cost little and do much, yet many of us are stingy with them. We think kind words and never say them. The sweetest words of all are God's: "How sweet are Your words to my taste, Sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Psalm 119:103). Jesus spoke them to the weary and the guilty. A heart that has tasted His words has honey to share.
units.application: This week, say aloud three kind words you have only thought: thank a teacher, encourage a discouraged coworker, bless your spouse in front of the children. Visit or call someone who is sick or grieving and bring words of comfort and Scripture. Leaders, notice who has gone weeks without encouragement. Parents, end the day with a specific word of delight to each child.

rel.note: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but the wise heed counsel.
The identical saying, where the warning is treated in full.
A man's ways look pure in his own eyes, which is why a deadly way can seem right.
The heart plans its way, but only the LORD's direction keeps the steps safe.

units.notes:
• The NKJV text of 16:25 is identical to 14:12. The two copies fall on either side of the division at 16:1, where a new movement of Solomon's sayings begins.
• "Seems right" is literally "is straight before a man": from where he stands, the road looks level and true.
• "The way of death" is plural in Hebrew, "the ways of death," as the KJV shows.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "And think not this a vain repetition; but know that it is thus redoubled, that it may be the better remarked and remembered." "Remarked" here means noticed.
• Compare 12:15; 14:12; 21:2; Matthew 7:13–14; John 14:6.
units.summary: Proverbs says it twice: feeling sure of the road does not make it safe.
units.principle: A path is proved by where it ends, not by how right it feels; plans made without God can be sincere and still deadly.
units.insight: Saul was sure he had obeyed the LORD when he spared King Agag and the best of the livestock. He even planned a sacrifice with the spoil. Samuel answered, "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul's way seemed right to him, and it cost him the kingdom. Paul once thought he was serving God by persecuting the church (Acts 26:9). Sincerity did not save either man. The warning appears twice because we need it twice. Bridges: "It is no proof that a way is right, because it seemeth right." Many ways seem right, but Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). The safest question is not "Do I feel sure?" but "Is this the LORD's way?"
units.application: Before you commit to a major plan this month, such as a move, a relationship, an investment or a church change, test it against Scripture, not only your feelings. Ask two mature believers to look at where the road ends, not just where it starts. Parents, help teenagers ask "Where does this lead?" instead of "Does this feel right?" If you are already on a road you suspect is wrong, turn back now.

rel.note: The one who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, the reward hunger drives the worker toward.
In all labor there is profit, while idle talk leads only to poverty.
The lazy man's way is a hedge of thorns, the opposite of the worker spurred on by need.
The ungodly man labors just as hard, but at digging up evil.

units.notes:
• "The person who labors" is literally "the soul of the laborer." The Hebrew word *nephesh*, often translated "soul," can also mean appetite or desire, so the ESV and NASB speak of "a worker's appetite."
• "Drives him on" pictures pressure bearing down on the worker. The ESV and NASB say his hunger "urges" him, and YLT pictures his mouth making him bend over his work.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "That is to say that hunger will make a man work when nothing else will."
• Compare 12:11; 14:23; Genesis 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 3:10; John 6:27.
units.summary: An empty stomach is one of God's ways of getting a worker out of bed.
units.principle: God has built the need for daily bread into human life to move people to honest work, and the worker rightly benefits from his labor.
units.insight: Ruth did not wait for bread to fall from heaven. She went out to glean behind the reapers and kept at it "from morning until now" (Ruth 2:7), and God used that ordinary hunger and labor to bring her to Boaz. Paul worked night and day with his own hands so as not to be a burden to anyone (2 Thessalonians 3:8). Hunger and need are not curses to resent; they are part of God's merciful design. Yet the verse raises a deeper question. Jesus said, "Do not labor for the food which perishes, but for the food which endures to everlasting life" (John 6:27). Bridges: "Our hands and our time are given to the world; our hearts to God." Work hard for bread, but do not let bread become your god.
units.application: If you are discouraged in an ordinary job, thank God this week that your work feeds your family; that is honorable. Parents, let teenagers earn something themselves instead of receiving everything freely. If you are able to work but have been avoiding it, take one concrete step toward employment. Employers, pay fairly and promptly. And everyone, set aside daily time to feed your soul as faithfully as you feed your body.

rel.note: Pleasant words heal like honey, while this man's words burn like fire.
The laborer works hard to feed himself, while the ungodly man works just as hard at digging up evil.
The perverse man and the whisperer continue the portrait of the troublemaker.
Gossip feeds the fire of strife the way wood feeds a flame.
The one who digs a pit falls into it, the end of the man who digs up evil.
The worthless person with a perverse mouth devises evil and sows discord, an earlier portrait of the same man.

units.notes:
• "An ungodly man" is literally "a man of Belial," a phrase for a worthless, good-for-nothing person; the ESV and NASB have "worthless." A similar description introduces the troublemaker of 6:12, "A worthless person, a wicked man." Paul later uses "Belial" as a name for the evil one (2 Corinthians 6:15).
• "Digs up" is the verb used for digging a pit, as in 26:27. The ESV has "plots"; the NASB keeps "digs up."
• Henry on the slanderer: "If none appear above ground, rather than want it they will dig for it". In plain words, if he cannot find a fault on the surface, he will dig until he does.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "What he finds he spreads; his speech is like scorching fire—the simile speaks of the devastating effect of his words."
• Compare 6:12–14; 26:20–21; Psalm 7:14–15; James 3:5–6.
units.summary: Some people dig for treasure; the worthless man digs for dirt and sets it on fire with his tongue.
units.principle: A worthless person spends his energy finding and spreading evil, and his words burn whatever they touch.
units.insight: When David fled from Saul, Doeg the Edomite saw the priest Ahimelech help him. Doeg dug it up and reported it to Saul, and the result was the slaughter of the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:9–19). Doeg did not need to lie; he took a fact and set it on fire. That is the danger for us too. We rarely invent evil, but we can go looking for it: searching someone's past online, asking leading questions, repeating the worst version of a story. The question is not only "Is it true?" but "Why am I digging?" Love "thinks no evil" and "bears all things" (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). Christ, who knows every hidden sin, came not to expose us to ruin but to cover us with His mercy.
units.application: When you feel the urge to dig into someone's failures, through searches, questions or stored-up grievances, stop and ask why. If you know something damaging about a coworker, church member or former friend, keep it buried unless love or safety requires telling the right person. Leaders, refuse to reward people who bring you dirt on others. Parents, teach children not to collect and repeat other children's mistakes.

rel.note: The worthless man who digs up evil supplies what the whisperer spreads.
Repeating a matter separates friends, while covering a transgression seeks love.
The talebearer's words go down into the inmost body, showing why whispers wound so deeply.
Where there is no talebearer, strife ceases, the reverse of strife sown by whispering.
One who sows discord among brethren is among the seven things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Sows" is literally "sends out," as strife is let loose among people. Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "It is, appropriately, the word used of the release of flaming foxes in the Philistines' corn, Judges 15:5." There Samson lit the torches and "let the foxes go into the standing grain."
• "A perverse man" is literally "a man of perversities," someone who overturns what is right.
• "Whisperer" describes someone who murmurs against others behind their backs. The same word is "talebearer" in 18:8 and 26:20–22. The ESV keeps "whisperer"; the NASB has "slanderer."
• Bridges on how the whisperer works: "He has seen or heard probably only a little. He guesses at the rest to make his story complete."
• Compare 6:16–19; 17:9; 26:20–22; 2 Corinthians 12:20.
units.summary: Strife is sown in whispers, and the harvest is broken friendships.
units.principle: Strife and broken friendships often begin with small, hidden words, and those who spread them do great harm.
units.insight: Absalom stood at the city gate day after day and quietly told each man with a complaint that his case was good, but the king had no one to hear it (2 Samuel 15:2–6). Whispered words, repeated for years, stole the hearts of Israel and split the kingdom. Whispering rarely feels like sin while we do it. It feels like concern, a prayer request or simply being open. But Paul lists "whisperings" among the sins he feared to find in the church (2 Corinthians 12:20). The gospel moves the other way. Christ came to break down "the middle wall of separation" and make peace (Ephesians 2:14). Those He has reconciled to God are sent out to reconcile others, not to separate them.
units.application: Before you repeat something about someone this week, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it necessary? Would I say it with that person present? If not, keep it to yourself. When someone brings you a story about a friend, ask, "Have you talked to them?" Church leaders, address whispering campaigns directly. If gossip has already separated you from a friend, take the first step toward that friend.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, the end of the neighbor who follows the violent man.
The schemer's face completes the portrait of the troublemaker begun in this cluster.
The father's first warning pictures sinners enticing a son into violence with the same verb.
Going with an angry man teaches his ways and sets a snare for the soul.
Do not envy the oppressor or choose any of his ways.

units.notes:
• "Entices" is the verb of 1:10, "if sinners entice you," where the father warns his son against joining a violent gang. In both places it means to persuade someone toward wrongdoing. The same root gives the word for "the simple," the open, easily persuaded person (1:4, 22).
• The father describes the same road in 1:15–16: "do not walk in the way with them … For their feet run to evil, And they make haste to shed blood."
• Ironside: "It is well not to be too easily persuaded."
• Compare 1:10–19; 3:31; 4:14–17; 22:24–25; 1 Corinthians 15:33.
units.summary: Violence rarely starts with a blow; it usually starts with an invitation.
units.principle: Violent and destructive people often work by recruitment, so the wise refuse to be drawn in by persuasive companions.
units.insight: Jehoshaphat was a good king, but he let wicked Ahab draw him into war with the words, "Will you go with me…?" He answered, "I am as you are, and my people as your people" (2 Chronicles 18:3). He nearly died in Ahab's battle, and a prophet asked him, "Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?" (2 Chronicles 19:2). Many good people have been led onto bad roads not because they loved evil but because they could not say no to a strong personality. The violent man's power lies in his persuasion. Jesus was enticed too, offered all the kingdoms of the world for a single act of worship, and He answered with Scripture (Matthew 4:8–10). Whose voice is pulling you along right now?
units.application: Young people, when friends pressure you to join a fight, a prank that hurts someone, an online pile-on or anything you would not do alone, walk away. Parents, know your children's friends and talk openly about peer pressure. Adults at work or church, beware of strong personalities recruiting you into a campaign against someone. Before you sign on to anything, take time to seek God's mind.

rel.note: The one who winks with the eye causes trouble.
The violent man who entices his neighbor is part of the same portrait of the troublemaker.
The worthless person winks with his eyes and devises evil, the same body language of scheming.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates, the inner source of these gestures.

units.notes:
• The KJV says he "shutteth his eyes," and the NASB renders "purses" as "compresses." The picture may be of a man narrowing his eyes in concentration or giving a sly signal.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Often people who are planning wicked things betray themselves with malicious expressions."
