• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "They search the devil's skull for new devices, and are very inventive to invent that which may do harm." "Devices" here means schemes.
• Compare 6:12–14; 10:10, "He who winks with the eye causes trouble"; Psalm 35:19.
units.summary: Evil plans often show on the face before they show in the deed.
units.principle: Hidden plans for evil tend to show themselves in small signals before they become deeds, and the wise learn to notice them, beginning with their own.
units.insight: Judas sat at the Last Supper among the disciples, outwardly one of them, already set on betrayal. Jesus saw through him and said, "What you do, do quickly" (John 13:27). The disciples missed every signal; the Lord missed none. This verse is first a warning to watch our own faces. Narrowed eyes during a meeting, tight lips when a rival is praised, a knowing glance to an ally: these can be the first visible signs of a scheme taking shape inside us. David prayed, "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart Be acceptable in Your sight" (Psalm 19:14), because the heart plots before the hands act. Bring the hidden plan to God before it reaches your face.
units.application: Notice what your face does when someone you resent is speaking: an eye-roll, a smirk, a look to a friend. Treat it as a warning light and deal with the heart behind it. Parents, when you catch a knowing glance between siblings, gently ask what is going on. Leaders and teachers, watch for signals of alliances forming against someone, and address them early and calmly.

rel.note: The upright who keep their way preserve their soul, the road on which the gray head is found.
Grandchildren are the crown of old men, another crown that a long, faithful life may bring.
The splendor of old men is their gray head, the same honor given to age.
Wisdom places a crown of glory on the head, the same phrase used of the righteous gray head.

units.notes:
• The NKJV, like the KJV, reads the second line as a condition with "If." The ESV, NASB and YLT read it as a statement of where the crown is gained: in a righteous life.
• "Crown of glory" joins a crown with beauty or splendor. The same phrase describes Wisdom's gift in 4:9: "A crown of glory she will deliver to you."
• Henry: "Let old people be old disciples". He means that the aged should keep walking in the way of righteousness they set out on long ago.
• Old age is often a blessing in Scripture (Genesis 15:15; 25:8), but not always: Hosea pictures Israel with gray hairs it does not even notice, aging without returning to God (Hosea 7:9).
• Compare 17:6; 20:29; Psalm 71:18; 92:14; Isaiah 46:4.
units.summary: Gray hair becomes a crown only when it has been earned on the road of righteousness.
units.principle: Old age deserves honor, and its true glory is a long life spent in righteousness; years alone do not make a crown.
units.insight: Caleb at eighty-five said, "I am as strong this day as on the day that Moses sent me," and asked for the hill country still held by giants (Joshua 14:10–12). He had "wholly followed the LORD God of Israel" for forty-five years (14:14). Anna, a widow of about eighty-four, served God with fastings and prayers night and day, and she was there to greet the infant Jesus (Luke 2:36–38). Their gray heads were crowns. Solomon is the sobering contrast: "when Solomon was old," his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). Age does not guarantee godliness. To the young, the crown is being shaped now, by daily choices. To the old, it is not too late to walk in righteousness. To all, honor the righteous aged among you.
units.application: Young people, find an older believer whose life you admire and ask how they stayed faithful; visit or call them this month. Churches, give the godly aged visible honor and real roles. Older believers, mentor someone younger and keep growing; make Psalm 71:18 your prayer. If you are older and carrying regrets, repent and begin walking righteously now. Families, show respect to grandparents in how you speak to them and about them.

rel.note: The one slow to wrath has great understanding, while the impulsive exalts folly.
The one slow to anger calms strife, while a wrathful man stirs it up.
Discretion makes a man slow to anger, and overlooking an offense is his glory.
The one with no rule over his spirit is like a city with broken walls, the opposite of the one who rules his spirit.
A fool vents all his feelings, while the wise holds them back.

units.notes:
• "Slow to anger" is literally "long of nostrils," a Hebrew picture of anger that takes a long time to heat up. Scripture uses the same description of God Himself, who is "Slow to anger" (Psalm 103:8; compare Exodus 34:6).
• "The mighty" translates a word for a warrior or hero, the word used for David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:8). The NLT has "Better to be patient than powerful."
• Bridges on why the inner battle is harder: "That is only the battle of a day. This, the weary, unceasing conflict of a life." A city falls once; the spirit must be ruled every day.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "There have been many kings who had conquered nations, and yet were slaves to their own passions."
• Compare 14:29; 15:18; 19:11; James 1:19–20; Galatians 5:22–23.
units.summary: The hardest city to conquer is the one inside your own chest.
units.principle: Mastery of one's own temper and spirit is a greater strength than any outward power or conquest.
units.insight: Gideon had just routed the Midianites when the men of Ephraim attacked him with sharp words for leaving them out. He answered gently, honoring their part, and "their anger toward him subsided" (Judges 8:1–3). His rule over his own spirit was a greater victory than the battle. Moses, the humblest man on earth (Numbers 12:3), struck the rock in anger and was barred from entering the land (Numbers 20:10–12). We tend to admire powerful people and excuse our own outbursts as personality. Scripture reverses that. Jesus, with all power at His command, "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). His Spirit produces self-control in His people (Galatians 5:23). Ruling your spirit is not a self-help project; it is the fruit of being ruled by Him.
units.application: Identify the situation where you most often lose your temper: traffic, a certain family member, criticism at work, a child's disobedience. Decide now what you will do when it comes: pause, breathe, pray and lower your voice. Parents, model apologizing after an outburst. Leaders, never make decisions while angry. If anger has hurt someone this week, go and make it right before the day ends (Ephesians 4:26).

rel.note: The chapter opens and closes with the same confession: the final answer and decision are "from the LORD."
The LORD has made all things for His purpose, so even what looks like chance serves Him.
Man plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps, the same rule over human choices.
Casting lots ends disputes between the powerful, because the decision is received as God's.
No counsel stands against the LORD, and victory belongs to Him however the horse is prepared.

units.notes:
• "Decision" translates *mishpat*, the ordinary word for judgment or verdict. It is the word behind "justice" in 16:8, "judgment" in 16:10 and "Honest" in 16:11. The KJV speaks of "the whole disposing thereof."
• Scripture records lots used to divide the land (Numbers 26:55; Joshua 18:10), to choose between the two goats on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:8), to single out Achan and Jonathan (Joshua 7:16–18; 1 Samuel 14:41–42) and to choose Matthias (Acts 1:26). Matthias is the last such use recorded among God's people; after Pentecost the church is led by the Spirit and the word.
• Even a pagan lot was ruled by God. Haman cast Pur, the lot, to pick a day to destroy the Jews, and the date it gave left time for their deliverance (Esther 3:7; 9:24–26).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Ultimately, the Lord, not the disciple's self-possession alone, rules his destiny, as illustrated by 'the lot.'"
• Compare 16:1; 18:18; Matthew 10:29–30; Romans 8:28.
units.summary: Nothing is random to God; even the lot falls where He decides.
units.principle: Nothing falls outside God's rule, not even what looks like chance, so His people can act, decide and rest in His sovereign care.
units.insight: Sailors on a storm-tossed ship cast lots to find out who had brought the trouble, and the lot fell on Jonah (Jonah 1:7). The pagan crew did not know the LORD, but the LORD ruled their lot. Then He prepared a great fish to swallow the runaway prophet (1:17). Nothing in Jonah's flight was out of God's hand. Life often feels random: a diagnosis, a layoff, a chance meeting that changes everything. This verse does not tell us to roll dice for guidance; we have God's word and Spirit. It tells us that what we call chance lies in our Father's hand. Jesus said not one sparrow falls apart from the Father, and "the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Matthew 10:29–30). That is solid ground to stand on.
units.application: When something unexpected happens this week, good or bad, pause and say, "This did not take God by surprise." Do not use chance or games to decide God's will; seek Scripture, prayer and godly counsel. Do not treat this verse as permission to gamble; it describes God's rule, not a way to make money. Parents, when a child is anxious about an uncertain outcome, such as a test, a tryout or a move, talk about God's care in the details.

rel.note: A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble.
A dinner of herbs with love outweighs a fatted calf with hatred, the same choice of peace over plenty.
The strife that spoils the feast here is best stopped at its first trickle.
A home ruled by contention is so miserable that the wilderness is preferable.

units.notes:
• *Feasting* translates zebach, the ordinary Hebrew word for a sacrifice, especially one whose meat was eaten at a family feast. The KJV keeps "sacrifices." The law told the worshiper to eat the meat of his peace offering on the day it was offered (Leviticus 7:15), so a house "full of sacrifices" was a house full of food and celebration.
• A house of sacrifices also looked godly. Ironside: such a feast "would be supposed to indicate great piety on the part of the host."
• Compare 15:16 ("Better is a little with the fear of the LORD, Than great treasure with trouble") and 15:17 ("Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, Than a fatted calf with hatred").
• Compare 21:19, where even the wilderness is better than a home ruled by contention.
units.summary: Peace turns a crust of bread into a feast; strife turns a feast into a battlefield.
units.principle: Peace in a home is worth more than prosperity or religious display, and neither can buy back what strife destroys.
units.insight: Every year Elkanah took his family to Shiloh to sacrifice, and every year the sacrificial feast became the place where Peninnah provoked Hannah until she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:3–7). The table was full; the home was not at peace. Centuries later the church at Corinth turned the Lord's Supper into a scene of division, and Paul said they came together "not for the better but for the worse" (1 Corinthians 11:17). A home can have a full table and a full calendar of church activity and still be empty of peace. Henry: "Love will sweeten a dry morsel, but strife will sour and embitter a house full of sacrifices." The peace this verse prizes is finally a gift of Christ, who "Himself is our peace" (Ephesians 2:14). What is your home really full of?
units.application: If money is tight, do not let financial worry turn the dinner table into a battleground; a simple meal shared in kindness is a real gift to your children. If you host holidays or church events, give more thought to the peace in the room than to the menu. Spouses: agree to save hard conversations for a calmer moment instead of spoiling a shared meal. Pastors and ministry leaders: do not let busy religious activity cover a fractured team.

rel.note: The same phrase, "a son who causes shame," describes the son who sleeps through harvest.
The fool ends up serving the wise of heart, the same reversal this verse describes.
The king favors a wise servant and turns his wrath on the one who causes shame.
A son who mistreats his parents is another "son who causes shame," showing what forfeits his place.

units.notes:
• *A son who causes shame* is the same phrase used of the son who sleeps through harvest (10:5) and of the son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother (19:26). In Proverbs it marks a son whose conduct disgraces his family.
• Henry: "True merit does not go by dignity." By "dignity" he means rank: worth is not settled by position.
• Jacob shows a hired worker overtaking the sons of a household. He arrived at Laban's house with nothing but a staff, and by faithful, shrewd service he came to hold so much of the family's wealth that Laban's sons complained, "Jacob has taken away all that was our father's" (Genesis 31:1).
• Compare 11:29, "the fool will be servant to the wise of heart," and 14:35, where the king favors a wise servant.
• Jesus draws on the same household picture: "a slave does not abide in the house forever, but a son abides forever" (John 8:35).
units.summary: Birth gives a son his place in the family, but only character lets him keep it.
units.principle: Privilege of birth can be forfeited by folly, and faithfulness can earn a trust that privilege throws away.
units.insight: Esau was the firstborn, yet he "despised his birthright" for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:34). Joseph arrived in Egypt as a slave, and his faithfulness made him overseer of Potiphar's whole house (Genesis 39:4–6). The proverb warns anyone who leans on privilege: a Christian home, a church upbringing, a respected family name. None of these replaces a life of wisdom. It also encourages anyone who started with nothing, because faithfulness is seen. The gospel goes further than this verse. In Christ, people with no claim on God's house are brought in and made heirs: "you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ" (Galatians 4:7). Grace, not birth, gives us the inheritance; a faithful life shows that we value it.
units.application: Young people raised with advantages: do not coast on your parents' name or faith; build your own faithfulness. Employers and church leaders: promote people for character and wisdom, not family connection. Employees and volunteers without a title: keep serving well where you are, because faithful work is noticed by God and often by people. Parents: do not assume an inheritance will make a child ready; train character first, and let responsibility follow it.

rel.note: If even Hell and Destruction lie open before the LORD, human hearts certainly do.
The LORD weighs the spirits, examining motives that people cannot see in themselves.
Every way seems right to a man, but the LORD weighs the hearts.
The same refining line is completed differently: praise becomes the test that reveals a person.

units.notes:
• *Tests* translates bachan, to examine something closely in order to prove what it really is. It is used of God in Psalm 7:9: "For the righteous God tests the hearts and minds." Here the word ties the refiner's fire to God's search of the heart.
• The first line returns word for word in 27:21, finished differently: "And a man is valued by what others say of him." There praise becomes the test that reveals a person.
• In 16:2 the LORD "weighs the spirits" as on a scale; here He tests them as with fire. Compare 15:11; 21:2; Jeremiah 17:10.
• Ironside pictures the divine Refiner who "sits by the fining pot, waiting till His own image be reflected in the soul." Compare Malachi 3:3: "He will sit as a refiner and a purifier of silver."
• Compare 1 Peter 1:7, where faith is "much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire."
units.summary: Fire proves silver and gold; only the LORD can prove a heart, and He tests in order to purify.
units.principle: The LORD alone sees the heart as it really is, and He tests it to prove and purify, not to destroy.
units.insight: Abraham was tested on Mount Moriah, and the test revealed what was already in him: "now I know that you fear God" (Genesis 22:12). Hezekiah was tested another way. When the Babylonian envoys came, "God withdrew from him, in order to test him, that He might know all that was in his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:31). We can fool others, and we are expert at fooling ourselves (Jeremiah 17:9). The LORD cannot be fooled. That is a fearful truth, and also a comfort, because a refiner does not waste fire on worthless metal. When Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-Nego were thrown into the furnace, a fourth figure walked with them in the fire (Daniel 3:25). Hard seasons are not always punishment; often they are where God brings out the gold. Pray with David, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23).
units.application: If you are in a hard season, do not assume God is punishing you; ask what He may be bringing to the surface and refining. If you lead or counsel others, resist judging hearts by appearances, and leave the final verdict on motives to the Lord (1 Corinthians 4:5). Before a major decision, pray Psalm 139:23–24 slowly and give God room to show you your real motives. Parents: teach children that God cares about why they act, not only what they do.

rel.note: The whisperer separates the best of friends, and his words travel only because someone is eager to hear them.
The one who repeats a matter separates friends, and he can only do it because someone listens.
The talebearer’s words are tasty trifles, which explains why spiteful talk finds willing ears.
Without a talebearer strife dies out; without a willing listener the talebearer has no fuel.
A ruler who pays attention to lies corrupts everyone under him, the same guilt of the eager listener.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV has "a spiteful tongue," the KJV has "a naughty tongue." In 1611 "naughty" meant wicked or worthless, not merely mischievous.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Evil words die without a welcome; and the welcome gives us away."
• Ahab kept four hundred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear, and he hated Micaiah because he would not (1 Kings 22:6–8). The lying spirit in their mouths found a willing ear (1 Kings 22:22–23).
• God said of Judah in Jeremiah's day, "The prophets prophesy falsely… And My people love to have it so" (Jeremiah 5:31). False teaching thrives where people want to hear it.
• Compare 18:8; 26:20; 29:12; Psalm 15:3.
units.summary: Lies need listeners, and what we love to hear tells the truth about us.
units.principle: Listening is a moral act: an appetite for lies and malice reveals a heart that shares them and gives them the audience they need.
units.insight: King Saul's jealousy made him an eager audience. David had to ask him, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Indeed David seeks your harm'?" (1 Samuel 24:9). At Jesus' trial the council went looking for false testimony because it already wanted Him dead (Matthew 26:59). Bridges: "the listening ears share the responsibility of the naughty tongue" ("naughty" in his day meant wicked). This verse searches more than our speech. Why does a rumor about a rival feel satisfying? Why do we click on the scandal? The appetite shows something in the heart that needs the Refiner of 17:3. Love "does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6), and Christ, who is the truth, can give us a new taste for what is true.
units.application: When someone starts to share a damaging story, ask: "Is this true? Why are you telling me? Have you talked to them?" If you lead a team or ministry, do not act on secondhand reports without hearing the other side. Notice which conversations, feeds or shows you return to for the pleasure of outrage, and cut one out this week. Parents: teach children that listening eagerly to gossip is a way of joining in.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor also reproaches his Maker; this verse shows that mockery alone does the same.
The one who pities the poor lends to the LORD, the opposite of the one who mocks them.
The LORD is the maker of rich and poor alike, which is why contempt for the poor insults Him.
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, for the LORD sees and is displeased.

units.notes:
• *Will not go unpunished*: the KJV margin reads "held innocent." The phrase is courtroom language: God will not acquit the one who gloats.
• Bridges: "To pour contempt upon the current coin with the king's image on it, is treason against the sovereign." The poor bear God's image as surely as the rich (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9).
• Proverbs gives a direct command on the same subject: "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, And do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles" (24:17).
• Edom gloated over Judah on the day of its disaster and was judged for it (Obadiah 12–15).
• Compare 14:31; 19:17; Matthew 25:40; James 2:5–6.
units.summary: Laugh at the poor and you are laughing at the God who made them.
units.principle: Every person bears the mark of the God who made him, so contempt for the poor and delight in another's ruin are sins against God Himself.
units.insight: Job could say he had never "rejoiced at the destruction of him who hated me" (Job 31:29). That is rare. Most of us know the small, secret pleasure when someone we resent stumbles. This verse names that pleasure as sin against God. It also condemns the casual contempt that jokes about "those people," the poor, the homeless, the struggling. Christ became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and on the cross passers-by wagged their heads and mocked Him in His calamity (Matthew 27:39). To sneer at the poor is to stand with that crowd. Bishop Reynolds, quoted by Bridges, gives the remedy: "One sun shines on both; one blood bought us both; one heaven will receive us both." Grace that reached down to us cannot leave us looking down on anyone.
units.application: Watch your humor: stop jokes that make poverty, accents, clothing or a struggling neighbor the punch line. When a rival at work or a critic at church falls, pray for them and refuse to pass the news along with satisfaction. Parents: correct a child who mocks a classmate's clothes or home, and explain that God made that child. If you serve the poor, guard against a superior tone and serve as one who has also received mercy.

rel.note: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, honor passed down the generations.
Where a fool is born, the joy that should flow between the generations is missing.
A foolish son brings grief and bitterness to the parents he should crown with honor.
The righteous man walks in integrity, and his children are blessed after him.

units.notes:
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Behind this apparently innocuous proverb is a profound assertion of the psychological interdependence of the generations." Each generation's honor and happiness depend in part on the other.
• Old Jacob, who had thought Joseph dead, said to him, "I had not thought to see your face; but in fact, God has also shown me your offspring!" (Genesis 48:11). Joseph himself lived to see Ephraim's children "to the third generation" (Genesis 50:23).
• On grandchildren as a crown and fathers as a glory, Henry adds a needed condition: "They are so, that is, they should be so, and, if they conduct themselves worthily, they are so."
• Compare 13:22; 20:7; Psalm 103:17; 127:3–5.
units.summary: Grandchildren crown the old, and a good father gives his children a name worth claiming.
units.principle: God designed families so that each generation brings honor to the other, and a life of integrity is the best legacy a parent can leave.
units.insight: Paul traced Timothy's faith back through his mother Eunice to his grandmother Lois (2 Timothy 1:5). Few things give an older believer more joy than seeing faith carried into a third generation. Yet Scripture is honest that the pattern often breaks. Godly Hezekiah was the son of Ahaz, a king who shut the doors of the LORD's house (2 Chronicles 28:24). If your father gave you little to be proud of, or you have no children at all, this verse is not a verdict on your worth. God is "A father of the fatherless" (Psalm 68:5), and in Christ believers belong to the Father "from whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named" (Ephesians 3:15). The question the verse puts to every parent and grandparent is simple: will the next generation be glad to bear my name?
units.application: Grandparents: be present. Pray for each grandchild by name and tell them stories of God's faithfulness in your family. Fathers: live this week in a way your children will be glad to remember, keeping your word and apologizing when you are wrong. Adult children: honor aging parents with time and patience, not obligation alone. Church leaders: create settings where older and younger believers actually know one another.

rel.note: A king's mouth must not transgress in judgment, which is why lying lips are so out of place in a ruler.
Righteous lips are the delight of kings, the speech that does befit those who rule.
The same word for nobles returns, now as upright men wrongly punished.
A proverb in a fool’s mouth hangs as limp as a lame man’s legs; fine words do not fit him.
When a ruler deals in lies, the corruption spreads to all who serve him.

units.notes:
• The word translated *fool* here is nabal, a person senseless toward God and coarse toward others. It is the name of the man of whom Abigail said, "Nabal is his name, and folly is with him!" (1 Samuel 25:25).
• The word translated *prince* is nadib, someone noble in rank and also noble and generous in character. Isaiah sets the two words side by side: "The foolish person will no longer be called generous" (Isaiah 32:5). So the nabal and the nadib are opposites in character as well as in station.
• *Excellent speech* is literally "a lip of excellency" (KJV margin), speech of abundance or superiority. Most versions take it as fine or eloquent speech; the 1984 NIV reads "Arrogant lips," hearing the excess as pride.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "God likes not fair words from a foul mouth."
• Compare 16:13; 26:7; Psalm 50:16–17.
units.summary: Fine words do not fit a fool, and lies fit a leader even less.
units.principle: Words must match the life behind them, and the greater a person's trust, the greater the betrayal when he lies.
units.insight: When Saul began prophesying, people asked in surprise, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (1 Samuel 10:11). Words that did not fit the man drew mockery. Abraham, the friend of God, lied about Sarah, and a pagan king had to rebuke him (Genesis 20:9). Ironside: "Men feel instinctively that he who leads others should be real himself." People forgive a leader for lacking polish far sooner than for lying. This verse searches anyone with a platform: parents, pastors, managers, Bible teachers. Do my words outrun my life? Is my spin a polite kind of lie? Christ our King is different. No deceit was found in His mouth (1 Peter 2:22), and He is "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5). Those who lead in His name must speak like Him.
units.application: If you lead at work, in church or at home, refuse to shade the truth to protect your image, and correct a misleading statement quickly, publicly if needed. Before you teach or give advice, ask whether your life backs your words. When your church or organization chooses leaders, weigh honesty above eloquence. Parents: let your children hear you admit it when you have spoken wrongly or broken your word.

rel.note: The one who hates bribes will live, while greed for gain troubles a man’s own house.
The same word returns as a bribe taken in secret to pervert justice, showing what the briber’s "lucky stone" really does.
A gift honestly given can open the way to great men without corrupting anyone’s judgment.
Another observation of how a secret gift works on people, again without approving it.

units.notes:
• The word translated *present* is shochad, a gift or payment given to win someone's favor. Most often it names a bribe, as in "you shall take no bribe" (Exodus 23:8). In 6:35, though, it describes gifts offered to a wronged husband. The setting decides when a corrupt payment is meant, and 17:23 settles it here.
• *Precious stone* is literally "a stone of favor," and the KJV margin has "a stone of grace." The NASB and the 1984 NIV render it "a charm," a lucky stone believed to bring good fortune, which suits a briber who expects his gift to win favor wherever he goes.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The proverb is expressing this reality from the viewpoint of the one giving the bribe—it works."
• Some older interpreters read the verse as praise of a gift given in love. Its link with 17:23 points the other way: the verse observes a briber's confidence without approving it.
• Compare 15:27; 21:14; 29:4; Deuteronomy 16:19.
units.summary: To the briber, his gift looks like a lucky charm, and for a while it seems to work.
units.principle: Money can seem to open every door, but what works is not the same as what is right, and success bought by bribery stands under God's judgment.
units.insight: Simon the sorcerer saw the apostles' power and assumed money could buy it. Peter's answer was blunt: "Your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be purchased with money!" (Acts 8:20). Felix kept Paul in prison for two years, hoping Paul would pay him to be released (Acts 24:26–27). The briber's faith in his "lucky stone" is a form of idolatry: he trusts money to do what only God does. Most of us are not tempted by envelopes of cash. We are tempted by subtler gifts: the favor done so someone owes us, the donation that expects influence, the present that makes it hard to say no. God's favor cannot be bought at all. It is given freely in Christ (Romans 3:24), and that frees us to give without strings.
units.application: If you hold any decision-making role, such as hiring, purchasing, grading or handling church finances, decline gifts that could tilt your judgment and disclose any you receive. Business owners: do not treat kickbacks or "facilitation payments" as normal costs of doing business. When you give to a church or ministry, give without expecting a vote or a favor in return. When someone's generosity starts to feel like leverage, name it kindly and step back.

rel.note: Love covers all sins, while hatred stirs up strife.
The whisperer separates the best of friends, just as the one who repeats a matter does.
The friend who loves at all times is the one who covers offenses instead of repeating them.
The one who repeats a matter needs listeners, and the eager listener shares his guilt.
It is a man’s glory to overlook a transgression.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb behind *repeats* means to do or say something a second time. It allows both senses: telling the matter to others, and raising it again with the offender.
• Covering is not the same as ignoring sin. Jesus' pattern is to go to the person privately first (Matthew 18:15). Once the matter is settled, it need not be spread.
• The same truth runs through the New Testament: "love will cover a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8; compare James 5:20).
• Ironside: "If such a mission is successful, the sin should never again be mentioned." By "mission" he means going to the erring person privately and gently.
• Compare 10:12; 11:13; 16:28; 19:11.
units.summary: Love lets a forgiven offense rest; repeating it, to others or to the offender, keeps the wound open.
units.principle: Love chooses to let a forgiven offense rest, while rehearsing wrongs slowly destroys friendship; yet covering never means hiding abuse or crime.
units.insight: When Noah lay exposed in his tent, Ham went out and told his brothers; Shem and Japheth walked in backward and covered their father (Genesis 9:22–23). The same choice faces us whenever we learn of someone's failure. Henry: "The ripping up of faults is the ripping out of love." Many friendships do not end in one explosion. They die from a hundred retellings and a dozen reminders: "You always…" "Remember when you…?" The gospel is the great covering. "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered" (Psalm 32:1), and God says of His people's sins, "I will remember no more" (Hebrews 8:12). Satan is called "the accuser of our brethren" (Revelation 12:10); Christ is the One who covers. Whom do you resemble when you talk about someone who hurt you?
units.application: Before you pass on a story about someone, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it kind? Is it necessary? Then add a fourth: Have I spoken to the person myself? If a friend or spouse has apologized, stop raising the offense in later arguments. Small-group leaders: do not let prayer requests become a channel for gossip. But if what you know involves abuse, danger or crime, do not cover it; report it to those responsible for protection.

rel.note: A wise son heeds instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.
The next verse shows the man who refuses correction and meets a cruel messenger instead.
Even grinding a fool in a mortar will not remove his foolishness, the same point as a hundred blows.
Rebuke a wise man and he will love you and grow wiser still.

units.notes:
• *Is more effective* translates a verb meaning to go down or sink in. The KJV keeps the picture: "A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool."
• The law limited a court-ordered beating: "Forty blows he may give him and no more" (Deuteronomy 25:3). A hundred blows is far beyond any lawful punishment, which marks the number as exaggeration for effect.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "The finer the disposition, the less is needed to correct it."
• Compare 9:8–9; 13:1; 15:31–32; 27:22, where even grinding a fool in a mortar will not remove his foolishness.
units.summary: A teachable heart turns at one word; a hardened heart shrugs off a hundred blows.
units.principle: Correction works according to the heart that receives it; a humble person is changed by a word that a proud person will not hear under any pressure.
units.insight: One sentence from Nathan, "You are the man!", broke David, and he confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). One look from Jesus sent Peter out to weep bitterly (Luke 22:61–62). Pharaoh endured plague after plague and only hardened his heart (Exodus 9:34–35). Bridges: "Stripes only scourge the fool's back. They never reach his heart." ("Stripes" are lashes.) The question is not how much correction we have received but how soft our hearts are when it comes. Does a word from a spouse, a friend or Scripture land, or do we wait until life hits us hard? The cure for a hard heart is not more blows but a new heart, which God promises: "I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26).
units.application: When someone corrects you, resist the urge to defend yourself first. Say, "Thank you; let me think about that," and then consider it. Parents and teachers: study each child, because a sensitive child may need only a quiet word, and harshness can crush rather than correct. Supervisors: give feedback early and plainly, while one word can still do its work. If you need repeated hard consequences before you change, ask God for a softer heart.

rel.note: The king’s wrath is pictured as messengers of death, the same royal setting.
The wise man is reached by one rebuke; the rebel refuses every correction.
Fear the LORD and the king, and avoid those given to change, for their ruin comes suddenly.
The one who hardens his neck against rebuke will suddenly be destroyed without remedy.

units.notes:
• The word translated *messenger* is the ordinary Hebrew word for a messenger, and also the word used for angels. Some readers hear an angel of judgment here (compare the "angels of destruction" in Psalm 78:49). A royal officer fits the immediate picture, as in "As messengers of death is the king's wrath" (16:14).
• The Hebrew of the first line can be read with either word as the subject. The NKJV, ESV and KJV have the evil man seeking rebellion; the NASB reads "A rebellious man seeks only evil." The sense is close either way.
• Sheba son of Bichri raised a revolt against David. Joab pursued him to the city of Abel, and the city ended the rebellion by throwing his head over the wall (2 Samuel 20:1, 21–22).
• Compare 24:21–22; 29:1; Romans 13:2.
units.summary: The man who refuses every correction will finally meet a messenger who does not negotiate.
units.principle: Settled rebellion against rightful authority invites a severity that gentler correction would have spared; whoever refuses the word will eventually meet the rod.
units.insight: Korah gathered men against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opened beneath him (Numbers 16:31–33). Absalom turned Israel's heart against his father and died caught in a tree, pierced by Joab's spears (2 Samuel 18:9–14). Bridges calls rebellion "the grand outbreaking of the stubborn will." It usually starts small, as a refusal to be told anything, long before it becomes open revolt. Every human heart carries that seed: "We have turned, every one, to his own way" (Isaiah 53:6). Yet the God who could send a cruel messenger sent His beloved Son to rebels instead (Mark 12:6), and "the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Where are you resisting the authority God has placed over you, at home, at work or in His word?
units.application: If you chafe under a boss, a parent or church leadership, voice disagreement openly and respectfully through proper channels, not through quiet sabotage or a campaign against them. Teenagers: settled defiance at home rarely stays at home. Leaders who must confront rebellion: act firmly but never cruelly, since the verse describes a consequence, not a model for leadership. And do not read every hard season, yours or anyone else's, as proof of rebellion.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, so keeping out of a fool’s path is wisdom.
Go from the presence of a foolish man; the wise course is to avoid him.
A fool’s wrath is heavier than stone and sand, again ranking the fool above a natural danger.
A wicked ruler is pictured as a charging bear, the same image of destructive power.

units.notes:
• The LORD uses the same image of His own judgment on Israel: "I will meet them like a bear deprived of her cubs" (Hosea 13:8). In the NKJV both verses use the verb "meet."
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, observes that a human being, who should be rational, "in such folly becomes more dangerous than the beast"; the bear at least has good reason for her rage.
• Scripture shows folly let loose: Simeon and Levi killed the men of a whole city over one man's crime (Genesis 34:25), and Saul had the priests of Nob put to death (1 Samuel 22:18).
• Compare 14:7; 27:3, where a fool's wrath is "heavier than both" stone and sand; 28:15, where a wicked ruler is like "a charging bear."
units.summary: A furious mother bear is dangerous, but a fool in full flow is worse.
units.principle: Folly in full flow is more dangerous than brute fury because it will not listen to reason, and wisdom knows when to stay out of its way.
units.insight: Nabal insulted David's men, and David strapped on his sword, vowing to wipe out Nabal's household. In that moment the man after God's own heart was the fool in his folly, and Abigail stepped into his path with wisdom and humility. David blessed her because she had "kept me this day from coming to bloodshed" (1 Samuel 25:13, 33). So the verse is not only about other people. Bridges asks: "Do we never see the Christian, whom his Master's discipline and example ought to have transformed to a lamb, still like the bear robbed of her whelps?" (Whelps are cubs.) The answer is the Lamb Himself, who "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). His Spirit can calm the rage that makes us dangerous.
units.application: When someone is in the grip of rage or reckless folly, do not argue, provoke or try to win the point; give them space and step away (14:7). Parents and spouses: in a heated moment, a calm "Let's talk later" is wisdom, not weakness. Employers and ministry leaders: do not put a known hothead in charge of others. And if you are the one who explodes, ask a trusted friend to tell you when you are becoming dangerous.

rel.note: He who troubles his own house inherits the wind, the household cost of wrongdoing.
Instead of repaying evil, the wise wait for the LORD to save them.
Wisdom goes the opposite way: it repays even an enemy with good.
The one who digs a pit falls into it; harm sent out tends to come back on the sender.

units.notes:
• The psalmist uses the same expression of his enemies: "They reward me evil for good, To the sorrow of my soul" (Psalm 35:12). Compare Psalm 109:5.
• Henry: "To render evil for evil is brutish, but to render evil for good is devilish."
• After Gideon's death Israel did not show kindness to his house "in accordance with the good he had done for Israel" (Judges 8:35). His son Abimelech murdered his brothers, and "God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech" and the men of Shechem who backed him (Judges 9:56–57).
• Nabal answered David's protection of his flocks with insults, and David said, "he has repaid me evil for good" (1 Samuel 25:21).
• Compare 20:22; 25:21–22; Romans 12:17, 21.
units.summary: Pay back kindness with harm, and the harm you sent out tends to move into your own house.
units.principle: Ingratitude that repays good with evil sows trouble that tends to settle on the ingrate's own household, while God calls His people to overcome evil with good.
units.insight: Jesus washed Judas's feet, handed him the bread and called him "Friend" in the garden, and Judas answered with a betraying kiss (John 13:5, 26; Matthew 26:49–50). Before we condemn him, we should see ourselves. The human story began with evil repaid for good: God gave Adam a garden full of gifts, and Adam reached for the one thing forbidden (Genesis 2:16–17; 3:6). We still repay grace with grumbling. The wonder of the gospel is that God answered our evil with good: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). That changes how we treat both those who help us and those who hurt us. Is there someone whose kindness you have repaid with coldness, criticism or neglect?
units.application: Think of a parent, teacher, pastor or employer who did you real good, and thank them this week. If you have answered someone's kindness with criticism or neglect, go and make it right. If someone has repaid your good with evil, do not retaliate; leave it with God and keep doing good (Romans 12:17–21). And never use this verse to explain a hurting family's troubles; it warns the ungrateful, not the suffering.

rel.note: The one who is slow to anger calms contention before it grows.
The peace that makes a dry morsel better than a feast is protected by stopping strife early.
The cluster on strife closes by tracing the love of quarrels to sin and pride.
It is honorable to stop striving, since any fool can start a quarrel.
Strife needs fuel; remove the talebearer and the contentious man, and it dies out.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV reads "before a quarrel starts," the ESV, NASB, 1984 NIV and NLT speak of the dispute before it "breaks out," which keeps the picture of water bursting through.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Opening such a sluice lets loose more than one can predict, control or retrieve."
• Henry: "Dread the breaking of the ice, for, if once broken, it will break further." A quarrel is like cracked ice: once it starts to give way, the crack keeps spreading.
• Abraham stopped the quarrel between his herdsmen and Lot's at once: "Please let there be no strife between you and me… for we are brethren" (Genesis 13:8).
• Compare 15:18; 20:3; 26:20–21; Ephesians 4:26.
units.summary: Quarrels start as a trickle and end as a flood, so close the breach while it is still a crack.
units.principle: Strife is far easier to prevent than to contain, so wisdom stops a quarrel at its first trickle.
units.insight: Abraham ended a quarrel by giving Lot first choice of the land (Genesis 13:8–9). Paul and Barnabas, both good men, let a disagreement run until "the contention became so sharp that they parted from one another" (Acts 15:39). A quarrel between Jephthah and the men of Ephraim ended in civil war (Judges 12:1–6). Most of our floods begin with a trickle: a tone of voice, a sarcastic reply, a text sent too fast. The heart that will not let the first word go is usually protecting its pride. Jesus calls peacemakers "sons of God" (Matthew 5:9), and Paul says, "do not let the sun go down on your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26). Where is a small leak running in one of your relationships right now?
units.application: When you feel the first heat in a conversation with your spouse, child or coworker, pause before you answer, lower your voice and ask a question instead of firing back. Decide in advance which issues are not worth a fight. If you lead a team or church board, address small frictions early and privately, before sides form. And before you go to bed tonight, settle anything you can settle.

rel.note: The bribe taken in secret is one of the main ways justice gets twisted.
Punishing the righteous and striking upright princes are further forms of condemning the just.
Showing partiality to the wicked or overthrowing the righteous in judgment is not good.
Whoever calls the wicked righteous is cursed by the people, while those who rebuke the wicked are blessed.

units.notes:
• The law describes the judge's task with the same pair of verbs used the right way round: "they justify the righteous and condemn the wicked" (Deuteronomy 25:1).
• Isaiah ties this injustice to bribery, the subject of 17:8 and 17:23: "Who justify the wicked for a bribe" (Isaiah 5:23).
• *Abomination* is one of Proverbs' strongest words for what the LORD finds detestable. This verse belongs with the book's other abominations, such as dishonest scales (11:1; 20:10, 23) and a proud heart (16:5).
• Ironside: "Observe that to justify necessarily means to clear, or to declare righteous; not, as some theologians would have it, to make righteous." The word is a verdict, not a change of character.
• Compare 18:5; 24:23–25; Isaiah 5:20.
units.summary: God hates a twisted verdict either way; only the cross acquits sinners without bending justice.
units.principle: Justice requires the right verdict for both the guilty and the innocent, and God's mercy to sinners never bends it, because in Christ the penalty was paid.
units.insight: At Jesus' trial both sins met in one verdict. Pilate said, "I find no fault in Him at all," then released Barabbas, a robber, and handed Jesus over to be crucified (John 18:38–40; 19:16). The guilty man went free and the Just One was condemned. Yet God turned that perfect injustice into the means of our justification. Bridges, speaking of God: "If he justifies the wicked, it is on account of righteousness," a righteousness God Himself provided in Christ (Romans 3:25–26). God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Every believer is Barabbas, set free because Another took his place. That grace should make us fiercely fair: in courtrooms and boardrooms, in family disputes and church conflicts, refusing to excuse our friends or condemn people we dislike.
units.application: If you serve on a jury, a hiring panel, a school board or a church discipline team, decide on the evidence, not on loyalty or dislike. Parents: do not automatically side with the child who complains first, or always blame the same one. Supervisors: do not cover for a favorite or scapegoat a weaker employee. When you hear one side of a conflict, wait to hear the other before you judge (18:17).

rel.note: The man "devoid of understanding" (literally "lacking heart") shows the same missing heart in a rash pledge.
The fool’s eyes wander to the ends of the earth while wisdom stands right before him.
Fools hate knowledge, which is why the price of wisdom in their hand goes unused.
Wisdom is to be bought and never sold, but the purchase requires a heart that values it.
Wisdom is the principal thing, worth getting at any cost, the very desire the fool lacks.

units.notes:
• *No heart for it*: the KJV reads "seeing he hath no heart to it." In Proverbs "heart" often means sense or good judgment. The same "lacking heart" language describes the man of 17:18 who rashly becomes surety.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The fool has no interest in obtaining wisdom in the way that it must be obtained."
• Wisdom's real price is set out in 2:1–5: receiving, treasuring, crying out and searching "as for hidden treasures." God's invitation in Isaiah 55:1 goes further still: "buy wine and milk Without money and without price."
• Simon the sorcerer tried to buy spiritual power with money (Acts 8:18–20).
• Compare 1:22; 4:7; 23:23.
units.summary: Money can buy books and teachers, but it cannot buy a heart that wants to learn.
units.principle: Wisdom cannot be bought with money or opportunity alone; it comes only to a heart that truly wants it.
units.insight: The rich young ruler had wealth, a moral life and a face-to-face meeting with Jesus, yet he "went away sorrowful," because his heart was set on his possessions (Mark 10:22). Herod was "exceedingly glad" to see Jesus, but only because he hoped to see a miracle (Luke 23:8). Most of us hold more of the price of wisdom than any generation before: Bibles in every translation, sermons on demand, classes and conferences. The question is not access but appetite. Ironside: "We only know truth as we walk in it." If the heart is missing, the remedy is not more information but honest prayer. Jesus said, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, For they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6). Ask Him for the hunger itself.
units.application: Students: tuition and good teachers will not make you wise unless you want to learn, so ask questions, do the reading and apply it. Parents: you can pay for lessons and a good school, but pray for and nurture your child's desire, not only their schedule. Church members: before buying another book or joining another class, put into practice one thing you already know. Leaders: invest training where there is hunger, not only where there is budget.

rel.note: The next saying shows that loyal love still needs wisdom and does not demand rash pledges.
Friendship is kept by covering offenses and lost by repeating them.
Proverbs returns to the faithful friend, one who sticks closer than a brother.
The poor man’s brothers and friends desert him, the opposite of love born for adversity.
Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend; loyal friendship holds over time.

units.notes:
• The NLT renders the second line "a brother is born to help in time of need," reading it as a statement of what a brother is for.
• Henry: "Swallow-friends, that fly to you in summer, but are gone in winter; such friends there is no loss of." Swallows leave when the weather turns cold, and so do false friends.
• Jonathan loved David "as his own soul" and stood by him when Saul turned against him (1 Samuel 18:1; 20:30–34). Ruth clung to Naomi in her bereavement: "wherever you go, I will go" (Ruth 1:16).
• Contrast 19:7, where the poor man's brothers and friends abandon him. Proverbs returns to the faithful friend in 18:24 and 27:10.
units.summary: Fair-weather friends vanish in the storm; a true friend and a real brother show up in it.
units.principle: Real friendship is proved by constancy, and loyal love shows its worth most clearly when trouble comes.
units.insight: When Saul hunted David, Jonathan went out to him in the woods "and strengthened his hand in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). When Paul sat in chains, Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found him and "was not ashamed of my chain" (2 Timothy 1:16–17). Such friends are rare, and the verse asks whether we are one. Do we drift from friends when they become hard work, poor, sick or embarrassing? No one has loved like Jesus. "Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end" (John 13:1), even when they slept, fled and denied Him. He is "not ashamed to call them brethren" (Hebrews 2:11). Loved like that, we can become a brother born for someone else's adversity.
units.application: Think of a friend going through a divorce, a diagnosis, a job loss or a public failure, and reach out this week without waiting to be asked. Bring a meal, sit in the waiting room, keep calling when they stop answering. Brothers and sisters estranged over small things: hardship is the time to come back. Church members: notice who has quietly disappeared after a crisis, and go after them.

rel.note: Surety for a stranger brings suffering, while the one who refuses it is secure.
The fool with no heart for wisdom is close kin to the man "lacking heart" who signs rashly.
The loyal love of the previous verse is balanced here by the wisdom that refuses rash pledges.
Do not shake hands in pledge, or you may lose your very bed.
The father urges a son who has pledged for a friend to free himself at once.

units.notes:
• *Devoid of understanding* reads literally "lacking heart." In Proverbs the heart is the center of thought and judgment, so the phrase means a man without sense. The KJV margin shows that "understanding" is literally "heart," and the YLT reads "A man lacking heart." The wording recalls the fool of 17:16, who has "no heart" for wisdom.
• Where the NKJV reads "for his friend," the KJV, ESV and NASB read that he becomes surety "in the presence of" his friend or neighbor, picturing a pledge made publicly before witnesses.
• Ironside: "Paul went surety for Onesimus, as Judah did for Benjamin; but each had counted the cost." See Philemon 18–19 and Genesis 43:9; 44:32–33.
• Compare 6:1–5; 11:15; 20:16; 22:26–27.
units.summary: Love your friend enough to help him, and wisely enough not to sign away your family's future for him.
units.principle: Faithful love must be guided by wisdom; helping a friend never requires rash promises that endanger your own household.
units.insight: Judah pledged himself for Benjamin with his eyes open, ready to stay as a slave in his brother's place (Genesis 43:9; 44:33). Paul told Philemon, "put that on my account" for the runaway Onesimus (Philemon 18). Both knew what it would cost them. The man in this verse does not. He wants to look generous, or he cannot bear to say no, so he signs. Sometimes such "kindness" is really a need to be needed or a fear of disappointing someone. The greatest Surety of all is Christ, who "has become a surety of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22) and paid our debt in full. Yet Bridges adds: "the eternal counsel is no pattern for our simple folly." God's eternal plan, in which Christ stood surety for sinners, does not license our rash pledges. Christ counted the cost perfectly; we must count ours with care.
units.application: Before you cosign a loan or lease for a friend, adult child or relative, ask whether you could pay all of it without harming your family; if not, say no kindly. If you want to help, give what you are able and willing to lose instead of guaranteeing what you cannot. Spouses: make such decisions together. Pastors and counselors: help people see that refusing a rash pledge is not a failure of love.

rel.note: Pride produces nothing but strife, linking the two lines of this verse.
Pride goes before destruction, the end the self-exalting man is unknowingly seeking.
The cluster on strife opens with the call to stop a quarrel before it starts.
Before destruction the heart of a man is haughty, but humility comes before honor.

units.notes:
• *Gate* means a doorway or entrance. The medieval Jewish commentators Rashi and Ibn Ezra took it as a picture of the mouth, so that the man exalts himself by boastful speech; some modern scholars point to Micah 7:5, "the doors of your mouth." That reading is possible but uncertain. Most versions keep the literal gate, and the warning against pride stands either way.
• A note in Bridges, drawn from a traveler's report, explains the image: "An allusion to the gates of splendid palaces in the East, generally elevated according to the vanity of their owner."
• Henry: the proud builder "makes his gate so large that his house and estate go out at it." His display costs him everything he owns.
• Compare 13:10; 16:18; 18:12; James 4:1.
units.summary: Love a fight and you love sin; build to show off and you build your own fall.
units.principle: Love of conflict is rooted in sin, and pride that builds itself up is already on the road to its own ruin.
units.insight: Adonijah "exalted himself, saying, 'I will be king'"; he gathered chariots, horsemen and fifty men to run before him (1 Kings 1:5). His bid failed, and his later scheming for the throne cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13–25). In the church John met Diotrephes, "who loves to have the preeminence," and who kept attacking others "with malicious words" (3 John 9–10). The lover of strife usually insists the other person started it. But if we are often in conflict, the verse asks us to look underneath. What am I defending? Whose gate am I raising? Jesus went the other way. Though He was in the form of God, "He humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death" (Philippians 2:8), and God highly exalted Him. In His kingdom the way up is down.
units.application: If you are often in conflict at work, online or at home, ask a trusted friend whether you enjoy the fight more than you admit. Leaders: watch for the team member who always has a cause to oppose, and lovingly name the pattern. Families: resist spending to impress, such as the bigger house or car that strains the budget and breeds tension. Before your next argument, ask whether pride is driving it.

rel.note: The perverse tongue will be cut out, while the righteous mouth brings forth wisdom.
The one who walks with integrity walks securely, while the one who perverts his ways will be found out.
Those of a perverse heart are an abomination to the LORD, while the blameless are His delight.
The one who is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall.
Wisdom hates the perverse mouth, because the fear of the LORD hates evil.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "He that hath a froward heart findeth no good." "Froward" is older English for perverse or contrary, a heart that will not go straight.
• The Hebrew word behind *evil* can mean harm or calamity as well as moral wrong. So the line pictures the perverse speaker falling into trouble of his own making; the KJV has "falleth into mischief."
• Henry: "Many a one has paid dearly for an unbridled tongue."
• Gehazi lied to Naaman and then to Elisha to get silver and clothing, and he left with Naaman's leprosy instead (2 Kings 5:20–27).
• Compare 8:13; 10:31; 11:20; 28:18; James 3:6.
units.summary: A crooked heart never reaches the good it schemes for, and a twisted tongue trips its owner.
units.principle: Crookedness of heart and speech never delivers the good it chases, and in the end it trips the one who practices it.
units.insight: Jacob schemed his way to his brother's blessing, and years later woke to find that Laban had out-schemed him: "Why then have you deceived me?" (Genesis 29:25). The deceiver was deceived, and the crooked path brought him twenty years of hard service and a divided home. The verse traces such ruin back to the heart. "The heart is deceitful above all things" (Jeremiah 17:9), and even believers find it bending toward self-interest, spin and half-truths. Bridges gives the prayer of a heart that knows this: "Let me have anything but my own way. Leave me not to my perverse heart." God answers that prayer. He promises a new heart and His own Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26–27), and in Christ He begins to straighten what we have twisted.
units.application: This week, catch yourself when you shade the truth to look better: the inflated résumé line, the half-true excuse to a teacher or boss, the spin in a family argument. Correct it on the spot. Salespeople and managers: refuse misleading language even when it works. Parents: teach children that a clever lie is still a lie, and praise them when they tell the truth at a cost to themselves.

rel.note: A foolish son is the grief of his mother, while a wise son makes a glad father.
The same grief returns, now naming the mother who bore the foolish son.
God’s design is for honor and joy to flow between the generations; folly breaks that flow.
A foolish son is the ruin of his father, another picture of the same sorrow.
The father of a wise child greatly rejoices, the joy this father lacks.

units.notes:
• The word behind *scoffer* in this verse is kesil, the word normally rendered "fool" in Proverbs; the ESV, NASB, 1984 NIV and KJV all read "fool." The second line uses nabal, the coarse fool of 17:7. Two words for folly, one grief.
• Henry: "The name of Absalom signifies his father's peace, but he was his greatest trouble."
• Solomon knew the fear behind this verse. He grieved that he must leave his labor to a successor, "And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?" (Ecclesiastes 2:19).
• Compare 10:1; 17:25; 19:13; 23:24–25.
units.summary: A father cannot stop loving a wayward child, and so he cannot stop hurting.
units.principle: A child's folly brings deep grief to a parent, a grief Scripture honors without assigning blame.
units.insight: David's cry over Absalom is one of the saddest in Scripture: "O my son Absalom—my son, my son Absalom—if only I had died in your place!" (2 Samuel 18:33). God Himself knows this grief: "I have nourished and brought up children, And they have rebelled against Me" (Isaiah 1:2). The perfect Father has wayward children, so a parent's pain is not proof of a parent's failure. If you carry this sorrow, the verse does not accuse you; it sits with you. Pour it out to a Father who understands. Keep watching the road, like the father in Jesus' parable who saw his son "when he was still a great way off" and ran to him (Luke 15:20). Hope is not a guarantee, but it is never wasted on the God of the prodigal.
units.application: Parents of a wayward child: grieve before God, keep praying, and keep the door open without excusing sin. Do not carry blame that God has not laid on you. Friends and church members: never treat a struggling child as a verdict on the parents; bring comfort, not commentary. Young people: remember that your choices land on hearts that love you, and one sincere phone call home can lift years of sorrow.

rel.note: Anxiety weighs a heart down, and a good word can make it glad, one way joy is given.
A sound heart is life to the body, again tying the inner life to physical health.
A merry heart shows in the face, while sorrow of heart breaks the spirit.
A man's spirit sustains him in sickness, but who can bear a broken spirit?

units.notes:
• The NKJV and KJV supply "like" before "medicine," while the ESV, NASB and 1984 NIV read "is good medicine." The KJV margin offers "to," and the YLT reads "doth good to the body." The short Hebrew line can be read more than one way; the point, that joy does real good, is the same in each.
• Elsewhere "a broken spirit" is a sacrifice God accepts (Psalm 51:17); there it means a repentant heart. Here it means a spirit crushed by grief or despair.
• Bridges, who urged believers toward cheerfulness, also wrote: "There is much in our physical economy rather within the province of the physician than the Minister." By "physical economy" he means the workings of the body: some troubles of the spirit call for a doctor's care more than a pastor's.
• Compare 12:25; 14:30; 15:13; 18:14.
units.summary: Joy is good medicine for the whole person, and a crushed spirit needs care, not blame.
units.principle: Inner joy strengthens the whole person and despair drains it, so a crushed spirit calls for compassion and care, never for blame.
units.insight: Paul and Silas sang hymns at midnight with their feet fastened in stocks (Acts 16:25), and Nehemiah told a weeping people, "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:10). Yet Scripture is just as frank about broken spirits. Elijah lay under a broom tree and asked to die, and God's first response was not a rebuke but sleep, food and water, twice (1 Kings 19:4–8). The Lord cared for the whole man. So should we. If your spirit is crushed, this verse is not an accusation; it names what you feel in your bones. Christ came "to heal the brokenhearted" (Luke 4:18), and His joy is given, not manufactured. Receive help from Him, from His people and, when needed, from doctors. If you are the cheerful one, let your gladness serve the weary rather than shame them.
units.application: If you are battling depression or long grief, tell someone and seek medical and pastoral help; both are gifts from God. Friends and church members: sit with the hurting instead of telling them to cheer up. Practice gladness in small ways this week: thank God aloud for three specific mercies, take a walk, share a meal and laugh with people you love. Leaders: build a team culture where joy is normal and burnout is noticed early.

rel.note: The one who hates bribes will live, the opposite of the wicked man who takes one in secret.
A bribe is the usual means of justifying the wicked and condemning the just.
Corrupt judgment goes on to punish the righteous and strike the upright.
The same word shows the briber’s view of his gift as a lucky charm; this verse shows what it really does.
The same phrase, "a bribe behind the back," describes how secret payments work on people.
The king establishes the land by justice, but the one who receives bribes overthrows it.

units.notes:
• *Behind the back* is literally "from the bosom," the fold of the robe above the belt, where a payment could be carried and passed unseen. The NASB keeps that wording and the KJV reads "out of the bosom." Proverbs uses the same picture in 21:14: "a bribe behind the back."
• *Bribe* translates shochad, the same word rendered "present" in 17:8. The two verses show the same payment from the giver's side and the taker's side.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The corrupt official defies God who has placed him over the community to protect the poor."
• Henry adds that guilt runs both ways, "for he is a bad man that gives bribes, as well as he that takes them."
• Compare 15:27; 29:4; Deuteronomy 16:19.
units.summary: Money slipped from a robe's fold shows the bribe for what it is: a secret purchase of injustice.
units.principle: Justice for sale is wickedness, and the secrecy bribery needs is its own confession of guilt.
units.insight: Samuel ended his years of leadership able to ask all Israel, "from whose hand have I received any bribe with which to blind my eyes?" No one could name one (1 Samuel 12:3–4). His own sons could not say the same (1 Samuel 8:3). Integrity is not inherited; each heart must choose it. Bribery also stood behind the Lord's own arrest: the chief priests counted out thirty pieces of silver to Judas (Matthew 26:15). The God we serve "shows no partiality nor takes a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). That is bad news for anyone hoping to buy His favor and good news for the poor, who cannot. Our acquittal before Him was never for sale; Christ paid for it. Where are you tempted to let a hidden advantage tilt your judgment?
units.application: Officials, inspectors, purchasing staff and anyone who decides who gets what: refuse every under-the-table payment, and report pressure to accept one. Business owners: build policies that make kickbacks hard and reward honesty. Ordinary citizens: refuse to pay a "fixer" to jump a queue or bend a rule. If you have ever taken something to look the other way, confess it and make restitution where you can.

rel.note: The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his own way, the near duty the fool overlooks.
The heart of understanding seeks knowledge, while the mouth of fools feeds on foolishness.
The fool holds the price of wisdom but has no heart for it; here he has no eyes for it.
The father urges his son not to let sound wisdom depart from his eyes, the very focus the fool lacks.
Let your eyes look straight ahead and do not turn to the right or the left.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "Wisdom is before him that hath understanding," keeping the picture of wisdom set right in front of him.
• Henry: "He lays his wisdom before him, as his card and compass which he steers by." A "card" was a sailor's chart; the wise man steers by wisdom as a pilot steers by chart and compass.
• Bridges: the fool's eyes are "rolling and wandering from one object to another."
• Moses told Israel that God's word is not far off, across the sea or up in heaven: "the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it" (Deuteronomy 30:11–14; compare Romans 10:6–8).
• Compare 4:25–27; 14:8; 15:14.
units.summary: The wise keep wisdom in plain view; the fool's eyes are always on some far horizon.
units.principle: Wisdom is usually found in faithful attention to what is near, while the restless search for something far away often becomes a way of avoiding it.
units.insight: When Jesus told Peter how he would die, Peter looked at John and asked, "But Lord, what about this man?" Jesus answered, "what is that to you? You follow Me" (John 21:21–22). Martha was "worried and troubled about many things," while Mary sat at Jesus' feet, and He said, "one thing is needed" (Luke 10:41–42). Our eyes are on the ends of the earth more than ever: news from everywhere, endless scrolling, the next big conference, speculation about distant questions. Meanwhile the plain duty in front of us waits: the spouse to love, the sin to confess, the verse we read this morning. Paul's secret was focus: "one thing I do" (Philippians 3:13). Keep your eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:2), and take the next step He has already shown you.
units.application: Before you look for new guidance, obey what you already know: the apology you owe, the bill you have delayed, the Bible reading you skipped. Students and young adults: resist the endless search for the perfect plan, and do today's work well. Leaders: keep the team on its present mission instead of chasing every new idea. Cut back one distraction this week, such as news or social media, and give that time to someone near you.

rel.note: A foolish son is the grief of his mother, the saying that opens Solomon’s proverbs.
The father’s sorrow over a foolish child, now joined by the mother’s.
Children should bring honor to the generations around them, not sorrow.
A foolish son is the ruin of his father.
A wise child lets father and mother rejoice, the opposite of grief and bitterness.

units.notes:
• *Grief* translates a word that carries vexation as well as sorrow. Henry draws out both sides: foolish children are "an occasion of anger to the father (so the word signifies)," but of "sorrow and bitterness to the mother."
• Esau's marriages to Hittite women "were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35), and Rebekah later said, "I am weary of my life" because of them (Genesis 27:46).
• Eve named her firstborn with hope, "I have acquired a man from the LORD" (Genesis 4:1), and lived to see him kill his brother.
• Compare 10:1; 17:21; 19:13; 23:25.
units.summary: A child's folly breaks two hearts at once: a father's grief and a mother's bitterness.
units.principle: A child's folly wounds both father and mother, and their grief is a sorrow to be honored, not a verdict on their parenting.
units.insight: Mothers often carry this bitterness quietly, in prayers no one hears and tears no one sees. Rebekah's weariness over Esau's choices shows how long such grief can last (Genesis 27:46). If that is you, God sees, and He speaks to His people with a mother's tenderness: "As one whom his mother comforts, So I will comfort you" (Isaiah 66:13). This verse also speaks to sons and daughters. Your choices are never only your own; they land on the hearts that carried you. Proverbs shows the better path: "Let your father and your mother be glad, And let her who bore you rejoice" (23:25). The prodigal's return turned his father's grief into a feast (Luke 15:23–24). With God it is never too late to come home.
units.application: Sons and daughters of any age: call your mother this week, and if you owe her an apology, give it. Mothers of wayward children: find a trusted friend or prayer partner, and do not carry the bitterness alone. Fathers: share the burden with your wife instead of withdrawing into anger. Churches: remember the parents who sit alone with this grief on Mother's Day, Father's Day and other family celebrations.

rel.note: Condemning the just is an abomination to the LORD, which shows how serious "not good" really is.
The bribe that perverts justice leads directly to punishing the upright.
The same word for nobles describes the prince whose lips should never lie.
It is not good to overthrow the righteous in judgment, the same understated protest.

units.notes:
• The word translated *punish* is anash, which most often means to impose a fine; the ESV, NASB, AMP and YLT read "fine" here. The same verb appears in the law's fine for injuring a pregnant woman (Exodus 21:22). If a fine is in view, the verse moves from a lesser penalty in the first line to a beating in the second, and both are unjust because they fall on the righteous.
• *Princes* translates nadib, the noble person of 17:7, noble in rank and in character.
• Bridges, on the understated "not good": "Often is the wise man's meaning much beyond his words." In other words, "not good" means far worse than it says. Compare the same understatement in 18:5.
• Ishmael son of Nethaniah murdered Gedaliah, the upright governor, while eating with him (Jeremiah 41:1–2). Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned for speaking God's word (Jeremiah 37:15).
• Compare 18:5; 24:23–24; 1 Peter 3:14.
units.summary: When integrity becomes the charge against a person, justice has been turned upside down.
units.principle: Penalizing people for doing right is a deep perversion of justice, and those who suffer for righteousness are seen and blessed by God.
units.insight: Daniel's enemies admitted they could find no fault in him "unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God" (Daniel 6:5). His faithfulness became the charge. When an officer struck Jesus before the high priest, the Lord asked, "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike Me?" (John 18:23). He was the upright One struck for His uprightness. The apostles were beaten for preaching and went away "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name" (Acts 5:41). If you are paying a price for doing right, at work, in your family or in public life, you stand in good company. And if you hold power, ask whether you have ever punished someone because their integrity made you uncomfortable.
units.application: Managers and leaders: protect the whistleblower and the employee who refused to cut corners, instead of sidelining them as "difficult." Parents: do not punish the child who told the truth about what happened. Church boards: never silence the person who raises a real concern. If you are suffering for doing right, keep doing it, keep records of what happens, and entrust yourself to God (1 Peter 2:23; 4:19).

rel.note: In many words sin is not lacking, but he who restrains his lips is wise.
The one slow to wrath has great understanding, the calm spirit of this verse.
The one who rules his spirit is better than the one who takes a city.
The next verse shows, with a touch of irony, how much wisdom a closed mouth holds.

units.notes:
• *Calm spirit*: the KJV reads "an excellent spirit," with "a cool" in the margin. The difference comes from the Hebrew text itself. The written consonants are read as qar, "cool," while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts is yeqar, "precious" or "excellent." The KJV follows the marginal reading; the NKJV, ESV, NASB and AMP follow the written text, which suits the parallel with restrained words.
• Henry: "A cool head with a warm heart is an admirable composition."
• Before Pilate, Jesus "answered him not one word" (Matthew 27:14). Nehemiah, angry at the oppression of the poor, rebuked the nobles only "After serious thought" (Nehemiah 5:6–7).
• Compare 10:19; 14:29; 16:32; 29:11; James 1:19.
units.summary: Real knowledge does not need to say everything it knows, and real understanding keeps a cool head.
units.principle: Understanding shows itself in measured words and a steady temper; the more a person truly knows, the less he needs to prove it by talking.
units.insight: Moses was the meekest of men, yet when Israel provoked him at Meribah, "he spoke rashly with his lips," and that moment cost him entry into the land (Psalm 106:32–33; Numbers 20:10–12). James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). Hot spirits spill words we cannot take back. Underneath is often fear or pride: we must be heard, we must win, we must show what we know. Jesus stood before His accusers with all knowledge and said little: "He opened not His mouth" (Isaiah 53:7). His calm was not weakness but complete trust in His Father. The Spirit who filled Him produces the same fruit of self-control in us (Galatians 5:22–23).
units.application: In your next tense meeting or family argument, let others finish, pause, and answer in fewer words than you planned. Experts and teachers: you do not have to correct every small error or show everything you know. Parents: lower your voice when your child raises theirs. Before replying to a provoking email or message, wait a day. Ask your spouse or a close friend to tell you when your temper starts to show.

rel.note: Restraining the lips is wise, because many words bring sin.
The prudent man conceals knowledge, while fools proclaim their foolishness.
The previous verse praises the one who spares his words; this one shows what silence can hide.
The fool delights in expressing his own heart, the very thing that exposes him.

units.notes:
• Job said nearly the same thing to his talkative friends: "Oh, that you would be silent, And it would be your wisdom!" (Job 13:5).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The dry advice of 28 is not purely ironical: the fool who takes it is no longer a complete fool." By "28" Kidner means this verse. Learning to be quiet is already a step toward wisdom.
• Henry adds a sober note: "when a fool holds his peace God knows his heart, and the folly that is bound up there." People may be fooled by silence; God is not.
• Compare 10:19; 12:23; 18:2; 29:11.
units.summary: Silence can make even a fool look wise, which shows how much wisdom a closed mouth holds.
units.principle: Restraint in speech is so much a part of wisdom that even a fool gains its reputation by keeping quiet, and the wise learn by listening.
units.insight: Job's friends were at their wisest in the first week, when "no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:13). When they began to speak, they made things worse, and God later rebuked them (Job 42:7). On the mount of transfiguration Peter blurted out a plan for three tabernacles, "not knowing what he said" (Luke 9:33). Many of us talk to fill silence, to be noticed or to prove we belong.
