The verse gently suggests a better way: listen first. Holding your tongue is not the whole of wisdom, but it is often where wisdom begins. James puts it plainly: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (James 1:19). The Lord who gives wisdom also gives the grace of a quiet tongue.
units.application: In your next meeting, class or small group, speak last rather than first, and ask one question before offering one opinion. When you visit someone who is grieving, sit with them and say little. Young people starting a new job: listen and learn before suggesting how things should change. In online discussions, let a day pass before weighing in, and often do not weigh in at all.

rel.note: The fool trusts his own way, while the wise man heeds the counsel this isolated man rages against.
Plans succeed in a multitude of counselors, the very company the self-willed man has left.
The same rare verb for a quarrel breaking out appears there, with counsel to stop strife before it starts.
One man withdraws so that no one can correct him, and the next talks so much that no one can teach him.

units.notes:
• *Rages against* translates a rare verb that pictures a quarrel bursting into the open. In the Old Testament it occurs only in Proverbs: here, in 17:14 ("stop contention before a quarrel starts") and in 20:3 ("any fool can start a quarrel"). The isolated man does not merely disagree with counsel; he picks a fight with it.
• *Wise judgment* translates tushiyyah, the word the NKJV renders "sound wisdom" in 3:21 and 8:14. It is practical wisdom that works in real life, the very thing this man has cut himself off from.
• The Hebrew of the verse is difficult and translations differ. The ESV and NASB are close to the NKJV, while the current NIV begins "An unfriendly person." The KJV reads the verse as praise of setting oneself apart to study ("seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom"), and older commentators who used the KJV, such as Bridges, expounded it that way; Henry offered both readings. The KJV margin comes closer to the NKJV: "He that separateth himself seeketh according to his desire."
• Ironside describes those who withdraw from fellow believers "not for the Lord's glory, but for their own pleasure."
• Compare Ecclesiastes 4:9–10, "woe to him who is alone when he falls," and Hebrews 10:24–25.
units.summary: Walling yourself off from every voice that might say no is not independence; it is a quarrel with wisdom.
units.principle: Separation chosen to protect our own desires soon turns into hostility toward the counsel that could save us.
units.insight: Self-willed isolation rarely announces itself. It sounds like "I just need space" or "No one understands my situation," and it ends with a heart that resents every voice of correction. Jonah shows the pattern. He fled toward Tarshish to escape God's word, and when God later questioned his anger he answered, "It is right for me to be angry, even to death!" (Jonah 4:9). The prodigal son also took his share and went "to a far country" where no one could check him (Luke 15:13). His way home began when he "came to himself" (Luke 15:17). Ask where you have pulled away, not to rest, but to keep something others would question. God does not leave us to ourselves. He sets us in the body of Christ, where no member can say, "I have no need of you" (1 Corinthians 12:21).
units.application: If you have stopped returning a mentor's calls or quietly left your small group because they questioned a decision, reach back out this week. Before a major choice about dating, money or a career move, ask one wise person, "What do you see that I don't?" Leaders, watch for the team member who withdraws after correction, and go to them. Introverts and the grieving, take the quiet you need; just keep one door open.

rel.note: The heart of fools proclaims foolishness, the same urge to put oneself on display.
The one with understanding seeks knowledge, while the fool's mouth feeds on foolishness.
The isolated man refuses correction by withdrawing; the fool refuses teaching by talking.
Answering before hearing is the fool's love of his own voice put into practice.
The prudent heart reaches for knowledge that the fool takes no delight in.

units.notes:
• *Expressing* translates a verb meaning to uncover or lay bare. Here it has a reflexive sense, "to uncover oneself," and with that sense it appears elsewhere only in Genesis 9:21, where Noah "was drunk, and became uncovered in his tent." The fool exposes what is inside him, and what is inside is only himself.
• The KJV reads "but that his heart may discover itself," using "discover" in its older sense of "uncover" or "reveal."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik, pictures the man who will not learn: "He is wilful, and so stands as a stake in the midst of a stream; lets all pass by him, but he stands where he was."
• Compare 12:23 ("the heart of fools proclaims foolishness"), 13:16, 15:2 and James 1:19.
units.summary: A fool's mouth is always open and his mind is always shut.
units.principle: Understanding grows only in a heart that would rather learn than be heard.
units.insight: On the Mount of Transfiguration Peter blurted out a plan for three tabernacles, "not knowing what he said" (Luke 9:33). The answer came from the cloud: "This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!" (Luke 9:35). Even a disciple can prefer speaking to listening. The Pharisees of John 9 show the hardened form. A healed man told them what Jesus had done, and they answered, "You were completely born in sins, and are you teaching us?" (John 9:34). They had no delight in understanding. Mary of Bethany chose the better part: she "sat at Jesus' feet and heard His word" (Luke 10:39). The fool in us loves the sound of our own opinions, on social media, in meetings, even in Bible studies. Grace makes us listeners again, because Christ is the Word we most need to hear.
units.application: In your next disagreement, at home or at work, ask two real questions before you state your view, and listen to the answers. If you post opinions online, try a week of reading more than you write. Small-group leaders, notice whether you are teaching or performing, and leave room for the quiet member to speak. Parents, model curiosity by asking your teenager what they think and learning something from the answer.

rel.note: When pride comes, shame comes with it, the same pairing of sin and disgrace.
The wicked man becomes loathsome and comes to shame.
What is true of one wicked person is true of a whole people: sin brings reproach.
The wise inherit glory while fools are left with shame as their legacy.

units.notes:
• Henry draws out both senses of the first line. Wicked people "are scornful people, and put contempt upon others"; they are also "shameful people, and bring contempt upon themselves."
• *Dishonor* is shameful conduct, the opposite of the honor Proverbs prizes; the KJV has "ignominy." *Reproach* is open blame or scorn spoken against someone.
• Bridges on how the scornful man treats godly people: "Their seriousness he calls gloom, their cheerfulness levity." Jesus described the same habit in His generation, which dismissed John as demon-possessed and Himself as a glutton (Matthew 11:18–19).
• Shame followed sin from the beginning: Adam and Eve hid from God as soon as they had disobeyed (Genesis 3:7–10).
• Compare 3:35 ("shame shall be the legacy of fools"), 11:2, 13:5 and 14:34.
units.summary: Sin never travels alone; contempt and disgrace ride along with it.
units.principle: Contempt for God and for others does not stay contained; it returns as disgrace on the one who carries it.
units.insight: Haman shows how contempt and disgrace travel together. When Mordecai would not bow, Haman scorned the idea of touching Mordecai alone and set out to destroy all his people (Esther 3:5–6). Soon afterward he was forced to lead Mordecai through the city in royal honor, and then he hurried home "mourning and with his head covered" (Esther 6:12). His contempt for others had come back on him as shame. The verse also exposes a quieter version in us: the eye-roll, the sarcastic comment, the settled habit of looking down on certain people. The gospel answers both. Jesus bore contempt He never deserved; He "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2), so that people who deserve reproach can be given honor. Those whom He has honored have no reason left to despise anyone.
units.application: Listen this week for contempt in your own speech: the sarcastic aside about a coworker, the dismissive tone with a spouse, the jokes at the expense of a group of people. Replace it with a plain, respectful word. Parents, correct contempt in your children early, before it hardens into character. If you are on the receiving end of someone's scorn, do not answer with scorn; entrust yourself to God and keep your own conduct honorable (1 Peter 2:23).

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life, the same picture of speech as life-giving water.
The mouth of fools also pours out, but what flows from it is foolishness.
Understanding is a wellspring of life to the one who has it.
Counsel in the heart is deep water that a person of understanding draws out.

units.notes:
• *Wellspring* translates maqor, a spring or fountain. The same word is behind "a well of life" (10:11), "a fountain of life" (13:14; 14:27) and "a wellspring of life" (16:22): in Proverbs, wise speech and wise living are pictured as water that gives life.
• *Flowing* translates a verb for water bubbling or gushing up. Proverbs uses the same verb when the mouth of fools "pours forth foolishness" (15:2) and the mouth of the wicked "pours forth evil" (15:28). Every mouth pours out what its source holds.
• Henry reads the pictures the other way round: the wise man's inner store is "as deep waters, which make no noise, but never run dry," and his words are the brook that flows from it.
• Jesus used similar language: "out of his heart will flow rivers of living water" (John 7:38). Some have wondered whether this proverb was among the Scriptures He had in mind; that remains a suggestion, not a certainty.
• Compare 10:11; 20:5; Matthew 12:34–35.
units.summary: Words are drawn from the deep well of the heart; wisdom turns them into a running stream.
units.principle: Speech is only as deep and fresh as its source; a heart filled with wisdom keeps giving life through its words.
units.insight: At a well in Samaria Jesus offered a weary woman water that would become "a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life" (John 4:14). She left her water pot and ran to tell her town (John 4:28–29). Words that give life to others start with a source that has been filled. When Jesus taught, the crowds "were astonished at His teaching" (Matthew 7:28), because the water came from the deepest spring there is. Many of us know the opposite: plenty of talk and little refreshment. Bridges describes such speech as "sometimes a torrent of words, yet without a drop of profitable matter." The cure is not more words but a fuller well. Time in God's word and in prayer keeps the brook running, so that a friend, a child or a struggling believer leaves our company refreshed.
units.application: Before you counsel a friend or teach a class, fill the well first with unhurried time in Scripture and prayer. When someone shares a problem, draw out the deep water with patient questions instead of rushing to answer (20:5). Parents, let your children hear wisdom flow naturally in ordinary conversation, not only in lectures. If your words have felt dry lately, look at the source before you work on the delivery.

rel.note: Justifying the wicked and condemning the just are both an abomination to the LORD.
The secret bribe is one of the main ways a verdict is bent toward the wicked.
Fair judgment hears both sides, the safeguard against deciding by the person instead of the case.
The same verdict, "It is not good," is passed on partiality in judgment.
Partiality is again called not good, and the verse shows how cheaply it can be bought.

units.notes:
• *Show partiality* is literally "lift up the face." To lift someone's face meant to receive him with favor; in a court it meant judging by the person instead of the facts. The KJV keeps the older phrase, "to accept the person of the wicked."
• "Not good" is deliberate understatement that carries strong disapproval. The companion saying 17:15 states it in full: acquitting the wicked and condemning the just are both "an abomination to the LORD."
• Proverbs repeats the warning at 24:23 ("It is not good to show partiality in judgment") and 28:21 ("To show partiality is not good").
• Bridges: "In judgment let the cause be heard, not the person."
• Naboth's trial is the classic case of both lines at once: false witnesses were believed, the elders went along, and an innocent man was stoned so a king could have a vineyard (1 Kings 21:8–13).
• Compare Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 16:19; James 2:1–4, 9.
units.summary: Bend a verdict toward the guilty and you bend it away from the innocent.
units.principle: Justice judges the deed, not the person; favoring the guilty and wronging the innocent are two sides of one corruption.
units.insight: The worst miscarriage of justice in history fulfilled both lines of this verse at once. Before Pilate the crowd asked for Barabbas, a murderer, and demanded that Jesus be crucified. Peter later told them, "you denied the Holy One and the Just, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you" (Acts 3:14). The guilty went free and the Righteous One was condemned. Yet God turned that unjust verdict into the place where He justifies sinners without bending His justice (Romans 3:26). We bend judgment in smaller ways: the favored child whose fault is overlooked, the generous donor whose behavior goes unaddressed, the friend we defend before we know the facts. Jehoshaphat reminded his judges that "there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, no partiality" (2 Chronicles 19:7). Those who judge for Him must judge like Him.
units.application: Parents, when two children quarrel, decide by what happened, not by which child usually behaves. Elders and church leaders, address sin in a prominent member or donor as you would in anyone else. Managers, when a complaint involves your best performer, let the facts decide. If you serve on a jury, a board or a hiring committee, set aside who the person is and weigh what was actually done.

rel.note: A soft answer turns away the wrath that the fool's words stir up.
The pair continues: here the fool's mouth draws blows from others, there it ruins him from within.
It is honorable to stop striving, while any fool can start a quarrel.
The contentious man kindles strife the way charcoal feeds burning coals.

units.notes:
• *Calls* translates qara', the ordinary verb for calling out, used when Wisdom "cries out in the chief concourses" (1:21). The fool's mouth calls too, but what it summons is a beating.
• *Blows* are strokes or beatings; the KJV has "strokes." Whether they come from an offended neighbor or from the authorities, the fool's own words have asked for them. Compare 19:29 and 26:3.
• Henry: "A wise man may, against his will, be drawn into a quarrel, but he is a fool that of choice enters into it when he might avoid it."
• Scripture gives a picture of this in the men of Succoth and Penuel, whose mocking refusal of Gideon brought punishment on them (Judges 8:4–17).
• Compare 17:14; 20:3; 26:17; 26:21.
units.summary: The fool's mouth sends out invitations to a fight, then he is surprised when the guests arrive.
units.principle: Provoking words rarely stay one-sided; the one who starts a quarrel with his mouth usually ends up paying for it.
units.insight: Nabal shows this verse in action. David's men had protected his flocks, and when they asked politely for provisions, Nabal answered, "Who is David?" and treated them like runaway servants (1 Samuel 25:10–11). Soon about four hundred armed men were on their way. Only his wife's humble, wise words turned the blows aside (1 Samuel 25:23–35). His own servant summed him up: "he is such a scoundrel that one cannot speak to him" (1 Samuel 25:17). Most of us have sent invitations like his: the sarcastic reply, the comment designed to sting, the text sent in anger. Jesus shows the other way. "When He was reviled, did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). His Spirit can set a guard on our lips.
units.application: Before you send the heated email or post the cutting reply, wait a day and read it again. Husbands and wives, notice the phrases that always start the same fight, and retire them. Young people, the insult that gets a laugh in the group chat can cost you a friendship or worse. If you supervise others, answer provocation with calm firmness instead of matching it (15:1).

rel.note: The mouth of the foolish is near destruction.
The wicked is ensnared by the transgression of his own lips.
The one who opens wide his lips shall have destruction, while the one who guards his mouth preserves his life.
The fool's mouth first draws blows from others; here it becomes his own destruction.
Whoever guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from the troubles the fool walks into.

units.notes:
• *Snare* translates moqesh, a fowler's trap that springs when touched. Compare 12:13: "The wicked is ensnared by the transgression of his lips."
• *Soul* here means the person's life, the whole self, not only his inner life.
• Bridges: "There is no need to dig a pit for the fool. He digs it for himself."
• Henry describes the fool who tries to talk his way out of trouble: "his defence proves his offence, and his lips are still the snare of his soul, entangling him yet more and more."
• Compare 10:14; 13:3; 14:3; Ecclesiastes 10:12 ("the lips of a fool shall swallow him up"); Matthew 12:37.
units.summary: The fool needs no enemy to trap him; his own tongue sets the snare.
units.principle: The person who will not govern his tongue is setting traps for himself, and more words only tighten them.
units.insight: Adonijah had already tried to seize the throne and been spared. Then he asked for Abishag, the young woman who had attended his father David, as his wife, a request that signaled a claim to the crown. Solomon answered, "Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life!" (1 Kings 2:23). One request sprang the trap. Jesus warned that "by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" (Matthew 12:37). If our words were the only evidence, every one of us would be caught. Isaiah knew it: "Woe is me... Because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5). God did not leave him in the snare. A coal from the altar touched his lips, and he heard, "Your iniquity is taken away" (Isaiah 6:7). Christ's sacrifice is that altar for us, and a cleansed mouth can learn to speak life.
units.application: When you are caught in a mistake, resist the urge to explain, excuse and blame; a short, honest admission closes the trap that more talking would tighten. Before a difficult meeting, decide what you will not say. Young people, remember that what you post can be read years later by an employer or a future spouse. If your words have already done damage, go and make it right instead of defending them.

rel.note: The faithful spirit conceals a matter that the talebearer reveals.
The whisperer separates the best of friends, the damage these swallowed words do.
Love covers a transgression, while repeating a matter separates friends.
Where there is no talebearer, strife dies out like a fire without wood.
The same saying is repeated word for word in the talebearer passage.

units.notes:
• *Talebearer* translates nirgan, a whisperer or murmurer. He is the "whisperer" who "separates the best of friends" (16:28) and the talebearer without whom "strife ceases" (26:20).
• *Tasty trifles* translates a rare word for delicacies, things swallowed eagerly. The KJV reads very differently, "as wounds," with a margin "like as when men are wounded"; modern versions follow the sense of choice morsels, as the NKJV does.
• *Inmost body* is literally "the chambers of the belly," the innermost rooms of a person. The same phrase appears at 20:27, "all the inner depths of his heart."
• The verse is repeated word for word at 26:22, in the talebearer passage of 26:20–22.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "When such tasty bits are taken into the innermost being, they stimulate the desire for more."
• Compare Leviticus 19:16 ("You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people"); Romans 1:29; James 4:11.
units.summary: Gossip goes down like candy and stays down like poison.
units.principle: Gossip harms because people want it; what is pleasant to hear about others lodges in the heart and poisons love.
units.insight: Doeg the Edomite told a jealous king only what he had seen: David at Nob, receiving food and Goliath's sword from the priest (1 Samuel 22:9–10). The report ended in the slaughter of the priests and their town (1 Samuel 22:18–19). David later wrote of him, "Your tongue devises destruction, Like a sharp razor" (Psalm 52:2). Most gossip never draws blood, but it still wounds. Bridges describes the hearer who claims to dismiss a rumor while thinking, "Suppose it should be true." From that moment suspicion has settled in. So the question is not only "Do I spread it?" but "Do I enjoy it?" Love "thinks no evil" (1 Corinthians 13:5). Christ, who knows every secret we have, has covered our sins instead of exposing them. Those who have been covered learn to cover others.
units.application: When a conversation turns to someone who is not there, ask, "Should we be talking about this?" or change the subject. If you hear a damaging report, take it to the person concerned or let it end with you. Small-group leaders, watch that prayer requests do not become a polite channel for gossip. Parents, keep other families' troubles off the dinner table, where your children are learning what tastes good.

rel.note: A slack hand leads to poverty, while the diligent hand makes rich.
The diligent hand rules, while the lazy man ends up under forced labor.
The lazy soul desires and has nothing, but the diligent soul is made rich.
The lazy man's overgrown field and broken wall show slow ruin by neglect.

units.notes:
• *Slothful* translates a verb meaning to be slack or to let the hands drop. The picture is of hands hanging down: the work is not refused, just never taken firmly in hand.
• *Great destroyer* is literally "master of destruction" (ba'al mashchit). The KJV has "great waster," the spendthrift who throws away what he has.
• The word "brother" links three sayings in this chapter: here, the offended brother of 18:19, and the friend who sticks closer than a brother in 18:24.
• Bridges sets the two side by side: "The one folds his arms in sloth. The other opens his hands in wastefulness."
• Compare Matthew 25:24–30, where the servant who buried his talent is called "wicked and lazy"; Luke 16:1, the steward accused of "wasting" his master's goods; James 4:17.
units.summary: You do not have to tear a house down to ruin it; you only have to stop keeping it up.
units.principle: Neglect is not neutral; leaving undone the work we are able to do destroys as surely as deliberate harm, only more slowly.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable the third servant did nothing wicked with his master's money. He simply buried it, and his master called him "wicked and lazy" (Matthew 25:26). Doing nothing with what God has entrusted is not neutral. The town of Meroz was cursed in Deborah's song, not for fighting against Israel but "Because they did not come to the help of the LORD" (Judges 5:23). G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "No living being can be merely a spectator. Each works or wastes." The same is true of the soul. Neglected prayer, a marriage left to drift, a gift never used: none of these is torn down in a day. They decay quietly. Jesus said, "I must work the works of Him who sent Me while it is day" (John 9:4). His faithfulness is our pattern, and His grace is our strength to begin again.
units.application: Employees, do the unseen tasks as carefully as the ones your manager checks; slack work wastes an employer's money as surely as careless spending. Homeowners, fix the small leak this week before it rots the floor. Students, the assignment you keep postponing is a grade slowly being torn down. If prayer or Bible reading has slid into silence, restart with ten honest minutes tomorrow. Those limited by illness are not in view here; do what you can.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence and a place of refuge for His children.
The rich man runs to a strong city of wealth that is high only in his own imagination.
Whoever trusts in the LORD shall be safe, while the fear of man is a snare.
God is a shield to those who put their trust in Him.
Trusting the LORD with all the heart, rather than one's own understanding, is what running to the tower means.

units.notes:
• *Strong tower* (migdal 'oz) is a fortified tower, the last stronghold of a city. When Abimelech attacked Thebez, the people "fled there and shut themselves in" a strong tower within the city (Judges 9:51).
• *Are safe* translates a verb meaning to be set on high, out of reach; the KJV margin has "set aloft." The same verb describes the rich man's "high wall" in 18:11, which sharpens the contrast between the two refuges.
• Bridges defines the name as "not the bare outward words, operating as a charm, but his character; that by which he is known, as a man by his name."
• *Run* pictures urgency and trust: the righteous do not stroll to the tower or merely know where it is.
• Compare Psalm 9:10 ("those who know Your name will put their trust in You"); Psalm 61:3 ("A strong tower from the enemy"); Joel 2:32 and Romans 10:13 ("whoever calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved").
units.summary: When danger comes, the righteous do not recite a name; they run to the God it reveals.
units.principle: True safety is found not in reciting God's name but in running to the God whose character that name reveals.
units.insight: At Ziklag David came home to a burned town and captured families, and his own men spoke of stoning him. "But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God" (1 Samuel 30:6). That is running to the tower. Contrast the seven sons of Sceva, who tried to use "the name of the Lord Jesus" as a formula over a demonized man. The spirit answered, "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?" and they fled wounded (Acts 19:13–16). The name protects those who know and trust the One it names. In the light of the New Testament, the LORD's name is fully revealed in Jesus, and "there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). When fear comes, where do you run first: to your phone, your savings, your own planning, or to Him?
units.application: When bad news comes, a diagnosis, a layoff, a child in crisis, make your first move toward God before any other: pray it out to Him, even in one sentence. Memorize one of His self-descriptions, such as Exodus 34:6 or Psalm 46:1, so you know where to run when you are afraid. Parents, teach your children to pray when they are frightened rather than to use Jesus' name like a magic word. Then help a frightened friend run there too.

rel.note: The same first line appears there as a plain observation, which this verse now qualifies.
He who trusts in his riches will fall.
Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, the very day the rich man expects his wall to hold.
The righteous run to the LORD's name and are truly set on high, while the rich man's wall is high only in his mind.
A heart lifted up by its own height is on the way to destruction.

units.notes:
• *Esteem* translates maskit, a word for an image or imagined picture. The ESV and NASB have "imagination," the KJV "conceit" in its older sense of "idea." The wall stands mainly in the rich man's mind.
• *High wall* uses the same verb as "are safe" (literally "set on high") in 18:10. The righteous are truly lifted high in the LORD; the rich man's wall is high only in his imagination.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, names the danger: wealth "gives its possessor the illusion of greater security than it can provide."
• Compare 10:15 (the same first line, without this qualification); 11:4; 11:28; 23:5; Psalm 49:6–9; 1 Timothy 6:17, "nor to trust in uncertain riches but in the living God."
units.summary: Money builds a wall that looks highest from the inside.
units.principle: Wealth offers real but limited protection; trusting it beyond those limits is a self-deception that fails when it is needed most.
units.insight: Jesus told of a farmer whose harvest outgrew his barns. He planned bigger ones and said to himself, "Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; take your ease." God answered, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:19–20). His wall was high only in his own esteem. Scott, quoted by Bridges: "Trouble will find an entrance into his castle. Death will storm, and take it." The danger is not only for the wealthy. Anyone can picture a savings account, a pension, a career or a good reputation as the thing that will keep them safe. The test is what we reach for first when we feel threatened. Christ, "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). In Him we have treasure no storm can take.
units.application: Save wisely, but notice when the balance in your account sets the level of your peace. If you have plenty, give generously enough this month that you feel it; generosity loosens money's grip on the heart (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Financial planners and business owners, be honest with clients about what money cannot do. When a crisis hits, pray before you call your banker or adviser.

rel.note: When pride comes, shame follows, but wisdom is with the humble.
The fear of the LORD teaches wisdom, and before honor is humility, the second line's first appearance.
Pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall, the first line said earlier.
The rich man's imagined high wall is one form of the haughty heart that comes before destruction.
Pride brings a man low, while the humble in spirit retain honor.

units.notes:
• *Haughty* translates a verb meaning to be high or lifted up. It carries on the picture of height from 18:10–11 with a different word: the heart lifts itself up, and that is the height that falls.
• Both lines appeared separately earlier, the first in 16:18 and the second at the close of 15:33. Proverbs repeats what people are slow to believe.
• Bridges: "It is hard to persuade a man that he is proud."
• Two kings of Judah show both lines. Of Uzziah: "when he was strong his heart was lifted up, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16). Of his son: "Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chronicles 27:6).
• Compare 11:2; 29:23; Luke 14:11; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5–6.
units.summary: The heart climbs before the fall, and the knees bend before the crown.
units.principle: Self-exaltation is the first step of a fall, and humility before God is the road He uses to bring honor.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar walked on his palace roof and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built... by my mighty power and for the honor of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30). Before the words had left his mouth, judgment fell. When his reason returned, he confessed that "those who walk in pride He is able to put down" (Daniel 4:37). The same pattern runs the other way in Christ. He "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also has highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:8–9). The humble path to honor was His path before it is ours. Pride is hard to see in ourselves; it hides in comparison, in defensiveness, in the need to be right. Ask God to show you where your heart is climbing, and take the low place before you are put there.
units.application: When you are praised at work, pass the credit to your team and thank God in the same breath. When you are corrected, say, "You may be right; let me think about that," before you defend yourself. Leaders, take on one humble task this week that no one expects you to do. Young people who succeed early, find an older believer who will tell you the truth about yourself. Before a big decision, ask, "Am I leaning on my own height?"

rel.note: The heart of the righteous studies how to answer instead of pouring out a reply.
The ear of the wise seeks knowledge before it speaks.
The first account seems right until the other side is heard, which is why answering early is folly.
The fool delights in airing his own heart, and answering before hearing is that delight in action.
There is more hope for a fool than for a man hasty in his words.

units.notes:
• *Answers a matter* is literally "returns a word" (KJV margin): he sends back a reply before the message has fully arrived.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, calls hasty answering "a special snare of the self-important."
• God Himself is described as investigating before He judges. Before judging Babel, "the LORD came down to see the city" (Genesis 11:5), and of Sodom He said, "I will go down now and see" (Genesis 18:21). His verdicts rest on full knowledge.
• Nicodemus appealed to the same principle in the council: "Does our law judge a man before it hears him and knows what he is doing?" (John 7:51).
• Compare 18:17; 29:20; Job 32:4, 11 (Elihu waits until the older men have finished speaking); James 1:19.
units.summary: Answering before you listen means replying to a conversation that happened only in your head.
units.principle: No one can answer rightly what he has not heard fully; listening is the first act of both wisdom and justice.
units.insight: Job's friends sat with him in silence for seven days, which was wise. Then they began to answer before they had truly heard him. They assumed his suffering proved hidden sin, and they argued it for chapter after chapter. In the end God told them, "you have not spoken of Me what is right, as My servant Job has" (Job 42:7). Their quick answers brought them folly and shame. Jesus did the opposite. A crowd pressed on Him, yet He stopped for one frightened woman, and she "told Him the whole truth" while He listened (Mark 5:33). Hasty answering grows from pride, the belief that my view is already complete. Before you reply to a spouse, a child or a critic, ask whether you are answering them or your assumption about them. The God who hears us fully is teaching us to do the same.
units.application: In your next hard conversation, let the other person finish, then repeat back what you heard before you respond. Parents, when your teenager starts a story, hold the lecture until you have heard the whole thing. Managers, gather the facts before you answer a complaint. In email threads, read the entire message before replying. Pastors and counselors, ask one more question than you think you need.

rel.note: Anxiety weighs the heart down, but a good word makes it glad, a way others help carry the load.
Sorrow of heart breaks the spirit, naming one cause of the wound this verse describes.
Perverse words can break the spirit, so speech can either wound or heal it.
A broken spirit dries the bones, the same crushed spirit affecting the whole person.

units.notes:
• *Broken* translates a word meaning stricken or wounded; the KJV has "a wounded spirit." The same phrase appears at 15:13 and 17:22, where it describes an inner life crushed by sorrow or despair.
• *Sustain* translates the verb used when Joseph "provided" for his father's household in Egypt (Genesis 47:12). A healthy spirit feeds and holds up the whole person the way Joseph kept his family alive through famine.
• *Sickness* here is bodily weakness or illness; the KJV has "infirmity."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "In physical sickness one can fall back on the will to live; but in depression the will to live may be gone".
• Compare 12:25; 15:13; 17:22; Psalm 34:18; Psalm 147:3; Isaiah 61:1.
units.summary: The body can lean on the spirit, but a broken spirit needs a stronger arm than its own.
units.principle: A wounded spirit is a real and heavy burden that human strength cannot carry alone, so it calls for compassion, not blame.
units.insight: Elijah had just seen fire fall on Mount Carmel, yet soon afterward he lay under a broom tree and prayed to die (1 Kings 19:4). God did not start with a rebuke. He sent an angel with bread and water, let him sleep, and said, "the journey is too great for you" (1 Kings 19:7). That is how the LORD treats a broken spirit. Bridges: "The suffering of the soul is the soul of suffering." Jesus knew that suffering from the inside. In Gethsemane He said, "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). From the start of His ministry He had announced that He was sent "to heal the brokenhearted" (Luke 4:18). If you are carrying a broken spirit, you are not weak for needing help. If someone near you is carrying one, bring bread before advice.
units.application: If a friend is depressed or grieving, do not tell them to cheer up or pray harder; bring a meal, sit with them, and keep showing up. Pastors and small-group leaders, learn the signs of depression and know when to encourage medical or counseling help. If your own spirit is crushed, tell one trusted person this week and ask for help. Caregivers, guard your own spirit too; rest is not selfishness.

rel.note: The heart of one with understanding seeks knowledge.
The seeking ear is the cure for answering a matter before hearing it.
The fool takes no delight in the understanding that the prudent heart pursues.
A wise man will hear and increase learning.
Instruct a wise man and he will be wiser still.

units.notes:
• The two verbs matter. *Acquires* is the word for getting or buying something as one's own, the verb of "Get wisdom! Get understanding!" (4:5). *Seeks* is the word for searching something out. Ironside, using the KJV words for "acquires" and "seeks": "Emphasize the 'getteth' and the 'seeketh.'"
• "Heart" and "ear" together describe the whole person learning, inward desire and outward attention. Compare 2:2, "incline your ear to wisdom, And apply your heart to understanding."
• The prudent and the wise are not beginners. Proverbs says the same of the wise in 1:5 and 9:9: they "increase learning."
• Compare 15:14; 22:17; Acts 17:11, where the Bereans "searched the Scriptures daily."
units.summary: The wise know enough to know how much they do not know, so they keep asking.
units.principle: The more truly a person grows in wisdom, the more eagerly he keeps learning, with both heart and ear.
units.insight: At twelve years old Jesus was found in the temple "sitting in the midst of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions" (Luke 2:46). In His true humanity the Son of God learned by listening. Ezra "had prepared his heart to seek the Law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10): seeking came before teaching. Near the end of his life, in prison, Paul still asked Timothy to bring "the books, especially the parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13). The danger for mature believers is to think they have arrived. Bridges recalls the confession of Ignatius, an early church leader: "I am now beginning to be a disciple." The prudent heart never outgrows that sentence. Where have you stopped being curious about God, His word, or the people around you?
units.application: Choose one area where you have stopped growing, such as Scripture, your marriage or your work, and take one concrete step: a book, a class, or a conversation with someone further along. Older believers, ask younger ones what they are learning; wisdom flows both ways. Teachers and pastors, keep reading beyond what you must prepare. In meetings, listen for what you do not already know instead of waiting for your turn to speak.

rel.note: The secret bribe that perverts justice is the corrupt counterpart of the open gift.
A present given to sway someone seems a precious stone to its owner, the self-serving use of giving that this verse does not approve.
Everyone is a friend to the one who gives gifts, the same observation of how gifts win favor.
A gift in secret pacifies anger, showing both the power of gifts and how close they come to bribery.

units.notes:
• *Gift* translates mattan, a general word for a present. It is different from shochad, the word for a bribe in 17:8 and 17:23. Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Matan ('gift') is more general than 'bribe'".
• *Makes room* is literally "makes wide": the gift widens a narrow way.
• Scripture shows such gifts in ordinary life. Jacob's sons carried "a present for the man" to Egypt (Genesis 43:11), and Abigail's provisions turned David away from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:18–35).
• The popular reading "your gift will make room for you," taking "gift" as a talent or spiritual gift, goes beyond the verse. The Hebrew word means a material present, and the setting in Proverbs supports that reading.
• Compare 17:8; 19:6; 21:14; 15:27 ("he who hates bribes will live").
units.summary: A gift can open doors that pressure cannot, so long as it is a gift and not a price.
units.principle: Generosity can rightly open doors, but a gift that is meant to buy a decision has become a bribe.
units.insight: Jacob sent drove after drove of animals ahead of him, saying, "I will appease him with the present that goes before me" (Genesis 32:20). The gift made room, and Esau met him with an embrace instead of a sword (Genesis 33:4). Proverbs is realistic: giving opens doors. But the verse also sets up a contrast with how we come to God. No present can buy a place before Him, and none is needed. Bridges: "Our welcome is free; our door of access ever open." Through Christ "we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand" (Romans 5:2). That frees us to give to people for the right reasons. Ask what your gifts are really for: honoring and serving someone, or securing an advantage you could not gain fairly. The first is generosity; the second is a bribe dressed as kindness.
units.application: A thoughtful gift to a new neighbor, a thank-you to a hard-working volunteer, or a meal for a coworker's family can open doors that words alone cannot; use it. Business owners and salespeople, keep a clear line: a courtesy may be given openly, but anything meant to buy a decision is a bribe. If you hold influence, ask whether a gift is shaping your judgment, and refuse it if it is.

rel.note: The simple believe every word, while the prudent consider carefully.
Answering before hearing is folly, and this verse shows how much a single account can hide.
Hearing both sides is the safeguard against overthrowing the righteous in judgment.
Going hastily to court can end in shame when the neighbor's side is heard.

units.notes:
• *Examines* translates chaqar, to search something out thoroughly. It is the verb of 25:2, "the glory of kings is to search out a matter," so the neighbor's questioning is a careful investigation, not a casual objection.
• *Plead his cause* is legal language; the KJV has "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just." The word for "cause" means a lawsuit or dispute.
• Henry: "We must therefore remember that we have two ears, to hear both sides before we give judgment."
• The law required the same care: "the judges shall make careful inquiry" (Deuteronomy 19:18), and a matter was established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).
• Compare 18:13; 14:15; John 7:51; Acts 25:16.
units.summary: Every story sounds complete until you hear the other side.
units.principle: One account, however convincing, is rarely the whole truth; fair judgment waits to hear the other side.
units.insight: Saul met Samuel with a confident first account: "I have performed the commandment of the LORD." Samuel examined him with one question: "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears?" (1 Samuel 15:13–14). The verse warns us about other people's stories, but it also warns us about our own. Each of us is the first to plead our own cause, and we usually sound right to ourselves. Bridges: "Here we are warned against justifying ourselves." Before God none of us could stand on our first account. Yet the Messiah does not judge "by the sight of His eyes, Nor decide by the hearing of His ears; But with righteousness He shall judge the poor" (Isaiah 11:3–4). Because He judges truly and mercifully, we can stop defending ourselves and invite His searching: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23).
units.application: When a friend tells you how badly someone treated them, sympathize, but hold your verdict until you have heard the other side or know you never will. Parents, hear both children before you decide who started it. Church leaders and HR managers, never act on one account alone; bring the parties together where possible. Online, wait for the second story before you share the first.

rel.note: Every decision of the lot is from the LORD, which is why both sides could accept it.
Strife is easier to stop at its beginning, before only an outside decision can end it.
The next verse shows how hard a quarrel becomes once it hardens between people who are close.
It is honorable to stop striving, the same goal of ending a contest of strength.

units.notes:
• *Lots* were objects thrown or drawn so that no one controlled the result; Scripture does not describe their exact form. Canaan was divided by lot among the tribes (Numbers 26:55; Joshua 18:10), and the priests' duties were assigned by lot (1 Chronicles 24:5, 31).
• *Keeps the mighty apart* is literally "separates between the mighty," the strong parties who could otherwise force their way.
• The apostles used the lot to choose Matthias after praying, "You, O Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two You have chosen" (Acts 1:24–26). The New Testament does not mention the practice again after Pentecost.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Today God's word and spiritual leaders figure prominently in divine arbitration (1 Corinthians 6:1-8)."
• Compare 16:33; 17:14; 20:3.
units.summary: When two strong wills reach a deadlock, a fair process trusted to God can do what force cannot.
units.principle: When agreement is impossible, peace is kept by a fair process both sides accept and a shared trust that God rules the outcome.
units.insight: When the herdsmen of Abram and his nephew Lot began to quarrel, Abram said, "Please let there be no strife between you and me... If you take the left, then I will go to the right" (Genesis 13:8–9). He let the younger man choose and trusted God with the outcome. Then God promised Abram all the land he could see (Genesis 13:14–15). Peace came because the stronger man refused to make strength the deciding factor. Bridges sees a harder test for believers: "Perhaps it is more easy to abide by the decision of the lot than of the word." Accepting a coin toss is easy; submitting our quarrels to Scripture's call to forgive and yield is harder. Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers, For they shall be called sons of God" (Matthew 5:9). Where are you insisting on winning instead of trusting God with the result?
units.application: When siblings or roommates deadlock over a small matter, let a coin, a rotation or a neutral friend decide, and agree beforehand to accept the result. Church boards and business partners, agree on a fair decision process before disputes arise, so no one wins by force. In serious disputes between believers, seek wise mediation within the church before going to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). Then receive the outcome as from God's hand.

rel.note: The whisperer separates the best of friends, one way such breaches begin.
Stopping strife before it starts prevents the barred gates this verse describes.
Covering a transgression seeks love, while repeating it separates friends.
The previous verse shows a way to end contentions before they harden into bars.
Against the offended brother stands the friend who sticks closer than a brother.

units.notes:
• *Offended* comes from the word for transgression or rebellion; the YLT has "A brother transgressed against." The word describes a real wrong done to him.
• The Hebrew line has no verb and reads literally "a brother offended—than a strong city," so every translation must supply the comparison. The KJV prints "is harder to be won" in italics to mark the added words; the ESV reads "more unyielding."
• *Bars* are the heavy beams or bolts that locked a city gate; compare Isaiah 45:2, "cut the bars of iron."
• Bridges: "as if the nearer the relation, the wider the breach." Kidner, quoted by Guzik, warns of "the strength of the invisible walls of estrangement."
• Compare 16:28; 17:9; 17:14; Matthew 5:23–24; 18:15.
units.summary: It is easier to take a fortress than to win back a brother you have wounded.
units.principle: The closer the bond, the harder the breach is to heal, so offense between loved ones must be avoided carefully and repaired patiently.
units.insight: Absalom said nothing to Amnon, "neither good nor bad," for two full years after Amnon wronged his sister (2 Samuel 13:22–23). The silence was a barred gate, and behind it hatred grew until it ended in murder. Jacob's story shows another road. Esau had vowed to kill him (Genesis 27:41). Twenty years later Jacob prayed for deliverance, sent gifts ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached. "But Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him" (Genesis 33:4). God opened a gate no siege could have opened. The gospel is the greatest reconciliation of all. Christ "Himself is our peace," who "has broken down the middle wall of separation" (Ephesians 2:14), and He gives His people "the ministry of reconciliation" (2 Corinthians 5:18). Is there someone whose gate you barred, or whose gate you have stopped knocking on?
units.application: If you have wronged a family member or close friend, go first, own it plainly without excuses, and expect healing to take time (Matthew 5:23–24). Do not add new bars by arguing over who was more at fault. If you are the one who was hurt, you can forgive and still move carefully; trust is rebuilt slowly. Parents, help siblings make peace the same day. Church leaders, address rifts early, before they harden.

rel.note: A man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth, the same harvest picture.
A man eats well by the fruit of his mouth, while the unfaithful feed on violence.
A man has joy by the answer of his mouth, one sweet fruit of wise words.
The next verse states the same truth in its strongest form: those who love the tongue will eat its fruit.

units.notes:
• *Stomach* is literally "belly," the KJV's word. Hebrew often uses the belly for a person's inner being, as in "the inmost body" of 18:8, so the harvest of words reaches the speaker's inner life, not only his circumstances.
• *Produce* is the word for the yield of a field or harvest, keeping the farming picture of the first line.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the image means "whatever a person dishes out, whether beneficial or harmful, he himself will feed on it".
• Ironside: "Words seldom fall idly to the ground."
• Compare 12:14; 13:2; Galatians 6:7–8; Matthew 12:36–37.
units.summary: Every word you speak is seed, and sooner or later you sit down to eat the harvest.
units.principle: Words are seed that return to the speaker; over time we live on the harvest of what we have habitually said.
units.insight: Rehoboam took the harsh advice of his young friends and told Israel, "My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scourges!" (1 Kings 12:14). Ten tribes walked away, and he ate the fruit of that sentence for the rest of his reign. Abigail's humble, wise words had the opposite harvest. David blessed her advice, which kept him from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:32–33). Most of us are eating some harvest right now: a relationship strained by years of criticism, or trust built by years of kept promises. The Servant of the LORD in Isaiah says, "The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary" (Isaiah 50:4). Christ can retrain our tongues to sow what we will be glad to eat.
units.application: Look at the harvest in one relationship, such as a marriage, a friendship or a workplace, and ask what kind of words have been sown there over the past year. Husbands and wives, plant one specific word of appreciation every day this week. Supervisors, notice whether your team hears more correction than encouragement. Young people, the way you speak to and about your parents now is shaping the relationship you will have with them later.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life.
Rash words pierce like a sword, while the tongue of the wise promotes health.
Guarding the mouth preserves life, while opening wide the lips brings destruction to the speaker.
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life, while perverse speech breaks the spirit.
The harvest of the lips in the previous verse is here given its highest stakes, death and life.

units.notes:
• *Power* translates yad, "hand," a common Hebrew picture of power or control, as when someone is said to be "in the hand" of another. The NKJV's "power" gives the sense.
• *Those who love it*: "it" is usually taken as the tongue, so the line speaks of people who love to use their tongues. The NLT reads, "those who love to talk will reap the consequences."
• Bridges: "It is, however, the habitual, not the occasional, use of this little member, that determines its fruit." ("This little member" is the tongue; compare James 3:5.)
• A rabbinic saying from the Midrash on the Psalms, quoted by Ross and cited by Guzik: "The evil tongue slays three, the slanderer, the slandered, and the listener".
• The New Testament gives speech the same weight: Matthew 12:36–37; Ephesians 4:29 ("what is good for necessary edification"); James 3:5–10. Confession "unto salvation" (Romans 10:10) is an act of faith in Christ, not a technique for getting results.
• Compare 10:11; 12:18; 13:3; 15:4.
units.summary: Words cannot conjure reality, but they can make or break a person.
units.principle: Speech carries real power to wound or to heal, and the one who loves to use it will live with its results, though words are not a formula for controlling outcomes.
units.insight: Nathan's words "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7) cut David to the heart, and they gave him life. David confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD," and heard, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Samuel 12:13). A true word, spoken in love, can rescue a soul. Peter shows another side. He declared, "I will never be made to stumble" (Matthew 26:33), and within hours he denied his Lord. Not every firm promise is sinful, and such words carry no automatic power. Yet words we settle on, "I will never" or "you always," can express fear or pride and harden the heart. They belong before God, to be examined and, where needed, repented of. Jesus restored Peter with three questions (John 21:15–17). Which words do you love to use, and what are they growing?
units.application: Speak life on purpose this week: tell a discouraged coworker exactly what they did well, or send a struggling friend a verse and a prayer. Parents, refuse labels like "you're lazy" or "you always"; correct the behavior, not the child's identity. If you have made an "I will never" vow out of hurt, bring it to God and ask whether it should be released. When you are ill, speak truthfully about it and pray; honesty is not unbelief.

rel.note: An excellent wife is her husband's crown, showing what makes a wife a good thing.
Houses come from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.
A contentious marriage is worse than a corner of the housetop, so the praise is for a good wife, not marriage at any cost.
The book's closing poem asks who can find a virtuous wife, the good thing this verse celebrates.
Whoever finds Wisdom obtains favor from the LORD, the same words used of finding a wife.

units.notes:
• *Obtains favor from the LORD* repeats word for word the phrase Wisdom uses in 8:35. The word for favor means goodwill, delight or acceptance. Finding a good wife and finding wisdom are described in the same terms.
• The Hebrew says simply "a wife," and the NKJV and other major English versions follow it. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads "a good wife," and the Clementine Latin Vulgate reads "a good woman," making explicit what the context of Proverbs implies.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Although it does not say it, the verse clearly means a 'good' wife."
• Single life is also honored as a calling from God (Matthew 19:11–12; 1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 32–35).
• Compare 12:4; 19:14; 31:10–31; Genesis 2:18–24; Ecclesiastes 9:9; Ephesians 5:31–32.
units.summary: A good wife is not a trophy a man wins but a gift he receives from God's hand.
units.principle: A good spouse is a gift of God's favor to be received with thanks, though His favor is never measured by whether a person is married.
units.insight: Abraham's servant went looking for a wife for Isaac with prayer, not just a plan, and when Rebekah appeared he bowed and said, "the LORD led me" (Genesis 24:27). Isaac "loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death" (Genesis 24:67). Bridges: "Isaac found it, where every Christian looks for his blessing, as an answer to prayer." A good wife is received, not merely chosen. That should humble husbands who take their wives for granted and steady young people tempted to settle for less than godliness. It should also comfort single men and women. In the light of the New Testament, marriage itself points to Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and the favor Wisdom promises is found fully in Him. Every believer, married or single, has been "accepted in the Beloved" (Ephesians 1:6).
units.application: Husbands, thank God for your wife by name this week, and tell her one specific way she has been God's favor to you. Young men and women, pray about marriage, and weigh character and the fear of the LORD above looks and status (31:30). Parents, teach your children that a spouse is a gift to receive from God, not a prize to win. Churches, honor single members as full partners in ministry, not as people waiting for life to begin.

rel.note: The poor are shunned while the rich have friends, yet despising one's neighbor is called sin.
Mercy to the needy honors God, while oppressing the poor reproaches Him.
The poor man pursues others with words and is still abandoned, the same pleading voice.
The rich and the poor share one Maker, which rebukes the rich man's rough answer.

units.notes:
• *Entreaties* translates a word for pleas for grace or favor, from the same root as the Hebrew word for "grace." It is the word behind "supplications" in Psalm 130:2: "Let Your ears be attentive To the voice of my supplications."
• *Roughly* is literally "strong" or "hard" things: blunt, forceful words. Compare Rehoboam, who "answered the people roughly" (1 Kings 12:13).
• Bridges on the rich man who is courteous in his own circle and rude to those beneath him: "His good breeding indeed is often only the polish of selfishness."
• Proverbs describes the rich man's tone here without approving it; elsewhere it condemns despising the poor (14:21, 31; 17:5).
• Compare 14:20; 19:7; 22:2; James 2:1–6.
units.summary: Need teaches the poor to say please; wealth can teach the rich to forget it.
units.principle: Power tempts people to speak harshly to those who depend on them, but God's people are to answer need with the gentleness He shows them.
units.insight: Blind Bartimaeus cried out from the roadside, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" The crowd "warned him to be quiet" (Mark 10:47–48). They answered his entreaty roughly. "So Jesus stood still and commanded him to be called" (Mark 10:49). The Lord of glory stopped for a beggar and asked, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51). Advantage of any kind, whether money, position, education or even spiritual maturity, can make us impatient with people who need something from us. The cure is to remember where we stand before God. Bridges: "all of us alike are poor before the throne of grace. All of us must use entreaties here." And we are invited to "come boldly to the throne of grace" (Hebrews 4:16), where no plea is answered with contempt. Those answered gently learn to answer others gently.
units.application: Notice how you speak to people who need something from you: the server, the cashier, the employee asking for time off, the person asking for help on the street. Managers and landlords, answer requests with courtesy even when the answer is no. Parents, teach your children to speak as kindly to the custodian as to the principal. If you are the one who must plead, keep your dignity; God hears you even when people do not.

rel.note: A friend loves at all times, the same loyal love that holds fast in adversity.
The offended brother who cannot be won stands against the friend who sticks closer than a brother.
Wealth makes many friends while the poor man is left alone, the fair-weather friendship that the clinging friend outlasts.
A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away, another case where friendship outweighs kinship.
The faithful friend's loyalty includes the honest wounds that flatterers never give.

units.notes:
• The first line is a well-known translation difficulty. The KJV and NKJV read a man with friends who must show himself friendly; the ESV has "A man of many companions may come to ruin," and the NASB (1995) "A man of too many friends comes to ruin." The difference turns on whether the Hebrew verb is read as "show oneself friendly" or as a verb meaning to be broken or ruined.
• *Friend* in the second line is a different word from "friends" in the first. It means literally "one who loves," a closer bond than the companions of the first line.
• *Sticks* translates the verb used for a man "joined to his wife" (Genesis 2:24) and for Ruth who "clung to" Naomi (Ruth 1:14): the language of the closest human bonds.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "It is better to have one good, faithful friend than numerous unreliable ones."
• Bridges sees the picture filled up in Christ, "who became our Brother, that he might cleave to us closer than a brother in tenderness and help" (compare Hebrews 2:11, 14–18).
• Compare 17:17; 27:10; John 15:13–15; Hebrews 13:5.
units.summary: To have friends you must be one, and the truest friend holds on when even family lets go.
units.principle: Friendship must be given to be received, and the most loyal love, found fully in Christ, holds fast when every natural tie fails.
units.insight: Jonathan was the king's son, yet "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David" (1 Samuel 18:1). He defended David before his own father at the risk of his life (1 Samuel 20:30–33). Such friends are rare, and the verse calls us to be one before we look for one. At a deeper, layered level, the verse points to Jesus. He was called "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19). On the night of His arrest His disciples "all forsook Him and fled" (Mark 14:50), yet He went to the cross for them. "Greater love has no one than this, than to lay down one's life for his friends" (John 15:13). If you feel friendless, He has promised, "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). His friendship makes us friends who stay.
units.application: If you are lonely, take the first step this week: invite someone for coffee, call an old friend, or sit with someone new at church. Be the friend who stays when trouble comes: visit the one in the hospital and keep calling the one who has gone quiet. Young people, a few loyal friends are worth more than a crowd of followers. If family has let you down, bring that grief to Christ, the Friend who will not let go.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, which explains why the poor man of 19:1 is better off.
A little with righteousness is better than great income gained without justice.
Later in the chapter a poor man is again ranked above a liar, so faithfulness, not wealth, is the measure of a person.
The same opening line sets the poor man of integrity above a rich man whose ways are crooked.

units.notes:
• Integrity means wholeness or completeness: a life without a hidden second self. Compare 10:9, "He who walks with integrity walks securely."
• Proverbs 28:6 repeats the first line exactly but ends "Than one perverse in his ways, though he be rich." In 19:1 the contrast falls on the lips, because crooked speech is the outward sign of a crooked heart.
• Verses 1 and 22 of this chapter make the same point from two angles: "a poor man is better than a liar" (19:22).
• Bridges: "Often man puts under his feet those, whom God lays in his bosom." He means that people trample the very ones God holds close.
• Compare Psalm 37:16, "A little that a righteous man has Is better than the riches of many wicked."
units.summary: Integrity is a wealth that poverty cannot take away and a crooked tongue cannot buy.
units.principle: Character is worth more than circumstances; an honest life with little outweighs a twisted tongue with much.
units.insight: We measure people by what they have; God measures them by what they are. Job sat among the ashes, stripped of everything, yet God called him "a blameless and upright man" who "holds fast to his integrity" (Job 2:3). Jesus told of a beggar named Lazarus at a rich man's gate, and in eternity their places were reversed (Luke 16:19–25). The verse searches us at two points. Do we quietly honor people for their money and overlook the poor believer whose word can be trusted? And would we bend our own words for advantage? The risen Christ said to a poor, persecuted church, "I know your works, tribulation, and poverty (but you are rich)" (Revelation 2:9). He Himself had nowhere to lay His head (Matthew 8:20), and no deceit was found in His mouth (1 Peter 2:22). In Him the poor man of integrity is never second best.
units.application: If you work in business or sales, refuse the gain that depends on a misleading word, even when it costs you the deal. Parents, praise your children for telling the truth when it was hard, not only for grades or trophies. If money is tight, do not let shame tell you that you count for less; your honesty is worth more than a bigger paycheck. In church, honor the faithful member with little as warmly as the generous donor.

rel.note: The prudent man considers well his steps, the opposite of the man who hastens with his feet.
Feet that rush ahead without knowledge lead to the twisted way and the fretting heart of the next verse.
The plans of everyone who is hasty lead to poverty, the practical cost of the hurry 19:2 calls sin.
The father's remedy for hasty feet is to ponder the path before taking it.

units.notes:
• *Soul* translates nefesh, which can mean a person, a life, or a person's appetite and desire. The ESV takes the last sense: "Desire without knowledge is not good."
• *Sins* translates chata', whose basic sense is to miss a target. Judges 20:16 uses it of the left-handed slingers who "could sling a stone at a hair's breadth and not miss." The ESV says the hasty man "misses his way," and the AMP reads "sins (misses the mark)," keeping both senses together.
• Ironside's translation offers "maketh false steps" (makes false steps) as an alternative to the KJV's "sinneth" (sins): the man who hurries stumbles.
• Samuel Johnson, quoted by Bridges: "He that is in a hurry proves, that the work in which he is engaged is too much for him."
• Compare 21:5 and 29:20 on haste, and Isaiah 28:16, "Whoever believes will not act hastily."
units.summary: Zeal without knowledge is a fast runner on the wrong road.
units.principle: Earnestness is no substitute for understanding; desire must be guided by knowledge, or speed will carry a person into sin.
units.insight: Some of the worst mistakes in Scripture were made in a hurry. Joshua's leaders examined the Gibeonites' moldy bread and made a treaty, "but they did not ask counsel of the LORD" (Joshua 9:14). King Saul would not wait for Samuel, offered the sacrifice himself, and lost the kingdom for his house (1 Samuel 13:8–14). Saul of Tarsus was sincere when he persecuted the church (Acts 26:9); he had the kind of zeal he later saw in his own people, "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge" (Romans 10:2). Our hurry often hides self-will: we do not want to wait for God or for wise counsel. The answer is not less zeal but zeal that kneels first. Jesus never rushed. When He heard Lazarus was sick, He stayed two more days where He was (John 11:6), because He did only what He saw the Father doing (John 5:19).
units.application: Before a big decision this week, such as a purchase, a job change, a hard conversation or a step in a relationship, give it a day, and ask God and one wise person before you move. Young people, enthusiasm is a gift, but learn the facts before you post, sign or commit. Leaders, when your team feels pressure to act now, ask what you do not yet know. Fast is not the same as faithful.

rel.note: Desire without knowledge and hasty feet are the folly that twists the way in 19:3.
Those who reject wisdom eat the fruit of their own way, the same self-made ruin 19:3 describes.
Instead of raging at God, the one who confesses and forsakes his sins finds mercy.
A man's own iniquities trap him, so the cause of his trouble lies in himself, not in God.

units.notes:
• *Twists* means to overturn or ruin; the KJV has "perverteth his way." The picture is a road wrecked by the traveler himself.
• *Frets* here is not mild worry but inward raging. The heart quarrels with God even when the mouth is silent.
• Bridges: "The malefactor blames the judge for his righteous sentence." A malefactor is a convicted criminal.
• Bridges on the man who thinks new circumstances would fix him: "he needs a change of heart, not a change of place."
• The first example in Scripture is Adam: "The woman whom You gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree" (Genesis 3:12). Compare James 1:13–14 and Lamentations 3:39–40.
units.summary: Folly wrecks the road, and then the fool blames the God who warned him.
units.principle: When our own folly brings trouble, the way forward is to own it before God, not to accuse Him of it.
units.insight: Blaming God is as old as the garden. Adam hid among the trees and pointed to "the woman whom You gave." Jonah ran from God's call, and later, when God spared Nineveh and took away his shade, he insisted, "It is right for me to be angry, even to death!" (Jonah 4:9). The same pattern lives in us. We neglect prayer, ignore counsel, overspend or overreach, and then ask why God let it happen. Lament is different. Job and the psalmists cried out in pain they had not caused, and God heard them. Jesus Himself prayed, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46), though He had never sinned. The prodigal son shows the way home from self-made ruin. He came to himself and said, "Father, I have sinned" (Luke 15:18). The Father runs to meet the one who owns his folly.
units.application: Think of a hardship you are angry about. Ask how much of it grew from your own choices, and confess that part plainly to God. If you counsel someone who rages at God over a crisis they caused, listen first, then gently help them trace cause and effect without crushing them. If your suffering is not your fault, you are free to lament. Bring your questions to Him, not away from Him.

rel.note: The same observation appears earlier: the poor man is hated even by his neighbor, while the rich has many friends.
A true friend loves at all times, unlike the friends who leave when wealth is gone.
Everyone is a friend to the gift-giver, which explains why wealth makes many friends.
The poor man's separation from his friend is drawn out in full: brothers and friends abandon him.
Proverbs condemns giving to the rich and oppressing the poor, so 19:4 describes favoritism without approving it.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "the poor is separated from his neighbour." The poor man is not only without a crowd; even the friend or neighbor he had pulls away.
• Compare 14:20: "The poor man is hated even by his own neighbor, But the rich has many friends."
• Henry on the rich man's crowd: they "really love what he has, or rather love themselves, hoping to get by him." To "get by him" means to gain something from him.
• Wealth can also win lasting friends when it relieves the needy. Jesus told His disciples, "make friends for yourselves by unrighteous mammon" (Luke 16:9).
• Compare 17:17, "A friend loves at all times," and James 2:1–9 on showing favoritism to the rich.
units.summary: Money draws a crowd, but only love stays when the money is gone.
units.principle: Friendship built on what a person has will leave when it is gone; true love attaches to the person, not the purse.
units.insight: The prodigal son had company while his money lasted. When it was spent and famine came, "no one gave him anything" (Luke 15:16). Many people learn after a job loss, a bankruptcy or a long illness who their friends really were. This verse does not sneer at the lonely poor man; it exposes the crowd. It also asks which kind of friend we are. Do we draw near to people who can help us and drift away from people who need us? Christ went the other way: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). For the poor believer there is a Friend who stays: "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). In Him the separated are brought near.
units.application: Call or visit someone who has lost income, status or health and has gone quiet; your presence matters more than your advice. Church leaders, notice who stops attending when they can no longer give or host, and go after them. If you have money or influence, test your friendships gently: who would still be there without it? If you are the one left alone, tell God and one trusted believer instead of withdrawing further.

rel.note: Truthful lips are established forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.
A true witness delivers souls, while a deceitful witness speaks lies that destroy them.
The warning returns almost word for word, adding that the liar shall perish.
A false witness who speaks lies is among the things the LORD hates, which is why he will not go unpunished.

units.notes:
• The law set the penalty: "then you shall do to him as he thought to have done to his brother" (Deuteronomy 19:19). The punishment matched the harm the witness intended.
• Ironside renders the second line as the one who breathes out lies, a picture of lying that comes as easily as breathing.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "This is a statement made in faith, for perjurers may escape human justice." Perjurers are people who lie under oath.
• Henry on where small lies lead: "Those that can swallow a false word debauch their consciences, so that a false oath will not choke them." To debauch is to corrupt.
• Compare 6:19; 14:5, 25; Exodus 20:16; Matthew 12:36.
units.summary: A lie can win in a courtroom, but it cannot win against God.
units.principle: Truth has the last word; every lie, especially one that harms another, will be answered before God.
units.insight: Jezebel arranged for two scoundrels to swear that Naboth had cursed God and the king, and an innocent man was stoned (1 Kings 21:10–13). The plan worked, but Elijah soon met Ahab in the stolen vineyard with God's sentence (1 Kings 21:17–19). Jesus Himself was condemned with the help of false witnesses whose testimonies did not even agree (Mark 14:56). He did not answer lie with lie but "committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). Christ's example is comfort for anyone who has been lied about. The verse is also a warning to our own hearts. False witness rarely begins in court. It starts with small untruths told for convenience, and the God who is truth sees both.
units.application: If you are asked to vouch for something you did not see, or to sign a statement you are unsure of, refuse until you know it is true. Employees, do not shade a report to protect yourself or a colleague. Parents, treat a child's "small" lie as a real matter, gently and firmly, because habits of truth are formed early. If someone has lied about you, keep telling the truth and leave the verdict with God.

rel.note: The rich has many friends, while the poor is hated even by his neighbor.
A man's gift makes room for him, so giving does open doors, though it cannot buy true friendship.
Wealth makes many friends, the same pull of money that draws everyone to the gift-giver.
When the gifts stop, the crowd vanishes: brothers and friends abandon the poor man.

units.notes:
• *Entreat the favor* joins a Hebrew verb meaning to soothe or entreat with the word for "face." It means seeking someone's goodwill by appealing to him in person. The same expression is used of prayer: "I entreated Your favor with my whole heart" (Psalm 119:58).
• *Nobility* translates nadib, a word that can describe someone noble in rank or noble and generous in character. The ESV and NASB read "a generous man," which ties the first line closely to the gift-giver of the second.
• Henry on the hangers-on around free spenders: they "will cry them up as long as it lasts, but will leave them when it is done." To "cry up" is to praise loudly.
• Compare Jude 16, people "flattering people to gain advantage," and 14:20; 18:16.
units.summary: Much of what passes for friendship is really a line at the gift table.
units.principle: Favor sought for profit is not friendship; love that wants only what another supplies vanishes when the supply ends.
units.insight: After Jesus fed the five thousand, crowds chased Him across the lake. He told them plainly, "you seek Me, not because you saw the signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled" (John 6:26). When His words grew hard, many "went back and walked with Him no more" (John 6:66). The same temptation lives in us. We can court people who have influence, and we can even seek God mainly for what He gives. Yet the Lord does not drive the needy away. He invites them to want Him, not only His gifts: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). Henry draws the lesson: "How earnest then should we be for the favour of God, which is far beyond that of any earthly prince." That favor cannot be bought. It is freely given in Christ to those who come with empty hands.
units.application: Leaders and donors, enjoy goodwill, but watch for people whose warmth rises and falls with your usefulness, and do not build decisions on their praise. Employees, serve your manager well without flattering for promotion. If you give generously, give without trying to buy loyalty, and let God be the one who rewards. In prayer this week, spend time thanking God for who He is before you ask Him for anything.

rel.note: The poor man is hated even by his own neighbor, the same rejection traced here through family and friends.
A brother is born for adversity, the very loyalty the poor man's brothers fail to show.
There is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, unlike the brothers and friends who go far away.
The poor man is separated from his friend; 19:7 shows that separation reaching even his brothers.
Everyone befriends the gift-giver, while the poor man who has nothing to give is abandoned.

units.notes:
