• The third line is difficult in Hebrew. The written text has a word meaning "not," while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has a word that sounds the same but means "to him." So translations differ: NKJV "they abandon him," ESV "but does not have them," NASB and AMP "they are gone," YLT "they are not!" Every reading leaves the poor man alone.
• Job knew this loss: "He has removed my brothers far from me... My relatives have failed" (Job 19:13–14).
• The law commands the opposite: "you shall open your hand wide to your brother, to your poor and your needy, in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11).
• Ironside sees the Lord in this verse: He "appeared on earth as one of the poor whom His brethren despised, and whose friends went far from Him."
• Compare 17:17, "a brother is born for adversity," the ideal this verse shows broken.
units.summary: Poverty can make a man a stranger to his own family.
units.principle: Poverty tests every relationship, and God calls His people to move toward the needy when others move away.
units.insight: Jesus knew this verse from the inside. His own brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5). At His arrest the disciples "all forsook Him and fled" (Mark 14:50). He called after His people with tender words: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37). So He understands the person whose phone has gone silent. Psalm 27:10 gives that person a promise: "When my father and my mother forsake me, Then the LORD will take care of me." The verse also turns a light on us. Is there a relative we avoid because their need is awkward, or a friend whose calls we let ring? Those whom Christ has gathered are sent to gather others.
units.application: Is there a brother, sister, cousin or old friend whose money troubles have made you keep your distance? Reach out this week, even if you cannot fix the problem. Families, talk together about how you will help a relative in need before a crisis comes. Churches, assign someone to stay in touch with members who fall on hard times. If you are the one calling after others, keep praying; God hears when people do not.

rel.note: The one who disdains instruction despises his own soul, the opposite of the one who gets wisdom.
He who heeds the word wisely will find good, as the one who keeps understanding does.
The father urges the son to take firm hold of instruction and keep it, the same move from getting to keeping.
Wisdom is the principal thing, so in all your getting, get understanding.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, and whoever sins against her wrongs his own soul.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV has "He who gets wisdom," the Hebrew words qoneh lev say literally "He who gets heart." The KJV margin notes that "wisdom" is literally "an heart," and the YLT reads "Whoso is getting heart is loving his soul."
• In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and judgment, not only of feeling, so to "get a heart" means to gain understanding. It is the opposite of the young man "devoid of understanding" in 7:7, literally one who lacks heart.
• Ironside calls the expression "a Hebraism, standing for sound judgment, or common sense." A Hebraism is a typically Hebrew way of speaking.
• Bridges on weighing Christ against the world: "It is like comparing pebbles with pearls, dust with diamonds, dross with gold."
• Compare 4:5–7; 8:35–36; 15:32, where the one who disdains instruction "despises his own soul."
units.summary: Refusing wisdom makes you your own worst enemy; getting it makes you your own best friend.
units.principle: Gaining and keeping wisdom is the truest care for oneself, because wisdom leads to life and refusing it harms one's own soul.
units.insight: Jesus asked, "For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?" (Mark 8:36). Many people love themselves in the wrong way, by feeding appetites that ruin them. This verse calls for the right kind of self-love. Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures from childhood, and Paul urged him to "continue in the things which you have learned" (2 Timothy 3:14–15). Getting was not enough; he had to keep. The man in Jesus' parable who found treasure hidden in a field sold all he had to buy that field (Matthew 13:44). In the light of the New Testament, the treasure of wisdom is found in Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). To pursue Him is not selfishness. It is life.
units.application: Treat time in Scripture and with wise counsel as care for your own soul, not as a duty that steals from your joy. Students and young adults, choose one book of wisdom to read slowly this month. If you learned something important in a sermon or a hard season, write it down and review it so you keep it. Parents, let your children see that you are still learning, not only teaching.

rel.note: Truthful lips are established forever, while a lying tongue lasts only a moment.
The worthless witness who scorns justice returns at the chapter's end, still facing judgment.
The first form of the warning says the liar will not escape; 19:9 adds that he shall perish.
A false witness shall perish, the same end announced here.

units.notes:
• Ironside: "The passage is not exactly a repetition of verse 5. There, we are reminded that the liar shall not escape. Here, we are told what his doom shall be."
• The twin warnings of 19:5 and 19:9 enclose verses 6–8, so the abandoned poor man of 19:7 stands inside a frame of judgment on liars.
• Compare 21:28, "A false witness shall perish," and Psalm 101:7, "He who tells lies shall not continue in my presence."
• Revelation 21:8 names "all liars" among those whose part is "in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone."
• Jesus called the devil "a liar and the father of it" (John 8:44), and called Himself "the truth" (John 14:6).
units.summary: The lie meant to destroy someone else ends by destroying the liar.
units.principle: God watches over the defenseless, and lies told against them end in the liar's ruin, whether soon or late.
units.insight: Ananias and Sapphira lied about a gift to look more generous than they were. Peter told Ananias, "You have not lied to men but to God" (Acts 5:4), and both husband and wife fell dead. Gehazi lied to Naaman to get silver and clothing, then lied to Elisha, and went out a leper (2 Kings 5:20–27). Most lies are not judged so quickly, but Scripture shows where the road leads. The deeper question is whose likeness we bear. Every lie takes after the father of lies, not after the One who is the truth. Yet the gospel offers more than a warning. Peter lied three times about knowing Jesus, and the risen Lord restored him with three questions of love (John 21:15–17). The Truth forgives liars who come to Him and makes them truthful.
units.application: Watch for the "small" lies you use to get out of trouble: the excuse to a boss, the shaded story to a spouse, the padded résumé. Confess one this week and set it right. If you supervise others, make it safe to tell the truth about mistakes, so no one feels a lie is the only way out. If someone has lied about you, write down the facts, speak the truth calmly and trust God to defend you.

rel.note: A wise servant rightly rules over a shameful son, so the problem in 19:10 is lack of wisdom, not low station.
Fine speech does not suit a fool, much less lying lips a prince, the same lesser-to-greater pattern.
Honor is not fitting for a fool, just as luxury is not.
A servant who reigns and a fool filled with food are named among the things the earth cannot bear.

units.notes:
• *Luxury* is delight, comfort and pleasant living; the KJV reads "Delight is not seemly for a fool." "Not fitting" means out of place, as honor is not fitting for a fool in 26:1.
• "Much less" argues from the lesser to the greater: if comfort does not suit a fool, rule over princes suits an unprepared servant even less.
• Proverbs 30:21–22 names "a servant when he reigns" and "a fool when he is filled with food" among the things under which the earth "cannot bear up."
• On a servant suddenly raised to rule, Bridges writes: "seldom is God's order reversed without anarchy and confusion." By "God's order" he means the settled order of society. In the same place he names Joseph as the great exception (Genesis 41:39–45).
• Compare 17:7 and Ecclesiastes 10:6–7, where folly is set in great dignity and servants ride on horses while princes walk.
units.summary: Prosperity and power are magnifying glasses: they enlarge whatever character is already there.
units.principle: Comfort and authority given to people without wisdom do harm; character must be ready before blessing or power arrives.
units.insight: Haman was set above all the princes of Persia, and power exposed his pride and cruelty until it destroyed him (Esther 3:1–2; 7:10). Saul began "little in your own eyes," Samuel reminded him, but the throne revealed a heart that would not obey (1 Samuel 15:17–23). By contrast, God prepared Joseph in a pit, a household and a prison before raising him over Egypt (Genesis 41:39–41). The verse asks what our comforts and positions are revealing. Do we want promotion, influence or ease more than the character to carry them? The gospel turns the world's ladder upside down. Christ took "the form of a bondservant," and the Father highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:7–9). He taught that whoever desires to be great must be a servant (Matthew 20:26). Greatness in His kingdom grows from humility, not from grasping.
units.application: Before you seek a promotion, a ministry platform or a bigger budget, ask whether your character is ready for it. Parents, do not hand a teenager freedom or money faster than they show the wisdom to use it. Church and business leaders, promote people for proven faithfulness, not only for talent or charm. If comfort has come to you, notice whether it is making you more thankful or more careless.

rel.note: He who is slow to wrath has great understanding, the same link between insight and patience.
The one slow to anger is better than the mighty, so patience is strength, not weakness.
He who covers a transgression seeks love, as the one who overlooks it finds glory.
Discretion that slows anger matters most in a ruler, whose wrath roars like a lion.
The man of great wrath brings repeated punishment on himself, the opposite of the man with a long fuse.

units.notes:
• *Slow to anger* is literally "makes his anger long." The KJV reads "deferreth his anger": discretion puts time between the provocation and the response.
• *Overlook* is literally "pass over." Micah uses the same verb with the same word for "transgression" when he praises God for "Pardoning iniquity And passing over the transgression" (Micah 7:18). The person who overlooks an offense acts as Scripture says God acts.
• *Discretion* comes from the same Hebrew root as "prudent" in 19:14, so the wise wife of that verse has the same insight this verse praises.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "The manlier any man is, the milder and readier to pass by an offence."
• Compare 12:16; 14:29; 16:32; 17:9; Colossians 3:13.
units.summary: The strongest person in the room is the one who can let an insult pass.
units.principle: Wisdom shows itself in patience and in letting personal wrongs go, while still confronting harm that must be corrected.
units.insight: Joseph had every reason to repay his brothers, yet he wept over them and said, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). David spared Saul in the cave and would not lift his hand against him (1 Samuel 24:4–7). Even Esau ran to embrace the brother who had cheated him (Genesis 33:4). These stories expose how much of our anger is wounded pride. We replay slights, rehearse comebacks and call it justice. Bridges calls this patience "likeness to God," and above all it is likeness to Christ, "who, when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). On the cross He prayed for those who crucified Him (Luke 23:34). Because God has passed over our great debt in Christ, we can pass over the small debts others owe us (Matthew 18:21–35).
units.application: When a coworker's comment stings or a family member forgets something important, wait before you respond; sleep on it if you can. Spouses, choose to drop a minor offense instead of keeping score. Leaders, do not punish every slight against your authority. But if someone is being harmed, or a pattern of sin needs correcting, overlooking is not the answer. Speak up, get help, and follow Matthew 18:15.

rel.note: The king's wrath is like messengers of death, but his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain.
The discretion that makes a man slow to anger is what a ruler with a lion's roar most needs.
The king's wrath is again compared to a lion's roar, and provoking it endangers one's life.
Patient forbearance and a gentle tongue persuade a ruler, the wise way to live under authority.

units.notes:
• Proverbs describes royal favor with a similar picture of moisture: "his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain" (16:15). Compare 16:14 and 20:2.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik, on the lion: "There is nothing more dreadful than the roaring of this tyrant of the forest."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "This proverb would advise the king's subjects to use tact and the king to cultivate kindness."
• Dew is a scriptural picture of quiet, life-giving blessing: "I will be like the dew to Israel" (Hosea 14:5). Compare Psalm 72:6 and 2 Samuel 23:3–4.
• Pharaoh showed both royal wrath and royal favor on one day: he restored his chief butler and hanged his chief baker (Genesis 40:20–22).
units.summary: The same throne can sound like a lion's roar or fall like morning dew.
units.principle: Authority magnifies a person's moods: anger from above wounds deeply and kindness from above gives life, so rulers must govern their temper and subjects must act wisely.
units.insight: Nehemiah knew how much rested on a king's face. When Artaxerxes noticed his sadness he became "dreadfully afraid," yet he prayed and spoke, and the king's favor opened the way to rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1–8). Esther risked the king's anger to plead for her people and found the golden scepter held out to her (Esther 5:2). The verse also invites a comparison with a greater King. Christ is "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5), and the psalm of the righteous King says, "He shall come down like rain upon the grass before mowing" (Psalm 72:6). His favor is not fickle as an earthly ruler's can be. And the verse searches all of us who hold any authority. A parent's anger or a manager's praise carries more weight than they realize.
units.application: If you lead a team, a classroom or a household, remember that your anger lands harder than you think and your encouragement refreshes more than you know; spend more of your words on the second. Employees, show respect to those over you, and when you must raise a hard matter, choose your words and timing with care, as Nehemiah did. Pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), whether they roar or refresh.

rel.note: A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to his mother.
The prudent wife, a gift from the LORD, stands beside the contentious one.
The son who brings shame on his parents returns later in the chapter in his worst form.
A corner of the housetop is better than a house shared with constant strife.
A contentious woman is again compared to a continual dripping on a rainy day.

units.notes:
• *Ruin* means calamity or disaster; the KJV has "the calamity of his father." Compare 17:25, "A foolish son is a grief to his father."
• The same image returns in 27:15: "A continual dripping on a very rainy day And a contentious woman are alike." Compare 21:9 and 25:24.
• Henry compares the drip to living in "a house so much out of repair that it rains in and a man cannot lie dry in it."
• Compare 17:21, "the father of a fool has no joy," and 10:1, where the foolish son grieves his mother too.
units.summary: Homes are seldom destroyed by one storm; they are worn away by a steady drip.
units.principle: The peace of a home is built or eroded by daily patterns, and a child's folly or constant quarreling can wear a family down over time.
units.insight: Esau's marriages to Hittite women "were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35), and David wept for Absalom, the son who had tried to take his throne: "O my son Absalom" (2 Samuel 18:33). Scripture lets such parents grieve without making every grieving parent guilty. The second line names a slower grief: the daily drip of criticism, complaint and the need to win every argument. Each of us should ask whether we are the leak in our own home. The gospel speaks to both pains. The LORD Himself said, "I have nourished and brought up children, And they have rebelled against Me" (Isaiah 1:2), and He still welcomes prodigals home. Christ, who "will not quarrel nor cry out" (Matthew 12:19), gives His Spirit, whose fruit is peace and gentleness (Galatians 5:22–23).
units.application: Spouses, listen to how you speak at home this week. If criticism, complaint or sarcasm has become a steady drip, name it, ask forgiveness, and replace one critical comment each day with thanks. Parents grieving a wayward son or daughter, keep praying and keep the door open, and do not carry blame that is not yours. Friends and church members, come alongside struggling families instead of judging them.

rel.note: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, showing why a prudent wife is a gift beyond riches.
A good man leaves an inheritance, the kind of gift fathers can pass down, unlike a prudent wife.
He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD.
The contentious wife's continual dripping stands opposite the prudent wife who comes from the LORD.
The virtuous wife's worth is far above rubies, a fuller portrait of the gift this verse names.

units.notes:
• *Prudent* describes insight and good sense. It comes from the same Hebrew root as the "discretion" of 19:11 that makes a man slow to anger, so the wife of 19:14 has the same wise insight.
• Compare 18:22, "He who finds a wife finds a good thing, And obtains favor from the LORD," and 31:10, "Who can find a virtuous wife?"
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Nature makes a woman, election a wife; but to be prudent, wise, and virtuous is of the Lord." By "election" he means a man's choice.
• Rebekah's story shows God's hand in a marriage. Abraham's servant prayed for success, and Laban and Bethuel answered, "The thing comes from the LORD" (Genesis 24:12, 50).
units.summary: A father can leave you a house, but only God can give you a wise spouse.
units.principle: Possessions can be passed down by people, but godly character in a spouse is a gift that comes from the LORD.
units.insight: Ruth was a Moabite widow with nothing to inherit, yet God led her to Boaz's field, and Boaz told her, "all the people of my town know that you are a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:11). Stories like hers teach us to receive a wise spouse with thanks rather than take credit for choosing well. Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "As a result, when a man has a competent wife, he praises God, not himself." The verse also checks what we value. Families often plan carefully for property and leave marriage to chance or attraction. And marriage itself points beyond itself. Paul says the union of husband and wife speaks of "Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32), whom Christ loved and gave Himself for. Every wise and faithful spouse is a gift that reflects that greater love.
units.application: Single adults, pray for a spouse with prudence and the fear of the LORD, and give that more weight than looks, money or family status. Parents, teach your children to value character in a future spouse above any inheritance. Married couples, thank God this week, aloud and in front of your spouse, for a specific way your husband or wife shows wisdom. If your marriage is hard, do not conclude God made a mistake; seek His help and wise counsel.

rel.note: The diligent hand and the son who gathers in summer prosper, unlike the slack soul who goes hungry.
Later in the chapter the lazy man is too slack even to lift food from the bowl to his mouth.
Loving sleep leads to poverty, while open eyes are satisfied with bread.
A little sleep and folding of the hands bring poverty like a prowler, the same road from sleep to want.

units.notes:
• *Deep sleep* translates tardemah, a heavy sleep from which a person is not easily roused. It is the word used when "the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam" (Genesis 2:21). The comparison concerns how deep the sleep is, not where it comes from.
• *Idle person* is literally "a slack soul"; the KJV reads "an idle soul shall suffer hunger." The slackness is in the will before it shows in the hands.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Laziness plunges him into a state of being so deep in sleep that he is totally unconscious of his situation."
• Ironside separates rest from idleness: "Needed rest is, of course, very right and proper." Jesus Himself told His tired disciples to "rest a while" (Mark 6:31).
• Compare 6:9–11; 10:4–5; 20:13; 24:33–34.
units.summary: Laziness begins as a little rest and ends at an empty table.
units.principle: Laziness is not harmless rest; settled unwillingness to work dulls a person and leads to want.
units.insight: Samson slept on Delilah's knees while his strength was taken from him (Judges 16:19). In Gethsemane the disciples slept while Jesus prayed, and He asked, "What! Could you not watch with Me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40). Laziness of soul works the same way. We drift into a deep sleep about prayer, Scripture or the needs around us, and we do not notice how hungry we have become. Paul's call fits: "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14). Grace does not excuse sloth; it wakes us up. Yet Christ knows the difference between the sluggard and the exhausted. He invites the weary to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28), and the LORD fed worn-out Elijah under the broom tree before sending him on (1 Kings 19:5–8).
units.application: Name one task you keep putting off at work, at home or in your walk with God, and do the first fifteen minutes of it today. Students, set a start time and keep it rather than waiting to feel like it. Parents, give children real responsibilities and let them taste the results. But if you are worn out by illness, grief or caring for others, this verse is not aimed at you. Rest is not laziness, and asking for help is wise.

rel.note: He who despises the word will be destroyed, but he who fears the commandment will be rewarded.
He who hates correction will die, the end of the one careless of his ways.
He who keeps his way preserves his soul, the same keeping that guards life.
The father's own teacher said, Keep my commands, and live.

units.notes:
• The repeated "keeps" carries the point: the one who keeps the commandment is himself kept. Compare 16:17, "He who keeps his way preserves his soul."
• *Careless* translates a word meaning to despise or hold in contempt. The KJV and ESV read "despises his ways," which shows that indifference is a form of contempt.
• Ironside's text reads "he that despiseth His ways," taking the ways as the LORD's. The NKJV takes them as the man's own, and either way the man is contemptuous of how he should walk.
• Henry on those who drift through life: "right or wrong, it is all one to them."
• Compare 4:4; 13:13; 15:10; John 14:15.
units.summary: The one who keeps God's word finds that God's word keeps him.
units.principle: Attention to God's instruction protects life, while indifference to the direction of one's life leads toward death.
units.insight: Solomon told Shimei he would live as long as he stayed in Jerusalem. Years later Shimei grew careless, went to Gath after two runaway servants, and died for it (1 Kings 2:36–46). Shimei's death took no rebellion, only indifference to a clear command. Many lives drift the same way. No one decides to despise God; we simply stop paying attention to where our habits are taking us. Jesus warned of the word choked by "the cares of this world" (Mark 4:19). Keeping the commandment is not a way of earning life. Christ kept the law perfectly for us, and He gives His Spirit so that we can keep His word from the heart: "If you love Me, keep My commandments" (John 14:15). The verse leaves a simple question: Do I care where my ways are going?
units.application: Take ten minutes this week to look at where your habits are heading: your spending, your screen time, your friendships, your prayer life. Ask, "If nothing changes, where will this be in five years?" Young adults, choose one command of Scripture you have been ignoring and begin to obey it. Small-group leaders, ask one another not only what you believe but how you are walking.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, while mercy to the needy honors Him.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry himself and not be heard.
The generous eye that gives bread to the poor will be blessed.
He who gives to the poor will not lack, the same assurance that God sees and repays.

units.notes:
• *Has pity* translates a verb meaning to be gracious or to show favor, a word often used of God's own graciousness. The one who pities the poor reflects the character of God.
• Compare 14:31: "He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker, But he who honors Him has mercy on the needy." Harm to the poor reaches God, and so does kindness.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "O what a word is this! God makes himself debtor for every thing that is given to the poor!"
• Henry: "Those that have not a penny for the poor, yet may have pity for them." Compassion begins in the heart, even where money is lacking.
• Compare 22:9; 28:27; Deuteronomy 15:10; Luke 6:38.
units.summary: Every gift to the poor is a loan that God Himself has signed for.
units.principle: God counts mercy to the needy as done to Himself, and no such kindness goes unrewarded, though He repays in His own way and time.
units.insight: The widow of Zarephath gave her last handful of flour to a hungry prophet, and "The bin of flour was not used up, nor did the jar of oil run dry" (1 Kings 17:16). Boaz let Ruth glean extra grain, and God wove that kindness into the line of David and of Christ (Ruth 2:15–16; 4:17). Yet the deepest repayment is not always material. Jesus said that when we give to those who cannot repay us, "you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the just" (Luke 14:14). The verse exposes our hearts at a tender point. We often give where we can see a return; God asks us to give where only He sees. And He gave first. He "did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). We lend to the Lord out of what He has already given.
units.application: Give this week to someone in need who cannot pay you back: a meal for a struggling family, groceries for a neighbor, a gift through your church's benevolence fund. Do it quietly. Business owners, look for ways to hire, pay or help people who are often overlooked. Families, involve your children in giving so they learn that kindness to the poor is service to God. Do not give expecting a financial return; give because God sees.

rel.note: The parent who loves a child disciplines him promptly, the same urgency as while there is hope.
After a word to parents comes a word to the son: listen to counsel and receive instruction.
Correcting a son brings rest and delight, the good that timely discipline aims at.
The LORD corrects those He loves, the pattern every earthly parent's discipline should follow.

units.notes:
• Translations of the second line vary widely. NKJV: "do not set your heart on his destruction"; ESV: "do not set your heart on putting him to death"; NASB (1995): "do not desire his death." The KJV reads "let not thy soul spare for his crying," with "to his destruction" or "to cause him to die" in its margin. The Hebrew can be read as a warning against neglect or against excess.
• Ironside: "Brutal punishments, even to endangering the life of the one chastised, are very wrong, and opposed to the Spirit of God."
• Compare 13:24, "he who loves him disciplines him promptly," and 29:17, "Correct your son, and he will give you rest."
• The LORD is the model parent: "whom the LORD loves He corrects" (3:12), and His discipline yields "the peaceable fruit of righteousness" (Hebrews 12:11).
• Compare Colossians 3:21, "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged."
units.summary: Correct while the clay is still soft, and never with a hand that wants to crush.
units.principle: Timely, loving correction is a parent's work of hope, always aimed at a child's life and good, never at harm.
units.insight: Eli knew his sons were sinning, yet the LORD said "he did not restrain them" (1 Samuel 3:13). David "had not rebuked" Adonijah "at any time" (1 Kings 1:6), and that son later reached for the throne. Saul shows the opposite failure: in a rage he hurled a spear at his own son Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:30–33). Both neglect and fury fail a child. The verse searches parents' hearts. Are we avoiding conflict because we are tired or want to be liked? Are we correcting mainly to relieve our own frustration? Our heavenly Father shows the better way. He corrects because He loves, and never to destroy (Hebrews 12:5–11). For parents who look back with regret, He is "the Father of mercies" (2 Corinthians 1:3), able to restore both parents and children.
units.application: Parents of young children, deal with patterns early and calmly rather than waiting for them to harden; be consistent more than severe. Parents of teenagers, keep correcting, but more by conversation, consequences and your own example. If you discipline in anger, stop, step away and come back calm, and apologize to your child when you get it wrong. If correction in a home is crossing into harm or abuse, get help from a pastor or a professional now.

rel.note: A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, bringing on himself the punishment 19:19 describes.
Discretion makes a man slow to anger and able to overlook offenses, the opposite of great wrath.
Close ties with an angry man can teach his ways and snare one's own soul, a reason for wise boundaries.
The angry man stirs up strife and abounds in transgression, the trouble that keeps needing rescue.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin notes that "do it again" is literally "add," and the YLT reads "yet again thou dost add." Each rescue adds another round to the cycle.
• In the first line the written Hebrew has a rare word meaning harsh or rough, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts is the common word for "great." The NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV follow the marginal reading, "great wrath"; either way the man's anger is out of control.
• Ironside: "He should be left to himself till he learns by punishment what he would not receive otherwise."
• Compare 14:17; 22:24–25; 29:22; Galatians 5:22–23.
units.summary: Rescuing a hothead without a changed heart only schedules the next rescue.
units.principle: Shielding an angry person from the consequences of his temper does not cure him; real change comes from a changed heart, and wise love sometimes lets consequences teach.
units.insight: Jonathan pleaded with his father Saul for David, and Saul swore to spare him, but before long his rage returned and he hurled a spear at David (1 Samuel 19:4–10). Samuel grieved over Saul until the LORD asked, "How long will you mourn for Saul?" (1 Samuel 16:1). Some of us are the rescuers. We pay the fines, smooth over the outbursts, make excuses, and call it love. Others of us are the man of wrath, counting on others to clean up after our temper. Both need the gospel. Jesus says, "learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29). Bridges trusts God for "the moulding of the man of great wrath into his image of meekness, gentleness, and love." What years of rescue cannot do, the Spirit of Christ can.
units.application: If you keep covering for someone's temper, whether a spouse, an adult child or a coworker, stop paying the price for them, and tell them kindly why. Family members, agree together on boundaries instead of each person quietly rescuing. If you are the one with the temper, ask a trusted friend to hold you accountable and get help. Where there is danger or abuse, do not wait: protect yourself and others, and seek help.

rel.note: He who heeds counsel is wise, while the fool is right in his own eyes.
The parent is told to chasten while there is hope; here the son is told to receive that instruction.
Receive counsel when you plan, but remember that the LORD's counsel is the one that stands.
The son who stops listening to instruction strays from knowledge, the opposite path.
A wise man will hear and increase learning, the teachability this verse calls for.

units.notes:
• *Counsel* is advice for decisions; *instruction* includes teaching and correction. The KJV reads "that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end."
• Henry: those who would be wise at the end "must be willing to be taught and ruled, willing to be advised and reproved, when they are young."
• Henry again: "Those that would be stored in winter must gather in summer." A well-supplied old age is gathered in youth.
• Solomon's later years are the warning: "when Solomon was old... his heart was not loyal to the LORD his God" (1 Kings 11:4).
• Compare 1:5; 12:15; 13:20; 15:22.
units.summary: The wise old man of tomorrow is the teachable young man of today.
units.principle: Teachability now shapes wisdom later; the person who keeps receiving counsel will be wise at the end of life.
units.insight: Rehoboam heard wise counsel from the older men who had served his father, rejected it for the advice of his peers, and the kingdom split in a day (1 Kings 12:6–16). Timothy received faith and instruction from his grandmother Lois, his mother Eunice and the apostle Paul, and he became a faithful pastor (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:14–15). Our hearts resist counsel because pride wants to be the expert on its own life. The verse asks whom we are listening to and whether we can still be corrected. Even old age is no guarantee, as Solomon's later years show. Jesus Himself, as a boy, sat among the teachers, "both listening to them and asking them questions," and He "increased in wisdom" (Luke 2:46, 52). If the Son of God listened and grew, we can too.
units.application: Young adults, find one older believer and ask for regular counsel about work, money or relationships, and then act on what you hear. Before your next major decision, ask two wise people what they see that you do not. Middle-aged and older readers, keep a teachable spirit: join a study, read a challenging book, ask your grown children what they wish you would hear. A wise old age is built one listening day at a time.

rel.note: The heart prepares, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD, the same pairing of human plans and divine rule.
A man's heart plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps.
Seeking human counsel is wise, and this verse sets it under the LORD's counsel, which has the final word.
A man's steps are of the LORD, so even his best plans depend on God.
No wisdom, understanding or counsel can stand against the LORD.

units.notes:
• *Plans* (KJV "devices") are the many intentions and schemes of the heart; *counsel* is the settled purpose of the LORD. The contrast is many against one.
• Bridges: "Man's devices are many; God's counsel is like himself—Unity." He means that God's purpose is single and undivided, as God Himself is one.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "The one thing in the heart that may be depended upon is the counsel or guidance of Jehovah."
• Compare 16:1, 9; 21:30; Psalm 33:11, "The counsel of the LORD stands forever"; James 4:13–15.
units.summary: We write our plans in pencil; the LORD's counsel is written in stone.
units.principle: Human plans are many and changeable, but the LORD's purpose stands; the wise plan humbly and rest in His counsel.
units.insight: Joseph's brothers sold him to be rid of a dreamer, and God used their scheme to keep many people alive (Genesis 45:5–8). The rulers of Jerusalem and Rome plotted against Jesus, yet they did "whatever Your hand and Your purpose determined before to be done" (Acts 4:28). The cross, the darkest human plan, became the place where God's counsel of salvation stood. God's sure counsel frees us from two errors. We need not fear that our failures or other people's schemes can overturn God's purpose for His people. And we must not cling to our own plans as though they were final. "If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that" (James 4:15). The heart that rests in God's counsel can plan carefully and still hold its plans loosely.
units.application: Write down your plans for the coming year, then pray over each one, "If the Lord wills." Business owners and leaders, plan diligently, but hold budgets and strategies with open hands when God closes a door. If a plan has collapsed, such as a job, a move or a relationship, tell God your disappointment and ask Him to show you His purpose in it. Parents, teach your children both to make plans and to pray over them.

rel.note: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, while those who deal truthfully are His delight.
The chapter opened by setting the poor man of integrity above the fool with twisted lips.
Many proclaim their own goodness, but a faithful man is hard to find, which is why loyal love is so desired.
Mercy and truth are to be bound around the neck, the two qualities 19:22 sets above wealth.

units.notes:
• *Kindness* translates chesed, loyal and faithful love that keeps its commitments. The ESV renders it "steadfast love."
• The first line can also be read as saying that a man's kindness is what makes him desirable, as the KJV takes it: "The desire of a man is his kindness." The NASB reads it the same way, and the sense is close either way.
• Henry: "A poor man, who wishes you well, but can promise you nothing, because he has nothing to be kind with, is better than a liar."
• Compare 3:3; 20:6, "But who can find a faithful man?"; 1 Corinthians 13:4.
units.summary: People long for loyal love, and an honest poor man gives more of it than a rich liar.
units.principle: Faithful love is what people most need from one another, and it is worth more than any wealth gained or kept by falsehood.
units.insight: Jesus watched a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury and said she had given more than all the rich (Mark 12:41–44). Peter and John had no silver or gold for the lame man at the temple gate, but they gave him what they had in the name of Jesus (Acts 3:6). Faithful love does not require wealth. Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "It is the comfort of poverty, that our affections are valued, not our presents." Yet the verse also searches those who promise much and do little. How often do we offer help we never mean to give, or say "I'll pray for you" and forget? Christ is the faithful One in whom "all the promises of God" are "Yes" and "Amen" (2 Corinthians 1:20). He keeps His word, and He makes His people keep theirs.
units.application: Do not promise help you have no intention of giving; a kind "I can't, but I will pray for you," followed by real prayer, is better than an empty "Sure." If money is tight, give what you can: time, a listening ear, a meal, a ride. Employers and leaders, value staff who keep their word over those who only impress. Parents, show your children that loyalty to friends and family matters more than anything anyone owns.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD prolongs days, another statement of the life it tends toward, read as a general pattern.
The fear of the LORD is strong confidence, a refuge and a fountain of life.
A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, the satisfaction 19:23 describes.
Whoever listens to Wisdom will dwell safely and be secure, without fear of evil.

units.notes:
• *Abide* translates a verb meaning to lodge or spend the night. The picture is a person lying down at night satisfied and safe.
• Henry quotes a Latin saying on this verse and translates it: "He shall not go supperless to bed." In other words, he will not lie down hungry.
• This verse belongs with 14:26–27, where the fear of the LORD is "strong confidence" and "a fountain of life." Compare Psalm 34:9, "There is no want to those who fear Him."
• Compare Psalm 91, the security of the one "who dwells in the secret place of the Most High."
• Compare 1:33; 10:27; 15:16; Romans 8:28.
units.summary: Reverence for God is not a cage of dread but a house where the soul can sleep in peace.
units.principle: A right view of God leads to life and settled rest; it does not exempt anyone from suffering, but it ensures that evil never has the final word.
units.insight: Joseph feared God in Potiphar's house and still went to prison, yet "the LORD was with Joseph" there (Genesis 39:21). Daniel feared God more than the king and was thrown to the lions, yet he could say, "My God sent His angel and shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22). The fear of the LORD did not keep them from trouble; it kept them in God through trouble. Many of us lie awake because we fear people, money or the future more than we fear God. Leighton, quoted by Bridges, puts it in six words: "He that so fears, fears not." When God is seen rightly, other fears shrink. Paul suffered prison, shipwreck and beatings, yet he was sure that nothing "shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39).
units.application: Tonight, before you sleep, name the fears that keep you awake and hand each one to God in prayer. If you are going through sickness or loss, do not read this verse as a verdict that you lack faith; it promises God's keeping, not a trouble-free life. Parents, teach your children awe and trust together, never dread alone. Counselors and friends, use this verse to comfort the suffering, never to blame them.

rel.note: The lazy man will not roast what he hunted, another failure to finish what is already within reach.
Laziness casts a person into deep sleep and hunger; here the hunger comes with food already in hand.
The lazy man's desire kills him because his hands refuse to labor.
The same picture returns: it wearies the lazy man to bring his hand back to his mouth.

units.notes:
• Proverbs 26:15 repeats the first line with a new ending: "It wearies him to bring it back to his mouth."
• The KJV reads "hideth his hand in his bosom," but modern versions, like the NKJV, read the Hebrew word as a bowl or dish, its usual meaning. Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The same word in 2 Kings 21:13 leaves no doubt of its meaning." There the LORD says He will wipe Jerusalem "as one wipes a dish."
• Compare 12:27, where the lazy man "does not roast what he took in hunting," and 13:4; 21:25.
units.summary: The lazy man has dinner in his hand and still goes hungry.
units.principle: Laziness can waste even what is already provided; the lazy fail not for lack of opportunity but for lack of will to finish.
units.insight: Many of us sit with the bowl already in our hands. We own Bibles we do not open, belong to churches whose fellowship we do not use, and know truths we never put into practice. Ironside makes the application: "The word of God is such a dish." The writer of Hebrews rebuked believers who had become "dull of hearing" and still needed milk when they ought to have been teachers (Hebrews 5:11–12). Spiritual hunger often comes not from God withholding food but from our refusing to lift the hand. Yet God does not stand over us with a sneer. He invites, "Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, And let your soul delight itself in abundance" (Isaiah 55:2). Christ, the bread of life, has done the hard work (John 6:35). Our part is to come, receive and eat.
units.application: Pick one thing you have already started but not finished: a Bible reading plan, a course, a home repair, an apology. Finish the last small step this week. Students, turn in the assignment that is ninety percent done. Small-group members, act on one thing you have learned instead of only discussing it. If you lead or parent others, help them break big tasks into small steps, and praise them when they finish something, not only when they start.

rel.note: A rebuke reaches a wise man more deeply than a hundred blows reach a fool.
The chapter ends by returning to the scoffer, for whom judgments are prepared.
When the scoffer is punished the simple is made wise, and the wise receive knowledge by instruction.
Correcting a scoffer brings shame, but instructing a wise man makes him wiser, the same three-way contrast.

units.notes:
• *Become wary* translates a verb meaning to become shrewd or prudent. It is related to the word for prudence that the book promises to give "to the simple" (1:4).
• Compare 21:11, "When the scoffer is punished, the simple is made wise," and 17:10, "Rebuke is more effective for a wise man Than a hundred blows on a fool."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik, on the scoffer: "Smite him never so much, there is no beating any wit into him." "Never so much" means however much.
• Henry on the scoffer's punishment: "If it cure not the infected, it may prevent the spreading of the infection."
• Compare 9:7–9 and 1 Timothy 5:20, "Those who are sinning rebuke in the presence of all, that the rest also may fear."
units.summary: The wise learn from a word, the simple from watching, and the scoffer not even from blows.
units.principle: Correction reaches people differently: the wise learn from a word, the simple from example, and the scoffer resists even blows, so it is wise to stay teachable.
units.insight: Pharaoh was struck by plague after plague and only hardened his heart (Exodus 8:15). Jethro heard what the LORD had done to Pharaoh and said, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods" (Exodus 18:11). David needed only Nathan's word, "You are the man!" and he confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). The verse asks each of us which one we are. Does it take a crisis to get our attention, or can a friend's gentle word turn us? God's correction is love, not rejection. The risen Christ says, "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. Therefore be zealous and repent" (Revelation 3:19). Blessed is the person who can be reached by a word.
units.application: When someone corrects you this week, whether a spouse, a boss or a friend, thank them before you defend yourself, and ask what you can learn. Parents and teachers, use consequences to teach, not to shame, and explain the lesson so that others learn too. Leaders who must address public wrongdoing, do it fairly and without humiliation. Young people, learn from the mistakes you see others pay for instead of repeating them.

rel.note: A foolish son is the ruin of his father, the grief this verse shows at its worst.
The one who curses his father or mother will have his lamp put out in deep darkness.
The son is told to listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old.
Whoever robs his father or mother and calls it no transgression is a companion to a destroyer.
The eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother comes to a terrible end.

units.notes:
• *Mistreats* translates a verb meaning to assault, plunder or devastate. The KJV has "wasteth his father," and Ironside "ruineth his father."
• Henry pictures a son who "wastes his estate which he should have to support him in his old age, wastes his spirits, and breaks his heart."
• Compare 28:24, the one who robs his father or mother "And says, 'It is no transgression'"; 20:20; 30:17.
• Jesus condemned those who used a religious vow as an excuse not to support their parents (Mark 7:10–13).
units.summary: His parents carried him when he was weak; he turns on them when they are weak.
units.principle: Honor for parents is tested when they are weak, and turning on them is a betrayal that brings shame and stands under God's judgment.
units.insight: Absalom plotted to seize his father's kingdom and drove David out of Jerusalem, and David climbed the Mount of Olives weeping (2 Samuel 15:13–14, 30). The prodigal son demanded his inheritance while his father still lived (Luke 15:12). This verse is not only about crimes that make the news. Adult children can plunder parents slowly: draining their money, neglecting them in old age, or pushing a widowed mother out of decisions about her own life. Jesus shows the opposite. While dying on the cross, He made sure His mother was cared for and entrusted her to John (John 19:26–27). For parents wronged by their children, God sees; He is "A father of the fatherless, a defender of widows" (Psalm 68:5). For children who have dishonored their parents, the way back begins with repentance and honor shown now.
units.application: Adult children, ask how your aging parents are really doing with money, health and loneliness. Visit, call and include them in decisions about their own lives. If you handle a parent's finances, keep careful, open records. Siblings, share the load rather than leaving it to one. Church leaders, watch for elderly members being taken advantage of by family, and step in. Parents who have been mistreated, tell someone you trust; you do not have to carry it alone.

rel.note: He who keeps instruction is in the way of life, but he who refuses correction goes astray.
The son who listens to counsel becomes wise in his latter days; the one who stops listening strays.
The father urges the son to take firm hold of instruction and not let go, the opposite of ceasing to listen.
The ruined man laments that he hated instruction and would not obey his teachers.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads the verse differently: "Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge," making it a warning against false teaching. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and NIV read it as a warning about what happens when a son stops listening to instruction.
• On the KJV reading, Ironside warns: "You cannot afford to trifle with unholy doctrine."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Without constant attention to wisdom depraved human beings unconsciously stray from it." "Depraved" means corrupted by sin.
• Compare 10:17, "he who refuses correction goes astray," and Hebrews 2:1, "we must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away."
units.summary: Drifting from God needs no rebellion; it only needs you to stop listening.
units.principle: Wisdom must be kept by continued listening; the person who stops hearing instruction begins to drift from what he knows.
units.insight: Solomon wrote many of these sayings, yet in his old age he stopped heeding them, and his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:4–9). Demas once worked beside Paul, but Paul later wrote, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Most spiritual decline is quiet. We miss a week of worship, then a month of prayer, and one day we find ourselves far from what we once knew. The father's warning is love, not threat. Christ the Good Shepherd says, "My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me" (John 10:27). Hearing and following go together. If you have drifted, His voice is still calling you home.
units.application: Notice where your listening has thinned: Sunday worship, personal Bible reading, honest friends who speak into your life. Restore one of them this week before the drift goes further. Parents of teenagers and college students, keep the conversation open even when they seem to have stopped listening, and ask what they are hearing elsewhere. When you weigh any teaching, test it by Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11).

rel.note: Judgments are prepared for those who scorn justice and feed on evil.
The false witness who will not go unpunished reappears here as the worthless witness who scorns justice.
The wicked eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence, as this mouth devours iniquity.
A worthless person, a wicked man, walks with a perverse mouth, the same corrupt character.

units.notes:
• *Disreputable witness* is literally "a witness of Belial," as the KJV margin notes. Belial means worthlessness, and the expression describes a worthless or wicked person whose testimony cannot be trusted.
• The men who gave false testimony against Naboth are called by the same Hebrew word, Belial (1 Kings 21:10, 13); the NKJV there calls them "scoundrels."
• *Devours* translates a verb meaning to swallow or gulp down; the ESV keeps "devours," and the YLT reads "swalloweth." The NASB and AMP read the second line "spreads iniquity," taking the verb in a different sense.
• Ironside: "His mouth devours iniquity. It is his food; he lives upon it."
• Compare 4:17, "they eat the bread of wickedness"; 6:12; Job 15:16, man "Who drinks iniquity like water!"
units.summary: The worthless witness laughs at justice and eats wrongdoing like bread.
units.principle: Contempt for justice and an appetite for wrongdoing grow together; what a person keeps feeding on, he comes to crave.
units.insight: The council that tried Jesus "sought false testimony against Jesus to put Him to death," and at last two false witnesses came forward (Matthew 26:59–61). They scorned justice in the very court built to uphold it. The second line warns how a heart gets there. No one starts by gulping evil. We taste a little gossip, a small dishonesty, a cynical laugh at what is right, and the appetite grows. Henry: "those that devour iniquity swallow the hook with the bait." What seems like food becomes a trap. Jesus offers a different hunger: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, For they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6). What we feed on, we come to love, so feed on what is good.
units.application: Notice what you take in for entertainment and conversation: shows, sites or friendships that make wrongdoing look funny or normal. Cut one this week and replace it with something good. If you serve on a jury, give testimony or write reports at work, treat truth as sacred even when no one would catch a slant. Parents, talk with your children about how small wrongs grow into appetites, and model honesty in front of them.

rel.note: A rod is for the back of him who lacks understanding, while wisdom is on the lips of the wise.
The scoffer struck so that the simple may learn returns here, now facing prepared judgments.
The worthless witness who scorns justice is the kind of scoffer for whom judgments are prepared.
A rod is for the fool's back, the same picture of correction in its harder form.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble.

units.notes:
• *Beatings* (KJV "stripes") are the marks of physical punishment. Proverbs uses the same picture in 10:13, "a rod is for the back of him who is devoid of understanding," and 26:3, "a rod for the fool's back."
• *Prepared* means made ready in advance: the consequence is already in place before the scoffer reaches it.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Profane and wicked men expose themselves to the punishments denounced against such by just laws." "Denounced" here means announced.
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "He that doth the work, earns the wages." The sinner earns the wages of his own sin.
• Compare 3:34; 9:12; Romans 6:23.
units.summary: Refuse every word of correction, and correction will come without words.
units.principle: Those who refuse every gentle word of correction will meet correction in a harder form; God warns before He judges.
units.insight: Jerusalem's leaders "mocked the messengers of God, despised His words, and scoffed at His prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against His people, till there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16). Judgment came late, and only after many warnings. The verse asks whether we are treating God's warnings lightly simply because they have not yet fallen. Yet the gospel holds out astonishing mercy. Isaiah says of the Servant of the LORD, "by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). The punishment that scoffers and fools deserve fell on Christ. One of the criminals crucified beside Jesus joined in the mockery, but the other rebuked him, turned to Jesus and heard, "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:39–43). No scoffer is beyond reach while he can still turn.
units.application: Ask yourself whether there is a warning you keep laughing off, whether from Scripture, a doctor, a spouse or a pastor. Respond to it this week before it becomes harder. Young people, do not join friends in mocking what is right; the laugh is cheap and the cost is high. Parents and leaders, warn clearly and early, and let consequences follow fairly, without cruelty. If you have been a scoffer, the cross is open to you today.

rel.note: The one who loves wine and pleasure will not prosper, another cost of being ruled by drink.
The father warns his son away from heavy drinkers, because drunkenness ends in poverty and rags.
The full portrait of the drunkard shows the wounds, confusion and craving that follow when drink leads a person astray.
Lemuel’s mother applies the warning to rulers, whose drinking would make them forget the law and pervert justice.

units.notes:
• *Led astray*: the KJV reads "whosoever is deceived thereby," stressing that drink fools the mind before it trips the feet. The NASB reads "whoever is intoxicated by it."
• *Brawler*: the KJV has "strong drink is raging." Either way, the picture is of drink that makes a person loud, reckless and ready to fight.
• Henry sums up the change drink makes in a person in an old saying: "When the wine is in the wit is out" (wit here means good sense).
• Proverbs’ fullest portrait of the drunkard ends with wine that "bites like a serpent, And stings like a viper" (23:32).
• Compare 23:20–21; 31:4–5; Isaiah 5:11; Ephesians 5:18.
units.summary: Drink comes in as a friend and stays as a mocker who picks fights.
units.principle: Whatever is allowed to take control of a person’s judgment will make a fool of him, however friendly it seems at first.
units.insight: Drink’s victims in Scripture include righteous men as well as scoffers. Noah, who walked with God through the flood, drank from his own vineyard and lay uncovered in his tent (Genesis 9:20–21). Lot’s daughters used wine to lead their father into shame (Genesis 19:30–36). Belshazzar drank from the holy vessels of God’s temple while praising his idols, and that night he was slain (Daniel 5:1–4, 30). No one is beyond this mocker’s reach: "let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). The deeper question is what we reach for when we want relief, courage or escape, and what we let lead us. Paul offers a better filling: "do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; but be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). Christ gives by His Spirit the joy and rest that drink only promises.
units.application: If drink has ever led you to say or do what a clear head would not, set your limit now, before the next party or office event, and ask a friend to hold you to it. Parents: talk with your teenagers about 23:29–35 before their friends talk with them about drinking. If someone you love is being led astray, do not mock or lecture. Speak plainly, offer help, and connect them with people who can walk with them.

rel.note: The king’s wrath is like messengers of death, and a wise man appeases it rather than provoking it.
The king’s wrath is again a lion’s roar, set against his favor, which is like dew on the grass.
The king whose wrath is feared here is truly secured by mercy and truth, not by terror.
After the danger of provoking a king comes the wider lesson that stepping back from strife brings honor.
The son is told to fear the LORD and the king and to keep away from rebels, whose ruin comes suddenly.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "The fear of a king," naming the terror the king’s anger stirs in others; the NKJV names the anger itself.
• *Sins against his own life*: the KJV has "sinneth against his own soul." The provoker damages his own life and future, not the king’s.
• Compare 16:14: "As messengers of death is the king’s wrath, But a wise man will appease it."
• Henry draws the contrast between two kinds of rulers. Kings who rule by wisdom and love reflect God, but "those that rule merely by terror, and with a high hand, do but rule like a lion in the forest, with a brutal power."
• Compare 19:12; 24:21–22; Ecclesiastes 10:4.
units.summary: Provoking those in power is like poking a lion: the wound comes back on you.
units.principle: Reckless provocation of those who hold power harms the provoker most; wisdom respects authority and chooses its battles.
units.insight: Adonijah had already lost one bid for the throne. Then he asked Solomon for Abishag, his father’s companion, a request that looked like a new claim to the crown, and it cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13–25). Hanun humiliated David’s messengers and brought war on his own people (2 Samuel 10:1–14). Both struck at a king and wounded themselves. Scripture then lifts our eyes higher. If an earthly king’s anger is a lion’s roar, what of the anger of the King of kings, provoked by our sin? Psalm 2:12 warns, "Kiss the Son, lest He be angry." Yet the Lion of the tribe of Judah is also the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:5–6). He bore the wrath that rebels deserved. Whoever has provoked Him need not wait for the roar; we may run to His mercy now.
units.application: Employees: when a manager is angry, do not add fuel with sarcasm, a reply-all email or a public challenge; ask for a calm, private conversation. Young people dealing with a teacher, coach or police officer: respect for the office protects you. When you must disagree with someone in authority, choose the right time and a gentle tone (25:15). Leaders: remember that your anger sounds louder to others than it does to you.

rel.note: The wrathful man stirs up strife, while the one slow to anger calms it.
Strife is like water breaking through a dam, so the wise stop contention before the quarrel bursts out.
A man’s glory is to overlook a transgression, the same honor found in stepping back from strife.
Provoking a king shows how dangerous a quarrel can become; this verse gives the wise alternative of stopping.
Refusing to repay evil is another way of ceasing from strife and leaving the outcome with the LORD.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb behind "start a quarrel" describes a dispute breaking out into the open. It occurs only three times in the Old Testament, all in Proverbs: here, in 17:14 ("before a quarrel starts") and in 18:1 ("rages against"). Each time it pictures conflict bursting out.
• The KJV reads "every fool will be meddling": the fool cannot keep himself out of a fight.
• Ironside: "A man of God will be ready to give up his fancied rights rather than to prolong strife" (fancied rights are rights he imagines he is owed). He adds that this holds "providing no divine principle is at stake."
• Compare 19:11 ("his glory is to overlook a transgression"); 15:18; 26:17; James 3:17–18.
units.summary: Starting a fight takes no talent; ending one takes character.
units.principle: Ending a quarrel takes more strength than starting one, and God counts that strength as honor.
units.insight: Abraham had every right to choose first, yet he said to Lot, "Please let there be no strife between you and me," and gave his nephew the pick of the land (Genesis 13:8–9). Isaac’s servants dug well after well, and when the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled over them, he moved on and dug again until there was room (Genesis 26:17–22). Both men looked weaker in the moment, and God honored both. What keeps a quarrel going is seldom principle; it is usually pride, the need to land the last word. Jesus calls peacemakers "sons of God" (Matthew 5:9), and "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace" (James 3:18). The question is not who started it, but whether you are willing to be the one who stops.
units.application: Spouses: in the middle of an argument, you can say, "I don’t need to win this; I want us to be okay," and mean it. Online, refuse the reply that only keeps a thread burning. Church members and coworkers: if an old dispute keeps flaring, go and end it, owning your part without waiting for the other person to own theirs. Parents: praise the child who walks away from a fight before you scold the one who started it.

rel.note: The son who sleeps through harvest brings shame, just as this man skips the season that decides the harvest.
The lazy man desires and has nothing, the same empty end as the one who would not plow.
Loving sleep leads to poverty, while open eyes lead to bread, the same lesson in the same chapter.
The field of the lazy man lies overgrown and broken down, and poverty comes on him like a prowler.
The ant gathers while the season is open, the opposite of the lazy man who lets planting time pass.

units.notes:
• *Winter* refers to the autumn and winter season after the early rains, when the ground was plowed. The ESV reads "in the autumn"; the KJV text reads "by reason of the cold," with "winter" in the margin.
• Bridges: "The sluggard always has his excuses ready to shift off any work, that requires exertion."
• Ironside, on the lazy man who blames bad luck for his empty field: "The fact is, fortune has nothing to do with it."
• The NKJV calls him "the lazy man" here; Proverbs calls the same figure "sluggard" in 6:6 and 6:9.
• Compare 10:5; 13:4; 24:30–34; Ecclesiastes 11:4; 2 Thessalonians 3:10.
units.summary: Skip the cold season of work and you will stand in an empty field at harvest.
units.principle: The harvest is decided at planting time; excuses that skip the hard season leave an empty field.
units.insight: The lazy man’s problem is not the weather but his heart. The ant has no overseer, yet she gathers while the season is open (6:6–8). Jesus told of ten virgins waiting for a bridegroom. The foolish five let their oil run low, went to buy more only when he was already coming, and found the door shut (Matthew 25:1–13). Many of us are diligent at our jobs and cold in prayer, Scripture and service, always waiting for a warmer season. Christ did not wait for comfort. "He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), and He could tell the Father, "I have finished the work which You have given Me to do" (John 17:4). Grace does not excuse the plowing; it gives strength for it: "in due season we shall reap if we do not lose heart" (Galatians 6:9).
units.application: Students: the hard weeks of the semester are the planting season; skipped work shows up at exam time. Employees and business owners: do the unpleasant task first instead of waiting for a better mood. Parents: teach children that chores come before play, even on cold mornings. In your walk with God, keep praying and reading Scripture through dry seasons; the harvest of a steady life comes later.

rel.note: Answering before hearing is folly and shame, the opposite of patiently drawing out what lies in another’s heart.
A man’s words are also called deep waters, while the wellspring of wisdom flows like a brook.
Plans are established by counsel, and the wise know how to draw that counsel out of others.
A wise man can draw out what is deep in a heart, but the LORD’s lamp searches all its inner depths.

units.notes:
• The ESV renders "counsel" as "purpose" and the NASB as "A plan," which brings out the sense of hidden intentions.
• Deep water can hide schemes as well as wisdom. Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Thus a person’s real motives are ‘deep’ in that they are difficult to extract; one must be wary of the pretenses of others."
• Henry: "We lose the benefit we might have by the conversation of wise men for want of the art of being inquisitive." In his older English, "conversation" means company and "for want of" means for lack of.
• The queen of Sheba drew out Solomon’s wisdom with hard questions (1 Kings 10:1–3).
• Compare 18:4; 20:18; James 1:19.
units.summary: The heart is a deep well; understanding brings a bucket and patience, not a drill.
units.principle: What matters most in a person often lies deep, and understanding draws it out with patience instead of force.
units.insight: Jesus was the master of drawing out deep water. At a well in Samaria He asked a woman for a drink, and by patient questions brought to the surface the thirst and the history she had kept hidden (John 4:7–18). On the road to Emmaus He asked two grieving disciples, "What kind of conversation is this that you have with one another as you walk and are sad?" He let them pour out their disappointment before He opened the Scriptures (Luke 24:17–27). He also "knew what was in man" (John 2:25), so nothing was too deep for Him. Most of us talk more than we listen, and we answer before we hear (18:13). The people near us may carry fears, plans or wisdom that will never surface unless someone cares enough to lower the bucket.
units.application: Parents: when your teenager comes home quiet, ask an open question and then wait through the silence. Pastors and small-group leaders: before giving advice, ask, "What do you think is really going on?" Managers: invite the quiet team member to speak in meetings; the best idea in the room may still be at the bottom of the well. Friends: when someone says "I’m fine," gently ask once more.

rel.note: A friend loves at all times, the faithful love that is proved in hard times rather than proclaimed.
The righteous man who walks in integrity is the faithful man this verse says is hard to find.
Trusting an unfaithful man in trouble is like leaning on a bad tooth or a foot out of joint.
Praise should come from another’s lips, not one’s own, the opposite of proclaiming one’s own goodness.
The same kind of question, "Who can find...?", marks the virtuous wife as rare and precious, as the faithful man is here.

units.notes:
• *Goodness* translates chesed, the Hebrew word for loyal love. The ESV reads "Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love." Seeing chesed here sharpens the contrast between the two lines: many claim loyal love, but few prove faithful.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "The paucity of pious persons makes them precious." Paucity means scarcity.
• Absalom stole the hearts of Israel by advertising how well he would care for them, while he plotted against his father (2 Samuel 15:1–6).
• Compare 27:2 ("Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth"); 25:19; Psalm 12:1; Luke 16:10.
units.summary: Everyone advertises loyalty; faithfulness is the rare thing that shows up when it costs.
units.principle: Loyalty is proved by what a person does over time, not by what he says about himself.
units.insight: Jehu told Jonadab, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD" (2 Kings 10:16). Yet Scripture says Jehu "took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart" (2 Kings 10:31). The Pharisee in the temple listed his virtues to God Himself (Luke 18:11–12). Self-advertised goodness is still with us, in résumés, online profiles and church conversation. The searching question is whether the people closest to us find us faithful when faithfulness costs something. Only one Man has perfectly matched His words with His life. Christ is "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5), and "If we are faithless, He remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself" (2 Timothy 2:13). His faithfulness to us is the soil in which our own faithfulness grows.
units.application: Before you tell anyone how loyal you are, ask whether your track record would say the same. Employees: keep small promises, like the email you said you would send or the shift you agreed to cover. Friends: show up for the hospital visit and the moving day, not only the celebration. Leaders choosing staff or volunteers: look for proven faithfulness in small things rather than impressive self-description (Luke 16:10).

rel.note: The posterity of the righteous will be delivered, another picture of a righteous life blessing those who come after.
A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, the lasting reach of a righteous life.
The fear of the LORD gives strong confidence, and His children have a place of refuge.
The same walk in integrity is worth more than wealth gained with crooked speech.
Children are blessed by a parent’s integrity, and their own deeds soon show what they are becoming.
The faithful man who is so hard to find is the righteous man walking in his integrity.

units.notes:
• *Integrity* means wholeness: a life that is the same in private as in public. Proverbs uses the same phrase, "walks in his integrity," for the poor man who is better off than a rich man with crooked lips or ways (19:1; 28:6).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "It answers the temptation to ‘get on’ at all costs ‘for the children’s sake’." He means that parents do more for their children by integrity than by compromising to get ahead.
• God told Abraham, "walk before Me and be blameless" (Genesis 17:1), and His covenant reached "your descendants after you" (Genesis 17:7).
• Compare 13:22; 14:26; Psalm 37:25–26; Psalm 112:1–2.
units.summary: The best inheritance a parent leaves is not an estate but a walk.
units.principle: A life of steady integrity leaves an inheritance of blessing that usually reaches beyond the one who lives it.
units.insight: Timothy grew up in a home where sincere faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5), and from childhood he knew the Holy Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15). Their quiet integrity became his inheritance. Scripture is just as honest that the pattern is not a formula. Hezekiah was among Judah’s most faithful kings, yet his son Manasseh became one of its worst (2 Kings 21:1–9). Even so, Manasseh found mercy when he humbled himself (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). So the verse calls us to walk with God, not to control our children’s outcomes. What are our children learning from our walk on ordinary weekdays, in how we speak, spend and repent? Our hope for them rests not on our record but on the God who keeps "mercy for thousands" (Exodus 34:7).
units.application: Parents: let your children see you tell the truth when a lie would be easier, admit when you are wrong, and keep your word to them. Grandparents: tell the stories of God’s faithfulness in your life. If you are grieving a wayward child, do not read this verse as a verdict on you; keep walking with God and keep praying. Business owners: refuse the shortcut you would not want your children to inherit.

rel.note: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, watching the evil and the good far more surely than any king.
The wise king again winnows out the wicked, now driving the threshing wheel over them.
If a just king’s eyes expose evil, no one can claim a clean heart before the eyes of God.
Removing the wicked from before the king is like removing dross from silver, and it establishes his throne.
The king establishes the land by justice, while bribery overthrows it.

units.notes:
• *Scatters* is the Hebrew verb for scattering or winnowing. It appears again in 20:26, where the wise king "sifts out the wicked." The ESV reads "winnows" in both verses, which keeps the farming picture of separating chaff from grain.
• Solomon judged the case of the two mothers himself, and all Israel "feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice" (1 Kings 3:28).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Righteousness at the top was necessary to undergird the whole judicial system."
• Compare 20:26; 25:4–5; 29:4; Psalm 101:3–8.
units.summary: When a just ruler is watching, evil loses its hiding places.
units.principle: Just leadership that pays close attention drives wrongdoing into the open, while evil grows where no one is watching.
units.insight: David resolved as king, "I will set nothing wicked before my eyes," and "Early I will destroy all the wicked of the land" (Psalm 101:3, 8). Scripture also shows the cost when a ruler looks away. David was angry at Amnon’s crime against Tamar but did nothing. Absalom took revenge into his own hands (2 Samuel 13:21–29) and later rose in revolt against his father (2 Samuel 15:1–12). Every earthly throne points beyond itself. "All things are naked and open to the eyes of Him to whom we must give account" (Hebrews 4:13). Such exposure is terrifying for anyone who hopes to hide. Yet the same passage goes on to our great High Priest, who sympathizes with our weaknesses and invites us to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:14–16). The safest place before the eyes of God is not hiding but confession.
units.application: Leaders in business, ministry or government: be present where decisions are made; wrongdoing grows where no one is looking. Managers: review what your people actually do, not only what they report. Parents: your attentive presence in the home deters more trouble than any rule. Church elders: do not leave known problems unexamined for years. In each case, let your eyes be fair as well as sharp.

rel.note: The next verse shows the uncleansed heart at work in false weights and measures.
Though no one can cleanse his own heart, even a child is still called to conduct that is pure and right.
The heart no one can cleanse alone is reached and cleansed by painful correction.
The just king’s eyes scatter evil, raising the question of who can stand clean before God’s eyes.
Since no one can claim a clean heart, mercy comes to the one who confesses and forsakes his sins.
A generation pure in its own eyes but unwashed makes the very claim this question exposes.

units.notes:
• The question "Who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean’?" stands right after the king who scatters evil with his eyes (20:8) and just before the false weights of 20:10. So the question of the clean heart sits between royal justice and everyday honesty.
• Bridges: "The clean heart therefore is not the heart pure from sin, but the heart cleansed and renewed by grace."
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "No man living upon earth can say this truly and sincerely."
• Contrast 30:12, "a generation that is pure in its own eyes, Yet is not washed from its filthiness."
• Compare 1 Kings 8:46; Ecclesiastes 7:20; Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:8–9.
units.summary: Self-made purity is the one claim no honest person can make.
units.principle: No one can cleanse his own heart; purity comes only as God forgives and renews those who confess.
units.insight: Isaiah was the great prophet of his day, yet when he saw the Lord he cried, "Woe is me, for I am undone! Because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5). Paul, after a life poured out for Christ, called himself the chief of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The closer people come to God, the less they claim for themselves. The opposite danger is common in church: confessing in general that we are sinners while defending ourselves against every particular charge. Yet this question is not meant to leave us in despair. What no one can do, Christ has done: "the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).
units.application: When a spouse, friend or pastor corrects you, resist the reflex to defend yourself; ask, "Is there truth in this?" Before you take communion or lead worship, confess specific sins, not just sin in general. Parents: model saying "I was wrong; please forgive me" to your children.
