If you have always thought of yourself as a good person who hardly needs grace, read Psalm 51 slowly this week and pray it.

rel.note: Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, while a just weight is His delight.
Honest weights and scales belong to the LORD, so tampering with them wrongs Him.
The seller’s false weights here are matched by the buyer’s false words in the same marketplace.
The same saying returns in nearly the same words, showing how much weight Proverbs gives to honest trade.
The heart no one can cleanse alone shows itself in everyday dishonesty like false weights.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew is literally "a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah." The stone was a weight used in a balance, and an ephah was a standard dry measure for grain. The doubled words describe two different weights and two different measures used for the same purpose.
• Henry describes the trick exactly: "an under-weight for what they paid and an over-weight for what they received."
• The prophets condemned the same fraud: "Making the ephah small and the shekel large, Falsifying the scales by deceit" (Amos 8:5; compare Micah 6:10–11).
• The saying returns almost word for word in 20:23. Compare 11:1; 16:11; Leviticus 19:35–36.
units.summary: Two sets of weights reveal one crooked heart, and God sees both.
units.principle: God hates a double standard, whether in a merchant’s scales or a person’s judgments, and He delights in honest dealing.
units.insight: Zacchaeus had grown rich by taking more than he was owed. When Jesus came to his house, his first response was to make his dealings honest: "if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Grace reached his heart and then his accounts. The "diverse weights" of this verse are not only found in the market. We use them whenever we excuse in ourselves what we condemn in others, judging ourselves by our good intentions and other people by their results. Jesus warned, "with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you" (Matthew 7:2). God is not like us. His scales are always true, and in Christ He shows grace without ever lowering His justice; He is "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26).
units.application: Business owners and salespeople: price, measure and describe goods the same way for every customer, whether or not they know the market. Employees: report hours and expenses exactly. Landlords and contractors: no hidden fees for the people least able to argue. At home and at work, notice when you hold a spouse, child or coworker to a standard you excuse in yourself, and use one scale for everyone.

rel.note: A parent’s walk of integrity blesses children whose own deeds soon reveal their character.
No one can make his own heart clean, yet the call to pure and right conduct remains from childhood on.
Foolishness bound up in a child’s heart shows itself in his deeds and calls for loving correction.
Because character shows early, parents are called to train a child in the way he should go.

units.notes:
• The verb behind "is known" is a form of the verb to recognize, and the ESV and YLT render it "makes himself known." The same verb form can elsewhere mean to disguise oneself, so the line may also hint that a child can mask his character for a time. The main versions follow the sense of being recognized by conduct.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "The future engineer is seen in the little handicraftsman of two years old." A handicraftsman is someone who makes things by hand.
• Samuel’s early faithfulness was plain to all: "the child Samuel grew in stature, and in favor both with the LORD and men" (1 Samuel 2:26).
• Compare 22:6; 22:15; Matthew 7:16–20; Luke 2:52.
units.summary: Character does not wait for adulthood; even a child’s deeds show who he is becoming.
units.principle: Conduct reveals character from the earliest years, and the call to live purely begins in childhood.
units.insight: Daniel was a young captive in Babylon when he "purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself" with the king’s food (Daniel 1:8), and that early choice set the course of his life. Jesus at twelve was already "about My Father’s business" (Luke 2:49). Character is being formed long before anyone calls it character. Children watch what we do more than what we hear us say, and our own deeds tell the truth about us too. If a child is known by his deeds, what do our habits at home, online and at work reveal? Only God can change the heart that shows itself in deeds. So parents bring their children to Christ, who said, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them" (Mark 10:14), and adults must come the same way.
units.application: Parents: notice patterns in your child’s behavior, such as truthfulness, temper or kindness, and address them early instead of saying "It’s just a phase." Praise right conduct specifically. Teachers and youth leaders: take children’s choices seriously; character is being formed now. Young people: what you do when no adult is watching already shows who you are becoming. Adults: ask what your own deeds say about you.

rel.note: The God who made the seeing eye has eyes in every place, watching the evil and the good.
The ear of the wise seeks knowledge, using the gift this verse says the LORD has made.
The LORD made the seeing eye, and the next verse commands the reader to open it.
Besides ear and eye, the LORD has given the human spirit as His lamp to search the heart.
The LORD gives light to the eyes of rich and poor alike, the same truth that He is the Maker of sight.

units.notes:
• Psalm 94:9 draws the same conclusion: "He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? He who formed the eye, shall He not see?"
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Since God made the eyes and ears, he is the infallible judge."
• Jesus spoke of the crowds, "seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear," and told His disciples, "blessed are your eyes for they see, and your ears for they hear" (Matthew 13:13, 16). Spiritual sight and hearing are God’s gift as much as the body’s.
• Compare 29:13 ("The LORD gives light to the eyes of both"); 18:15; Exodus 4:11.
units.summary: The Maker of every ear hears everything, and He gave you ears to hear Him.
units.principle: The God who made our eyes and ears sees and hears everything, and He calls us to use those gifts to receive His wisdom.
units.insight: When Moses protested that he was slow of speech, the LORD answered, "Who has made man’s mouth? Or who makes the mute, the deaf, the seeing, or the blind? Have not I, the LORD?" (Exodus 4:11). Our weakness does not limit the God who made our senses. Lydia listened to Paul by a riverside, and "The Lord opened her heart to heed the things spoken by Paul" (Acts 16:14). Jesus opened deaf ears and blind eyes (Mark 7:32–35; 8:22–25), signs that He gives spiritual hearing and sight. So it is fair to ask what our eyes and ears are given to. What we watch and listen to shapes the heart. The boy Samuel learned the right prayer: "Speak, for Your servant hears" (1 Samuel 3:10).
units.application: This week, take stock of what fills your eyes and ears: the shows, feeds, music and conversations that fill your hours. Thank God for your senses, and give Him the first look and listen of the day in Scripture and prayer. Parents: help children choose what they watch and hear, and explain why. In a meeting or a conflict, listen fully and look closely before you judge.

rel.note: The one who works his land is satisfied with bread, the same reward promised to open eyes.
Laziness casts a person into deep sleep, and the idle one goes hungry.
The LORD made the seeing eye, and this verse commands the reader to open it and work.
The lazy man who will not plow in winter ends with nothing, another picture of ease leading to want.
A little more sleep and slumber brings poverty like a prowler, the same warning against loving sleep.

units.notes:
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The number of hours one sleeps per day is not the point here." The issue is the love of ease, not a set amount of rest.
• Henry: "Love not sleep for its own sake, but only as it fits for further work." By "fits" he means prepares a person for work.
• Scripture treats sleep as a gift: "For so He gives His beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2).
• Compare 6:9–11; 19:15; 12:11 ("He who tills his land will be satisfied with bread"); 23:21 ("drowsiness will clothe a man with rags").
units.summary: Sleep is a gift to enjoy, not a master to love.
units.principle: Rest is a gift, but loving ease leads to want; alert, willing work is the ordinary path to provision.
units.insight: David’s great fall began in a season of ease. "In the spring of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle," he stayed home, rose from his bed one evening, and saw Bathsheba from the roof (2 Samuel 11:1–2). Comfort left him with idle hours and an unguarded heart. In Gethsemane Jesus found His disciples sleeping and asked, "What! Could you not watch with Me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40). He was not scorning tiredness; He knew "the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:41). Our drowsiness is often spiritual before it is physical. We drift, scroll and postpone. Paul’s wake-up call is for every believer: "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14).
units.application: Students and young adults: set an alarm you actually obey, and do your hardest work in your best hours. If you are between jobs, treat the search as a full day’s work. Anyone who loves comfort: notice where ease has become your master, whether endless scrolling, a lingering bed or a postponed task. Rest well and on purpose, then rise and work. Parents: teach children to finish their work before they rest.

rel.note: The LORD hates dishonest scales and delights in a just weight, a standard that covers the buyer’s words as well as the seller’s balance.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, including the convenient lies of the market.
The seller’s false weights are matched by the buyer’s false words in the same marketplace.
Gain won by deceit tastes sweet at first, like the buyer’s bargain, but turns to gravel.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the buyer’s complaint is the word for "bad" said twice, "Bad, bad," as the ESV and NASB render it. Ironside’s translation reads "Bad! bad! saith the buyer."
• Henry: "a fraud and a lie are what a man ought to be ashamed of, though he have gained ever so much by them."
• The seller often plays the same game from the other side, praising his goods beyond their worth. Both use words to win, not to tell the truth.
• Contrast Abraham, who refused a gift and paid Ephron the full price openly before witnesses (Genesis 23:10–16).
• Compare 11:1; 20:10; 20:23; Ephesians 4:25.
units.summary: The buyer who calls it junk at the counter brags about his bargain in the parking lot.
units.principle: Honest speech belongs in the marketplace too; words used as tools to deceive are lies, however common the practice.
units.insight: When Abraham needed a burial place for Sarah, Ephron offered him the field as a gift. Abraham insisted on paying the full price in front of everyone at the city gate (Genesis 23:10–16). There was no pose, no running down the goods, and no boasting afterward. His dealings were as clean as his worship. The buyer in this proverb thinks his little lie is simply how business works. Jesus set a different standard: "let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’" (Matthew 5:37). The searching question is whether our words serve the truth or serve our wallet. Ananias and Sapphira learned that a lie about money is a lie told before God (Acts 5:1–11). A heart made new in Christ wants its words to match its thoughts, even when money is on the table.
units.application: Buyers: negotiate truthfully. You may ask for a better price, but do not invent flaws or pretend you are not interested. Sellers and small business owners: describe your goods truthfully, defects included. Anyone selling a car, a house or items online: put in the listing what you would tell a friend. And when you get a bargain, ask whether you would be comfortable if the seller heard how you describe it afterward.

rel.note: The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, another picture of speech as treasure.
Getting wisdom is far better than getting gold, the same scale of value.
Lips of knowledge are a jewel, while the flattering lips of the talebearer are to be avoided.
Wisdom is more precious than rubies, the same comparison applied here to wise lips.
Wisdom is better than rubies, and nothing one desires can compare with her.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew phrase behind "precious jewel" is literally "a vessel of preciousness," an object of great value; the YLT renders it "a precious vessel." After the gold and rubies of the first line, the wording places wise speech among a person’s treasured possessions, something to value and keep.
• Henry: "There is gold in many a man’s pocket that has no grace in his heart."
• Solomon’s court was so rich that its drinking vessels were gold (1 Kings 10:21), yet the gift he had asked of God was "an understanding heart" (1 Kings 3:9).
• Compare 3:15; 10:20; 15:7; 16:16; 25:11.
units.summary: Gold and rubies can be bought; a mouth full of true knowledge is the rarer jewel.
units.principle: Wise and truthful speech is rarer and more valuable than wealth, because it does good that money cannot do.
units.insight: A rich man ran to Jesus asking about eternal life, then went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:17–22). Peter, with nothing in his hands, answered for the disciples: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:68). Later Peter told a lame beggar, "Silver and gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you," and the man walked (Acts 3:6–8). Few of us will ever hold a multitude of rubies. Anyone can become a person whose words carry knowledge that heals. Most of us spend far more effort building wealth than storing up wisdom to speak. Yet the best gift for a struggling friend is often a true word at the right time, drawn from Christ, in whom "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).
units.application: Value wise counsel above financial gain when you choose a job, a church or a mentor. Young people: seek out older believers whose words carry knowledge, and listen to them. Parents: let your children hear you prize wisdom more than possessions. Teachers, pastors and friends: handle your words as carefully as a jeweler handles a stone; a true, encouraging word at the right moment can be worth more than any gift you could buy.

rel.note: Whoever becomes surety for a stranger will suffer, while the one who refuses is secure.
Shaking hands in pledge marks a man devoid of understanding.
Pledging for debts you cannot pay can cost you the bed from under you.
The same counsel to take the garment of a rash guarantor appears again almost word for word.
The father urges the son who has become surety to free himself quickly, the guarantor’s side of this warning.

units.notes:
• To be *surety* is to guarantee someone else’s debt, much like cosigning a loan today.
• The Hebrew text has two readings in the second line. The written text has "foreigners," while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has "a foreign woman." The NKJV and KJV follow the marginal reading; the ESV and NASB follow the written text.
• The verse is repeated almost exactly at 27:13. There the Hebrew has only the feminine form, and the NKJV again reads "seductress."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Take his garment means: ‘Don’t lend to him without security (Exodus 22:26); he is a bad risk!’"
• Compare 6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 22:26–27.
units.summary: Sign carelessly for strangers, and soon no one will trust your own signature.
units.principle: A person who pledges rashly loses the trust of others; wisdom guards against careless commitments while still helping with open hands.
units.insight: Judah gave his signet, cord and staff as a pledge to a woman he took for a harlot, and those very pledges later exposed him (Genesis 38:16–26). A rash promise and careless company left him at the mercy of others. Proverbs is not cold toward people in need; the law commanded mercy to the poor borrower (Exodus 22:25–27). What it exposes is the heart that commits without thinking, whether to win approval or to satisfy desire. Yet the gospel shows one pledge that was never rash. Jesus "has become a surety of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). He knew exactly what our debt would cost, counted it, and paid it in full. Because He stood surety for strangers like us, we can be generous wisely, giving freely where we can rather than signing what we cannot pay.
units.application: Before you cosign a loan, ask whether you could pay the whole debt without resentment; if not, do not sign. Parents of young adults: give a smaller gift you can afford rather than guarantee a debt you cannot. Lenders, landlords and business owners: it is not unkind to require security from someone with a record of careless commitments. Young men: notice how desire can rush you into promises you would never make with a clear head.

rel.note: The buyer’s bargain won by false words is one form of bread gained by deceit.
An inheritance grabbed too soon also looks like gain at the beginning and is not blessed at the end.
Treasure gained by a lying tongue is a fleeting fantasy that leads toward death.
Wine goes down smoothly but bites like a serpent at the last, the same sweet start and bitter end.
Folly’s secret bread is pleasant, but her guests end in the depths of hell.

units.notes:
• *Bread* stands for whatever is gained, whether food, money or advantage, not only a loaf.
• Bridges quotes Bishop Hall on the deceiver who chews his bread until "he shall find it to be but harsh gravel, that crasheth between his teeth, galls his jaws, wounds his tongue, and offends his palate." In older English, "crasheth" means crunches and "galls" means rubs raw.
• Wine shows the same pattern: it "swirls around smoothly; At the last it bites like a serpent" (23:31–32).
• Compare 9:17–18; 21:6; Job 20:12–14; Hebrews 11:25.
units.summary: Cheating tastes like fresh bread on the first bite and like gravel on the last.
units.principle: Sin is sweet at first and bitter at the end, so every choice must be judged by where it leads, not by its first taste.
units.insight: Achan saw a beautiful garment, silver and a wedge of gold among the spoils of Jericho. He coveted them, took them and hid them in his tent (Joshua 7:21). The sweetness was brief, and it brought ruin on him and his household (Joshua 7:24–25). Gehazi lied to get silver and clothing from Naaman and walked away with leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27). Judas took thirty pieces of silver and soon threw them down in the temple in despair (Matthew 27:3–5). Temptation always shows us the first bite and hides the gravel. Moses chose differently, "choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin" (Hebrews 11:25). Christ offers bread that never turns to grit: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35).
units.application: Employees tempted to pad a timesheet or expense report: picture the conversation when it is discovered. Students: a grade gained by cheating sours at the next exam and in your conscience. Business owners: refuse the deal that depends on a lie, even if it would close today. If you are already eating bread gained by deceit, stop now, confess it, and make it right where you can, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8).

rel.note: Without counsel plans go awry, but with many counselors they are established.
The next verse shows whom not to trust with your plans: the talebearer and the flatterer.
A rash vow made without thought is the opposite of plans weighed with counsel.
Counsel lies deep in the heart, and a man of understanding draws it out before acting.
By wise counsel you will wage your war, the same instruction repeated.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word rendered "wise counsel" in the second line means guidance or direction. It is the word used in 1:5 ("wise counsel") and 24:6, where it describes the skilled guidance a wise person acquires and a nation needs in war.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Perhaps there is not a precept in this whole book so little regarded as this."
• Jesus used the same picture: what king going to war "does not sit down first and consider whether he is able" to meet the enemy (Luke 14:31)?
• Compare 11:14; 15:22; 24:6; 1 Kings 12:6–16.
units.summary: The bigger the battle, the more you need advice before you march.
units.principle: Plans grow firm through wise counsel, and the greater the stakes, the more counsel is needed before acting.
units.insight: Rehoboam asked for counsel, then rejected the elders who had served his father and followed the young men he grew up with. He answered the people harshly, and ten tribes broke away (1 Kings 12:6–16). He had advice; he simply chose the counsel that flattered him. David, by contrast, "inquired of the LORD" before battle and waited for His direction, even on how to attack (2 Samuel 5:19, 23–24). Our spiritual battles need counsel too. We fight temptation, discouragement and conflict, and pride tells us to go it alone. The wisest counsel begins with the One whose name is "Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6), and He gives His people one another. Whom have you invited to speak into your biggest decisions, and do you consult only those who will agree?
units.application: Before a major decision, such as a job change, a move, a marriage, a large purchase or a church building project, bring it to at least two wise people who will tell you the truth. Leaders: build a team that includes people who see differently from you. Couples: plan your finances together, not alone. Before a hard confrontation, pray and seek counsel first; it is a kind of battle too.

rel.note: A talebearer reveals secrets, but a faithful spirit conceals a matter.
The talebearer’s words are tasty trifles that sink deep into the listener.
Lips of knowledge are a precious jewel, unlike the loose and flattering lips of the talebearer.
Plans need counsel, and this verse warns not to share them with a talebearer.
The man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb behind "one who flatters with his lips" can be connected with a verb meaning to open wide, so the phrase may describe one who opens his lips wide, a loose talker. A verb of the same spelling means to entice or deceive, which lies behind the NKJV’s "flatters" and the KJV margin’s "enticeth." The ESV reads "a simple babbler."
• Ironside: "He who flatters to the face will as readily scandalize behind the back." To scandalize here means to slander.
• Compare 11:13 ("he who is of a faithful spirit conceals a matter"); 18:8; 26:20–22; 29:5.
• Paul warns of people who become "gossips and busybodies, saying things which they ought not" (1 Timothy 5:13).
units.summary: Flattery opens your mouth, and gossip carries what you said to the next house.
units.principle: Whoever carries other people’s secrets to you will carry yours to others, so choose confidants who can keep a confidence.
units.insight: Ziba came to David with gifts and a damaging story about his master Mephibosheth, and David believed him without hearing the other side (2 Samuel 16:1–4). The report cost an innocent man dearly (2 Samuel 19:24–30). Gossip feels like closeness: someone trusts us with inside information, and we feel included. But the mouth that carries others’ secrets to us will carry ours away. The harder question is which side of this verse we stand on. Do we enjoy hearing secrets, and pass them on with a pious "just so you can pray"? Christ knows every secret of our hearts, and instead of exposing us, He covered our sins at the cost of His life. His people are called to the same love, for "love covers all sins" (10:12).
units.application: When someone begins, "Don’t tell anyone, but…," you can kindly say, "I’d rather not hear that." Small-group members and church staff: keep what is shared in confidence, including prayer requests, unless someone is in danger. Employees: be wary of the coworker who praises you warmly and criticizes everyone else. Parents: teach teenagers that friends who spread others’ secrets will spread theirs too.

rel.note: The son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother brings shame and reproach.
The next verse warns against grabbing an inheritance too early, another way of dishonoring parents.
The son is told to listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old, the honor this verse’s curser refuses.
The lamp of the wicked will be put out, the same image of a life and future extinguished.
The eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother comes to a terrible end, the same judgment on contempt for parents.

units.notes:
• The phrase rendered "deep darkness" is unusual. The Hebrew says literally "the pupil of darkness," an expression for the blackest middle of the night. The ESV has "utter darkness," the YLT "blackness of darkness," and the NASB "in time of darkness."
• Ironside: "No parents are perfect in all their ways, but, like civil authorities, they are to be honored because of their position."
• Jesus quoted this law, "He who curses father or mother, let him be put to death," against those who used religious excuses to avoid caring for their parents (Matthew 15:4–6).
• Compare 30:17; 19:26; 24:20 ("The lamp of the wicked will be put out"); Ephesians 6:2–3.
units.summary: Curse the people who gave you life, and you put out the light in your own.
units.principle: Contempt for one’s parents darkens a person’s own life, while honoring them is the path God blesses.
units.insight: Ham saw his father’s shame and told his brothers; Shem and Japheth walked backward and covered it (Genesis 9:22–23). The difference between contempt and honor showed in a single moment. Absalom went much further, stealing his father’s throne and openly dishonoring him, and his life ended young, caught in a tree (2 Samuel 18:9–15). Contempt for parents often starts small: a sneer, a dismissive word, a rolled eye that hardens over years into a heart that curses. Jesus showed the other way. In agony on the cross He still provided for His mother, giving her into John’s care (John 19:26–27). The command to honor father and mother is "the first commandment with promise" (Ephesians 6:2). For anyone who has spoken contempt, there is mercy in Christ, and a new beginning can start with a phone call.
units.application: Teenagers and young adults: you can disagree with your parents without contempt; watch your tone, your texts and what you say about them to friends. Adult children: speak of aging parents with respect, and provide for them where you can (1 Timothy 5:4). If your parents wounded you deeply, honoring them does not mean pretending; it means refusing contempt, setting wise boundaries with good counsel, and leaving judgment to God. Parents: model honor in how you speak of your own parents.

rel.note: Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles, while wealth gathered by labor grows.
Bread gained by deceit is sweet at first and gravel afterward, the same sweet beginning and bitter end.
Cursing parents and grabbing their goods early are two forms of the same dishonor.
The one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished, while the faithful man abounds with blessings.
Robbing one’s father or mother and calling it no sin is the grasping heart behind a hasty inheritance.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew text has two readings of one word here. The written text has a word meaning gained by greed, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts means hurried or hastened. The NKJV, ESV and NASB follow the marginal reading, "hastily" or its equivalent. The YLT’s "An inheritance gotten wrongly at first" appears to reflect the written reading.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Easy money does not foster financial responsibility."
• Proverbs condemns the child who "robs his father or his mother, And says, ‘It is no transgression’" (28:24): grasping from parents while excusing it.
• Compare 13:11; 28:20; 1 Timothy 6:9–10.
units.summary: An inheritance grabbed too early is a gift without the blessing.
units.principle: Wealth grabbed before its time rarely brings blessing, because blessing comes with patience, honesty and trust in God’s timing.
units.insight: The younger son in Jesus’ parable said, "Father, give me the portion of goods that falls to me" (Luke 15:12). He took his inheritance early, wasted it all, and soon was feeding pigs (Luke 15:13–16). Ahab grabbed Naboth’s vineyard, the family inheritance Naboth would not sell, and the prize brought God’s judgment on his house (1 Kings 21:1–19). The hasty grab always reveals the heart: I want it now, and I do not trust the giver’s timing. Yet Jesus’ parable does not end with the pigs. The father ran to meet the son who came home with nothing (Luke 15:20). In Christ we are given "an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and that does not fade away" (1 Peter 1:4), and it is worth the wait.
units.application: Adult children: do not pressure aging parents for money or property, and refuse family schemes that hurry an estate along. Heirs: if an inheritance comes, receive it with gratitude and make a plan before you spend. Young adults: be wary of gambling and online get-rich offers that promise wealth at the beginning. Parents: talk openly with your children about money, so that what you leave them blesses rather than ruins them.

rel.note: The God who will right wrongs done to His people also hates the quiet theft of false scales.
Waiting for the LORD rests on the truth that He directs a person’s steps.
Stepping back from strife brings honor, and refusing revenge is one form of that honor.
Do not say you will do to him as he did to you, the same refusal of personal payback.
Instead of revenge, feed your hungry enemy, and the LORD will reward you.

units.notes:
• Paul’s words in Romans 12:19 quote Deuteronomy 32:35, "Vengeance is Mine, and recompense," rather than this proverb, though the teaching is closely related.
• The promise "He will save you" is made to the one wronged; it is not a threat against the offender. Henry: "he will save thee, and that is enough."
• Bridges quotes Francis Bacon: "He that studieth revenge, keepeth his own wounds open."
• Compare 24:29; 25:21–22; Romans 12:17–21; 1 Thessalonians 5:15.
units.summary: Revenge chains you to the one who hurt you; waiting on God sets you free.
units.principle: Personal revenge belongs to God alone; the wronged entrust their cause to Him while still seeking lawful justice and protection.
units.insight: Shimei cursed David and threw stones at him as he fled from Absalom. Abishai offered to cut off his head, but David said, "Let him alone, and let him curse," and added, "It may be that the LORD will look on my affliction" (2 Samuel 16:5–12). He left his reputation and his enemy with God. David’s greater Son went further. "When He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). Revenge promises relief and never delivers it. The hardest wrongs are the ones that replay at night, when we rehearse what we will say or do to get even. Waiting for the LORD means handing Him that rehearsal, again and again, until His peace replaces it and we can pray for the one who hurt us.
units.application: If someone has wronged you, bring it to God in prayer before you speak about it to anyone else. Where there is a crime, abuse or danger, report it and seek protection; that is not revenge. Employees treated unfairly: use proper channels, not sabotage or gossip. Spouses and family members: refuse the cold silence or cutting remark meant to make the other person pay. Ask God to bless the one who hurt you, and to deliver you.

rel.note: Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is His delight.
Honest weights and scales belong to the LORD, so cheating with them is an offense against Him.
The same condemnation of diverse weights and measures appears earlier in the chapter.
The one who waits for the LORD to save him has no need to secure himself by cheating.
Because the LORD directs a man’s steps, honest dealing can trust Him with the outcome.

units.notes:
• The law required one honest standard: "You shall have honest scales, honest weights" (Leviticus 19:36).
• Henry on why the second line says such scales are "not good": "a bargain made by fraud will prove a losing bargain in the end."
• Proverbs speaks of false or honest weights in 11:1, 16:11, 20:10 and here. The repetition shows how seriously it takes everyday honesty.
• Compare Deuteronomy 25:13–16; Micah 6:11.
units.summary: A thumb on the scale is a vote of no confidence in God.
units.principle: Honest dealing is an act of trust in God; whoever believes He will provide does not need to tip the scales.
units.insight: Laban cheated his nephew Jacob and changed his wages ten times (Genesis 31:7). Yet God watched over Jacob and told him, "I have seen all that Laban is doing to you" (Genesis 31:12). The God who sees crooked dealing is the God who defends those it harms. God’s care for the wronged explains why this verse sits beside the call to wait for the LORD. When we cheat, we do more than take from people. We act as if God will not provide for us unless we cheat. Small dishonesty is a quiet form of unbelief. In Christ we have a Father who knows what we need: "your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things" (Matthew 6:32). We do not need a thumb on the scale. We can deal fairly and leave the outcome with Him.
units.application: Tradespeople and contractors: bill only the hours and materials you actually used. Online sellers: show the flaws in the photos. Employees who handle cash or inventory: count the same way whether or not anyone checks. Customers: when a cashier gives you too much change, give it back. When money is tight, resist the small cheat, pray instead, and trust that God sees and provides.

rel.note: A man’s heart plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps.
Many plans fill a man’s heart, but the LORD’s counsel is what stands.
The God who directs every step is the One the wronged can wait for.
Trusting the LORD with one’s steps frees a person from tipping the scales in his own favor.
Since no one fully understands his own way, he must trust the LORD and not lean on his own understanding.

units.notes:
• Henry: "The goings even of a strong man (so the word signifies) are of the Lord." The word translated "man" in the first line suggests strength, so even the strongest person depends on God for every step.
• Jeremiah expresses the same truth: "It is not in man who walks to direct his own steps" (Jeremiah 10:23).
• Bridges: "Here is dependence without passive inertion; diligence without presumption or self-confidence." "Inertion" is an old word for inactivity: trusting God does not mean sitting still.
• Compare 16:9; 19:21; 21:30–31; 27:1; Psalm 37:23.
units.summary: You cannot see the whole map of your life, but the One directing your steps can.
units.principle: God directs the course of every life, so wisdom plans diligently but trusts Him rather than its own understanding.
units.insight: Joseph went out one day to check on his brothers and did not see his father again for more than twenty years (Genesis 37:13–28). Sold, falsely accused and forgotten in prison, he could not have explained his way at any point along it. Only at the end could he say, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Ruth "happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz" (Ruth 2:3), and the line of David began there. Our lives are full of turns we did not plan and do not understand. The anxious heart demands an explanation before it will trust. Faith keeps walking with the One who knows the way, as Jesus did when He prayed, "not My will, but Yours, be done" (Luke 22:42).
units.application: Make plans this week, and hold them with open hands; pray over your calendar instead of only filling it. If you are in a season you do not understand, such as a closed door, a job loss or a hard diagnosis, write down the ways God has led you before, and trust Him for the next step. Young people anxious about the future: you do not need the whole map. Leaders: say "if the Lord wills" and mean it (James 4:15).

rel.note: He who hastens with his feet sins, the same danger of acting before thinking.
Plans are established by counsel, the careful thought a rash vow skips.
There is more hope for a fool than for a man hasty in his words, and a rash vow is hasty speech toward God.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb in the first line can mean to speak rashly or to swallow. The ESV and NASB take the first sense and render the line as saying rashly, "It is holy." The KJV takes the second and reads "devoureth that which is holy."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "To pronounce a thing sacred is to dedicate it."
• The law left a person free not to vow, but bound him once he had: "if you abstain from vowing, it shall not be sin to you" (Deuteronomy 23:22; compare 23:21–23).
• Compare Ecclesiastes 5:4–6; Leviticus 27; Acts 5:1–4.
units.summary: Count the cost before you make a vow to God, not after.
units.principle: Promises to God are serious, so they should be weighed before they are made and kept once they are made.
units.insight: Jephthah vowed that whatever came out of his house first to meet him would be the LORD’s, and his only daughter came out dancing (Judges 11:30–35). His rash words became a lifelong grief. Ananias and Sapphira wanted the praise of a generous gift without its cost, and their lie about what they had given was a lie "to God" (Acts 5:1–4). Many believers have made promises in an emotional moment, at an altar call, in a hospital or in a crisis, and later quietly backed away. God does not want frightened silence; He wants honest hearts. Jesus knew the full cost of His commitment and kept it: He "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2). If you have broken a vow, confess it; His faithfulness covers what ours could not keep.
units.application: Before you pledge money, time or service to God, whether in a church campaign, a mission commitment or a promise made in a crisis, pause, pray and talk it over with your spouse or a wise friend. Pastors: do not pressure people into on-the-spot vows. If you made a promise to God that you have neglected, bring it to Him openly and keep it where you can. Then make your next commitment slowly, and keep it gladly.

rel.note: A throne is established by righteousness, the reason a wise king removes wickedness.
The firm justice of the threshing wheel is balanced by the mercy and truth that uphold the throne.
The king on the throne of judgment already winnows evil with his eyes; here he acts on what he sees.
Taking the wicked away from before the king is like removing dross from silver, and it establishes his throne.

units.notes:
• *Sifts out* is the same Hebrew verb as "scatters" in 20:8, the word for winnowing. The ESV reads "winnows" in both verses.
• Bridges describes one ancient threshing cart: "a wain, which had wheels with iron teeth like a saw." A wain is a farm wagon; its wheels cut the straw and freed the grain.
• Isaiah says a farmer rolls the cartwheel over his grain but does not thresh it forever (Isaiah 28:27–28). Threshing has a purpose and a limit.
• Compare 20:8; 25:4–5; 16:12; Romans 13:3–4.
units.summary: Wise leadership does not leave the chaff mixed in with the wheat.
units.principle: Wise authority does not tolerate evil but separates it from the good, firmly and justly, to protect those in its care.
units.insight: Asa removed his own grandmother Maachah from her place as queen mother because she had made an obscene idol (1 Kings 15:13). He did not let family ties shield evil in his kingdom. Leaders who will not confront evil let it spread through everyone they serve. Scripture also speaks of a greater sifting. John the Baptist said of Christ, "His winnowing fan is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clean out His threshing floor" (Matthew 3:12). That day will separate wheat from chaff completely, and it is sobering for every heart, not only for kings. Yet the One who winnows is the One who "was bruised for our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5). All who trust Him are gathered as wheat into His barn.
units.application: Pastors and elders: do not let destructive, unrepentant behavior go unaddressed out of a wish to seem kind (1 Corinthians 5:6). Business leaders: deal promptly and fairly with theft, harassment or bullying on your team. Parents: firm, fair consequences protect the rest of the household. In every case, act on facts, follow a fair process, and aim at protecting the good rather than punishing for its own sake.

rel.note: If even Hell and Destruction lie open before the LORD, the hearts of people are surely open to His searching.
A person’s ways seem pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirits.
The LORD made the ear and the eye, and He has also given the human spirit as His lamp within.
The inner depths the LORD’s lamp searches are the same inner depths His correction reaches and cleanses.
A wise man can draw out what lies deep in a heart, but the LORD’s lamp searches all its depths.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "spirit" here is neshamah, "breath." It is the word used in Genesis 2:7, where God "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life," so the verse ties the lamp of the LORD to the life God Himself breathed into human beings.
• The phrase behind "inner depths" is literally "chambers of the belly," a picture of a person’s hidden inner life. The same phrase lies behind "inmost body" in 18:8 and "inner depths" in 20:30.
• The first line has no verb in Hebrew. It sets "the lamp of the LORD" beside "the breath of man," and the NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV supply "is," identifying the human spirit as the LORD’s lamp. Exactly what "spirit" means here is debated; conscience and self-awareness are the common understanding.
• Ironside: "The lamp is the vessel that holds the light, which itself is divine, proceeding from God." In other words, the human spirit is only the lamp; the light by which it searches comes from God.
• Compare 15:11; 16:2; 1 Corinthians 2:11 ("the spirit of the man which is in him"); Psalm 139:23–24.
units.summary: God has set a lamp inside you that shines into rooms you would rather keep dark.
units.principle: God searches the human heart through the spirit He has placed within it; heeding that inner light leads to healing, while silencing it leads to darkness.
units.insight: After David cut off a corner of Saul’s robe in the cave, "David’s heart troubled him" (1 Samuel 24:5). The lamp of the LORD was shining. When David later kept silent about his sin, he felt his strength drain away until he confessed (Psalm 32:3–5). Many of us treat conscience as an intruder to be silenced with busyness, noise or excuses. Proverbs calls it the LORD’s lamp, His mercy searching the rooms we would rather keep dark. When it shows us sin, the answer is not to blow out the lamp but to bring what it reveals to Christ. His blood cleanses the conscience "from dead works to serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). David’s prayer is the right response: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23).
units.application: When your conscience troubles you about a conversation, a purchase or a habit, stop and ask God what He is showing you before you explain it away. Set aside quiet time this week, without phone or music, and pray Psalm 139:23–24. Parents: help children notice and name what their conscience tells them, not only what the rules say. Counselors and friends: ask questions that help people listen to their own conscience.

rel.note: A throne is established by righteousness, set here beside mercy and truth.
A king’s wrath is feared like a lion’s roar, yet his throne is truly secured by mercy and truth.
The wise king’s firm justice against the wicked is balanced by the mercy that upholds his throne.
The king who judges the poor with truth has his throne established forever.
The same pair, mercy and truth, is to be bound around the neck of every son of wisdom.

units.notes:
• The ESV renders the word as "steadfast love" in both lines, showing that the same Hebrew word stands behind the NKJV’s "Mercy" and "lovingkindness." It is also the word behind "goodness" in 20:6.
• Proverbs’ early call to the son uses the same pair: "Let not mercy and truth forsake you" (3:3).
• Bridges: "while truth commands reverence, it is mercy that wins the heart."
• Isaiah pictures a coming throne in the tent of David built the same way, established in mercy, with One seated on it in truth (Isaiah 16:5).
• Compare 16:12; 29:14; Psalm 89:14.
units.summary: Thrones held up by fear wobble; thrones held up by faithful love stand.
units.principle: Lasting authority rests on faithful love and truthfulness, not on force alone; justice and mercy belong together.
units.insight: Saul tried to hold his throne by suspicion and spears, hurling one at David as he played the harp (1 Samuel 18:10–11), and he lost the kingdom anyway. David, for all his failures, sought out Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth and gave him a place at the king’s table for Jonathan’s sake (2 Samuel 9:1–7). Every earthly throne is a small picture of a greater one: "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; Mercy and truth go before Your face" (Psalm 89:14). In the light of the New Testament, these meet perfectly in Christ, who came "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). Whatever authority we hold, in a home, a classroom or a church, it is held steady not by fear but by faithful love and truthfulness.
units.application: Parents: enforce rules with steady love and honest words, not fear or sarcasm. Managers and pastors: keep your promises to your team, and show mercy when someone fails and owns it. Teachers and coaches: let correction and kindness travel together. Anyone in authority: before a hard decision, ask both questions, "Is this true and just?" and "Is this kind and loyal?" Authority built on both is the kind that lasts.

rel.note: The silver-haired head is a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness.
Grandchildren are the crown of old men, another honor that belongs to age.
The young are told not to despise their mother when she is old, honoring the splendor of age.

units.notes:
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Each age has its appointed excellence, to be respected and enjoyed in its time."
• Bridges, citing an older writer, says the world and the church need both: "the strength of youth for energy, and the maturity of age for wisdom."
• The apostle John writes to young men because they are strong and to fathers because they have known Him who is from the beginning (1 John 2:13–14).
• Compare 16:31; 17:6; Leviticus 19:32 ("You shall rise before the gray headed").
units.summary: Youth brings the muscle, age brings the map, and God’s people need both.
units.principle: Every season of life carries its own God-given honor, and the young and the old need each other’s gifts.
units.insight: Elihu waited while Job and his older friends spoke, saying, "Age should speak, And multitude of years should teach wisdom" (Job 32:7). Caleb, at eighty-five, still asked for the hill country: "As yet I am as strong this day as on the day that Moses sent me" (Joshua 14:10–12). Paul told young Timothy, "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Timothy 4:12). God gives each season its glory, and pride can spoil either one. The young are tempted to scorn the slow, and the old to scorn the restless. Strength fades, and gray hair alone is no virtue. The question is whether we spend our strength on God while we have it and grow wiser as it fades. In Christ, "Even though our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16).
units.application: Churches: put young adults and older saints on the same teams, so energy and wisdom work side by side. Young people: ask an older believer to mentor you, and offer your strength in return, such as helping with a move or a repair. Older believers: do not retire from serving; your experience is a gift. Families: bring grandparents’ stories and children’s energy into the same evening.

rel.note: A rebuke reaches a wise man more than a hundred blows reach a fool, a reminder that correction should use the least force that works.
Correction teaches both the one corrected and those who watch.
The inner depths that correction reaches are the same depths the LORD’s lamp searches.
No one can cleanse his own heart, but God uses correction to cleanse away evil.
The LORD corrects those He loves, so painful correction is a sign of His care, not His rejection.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. In the first line the written text has a verb meaning to scour or polish, while the reading noted in the margin of the Hebrew manuscripts has a related noun meaning a scouring or remedy. The KJV reads "The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil." The NKJV, ESV, NASB and AMP agree on the main sense of painful correction that cleanses.
• Bridges insists that true discipline is given "not in pleasure or caprice, much less in anger, but for profit." Caprice means whim; profit means the good of the one corrected.
• Ironside compares God’s dealings to a surgeon cleaning a wound: the probing is "very painful, but good in result."
• God’s discipline "yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it" (Hebrews 12:11).
• Compare 3:11–12; 17:10; 19:25; Psalm 119:71.
units.summary: Some wounds heal: God’s correction hurts in order to make the heart clean.
units.principle: Painful correction given in love can reach and cleanse the heart in ways words alone cannot, but it must always aim at restoration, never at harm.
units.insight: Manasseh filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood. Only when he was bound with bronze fetters and carried to Babylon did he humble himself, and God heard him and brought him home (2 Chronicles 33:10–13). The prodigal "came to himself" in a pigsty, not at a banquet (Luke 15:17). The psalmist confessed, "Before I was afflicted I went astray, But now I keep Your word" (Psalm 119:67). God’s correction is never rejection: "whom the LORD loves He corrects" (3:12). Yet the deepest cleansing came through stripes laid on Another. Isaiah saw the Servant "wounded for our transgressions," and wrote, "by His stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). The punishment our sin deserved fell on Christ. What His people now receive is a Father’s loving discipline, aimed at making them whole.
units.application: Parents: correct calmly and never in anger; explain the wrong, keep restoration in view, and never humiliate. If your discipline has crossed into harshness, stop, apologize and seek help. Anyone facing hard consequences of their own choices: ask what God is cleansing, not only how to escape the pain. Church leaders: let every correction of a member aim at restoring that person "in a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1).

rel.note: A man plans his way but the LORD directs his steps, the same rule of providence applied to every person.
A man's steps are of the LORD, the saying just before this chapter that 21:1 carries up to the king's heart.
The LORD who directs the king's heart also weighs every human heart.
The chapter closes as it opens, with no counsel standing against the LORD and victory belonging to Him.
Many seek the ruler's favor, but justice comes from the LORD, who holds the ruler's heart.

units.notes:
• The word translated "rivers" means a channel or stream, often a ditch cut to water a field, not a great river. The same phrase, "rivers of water," describes the streams beside the fruitful tree of Psalm 1:3. The ESV and NLT have "stream."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "As a farmer channels the water where he wants and regulates its flow, so does the Lord with the king."
• Scripture shows the LORD turning rulers who did not know Him: Cyrus, whose spirit He "stirred up" to send the exiles home (Ezra 1:1), and Artaxerxes, in whose heart God put the desire to beautify His house (Ezra 7:27). Even hostile kings serve His purpose (Revelation 17:17).
• The chapter opens and closes with the LORD ruling the two great powers of Solomon's world: the throne here, and the army in 21:30–31.
• Compare 16:9; 20:24; Daniel 4:32; Acts 4:27–28.
units.summary: No throne sits above God's hand; even a king's heart flows where the LORD channels it.
units.principle: God governs the hearts of the powerful without erasing their responsibility, so His people can trust Him above every throne and pray for those who sit on them.
units.insight: Nehemiah stood before Artaxerxes with the king's cup in his hand, knowing a sad face could cost him his life. When the king asked what he wanted, "I prayed to the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 2:4), and then he spoke. The king granted his request, "according to the good hand of my God upon me" (Nehemiah 2:8). Our hearts swing between fearing the powerful and trusting them too much. This verse cures both. Bridges draws the comfort: "not kings, but the King of kings reigneth." The clearest proof came at the cross. Herod and Pilate gathered against Jesus and did only what God's hand had determined beforehand (Acts 4:27–28). The same verse asks a question of us. A king's heart yields to God like water to a farmer's hoe. Does yours, or does it resist every turn He makes?
units.application: If you are anxious about an election, a court ruling or a decision made above your head, turn the worry into specific prayer for the person who holds that power (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Employees: before you raise a hard matter with a difficult manager, pray as Nehemiah did, then speak respectfully and plainly. Leaders and parents: your decisions answer to Someone greater, so ask Him this week to steer the one you are weighing.

rel.note: The near-twin saying: ways that seem pure to a man are weighed by the LORD, who weighs the spirits.
The God who holds the king's heart weighs every other heart as well.
The LORD who weighs hearts sees the wicked intent behind an offering.
Because the LORD weighs hearts, the next saying ranks a just life above ritual.
The pure man's work actually is right, set against the man whose way is only right in his own eyes.
He who weighs the hearts will not accept the excuse "we did not know," applying this truth to neglected duty.

units.notes:
• This saying nearly repeats 16:2, "All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, But the LORD weighs the spirits." Solomon's collection often repeats a saying with small changes, pressing the point home. The same title, "He who weighs the hearts," returns in 24:12 as a warning against pleading ignorance.
• The KJV has "pondereth the hearts." The picture is a merchant's balance: God's verdict on a person is measured exactly, not guessed.
• Bridges: "There are no persons in the world, about whom we make so many mistakes as ourselves."
• Jehu and Jehonadab rode together in the same campaign against Baal worship (2 Kings 10:15–28). Jehonadab's house was later commended for its faithfulness (Jeremiah 35:18–19), while Jehu did not walk in the law of the LORD with all his heart (2 Kings 10:31). The same outward work was weighed differently.
• Compare 14:12; 1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Hebrews 4:12–13.
units.summary: We are rarely the villains of our own stories, but God weighs what we cannot see in ourselves.
units.principle: Self-approval proves nothing; God judges motives as well as actions, so the only safe verdict on a life is His.
units.insight: Saul was sure he had obeyed. He spared the best of Amalek's flocks and told Samuel, "I have performed the commandment of the LORD" (1 Samuel 15:13). God saw a man who feared the people more than Him (1 Samuel 15:24). Paul had a clear conscience and still refused to rest on it: "I know of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this; but He who judges me is the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:4). Where are you most certain you are right? That may be the place to ask God to weigh you, with David's prayer: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23). The scale that exposes us is held by the God who justifies the ungodly who trust in Christ (Romans 4:5). He weighs our hearts, finds them wanting, and gives His Son's righteousness in their place.
units.application: Choose one conflict where you feel fully justified and write down what you want out of it, not only what you did. Ask your spouse or a trusted friend, "Where do you see me excusing myself?" and listen without defending. Parents: when you correct a child, ask about the motive as well as the behavior. Leaders: invite honest review of a plan before you call it right, especially from people who see it differently.

rel.note: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination while the prayer of the upright is His delight, the same ranking of heart over ritual.
Doing justice pleases the LORD and is also the joy of the just.
The LORD weighs hearts, which is why ritual alone cannot satisfy Him.
The chapter's second sacrifice saying shows the other side: the offering of the wicked is an abomination.
The wicked refuse to do the very justice this verse says God prizes above sacrifice.
Even the prayer of one who turns his ear from God's law is an abomination.

units.notes:
• "Righteousness and justice" are a frequent pair in Scripture for a life and a society set right before God, as in Amos 5:24: "But let justice run down like water, And righteousness like a mighty stream."
• Sacrifice brackets the chapter. Here justice pleases God more than sacrifice; in 21:27 the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination.
• Jesus twice quoted Hosea 6:6, "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), and He rebuked those who tithed garden herbs while neglecting "justice and mercy and faith" (Matthew 23:23).
• Bridges: "He has accepted the moral without the ceremonial; but never the ceremonial without the moral". In plain terms, God has received obedience that came without ritual, but never ritual that came without obedience.
• Compare 15:8; Isaiah 1:11–17; Micah 6:6–8; Mark 12:32–33.
units.summary: God would rather have a just life than a crowded altar.
units.principle: Worship pleases God when it comes from a life that does what is right; no religious act can replace justice and mercy toward others.
units.insight: Saul wanted to offer God the plunder he had been told to destroy, and Samuel's answer still stands: "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Israel kept its feasts while neglecting the fatherless and the widow, and God said He was weary of their offerings (Isaiah 1:13–17). We have our own versions: the faithful attender who cheats his customers, the generous giver who will not speak to her sister. Jesus said to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled first (Matthew 5:23–24). Bridges names the root in one line: "Cain brought the sacrifice, not the heart." The gospel does not lower this standard. Christ offered the one sacrifice that truly takes away sin (Hebrews 10:12), and those He cleanses present themselves as "a living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1). That is worship that reaches Monday's business as well as Sunday's service.
units.application: Before Sunday, ask whether there is a debt you owe, a wage you have held back or a wrong you have not made right, and settle it first (Matthew 5:23–24). Business owners: test your prices, contracts and pay against righteousness and justice, not only against the law. Worship leaders and volunteers: let how you treat people off the platform match what you sing on it. Keep worshiping; bring a just life with your offering.

rel.note: The lamp of the wicked will be put out, the image behind the alternative reading "lamp" in this verse.
Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD, the inward pride this verse names.
The proud heart of this verse grows into the full portrait of the scoffer who acts with arrogant pride.
Even the worship of the wicked is an abomination, as even his plowing is counted sin.
A proud look heads the list of things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "A haughty look" is literally "height of eyes," eyes lifted above others. David disowns the same posture: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, Nor my eyes lofty" (Psalm 131:1).
• The Hebrew word rendered "plowing" can also be read as "lamp," and the ESV and NASB (1995) translate it that way. On that reading the line speaks of the outward prosperity of the wicked, since a burning lamp pictures life and well-being in Proverbs (13:9). The KJV, like the NKJV, has "plowing," with "light" in its margin.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "This figure indicates that the product of the wicked is sin." Whether the word is "plowing" or "lamp," what the proud produce is tainted by its source.
• Bridges: "The motive determines the act." Plowing done in dependence on God honors Him; the same plowing done with no thought of God becomes part of a life lived against Him.
• Compare 6:16–17; 16:5; 1 Corinthians 10:31; Titus 1:15.
units.summary: Pride stains everything it touches, even an honest day's plowing.
units.principle: Pride corrupts not only what a person does but why he does it; even ordinary work done for self alone, without regard for God, falls short in His sight.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar walked on his palace roof and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…?" (Daniel 4:30). Building a city was not his sin; claiming the glory was. He was driven out until he learned "that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men" (Daniel 4:32). Jesus told of a rich farmer whose fields yielded well. He planned bigger barns and told himself, "eat, drink, and be merry," and God called him a fool (Luke 12:16–20). His farming was fine; his heart left God out. Busy, capable people can be diligent, productive, even generous, and still do it all for themselves. The cure is not to stop working but to receive a new heart. "To the pure all things are pure" (Titus 1:15), and those Christ has cleansed can plow, cook, code and teach "as to the Lord" (Colossians 3:23).
units.application: Before your workday starts, offer it to God in one sentence and ask Him to show you any pride driving it. Students and young professionals: notice the "haughty look" toward classmates or coworkers you consider beneath you, and do one kind thing for one of them this week. Business owners and high achievers: when a project succeeds, thank God and the people who helped before you tell anyone about your own part.

rel.note: The diligent set against the slack hand is the book's usual contrast, which this verse varies by naming the hasty instead.
What is gathered by labor increases, the slow and steady growth this verse commends.
He sins who hastens with his feet, the same danger of action that outruns thought.
The next saying shows where the rush to get rich often turns: to treasure gained by lying.
He who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished, haste applied to the pursuit of wealth.

units.notes:
• "Plans" are the thoughts or devisings behind the work; the KJV reads "The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness." The verse values thinking ahead as much as working hard.
• The hasty person appears elsewhere in the book: "he sins who hastens with his feet" (19:2), and "he who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished" (28:20).
• Henry: "Forecast is as good as work." By "forecast" he means planning ahead; thinking the job through is part of diligence, not a delay to it.
• Esau traded his birthright for one meal because he wanted it at once (Genesis 25:29–34; Hebrews 12:16). Haste gave up what could only be gained over time.
• Compare 13:11; 20:21; 24:27; Luke 14:28–30.
units.summary: Steady beats speedy: careful plans grow into plenty, while hurry runs toward want.
units.principle: Careful plans joined to patient effort tend toward fruitfulness, while haste that skips thinking and grabs for quick returns tends toward loss.
units.insight: Esau came in from the field hungry and sold his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34). Abraham and Sarah tried to hurry God's promise through Hagar and reaped years of grief (Genesis 16). Haste is often the impatience of a heart that does not trust God's timing. It hides in good things too: the ministry built too fast, the relationship rushed, the investment that promised to double. Isaiah's word steadies us: "Whoever believes will not act hastily" (Isaiah 28:16). Jesus was never in a hurry. He stayed two more days when Lazarus was sick (John 11:6), yet He finished the work the Father gave Him to do (John 17:4). Where are you rushing because you do not trust God to provide in His time?
units.application: Before a major purchase, job change or investment, write a plan, count the cost (Luke 14:28) and wait a set time before you sign. Young adults: be wary of any scheme that promises quick money for little work. Small-business owners: choose steady growth you can sustain over a rush that cuts corners on quality or honesty. Parents: teach children to save toward something rather than buy it today.

rel.note: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, the same verdict on ill-gotten wealth.
Wealth gained by dishonesty dwindles, the vanishing this verse pictures as vapor.
Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet at first and turns to gravel, the bitter end of lying gain.
Another road in this chapter ends among the dead, the end those who seek death will reach.
The hasty push for gain in the previous verse often turns into the lying tongue of this one.

units.notes:
• Behind "fleeting fantasy" stand two Hebrew words. The first, hebel, means vapor or breath; it is the word Ecclesiastes uses for "vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The second means driven away. Together they picture a breath of vapor blown off by the wind. The KJV has "a vanity tossed to and fro."
• The ESV ends the verse with "a snare of death." The ancient Greek and Latin translations read "snares of death," and some Hebrew manuscripts have the word for "snares," which differs by one letter from the word for "those who seek." Most Hebrew manuscripts, followed by the NKJV and KJV, read "those who seek death."
• Bridges: "Unrighteous gain is a dear bargain." "Dear" here means costly: what is gained by lies costs far more than it brings.
• Scripture shows the pattern in Gehazi, whose lie to win Naaman's silver ended in leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27), and in Ananias and Sapphira, who lied about the price of their land and died (Acts 5:1–10).
• Compare 10:2; 13:11; 20:17; Jeremiah 17:11; James 5:1–4.
units.summary: Wealth won by lies is a breath on a cold morning, and the liar is walking toward death.
units.principle: Riches gained by deceit cannot last, and the pursuit of them leads toward ruin, because a life built on lies is built on vapor.
units.insight: Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver and got his money. Within hours it was unbearable. He threw it down in the temple and went out and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5). The treasure was vapor, and the road ended in death, just as this verse says. Jesus asked, "For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his own soul?" (Matthew 16:26). Most of the lies that build wealth are small: an inflated expense report, a hidden defect, a padded résumé. Look closely at your own dealings. Christ offers treasure that does not vanish (Matthew 6:19–20), and He welcomes the dishonest who come clean, as He welcomed Zacchaeus (Luke 19:8–10).
units.application: Salespeople and business owners: refuse the small lie that closes the deal, such as the hidden fee or the overstated claim. Employees: keep expense reports, timesheets and résumés exact. If you already hold something gained by deceit, make it right as Zacchaeus did, with restitution where you can (Luke 19:8). Parents: praise a child's truthfulness when it costs them something, so they learn that truth is worth more than gain.

rel.note: The wicked will fall by his own wickedness, the principle behind violence that destroys its users.
The violent gang lies in wait for its own blood, the same recoil of violence on those who use it.
The wicked becoming a ransom for the righteous is another form of the same recoil of evil on its authors.
The same verb "refuse" describes the lazy man's hands, showing that both injustice and laziness are choices of the will.
The LORD prizes doing justice above sacrifice, the very justice the wicked here refuse to do.
Whoever digs a pit falls into it, a picture of harm that comes back on the one who plans it.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NLT render the verb "sweep" and "sweeps," closer to the Hebrew picture of dragging something away than the NKJV's "destroy." The KJV calls the violence "robbery," with "saw" in the margin for "destroy," that is, the violence will saw them apart.
• The verb translated "refuse" returns at 21:25, where the lazy man's hands "refuse to labor." In both sayings the trouble lies in the will, not in a lack of knowledge or ability.
• Bridges: "It is not ignorance or inconsideration, but wilfulness, that destroys". "Inconsideration" means thoughtlessness, and "wilfulness" means a stubborn choice.
• Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it (Esther 7:10). The men who had Daniel thrown to the lions were thrown in themselves (Daniel 6:24).
• Compare 1:18–19; 11:5; 26:27; Psalm 7:15–16.
units.summary: Violence is a net the wicked throw at others and end up caught in themselves.
units.principle: Those who choose force over justice set in motion the ruin they plan for others; the refusal to do right is itself the seed of destruction.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard. Jezebel arranged false witnesses, Naboth was stoned, and Ahab went down to take possession (1 Kings 21:1–16). Elijah met him in the vineyard with God's sentence: where dogs licked Naboth's blood, they would lick his (1 Kings 21:19). Violence looked efficient, but it dragged the whole house down (2 Kings 9:30–37). Most of us will never seize a vineyard. Yet the same choice of force over justice can live in us: the habit of winning by force of voice or position, the pressure that bends others to our will. Jesus took the opposite path. When Peter drew a sword, He said, "all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). He refused force in His own defense and bore the violence of others to save them (Isaiah 53:5). Those who follow Him can lay down force and take up justice.
units.application: If you lead a team, a classroom or a household, look at how you get people to comply: by fairness and reason, or by intimidation and a raised voice? Change one pattern this week. Business leaders: refuse practices that squeeze workers or suppliers simply because you can. If you are living under someone else's force, seek safety and help; you may leave final justice to God (Romans 12:19) without staying in harm's way.

rel.note: He who walks with integrity walks securely, while the one who perverts his ways will become known.
Integrity guides the upright while perversity destroys the unfaithful, the same two paths.
Even a child is known by whether his deeds are pure and right, the outward life revealing the inner one.
The man whose way is right in his own eyes stands beside the pure man whose work is right in fact.
Covering sin does not prosper, but confession brings mercy, the way out of the guilty man's crooked path.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word translated "guilty" occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its meaning has been debated. The KJV rendered the line "The way of man is froward and strange," while modern versions agree with the NKJV's "guilty."
• "Right" here is the same Hebrew word as "right" in 21:2. The wording itself sets the man who only seems right in his own eyes beside the man whose work is right.
• Ironside: "Like the trail of the serpent are the ways of a guilty man."
• Daniel shows the straight path of the pure. His enemies examined his conduct, "but they could find no charge or fault, because he was faithful" (Daniel 6:4).
• Compare 10:9; 11:3; 20:11; Matthew 5:8.
units.summary: A guilty conscience cannot walk a straight line, but a clean heart leaves a plain path.
units.principle: What a person is inside shows in how he lives; guilt twists the path into concealment, while a clean heart produces plain, honest work.
units.insight: David's sin with Bathsheba drove him down a crooked road: a summons, a cover story, a loyal soldier who would not go home, and finally a death arranged in battle (2 Samuel 11). Each lie needed another. Only when Nathan said, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7) did the path begin to straighten, through confession. David later described what concealment had done to him: "When I kept silent, my bones grew old" (Psalm 32:3). Many of us know the tiring work of managing a story. The way out is not better management but cleansing: "if we walk in the light as He is in the light… the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). A forgiven person has nothing left to hide, and so can walk straight.
units.application: If you catch yourself rehearsing explanations or keeping track of what you told whom, stop and ask what you are hiding. Confess it to God and, where needed, to the person (James 5:16). Parents: make it safe for children to tell the truth about wrongdoing, so they learn that confession straightens a path. Employees and managers: do the plain, honest version of the job even when no one is checking.

rel.note: A dry morsel with quietness is better than a feast with strife, the same preference of peace over comfort.
The chapter restates the thought with the harsher picture of the wilderness, closing the section this verse opens.
The same saying repeated almost word for word in the Hezekiah collection.
A contentious man kindles strife like charcoal on coals, showing that the warning applies to husbands as well.
A contentious woman is like a continual dripping on a rainy day, another picture of strife that wears a home down.

units.notes:
• "A house shared" is literally "a house of company," a household where people live and gather together; the KJV margin reads "a house of society." The house is roomy and full of life, yet a quarrelsome spirit spoils all of it.
• The saying is repeated almost word for word in 25:24, and 21:19 restates it with a harsher picture. In 19:13 and 27:15 a wife's contentions are "a continual dripping."
• Flat roofs were real living space: Rahab hid the spies on hers (Joshua 2:6), and Peter went up on the housetop to pray (Acts 10:9).
• Bridges: "A solitary life without would be better than a quarrelsome life within." "Without" here means outside the house.
• Compare 17:1; 26:21; Colossians 3:19; 1 Peter 3:7.
units.summary: A cramped corner in peace is worth more than a spacious house full of quarreling.
units.principle: The worth of a home lies in its peace more than its size, and every member of the household either builds that peace or wears it down.
units.insight: On the day David brought the ark to Jerusalem, Michal met him with contempt instead of joy, and the account closes with a marriage that bore no children (2 Samuel 6:20–23). Nabal shows the same spirit in a husband. His own servant said he was "such a scoundrel that one cannot speak to him" (1 Samuel 25:17). Contention is not a woman's sin or a man's sin; it is a heart sin. So what is living with us like? Do our spouses and children find refuge in us, or are they looking for a corner of the roof? James traces quarrels to desires at war within us (James 4:1). Christ came to make peace and to break down the walls of hostility (Ephesians 2:14), and His Spirit grows gentleness where strife ruled (Galatians 5:22–23). A home becomes spacious again when He rules it.
units.application: Husbands and wives: this week, listen to your tone in small disagreements, and drop one recurring complaint for seven days. Parents: ask your teenagers whether home feels peaceful or tense, and listen without defending. If your home is marked by constant quarreling, do not retreat to the roof for good; seek help from a pastor or Christian counselor. Singles thinking about marriage: weigh a person's temper and peaceableness above looks or status.

rel.note: He who despises his neighbor sins, but he who has mercy on the poor is happy, the opposite of the man who shows no favor.
The hardness that shows the neighbor no favor becomes the closed ear toward the poor.
The righteous gives and does not spare, the open hand set against this closed heart.
The wicked rejoice in doing evil, the same appetite for wrongdoing.
The wicked cannot sleep unless they have done evil, a portrait of evil craved like food.

units.notes:
• "Desires" is the language of craving. The NKJV's "soul" is the seat of appetite in Hebrew thought, so the line pictures a hunger for evil, not a mere slip.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "An important truth about depravity: men can sin not merely from weakness but eagerly and ruthlessly."
• Bridges contrasts the believer and the wicked man: "the one does it from constraint, the other from delight." He means that a believer still sins, but against the grain of his renewed will (Romans 7:15–19), while the wicked man sins because he loves it.
• Nabal shows a neighbor finding no favor. David's men had protected his flocks, yet he refused them even bread and water (1 Samuel 25:7–11).
• Compare 2:14; 4:16; 14:21; Luke 10:31–32.
units.summary: Wickedness starts as an appetite and ends with no mercy even for the man next door.
units.principle: Conduct grows from desire; a heart that craves evil will show no mercy even to those closest to it, so the heart's appetites must be changed at the root.
units.insight: Jesus told of a man beaten and left half dead on the road. A priest and a Levite saw him and passed by on the other side (Luke 10:31–32). They were not plotting harm, but their hearts had no room for the man in the ditch. The Samaritan, a despised outsider, "had compassion" (Luke 10:33). This verse shows where their road ends. A heart that follows its own desires slowly loses sight of the neighbor. So the question is not only whether we do harm, but whom we no longer notice. Only God can change what a heart craves. He promises a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26), and the love of Christ, who stopped for us when we lay helpless, teaches us to see even the inconvenient neighbor as someone to show favor to.
units.application: Learn the name and one need of a neighbor you usually pass without speaking, and do one practical kindness for them this month. Parents: when siblings fight, ask each child what they wanted, so they learn that actions grow from desires. Anyone who notices a secret pleasure in another's trouble, such as a rival's failure or an enemy's embarrassment, should name it to God as sin and ask Him to change the craving.

rel.note: A scoffer does not listen to rebuke, which is why he may learn nothing even from punishment.
Striking a scoffer makes the simple wary while the man of understanding learns from rebuke, the same three learners.
A wise man will hear and increase learning, the wise learner of this verse's second line.
The verb of insight behind "instructed" returns as the Righteous One "wisely considers" the house of the wicked.
