The chapter later names the scoffer and traces his scoffing to arrogant pride.
The portrait of the scoffer who hates correction and the wise man who grows wiser when taught.

units.notes:
• Proverbs 19:25 makes the same point in different words: "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will become wary; Rebuke one who has understanding, and he will discern knowledge."
• The verb behind "instructed" has to do with insight. The same verb is translated "wisely considers" in 21:12, and "understanding" in 21:16 is its noun form. The repeated word links three sayings: the wise gain insight when taught, the Righteous One considers the wicked with full insight, and the wanderer leaves the way of insight.
• Bridges: "The blow that strikes one, reaches two—the scorner for punishment; the simple for improvement." "Scorner" is the KJV word for the scoffer.
• Paul applies the principle to church discipline: "Those who are sinning rebuke in the presence of all, that the rest also may fear" (1 Timothy 5:20).
• Compare 1:5; 9:7–9; 13:1; Psalm 32:8–9.
units.summary: Some learn from a word, some from watching others fall, and the scoffer from neither.
units.principle: Wisdom can be learned the easy way, by receiving instruction, or the hard way, by watching others suffer for folly; the scoffer refuses both.
units.insight: When Ananias and Sapphira fell dead for lying to the Holy Spirit, "great fear came upon all the church" (Acts 5:11). Others learned from what they saw. Paul says Israel's failures in the wilderness "were written for our admonition" (1 Corinthians 10:11), so that we would not repeat them. God is kind to teach us by both word and example. The psalmist pleads with us not to be like the horse or mule that must be steered with bit and bridle (Psalm 32:9). Which kind of learner are you? Some of us change only after pain, and the scoffer will not change even then. Jesus describes a better way: the one who hears His sayings and does them builds on the rock before the storm comes (Matthew 7:24–25). His word is meant to spare us the lessons the scoffer learns too late.
units.application: When a colleague, friend or public figure suffers for a foolish choice, do not only shake your head; ask what that choice would look like in your own life. Parents: talk with children about the consequences others face, without gloating. Pastors and leaders: when correction must be public, give it in a way that teaches others too (1 Timothy 5:20). Practice receiving correction the first time it is given.

rel.note: The house of the wicked will be overthrown while the tent of the upright flourishes.
The LORD will destroy the house of the proud, God's judgment on a household built in pride.
The same verb of insight links the wise who are instructed with the Righteous One who considers the wicked.
God's overthrow of the wicked appears again as the wicked becoming a ransom for the righteous.
Do not fret or envy the wicked, for the lamp of the wicked will be put out, the comfort this verse gives the troubled believer.
The curse of the LORD is on the house of the wicked, the same house God considers and overthrows.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew has no separate word for "God" in the first line. It uses "righteous" as a title, the Righteous One, and the NKJV supplies "God" to make the subject clear. The KJV instead reads the first line of "the righteous man" who considers the house of the wicked, and supplies "God" as the subject of the second line. The NKJV reading fits the second line, since overthrowing the wicked is God's work.
• "Wisely considers" is the same verb translated "instructed" in 21:11. God looks at the wicked house with complete insight.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "The destruction of others should be an instruction to us." When God brings down a wicked house, those who watch should take warning and turn from the same sins.
• Psalm 73 tells of a believer who envied the prosperous wicked until he went into God's sanctuary; "then I understood their end" (Psalm 73:17).
• Compare 3:33; 14:11; 15:25; Genesis 18:25.
units.summary: The house of the wicked may look secure from the street, but the Righteous One sees inside.
units.principle: God sees fully into every house that seems secure in its wickedness, and His judgment, though it may wait, is careful and just.
units.insight: Ahab's house in Samaria looked unshakable. He built an ivory palace and left seventy sons (1 Kings 22:39; 2 Kings 10:1). Yet God had weighed that house, and in His time it fell (2 Kings 10:1–11). Asaph nearly lost his footing watching the wicked prosper, until he entered God's sanctuary and saw their end (Psalm 73:2–3, 16–17). Envy and despair at the success of the wicked both forget that God is looking. The verse also searches our own homes. What would the Righteous One find if He considered ours? His gaze is not only judgment. The same God sent His Son, "Jesus Christ the righteous," to be the Advocate of all who turn to Him (1 John 2:1). The house that is weighed and found wanting can be rebuilt on Him.
units.application: If the success of a dishonest coworker, competitor or public figure is eating at you, read Psalm 73 slowly and hand the matter to God. Those who have been wronged: pursue proper remedies, but leave the timing of final justice with Him. Families: take an honest look at what goes on inside your own home, the things neighbors never see, and bring one hidden pattern into the light this week.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, which is why God stands behind their cry.
He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD, the reward of the open ear set against this closed one.
The heart that shows its neighbor no favor is the same heart that shuts its ears to the poor.
He who hides his eyes from the poor will have many curses, the same refusal and its cost.
The righteous considers the cause of the poor, the attentive heart this verse's man refuses to have.

units.notes:
• "Shuts his ears" means stopping them up on purpose; the KJV has "stoppeth his ears." It is the opposite of the righteous man who "considers the cause of the poor" (29:7).
• The Law put God's hearing behind the cry of the weak. Of the widow and the fatherless He said, "I will surely hear their cry" (Exodus 22:23).
• Bridges: "Covetousness and sensuality harden the heart; and when the heart is hard, the ear is deaf." Covetousness is greed for more, and sensuality is living for bodily comfort and pleasure.
• Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus shows the reversal. The man who ignored the beggar at his gate later begged for a drop of water and was refused (Luke 16:19–26).
• Compare 14:31; 19:17; 28:27; 1 John 3:17.
units.summary: Mercy refused to the poor is mercy we cannot expect for ourselves.
units.principle: Hardness toward the needy closes a person off from the mercy he will one day need; mercy received and mercy shown belong together.
units.insight: Nabal heard David's request for food for his men and answered, "Who is David?" (1 Samuel 25:10). He shut his ears, and within days he was dead (1 Samuel 25:38). The rich man in Jesus' story stepped past Lazarus at his gate, and later he was the one crying, "Father Abraham, have mercy on me" (Luke 16:24). Few of us refuse the poor in one dramatic act. We stop our ears gradually, by crossing the street or assuming someone else will help. John asks how God's love can abide in anyone who sees a brother in need "and shuts up his heart from him" (1 John 3:17). Christ heard our cry when we were poor in every way: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). Those who have been heard learn to listen.
units.application: Choose one person in need you have been avoiding, such as a struggling neighbor, a relative behind on bills or someone you pass on the street each day, and stop to listen to them this week. Church leaders: make sure members have a simple way to make needs known. Employers: hear out the worker who says the pay or hours are not enough to live on. Give with wisdom, but do not let caution become a closed ear.

rel.note: A soft answer turns away wrath, the gift of gentle words that also calms anger.
The same "bribe behind the back" is condemned when a wicked man takes it to pervert justice.
A present is like a precious stone to its owner, the power of gifts observed without approval.
A man's gift makes room for him, another observation of how gifts open doors.
The king who receives bribes overthrows the land, the public harm of the bribe this verse describes.

units.notes:
• "Behind the back" renders a Hebrew word for the bosom, the fold of the robe where something could be carried out of sight. The NASB and KJV translate it "bosom."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The verse does not condemn or condone; it merely observes the effectiveness of the practice."
• Abigail met David with bread, wine and figs and a humble plea, and turned him back from shedding blood (1 Samuel 25:18–35). A gift made peace without perverting justice.
• The Law forbids the bribe, "for a bribe blinds the discerning and perverts the words of the righteous" (Exodus 23:8). Samuel's sons "took bribes, and perverted justice" (1 Samuel 8:3), and Felix kept Paul in prison hoping for money (Acts 24:26).
• Compare 17:8; 17:23; 18:16; 29:4.
units.summary: Money can quiet anger, which is exactly why it can also buy injustice.
units.principle: Gifts have real power to calm anger; that power is wise when it restores peace and wicked when it buys favor or bends justice.
units.insight: Abigail heard that David was coming to destroy her household. She hurried out with food and a humble plea, calmed a furious man and kept him from bloodshed, and David blessed God for her (1 Samuel 25:18–33). Judas, by contrast, took money in secret to hand over an innocent man (Matthew 26:14–16). Both used the power this verse describes; their purposes made all the difference. Our hearts are skilled at dressing bribes up as gifts: the favor done to buy silence, the donation that expects influence, the present that makes a complaint go away. Ask what your gifts are meant to purchase. No gift of ours could buy peace with God. Christ made that peace "through the blood of His cross" (Colossians 1:20), a gift given openly so that we would never need to buy His favor.
units.application: When you have offended someone, a thoughtful gift with a sincere apology can help restore peace; let the apology carry the weight. Officials, managers and anyone who decides between people: refuse gifts that come with expectations, and disclose any that might look like one. Donors to churches and charities: give without strings that buy influence. Board and committee members: ask whether money is shaping a decision more than justice is.

rel.note: The LORD's way is strength for the upright and destruction for the workers of iniquity, with the same second line.
The city rejoices when it goes well with the righteous and when the wicked perish, justice as public gladness.
The same word appears as "pleasure": joy in doing justice is set against the love of pleasure that makes a man poor.
Doing justice pleases the LORD more than sacrifice, and here it also gladdens the just.
When the righteous rule the people rejoice, the joy that just government brings.

units.notes:
• The first line can be read as the just person's own delight in doing justice, as in the NKJV, or as a statement about what happens when justice is done in the land. The ESV takes the second view: "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers."
• The second line is identical in the NKJV to the second line of 10:29, "But destruction will come to the workers of iniquity."
• The word for "joy" here is the same Hebrew word translated "pleasure" in 21:17. The just find joy in doing justice, while the man who loves joy for its own sake ends poor.
• Paul says the same of rightful government: "rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil" (Romans 13:3).
• Compare 10:29; 11:10; 29:2; Psalm 1:1–2.
units.summary: Justice is music to the righteous and an alarm bell to the wicked.
units.principle: Justice gladdens those who love what is right and alarms those who practice wrong; how a person feels about justice reveals which way his heart is set.
units.insight: Jesus said, "My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me, and to finish His work" (John 4:34). Obedience was not His burden but His nourishment, as the psalm says: "I delight to do Your will, O my God" (Psalm 40:8). Felix heard the same message and reacted the opposite way. When Paul reasoned with him about "righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was afraid" (Acts 24:25). The same truth that gladdens one person frightens another. Where do you stand when justice comes near: when an audit is announced, when the truth comes out, when someone asks hard questions? Dread can be a mercy, a warning to turn while there is time. Joy in doing right is not something we manufacture. It is the fruit of a heart God has made new, with His law written within (Hebrews 8:10).
units.application: Notice your reaction the next time a rule is enforced, an error is discovered or a hard truth is told: relief or dread? Let it show you your heart. Managers and parents: make doing right a matter of gladness by noticing and thanking fairness, not only punishing wrongs. Jurors, officials and anyone who must judge between people: take joy in a fair decision, even when it costs you popularity.

rel.note: A way can seem right and still end in death, which is why drift feels harmless.
Ceasing to listen to instruction makes a son stray from knowledge, the first step of the drift this verse traces to its end.
The turning away of the simple will slay them, the deadly drift this verse describes.
Another road in this chapter, the pursuit of lying gain, also ends in death.
The paths of the immoral woman lead to the dead, using the same word for the departed.
The dead are already in Folly's house, the same company the wanderer joins.

units.notes:
• The word for "the dead" here, rephaim, is the one used in 2:18 and 9:18, which the NKJV also renders "the dead." It refers to the departed in the realm of the dead.
• "Understanding" is the noun form of the verb translated "instructed" in 21:11 and "wisely considers" in 21:12. The wanderer leaves the very way of insight that the wise receive.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "As every motion has an end, so every journey has a goal."
• Bridges: "Beware of the first wandering step, whether it may be in doctrine or in practice." Drift can begin in what we believe or in how we live.
• Compare 1:32; 2:18–19; 14:12; Hebrews 2:1; James 5:19–20.
units.summary: No one plans to end up among the dead; they simply stop watching the path.
units.principle: Drifting from wisdom is never harmless; every path has an end, and the one that leaves understanding leads to death unless the wanderer turns back.
units.insight: Lot did not move into Sodom all at once. He chose the well-watered plain and "pitched his tent even as far as Sodom" (Genesis 13:12); later he was sitting in its gate (Genesis 19:1). Demas served beside Paul, then forsook him, "having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Even Solomon, whose collection this is, let his heart be turned away in old age (1 Kings 11:4). Drift rarely feels like rebellion. It feels like a few missed weeks, a softened conviction, a new circle of friends. Hebrews warns, "we must give the more earnest heed to the things we have heard, lest we drift away" (Hebrews 2:1). Yet the Good Shepherd goes after the one sheep that wandered (Luke 15:4–7). If you have drifted, the way back is still open today.
units.application: Look back over the last three months and ask what you have quietly dropped: prayer, Scripture, fellowship or accountability. Restart one this week. Friends and small-group leaders: when someone stops showing up, reach out within the week instead of waiting (James 5:19–20). Parents of young adults: keep the door open and the conversation warm; drift is reversed more often by patient love than by lectures.

rel.note: Wine is a mocker that leads people astray, one way the love of wine brings loss.
The same word is the just person's joy in doing justice, set against the love of pleasure for its own sake.
The wise keep oil stored in their dwelling, while the lover of wine and oil spends it.
The drunkard and the glutton come to poverty, the same ruin of a life given to feasting.

units.notes:
• The word translated "pleasure" is the same Hebrew word translated "joy" in 21:15. The just find joy in doing justice, while the man who loves joy for its own sake ends poor.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The 'love' that is here portrayed must be excessive or uncontrolled, because it brings one to poverty."
• Bridges: "the way to enjoy pleasure is not to love it". Pleasure is best enjoyed by someone who does not live for it.
• The prodigal son "wasted his possessions with prodigal living" and ended up longing for the food of the pigs he fed (Luke 15:13–16).
• Compare 21:20; 23:20–21; 1 Timothy 6:17; 2 Timothy 3:4.
units.summary: Love the gift more than the Giver, and the gift will leave you poor.
units.principle: God's gifts are meant to be enjoyed with thanks, not loved for their own sake; a life organized around pleasure drains the very resources it spends.
units.insight: The prodigal son took his inheritance to a far country and "wasted his possessions with prodigal living" (Luke 15:13). Within a season he was hungry enough to envy pigs. Jesus' story does not end in the pigsty, though. The son came to himself and went home, and his father ran to meet him (Luke 15:17–20). Paul warns of people who are "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God" (2 Timothy 3:4). Our age offers endless ways to spend on the next good time: dining, travel, entertainment, subscriptions. None of these is wrong in itself; the question is what we love. God "gives us richly all things to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17), and at His right hand "are pleasures forevermore" (Psalm 16:11). The lover of pleasure is not wrong to want joy. He is looking for it in too small a place.
units.application: Review last month's spending and ask which purchases were gifts received with thanks and which were attempts to fill an emptiness. Young adults with a first paycheck: set aside giving and saving before you budget for fun. Families: plan celebrations that are generous but not ruinous, and teach children to thank God for good things. If drinking, gambling or spending feels out of control, tell someone you trust and get help.

rel.note: The righteous is delivered from trouble and it comes to the wicked instead, the plainest statement of this reversal.
The Righteous One who overthrows the wicked is the God who turns their trouble back on them.
The violence of the wicked sweeps them away, another form of the same reversal.
Whoever digs a pit falls into it, the same recoil of evil on its author.
Whoever leads the upright astray falls into his own pit, the scheme turning back on the schemer.

units.notes:
• "Ransom" translates kopher, a payment given to redeem or cover a life, as in Exodus 21:30. Isaiah uses it of nations given in Israel's place: "I gave Egypt for your ransom" (Isaiah 43:3).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The metaphor should not be pushed to walk on all fours by asking to whom the ransom is paid." In other words, the picture makes one point, the reversal, and should not be pressed for every detail.
• Ironside: "Justice demands the punishment of the guilty, in order that the guiltless may be delivered; but love gave the Guiltless to die that the guilty might be justified."
• Daniel's accusers show the same reversal: the men who had him thrown to the lions were thrown in themselves (Daniel 6:24).
• Compare 11:8; 28:10; Isaiah 43:3–4; Mark 10:45; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
units.summary: The wicked fall into the trouble they planned; at the cross, the Just took the place of the unjust.
units.principle: Under God's justice the harm the wicked plan for the righteous tends to fall on themselves, while in Christ God's grace provides the Righteous One in place of the unrighteous.
units.insight: Barabbas was a robber, held with rebels who had committed murder (Mark 15:7; John 18:40). By every rule of justice he should have died, and Jesus should have gone free. Instead the crowd chose Barabbas, and the innocent One went to the cross in his place. This proverb shows God's justice, the wicked falling into the trouble meant for the righteous. The cross shows what Proverbs does not say, God's mercy giving the Righteous for the unrighteous: "the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). Every one of us stands where Barabbas stood. Those who trust Christ need not fear standing among the wicked on whom judgment falls, because He has already taken their place. Since God deals justly with those who plot against His people, we can leave revenge to Him.
units.application: If someone is scheming against you at work or in your family, keep doing right, keep careful records where needed, and leave the outcome to God instead of plotting a counterattack (Romans 12:19). If you have been tempted to set a trap for a rival, drop it now. This week, thank Christ by name for taking your place, and let that gratitude shape how you treat someone who has wronged you.

rel.note: A wrathful man stirs up strife while one slow to anger calms it, showing anger as the fuel of household conflict.
The first form of the saying, with the corner of the housetop, opens the section this verse closes.
The housetop saying repeated in the Hezekiah collection.
A contentious woman is a continual dripping that cannot be restrained, another picture of a strife-filled home.
An angry man stirs up strife, the same warning applied to men.

units.notes:
• "Angry" translates a word for vexation or provocation, the irritability that keeps others on edge. The ESV has "a quarrelsome and fretful woman."
• Bridges: "The woman only is mentioned. Yet the disruption is as frequent, and at least as guilty, from an imperious husband, as from a scolding wife." "Imperious" means domineering.
• The wilderness was the place of hardship and solitude, where Hagar wandered with her son (Genesis 21:14) and David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14).
• Paul gives the remedy to every household: "Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and evil speaking be put away from you" (Ephesians 4:31).
• Compare 15:18; 21:9; 25:24; 27:15–16; 29:22.
units.summary: A lonely desert is easier to live in than a home where anger never rests.
units.principle: Constant anger can make a home lonelier than a desert; peace in a household is worth more than comfort, and every member is responsible for it.
units.insight: Each year Elkanah's family went up to worship at Shiloh, and each year Peninnah "provoked her severely, to make her miserable" (1 Samuel 1:6), until Hannah wept and would not eat. A home that should have been a refuge had become a wilderness. Anger in a household often hides hurt, rivalry or fear, and we can be the provoking one without seeing it. "For the wrath of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:20). Hannah shows another way. She did not answer provocation with provocation but poured out her soul before the LORD (1 Samuel 1:10–15). Christ walked that way perfectly: "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). He gives His peace to those who come to Him (John 14:27), and His peace can turn a wilderness home back into a dwelling.
units.application: Ask your spouse or the people you live with, "Do I make home feel tense?" and receive the answer without arguing. If anger is the climate of your home, get help early from a pastor or Christian counselor instead of simply withdrawing. Parents: model how to disagree without contempt, and apologize to your children when you lose your temper. If you are ever unsafe at home, seek protection at once.

rel.note: A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren, the long view that wise saving makes possible.
The lover of wine and oil will not be rich, the spender who empties what the wise keep.
The righteous give and do not spare, so the reserves of the wise are kept for sharing, not hoarding.
By knowledge the rooms of a house are filled with precious riches, the well-stocked dwelling of the wise.
The ant gathers food in harvest for the season ahead, the same wisdom of storing up.

units.notes:
• "Squanders" pictures swallowing something down. The KJV has "spendeth it up," and the ESV "devours it."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The verse basically means that the wise gain wealth but the foolish squander it."
• Henry: "Foolish children spend what their wise parents have laid up." The saving of one generation can be swallowed by the next.
• Joseph stored grain in the years of plenty so that Egypt could live through the famine (Genesis 41:35–36, 53–57). In Jesus' parable of the ten virgins, the wise took oil in their vessels and the foolish took none (Matthew 25:1–13).
• Compare 6:6–8; 13:22; 24:3–4; 30:25.
units.summary: Wisdom keeps something back for tomorrow; folly swallows whatever comes in today.
units.principle: Wisdom stores up and stewards what God provides, so there is enough for tomorrow and for others, while folly consumes everything as fast as it comes.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable ten virgins waited for the bridegroom. Five were wise and took oil in their vessels; five took none. When the cry came at midnight, the foolish had run out, and the door was shut before they returned (Matthew 25:1–13). The parable is about being ready for Christ's coming, and it draws on the same picture of a wise house with oil in store. The heart that cannot save money often cannot wait for anything; it lives for now. Yet the answer is not hoarding. The rich fool stored up for himself and lost his soul (Luke 12:20–21). The answer is faithful stewardship. What are you storing up: in the bank, in your character, in your walk with God? Jesus said, "lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:20).
units.application: Start or rebuild an emergency fund this month, even if it is a small amount set aside each payday. Young couples: agree on a budget that saves before it spends. Parents: teach children to divide money into giving, saving and spending. Church treasurers and ministry leaders: keep sensible reserves so the work is not one crisis from collapse. And keep your own lamp supplied with daily time in God's word.

rel.note: Righteousness leads to life, the first of the gifts this verse names.
The LORD loves him who follows righteousness, the same pursuit with God's love as its reward.
The righteous person who gives and does not spare is the one who pursues mercy as well as righteousness.
Humility and the fear of the LORD bring riches, honor and life, a related list of the fruit of godliness.
Keeping mercy and truth brings favor and high esteem with God and man.

units.notes:
• "Mercy" translates chesed, steadfast and loyal love, the word often used of God's faithful love for His people. The ESV has "kindness."
• In the second line the word translated "righteousness" can also mean vindication or well-being: being shown to be in the right and enjoying the blessing that follows. Some translations take it that way and render it "prosperity." The NKJV, ESV, NASB and NLT repeat "righteousness."
• Henry, on the word "follows": "though we cannot attain to perfection, yet it will be a comfort to us if we aim at it and follow after it."
• Jesus gave the same order: "seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matthew 6:33). Paul told Timothy to "pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness" (1 Timothy 6:11).
• Compare 3:3–4; 11:19; 15:9; 22:4; Micah 6:8.
units.summary: Chase righteousness and kindness, and you will find more than you were chasing.
units.principle: Those who pursue right living and faithful love tend to find life, righteousness and honor along the way, because God delights to give more than is sought.
units.insight: Boaz shows this verse in a life. He dealt rightly with the law of redemption and showed a foreign widow kindness far beyond duty (Ruth 2:8–16; 4:1–10). He was not chasing fame, yet his name stands in the line of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:21–22; Matthew 1:5). Many people chase life and honor directly and never catch them. This verse redirects the chase: pursue righteousness and mercy, and leave the rest to God. Jesus is the fullest picture of both, "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). In Him the reward becomes a gift, for He Himself became our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). Even when honor is withheld in this life, He has promised, "If anyone serves Me, him My Father will honor" (John 12:26). Which half of the pair comes harder to you, righteousness or mercy?
units.application: Pick one relationship where you have been right but not kind, or kind but not truthful, and work on the missing half this week. Young people planning a career: ask what kind of person you want to become before you ask how much you want to earn. Leaders: build a culture that rewards integrity and loyalty, not only results. When doing right goes unnoticed, keep at it and leave the honor to God.

rel.note: Ruling one's spirit is greater than taking a city, a reminder of the hardest stronghold of all.
The LORD's name is a strong tower, while the rich man's wealth is a strong city only in his own esteem, like the stronghold the mighty trusted.
Plans are established by counsel and war is waged by wise guidance.
Wisdom overcomes strength, yet no wisdom stands against the LORD, and victory is His.
A wise man is strong and by wise counsel wages war, the same triumph of wisdom over force.

units.notes:
• "Trusted stronghold" renders a phrase meaning literally "the strength in which it trusted," which puts the stress on the defenders' confidence. The KJV has "the strength of the confidence thereof."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "It is more effective to use wisdom than to rely on strength."
• David took the stronghold of Jebus, whose defenders boasted that even the blind and lame could hold it, by sending men up the water shaft (2 Samuel 5:6–8). Joshua took Ai by an ambush after a frontal attack had failed (Joshua 7:2–5; 8:1–22).
• Paul applies the image to spiritual battle: "the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty in God for pulling down strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4).
• Compare 16:32; 20:18; 24:5–6; Ecclesiastes 9:13–18.
units.summary: Walls stop armies; wisdom finds the way over them.
units.principle: Wisdom can overcome what strength and fortifications cannot, and confidence placed in walls, numbers or force is weaker than it looks.
units.insight: Ecclesiastes tells of a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man whom no one remembered afterward (Ecclesiastes 9:14–15). Wisdom often works quietly and goes unthanked, yet it brings down walls that force cannot. Many of us face strongholds that feel impregnable: a habit that has held for years, a fear, a family pattern, an argument raised against God. Paul says such strongholds fall not to human force but to weapons "mighty in God," as every thought is brought captive to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:4–5). Jesus pictured Satan as a strong man guarding his palace, until "a stronger than he" overcomes him and "takes from him all his armor in which he trusted" (Luke 11:21–22). Christ, "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), has already breached that fortress. What stronghold are you still treating as unbeatable?
units.application: Leaders facing a problem bigger than your resources: before adding more force or money, gather wise counsel and think through a better strategy (20:18). Parents facing a strong-willed child: wisdom and patience will accomplish what volume cannot. Anyone fighting a long-standing sin: name the stronghold, bring Scripture against it, ask a trusted believer to pray with you, and stop relying on willpower alone.

rel.note: In many words sin is not lacking, but restraining the lips is wise.
He who guards his mouth preserves his life, the same saying in nearly the same words.
The person of understanding spares his words, the restraint this verse calls a guard.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, the stakes of guarding it.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the same verb, shamar, stands behind "guards" and "keeps." The guard set over the mouth becomes a guard over the life.
• "Soul" here means the whole person and his life, not only the inner spirit.
• Henry: "Keep thy heart, and that will keep thy tongue from sin; keep thy tongue, and that will keep thy heart from trouble."
• David prayed for this guard: "Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; Keep watch over the door of my lips" (Psalm 141:3). Moses, provoked at Meribah, "spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33) and was barred from leading Israel into the land (Numbers 20:10–12).
• Compare 10:19; 13:3; 18:21; James 3:2–10.
units.summary: Many of life's troubles walk in through the front door of our own mouths.
units.principle: Much avoidable trouble comes through careless words, so guarding what we say is one of the surest ways to guard our lives.
units.insight: Jephthah made a rash vow before battle, and his own daughter came out to meet him on his return (Judges 11:30–35). Peter swore he would never deny Jesus, and within hours he swore he did not know Him (Matthew 26:33–35, 69–74). Most of us can name troubles that began with our own words. James says no one can tame the tongue (James 3:8), so a guarded mouth must begin with a changed heart: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). Jesus is the perfect pattern. He "committed no sin, Nor was deceit found in His mouth" (1 Peter 2:22), and before His accusers He was silent when silence was wisdom (Isaiah 53:7). The Spirit He gives can set the guard David prayed for. Where will you most need that guard on your words this week?
units.application: Before you post, text or reply in anger this week, wait an hour and reread it. Married couples: agree on a signal for when a conversation is getting heated, and pause. Employees and team members: refuse to pass along gossip about a coworker; change the subject or speak well of them. Parents: think through your words before a hard conversation with a teenager. Make no promise you have not thought through.

rel.note: A scoffer does not listen to rebuke, the behavior that pride produces.
Pride goes before destruction, the end of the arrogant path this verse names.
The scoffer named here is the one whose punishment teaches the simple.
The proud heart and haughty look of 21:4 grow here into a whole character.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble, the alternative set beside this portrait.
The gallery portrait of the scoffer who hates correction, to which this verse adds the root of pride.

units.notes:
• The KJV renders the verse, "Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath." The scoffer's pride spills over into angry contempt for others.
• Henry: "Most of the wrath that inflames the spirits and societies of men is proud wrath." He means that most of the anger that sets people and communities on fire comes from wounded pride.
• Ironside sets this man apart from someone who loses his temper under strong provocation and grieves over it afterward; the scoffer "has no compunction of conscience because of his wrong spirit." "Compunction" means remorse.
• Pharaoh shows the type: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go?" (Exodus 5:2).
• Compare 1:22; 3:34; 9:7–9; 13:1; 16:18; James 4:6.
units.summary: Pride practiced long enough becomes a name: Scoffer.
units.principle: Pride left unchecked hardens into a settled character of contempt, and the one who scorns correction becomes known by the pride he refuses to confess.
units.insight: Pharaoh met God's command with a sneer, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice…?" (Exodus 5:2), and hardened himself plague after plague until his army lay in the sea. Haman's pride could not bear one man who would not bow, so he plotted to destroy a whole people (Esther 3:5–6). Yet Scripture also shows pride broken. Nebuchadnezzar, humbled, confessed that "those who walk in pride He is able to put down" (Daniel 4:37). A scoffer's name is not fixed until he refuses to the end. What name are your habits writing for you? Christ, though equal with God, "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death" (Philippians 2:8). He calls the proud to learn from Him, "for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29), and God still "gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6).
units.application: Notice when you roll your eyes at, mock or dismiss someone who corrects you; that reflex is where the scoffer begins. This week, thank one person for a correction you resented. Parents: do not let sarcasm become the language of your home, especially toward authority. Leaders: receive criticism graciously in front of others. Teens and students: refuse to join online mockery or the laugh at someone's expense.

rel.note: The soul of a lazy man desires and has nothing, the same craving without labor.
The lazy man will not even lift his hand from the bowl to his mouth, a picture of hands that refuse.
The next verse continues the portrait, setting the lazy man's endless craving against the generosity of the righteous.
The same verb "refuse" describes the wicked who will not do justice, showing laziness as a choice of the will.
The overgrown field of the lazy man shows the slow ruin this verse calls death.
A little sleep and folding of the hands bring poverty like an armed man, the end of refusing to work.

units.notes:
• "Desire" is a word for craving or longing. The next verse doubles it: "He covets greedily" is literally "he desires a desire" (21:26).
• Bridges: "He thinks to live by wishing, not by working."
• Henry: "their desires at the same time stab them." The lazy man suffers twice, from the want his idleness causes and from the cravings that torment him.
• Work was given before the fall: God put Adam in the garden "to tend and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Paul wrote, "If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
• Compare 6:9–11; 13:4; 19:24; 20:4; 24:30–34.
units.summary: Wanting without working does not only leave a man empty; it slowly kills him.
units.principle: Desire without diligence destroys; the one who could work but will not is ruined by the very wants he refuses to labor for.
units.insight: Jesus told of a servant who received one talent, buried it and blamed his master's hardness. The master called him "You wicked and lazy servant" (Matthew 25:26). His hands refused, and he lost even what he had. Laziness is rarely called by its name. It dresses up as waiting, perfectionism or "someday." It can be spiritual too. We want to know God, to be free from a sin, to see our children walk with the Lord, yet we will not pray, study or take the hard step. The gospel does not shame the weary. Christ worked until He could say, "It is finished!" (John 19:30), and He "gives power to the weak" (Isaiah 40:29). Grace does not cancel effort; Paul says he "labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10).
units.application: Write down one thing you keep wishing for, such as a degree, a tidier home, better health or a deeper prayer life, and name the first small step it requires; take it today. Parents: give children real chores and let them taste the reward of finished work. Employees: do the task you have been avoiding first thing tomorrow. If illness or disability keeps you from working, this verse is not about you; ask for help without shame.

rel.note: The one who scatters increases and the generous soul is made rich, the open hand of the righteous.
The wicked man shows his neighbor no favor, the closed heart opposite the righteous who gives.
The reserves in the dwelling of the wise make generous giving possible.
The one who gives without holding back is pursuing mercy, the path that finds life and honor.
The lazy man whose desire kills him is the one who covets greedily all day long.
He who has a generous eye gives his bread to the poor, the same generosity named as a mark of righteousness.

units.notes:
• "He covets greedily" is literally "he desires a desire." The verb and the noun share the root of the word "desire" in 21:25, so the repetition stresses how intense the craving is and ties this saying to the lazy man.
• The NLT treats the first line as a general statement about greedy people rather than a continuation of 21:25. The NKJV, ESV and NASB (1995) keep the singular "he," which most naturally refers back to the lazy man.
• Henry: "The slothful are always craving and gaping to receive, but the righteous are always full and contriving to give". "Contriving" means planning.
• Giving without holding back describes God Himself: "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?" (Romans 8:32).
• Compare 11:24–25; 22:9; Acts 20:35; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7.
units.summary: The idle hand is always open to take; the righteous hand is open to give.
units.principle: Righteousness turns a life outward; those who work and trust God are free to give generously, while the idle heart only craves more.
units.insight: Achan saw a fine garment and silver among the spoils of Jericho and confessed, "I coveted them and took them" (Joshua 7:21). The Macedonian believers, in deep poverty, gave beyond their ability and begged Paul for the privilege of giving (2 Corinthians 8:1–4). The difference was not money but the direction of the heart. Craving is a tiring way to live, because it is never full. Generosity is freedom. Jesus said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Acts 20:35), and He lived it. God "did not spare His own Son" (Romans 8:32), and Christ gave Himself completely. Those who have received such a gift are set free from grasping. Are your days spent mostly wanting, or mostly giving?
units.application: Set a giving amount this month before you look at what is left over, and give it gladly (2 Corinthians 9:7). Students and young workers: start the habit of giving now, even if the sum is small. When a want grips you, such as a new phone or a bigger house, give something away first and see what it does to the craving. Retirees and the well-off: look for one person or ministry you can help without holding back.

rel.note: The same first line, with the added contrast that the prayer of the upright is His delight.
The LORD who weighs hearts sees the intent behind the offering.
Near the chapter's start, doing justice is ranked above sacrifice; here sacrifice without justice is rejected.
Even the plowing of the wicked is sin, as here even his sacrifice is an abomination.
Even the prayer of one who turns from the law is an abomination.
The seductress boasts of her peace offerings and paid vows, religion used as cover for sin.

units.notes:
• The KJV has "with a wicked mind," with "in wickedness" in its margin. The NKJV "wicked intent" points to a scheme: the offering is part of a plan.
• Henry: "when holiness is pretended, but some wickedness intended, then especially the performance is an abomination". By "the performance" Henry means the act of worship itself.
• Jezebel proclaimed a fast as the setting for Naboth's false trial (1 Kings 21:9–13). The chief priests would not enter Pilate's headquarters, "lest they should be defiled," while they pressed for Jesus' death (John 18:28).
• Proverbs gathers several sayings about what the LORD detests, and outward religion without an upright heart is among them (15:8; 28:9). The God who "weighs the hearts" (21:2) sees the intent behind every offering.
• Compare 7:14; 15:8; 28:9; Isaiah 1:13–17; Mark 12:40.
units.summary: Worship without repentance offends God; worship used as a cover for evil offends Him twice.
units.principle: God rejects worship from a heart that clings to wickedness, and most of all religion used as a mask for evil plans.
units.insight: Absalom wrapped his rebellion in a vow to the LORD (2 Samuel 15:7–12). Jezebel staged a fast to murder a neighbor (1 Kings 21:9–13). Some scribes made long prayers while they devoured widows' houses (Mark 12:40). Religion makes a powerful disguise, and the human heart is skilled at wearing it: the church office sought for status, the gift that buys silence, the Scripture quoted to win a fight. God sees through all of it. Yet the verse is meant to bring the guilty to worship with a true heart, not to drive them away. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, A broken and a contrite heart—These, O God, You will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). Christ "offered Himself without spot to God" (Hebrews 9:14), the one sacrifice with no hidden motive, and through Him sinners may draw near.
units.application: Before you serve, give or pray in public this week, ask, "What am I hoping this will get me?" Church leaders: watch for anyone seeking a role to gain influence rather than to serve, beginning with yourself. If you are holding on to an unresolved wrong, deal with it before you lead worship or come to the Lord's Table (Matthew 5:23–24; 1 Corinthians 11:28). Never use Scripture or prayer as a weapon in a personal conflict.

rel.note: The truthful lip is established forever while a lying tongue lasts a moment, the same contrast of lasting and perishing words.
A true witness delivers souls, while a deceitful witness speaks lies.
A false witness will not go unpunished and he who speaks lies shall perish, the same end.
A false witness is like a club, a sword and an arrow, the damage that explains his punishment.
A false witness who speaks lies is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew has no object after "hears"; the NKJV supplies "him." The final phrase means literally "to perpetuity," which the NKJV renders "endlessly" and the KJV "speaketh constantly."
• Translations divide over the second line. The ESV and NASB (1995) take it as the lasting word of a man who listens, close to the NKJV. Earlier editions of the NIV read it the opposite way, that whoever listens to the false witness will be "destroyed forever." The current NIV (2011) has a "careful listener" who will "testify successfully," and the NLT speaks of a credible witness being allowed to speak.
• Bridges, on the true witness: "He holds to his testimony and never contradicts himself."
• Jezebel hired two scoundrels to testify falsely against Naboth (1 Kings 21:10–13). At Jesus' trial "many bore false witness against Him, but their testimonies did not agree" (Mark 14:56).
• Compare 12:19; 14:5; 19:5, 9; Deuteronomy 19:16–19.
units.summary: A lie dies with the liar, but the word of one who truly listened still stands.
units.principle: False testimony does not last, while the word of a careful, truthful witness who speaks only what he knows will stand.
units.insight: The apostles were careful witnesses. They chose Judas's replacement from men who had been with Jesus from the beginning (Acts 1:21–22), and before the council they said, "we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20). Their testimony still speaks. The false witnesses at Jesus' trial could not even agree with one another (Mark 14:56), and their words have perished. Jesus Himself is "the Faithful and True Witness" (Revelation 3:14), who said, "We speak what We know and testify what We have seen" (John 3:11). Much false witness today is careless repetition: the rumor forwarded, the secondhand story told as fact. Being a true witness begins with hearing well. Are you careful to speak only what you know, about others and about Christ?
units.application: Before you repeat a story about someone, ask, "Did I see or hear this myself?" If not, do not pass it on. Anyone called as a witness, writing a reference or filing a report: state only what you know, and say plainly what you do not know. Anyone who posts news or opinions online: check before you share. When you tell others about Jesus, speak from what you have actually known of Him.

rel.note: The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way, the careful thought behind the upright man's established course.
He who hardens his heart will fall into calamity, the inner hardness behind the hard face.
One often rebuked who hardens his neck will be suddenly destroyed, the end of resisting correction.
Acknowledging the LORD in all your ways is how the upright find their path made straight.
Ponder the path of your feet and let your ways be established, the upright man's careful course.
The immoral woman meets the young man with an impudent face, the same brazen look.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew text preserves two readings of the verb in the second line. The letters written in the text give "establishes," which the NKJV follows. A note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to a word that differs by one letter and means "understands" or "considers." The ESV follows the margin: the upright "gives thought to his ways." Either reading fits the contrast with the wicked man's hard face.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Kidner summarizes the verse to say that a bold front is no substitute for sound principles."
• Bridges gives the first example in Scripture: "Cain standing boldly in the presence of his God, with his hands reeking with his brother's blood". Cain's answer was "Am I my brother's keeper?" (Genesis 4:9).
• The same image can be holy. Jeremiah's hearers "made their faces harder than rock" against God (Jeremiah 5:3), but the Servant of the LORD says, "I have set My face like a flint" (Isaiah 50:7), trusting the Lord GOD to help Him.
• Compare 3:5–6; 4:26; 7:13; 28:14; 29:1.
units.summary: Some faces are set hard against the truth; others are set on walking in it.
units.principle: Firmness is a virtue only when it rests on truth; the hardened face resists correction, while the upright are steady because they have thought their way through before God.
units.insight: Gehazi took Naaman's silver, hid it, then stood before Elisha and said, "Your servant did not go anywhere" (2 Kings 5:25). A hard face is the outward sign of a heart that has stopped blushing. Jesus also set His face, but in the opposite direction: "He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), toward the cross, steady because He was set on the Father's will. Daniel "purposed in his heart" not to defile himself (Daniel 1:8), yet his firmness was courteous and respectful. Where are you stubborn? It may be holy steadiness, or it may be a hardened face against something God is trying to tell you. A soft heart before God and a steady face before people is the combination this verse commends.
units.application: The next time someone confronts you, notice whether your first reflex is to harden your face or to listen. Parents: when a child bluffs through a lie, address the hardness gently but firmly, and model admitting your own wrongs. Young people facing pressure: decide ahead of time, as Daniel did, what you will and will not do, so your firmness rests on thought, not stubbornness. Leaders: before a major decision, write down your reasons and ask God to establish your way.

rel.note: A man plans his way but the LORD directs his steps, the right place for human planning under God.
Many plans fill a man's heart, but the LORD's counsel will stand, the same supremacy of God's purpose.
The chapter began with the king's heart in the LORD's hand and ends with all counsel beneath Him.
Wisdom can overcome strength, but no wisdom can overcome the LORD.
The next verse carries the thought from the council room to the battlefield: victory is the LORD's.
Wisdom claims counsel, sound wisdom and understanding as her own, the qualities this verse places beneath the LORD.

units.notes:
• The three words resemble the qualities Wisdom claims in 8:14, "Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom; I am understanding." The link is one of meaning rather than identical wording. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for "counsel," but the words behind "wisdom" and "understanding" differ. Here the book places such qualities beneath the LORD.
• Ahithophel's advice was treated "as if one had inquired at the oracle of God" (2 Samuel 16:23), yet God overturned it in answer to David's prayer, "turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!" (2 Samuel 15:31; 17:14).
• Henry: "He that sits in heaven laughs at men's projects against him and his anointed". He is echoing Psalm 2:1–4.
• Gamaliel warned the council about the apostles: "if it is of God, you cannot overthrow it—lest you even be found to fight against God" (Acts 5:39).
• Compare 16:1, 9; 19:21; Psalm 33:10–11; Isaiah 8:10; 1 Corinthians 1:25.
units.summary: Every plan made against God has already lost.
units.principle: No human wisdom, insight or strategy can overturn the LORD's purpose; every plan is finally answerable to Him, which warns the proud and comforts those who trust Him.
units.insight: The greatest counsel ever taken against the LORD was the plot against His Son. Herod and Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel gathered "to do whatever Your hand and Your purpose determined before to be done" (Acts 4:27–28). Their shrewdest scheme became the means of our salvation. Joseph's brothers meant evil against him, "but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). This verse warns anyone fighting God, whether in open rebellion or in quiet resistance to His will in one corner of life. You cannot win, and you do not need to. It also steadies anyone who feels outmaneuvered by powerful people. Their counsel is real, but it is not final. The God who overturned Ahithophel's advice and raised Jesus from the dead holds your situation too. Yielding to Him is not defeat, because He is wiser than all counsel.
units.application: Before you finalize a major plan, ask whether any part of it works against what God has said, and change that part. Church and business leaders: pray over strategy at the start, not only after it fails. If you feel outmatched by someone's influence at work, in court or in your family, do what is right, pray as David did (2 Samuel 15:31), and rest in God's final word. Students: learn eagerly, but hold every idea under God.

rel.note: The lot is cast but every decision is from the LORD, human action with a God-given outcome.
A man plans his way but the LORD directs his steps, preparation under God's direction.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous are safe, the true source of deliverance.
The chapter opens with the throne in the LORD's hand and closes with the battle in His hand.
Wisdom overcomes the stronghold of the mighty, yet the victory itself still belongs to the LORD.
No counsel stands against the LORD, so no battle plan can secure victory without Him.

units.notes:
• "Deliverance" is a broad word for rescue, victory and salvation. The KJV has "safety," with "victory" in its margin.
• The law of the king said that he "shall not multiply horses for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:16), which gives the saying added point in a collection associated with Israel's kings. Compare Psalm 33:17: "A horse is a vain hope for safety."
• Bridges: "Use the means, but idolize them not." In other words, prepare well, but do not put your trust in the preparations.
• Nehemiah held both halves of the verse together: "we made our prayer to our God, and because of them we set a watch against them day and night" (Nehemiah 4:9).
• Compare 16:33; 18:10; 1 Samuel 17:47; Isaiah 31:1; Jonah 2:9.
units.summary: Saddle the horse and train the troops, but look to the LORD for the victory.
units.principle: Preparation is a duty, but victory belongs to the LORD; the wise prepare fully and rest their confidence entirely in God.
units.insight: King Asa faced a vast Ethiopian army. He set his troops in battle array, then cried to the LORD that it was nothing for Him to help, whether with many or with the powerless, "for we rest on You" (2 Chronicles 14:8–12). The LORD struck the enemy before him. Years later the same Asa leaned on a foreign king and, in his illness, "did not seek the LORD, but the physicians," and his story ended in sorrow (2 Chronicles 16:7–12). Our horses are savings, credentials, connections and careful plans. Prepare them, but do not trust them. "Salvation is of the LORD" (Jonah 2:9) reaches its fullest meaning at the cross. The decisive battle against sin and death was won by Christ alone: "thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 15:57).
units.application: Prepare thoroughly for the exam, the interview, the surgery or the hard conversation, then pray and leave the outcome with God. Business owners and leaders: plan carefully, but do not let reserves or strategies become your confidence. Parents: train your children diligently, and entrust their hearts to the Lord who alone saves. When the outcome goes your way, thank God first; when it does not, keep trusting Him.

rel.note: The righteous leave a blessed memory while the name of the wicked rots, showing why a good name is worth choosing.
The gracious keep honor while the ruthless keep riches, the same choice between two treasures.
The next saying turns from riches themselves to the rich and the poor, who share one Maker.
A poor man with integrity is better than a rich man with crooked ways, the same ranking of character over wealth.
Mercy and truth bound to the heart bring the same favor and high esteem with God and man that this verse prizes.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the first line says simply “name.” The NKJV and most English versions add “good” to bring out the sense, and the KJV prints the added word in italics. The sense is a good reputation, a name worth having.
• The builders of Babel said, “let us make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). That was a name grasped in pride; the name this verse commends is earned by faithful character.
• “Loving favor” is goodwill and esteem. Jesus “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52).
• As Kidner puts it, quoted by Guzik, “not the power we wield, but the love in which we are held, is our proper joy.”
• Compare Ecclesiastes 7:1, “A good name is better than precious ointment,” and Proverbs 10:7, “The memory of the righteous is blessed, But the name of the wicked will rot.”
units.summary: Riches show what a person owns; a good name shows what he can be trusted to do.
units.principle: Trustworthy character is worth more than wealth, because money can be replaced but trust lost through dishonesty is slow to return.
units.insight: This verse exposes what we really treasure. Gehazi watched Elisha refuse Naaman’s gifts, then ran after the general, lied to get silver and clothing, and went home with Naaman’s leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27). He traded his name for silver and lost both. Our temptations are usually quieter: the padded expense report, the inflated résumé, the promise we hope no one remembers. Yet reputation must never become an idol either. Bridges: “Far better that others should blot our name, than that we should wound our consciences.” The deepest comfort is in Christ, who “made Himself of no reputation” (Philippians 2:7) and bore the shame our names deserved. God has given Him “the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9), and in Him our names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). That frees us to live with integrity before people.
units.application: Before you take a deal, a shortcut or a convenient exaggeration this week, ask what it would cost your name if it came to light. Employees: be the one whose hours and expenses never need checking. Parents: let your children watch you keep a costly promise. If your own failure has damaged your name, start rebuilding with small, consistent honesty; trust returns slowly. If you are slandered while doing right, keep your conscience clean and leave your name with God.

rel.note: Because the LORD made the poor, oppressing them insults their Maker, the practical conclusion of this verse.
Mocking the poor also reproaches his Maker, applying the shared creation of rich and poor to speech.
The saying before it ranks a good name above riches; this one denies that riches make one person worth more than another.
The Maker of rich and poor stands up as the advocate of the poor against those who rob them.
The poor man and the oppressor share the same LORD who gives light to the eyes of both.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads, “The rich and poor meet together.” However far apart they live, rich and poor meet on the same ground before their Maker.
• Proverbs draws the practical conclusion twice: “He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker” (14:31), and “He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker” (17:5). To despise a poor person is to insult the God who made him.
• A similar saying appears in 29:13: “The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both.”
• Bridges: “At the gate of the invisible world the distinction of riches and poverty is dropped.” At death, wealth no longer separates anyone.
• Compare Job 31:15, where Job refuses to despise his servants because the same God made them in the womb, and Malachi 2:10, “Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?”
units.summary: Whatever separates the rich and the poor, both were shaped by the same divine hands.
units.principle: Every person bears the dignity of being made by God, so wealth can never measure a person’s worth or excuse contempt for the poor.
units.insight: We sort people quickly by what they drive, where they live and what they wear. Scripture refuses that sorting. The rich man in Jesus’ parable passed Lazarus at his gate every day and never truly saw him; death erased the difference between them and then reversed it (Luke 16:19–25). James rebuked a church that gave the good seat to the man with the gold ring and told the poor man to stand (James 2:1–4). The gospel goes further than creation. Rich and poor also meet as sinners at the same cross, saved by the same blood. Christ, “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Ask yourself whose company you seek and whose you avoid. The answer shows whether you see people as God’s handiwork or as their bank balance.
units.application: This week, learn the name of someone you usually look past: the office cleaner, the cashier, the man at the shelter. If you hire or manage people, check that your pay and policies treat the lowest-paid worker as made by the same Maker as you. At church, notice who sits alone and sit with them. If you are poor, refuse the lie that you are worth less; God made you as surely as He made anyone.

rel.note: The simple believes everything while the prudent considers his steps, the same contrast of carelessness and forethought.
The book was written to give prudence to the simple, the very quality they lack here.
The person who guards his soul keeps far from the snares, the same foresight applied to the crooked road.
The same saying is repeated almost word for word, underlining the value of foresight.
The simple young man who followed the seductress shows a person walking straight into a snare without knowing it would cost his life.

units.notes:
• The saying is repeated almost word for word in 27:12.
• In Proverbs the “simple” person is open to any influence and has not yet chosen wisdom: “The simple believes every word, But the prudent considers well his steps” (14:15).
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: “Prevision is the best means of prevention.” Seeing trouble ahead is the surest way to avoid it.
• Scripture gives a picture of both responses in Exodus 9:20–21. Before the hail, Pharaoh’s servants who feared the word of the LORD brought their servants and livestock indoors; those who ignored the warning left them in the field.
• Compare Hebrews 11:7: Noah, “being divinely warned of things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared an ark for the saving of his household.”
units.summary: Wisdom sees the storm coming and takes shelter; folly keeps walking until the storm breaks over it.
units.principle: Wisdom looks ahead and acts before trouble arrives, while carelessness walks into consequences it could have avoided.
units.insight: The simple person’s motto is “It won’t happen to me.” Lot’s sons-in-law heard that Sodom would be destroyed and thought he was joking (Genesis 19:14). Abigail, by contrast, saw that David was coming to destroy her household, acted at once, and turned the danger aside (1 Samuel 25:14–35). Most of us know where our own roads lead: the habit that is tightening, the debt that is growing, the friendship that is pulling us down. We simply prefer not to look. Scripture’s gravest warning is of judgment to come, and the gospel gives the prudent a hiding place. Christ took the storm of judgment on Himself, and all who run to Him are sheltered. “Whoever trusts in the LORD shall be safe” (29:25).
units.application: Name one danger you can see coming, such as a credit card balance, a relationship moving too fast, or a schedule crowding out prayer, and take one step out of its path this week. Young people: before a party or a trip, decide your limits and how you will leave if you need to. Parents: talk with your teenagers about what trouble looks like before it arrives. Leaders: ask your team which problem everyone is quietly ignoring.

rel.note: The LORD’s blessing makes rich without adding sorrow, placing every such gift in His hands.
The fear of the LORD is joined to humility, and humility comes before honor, the same root and fruit.
A haughty heart comes before destruction and humility before honor, showing the path this verse commends.
Riches fly away like an eagle, a warning that keeps this verse from becoming a formula for wealth.
Wisdom holds length of days, riches and honor, the same blessings named here.

units.notes:
• The NKJV’s first word, “By,” translates a Hebrew noun meaning consequence or reward. The ESV and NASB (1995) translate it “reward,” and the KJV margin offers the same reading: riches, honor and life are what humility and the fear of the LORD lead to.
• Proverbs twice says, “before honor is humility” (15:33; 18:12). Honor follows humility; it is not seized by pride.
• “Life” here is more than length of days. It is life under God’s favor, which the New Testament opens into eternal life.
• Bridges: “The most humble is the most triumphant Christian.”
• Compare Micah 6:8, “to walk humbly with your God,” and James 4:10, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up.”
units.summary: The road to true riches and lasting honor begins on your knees before God.
units.principle: God’s blessing grows from humility and reverence toward Him, though He alone decides what form and measure that blessing takes.
units.insight: At the start of his reign Solomon called himself “a little child” who did not know how to go out or come in, and he asked God for an understanding heart. God gave him wisdom, and riches and honor besides (1 Kings 3:7–13). Yet the same king later lost that humility and drifted from the LORD. The blessings did not keep him; only the fear of the LORD could. Jesus is the full picture of this verse. He had nowhere to lay His head (Matthew 8:20), yet He “humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death,” and God “highly exalted Him” (Philippians 2:8–9). The true riches, honor and life are His, and He shares them with all who bow to Him. So the question for us is not “How can I be blessed?” but “Am I bowed before God?”
units.application: Begin each day this week by naming before God one thing you cannot do without Him. When you are praised at work, pass the credit to God and to the people who helped. Young believers chasing success: set your heart first on fearing God, and leave the timing and size of His blessing to Him. If you are faithful and still struggling financially, do not read this verse as a verdict on you. God’s riches include provision, honor and life that no market can touch.

rel.note: The way of the unfaithful is hard, naming the trouble that fills the crooked road.
The lazy man’s way is a hedge of thorns, the same picture of a road made painful by the traveler’s character.
Keeping one’s way preserves the soul, the same guarding commended here.
Refusing friendship with an angry man is one concrete way to guard the soul from a snare.
The prudent man foresees evil and hides himself, the same foresight that keeps a person far from snares.

units.notes:
• The KJV has “the froward,” an older word for people who are stubbornly contrary. The NKJV’s “perverse” means twisted or crooked.
• To “guard his soul” is to watch over his whole life. Compare 16:17, “He who keeps his way preserves his soul,” and 4:23, “Keep your heart with all diligence.”
• Bridges: “A forcible image to shew, that nothing stands so much in a man’s way, as the indulgence of his own unbridled will.” (“Shew” is an older spelling of “show.”) The crooked man’s worst obstacle is his own stubborn will.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “The metaphor refers to temptations such as easy sex and easy money that tempt youth.”
• Compare 15:19, “The way of the lazy man is like a hedge of thorns,” and 13:15, “the way of the unfaithful is hard.”
units.summary: Crooked paths are lined with thorns and traps; the wise simply stay off them.
units.principle: A crooked life creates its own pain and traps, while the person who watches over his path is kept clear of much of that harm.
units.insight: Balaam set out on a road God had forbidden, chasing a reward. An angel blocked the narrow path between the vineyard walls, his donkey crushed his foot against the wall, and the angel told him, “your way is perverse before Me” (Numbers 22:22–32). The pain on the crooked road was mercy, a warning to turn. Hunger did the same for the prodigal son, bringing him to himself (Luke 15:14–20). Ask where you keep getting scratched: the same conflict, the same exposure, the same regret. The pattern may point to a crooked path you keep choosing. The gospel holds a deeper wonder. Thorns sprang up with the curse (Genesis 3:18), and soldiers twisted thorns into a crown and pressed it on Christ’s head (Matthew 27:29). He bore the curse so that crooked people could be brought onto a straight road.
units.application: Guarding your soul is practical. If certain websites, places or people keep pulling you into sin, put distance between you and them this week: an app blocker, a different route home, lunch with someone else. Parents: help your children name the snares in their world, such as group chats or pressure to cheat, and plan how to avoid them. If you are caught in thorns of your own making, stop pressing forward; confess, turn and ask someone for help.

rel.note: Chastening a son while there is hope stresses the same early window for formation.
The son is called to hear his father’s instruction and his mother’s law, the other side of parental training.
Folly is bound up in a child’s heart, which is why the training commanded here is needed.
A child left to himself brings shame, the opposite of a child trained in the way he should go.
The father passes on what his own father taught him as a child, a picture of training handed down.

units.notes:
• The verb translated “train up” (chanak) appears elsewhere only for dedicating a new house (Deuteronomy 20:5) and the temple (1 Kings 8:63; 2 Chronicles 7:5). In those places it marks the start of a building’s intended use, which fits the picture of starting a child on his course.
• “In the way he should go” is shorter in Hebrew, literally “in his way,” as the KJV margin notes. The Hebrew does not say whose standard defines “his way,” which is why two readings exist.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, takes the second reading: training that shows “respect for his individuality and vocation, though not for his selfwill.” Even on that reading, the child’s self-will is not the guide.
• The KJV margin offers “Catechise” for “Train,” reflecting the older understanding of training as instruction.
• Henry admits the hard case plainly: “Many indeed have departed from the good way in which they were trained up; Solomon himself did so.”
• Compare Deuteronomy 6:6–7 and 2 Timothy 3:15, “from childhood you have known the Holy Scriptures.”
units.summary: Set a child's feet on God's road early; the first steps often set the direction for a lifetime.
units.principle: Faithful early training in God’s way usually shapes a whole life, but it is a calling for parents to fulfill, not a guarantee to claim.
units.insight: Timothy’s faith first lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and from childhood he knew the Holy Scriptures (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). That is the pattern this verse commends: faith handed on day after ordinary day. Yet parents who have done their best sometimes watch a child walk away. Samuel’s sons “did not walk in his ways” (1 Samuel 8:3). God Himself, the perfect Father, says, “I have nourished and brought up children, And they have rebelled against Me” (Isaiah 1:2). A grieving parent is not condemned by this verse. Train faithfully, then pray and wait like the father in Jesus’ parable, who saw his son “a great way off” because he was still watching the road (Luke 15:20). The harvest belongs to God, and His grace reaches farther than our training.
units.application: Parents and grandparents: choose one daily habit to build this week, such as reading a psalm at breakfast or praying at bedtime, and keep it simple enough to last. Study each child, and shape how you teach to how he learns, while keeping God’s way as the goal. Let your children see your faith at work when things go wrong. If a grown child has strayed, stop rehearsing your failures. Confess what you need to, keep loving, and keep praying.

rel.note: The poor man pleads while the rich answers roughly, the same imbalance of power described here.
The rich who use their power to oppress the poor are warned that they will come to poverty themselves.
The warning against surety shows the same danger of debt reaching even a person’s bed.
The father urges a son caught in a pledge to free himself quickly, applying the dependence that debt creates.

units.notes:
• The ESV has “the borrower is the slave of the lender,” bringing out how complete the dependence could become.
• A prophet’s widow told Elisha, “the creditor is coming to take my two sons to be his slaves” (2 Kings 4:1). In Nehemiah 5:1–5 families mortgaged their fields and saw their children forced into bondage to pay debts.
• The law did not ban lending. It told Israel to lend to the poor without charging them interest (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8) and counted it a blessing to lend rather than borrow (Deuteronomy 28:12).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, counsels that “one must regard indebtedness only as a last resort.”
• Compare Romans 13:8, “Owe no one anything except to love one another,” a New Testament command that sits naturally beside this proverb.
units.summary: Debt is a leash: whoever holds your loan holds a piece of your freedom.
units.principle: Debt places a person under another’s power, so wisdom borrows cautiously, avoids debt for luxuries and pays what it owes.
units.insight: Behind much debt lies a heart that cannot wait. We want now what God has not yet provided, and we sign away tomorrow’s freedom to get it. Scripture also shows debt’s cruelty. A prophet’s widow cried to Elisha that the creditor was coming for her sons, and God met her with oil enough to pay what she owed and live on the rest (2 Kings 4:1–7). Nehemiah rebuked the nobles of Jerusalem for exacting interest from their own poor brothers until their children were sold into bondage (Nehemiah 5:6–13). The gospel speaks of a greater debt. We owed God what we could never pay, and Christ cancelled it, “having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us” (Colossians 2:14). Freed from that debt, we are free to live content and generous.
units.application: Before you borrow this week, ask whether this is a need or a want, and whether you could wait and save instead. If you carry debt, list what you owe and start paying down one balance on purpose; pay every bill on time. Young adults: refuse debt for luxuries before it becomes a habit. If you lend, especially to someone struggling, do not use that power to control or shame them.

rel.note: The one who sows righteousness has a sure reward, the opposite harvest from sowing iniquity.
Those who reject wisdom eat the fruit of their own way, the same law of harvest.
The oppressor of the poor comes to poverty, the same harvest applied to money.
The next verse shows the generous person, who sows kindness to the poor and is blessed.

units.notes:
• The second line is difficult, and translations vary. The NKJV, ESV and KJV say the rod “will fail”; the NASB (1995) says it “will perish.” The KJV margin reads, “with the rod of his anger he shall be consumed.”
• Where the NKJV has “reap sorrow,” the KJV has “reap vanity,” meaning emptiness: the harvest has nothing in it.
• The ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) adds a line here saying that God blesses a cheerful and generous man. Paul’s “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7) closely resembles it and may echo it. The added line is not part of the Hebrew text the NKJV translates.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: “The crop must be according to the seed.”
• Compare Job 4:8, “Those who plow iniquity And sow trouble reap the same”; Hosea 8:7; Galatians 6:7; and Isaiah 10:5, 24–25, where Assyria is God’s rod for a time and then is broken.
units.summary: Plant injustice and the harvest is grief; the oppressor's rod does not last.
units.principle: Injustice carries the seed of its own sorrow, and power used in anger will not endure, though God sets the time of the harvest.
units.insight: Pharaoh ruled Israel with a hard rod. He set taskmasters over them, ordered their baby boys thrown into the Nile, and answered every plea with heavier burdens (Exodus 1:11–22; 5:6–9). He sowed iniquity for years, and the harvest was a great cry in every Egyptian home on the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:29–30). His rod failed at the Red Sea. Most of us hold some smaller rod: authority over children, employees, a team or a congregation. When anger drives how we use it, we are sowing a crop we will not want to reap. For those under an oppressor’s rod there is hope. Christ Himself was struck by angry men (Matthew 27:30), and “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). He knows that rod from the inside, and He will judge every rod raised unjustly.
units.application: Parents: never discipline while anger is in charge; step away, cool down, then correct. Managers and pastors: ask whether people follow you out of respect or out of fear of your temper. If you have been sowing harshness, begin sowing differently this week with an apology and a changed tone. If you live under someone’s harsh rule, seek safety and help where you need it, and do not let bitterness plant a crop of its own.

rel.note: The generous soul is made rich and the one who waters is watered, the same pattern of blessing.
Pity on the poor is a loan to the LORD, who repays it, the same blessing on generosity.
The verse before shows a man sowing injustice; this one sows kindness and is blessed.
The man with an evil eye hastens after riches, the stingy opposite of the good eye.
