The one who gives to the poor will not lack, while the one who hides his eyes from them is cursed.

units.notes:
• The opposite Hebrew expression, a bad or evil eye, describes a stingy, grasping person in 23:6 (“miser”) and 28:22 (“evil eye”). In Proverbs the eye stands for a person’s attitude toward what he has and toward others’ needs.
• Jesus uses the same language: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15). Compare Matthew 6:22–23.
• Henry notices the word “of”: “he does not give all his bread, but of his bread; the poor shall have their share with his own family.” The generous man treats the poor as if they had a place at his table.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “the liberal participates in a cycle of endless enrichment.” By “the liberal” he means the generous person.
• Compare 19:17, “He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD,” and Luke 14:13–14.
units.summary: Generosity starts with the eyes: it notices the need, then opens the hand.
units.principle: Generosity begins with eyes that notice need, and God blesses those who share what sustains them with people who lack it.
units.insight: Boaz noticed a foreign widow gleaning in his field, asked who she was, and quietly told his reapers to let grain fall for her on purpose (Ruth 2:5–16). That is a good eye: it sees before it is asked. The priest and the Levite in Jesus’ parable saw the wounded man too, but they “passed by on the other side” (Luke 10:31–32). The difference was not eyesight but heart. Our eyes go easily to what we want, and the needs around us blur. Jesus saw the hungry crowds and was moved with compassion (Matthew 9:36). He fed them with bread, and then gave Himself as the living bread for the life of the world (John 6:51). Those who have been fed by Him learn to look up from their own plates.
units.application: This week, ask God to show you one need you would normally miss, then meet it: a meal for a new mother, groceries for a struggling neighbor, a bag of food for the church pantry. Families: let your children help choose and deliver what you give. If you lead a business or ministry, build generosity into the budget instead of leaving it to leftovers. Give cheerfully, and give from what costs you something.

rel.note: The proud and haughty man is named “Scoffer,” describing the person this verse says to remove.
Where there is no talebearer, strife ceases, the same link between one troublemaker and ongoing conflict.
Scoffers set a whole city aflame, showing how far one mocker’s contention spreads.
Correcting a scoffer brings only shame and hatred, which is why removal eventually becomes necessary.

units.notes:
• The KJV calls him “the scorner”; the NKJV’s “scoffer” names the same figure, the most hardened kind of fool: “A proud and haughty man—‘Scoffer’ is his name; He acts with arrogant pride” (21:24).
• Scripture gives a picture of this in Genesis 21:9–10. When Ishmael mocked Isaac, Sarah said, “Cast out this bondwoman and her son.”
• The New Testament follows the same pattern with careful steps: Matthew 18:15–17; Titus 3:10, “Reject a divisive man after the first and second admonition”; and 1 Corinthians 5:11–13.
• Bridges keeps mercy in view: “Yet if we cast him out, cast him not off. Pray for him.” Removing him from the group is not giving up on him.
• Compare 26:20, “where there is no talebearer, strife ceases,” and 29:8, “Scoffers set a city aflame.”
units.summary: Some quarrels end only when the person who keeps starting them is asked to leave.
units.principle: Patient correction comes first, but peace sometimes requires removing a proud troublemaker who refuses every correction.
units.insight: John wrote of Diotrephes, who loved to have first place, spoke against the apostles with malicious words, and put faithful believers out of the church (3 John 9–10). One proud scoffer can sour a whole fellowship. Yet before we look for the scoffer in others, we should check our own mouths. The cynical comment in a meeting, the eye-roll at a leader, and the habit of mocking what others hold dear are seeds of the same spirit. And removal is never the end of hope. Paul had once been “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man,” yet he “obtained mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). He handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over so that they would “learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20). Even discipline aims at restoration, because Christ came to save scoffers too.
units.application: Leaders of churches, teams or ministries: when one person keeps stirring contempt, follow the steps of Matthew 18:15–17 patiently, but do not let the whole group suffer indefinitely. Parents: you cannot cast out a child, but you can refuse to let mockery rule your home, with clear limits and steady love. Everyone: if your sarcasm keeps others on edge, repent before someone has to ask you to leave.

rel.note: The king’s favor rests on a wise servant, as it rests here on the pure and gracious.
Righteous lips are the delight of kings, the same royal favor toward honest speech.
The skilled worker also stands before kings; character and competence both earn a place near the throne.
A throne is established when the wicked are removed from the king, the other side of welcoming the pure.
Keeping the heart with all diligence is the source of the pure heart this verse commends.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew of this verse is compact. The KJV reads it differently: “for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend,” that is, the king befriends him because of his gracious speech. The KJV margin gives the reading the NKJV follows.
• “The king’s friend” was an actual role at court: Hushai was “David’s friend” (2 Samuel 15:37), and Zabud was “a priest and the king’s friend” under Solomon (1 Kings 4:5).
• Bridges adds a realistic note: “Yet this choice of the gracious lips is too often rather what ought to be, than what is.” Not every king chooses so well.
• Compare 16:13, “Righteous lips are the delight of kings,” and 14:35.
• Compare Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart, For they shall see God,” and Colossians 4:6, where speech is to be “always with grace, seasoned with salt.”
units.summary: A clean heart and a gracious tongue open doors that flattery never can.
units.principle: Integrity of heart joined to gracious speech earns trust, even among the powerful, because such people are rare and valuable.
units.insight: Daniel served kings who did not share his faith, yet Darius planned to set him over the whole realm “because an excellent spirit was in him.” His rivals searched his conduct and “could find no charge or fault” (Daniel 6:3–4). A pure heart showed in faithful work and respectful words. Many of us split the two. Some guard their hearts but speak harshly and call it honesty. Others master pleasant speech while their motives stay mixed. Jesus joined them perfectly. People “marveled at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth” (Luke 4:22), and no deceit was found in Him. Now the King of kings calls His servants friends (John 15:15). Ask Him for a clean heart first, and gracious words will have something true to carry.
units.application: If you serve a leader, be the person whose reports never need second-guessing, and deliver hard news with courtesy. Leaders: look for people like this and keep them close, instead of rewarding flatterers. Before you send a sharp email or text this week, ask whether it is both true and gracious. Pray Psalm 51:10 each morning, because clean words flow from a clean heart.

rel.note: Truthful lips endure while a lying tongue lasts a moment, the same outcome for truth and deceit.
The eyes of the LORD watch the evil and the good everywhere, the same watchful care named here.
The false witness will not go unpunished, one way God overthrows the words of the faithless.
No wisdom or counsel stands against the LORD, so the words of the faithless cannot stand either.
The LORD stores up wisdom for the upright and guards the way of His saints, the same protection this verse describes for knowledge and those who hold it.

units.notes:
• “Preserve knowledge” can be read of God guarding true knowledge itself or guarding the people who hold it. Both fit, because God keeps His truth by keeping those who know and speak it.
• The KJV has “the transgressor” where the NKJV has “the faithless”; the word describes those who betray trust and deal treacherously.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: “God causes their distortions of the truth to be shown for what they are.”
• Compare 15:3, “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, Keeping watch on the evil and the good,” and 2 Chronicles 16:9.
• Compare 12:19, “The truthful lip shall be established forever, But a lying tongue is but for a moment,” and Isaiah 40:8, “the word of our God stands forever.”
units.summary: Lies may win a day, but God keeps watch over the truth and has the last word.
units.principle: God watches over the truth and those who hold it, and the words of the treacherous will not have the final say.
units.insight: King Jehoiakim had Jeremiah’s scroll read to him, cut it piece by piece with a scribe’s knife, and burned it. God simply told Jeremiah to write it again, with more words added (Jeremiah 36:23, 27–32). The king’s contempt did not erase one word. At Jesus’ trial many bore false witness, though their testimonies did not agree (Mark 14:56). Later the leaders paid soldiers to spread a lie about the empty tomb (Matthew 28:12–15). The resurrection overturned them all. This verse searches us too. Do we bend the truth when it serves us, trusting that no one will check? And it steadies us when lies are told about us or about the gospel. The eyes of the LORD are on the truth, and He will have the final word.
units.application: If you have been misrepresented at work or in your family, state the truth plainly once, then resist the urge to fight every rumor; God keeps watch. Teachers and parents: hand on what is true with care, because God preserves His word through faithful people. Before you repeat a story or share a post this week, check whether it is true. Do not lend your words to what God will overthrow.

rel.note: The lazy man’s way looks like a hedge of thorns to him, another obstacle seen mainly by the unwilling.
The lazy man’s desire kills him because his hands refuse to labor, the real danger behind his excuses.
The man who excels in his work stands before kings, while the lazy man will not even step into the street.
The lazy man again cries that a lion is in the road, the same invented excuse.
The sluggard is sent to learn from the ant, the book’s fullest treatment of laziness.

units.notes:
• The NKJV calls him “the lazy man” (KJV “slothful man”); it uses “sluggard” only in 6:6 and 6:9. All describe the same figure.
• The saying is nearly repeated in 26:13. The fuller portrait appears in 6:6–11; 15:19; 19:24; 21:25; 24:30–34; and 26:13–16.
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: “lions abide in the woods or fields, not in the streets of towns or cities.” The excuse fails on its own terms.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: “Laziness is a great lion-maker.”
• Contrast Benaiah, one of David’s mighty men, who went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion (2 Samuel 23:20).
units.summary: When we do not want to go, there is always a lion in the street.
units.principle: Laziness disguises itself as caution, inventing dangers to escape duties that are hard but not harmful.
units.insight: Ten of the spies came back from Canaan carrying real fruit and imagined defeat: “we were like grasshoppers in our own sight” (Numbers 13:33). Their fear dressed itself as realism, and a whole generation stayed in the wilderness. Moses himself piled up excuses when God called him, until he said, “O my Lord, please send by the hand of whomever else You may send” (Exodus 4:13). Our lions have modern names: “I’m not gifted for that,” “The timing isn’t right,” “Someone else will do it better.” The real danger is not in the street but in the comfortable bed, where obedience slowly dies. Jesus faced real dangers and “steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). Because He went, we can go where He sends us.
units.application: Write down the task you keep putting off and the reason you keep giving. Ask whether the reason is real or a lion. Then take the smallest first step today: one phone call, one page, one hour. Students: start the paper before the deadline starts roaring. Employees: tackle the dreaded task first thing in the morning. Church members: say yes to the service you have been dodging. If illness or real limits hold you back, say so plainly and ask for help.

rel.note: The harlot is a deep pit and the seductress a narrow well, the same image of a trap that is hard to escape.
Wisdom delivers from the immoral woman whose paths lead to death, the rescue this verse assumes.
Her lips drip honey but her steps lead to death, the sweetness and danger of her mouth.
God’s commandment is a lamp that keeps a person from the seductress’s flattering tongue, the guard missing from the man who falls here.
Her enticing speech made the young man yield, and he went like an ox to the slaughter.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind “immoral woman” is plural here, literally “strange women.” The KJV has “strange women” and the ESV “forbidden women”; the NKJV and NASB (1995) use the singular to describe a type of woman.
• Proverbs uses the same image in 23:27: “For a harlot is a deep pit, And a seductress is a narrow well.”
• Her mouth was described in 5:3: “the lips of an immoral woman drip honey, And her mouth is smoother than oil.” The father’s fuller warnings are in 2:16–19; 5:1–23; 6:20–35; and 7:1–27.
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, describes the pit as one “Into which it is easy to fall, but hard, if not impossible, to get out of it.”
• Compare Romans 1:24, 28, where God gives people over to what they have already chosen.
units.summary: Seduction begins with listening; the deepest pits are dug with sweet words.
units.principle: Seductive words are a trap that most easily catches a heart already turned from God, so the surest guard is a life that keeps listening to Him.
units.insight: Samson was not ruined in a moment. He had treated his vow lightly for years, and when Delilah “pestered him daily with her words and pressed him,” he finally told her everything (Judges 16:16–17). The pit opened under a man who had already drifted from God. That is the sober point here: the fall is usually the end of a long walk away from the LORD. The warning is not that women are dangerous. It is that seductive words find their mark in a heart that has stopped listening to God, and each of us is responsible for the voices we entertain. Yet there is hope even at the bottom of the pit. David sang, “He also brought me up out of a horrible pit, Out of the miry clay” (Psalm 40:2). Christ came down into our pit to lift sinners out.
units.application: Men and women alike: notice the voices you entertain, such as flirtatious messages, private conversations that drift, or content that stirs desire, and close those doors this week. Young people: tell a trusted adult or friend where you are tempted, so you are not walking alone. If you are married, keep your heart turned toward your spouse and toward God’s word every day. If you are already in the pit, do not try to climb out alone; confess and get help now.

rel.note: The parent who loves his son disciplines him promptly, the fuller statement of loving correction.
Training a child in God’s way is the positive work that correction serves.
Correction that does not kill but delivers the child’s soul shows the rescuing aim of discipline.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, while a child left to himself brings shame.
The LORD corrects the son He loves, the pattern that parental correction must reflect.

units.notes:
• “Bound up” pictures something knotted or tied tight. Folly is not a surface habit easily brushed off; it is knotted into the heart.
• Bridges stresses that the verse speaks of moral folly, not ordinary immaturity: “it is foolishness, not childishness.” A child is corrected for willful wrong, not for being young.
• Ironside on the rod: “Corporal punishment is not always required, and might at times be very unwise.” The aim is firm, kindly discipline.
• Proverbs speaks of the rod in correcting children at 13:24, 22:15, 23:13–14 and 29:15. The fuller discussion belongs to 13:24; here the stress falls on the folly already present in a child’s heart.
• Compare Ephesians 6:4, “do not provoke your children to wrath, but bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord,” and Hebrews 12:5–11.
units.summary: Folly comes naturally to every child; wisdom has to be taught, patiently and with love.
units.principle: Because folly is natural to every child, loving and consistent correction is a parent’s duty, and it must never become harshness or abuse.
units.insight: Scripture records parents who would not correct. Eli knew his sons were making themselves vile, and “he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). David never once asked Adonijah, “Why have you done so?” and that son grew up to grasp at the throne (1 Kings 1:5–6). Neglect is not kindness. Yet harshness is not wisdom either, and Paul warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4). The test is the heart behind the correction. God disciplines His children “for our profit, that we may be partakers of His holiness” (Hebrews 12:10); He never disciplines in a temper. For those in Christ, the punishment for sin has already fallen on Him: “The chastisement for our peace was upon Him” (Isaiah 53:5). Parents who have received that grace can correct as they have been corrected.
units.application: Parents: decide calmly in advance how you will respond to defiance, and never correct while angry. Explain the wrong, apply a fitting consequence, then restore warmth quickly with a hug and a prayer. Fit the form of correction to the child’s age and to wise care for children today; the goal is a changed heart, not a frightened child. Grandparents and teachers: back parents up with consistency. If you were treated harshly as a child, seek help so the pattern stops with you.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, the sin that sets the oppressor against God.
The LORD pleads the cause of the poor and plunders their plunderers, the reason oppression ends in want.
The rich rule over the poor; this verse warns the rich against abusing that rule.
Sowing iniquity reaps sorrow, the same harvest applied here to unjust gain.
Wealth gained by usury and extortion is gathered for someone who will pity the poor, so the oppressor does not keep it.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew of this verse is compressed, and translations arrange it differently. The 1984 NIV adds “both” to make clear that the two figures share one end.
• With this saying the collection headed “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1) comes to an end, and a new call to listen begins at 22:17.
• Bridges: “These two cases seem to be at opposites. Yet they meet at the same centre.” Both men are serving themselves.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, calls giving to the rich “a waste of money to try to buy a patron.” A patron is a powerful sponsor.
• Compare 14:31; 28:8; Luke 14:12–14, where Jesus says not to invite rich neighbors who can repay; and James 5:1–4 on wages withheld from workers.
units.summary: Squeezing the weak and flattering the strong look like two roads to wealth; both end in want.
units.principle: Wealth pursued by using people, whether by exploiting the weak or courting the powerful, sets a person against God and does not last.
units.insight: Haman did both things this verse condemns. He offered the king ten thousand talents of silver for permission to destroy a people who had no defender (Esther 3:8–11). He courted the powerful and crushed the weak in one move. Within the year he was hanged on his own gallows, and his house was given to Esther (Esther 7:10; 8:1). Most of us are subtler. We spend our attention on people who can advance us and spare little for those who cannot. We are generous upward and stingy downward. Jesus turned that around. He told His host to invite “the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind,” because they cannot repay (Luke 14:13–14). He Himself gave everything to people who had nothing to give back, and that grace frees us from using people.
units.application: Look at your giving and your attention this week. Whom do you take to lunch, call back first, or remember at Christmas: people who can help you, or people who need help? Business owners: pay fair wages promptly and never profit from a worker’s desperation. Employees: seek favor through good work, not gifts or flattery. Church leaders: make sure the influential are not served better than the poor.

rel.note: The book promised at the start to help the reader understand “the words of the wise,” the collection that begins here.
The teacher states the purpose of this call to listen: that the learner’s trust may be in the LORD.
“These things also belong to the wise” introduces a second short collection, confirming that this phrase heads a body of sayings.
Agur’s words open another collection from wise men beyond Solomon.
The father’s call to incline the ear and keep his words in the heart uses the same language of attentive listening.

units.notes:
• “The words of the wise” names a body of sayings. A second short collection is introduced at 24:23 with “These things also belong to the wise,” which confirms the phrase as a heading. The teachers are not named; the book credits these sections to “the wise,” not to Solomon by name.
• The command to hear and to set the heart, followed by reasons (22:18–21), echoes the father’s appeals: “My son, give attention to my words; Incline your ear to my sayings” (4:20). Compare 2:2 and 23:12.
• The KJV has “Bow down thine ear,” a picture of bending low to catch every word.
• Henry: “The ear will not serve without the heart.”
• Compare the call repeated to the churches in Revelation 2–3, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2:7).
units.summary: The words of the wise reach only those who lean in with the ear and open the heart.
units.principle: Wisdom is received by those who listen closely and set their hearts on it, not by those who merely hear.
units.insight: Long familiarity can make us deaf. After twenty-one chapters of proverbs a reader may start to skim, and a churchgoer who has heard sermons for years may stop listening. So the teacher stops and calls for fresh attention. Samuel learned to say, “Speak, for Your servant hears” (1 Samuel 3:10). Mary of Bethany “sat at Jesus’ feet and heard His word,” and Jesus said she had chosen “that good part” (Luke 10:39, 42), while Martha, busy serving, missed what mattered most. Ask yourself whether your heart is bowed or only your head. For the Christian, the voice most worth leaning toward is Christ’s, of whom the Father said, “This is My beloved Son. Hear Him!” (Mark 9:7). An open heart before Him is the beginning of every lesson that follows.
units.application: Before you read Scripture or hear a sermon this week, put your phone in another room and ask God to open your ears. Carry one line from what you hear through the day. Parents and mentors: like this teacher, make the truth your own before you pass it on, and speak to your child or student personally, not to a crowd. Students and young believers: find a wise teacher and listen with a pen in hand.

rel.note: The lips of the righteous feed many, showing why stored wisdom must reach the mouth.
A word spoken in due season is good, the fruit of having wise words ready on the lips.
The words fixed on the lips are what the son will use to answer others with words of truth.
When wisdom enters the heart, knowledge is pleasant to the soul, the same pleasure promised here.
The father tells the son to treasure his commands within and write them on his heart, the same inward keeping.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, “within you” is literally “in your belly,” as the KJV margin notes. The belly stands for the innermost part of a person, the place where the sayings are to be kept. Poole, quoted by Guzik, explains it as “in thine heart, which implies receiving them in love.”
• Henry: “those only that submit to the power of godliness, and make heart-work of it, find the pleasure of it.” The pleasure belongs to those who take the words to heart, not to those who only know them.
• The KJV reads, “they shall withal be fitted in thy lips”: the words are to fit the mouth, ready and suitable for use.
• Compare 2:10, “knowledge is pleasant to your soul”; Psalm 119:11, “Your word I have hidden in my heart”; and Colossians 3:16.
units.summary: Truth stored deep in the heart is ready on the lips when the moment comes.
units.principle: Wisdom brings joy when it is stored in the heart, and it serves others when it is ready on the lips.
units.insight: When Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness, He answered three times, “It is written,” each time with words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1–11). The Scriptures were stored within Him and fixed on His lips, ready at the moment of testing. That is the life this verse describes. Many of us treat God’s word like a reference book on a shelf, consulted in emergencies, rather than food we have eaten. Jeremiah knew the difference: “Your words were found, and I ate them, And Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart” (Jeremiah 15:16). Truth kept within is not a burden but a pleasure, “Sweeter also than honey” (Psalm 19:10). Ask what fills your inner store, because that is what will come out of your mouth when you are pressed.
units.application: Choose one verse this week, write it on a card, and say it aloud each morning until it is fixed on your lips. Parents: memorize a verse together at dinner and use it when a real situation arises. Small-group leaders and teachers: ask people to recite, not only to discuss. When a friend is struggling, be ready to offer a word of Scripture gently instead of a slogan.

rel.note: The one who heeds the word wisely finds good, and whoever trusts in the LORD is happy, joining instruction to trust.
Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD, and this collection aims at the same reliance on Him, stated here as trust in the LORD.
The call to hear the words of the wise is explained here by its purpose.
Whoever trusts in the LORD shall be safe, naming the security this instruction aims at.
Trusting the LORD with all the heart instead of one’s own understanding is the aim stated here.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads, “That thy trust may be in the LORD, I have made known to thee this day, even to thee.” The repeated “thee” (in the NKJV, “you today, even you”) presses the message home to one person.
• This purpose governs the whole collection that follows (22:17–24:22). Whatever its subject, each saying is meant to bring the learner to trust the LORD.
• Henry: “We cannot trust in God except in the way of duty; we are therefore taught our duty, that we may have reason to trust in God.”
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “Even the most brilliant, moral sayings are powerless without personal application.”
• Compare 3:5–6; 16:20, “whoever trusts in the LORD, happy is he”; and Psalm 95:7, “Today, if you will hear His voice.”
units.summary: Every lesson about money, words and friends has one goal: a heart that leans on God.
units.principle: The purpose of God’s practical wisdom is not self-sufficiency but trust in Him, and His word is addressed personally to each reader.
units.insight: It is possible to learn wise principles and still trust only yourself. Budgeting, careful speech and good habits can become a quieter kind of self-reliance. Solomon knew more proverbs than anyone, yet “when Solomon was old . . . his heart was not loyal to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 11:4). Wisdom that did not end in trust could not keep him. The rich man in Jesus’ parable planned carefully for his barns and forgot God, and God called him a fool (Luke 12:16–21). This verse aims every practical lesson at the heart. Jesus lived it perfectly; even His mockers at the cross admitted, “He trusted in God” (Matthew 27:43). Ask whether your good habits are drawing you closer to God or making you feel you need Him less.
units.application: When you make a financial plan, a hard decision or a schedule this week, finish by praying over it and handing the outcome to God in so many words. Parents: when you teach your children practical skills, tell them why God cares about those things. Teachers and preachers: aim every lesson at trust in the LORD, not only better behavior. Read today’s portion of Scripture as a letter addressed to you, “even you.”

rel.note: A faithful witness does not lie, describing the reliable speech this instruction aims to produce.
The book’s opening purpose, to know wisdom and understand the words of the wise, is restated here for the new collection.
The words fixed on the son’s lips are what he uses to answer others with truth.
A faithful messenger refreshes those who send him, a picture that fits the reading of 22:21 in which the son brings back a true report.
Wisdom speaks “excellent things” and truth, with nothing crooked in her words, the same quality claimed for these writings.

units.notes:
• “Excellent things” is one of the hardest words in the chapter. The letters in the Hebrew text spell a word meaning “the day before yesterday,” used in expressions for “formerly.” A note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to a different word, which the NKJV, NASB (1995) and KJV understand as excellent or noble things. The ancient Greek, Syriac, Aramaic and Latin translations have “three times,” as does the YLT.
• Hebrew was first written without vowels, so the same letters can sometimes be read as different words. Many modern scholars read the margin’s word with different vowels as “thirty,” and the ESV and NLT translate “thirty sayings.” That reading is tied to an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope, arranged in thirty chapters. In 1924 Adolf Erman pointed out close parallels with the sayings that follow, especially 22:17–23:11. How the two are related, and which way any influence ran, is debated. Whatever their history, these sayings stand in Scripture as inspired words, given “So that your trust may be in the LORD” (22:19).
• Henry on “excellent things”: “they are princely things (so the word is), fit for kings to speak and senates to hear.”
• Translations differ on the last phrase. The NKJV and KJV have people who send to the son. The KJV margin, ESV, NASB and NLT read it as those who sent him, picturing the son as a messenger who brings back an accurate report (compare 25:13).
• Compare Luke 1:4, written “that you may know the certainty of those things in which you were instructed,” and 1 Peter 3:15.
units.summary: Wisdom was written down so we could stand on the truth and give others a true answer.
units.principle: God’s word was written so that we may be sure of the truth and able to give a true and reliable answer to others.
units.insight: Many believers live with a low hum of uncertainty. They believe, but when a friend asks a hard question they have nothing solid to say. God did not leave us to guess. He had His words written so that we could “know the certainty” of them. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus, “beginning at Moses and all the Prophets,” explained the Scriptures concerning Himself (Luke 24:27). The two disciples’ hearts burned within them, and they hurried back to Jerusalem to tell what they had heard (Luke 24:32–35). Certainty received became testimony given. Christ is the truth itself (John 14:6). The more firmly we stand on His written word, the more steadily we can answer those who come to us.
units.application: If there is a question about your faith you cannot answer, write it down this week and look for the answer in Scripture with a pastor or a trusted book. Parents: when your children ask why, show them where the Bible says it. Employees and friends: be the person whose report can be relied on, who does not exaggerate or shade the facts. Teachers: aim to leave people sure of God’s word, not only interested in it.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, the God who here pleads their cause.
The one who oppresses the poor to grow rich comes to poverty, because the LORD takes up their case.
The LORD is Maker of rich and poor alike, which is why He defends the poor against the rich who rob them.
Moving a weak neighbor’s boundary stone is another way of robbing those who cannot defend themselves.
The Redeemer of the fatherless will plead their cause against those who take their fields, the same divine advocacy.
Lemuel’s mother tells the king to plead the cause of the poor, calling human authority to do what the LORD does here.

units.notes:
• To “plead their cause” is to argue a case as an advocate. The promise returns at 23:10–11: “For their Redeemer is mighty; He will plead their cause against you.”
• The city gate served as the court. Boaz settled Ruth’s case before the elders at the gate (Ruth 4:1–11), and Amos called Israel to “Establish justice in the gate” (Amos 5:15).
• The KJV has “spoil the soul of those that spoiled them.” The same verb is used twice, so the punishment mirrors the crime exactly.
• Henry: “It is bad to rob any man, but most absurd to rob the poor, whom we should relieve”.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: “Woe therefore to them that oppress them, for they will have God, not the poor, to deal with.”
• Compare Exodus 22:22–24 and Psalm 140:12, “I know that the LORD will maintain The cause of the afflicted, And justice for the poor.”
units.summary: The poor may have no lawyer, but they have an Advocate no oppressor can outlast.
units.principle: God Himself defends the poor against those who exploit them, so injustice toward the weak is a fight with Him.
units.insight: Nathan told David of a rich man who, with flocks of his own, took a poor man’s one little lamb to feed a guest. David burned with anger and said the man deserved to die. Then Nathan said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:1–7). David had used his power against a man who could not resist him. It is easy to condemn oppression in others and miss it in our own dealings. The poor have a Defender who sees what we hide. In Jesus that Defender came near. He was condemned by a corrupt court and “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), and now He is our “Advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1). The One who pleads for sinners also pleads for the poor, and He calls His people to stand where He stands.
units.application: If you manage people, set prices, lend money or collect rent, check this week whether any of your practices profit from someone’s lack of options: late fees, unpaid overtime, fine print. Fix one. If you serve on a board, jury or committee, give the person without power the same hearing as the person with it. Churches: learn which neighbors are being exploited, and offer advocacy as well as charity.

rel.note: The righteous should choose friends carefully, because the way of the wicked leads them astray.
Walking with the wise makes a person wise and the companion of fools is destroyed, the same power of companionship.
The wrathful man stirs up strife, while the one slow to anger calms it, the better example to learn from.
The one who guards his soul stays far from snares; avoiding an angry companion is one way to do that.
The angry and furious man stirs up strife and abounds in sin, showing the ways the son would learn.

units.notes:
• The same pair of words appears in 29:22: “An angry man stirs up strife, And a furious man abounds in transgression.”
• “Lest you learn his ways”: friendship is a school, whether we intend it or not. Compare 13:20, “He who walks with wise men will be wise,” and 1 Corinthians 15:33, “Evil company corrupts good habits.”
• Bridges: “We learn anger easier than meekness.”
• Henry: “Those we go with we are apt to grow like.” The danger is not only being hurt by the angry man, but becoming like him.
• “Snare” links this warning to 22:5, where the person who guards his soul stays far from snares.
units.summary: Anger is contagious: spend your days with a hothead and you will catch his temper.
units.principle: We grow like the people we walk with, so close friendship with an angry person endangers our own soul.
units.insight: Rehoboam rejected the counsel of the elders and consulted “the young men who had grown up with him.” They taught him to answer the people with threats, and he did: “My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scourges!” The ten northern tribes broke away from him (1 Kings 12:8–19). We become like the people we keep closest. Some of us caught a temper from a friend, a parent or a workplace, and now we pass it on at home. Jesus offers a different companionship: “Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The more time we spend with Him, the more His ways become ours. To the angry person reading this, the same invitation stands: come to Him and learn.
units.application: Young people: look at your closest friends and ask whose temper you are starting to share. Choose your nearest companions for their character, while staying kind to everyone. Parents: notice who is shaping your children’s reactions, including voices online. If you work under an angry boss, refuse to pass his tone on to others. If you are the angry one, ask a calm, godly friend to hold you accountable.

rel.note: The one who is surety for a stranger will suffer, while the one who refuses is secure.
Shaking hands in a pledge is called the act of a man devoid of understanding.
The creditor takes the garment of one who is surety for a stranger, showing what the guarantor can lose.
The borrower is servant to the lender, the dependence a rash pledge brings on the guarantor.
The father urges the son who has shaken hands in pledge to free himself at once, the fullest treatment of surety.

units.notes:
• Proverbs repeats this warning often: 6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 27:13. “A man devoid of understanding shakes hands in a pledge, And becomes surety for his friend” (17:18).
• The law protected the poor borrower: a cloak taken as a pledge had to be returned by sunset, “For that is his only covering . . . What will he sleep in?” (Exodus 22:26–27; compare Deuteronomy 24:12–13). The guarantor who promised beyond his means could still be stripped of his bed.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: “The risk is that if someone lacks the means to pay, his creditors may take his bed”.
• Bridges guards against the opposite error: “There is, however, so much danger of erring in over-caution, and of indulging selfishness under the cover of prudence, that these wholesome cautions must be considerately applied.”
• Compare 22:7, “the borrower is servant to the lender.”
units.summary: A careless handshake can cost you the very bed you sleep on.
units.principle: Wisdom does not guarantee debts it cannot pay; love gives what it can afford to lose rather than promising what it cannot keep.
units.insight: Most cosigning begins with a hard conversation and a soft heart. We want to help, we cannot bear to say no, and we sign for more than we could ever cover. Scripture does honor a surety who counts the cost. Judah told his father, “I myself will be surety for him” (Genesis 43:9), and later offered to stay as a slave in Benjamin’s place (Genesis 44:32–33). Paul wrote to Philemon about Onesimus, “if he has wronged you or owes anything, put that on my account” (Philemon 18). Above all, “Jesus has become a surety of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). He pledged Himself for debtors who had nothing to pay, knowing the full price, and He paid it. We cannot be anyone’s savior. Love sometimes means giving what we can and refusing to promise what we cannot.
units.application: If a family member or friend asks you to cosign a loan or lease, ask one question: could I pay this whole debt myself without harming my household? If not, say no kindly, and consider giving a smaller gift you can afford. Parents of young adults: talk this through before the request comes. Spouses: never sign for anyone without agreeing together. If you have already cosigned, stay in touch with the borrower and plan for the worst.

rel.note: A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren, the family portion the landmark protects.
The LORD establishes the boundary of the widow, guarding the very stones this verse forbids moving.
Robbing the poor and moving a weak neighbor’s boundary are both theft from people who cannot defend themselves.
The same command not to move the ancient landmark is repeated with a warning that the Redeemer of the fatherless defends their fields.

units.notes:
• Moving a boundary stone fell under a public curse, pronounced before all the people: “Cursed is the one who moves his neighbor’s landmark” (Deuteronomy 27:17).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: “Unfortunately, the crime was easy to accomplish and difficult to prove.” That is why the law and this proverb appeal to conscience and to God.
• Job lists those who “remove landmarks” among the oppressors of the poor (Job 24:2), and Hosea compares Judah’s princes to “those who remove a landmark” (Hosea 5:10).
• Compare 15:25, “He will establish the boundary of the widow,” and 23:10–11.
• The verse is often applied to long-tested truths handed down from earlier generations of believers (compare Jude 3). That is a secondary application; the verse itself concerns land and inheritance.
units.summary: Shifting a boundary stone a few feet is still theft, and God sees every inch.
units.principle: God guards the rightful portion of every family, so quietly taking what belongs to another, especially the weak, is theft against both neighbor and God.
units.insight: Naboth refused to sell his family vineyard to King Ahab: “The LORD forbid that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!” (1 Kings 21:3). Jezebel hired false witnesses, Naboth was stoned, and Ahab went down to take the land. Elijah met him there with God’s question: “Have you murdered and also taken possession?” (1 Kings 21:19). Few of us would go that far, but boundary stones still move quietly: a property line fudged, credit taken for someone else’s work, a little more taken from an elderly relative’s estate than was agreed. God sees every inch. For believers there is also deep comfort here. Our inheritance in Christ is “incorruptible and undefiled,” “reserved in heaven” (1 Peter 1:4). No one can move its boundary.
units.application: Business owners and contractors: honor every boundary, from property lines to contract terms, even when no one would notice. Families settling an estate: divide it as agreed and protect the share of the weakest member. Anyone handling another person’s money, such as a guardian, executor or treasurer, should keep clear records and invite someone to check them. If you have moved a boundary, make it right this week.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent makes rich, while a slack hand brings poverty.
The hand of the diligent will rule, the same rise of the faithful worker.
The king’s favor rests on a wise servant, as here the skilled worker stands before kings.
The pure-hearted and gracious also win the king’s friendship; character and skill both earn a place near the throne.
The lazy man invents a lion to avoid work, while this man excels in his work and is honored.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind “excels” means quick and skilled. The same word describes Ezra as “a skilled scribe in the Law of Moses” (Ezra 7:6).
• Where the NKJV has “unknown men,” the ESV and NASB (1995) have “obscure men,” and the KJV has “mean men,” with a margin note that the Hebrew means “obscure men.” In older English “mean” meant low in rank, not unkind.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: “Anyone who puts his workmanship before his prospects towers above the thrusters and climbers of the adjacent paragraphs.” The person who cares more about the work than about getting ahead stands far above ambitious schemers.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: “A diligent man shall not sit long in a low place.”
• Compare 12:24, “The hand of the diligent will rule,” and Romans 12:11, “not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord.”
units.summary: Excellent work rarely stays hidden; skill and faithfulness open doors to high places.
units.principle: Skill and faithfulness in ordinary work usually earn trust and honor, and God values excellent work whether or not people notice it.
units.insight: God filled Bezalel, a craftsman, “with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–5). Skilled work is not unspiritual. Jesus Himself was known in Nazareth as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3), and before He had preached a sermon or worked a miracle, the Father said, “You are My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11). Our hearts tend toward one of two errors. Either we despise ordinary work as unimportant, or we treat our careers as the measure of our worth. This verse corrects both. Do the work well, and leave the recognition to God. One day the King of kings will say to His faithful servants, “Well done” (Matthew 25:21).
units.application: Choose one ordinary task this week, such as a report, a meal or a repair, and do it as well as you can, “as to the Lord and not to men” (Colossians 3:23). Students: master the basics instead of cramming for the grade. Employers: notice and promote skill and faithfulness, not self-promotion. If your good work has gone unrecognized, do not grow bitter; God sees it, and your work still matters.

rel.note: The knife at the throat names the decisive restraint that careful consideration at the ruler's table requires.
The ruler's delicacies are called deceptive food, which explains why the guest must consider carefully what is before him.
The miser's table is a second meal where the welcome is not what it seems, so the same watchfulness is required.
Conduct in the king's presence calls for the same restraint and self-awareness as eating at a ruler's table.
Many seek a ruler's favor, but justice comes from the LORD, so the son need not sell his judgment for access to the great.

units.notes:
• "Consider carefully" repeats the Hebrew verb for understanding, literally "understanding, understand." The doubling presses the son to give the scene his full attention, not a passing glance. The KJV has "consider diligently."
• "What is before you" can also be read "who is before you." Ironside renders the line, "Consider well who is before thee." Most versions, including the ESV and KJV, have "what," and both senses fit: the food and the host must both be weighed.
• Daniel and his friends faced this test at Nebuchadnezzar's court. Daniel "purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's delicacies" and asked for vegetables and water instead (Daniel 1:8, 12).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The rich do not give away their favors for free."
• Compare 25:6–7; 29:26; Luke 14:1, where Jesus ate in the house of a ruler of the Pharisees and "they watched Him closely."
units.summary: An invitation to a powerful man's table is an honor, a test and sometimes a trap.
units.principle: Honor and generosity from the powerful call for clear eyes, because an offer is never only about what is on the table.
units.insight: Haman went home from Queen Esther's private banquet glowing, boasting that no one but he had been invited with the king (Esther 5:12). He never considered carefully what was before him, and the next banquet exposed him (Esther 7:1–10). Invitations from important people do their quiet work on us because we want to be noticed. The verse asks what we are really hungry for when we sit at the great man's table: the food, the approval, the access? Jesus sat at such tables too. He ate in the house of a ruler of the Pharisees while they watched Him closely (Luke 14:1). He was neither flattered nor afraid, and He even told His host whom he ought to invite (Luke 14:12–14). Secure in His Father's love, He did not need the host's favor, and He was free to be faithful.
units.application: Before you accept the dinner with the senior partner, the donor or the official, ask what is being offered and why. Go, if it is right to go, but keep your judgment awake: eat moderately, drink little, and promise nothing you would not promise in daylight. Young professionals and new leaders are especially exposed, because a powerful person's attention feels like arrival. Pastors and church leaders, weigh gifts and hospitality from people who may want influence in return.

rel.note: The call to consider the ruler's table carefully sets the scene in which appetite must be restrained.
The glutton's company and end are described later in the chapter, showing where an unchecked appetite leads.
Honey eaten past need ends in vomiting, another call to set a firm limit on a pleasant food.
A person with no rule over his own spirit is a city without walls, the danger the knife at the throat is meant to prevent.

units.notes:
• "Appetite" translates nephesh, the common Hebrew word often rendered "soul." It can name a person's hunger or desire, and here it is the craving the knife is meant to stop. The word for "throat" in the first line is a different Hebrew word.
• "Given to appetite" is literally "a master of appetite." The phrase carries an irony: the one who seems to own his appetite is in fact owned by it.
• Henry explains the image: "restrain thyself, as it were with a sword hanging over thy head, from all excess."
• Jesus used the same kind of overstatement: "If your right eye causes you to sin, pluck it out and cast it from you" (Matthew 5:29). Neither saying calls for bodily harm; both call for decisive action against sin.
• Compare 25:16; 25:28; 1 Corinthians 9:27; Galatians 5:22–23.
units.summary: Where appetite is strong, restraint must be stronger, as if your life depended on it.
units.principle: Where a desire is strong, wisdom answers with decisive restraint, not with small bargains that let the desire win a little at a time.
units.insight: Esau came in from the field weary and traded his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34). One meal, eaten in the grip of appetite, cost him what he could never recover (Hebrews 12:16–17). Appetite rarely announces itself as a threat; it simply feels like need. Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "It is a shame for a saint to be a slave to his palate." Most of us know where we are "given to appetite," whether food, drink, screens or spending. The gospel does more than tell us to clench our teeth. Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, refused bread on the devil's terms and answered that man lives "by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). His Spirit now produces self-control in those who belong to Him (Galatians 5:22–23).
units.application: Name your weak point before you walk into the situation that feeds it: the business dinner with an open bar, the buffet, the late-night scrolling, the shopping site. Decide in advance what you will take, and stop there. If you struggle with drink, skip the event that centers on it, or bring a friend who knows. Parents, help a teenager plan a firm "no" before the party, not during it.

rel.note: Bread gained by deceit tastes sweet and then turns to gravel, the same gap between a pleasant meal and its hidden cost.
The command to consider carefully what is before you opens the warning that this verse completes.
The miser's delicacies are another meal whose welcome is false, and the same words, "desire his delicacies," join the two scenes.
Flattery spreads a net for a neighbor's feet, which is what a lavish table can do when it is used to win a guest.

units.notes:
• "Deceptive food" is literally "bread of lies." The lie is not in the food itself but in what the meal pretends to say about the host's goodwill. The KJV has "deceitful meat," using "meat" in its old sense of food.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "So the warning is not to indulge in his impressive feast—the ruler wants something from you or is observing you."
• The words "desire his delicacies" return in 23:6 ("Nor desire his delicacies"), tying the ruler's table to the miser's.
• David prayed against this kind of table: "do not let me eat of their delicacies" (Psalm 141:4). Compare Daniel 11:26, where those who eat from a king's table bring him down.
• Compare 20:17: "Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, But afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel."
units.summary: Some generosity is bait: the food is real, but the friendship it seems to offer may be a lie.
units.principle: Not every generous gift is a kindness, and desire that cannot see past the gift is easily bought.
units.insight: The first temptation came as food that was "good for food" and "pleasant to the eyes" (Genesis 3:6). Behind the fruit was a lie about God. Isaac's love of savory food became the doorway through which Jacob deceived him (Genesis 27:4, 25). The ruler's delicacies work the same way: the gift is real, the message is false. We are most easily used where we most want something, whether approval, comfort, access or a seat at the right table. Jesus answers that hunger with a better table. He is "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and His invitation hides no agenda. He does not offer Himself as a hook but as the gift itself. A heart already fed by Him is much harder to buy.
units.application: When a perk seems too generous, ask what it is meant to buy: the trip from a vendor, the expensive meal from someone seeking a contract, the gift that arrives just before a vote. Employees and purchasing managers, follow a simple rule: accept nothing you would be uncomfortable disclosing to your supervisor. Young adults courted with lavish attention by a group, a recruiter or a suitor, slow down and find out what is expected in return.

rel.note: The diligent hand is commended, a balance that keeps this warning from becoming an excuse for idleness.
A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, showing what is worth the effort instead.
Riches sprouting wings and flying away give the reason the son should stop wearing himself out for them.
The one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished, the same warning against making wealth the race of life.
The KJV reading, "cease from thine own wisdom," echoes the call not to lean on one's own understanding.

units.notes:
• "Overwork" describes toil that wears a person out. The verse targets exhausting effort spent for riches, not the ordinary diligence Proverbs praises.
• The second line has been read in three ways. The NKJV, ESV and NLT take it as using good sense to stop. The NASB (1995) reads it as ceasing from one's consideration of wealth, that is, stop thinking about it. The KJV has "cease from thine own wisdom": stop relying on your own cleverness to get rich, which recalls "lean not on your own understanding" (3:5).
• Henry draws the line between work and greed: "Immoderate labour, that we may have to hoard, is our sin and folly."
• Paul makes the same distinction: "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and a snare" (1 Timothy 6:9), while "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1 Timothy 6:6).
• Compare 28:20; 15:16; Psalm 127:2; Ecclesiastes 4:8.
units.summary: Work hard, but do not wear yourself out chasing money; have the sense to know when enough is enough.
units.principle: Work is a gift and a duty, but wealth pursued as life's goal drains the strength it was meant to serve.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man whose land yielded so much that he planned bigger barns and said to his soul, "take your ease; eat, drink, and be merry." God said to him, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:19–20). He had worked hard and planned well; his folly was that wealth had become the point. The verse diagnoses a heart that cannot stop. Often the drive to get more is fear in disguise, a belief that security lies one more raise away. The gospel answers that fear. Our Father knows what we need, so we can seek first His kingdom (Matthew 6:31–33). Christ, though He was rich, became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9). Those who have Him have enough to rest.
units.application: If you are working evenings and weekends mainly to get ahead financially, ask what "enough" would look like and write it down. Business owners and ambitious employees, set a stopping point, protect a weekly day of rest, and let some opportunities go. Parents, notice whether your children are getting your strength or only your paycheck. Give generously this month; giving is one of the surest ways to loosen money's grip.

rel.note: The one who trusts in his riches will fall, because what he leaned on does not stay.
The rich man imagines his wealth as a strong city and a high wall, the very security this verse shows to be imaginary.
Truth and wisdom are to be bought and never sold, treasures that stay when riches fly away.
The command not to wear oneself out for riches is the instruction this verse supports with its reason.
Riches are not forever, the plain statement behind the picture of wings.

units.notes:
• "Set your eyes" is literally "cause your eyes to fly," as the KJV margin notes. The eyes swoop down on money, and the money flies off: the verse plays on the same picture of flight in both lines.
• Bridges: "One moment it seems to be within reach. The next it has eluded our grasp, and flown away as an eagle towards heaven."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Riches will certainly disappear, and once gone, they are gone forever."
• The eagle is Scripture's picture of speed (Deuteronomy 28:49; 2 Samuel 1:23; Lamentations 4:19).
• Compare 11:28; 27:24 ("riches are not forever"); Matthew 6:19–21; 1 Timothy 6:17.
units.summary: Money grows wings: chase it, and you are watching an eagle disappear into the sky.
units.principle: Wealth is real but never secure, so it must never become the place where the heart rests.
units.insight: Job lost his livestock, his servants and his children in a single day (Job 1:13–19). His wealth flew off like an eagle, yet he worshiped: "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; Blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21). His heart had been anchored elsewhere. The verse asks where our eyes are set. When markets fall or a job ends, the panic we feel shows how much weight we had put on what cannot hold it. Jesus told us to lay up treasure in heaven, "where neither moth nor rust destroys" (Matthew 6:20). Paul tells the rich not to trust "in uncertain riches but in the living God, who gives us richly all things to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17). In Christ we have an inheritance that "does not fade away" (1 Peter 1:4).
units.application: Notice where your eyes go: the account balance you keep refreshing, the investment you think about at night. Investors and savers, plan wisely, but hold your plans with an open hand and give regularly so money stays a servant. If you have recently lost income or savings, grieve the loss, then name what did not fly away: God's care, your family, your salvation. Young adults choosing a career, weigh calling and character, not salary alone.

rel.note: A plain meal with love is better than a feast with hatred, the value that makes the miser's fine food worthless.
The man with a generous eye gladly shares his bread, the opposite of the evil-eyed miser.
The ruler's table also serves deceptive delicacies, and the repeated words "desire his delicacies" join the two tables.
The miser's inner reckoning and false welcome explain why his bread should be refused.
The same man with an evil eye hastens after riches, showing the greed behind his grudging table.

units.notes:
• "Miser" is literally "one who is evil of eye." In Hebrew idiom the eye shows a person's attitude toward others: a good eye is generous (22:9), an evil eye grudging. The same expression appears in 28:22, where such a man "hastens after riches." The KJV keeps "him that hath an evil eye"; the ESV has "a man who is stingy."
• Jesus used the same idiom in His parable of the workers: "Is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15). The grumblers begrudged the owner's generosity.
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik, pictures the miser as one "that wisheth thee choked for so doing," that is, he silently wishes his guest would choke for eating his food.
• Compare 15:17: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, Than a fatted calf with hatred." Compare also 17:1.
units.summary: A grudging host serves bitterness with every course, however fine the food looks.
units.principle: Hospitality is measured by the heart behind it, and a gift given grudgingly is a debt in disguise.
units.insight: Nabal was rich and refused David's men even bread and water; his wife Abigail brought bread, wine and meat freely and turned away disaster (1 Samuel 25:10–11, 18–35). The evil eye and the generous eye can live in the same house. The verse warns guests, but it also holds up a mirror to hosts. Do we feed people while privately counting the cost and keeping score of every favor? God's own invitation is the opposite of the miser's: "Ho! Everyone who thirsts, Come to the waters... Yes, come, buy wine and milk Without money and without price" (Isaiah 55:1). Bridges: "No such danger attaches to the invitations of the Gospel." In Christ, God gives with His whole heart, and He teaches us to give the same way, not "grudgingly or of necessity" (2 Corinthians 9:7).
units.application: If someone's hospitality always comes with a bill, a favor expected or a guilt trip later, you are free to decline graciously; accepting every invitation is not a duty. When you host, settle your heart before guests arrive and give the meal as a gift, not a loan. Church members who serve meals and families who host relatives over the holidays, ask God for a glad eye, and give only what you can give without resentment.

rel.note: The command not to eat the miser's bread is the instruction this verse explains.
The meal turns sour once the guest discovers the heart behind the welcome.
The one who hides hatred behind gracious words is not to be believed, the same gap between lips and heart seen in the miser.
A man's heart reveals the man, the principle behind "as he thinks in his heart, so is he."

units.notes:
• "Thinks" translates a Hebrew verb found only here in the Old Testament, so its exact sense has been debated. It is usually understood as calculating or reckoning; the ESV has "calculating," and the NLT speaks of thinking about the cost. The NKJV and KJV keep the more general "thinks."
• The first line is often quoted on its own as a saying about the power of thought to shape character. In context it unmasks the miser: his inner reckoning, not his outward welcome, shows who he really is.
• Henry: "We are that really, both to God and man, which we are inwardly."
• Compare 26:24–25, the man who hides hatred behind gracious speech, and 27:19: "As in water face reflects face, So a man's heart reveals the man." Compare also 1 Samuel 16:7.
units.summary: Listen past the warm welcome to the heart doing the math behind it.
units.principle: A person is what he is in his heart, so words of welcome must be weighed by the character behind them.
units.insight: The old prophet of Bethel urged the man of God to come home and eat bread, claiming an angel had told him to. "He was lying to him" (1 Kings 13:18), and that meal cost the man of God his life. Not every warm voice wishes us well. Yet the verse searches the host as well as the guest. Jesus exposed the same gap in the religious leaders of His day: "These people draw near to Me with their mouth, And honor Me with their lips, But their heart is far from Me" (Matthew 15:8). We can say "Eat and drink!" while resenting the people at our table, or sing praise while keeping score. The cure is not better acting but a new heart. God promises, "I will give you a new heart" (Ezekiel 36:26), so that our welcome can be real.
units.application: When someone's welcome feels warm but their pattern is to resent, keep score or use favors as leverage, trust the pattern. You can be courteous without placing yourself in their debt. Hosts, before you open your door this week, examine your heart toward your guests; if you resent the cost, settle it with God or give less and give gladly. Leaders, let your praise of your team in public match what you say about them in private.

rel.note: A dry morsel eaten in peace is better than a feast with strife, the opposite of a fine meal eaten under a false welcome.
Bread gained by deceit turns to gravel, the same bitter aftertaste that follows the miser's meal.
The miser's grudging heart, described in the verses before, is what turns this meal sour.
The next verse turns from wasted thanks to wasted wisdom, words spent where they are despised.
Too much honey also ends in vomiting, another picture of pleasure that turns to sickness.

units.notes:
• The "morsel" is only a small bite, yet it costs the guest a great deal of discomfort. Even a little taken from a grudging host sits badly.
• "Pleasant words" are a guest's compliments and thanks; the KJV has "sweet words." Henry pictures the guest wishing he could take them back, as if he must "eat the words thou has spoken in returning his compliments."
• Vomiting appears again in 25:16 as the result of taking more honey than one needs: both sayings picture pleasure that turns to sickness.
• Compare 20:17, where bread gained by deceit turns to gravel in the mouth, and 17:1: "Better is a dry morsel with quietness, Than a house full of feasting with strife."
units.summary: A meal eaten under a false welcome turns sour, and every polite thank-you spent on it is wasted.
units.principle: Courtesy spent on an insincere heart is often wasted, so wisdom chooses carefully whose favors it receives.
units.insight: Most of us know the sick feeling of discovering that someone's welcome was a performance: the relative who resented our visit, the colleague whose praise was strategy. The verse names that feeling plainly. Jacob spent twenty years of hard work and courtesy on Laban, who changed his wages "ten times" (Genesis 31:7, 41). Yet God saw it and defended him (Genesis 31:42). At the Last Supper the roles were reversed. The Host's heart was wholly with His guests, and one guest's heart was not. Jesus still dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas (John 13:26), having loved His own "to the end" (John 13:1). Kindness spent on the ungrateful is never lost to God, and His table is the one place where no welcome is false.
units.application: If you keep leaving someone's company feeling used, treat that as information, not merely hurt feelings, and limit the time and favors you give. Employees who keep pouring compliments and extra effort into a boss who never returns goodwill, give honest courtesy, but stop spending yourself to win a welcome that is not there. If you have been burned by false hospitality, resist bitterness: thank God that He saw it, and keep your own welcome toward others sincere.

rel.note: The fool takes no delight in understanding, only in airing his own opinions, which is why he despises wise words.
Fools despise wisdom and instruction, the same contempt this verse expects.
Pleasant words wasted on the miser lead into wise words wasted on the fool.
The paired sayings on answering a fool show that wisdom discerns when to speak and when to keep silent.
Correcting a scoffer brings shame and hatred, so the wise choose where to spend rebuke.

units.notes:
• "In the hearing of" is literally "in the ears of," as the KJV renders it. Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "it is direct address, not something overheard." The warning concerns deliberately addressing the fool.
• "Despise" means to treat as worthless. It is the same contempt that fools show for "wisdom and instruction" in 1:7.
• Jesus gave Herod no answer when Herod wanted only a show: "he questioned Him with many words, but He answered him nothing" (Luke 23:9).
• Compare 9:7–8; 18:2; 26:4–5; Matthew 7:6; Ecclesiastes 3:7 ("A time to keep silence, And a time to speak").
units.summary: Wise words are pearls; do not keep pouring them into an ear that only sneers.
units.principle: Wisdom must be offered where it can be received; knowing when to be silent is part of loving well.
units.insight: Herod had long wanted to see Jesus and hoped for a miracle. He questioned Him at length, and Jesus kept silent (Luke 23:8–9). The One who ate with sinners and wept over Jerusalem also knew when words would only be trampled. We tend to fail on one side or the other. Some of us keep arguing with people who mock everything we say, and our "wisdom" becomes a way to win. Others use this verse to excuse never speaking at all. Bridges warns against that second failure: "never make the rule of prudence the excuse for indolence," that is, do not let caution become an excuse for laziness. The heart question is whether we speak or keep silent out of love. When words have to stop, prayer does not.
units.application: If a family member mocks your faith every time you raise it, stop forcing the conversation; live it, pray, and wait for an opening. On social media, refuse the endless reply thread with someone who only wants to ridicule. Parents of a scornful teenager, say less, and say it once, calmly. But watch your own heart: do not label someone a fool just because they disagree with you or ask hard questions.

rel.note: The LORD establishes the boundary of the widow, guarding the land of the vulnerable as this verse commands.
Robbing the poor because they are poor is forbidden, because the LORD pleads their cause.
The same command forbids moving the ancient landmark, here extended to the fields of orphans.
The mighty Redeemer of the fatherless is the reason no one may encroach on their land.

units.notes:
• The law of Moses protected the boundary stone: "You shall not remove your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set" (Deuteronomy 19:14), and it pronounced a curse on anyone who moved it (Deuteronomy 27:17).
• Family land in Israel was an inheritance from the LORD, meant to stay in the family (Leviticus 25:23). That is why Naboth refused to sell his vineyard: "The LORD forbid that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!" (1 Kings 21:3).
• In 22:28 the landmark is the one "your fathers have set." Here the concern is the fatherless, who have no father left to guard it.
• Bridges: "Many would not dare to touch the rich, while they oppress the poor at their will."
• Compare 15:25; Exodus 22:22–24; Isaiah 10:1–2; Hosea 5:10.
units.summary: The quietest theft is taking land from someone who has no one to object.
units.principle: Injustice often hides in small encroachments on those too weak to object, and God counts such quiet theft as serious sin.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard. When Naboth would not sell his family inheritance, Jezebel arranged false charges and his death so the king could take the land (1 Kings 21:1–16). Elijah met Ahab in that very vineyard with the word of the LORD (1 Kings 21:17–19). The powerful seldom think of themselves as thieves; they are only "adjusting boundaries." The verse asks where we take a little from those who cannot push back: an elderly relative's estate, an employee who will not complain, a tenant who does not know the law. Jesus condemned those who "devour widows' houses, and for a pretense make long prayers" (Mark 12:40). A heart that loves Christ guards the field of the defenseless instead of entering it.
units.application: If you hold power over someone who cannot easily defend themselves, such as an aging parent's finances, a foster child's benefits, a worker afraid to complain or a tenant, make sure every line is fair and documented. Executors and trustees, handle estates as if the heirs were watching. Churches, ask whether anyone among you is being quietly taken advantage of, and step in. If you have moved a boundary, restore it.

rel.note: The LORD establishes the widow's boundary, acting as the defender of those who have no one else.
The LORD pleads the cause of the poor against those who rob them, the same divine advocacy promised to the fatherless.
The command not to enter the fields of the fatherless is the instruction this verse backs with its reason.
Those with power are told to open their mouths for the speechless, imitating the Redeemer who pleads the cause of the weak.

units.notes:
• "Redeemer" translates go'el, the kinsman-redeemer of Leviticus 25 and the Book of Ruth: the close relative bound to buy back lost land, free a relative from servitude and take up his cause (Ruth 3:12–13; 4:1–10). Applied to the LORD here, it means the fatherless have God Himself as their next of kin. Ironside: "they have a Goel, or Kinsman-Redeemer, in Jehovah Himself."
• "Plead their cause" is courtroom language: to argue a case as an advocate. The same words describe the LORD's defense of the poor in 22:23.
• Jeremiah uses closely similar words of the LORD's defense of His exiled people: "Their Redeemer is strong; The LORD of hosts is His name. He will thoroughly plead their case" (Jeremiah 50:34).
• God names Himself "A father of the fatherless, a defender of widows" (Psalm 68:5). Compare Exodus 22:22–24; Psalm 10:14, 18; Isaiah 41:14.
units.summary: The orphan who seems to have no one has the strongest Kinsman of all.
units.principle: God takes the side of those with no defender, and whoever exploits them must answer to Him.
units.insight: Naomi came home to Bethlehem empty, a widow with no sons and no way to hold her family's land. Then Boaz, a near kinsman, stepped in, redeemed the land and married Ruth (Ruth 4:9–10). This verse says the LORD does that for every orphan who has no Boaz. It is a warning to anyone who preys on the weak and a comfort to anyone who has been wronged and has no one to plead their case. In the light of the New Testament, the Redeemer has a name. Christ shared our flesh and blood so that He could be our kinsman (Hebrews 2:14–15), and He "always lives to make intercession" for those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25). If you feel defenseless, you are not. Your Redeemer is mighty.
units.application: If you have been cheated and have no one to stand up for you, bring the whole case to God, as David did ("Plead my cause, O LORD," Psalm 35:1), and seek honest legal help where it exists. If you have influence, be a kinsman to someone who has none: volunteer as a child advocate, mentor a foster youth, or help a widow understand her paperwork. Business owners, never build profit on people too weak to object.

rel.note: The heart of the prudent acquires knowledge and the ear of the wise seeks it, the same two organs at work.
The collection opens with the same pairing of an inclined ear and an applied heart.
The word for instruction here is translated correction in the next verse, so the call to listen leads straight into discipline.
The call to hear and be wise returns, again aimed at the heart.
The father earlier called for the ear inclined to wisdom and the heart applied to understanding.

units.notes:
• The word for "instruction" here means discipline and training. It is the same word translated "correction" in 23:13, which ties this call to listen to the saying on discipline that follows.
• Heart and ear are paired throughout Proverbs: "Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, And apply your heart to my knowledge" (22:17). Compare 2:2 and 18:15.
• Henry: "The heart is then applied to the instruction when the instruction is applied to the heart."
• Lydia shows how this happens: "The Lord opened her heart to heed the things spoken by Paul" (Acts 16:14).
• Compare Jeremiah 15:16; James 1:21–22.
units.summary: Wisdom has to get past the ear and into the heart, or it never changes a life.
units.principle: Truth changes a person only when the ear hears it and the heart receives it.
units.insight: Ezra "had prepared his heart to seek the Law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10). He did not only read; he set his heart. Many of us hear a great deal of teaching through sermons, podcasts and studies, and remain largely unchanged, because the words reach the ear but never the heart. Jesus warned of seed that falls by the wayside and is snatched away before it takes root (Matthew 13:19). The repeated call to listen in Proverbs implies a humbling truth: we drift from instruction and need to be called back again and again. Yet the One who calls also opens hearts, as He did for Lydia (Acts 16:14). Ask Him to do that before you read or listen.
units.application: Before the sermon on Sunday or your Bible reading this week, pray one sentence: "Lord, open my heart to receive this." Then write down one thing to do and do it within a day. Students, give your full attention in class instead of half-listening. Small-group leaders, ask "What will you do with this?" and not only "What did you learn?" Parents, let your children see you receive correction well.

rel.note: The parent who loves his son disciplines him promptly, the same love that refuses to withhold correction.
The rod of correction drives foolishness from a child's heart, naming the aim of the discipline commanded here.
The word for instruction in the call to listen is the word for correction here, so receiving and giving correction belong together.
The next verse names the goal: delivering the child's life from the path that ends in death.
The LORD corrects the son He loves, the pattern that every parent's correction should follow.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV and KJV have "beat," the ESV and NASB (1995) have "strike." The Hebrew verb is the common word for striking, used of blows of every kind; the setting here is a parent's measured correction.
• "He will not die" most likely means that correction will not destroy him, while its absence may lead to ruin. Ironside: "Discipline, administered seasonably (not in harshness, or undue severity), is for the profit of the child." "Seasonably" means at the right time.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "This text does not justify brutalizing children."
• Compare 13:24; 19:18; 22:15; 29:15, 17; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:10–11.
units.summary: Loving correction will not destroy a child; leaving him uncorrected might.
units.principle: Loving correction is an act of care, not cruelty, and it must never become harshness, rage or abuse.
units.insight: Eli loved his sons, rebuked them gently and never restrained them, and the LORD judged his house (1 Samuel 3:13). David never once asked his son Adonijah, "Why have you done so?" (1 Kings 1:6), and that son grew up to grab the throne. Withheld correction is often our own comfort dressed up as kindness. Yet some parents fail the other way, correcting in anger and calling it obedience to Scripture. The Bible holds both together. Our heavenly Father disciplines "for our profit, that we may be partakers of His holiness" (Hebrews 12:10), and He tells fathers, "do not provoke your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4). His correction of us is never rejection: "whom the LORD loves He corrects" (3:12). That is the pattern for every parent.
units.application: Parents, if you have been avoiding correction because you are tired or dread the conflict, pick one behavior and address it calmly and consistently this week. If you tend to correct in anger, wait until you are calm, explain what was wrong, and end by reassuring your child of your love. Grandparents and teachers, support parents' fair correction.
