If you were harmed by harsh discipline as a child, know that this verse never justified it.

rel.note: The way of life leads the wise away from Sheol below, the very rescue correction aims at.
Chastening a son while there is hope aims at the same rescue from destruction.
The rod of correction drives foolishness far from a child, the same rescue from folly that this verse names as the goal of discipline.
The previous verse gives the command and the reassurance that this verse completes with its goal.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, while a child left to himself brings shame.

units.notes:
• "Hell" translates Sheol, the Old Testament name for the grave and the realm of the dead. The ESV and NASB (1995) keep "Sheol," and the NLT renders it "death." Ironside: "Sheol is not exactly hell," but the place to which a reckless life soon leads.
• "Soul" here means the child's life or self, so "deliver his soul" means rescue his life.
• Henry: "The rod will not kill him; nay, it will prevent his killing himself" through the reckless ways it restrains.
• Compare 15:24 ("That he may turn away from hell below"); 19:18; 22:15; Hebrews 12:11; James 5:20.
units.summary: Correction is a rescue: it pulls a child off the road whose end is death.
units.principle: Faithful correction aims at rescue; it cannot save a soul, but it can turn a young life from the way that leads to death.
units.insight: Manoah asked the angel, "What will be the boy's rule of life, and his work?" (Judges 13:12). He wanted to raise his son rightly from the start. Yet Samson still chose his own way, a reminder that correction aims at rescue but does not guarantee the outcome. Parents carry great responsibility and limited control. This verse lifts the eyes of a weary parent to what discipline is for: not winning arguments or keeping the house quiet, but pulling a beloved child back from a road that ends in death. Only God saves. In the light of the New Testament, the Father disciplines us as sons (Hebrews 12:7) and "has delivered us from the power of darkness" through His Son (Colossians 1:13). Parents grieving a wayward child are not condemned by this verse.
units.application: Parents, when you correct, tell your child why: name the road you are steering them away from and the good you want for them. Pray before and after. If your child is grown and wandering, keep praying and loving; your earlier faithfulness is not wasted, and the outcome rests with God. Youth leaders and teachers, do not let fear of conflict stop you from lovingly confronting a young person heading toward danger.

rel.note: A wise son makes a glad father, the saying that opened Solomon's collection on the same note.
The father of a fool has no joy, the opposite of the gladness a wise heart brings.
The next verse shows the wise heart reaching the lips and the father's joy reaching his inmost being.
The father of the righteous greatly rejoices, as the chapter returns to a parent's joy in a wise child.
The father again asks his son to be wise and make his heart glad.

units.notes:
• The verse is built as a mirror: "your heart" in the first line answers "My heart" in the second. What happens in the son's heart reaches the father's.
• The added words "indeed, I myself" (KJV "even mine") make the father's joy emphatic and personal, not a formal approval.
• At a deeper level the father's voice carries the voice of God's fatherly care. Ironside: "We may hear, in these words of a father addressed to his son, the desire of our Father, God, that His children walk in the truth."
• Compare 10:1; 15:20; 27:11 ("My son, be wise, and make my heart glad"); 3 John 4.
units.summary: A father's deepest joy is not a child's success but a child's wise heart.
units.principle: Wisdom in a child's heart brings a parent a joy that no achievement can give, and the Father in heaven delights in the same way.
units.insight: When the prodigal came home, his father ran to him, embraced him and called for a feast: "for this my son was dead and is alive again" (Luke 15:24). Jesus told that story to show the joy of God over one who returns. This verse lets a son glimpse his father's heart, and it lets us glimpse God's. We often imagine God as a stern examiner waiting for us to fail. The father here begins with delight, not threat. The apostle John wrote, "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth" (3 John 4). Parents and spiritual mentors know that joy. The question for each of us is simple: what would make the heart of the One who loves us most rejoice today?
units.application: Parents, tell your children specifically when you see wisdom in them: a kind choice, an honest admission, a wise decision. Let them hear that you are glad in them, not only in their grades or games. Young adults, call a parent or mentor this week and tell them about a wise step you have taken; it will do them good. Mentors and pastors, name the growth you see in those you disciple.

rel.note: The heart of the wise teaches his mouth, the same link between a wise heart and right speech.
The wise heart of the previous verse is what produces the right words that bring the father joy.
The same word for what is upright describes the wine that merely goes down smoothly, setting true rightness against easy pleasure.
The drunkard's heart utters perverse things, the opposite of the son's right speech.
Wisdom promises that right things will come from her lips, the speech the father hopes to hear from his son.

units.notes:
• "Inmost being" is literally "kidneys"; the KJV has "reins," an old word for kidneys. In Hebrew idiom the kidneys stand for the deepest emotions and thoughts, much as we speak of the heart or the gut.
• Waltke, quoting Kellermann (cited by Guzik): "Of all human organs, the Old Testament associates the kidneys in particular with a variety of emotions."
• "Right things" translates a word meaning what is level, straight or upright. The same word describes the wine that goes down "smoothly" in 23:31: the son's lips speak what is upright, while the wine merely slides down easily.
• Wisdom herself says, "from the opening of my lips will come right things" (8:6). Compare 16:23; Matthew 12:34.
units.summary: A wise heart shows itself in right words, and right words make a father glad to the core.
units.principle: Speech shows the heart, and upright words from a wise heart bring deep joy to those who love us.
units.insight: Timothy grew up hearing the Scriptures from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and Paul called him "a beloved son" (2 Timothy 1:2). What delights those who raise us is not polish but truth in our mouths. Jesus said, "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). Our words are a window. What would the people who love us hear if they listened to us this week, in the car, online or at work? Speech cannot be fixed only at the lips. The heart must be changed, and God does that work by His Spirit. When He does, our words become a joy to our parents, our mentors and our Father in heaven.
units.application: Parents, notice and praise right speech in your children: the apology offered, the truth told when a lie was easier, the kind word to a sibling. Teens and young adults, watch your words in the places your parents never see, especially online. Leaders and teachers, thank people when they speak up for what is right in a meeting, so that upright speech is honored, not merely tolerated.

rel.note: Envy is rottenness to the bones, describing what envy does to the one who harbors it.
The next verse gives the reason not to envy: the righteous have a sure future.
Do not be envious of evil men or desire to be with them, the same warning against admiring sinners.
The son is again told not to envy the wicked, because the evil man has no future.
Do not envy the oppressor or choose any of his ways, showing how envy leads to imitation.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb for "envy" can also mean "be zealous," and it carries over into the second line, which has no verb of its own. The NKJV brings this out with "be zealous," while the ESV and NLT supply "continue." One verb names both the wrong passion and the right one.
• "All the day" means continually, not only at times of worship. Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "Men must wake with God, walk with him, and lie down with him."
• Compare 3:31; 14:30; 24:1, 19; Psalm 37:1–2; Psalm 73.
units.summary: Envy stares at what sinners have; zeal for God looks at Him until their glitter fades.
units.principle: Envy of the wicked is cured not by wanting less but by loving and fearing God more, all day long.
units.insight: Asaph confessed, "my feet had almost stumbled; My steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the boastful" (Psalm 73:2–3). He watched the arrogant prosper and wondered whether his own purity had been in vain. The turning point came when he "went into the sanctuary of God" (Psalm 73:17). Seeing God rightly changed how everything else looked. Envy often hides behind respectable words like fairness and frustration. It quietly whispers that obedience does not pay. The answer is not to stare harder at the sinner's life but to look longer at the LORD. Asaph ended, "Whom have I in heaven but You?" and called God "my portion forever" (Psalm 73:25–26). In Christ we have that portion, and it changes what we want.
units.application: When scrolling through other people's success leaves you resentful, close the app and spend five minutes in worship or Scripture instead; Psalm 73 is a good place to start. Employees watching a dishonest coworker get promoted, keep your integrity and take your frustration to God, not to gossip. Young people tempted by peers who seem to have more fun without restraint, fill your days with what keeps God in view: prayer, worship and godly friends.

rel.note: The hope of the righteous ends in gladness while the expectation of the wicked perishes.
The command not to envy sinners is the instruction this verse supports with its reason.
The same word for the end describes the drinker's last state, a serpent's bite instead of a hope that is not cut off.
The same assurance appears almost word for word: there is a prospect, and your hope will not be cut off.
The evil man has no prospect, the opposite of the sure future of the one who fears the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Hereafter" translates acharit, meaning the end, the latter part or the outcome. The same word is translated "prospect" in 24:14 and 24:20 and "At the last" in 23:32. The KJV has "an end," with "reward" in the margin; the ESV and NASB have "future."
• Whether the word here points beyond death or to an outcome within this life is debated. Ironside thought "the doctrine of future retribution is more than hinted at"; the verse itself names a sure outcome without describing it.
• Bridges: "Pronounce nothing upon an unfinished work." In other words, do not judge God's dealings before the story is finished.
• Compare 10:28; 24:14, 19–20; Psalm 37:37 ("the future of that man is peace"); Jeremiah 29:11.
units.summary: Do not envy a life with no future when your own story is heading somewhere good.
units.principle: The outcome of a life matters more than its present appearance, and the God who is feared holds a good end for those who fear Him.
units.insight: Abraham lived in tents all his life and owned no more of the promised land than a burial field (Genesis 23:17–20). Yet "he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:10). His neighbors had more land; he had a future. Much of our envy comes from judging a story by its middle chapter. The sinner seems ahead and the faithful seem slow. This verse teaches us to wait for the last page. In the light of the New Testament, the hope of the righteous rests on the risen Christ, and that hope "does not disappoint" (Romans 5:5). We do not wait for nothing. We wait for Him, and with Him for an end that is good.
units.application: If you are tired of doing right with little to show for it, write down where you trust God to bring your life, in this world and in the next, and pray over it. Caregivers, faithful workers passed over for promotion, and believers waiting on long-unanswered prayers, hold on; the outcome is with God. Parents, when your children ask why the wicked seem to win, tell them the end of the story, not only the middle.

rel.note: Listening to counsel and receiving instruction is the way to become wise.
The earlier call to apply the heart and ear to instruction returns here as a call to hear and be wise.
The following verses name the drinking and gluttony the heart must be steered away from.
The appeal that begins with guiding the heart reaches its center in the call to give the heart to the father.
Keeping the heart with all diligence is the same task as guiding it in the way, because life flows from it.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV says "guide your heart in the way," the ESV has "direct your heart in the way." The son is not only to receive direction but to take the wheel of his own inner life.
• Hearing comes before wisdom throughout Proverbs (1:5; 19:20). Bridges links this to the gospel: "For wisdom, no less than 'faith, cometh by hearing.'" The words he quotes are Paul's in Romans 10:17, "faith comes by hearing."
• "The way" is the book's central picture of life as a walk on one of two roads, the path of the just that shines brighter and the way of the wicked that is like darkness (4:18–19). Compare Psalm 1:6; Matthew 7:13–14.
• Compare 4:23–27; 23:12, 26.
units.summary: Steer your heart, and the rest of your life will follow where it goes.
units.principle: Life goes where the heart is steered, so wisdom begins by listening and then guiding the heart along God's way.
units.insight: Samson's heart was never steered. It went wherever his eyes and appetites pulled it, from Timnah to Gaza to the Valley of Sorek (Judges 14:1–3; 16:1, 4). His great strength could not make up for an unguided heart. Most drift is not dramatic rebellion but a heart left to wander. The father's call assumes we can and must take the wheel: notice where our desires are heading and turn them. Yet we cannot steer by willpower alone. David prayed, "Unite my heart to fear Your name" (Psalm 86:11). Jesus is "the way" (John 14:6), and "as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God" (Romans 8:14). We guide our hearts best by keeping them close to Him.
units.application: Take a quick inventory: where have your thoughts drifted this week when you were not choosing them? Cut one input that pulls you off course, such as a show, a feed or a habit, and add one that steadies you, such as Scripture, prayer or a wise friend. Parents, teach teens that guarding the heart means choosing what to watch and whom to follow. New believers, set your heart's direction each morning with a short prayer.

rel.note: The companion of fools will be destroyed, because people become like those they walk with.
Whoever is led astray by wine and strong drink is not wise.
The call to guide the heart in the way comes just before this verse names the company the heart must be steered away from.
The next verse gives the reason: drunkenness and gluttony end in poverty and rags.
The poem on drunkenness shows in full where the drinking life leads.
A companion of gluttons shames his father, the same warning about the company of the indulgent.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew words behind "winebibbers" and "gluttonous" here, and "drunkard" and "glutton" in 23:21, are the pair used of the stubborn and rebellious son in the law: "he is a glutton and a drunkard" (Deuteronomy 21:20).
• Jesus' enemies threw the same pair of words at Him: "Look, a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" (Matthew 11:19). Compare Luke 5:31–32.
• "Mix with" is literally "be among," as the KJV has it: "Be not among winebibbers." Bridges: "Not only be not one of them, but be not amongst them."
• Compare 13:20; 28:7; Romans 13:13; 1 Corinthians 15:33.
units.summary: Choose your table carefully; the company you keep shapes the appetites you develop.
units.principle: Appetites are shaped by company, so the wise choose companions who will not pull them into excess.
units.insight: Lot "pitched his tent even as far as Sodom" (Genesis 13:12), and in time Sodom's ways were in his house. We rarely fall alone; usually we drift into the habits of the people we enjoy. Paul warns, "Evil company corrupts good habits" (1 Corinthians 15:33). Yet this verse must be read beside the life of Jesus. He was called "a glutton and a winebibber" because He ate with sinners (Matthew 11:19). He was among them to rescue them, and He never became like them. The heart question is why we are at the table. Are we there as a friend who brings Christ, or as someone quietly hungry for what the table offers? The answer decides whether we influence the company or the company influences us.
units.application: If most of your free time is spent with people whose evenings center on drinking or bingeing, make one change this month: start a different tradition, invite a different friend, or leave earlier. College students, choose your housing and your clubs with this in mind. Parents, know who your teenagers are with on weekends. If you are reaching out to friends who party, go with a clear purpose and a plan to leave, and bring a believer with you.

rel.note: Loving sleep leads to poverty, the drowsiness that clothes a man in rags.
The one who loves pleasure and wine will be poor, the same outcome of a life given to appetite.
The warning against the company of drunkards and gluttons is the instruction this verse explains.
A little sleep and slumber bring poverty like a prowler, the same slide from sluggishness to want.

units.notes:
• "Drunkard" and "glutton" are the same pair used of the rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20, a son whose appetites have overruled his parents' voice.
• "Drowsiness" is the heavy, half-asleep dullness that follows overindulgence. Proverbs ties sleep and slackness to poverty elsewhere too (6:9–11; 20:13).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Their full stomachs empty their minds."
• Compare 21:17; Luke 21:34; Romans 13:13.
units.summary: A life lived for the next feast tends to end in rags.
units.principle: Habitual indulgence tends to drain both resources and diligence, though poverty itself is never proof of a person's sin.
units.insight: The prodigal son spent his inheritance "with prodigal living" and ended up longing to eat the pods he fed to the pigs (Luke 15:13–16). Then "he came to himself" (Luke 15:17). The rags were not the end of his story; they were the beginning of his return. Many who read this verse are not wealthy drinkers but people quietly losing ground to a habit: the nightly bottle, the binge, the spending that numbs the evening. The verse is a warning, not a sneer. It names where the road goes so we can turn sooner. And the father in Jesus' story ran to meet a son in rags, called for "the best robe" and celebrated (Luke 15:20–24). There is grace for those already in rags.
units.application: Add up what you spent last month on alcohol, takeout and impulse indulgence; the number may surprise you. If a habit is draining your money or making you sluggish at work, tell a trusted friend and ask for accountability, or join a recovery group. Employers and pastors, when someone's work is slipping because of drinking, speak privately and point them to help. Never use this verse to judge a poor neighbor.

rel.note: The son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother brings shame, the contempt this verse forbids.
The son is told to hear his father's instruction and not forsake his mother's teaching.
The call to let father and mother be glad shows the joy that honoring them brings.
The eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother comes to a terrible end, the opposite of the honor commanded here.

units.notes:
• "Who begot you" grounds the command in the parent's gift of life. Listening is the first form that honor takes.
• "Despise" means to look down on, to treat as worthless. It is the same verb used of the fool who "will despise the wisdom of your words" in 23:9.
• Honor does not end when a child becomes independent: Esther, already queen, still obeyed Mordecai, the cousin who had raised her (Esther 2:20).
• Henry, speaking of grown children and their aged mother: "let them not think themselves past being taught, even by her, but rather respect her the more for the multitude of her years."
• Compare 1:8; 19:26; 20:20; 30:17; Leviticus 19:32; 1 Timothy 5:4.
units.summary: Honor does not retire when a parent grows old; that is when it costs the most.
units.principle: Honor for parents is lifelong, and it is tested most when they grow old and slow, when listening to them takes patience.
units.insight: Joseph, ruler of Egypt, brought his aged father before Pharaoh and provided for him through the famine (Genesis 47:7, 12). Greatness did not end his honor. On the cross, in agony, Jesus looked down at His mother and entrusted her to John (John 19:26–27). Caring for her was part of His obedience to the Father. Many adult children feel the strain this verse anticipates: repeated stories, slower steps, decisions that need patience. Contempt can creep in through impatience and neglect as easily as through harsh words. We may honor our parents in public and sigh at them in private. Christ, who honored His mother while bearing the sin of the world, gives grace to honor ours.
units.application: Call or visit an aging parent this week and listen without hurrying, even to the familiar stories. Ask their advice about something real. If you are a caregiver worn down by the work, ask siblings or your church for help before resentment grows. Teenagers, speak to your mother and father with respect, especially when you disagree. Churches, honor older members by seeking their wisdom, not only their attendance.

rel.note: Getting wisdom is far better than gold, the value that makes truth worth any price.
Riches fly away like an eagle, while truth and wisdom, once bought and kept, remain.
The father urges the son to get wisdom and understanding above everything else, using the same verb as "buy."
Wisdom's instruction is to be chosen over silver and gold, because nothing desirable compares with her.

units.notes:
• "Buy" is the same verb translated "get" in 4:5 and 4:7 ("Get wisdom! Get understanding!"). Acquiring wisdom is pictured as a purchase that costs something.
• The verse allows a purchase but forbids a sale: there is no proper price at which truth may be given up.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "Buy the truth; that is, be willing at all risks to hold to the truth."
• Jesus pictured the same purchase in the merchant who sold all he had for one pearl of great price (Matthew 13:45–46). Esau and Judas show the opposite trade, selling what was priceless for a meal and for silver (Hebrews 12:16; Matthew 26:14–16).
• Compare 3:15; 8:10–11; 16:16; Revelation 3:18.
units.summary: Truth is the one purchase worth any price and the one possession worth never selling.
units.principle: Truth and wisdom are worth any cost to gain and are never worth trading away for any gain.
units.insight: Paul had a record most men would envy, and he counted it all "loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). He bought the truth. Demas, once his fellow worker, left him, "having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). He sold it. Bridges: "For those who sell the truth, sell their own souls with it." Truth is rarely sold in one dramatic moment. It is traded in small pieces: a shaded fact to close a deal, a silence to keep the peace, a doctrine softened to stay popular. In the end truth is a Person. Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). To hold on to the truth is to hold on to Him.
units.application: Ask where you are tempted to sell truth cheaply this week: inflating a report, staying silent while a coworker takes the blame, nodding along with teaching you know is false. Decide now not to. Students, invest time in learning Scripture well; it costs hours and pays for a lifetime. Parents, let your children see you tell the truth when it costs you. Teachers and pastors, refuse to trim the message to keep an audience.

rel.note: A wise son makes a glad father, the same joy described here.
The father of a fool has no joy, the reverse of the father of the righteous.
The father's personal joy in his son's wise heart and right speech is the gladness this verse states as a general truth.
The next verse calls the son to give his father and mother this joy.
Whoever loves wisdom makes his father rejoice.

units.notes:
• "Greatly rejoice" renders a Hebrew phrase that repeats the verb for rejoicing, something like "rejoicing, he will rejoice." The doubling expresses overflowing joy.
• Ironside: "Righteousness and wisdom in their children fill the hearts of parents with a joy beyond telling."
• The opposite is stated in 17:21: "the father of a fool has no joy."
• Compare 10:1; 15:20; 23:15–16; 29:3; 3 John 4.
units.summary: No trophy or paycheck can make a parent as glad as a child who walks with God.
units.principle: A child's righteousness and wisdom are a parent's richest reward, and children's choices shape their parents' joy.
units.insight: When Jacob heard that Joseph was alive and ruling Egypt, his spirit revived, and he said, "It is enough. Joseph my son is still alive" (Genesis 45:27–28). Joseph had stayed faithful through slavery, temptation and prison, and his father's joy was full. Young people often underestimate how much their lives weigh on their parents' hearts. Parents, for their part, can slip into wanting a child's success more than a child's righteousness. The verse sets the priorities right. Scripture also speaks of joy in heaven "over one sinner who repents" (Luke 15:7). If you have grieved your parents, it is not too late to give them this joy. If you are a parent still waiting, keep praying; the Father who rejoices over returning children hears you.
units.application: Parents, look at what you celebrate most at home: grades and games, or honesty, kindness and faith? Celebrate character out loud. Adult children, if you have found your way back to God, tell your parents; it may be the best news they hear this year. Grandparents and mentors, write a note to a young person whose godliness you have noticed, and tell their parents too.

rel.note: A wise son makes a glad father, while a foolish son is his mother's grief.
A foolish son is bitterness to her who bore him, the opposite of the joy this verse invites.
Both parents are named again, as in the command to listen to the father and not despise the aging mother.
The father's great joy in a righteous child is the gladness the son is now urged to give.

units.notes:
• The NKJV reads the verbs as an invitation ("Let... be glad"), placing the parents' joy partly in the son's hands. The KJV reads them as a statement about the future: "Thy father and thy mother shall be glad."
• "Her who bore you" is the same phrase used in 17:25, where the foolish son is "bitterness to her who bore him."
• Henry: "she that bore them with pain, and nursed them with pains, will rejoice in them."
• Jesus spoke of a mother's anguish in labor giving way to joy once the child is born (John 16:21). Compare 10:1; 15:20; 29:3.
units.summary: A child's wise life is the best thank-you a mother ever receives.
units.principle: Children can repay a measure of their parents' love by living wisely, and a mother's sacrifice deserves that joy.
units.insight: Hannah prayed through tears for a son, then gave him to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:10–11, 27–28). Year by year she made him "a little robe" and brought it to the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:19), and the boy Samuel grew "in favor both with the LORD and men" (1 Samuel 2:26). Few mothers' prayers are so plainly answered, and few sons repaid them so well. The verse invites every son and daughter to ask a simple question: does the way I live give my mother joy or grief? It also comforts mothers who sacrificed much and still wait to see the fruit. The LORD who remembered Hannah (1 Samuel 1:19) sees a mother's labor, and He is able to finish what her prayers began.
units.application: Sons and daughters, write or say a specific thank-you to your mother this week, and name one way you are living wisely because of what she taught you. If the relationship is strained, take one honest step toward peace. Fathers, teach your children to honor their mother by honoring her yourself. Churches, remember single mothers and widowed mothers, whose sacrifices often go unseen.

rel.note: The appeal that began with guiding the heart in the way reaches its center in giving the heart to the father.
The harlot's deep pit gives the reason the heart must already belong to the father.
The son is asked to let his heart keep his father's commands, an obedience that comes from within.
The father has taught his son the way of wisdom and led him in right paths, the ways the son's eyes are now asked to observe.
Keeping the heart with all diligence is the same concern: whoever holds the heart directs the life.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew text preserves two readings in the second line. The letters written in the text give a verb meaning "delight in"; a note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to a verb meaning "keep" or "observe." The NKJV, ESV and KJV follow the margin ("observe"); the NASB (1995) and NLT follow the written text ("delight"). Either way, the request flows from a heart given to the father.
• Bridges: "Many are the claimants for the heart. Heaven and hell contend for it."
• The heart's surrender lies behind the great commandment: "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37).
• Compare 3:1; 4:20–23; Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 11:1 ("Imitate me, just as I also imitate Christ").
units.summary: Everything in life bids for the heart; the father who loves you asks for it first.
units.principle: God asks first for the heart, because a heart given to Him turns the eyes, the habits and the whole life toward His ways.
units.insight: Martha served Jesus busily while Mary sat at His feet and listened, and Jesus said Mary had "chosen that good part" (Luke 10:39–42). Ironside: "It is not mere service as in Martha's case, but heart-occupation with Himself that he yearns for, as illustrated in Mary." The verse exposes a common evasion. We offer God our time, our money and our activity while keeping our heart for ourselves. The father will not settle for that, and neither will God. Yet the request is an invitation of love, not the demand of a tyrant. In the light of the New Testament, the Father who asks for our heart gave His Son for us, the Son "who loved me and gave Himself for me" (Galatians 2:20). Give Him your heart again today. He has already given His.
units.application: Ask which claimant is pulling hardest at your heart right now: a relationship, a career goal, a habit, a fear. Name it before God and hand it over in prayer. Parents and mentors, ask for your children's hearts, not just their compliance: spend unhurried time with them and let them watch how you live, including how you repent. Young people, choose an older believer whose ways are worth observing, and watch closely.

rel.note: The mouth of the immoral woman is called a deep pit, the same trap pictured here.
The call to give the father one's heart is the protection this verse explains.
The next verse shows the trap is active: she lies in wait and multiplies the unfaithful.
The lover of wisdom makes his father rejoice, while a companion of harlots wastes his wealth.
The seductress's sweet start and bitter end lead down to death, the depth of the pit described here.

units.notes:
• "Seductress" translates a Hebrew word for an outsider or stranger. Proverbs uses it for the woman outside a man's marriage and outside God's ways (2:16; 5:20; 6:24; 7:5). The word marks her as an outsider to his home; it does not settle her nationality.
• A "narrow well" is a deep shaft with no room to turn or climb. Pits and cisterns served as prisons, as when Joseph was cast into a pit (Genesis 37:24) and Jeremiah was let down into a cistern of mire (Jeremiah 38:6).
• Ironside: "Like a deep ditch, hidden until one has stumbled into it, is the unholy woman who has been so frequently warned against."
• Compare 5:3–5; 6:26; 7:26–27; 22:14; 1 Corinthians 6:18.
units.summary: Sexual sin is a pit easy to slip into and a narrow well almost impossible to climb out of.
units.principle: Sexual sin is far easier to enter than to escape, so the surest guard is a heart already given to God.
units.insight: Samson tore a lion apart with his bare hands, yet he could not climb out of Delilah's snare (Judges 14:6; 16:4–21). He lost his eyes, his strength and his freedom. The verse speaks plainly because the danger is real and many strong people have fallen. It does not call women the problem. It names the snare of sexual sin and puts responsibility on the one who walks near the edge. Joseph shows the other way. When his master's wife pressed him, he "fled and ran outside" (Genesis 39:12). For those already in the pit, there is hope. Proverbs holds out mercy to "whoever confesses and forsakes" his sins (28:13), and Jesus said to the woman others wanted to stone, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:11).
units.application: Men and women alike, identify the edges of your pit: the late-night messages, the private browser, the friendship that is becoming secret. Set phone boundaries, use accountability, and tell a trusted friend where you are weak. Married couples, invest in your own marriage (5:15–19). Parents and youth leaders, speak about sexual temptation openly, as this father does. If you have already fallen, confess it to God and to a mature believer this week.

rel.note: The deep pit and narrow well of the previous verse are the trap she now sets actively.
Whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy, the way back for those she has caught.
The immoral woman lurks at every corner, lying in wait for the young man as she does here.
She has cast down many, and strong men among them, the multiplying harm of the second line.

units.notes:
• "As for a victim" translates a word that has been understood in two ways, as prey or as a robber. The NKJV and KJV take it as prey, picturing the man she catches. The ESV, NASB (1995) and NLT read "robber," picturing the woman herself lying in ambush; the KJV margin also offers this reading.
• "The unfaithful" are those who break faith, betraying a covenant or a trust; the KJV has "transgressors."
• Henry: "One adulteress may be the ruin of many a precious soul."
• Compare 6:26; 7:12, 22–23, 26; 1 Corinthians 6:18–20.
units.summary: The young man drawn to the seductress thinks he is the hunter, but he is the prey.
units.principle: Sexual sin hunts its victims and spreads faithlessness, yet confessing and forsaking it still opens the way to mercy.
units.insight: David's adultery did not stay private. To cover it he made Uriah drunk, then made Joab his accomplice in Uriah's death, and the sword never departed from his house (2 Samuel 11:13–17; 12:10). One man's unfaithfulness spread to many. That is the second line of this verse: sexual sin is never only personal; it multiplies betrayal in families, churches and communities. The first line corrects our self-image, because many who fall thought they were in control. Yet the same David prayed, "Have mercy upon me, O God... Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity" (Psalm 51:1–2), and Nathan told him, "The LORD also has put away your sin" (2 Samuel 12:13). In Christ the hunted can be rescued and the unfaithful made clean (1 Corinthians 6:11).
units.application: If someone keeps seeking you out with flattery and secrecy, recognize the hunter's pattern and step away early. Married people, keep conversations and meetings with the opposite sex transparent to your spouse. Pastors and leaders, remember that a fall rarely harms only one person, and guard yourself for the sake of those you lead. If unfaithfulness has already spread through your family, seek help from a pastor or counselor, and begin with honest confession.

rel.note: Wine is a mocker and strong drink a brawler, the quarrels and wounds that the questions list.
The earlier warning against the company of drunkards is filled out here with the full cost of drink.
The next verse answers the riddle by naming those who linger long at the wine.
The wounds without cause return at the poem's end in the drinker's boast that he did not feel the blows.
Lemuel's mother warns kings that wine makes them forget the law, another picture of what drink does to judgment.

units.notes:
• The poem moves in five steps: questions (23:29), the cause (23:30), a warning (23:31–32), the effects (23:33–34), and the drinker's own words (23:35).
• "Complaints" is rendered "babbling" in the KJV and "anxiety" by Ironside: the restless, troubled talk of a man whose life is in disorder.
• Bridges calls the poem "the drunkard's looking-glass," that is, a mirror held up so the drinker can see his own face.
• Compare 20:1; Isaiah 5:11, 22; Ephesians 5:18.
units.summary: Six questions trace a ruined life backward from the bruises to the bottle.
units.principle: Drunkenness promises pleasure but gathers sorrow, conflict and needless wounds into one damaged life.
units.insight: Noah, the righteous man who came through the flood, drank wine, became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent, and shame and a curse followed in his family (Genesis 9:20–25). Even a great saint was not immune. The questions of this verse are asked of every reader, not only of the hopeless drunk. Where does my sorrow come from? Why so many quarrels? Some of our wounds are "without cause," self-inflicted through habits we defend. Many who read this also love someone whose life fits these questions, and they carry the bruises of that love. God sees both. Jesus came "to heal the brokenhearted" and "to proclaim liberty to the captives" (Luke 4:18), and that includes the captive to drink and the family hurt by it.
units.application: Ask yourself plainly whether drinking is connected to the arguments, injuries or regrets in your life. If it is, talk to someone this week: a pastor, a doctor, a recovery group or a trusted friend. Families of a heavy drinker, you did not cause it and cannot cure it alone; find support through your church or a group for families. Youth leaders, read this poem with teenagers and let the questions do their work.

rel.note: The one who loves pleasure and wine will be poor, the cost of making drink a pursuit.
The six questions of misery are answered by this verse.
The drinker's last words, planning another drink, show the seeking of this verse hardened into bondage.
Wisdom also mixes her wine, but her table leads to life while the drinker's search leads to woe.

units.notes:
• Isaiah describes the same people: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning, That they may follow intoxicating drink; Who continue until night, till wine inflames them!" (Isaiah 5:11). He also condemns those "valiant for mixing intoxicating drink" (Isaiah 5:22).
• The Hebrew word behind "mixed wine" comes from the same root as the verb in Wisdom's banquet: "She has mixed her wine" (9:2). Wisdom's table leads to life; the drinker's search leads to the woe of 23:29.
• Henry pictures the seekers going from place to place: "their great enquiry is, 'Where is the best liquor?'"
• Compare 20:1; 21:17; Ephesians 5:18.
units.summary: The bruises and quarrels belong to those who do not just drink but go looking for it.
units.principle: Misery gathers where drinking becomes a pursuit, so the pattern of lingering and seeking is itself a warning sign.
units.insight: Belshazzar held a great feast and drank wine before a thousand lords. While he tasted the wine, he called for the holy vessels from God's temple, and the handwriting appeared on the wall; that very night he was slain (Daniel 5:1–5, 30). His kingdom ended at the wine table. The verse names a pattern, not a single mistake. Those who "linger long" have usually moved from enjoying a drink to needing one. The heart question is what we go searching for. Many seek in drink what only God can give: rest, courage, comfort or escape from pain. Jesus stood up at a feast and cried, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink" (John 7:37). He is the better answer to the thirst that sends us searching.
units.application: Notice your patterns: do you plan evenings around drinking, stay longer than you intended, or look forward to the drink more than to the people? Those are signals to act now. Set limits and tell someone about them, or stop entirely if you cannot keep them. Hosts, make your gatherings about people, not the bar. Friends, if someone you love always lingers longest at the wine, speak to them privately and kindly.

rel.note: Whoever is led astray by wine is not wise, the danger this warning tries to stop at its start.
The same word describes the son's upright speech and the wine's smooth slide, setting true rightness against mere smoothness.
The sparkle of this verse ends in the serpent's bite of the next.
Kings are warned away from wine because it makes them forget the law.
The son is told to keep his eyes looking straight ahead, the discipline of the eyes this verse requires.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV says the wine "sparkles in the cup," the KJV says it "giveth his colour in the cup." Either way, the wine's gleam is what catches the drinker's eye.
• "Smoothly" translates a word meaning what is level, straight or upright. It is the word translated "right things" in 23:16: the son's lips speak what is upright, while the wine merely slides down. The ESV, NASB and NLT also have the wine going down smoothly; compare Song of Solomon 7:9.
• Henry says some wine "looks so well that it even says, 'Come and drink me.'"
• Compare 20:1; 31:4–5; Genesis 3:6; Psalm 104:15; Ephesians 5:18.
units.summary: Temptation begins with a look; stop at the gaze and you never feel the sting.
units.principle: The battle against enslaving desire is won earliest at the eyes, before attraction becomes indulgence.
units.insight: David's fall began on a rooftop: "he saw a woman bathing" (2 Samuel 11:2). Achan's began among the spoils of Jericho: "When I saw... I coveted them and took them" (Joshua 7:21). Sin usually comes as beauty before it comes as bondage. This verse is honest about the attraction; it does not call wine ugly. It tells us to stop at the look, because the look is where we are still free. Many who struggle with drink say the hardest moment is not the third glass but the first glance at the bottle. Jesus taught that "The lamp of the body is the eye" (Matthew 6:22). He was "in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15), and He gives grace to turn our eyes away when the cup begins to sparkle.
units.application: If alcohol has a pull on you, plan where your eyes will not go: skip the wine aisle, keep it out of the house, decline the tasting. Parents, notice how drink is presented to your children in ads and media, and talk about it openly. Restaurant and hospitality workers in recovery, ask for accountability at work. Believers who drink in freedom, be mindful of friends for whom the sparkle is a snare (Romans 14:21).

rel.note: A way that seems right ends in death, the hidden end of a pleasant beginning.
Bread gained by deceit is sweet and then fills the mouth with gravel, another pleasure that turns.
The same word for the end describes the sure future of the one who fears the LORD, set against the drinker's bitter end.
The sparkling cup of the previous verse is the beginning whose end this verse reveals.
The seductress's honeyed lips end as bitter as wormwood, the same sweet start and bitter end.

units.notes:
• "At the last" translates the same Hebrew word rendered "hereafter" in 23:18. The one who fears the LORD has a good end (23:18); the drinker's end is the serpent's bite.
• "Viper" names a poisonous snake; the KJV has "adder."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Both the vixen and wine are hidden and deadly traps." By "vixen" he means the seductive woman of 23:27–28; the chapter sets wine beside her.
• Bridges: "Did it bite first, who would touch it?"
• Compare 5:3–4; 14:12; 20:17; Romans 6:21–23.
units.summary: Wine that sparkles at the start can bite like a snake at the end.
units.principle: Sin's pleasure comes first and its poison later, so wisdom judges a choice by its end, not its beginning.
units.insight: In the wilderness, Israel was bitten by fiery serpents for their rebellion, and many died. God told Moses to lift a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived (Numbers 21:6–9). Jesus took that story as a picture of Himself: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up" (John 3:14). This verse warns that wine abused bites like a serpent. Many readers already carry that venom: a damaged body, a broken marriage, a record, a load of shame. The verse is true, but it is not the last word. The One lifted up on the cross bore sin's curse so that those bitten by it may look to Him and live (John 3:15).
units.application: Before the first drink, picture the morning after: the conversation you will regret, the drive you should not make, the money gone. Judge by the end. If you already feel the bite, do not hide it; see a doctor, call a recovery ministry, or talk to your pastor this week. Parents and youth workers, tell young people the truth: drinking feels good at first, and explain what follows.

rel.note: Wine is a mocker, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
The same plural word stands behind "immoral woman" in 22:14, which is why the KJV reads "strange women" here.
The son's lips speak right things, while the drunken heart utters perverse things.
The next verse moves from the drinker's distorted mind to his reeling body.
Wine makes rulers forget the law and pervert justice, the same distortion of mind and judgment.

units.notes:
• "Strange things" translates a plural word that can also mean "strange women"; the KJV renders it "strange women," and Ironside follows. The same plural word stands behind "immoral woman" in 22:14. Most modern versions agree with the NKJV's "strange things." On either reading, drink removes restraint.
• "Perverse things" are twisted, upside-down words. The same word describes the man "who speaks perverse things" in 2:12 and "the perverse mouth" Wisdom hates in 8:13.
• Henry, following the KJV reading "strange women": "Wine is oil to the fire of lust."
• Compare 20:1; 31:4–5; Isaiah 28:7; Hosea 4:11; Ephesians 5:18.
units.summary: Drink twists the eyes that see and the heart that speaks, until nothing true comes out.
units.principle: Drunkenness clouds perception and loosens the tongue, exposing and multiplying what is twisted in the heart.
units.insight: Noah's drunkenness left him exposed in his tent; Lot's left him unaware of what was done to him (Genesis 9:21; 19:33, 35). Wine did not create what was in their hearts or families, but it removed the guard. That is why "I was drunk" is never an excuse for what was said or done. The verse turns the question inward: what would come out of my heart if every restraint were removed? Paul sets the answer beside the warning: "do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; but be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). Wine loosens the tongue toward what is twisted. The Spirit fills the heart, so that the mouth speaks "in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (Ephesians 5:19).
units.application: If you have said things while drinking that you deeply regret, apologize sober and specifically, and do not blame the alcohol. Then ask whether you should drink at all. Spouses and friends, if someone you love becomes cruel or careless when drunk, address it calmly the next day, not in the moment. Students, decide before the party that you will stay clear-headed enough to see and speak truly.

rel.note: Whoever is led astray by wine is not wise, and this verse shows how far astray he goes.
The prudent man sees danger and hides, while the drinker lies down in the middle of it.
The distorted sight and speech of the previous verse lead into the reeling helplessness of this one.
The word "saying" introduces the drinker's own words in the next verse.

units.notes:
• "In the midst of the sea" is literally "in the heart of the sea," as Ironside renders it: the open water, far from any shore.
• The top of a mast is where a ship's roll is felt most. A man lying there sways far more widely than one on deck.
• Henry: "Their heads are giddy, and when they lie down to sleep they are as if they were tossed by the rolling waves of the sea."
• Isaiah uses the same picture of a world under judgment: "The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard" (Isaiah 24:20). Compare Isaiah 28:7.
units.summary: The drunk sleeps easy in places where any sober man would see death.
units.principle: Drunkenness steals both balance and the sense of danger, leaving a person careless at the very edge of ruin.
units.insight: Nabal held a feast "like the feast of a king" and "was very drunk" on the very night his household had narrowly escaped David's sword through his wife's quick wisdom. He had no idea how close he had come. In the morning, when he heard, "his heart died within him," and about ten days later he died (1 Samuel 25:36–38). Drunkenness rocks a person to sleep in the middle of danger. The deepest peril is not dizziness but indifference, and any sin that numbs us can do the same: we sleep on the mast and call it rest. God, in mercy, wakes us: "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14). His wake-up call is not cruelty but rescue.
units.application: Never drive, swim or care for small children after drinking; the danger is real even when you feel fine. Friends, take the keys and make the call; do not let someone sleep it off in a dangerous place. Parents of college students, talk plainly about alcohol poisoning and stay reachable. If you have woken up in places you do not remember reaching, treat that as God's warning and seek help now.

rel.note: The wounds without cause in the opening questions are the blows the drinker now says he did not feel.
Those who go in search of mixed wine are the ones whose search ends in this plan to drink again.
The word "saying" at the end of the previous verse introduces these words of the drinker.
A fool repeats his folly as a dog returns to its vomit, the same compulsive return to what harms him.
The wicked man is caught in the cords of his own sin, the bondage the drinker voices here.

units.notes:
• The last line is literally "I will seek it yet again," as the KJV has it. The drinker's final words are a plan to return.
• Aitken, quoted by Waltke and cited by Guzik: "The passage describes more than a night's drinking and a morning's hangover." The poem portrays a settled bondage, what we now call addiction.
• Bridges: "The love of Christ overpowers the love of sin."
• Jeremiah gives the same voice of compulsion to Israel in her idolatry: "There is no hope. No! For I have loved aliens, and after them I will go" (Jeremiah 2:25).
• Compare 26:11; 5:22; John 8:34–36; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
units.summary: The cruelest part of addiction is waking up bruised and reaching for the thing that bruised you.
units.principle: Addiction numbs a person to the harm it does and binds him to repeat it, but no bondage is beyond God's power to wash and set free.
units.insight: Jesus said, "whoever commits sin is a slave of sin," and then, "if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed" (John 8:34, 36). The drinker of this verse is the slave: struck, numb and already planning the next drink. Many readers know that voice from the inside, or from someone they love. The poem does not mock him. It tells the truth so that the son will never start down that road, and it leaves the drinker waiting for an awakening he cannot produce. The gospel brings that awakening, and it does not give up on those who fall again. Peter denied Jesus three times in one night, yet the risen Lord sought him out by the sea and restored him (John 21:15–17). Recovery is often slow and marked by relapse, but Christ does not abandon those who keep turning to Him.
units.application: If your first thought on waking is the next drink, you are not beyond help, but you need more than willpower. This week tell a pastor or trusted friend, see a doctor, and join a Christ-centered recovery group. Families, set loving boundaries instead of covering for the drinker, and get support for yourselves. Churches, make room for people in recovery: welcome them, walk with them through relapses, and celebrate every step of freedom.

rel.note: Companions shape character, which is why the wish to be with evil men is dangerous.
The father's first warning shows the goal of envy, when sinners invite the son to "Come with us."
The same command not to envy sinners, turned toward zeal for the fear of the LORD.
The chapter repeats the warning against envying the wicked and adds that they have no future.
The next verse gives the reason: the hearts and lips of evil men are set on harm.

units.notes:
• The same command came in 23:17: "Do not let your heart envy sinners, But be zealous for the fear of the LORD all the day." Chapter 24 raises it again in 24:19, which shows how stubborn this temptation is.
• The two lines move from feeling to belonging. Envy lives in the heart (line 1); the wish "to be with them" reaches for their company (line 2). Compare the father's first warning: "My son, if sinners entice you, Do not consent" (1:10).
• Bridges on the spirit of envy: it "curses our blessings, withers our graces, cankers our peace." To canker is to eat away like a spreading sore.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The antidote to envy is the long view: the glory (Proverbs 23:18) or darkness (Proverbs 24:20) to come."
• Compare 3:31; Psalm 37:1; 73:2–3, 16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:33 ("Evil company corrupts good habits").
units.summary: What you envy today you will want to join tomorrow.
units.principle: What we envy we begin to imitate, so guarding what the heart admires is the first defense against bad company.
units.insight: Asaph nearly slipped here. "I was envious of the boastful, When I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Psalm 73:3), until he went into the sanctuary of God and understood their end (Psalm 73:17). Lot walked the same road. He looked at the well-watered plain, pitched his tent toward Sodom, and ended up living inside it (Genesis 13:10–12; 19:1). Envy rarely begins with a decision to sin. It begins with a long look and a quiet "if only." The deeper question is whom we secretly admire. Moses chose "rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin," because he esteemed "the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt" (Hebrews 11:25–26). The cure for envy is a greater treasure, and in Christ we have one.
units.application: Young people: notice whose life you scroll past with a twinge of longing, and ask what exactly you envy in it. Employees: when a colleague gets ahead by cutting corners, refuse to resent it and refuse to copy it. Parents: talk with your children about the people they admire, not only the people they spend time with. If an invitation this week would require you to share in wrongdoing, decline it before admiration becomes membership.

rel.note: This verse supplies the reason for the command not to envy evil men or seek their company.
The wicked plan destruction, while wisdom builds and establishes a house.
The wicked are so set on harm that they cannot sleep until they have done evil.
The worthless man also devises evil in his heart and spreads trouble with his mouth.

units.notes:
• The word translated "devises," hagah, means to ponder or murmur over something. It is the verb used of the blessed man who meditates on God's law "day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The wicked meditate too, but on harm.
• "Violence" translates a word for destruction or ruin; the KJV has "their heart studieth destruction." "Troublemaking" (KJV "mischief") is trouble or harm brought on others.
• Henry: "their heart studies destruction to others, but it will prove destruction to themselves."
• Compare 4:16 ("For they do not sleep unless they have done evil"), 6:14, Psalm 36:4, Micah 2:1 and Matthew 15:19.
units.summary: Behind the success you envy is a heart planning harm and a mouth talking trouble.
units.principle: Judge a way of life by the heart and speech it produces, not by the success it displays.
units.insight: Haman had wealth, honor and the king's favor, yet he said, "all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (Esther 5:13). His heart was busy planning the destruction of a whole people (Esther 3:6–9), and that plan became his own ruin (Esther 7:10). That is the life the envious heart overlooks. Jesus traced it to its source: "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders" (Matthew 15:19). Before we envy anyone, we should ask what fills their heart and their mouth. The same question searches us. What do we turn over in our minds when we lie awake? What does our talk drift toward among friends? The gospel offers more than better plans. God promises a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), one that meditates on His word instead of on harm.
units.application: When you are drawn to someone's lifestyle, listen for a few weeks to how they talk about other people. Leaders: if a group's conversation keeps returning to who can be pushed aside or taken down, do not build with that group. In your own speech, catch the moment when venting turns into planning harm, and stop there. At night, instead of replaying grievances, meditate on a psalm, as the blessed man of Psalm 1:2 meditates on God's law.

rel.note: The wise woman builds her house, while folly pulls it down with her own hands.
The wicked plan violence and destruction, while wisdom builds.
The lazy man's field, with its wall broken down, shows what neglect does to what was once built.
The building picture continues as knowledge fills the rooms of the house wisdom has built.
The LORD made the world with the same wisdom, understanding and knowledge that build a household.
Wisdom herself is pictured as the builder of a house.

units.notes:
• The three words in 24:3–4, wisdom, understanding and knowledge, are the same three used of the LORD's own work in creation, and "established" is the verb used there of the heavens: "By understanding He established the heavens" (3:19–20). The builder of a household works with the qualities by which God made the world.
• "House" can mean a building, a household or a family line. When God told David, "the LORD tells you that He will make you a house" (2 Samuel 7:11), He meant a dynasty, not a building.
• Geier, quoted by Bridges, on a house built by wickedness: "It is only the snow-palace built in the winter, and melting away under the power of the summer's sun."
• Compare Psalm 127:1 ("Unless the LORD builds the house, They labor in vain who build it"), Matthew 7:24–27 and 1 Corinthians 3:10–15.
units.summary: Every life is building a house; wisdom decides whether it will stand.
units.principle: Whatever we build, whether a home, a work or a ministry, lasts only as well as the wisdom it is built with.
units.insight: Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders whose houses faced the same storm. The difference was the foundation: the one who heard His sayings and did them built on the rock, and his house stood (Matthew 7:24–27). Jesus' parable makes the same point as this proverb: what is built wisely stands. Wisdom leaves its signature on what is built in a life. A marriage, a home, a business or a church shows over time the wisdom or folly that went into it. That truth is meant as an examination, not a verdict. Some houses have been shaken by storms their builders did not cause. The question is what you are building with now. The one sure foundation is Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and He is building the one house that will never fall: "I will build My church" (Matthew 16:18).
units.application: Husbands and wives: choose one area of your home, such as money, conversation or rest, and ask together what wisdom would build there this month. Parents: build habits of prayer and Scripture into family life before the storms come. Business owners and ministry leaders: before adding a new program or expansion, ask whether it rests on understanding or on impulse. If your home has suffered losses you did not choose, do not condemn yourself; ask God what to build next.

rel.note: The house of the righteous holds much treasure, while the revenue of the wicked brings trouble.
The enticers promise to fill their houses with precious things by robbery instead of by wisdom.
Wisdom builds and understanding establishes the house that knowledge here furnishes.
The neglected field, overgrown and unwalled, is the opposite of rooms filled by knowledge.
Wisdom gives enduring riches with righteousness and fills the treasuries of those who love her.

units.notes:
• "Rooms" means the inner rooms or chambers of a house; Ironside renders it "inner-chambers." Wisdom's work reaches the private life of a home, not only its public face.
• The enticers of chapter 1 promised to fill a house by robbery: "We shall find all kinds of precious possessions, We shall fill our houses with spoil" (1:13). Proverbs sets the two ways of filling a house side by side.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The precious jewels that fill the house are a harmonious, loving family and a sense of security and stability."
• Henry calls such riches "precious because got by honest labour" and "pleasant because enjoyed with holy cheerfulness."
• Compare 8:18–21; 15:6 ("In the house of the righteous there is much treasure"); Colossians 2:3.
units.summary: Wisdom does not stop at the walls; it fills the rooms with what makes a house a home.
units.principle: The truest riches wisdom brings are measured in the life of a home, not only in what it owns.
units.insight: Some of the wealthiest houses are empty, and some plain homes are full. Naomi came back to Bethlehem saying, "I went out full, and the LORD has brought me home again empty" (Ruth 1:21). Yet her household with Ruth became rich in loyalty and kindness, and God built from it the line of David (Ruth 4:13–17). Solomon filled his palace with gold, yet in old age his heart turned after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). So the question is not how much our rooms hold but what fills them. Is there peace at the table and forgiveness in the hallway? Paul prayed that Christ would "dwell in your hearts through faith," so that believers would be "filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:17, 19). In Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).
units.application: Parents: this week, fill your home with something precious that costs no money, such as a shared meal without screens, a family prayer, or a story of God's faithfulness to you. Spouses: name one "pleasant riches" your home is missing, perhaps kindness in speech, and begin supplying it yourself. Anyone setting up a first home: learn budgeting, planning and household order; that practical knowledge is part of how wisdom furnishes a house.

rel.note: A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold they trusted.
Strength that faints in adversity is small; wisdom is the strength that holds.
The same wisdom and knowledge that build and fill a house also make a person strong.
The next verse shows wisdom's strength at work through wise counsel in war.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew wording is more vivid than the English. The KJV margin gives the literal sense: a wise man is "in strength," and a man of knowledge "strengtheneth might," that is, makes his strength greater. Knowledge does not merely possess strength; it builds it up.
• Henry: "A wise man will compass that by his wisdom which a strong man cannot effect by force of arms." To compass something is to accomplish it.
• Scripture gives a picture of this in the wise woman of Abel, who saved her city from Joab's besieging army with a few wise words (2 Samuel 20:16–22), and in the poor wise man who delivered a city by his wisdom (Ecclesiastes 9:14–16).
• Compare 21:22; Ecclesiastes 7:19; 1 Corinthians 1:25.
units.summary: Muscle wins a moment; wisdom multiplies whatever strength you have.
units.principle: Wisdom is a deeper strength than force, because it directs and multiplies whatever power a person has.
units.insight: When Joab's army besieged Abel and began battering its wall, one wise woman called out from the city. She reasoned with Joab, counseled her people, and the city was spared without another blow (2 Samuel 20:16–22). Her strength was her wisdom. We are tempted to measure strength by volume, size and force. God measures it differently: "the weakness of God is stronger than men" (1 Corinthians 1:25). The cross looked like defeat and was the power of God. Christ is "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and those joined to Him are told to "be strong in the Lord and in the power of His might" (Ephesians 6:10). When you feel weak, where do you reach first: for more force, or for wisdom from God?
units.application: Leaders: before you push harder on a stalled project, stop and ask what you do not yet understand about it. Parents of a strong-willed child: aim to win with wisdom and patience, not volume. Anyone facing a conflict at work: gather the facts and think before you act; a calm, well-reasoned word often does what pressure cannot. This week, invest in knowledge through Scripture, a good book or a wise mentor, as a way of building strength.

rel.note: The second line of 11:14 is repeated here: in the multitude of counselors there is safety.
The fool trusts his own way, while the wise man heeds counsel.
Plans go wrong without counsel and stand firm when many counselors are heard.
Plans are established by counsel, and war is to be waged by wise counsel.
Wise counsel is the reason the wise man is strong.

units.notes:
• The second line repeats the second line of 11:14, "But in the multitude of counselors there is safety," and 15:22 says the same of plans in general: "in the multitude of counselors they are established."
• A "multitude of counselors" does not mean deciding by majority vote. The point is wise advisers, enough of them to catch what one person misses. Rehoboam had advisers on both sides and chose the ones who told him what he wanted (1 Kings 12:6–14).
• Ironside on the wise man: "He is not an egoist. His safety is in his willingness to hear what others soberly present." An egoist is a man who thinks only of himself.
• Jesus used the same picture of a king going to war who "does not sit down first and consider whether he is able" to meet a larger army (Luke 14:31).
• Compare 12:15; 20:18; Exodus 18:13–24.
units.summary: No one wins life's battles alone; the safest plans are the ones many wise people have tested.
units.principle: Wise people seek counsel before they act, because several good advisers see dangers that one person misses.
units.insight: Rehoboam had two sets of counselors. The elders who had served Solomon urged him to lighten the people's load; the young men he grew up with told him to make it heavier. He took the advice he wanted to hear, and the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:6–16). Moses, by contrast, listened when his father-in-law told him he was wearing himself out, and the whole nation was better served (Exodus 18:17–24). Refusing counsel usually comes from pride or fear: pride that thinks it needs no help, or fear of hearing what it does not want to hear. Which one keeps you from asking? God made the church a body so that no member fights alone (1 Corinthians 12:21). Above all, believers have the One called "Wonderful, Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), and His counsel never fails.
units.application: Before a major decision, such as a move, a job change, a large purchase or a new ministry, ask two or three mature believers to look at your plan and tell you what they see. Leaders: build a small circle of advisers who are free to disagree with you, and listen when they do. Young adults: find an older believer who will walk with you through hard choices. Pray over the plan before you present it to anyone.

rel.note: The scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it, while knowledge comes easily to the one who understands.
The fool may hold the price of wisdom in his hand, but he has no heart for it.
The fool loves to air his own opinions, yet he has no word where wisdom is needed.
Wisdom calls openly at the gates, so the fool's lack of wisdom is not for want of access.
The respected husband sits among the elders at the gates, where the fool has nothing to say.

units.notes:
• The word for "wisdom" here is plural in Hebrew, literally "wisdoms," the same form used when Wisdom "calls aloud outside" (1:20) and "has built her house" (9:1). Hebrew sometimes uses a plural to express fullness: wisdom in all its richness is beyond the fool.
• The city gate was the place of public business. Boaz settled the matter of Ruth's redemption there before the elders (Ruth 4:1–11), and the husband of 31:23 "is known in the gates, When he sits among the elders of the land."
• Henry on fools in public counsel: "they say nothing, because they have nothing to say."
• Compare 14:6 ("A scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it"); 17:16; Job 29:7–10; James 1:5.
units.summary: Wisdom calls in the open street; the fool cannot reach it because he will not stoop to learn.
units.principle: Wisdom is open to all who will humble themselves to learn, and those who scorn it have nothing to give when it matters most.
units.insight: Wisdom is not reserved for the clever. "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach" (James 1:5). The fool's real problem is not his mind but his pride. Think of Job in his days of honor. When he took his seat at the city gate, the young men stepped aside and the elders stood, waiting for his words (Job 29:7–10). Trust like that is earned slowly, by years of listening to God. What will you have to say when a friend's marriage is failing or your church faces a hard decision? Only those who have been learning in private will have something to offer in public. Christ "became for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30), so no one who comes to Him is shut out.
units.application: Young people: start now to gather wisdom through Scripture, good books and older believers, so that you have something to offer when friends come to you in crisis. If you serve on a church board, a school committee or a family decision, prepare and pray before you speak. If you notice that you have little to say when serious matters come up, do not fake it; ask God for wisdom and become a learner.

rel.note: The LORD condemns the man of wicked intentions.
Those who devise evil go astray, while mercy and truth belong to those who devise good.
The proud man earns the name "Scoffer" just as the plotter earns the name schemer.
The next verse judges the devising of folly itself as sin.
A heart that devises wicked plans is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Schemer" is literally "master of schemes." The word for schemes, mezimmah, is the word Proverbs uses in a good sense for "discretion," the ability to plan wisely (1:4; 2:11). The schemer has the gift of planning and has turned it to evil.
• Henry calls him "a master of mischief, which perhaps was then a common name of reproach," that is, a byword or insult.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, describes him as "a cold, calculating, active person."
• Scripture shows a scheme becoming a name in Jeroboam. His golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:26–30) became his permanent title: "Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had made Israel sin" (2 Kings 10:29).
• Compare 6:18; 12:2; 14:22; Romans 1:30 ("inventors of evil things").
units.summary: Plan evil long enough and it becomes your name.
units.principle: What we repeatedly plan in private becomes, in time, the name we carry in public.
units.insight: Jacob was a schemer whose name fit him. When he took Esau's blessing, Esau cried, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times" (Genesis 27:36). His plans had become his name. Yet his story does not end there. At the Jabbok, God wrestled with the schemer, broke his strength and gave him a new name, Israel (Genesis 32:24–28). That is the hope of the gospel for anyone whose reputation has caught up with him. Our schemes may have named us, but God can rename us: "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17). The verse still asks a searching question. If the people around you named you by what you plan when no one is watching, what would they call you? Bring those plans into the light before they become your name.
units.application: Notice the plans you rehearse in the car or the shower: the clever comeback, the way to get even, the angle that gets you ahead at someone else's expense. Drop them before they harden into habit. Parents: when a child begins to plan mischief, address the planning, not only the act. Employees and managers: refuse to become known as the one who works the system. If past scheming has damaged your name, confess it and start building a new reputation through honest dealing.

rel.note: Fools mock at sin, treating as a joke what God takes seriously.
The proud and haughty man earns the name "Scoffer."
Removing the scoffer ends contention, showing why people find him hard to bear.
The plotter of the previous verse is named a schemer; here his plotting is called sin.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble.

units.notes:
• The KJV has "The thought of foolishness is sin." The word translated "devising" means a plan or purpose, so the verse speaks of folly that has been deliberately intended, not a passing thought that is resisted.
• Bridges: "as the thought is the fountain of the act, God counts it in the act." A fountain here means a spring, the source from which the act flows.
• Henry: such devising "is made light of, and turned off with a jest, as only a foolish thing, but really it is sin."
• The scoffer is the proud mocker of 21:24 ("Scoffer" is his name; He acts with arrogant pride). Proverbs adds, "Cast out the scoffer, and contention will leave" (22:10).
• Compare Genesis 6:5; Psalm 1:1; Matthew 5:21–22, 27–28; 2 Corinthians 10:5.
units.summary: God counts the plotting as sin, and people cannot stand the mocker.
units.principle: Sin begins in what we deliberately plan, and contempt for correction poisons a person's relationships long before it ruins his life.
units.insight: Jesus pressed this verse to its depths. He taught that anger in the heart breaks the command against murder, and that looking with lust is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22, 27–28). None of us survives that standard, which is why we need a Savior and not merely a better plan. The scoffer shows where unconfessed thoughts lead. Sanballat's resentment ended in public mockery of Nehemiah's builders: "What are these feeble Jews doing?" (Nehemiah 4:2). Mockers stood at the cross too, wagging their heads at Jesus (Matthew 27:39). He bore their scorn and our sinful thoughts alike. Now He calls us to bring "every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5). What thought have you been entertaining that you would not want spoken aloud?
units.application: When a scheme or fantasy begins to take shape in your mind, name it as sin and confess it before it grows. Deal with resentment when you first notice it, not when it boils over. Leaders and teachers: refuse sarcasm as a way of managing or teaching; it makes you a scoffer to the people under you. If your humor regularly mocks people or holy things, ask a trusted friend whether it has made you hard to be around.

rel.note: A true brother is born for adversity, showing that hard days reveal character in friendship too.
The costly duty to rescue those in danger demands the strength this verse tests.
Wisdom makes a person strong, and adversity tests how much strength is really there.
The LORD is the believer's confidence when sudden trouble comes.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, "adversity" (tsarah) and "small" (tsar) sound alike, and both come from words for narrowness. The day of adversity is a day of tight straits, and strength that gives way in it is narrow strength. The KJV margin renders "small" as "narrow."
• Ironside: "It is the hour of trial that manifests whatever strength one really has." To manifest is to show.
• Bridges: "If thy strength be small, go to the strong for strength."
• Scripture sets two responses side by side. Elijah, threatened by Jezebel, asked to die (1 Kings 19:2–4), while David at Ziklag "strengthened himself in the LORD his God" (1 Samuel 30:6).
• Compare 17:17 ("a brother is born for adversity"); Isaiah 40:29–31; Galatians 6:9.
units.summary: Hard days do not create weakness; they reveal how much strength was there.
units.principle: Trouble does not create weakness but exposes it, and lasting strength is strength drawn from God.
units.insight: Ziklag was David's lowest day. Raiders had burned the town and carried off every family, and his own men spoke of stoning him. "But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God" (1 Samuel 30:6). He did not find strength in himself; he went to its source. Elijah fainted under Jezebel's threat, and God met him under the broom tree with bread, sleep and a still small voice (1 Kings 19:4–8, 12). Even this rebuke is meant to send us to God, not to shame us. Hebrews tells weary believers to "consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners against Himself, lest you become weary and discouraged in your souls" (Hebrews 12:3). Christ did not faint in His day of adversity, and He offers His strength to those whose strength is small: "My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9).
units.application: If you are in a day of adversity now, through illness, job loss or family trouble, do not measure your faith by your feelings. Go to the source of strength: read Isaiah 40:28–31 aloud each morning this week. Friends and pastors: when someone is fainting, bring practical help first, as God did for Elijah. Young believers: build habits of prayer and Scripture in easier days, so that you have reserves when the hard day comes.

rel.note: The LORD Himself pleads the cause of the oppressed whom others abandon.
Rescue takes the strength that fainting in adversity lacks.
The next verse answers the excuse "we did not know" and warns of God's judgment on indifference.
Lemuel's mother also calls for speaking up for all who are appointed to die.
Do not withhold good when it is in the power of your hand to do it.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads the verse as a condition, "If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death," which runs on into the warning of verse 12. The NKJV, NASB and ESV read it as a direct command.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "These could be literal prisoners who have been (presumably wrongfully) condemned to die." The words also fit people stumbling toward death through moral and spiritual blindness.
