• Scripture is full of such rescuers: the Hebrew midwives who would not kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), Obadiah hiding a hundred prophets in caves (1 Kings 18:4), Esther pleading for her people (Esther 4:16; 7:3–4), and Ebed-Melech lifting Jeremiah out of the cistern (Jeremiah 38:7–13).
• Compare 31:8 ("Open your mouth for the speechless, In the cause of all who are appointed to die"); Psalm 82:3–4; Luke 10:30–37; Jude 23.
units.summary: Wisdom does not stand on the sidewalk while others are led to the slaughter.
units.principle: Those who are able to help people heading toward destruction are responsible to act, not merely to sympathize.
units.insight: Esther had every reason to stay quiet. Going to the king uninvited could cost her life. Mordecai's words cut through her hesitation: "Yet who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" She answered, "If I perish, I perish!" (Esther 4:14, 16), and a people drawn toward death was delivered. In Jesus' parable, a priest and a Levite saw the wounded man and "passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31–32). The Samaritan stopped. The verse exposes our love of comfort and our fear of cost. It also shows us Christ. We were the ones stumbling toward the slaughter, and He did not pass by: "the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). Those He has rescued are sent to rescue others.
units.application: Ask where someone near you is being drawn toward harm: a teenager sliding into addiction, a neighbor in an abusive home, a coworker facing an unjust accusation, a friend drifting from God. Do one concrete thing this week. Make the call, speak up in the meeting, offer the ride, report what must be reported. Church leaders: train your people to recognize danger and respond. Do not wait to feel brave; courage usually follows obedience.

rel.note: If even the depths of death lie open before the LORD, so do human hearts.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard.
Every way seems right to a man, but the LORD weighs the hearts.
This verse answers the excuse a person might give for ignoring the command to rescue.
The same words for repaying a man "according to his work" belong to God here and are forbidden to us there.

units.notes:
• "Weighs" pictures God testing the heart as a merchant weighs goods on scales. Proverbs uses the same picture in 16:2 ("the LORD weighs the spirits") and 21:2 ("the LORD weighs the hearts"); the KJV has "pondereth the heart."
• Paul states the same principle: God "will render to each one according to his deeds" (Romans 2:6). Psalm 62:12 says the same of God in different Hebrew words.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The omniscient and omnipotent Sovereign will act justly, unlike the passive coward." Omniscient means all-knowing; omnipotent means all-powerful.
• Henry: God will judge "not only the commission of evil works, but the omission of good works."
• Compare Ezekiel 33:6; Matthew 25:41–45; James 4:17; Revelation 2:23.
units.summary: "I didn't know" may satisfy people, but never the God who weighs the heart.
units.principle: Before God, willful ignorance is no excuse, because He who weighs the heart knows what we chose not to see.
units.insight: Cain's answer has echoed through history: "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" (Genesis 4:9). The God who questioned Cain questions us. Jesus told of people who will ask, "Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?" His answer searches us: "inasmuch as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to Me" (Matthew 25:44–45). Indifference often hides behind not wanting to know. We avoid the hard story, the awkward conversation, the neighborhood we would rather not drive through. Yet the verse is also tender. The One who weighs the heart is the One who "keeps your soul." He has kept us, and He asks us to care for others as He has cared for us.
units.application: Ask God this week, "What have I chosen not to know?" It may be a lonely member of your church, a coworker's obvious distress, or suffering in your own city. Parents: teach your children that looking away is a choice. Church members: learn the real needs of your community instead of assuming someone else is meeting them. If you realize you have been looking away, confess it plainly and take one step toward the person you avoided.

rel.note: Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healthy to the body.
The next verse completes the comparison: wisdom is as sweet to the soul as honey to the taste.
Honey is good, but it must be enjoyed in measure.
The immoral woman offers a honeyed sweetness that turns bitter in the end.

units.notes:
• Honey was both a staple and a delight in Israel. Canaan was "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8), and when Jonathan tasted a little honey in battle, "his countenance brightened" (1 Samuel 14:27).
• Proverbs also knows honey's limits: "Have you found honey? Eat only as much as you need" (25:16), and "It is not good to eat much honey" (25:27). The pleasure is good, but it is not the highest good.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The proverb draws on the image of honey; its health-giving properties make a good analogy to wisdom."
• Proverbs warns of a counterfeit sweetness: "the lips of an immoral woman drip honey" (5:3), "But in the end she is bitter as wormwood" (5:4).
• Compare 16:24; Judges 14:8–9, 18; Psalm 19:10; 119:103.
units.summary: Enjoy the honey, then let its sweetness teach you what wisdom tastes like.
units.principle: God's good gifts are meant to be enjoyed, and their goodness points beyond themselves to the greater sweetness of wisdom.
units.insight: Some believers treat every pleasure as suspect. This verse opens with a father telling his son to enjoy honey because it is good. God made the honeycomb and the tongue that tastes it. Yet the father has more in mind than food. He wants his son to learn, from a small sweetness, what a greater sweetness is like. The danger is to stop at the honey. Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of stew because he wanted the taste in front of him more than the lasting gift (Genesis 25:29–34). Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, answered the tempter, "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). Every good taste in life is a small invitation to "taste and see that the LORD is good" (Psalm 34:8).
units.application: Thank God this week for one ordinary pleasure, such as a meal, a sunrise or a child's laugh, and let it lead you to worship. Parents: teach your children to enjoy good gifts with gratitude, not guilt, and to see the Giver behind them. If faith has become only duty for you, ask God to restore the taste of His word, and read one psalm slowly, looking for what is sweet in it. Watch for the counterfeit sweetness that ends in bitterness (5:3–4).

rel.note: The same promise in nearly the same words: there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
The honey of the previous verse is the picture this verse explains.
The evil man has no prospect, while the one who finds wisdom has a future.
When wisdom enters the heart, knowledge becomes pleasant to the soul.
Wisdom's ways are pleasant, and she is a tree of life to those who hold her.

units.notes:
• "Prospect" is the same Hebrew word rendered "hereafter" in 23:18 and "prospect" again in 24:20, a word for an end or future outcome. The KJV has "reward" here and in 24:20, but "end" in 23:18. The final line of 24:14 and 23:18 is identical in the NKJV: "And your hope will not be cut off."
• Wisdom's sweetness is known by tasting, not by description. Henry: "Those that have tasted honey need no further proof that it is sweet."
• Bridges says the joys of wisdom "are not opiates, but cordials." An opiate dulls a person; a cordial was a reviving drink. Wisdom's delights do not make us drowsy; they strengthen us.
• Compare 2:10 ("knowledge is pleasant to your soul"); 3:17; Psalm 119:103; Romans 5:5.
units.summary: Honey's sweetness fades in a moment; wisdom's sweetness carries a hope that cannot be cut off.
units.principle: Wisdom is both sweet now and secure for the future; it delights the soul and anchors a hope that will not fail.
units.insight: Many people imagine that following God means trading sweetness for duty. This verse says the opposite. Jeremiah said, "Your words were found, and I ate them, And Your word was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart" (Jeremiah 15:16). When Jesus' hard sayings drove others away, Peter answered, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:68). Wisdom tastes good, and it also leads somewhere. The world's sweetness fades and leaves a bitter aftertaste. The sweetness of Christ grows and ends in glory, for He is "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). In Him the believer's hope will not be cut off. If wisdom has lost its taste for you, ask God to restore your appetite. The honey has not changed.
units.application: Read Scripture this week to enjoy it, not only to study it; choose one psalm and linger over a line that is sweet to you. Parents and teachers: let young people see that you delight in God's word, not only that you require it. If you are discouraged about the future, write out 24:14 and 23:18 and pray them back to God. Mentors: tell those you disciple how wisdom has borne fruit in your life over the years.

rel.note: The wicked are overthrown, but the house of the righteous will stand.
The enticers also plan to lie in wait for the innocent.
Those who lie in wait for others are lying in wait for their own lives.
The next verse explains why the plot will fail: the righteous rises again, but the wicked falls.
The LORD curses the house of the wicked and blesses the home of the just.

units.notes:
• "Lie in wait" is the language of ambush, the same NKJV phrase the enticers use in 1:11, "Let us lie in wait to shed blood." Proverbs answers them in 1:18: "But they lie in wait for their own blood."
• Proverbs usually speaks to the son; addressing the wicked man is unusual. Henry says the verse is spoken "not so much by way of counsel to wicked men" but "rather in defiance of them, for the encouragement of good people."
• Scripture gives a picture of this ambush when Saul sent men to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, and Michal let David down through a window (1 Samuel 19:11–12). The title of Psalm 59 ties that psalm to that night.
• Compare 3:33 ("He blesses the home of the just"); 12:7; 14:11; Zechariah 2:8.
units.summary: The wicked man who ambushes the home of the righteous is picking a fight he cannot win.
units.principle: Those who plot against God's people are plotting against God's purposes, and their plans will not have the last word.
units.insight: When Saul of Tarsus was "breathing threats and murder against the disciples," the risen Christ stopped him on the road and asked, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?" (Acts 9:1, 4). Jesus counted the attack on His people as an attack on Himself. That is why the wicked man of this verse is warned: the righteous are not unguarded. God says of His people, "he who touches you touches the apple of His eye" (Zechariah 2:8). Some readers lie awake fearing someone who wishes them harm. This verse does not promise that no harm will come, but it assures them that the plotter does not have the last word. It also holds out hope for the plotter, for the persecutor Saul became the apostle Paul. And it searches the rest of us. Have we ever lain in wait to catch a godly person in a fault?
units.application: If someone is plotting against you, commit your home and family to God in prayer, take sensible precautions, and seek help from the proper authorities where needed; trust and prudence go together. Do not answer plotting with plotting. If you hold power over others, as an employer, landlord or official, never use it to trap a godly person or strip him of what he has. Pray for those who oppose you; God still turns persecutors into brothers.

rel.note: The wicked fall by their own wickedness.
The righteous will come through trouble, while the wicked is ensnared.
The wicked is banished, but the righteous has a refuge even in death.
This verse gives the reason the wicked man should not plot against the righteous.
The next verse turns to the right response when an enemy falls.

units.notes:
• Seven is the number of fullness: the righteous may fall as often as trouble comes. The popular form "seven times a day" adds to the text; Bishop Patrick, quoted by Bridges, says it has "no authority but some corrupt edition of the Vulgate," the Latin Bible of the medieval church.
• Bridges on the word "fall": "The word fall frequently occurs in this book; but always in reference to trouble, not sin."
• Where the verse is applied to moral failure, Scripture's picture is Peter, who denied Christ, wept bitterly and was restored (Matthew 26:75; John 21:15–17), set beside Judas, who fell and did not rise (Matthew 27:3–5). The difference was repentance.
• Compare Psalm 37:24 ("Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down; For the LORD upholds him with His hand"); Micah 7:8 ("When I fall, I will arise"); 2 Corinthians 4:8–9.
units.summary: Knock the righteous down seven times and, by God's hand, he gets up again.
units.principle: Under God's care the righteous are not finally overthrown by repeated troubles, while the wicked have no such hope of rising.
units.insight: Joseph fell again and again. His brothers sold him, his master's wife slandered him, and the butler forgot him in prison. Each time he was knocked down, and each time God lifted him, until he could say, "you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Paul described the same life: "struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:9). Not every believer's rising comes quickly. Some wait years; some rise only at the resurrection. But the one God upholds is never finally overthrown. That hope rests on Christ, whom God raised up, "having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that He should be held by it" (Acts 2:24). If you have been knocked down, you are not finished. If you have fallen through sin, the way up is the way Peter took: repentance and the restoring love of Jesus.
units.application: If you are on the ground right now, through a lost job, a betrayal or a long illness, tell God plainly that you cannot rise without Him, and ask one friend to pray with you this week. Friends and church members: help the fallen up instead of analyzing why they fell. If your fall has been moral, do not use this verse to excuse it; confess the sin, make right what you can, and receive the restoration Christ offers.

rel.note: Whoever is glad at calamity will not go unpunished.
The wicked do fall, but the righteous must not take pleasure in it.
The next verse gives the reason: the LORD sees gloating and is displeased.
The same chapter forbids paying back an enemy for what he has done.
Wisdom goes beyond refusing to gloat and actively meets an enemy's need.

units.notes:
• "Falls" and "stumbles" pick up the language of 24:16, where the righteous rise and the wicked fall by calamity. The teacher immediately guards the son's heart: knowing the wicked will fall is no license to enjoy it.
• Proverbs elsewhere calls for kindness to an enemy in need: "If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat" (25:21). Compare 17:5: "He who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished."
• Ironside: "Love does not gloat over the sorrows of others, even though richly deserved."
• Bridges sets joy in God's justice apart from "the malignant joy of private revenge." Malignant here means spiteful.
• Scripture judges Edom for exactly this sin: Obadiah condemns Edom for gloating over Judah on the day of its destruction (Obadiah 12–15).
• Compare Psalm 35:13–14; Matthew 5:44; Luke 19:41–44.
units.summary: When your enemy falls, do not celebrate; God is watching your heart.
units.principle: Gloating over an enemy's ruin is itself a sin, because God judges the heart's private delight in another's suffering.
units.insight: David had every reason to celebrate Saul's death. Saul had hunted him for years. Yet when the news came, David tore his clothes, wept and fasted, and wrote a lament: "How the mighty have fallen!" (2 Samuel 1:11–12, 19). Of enemies who were sick he could say, "I humbled myself with fasting" (Psalm 35:13). Jesus went further still. He wept over the city that would reject Him (Luke 19:41), and from the cross He prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do" (Luke 23:34). He calls us to "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44). The natural heart cannot do it. It becomes possible when we remember how God treated us "when we were enemies" (Romans 5:10). Whose trouble would secretly please you?
units.application: When news comes that someone who hurt you has failed, been exposed or fallen ill, guard your first reaction, including the private smile. Pray for that person by name. Leaders: do not let your team celebrate a rival's collapse. Parents: teach children not to cheer when a brother or sister gets in trouble. If you catch yourself enjoying an enemy's misfortune online or in conversation, stop, confess it, and speak a kind word if you can.

rel.note: The one who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished.
Repayment is left to the LORD; the wronged person waits for Him.
The LORD who weighs the hearts sees the private joy of the gloater.
This verse supplies the reason for the command not to rejoice when an enemy falls.

units.notes:
• "And it displease Him" is literally "and it be evil in His eyes," as Ironside renders it. The gloater's joy looks to God like the very evil he is glad to see punished.
• The verse must not be read as advice on how to make God punish an enemy more by keeping quiet until He does. That reading turns a warning about the gloater's heart into a new way to gloat.
• Henry: "the righteousness of God was never intended to gratify the wrath of man." To gratify is to satisfy.
• Compare 17:5; 20:22 ("Wait for the LORD, and He will save you"); Romans 12:19; James 2:13 ("Mercy triumphs over judgment").
units.summary: Gloating over an enemy can turn God's attention from his sin to yours.
units.principle: Judgment belongs to God alone, and those who celebrate another's punishment invite His displeasure on themselves.
units.insight: Jonah sat outside Nineveh hoping to watch it burn. When God spared the city, Jonah was angry enough to want to die (Jonah 4:1–3, 9). God's question to him is His question to every gloating heart: "should I not pity Nineveh, that great city?" (Jonah 4:11). Jonah wanted wrath on his enemies and forgot that he had just been rescued from the deep himself. That is the gloater's blindness: he forgets that he too lives by mercy. Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant makes the same point. The man forgiven a vast debt seized his fellow servant by the throat, and the master's anger turned on him (Matthew 18:28–34). Whenever we wish God would be harder on someone else, we need to go back to the cross. There the wrath we deserved was turned away from us and fell on Christ.
units.application: If you have been wronged, hand the case to God and stop checking whether your enemy is getting what he deserves. Notice when you follow news of someone's downfall with eager interest. Pastors and counselors: help the wounded release their need to see the offender punished, without pretending the offense did not matter. Parents: when one child is disciplined, do not let the others gloat. This week, pray for mercy on someone you would rather see judged.

rel.note: Envy of sinners is to be replaced by zeal for the fear of the LORD.
The chapter opened with the same warning against envying evil men.
The next verse gives the reason: the wicked have no future.
Do not envy the oppressor or choose any of his ways.

units.notes:
• The first line matches Psalm 37:1 in the NKJV: "Do not fret because of evildoers." The psalm goes on, "For they shall soon be cut down like the grass" (Psalm 37:2), and "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for Him" (Psalm 37:7).
• The Hebrew word behind "fret" comes from a verb meaning to burn or grow hot. It describes anger kindled inside, not mild worry; the KJV has "Fret not thyself."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Those who love the truth are naturally enraged by the effrontery of those who promote or practice godless behavior." Effrontery is shameless boldness.
• Compare 3:31; 23:17; Psalm 73:2–3; Habakkuk 1:13.
units.summary: Fretting and envy both hand the wicked control of your inner life.
units.principle: Envy and anxious anger over the wicked both come from a short view of life; trust in God frees the heart from both.
units.insight: Asaph confessed, "my feet had almost stumbled; My steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the boastful" (Psalm 73:2–3). Habakkuk asked God why He stayed silent while the wicked devoured people more righteous than they (Habakkuk 1:13). Fretting over evildoers is an old and honest struggle. Scripture does not shame it; it answers it. The answer is not to stop caring about justice, but to bring our heat to God instead of letting it burn inside us. Jesus told of wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). God is not careless; He is patient, and His timing is wiser than ours. What do you feel when a dishonest coworker is promoted or a scoffer prospers? Bring that feeling to the One who judges rightly, and let Him carry it.
units.application: When the news or your workplace stirs up anger over people getting away with wrong, turn it into prayer instead of brooding. Read Psalm 37 this week, a few verses each day. If social media keeps you fretting over evildoers, cut back. Young people tempted to envy peers who cheat or party their way to popularity: write down what you would lose by becoming like them. Leaders: correct wrongdoing where it is your responsibility, then leave the rest to God.

rel.note: The same line: the lamp of the wicked will be put out.
The lamp of the one who curses his parents goes out in deep darkness.
The one who fears the LORD has a hereafter, a future the evil man lacks.
The one who finds wisdom has a prospect and a hope that will not be cut off.
This verse is the reason not to fret over evildoers or envy the wicked.

units.notes:
• The second line repeats 13:9 word for word in the NKJV: "But the lamp of the wicked will be put out." Compare 20:20, where the lamp of one who curses his parents "will be put out in deep darkness."
• "Prospect" is the word for an end or future outcome used in 23:18 and 24:14. The KJV has "there shall be no reward to the evil man." The wise have a future; the evil man has none.
• A lamp kept burning through the night was a sign of a living, well-run household; of the virtuous wife Proverbs says, "her lamp does not go out by night" (31:18).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Keeping the extinction of their lamp in view will extinguish burning envy."
• Compare Job 18:5–6; Psalm 37:35–36; Luke 12:20.
units.summary: The wicked man's lamp may blaze tonight, but it is already burning down.
units.principle: Whatever the wicked possess has no future, so envying them means envying something already passing away.
units.insight: Herod Agrippa sat on his throne in royal robes while the crowd shouted, "The voice of a god and not of a man!" At once an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give glory to God (Acts 12:21–23). His lamp went out at its brightest moment. Jesus told of a rich man who planned bigger barns, and God said, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). Not every lamp goes out so suddenly, but none burns forever. Christ says, "I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life" (John 8:12). The envious heart is cured by looking at the end. Why envy a lamp that is burning down, when you have been given a light that never goes out?
units.application: When you are tempted to envy someone's success built on wrong, picture the end of that road as Scripture describes it, then pray for the person, since the lamp of the wicked can still be exchanged for the light of life. Parents: teach teenagers to measure lives by where they end, not by how they look now. If a wicked person's success troubles you, read Psalm 37:35–40 and trust God with the timing.

rel.note: The evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger is sent against him.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, which is why it comes first in this verse.
Whoever provokes a king sins against his own life.
The next verse gives the reason: sudden ruin comes from the LORD and the king on those who rebel.
Kings reign and rulers decree justice by wisdom, which grounds respect for rightful authority.

units.notes:
• The meaning of "those given to change" is debated. The Hebrew is a form of the verb "to change," which the KJV margin renders literally "changers." Earlier editions of the NIV and the NLT take it as rebels; the ESV has "those who do otherwise," meaning those who do not fear the LORD and the king.
• Matthew Poole, quoted by Bridges, says Solomon "puts God before the king, because God is to be served in the first place."
• Bridges guards against the opposite error: "To oppose all change, indeed, is to set up a plea of perfection." That is, refusing every change amounts to claiming things are already perfect.
• Daniel shows the order in practice. He served the kings of Babylon and Persia faithfully, yet when the law forbade prayer, he prayed to God as before (Daniel 6:4, 10).
• Compare 8:15–16; 20:2; Matthew 22:21; Romans 13:1–7.
units.summary: Fear God first, honor the king second, and never confuse the order.
units.principle: Reverence for God comes first and respect for rightful authority follows; wisdom chooses neither reckless rebellion nor blind obedience.
units.insight: Daniel lived this verse in a foreign court. He served so faithfully that his enemies "could find no charge or fault" in him except concerning the law of his God (Daniel 6:4–5). When the king's decree forbade prayer, Daniel opened his windows toward Jerusalem and prayed three times that day, "as was his custom since early days" (Daniel 6:10). He honored the king and feared God, in that order. Jesus held the same balance: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matthew 22:21). Our hearts drift toward one error or the other: contempt for every authority, or a fear of people that silences conscience. Where are you tempted to fear your boss, the government or public opinion more than God? Begin with the fear of the LORD, and everything else finds its place.
units.application: Citizens: pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), pay what you owe, and speak respectfully even when you disagree. Employees: honor your employer's rightful direction, but refuse any instruction to lie or cheat. Young people: be wary of groups that thrive on contempt for every authority, online or in person. If obeying a ruler would mean disobeying God, obey God and accept the cost with Daniel's respectful firmness.

rel.note: The rebel who seeks only rebellion has a cruel messenger sent against him.
The wrath of a king is like a lion's roar to the one who provokes him.
"Those two" are the LORD and the king whom the previous verse commands the son to fear.
The one who hardens his neck against correction is suddenly destroyed.
The troublemaker's calamity also comes suddenly and without remedy.

units.notes:
• "Those two" points back to "the LORD and the king" of 24:21; the KJV asks, "who knoweth the ruin of them both?" The Greek translation known as the Septuagint, as Bridges quotes it, makes the sense plain: "Do not disobey either of them, who knoweth their vengeance?"
• Some older writers, Ironside among them, take "them both" as the rebel leader and his followers. The reading that points back to the LORD and the king fits the flow from 24:21 best.
• Scripture gives pictures of sudden collapse in Korah's revolt, when the ground opened beneath the rebels (Numbers 16:31–33), and in Absalom's, which ended with his head caught in a terebinth tree (2 Samuel 18:9–15).
• Compare 6:15 ("Therefore his calamity shall come suddenly"); 17:11; 29:1; Acts 5:36–37.
units.summary: Rebellion against God and rightful order promises freedom but can collapse in a single day.
units.principle: Rebellion against God and rightful authority carries hidden ruin, and its collapse often comes without warning.
units.insight: Absalom's revolt looked unstoppable. He stole the hearts of Israel (2 Samuel 15:6), drove his father from Jerusalem and gathered a great army. Then in one day it was over. His army was routed in the forest, and Absalom hung by his head in a tree until Joab's men killed him (2 Samuel 18:7–15). Calamity rose suddenly. Psalm 2 pictures earthly rulers taking counsel "Against the LORD and against His Anointed," and it warns them, "Kiss the Son, lest He be angry, And you perish in the way" (Psalm 2:2, 12). In the light of the New Testament, the Anointed King is Christ (Acts 4:25–27). The deepest rebellion is not against a government but against Him. Yet the same psalm ends with an open door: "Blessed are all those who put their trust in Him." The way out of ruin is surrender.
units.application: Before you join a cause, a faction or a church split, ask whether it fears God and respects rightful order, or whether it feeds on anger and the thrill of tearing down. Church members: refuse to join whispering campaigns against leaders; raise concerns openly and humbly. Young people: notice how quickly online movements of outrage rise and collapse. If you are resisting God Himself, the call of Psalm 2 is for you: turn to the Son and trust Him.

rel.note: The bribe taken behind the back is one of the chief causes of partial judgment.
It is not good to show partiality to the wicked or to overthrow the righteous in judgment.
The heading "These things also" adds to the collection of the words of the wise that begins here.
The next verse shows partiality at its worst: calling the guilty righteous.
The same verdict, "not good," is passed on partiality, which can be bought for a piece of bread.

units.notes:
• The heading reads in Hebrew simply, "These also are of the wise." It is one of the book's section markers (1:1; 10:1; 22:17; 24:23; 25:1; 30:1; 31:1). The word "also" ties this short collection to the longer one that began, "Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise" (22:17).
• The short collection takes up four subjects: fairness and honesty in judgment (24:23–26), ordering one's work (24:27), false witness and revenge (24:28–29), and the lazy man's field (24:30–34).
• "Partiality" is literally "recognizing faces." Trapp, quoted by Guzik, explains it as "to regard not so much the matter as the man."
• Henry: a good judge "will know the truth, not know faces."
• The rule recurs in 18:5 and 28:21 ("To show partiality is not good"). Compare Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 16:19; James 2:1–4.
units.summary: The further sayings of the wise open in the courtroom: true justice weighs the case, not the face.
units.principle: Justice must weigh the case, not the person, because favoritism quietly robs those who have no one to speak for them.
units.insight: Samuel's sons sat as judges in Israel, but "they turned aside after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice" (1 Samuel 8:3), and the people demanded a king. Partiality rarely announces itself. It shows up as a softer tone for the donor, a quicker hearing for the friend, a harsher word for the person we find difficult. James saw it in church, where the man with a gold ring was given a good seat and the poor man told to stand (James 2:1–4). God is not like that. He "shows no partiality" (Acts 10:34). Even Jesus' opponents admitted, "You do not regard the person of men" (Matthew 22:16). The gospel itself is impartial, for rich and poor come to the cross on the same terms. Where do you treat people differently because of who they are?
units.application: Parents: settle quarrels between children on the facts, not on which child is easier to like. Supervisors: apply the same standards to your friends on the team as to everyone else. Church leaders: notice whether visitors, donors and long-time members receive the same welcome and the same correction. Anyone asked to give a reference or a verdict: weigh the matter, not the person. Start this week with one decision where you know your bias.

rel.note: Justifying the wicked and condemning the just are both an abomination to the LORD.
Showing partiality to the wicked is not good.
Partiality in judgment leads to the false verdict this verse condemns.
Those who rebuke the wicked receive delight and blessing instead of curses.
Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, while those who keep it contend with them.

units.notes:
• "You are righteous" is the language of a court verdict, declaring someone in the right. Said of the guilty, it is what 17:15 calls "an abomination to the LORD."
• Henry applies the verse beyond the courtroom: to excuse a wicked man and keep company with him is, "in effect, to say, Thou art righteous."
• Isaiah pronounces woe on "those who call evil good, and good evil" (Isaiah 5:20), and on those "Who justify the wicked for a bribe" (Isaiah 5:23).
• Compare 17:15; 18:5; 28:4; Exodus 23:7.
units.summary: Call the guilty innocent and you will lose the respect of everyone who loves justice.
units.principle: Calling evil good corrupts justice and stirs the rightful outrage of everyone with a conscience.
units.insight: Pilate examined Jesus and said, "I find no fault in Him" (John 19:4). Then, under pressure from the crowd, he released Barabbas, a man imprisoned for rebellion and murder, and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Luke 23:18–25). In one afternoon he justified the wicked and condemned the just. Yet God was doing something there that turns this verse inside out. Scripture says God "justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). How can He, when 17:15 calls that an abomination? Only because the Just One took the condemnation of the unjust, so that God could be "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). God never calls sin righteous. He punishes it in Christ and clothes sinners in Christ's righteousness. Where are we tempted to excuse wrong to keep the peace?
units.application: Parents: do not tell a child who lied that it was fine because you are tired of conflict; name the wrong and offer forgiveness. Managers and church leaders: when a popular or useful person does wrong, deal with it as you would with anyone else. Friends: comfort a friend who has sinned without telling him he did nothing wrong. Citizens: refuse to cheer leaders who excuse corruption simply because it serves your side.

rel.note: The one who calls the wicked righteous is cursed, while the one who rebukes them is blessed.
The honest, right answer is compared to a kiss on the lips.
Open rebuke and a friend's faithful wounds are better than concealed love.
The one who rebukes finds more favor afterward than the flatterer.
Rebuke is welcomed by the wise but hated by the scoffer, so it calls for discernment.

units.notes:
• To "rebuke" is to correct someone openly for wrongdoing: in court by a just verdict, and in daily life by a plain word. Proverbs adds that over time such honesty wins out: "He who rebukes a man will find more favor afterward Than he who flatters with the tongue" (28:23).
• Henry says those who rebuke the wicked "shall have the comfort of it in their own bosoms," that is, the inner peace of a clear conscience.
• Scripture shows both sides of the blessing. Nathan's rebuke, "You are the man!", brought David to repentance (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). John the Baptist's rebuke of Herod cost him his life (Mark 6:18, 27), yet Jesus said none born of women was greater than John (Luke 7:28).
• Compare 9:8; 27:5–6; Leviticus 19:17; Ephesians 5:11.
units.summary: Telling the truth about wrong may cost you at first, but it carries a blessing flattery never earns.
units.principle: Speaking the truth about wrong, with courage and love, is blessed by God even when it costs something at first.
units.insight: Nathan walked into the palace of a king who had already killed one man to cover his sin. He told a story about a poor man's stolen lamb and then said four words: "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). That rebuke saved David. He confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13), and Psalm 51 grew out of that day. Rebuking the wicked is not the same as being harsh. It is love that refuses to leave a person in his sin. Many of us avoid hard conversations to keep the peace and call it kindness. Jesus told Peter the hardest truth, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23), and later restored him with great tenderness (John 21:15–17). Both were love. Whom have you been flattering because you were afraid to tell the truth?
units.application: Parents: correct your children's wrongdoing plainly instead of joking it away. Elders and small-group leaders: when a member is clearly sinning, go to him privately and humbly (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). Employees: report fraud through proper channels even if it makes you unpopular. Friends: before you rebuke, pray, examine your own heart and choose your words; then speak. Expect that some will thank you later (28:23).

rel.note: Kings love the one who speaks what is right.
The one who rebukes the wicked is blessed, and his honest answer is a sign of love.
The false witness uses his lips to deceive; the right answer uses them to love.
The kisses of an enemy are deceitful, while a friend's honest wounds are faithful.
Honest rebuke wins more favor in the end than flattery.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "right" means straight. The KJV margin gives the line as one "that answereth right words," a man who replies with straight, honest words. The KJV text reads it the other way round: "Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer," picturing others honoring the honest man.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The symbol of specifically kissing on the lips is mentioned only here in the Bible."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Note the paradox, that a proper forthrightness, costly though it may seem, wins gratitude, and has its special charm." Forthrightness means directness.
• Contrast 27:6: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend, But the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." Compare 16:13; 28:23; Psalm 85:10 ("Righteousness and peace have kissed").
units.summary: An honest answer is a kiss on the lips; flattery only pretends to be kind.
units.principle: Honest words given in love are a true mark of affection, while flattery only imitates kindness.
units.insight: Judas greeted Jesus with a kiss and betrayed Him by it (Luke 22:47–48). That is the kiss of an enemy (27:6), warm on the surface and false underneath. This proverb describes the opposite, a kiss given in honest words. Jesus gave such answers. When the Samaritan woman said, "I have no husband," He replied, "You have well said, 'I have no husband,' for you have had five husbands" (John 4:17–18). He told her the truth without contempt, and she ran to tell her town about Him. Many of us offer the false kiss of flattery because we fear conflict or want to be liked. Yet people are rarely helped by hearing only what they want to hear. Who in your life needs a straight answer from you, given with love?
units.application: When a friend asks, "What do you think?", give your real opinion, kindly and clearly. Managers and employees: give honest feedback instead of vague praise, and welcome it in return. Parents: when your teenager asks a hard question about faith or life, answer straight, and admit what you do not know. Pastors: preach what the text says, not only what the room wants. This week, give one honest answer where you would normally dodge.

rel.note: The one who tills his land will be satisfied with bread.
The plans of the diligent lead to plenty, while haste leads to poverty.
Wisdom builds a house; this verse adds that a wise builder first secures the means to sustain it.
The lazy man left his field unprepared and his wall in ruins.
Attention to flocks and fields provides food for the whole household.

units.notes:
• "House" can mean a building or a household, as in 24:3. Henry mentions those who read the verse as "advice to young men not to marry (for by that the house is built) till they have set up in the world," that is, until they can support a family.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "It emphasizes the practical rule of producing before consuming, a rule the slothful do not accept."
• Scripture gives a picture of this order in Solomon's temple. Its stones were finished at the quarry, so that no hammer or chisel was heard at the building site (1 Kings 6:7).
• Jesus taught the same order: "which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost, whether he has enough to finish it" (Luke 14:28).
• Compare 21:5; 27:23–27; 1 Timothy 5:8.
units.summary: Plow the field before you build the house: secure the livelihood before you take on the costs.
units.principle: Wisdom puts first things first, building a sound livelihood before taking on the costs of the household it must support.
units.insight: Jesus warned of the man who laid a foundation and could not finish, so that onlookers mocked him: "This man began to build and was not able to finish" (Luke 14:30). Many households carry that burden today: a house bought before the income was there, a wedding planned with no plan for the marriage, a ministry launched without counting the cost. The root is often impatience, the wish to have the house before doing the fieldwork. Think of Jacob, who served seven years for Rachel, "and they seemed only a few days to him because of the love he had for her" (Genesis 29:20). This verse is not against homes or marriage; it is for building them on solid ground. Patience in preparation is a form of faith. It trusts God to provide the house in His time.
units.application: Young couples: build a realistic budget and steady income before taking on a large mortgage or loan. Young adults: finish your training and learn a skill before rushing into commitments you cannot sustain. Church and ministry leaders: secure people, funding and prayer before launching a building program. Parents: teach children to save before they spend. Choose one plan this week and ask, "Have I prepared the field?"

rel.note: A faithful witness does not lie, while a false witness pours out lies.
An accusation must be examined, because the first to plead his case seems right until he is questioned.
The right answer uses the lips to love; the false witness uses them to deceive.
The next verse names revenge, a common motive for testifying without cause.
A false witness against a neighbor is like a club, a sword and a sharp arrow.

units.notes:
• "Without cause" translates chinnam, a Hebrew word meaning freely, for nothing, without reason. It is the word in "Let us lurk secretly for the innocent without cause" (1:11), and in the psalm Jesus applied to Himself: "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25; Psalm 69:4).
• The KJV has a command, "and deceive not with thy lips"; the NKJV turns it into a pointed question.
• Henry warns against deceiving even with words that are technically true, "by innuendos or hyperboles," that is, by hints and exaggerations.
• Scripture's pictures of false witness include the two scoundrels who testified against Naboth (1 Kings 21:10–13) and the many who "bore false witness against Him" at Jesus' trial (Mark 14:56).
• Compare 14:5; 19:5; 25:18 ("A man who bears false witness against his neighbor Is like a club, a sword, and a sharp arrow").
units.summary: A witness without cause turns the mouth into a weapon against a neighbor.
units.principle: Speech that accuses a neighbor without cause is deceit, however it is dressed, and it betrays both the neighbor and justice.
units.insight: Jezebel needed only two worthless men and a public fast to destroy Naboth. They sat before the people and said, "Naboth has blasphemed God and the king!" and he was stoned (1 Kings 21:13). Jesus faced the same weapon. Many testified falsely against Him, and their stories did not agree (Mark 14:56). He stood silent, "as a sheep before its shearers is silent" (Isaiah 53:7), and bore the lie for us. Few of us will stand in a courtroom, but we testify about our neighbors all the time: in a review, a staff meeting, a conversation after church. The careless report, the exaggerated story and the half-truth that leaves a wrong impression all fall under this verse. Before we speak about someone, the question remains: would you deceive with your lips?
units.application: Before you report on a coworker, write a review or share a concern about someone, ask three questions: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it the whole picture? Managers: hear both sides before you act on an accusation (18:17). Church members: refuse to pass on unverified stories about leaders or fellow believers. If you have spoken against someone without cause, go back and correct it with the people who heard you.

rel.note: Do not vow to repay evil; wait for the LORD, and He will save you.
God is the One who will render to each man according to his deeds.
The same chapter forbids even private gladness when an enemy falls.
False testimony is often the tool of the revenge this verse forbids.
Instead of repaying an enemy, wisdom feeds him and leaves the reward to the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Render to the man according to his work" repeats the language God uses of Himself in 24:12. The person who vows revenge is claiming a role that belongs to God alone.
• Bridges: "Far sweeter will be the recollection of injuries forgotten than revenged." It is better to remember an injury you let go than one you paid back.
• Henry on repaying a wrong: "it is God's prerogative to do so, and we must leave it to him." A prerogative is a right that belongs to one person alone.
• Paul gives the same teaching: "Repay no one evil for evil" (Romans 12:17), "for it is written, 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' says the Lord" (Romans 12:19).
• Compare 20:22; 25:21–22; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 5:38–44.
units.summary: Revenge calls itself fairness, but repayment belongs to God, not to you.
units.principle: Personal revenge takes over God's place as judge, even when it calls itself fairness.
units.insight: David had Saul at his mercy in a dark cave. His men whispered that God had delivered his enemy into his hand. David cut off only the corner of Saul's robe, and even that troubled his conscience. Then he said, "Let the LORD judge between you and me, and let the LORD avenge me on you. But my hand shall not be against you" (1 Samuel 24:12). Joseph, holding power over the brothers who sold him, asked, "am I in the place of God?" (Genesis 50:19). Above all, Christ, "when He was reviled, did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten, but committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). The urge to even the score is strong. What wrong are you still replaying, waiting to pay back? Hand it to the Judge who will do right.
units.application: If you have been wronged by a spouse, a coworker or a former friend, refuse the small revenges: the cold shoulder, the leaked story, the payback comment. Tell God plainly what was done and ask Him to judge. Where a crime has been committed, let the proper authorities handle it, without malice. Parents: when siblings retaliate, teach them that "he did it first" is no defense. This week, do one good thing for someone you would like to repay with evil (Romans 12:20).

rel.note: The one who tills his land is satisfied, while the one devoid of understanding chases frivolity.
Wisdom prepares the field first; the lazy man has left his untended.
The next verse describes what the wise man saw in the neglected field.
The lazy man thinks himself wise, though he is devoid of understanding.
The first portrait of the sluggard ends with the same lesson of sleep and sudden poverty.

units.notes:
• "Lazy man" translates 'atsel, the sluggard of Proverbs. The NKJV uses "sluggard" only in 6:6 and 6:9 and "lazy man" elsewhere; the KJV has "the slothful." Compare the portraits in 6:6–11; 19:24; 22:13; 26:13–16.
• "Devoid of understanding," literally "lacking heart," also describes the young man led astray in 7:7 and the man who chases frivolity instead of tilling his land in 12:11. Laziness is a failure of wisdom, not of ability.
• Bridges: "by some strange delusion, the slothful conceives himself to be wise." Compare 26:16: "The lazy man is wiser in his own eyes Than seven men who can answer sensibly."
• Laziness must be distinguished from inability, illness or genuine need. The field here belongs to a man who could have worked it and did not.
units.summary: The lazy man had a field and a vineyard; what he lacked was not land but sense.
units.principle: Laziness is not a lack of opportunity but a lack of wisdom; it wastes what God has already put in our hands.
units.insight: Jesus told of a servant who was given a talent and buried it. He had not stolen it or squandered it; he simply did nothing. His master called him a "wicked and lazy servant" (Matthew 25:26). The lazy man of this verse is the same kind of person. He has a field and a vineyard, real gifts from God, and he leaves them alone. Laziness rarely looks dramatic, yet it is a quiet rebellion against the work God gave people from the beginning (Genesis 2:15). The verse calls the lazy man "devoid of understanding," so the cure begins in the heart. Every believer has fields: a family, a job, a gift, a walk with God. Which field have you been walking past? Jesus said, "My Father has been working until now, and I have been working" (John 5:17), and He gives grace to begin again.
units.application: Name one "field" you have been neglecting: a repair, a relationship, a responsibility at work, your prayer life. Do one concrete piece of work on it this week. Parents: give children real responsibilities and follow up. Employers: deal with chronic idleness directly and fairly. Be careful not to call laziness what is really illness, grief or exhaustion; offer help and patience there. Pray for grace to work, not only for the work to be done.

rel.note: The way of the lazy man is like a hedge of thorns.
The lazy man will not plow, and at harvest he has nothing.
Wisdom builds a house and fills its rooms, while neglect lets the wall fall and the weeds take over.
The previous verse introduces the field and its lazy owner.
The next verse tells how the wise man learned from what he saw.

units.notes:
• Thorns and nettles are the weeds of a cursed ground left to itself: "Both thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you" (Genesis 3:18). Without labor, land goes back to wilderness.
• Stone walls around vineyards kept out animals and intruders. Isaiah's song of the vineyard pictures judgment as the removal of that protection: "I will take away its hedge, and it shall be burned; And break down its wall" (Isaiah 5:5).
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "Neglect is all that is needed to produce evil."
• Compare 15:19 ("The way of the lazy man is like a hedge of thorns"); 20:4; Song of Solomon 2:15; Matthew 13:7, 22.
units.summary: No one plants the thorns or tears down the wall; neglect does both on its own.
units.principle: Neglect is never neutral; whatever is left untended slowly fills with what we did not plant and loses the protection we did not keep.
units.insight: When Nehemiah heard, "The wall of Jerusalem is also broken down" (Nehemiah 1:3), he wept, prayed and went to work, and the broken wall of this verse calls for the same response. Jesus warned that the seed of God's word can be choked by thorns: "the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful" (Matthew 13:22). No one decides to let thorns win. They simply grow while we attend to other things. Applied to the life of faith, the overgrown field is the soul where prayer has lapsed, Scripture has gone unread, and the walls of conviction and accountability have crumbled one stone at a time. This is an invitation to look, not an accusation. Walls can be rebuilt. The God who helped Nehemiah finish Jerusalem's wall in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15) can help you rebuild yours.
units.application: Walk around your life this week the way the wise man walked past the field: your home, your finances, your marriage, your devotional life. Where are weeds spreading, and where is a wall down? Choose one wall to rebuild, such as a weekly time of prayer with your spouse or a budget you actually keep. Church leaders: check the walls of your congregation too, such as care for new believers. Small, regular weeding beats occasional heroic cleanups.

rel.note: The simple are made wise by seeing the scoffer punished.
The ruined field of the previous verse is what the wise man considered.
These verses state the instruction he received.
The sluggard is told to consider the ant and be wise, learning by observation.

units.notes:
• "Considered it well" is literally "set my heart" on it, as the KJV margin gives it: he gave the scene his full attention. "Received instruction" echoes the book's opening purpose, "To receive the instruction of wisdom" (1:3).
• Henry: the observer "did not call him any ill names, but he endeavoured himself to get good by the observation." To endeavour oneself is to make the effort.
• Henry also passes on a saying of Cato, recorded by Plutarch: "That wise men profit more by fools than fools by wise men."
• Compare 6:6 ("Consider her ways and be wise"); 21:11; 1 Corinthians 10:6, 11; Hebrews 5:14.
units.summary: The wise learn from other people's ruin so they do not have to learn from their own.
units.principle: Wisdom pays attention; the wise turn what they see in other lives into instruction for their own.
units.insight: Paul looked back at Israel's failures in the wilderness and wrote, "Now all these things happened to them as examples, and they were written for our admonition" (1 Corinthians 10:11). The wise man of this verse does the same with a weedy field. He does not gossip about the owner or mock the mess. He considers, and he learns. Jesus taught His disciples to look the same way: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow" (Matthew 6:28), and "lift up your eyes and look at the fields" (John 4:35). Many of us see plenty and learn little. We notice other people's ruined marriages, debts or broken faith, and we feel either smug or sad. We rarely ask, "What is this teaching me?" The difference between the fool and the wise is often not what they see but what they do with it.
units.application: When you see someone's life unravel, through debt, divorce, addiction or spiritual drift, resist both gossip and smugness. Ask quietly, "Where am I open to the same thing?" and act on the answer. Parents: talk with your children about what you observe in the world, and draw out the lesson together. Mentors: pass on what you learned by watching others, not only from your own failures. Keep a short journal of such lessons this month.

rel.note: Laziness casts a person into deep sleep, and the idle go hungry.
Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty.
These words are the instruction the wise man received when he considered the ruined field.
The next verse names where the little sleep leads: sudden poverty.
The same words first warned the sluggard after the lesson of the ant.
The question "How long will you slumber?" exposes the endless "little" of the sluggard.

units.notes:
• Proverbs 6:10 has almost the same words. The NKJV ends 6:10 with "to sleep" and 24:33 with "to rest"; the KJV has "to sleep" in both places.
• Bridges: "But this little insensibly increases." Insensibly means without being noticed: the "little" keeps growing while the sleeper does not see it.
• Henry pictures the sluggard's "a little sleep" becoming "a little more, till he has slept his eyes out."
• Compare 6:9 ("How long will you slumber, O sluggard?"); 19:15; 20:13 ("Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty"); 26:14; Romans 13:11.
units.summary: Ruin rarely comes from one big decision; it comes from a hundred small delays.
units.principle: Small, repeated indulgences of ease, each harmless in appearance, add up to ruin; faithfulness is built the same way, a little at a time.
units.insight: In Gethsemane Jesus asked His closest disciples to watch with Him, and three times He found them sleeping. "What! Could you not watch with Me one hour?... The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:40–41). They did not plan to fail Him. They only closed their eyes for a little while. Spiritual drift usually works the same way. A skipped prayer becomes a skipped week; a missed Sunday becomes a habit. Applied to the life of faith, "a little slumber" may be the most dangerous phrase in the chapter. Paul's call fits it: "it is high time to awake out of sleep" (Romans 13:11). The good news is that small steps work in the other direction too. A little prayer, a little Scripture and a little obedience, repeated daily by God's grace, build a fruitful field.
units.application: Notice your own "a little" phrases: "just one more episode," "I'll answer that tomorrow," "I'll start praying again next week." Replace one of them this week with a small, immediate action. Students: break big assignments into daily portions. Employees: tackle the task you keep postponing first thing in the morning. Parents: model getting up and getting on with the day. If exhaustion or depression is the real issue, seek help; that is not laziness.

rel.note: A slack hand makes poor, but the diligent hand makes rich.
Some poverty comes from injustice, so this warning must not be used to blame every poor person.
The lazy man's desire kills him, because his hands refuse to work.
The little sleep of the previous verse is what brings this sudden want.
The same words close the first warning to the sluggard.

units.notes:
• The verse repeats 6:11 almost exactly: "So shall your poverty come on you like a prowler, And your need like an armed man." Here the words "on you" are left out.
• "Prowler" is literally one who walks about. The KJV has "as one that travelleth," and its margin gives "a man of shield" for "an armed man." The ESV has "like a robber."
• Ironside: the sluggard "will be awakened too late to realize that his wasted opportunities have gone beyond recall."
• Proverbs itself warns against blaming every poor person: "Much food is in the fallow ground of the poor, And for lack of justice there is waste" (13:23). Some poverty comes from injustice, not laziness.
• Compare 10:4; 20:4; 21:25; 2 Thessalonians 3:10; Revelation 16:15.
units.summary: Poverty does not knock; it slips in like a prowler while the lazy man sleeps.
units.principle: Willful neglect brings want suddenly and with force, though not all poverty comes from laziness.
units.insight: The lazy man never meant to become poor. He meant to get up soon. That is why poverty comes "like a prowler": it arrives while the excuses are still being made. Jesus used a similar picture of His own return: "Behold, I am coming as a thief. Blessed is he who watches" (Revelation 16:15). Applied to the life of faith, the verse asks whether we are awake. Yet it must be handled with care. Ruth gleaned behind the reapers because she was poor, not lazy, and Boaz honored her for it (Ruth 2:2, 11–12). Jesus Himself had "nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20). Never use this proverb to judge the poor; use it to examine yourself. And remember that Christ "became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). His grace meets us in every kind of need.
units.application: If you are able to work and have been drifting, start today: apply for the job, finish the task, open the bills. Parents of young adults: love them enough to require responsibility. Churches: help the poor generously, and where laziness is part of the problem, pair help with accountability (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12). Never assume someone's poverty is his own fault; ask, listen and learn the story before you judge.

rel.note: The earlier heading over Solomon's proverbs, to which the word "also" in 25:1 ties this second collection.
The book's opening heading also names Solomon, showing that his sayings were gathered under his name more than once.
Another heading that uses "also" to mark a further collection added to the book.

units.notes:
• "Copied" translates a Hebrew verb whose basic meaning is to move or transfer something. Here it describes carrying sayings over into a new written collection. The text does not say whether Hezekiah's men worked from older written records, from sayings handed down by memory, or from both.
• The Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) calls these men the friends of Hezekiah. The Hebrew simply says "the men of Hezekiah," people in the king's service.
• This is the third heading in Proverbs to carry Solomon's name (1:1; 10:1; 25:1). Many sayings in chapters 25–27 are comparisons built with "like" or "as," while chapters 28–29 return to the righteous-and-wicked contrasts of 10:1–22:16.
• Bridges: "The Holy Spirit mentions not only the author, but the copyists, of these proverbs."
• Compare 1 Kings 4:32; Ecclesiastes 12:9, where the Preacher "set in order many proverbs"; and 2 Chronicles 29–31, the account of Hezekiah's reform.
units.summary: Solomon spoke these sayings, but faithful men two centuries later made sure we would hear them.
units.principle: God preserves His word through faithful people in every generation, and the hands that pass it on do not lessen its authority.
units.insight: No one remembers the names of Hezekiah's men, yet every reader of Proverbs 25–29 owes them a debt. Scripture gives other pictures of this hidden service. Baruch wrote Jeremiah's words on a scroll, and when the king burned it, he wrote them all out again (Jeremiah 36:4, 32). In Josiah's day the Book of the Law was found in the temple and read aloud, and the king tore his clothes and led the people in renewing the covenant (2 Kings 22:8–23:3). Revival and the word of God belong together. Serving God's word is often quiet work: copying, teaching, keeping. Paul charged Timothy to commit what he had heard "to faithful men who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). The question for each of us is whether the truth we received will reach the next generation through us.
units.application: Thank God this week for the people who handed Scripture on to you: a parent, a Sunday school teacher, a translator you will never meet. If you teach children or lead a small group, remember that your work is like theirs: keeping God's word safe for people who will need it later. Young people: try copying out one verse a day by hand; it slows you down enough to hear it. Pastors and teachers: pass on what you received faithfully, without decorating it.

rel.note: A ruler must search a matter out because the first account heard often seems right until it is examined.
The chapter opens with true glory and closes by warning that seeking one's own glory is no glory.
The king who searches matters out has a heart his subjects cannot search; the two sayings share one Hebrew root.
Whoever searches for wisdom as for hidden treasure finds the knowledge of God, so searching is honored there too.

units.notes:
• The same Hebrew word stands behind "glory" in both lines, so God and king are measured on one scale. The chapter returns to the word in 25:27, where seeking one's own glory "is not glory."
• "Search out" comes from the same Hebrew root as "unsearchable" in 25:3. The wordplay binds the two sayings: kings search matters out, yet their own hearts cannot be searched.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Proverbs 25:2 appears to be an intentional tribute to Solomon and Hezekiah as scholar-kings."
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "It is happy for me, that God makes me of his court, though not of his council." In other words, God welcomes us into His presence without telling us all His plans.
• Compare Deuteronomy 29:29 ("The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but those things which are revealed belong to us and to our children forever"); Job 11:7; Romans 11:33.
units.summary: God is honored by the depths He keeps; a ruler is honored by the truth he digs out.
units.principle: God's greatness includes what He has not explained, and those who govern others honor their trust by searching out the truth before they judge.
units.insight: This verse humbles two kinds of pride. One demands that God explain Himself. Job wanted a hearing, and when God answered out of the whirlwind He gave no reason for Job's suffering, only a vision of His own greatness, and Job bowed in worship (Job 38–42). Paul ended his deepest reflection on God's ways not with an answer but with praise: "Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" (Romans 11:33). The other pride judges quickly and searches little. Solomon's ruling over the two mothers shows the opposite: patient searching that found the truth. God's hidden things are not locked away from the humble. Jesus thanked the Father for revealing to little children what He had hidden from the wise (Matthew 11:25). Where are you demanding answers when God is asking for trust?
units.application: When God has not explained a loss or a delay, tell Him so plainly, then choose to trust Him with what He has kept hidden. When you must decide between people, as a parent, a manager or a church leader, search before you judge: hear both sides, ask questions, check the facts and wait for the second account (18:17). In your Bible reading, dig. Slow down over a passage, compare Scripture with Scripture, and let the searching become worship.

rel.note: No heart, however hidden from people, is hidden from the LORD, who weighs the spirits.
A heart's counsel is deep water, yet a person of understanding can draw it out.
The king's heart, hidden from his subjects, is in the LORD's hand.
Kings search matters out, yet their own hearts cannot be searched; the same Hebrew root joins the two sayings.

units.notes:
• "Unsearchable" renders a Hebrew phrase that means literally "there is no searching." It comes from the same root as "search out" in 25:2, so the two sayings play on one word: the searcher cannot be searched.
• Henry compares the hearts of wise rulers to the height of heaven and the depth of the earth, "which we may guess at, but cannot measure."
• Bridges draws a lesson for subjects: "Ought not this to teach forbearance in pronouncing judgment?" People who cannot see a ruler's reasons should be slow to condemn him.
• Compare 21:1; 16:2; Psalm 139:1–6; Jeremiah 17:10 ("I, the LORD, search the heart"); 1 Timothy 2:1–2.
units.summary: You cannot measure the sky or sound the earth's depths, and you cannot fully read a ruler's heart.
units.principle: Leaders carry counsel others cannot see, so those under them owe humility and restraint in judging, while every heart, however high, lies open to God.
units.insight: We are quick to judge those above us. We assume we know why a pastor, a boss or a government made a decision, and we fill the silence with suspicion. This verse asks for humility. David refused to lift his hand against Saul, though Saul was in the wrong and David had the chance (1 Samuel 24:6). Paul told believers to pray "for kings and all who are in authority" (1 Timothy 2:1–2), not to tear them down. The verse also comforts. No human heart is unsearchable to God, for "the LORD weighs the spirits" (16:2), and Jesus "knew what was in man" (John 2:25). Rulers who hide wrong cannot hide it from Him. Even our own hearts, which we cannot fully read, are known by a God who searches them in order to lead us in the way everlasting (Psalm 139:23–24).
units.application: When leaders make a decision you do not understand, at work, in church or in government, ask before you assume, and pray before you criticize (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Employees: give your supervisor the benefit of the doubt you would want yourself. Leaders: the privacy of your counsel is a trust, not a cover; you answer to the One who weighs every heart. All of us: ask God to search what we cannot see in ourselves (Psalm 139:23–24).

rel.note: The refining pot is for silver, and the LORD tests hearts the way fire tests metal.
The refiner's picture is applied to the court: remove the wicked and the throne stands in righteousness.
There the silver dross is not removed but used to coat a worthless pot, a picture of fine words over a wicked heart.

units.notes:
• The NKJV's "jewelry" renders a general Hebrew word for an object, article or vessel; the ESV has "a vessel." The KJV reads "there shall come forth a vessel for the finer," that is, for the refiner. Every translation keeps the picture of purified silver becoming something useful.
• Dross is the scum of impurities that separates from molten metal. In 26:23 the same worthless "silver dross" becomes a shiny coating on a cheap clay pot, a picture of warm words covering a wicked heart.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "You cannot have a pure silver vessel till you have purified the silver."
• Scripture often uses refining for God's work in His people: Isaiah 1:22, 25; Malachi 3:2–3; 1 Peter 1:7.
• Compare 2 Timothy 2:21, where whoever cleanses himself becomes "a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful for the Master."
units.summary: Before the craftsman can make anything fine, the fire must take away what does not belong.
units.principle: What is valuable becomes useful only when what corrupts it is removed; purity comes before usefulness.
units.insight: God is a refiner, and He does with His people what the silversmith does with ore. Malachi pictures the Lord sitting "as a refiner and a purifier of silver" (Malachi 3:3), patient over the fire until the dross is gone. Peter told suffering believers that their faith, "much more precious than gold that perishes," was being tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7). Think of Jacob, whose scheming was worn away through twenty hard years with Laban until he limped away from Peniel a changed man (Genesis 31:38–41; 32:24–31). The fire is not God's rejection. He refines silver because it is worth refining. The question this verse puts to us is not whether we are valuable but what dross we are holding onto that keeps us from being useful: bitterness, pride, or a habit we will not surrender.
units.application: Ask God to show you one piece of dross in your life: a resentment, a habit, a pride you keep defending. Name it to Him and confess it. If you are in a season of hardship, ask not only "When will this end?" but "What is God removing?" Parents and mentors: help a young person see that correction is refining, not rejection. Leaders: before you ask God to use your ministry or business, ask Him to purify it.

rel.note: A throne is established by righteousness, the same truth stated directly.
A king on the throne of judgment scatters evil with his eyes, removing it from his presence.
The refiner's picture explains this command: wicked advisers are the dross of a kingdom.
A ruler who listens to lies ends up with wicked servants, the opposite of a court cleared of the wicked.

units.notes:
• Other sayings show the king himself removing evil: he "Scatters all evil with his eyes" (20:8) and "sifts out the wicked" (20:26). The refining picture of 25:4–5 makes the same point with silver and dross.
• Solomon's own reign began this way. After Joab and Shimei were dealt with, the text says, "Thus the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon" (1 Kings 2:46).
• Henry: "The reformation of the court will promote the reformation of the kingdom." Reform at the top spreads downward.
• Psalm 101 is a king's vow to keep the wicked out of his house: "He who works deceit shall not dwell within my house" (Psalm 101:7).
• Scripture sets this pattern beside Christ's own rule: at the end of the age He will gather out of His kingdom "all things that offend, and those who practice lawlessness" (Matthew 13:41).
units.summary: A leader is only as righteous as the people he keeps closest to him.
units.principle: Leadership is shaped by the people a leader keeps close, and righteousness, not cleverness, makes any rule secure.
units.insight: Rehoboam lost ten tribes in a day because he listened to the young men he had grown up with instead of the elders (1 Kings 12:8–16). Joash did what was right all the days of Jehoiada the priest, but after Jehoiada died he listened to the leaders of Judah and turned to idols (2 Chronicles 24:2, 17–18). The people around a leader shape him more than he knows. Scripture also sets this verse beside a greater throne. Christ's throne is forever, and "A scepter of righteousness is the scepter of Your kingdom" (Hebrews 1:8); when He returns He will remove from His kingdom everything that offends (Matthew 13:41–43). The question for us is personal. Who has the king's ear in your life? Whose voices are shaping your decisions, and would they help your throne stand in righteousness?
units.application: If you lead a team, a church or a household, take a hard look at your inner circle. Who flatters, who gossips, who bends the truth? Move such people away from places of influence, kindly but firmly, and choose advisers who will tell you the truth. If you serve near a leader, be the kind of counsel that steadies a throne, not one that corrupts it. Young people: the friends you keep closest will shape the person you become.

rel.note: Before honor is humility, the principle behind taking the lower place.
Pride goes before destruction, the fall that awaits the one who seizes the place of the great.
Seeking one's own glory is not glory, so the chapter closes by returning to the self-promotion warned against here.
Let another praise you and not your own mouth; honor should come from someone else.
Pride brings a person low, while the humble in spirit retain honor.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin renders the first line of 25:6 "set not out thy glory": do not put your own splendor on display before the king.
• The ESV and the 1984 NIV join the last line of 25:7 to 25:8, so that it warns against rushing to court over what you have seen with your own eyes. The NKJV, NASB and KJV keep it with 25:7 as a description of the prince. The Hebrew can be read either way.
• Jesus told guests to take the lowest place so that the host may say, "Friend, go up higher," and gave the principle: "whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 14:10–11).
• Henry warns against turning humility into a technique: "Not that we must therefore pretend modesty and humility, and make a stratagem of it, for the courting of honour." A stratagem is a scheme.
• Compare 15:33; 29:23; James 4:10; 1 Peter 5:5–6.
units.summary: Better to be invited higher than to be sent lower in front of everyone.
units.principle: True honor is received, not seized; the humble leave their standing in the hands of the One who has the right to give it.
units.insight: The hunger for the best seat runs deep. The disciples argued about which of them was greatest at the Last Supper itself (Luke 22:24). Saul was once "little in your own eyes" (1 Samuel 15:17), but he came to grasp at honor and lost his kingdom. Jesus did more than retell this proverb; He lived it. He "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death," and therefore God "highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:8–9). He took the lowest place and was called up to the highest. That is the pattern for His people, not as a strategy but as a heart that trusts the Host. So the question is where we are quietly maneuvering for a better seat, and whether we could be content if the call to come up higher never came in this life.
units.application: At the next dinner, meeting or church event, take the lesser seat and let someone else have the attention. In meetings, resist the urge to make sure everyone knows your contribution. Young professionals: do excellent work and let it be noticed rather than lobbying for promotion. Leaders and hosts: look for the humble people at the back and call them up higher, as the host does in Jesus' parable.

rel.note: Strife once released is hard to hold back, so contention should be stopped before a quarrel starts.
The first to plead his cause seems right until his neighbor examines him, the very reversal the hasty accuser risks.
The next sayings give the better way: settle the matter directly with the neighbor and never win by betrayal.
Do not strive with a man without cause, a limit on quarrels that haste ignores.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew behind "go hastily to court" is a verb meaning to contend or quarrel, and the same verb is used for pleading a case before judges. The KJV has "Go not forth hastily to strive." The NKJV's "court" brings out the legal setting, while the Hebrew covers any quarrel pressed too quickly.
• Shame links this small group of sayings with the one before it: the proud guest may be "put lower" (25:7), the hasty accuser may be put to shame (25:8), and the betrayer of a secret may have his own shame exposed (25:10).
• Henry: "we are apt to be partial in our own cause." We see our side of a dispute more favorably than the facts may warrant.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Jesus gave a similar teaching in Luke 12:57-59." There Jesus urges making peace with an adversary on the way, before the judge hears the case.
• Compare 17:14; 20:3; Matthew 5:25; 1 Corinthians 6:1–7.
units.summary: Before you rush to court, ask where the case will end; it may end with you ashamed.
units.principle: Haste in conflict rarely ends well; think through where a quarrel will lead and hear the other side before you press it.
units.insight: Josiah was one of Judah's best kings, yet he died because he went out hastily to fight Pharaoh Necho in a quarrel that was not his, ignoring the warning that came to him (2 Chronicles 35:20–24). Haste can undo a lifetime of faithfulness. Abram shows the better way. When strife broke out between his herdsmen and Lot's, he gave up his rights rather than press them: "Please let there be no strife between you and me" (Genesis 13:8). The rush to court usually comes from wounded pride. We want to be proved right, and we want it now. Paul asked the Corinthians, who were suing one another, "Why do you not rather accept wrong?" (1 Corinthians 6:7). Jesus, wronged more than anyone, "committed Himself to Him who judges righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). Where are you rushing to be vindicated when God is asking you to wait?
units.application: Before you file the complaint, send the angry email or report someone to a supervisor, wait a day. Write down the other person's likely answer and ask whether you could be wrong. Neighbors in a property dispute, church members with a grievance, employees with a complaint: talk to the person first (Matthew 18:15). Leaders hearing a complaint: do not act on one side of the story. Ask what the end will be before you begin.

rel.note: The talebearer reveals secrets, while the one with a faithful spirit conceals a matter.
Repeating a matter separates friends, while covering a transgression seeks love.
A talebearer reveals secrets, so the one who betrays confidences becomes someone others learn to avoid.
