A good name is worth more than great riches, and betraying a confidence can ruin it for good.
The warning against rushing to court is the first step of the same counsel for conflict.

units.notes:
• The ESV, the 1984 NIV and the NLT take "the secret" to mean another person's secret, so the forbidden act is betraying a confidence that belongs to someone else, the neighbor or a third party. The NKJV's wording can carry the same sense, and the KJV margin reads "of another."
• "Your reputation be ruined" uses a Hebrew word for an evil report, the damaging talk that spreads about a person, and says literally that this report will not turn back. The ESV renders the sense as ill repute that will have "no end." The betrayer cannot call back the damage to his name.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "To run to the law or to the neighbours is usually to run away from the duty of personal relationship."
• Bridges on the cost of betraying a confidence: "Backbiter will be the stamp on our name." A backbiter is someone who speaks against people behind their backs, and that label sticks.
• Compare 11:13 ("he who is of a faithful spirit conceals a matter"); 17:9; 20:19; Matthew 18:15.
units.summary: Settle it face to face, and never win an argument by spending someone else's secret.
units.principle: Conflict is best settled directly and privately, and a confidence must be kept even when breaking it would win the argument.
units.insight: Jesus gave the same order for His people: "if your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone" (Matthew 18:15). We tend to tell everyone except the person. When the king of Ammon came against Israel, Jephthah first sent messengers to reason with the king himself (Judges 11:12–27). Abigail went straight to David and turned him back from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–33). Betraying a secret is a deeper sin than it looks, because it turns another person's trust into a weapon. The heart behind it wants to win more than it wants to be reconciled. God knows every secret of ours and does not use them against us. He covers the sin of those who come to Him (Psalm 32:1; Romans 4:7), and those who have been covered can learn to cover others in love (1 Peter 4:8).
units.application: When you are in a conflict with a coworker, family member or fellow church member, go to the person first, before you tell anyone else. Keep the conversation on the issue, not on everything you know about their past. If someone once confided in you and is now at odds with you, guard that confidence all the more. Leaders and counselors: never use what you heard in private to win a public argument. If you have already spread it, go back and make it right.

rel.note: The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, the instinct that makes a word fit its hearer.
A word spoken in due season is called good, the same praise of timely speech without the picture.
The gold-and-silver picture continues and is applied to a rebuke that meets an obedient ear.
Cheerful songs sung to a heavy heart are the opposite of a fitting word: pleasant in themselves but wrong for the moment.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind "fitly" is rare, and its meaning is debated. It seems to come from a root meaning to turn, and the KJV margin reads "spoken upon his wheels," as though the word runs smoothly in its proper course. The YLT has "fit times" and the NASB "right circumstances." All agree that the saying is about timing and suitability.
• The word rendered "settings" elsewhere means a carved figure or image, so the picture may be carved silver work framing golden fruit. The KJV has "pictures of silver," the NLT "a silver basket."
• Trapp, quoted by Guzik: "It is an excellent skill to be able to time a word."
• Bridges on the "wheels" of the KJV margin: a fit word is "not forced or dragged, but rolling smoothly along, like the chariot-wheels."
• Compare 15:23; 24:26; Isaiah 50:4; Colossians 4:6 ("Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt").
units.summary: The right word is precious; the right word at the right moment is a work of art.
units.principle: Truth does its best work when it is spoken at the right time and in the right way; wisdom weighs both the word and its setting.
units.insight: Many of us have the right words and the wrong timing. Job's friends said many true things about God, yet their words fell on Job like blows because they did not fit his need, and he called them "Miserable comforters" (Job 16:2). Boaz, by contrast, spoke kind words to a weary foreigner gleaning in his field, and they were exactly what Ruth needed to hear (Ruth 2:8–13). The Servant of the LORD says, "The Lord GOD has given Me The tongue of the learned, That I should know how to speak A word in season to him who is weary" (Isaiah 50:4). Jesus did this often. To a thirsty Samaritan woman He spoke of living water; to grieving Martha He said, "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 4:10; 11:25). The fitting word begins with listening. Before we speak, we must understand the person in front of us.
units.application: Before you give advice this week, ask three questions: Is it true? Is this the moment? Is this the way to say it? Parents: correct a child privately and calmly, not in front of siblings in the heat of the moment. Friends: when someone is hurting, comfort first and counsel later. Preachers and teachers: build the frame as carefully as you choose the content, because tone, illustration and timing are the silver setting for the gold.

rel.note: The ear that hears the rebukes of life will abide among the wise.
Instruction from father and mother is a graceful ornament, the same picture of teaching worn as jewelry.
The gold-and-silver picture of a fitting word leads straight into this gold ornament of a fitting rebuke.
Faithful are the wounds of a friend, the kind of rebuke worth wearing.
Rebuke a wise man and he will love you; the receptive hearer grows wiser.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "earring" is also used for a nose ring, as in Genesis 24:47, where the NKJV has "nose ring."
• Earlier the father said that the instruction of father and mother would be "a graceful ornament on your head" (1:9). Here the ornament belongs to the ear that receives a wise rebuke.
• The ESV has "a listening ear"; the KJV keeps "an obedient ear." The point is an ear that hears in order to act.
• Henry: both "will have their praise, the reprover for giving it so prudently and the reproved for taking it so patiently."
• Compare 9:8–9; 15:31; 27:6; Psalm 141:5 ("Let the righteous strike me; It shall be a kindness").
units.summary: Correction becomes jewelry when a wise mouth meets a willing ear.
units.principle: Correction given wisely and received humbly honors both people; a willing ear turns a rebuke into an ornament.
units.insight: Nathan's rebuke of David is the great example. He came first with a story, then with four words: "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). David did not defend himself. He said, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13), and out of that moment came Psalm 51. A wise rebuker met an obedient ear, and the rebuke became an ornament David still wears in Scripture. Saul, rebuked by Samuel, made excuses and blamed the people (1 Samuel 15:20–21), and the same kind of word became his undoing. Which ear do we have? Most of us would rather be the wise rebuker than the obedient ear. Yet the Lord Jesus says, "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19). His correction is never rejection. It is love fitting us with gold.
units.application: The next time someone corrects you, whether a spouse, a boss or a small-group leader, say "Thank you" before anything else, and take a day before defending yourself. If you must correct someone, do it privately, specifically and with evident care, and pray first. Parents: let your children see you receive correction well. Leaders: make it safe for people to tell you hard things, and treat their faithful words as gold.

rel.note: The lazy messenger is vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes of those who send him.
A faithful ambassador brings health, while a wicked messenger falls into trouble.
The boaster who promises and never gives disappoints like clouds without rain.
An unfaithful man fails like a bad tooth just when he is relied on, the opposite of the messenger who refreshes.
Good news from far away refreshes like cold water; the chapter pairs the faithful messenger with the good report he carries.

units.notes:
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Probably the reference is to drink cooled with snow."
• The Greek writer Xenophon, in his Memorabilia, mentions people hunting for snow in summer to chill their wine. Cooling drinks with snow was known in the ancient world, though the proverb itself does not describe the custom.
• "Refreshes the soul" translates a Hebrew expression meaning to bring back or restore the soul, used of reviving someone who is exhausted. A related expression appears in Psalm 23:3, "He restores my soul."
• Abraham's servant is Scripture's portrait of this messenger. He prayed for success, refused to eat until he had told his errand, and would not let the family delay his return (Genesis 24:12–14, 33, 56).
• Compare 13:17 ("a faithful ambassador brings health"); 10:26; 26:6.
units.summary: A dependable person is as refreshing as a cold drink in the heat of harvest.
units.principle: Faithfulness in small errands refreshes the people who depend on us; reliability is a ministry, not a minor virtue.
units.insight: Dependability can look like a plain virtue, but this saying ranks it among the things that revive people. Paul knew that refreshment. When Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus arrived from Corinth, he wrote, "they refreshed my spirit" (1 Corinthians 16:17–18). Epaphroditus risked his life to bring the Philippians' gift to Paul (Philippians 2:25–30). The greatest faithful messenger is Jesus Himself. He spoke only what the Father gave Him to speak (John 12:49), and He could say, "I have finished the work which You have given Me to do" (John 17:4). Every believer is now sent as well, an ambassador for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20). So the question is whether the people who depend on us, at home, at work and in God's work, find us like cold water or like smoke in the eyes.
units.application: This week, do the small things you said you would do: return the call, pass on the message accurately, finish the task without being chased. Employees and volunteers: report back when the job is done, so the person who sent you can rest. Young people: when your parents send you on an errand, do it fully and promptly. Leaders: thank the faithful messengers around you; they are cold water in your harvest.

rel.note: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, the very damage that empty promises of giving do.
Many proclaim their own goodness, but a faithful man is hard to find.
The faithful messenger refreshes like cold at harvest; the boaster disappoints like clouds without rain.
Do not withhold good or tell your neighbor to come back tomorrow when you have it with you.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin gives the Hebrew of the first line literally as boasting "in a gift of falsehood," a gift that is never actually given.
• Bishop Coverdale's rendering, quoted by Bridges: "Whoso maketh greate boastes, and giveth nothing."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The lesson, of course, is not to make false promises."
• Jude uses the same picture for false teachers who promise much and give nothing: "clouds without water, carried about by the winds" (Jude 12).
• Contrast 1 Kings 18:44–45, where after years of drought "a cloud, as small as a man's hand" rose from the sea and real rain followed. Compare also 20:6; 3:27–28; Matthew 6:1–4.
units.summary: Clouds that bring no rain are worse than a clear sky, and so are promises no one keeps.
units.principle: Promised generosity that never arrives does more harm than a plain refusal; let your giving be real before it is ever spoken of.
units.insight: Ananias and Sapphira are this proverb's sharpest example. Barnabas had sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:36–37). Ananias and his wife wanted the same reputation, so they sold land, kept back part of the price, and presented the rest as the whole (Acts 5:1–11). They wanted the clouds without the rain. Their sin was not keeping some of the money, which was theirs to keep (Acts 5:4), but lying to win admiration. Jesus warned against giving in order to be seen (Matthew 6:1–4). The gospel turns this sin on its head. God did not boast of a gift He would not give. He promised a Savior and gave Him: "He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). Our giving should look like His: quiet, real and costly.
units.application: Do not announce a gift, a donation or a favor until you are sure you will give it. If you promised something to a friend, a ministry or your children and have not delivered, keep the promise this week or go back and tell them the truth. Leaders and fundraisers: never inflate pledges or claim generosity you have not shown. Parents: let your children see you give quietly and keep your word.

rel.note: Being slow to wrath shows great understanding, while impulsiveness exalts folly.
A soft answer turns away wrath; here gentle speech goes further and changes a mind.
A wise man appeases the king's wrath, persuading power by wisdom rather than force.
He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, the strength behind long forbearance.

units.notes:
• "Long forbearance" translates a Hebrew phrase built from the words for "length" and "anger," describing a long delay before anger rises. A closely related phrase is rendered "slow to wrath" or "slow to anger" elsewhere in Proverbs (14:29; 15:18; 16:32).
• The word translated "ruler" (KJV "prince") is not the usual Hebrew word for king. It is used for a commander or chief official, so the saying fits anyone with power over the speaker, not only a monarch.
• Henry: "Hard words, we say, break no bones, and therefore we should bear them patiently; but, it seems, soft words do, and therefore we should, on all occasions, give them prudently."
• Gideon calmed the angry men of Ephraim with a humble answer, and "their anger toward him subsided" (Judges 8:1–3).
• Compare 15:1; 16:14; Ecclesiastes 10:4; 2 Timothy 2:24–25.
units.summary: Soft words can break what hard words only harden.
units.principle: Patience and gentleness often move what force cannot, and they remain the way of wisdom whether or not they succeed.
units.insight: David spared Saul's life and then spoke to him gently from a distance. Saul wept and said, "You are more righteous than I" (1 Samuel 24:16–17). Abigail met an angry David on the road with humble words and a generous gift, and he turned back from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–35). When God restored Elijah, He did not speak in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12). Our flesh believes that pressure wins. The gospel shows otherwise. Christ, who is "gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29), won us not by force but by patient love, and "the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation" (2 Peter 3:15). Where are you pushing harder when God is asking you to be patient and speak more softly?
units.application: When you need a decision from someone above you, such as a boss, a landlord or an official, ask calmly, give your reasons, and be willing to ask again later rather than pressing in anger. Spouses and parents: lower your voice when a conversation heats up; a gentle reply often breaks a stalemate. When you share your faith, choose patience over pressure. If someone stays hard, keep being kind and leave the outcome with God.

rel.note: At a ruler's table the one given to appetite must restrain himself, the same call to self-control with food.
Eat honey because it is good; the gift is affirmed before the limit is set.
The same Hebrew word for being full links overeating honey with wearing out a neighbor's welcome.
Honey returns at the chapter's close: eating much is not good, and neither is seeking one's own glory.
A satisfied soul loathes the honeycomb, the end of an appetite pushed past its need.

units.notes:
• "Filled with it" here and "weary of you" in 25:17 translate the same Hebrew verb, which means to be satisfied or full. The shared word links the two sayings: too much honey and too much of a visitor produce the same overfullness.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "Since Eden, man has wanted the last ounce out of life."
• Henry: "Enough is as good as a feast."
• Israel's craving in the wilderness shows the same pattern on a larger scale. God gave them meat for a whole month, "until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you" (Numbers 11:20).
• Compare 24:13; 27:7; 23:1–3; 1 Timothy 4:4 ("every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be refused if it is received with thanksgiving").
units.summary: God gives the honey; wisdom knows when to put the spoon down.
units.principle: God's good gifts are meant to be enjoyed with thanks and within limits; an appetite that will not stop turns sweetness into sickness.
units.insight: Esau came in from the field hungry and traded his birthright for one bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34). The food was not evil; the appetite that would not wait was. Israel complained for meat in the wilderness, and God gave them so much that it became loathsome to them (Numbers 11:18–20). Our age knows this sickness well: too much food, too much screen time, too much shopping, even too much of good things like work or entertainment. The problem is not the gift but a heart that always wants one more taste. The answer is not to despise God's gifts but to find our deepest satisfaction in Him. Jesus said, "I am the bread of life. He who comes to Me shall never hunger" (John 6:35). A soul satisfied in Christ can enjoy honey without being ruled by it.
units.application: Pick one good thing you tend to overdo, such as dessert, your phone, streaming, online shopping or even overtime, and set a simple limit for this week. Stop before you are full, and thank God for the gift as you enjoy it. Parents: teach children to enjoy treats and to stop, without making food or fun the enemy. If unexpected money or free time comes your way, decide your limits before the abundance decides for you.

rel.note: A man who has friends must himself be friendly, and part of friendliness is knowing when to give space.
Honey and visits are paired: both are good, and both turn sour when taken past their measure.
A loud blessing early in the morning is counted a curse, so friendship needs sensitivity to timing.

units.notes:
• "Seldom set foot" translates Hebrew that says literally "make your foot rare." The verb belongs to the same word family as "rare" in "the word of the LORD was rare in those days" (1 Samuel 3:1), a word that can also mean precious. A visit that stays rare stays precious.
• "Weary of you" uses the same Hebrew verb as "filled with it" in 25:16. A neighbor can have his fill of a visitor as a person can have his fill of honey.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Friendship ripens through discreet sensitivity not to intrude on privacy."
• Compare 27:14; 1 Timothy 5:13; 2 Thessalonians 3:11.
units.summary: Make your visits rare enough to be welcome, and your friendship will stay sweet.
units.principle: Love respects another person's limits; even a good friendship needs restraint to stay welcome.
units.insight: Paul warned about people who learn to be idle, "wandering about from house to house," and become "busybodies" (1 Timothy 5:13). Sometimes our visiting serves our own loneliness or curiosity more than our neighbor's good. This verse asks us to love people enough to notice when we are too much. It also sets up a contrast. There is one door we can never knock on too often. Jesus told the parable of the friend at midnight to teach persistence in prayer (Luke 11:5–9), and we are invited to "come boldly to the throne of grace" (Hebrews 4:16). Henry says of God's house: "the oftener we come to him the better and the more welcome." Earthly friendships need measure; our friendship with God never wears out His welcome. If you find yourself pressing too hard on people, it may be a sign that you need to press more into Him.
units.application: Before you drop in on a neighbor, a friend or an adult child, ask whether it is a good time, and keep visits short enough that they want you back. If someone's replies are getting shorter, give them space without taking offense. Parents of grown children, and grown children near their parents: respect each other's time. Church members: welcome newcomers warmly without crowding them. When loneliness pushes you toward people, bring it first to God in prayer.

rel.note: Some speak like the piercings of a sword, the same picture of words as weapons.
A false witness will not go unpunished, the judgment that answers this violence.
Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause, the same command stated directly.
A false witness who speaks lies is among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• "Club" is a war club or battle hammer; the KJV has "maul," a heavy hammer.
• The word "neighbor" runs through this part of the chapter (25:8, 9, 17, 18), keeping attention on the people who live nearby: disputes, secrets, visits and testimony.
• Henry: the false witness is "a sword to wound near at hand and a sharp arrow to wound at a distance."
• Scripture records the damage. Potiphar's wife's lie put Joseph in prison (Genesis 39:14–20); false witnesses cost Naboth his vineyard and his life (1 Kings 21:10–13); false witnesses were brought against Jesus and against Stephen (Matthew 26:59–61; Acts 6:13).
• Compare 24:28; 12:18; 6:16–19; 19:5.
units.summary: A lie about your neighbor is not just talk; it is a weapon.
units.principle: False words about another person are acts of violence, and God holds the witness responsible for the damage his tongue does.
units.insight: Naboth refused to sell his family inheritance, so Jezebel hired two scoundrels to swear that he had cursed God and the king. Their words did a sword's work: Naboth was stoned and his vineyard taken (1 Kings 21:8–16). The worst false witness in history came against Jesus. Many false witnesses came forward, and their lies helped condemn the only truly innocent man (Matthew 26:59–61). He bore it in silence, and through His death the guilty are set free. His silence under false witness speaks to both sides of this sin. If you have been lied about, you can entrust your name to God, as Jesus did (1 Peter 2:23). If you have passed on what you did not know to be true, you can repent and make it right. Before you repeat a story about someone who is not present, ask whether you are holding a weapon.
units.application: This week, refuse to pass on any report about someone that you have not verified, whether at work, online or in church conversation. If you have shared something false or exaggerated, go back to the people you told and correct it. If you serve on a board, a jury or a church council, insist on facts and on hearing the accused. If you have been falsely accused, speak the truth calmly and leave your vindication with God.

rel.note: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity, the reverse of the man who fails in trouble.
There is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, unlike the one who gives way when leaned on.
A faithful man is hard to find, so trust must be given with care.
The faithful messenger refreshes those who rely on him; the unfaithful man fails them at the point of pressure.

units.notes:
• "Unfaithful" translates a word for someone who acts treacherously, breaking faith with those who trusted him. The ESV has "a treacherous man" and "a foot that slips."
• Some older interpreters read the first line as the unfaithful man's own confidence, which fails him in trouble, like the man in Psalm 52:7 who trusted in his riches instead of God. The NKJV and most translations read it as confidence placed in him.
• Bridges on false friends: "Very friendly are they, when they are not needed."
• Egypt was Judah's bad tooth. The Assyrian commander called it "this broken reed," which pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it (Isaiah 36:6).
• Compare 17:17; 20:6; Psalm 55:12–14; Jeremiah 17:5–8.
units.summary: An unfaithful friend is like a bad tooth: fine until you lean on him.
units.principle: Trust is tested in trouble; choose carefully whom you lean on, and be the kind of person who holds when others lean on you.
units.insight: Near the end of his life Paul wrote, "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me" (2 Timothy 4:16). David was betrayed by his trusted counselor Ahithophel in the dark days of Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:31). Jesus Himself, in His hour of trouble, watched His disciples forsake Him and flee (Matthew 26:56). Yet Paul's next words were, "But the Lord stood with me and strengthened me" (2 Timothy 4:17). People will sometimes fail us, but God does not: "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). This truth guards us from bitterness and from putting our full weight on any human being. It also searches us. When a friend leans on us in trouble, do we hold?
units.application: Before you depend on someone for something important, such as a business deal, a loan, a ministry role or a confidence, look at how they have handled small trusts and hard times. When a friend is in trouble this week, be the one who shows up: make the call, bring the meal, stay. Leaders: place people in critical roles only after they have proved faithful. If someone failed you, grieve it, forgive, and lean harder on the Lord.

rel.note: A good word makes a heavy heart glad, the kind of word that fits the grieving.
Even in laughter the heart may sorrow, so surface cheer is no measure of what someone carries.
A broken spirit is hard to bear, so the heavy heart needs gentleness, not mirth.
A word fitly spoken suits its hearer; songs sung to a heavy heart do not.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word translated "soda" occurs elsewhere in the Old Testament only in Jeremiah 2:22, where the NKJV renders it "lye" and it is used for washing.
• The NLT reads the second line as "pouring vinegar in a wound," following the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint). The NKJV, ESV and NASB follow the Hebrew "soda."
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "The proverb indicates the impropriety of making merry in the presence of sorrow." Impropriety means unfitness.
• Psalm 137 gives the cruelest example: the captors of exiles who had hung up their harps demanded, "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!" (Psalm 137:2–4).
• Compare 14:13; 18:14; Ecclesiastes 3:4 ("A time to weep, And a time to laugh"); Romans 12:15.
units.summary: Cheerful songs for a grieving heart are like stripping a coat off someone in the cold.
units.principle: Comfort must fit the sufferer; compassion meets grief where it is before trying to lift it.
units.insight: Job's friends did their best work in the first week, when they sat with him on the ground seven days and said nothing, "for they saw that his grief was very great" (Job 2:13). Their trouble began when they started talking. Jesus knew He would raise Lazarus, yet at the tomb He wept with Mary and Martha (John 11:33–35). He did not rush past their grief to the miracle. Many of us find another's sorrow uncomfortable, and we hurry to fix it with cheerful words, a verse quoted too quickly or a change of subject. Often we are relieving our own discomfort, not their pain. Paul's command is simple: "weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). Christ is a High Priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and His people can learn to sit with the grieving as He sits with us.
units.application: When you visit someone who is grieving this week, say less. Sit with them, listen, and let them talk about the person or the loss if they want to. Avoid quick fixes such as "Everything happens for a reason." Worship leaders and pastors: remember the grieving in the room when you choose songs and words. Friends of the bereaved: keep showing up after the funeral, when everyone else has gone back to normal.

rel.note: When a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.
Revenge is forbidden there; here wisdom goes further and does active good to the enemy while waiting for the LORD.
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, a heart posture that must lie beneath real kindness.
Refusing to repay a man as he has done is the first step; feeding him is the next.

units.notes:
• Paul places this saying right after his call to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19). In Romans 12:20 he quotes the commands of 25:21, with slightly different wording, "feed him" and "give him a drink," and the coals clause of 25:22. He leaves out only the closing line about the LORD's reward, and concludes, "overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:21).
• Some early interpreters, including John Chrysostom, took the coals as a sign of God's judgment, since burning coals elsewhere picture His punishment: "Let burning coals fall upon them" (Psalm 140:10). On that reading, kindness leaves a stubborn enemy more accountable before God. Paul's conclusion favors the restorative reading.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Not to consume, but to melt him into kindness; a metaphor taken from smelting metallic ores." A metalworker heaps coals on ore to melt it, not to destroy it.
• Bridges: "No man ever conquered his enemy's heart by revenge; many by love."
• Compare 20:22; 24:17–18, 29; Exodus 23:4–5; Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27–28.
units.summary: Feed your enemy, and let God do with your kindness what revenge never could.
units.principle: Evil is overcome by good, not by revenge; practical kindness to an enemy leaves room for his repentance and leaves the reward to God.
units.insight: When the Syrian army came to seize Elisha, God struck them blind and Elisha led them into Samaria. The king of Israel asked, "Shall I kill them?" Elisha told him to set food and water before them and send them home, and the text adds, "So the bands of Syrian raiders came no more into the land of Israel" (2 Kings 6:21–23). When David spared Saul's life, even Saul wept (1 Samuel 24:16–19). This is not weakness or a clever tactic. It is the heart of God: "when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son" (Romans 5:10). On the cross Jesus prayed for those who crucified Him (Luke 23:34). Every Christian is a former enemy whom God fed. So the question is whether we will feed ours, or whether our forgiveness is only a quieter way of waiting for them to suffer.
units.application: Think of one person who has opposed or wronged you. This week, do one concrete good for them: a meal, a good word on their behalf, practical help in a crisis, a prayer for their blessing by name. Do it without announcing it and without demanding that they change. Families divided by a feud, coworkers in a rivalry, church members hurt by one another: let kindness make the next move, and leave the outcome, and any justice still owed, with the LORD.

rel.note: Whoever spreads slander is a fool.
A whisperer separates the best of friends, the broken relationships that secret talk leaves behind.
The talebearer's words go down into the inmost body, which is why they do such lasting harm.
Where there is no talebearer, strife ceases, the reverse of the storm that backbiting produces.

units.notes:
• In Israel rain usually comes from the west, off the Mediterranean (compare 1 Kings 18:44; Luke 12:54), and the north wind is more often linked with cool, clear weather. Some commentators, among them Keil and Delitzsch, suggest that "north" here may include the northwest, the direction from which rain does come.
• The KJV reverses the comparison: "The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue." On that reading an angry face silences the slanderer. The KJV margin gives the reading the NKJV and most modern translations follow.
• "A backbiting tongue" is literally "a tongue of secrecy," a tongue that slanders in secret; the YLT has "secret tongue." The Hebrew word for secrecy comes from the same root as "conceal" in 25:2, so the chapter sets God's glorious concealing beside the slanderer's harmful secrecy.
• Henry, on the KJV reading: "Slanders would not be so readily spoken as they are if they were not readily heard."
• Bridges: "This tongue wounds four at one stroke." He names the backbiter himself, the person attacked, the hearer, and the name of God.
• Compare 16:28; 26:20; James 3:5–6.
units.summary: Whisper about someone behind their back, and a storm of anger will follow.
units.principle: Secret slander never stays secret in its effects; words spoken behind someone's back bring open anger and broken relationships.
units.insight: During Absalom's revolt Ziba came to David with gifts and a story: his master Mephibosheth had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to regain his grandfather's kingdom. David believed the absent man's accuser and gave Ziba everything Mephibosheth owned (2 Samuel 16:1–4). Later Mephibosheth came, unwashed and grieving, and the truth looked very different (2 Samuel 19:24–30). Backbiting does damage on every side, and the heart behind it is often envy or resentment dressed up as concern. Jesus shows another way. He warned Peter to his face that he would fall, and He told him plainly that He had been praying for him: "I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail" (Luke 22:31–34). The cure for a backbiting tongue is a heart that has received grace, and so can say to people's faces what it would otherwise say about them.
units.application: When someone starts telling you about a person who is not present, gently ask, "Have you talked to them about this?" A cool face and a change of subject often end it. If you catch yourself venting about a coworker, family member or church leader, take the concern to the person instead, or to God. Group chats and social media count. Leaders: do not act on reports gathered behind someone's back without hearing that person first.

rel.note: A dry morsel with quietness is better than a feast with strife; peace outweighs plenty.
The contentions of a wife are a continual dripping, the wearing effect of constant strife.
The wilderness is better than living with a contentious and angry woman, the same point with a harsher picture.
The same saying appears in the earlier Solomon collection, almost word for word.
A contentious man kindles strife, so the warning applies to husbands as much as to wives.

units.notes:
• In the NKJV the saying differs from 21:9 only in its opening words, "It is better" instead of "Better." The heading in 25:1 presents chapters 25–29 as a separate gathering of Solomon's proverbs, so some sayings from the earlier collection naturally appear again.
• Bridges: "Scriptural repetitions shew not want of matter, but the deep importance of the matter laid out." That is, a saying is repeated not because material ran short but because it matters.
• Henry applies the saying to husband and wife alike: "for it is equally true of both."
• "Contentious" comes from a Hebrew word for strife or quarreling. The same idea appears in 19:13, "the contentions of a wife are a continual dripping," and in 27:15.
• Compare 21:9, 19; 17:1; 26:21; James 3:16–18; 1 Peter 3:7.
units.summary: A cramped corner of the roof beats a spacious house filled with quarreling.
units.principle: Peace in a home is worth more than space or comfort, and every member of a household is responsible for the strife he or she brings into it.
units.insight: Peninnah made Elkanah's home a misery for Hannah. Year after year she "provoked her severely, to make her miserable," until Hannah wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:6–7). The house was full, but there was no peace in it. Strife at home rarely begins with one great blow-up. It grows through a hundred small criticisms, complaints and corrections. This proverb is not a weapon for one spouse to aim at the other. It is a mirror for each of us: am I the one who makes the corner of the roof look inviting? The gospel speaks into such homes. Christ Himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Paul told believers, "Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and evil speaking be put away from you," and to forgive one another "even as God in Christ forgave you" (Ephesians 4:31–32).
units.application: Husbands and wives: this week, count your criticisms and complaints, and replace one with thanks each day. If a disagreement keeps recurring, set a calm time to talk it through instead of skirmishing daily. Parents and teenagers: notice the tone you bring through the door. If you live in a home full of strife, seek help from a pastor or counselor rather than suffering in silence, and pray for peace, beginning with your own words.

rel.note: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life, which is why long-awaited news refreshes so deeply.
A good report makes the bones healthy, the same reviving power of good news.
The faithful messenger refreshes like cold at harvest; here the good report he carries refreshes like cold water.

units.notes:
• "Weary" describes someone faint or exhausted; the KJV has "a thirsty soul." Both point to a person drained and in need of reviving.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "In the Biblical world news traveled agonizingly slow and was delivered with great difficulty."
• Solomon's own fleets sailed to distant Ophir and came back with gold after long voyages (1 Kings 9:26–28; 10:22), so news from far away was part of his world.
• Scripture also shows the reverse: Nehemiah heard bad news from far-off Jerusalem and wept and mourned for days (Nehemiah 1:2–4).
• Compare 15:30 ("a good report makes the bones healthy"); 13:12; Isaiah 52:7.
units.summary: After long waiting, good news from far away is cold water to a parched soul.
units.principle: Good news after long uncertainty revives the whole person, and those who carry it bring life to the weary.
units.insight: Paul arrived in Macedonia exhausted: "Outside were conflicts, inside were fears." Then Titus came with news that the Corinthians had repented, and Paul wrote, "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus" (2 Corinthians 7:5–7). Later Timothy brought a good report from Thessalonica, and Paul said, "For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 3:6–8). Good news can make a weary person live again. The proverb speaks of ordinary news, yet it helps us feel the wonder of the best news of all. It came from the farthest country there is, when angels announced "good tidings of great joy" because a Savior was born (Luke 2:10–11). Whoever is thirsty and hears it finds living water (John 4:14). Who is waiting for good word from you, and who around you has not yet heard the gospel?
units.application: Who is waiting to hear from you? Call the parent who wonders how you are, answer the missionary's update, tell the friend that the test results came back clear. Parents of grown children far away: a short good report is cold water. Church leaders: share good news from missionaries and partner churches with your people. And carry the gospel to the people around you who are still thirsty for it.

rel.note: The mouth of the righteous is a well of life; here that well has been fouled.
Fainting in the day of adversity shows how small one's strength is.
The righteous are bold as a lion, the opposite of faltering before the wicked.
The fear of man brings a snare, the usual root of yielding to the wicked.

units.notes:
• "Murky" translates a Hebrew verb meaning to trample and so to muddy water. The same verb appears in Ezekiel 34:18, where God rebukes the strong sheep of His flock, who drink the clear water and then "foul the residue with your feet."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, names "the profound disillusionment one feels when the righteous yield to evil."
• Flavel, quoted by Bridges: "the scandalous falls of good men are like a bag of poison cast by Satan into the spring, from whence the whole town is supplied with water."
• Some older interpreters also read the verse as the righteous being overthrown or oppressed by the wicked, which troubles the springs of justice. The NKJV's "falters" means yielding, and the picture of a fouled well fits that reading.
• Compare 10:11; 28:1; 29:25; Galatians 2:11–14.
units.summary: When a righteous person caves to evil, everyone who drew from his life is left with mud.
units.principle: The righteous carry a public trust; when they yield to evil under pressure, the people who depend on them are harmed too.
units.insight: At Antioch Peter ate freely with Gentile believers until certain men came from James. Then, "fearing those who were of the circumcision," he withdrew, and "even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy" (Galatians 2:12–13). One respected man's faltering muddied the well for a whole church. Abraham, the friend of God, lied about Sarah out of fear and was rebuked by a pagan king (Genesis 20:9–10). The fear of man is usually the root (29:25). We want approval, or we want to avoid trouble. Jesus stood before Pilate and did not falter; He "witnessed the good confession" (1 Timothy 6:13). Peter had faltered before, when he denied Jesus, and Jesus restored him (John 21:15–19); soon after, Peter stood firm before the council in Jerusalem (Acts 4:5–20). Faltering need not be the end of the story. Others are drawing from your life. Where is pressure tempting you to give way?
units.application: Ask where pressure is pushing you to compromise: laughing along with what is wrong at work, staying silent when a colleague is mistreated, bending the truth to please a client. Decide now what you will say. Parents: your children are drinking from your example; let them see you stand. Church leaders: do not quietly give way to a powerful member's wrong demands. If you have faltered, confess it, repair what you can, and stand again.

rel.note: The first honey saying sets the limit that this one applies to glory.
The chapter that opened with the glory of God and of kings closes by warning against grasping one's own glory.
The king who calls the humble guest higher shows where true honor comes from.
Let another praise you, not your own mouth, the same refusal of self-glory.

units.notes:
• Translations supply words to make sense of the short Hebrew of the second line. The NASB has "Nor is it glory to search out one's own glory," because the Hebrew word there comes from the same root as "search out" in 25:2. Read that way, the chapter opens and closes with glory and searching.
• The Latin Vulgate takes the line differently, and the Douay-Rheims follows it: whoever searches into majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. On that reading the line warns against prying into God's majesty. The NKJV's rendering fits the parallel with honey and the chapter's warning against self-promotion.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "Much honey produces nausea. So eventually does self-glorification."
• Bridges: "Oh! it is a mighty victory over self, to trample man's judgment under foot, and eye only God's approval."
• Compare 25:6–7; 27:2; John 5:44; John 8:50 ("I do not seek My own glory").
units.summary: Glory you chase for yourself turns sour, like honey eaten past its limit.
units.principle: Honor pursued for its own sake turns to emptiness; lasting honor is received from God, not seized for oneself.
units.insight: Herod Agrippa sat on his throne in royal robes, and when the crowd shouted, "The voice of a god and not of a man!" he accepted it. "Then immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give glory to God" (Acts 12:21–23). Nebuchadnezzar admired "this great Babylon, that I have built," and was driven from men until he learned to honor the Most High (Daniel 4:30–37). John the Baptist shows the opposite spirit: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). Jesus asked, "How can you believe, who receive honor from one another, and do not seek the honor that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44). Self-glory is a sweet taste that leaves the soul sick. The freedom of the gospel is that in Christ we no longer need to make a name for ourselves.
units.application: This week, notice how often you steer conversations toward your achievements, and let one go unmentioned. Give others credit for shared work, in meetings and online. Leaders and pastors: ask whether you are building God's work or your own platform. Young people: resist measuring your worth by likes and followers. When praise comes, receive it gratefully, give the glory to God, and move on without feeding on it.

rel.note: Being slow to wrath shows great understanding, while impulsiveness exalts folly.
The one who rules his spirit is better than the one who takes a city; here the one who cannot rule it is a city taken.
Discretion makes a person slow to anger, the inner rule that keeps the walls standing.
A fool vents all his feelings, but a wise man holds them back.

units.notes:
• Hezekiah himself "built up all the wall that was broken" in Jerusalem when Assyria threatened (2 Chronicles 32:5), so the image may have been especially vivid in his court. The proverb is Solomon's, however, and does not refer to that event.
• A broken wall meant disgrace as well as danger. Nehemiah wept when he heard that "The wall of Jerusalem is also broken down" (Nehemiah 1:3) and rebuilt it so that the people would "no longer be a reproach" (Nehemiah 2:17).
• Bridges: "Certainly the noblest conquests are gained or lost over ourselves."
• Henry: "All that is good goes out, and forsakes him; all that is evil breaks in upon him."
• Compare 16:32; 29:11; Galatians 5:22–23; Titus 2:11–12; 2 Peter 1:5–6.
units.summary: A life without self-control is a city with its walls down, open to every enemy.
units.principle: Self-control is the wall that protects a life; without it, every passion and every enemy finds an open way in.
units.insight: Samson tore a lion apart and carried off the gates of Gaza, yet he could not rule his own desires, and Delilah brought him down (Judges 14–16). His strength was great, but his walls were down. Cain let his anger rule him, though God warned that sin lay at the door and "you should rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). Even Moses, the humblest of men, lost his temper at Meribah and was kept out of the promised land (Numbers 20:10–12). None of us builds these walls by willpower alone. "The grace of God that brings salvation" teaches us to deny "ungodliness and worldly lusts" and to "live soberly" (Titus 2:11–12). Christ, tempted in every way yet without sin, gives His Spirit, whose fruit includes self-control. Where are your walls broken down?
units.application: Name the gate where your wall is weakest: temper, appetite, spending, lust, the urge to fire back a reply. Put up one guard this week, such as waiting an hour before answering an angry message, or a filter on your devices. Parents: help children learn to pause and name their feelings before they act. Anyone fighting a habit: invite one trusted friend to check on you. Pray each morning for the Spirit's fruit of self-control.

rel.note: "Luxury is not fitting for a fool" uses the same language of what does not suit a fool.
There snow at harvest is a welcome coolness; here weather out of season pictures what is unfitting.
Honor does not fit the fool, but the rod does; the two verses frame what the fool has earned.
Both sayings teach that giving honor to a fool is unfitting and self-defeating.

units.notes:
• Eleven of the twelve sayings in 26:1–12 name the fool; only 26:2 does not. Placing them together gathers the book's scattered sayings about the fool into one concentrated portrait.
• Rain at harvest was a real disaster, not a small inconvenience. When Samuel called for thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, the people took it as a sign of God's displeasure and "greatly feared the LORD" (1 Samuel 12:17–18).
• Snow appears in 25:13 as something welcome: "Like the cold of snow in time of harvest Is a faithful messenger." Here the same weather out of season pictures what does not belong.
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, on why honor does not suit a fool: "Because he neither deserves it, nor knows how to use it, but his folly is both increased and publicly manifested by it."
• Compare 19:10 ("Luxury is not fitting for a fool"), 30:21–22 and Ecclesiastes 10:5–7, where folly is set in high places.
units.summary: What a community honors, it multiplies; honor a fool and you will harvest folly.
units.principle: Honor belongs with character that can carry it; given to someone who rejects wisdom, it spreads his folly and teaches others that folly pays.
units.insight: Scripture shows both sides of this proverb. When Pharaoh honored Joseph and Darius raised Daniel to high office, honor fit their character, and the kingdoms they served were blessed (Genesis 41:38–40; Daniel 6:1–3). When Ahasuerus promoted Haman, the honor only fed his pride and nearly destroyed a people (Esther 3:1–6). The proverb searches us in two directions. First, what do we applaud? A church or family that celebrates charm, talent or boldness without character teaches its children that folly pays. Second, what do we crave? Many of us want honor before we have the character to carry it. Jesus shows the right order. He humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross, and God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:8–9). He teaches His people the same path: faithfulness in little before honor in much (Luke 16:10; 1 Peter 5:6).
units.application: Leaders and church boards: before you promote someone or give them a platform, look at how they handle correction and small responsibilities, not only at their gifts. Parents: notice what you praise at the dinner table, and praise faithfulness and honesty more than cleverness or winning. If you are eager for recognition yourself, ask whether your character is ready to carry it, and be faithful where you are first.

rel.note: The lying tongue that crushes its victims keeps 26:2 from being turned into a promise that malicious words never cause any harm.
The innocent need not fear sudden terror, because the LORD is their confidence, the same freedom from fear 26:2 gives.
A curse with cause does land: the curse of the LORD rests on the house of the wicked, while He blesses the home of the just.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew text handed down by the Jewish scribes carries a note on one small word in the last line. The word written in the text means "not"; the scribes' marginal reading is a word that sounds the same but means "to him." On that marginal reading some take the line to mean that a causeless curse comes back on the one who spoke it. The NKJV, like the KJV, ESV and NASB, follows the written word, "not."
• The KJV reads "As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying." Either way the picture is restless flight that never settles.
• Bridges asks how Shimei's curse harmed David, or the curses of his persecutors harmed Jeremiah: "What was David the worse for Shimei's curse; or Jeremiah for the curse of his persecutors?" (2 Samuel 16:5–13; Jeremiah 15:10).
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "Therefore, if the heart knows that a curse is unjust it may rest in the certainty that it cannot harm."
• Compare Deuteronomy 23:5, where the LORD "turned the curse into a blessing" because He loved Israel, and Psalm 109:28, "Let them curse, but You bless."
units.summary: An undeserved curse is a bird with nowhere to land.
units.principle: Words of harm spoken against the innocent have no power of their own; the LORD, not the one who curses, governs what comes to pass.
units.insight: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, yet each time the curse turned to blessing (Numbers 23–24). Goliath cursed David by his gods and fell to a shepherd's stone (1 Samuel 17:43–50). Many believers still live under words like these: a parent's "You'll never amount to anything," an enemy's threat, a superstition about bad luck. This proverb lifts that weight. The LORD rules your life, not the person who wishes you harm. There is one curse that was not without cause: the curse our sin deserved under God's law. In the light of the New Testament, Christ took that curse on Himself, "having become a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). For those who are in Him, "there is therefore now no condemnation" (Romans 8:1), and no curse is left to land.
units.application: Someone may have spoken harm over you: a bitter relative, an angry former spouse or a coworker who wishes you ill. Bring it to God and refuse to live in fear of it. If you have done wrong, deal with the wrong, not the words. Parents and leaders: guard your own mouths, because careless curses still wound even though they cannot rule. When you are cursed, answer as Scripture teaches, by blessing and trusting God (Psalm 109:28; Romans 12:14).

rel.note: Both sayings assign the rod to the back of the one who lacks understanding.
A wise man learns from one rebuke, while a fool is not reached even by a hundred blows.
"Beatings for the backs of fools" states the same pattern of hard consequences for those who refuse wisdom.
Honor does not fit a fool (26:1); the rod does (26:3).

units.notes:
• The order may surprise a modern reader, who might expect the bridle for the horse and the whip for the donkey. In Bible lands donkeys were often prized animals that leading families rode (Judges 10:4; 12:14). Each creature simply receives the control that suits it.
• Psalm 32:9 uses the same picture as a warning to believers: "Do not be like the horse or like the mule, Which have no understanding, Which must be harnessed with bit and bridle."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, on fools who will not listen to reason: "Like brute animals, force is the only language they understand."
• Compare 10:13; 19:29 ("Judgments are prepared for scoffers, And beatings for the backs of fools"); 17:10, where a rebuke does more for a wise man than a hundred blows on a fool.
units.summary: A person made to be led by wisdom can end up being driven by pain.
units.principle: Whoever refuses to be guided by wisdom will in the end be governed by consequences.
units.insight: Daniel urged Nebuchadnezzar to "break off your sins by being righteous" (Daniel 4:27), but the king would not listen. So he was driven from men to eat grass like an ox until, as he said, he "lifted my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me" (Daniel 4:34). God had to drive a king who would not be led. The LORD prefers to lead: "I will guide you with My eye. Do not be like the horse or like the mule" (Psalm 32:8–9). Speaking of the rod God uses to correct His own children, Bridges writes, "never does his loving Father use it, till gentle means have been tried in vain." So ask where God has already spoken gently to you, through His word, a friend or your conscience. Jesus still offers His easy yoke to all who will learn from Him (Matthew 11:29–30).
units.application: A habit may keep costing you, through a lost job, a strained marriage or a repeated rebuke. Ask what gentler warnings you ignored before the pain came, and respond quickly to the next one. Parents: this verse is about the adult fool, not a license for harshness; correct your children with patience and self-control. If you love an adult who keeps refusing counsel, stop rescuing him from every consequence. Sometimes love lets hard results teach what words could not.

rel.note: A word spoken in due season is good; wisdom lies in knowing which season it is.
Supports 26:4: it is honorable to stop striving, since any fool can start a quarrel.
Like 26:4, it counsels against speaking to a fool who will despise wise words.
Shows why leaving the fool wise in his own eyes (26:5) is so serious: there is more hope for a fool than for such a man.
The lazy man is also wise in his own eyes, the same condition 26:5 warns an unanswered fool may fall into.
Names the danger 26:5 guards against: being wise in one's own eyes.

units.notes:
• The phrase "according to his folly" carries two senses. In v4 it means in his manner, on his terms; in v5 it means in the way his folly deserves. The reason attached to each saying, "Lest you also be like him" and "Lest he be wise in his own eyes," shows which sense is meant.
• "Wise in his own eyes" returns in 26:12 and 26:16, linking the unanswered fool, the self-satisfied man and the lazy man. Compare 3:7, "Do not be wise in your own eyes."
• The tension was noticed early. The Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 30b) applies "answer a fool" to matters of God's law and "do not answer" to ordinary worldly affairs. That is its own way of dividing the cases, but it agrees that each saying fits a different situation.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, says the two sayings stand together because "human problems are often complicated and cannot always be solved by appealing to a single rule."
• Bridges sums up the right kind of reply: "not in folly, but to folly." In other words, answer the fool's folly, but not in a foolish way.
• Compare Ecclesiastes 3:7 ("A time to keep silence, And a time to speak"); 1 Peter 3:9, 15.
units.summary: Wisdom is a skill, not a rulebook: it knows when silence is wiser and when an answer is.
units.principle: Wisdom reads the person and the moment instead of applying one rule mechanically; sometimes silence is wise, and sometimes love requires a plain answer.
units.insight: When Rabshakeh mocked the LORD outside Jerusalem's walls, the people "held their peace and answered him not a word," as King Hezekiah had commanded (2 Kings 18:36). When Sanballat spread lies, Nehemiah answered plainly: "you invent them in your own heart" (Nehemiah 6:8). Both were right. Jesus showed this wisdom perfectly. He gave Herod no answer at all (Luke 23:9), yet He so answered His critics in the temple that "no one was able to answer Him a word" (Matthew 22:46). Our failures here usually come from the heart, not from missing rules. We answer because we must win, or we stay silent because we fear conflict. Before you reply, ask: Am I protecting my pride, or serving the truth and the people listening? God gives this wisdom to those who ask Him (James 1:5).
units.application: Online, at a family dinner or in a staff meeting, pause before replying to a foolish comment. Ask three questions: Will answering drag me into his tone? Will silence leave him or others misled? Who is listening? Parents of teenagers: some provocations deserve calm silence, and some false claims need a clear, kind answer. Pastors and teachers: refuse to be drawn into mockery, but do not leave error unanswered where people are being harmed by it.

rel.note: The lazy man is vinegar and smoke to those who send him, another picture of the cost of an unfit messenger.
A wicked messenger falls into trouble himself; 26:6 adds that the sender also pays for choosing him.
The faithful messenger refreshes those who send him; the fool as messenger harms the one who sends him.
Together the two sayings warn those who appoint and promote others to look at character before handing out responsibility or honor.

units.notes:
• The word translated "violence," chamas, usually means violent wrong or injury. The KJV has "drinketh damage." The picture is of a man gulping down the harm his own choice has brought on him.
• The KJV reads "cutteth off the feet." Some take the feet to be the messenger's, since a fool is as useless as a runner with no feet; others take them to be the sender's, as the NKJV's "his own feet" makes plain. Either way the errand fails and the sender suffers.
• Henry: "people will be apt to judge of the master by his messenger."
• Compare 10:26 (the lazy man is "vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes" of those who send him); 13:17 ("A wicked messenger falls into trouble, But a faithful ambassador brings health"); 25:13.
units.summary: A messenger is your feet in places you cannot go; send a fool and you have cut them off.
units.principle: Responsibility should go to those whose character can carry it; trusting important work to the careless or dishonest harms the one who sends them.
units.insight: Ten of the twelve spies sent into Canaan came back with a bad report that turned a whole nation toward rebellion (Numbers 13:32–14:4). An unfaithful messenger does damage far beyond himself. Ben-Hadad sent Hazael to Elisha with a gift and a question, and Hazael went home and murdered his master (2 Kings 8:7–15). The king drank the violence of a poor choice. The verse also asks what kind of messenger you are. God has entrusted His people with His own message and calls them "ambassadors for Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:20). Jesus is the perfectly faithful Messenger. He told the Father, "I have given to them the words which You have given Me" (John 17:8), and nothing was lost or twisted on the way. Those who carry His word are called to the same faithfulness, for "it is required in stewards that one be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2).
units.application: Managers and ministry leaders: before you hand someone a client, a sensitive conversation or the church's money, look at how they have handled small tasks and confidences. Parents: train children to carry messages exactly and report truthfully, and give larger errands as they prove faithful. Employees and volunteers: when you are sent, be the messenger people can trust. Deliver the whole message, on time, without adding your own spin.

rel.note: "Excellent speech is not becoming to a fool" also says fine words do not suit a fool.
A fool has no delight in understanding, which explains why the proverbs he repeats never carry him anywhere.
Shares the same second line; there the proverb in a fool's mouth becomes harmful rather than merely useless.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew verb in the first line is uncertain. The KJV reads "The legs of the lame are not equal"; the NKJV and ESV picture legs that hang limp or useless. The point of the comparison is the same in each rendering.
• The word translated "proverb," mashal, is the word in the book's title (1:1): a proverb, parable or comparable saying. The very thing this book is made of becomes useless in the wrong mouth.
• Henry, working from the KJV's "not equal": "His good words raise him up, but then his bad life takes him down, and so his legs are not equal." The fool's words and his life do not match, so he limps.
• Compare 17:7 ("Excellent speech is not becoming to a fool"); Romans 2:21 ("You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself?"); James 1:22.
units.summary: A fool can own a proverb the way limp legs belong to a body: present, but carrying him nowhere.
units.principle: Knowing wise words is not the same as being wise; truth helps only the person who lives it.
units.insight: Jesus said of the scribes and Pharisees, "they say, and do not do" (Matthew 23:3). They could quote the law with precision, yet it carried them nowhere near the God who gave it. He ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders who both heard His words. Only the one who did them built on the rock (Matthew 7:24–27). This proverb is aimed less at the obvious fool than at people who know a great deal of Scripture. It is possible to have a verse for every occasion and still walk in the wrong direction. In Jesus, word and life were one; He is the Word who "became flesh" (John 1:14). He does not only hand us wise sayings. He gives the life that puts legs under them. Ask yourself which truth you can quote that you have not yet obeyed.
units.application: Before you quote a verse to your spouse, child or friend in an argument, ask whether you are living it. Small-group leaders and teachers: measure growth by changed habits, not by how many verses people can recite. Young believers: choose one proverb this week, such as "A soft answer turns away wrath" (15:1), and practice it at home or work until it shapes what you actually do.

rel.note: Luxury and rule do not fit a fool or an unfit servant, the same misfit of honor and character.
Both sayings teach that honor does not belong with a fool.
Together the two sayings warn those who appoint and praise others to look at character before handing out honor or responsibility.
When the wicked rule the people groan, which shows what honor misplaced does to everyone under it.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin records an older understanding of the line: putting a precious stone into a heap of stones, which would picture honor wasted and lost on a fool. The NKJV and most modern translations read the picture of a sling.
• Slings were serious weapons, not toys. David killed Goliath with one (1 Samuel 17:49), and Benjamin had seven hundred slingers who "could sling a stone at a hair's breadth and not miss" (Judges 20:16). Tying the stone in defeats the whole purpose of such a weapon.
• Henry: "To give honour to a fool is to put a sword in a madman's hand."
• Compare 26:1; 19:10; 29:2.
units.summary: Honor tied to a fool is a stone that will not fly and may swing back on you.
units.principle: Honor and influence given to people without character fail in their purpose and often injure the ones who gave them.
units.insight: The men of Shechem made Abimelech king, though he had murdered his brothers to get the throne (Judges 9:5–6). Jotham warned them with a parable: the trees had anointed a bramble, and fire would come out of the bramble to devour them (Judges 9:15, 20). Within a few years Abimelech burned their stronghold over their heads (Judges 9:46–49). The honor they gave him swung back and struck them. We still do this when we honor people for what they can do for us: their money, their following or their charm. Jesus asked, "How can you believe, who receive honor from one another, and do not seek the honor that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44). The cure is to value what God values. He says, "those who honor Me I will honor" (1 Samuel 2:30).
units.application: Church leaders and nominating committees: do not hand a microphone, a title or a budget to someone because they are talented, wealthy or popular. Look for humility, teachability and faithfulness over time (1 Timothy 3:6; 5:22). Employers: promote for character as well as skill. All of us: be slow to cheer a public figure whose life contradicts what he claims to stand for, because applause is a kind of honor too.

rel.note: Careless words pierce like a sword, while the tongue of the wise brings health, the same contrast between wounding and wise use of words.
Excellent speech does not suit a fool, because his character cannot carry it.
Shares the same second line; there the proverb in a fool's mouth is useless, here it is harmful.

units.notes:
• The NKJV pictures a thorn that "goes into" the drunkard's hand, and the ESV a thorn that "goes up" into it, as the KJV also reads. The NLT has "a thorny branch brandished by a drunk." Each rendering keeps the point: something hurtful is in hands that cannot manage it.
• The picture can be read two ways, and both fit the chapter. Either the drunkard does not feel the thorn in his own hand, as the fool is unmoved by the proverb he quotes, or he waves a thorny branch and wounds those around him, as the fool hurts others with wise words.
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "It is no more fit for a fool to meddle with a wise speech, than for a drunken man to handle a thorn bush."
• Compare 26:7; 12:18 ("There is one who speaks like the piercings of a sword"); 2 Peter 3:16, where untaught people twist the Scriptures "to their own destruction."
units.summary: In a fool's mouth even true words become a weapon he cannot handle.
units.principle: Truth handled without wisdom and humility becomes a weapon that wounds both the speaker and others.
units.insight: Job's friends were full of true sayings about God's justice. But they pressed them on a suffering man who did not fit their theory, and their proverbs became thorns in his wound. In the end God told them, "you have not spoken of Me what is right" (Job 42:7). Satan himself quoted Scripture to Jesus in the wilderness, twisting a promise into a temptation (Matthew 4:6). Jesus answered, "It is written again" (Matthew 4:7), handling the word with the wisdom the tempter lacked. This proverb warns everyone who loves Bible verses. A verse thrown at a grieving friend, a spouse or a struggling believer can do real harm. The problem is not the truth of the words but the heart and judgment of the one holding them. Ask the Spirit for wisdom before you take up His sword (Ephesians 6:17).
units.application: Before you quote a verse to someone who is hurting, ask whether it fits their situation and whether you are offering it in love. Parents: do not use Scripture to win arguments with your children; let it correct you first. On social media, resist posting verses as weapons against people you dislike. Teachers and small-group leaders: handle hard texts carefully, so you do not wound the people you mean to help.

rel.note: Affirms that the wicked will not go unpunished.
The LORD made all things for His purpose, even the wicked for the day of doom, the same Creator's rule over the wicked.
States plainly that God will "render to each man according to his deeds," the point the NKJV reading of 26:10 makes.
The alternative translation of 26:10, about hiring a fool, fits the theme of 26:6.

units.notes:
• The word "God" is not in the Hebrew; the KJV prints it in italics to show that the translators supplied it.
• Translations differ widely because the Hebrew can be read more than one way. The first word can mean "great" or "archer," and the verb that follows can mean forming something or wounding. So the ESV and NASB speak of an "archer" and of one who hires a fool or passers-by, and the NLT compares hiring a fool or a bystander to an archer "who shoots at random." The NKJV follows the line of the KJV and YLT.
• On the "archer" reading the verse fits 26:6: entrusting work to a fool is as dangerous as an archer shooting at everyone.
• Ironside keeps the KJV reading (he calls the KJV "the authorized version"): "For want of better authority we keep to the authorized version, which at least expresses a solemn truth that is often insisted on in the word of God."
• Compare 24:12 ("And will He not render to each man according to his deeds?"); 11:21; Romans 2:6; Luke 12:47–48.
units.summary: The God who made the world keeps its accounts; folly is paid what it has earned.
units.principle: The Creator who set the world's order sees that folly and sin receive their due in His time.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns and said to his soul, "take your ease." But God said to him, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:19–20). The man had planned for everything except his meeting with the God who made him. When fools seem to prosper, this verse steadies us. The Creator keeps the accounts, and no one is overlooked (Psalm 73:16–19). It also humbles us, because we have all earned wages we would not want paid. "For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). The God who pays wages also gives gifts. At the cross Christ received what we had earned, so that we could receive what we never could earn.
units.application: When a dishonest coworker gets ahead or a mocking relative seems untouched, leave the reckoning to God instead of keeping score yourself. Young people tempted to think folly costs nothing: every choice is paid for in the end. Bible teachers: when a verse is hard to translate, say so plainly, teach its clear point, and send people to the plain passages that say the same thing (24:12; Romans 2:6).

rel.note: Even when ground in a mortar, the fool's foolishness does not depart from him; both sayings picture folly that does not learn.
The one who confesses and forsakes his sins finds mercy, the opposite of returning to them.
The one who is often rebuked and hardens his neck is destroyed without remedy, the end of the fool's repeated return.

units.notes:
• Peter cites the saying as a "true proverb" and joins it with a second saying, "a sow, having washed, to her wallowing in the mire" (2 Peter 2:22). The second saying is not found in Proverbs.
• In 2 Peter 2 the warning concerns false teachers and those drawn after them: people who had known "the way of righteousness" and then turned from it (2 Peter 2:1–3, 21).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "An intentionally repulsive simile. It juxtaposes a fool with the contemptible dog" (a simile is a comparison using "as" or "like"; "juxtaposes" means sets side by side.)
• Pharaoh is the Bible's clearest case of the pattern. He begged for relief under the plagues, and "when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart" (Exodus 8:15; compare 9:27, 34).
• Compare 27:22 (grind a fool in a mortar, "Yet his foolishness will not depart from him"); Matthew 12:43–45.
units.summary: Folly's deepest sickness is not that it hurts us once, but that we go back for more.
units.principle: Sin that is not hated will be repeated; relief from consequences without a changed heart leads back to the same folly.
units.insight: The fool's cycle lives in every heart. We feel sick after the outburst, the binge or the lie, and we promise never again. Then the sickness fades and the old appetite returns. Jesus warned that a house swept clean but left empty does not stay empty (Matthew 12:43–45). Bridges: "Would that we had the same disgust at the sin, which it so graphically pourtrays!" (an old spelling of "portrays"). Peter shows the way out of the cycle. He denied his Lord, but when Jesus looked at him he "went out and wept bitterly" (Luke 22:61–62). He did not go back to the denial; he was restored and fed Christ's sheep (John 21:15–17). The way out is not regret alone but "godly sorrow" that "produces repentance" (2 Corinthians 7:10). Christ gives what a dog never has: a new heart, so that "old things have passed away" (2 Corinthians 5:17).
units.application: Name the folly you keep returning to: an old relationship, a habit, a way of speaking to your spouse. When you feel sick of it, use that moment to put real barriers in place, and ask a friend to hold you to them. Parents: when a child repeats the same wrong, look past the behavior to the heart. Mentors and pastors: celebrate repentance, but watch for the quiet return once the pain has passed.

rel.note: The fool is right in his own eyes, while the wise person listens to counsel.
The lazy man wiser in his own eyes shows the same self-deception.
The fool left unanswered becomes wise in his own eyes, the condition 26:12 judges so severely.
Uses the same comparison, placing the man hasty in his words below the fool.
Gives the command and the remedy: do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD.

units.notes:
• "Wise in his own eyes" links this verse with 26:5, where the unanswered fool becomes wise in his own eyes, and 26:16, where the lazy man is. The chapter traces one disease in three forms.
• The same comparison appears in 29:20: "Do you see a man hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him." Both sayings measure a person against the fool to show how serious his condition is.
• Bridges: "The false persuasion that he has gained wisdom, utterly precludes him from gaining it." In plain words, believing he is already wise is the very thing that keeps him from becoming wise.
• Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "The greatest fool is the fool who does not know he is a fool."
• Compare 3:7 ("Do not be wise in your own eyes; Fear the LORD and depart from evil"); 12:15; Isaiah 5:21; Romans 12:16; 1 Corinthians 3:18.
units.summary: The most hopeless fool is the one who is sure he is not one.
units.principle: Self-satisfaction is more hopeless than ignorance, because the one who thinks he knows enough will not learn; humility before God is where wisdom starts.
units.insight: Jesus told a parable "to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous" (Luke 18:9). The Pharisee thanked God he was not like other men; the tax collector beat his breast and asked for mercy. Only the second went home justified (Luke 18:14). Jesus told the religious leaders that "tax collectors and harlots enter the kingdom of God before you" (Matthew 21:31). To those who claimed to see, He said, "Therefore your sin remains" (John 9:41). This verse aims at the reader, not only at others. Religious people are especially at risk, because knowing a great deal can feel like being wise. The question is not only "Do you see that man?" but "Do you see yourself?" The hope for all of us is the same: come as the tax collector came, asking for mercy, and Christ receives the humble.
units.application: This week, ask someone who knows you well, such as a spouse, a friend or a coworker, "Where am I hard to correct?" Then listen without defending yourself. Leaders: notice whether anyone around you still disagrees with you, and if no one does, ask why. Parents: say "I was wrong" in front of your children. Students and young adults: when you feel sure you have outgrown your parents' or pastor's counsel, slow down and listen again.

rel.note: The lazy man's way seems a hedge of thorns to him, the same imagined obstacles that his lion represents.
The lazy man uses almost the same excuse: a lion outside, and danger in the streets.
The lazy man's overgrown field shows the result of the excuses voiced in 26:13.
The lazy man who invents excuses also thinks himself wiser than all who could answer them.
The earlier portrait of the sluggard shows where excuses and sleep lead: poverty that comes like a prowler.

units.notes:
• The NKJV's "a lion" and "A fierce lion" render two different Hebrew words for lion. Piling up the terms makes the excuse sound more dramatic.
• The NKJV uses "lazy man" in all four sayings of 26:13–16, while the ESV and NASB use "sluggard." The NKJV keeps "sluggard" for 6:6 and 6:9.
• Henry: "It is a foolish thing to frighten ourselves from real duties by fancied difficulties."
• Bishop Patrick, quoted by Bridges: "he, who has no mind to labour, never wants pretences for idleness." Here "never wants" means "never lacks": the unwilling worker always has an excuse ready.
• Compare 22:13 ("There is a lion outside! I shall be slain in the streets!"); Ecclesiastes 11:4 ("He who observes the wind will not sow"); and the earlier portraits of the lazy man in 6:6–11 and 24:30–34.
units.summary: The lazy man's lion lives mostly in his imagination, and it always blocks the road to work.
units.principle: Excuses can be dressed up as prudence; often the problem is not the danger outside but the unwillingness inside.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable, the servant who buried his master's money explained, "I was afraid, and went and hid your talent in the ground." His master called it what it was: "You wicked and lazy servant" (Matthew 25:25–26). Fear was the lion; laziness was the reason. Our excuses are spiritual as often as practical. We would share the gospel, but a coworker might laugh. We would start the hard conversation, the ministry or the Bible reading plan, but the timing is wrong. Some fears are real, and wisdom weighs them. But often the lion grows larger the longer we stay in bed. David met real lions and went out anyway, trusting "The LORD, who delivered me from the paw of the lion" (1 Samuel 17:37). The Lord who sends His people promises, "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20).
units.application: Write down the task you keep postponing, then the reason you give. Ask whether the danger is real or only the dread is. If it is real, plan around it; if it is dread, take the first small step today.
