Students facing a hard assignment, employees avoiding a difficult call, believers avoiding a conversation about faith: name the lion out loud. Friends and parents: be gentle with those whose limits are real, and patient but direct with excuses.

rel.note: Laziness casts a person into deep sleep and leaves him hungry, the same bed and the same outcome.
The command not to love sleep, but to open one's eyes and be satisfied, is the remedy for the door-turning man.
The neglected field of the lazy man shows where this pattern leads.
The sluggard's "little sleep, a little slumber" and its end in poverty describe the same man fastened to his bed.

units.notes:
• Ancient doors commonly turned on pivots set into sockets above and below, not on hinges as we know them. The door turned all day but never left its place, which makes the comparison sharper.
• Henry: "as the door is moved, but not removed."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The humor in this verse is based on the analogy with a door—it moves but goes nowhere."
• Compare 6:9–11; 19:15 ("Laziness casts one into a deep sleep"); 20:13 ("Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty"); 24:33–34.
units.summary: The lazy man is always moving and never going anywhere, like a door on its hinges.
units.principle: Activity is not progress; a life can be full of motion and still never rise to the work God has given.
units.insight: "It happened in the spring of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle," that David stayed behind in Jerusalem. One evening he rose from his bed, walked on the roof and saw Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:1–2). The bed where duty is avoided easily becomes the place where temptation finds us. The door also pictures a spiritual condition: the same resolutions every January, the same intention to pray more, the same confession of the same neglect, and no movement. Jesus rose "a long while before daylight" to pray (Mark 1:35). At the end He could say to the Father, "I have finished the work which You have given Me to do" (John 17:4). His call still comes to every door-turning soul: "Awake, you who sleep, Arise from the dead, And Christ will give you light" (Ephesians 5:14).
units.application: If you hit snooze three times every morning, set one rising time and one first task, and keep them for a week. Students and people who work from home: notice the difference between being busy and finishing something, and measure the day by what was completed. If weariness comes from illness, grief or depression, that is not laziness; talk to a doctor or a trusted friend. Parents: help teenagers build a morning routine instead of only scolding.

rel.note: The lazy man does not roast what he caught in hunting, another picture of failing to finish what would feed him.
The lazy man desires and has nothing, the hunger 26:15 shows him bringing on himself.
Nearly the same saying: the lazy man buries his hand in the bowl and will not bring it to his mouth.
The desire of the lazy man kills him because his hands refuse to labor, the end of the habit pictured here.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV has "bowl," the KJV reads "bosom," picturing a man with his hands tucked into the folds of his garment. Most modern translations, like the NKJV, read a dish or bowl.
• "It wearies him" (KJV "it grieveth him") describes being worn out. The effort he dreads is the smallest one imaginable, which is the joke and the warning.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The sluggard so dislikes any form of work that the very thought of exerting himself exhausts him."
• Compare 19:24 ("A lazy man buries his hand in the bowl, And will not so much as bring it to his mouth again"); 12:27; 13:4 ("The soul of a lazy man desires, and has nothing"); 21:25.
units.summary: Laziness at its worst will not even finish what would feed it.
units.principle: Laziness does not only neglect the needs of others; in the end it starves itself, leaving undone even the effort that would bring life.
units.insight: God fed Israel in the wilderness with bread from heaven, yet the people still had to go out each morning and gather it (Exodus 16:4, 21). Provision came as a gift, and receiving it took a small daily effort. Jesus calls Himself "the bread of life" (John 6:35). Many believers have His word on the nightstand and His promises within reach, yet they go hungry because they will not lift the hand from bowl to mouth. Henry: "Those that are slothful in the business of religion will not be at the pains to feed their own souls with the word of God, the bread of life." In plain words, spiritual laziness will not take the trouble to eat. The problem is rarely access; it is appetite and will. Ask the Lord to renew your hunger, then take the small step of opening the book (Psalm 81:10).
units.application: Finish one thing you started and left: the half-painted room, the unanswered email, the online course, the Bible reading plan. Parents: teach children to complete small tasks, such as clearing their plate or finishing homework, before starting something new. Believers who feel spiritually dry: before asking why God feels distant, eat what is already set before you. Read one chapter and pray one simple prayer each morning this week.

rel.note: The fool is right in his own eyes, but the one who heeds counsel is wise; the lazy man refuses even seven counselors.
The man wise in his own eyes has less hope than a fool; the lazy man shares that self-deception.
The invented lion of 26:13 is the kind of excuse his self-confidence defends.
The same phrase, "wise in his own eyes," describes the fool left unanswered.

units.notes:
• "Answer sensibly" describes people who can give a fitting, discerning reply; the KJV has "that can render a reason." They can explain why they do what they do. The lazy man cannot, yet thinks himself wiser than all of them.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Seven here only means perfection, abundance, or multitude."
• Henry: "A conceit of the sufficiency of our attainments is a great enemy to our improvement." In modern terms, thinking we already know enough is the great enemy of growth.
• The lazy man is the third figure in the chapter called "wise in his own eyes," after the unanswered fool (26:5) and the self-satisfied man (26:12).
• Compare 3:7; 12:15; 28:11 ("The rich man is wise in his own eyes").
units.summary: The lazy man's last defense is his certainty that he is smarter than everyone telling him to work.
units.principle: Self-deception is laziness's best defense; the person who cannot see his fault will out-argue every counselor and stay where he is.
units.insight: Jesus' letter to Laodicea describes this man in church clothes. The church was lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, yet it said, "I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing." It did not know it was "wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:15–17). Spiritual sloth and self-satisfaction live together. The less effort we give, the more reasons we find to approve of ourselves. The lazy man of this verse can out-argue seven counselors, and many of us can out-argue our pastor, our spouse and our conscience. Yet Christ does not abandon the lukewarm. He says, "be zealous and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock" (Revelation 3:19–20). The lazy man of 26:14 swung like a door on its hinges and never went anywhere; the door of the heart can still be opened to Christ.
units.application: Notice the moment you begin explaining why the advice you were given does not apply to you. Write down the counsel you keep dismissing, then ask two people you respect whether they agree with it. Parents of grown children who will not work: stop debating every excuse, set clear expectations and keep them. Employees: when your manager and coworkers all name the same weakness, assume they see something you do not.

rel.note: Strife spreads like released water, so wisdom stops contention early instead of joining it.
It is honorable to stop striving; the passer-by does the opposite by entering strife that is not his.
If one should not rush into a dispute of one's own, still less into someone else's.
The contentious man kindles strife; the meddler adds heat to strife already burning.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, the words for "passes by" and "meddles" are built on the same three letters and sound alike. The sound play carries the point: the man who was only passing by becomes, in the very next word, the man caught up in someone else's quarrel.
• The word for "meddles" can also suggest becoming worked up or angry. That is why the KJV margin gives "is enraged" as an alternative to "meddleth," and the YLT speaks of the passer-by making himself angry over strife not his own.
• Henry: "He that has got a dog by the ears, if he lets him go he flies at him, if he keeps his hold, he has his hands full, and can do nothing else."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Not even Samson grabbed the foxes by their ears (Judges 15:4)." Samson tied his foxes tail to tail; even he did not try to hold a wild animal by the ears.
• Compare 20:3; 25:8; 1 Thessalonians 4:11 ("lead a quiet life, to mind your own business"); 1 Peter 4:15, which lists "a busybody in other people's matters" beside the murderer and the thief.
units.summary: Grabbing someone else's quarrel is like grabbing a stray dog's ears: easy to start, painful to stop.
units.principle: Stepping uninvited into a quarrel that is not yours brings trouble on yourself; true peacemaking needs a rightful place and a heart for peace.
units.insight: Jehoshaphat told Ahab, "I am as you are," and rode into a war that was not his. Mistaken for the king of Israel, he barely escaped with his life (1 Kings 22:4, 32–33). Jesus, by contrast, refused to be drawn into a family dispute over an inheritance: "Man, who made Me a judge or an arbitrator over you?" (Luke 12:14). Yet Abigail rode out between David and her husband's household and turned away bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–35). She had a rightful place, and she came to make peace. Our hearts often meddle for the excitement of drama or the pleasure of being right. Christ made peace in the costliest way, "through the blood of His cross" (Colossians 1:20). Those who follow Him enter conflicts to heal them, not to feed them.
units.application: Before you jump into a coworker's dispute, a family argument at the holidays or a heated comment thread, ask: Is this mine? Was I asked? Will I bring peace or only take a side? If you are a leader with real responsibility, step in to reconcile. If you are a bystander, pray, keep confidences and, where fitting, point the parties toward each other (Matthew 18:15). Parents: teach children to stay out of fights that are not theirs.

rel.note: "To do evil is like sport to a fool" describes the same attitude that treats wrongdoing as play.
Reckless words pierce like a sword, the same wounding the madman's arrows picture.
The firebrands of 26:18 begin the fire language that continues with the contentious man who kindles strife.
The lying tongue that hates its victims shows what lies beneath deceit passed off as a joke.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the excuse is a question, asking in effect, "Was I not just playing?" The KJV keeps the question ("Am not I in sport?"), as do the NASB and YLT; the NKJV, ESV and NLT turn it into a statement.
• The "madman" of v18 is someone acting wildly, as if out of his mind. The point is not his illness but the damage that flies from his hands.
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "There is little difference in this case betwixt fraud and fury." ("Betwixt" means "between": deceit dressed as a joke does as much harm as rage.)
• Henry, quoted by Bridges: "He that sins in jest, must repent in earnest; or his sin will be his ruin."
• Compare 10:23 ("To do evil is like sport to a fool"); Ephesians 4:25; 5:4; James 3:5–6.
units.summary: A lie does not become harmless because you laugh after telling it.
units.principle: We are responsible for the harm our words and tricks do, whatever we claim about our intentions afterward; humor is no cover for deceit.
units.insight: Genesis says Ishmael was "scoffing" at young Isaac (Genesis 21:9). It may have looked like an older brother's teasing, but Paul calls it what it was: he "persecuted" him (Galatians 4:29). God measures our words by what they do, not by the label we give them. Jesus said we will give account for "every idle word" (Matthew 12:36). The heart behind "I was only joking" is usually one of two things: cruelty that wants to wound without being blamed, or pride that will not say, "I was wrong." Both shrink from the light. The gospel makes confession possible, because in Christ we no longer need to defend ourselves; "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us" (1 John 1:9). The person who knows he is forgiven can stop hiding behind a laugh and say, "That hurt you. I am sorry."
units.application: If you have said "just kidding" after a comment that stung, go back and apologize without the qualifier. Parents: do not let siblings excuse cruelty or tricks as fun; teach them to own the hurt. At work and online, refuse pranks and "jokes" that mislead or humiliate a coworker, and do not laugh along. Youth leaders: watch for teasing that has turned into bullying. When someone tells you your joke hurt, believe them first.

rel.note: A whisperer separates the best of friends, another picture of talebearing that sustains strife.
Covering a transgression seeks love, while repeating a matter separates friends, the same choice between starving and feeding strife.
There the contentious man keeps adding fuel; here strife dies when the fuel is removed.
Explains why the talebearer's fuel keeps coming: hearers find gossip tasty and willingly take it in.
Among the things the LORD hates is "one who sows discord among brethren"; 26:20 shows how such discord is kept alive.

units.notes:
• "Talebearer" translates a word for a whisperer, one who passes along tales quietly. The same word appears in 16:28 ("a whisperer separates the best of friends"), 18:8 and 26:22.
• Where the NKJV has "strife ceases," the KJV margin reads "is silent." When the whispering stops, the quarrel goes quiet too.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "The tale-receiver and the tale-bearer are the agents of discord."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, on the talebearer: "In the absence of such a person, old hurts can be set aside, and discord can die a natural death."
• Compare 6:19; 16:28; 17:9 ("he who repeats a matter separates friends"); James 3:5–6.
units.summary: Gossip is firewood; stop carrying it and the quarrel burns itself out.
units.principle: Most quarrels live on repetition; when people refuse to carry and receive tales, strife loses its fuel and dies.
units.insight: Doeg the Edomite saw David receive bread and a sword from the priest at Nob, and he carried the story to Saul. Out of that one report came the slaughter of eighty-five priests and their whole town (1 Samuel 22:9–19). A tale can feed a fire far larger than the teller imagined. Most of us would never call ourselves talebearers. Yet we "just share a concern," pass on a prayer request with too many details, or keep a family grievance alive by retelling it. The heart that carries tales usually enjoys being in the know, or wants others on its side. The gospel offers another way. Christ's love covers our sins instead of broadcasting them, and He calls us to the same love, for "love will cover a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8).
units.application: When someone starts a story about a person who is not present, decline to pass it on. That holds at work, at church and in the family group chat. Where wise, ask, "Have you talked to them?" If you are caught in a long-running family or church conflict, stop retelling the old offense, even to sympathetic friends. Leaders: do not act on secondhand reports until you have heard the other side (18:17).

rel.note: "A wrathful man stirs up strife" states the same pattern, while the one slow to anger calms it.
When the scoffer is cast out, contention leaves, which shows how much strife depends on one person.
Uses similar language of a contentious woman, showing the warning applies to men and women alike.
The meddler adds heat to someone else's quarrel; the contentious man kindles quarrels of his own.
The madman's firebrands in 26:18–19 begin the fire language that the contentious man's charcoal continues.
There strife dies when fuel is removed; here the contentious man keeps adding it.

units.notes:
• Charcoal was a common fuel for braziers and cooking fires in Bible times; compare the "fire of coals" in John 18:18 and 21:9.
• "Contentious" comes from the Hebrew word for strife or quarreling. The same word describes the contentious woman of 21:9, 25:24 and 27:15, so the warning covers both sexes.
• Bridges, on the contentious man: "His determination to have the last word is as coals to burning coals, and wood to the fire."
• Henry: "it will be very difficult to avoid quarrelling with those that are quarrelsome."
• Compare 15:18 ("A wrathful man stirs up strife, But he who is slow to anger allays contention"); 22:10; 29:22.
units.summary: Some people put out fires; the contentious man carries charcoal wherever he goes.
units.principle: Strife does not burn long on its own; it lasts because someone keeps feeding it, and each of us chooses whether to add fuel or let it die.
units.insight: John wrote of Diotrephes, "who loves to have the preeminence," and who was "prating against us with malicious words," turning away visitors and putting others out of the church (3 John 9–10). One quarrelsome man kept a whole congregation smoldering. Contention usually grows from pride: the need to win, to be right and to have the last word. "By pride comes nothing but strife" (13:10). If conflict seems to follow you from job to job, church to church or relationship to relationship, the common factor may be the one carrying the charcoal. Jesus is the opposite. Of Him it was written, "He will not quarrel nor cry out" (Matthew 12:19). When He was reviled, He did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and His Spirit makes quarrelsome people gentle (Galatians 5:22–23).
units.application: In your next disagreement, at home, at work or online, let the other person have the last word once. Husbands and wives: stop reopening settled arguments. If you work beside a contentious person, keep your replies brief, calm and factual, and do not match their heat (15:1). Church leaders: address a habitually divisive member directly and lovingly before the fire spreads (Titus 3:10).

rel.note: The talebearer reveals secrets, but the faithful spirit conceals a matter.
An evildoer gives heed to false lips, which places responsibility on the eager listener as well as the teller.
The NKJV wording of 18:8 is identical to 26:22.
26:20 shows the talebearer supplying the fuel for strife; 26:22 explains why that fuel is accepted.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word behind "tasty trifles" occurs only here and in 18:8. The KJV reads "as wounds," following an older understanding of the word as something that burns or rankles. Hebrew dictionaries today take it as food swallowed greedily, and most modern translations, like the NKJV, read it as tasty morsels.
• "Inmost body" is literally "the chambers of the belly," the deepest inner rooms of a person. The same expression appears in 20:27, where the LORD's lamp searches "all the inner depths of his heart."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, on gossip: "When such tasty bits are taken into the innermost being, they stimulate the desire for more."
• Compare 18:8; 11:13 ("he who is of a faithful spirit conceals a matter"); 17:4; 20:19.
units.summary: Gossip tastes sweet going down, and it stays down long after the taste is gone.
units.principle: Gossip spreads because hearers enjoy it, and what is heard settles deep; refusing to receive it matters as much as refusing to tell it.
units.insight: When David fled from Absalom, Ziba told him that Mephibosheth had stayed behind hoping to take the throne. David swallowed the story at once and gave Ziba everything Mephibosheth owned (2 Samuel 16:1–4). Later Mephibosheth explained that his servant had deceived him, and that he had mourned for the king the whole time. Yet David still divided the land between them (2 Samuel 19:24–29). The morsel had gone down deep. That is the power of what we choose to hear. Our appetite for gossip often reveals a heart that enjoys feeling above others, or that wants a reason to think less of someone. Christ shows the opposite spirit. Of the coming King it was written, "He shall not judge by the sight of His eyes, Nor decide by the hearing of His ears" (Isaiah 11:3). Ask Him for that same fairness.
units.application: When a juicy story starts, change the subject or say, "I'd rather not hear this unless I can help." Before you believe a report about a coworker, church member or relative, wait until you have heard from them (18:17). Parents of teenagers: talk about how group chats spread rumors, and show them by example how to refuse to forward one. If gossip has already shaped how you see someone, ask God to help you see that person freshly.

rel.note: The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; here the silver is only a coating over clay.
There dross is removed so silver can become fine; here dross itself is the deceptive coating.
Develops the same theme of hatred hidden behind pleasant speech.

units.notes:
• The word translated "fervent," dalaq, means burning or hotly pursuing; the KJV, NASB and YLT have "burning lips." The phrase can be read two ways: lips burning with rage, or lips burning with warm professions of love. The second fits verses 24–26, which describe hatred hidden behind kind words.
• "Silver dross." The NKJV keeps the traditional reading. The ESV and NLT have "glaze," following a proposal by the scholar H. L. Ginsberg based on a word for glaze in Ugaritic, an ancient language related to Hebrew. The traditional picture also fits real practice. Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Because of its silvery gloss, this slag was used as a glaze for ceramics." Either way the picture is a cheap pot with a shiny surface.
• Proverbs 10:20 says, "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver." Setting that verse beside this one, Bridges writes: "Here is only silver dross."
• Compare Psalm 12:2 ("With flattering lips and a double heart they speak"), Psalm 55:21 and Matthew 23:27.
units.summary: A silver coating cannot turn clay into silver, and warm words cannot make a wicked heart good.
units.principle: Words are worth only what the heart behind them is worth; polished speech can coat a worthless heart.
units.insight: This verse exposes how easily we are impressed. We trust warmth, eloquence and enthusiasm, and the hypocrite counts on that. Absalom won Israel's heart at the city gate with warm words and kisses while he plotted to take his father's throne (2 Samuel 15:1–6). Jesus pronounced woe on whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of death within (Matthew 23:27). The verse also turns inward, because "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). The cure for a glazed-over heart is not a better glaze but a new heart, which only God gives (Ezekiel 36:26; Psalm 51:10).
units.application: Whether you are hiring, dating or choosing a business partner, judge people over time by what they do, not by how warmly they speak. Be especially careful when the warmth comes fast and wants something from you. In your own speech, notice when your words run warmer than your heart, and deal with the heart before you open your mouth.

rel.note: "Whoever hides hatred has lying lips" states the same truth about concealed hatred.
The image of a silver-coated clay pot introduces the hidden hatred these verses describe.
The hidden hater's schemes recoil on him, like the pit that swallows its digger.
Names the root of the hidden hatred in these verses: lies that crush and flattery that charms both come from a heart that does not love.
"The kisses of an enemy are deceitful" also warns that warm gestures can hide hostility.

Uses the same verb for covering: in 26:26 deceit covers hatred until it is uncovered, and in 28:13 the one who covers his sins does not prosper, while the one who confesses and forsakes them finds mercy.

The things the LORD hates, including "A lying tongue" and "A heart that devises wicked plans," share the language of detestable conduct with 26:25, though the "seven abominations" of 26:25 express fullness rather than pointing to that list.

units.notes:
• v24 "disguises" means making oneself unrecognizable. The same Hebrew verb is used in 1 Kings 14:5–6, where Jeroboam's wife pretends to be another woman to fool the prophet Ahijah.
• v25 "speaks kindly" is literally "makes his voice gracious." His pleasant tone is deliberate, part of the disguise.
• v25 "seven abominations": Waltke, quoted by Guzik, calls the phrase "an abstraction for the full panoply of his wicked thoughts and deeds." In plain words, it stands for the whole array of his evil, not a count of seven sins.
• v26 "covered" is answered by "revealed," a verb meaning "uncovered": what deceit has covered, the assembly will see uncovered. The same verb for covering appears in 28:13, "He who covers his sins will not prosper." The "assembly" is the community gathered for public business and judgment.
• Compare 10:18 ("Whoever hides hatred has lying lips"), Psalm 55:12–14, 21 and Jeremiah 9:8 ("One speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, But in his heart he lies in wait").
units.summary: The friendliest face can hide the deepest hatred, but what is hidden does not stay hidden forever.
units.principle: Hatred dressed in kind words is the most dangerous kind, and God does not let it stay hidden.
units.insight: Scripture is full of this man. Cain talked with his brother, then rose against him in the field (Genesis 4:8). Joab asked Amasa, "Are you in health, my brother?" as he took his beard to kiss him, then stabbed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). Judas betrayed the Son of Man with a kiss (Luke 22:48). David felt this wound most deeply: "It is not an enemy who reproaches me… But it was you, a man my equal" (Psalm 55:12–13). There are two errors here: being so naive that we are taken in, and being so wicked that we do the deceiving. So the question is not only "Who is hiding hatred from me?" but "What am I storing up behind my smile?" Resentment kept behind polite church courtesy is this same sin in its early stage. The way out is 28:13: whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will have mercy.
units.application: When someone's kind words do not match their track record, believe the track record. You can wish someone well and still not hand them your trust (Matthew 10:16). If a friendly face has betrayed you, leave the exposing to God instead of plotting it yourself. If you are smiling at someone you resent, stop storing it: name it to God and, where needed, go to the person (Matthew 18:15) before it hardens.

rel.note: Those who lie in wait for others "lie in wait for their own blood," the same recoil of planned harm.
The hidden hater schemes against others; this saying shows how his trap recoils on him.
The one who leads the upright astray "will fall into his own pit."

units.notes:
• The saying recurs across Scripture: Psalm 7:15–16 ("He made a pit and dug it out, And has fallen into the ditch which he made"); 9:15; 57:6; Ecclesiastes 10:8; Proverbs 28:10.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "For samples consider Haman (Esther 7:10) and Daniel's enemies (Daniel 6:24-28)."
• Henry, translating a Latin poet: "Nor is there any law more just than that the contrivers of destruction should perish by their own arts." In other words, nothing is more fitting than schemers being caught by their own schemes.
• Compare Galatians 6:7, "whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."
units.summary: The pit you dig for someone else is the pit you will fall into.
units.principle: Evil planned against others carries the seed of its own judgment; the schemer builds his own trap.
units.insight: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it (Esther 7:10). The officials who trapped Daniel with a royal decree were thrown to the lions themselves (Daniel 6:24). The greatest example is the cross. There the powers of evil dug their deepest pit for the Son of God, and in that very act their own defeat was sealed (1 Corinthians 2:8; Colossians 2:15). This truth frees the wronged person from revenge (Romans 12:19), because the scheme is already working against the schemer. It also sobers anyone tempted to set someone up, because every trap we dig, we dig in our own path.
units.application: When you are tempted to set someone up, whether through the leaked comment, the arranged embarrassment or the quiet campaign to push someone out, stop digging. When a coworker or relative is digging for you, do not dig back. Keep doing right and trust God with the outcome (Psalm 37:1–7; Romans 12:19–21).

rel.note: The deceiver who claims he was only joking shows another face of the lying tongue that does not love its victims.
Traces the same hatred hidden behind pleasant lips that 26:28 names at its root.
The faithful wounds of a friend stand against the ruin that flattery works.
The one who rebukes finds more favor afterward than the one who flatters.
The flatterer spreads a net for his neighbor's feet; flattery works ruin.

units.notes:
• "Crushed" is literally "its crushed ones," the people the lie has crushed or oppressed. The ESV and NLT have "its victims," the KJV "afflicted."
• "Flattering" means smooth or slippery. The same word describes the seductress's speech, "smoother than oil" (5:3).
• "Ruin" translates a Hebrew word found only here in the Old Testament. It means something that makes a person stumble and fall, an overthrow.
• Derek Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "deceit, whether it hurts or soothes, is practical hatred, since truth is vital, and pride fatal, to right decisions."
• Amnon shows the first line at work: after he wronged his sister Tamar, he "hated her exceedingly" (2 Samuel 13:15).
• Compare 27:6; 29:5; Psalm 12:2–3; Romans 16:18; 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
units.summary: You cannot lie to someone you love, and flattery is a lie with a smile.
units.principle: Every deliberate deception is a failure of love, whether it wounds or flatters; only truth spoken in love builds people up.
units.insight: The first flattery in the Bible was the serpent's "you will be like God" (Genesis 3:5), and it ruined the world. As Bridges puts it, the flatterer's great advantage is that "he has a friend in his own bosom": part of us wants to believe him. King Ahab kept four hundred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear, and he hated Micaiah because he did not (1 Kings 22:8). The pleasant voices led him to his death. Against both kinds of lie stands Jesus, in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22). He looked at the rich young ruler and loved him, and so He told him the hardest truth he would ever hear (Mark 10:21). "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" (27:6).
units.application: Before you praise someone, ask whether it is true and whether it is for them or for you. Give encouragement that is specific and truthful. If you lead, notice who only ever agrees with you, and keep at least one Micaiah close. When praise comes your way, follow the old counsel to be as troubled by unjust praise as by unjust slander.

rel.note: A man plans his way, but the LORD directs his steps, which is why no one can boast about tomorrow.
Many plans fill the human heart, but only the LORD's counsel stands, so every plan is held under His hand.
The plans of the diligent are commended, showing that this verse forbids presumption, not planning.
The next verse uses a verb from the same root to forbid praising oneself, as this one forbids praising one's future.

units.notes:
• "Bring forth" translates the ordinary Hebrew verb for giving birth. Each day is pictured as about to deliver something no one has yet seen.
• "Boast" in this verse and "praise" in 27:2 come from the same Hebrew root, halal, the root behind "hallelujah." The two sayings belong together: do not praise your own future, and do not praise yourself.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The verse is not ruling out wise planning for the future, only one's overconfident sense of ability to control the future."
• Compare James 4:13–16, which calls such boasting evil; Proverbs 16:9; 19:21; Luke 12:16–21.
units.summary: Tomorrow is God's to give; plan for it, but never brag about it.
units.principle: Plan carefully, but hold every plan humbly, because only God commands what tomorrow brings.
units.insight: Haman left Esther's first banquet boasting that he was invited again "tomorrow" (Esther 5:12). The next day he was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). Jesus told of a farmer who planned bigger barns for many years to come, and God said, "Fool! This night your soul will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). Such boasting does more than misjudge the calendar. As Bridges puts it, people who boast of tomorrow "virtually put God out of his own world." Where do you speak as though tomorrow were yours? The gravest form of this boast is putting off God, as Felix did while he waited for "a convenient time" (Acts 24:25). Scripture answers, "now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). Those who belong to Christ need not know tomorrow or worry about it (Matthew 6:34), because they know the One who holds it.
units.application: If you lead a business, a ministry or a family, keep planning, but let "if the Lord wills" shape how you speak about the plan (James 4:15). Announce next year's goals with an open hand. If you are a young person who assumes there is plenty of time to get serious about God, settle it today. And if a plan has just collapsed, take it as a reminder that tomorrow was always God's, not as proof that He has abandoned you.

rel.note: Most men proclaim their own goodness, but a faithful man is hard to find; self-praise is common and proves nothing.
Seeking one's own glory "is not glory," the same verdict this verse passes on self-praise.
The preceding verse forbids boasting about tomorrow with a verb from the same root as "praise" here.
Praise from others is the right kind, yet it becomes a test that shows what a person is made of.
The virtuous woman's own works praise her in the gates, the kind of praise this verse commends.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew words behind "another man" and "a stranger" often describe outsiders or foreigners. Here they simply mean anyone other than yourself.
• An old writer, Jermin, quoted by Bridges, says that praise "is a comely garment. But though thyself doth wear it, another must put it on, or else it will never sit well about thee." Comely means attractive and fitting.
• Speaking up is sometimes right. Samuel defended his integrity before Israel (1 Samuel 12:3–5), and Paul, forced to defend his apostleship, called his own boasting foolishness (2 Corinthians 11:16–23; 12:11). Defending the truth differs from advertising yourself.
• Compare 25:27; 31:31; Matthew 6:1–4; 2 Corinthians 10:18, "For not he who commends himself is approved, but whom the Lord commends."
units.summary: Your own mouth is the one voice whose praise of you counts for nothing.
units.principle: Honor is real only when others give it; the moment we supply it ourselves, it loses its worth.
units.insight: Scripture shows this verse at work again and again. John the Baptist said he was not worthy to loose Jesus' sandal strap (John 1:27), and Jesus said no one born of women was greater (Matthew 11:11). The centurion said, "I am not worthy" (Luke 7:6); the elders had already called him worthy (Luke 7:4), and Jesus praised his faith above any in Israel (Luke 7:9). Above all, Christ did not seek His own glory (John 8:50). He humbled Himself to the cross, "Therefore God also has highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:9). Self-praise usually grows from a hungry heart that needs to be noticed. The cure is not pretending we did nothing. It is resting in the approval of the Father, who sees in secret (Matthew 6:4). A person secure in that approval can let others speak, or let silence speak.
units.application: In a job interview or a performance review, state your work accurately, then let the facts and other people speak for you. Before you post your latest success online, ask whether it is written mainly to be admired, and leave it unposted if it is. Parents and leaders: be quick to praise others specifically and sincerely, since you are the "another man" this verse needs. When praise comes to you, say thank you and pass the glory on to God.

rel.note: The same word for a fool's wrath appears there: it shows itself at once, while the prudent man covers shame.
Meeting a robbed she-bear is safer than meeting a fool in his folly, another picture of how dangerous he is to others.
The next verse sets wrath and anger beside jealousy, a passion even harder to withstand.
An angry man stirs up strife, showing how one person's temper spreads trouble to others.
Whether a fool rages or laughs, the wise man who contends with him finds no peace.

units.notes:
• The word translated "wrath," ka'as, means vexation or provocation: the irritable resentment a fool feels and stirs up in others. The same word appears in 12:16, "A fool's wrath is known at once."
• Matthew Poole, quoted by Bridges, calls a fool's wrath intolerable, "being without cause, measure, or end."
• Matthew Henry adds that the fool's anger crushes the fool too: "It lies heavily upon himself."
• Hezekiah's officials show a wise response to a raging fool. When the Rabshakeh taunted them, "they held their peace and answered him not a word" (Isaiah 36:21).
• Compare 12:16; 17:12; 29:9; Ecclesiastes 7:9.
units.summary: You can set down a sack of sand, but a fool's anger follows you home.
units.principle: Uncontrolled anger is never a private matter; its weight falls on everyone who has to live beside it.
units.insight: Saul's household learned what this verse means. In his dark moods he hurled a spear at David, and later at his own son Jonathan (1 Samuel 18:10–11; 20:33). Nabal's servants said of their master, "he is such a scoundrel that one cannot speak to him" (1 Samuel 25:17). Everyone around these men walked carefully. The verse asks a searching question: who has to carry my moods? A parent's sulking, a boss's temper or a spouse's simmering resentment can become the heaviest load in a home or workplace. Jesus is the opposite of the fool. He is "gentle and lowly in heart," and the burden He gives is light (Matthew 11:29–30). He carries what others lay on Him instead of loading His anger onto them. Those who come to Him learn to set their own anger down.
units.application: If you live or work with someone whose anger is unreasonable, do not feed it with argument. Answer briefly, step away, and get help from a pastor or counselor; if the anger turns threatening, seek safety first. If you are the one others tiptoe around, ask your spouse, children or coworkers how your moods affect them, and listen without defending yourself. Confess the grudge you have been nursing, and lay it down before God tonight.

rel.note: Envy rots the bones of the one who harbors it, while this verse shows its power over its victims.
The son is told not to let his heart envy sinners, the guard this verse calls for.
The fool's wrath in the previous verse is heavy, but jealousy is harder still to withstand.
A husband's jealousy will not spare in the day of vengeance, showing the relentless force this verse describes.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "envy," the NKJV "jealousy." One Hebrew word, qin'ah, covers zeal, jealousy and envy, and the context decides. Elsewhere it can describe the LORD's righteous zeal; here it is the dark jealousy of a sinful heart.
• For "cruel" and "outrageous" (the KJV wording of the first line), the KJV margin offers "cruelty" and "an overflowing," picturing anger as a river bursting its banks, the picture behind the NKJV's "torrent."
• Matthew Henry contrasts a passing outburst ("a sudden heat") with settled envy: "One may avoid a sudden heat, as David escaped Saul's javelin, but when it grows, as Saul's did, to a settled envy, there is no standing before it."
• Compare 6:34; 14:30, "envy is rottenness to the bones"; Song of Solomon 8:6, where jealousy is "as cruel as the grave"; James 3:16.
units.summary: Anger floods and then recedes; jealousy settles in and never stops working.
units.principle: Anger that flares can cool, but jealousy that is fed becomes a settled force that few can withstand.
units.insight: Jealousy shed the first human blood. Cain, angry that God accepted Abel's offering and not his, killed his brother (Genesis 4:5–8). Joseph's brothers "envied him" and then sold him (Genesis 37:11, 28). After the women sang David's praise, "Saul eyed David from that day forward" (1 Samuel 18:9), and years of pursuit followed. Most solemn of all, Pilate "knew that they had handed Him over because of envy" (Matthew 27:18). Envy helped bring the Son of God to the cross, and God turned even that sin into the means of our salvation. So the question comes home: whose success do I find hard to celebrate? Jealousy rarely announces itself; it hides behind criticism and quiet comparison. The answer is a heart secure in Christ, able to say with John the Baptist, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).
units.application: Watch for the early signs of jealousy: the quick criticism of a coworker's promotion, the secret pleasure at a rival's setback, the friend whose good news you cannot bring yourself to celebrate. Name it to God before it settles in. Then do the opposite, and praise that person to someone else this week. If you are on the receiving end of someone's jealousy, do not argue with it. Guard your conduct, give the person room, and pray for them.

rel.note: A wise rebuker received by an obedient ear is as precious as fine gold.
Honest correction is part of the friction by which friends sharpen one another.
The next verse explains why a friend's painful words can be trusted: they are faithful wounds.
The one who rebukes finds more favor in the end than the one who flatters.
A wise person loves the one who rebukes him, which is why open rebuke can strengthen a friendship.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "secret love." The NKJV's "love carefully concealed" brings out that the silence is chosen: love kept hidden when it ought to speak.
• Bridges explains what "open" means: "The openness of the rebuke describes the free and unreserved sincerity of the heart, not necessarily the public exposure of the offender."
• The Law already joined rebuke and love: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him" (Leviticus 19:17).
• Jesus gives the right order for correcting a brother: first "between you and him alone" (Matthew 18:15).
• Compare 9:8; 25:12; 28:23; Galatians 6:1.
units.summary: Love that never speaks up is love that never helps.
units.principle: Love proves itself by telling the truth that helps, not by a silence that only keeps the peace.
units.insight: Eli loved his sons, but when they defiled the priesthood he spoke only mildly, and God said "he did not restrain them" (1 Samuel 3:13). His concealed love left them to ruin. Paul loved Peter, yet when Peter drew back from Gentile believers, Paul "withstood him to his face" (Galatians 2:11), and the gospel was protected. Our silence is often less about love for the other person than love for our own comfort. We fear the awkward moment, or losing their good opinion of us. Christ's love is not like that: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19). He tells us the truth because He means to save us. Those who have received His loving rebuke learn to give it, and to welcome it.
units.application: Think of one friend you have watched drift into a harmful relationship, habit or decision. Pray, check your facts and your motives, then speak privately, plainly and kindly. Parents of grown children and small-group leaders face this often; choose the hard conversation over the silent worry. And when a friend corrects you, thank them before you explain yourself. Their courage is a gift.

rel.note: Hatred disguised by kind words is the enemy's kiss in fuller portrait.
Loud, ill-timed blessing is another form of affection that cannot be trusted.
A friend's faithful wounds are part of the friction by which iron sharpens iron.
Open rebuke is better than silent love, and this verse explains why a friend's wounds can be trusted.
The same friend who wounds faithfully also delights the heart with hearty counsel.
A flatterer spreads a net for his neighbor's feet, showing where the enemy's kisses lead.

units.notes:
• Translations differ on the last word. The Hebrew word behind "deceitful" comes from a verb that lexicons define as to be abundant. The ESV reads "profuse," the YLT "abundant," and the 1984 NIV says an enemy "multiplies" kisses; the NKJV, NASB and KJV read "deceitful." Either way, the enemy's kisses are excessive and cannot be trusted.
• The word translated "faithful" comes from the same root as "amen": what is firm, reliable and trustworthy. A friend's wounds are "faithful" because they can be relied on to serve your good.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The 'wounds' are a metaphor for the painful and plain words that must be spoken in a true friendship."
• Compare 26:24–26; 28:23; 29:5; 2 Samuel 20:9–10; Psalm 141:5, "Let the righteous strike me; It shall be a kindness."
units.summary: A friend's honesty may hurt you, but an enemy's affection can ruin you.
units.principle: Love is measured by its aim, not its feel: truth that wounds for our good is kinder than warmth that hides ill will.
units.insight: Judas came to Gethsemane with a greeting, "Greetings, Rabbi!" and a kiss (Matthew 26:49). No kiss in history was more deceitful. Jesus' wounds were of the other kind. He rebuked Peter sharply, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23). After Peter's denials He asked him three times, "Do you love Me?" until Peter was grieved (John 21:17), and that painful question restored him. Bridges, speaking of Christ: "The truest friend of man—his wounds are faithful." The verse exposes what we prefer. Many of us choose the friend who always agrees and resent the one who tells us the truth. Ask whose voice you trust more, and why. Jesus Himself "was wounded for our transgressions" (Isaiah 53:5). Because the Friend who corrects us was wounded for us, we can receive His corrections as love.
units.application: When you must correct a friend, make sure the wound is faithful: true, private, kind in tone and aimed at their good, not at your own relief. Correction that only vents frustration is not what this verse praises. When someone flatters you while working against you, in office politics or a manipulative relationship, look past the warmth to the track record. And keep near you at least one friend who loves you enough to disagree with you.

rel.note: A worker's hungry mouth drives him on, showing how need sharpens desire.
Honey eaten past need turns from pleasure to sickness, another picture of fullness spoiling a good gift.
A friend's hearty counsel is sweet, and it is sweetest to the one who knows his need.
Agur fears that fullness could lead him to deny the LORD, the spiritual danger of the satisfied soul.

units.notes:
• The word translated "loathes" is strong. For it the KJV margin has "treadeth under foot" (tramples), and Ironside renders the line, "The full soul tramples on a honeycomb." The full man does not merely decline the honey; he pushes it away.
• Israel in the wilderness shows the full soul. Fed each day with manna, the people complained, "our soul loathes this worthless bread" (Numbers 21:5).
• Bridges applies the verse to people who have every spiritual privilege and no appetite for it: "May not satiety be as great a curse as famine?" Satiety means being too full.
• Compare 16:26; 25:16; 30:8–9; Luke 1:53; Revelation 3:17.
units.summary: Hunger makes bitter things sweet; fullness makes even honey dull.
units.principle: Need sharpens gratitude and fullness dulls it, so the comfortable must guard against despising good gifts.
units.insight: The prodigal son, starving in a far country, "would gladly have filled his stomach with the pods that the swine ate" (Luke 15:16). Hunger brought him home, and his father's welcome tasted sweet. His older brother, who had never left the table, could not enjoy the feast at all (Luke 15:28–30). The same thing happens in the soul. A church that says, "I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing" (Revelation 3:17) finds the gospel tasteless. A person aware of his need finds even hard truths sweet, because they lead him to Christ. Ask whether God's word has grown dull to you because you are full of other things. Jesus promises, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, For they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6).
units.application: If you have plenty, practice gratitude on purpose: give thanks before meals, fast now and then, and notice the gifts you have stopped seeing. Parents in comfortable homes, teach your children to say thank you for ordinary things. When you counsel someone who is broken and hungry for help, speak with care, because he will take in every word. And if Scripture tastes flat, cut back on what fills you before you open it.

rel.note: The man who wanders from the way of understanding ends among the dead, the spiritual end of restless straying.
Keeping old friendships and staying near one's neighbors is the settled life this verse commends.
The closing poem calls for steady attention to one's own flocks, the duties the wanderer leaves behind.
The son is told to ponder the path of his feet and not turn aside, the steadiness the wanderer lacks.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew, as in the NKJV, one verb, "wanders," describes both the bird and the man, so the two lines mirror each other: the same restless straying in each.
• Matthew Henry on what the wanderer leaves behind: "When the bird wanders from her nest the eggs and young ones there are neglected. Those that love to be abroad leave their work at home undone." "Abroad" here means away from home.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "Those who wander lack the security of their home and can no longer contribute to their community life."
• Not every move is wandering. Abraham left his country at God's call (Genesis 12:1), and Paul traveled where the Spirit directed (Acts 16:6–10).
• Compare 21:16; 1 Corinthians 7:20, 24; 1 Thessalonians 4:11.
units.summary: A bird off its nest is exposed, and so is the person who drifts from where God placed him.
units.principle: Faithfulness grows where a person stays with the people and duties God has given; restless drifting leaves both the wanderer and those who need him exposed.
units.insight: Jonah was sent to Nineveh, but he "arose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD" (Jonah 1:3). Out of his place, he slept through a storm that endangered everyone on board. Demas served beside Paul, yet Paul had to write, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10). Wandering usually begins in the heart, with restlessness, discontent or the wish to escape a hard duty. Behind it lies the belief that life would be better somewhere else. So ask whether you are being called away, or simply running. The gospel speaks to wanderers. "All we like sheep have gone astray" (Isaiah 53:6), and the Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one, carrying it home on His shoulders (Luke 15:4–5).
units.application: Before you leave a job, a church or a commitment in search of something better, ask whether God is sending you or you are running from a duty. Husbands and fathers especially: be present where your family needs you, not always somewhere else. If you have drifted from your church family, go back this Sunday and take your place again. And if you are moving for good reasons, leave well, with your responsibilities handed on to someone who will carry them.

rel.note: The wise man heeds counsel, so a friend's advice is a gift worth receiving.
A friend loves at all times, the steady love from which hearty counsel flows.
The next verse urges keeping the old friends whose counsel has proved sweet.
Hearty counsel is part of how friends sharpen one another.
The same friendship that comforts with sweet counsel can also wound faithfully when the truth hurts.
Need makes even bitter things sweet, and a friend's counsel is sweetest to the one who knows his need.

units.notes:
• The KJV margin gives the Hebrew behind "hearty counsel" as "counsel of the soul": advice that comes from the friend's inner self, not from duty or mere cleverness.
• The NASB takes the line differently, as a man's counsel being sweet to his friend, but the main translations agree that a friend's sincere advice is the source of delight.
• Matthew Henry: "The sweetness of friendship lies not in hearty mirth, and hearty laughter, but in hearty counsel."
• Anointing a guest with oil was a mark of welcome and refreshment (Psalm 23:5; Luke 7:46).
• Compare 12:15; 15:22; 17:17; 18:24; 27:6, 17; Psalm 133.
units.summary: A true friend's heartfelt advice is perfume for a weary soul.
units.principle: Counsel given from a loving heart is one of friendship's sweetest gifts, refreshing the soul as fragrance refreshes the senses.
units.insight: When David was hunted in the wilderness, "Jonathan, Saul's son, arose and went to David in the woods and strengthened his hand in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). That visit was perfume to a weary man. Jethro's counsel did the same for Moses, lifting a load he could not carry alone (Exodus 18:17–24). The gospel gives us a Friend whose counsel is sweeter still. Jesus is called "Wonderful, Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), and He says, "I have called you friends, for all things that I heard from My Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). Ask two questions. Do I have friends whose counsel comes from the heart, and do I listen to them? And am I that kind of friend, or do I offer only quick opinions?
units.application: This week, reach out to a friend who is carrying a heavy decision, a hard diagnosis or a discouraging season. Listen first, pray with them, and then offer counsel from your heart, not a quick fix. If you lead a small group or mentor a younger believer, make room for unhurried conversation, not only teaching. And when you face a decision of your own, seek out the friend who will tell you the truth kindly.

rel.note: A brother is born for adversity, the balance that keeps this verse from discounting family.
There is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, the same truth that a faithful friend may help more than kin.
The poor man's own brothers hate him and his friends go far from him, the opposite of the near neighbor.
The wanderer loses his settled ties, while this verse urges keeping them.
The sweetness of a friend's counsel is the reason old friendships are worth keeping.

units.notes:
• This saying has three lines instead of the usual two. The NLT reads the middle line as a reassurance ("When disaster strikes, you won't have to ask your brother for assistance"), while the NKJV, ESV and NASB read it as a warning against going to a brother's house.
• Solomon kept his father's friend. Hiram king of Tyre "had always loved David," and Solomon renewed that friendship to build the temple (1 Kings 5:1–12). His son Rehoboam "rejected the advice which the elders had given him," the men who had served his father, and lost most of the kingdom (1 Kings 12:8, 16–19).
• Duane Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The 'brother' in Proverbs 27:10 is a close relative, one to whom people naturally turn in difficult times."
• Compare 17:17; 18:24; 19:7; Luke 10:29–37.
units.summary: In a crisis, the friend next door can do more than the relative far away.
units.principle: Long-tested friendships are a treasure to keep, because faithful people close at hand often help most when trouble comes.
units.insight: Jesus knew what this verse describes. His own brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5), yet He could say to His disciples, "you are those who have continued with Me in My trials" (Luke 22:28). In His parable, a wounded man was passed by a priest and a Levite, men of his own people, and was saved by a Samaritan who came near (Luke 10:30–35). Nearness and willingness made the difference. This verse searches our loyalty. Some of us let old friendships lapse because new ones are more exciting or more useful. Others assume family will always be there and invest nowhere else. Ask who would come if your phone rang in the night, and whose call you would answer. Christ, who calls His people friends (John 15:15), never forsakes His own (Hebrews 13:5).
units.application: Call an old friend you have neglected, or a friend of your parents who has known your family for years, and renew the tie. Get to know the neighbors on your street; they are the ones who can come quickly in an emergency. If you live far from aging parents, help them build a circle of nearby friends and church members. And be that near neighbor yourself for someone whose family is far away.

rel.note: A wise son makes a glad father, the joy this verse appeals to.
The father rejoices when his son's heart is wise and his lips speak right things.
The father of the righteous greatly rejoices, and the son is urged to let his parents be glad.
Whoever loves wisdom makes his father rejoice, while a companion of harlots wastes his wealth.

units.notes:
• "Reproaches" means taunts or scorn. The father pictures someone mocking him or his teaching, and his son's wise life as his reply.
• "My son" runs through the father's lessons in chapters 1–9 and returns in 23:15, 19, 26 and 24:13, 21. This is its last appearance before Lemuel's mother uses the address in 31:2.
• Duane Garrett, quoted by Guzik, sums up the stakes: "his son will either publicly disgrace the father or enable him to stand proudly before even his enemies."
• Compare 10:1; 15:20; 23:15–16, 24–25; 29:3; 3 John 4.
units.summary: A child's wise life is a father's best answer to his critics.
units.principle: The way children live reflects on those who raised them, so a wise life is both a gift to parents and a defense of their teaching.
units.insight: Paul traced Timothy's sincere faith to "your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5); Timothy's life honored their teaching. David's sin brought reproach on the God he served: it gave "great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme" (2 Samuel 12:14). In the light of the New Testament, the father's appeal is also the voice of our heavenly Father to His children (Hebrews 12:5–6). Jesus perfectly gladdened the Father's heart: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). Through Him we too are sons and daughters, and our lives either adorn or shame His name (Titus 2:10). A caution for parents: critics do not always judge fairly, and a child's folly is not always the parent's failure. The father here appeals; he cannot compel.
units.application: Young people: your choices are not only your own business. Let your parents, or the spiritual mothers and fathers who invested in you, hear how their teaching is bearing fruit, and thank them. Parents: like this father, tell your children what their wisdom means to you instead of only issuing commands. If your grown child has wandered, refuse the shame others heap on you, keep praying, and leave room for the Father who welcomes prodigals home.

rel.note: The simple believe every word, while the prudent consider their steps and depart from evil.
The book was written to give prudence to the simple, the remedy for the drift this verse describes.
The earlier collection gives nearly the same saying, word for word.
The next verse applies prudence to lending: see the risk and protect yourself.

units.notes:
• The only difference from 22:3 in the NKJV is the opening of the second line, which there begins with "But." The heading in 25:1 presents these chapters as a further collection of Solomon's proverbs, so a saying from the earlier collection naturally appears again.
• "The simple" in Proverbs are not slow-witted but untaught and easily led. They can still learn, and Wisdom calls them: "O you simple ones, understand prudence" (8:5).
• Matthew Henry on why the evil can be seen in time: "commonly, God warns before he wounds."
• Compare 14:15–16; 22:3; Hebrews 11:7.
units.summary: Foresight sees trouble coming and takes cover; carelessness walks straight into it.
units.principle: Wisdom looks ahead and acts on what it sees; folly drifts forward and meets consequences it never stopped to consider.
units.insight: Noah saw judgment coming. "Moved with godly fear," he "prepared an ark for the saving of his household" (Hebrews 11:7). His neighbors kept eating, drinking and marrying, and "did not know until the flood came and took them all away" (Matthew 24:39). That is the difference this verse draws. The greatest evil anyone can foresee is standing before God unprepared, and the gospel provides the hiding place. Believers are those "who have fled for refuge to lay hold of the hope set before us" (Hebrews 6:18), and that refuge is Christ. Yet the verse also reaches into daily life. Ask where you are drifting toward a danger you could see if you stopped to look: a temptation, a debt or a cooling heart.
units.application: Name one situation where you can already see trouble ahead: a relationship heading toward compromise, spending that outruns income, a schedule with no room for God. Take cover now by changing course, setting a boundary or asking for help. Parents, teach teenagers to ask before a party or a trip, "What could go wrong here, and what will I do?" Leaders, listen to the staff member who raises a concern before it becomes a crisis.

rel.note: He who is surety for a stranger will suffer, the risk that makes such a man a poor credit.
The earlier collection gives almost the same counsel about taking a garment as security.
Do not be one who shakes hands in pledge, or your own bed may be taken.
The prudent foresee evil and hide themselves, and this verse applies that foresight to lending.
The father's fuller warning urges a son to free himself quickly from a rash pledge.

units.notes:
• Taking a garment as security was a recognized practice. The Law required that a neighbor's garment taken in pledge be returned before sundown, since it might be his only covering at night (Exodus 22:26–27).
• The KJV reads "a strange woman," the NKJV "a seductress," the language Proverbs uses for the immoral woman of chapters 5–7.
• Matthew Henry on the cost to a household: "Foolish lending is injustice to our families."
• Bridges on keeping kindness and good sense together: "Kindness loses the name of virtue, when shewn at the expense of prudence." Shewn is an old spelling of shown.
• Compare 6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27.
units.summary: A man who will guarantee anyone's debt should not be trusted without a pledge in hand.
units.principle: Generosity must walk with prudence; whoever binds himself rashly for the untrustworthy endangers his own household and those who rely on him.
units.insight: Judah once said of his young brother Benjamin, "I myself will be surety for him" (Genesis 43:9). When the moment came, he offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (Genesis 44:33). That was surety at its noblest, for a brother he knew and loved. The gospel goes further: "Jesus has become a surety of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). He bound Himself for people who were strangers to God (Ephesians 2:12), unfaithful and unable to pay, and He paid the whole debt at the cross. What no prudent lender would do, Christ did out of love. That should humble us and make us grateful. It should not make us careless. Because only He could bear such a debt, we are called to steady, wise generosity, not reckless promises.
units.application: Before you cosign a loan, a lease or a credit card for anyone, ask whether you could pay the whole amount yourself without harming your family. If not, give a smaller gift instead of a guarantee. If you lend money or rent out property, protect yourself when a borrower has a record of reckless promises. Parents, teach young adults this verse before their first friend asks them to cosign. Helping is good; binding yourself blindly is not.

rel.note: A word spoken in due season is good, unlike the ill-timed blessing of this verse.
Too many visits make a neighbor weary, as too much praise makes a friend suspicious.
Singing songs to a heavy heart is another kindness that ignores the person and the moment.
Fervent lips can cover a wicked heart, the danger loud praise raises.
The enemy's profuse kisses and this loud blessing are both affection that cannot be trusted.

units.notes:
• "Counted" means reckoned or regarded. The friend hears the noisy blessing as if it were a curse, and the praise loses all its value.
• Ironside quotes an Italian saying: "He who praises you more than he is wont to do, either has deceived you, or is about to do it." "Wont" means accustomed.
• Absalom would "rise early and stand beside the way to the gate," greeting every man with a kiss, and "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:2–6).
• Compare 15:23; 25:17, 20; 26:23–25; 1 John 3:18.
units.summary: Praise shouted at dawn sounds less like a blessing than a sales pitch.
units.principle: Love shows itself with sensitivity to the person and the moment; praise that ignores both sounds false, however loud it is.
units.insight: When the people of Tyre and Sidon needed Herod's favor, they kept shouting over his speech, "The voice of a god and not of a man!" (Acts 12:20–22). Their loud blessing became a curse to him: he took the glory, and God struck him (Acts 12:23). Overdone praise often has a motive behind it, such as winning favor, covering guilt or being seen as generous. Bridges: "One act of love is more than many loud blessings." The verse asks us to examine our own affection. Is my praise for the other person's good, or for mine? Christ's love was never loud talk. He showed it by laying down His life (1 John 3:16). So John writes, "let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3:18).
units.application: Before you send the gushing message or give the public tribute, ask whether it is true, timely and for the other person's good. A grieving friend, an exhausted new parent or a coworker under pressure may need quiet help more than loud words. Leaders, beware the person whose praise of you suddenly grows louder, and ask what he wants. And replace one compliment this week with one concrete act of kindness.

rel.note: The earlier saying also compares the contentions of a wife to a continual dripping.
Living in the wilderness is better than living with a contentious and angry woman.
A corner of the housetop is better than a house shared with a contentious woman, the same portrait of strife at home.
The Hezekiah collection repeats the housetop saying, keeping this portrait of strife before the reader.
The contentious man kindles strife like charcoal on coals, showing that the warning is not about women alone.

units.notes:
• Many houses in Israel had flat roofs of packed earth. Ironside quotes a Dr. Thompson's description of a rainstorm in Palestine: the heavy rains "thoroughly soak through the flat earthen roofs of these mountain houses."
• The Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult. Its first verb usually means to hide or store up, so the KJV reads, "Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, which bewrayeth itself." Bewrayeth means betrays: a man can no more hide the strife at home than hide the wind or the smell of perfume on his hand. The NKJV, ESV and NASB take the sense of holding back, and picture restraining the wind and grasping oil.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, describes such contention as "as unpredictable and uncontrollable as a gust of wind or a hand grasping oil."
• Compare 19:13; 21:9, 19; 25:24; 26:21.
units.summary: Constant quarreling wears a home down like a roof leaking all day, and force cannot stop it.
units.principle: Strife that never lets up wears down everyone who lives with it and yields to no amount of force, so each person must guard against becoming its source.
units.insight: Hannah lived with this kind of dripping. Her rival Peninnah "provoked her severely, to make her miserable," and it went on "year by year" (1 Samuel 1:6–7). Hannah did not answer in kind; she poured out her soul before the LORD (1 Samuel 1:15). Contention is not a woman's sin only. Jesus' disciples argued about who was the greatest even at the Last Supper (Luke 22:24). So the verse asks every reader, husband or wife, whether he or she is the steady drip in someone's home: the nagging, the sarcasm, the complaint that never rests. Force will not cure it, but Christ can. "He Himself is our peace" (Ephesians 2:14), and in Him believers are told, "Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, and evil speaking be put away from you" (Ephesians 4:31).
units.application: If you live with constant quarreling, do not try to win by force or by matching complaint with complaint; that only makes the wind blow harder. Pray, choose your words carefully, and seek help together from a pastor or a Christian counselor. Husbands and wives, ask your spouse this week, "What do I say too often?" and listen without arguing. Parents, notice whether criticism has become the background noise of your home, and replace some of it with thanks.

rel.note: He who walks with wise men will be wise, because companions shape one another as iron sharpens iron.
A friend loves at all times, and that loyal love is what makes his sharpening safe to receive.
The friction that sharpens a friend does nothing for the fool who will not be changed.
Open rebuke is part of the friction by which friends sharpen one another.
A friend's faithful wounds are one way he sharpens his friend.
Hearty counsel is the gentler side of the same sharpening friendship.

units.notes:
• The NKJV, KJV and YLT keep the Hebrew word for "face," translating it "countenance" or "face," while the ESV and NASB render the line more generally as one man sharpening another.
• Derek Kidner, quoted by Guzik, on the word "countenance": it "almost equals 'personality' here. Like 'soul', it can stand for the man himself."
• A dull blade was a real loss. In Saul's day Israel had no blacksmith, and the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen their tools (1 Samuel 13:19–21).
• Sharpening can run the wrong way too. Companions can just as easily sharpen one another's worst desires, which is why the company we keep matters so much (13:20; 1 Corinthians 15:33).
• Compare 13:20; 17:17; 18:24; 27:5–6, 9; Ecclesiastes 4:9–10; Hebrews 10:24–25.
units.summary: Friends who never rub against each other never sharpen each other.
units.principle: People grow sharper through honest, two-way friendship, and whoever isolates himself loses the edge that only others can give.
units.insight: Paul and Timothy show this verse at its best. Timothy had "carefully followed" Paul's doctrine and manner of life (2 Timothy 3:10), and Paul said of him, "I have no one like-minded" (Philippians 2:20). Sharpening can also hurt. Paul and Barnabas once parted after a sharp disagreement over Mark (Acts 15:39), yet years later Paul wrote that Mark was "useful to me for ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). On the Emmaus road the risen Christ walked with two discouraged disciples, and afterward they said, "Did not our heart burn within us while He talked with us on the road" (Luke 24:32). Ask who sharpens you, and whom you sharpen. Bridges: "If a brother seems to walk alone, sharpen his iron by godly communication." Communication here means fellowship and conversation.
units.application: Find one or two believers who will ask you hard questions, and meet with them regularly over Scripture and prayer; the lone believer grows dull. In a disagreement with a coworker or a fellow church member, listen for what might sharpen you before you defend yourself. Leaders, invite pushback from your team instead of surrounding yourself with agreement. Young people, notice whether your closest friends are making you better or only sharper in the wrong direction.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent will rule, the same pattern of faithful work bringing advancement.
A wise servant can rise to rule over a shameful son and share the inheritance.
A man who excels in his work will stand before kings, another picture of diligence leading to honor.
Well-tended flocks repay their keeper with clothing and land, as the kept fig tree yields its fruit.

units.notes:
• The two Hebrew verbs behind "keeps" and "waits on" both mean to guard or watch over. The parallel ties the tending of a tree to the attentive service of a master.
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The fig tree needed closer attention than other plants; so the point would include the diligent tending of it."
• The KJV reads "he that waiteth on his master"; Ironside renders it "he that regardeth his master," the servant who pays close attention to his master's interests.
• Compare 12:24; 17:2; 22:29; 1 Corinthians 9:7; 2 Timothy 2:6; Colossians 3:22–24.
units.summary: Tend the tree and you will eat the figs; serve faithfully and honor comes in its season.
units.principle: Patient, faithful service ordinarily bears fruit and honor in time, and God sees the faithfulness that people overlook.
units.insight: Joseph served Potiphar so faithfully that his master put everything under his authority (Genesis 39:4). Later, in prison, he helped Pharaoh's butler, yet "the chief butler did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (Genesis 40:23). Two more years passed before honor came, and it came from God. Elisha was known simply as the man "who poured water on the hands of Elijah" (2 Kings 3:11), and that humble service prepared him to carry on Elijah's work. Faithfulness that waits for applause soon quits; faithfulness that serves the Lord keeps going. Jesus promises, "If anyone serves Me, him My Father will honor" (John 12:26). The servant overlooked by every earthly master will still hear, "Well done, good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:21).
units.application: Employees: do the unseen parts of your job well, guard your employer's interests, and be the person others can count on, even when no one notices. Volunteers and church workers: keep tending your fig tree, because fruit often comes late. If you supervise others, make sure faithful people are honored, not overlooked. And if you have served well and been passed over, take your disappointment to the Master who sees in secret.

rel.note: The LORD's lamp searches the inner depths of the heart, the searching this verse calls for.
The heart's counsel is deep water that only understanding draws out.
As a man thinks in his heart, so is he, the same truth that the heart reveals the man.
The next verse shows what the human heart is like when its desires are left to themselves.
Out of the heart spring the issues of life, which is why the heart shows who a person is.

units.notes:
• Derek Kidner, quoted by Guzik: "The Hebrew is very cryptic: literally, 'As the water the face to the face, so the man's heart to the man.'" The KJV and YLT keep that terseness, while the ESV, NASB and NLT, like the NKJV, supply a verb such as "reflects" or "reveals."
• Interpreters differ on whether the second line means that a person's own heart shows him what he is, or that one person can know another by looking into his own heart. The NKJV favors the first.
• Ironside takes the second view: "As the reflected image answers to the face of him who is looking into it, so does one man's heart answer to another's."
• Compare 4:23; 20:5, 27; 23:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; James 1:23–25.
units.summary: Still water shows your face; your heart shows who you really are.
units.principle: A person is what his heart is, so true self-knowledge looks past the public image to the desires and motives within.
units.insight: When Samuel admired Eliab's appearance, the LORD told him, "man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Jesus "knew what was in man" (John 2:25). Peter was sure of his own heart: "I will never be made to stumble" (Matthew 26:33). Before morning his denials showed what was really there. The heart is "deceitful above all things" (Jeremiah 17:9), so we cannot read it accurately on our own. That is why David prayed, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalm 139:23). The second reading of the verse humbles us too: the sins we despise in others usually have a reflection in ourselves. Christ does not merely expose the heart. He gives a new one (Ezekiel 36:26).
units.application: Take ten quiet minutes this week to ask what you have been loving, thinking about and wanting most; the answers will show your heart more truly than your reputation does. Leaders and anyone with a public role especially need this, because the gap between image and heart can grow unnoticed. Before you criticize someone, ask whether the same fault is reflected in you. And ask a trusted friend what they see in you that you might be missing.

rel.note: Hell and Destruction lie open before the LORD, the same pair named here.
Do not overwork to be rich, because riches fly away; chasing more never satisfies.
The heart reveals the man, and its endless desires are part of what it reveals.
The grave appears among the things that never say "Enough!", the same picture of endless appetite.
Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches, the contentment that answers never-satisfied eyes.

units.notes:
• The same pair, "Hell and Destruction" (Sheol and Abaddon), appears in 15:11, where they lie open before the LORD. In both verses the two names together stand for death and the grave.
• Agur lists the grave among the things that never say "Enough!" (30:15–16), using a similar picture of endless appetite.
• "Eyes" stand for desire, the wanting that begins with looking. Eve saw that the tree "was pleasant to the eyes" (Genesis 3:6), and Achan confessed of the plunder, "I coveted them and took them" (Joshua 7:21).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, on endless desire: "It is the bane of humanity, and this truism should drive the son to examine his own lusts." Bane means ruin; the "son" is the young learner Proverbs addresses.
• Compare Ecclesiastes 1:8; 5:10; Habakkuk 2:5; 1 John 2:16.
units.summary: The grave never says "enough," and neither do eyes that live for more.
units.principle: Desire left to itself never says enough, so contentment must be learned from God, not purchased with more.
units.insight: Solomon tested this verse on himself: "Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them" (Ecclesiastes 2:10). At the end he called it all "vanity and grasping for the wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). The Samaritan woman had had five husbands and was still thirsty when she met Jesus at the well. He told her, "whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst" (John 4:14). Augustine's prayer, quoted by Bridges, names the reason: "Thou hast made us for thyself; and our heart can have no rest, till it rests in thee." Restless eyes are often the symptom of a heart looking for God in things. Paul could say, "I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). He learned it by finding his satisfaction in Christ.
