units.application: Notice what your eyes feed on: shopping sites, social media, a neighbor's new car, images that stir lust. Choose one feed to cut off this week. Before a purchase, wait a day and give thanks for what you already have. Parents, model contentment by talking more about gratitude than about upgrades. And when the old craving rises, turn it into prayer, asking Christ to satisfy what things cannot.

rel.note: The same refining image there introduces the LORD's testing of hearts.
Taking the dross from silver yields a vessel for the smith, the purifying that praise can expose the need for.
Praise should come from others, and this verse shows that such praise is itself a test.
Pride brings a man low while the humble in spirit retain honor, the two outcomes of praise's furnace.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the second line says literally that a man is "according to his praise," and the YLT keeps that wording. The ESV says a man is "tested by" his praise, focusing on how he handles admiration, while the NKJV says he is valued by what others say of him. Both fit the refining pot.
• In 17:3 the same first line continues, "But the LORD tests the hearts." Here the testing comes through human praise.
• Bridges: "He that is praised is not only much approved, but much proved." Proved here means tested.
• Ironside: "There is no hotter crucible to test a man than when he is put through a fire of praise and adulation."
• Compare 17:3; 25:4; 27:2; 1 Peter 1:7.
units.summary: Fire tests gold, and praise tests people; applause shows what we are made of.
units.principle: Praise is a furnace that reveals character: the humble come through it purer, and the proud are exposed by it.
units.insight: One song tested two men. The women sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, And David his ten thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7). Saul burned with jealousy, while "David behaved wisely in all his ways" (1 Samuel 18:14). At Lystra, when crowds tried to worship Paul and Barnabas, they tore their clothes and pointed the people to the living God (Acts 14:14–15). Hezekiah failed the test. When envoys from Babylon came with letters and a gift, he showed them all his treasures (2 Kings 20:12–13). Scripture says God withdrew from him "to test him, that He might know all that was in his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:31). When crowds wanted to make Jesus king, He withdrew to the mountain alone (John 6:15). So ask what praise does in you. Do you replay it, fish for more, or pass it on to God?
units.application: When you are praised this week, say thank you, then privately give the credit to God and get back to work. Pastors, worship leaders and anyone with a platform: ask a trusted friend to tell you when success is changing you. Parents, praise your children's character and effort more than their image. And be careful how you praise others, because extravagant praise can feed pride in someone already struggling with it.

rel.note: A hundred blows do less for a fool than one rebuke for a wise man, the same limit of force.
In a child, folly can still be driven out by loving correction; in the hardened fool it cannot.
The fool returns to his folly like a dog to its vomit, showing how firmly he clings to it.
The friction that sharpens a friend leaves the fool unchanged.

units.notes:
• The KJV's "bray" is an older English word meaning to pound or crush, as in a mortar.
• Bridges: "the husk sticks not so close to the grain, as foolishness to the fool."
• Folly can be corrected early: "Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child; The rod of correction will drive it far from him" (22:15). The fool of this verse has hardened past that stage.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, on the limits of punishment: "Prisons were made into penitentiaries through the mistaken notion that confinement would bring repentance and effect a cure."
• Compare 17:10; 26:11; Jeremiah 13:23.
units.summary: You can pound the husk off grain, but you cannot pound folly out of a fool who loves it.
units.principle: Pressure and punishment cannot by themselves make a person wise; only a changed heart lets go of folly.
units.insight: Pharaoh was struck by plague after plague, yet each time relief came, "he hardened his heart" (Exodus 8:15). King Ahaz, in his distress, "became increasingly unfaithful to the LORD. This is that King Ahaz" (2 Chronicles 28:22). Suffering alone changed neither man. Manasseh, by contrast, "humbled himself greatly" in his affliction and prayed (2 Chronicles 33:12). The difference was not the force of the blows but the grace of God. This is sobering for anyone who has been through hard things and stayed the same. Pain can open a door, but only God can turn the heart. He promises, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you" (Ezekiel 36:26). Ask Him for that, instead of waiting for one more blow.
units.application: Parents of a grown child, spouses and friends: you cannot pound wisdom into someone who loves folly. Stop escalating pressure; pray, speak the truth once with love, and leave room for God. Pastors and counselors, do not mistake compliance under pressure for repentance. And if you keep meeting the same painful consequences, ask God for a new heart, not just relief. Folly yields to grace, not to force.

rel.note: A righteous man regards the life of his animal, the same personal care this verse commands.
The lazy man's overgrown field shows what happens when no one attends to what has been entrusted.
The next verse gives the reason for this diligence: riches and crowns do not last.
The man who wanders from his place leaves undone the very duties this verse calls him to attend.

units.notes:
• "Be diligent to know" repeats the verb "know" in Hebrew, literally "knowing, know." Hebrew repeats a verb this way for emphasis, so the line stresses careful, firsthand knowledge of the flock.
• The word behind "state" is literally "face," and "attend to" is literally to set one's heart on something, as the KJV margin notes. The owner is to know the face of his flock and set his heart on his herds.
• The word translated "herds" in the second line can mean either a flock or a herd, so the line repeats the first with a second word for the animals in one's care.
• Derek Kidner, quoted by Guzik, on the scope of the poem: "This country scene is not designed to make farmers of everybody…" The principle of attentive care reaches every kind of work.
• The five verses move from command (27:23) through reason (27:24) and the cycle of the seasons (27:25) to the provision the flocks supply (27:26–27). Compare 12:10; 24:30–34; Genesis 31:38–40.
units.summary: You cannot care well for what you do not know well.
units.principle: Faithful stewardship requires personal, attentive knowledge of what God has entrusted to us; neglect from a distance wastes it.
units.insight: Jacob could tell Laban what faithful shepherding cost: "in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep departed from my eyes" (Genesis 31:40). Years later he refused to drive his flocks hard, because he knew the young ones could not bear it (Genesis 33:13). He knew the state of his flock. Neglect usually begins quietly. We stop looking closely at our accounts, our work, our children or our own souls, and assume all is well. The deeper question is whether we treat what we have as a trust from God. Applied to the care of people, the same attentiveness reflects Christ, the Good Shepherd, who says, "I know My sheep, and am known by My own" (John 10:14). He knows the state of His flock better than any of us knows ours.
units.application: Business owners and managers: walk the floor, look at the numbers yourself, and know how your people are doing. Parents: know your children's friends, moods and struggles, not only their grades. Look closely at your budget this month instead of guessing. Pastors and small-group leaders, applying this verse to the care of people, know those in your care by name, and visit the one who has gone quiet.

rel.note: He who trusts in his riches will fall, the danger of resting on what may vanish.
The rich man imagines his wealth a high wall, the false security this verse exposes.
Riches make themselves wings and fly away, the same impermanence named here.
Because riches do not last, the previous verse commands diligent care of the flocks.
Stored riches may vanish, but the well-tended flock keeps feeding the whole household.

units.notes:
• The KJV words the second line as a question, "doth the crown endure to every generation?" The NKJV makes it a statement. Either way, the expected answer is no.
• Solomon's own crown proves the point. Right after his death, ten tribes broke away from his son Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:16–20).
• Matthew Henry on why even a king should tend his flocks: "Though David had the crown entailed on his family, yet he looked well to his flocks." Entailed means legally secured to his descendants; David still kept overseers over his herds (1 Chronicles 27:29–31).
• Compare 11:28; 18:11; 23:4–5; 1 Timothy 6:17.
units.summary: Money can vanish and thrones can fall, so keep tending what keeps on providing.
units.principle: Accumulated wealth and position are never secure, so wisdom trusts God and faithfully tends what He provides instead of resting on what has been stored up.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar walked in his royal palace and boasted of "this great Babylon, that I have built" (Daniel 4:30). While the words were still in his mouth, a voice said, "the kingdom has departed from you!" (Daniel 4:31). Saul's house lost the throne within a few years of his death. Where do you rest your security: in savings, a position, a title? Each is a gift to steward, but none can carry the weight of trust. Paul tells the rich "not to be haughty, nor to trust in uncertain riches but in the living God" (1 Timothy 6:17). Only one throne lasts: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" (Hebrews 1:8). And Christ's faithful servants are promised "the crown of glory that does not fade away" (1 Peter 5:4).
units.application: If your savings or retirement account is your main source of peace, give some of it away this year as a declaration of trust in God. Business owners, keep tending the daily work that produces, instead of living off past success. Leaders in any role, remember that your position is temporary, and use it to serve while you have it. Parents, teach your children to value skill and faithfulness over money they did not earn.

rel.note: The wise son gathers in summer, while the shameful son sleeps through the harvest.
The sentence that begins here continues with the provision the well-fed flocks supply.
The faithful man abounds with blessings, but the one who hastens to be rich is punished.
The ant gathers her food in harvest, working with the season as the farmer does here.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads, "The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself," picturing the growth of the year; the NKJV's "When the hay is removed" pictures the mown field where new growth comes up. Both describe the turning seasons that feed the flock.
• Matthew Henry on God's part and the farmer's: "God has done his part; thou art ungrateful to him, and unjustly refusest to serve his providence, if thou dost not do thine." God grows the grass; the farmer must gather it.
• The promise behind the rhythm: "While the earth remains, Seedtime and harvest, Cold and heat, Winter and summer, And day and night Shall not cease" (Genesis 8:22).
• Compare 6:6–8; 10:5; Psalm 104:14; Acts 14:17.
units.summary: God keeps the seasons turning; the wise do each season's work and trust Him for the harvest.
units.principle: God provides through the faithful order of His creation, and the wise cooperate with it by doing the right work in its season.
units.insight: Joseph read God's seasons and acted on them, gathering grain in the seven plentiful years so that there was bread when famine came (Genesis 41:47–49, 54). Paul told the people of Lystra that God "did not leave Himself without witness," giving "rain from heaven and fruitful seasons" (Acts 14:17). Every spring the new grass preaches that same faithfulness. Jesus used this rhythm to describe His kingdom: the earth yields "first the blade, then the head, after that the full grain in the head," and when it ripens the farmer puts in the sickle (Mark 4:28–29). Our hearts are often impatient with slow seasons and drawn to shortcuts. The verse calls us to trust God's timing, do today's work, and wait for His harvest without losing heart (Galatians 6:9).
units.application: Look at your work and family life by seasons. What needs gathering now, while the hay is ready: savings in a good year, time with children while they are young, study while you are free? Do it before the season passes. If you are tempted by a get-rich-quick scheme, choose steady work instead. Gardeners, farmers and anyone who works outdoors: this week, thank God aloud for the seasons He keeps.

rel.note: He who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, the same reward of faithful work.
He who gathers by labor will increase, the steady growth pictured in the goats' price.
Whoever keeps the fig tree eats its fruit, as whoever tends the flock is clothed and enriched by it.
The turning seasons described there feed the flock that now provides for the household.
The virtuous woman considers a field and buys it from the fruit of her diligent work.

units.notes:
• Matthew Henry sums up the exchange: "Keep thy sheep, and thy sheep will help to keep thee."
• John Trapp, quoted by Guzik, on what the goats' price could do: "Wherewith thou mayest pay thy rent, and besides hire tillage, or it may be purchase land…" To hire tillage is to pay for plowing.
• The virtuous woman shows the same fruit of steady work: she seeks wool, and "She considers a field and buys it" (31:13, 16).
• Compare 12:11; 13:11; 27:18.
units.summary: Care for the flock, and in time the flock will care for you.
units.principle: Faithful care of what God entrusts ordinarily turns into provision and even growth, though it never guarantees against loss.
units.insight: Jacob crossed the Jordan with nothing but his staff (Genesis 32:10). Through years of faithful shepherding, and God's blessing on it, he "became exceedingly prosperous" (Genesis 30:43). Job's flocks clothed more than his own family; the poor were "warmed with the fleece of my sheep" (Job 31:20). Faithful provision is meant to overflow. Our hearts often want the field without tending the lambs, the result without the years of care. Jesus speaks to the worry behind that hurry. Our Father knows we need food and clothing, and Jesus tells us to "seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matthew 6:33). Steady faithfulness rests on that promise, not on luck or shortcuts.
units.application: Small business owners and farmers: reinvest in what produces, and resist draining it for short-term comfort. Employees: keep growing your skills, because they are your flock. Families: build modest savings so that a good year can become room to grow or to give. And when your work does provide extra, ask whom your fleece could warm: a neighbor, a missionary or a struggling family at church.

rel.note: He who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, the sufficiency that faithful work ordinarily brings.
Riches and crowns pass away, while the well-tended flock keeps the household fed.
Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches but the food allotted to him, the contentment this poem ends on.
The virtuous woman provides food for her household and a portion for her maidservants, the same provision that reaches everyone.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word rendered "nourishment" is chayyim, the ordinary word for "life," which can also mean sustenance. The flock is pictured as sustaining the very lives of those who depend on the household.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "goat's milk was by far the animal nutrient of choice in the ancient Near East."
• Matthew Henry, on the household fed with plain food: "enough is as good as a feast."
• Boaz shows a household whose provision reached its young workers. He told Ruth to stay close to "my young women," and at mealtime she "ate and was satisfied" (Ruth 2:8, 14).
• Compare 12:11; 30:8; 31:15.
units.summary: The poem ends not with luxury but with enough, and enough for everyone in the house.
units.principle: Diligent stewardship aims at enough for everyone in one's care, a sufficiency steadier and better than the pursuit of riches.
units.insight: In the wilderness God gave Israel manna each morning, and "he who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack" (Exodus 16:18). His provision was enough, and enough for everyone. Jesus taught us to ask for "daily bread" (Matthew 6:11), and on a hillside He fed thousands until "they all ate and were filled" (Matthew 14:20). This verse asks two heart questions. Is enough truly enough for me, or do I always need a little more? And do the least people in my care, the employee, the caregiver, the child, share in what I have? Paul gives the measure: "having food and clothing, with these we shall be content" (1 Timothy 6:8). A heart that has found Christ sufficient can rest in enough.
units.application: Sit down this month and name what "enough" looks like for your household, then thank God for it at the table. If you employ others, whether a nanny, a cleaner or a small staff, make sure they are paid fairly and on time. Parents, let your children see you choose contentment over upgrades. And if this year has brought loss despite your diligence, bring your need to the Father who still provides daily bread.

rel.note: The one who walks with integrity walks securely, while the crooked will be found out.
In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, the true source of the righteous man's boldness.
The guilty who run from no one find the way to peace a few verses later: confession and forsaking bring mercy.
The lion returns as a picture of a wicked ruler's cruelty, the opposite of the righteous man's lion-like courage.
The fear of the guilty reaches its heaviest form in the man burdened with bloodshed, fleeing toward the pit.
Describes the lion that turns away from no beast, the picture behind the boldness of the righteous.

units.notes:
• *Bold* translates batach, the usual Hebrew verb for trusting or feeling secure. The same verb returns near the end of the chapter: "he who trusts in the LORD" (28:25) and "He who trusts in his own heart" (28:26). The lion-like boldness of the righteous is the security of someone whose trust is rightly placed.
• Among the curses for disobedience the Law said, "the sound of a shaken leaf shall cause them to flee" (Leviticus 26:36; compare 26:17). The first line of this proverb describes that same groundless fear.
• Bridges: "But if guilt brings fear, the removal of guilt gives confidence." The boldness of the righteous is not natural toughness but the fruit of guilt removed.
• The first fear in Scripture follows the first sin. Adam told God, "I was afraid because I was naked; and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10).
• Compare 10:9; 14:26; Psalm 27:1–3; Hebrews 10:22; 1 John 3:21.
units.summary: Guilt hears footsteps that are not there; a clear conscience stands its ground like a lion.
units.principle: Guilt makes a person afraid even when no one threatens him, while a conscience at peace with God gives steady courage.
units.insight: Cain killed his brother and from then on expected to be hunted: "anyone who finds me will kill me" (Genesis 4:14). Elisha shows the opposite. When an army surrounded Dothan, his servant panicked, but Elisha said, "Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them" (2 Kings 6:16). In another siege the LORD made a Syrian army hear the noise of chariots, and they fled their own camp though no one was attacking (2 Kings 7:6–7). Where does your own unease come from? Some of our fear has nothing to do with circumstances; it is unconfessed sin keeping us on edge. The gospel does more than calm nerves. Christ cleanses the conscience (Hebrews 10:22), and forgiven people can stand before God and others with the boldness Peter and John showed before the council (Acts 4:13).
units.application: If you notice that you are jumpy, defensive or quick to cover your tracks, ask whether something is unconfessed, and bring it to God and, where needed, to the person you wronged. If you lead a team or a family, model the courage of a clear conscience by admitting mistakes quickly, so that others learn that honesty, not image, is what lets a person stand firm. Courage that comes from a clear conscience never needs to bully.

rel.note: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people, the root of the turmoil in the first line.
Shows the same link from the side of the people: the rise of the righteous or the wicked changes the life of the whole land.
Describes the ruler of understanding who hates covetousness and prolongs his days.
A king establishes the land by justice, while one who takes bribes overthrows it; a ruler's character decides a land's stability.

units.notes:
• The northern kingdom of Israel illustrates the first line. In its last decades kings rose and fell quickly, several by assassination: Zechariah reigned six months and Shallum one month (2 Kings 15:8–15). Earlier, Zimri reigned seven days (1 Kings 16:15). The proverb itself names no nation.
• The second line is compressed in Hebrew. The word translated "Right," ken, can mean right or just, and a word spelled the same way is the ordinary Hebrew word for "so," which is how the NASB reads it. The KJV has "the state thereof shall be prolonged." Each reading pictures lasting order under a wise ruler.
• Ironside reports an Arab curse that captures the first line: "May God multiply your sheiks." A land with many rulers is a land in trouble.
• Joseph shows the second line at work. Pharaoh recognized him as "a man in whom is the Spirit of God" (Genesis 41:38), and his wisdom preserved Egypt through seven years of famine.
• Compare 14:34; 29:4; 1 Timothy 2:1–2.
units.summary: A nation's sin shows up in the turnover at the top; one wise leader can steady a whole land.
units.principle: A people's moral condition shapes its stability, and wise, righteous leadership lets what is right endure.
units.insight: We usually blame unstable leadership on politics, economics or personalities. Proverbs looks deeper, at the moral condition of the people. Israel's northern kingdom began with Jeroboam's golden calves (1 Kings 12:28–30). In about two centuries it suffered repeated assassinations and changes of dynasty, and then Assyria carried it away (2 Kings 17:6–18). Scripture also shows the other side: in Egypt, Joseph, one man of understanding, preserved a nation through famine. The verse turns to our own part. A household, church or nation is shaped by the private faithfulness of its members, so repentance is a service to the community as well as a personal duty (2 Chronicles 7:14). The verse also directs our prayers "for kings and all who are in authority" (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Above every unstable throne, God's people look to the King of whose government "there will be no end" (Isaiah 9:7).
units.application: If you lead a church, business or family, pursue understanding before influence: study Scripture, seek counsel and deal with what is wrong in your own life first. If the place where you serve keeps churning through leaders, look past the personalities and ask what sin or broken trust lies underneath. This week, pray by name for those in authority over you, including the ones you did not vote for.

rel.note: Whoever oppresses the poor reproaches their Maker, whoever the oppressor is.
The LORD pleads the cause of the poor against those who rob them.
Another picture of power turned against the poor, there a wicked ruler like a lion or a bear.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew describes the man in the first line with a word meaning "poor," and the NKJV, ESV, NASB, KJV and NLT translate it that way. The 1984 NIV reads "A ruler" instead.
• *Driving rain*: the KJV has "sweeping rain." Rain in its season was God's blessing on the land (Deuteronomy 11:14), but a beating storm on ripening grain could destroy a year's food. The picture is of something meant to give life that destroys instead.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "The comparatively poor are often shockingly uncharitable and unfeeling towards the real poor."
• Bridges: "a base mind becomes more corrupt from a hasty elevation." In other words, sudden power tends to make a small-hearted person worse, not better.
• Compare 14:31; 22:22–23; Matthew 18:28–30; Psalm 72:12–14.
units.summary: Rain should feed a field; a poor man who preys on the poor is a storm that leaves nothing.
units.principle: Having known hardship does not by itself make a person kind; power in the hands of an unchanged heart oppresses, whoever holds it.
units.insight: Jesus told of a servant who was forgiven a debt he could never repay. He went out, found a fellow servant who owed him a little, "laid hands on him and took him by the throat" (Matthew 18:28). He had received mercy and still showed none. In Jesus' day many tax collectors were Jews who served Rome and squeezed their own people; Zacchaeus became a different man when Jesus came to his house (Luke 19:8). This proverb searches anyone who has risen a little, such as a first-time supervisor or a new church leader. Remembered hardship can make us gentle or harsh. Christ is the opposite of the driving rain. Psalm 72 pictures the King who "will spare the poor and needy" and comes down "like rain upon the grass before mowing" (Psalm 72:6, 13).
units.application: If you have just been given authority, as a new manager, team leader or the older sibling left in charge, treat those under you as you wanted to be treated when you stood where they stand. If you have come through hard times, let that history make you generous toward people still in them, not impatient. This week, ask someone who works under you how your decisions land on them, and listen.

rel.note: Whoever tells the wicked "You are righteous" is cursed, while those who rebuke the wicked find delight; both lines of this verse in another form.
The one who rebukes finds more favor than the flatterer, the same courage to confront wrong instead of praising it.
God's law appears again: keeping it marks the discerning son.
The same law: refusing to hear it makes even prayer an abomination.
The righteous and the wicked find each other abhorrent, the opposition that "contend with them" describes.

units.notes:
• *Law* is torah, which basically means instruction or teaching. It appears four times in this cluster: twice here and once each in 28:7 and 28:9. In Proverbs the word can mean a parent's teaching (1:8), but in these sayings it stands for God's instruction to His people.
• The psalmist felt the same tension: "Indignation has taken hold of me Because of the wicked, who forsake Your law" (Psalm 119:53).
• Bishop Hall, quoted by Bridges: "It is fearful to sin; more fearful to delight in sin; yet more to defend it."
• Bridges on those who keep the law: they "cannot call sin by smooth names, and gloss over an ungodly character."
• Compare 17:15; 24:24–25; Romans 1:32; Ephesians 5:11; Isaiah 5:20.
units.summary: What a person applauds reveals what he has done with God's law.
units.principle: What we praise reveals what we have done with God's word; keeping His instruction makes a person unwilling to applaud evil.
units.insight: Elijah would not flatter Ahab. When the king called him "troubler of Israel," Elijah answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father's house have, in that you have forsaken the commandments of the LORD" (1 Kings 18:17–18). John the Baptist told Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have her," and it cost him his life (Matthew 14:4, 10). Paul describes a darkened mind in its last stage: people not only do wrong but "approve of those who practice them" (Romans 1:32). Look closely at what you laugh at, share and admire. Our applause often drifts before our conduct does. The answer is not a combative spirit. Jesus opposed evil while He welcomed sinners, and He calls His people to "expose" darkness (Ephesians 5:11) with that same mix of truth and love.
units.application: This week, notice which public figures, characters or coworkers you find yourself excusing or admiring for conduct God calls sin. Parents: when your children praise someone for cruelty, cheating or crude humor, talk it through instead of laughing along. At church or at work, when wrongdoing is being smoothed over with soft names, say plainly and kindly what it is. Contending for what is right does not require a harsh tone.

rel.note: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, the root of the understanding this verse describes.
The righteous considers the cause of the poor, while the wicked does not understand such knowledge.
The LORD gives wisdom, and with it the understanding of righteousness and justice.
The knowledge of the Holy One is understanding; seeking the LORD is the path to it.

units.notes:
• *Justice* is mishpat, the word for right judgment and fair decisions; the KJV has "judgment." What evil men lack is not information but the moral sight to judge rightly.
• *Understand all* refers to everything needed for upright living and just judgment, not to unlimited knowledge. The verb "understand" appears in both lines. What separates the two groups is not intelligence but their relationship to God: one group is evil, the other seeks the LORD.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "There are always those who believe justice is that which benefits them—otherwise it is not justice."
• Paul draws the same contrast: "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God ... But he who is spiritual judges all things" (1 Corinthians 2:14–15).
• Compare 2:6–9; 9:10; 29:7; John 7:17; Ephesians 4:18.
units.summary: Justice is not learned by cleverness; it is learned by seeking the One who is just.
units.principle: Moral understanding grows from seeking God, while persistent evil blinds a person to what is just.
units.insight: Jesus thanked His Father that He had "hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to babes" (Matthew 11:25). Learned Pharisees missed the Messiah standing in front of them, while a man born blind said, "One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see" (John 9:25). Bridges: "What a curse are learning and intellect without an humble heart!" The problem is not a lack of intelligence but the direction of the heart. Jesus said that anyone who "wills to do His will" will know whether His teaching is from God (John 7:17). So when something right looks unclear to us, it is worth asking whether we want to know. Sin first bends the will and then blurs the sight. Seeking the LORD reverses that order: the heart bows, and the eyes begin to see.
units.application: Before a hard ethical decision at work or at home, seek the LORD first: pray, open Scripture and ask, "What would I see if I wanted God's will more than my own?" If you are a student or professional surrounded by brilliant people who dismiss God, do not mistake their cleverness for wisdom. Parents: teach your children that understanding right and wrong begins with knowing God, not with winning arguments.

rel.note: A little with righteousness is better than vast revenues without justice.
Nearly the same saying: the poor man who walks in integrity is better than the perverse fool.
Another poor man who outranks a rich one, there in understanding.
Uses the same expression, "perverse in his ways," and shows where the straight and crooked roads end.

units.notes:
• *Perverse in his ways*: in the Hebrew, "ways" has a special form used for things that come in pairs. The wording pictures a man trying to walk two roads at once, living a double or two-faced life. Compare James 1:8, "a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways." The same expression returns in 28:18.
• 19:1 has nearly the same first line but ends "Than one who is perverse in his lips, and is a fool." Here the contrast moves from crooked speech to a crooked way of life, and it adds "though he be rich."
• Henry tells of the Greek statesman Aristides, who answered a rich man who mocked his poverty: "Thy riches do thee more hurt than my poverty does me."
• Compare 15:16; 16:8; Mark 8:36; Luke 16:19–31.
units.summary: An honest poor man is richer than a crooked rich man, whatever their bank balances say.
units.principle: Integrity is worth more than wealth; a straight life with little is better than riches held by crooked ways.
units.insight: Paul stood in chains before the governor Felix, who was afraid at his words yet kept hoping for a bribe (Acts 24:24–26). Which man was better off? Jesus told of a rich man who "fared sumptuously every day" and a beggar named Lazarus at his gate, and death revealed which life had been rich (Luke 16:19–25). The proverb challenges how we measure success and what we quietly envy. It also exposes the temptation to walk two roads, keeping a respectable face while cutting corners in private. Christ chose the poor man's road: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). In Him, the poor who walk in integrity lack nothing that matters most.
units.application: If you are offered a deal, a promotion or a shortcut that requires shading the truth, choose the straight road even if it costs you. Parents: praise your children's honesty more than their achievements. If you have less than the people around you, refuse to measure your worth by your income. If you have more, examine whether any part of it rests on a double standard, and set it right.

rel.note: Companions shape a person: walk with the wise and become wise.
The earlier warning not to mix with winebibbers and gluttonous eaters, who come to poverty.
A wise son makes his father's heart glad, the honor this verse implies.
Another son who wrongs his parents, there by robbing them and excusing it.
Keeping the law appears in both verses; there it means resisting the wicked, here it marks the discerning son.

units.notes:
• *Gluttons* translates a word for squanderers, people who treat what is valuable as cheap, especially through excess in eating. The same word stands in 23:20–21 ("gluttonous eaters," "the glutton") and in Deuteronomy 21:20, where parents describe a stubborn and rebellious son as "a glutton and a drunkard."
• *Discerning* translates a word from the Hebrew family for understanding. The KJV has "a wise son." The same family of words runs through the chapter: the "man of understanding" (28:2), those who "understand all" (28:5), the poor man "who has understanding" (28:11) and the ruler who "lacks understanding" (28:16).
• Henry: "Bad company is a great hindrance to religion." By "religion" he means a life of godliness.
• Compare 10:1; 13:20; 27:11; Psalm 119:63; 1 Corinthians 15:33.
units.summary: Show me a son's friends, and I will show you what he did with his father's teaching.
units.principle: Obedience to God and the company we keep go together, and both shape the honor or shame we bring to those who raised us.
units.insight: Daniel was a young man far from home in a palace of plenty, yet he "purposed in his heart" not to defile himself with the king's delicacies, and his friends stood with him (Daniel 1:8–16). Their faithfulness honored the God of their fathers. The prodigal son took the opposite road. He "wasted his possessions with prodigal living" (Luke 15:13). Yet when he came home, his father ran to meet him and kissed him (Luke 15:20). Here is the gospel inside this proverb: our heavenly Father has been shamed by His children, and still He runs to welcome those who return. Ask whose company is quietly forming you. The psalmist chose his circle on purpose: "I am a companion of all who fear You, And of those who keep Your precepts" (Psalm 119:63).
units.application: Young people: look at the three or four people you spend the most time with, and ask whether they help you keep God's word or make it easier to drift. Parents: know your children's friends by name, open your home to them, and talk with your children about why companions matter. If you have brought shame on your family, do not stay away; come home, own it and begin again.

rel.note: The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.
Pity on the poor is a loan to the LORD, who repays it.
Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his riches will come to poverty.
The one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.
The one who gives to the poor will not lack, the kind of person who ends up holding the exploiter's wealth.

units.notes:
• The Law was plain: "If you lend money to any of My people who are poor among you, you shall not be like a moneylender to him; you shall not charge him interest" (Exodus 22:25). Leviticus 25:36–37 forbade profit on food lent to a poor brother as well.
• The two Hebrew words behind "usury and extortion" both refer to forms of interest or profit taken on a loan. The first, neshek, is related to a verb meaning "to bite": interest that takes a bite out of the borrower. The KJV has "usury and unjust gain."
• Deuteronomy 23:19–20 allowed interest on a loan to a foreigner but not to a fellow Israelite. The concern is not lending as such but profiting from a brother's need.
• Henry: "That which is ill-got, though it may increase much, will not last long."
• Compare 13:22; 22:16; Psalm 15:5; Nehemiah 5:1–13; James 5:1–4.
units.summary: Money squeezed out of the poor does not stay put; God has ways of sending it back to them.
units.principle: Wealth taken from the vulnerable is never secure, because God sees the poor and turns the course of events toward their good.
units.insight: In Nehemiah's day, Jewish nobles were lending at interest to their own poor brothers, who mortgaged their fields and saw their children sold into slavery to pay. Nehemiah rebuked them, and they promised, "We will restore it, and will require nothing from them" (Nehemiah 5:1–12). Zacchaeus had grown rich by overcharging his own people. When Jesus came to his house, he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). His wealth went to the poor, given by a man who had learned to pity them. The proverb asks where our profit comes from. Does any of it rest on someone else's desperation? Christ is the opposite of the lender who profits from another's need. The Son of Man came "not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).
units.application: If you run a business, lend money or set prices, ask whether any of your profit depends on someone's desperation, such as predatory fees, hidden charges or rent hikes on people with no other options. If you have the means, find a way to help someone in a tight place without squeezing them. If you are trapped in an exploitative loan, take heart that God sees you, and seek honest help.

rel.note: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, but the prayer of the upright is God's delight.
Wisdom warns that those who refused her call will call on her and not be answered.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, all the more when brought with wicked intent.
The one who confesses and forsakes his sins finds mercy; the closed ear and the confessing mouth are opposite responses to God.
The same law: forsaking it shows in what a person praises.

units.notes:
• *Abomination* is the strong word Proverbs uses for what the LORD finds detestable (6:16; 15:8; 21:27). Applying it to prayer itself shows how seriously God takes a closed ear.
• Bridges: "The case described is that habitual and obstinate rejection of God." The verse does not describe the weakness or distraction that sometimes interrupts a believer's hearing, but a settled refusal.
• Bishop Reynolds, quoted by Bridges: "Great reason that God shall refuse to hear him, who refuseth to hear God."
• God said the same through Isaiah to worshipers whose hands were stained with violence: "Even though you make many prayers, I will not hear" (Isaiah 1:15). Compare Zechariah 7:11–13 and Psalm 66:18.
• Compare 1:24–28; 15:8, 29; 21:27; 28:13.
units.summary: You cannot shut your ear to God's word and expect Him to open His ear to your prayer.
units.principle: God will not be used by those who refuse to hear Him; prayer is welcomed from a listening heart, and the returning sinner is always heard.
units.insight: King Saul disobeyed the LORD's plain command and covered it with talk of sacrifice. Samuel answered, "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Years later, when Saul inquired of the LORD, "the LORD did not answer him" (1 Samuel 28:6). Yet Manasseh, one of Judah's worst kings, humbled himself in his distress and prayed, and God "received his entreaty" (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). The difference was not the size of the sin but the turning of the heart. This verse searches anyone who prays regularly but reads Scripture selectively, skipping the parts that confront them. It is no word against the struggling believer or the returning prodigal. The tax collector who prayed, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" went home justified (Luke 18:13–14).
units.application: If there is a passage of Scripture or a command you have been avoiding because it confronts you, stop avoiding it this week: read it and pray it back to God. Small-group leaders and pastors: when someone asks for prayer while refusing counsel, lovingly name the gap. If you have been away from God and fear He will not hear you, come anyway, just as you are; He hears the returning heart.

rel.note: The righteous is delivered from trouble, and it comes to the wicked instead.
The father warns his son not to consent when sinners entice him, the very tempter this verse judges.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it.
The one who walks blamelessly is kept safe, while the crooked suddenly fall.

units.notes:
• The three-line form is unusual among the two-line sayings of chapters 10–29. The extra line lets the verse give an outcome for each party, the tempter and the blameless.
• Jesus spoke strongly about this sin: "whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to sin, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck, and he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matthew 18:6).
• Balaam taught Balak "to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel" (Revelation 2:14; Numbers 31:16), and he was killed among Israel's enemies (Numbers 31:8).
• Bridges on the corrupter's moment of triumph: "Success is his ruin."
• Compare 1:10–19; 11:8; 26:27; Psalm 7:15–16.
units.summary: Whoever sets a trap for someone else's integrity is digging his own pit.
units.principle: Leading others into sin is a trap that closes on the tempter, while those who keep their integrity have good laid up for them.
units.insight: Jeroboam set up golden calves so his people would not worship in Jerusalem, and Scripture repeats his epitaph again and again: he "made Israel sin" (1 Kings 14:16). His whole house was cut off (1 Kings 15:29–30). Joseph shows the other side. Potiphar's wife pressed him "day by day," and he refused: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9–10). Prison followed, but so did the good God had planned for him. Consider your own influence. Do you make it easier or harder for others to stay faithful? Think of the coworker you draw into gossip or the friend you talk into a compromise. Christ is the true Shepherd, who leads His sheep in paths of righteousness (Psalm 23:3), and no one can snatch them out of His hand (John 10:28).
units.application: If you have influence over others, as a boss, coach, older friend or popular student, never use it to pull someone toward what you know is wrong, even "small" things like padding hours or crude jokes. If someone is pressuring you to compromise, refuse plainly, as Joseph did, and leave the outcome with God. Parents: talk openly with your children about friends who mock their faith or push them toward wrong.

rel.note: The rich man's wealth is a high wall in his own esteem.
There is more hope for a fool than for a man wise in his own eyes.
Trusting one's own heart is folly, the root of the rich man's inflated view of himself.
Another poor man who outranks a rich one, there in integrity.
Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and depart from evil.

units.notes:
• *Searches him out* is the language of examining or probing. The same verb is used in 25:2: "the glory of kings is to search out a matter." The poor man of insight examines the rich man and sees him as he really is.
• "Wise in his own eyes" is one of the gravest dangers in Proverbs: "Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him" (26:12).
• Bridges: "The atmosphere of flattery clouds that faculty of self-knowledge, which is the basis of true wisdom."
• Naaman, a great and wealthy commander, was ready to walk away from his healing in a rage until his servants reasoned with him (2 Kings 5:11–14). The people with less status saw more clearly.
• Compare 18:11; Ezekiel 28:2–5; 1 Timothy 6:17.
units.summary: Money can buy a man flattery but not self-knowledge; a poor man with insight sees right through him.
units.principle: Success can persuade a person that he is wise, but true understanding is something money cannot buy and poverty cannot take away.
units.insight: The church at Laodicea said, "I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing," and Christ answered that they did not know they were "wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). Jesus told of a rich farmer who planned bigger barns and congratulated his own soul; God said to him, "Fool!" (Luke 12:19–20). The danger is not money itself but the self-confidence it breeds, often fed by people who depend on us. If you have done well, ask who still feels free to tell you that you are wrong. If you are poor, do not despise the understanding God has given you. God has chosen "the poor of this world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5), and Christ Himself took the place of the poor.
units.application: If you are successful in business, ministry or family life, invite correction from people with less status than you, such as an employee, a younger believer or your own children. Ask them, "What am I not seeing?" and never punish an honest answer. If you work for someone who is wise in his own eyes, speak the truth respectfully and patiently, as Naaman's servants did. Do not let anyone's wealth decide whose counsel you trust.

rel.note: When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices.
A land's condition follows its rulers: rebellion multiplies princes, while a man of understanding makes right endure.
Repeats the second line almost exactly, so the two verses frame the chapter's sayings about rule.
When the righteous are in authority the people rejoice; when a wicked man rules they groan.

units.notes:
• *Men hide themselves*: the Hebrew says literally that a man "is searched for." The KJV has "a man is hidden," with "sought for" in its margin. The picture is of people who disappear so completely that they have to be searched out.
• Hiding and covering run through the chapter: people hide themselves when the wicked rise (28:12, 28), the sinner covers his sins (28:13), and the stingy man hides his eyes from the poor (28:27).
• Under Ahab and Jezebel, Obadiah hid a hundred of the LORD's prophets in caves and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4). When Mordecai was raised to honor, "the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad" (Esther 8:15).
• Henry: "The advancement of the wicked is the eclipsing of the beauty of a nation." When the wicked rise, what was fine and good in a land is hidden from view.
• Compare 11:10; 29:2, 16.
units.summary: Watch who rises to power: under the righteous a city celebrates; under the wicked its people disappear.
units.principle: The character of those who hold power shapes the life of everyone under them, bringing either open joy or fearful hiding.
units.insight: Scripture shows both scenes. Under Ahab, faithful people lived in caves, and Elijah himself fled into the wilderness (1 Kings 19:3–4). When Joseph and Mary took the child Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod, the Son of God Himself was among those who had to hide (Matthew 2:13–15). But when Mordecai was honored, "The Jews had light and gladness, joy and honor" (Esther 8:16). The proverb asks what kind of presence we bring wherever we have influence. Do people relax and flourish when we walk into a room, or do they go quiet? For those living under hostile power, it offers patience, because seasons of hiding do not last forever (28:28). The greatest rejoicing of the righteous lies ahead, when Christ the righteous King reigns openly and every knee bows to Him (Philippians 2:10–11).
units.application: If you hold authority as a manager, pastor, coach or parent, ask whether the people under you feel free to speak, or whether they keep their heads down when you arrive. Invite honest feedback and reward it. If you serve under a harsh leader, it may be wise to keep a low profile for a season, as Obadiah's prophets did, without giving up your integrity. Pray for righteous people to rise in your community, and support them when they do.

rel.note: Hatred covered by deceit is exposed before the assembly; the same verb for covering, with no confession.
The guilty flee when no one pursues; confession and forsaking are the way out of that fear.
Confession deals with sin already committed; constant reverence keeps the heart from hardening in the first place.
Even the man burdened with bloodshed, whom justice must not shield, is not beyond the mercy promised to the one who confesses and forsakes his sin.
The man who will not hear God finds even his prayer rejected, while the one who confesses finds mercy.

units.notes:
• *Covers* is kasah, the same verb used in 26:26 of hatred "covered by deceit." There the covering is exposed before the assembly; here the alternative to covering is confession.
• *Will have mercy* translates a verb meaning to love deeply or to show tender compassion. The same verb appears twice in Psalm 103:13: "As a father pities his children, So the LORD pities those who fear Him." The mercy promised here is a father's compassion.
• David describes both sides of this verse in Psalm 32. Silence wasted him: "When I kept silent, my bones grew old Through my groaning all the day long" (32:3). Confession freed him: "I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,' And You forgave the iniquity of my sin" (32:5).
• Bridges: "The contrast is not between great sins and small, but between sins covered, and sins confessed and forsaken."
• Meyer, quoted by Guzik: "Confession is to take God's side against sin."
• Compare 1 John 1:8–9; James 5:16; Psalm 32:1–5.
units.summary: Sin you hide will keep you from flourishing; sin you confess and forsake meets the mercy of God.
units.principle: Concealed sin blocks the way to peace, but God freely gives mercy to the one who confesses sin and turns from it.
units.insight: Hiding sin is as old as Eden, where Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves and hid among the trees (Genesis 3:7–8). Achan buried what he had stolen under his tent, and it brought ruin on him and his family (Joshua 7:21–26). David covered his adultery with murder, and the covering nearly crushed him until Nathan's rebuke led him to say, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). Where are you still covering? We cover with excuses, silence, busyness and comparison. God offers a better covering: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, Whose sin is covered" (Psalm 32:1). In Christ, God Himself covers what we stop hiding: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).
units.application: Name one thing you have been covering, and confess it to God today in plain words, without excuses. Where your sin has wronged someone, such as a spouse, coworker or friend, go to that person, own it and make it right where you can. Then take a concrete step to forsake it: remove the access, change the habit or ask a mature believer to check on you. Parents: make your home a place where confession is met with mercy, not only punishment.

rel.note: A wise man fears and departs from evil, but a fool rages and is self-confident.
Be zealous for the fear of the LORD all the day, the "always" of this verse.
Confession brings mercy for sin committed; reverence keeps the forgiven heart soft.
The one who is often rebuked and hardens his neck will suddenly be destroyed.

units.notes:
• *Always reverent* is literally "fears continually," without naming the object; the KJV has "feareth alway." The ESV supplies "the LORD," and the NLT reads "fear to do wrong." The NKJV's "always reverent" understands the fear as reverence toward God.
• *Happy* translates the same Hebrew word that opens Psalm 1, "Blessed is the man." It describes the good condition of a person rightly related to God, not a passing mood.
• Bridges: "Fear keeps the heart tender, and the soul safe."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "When one hardens his heart his psyche can no longer feel, respond, and opt for a new direction." By "psyche" he means the inner self.
• Scripture warns often against hardening: Pharaoh "hardened his heart" (Exodus 8:15), and the psalm pleads, "Do not harden your hearts" (Psalm 95:8; Hebrews 3:7–8). Compare 14:16; 23:17; 29:1.
units.summary: The happiest heart is not the fearless one but the one that never stops revering God.
units.principle: Lasting reverence for God keeps the heart soft and safe, while a heart that hardens itself against Him is headed for ruin.
units.insight: How can someone be happy and always afraid? Because the fear of the LORD is not terror of a hostile God but awe of a holy one. Joseph showed it when he refused his master's wife: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). Pharaoh took the other road. Plague after plague, he hardened his heart, until the sea closed over his army (Exodus 14:23–28). Peter shows that even a sincere believer can drift toward hardness through self-confidence: "Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble" (Matthew 26:33). That same night he denied Jesus three times. Hardening usually begins small, with one warning ignored and one conviction brushed aside. Christ gives His people a heart of flesh in place of stone (Ezekiel 36:26), and daily reverence keeps it soft.
units.application: Notice the warnings you have learned to ignore: the check in your conscience, the verse that keeps coming up, the friend who keeps raising the same concern. Respond to one of them this week. Build small daily habits of reverence, such as reading Scripture with prayer and pausing before decisions to ask what pleases God. Parents and mentors: when a young person's heart seems to be hardening, keep speaking the truth with patience and love, and do not give up on them.

rel.note: The king's wrath is like the roaring of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.
The same lion pictures the courage of the righteous instead of the cruelty of the wicked.
The next verse traces the oppressive ruler's cruelty to lack of understanding and greed.
Another picture of power turned against the poor, there a poor man who oppresses the poor.
When a wicked man rules, the people groan.

units.notes:
• In 28:1 the righteous are "bold as a lion." Here the lion returns as a picture of a ruler's cruelty. The same image can stand for courage or for menace, depending on whether strength serves others or devours them.
• *Charging bear*: the KJV has "ranging bear," a bear roaming in search of prey. David had faced both animals while guarding his father's sheep (1 Samuel 17:34–36), so Israel knew exactly what these pictures meant.
• Daniel's visions use beasts, including a lion and a bear, to picture cruel empires (Daniel 7:4–5).
• Henry on the wicked ruler: "whatever we may call him, this scripture calls him a roaring lion and a ranging bear."
• Compare 19:12; 28:3; 29:2; Zephaniah 3:3; 1 Peter 5:8.
units.summary: A ruler meant to protect the weak can become the very beast they need protection from.
units.principle: Power given to protect the weak becomes predatory in wicked hands, and everyone who holds authority must guard against using it to devour.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard. When Naboth would not sell his family inheritance, Jezebel arranged false witnesses, and Naboth was stoned so the king could take his land (1 Kings 21:1–16). That is the lion and the bear in royal robes. Scripture names Satan as the ultimate predator, who "walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Peter 5:8), and every abuse of power echoes him. The verse searches anyone with authority: the parent who rules by fear, the boss who exploits workers who cannot afford to quit, the church leader who silences the weak. The gospel shows power used the other way. Christ, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah," appeared as a Lamb that had been slain (Revelation 5:5–6). He is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11).
units.application: If you have power over others, as a parent, employer, landlord, officer or ministry leader, ask the people under you whether they feel safe with you, and listen without defending yourself. Refuse to use your position to take what is not yours. If you live or work under a predatory authority, keep a record of the wrongs, seek help from those who can step in, and remember that God sees the poor.

rel.note: Whoever is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but whoever hates bribes will live.
The wicked ruler pictured as a lion and a bear; this verse names the folly and greed behind his cruelty.
By a man of understanding and knowledge what is right is prolonged.
The king who judges the poor with truth will have his throne established.
The king establishes the land by justice, but one who receives bribes overthrows it.

units.notes:
• *Covetousness* is rendered "unjust gain" in the ESV and NASB, pointing to profit taken unjustly. It is the same word used in Exodus 18:21, where Jethro told Moses to appoint leaders "hating covetousness": greed disqualifies a leader.
• *Lacks understanding* uses the same family of words as the "man of understanding" in 28:2. The two verses describe two kinds of leader: one whose wisdom lets what is right endure, and one whose folly makes him an oppressor.
• Rehoboam shows the first line. He rejected the elders' counsel to serve the people, promised a heavier yoke, and ten tribes broke away (1 Kings 12:6–19).
• Henry: "Oppressors therefore and tyrants are the greatest fools in the world; they want understanding." In older English "want" means lack.
• Compare 15:27; 29:4, 14; 1 Samuel 12:3–4.
units.summary: A ruler who loves gain grinds his people down; one who hates it builds something that lasts.
units.principle: Greed is the root of oppressive leadership, and leaders who refuse unjust gain tend to build authority that lasts.
units.insight: Samuel ended a lifetime of leadership by asking Israel, "Whose ox have I taken, or whose donkey have I taken, or whom have I cheated?" No one could name anything (1 Samuel 12:3–4). Nehemiah served as governor for twelve years without taking the governor's food allowance, "because of the fear of God" (Nehemiah 5:14–15). Rehoboam chose the opposite way, and his harsh answer split the kingdom. Every leader should ask what he is quietly taking. Greed rarely calls itself greed; it calls itself what we deserve. Christ is the King who never grasped for gain. He had "nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20), yet of His kingdom "there will be no end" (Luke 1:33), because His rule rests on righteousness and self-giving love.
units.application: If you lead a company, ministry, team or household budget, look for ways your position lets you take more than is fair: perks, credit, time or money. Set limits before the temptation comes, and ask someone to hold you to them. Church members and boards: choose leaders, as Moses did, who hate unjust gain, and give them accountability that protects both them and the people they serve.

rel.note: Those who lie in wait for blood are ambushing their own lives.
The guilty flee when no one pursues; here the flight of guilt is at its heaviest.
Mercy remains open to whoever confesses and forsakes sin, even after grave wrong.
Hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• *Burdened* pictures guilt as a crushing load. The ESV and NASB render the first line as the man being a "fugitive" until death; the NKJV, KJV and YLT speak of his fleeing to the pit.
• The Law provided cities of refuge for someone who killed by accident, but not for a deliberate murderer. The elders were to hand such a man over to justice, and "Your eye shall not pity him" (Deuteronomy 19:11–13; compare Numbers 35:16–25).
• Joab took hold of the horns of the altar after shedding innocent blood, but Solomon did not let even the altar shelter him (1 Kings 2:28–34; compare Exodus 21:14).
• Bridges holds both sides of the verse together. On justice: "Let God's law take its course." On the guilty man himself: "Yet we must not cast off his soul."
• Compare 1:16–18; 6:16–17; Genesis 9:6.
units.summary: The guilt of innocent blood drives a man toward the grave; let no one stand in justice's way.
units.principle: Justice for innocent blood must not be obstructed, yet no guilt lies beyond the reach of God's mercy for the one who confesses.
units.insight: After killing Abel, Cain became "a fugitive and a vagabond" (Genesis 4:12), the first man to carry this burden. Scripture does not soften the guilt of bloodshed. Yet it also records killers who found mercy. David arranged Uriah's death, and when he confessed, Nathan said, "The LORD also has put away your sin" (2 Samuel 12:13). Saul of Tarsus consented to Stephen's death and later called himself the chief of sinners, saved by grace (Acts 8:1; 1 Timothy 1:15). Mercy did not cancel the earthly consequences for David, but it reached his soul. That is the balance of this verse: let justice run its course, and still bring the gospel to the guilty. Christ's blood "speaks better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:24).
units.application: If you know of violence or abuse, do not help cover it up out of loyalty, fear or family pressure; report it to those responsible for justice. Church leaders: protect victims first, cooperate fully with the authorities, and never treat forgiveness as a reason to hide a crime. If you carry the guilt of a grave wrong, bring it into the light before God and the proper authorities. Mercy is still offered to you.

rel.note: Whoever walks with integrity walks securely, but whoever perverts his ways will become known.
The righteousness of the blameless directs his way, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness.
The blameless will inherit good, while the corrupter falls into his own pit.
The same two figures, the poor man of integrity and the man perverse in his ways, now with their outcomes.
The hardened man will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.

units.notes:
• *Perverse in his ways* is the same Hebrew expression as in 28:6, with "ways" in the form used for pairs: the man is trying to walk two roads at once.
• *Suddenly* is literally "in one," understood as "all at once"; the KJV has "shall fall at once." The fall of the double-minded man comes in a single stroke.
• Ironside: "It is not the salvation of the soul that is here contemplated." The "saving" here is practical: being kept, day by day, from failure and sin and the sorrows they bring.
• Henry on the upright: "They may be injured, but they cannot be hurt." Others may wrong them, but they cannot do them lasting harm.
• Compare 10:9; 11:5; 28:10; Psalm 15:1–2; 26:11.
units.summary: Integrity is a road that keeps you; a double life is a cliff edge that gives way all at once.
units.principle: A life of integrity is a safer road than a double life, whose collapse often comes suddenly and without warning.
units.insight: Gehazi lived a double life for one afternoon. He chased Naaman to collect the gifts Elisha had refused, hid them, and lied to his master's face, and he walked out a leper (2 Kings 5:20–27). Ananias and Sapphira kept up a generous image while holding back part of the price, and both fell dead the same day (Acts 5:1–10). By contrast, Daniel's enemies searched his life and "could find no charge or fault" (Daniel 6:4). Where are you walking two roads, one for church and another for the rest of the week? Even the upright still need mercy. David, who walked in integrity, prayed, "Redeem me and be merciful to me" (Psalm 26:11). Christ alone walked perfectly blameless, and in Him the double-minded can be made whole.
units.application: Look for the places where your private life and public face do not match, such as your browsing history, your expense reports or the way you speak about people behind their backs, and bring them into line this week. Leaders: build accountability before you need it. Parents: let your children see at home the same person the church sees on Sunday. If you think a hidden compromise is safe, remember that crooked roads often give way without warning.

rel.note: Nearly the same saying: the one who tills his land will be satisfied with bread, but the one who follows frivolity lacks understanding.
In all labor there is profit, but idle chatter leads only to poverty.
The next step in the section sets steady faithfulness against haste to be rich.
The man who hastens after riches does not see that poverty is coming, the "poverty enough" of the frivolous.

units.notes:
• The same Hebrew verb, meaning to be satisfied or to have one's fill, stands behind "will have plenty of bread" and "will have poverty enough." The worker is filled with bread; the dreamer is filled with want. The repeated verb gives the contrast its ironic edge.
• *Frivolity* translates a word for empty, worthless things. The KJV reads "vain persons," meaning worthless companions. Either way, the man is chasing what has no substance.
• Bridges: "The blessing comes, not by miracle, to encourage sloth; but in use of means, to stimulate exertion." God's blessing usually comes through ordinary work, not around it.
• The prodigal son shows the second line. He left a home where there was "bread enough and to spare" and ended up saying, "I perish with hunger!" (Luke 15:17).
• Compare 12:11; 14:23; 24:30–34; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12.
units.summary: Till your own field and you fill up on bread; chase empty dreams and you fill up on want.
units.principle: Faithful work on what God has entrusted to us is the ordinary path to provision, while chasing empty things fills a life with want.
units.insight: Before sin entered the world, God put Adam in the garden "to tend and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Work is part of God's good design, not only a result of the curse. The proverb warns against despising ordinary faithfulness while chasing the scheme, the shortcut or the crowd with big talk and no fruit. Paul told the Thessalonians to "work in quietness and eat their own bread" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). The principle reaches the spiritual life too. A believer who keeps tilling the field of Scripture and prayer is fed, while one who drifts after empty things grows thin. Are you tending your own field, or watching someone else's dream? In Nazareth Jesus was known as "the carpenter" (Mark 6:3). Before He had preached a sermon, the Father said at His baptism, "You are My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mark 1:11). Ordinary faithfulness pleases God.
units.application: If you are drawn to quick-money schemes, online hype or a crowd that talks big and produces little, step back and invest in the work actually in front of you. Young adults: learn a skill, show up and finish what you start; steady work builds more than any shortcut. Parents: give your children real responsibilities at home. If you are out of work through no fault of your own, take heart: this proverb describes a pattern, not a verdict on you.

rel.note: Wealth gained by dishonesty will be diminished, but whoever gathers by labor will increase.
The plans of the diligent lead to plenty, but everyone who is hasty comes to poverty.
Steady work on one's own field yields bread, the ordinary faithfulness this verse blesses.
Completes the portrait: the man with an evil eye hastens after riches and does not see poverty coming.
Wealth piled up by usury does not stay with the one who gathered it, one way haste for gain goes unpunished.

units.notes:
• *Will not go unpunished* is literally "will not be innocent." The KJV reads "shall not be innocent," with "unpunished" in its margin. The man in a hurry for wealth rarely stays clean.
• The contrast is carefully drawn. The faithful man is set against the man who "hastens to be rich," not against the rich as such. Wealth can come by God's blessing (10:22); haste for it is the danger.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "While not condemning possessions in themselves, Proverbs always rejects greed."
• Bridges on the faithful man: "He would rather be poor by Providence, than rich by sin." In other words, he would rather accept the little God gives than gain much by doing wrong.
• Compare 13:11; 20:21; 21:5; 1 Timothy 6:9–10.
units.summary: Faithfulness gathers blessings slowly; haste for riches gathers trouble fast.
units.principle: God blesses steady faithfulness in many ways, while the rush to get rich draws a person into wrongs that do not go unpunished.
units.insight: Jacob served Laban faithfully for twenty years. Laban changed his wages ten times, yet God prospered Jacob (Genesis 31:7–9, 41). Judas went to the chief priests and asked, "What are you willing to give me if I deliver Him to you?" (Matthew 26:15). The silver brought him only anguish (Matthew 27:3–5). Jesus praised the servant who was "faithful over a few things" (Matthew 25:21). Faithfulness is measured in small things kept over long seasons. The proverb searches what drives us. Are we impatient to have now what God may give later, or not at all? Christ is the faithful One. "For the joy that was set before Him" He "endured the cross, despising the shame" (Hebrews 12:2). He did not seize glory in haste, and the Father highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:9).
units.application: Employees and business owners: choose the slower honest path over the fast questionable one, whether that means refusing to inflate numbers or turning down a deal that depends on cutting corners. If you feel pressure to "get ahead" quickly, examine where it comes from: envy, fear or comparison. Young people: be faithful now in small jobs and small amounts of money. Count blessings other than money, such as a good name and trusted friendships.

rel.note: A wicked man accepts a bribe behind the back to pervert the ways of justice.
It is not good to show partiality to the wicked or to overthrow the righteous in judgment.
It is not good to show partiality in judgment.
The king who receives bribes overthrows the land he should establish.

units.notes:
• *Show partiality* is literally "to recognize faces"; the YLT has "To discern faces." The phrase describes judging a case by the person instead of by the facts.
• The Law set the standard: "You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great" (Deuteronomy 1:17).
• Ezekiel condemned women who prophesied lies to God's people "for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread" (Ezekiel 13:19).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, on how cheap corruption can become: "The price can go still lower."
• Henry: "Those that are partial will be paltry." In other words, once a person starts favoring people for gain, he soon sells his judgment for trifles.
• Compare 17:23; 18:5; James 2:1–4.
units.summary: Partiality rarely starts with a fortune; a crust of bread can be enough to bend a judgment.
units.principle: Justice must not bend to faces or favors, because a conscience that bends for a small gain will soon bend for anything.
units.insight: Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34), and Hebrews remembers him as one "who for one morsel of food sold his birthright" (Hebrews 12:16). James rebukes churches that give the rich man a good seat and tell the poor man to stand (James 2:1–4). The verse searches the small ways we tilt toward people who can do something for us: the donor, the boss, the attractive, the influential. God is not like that. "God shows no partiality" (Acts 10:34), and the gospel itself is God's refusal to judge by faces. Christ welcomed tax collectors and lepers, and even His enemies admitted, "You do not regard the person of men" (Mark 12:14). He calls His people to judge with the same fairness.
units.application: If you make decisions about others, as a supervisor, teacher, coach, referee, parent or church leader, ask whether anyone gets a better hearing because of what they can do for you. Turn down small gifts or favors that come with strings. At church, greet the newcomer who has nothing to offer as warmly as the influential member. Parents: settle your children's disputes on the facts, not on which child is easiest to please.

rel.note: The generous eye is blessed because it gives bread to the poor.
Do not overwork to be rich, for riches make themselves wings and fly away.
The same "evil eye," translated "miser," describes the stingy host.
The one who chases empty things "will have poverty enough," the same poverty the hasty man does not see coming.
Opens the warning this verse completes: the one who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.
The one who gives to the poor will not lack, the opposite of the grasping man whom poverty overtakes.

units.notes:
• *An evil eye* is the Hebrew expression behind the "miser" of 23:6, and its opposite is the "generous eye," literally a good eye, of 22:9. The ESV renders it "stingy" here. Jesus used the same picture for greed and generosity (Matthew 6:22–23; 20:15).
• Paul's warning echoes this verse: "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition" (1 Timothy 6:9).
• Henry: "while they are making haste to be rich they are really making haste to be poor."
• *Does not consider*: the man never stops to think. Riches "make themselves wings" (23:5), but he is too busy chasing to notice.
• Compare 22:9; 23:4–6; 28:20, 27.
units.summary: The man racing toward riches does not see poverty running to meet him.
units.principle: Greed that rushes after wealth blinds a person to the poverty it is bringing, while a generous eye sees both God's provision and a neighbor's need.
units.insight: Lot lifted his eyes, saw the well-watered plain of the Jordan and chose it for himself (Genesis 13:10–11). Step by step he moved toward Sodom, and he ended up fleeing with almost nothing and living in a cave (Genesis 19:30). Abraham let Lot choose first, and God gave Abraham the whole land (Genesis 13:14–17). The evil eye always sees what it lacks and never what it has. Jesus warned, "Take heed and beware of covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses" (Luke 12:15). Ask where your eye has been resting: on what others have, on the next purchase, on the deal that will finally be enough. Christ frees the grasping heart by giving it a treasure no one can take, for "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21).
units.application: Before your next big financial decision, ask whether you are hurrying because of a real need or because you want more than others have. If you feel envy every time a friend buys something new, practice thanking God for what you already have. Business owners and investors: be wary of any opportunity whose main appeal is speed. Parents: let your children see you give generously, not only acquire.

rel.note: A flattering mouth works ruin.
Open rebuke is better than concealed love; faithful are the wounds of a friend.
Those who keep the law contend with the wicked, the same courage to confront what is wrong.
The flatterer spreads a net for his neighbor's feet, the harm behind his pleasant words.
Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you, the "favor afterward" this verse describes.

units.notes:
• *Afterward* is the key word. A rebuke is measured over time, not in the moment; the favor it earns usually comes later, once the sting has passed and the benefit is clear.
• Henry: "He that cries out against his surgeon for hurting him when he is searching his wound will yet pay him well, and thank him too, when he has cured it."
• Dr. South, quoted by Bridges: "Few people have the wisdom to like reproofs that would do them good, better than praises that do them hurt."
• Paul rebuked Peter to his face at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14), yet years later Peter wrote of "our beloved brother Paul" (2 Peter 3:15).
• Compare 9:8; 27:5–6; 29:5; Psalm 141:5.
units.summary: Flattery wins applause today; faithful rebuke wins gratitude that lasts.
units.principle: Truth spoken in love may cost favor at first, but it earns a deeper and more lasting trust than flattery ever can.
units.insight: Nathan risked a king's anger to tell David, "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). David repented, and Psalm 51, written "when Nathan the prophet went to him," still helps sinners pray. Jesus' sharpest words to Peter, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23), came from love, and Peter followed Him to the end. The verse asks two things. Do you love people enough to risk their displeasure? And can you receive correction without punishing the one who brings it? Rebuke given in the spirit of Christ is gentle (Galatians 6:1), well timed and aimed at restoring a person, not winning an argument. Christ wounds in order to heal: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Revelation 3:19).
units.application: If a friend, child or coworker is heading somewhere harmful, speak up this week, privately, gently and specifically, after praying. Do not wait until you are angry. Leaders: reward the people who tell you hard truths, and notice whether your team only ever agrees with you. When someone corrects you, thank them before you defend yourself, then take a day to weigh what they said.

rel.note: The son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother causes shame and brings reproach.
Whoever curses father or mother will have his lamp put out in deep darkness.
The deceiver who says "I was only joking!" adds an excuse to his wrong, as the robber says "It is no transgression."
Another son who shames his father, there through the company he keeps.
Agur describes a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother.

units.notes:
• *Companion to a destroyer*: the son who calls his theft "no transgression" is placed in the company of those who ruin and destroy. The KJV has "the companion of a destroyer." A similar saying calls the slacker "a brother to him who is a great destroyer" (18:9): whether by theft or by neglect, he ruins what others built.
• Jesus exposed a religious form of this sin. Some declared their money "Corban," a gift devoted to God, and so refused to support their parents (Mark 7:10–13; Matthew 15:4–6).
