• Henry gives the son's excuses in his own words: "It is no transgression, for it will be our own shortly, our parents can well enough spare it."
• Honoring parents carries a promise: "Honor your father and mother ... that it may be well with you" (Ephesians 6:2–3).
• Compare 19:26; 20:20; 30:11, 17; 1 Timothy 5:4.
units.summary: Stealing from your parents is still stealing, however you excuse it.
units.principle: A wrong done within the family is still a wrong, and excuses that rename sin only add to its guilt.
units.insight: Micah stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his mother and admitted it only after hearing her curse the thief (Judges 17:1–2). Absalom went further and "stole the hearts of the men of Israel," taking his father's kingdom (2 Samuel 15:6). We are skilled at renaming sin, especially at home: "borrowing," "it's family money," "they owe me." Honoring parents includes their property, their time and, as they grow old, their care (1 Timothy 5:4). See how Jesus honored His mother. While He hung on the cross bearing the sins of the world, He made sure she would be cared for, saying to John, "Behold your mother!" (John 19:26–27). The Son who gave everything shows what children owe their parents.
units.application: Adult children: if you handle your parents' money, property or care, keep clear records, ask permission, and never treat their resources as yours before they are. If you have taken something from your parents and called it nothing, name it, return it and ask forgiveness. Young people: respect your parents' things and their trust. Families: talk openly about money and inheritance so that resentment and excuses have no room to grow.

rel.note: By pride comes nothing but strife.
Whoever trusts in the LORD, happy is he.
Trust appears again, this time misplaced in one's own heart.
Whoever trusts in the LORD shall be safe.

units.notes:
• *Of a proud heart* is literally "wide of soul." The Hebrew word for soul can also mean appetite or desire, so the phrase pictures a desire that is never full. The ESV renders it "greedy," the NASB "arrogant"; the NKJV and KJV read "proud heart."
• *Will be prospered* is literally "will be made fat"; the KJV has "shall be made fat." In a land that often knew hunger, fatness pictured plenty and well-being. The same verb appears in 11:25, where the KJV reads "The liberal soul shall be made fat" and the NKJV "The generous soul will be made rich."
• *Trusts* is the verb behind the boldness of the righteous in 28:1, and it returns in 28:26 for the fool who trusts his own heart. Proverbs asks not whether a person trusts, but in what.
• Bridges: "It shews that pride is the root of unbelief." The proud man grasps because he does not believe God will provide.
• Compare 13:10; 16:20; 29:25; James 4:1–2.
units.summary: A grasping heart starts fights to get more; a trusting heart rests and receives from God.
units.principle: Pride grasps and quarrels to secure its own good, while trust in the LORD rests in His provision and finds peace.
units.insight: Haman had wealth, honor and the king's favor, yet because Mordecai would not bow, he said, "all this avails me nothing" (Esther 5:11–13). His wounded pride stirred up a plot against a whole people. Diotrephes "loves to have the preeminence," and he put believers out of the church (3 John 9–10). Even the disciples argued on the road about "who would be the greatest" while Jesus was speaking of His cross (Mark 9:31–34). James traces our fights to desires at war within us (James 4:1–2). Where are you striving to secure something for yourself? Ask what you are afraid God will not give. Christ shows the trusting heart. He did not grasp at equality with God but humbled Himself, and the Father exalted Him (Philippians 2:6–9). Those who rest in Him can stop fighting for their place.
units.application: Before your next argument at home, at work or in a church meeting, ask, "What am I trying to get, and do I trust God for it?" If you keep finding yourself in conflict, look for the pride underneath: the need to be right, recognized or ahead. Leaders: refuse to compete with the people you serve. When you feel overlooked, take it to God in prayer instead of taking it out on others.

rel.note: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but whoever heeds counsel is wise.
The rich man wise in his own eyes is one example of trusting one's own heart.
Trust in the LORD stands opposite trust in one's own heart.
Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding.
Keep your heart with all diligence: the heart is to be guarded, not simply followed.

units.notes:
• *Trusts* is the same verb as in 28:25, "he who trusts in the LORD." Side by side, the two verses name the two places a person can rest his confidence: the LORD or himself.
• Jeremiah gives the reason: "The heart is deceitful above all things, And desperately wicked; Who can know it?" (Jeremiah 17:9).
• Bridges: "To trust an impostor, who has deceived us an hundred times ... is surely to deserve the name of fool." The impostor he means is our own heart.
• Jesus' story of the two builders makes the same contrast: the one who hears His words and does them builds on rock, while the other builds on sand (Matthew 7:24–27).
• Compare 3:5–7; 4:23; 12:15; 14:12.
units.summary: Follow your heart, and you follow the one guide that has fooled you most often.
units.principle: The human heart is not a safe final guide; deliverance comes to those who let God's wisdom direct their steps.
units.insight: Our culture says, "Follow your heart." Scripture says to guard it. Solomon, the wisest of men, followed his heart after foreign wives and their gods, and "his heart was not loyal to the LORD his God" (1 Kings 11:4). Peter trusted his own courage, "I will lay down my life for Your sake" (John 13:37), and denied his Lord before dawn. If they could be misled by their own hearts, so can we. This is not a call to despise feelings but to submit them to God. The good news is that God does not leave us alone with our hearts. He gives His word and His Spirit, and He promised a covenant in which He would write His law on His people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Those who walk by His wisdom are delivered.
units.application: Before a major decision about a relationship, a job or a move, write down what Scripture says, what wise counselors say and what your feelings say, and do not let the last outvote the first two. Young people: when you hear "just follow your heart," ask who is guiding your heart. Parents: teach your children to test their feelings against God's word. Mentors: ask good questions instead of simply affirming whatever someone feels.

rel.note: Pity on the poor is a loan to the LORD, who will repay it.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry himself and not be heard.
The one with a generous eye will be blessed, for he gives of his bread to the poor.
The grasping man is overtaken by poverty, while the giver does not lack.
Wealth taken by usury ends up with the one who pities the poor.

units.notes:
• *Hides his eyes* pictures a deliberate choice not to look. Morgan, quoted by Guzik: "To hide the eyes means to refuse to see poverty."
• Hiding runs through the chapter: people hide from wicked rulers (28:12, 28), the sinner covers his sins (28:13), and here a man hides his own eyes from need.
• The widow of Zarephath shared her last flour with Elijah, and "The bin of flour was not used up, nor did the jar of oil run dry" (1 Kings 17:16).
• Henry: "What we gave we have." What is given in love is not lost.
• Compare 11:24–25; 19:17; 21:13; 22:9; 2 Corinthians 9:6–8.
units.summary: The hand that opens to the poor rests in God's care; the eye that looks away gathers curses.
units.principle: God cares for those who open their hands to the poor, and deliberately looking away from need is a sin, not a neutral choice.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable, a priest and a Levite saw the wounded man and "passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31–32). Hiding the eyes is often that simple: crossing the street, scrolling past, changing the subject. Nabal refused bread to David's hungry men, and only Abigail's generosity kept his household from disaster (1 Samuel 25:10–35). The verse searches what we choose not to see. Often we look away because seeing would cost us something. Christ did the opposite. When He saw the multitudes, "He was moved with compassion for them" (Matthew 9:36), and in the end He gave Himself. People who have received such grace can give freely, trusting their Father to supply what they need (Philippians 4:19).
units.application: This week, do not look away from one need you would normally pass by: the coworker who is struggling, the neighbor who is alone, the person asking for help. Give something real, such as time, money or a meal. Families: decide together how you will give regularly, so generosity is planned and not only impulsive. If you fear that giving will leave you short, start small and give in faith, not as an investment that must pay you back.

rel.note: When the wicked perish, there is jubilation.
Its second line is repeated here almost exactly, so the two verses frame the chapter.
When the wicked are multiplied transgression increases, but the righteous will see their fall.
When the righteous are in authority the people rejoice; when a wicked man rules they groan.

units.notes:
• The first line repeats the second line of 28:12 almost exactly, so the chapter is framed by sayings about the rise of the wicked and the hiding of ordinary people. The next chapter continues the theme in 29:2 and 29:16.
• *Increase* means to grow many. When the wicked are removed, the righteous come out of hiding and multiply in number and influence.
• Bridges: "The power of the wicked even here however is but for a moment."
• After Herod persecuted the church and died under God's judgment, "the word of God grew and multiplied" (Acts 12:23–24).
• Compare 11:10; 29:2, 16; Psalm 37:10–11, 35–36.
units.summary: The wicked can drive good people into hiding, but they cannot keep them there forever.
units.principle: Wicked power can force the righteous into hiding for a season, but God sets limits on it, and when it falls His people flourish again.
units.insight: Under Haman's decree the Jews faced destruction, but when Haman fell, "many of the people of the land became Jews" (Esther 8:17). Ahaz shut the doors of the LORD's house, and his son Hezekiah, whose men later copied these proverbs (25:1), opened them in the first month of his reign (2 Chronicles 28:24; 29:3). Herod killed James and imprisoned Peter, then died under God's hand, and the church grew (Acts 12:1–2, 23–24). The verse speaks to anyone living through a dark season, under a hostile boss, a corrupt government or pressure on their faith. Wicked power is real, but it is temporary. The final fulfillment lies ahead. Christ will put an end to every opposing rule and authority (1 Corinthians 15:24), and "the righteous will shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father" (Matthew 13:43).
units.application: If you live under a harsh authority at work, in your community or in your nation, keep doing right, pray, and wait with hope instead of despair. When a season of oppression ends, step back into the open: serve, speak and rebuild. Church members and leaders: when freedom returns, use it to strengthen what is good instead of settling scores. Parents: teach your children that God, not the powerful, has the last word.

rel.note: Wisdom warns that those who despise her every rebuke will eat the fruit of their own way.
The door of mercy stays open for the one who confesses and forsakes his sin, which keeps the warning hopeful.
The one who hardens his heart will fall into calamity, the same end as the hardened neck.
The servant who understands but will not respond shows the same refusal that hardens the neck.
The troublemaker's end uses nearly the same words: suddenly broken, without remedy.

units.notes:
• "Often rebuked" is literally "a man of reproofs" in Hebrew, a person marked by correction received again and again. The 1611 KJV gives this wording in its margin. The word for reproof, tokachat, is the "rebuke" Wisdom offered and the scornful refused in 1:23–30.
• "Hardens his neck" pictures an ox stiffening against the yoke. The LORD called Israel "a stiff-necked people" at the golden calf (Exodus 32:9), and Stephen brought the same charge against the council (Acts 7:51).
• "Without remedy" translates marpe, a word for healing; the same word is rendered "health" in 4:22 and 12:18. The ruin is a wound that will not heal. The line nearly repeats 6:15, "Suddenly he shall be broken without remedy," and the ESV and YLT also say "broken" here.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The opposite of the stiff neck would be a bending neck, i.e., submission."
• Compare 1:24–31; 15:32; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16, where God's warnings were mocked "till there was no remedy"; Hebrews 3:13–15.
units.summary: Every rebuke is a door held open, and the man who keeps refusing will one day find it shut.
units.principle: Correction refused again and again hardens the heart toward sudden ruin, so the time to turn is while the warning is still being given.
units.insight: Pharaoh shows how hardening works. Plague after plague came as warning, and each time he hardened his heart again, until the sea closed over his army (Exodus 14:28). Eli's sons "did not heed the voice of their father," and both died on the same day, as the LORD had warned (1 Samuel 2:25, 34; 4:11). Jesus wept over a city that had heard prophet after prophet: "How often I wanted to gather your children together… but you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37). Bridges: "Truly Divine patience has its end." Yet patience has not ended for anyone still hearing the rebuke. The question is not whether you have been warned, but what you are doing with the warning in front of you now. The Spirit still says "Today" (Hebrews 3:15), and Christ still receives everyone who turns.
units.application: If the same correction keeps reaching you from different directions, such as a spouse, a friend, an elder or your own conscience, stop defending yourself and ask God whether it is true. Act on one long-ignored rebuke this week. Parents, when a teenager keeps hearing the same warning, pray for a soft heart more than for outward compliance. Leaders, ask the people closest to you what they have stopped telling you, and do not punish the answer.

rel.note: A city rejoices when it goes well with the righteous, showing the public joy of righteous influence.
The rise of the righteous brings glory, while the rise of the wicked sends people into hiding.
When the wicked perish the righteous increase, the same shift in public life this verse describes.
The opposite increase, of the wicked, multiplies transgression, though the righteous will see their fall.

units.notes:
• "Are in authority" is literally "increase" (rabah); the ESV and NASB read "increase," and the KJV margin "increased." The same word describes the wicked being "multiplied" in 29:16, so the two sayings answer each other across the chapter.
• "Groan" (KJV "mourn") is the sigh of people under a heavy load. When Israel cried out under Pharaoh, "God heard their groaning" (Exodus 2:24).
• Esther shows both halves of the verse. When Haman's decree went out, "the city of Shushan was perplexed"; when Mordecai was honored, "the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad" (Esther 3:15; 8:15).
• Bridges: "The tyrant rules for his own sinful ends. The Christian sovereign for the good of the people."
• Compare 11:10; 28:12, 28; 2 Samuel 23:3–4; 1 Timothy 2:1–2.
units.summary: You can measure a ruler by the sound his people make: rejoicing or groaning.
units.principle: Authority is measured by what it does to the people under it: righteous rule brings joy, and self-serving rule brings groaning.
units.insight: David's last words describe the ruler this verse celebrates: "He who rules over men must be just, Ruling in the fear of God," and such a ruler is like morning light after rain (2 Samuel 23:3–4). His grandson Rehoboam chose the opposite. When the people asked relief from a heavy yoke, he promised a heavier one, and the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:4, 14–16). Most of us hold some authority, over children, employees, a classroom or a ministry team. What would the people under us say if they spoke freely? Do they breathe easier when we arrive, or tense up? Scripture holds out one King whose rule brings unmixed joy. Of the increase of His government and peace "there will be no end," and His kingdom is established "with judgment and justice" (Isaiah 9:7). Under Him even the groaning creation will be set free (Romans 8:21–22).
units.application: If you lead at work, at church or at home, ask what your people feel when you walk in: relief or dread. Then fix one thing that makes them groan. Pray by name for those who govern, whatever their party (1 Timothy 2:1–2). If you live or work under a leader who burdens people, do not lose heart. God hears groaning, and your own faithful conduct is a piece of righteous influence where you are.

rel.note: A wise son makes a glad father, the theme of this verse's first line.
A son's companions again decide whether his father is gladdened or shamed.
Going near the immoral woman's house gives away strength and wealth to strangers.
The father's earlier warning that a harlot reduces a man to a crust of bread explains the waste.

units.notes:
• "Companion" is the same word used in 28:7 ("a companion of gluttons") and 13:20 ("the companion of fools"). In each saying a man's chosen company both reveals and shapes his character.
• "Wastes his wealth" is "spendeth his substance" in the KJV. Compare 5:10, where the immoral woman leaves strangers "filled with your wealth."
• Jesus' parable pictures the same waste. The younger son "wasted his possessions with prodigal living" (Luke 15:13), and his angry brother later charged that he had "devoured your livelihood with harlots" (Luke 15:30). That charge is the brother's accusation within the story, not the narrator's report.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "it would break a father's heart to see his son become a pauper through vice."
• Compare 5:8–11; 23:15–16, 24–25; 27:11; 1 Corinthians 6:18.
units.summary: A son's loves set his course: love wisdom and gladden a father, love harlots and lose everything.
units.principle: What a person loves shapes the company he keeps and the life he builds; love for wisdom blesses a family, while sexual sin squanders what God has given.
units.insight: Samson shows how sexual sin drains a strong man. He went in to a harlot at Gaza, later gave his secret to Delilah, and ended blind and grinding grain in a Philistine prison (Judges 16:1, 21). The waste is never only money. It is strength, sight, years and the joy of a father's house. Yet the deeper question of this verse is what we love. No one drifts toward wisdom; we go after what our hearts want. So it is not enough to fear the harlot's house. We need a stronger love. The parable of the prodigal turns on a father rejoicing, not over a son who never strayed, but over one who came home: "this my son was dead and is alive again" (Luke 15:24). The heavenly Father's joy is still open to anyone who turns from wasted years.
units.application: Young men, look at your friendships and your screens: what company is shaping your desires? Cut off one source of sexual temptation this week, and seek out one wise older man to walk with. Parents, tell your children specifically when their choices make you glad, not only when they disappoint you. If you have wasted money or years through sexual sin, do not stay in the far country. Confess it to God and to a trusted believer, and come home.

rel.note: The one who hates bribes will live, while greed for gain troubles his own house.
A throne is established by righteousness, as the land is established by justice.
A bribe taken in secret perverts the ways of justice, the corruption that overthrows a land.
The king who judges the poor with truth has an established throne, the same stability seen from the side of the weak.

units.notes:
• "He who receives bribes" is literally "a man of contributions" (terumot). The word is often used for offerings brought to the LORD, which is why the 1611 KJV margin reads "a man of oblations." Here it most likely describes a ruler who demands gifts or payments for himself. The NKJV and NASB read "bribes"; the ESV reads "exacts gifts," pointing to heavy demands laid on the people.
• Samuel's sons show the overthrow. They "took bribes, and perverted justice," and Israel's elders used that corruption as their reason to demand a king (1 Samuel 8:3–5).
• Bridges: "Of what avail are the best laws, if they be badly administered?"
• Compare 16:12; 17:23; 20:8; 25:5; Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19.
units.summary: Justice holds a nation up; bribes pull it down from the top.
units.principle: Stability in any community rests on justice that cannot be bought; when those in charge sell their judgment, everything under them begins to give way.
units.insight: When King Jehoshaphat appointed judges, he told them why bribes were unthinkable: "there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, no partiality, nor taking of bribes" (2 Chronicles 19:7). Human judges were to reflect the Judge of all. Felix shows the opposite. He kept Paul in prison for two years, hoping Paul would pay for his release (Acts 24:26–27). Few of us are offered envelopes of cash, but the same sin works in smaller ways. We favor the person who praises us, gives to our cause or can do something for us in return (James 2:1–4). The gospel exposes this, because no one could buy God's favor. We were redeemed "not with corruptible things, like silver or gold," but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). His kingdom cannot be bought, and His scepter is "a scepter of righteousness" (Hebrews 1:8).
units.application: If you hold any decision-making role, as a manager, board member, elder or official, refuse gifts or favors that could bend your judgment, and disclose any conflict of interest. Parents, settle your children's disputes on the facts, not by who pleads loudest or pleases you most. Employees, if you are asked to look away from a kickback or a doctored report, say no. Small corruption is how a whole organization is overthrown.

rel.note: The one who sets a trap often falls into it himself, which explains why the net may catch the flatterer.
A flattering mouth works ruin, the same harm pictured here as a net.
The faithful wounds of a friend stand against the pleasant but deceitful words of an enemy.
Honest rebuke wins more favor in the end than flattering words.
The next saying continues the trap image: the evil man is snared by his own transgression.

units.notes:
• "Flatters" comes from chalaq, a word meaning smooth or slippery. The same word describes the immoral woman's mouth, "smoother than oil" (5:3), and the "flattering mouth" of 26:28.
• The NASB reads "his steps" where the NKJV has "his feet," keeping the picture of a trap laid along the path a person walks.
• Older interpreters read "his feet" two ways: the neighbor's, whom the flatterer means to use or puff up, and the flatterer's own, since insincere praise often turns back on the one who gives it.
• Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "Beware of a flatterer; he does not flatter merely to please you, but to deceive you and profit himself."
• Compare 26:28; 27:6; 28:23; Psalm 12:2–3; Romans 16:18; 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
units.summary: Flattery feels like a gift but works like a trap laid across someone's path.
units.principle: Praise that is not true is not kindness; it lays a trap for the one who believes it, whatever the speaker hopes to gain.
units.insight: The enemies of Jesus once came with smooth words: "Teacher, we know that You are true, and teach the way of God in truth" (Matthew 22:16). The praise was bait for a trap about taxes. Jesus "perceived their wickedness" and walked straight through the net (Matthew 22:18). Herod was not so wise. When a crowd shouted that his voice was "the voice of a god and not of a man," he accepted it, and an angel of the Lord struck him (Acts 12:22–23). Ironside describes flattering words as "but as fuel to the fire of pride": they only feed a pride already burning in us. That is why flattery works: part of us wants to believe it. Before we blame the flatterer, we need to ask why we enjoy his words so much, and whether we ourselves use praise to get what we want from others.
units.application: When someone praises you lavishly and then asks for something, separate the two and judge the request on its own merits. Leaders and pastors, keep close the people who tell you the truth, and be wary of those who only admire. Parents and managers, praise specific, real things instead of inflating. Before you compliment anyone this week, ask two questions: Is it true? Is it for their good or for mine?

rel.note: The wicked is ensnared by his own transgression, while the righteous come through trouble.
The guilty flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold, free of the fear sin creates.
The same word for snare names the trap set by the fear of man.
The flatterer's net leads straight into this saying about the snare hidden in sin.
The wicked man's own iniquities entrap him and hold him in the cords of his sin.

units.notes:
• The KJV keeps the Hebrew word order: "In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare." The wording puts the trap inside the sin, not beside it.
• "Snare" (moqesh) is a hunter's noose or trap. The same word returns in 29:25, "The fear of man brings a snare," so the chapter names two traps: one built by sin, one by fear.
• Ronald Knox's translation, quoted by Kidner and cited by Guzik, renders the second line: "innocence goes singing and rejoicing on its way."
• Compare 5:22; 11:6; 12:13; 28:1; Psalm 7:15–16.
units.summary: Sin needs no hunter, for it is its own trap; a clear conscience leaves the heart free to sing.
units.principle: Sin carries its own trap and binds the one who commits it, while a life lived openly before God is free to rejoice even in trouble.
units.insight: Two scenes show the contrast. Joseph's brothers, years after selling him, stood accused before a stern Egyptian governor, and their hidden sin rose up at once: "We are truly guilty concerning our brother" (Genesis 42:21). Paul and Silas sat beaten and chained in a Philippian jail, yet at midnight they "were praying and singing hymns to God" (Acts 16:25). The real prison is the one sin builds inside. David knew both. While he kept silent about his sin, "my bones grew old," but once forgiven he spoke of "songs of deliverance" (Psalm 32:3, 7). Jesus said, "whoever commits sin is a slave of sin," and then, "if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed" (John 8:34, 36). If you are tired of covering, the way out of the snare is not a better cover. It is confession to the One who sets captives free.
units.application: If you are keeping a secret sin going, such as a hidden debt, an affair or a lie at work, notice how much energy the cover-up takes. Bring it into the light this week, before God and one trusted person. Parents, show your children that confessing early is safer than hiding, by receiving their confessions with grace. When a shortcut tempts you that would need a lie to protect it, picture the snare and walk around it.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, which shows why caring to know their cause matters to God.
The LORD Himself pleads the cause of the poor who are oppressed at the gate.
The king who judges the poor with truth does at the throne what the righteous do here.
Lemuel's mother charges the king to plead the cause of the poor and needy.

units.notes:
• "Considers" is the Hebrew verb for knowing (yada), and "cause" (din) is a legal case or claim. The ESV keeps both senses: "knows the rights of the poor."
• Job described this kind of righteousness: "I was a father to the poor, And I searched out the case that I did not know" (Job 29:16).
• The LORD said of King Josiah, "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; Then it was well. Was not this knowing Me?" (Jeremiah 22:16). Knowing the poor man's cause and knowing God belong together.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "His ignorance and lack of understanding is not an intellectual defect but the expression of an evil perversion."
• Compare 14:31; 22:22–23; 31:8–9; Psalm 41:1; 82:3–4.
units.summary: The righteous take the trouble to learn the poor man's case; the wicked never care to know it.
units.principle: Righteousness does not stop at sympathy for the poor; it takes the trouble to learn their situation and to stand for what is right on their behalf.
units.insight: The priest and the Levite in Jesus' parable both saw the wounded man and "passed by on the other side" (Luke 10:31–32). They did not lack information; they chose not to know more. The Samaritan came near, looked and stayed. This verse names the wicked man's failure the same way: he does not want the knowledge, because knowing would cost him. Bridges: "Consideration of the poor is the true spirit of Christian sympathy; putting ourselves as far as may be in their place." That is what Christ did for us. "Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor" (2 Corinthians 8:9). He did not consider our case from a distance; He entered it. Each of us has to ask where we have avoided learning the details of someone's need so that we would not feel bound to act.
units.application: If you serve on a benevolence team, a school board or a jury, take time to learn the whole story before deciding, especially when the person has no advocate. Employers, find out what your lowest-paid workers face before you set policy. Church members, get to know one struggling family by name instead of giving only from a distance. Ask questions, listen to the answers, and then act on what you learn.

rel.note: The upright build a city up while the mouth of the wicked overthrows it.
A soft answer turns away wrath, the tool wise men use to calm a city.
Casting out the scoffer ends contention, the remedy for the fire this verse describes.
The contentious man kindles strife like charcoal on burning coals, the same fire image.
The next saying shows how fruitless it is to argue with the foolish once they rage or mock.

units.notes:
• "Scoffers" is literally "men of scorn," people whose settled attitude toward God, truth and authority is contempt.
• "Set a city aflame" comes from a Hebrew verb whose basic meaning is to breathe or blow. The picture is breath fanning a fire until it spreads. The KJV main text reads "bring a city into a snare," and its 1611 margin gives "set the city on fire."
• Rehoboam showed the scoffer's spirit in a ruler. When Israel asked for relief, he answered with contempt, and the northern tribes broke away (1 Kings 12:13–16).
• Henry: "Proud and foolish men kindle the fires which wise and good men must extinguish."
• Compare 11:11; 15:18; 26:20–21; Ecclesiastes 9:14–15; James 3:5–6.
units.summary: Mockers can set a whole town on fire with words; one wise voice can put the fire out.
units.principle: Contempt spreads through a community like fire, and the patient, truthful words of the wise are what put it out.
units.insight: Scripture gives a picture of this in the wise woman of Abel. Joab's army was battering her city's wall, and she called down to him, reasoned with him and saved the city (2 Samuel 20:16–22). Abigail did the same when she met David's angry men with humility and gifts and turned him back from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–33). James warns that "the tongue is a fire" (James 3:6), and every one of us has struck that match. The scoffer's spirit is easy to fall into: the sarcastic post, the eye-roll at leaders, the joke that makes a grievance burn hotter. Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9), and He is the great Peacemaker, who made peace "through the blood of His cross" (Colossians 1:20). Those who belong to Him are sent to calm fires, not to fan them.
units.application: When a church, workplace or family is heated, refuse to be the one who adds fuel. Do not forward the angry message or repeat the cutting joke. If you lead, deal early and directly with a person whose mockery keeps stirring division, as 22:10 counsels. If you are a natural peacemaker, go to the people involved with calm, truthful words. Before you post about a public controversy this week, ask whether your words will cool it or spread it.

rel.note: The fool despises wise words, so speaking into his hearing settles nothing.
The paired sayings on answering a fool show that wisdom must judge when to engage and when to stop.
The scoffers who inflame a city are the same kind of people who rage or laugh in a dispute.
Correcting a scoffer brings shame and hatred, the same dead end this verse describes.

units.notes:
• "Contends" comes from the Hebrew word for judging, so the dispute may be a case at law. Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The setting of Proverbs 29:9 is the court, in which the recklessness of the fool is given full vent."
• The Hebrew of the second line does not name who rages or laughs. The NKJV and ESV supply "the fool," and the NASB names the foolish man, while the KJV keeps the open "he rage or laugh." That open wording allows another sense: whether the wise man answers angrily or lightly, nothing is settled. Either reading ends without rest.
• The NASB and KJV render the final phrase "no rest."
• Jesus described a generation that, like the fool, would not respond to any approach, mournful or joyful: "We played the flute for you, And you did not dance; We mourned to you, And you did not lament" (Matthew 11:17). They said John had a demon and called Jesus a glutton (Matthew 11:18–19).
• Compare 9:7–8; 23:9; 26:4–5; 2 Timothy 2:23–25.
units.summary: Argue with a fool and it ends the same whether he storms or sneers: no settlement and no rest.
units.principle: Some disputes cannot be settled by better arguments, because the fool answers truth with anger or mockery; wisdom knows when to stop.
units.insight: Nehemiah met both of the fool's responses. Sanballat was furious and mocked the wall-building (Nehemiah 4:1–3), then tried to draw Nehemiah away to a meeting. Nehemiah replied, "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" (Nehemiah 6:3). He did not need to win the argument to finish the work. Jesus stood before Herod, who wanted a show and then mocked Him, and "He answered him nothing" (Luke 23:9–11). His silence there was wisdom, not weakness. The verse also asks a hard question of us. When we are corrected, do we rage or laugh it off? The fool's two responses can be ours too. Grace makes a person able to stay in the conversation, hear the truth and change. The grace that changed us can reach the fool, so we keep praying for him even when we stop arguing.
units.application: If you keep having the same argument with someone who only rages or ridicules, say your piece once, clearly and kindly, and then stop. Parents of grown children, elders and managers: you do not owe anyone an endless debate. Pray instead of answering the fifth angry email. And when you are the one being corrected, notice whether your reflex is anger or a joke, and choose to listen instead.

rel.note: The wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers, the same two responses.
The enticers who lurk to shed innocent blood are the bloodthirsty of this verse.
The call to rescue those drawn toward death describes what the upright do when they seek the blameless man's life.
The upright are an abomination to the wicked, the same hostility that ends the chapter.

units.notes:
• "Seek his life" usually describes hostility, as when Moses was told, "all the men who sought your life are dead" (Exodus 4:19), and when David asked why Saul "seeks my life" (1 Samuel 20:1). Here the upright seek the blameless man's life in order to keep him alive.
• The line is read two ways. The NKJV, NASB and NLT take it as protection of the blameless. The ESV takes "the upright" as the object of the bloodthirsty, so both lines describe hostility: they hate the blameless "and seek the life of the upright." The NKJV reading fits the contrast that usually marks the two lines of these sayings.
• "Blameless" (tam) describes a person who is whole and consistent, the word used of Job, "blameless and upright" (Job 1:1).
• Compare 1:11; 12:6; 29:27; Psalm 37:12–14, 32; John 15:18–19.
units.summary: Integrity draws two crowds: one wants the blameless man dead, and the other guards his life.
units.principle: Integrity provokes the hatred of the violent and the protection of the upright, and each response exposes the heart behind it.
units.insight: Scripture is full of both crowds. Saul hunted David, while Jonathan risked his own life to shield him (1 Samuel 20). Jezebel killed the LORD's prophets, while Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them (1 Kings 18:4). Jeremiah's enemies lowered him into a muddy cistern, and Ebed-Melech the Ethiopian pulled him out with ropes and old rags (Jeremiah 38:6–13). The upright, in Ironside's words, are "glad to be what Cain was not—their brother's keeper." At the center stands the only fully blameless Man. Jesus said, "They hated Me without a cause" (John 15:25), and men of blood called for His crucifixion. The verse asks which crowd we join. Do we quietly resent the person whose integrity makes us uncomfortable? Or do we stand beside the one who is targeted for doing right?
units.application: When a coworker is being pushed out for refusing to cut corners, stand with them openly, and put your support in writing if needed. Pastors and elders, protect members who are slandered for their faithfulness. If you notice resentment toward someone whose integrity convicts you, name it before God instead of acting on it. This week, pray for believers who face violence for their faith, and support one ministry that serves them.

rel.note: A fool's wrath is known at once, while the prudent man holds back.
Ruling one's spirit is greater strength than taking a city.
The man of understanding spares his words and keeps a calm spirit.
The man hasty in his words shows the same lack of restraint in speech.
The angry man who stirs up strife shows where unrestrained feelings lead.

units.notes:
• "Vents all his feelings" is literally "brings out all his spirit." The NASB and NLT narrow the line to anger or temper; the NKJV and ESV keep the broader sense of everything a person feels, and the KJV's "mind" is similarly broad.
• "Holds them back" translates shabach, a verb meaning to calm or still. It is used of God in "When its waves rise, You still them" (Psalm 89:9). The wise man quiets his feelings the way the LORD quiets a stormy sea. As Kidner puts it, quoted by Guzik, the verb "speaks of anger overcome, not merely checked."
• The line also contains a Hebrew word meaning "back" or "behind." Most modern versions join it to the verb ("holds them back"). The KJV and YLT read it as "till afterwards," meaning that the wise man waits for a fitting time to speak.
• Compare 12:16; 14:29; 17:27–28; Ecclesiastes 3:7; James 1:19–20.
units.summary: A fool empties every feeling onto the room; a wise man calms the storm before he speaks.
units.principle: Wisdom does not deny feelings but governs them, choosing the time and the way to express them.
units.insight: Joseph shows restraint without coldness. When his brothers stood before him, he held back his feelings, tested them, and turned aside to weep in private (Genesis 42:24). When the moment was right, he "could not restrain himself" and wept aloud as he made himself known (Genesis 45:1–2). Moses shows the cost of venting. Worn down by complaints, he cried, "Hear now, you rebels!" and struck the rock, and that outburst kept him out of the land (Numbers 20:10–12). Jesus felt fully: He wept at Lazarus's tomb and cleared the temple. Yet "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23). Self-control is the Spirit's fruit, not a personality type (Galatians 5:22–23). The question is not whether you feel strongly, but who is ruling: your feelings, or the Lord in you.
units.application: Before you send the email you wrote in anger, wait a night and read it again. Parents, when a child's behavior provokes you, quiet your own spirit first, then correct. Spouses, choose a calm time to raise what hurts instead of unloading everything in the heat of an argument. If you tend to bottle feelings up, this verse is not telling you to bury them. Pour them out to God, as the psalmists did, and then speak wisely.

rel.note: Righteous lips are the delight of kings, the opposite of a ruler who welcomes lies.
An evildoer gives heed to false lips, the same eager ear for lies.
Removing the wicked from the king's presence establishes his throne, the cure for a corrupted court.
The king who judges with truth has an established throne, while the ruler who listens to lies corrupts his whole court.

units.notes:
• The ESV renders "servants" as "officials," and the NASB reads "ministers," making clear that a ruler's court and government are in view.
• Ahab shows the pattern. He kept four hundred prophets who all told him what he wanted to hear, and he said of the one who would not, "I hate him" (1 Kings 22:6–8).
• Henry: "Lies will be told to those that will hearken to them; but the receiver, in this case, is as bad as the thief." ("Hearken" means listen.)
• Compare 16:13; 17:4; 20:28; 25:5; Psalm 101:5–7.
units.summary: A leader does not have to lie to fill his house with liars; he only has to listen to them.
units.principle: Leaders set the standard of truth for those under them by what they are willing to hear; a leader who welcomes lies will be surrounded by liars.
units.insight: Even David once listened to a lie. As he fled from Absalom, Ziba met him with supplies and a false report that Mephibosheth hoped to take the throne, and David handed Ziba his master's property on the spot (2 Samuel 16:1–4). In Psalm 101 David had resolved, "He who tells lies shall not continue in my presence" (Psalm 101:7). Every leader faces that choice, and so does every listener. We pay attention to lies whenever we enjoy a damaging report, never check it, and reward the one who brought it. The Messiah stands in contrast. Isaiah says He "shall not judge by the sight of His eyes, Nor decide by the hearing of His ears" (Isaiah 11:3). His court has no room for lies, and those who serve Him are called to share His love of truth.
units.application: If you lead a team, a ministry or a family, notice what kind of reports you reward. Thank the person who brings bad news truthfully, and refuse to act on a damaging story until you have heard the other side. When someone says, "Don't tell anyone I told you," ask whether you should be hearing it at all. Employees, do not shade the truth to please your boss; your truthfulness may be what keeps the culture from rotting.

rel.note: Oppressing the poor reproaches their Maker, the consequence of forgetting that God gives both their life.
Mocking the poor insults the God who made them.
The rich and the poor meet together because the LORD made them all, the same pattern and wording.
The next saying shows what a just king does for the poor whom God has given light.

units.notes:
• "Have this in common" is literally "meet together," as the ESV and KJV keep it; the same expression joins the rich and the poor in 22:2.
• "The oppressor" is literally "a man of oppressions," someone who takes advantage of others. The KJV reads "deceitful," with "the usurer," a lender who charges crushing interest, in its 1611 margin. Modern versions agree on "oppressor."
• Jesus spoke of the same impartial kindness: the Father "makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good" (Matthew 5:45).
• Bridges, picturing the poor man Lazarus and the rich tax collector Zacchaeus together in glory: "both alike the undeserved monuments of wondrous everlasting mercy."
• Compare 14:31; 17:5; 22:2; Job 31:13–15; Acts 10:34.
units.summary: Oppressor and oppressed see by the same borrowed light, and both will answer to the One who gives it.
units.principle: Every person, rich or poor, oppressor or oppressed, receives life from the same God, so no one has ground to despise another, and all will answer to Him.
units.insight: Jesus told of a rich man and a beggar named Lazarus who lay at the rich man's gate. The rich man did nothing for him; then both died, and both stood before God (Luke 16:19–23). The same God had given light to the eyes of both, and the one who despised that shared gift answered for it. Yet the verse also holds out hope for the oppressor. Zacchaeus had grown rich by cheating, but when Jesus came to his house, his eyes were opened. He gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold, and Jesus said, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:8–9). Think of the person you are tempted to look down on, whether the beggar on the corner or the powerful man who wronged you. Both breathe by God's gift, both answer to Him, and both can be reached by His grace.
units.application: Treat the cashier, the custodian and the person asking for help with the same respect you give the boss; each one's life is God's gift. Employers and landlords, remember that your power over others is held before a God who sees both of you. If you have been oppressed, take comfort that God has not forgotten you; He keeps your eyes alight. This week, pray for someone who has wronged you, that God would open his eyes.

rel.note: Mercy and truth preserve the king and uphold his throne.
The ruler who listens to lies corrupts his court, while the king who judges with truth is established.
The poor man's life is God's gift as much as the oppressor's, which is why the king must judge him with truth.
The king establishes the land by justice, the same stability gained by faithful judgment.
The righteous consider the cause of the poor, which a just king does from the throne.

units.notes:
• The word translated "truth," emet, also means faithfulness or reliability, which is why the ESV and KJV render "with truth" as "faithfully." The point is dependable, faithful judgment, not only accurate information.
• Psalm 72, a prayer for the king, describes this kind of reign: "He will bring justice to the poor of the people" and "He will spare the poor and needy" (Psalm 72:4, 13).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The poor are no less created in the image of God than the rich…"
• Compare 16:12; 20:28; 25:5; 29:4; 31:8–9; Jeremiah 22:15–16.
units.summary: The surest foundation for a throne is fairness to the people who can give the king nothing.
units.principle: Authority is made secure by faithful justice for those who cannot repay it, and only Christ's reign fulfills that pattern perfectly and forever.
units.insight: Solomon's best-known case came from two harlots with one living baby between them. They were women of no standing, yet the king gave them his full attention, found the truth and gave the child to its real mother. Then all Israel "feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him" (1 Kings 3:28). Justice for the lowest strengthened his throne. Solomon's kingdom later divided, but the promise points past him to a King of whose kingdom "there will be no end" (Luke 1:33). Jesus began His ministry by announcing good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). The test of this verse comes to each of us in small ways: How do we treat those who can never repay us? In Christ's kingdom, they are the ones He honors first.
units.application: If you supervise people, give the same care to the complaint of a part-time worker as to that of a senior partner or major donor. Parents and teachers, listen fully to the quiet child before siding with the confident one. Church leaders, make sure the poor have a real voice in your decisions, not only a line in your budget. This week, find one person who cannot repay you and make sure they are treated fairly.

rel.note: The parent who loves his child disciplines him promptly, while sparing the rod is a failure of love.
Correction drives out the foolishness bound up in a child's heart, the same goal of wisdom.
The chapter returns to the same theme, showing the rest and delight that correction usually brings.
The pampered servant shows the same harm in a household when care is given without training.
The LORD corrects those He loves, the pattern that keeps parental correction loving rather than harsh.

units.notes:
• "Left to himself" comes from the common Hebrew verb for sending. Its form here pictures a child sent off or let loose without restraint. The NASB (1995) interprets the phrase as a child "who gets his own way."
• "Rebuke" is tokachat, the same word for reproof used in 29:1, where the hardened man is "a man of reproofs." The chapter shows both ends of correction: received in childhood it gives wisdom, refused again and again it ends in ruin.
• The verse names the mother, as 10:1 calls a foolish son "the grief of his mother."
• Bridges: "Discipline is the order of God's government." Parents who correct with love are following the way God Himself governs His children (Hebrews 12:5–11).
• Compare 13:24; 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:17; Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21.
units.summary: Loving correction grows wisdom; a child left to himself is not free, only abandoned.
units.principle: Children grow wise through loving correction in word and deed, while neglect, not discipline, leaves them to their own folly.
units.insight: Scripture records a quiet failure behind a royal crisis. David "had not rebuked him at any time by saying, 'Why have you done so?'" and his son Adonijah grew up to try to seize the throne (1 Kings 1:5–6). Love that never says no is not love at all. Yet the opposite failure is just as real, and Paul warns fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). The model for every parent is the heavenly Father. He disciplines us "for our profit, that we may be partakers of His holiness" (Hebrews 12:10), and He never corrects in rage. Some readers were raised without guidance; others were harmed by harshness that was called discipline. Both can find in God the Father they needed, whose correction is always love. Parents who look back with regret can bring their failures to Him as well. His grace reaches both parent and child.
units.application: Parents, pair every consequence with words that explain it, so the goal is understanding, not only obedience. Never correct in anger; step away, calm down, then act. Set a few clear expectations and follow through consistently. Grandparents and mentors, support parents who are trying to correct instead of undercutting them. If you were wounded by harsh discipline, talk with a pastor or counselor and seek healing rather than repeating the pattern.

rel.note: The wicked pass like a whirlwind, while the righteous have an everlasting foundation.
Seeing the fall of the wicked gives no license to rejoice when an enemy stumbles.
Do not fret over evildoers, for the lamp of the wicked will be put out.
When the wicked arise people hide, but when they perish the righteous increase.
The increase of the righteous makes the people rejoice, the opposite increase from this verse.

units.notes:
• "Are multiplied" and "increases" translate the same Hebrew verb, rabah, so the line echoes itself: as the wicked increase, transgression increases. The ESV brings this out with "increase" in both places. The same verb lies behind "are in authority" in 29:2.
• Sayings about the rise and fall of the wicked and the increase of the righteous recur through the end of this collection (28:12, 28; 29:2, 16).
• Asaph wrestled with the problem this verse answers, the success of the wicked. He envied them until he went into God's sanctuary: "Then I understood their end" (Psalm 73:17).
• Compare 10:25; 11:10; 24:17–20; Psalm 37:34–36; Revelation 11:15.
units.summary: Evil grows louder as its numbers grow, but it never gets the last word.
units.principle: When the wicked multiply, sin multiplies with them, but God has not lost control, and His people can wait for His justice without despair or gloating.
units.insight: In Noah's day "the wickedness of man was great in the earth" (Genesis 6:5), and one family kept walking with God while the multitude went the other way. Generations later, Israel stood on the far side of the sea and "saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore" (Exodus 14:30). The oppressor who had multiplied their burdens was gone. Many believers today feel the first line of this verse more than the second, as if the news reported only increasing sin. Faith remembers that the last word belongs to God: "The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ" (Revelation 11:15). That hope does not make us gloat over anyone's fall, for we too were rescued by mercy. It makes us steady. We can keep doing right, pray for our enemies and wait for Him.
units.application: When the culture around you seems to grow darker, limit the news that feeds despair and spend that time in Psalm 37 or Psalm 73. Parents, explain to your children that God sees and will judge, so they need not copy what everyone else does. Believers in hard workplaces, keep doing right even when wrongdoing is rewarded. If you are tempted to celebrate an opponent's downfall, pray for him instead.

rel.note: Chasten your son while there is hope, the same call to timely correction.
Training a child in the way he should go is another general principle of formation, not a guarantee.
The father of a wise child delights in him, the joy described in the second line.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, the correction whose fruit this verse describes.

units.notes:
• "Delight" translates ma'adannim, a word that usually means rich, choice food. Jacob uses it of the "royal dainties" Asher's land would yield (Genesis 49:20). Applied to a son, it pictures the deep satisfaction a wise child brings a parent, like the enjoyment of a fine meal.
• The ESV reads "Discipline" for "Correct," and the NASB reads "comfort" for "rest."
• Bridges describes the balance this verse needs: discipline "not relaxed in fondness, not pushed on in harshness; but authority tempered with love."
• Compare 19:18; 22:6; 23:24–25; 29:15; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:11.
units.summary: Correction costs a parent effort now and usually repays it later in rest and delight.
units.principle: Patient, loving correction usually bears fruit in a child's character and a parent's peace, though each child remains responsible for his own choices.
units.insight: Timothy shows the fruit of patient training. From childhood he had known the Holy Scriptures, taught by his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and he grew into a man Paul could trust with churches (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). Yet Scripture also shows that the pattern is not a formula. Godly Hezekiah's son Manasseh became one of Judah's worst kings, and only after years of rebellion did he humble himself before God (2 Chronicles 33:1–2, 12–13). Parents carry real responsibility, but they cannot carry a child's heart; that belongs to God. The deeper picture is the Father Himself, who corrects His children and delights in them: "He will rejoice over you with gladness" (Zephaniah 3:17). Parents who correct in that spirit share His joy, and parents who grieve over a wandering child can rest in His care.
units.application: Parents of young children, set aside time this week to teach one clear expectation and follow through calmly, instead of reacting only when you are exhausted. When you correct, finish by restoring warmth with a hug or a word of love. Parents of teenagers, keep correcting with respect, and explain your reasons. If your grown child has strayed despite your care, stop blaming yourself for choices that were his. Keep praying, and keep the door open.

rel.note: Keeping the commandment keeps a person's soul, while carelessness of God's ways leads to death.
Whoever keeps the law is a discerning son, the blessed obedience of the second line.
The one who turns his ear from the law finds even his prayer an abomination, the opposite of keeping it.
Wisdom calls those who keep her ways and listen at her gates blessed.

units.notes:
• "Revelation" translates chazon, a vision God gives a prophet, a message from Him rather than human foresight. The ESV renders it "prophetic vision," the KJV "vision." The same word opens Isaiah's book: "The vision of Isaiah" (Isaiah 1:1).
• "Cast off restraint" comes from a verb meaning to let go or let loose; elsewhere it describes hair let down loose. The same verb describes Israel at the golden calf: "Moses saw that the people were unrestrained" (Exodus 32:25).
• The KJV's familiar "the people perish" differs from modern versions, which read "cast off restraint" or "unrestrained"; the 1611 margin offers "is made naked," closer to the sense of being let loose. Quoting the KJV line as a motto for organizational vision misses the verse's meaning.
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, says the word "is to be taken in its exact sense of the revelation a prophet receives."
• Compare 28:4, 7, 9; 8:32–34; Psalm 19:7–11; Luke 11:28; James 1:22–25.
units.summary: When God's voice goes unheard, people run loose; blessed is the one who obeys what He has already said.
units.principle: A people needs God's revealed word to hold it steady, and the person who obeys what God has already spoken is blessed.
units.insight: Israel's darkest days show what this verse means. In the time of the judges, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25), and the book closes in moral chaos. Under King Josiah, a lost Book of the Law was found in the temple. When it was read, the king tore his clothes, and the nation turned back to God (2 Kings 22:8–13; 23:1–3). God's word restrained and renewed them. We live after the fullest revelation of all, for God "has in these last days spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:2). Our danger is seldom a lack of Bibles. It is a famine we choose by leaving them closed, or by hearing without obeying. Jesus pronounced the same blessing as this verse: "blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it!" (Luke 11:28).
units.application: Make God's word, not your own plans, the anchor of your week: read a passage daily and obey one specific thing it says. Pastors and teachers, preach and teach Scripture itself, not only principles for success. Church leaders, when you set goals, do not borrow this verse to support them; seek God's word and obey it. Parents, read the Bible with your children so they learn where restraint and blessing come from.

rel.note: A rebuke reaches the wise man more than a hundred blows reach a fool, while this servant ignores words.
The rod for the fool's back shows that some people need more than words before they change.
The man who hardens his neck under repeated rebuke shows where unresponsive understanding leads.
The pampered servant is the opposite problem, showing that wise oversight needs both kindness and correction.

units.notes:
• "He will not respond" is literally "and there is no answer." The NASB renders it "no response," and the NASB (1995) reads "slave" for "servant."
• Ironside: "The Septuagint reads, 'a stubborn servant,' which seems to convey the right thought." The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament; its wording shows the verse was understood to describe a certain kind of servant, not every servant.
• "Mere words" are set against the stronger correction a stubborn person may need, the same contrast drawn in 17:10 and 26:3.
• Compare 17:10; 26:3; 29:1, 21; Ephesians 6:5–9; James 1:22–24.
units.summary: Understanding is not obedience; some hear every word and still will not answer.
units.principle: Knowing what is right is not the same as doing it, and a heart that understands but will not respond needs more than words to change.
units.insight: Jonah understood God's command perfectly. "Arise, go to Nineveh" could not have been clearer, yet he went the other way, and it took a storm and a great fish before he answered (Jonah 1:1–3, 17; 3:1–3). Jesus told of a son who said, "I go, sir," but did not go (Matthew 21:30). The servant of this verse sits in many church pews. We hear sermon after sermon, nod in agreement and change nothing. God is patient with such servants, and He often adds hard providences to His words, as He did with Jonah. Against every unresponsive servant stands the one perfect Servant. Jesus said, "I always do those things that please Him" (John 8:29), and in Gethsemane, "not My will, but Yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). His obedience covers our failures and teaches us to answer when God speaks.
units.application: Supervisors, when an employee keeps ignoring clear instructions, move from repeated talks to clear, fair consequences, and put them in writing. Parents, stop repeating the same warning; follow through calmly. All of us can pick one instruction from Scripture we already understand but have not obeyed, and act on it this week. Understanding it longer will not change us; responding will.

rel.note: The one who restrains his lips is wise, unlike the man who rushes into words.
Guarding the mouth preserves life, while opening wide the lips brings destruction.
Answering before hearing is folly and shame, the hasty speaker's habit.
The same formula says there is more hope for a fool than for the man wise in his own eyes.
The fool who vents all his feelings shares the hasty speaker's lack of restraint.

units.notes:
• The formula "There is more hope for a fool than for him" appears only here and at 26:12.
• The 1611 KJV margin offers "matters" for "words," because the Hebrew noun can mean a matter or affair as well as a spoken word. On that reading he is rash in action as well as in speech.
• Saul's hasty oath nearly cost Jonathan his life (1 Samuel 14:24, 43–45), and Jephthah's rash vow brought grief on his own household (Judges 11:30–35).
• Bridges: the man who distrusts himself "is more likely to be led right, than he, who thinks himself to be right already."
• Compare 10:19; 13:3; 18:13; 19:2; Ecclesiastes 5:2; James 1:19.
units.summary: A fool has more hope than the man whose mouth always outruns his mind.
units.principle: Rash words shut out correction, so the person who will not slow down to listen is in greater danger than the plain fool.
units.insight: Peter was a man hasty in his words. He rebuked Jesus for speaking of the cross (Matthew 16:22), and on the night of the betrayal he declared, "Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble" (Matthew 26:33). Within hours he denied Jesus three times. Yet the story did not end there. The risen Lord met him by the sea and asked three times, "Do you love Me?" (John 21:15–17). Peter's answers this time were humbler and slower. The verse is a warning, but Peter shows that grace can change the hasty talker. Most of us know the feeling of hearing our own words a second too late. The cure begins where Peter's did, with the Lord's searching question and a heart willing to listen before it speaks.
units.application: In meetings, let others finish before you answer, and ask one clarifying question before giving your view. Before replying to a text or comment that stirs you, wait. Parents, model slowness by saying, "Let me think about that," instead of an instant yes or no. Leaders, never make promises or announcements in the heat of the moment. If your quick words hurt someone this week, go back and make it right.

rel.note: A wise servant may rightly rise over a shameful son, unlike the pampered servant who grasps a son's place.
Luxury does not fit a fool, nor rule a servant, the same disorder of roles.
A child left to himself shows the same harm that comes from care without correction.
The stubborn servant who ignores words is the opposite problem, and together they show the need for balanced oversight.
A servant when he reigns is among the things the earth cannot bear.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word translated "son," manon, occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its meaning is uncertain. The NKJV, KJV and NASB read "son," the ESV "his heir," the current NIV (2011) "insolent," and the NLT "a rebel." Each rendering describes a servant who no longer keeps his proper place.
• The KJV renders "pampers" as "delicately bringeth up," the picture of a servant raised in comfort and never trained.
• Abraham's fear that his servant Eliezer of Damascus would become his heir shows how a household servant could end up in a son's place (Genesis 15:2–3).
• Henry: "Let masters give their servants that which is equal and fit for them, and neither more nor less." Compare Colossians 4:1.
• Compare 17:2; 19:10; 29:19; 30:21–22.
units.summary: Kindness without training does not make a grateful servant; it makes a presumptuous one.
units.principle: Indulgence that never trains or corrects breeds presumption, so real care for those under our authority joins kindness with responsibility.
units.insight: Henry draws a striking contrast: "The humble prodigal thinks himself unworthy to be called a son, and is content to be a servant; the pampered slave thinks himself too good to be called a servant." The verse warns against grasping a place we were never given. Yet the gospel tells of another way to become a son. The prodigal came home asking only to be a hired servant, and his father put a robe on him, a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet (Luke 15:19–22). Paul tells believers, "you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ" (Galatians 4:7). That sonship comes by grace, not presumption, and those who receive it serve more gladly, not less. Do you treat God's kindness as a reason to obey or as an excuse to presume?
units.application: Managers and business owners, be generous with your employees, but pair privileges with clear expectations and truthful feedback. Parents of adult children living at home, show love without removing all responsibility; agree on what each person contributes. Ministry leaders, train volunteers before handing them authority. If an employer, a parent or a church has shown you great kindness, let it make you more faithful, not more entitled.

rel.note: The quick-tempered man acts foolishly, showing how anger multiplies wrongdoing.
A wrathful man stirs up strife, nearly the same words as the first line.
The one who is slow to anger and rules his spirit is stronger than a conqueror.
A contentious man kindles strife like wood on a fire.
The wise man who quiets his feelings shows the restraint the furious man lacks.

units.notes:
• "A furious man" is literally "a master of wrath" (ba'al chemah), a Hebrew way of describing a person characterized by rage.
• The word for "angry" in the first line, aph, also means nose or nostrils. Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says it "describes his outward visage of snorting nostrils," that is, the flaring face of a man in a rage.
• The ESV renders the second line with the verb "causes" ("causes much transgression"), suggesting that his anger leads others into sin as well as himself.
• Bridges guards against misreading the verse: "Anger is not necessarily a sinful passion." Jesus' anger at the temple was holy (John 2:15–17); the verse condemns anger that rules a person.
• Compare 14:17; 15:18; 26:21; 30:33; James 1:19–20.
units.summary: Anger does not stay a feeling; left unruled, it starts fights and multiplies sins.
units.principle: Anger that is not ruled becomes a ruler, stirring up conflict and multiplying sin in everything it touches.
units.insight: God warned Cain while his anger was still smoldering: "sin lies at the door. And its desire is for you, but you should rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). Cain did not rule it, and anger became murder. Saul's jealous rage showed the same multiplying power. It led him to hurl a spear at David, to hunt him for years and finally to have the priests of Nob slaughtered (1 Samuel 18:10–11; 22:17–19). One unruled passion produced sin after sin. Most of us do not throw spears, but we know the slammed door, the cutting text and the cold silence that follow anger. Jesus felt holy anger, yet on the cross He prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Only a heart changed by that mercy learns to rule its anger instead of serving it.
units.application: If people around you walk on eggshells, take that as evidence about you, not as their problem. Ask your spouse or a close friend how your anger affects them, and listen without defending yourself. Parents, deal with your own temper before you correct a child's. Leaders, never make decisions or send messages while angry. If anger has become a pattern, confess it, ask someone to hold you accountable, and seek pastoral counsel.

rel.note: Pride brings shame, while wisdom is with the humble.
Before honor is humility, the path the second line describes.
Pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall.
A haughty heart comes before destruction, and humility before honor, the same reversal.
The LORD scorns the scornful but gives grace to the humble, the source of the honor that holds them.

units.notes:
• "Bring him low" and "humble" come from the same Hebrew root, shaphel, a word meaning low. Pride makes a man low against his will, while the humble, literally "the low in spirit," choose lowliness and receive honor.
• The word for "pride" comes from a root meaning to be high or lifted up. So the verse sets high against low: the man who lifts himself up is brought low, and the one who is low in spirit is held up.
• The ESV and NASB read "obtain honor," and the KJV makes honor the subject: honour shall "uphold" the humble.
• Poole, quoted by Guzik: "Thus honour, like a shadow, flees from them that pursue it, and follows them who flee from it."
• Compare 11:2; 15:33; 16:18–19; 18:12; Luke 14:7–11; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5–6.
units.summary: Pride climbs for honor and falls; humility bows low and finds honor holding on to it.
units.principle: Pride grasps for height and ends low, while humility before God and others is the path on which honor comes.
units.insight: The book of Esther acts out this verse. Haman built a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it, while Mordecai was led through the city in royal robes (Esther 6:10–11; 7:10). Nebuchadnezzar looked over his city and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…?" He was driven out to live like an animal until he learned that heaven rules, and then confessed, "those who walk in pride He is able to put down" (Daniel 4:30–37). The supreme picture of the second line is Christ, who "humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death." Therefore God "has highly exalted Him" (Philippians 2:8–9). Pride is rarely loud in church. It hides in needing credit, resenting correction and comparing ourselves with others. Grace meets us at the low place, for God "gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6).
units.application: This week, give credit away: name someone else's contribution in a meeting or at home. When you are corrected, say "thank you" before you explain yourself. Leaders, do a task no one will notice. Young people tempted to build an image online, spend that energy serving someone in secret. If you have been passed over while others promote themselves, keep serving faithfully and leave your honor with God.

rel.note: A false witness will not go unpunished, the end of the partner's sworn silence.
Joining sinners for a share of the plunder takes away the life of those who do it.
The one who robs and calls it no transgression is a companion to a destroyer.
The fear of man is the snare that keeps the partner silent under oath.
Those who sin against Wisdom wrong their own soul, as the thief's partner hates his own life.

units.notes:
• "He swears to tell the truth" is literally "he hears the oath." The word refers to an oath that calls down a curse on anyone who withholds testimony, the situation addressed in Leviticus 5:1. The ESV speaks of hearing "the curse," and the KJV reads "heareth cursing."
• "Hates his own life" echoes Wisdom's warning that "he who sins against me wrongs his own soul; All those who hate me love death" (8:36).
• Bridges: "The law acknowledges no difference between the thief and his partner."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The call to testify is actually a curse pronounced on anyone who will not testify."
• Compare 1:10–19; 28:24; Psalm 50:18; Ephesians 5:11; 1 Timothy 5:22.
units.summary: Take a share of a thief's profit and you inherit his guilt; silence under oath only deepens it.
units.principle: Sharing in another's wrongdoing, even quietly, binds us to its guilt, and covering it up only adds sin to sin.
units.insight: Sapphira did not plan the lie alone. She agreed with her husband to keep back part of the money and present the rest as the whole. When Peter asked her directly, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much?" she answered, "Yes, for so much," and she shared his judgment (Acts 5:1–10). Partnership in sin is still sin, and silence when the truth is asked for is still a lie. Yet the gospel reaches accomplices too. Saul of Tarsus stood by "consenting to his death" while Stephen was stoned (Acts 22:20). The same man became Paul, who called himself the chief of sinners and found mercy (1 Timothy 1:15–16). If you are holding someone else's guilty secret to protect yourself, the way out is not more silence. It is confession and the mercy promised in 28:13.
units.application: If a coworker or friend is stealing, padding expenses or cheating customers, do not accept a share or a favor to keep quiet. Employees, when you are questioned in an audit or investigation, tell the truth even if it costs you. Young people, refuse to cover for a friend's shoplifting or cheating. If you already have, go to the right person, whether a parent, pastor or supervisor, and set it right before it hardens into a pattern.

rel.note: The righteous run to the LORD's name and are safe, the same verb for being set on high.
The thief's partner, silent under oath, is caught in the snare of fearing exposure.
The next saying turns from fearing people to seeking their favor, and gives the same answer: justice comes from the LORD.
The same word for snare names the trap hidden in an evil man's transgression.
Trusting the LORD with all the heart, rather than leaning on human opinion or understanding, is the way of safety.

units.notes:
• "Fear" here is a word for trembling or dread, charadah, stronger than mere respect. The same word describes Isaac when he "trembled exceedingly" on learning that Jacob had taken the blessing (Genesis 27:33).
• "Snare" is the hunter's trap already seen in 29:6, where the evil man is caught in his own transgression. The chapter sets two traps side by side: one built by sin and one by fear.
• "Safe" translates a verb meaning to be set high, out of an enemy's reach. Its form is passive: the one who trusts is set on high instead of climbing there himself. The 1611 KJV margin gives "set on high," and the NASB (1995) "exalted." The same verb appears in "The name of the LORD is a strong tower; The righteous run to it and are safe" (18:10).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "The 'fear of man' describes any situation in which one is anxious about not offending another person."
• Compare 1:7; 3:5–6; Psalm 56:3–4; 118:6; Isaiah 51:12–13; Galatians 1:10.
units.summary: The fear of man is a trap; trust in the LORD is a high tower.
units.principle: Fear of people traps us into compromise, but trust in the LORD, grounded in a right view of Him, keeps us secure in His hands even when harm still comes.
units.insight: Pilate found no fault in Jesus, yet when the crowd cried, "If you let this Man go, you are not Caesar's friend," he gave in (John 19:12–16). Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "It was the fear of man that caused Pilate's name to become infamous in the history of the world…" Peter denied his Lord before a servant girl, yet later told the council, "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). Three young men in Babylon show what "safe" means. They trusted God to deliver them, "But if not," they would still not bow (Daniel 3:17–18). Their safety was in God, whatever the furnace did. Whose opinion controls you? Jesus answers the fear of man with a greater fear and a greater love: fear Him who holds the soul, and know that you are worth more than many sparrows (Matthew 10:28–31).
units.application: Name one decision this week that you are making mainly to avoid someone's disapproval, and make it before God instead. Employees, if you are pressured to sign off on something false, refuse, and trust God with your job. Teenagers, choose one way to stand openly as a believer among your friends. Pastors, preach what the text says even when it is unpopular. Parents, let your children see you confess your faith where it costs you something.

rel.note: Every decision of the lot is from the LORD, the same truth applied to outcomes.
Many entreat the favor of the nobility, the same crowd around those in power.
The king's heart is in the LORD's hand, which is why justice finally comes from Him.
Trust in the LORD, not fear of people, frees a person from courting human favor.

units.notes:
• "The ruler's favor" is literally "the face of a ruler," as the 1611 KJV margin notes. To seek a ruler's face was to ask for an audience, a chance to stand before him and be heard. The ESV keeps the image with "the face."
• The KJV reads the second line "every man's judgment cometh from the LORD": the decision in each person's case finally rests with God.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, notes the balance: the verse "does not forbid seeking relief from injustice through the legal system."
• Esther both sought a ruler's favor and looked beyond it. She went to the king to seek his favor, at the risk of her life, but only after she and her people had fasted (Esther 4:16; 5:1–2).
• Compare 16:33; 19:6; 21:1; Psalm 62:9–10; 146:3–5.
units.summary: Crowds wait for the ruler's smile, but the verdict that matters comes from the LORD.
units.principle: It is right to seek fair treatment from those in authority, but our final hope rests on the LORD, from whom every true verdict comes.
units.insight: Joseph asked Pharaoh's cupbearer to "remember me" and to "make mention of me to Pharaoh" (Genesis 40:14). It was a fair request. But "the chief butler did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (Genesis 40:23), and two more years passed in prison. When Joseph's moment came, it came from God, not from the cupbearer's influence. Haman shows the other side. He enjoyed the king's highest favor and lost it, with his life, in a single evening (Esther 7:6–10). Jesus stood before Pilate, the man who held His earthly case, and told him, "You could have no power at all against Me unless it had been given you from above" (John 19:11). Every human judge sits under a higher court. Whose favor are you working hardest to win? Bring your case to the Judge whose verdict stands.
units.application: If you are waiting on a court date, a hiring decision, a promotion or an immigration ruling, do what is right and reasonable to present your case, and pray before you plead. Refuse to flatter or bend the truth to win favor. Leaders, remember that you too answer to God for every decision. When a human verdict goes against you, take your grief to God, who sees the whole case.

rel.note: The perverse are an abomination to the LORD while the blameless are His delight, the view the righteous share.
