The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, who loves the one who follows righteousness.
Doing good to an enemy keeps the righteous from turning their hatred of injustice into hatred of persons.
The bloodthirsty hate the blameless, the same hostility of the wicked toward the upright.
The path of the just shines brighter while the way of the wicked is darkness, the two roads this verse leaves opposed.

units.notes:
• "Abomination" (to'evah) is the word Proverbs uses for what the LORD detests (3:32; 11:1, 20; 15:8–9). Here the righteous and the wicked each apply it to the other.
• This verse closes the proverbs of Solomon copied by Hezekiah's men, which began at 25:1, and with them the sayings attributed to Solomon in the book.
• Bridges: "Here is the oldest, the most rooted, the most universal quarrel in the world." The quarrel goes back to the enmity announced in Genesis 3:15.
• Bridges also draws the line the verse requires: "The enmity of the just is against the sins, not the persons, of the wicked."
• Compare 4:18–19; 29:10; John 15:18–19; 1 John 3:12–13.
units.summary: Solomon's proverbs end with two roads that can never make peace, and every reader must choose one.
units.principle: Righteousness and wickedness cannot be reconciled, yet the righteous oppose the sin and not the sinner, and keep doing good even to those who oppose them.
units.insight: Jesus told His brothers, "The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me because I testify of it that its works are evil" (John 7:7). His uprightness offended the wicked, and they did not rest until He was crucified. Yet the One most opposed to sin loved sinners most. Paul writes that "when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son" (Romans 5:10). Every believer once walked the other road, and that memory keeps the righteous from contempt. We can detest injustice, refuse to make peace with it, and still pray for the unjust and do them good. Two questions search the heart. Does wrongdoing still grieve you, or has it become normal? And when you oppose it, is your heart set against the sin, or against the person God may yet save?
units.application: When you face open hostility for doing right at work or school, do not be surprised; keep walking upright and answer with kindness. Parents, teach your children to stand against cruelty without mocking the cruel. Church members, oppose injustice firmly in public discussion, but never speak of opponents with contempt. This week, pray by name for someone who opposes you, and look for one practical way to do him good (25:21).

rel.note: Another collection from wise men beyond Solomon opens with a call to hear "the words of the wise."
The utterance this heading introduces begins with Agur's confession of his own limits.
The next heading also introduces a distinct, otherwise unknown voice and calls his words an "utterance."

units.notes:
• The word translated "utterance," massa, means a weighty message. Other versions render it "oracle" (ESV, NASB) or "prophecy" (KJV). Some take it instead as the name of a people, Massa, descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14). The same word heads Lemuel's words in 31:1.
• "Ithiel and Ucal." Dividing the Hebrew letters differently produces a lament, "I am weary, O God" (ESV, NLT). The NKJV, NASB and KJV keep the names.
• The name Agur is often explained as "gatherer." The medieval Jewish commentator Rashi took it as a name for Solomon, and some older Christian writers read Ithiel and Ucal as veiled names of the Messiah. The text supports neither: the heading presents a separate collection spoken to real hearers.
• Bridges, on the questions no one can answer about Agur: "it is vain to speculate, where God is silent."
• Compare 1 Kings 4:30–31, which names other wise men of Solomon's day.
units.summary: A man the world never heard of stands beside Solomon, because wisdom is God's gift, not a famous name's.
units.principle: God's wisdom is not limited to famous voices; His word deserves a hearing whoever carries it.
units.insight: We know almost nothing about Agur, and that is part of the lesson. God placed the words of an unknown man beside the proverbs of Israel's greatest king, just as He called Amos from following the flock (Amos 7:14–15) and spoke through unschooled fishermen (Acts 4:13). We do not know who wrote many of the Psalms either, and they lose nothing by it. As Bridges puts it, "We know their author, when the penmen are hid": God is the author, even when the human writers are hidden. Many faithful teachers and praying grandparents will never be known beyond a small circle, yet God uses them to hand wisdom to an Ithiel and a Ucal. Being unknown is no barrier to being used.
units.application: Listen for God's wisdom from people without a title or platform, such as the older believer in the back row or the quiet small-group leader. If you teach or mentor, do not wait to be recognized. Pour what God has given you into the one or two people in front of you, as Agur did with Ithiel and Ucal.

rel.note: Wisdom is found with the humble, and Agur's humble confession is where his wisdom begins.
Proverbs uses the same word "stupid" for the man who hates correction; Agur applies it to himself and so becomes teachable.
The man wise in his own eyes is the opposite of Agur, who calls himself stupid and so remains teachable.
Agur confesses his lack before God, while that generation is pure in its own eyes and blind to its filth.
Agur begins with humble confession and ends by warning those who foolishly exalt themselves.

units.notes:
• The word translated "stupid," ba'ar, means brutish or beast-like; the KJV has "brutish." The same word describes the man who hates correction (12:1), and Asaph uses it in his own confession: "I was so foolish and ignorant; I was like a beast before You" (Psalm 73:22).
• "More stupid than any man" is poetic intensity, not a literal ranking. Agur is not claiming to be the least intelligent person alive; he is describing how small his understanding looks before God.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "Philosophy had failed him, and revelation was his sole confidence."
• Compare Job 42:6; Isaiah 6:5; 1 Corinthians 3:18; 8:2.
units.summary: The wisest thing Agur ever said was that he was not wise.
units.principle: Wisdom begins where pretending ends; the person who admits how little he understands is the one God can teach.
units.insight: Agur stands in a long line of believers who saw themselves most clearly when they saw God most clearly. Isaiah cried, "Woe is me, for I am undone" (Isaiah 6:5). Job said, "I abhor myself" (Job 42:6). Paul called himself the chief of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). Bridges: "The nearer our contemplation of God, the closer our communion with him, the deeper will be our self-abasement before him." Agur is the opposite of the man wise in his own eyes, for whom there is less hope than for a fool (26:12). Yet his confession is not self-hatred. His low view of himself drives him to God's word (30:5), not to despair. Humility that ends in God is health; self-criticism that ends in self-pity is only another way of looking at ourselves.
units.application: Practice saying "I don't know" instead of bluffing, whether in a Bible study, a counseling conversation or an argument. Before you open Scripture, take Agur's posture: "I cannot reach this on my own; teach me." If people look to you for answers, admit the limits of what you know. It frees them to learn as well.

rel.note: Agur's humble confession shows the fear of the LORD that the book names as the beginning of knowledge.
The wisdom Agur cannot reach by study is given by the LORD from His own mouth.
The man who confesses he cannot grasp the Holy One later stands in wonder at things too wonderful for him.
Agur echoes the words "knowledge of the Holy One," which 9:10 pairs with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew word for "Holy One" is plural in form, as in 9:10; the KJV has "the holy." Hebrew sometimes uses a plural to stress greatness. Here it refers to the one God in the fullness of His holiness; it does not mean more than one God.
• "Have knowledge" is literally "know the knowledge": Agur says he does not know the knowledge of the Holy One.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Earthbound mortals cannot find transcendent wisdom apart from the transcendent Lord." In plain words, people bound to the earth cannot reach the wisdom that is above it unless the Lord who is above it gives it.
• Socrates, quoted by Bridges: "I only know one thing—that I know nothing." Agur's confession goes further, because it is made before the Holy One.
• Compare Job 11:7; 28:12–28; Matthew 11:27; 1 Corinthians 2:11–14.
units.summary: You can study about God for a lifetime, but you know Him only as He makes Himself known.
units.principle: God cannot be mastered by human effort; He is known only as He reveals Himself, and the humble are the ones who receive it.
units.insight: There is a kind of Bible knowledge that puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1–2) and a kind that bows down. Agur had the second. Job's great poem asks where wisdom can be found and answers that only God knows the way to it (Job 28:12, 23). Jesus said no one knows the Father "except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him" (Matthew 11:27). So Agur's confession is not the end of hope but the doorway to grace. The Holy One who cannot be reached has come near and made Himself known in His word and, finally, in His Son (John 1:18). This is a word for seminarians and lifelong believers as much as for new Christians: knowing about God is never the same as knowing God.
units.application: Come to Scripture to meet God, not only to gather information, and pray before you read, "Open my eyes" (Psalm 119:18). If you teach, do not let mastery of the material replace awe at the Person. When someone admits they are struggling with questions about God, honor the honesty and point them to the God who reveals Himself, instead of pretending every question is easy.

rel.note: Agur's unanswerable questions find their resting place in God's pure word.
The LORD founded the earth and set the clouds and depths by wisdom, the works Agur's questions ascribe to Him.
Wisdom's creation poem portrays the same divine ordering of the heavens, waters and earth that Agur's questions point to.

units.notes:
• The word translated "fists" means the hollows of the hands. Compare Isaiah 40:12, "measured the waters in the hollow of His hand."
• "Bound the waters in a garment" pictures the clouds holding rain like a tied-up cloak (Job 26:8) and the sea wrapped in swaddling bands (Job 38:8–9).
• The last line can be read as a question (NKJV, KJV) or an exclamation, "Surely you know!" (ESV, NASB); the NLT has "Tell me if you know!"
• Ironside: "No man, apart from divine revelation, could reply to the questions here asked."
• Bridges, on how far to press the question: "Be careful that we stop, where Revelation stops." In other words, go as far as Scripture goes, and no further.
• Compare 8:22–31; John 1:1–3, 18; Ephesians 4:9–10.
units.summary: Agur asked the name of God's Son and left the answer blank; the Gospels fill it in.
units.principle: The Creator is beyond human reach, and He is known only because He has come down and made Himself known in His Son.
units.insight: Agur's questions leave every human reader empty-handed, and that is their purpose. No one climbed to heaven to bring God down. Instead the Son came down (John 3:13), and with His work finished He ascended "far above all the heavens" (Ephesians 4:10). Enoch and Elijah were taken up to God (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:11), but Jesus ascended in His own power. Paul uses the same picture: we need not ask "Who will ascend into heaven?" to bring Christ down, because the word of faith is near us (Romans 10:6–9). The One who gathers the wind in His fists rebuked the wind on Galilee, and His disciples asked Agur's question again: "Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?" (Matthew 8:27). We now know the name Agur could only ask about (Philippians 2:9–11).
units.application: When God feels distant or hard to understand, start where Agur ended, with the Son who came down; read John 1:18 and 3:13 beside this verse. When creation overwhelms you, in a storm or under a night sky, let it lead you to worship the One who holds it. Then share His name: Agur's question still hangs over people who have never heard the answer.

rel.note: The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous are safe, as God is a shield to those who trust Him.
Whoever trusts in the LORD shall be safe, the same protection promised to those who trust Him here.
God's pure word answers the questions about heaven and the Creator that no human can answer.
Because every word of God is pure, nothing may be added to it.
Trusting the LORD rather than one's own understanding is the posture Agur takes after confessing his limits.

units.notes:
• The word translated "pure" means refined, the way metal is purified in a furnace until no impurity remains. The KJV margin reads "purified," the NASB "tested," and the ESV and NLT "proves true."
• Psalm 12:6 uses the same picture: "The words of the LORD are pure words, Like silver tried in a furnace of earth, Purified seven times."
• The verse closely matches Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, which also join the proven word of the LORD with the LORD as "a shield to all who trust in Him."
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, on the second line: "the aim of revelation is to promote trust, not bare knowledge." God speaks so that we will rely on Him, not merely so that we will know more.
• Bridges: "Nothing is learned solidly by abstract speculation. Go to the book." After the unanswerable questions of 30:4, Agur turns to what God has actually said.
• Compare Genesis 15:1 ("I am your shield"); Psalm 119:140; John 17:17.
units.summary: When you cannot climb up to God, you can still lean your whole weight on what He has said.
units.principle: Every word God speaks is tested and true, and the God behind that word is the shelter of all who trust Him.
units.insight: Every honest believer makes Agur's move: from confessing what he does not know (30:2–3) to resting on what God has spoken (30:5). Abram, afraid and still childless, heard God say, "I am your shield" (Genesis 15:1). When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He met each lie with "It is written" (Matthew 4:4–10). Being shielded does not mean nothing hurts. David wrote the song of Psalm 18 after years of being hunted by Saul, yet he could say that the word of the LORD is proven. Many of us trust God's word in theory but run to other shelters when trouble comes: our savings, our reputation, our own explanations. In Jesus all God's promises are "Yes" (2 Corinthians 1:20). The question is not whether God's word is pure, but whether we are hiding in the God who gave it.
units.application: When doubts crowd in, choose one promise of Scripture and pray it back to God, resting on what He has said. If you counsel an anxious friend, open the Bible with them instead of offering only your own reassurance. Parents: let your children hear you say, "I don't know how this will turn out, but I know what God has said." Notice where you run first when trouble hits, and run to Him.

rel.note: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, and claiming His authority for human words is lying about Him.
The one who speaks lies will not escape, as the one who adds to God's words will be exposed.
The purity of every word of God is the reason nothing may be added to it.
The word for "liar" shares its root with the "lies" Agur asks God to keep far from him.

units.notes:
• The word for "liar" comes from the same Hebrew root as "lies" in 30:8, where Agur asks God to keep lies far from him. The man who warns others against adding lies to God's word prays to be kept from lies himself.
• Scripture repeats the warning near its beginning and at its end (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32; Revelation 22:18–19). Jesus rebuked teachers who taught "as doctrines the commandments of men" (Mark 7:7).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, names the usual form of the danger: "The temptation is to improve on the text." Few people write a new Bible; many quietly improve on the one they have.
• Bridges urges teachers "to add not to the pure word by the glosses of false interpretation; not to expound their own minds, instead of the mind of God." A gloss is an added explanation; Bridges means explanations that put the teacher's ideas in God's mouth.
• Compare 30:5; 1 Corinthians 4:6 ("not to think beyond what is written"); Galatians 1:8.
units.summary: Adding to God's word does not make it bigger; it makes the one who adds a liar.
units.principle: God's word needs no additions; claiming His authority for our own ideas misrepresents God and exposes the speaker as false.
units.insight: The first addition to God's word came early. God told Adam not to eat from one tree; Eve reported that God had also said, "nor shall you touch it" (Genesis 3:3), and the serpent worked in the gap between what God said and what was believed. The Pharisees built fences of tradition around the law until their rules canceled God's command (Mark 7:8–13). Jesus did the opposite: He spoke what the Father gave Him to say (John 12:49). The temptation is near at hand. It is the preacher who says "God told me" to win an argument, the parent who uses a verse to back a house rule, the believer who turns personal convictions into tests for others. Each of these makes us liars about God. The safe place is the one Agur chose: humble about our own words, confident in His (30:5).
units.application: Preachers and teachers: keep clear what the text says and what you take it to mean, and say so out loud: "Scripture says… I think this means…." Before you say "God told me," ask whether you could show it from Scripture. Parents: do not use a verse to settle an argument it was never written to settle. In a small group, when someone shares a striking idea about a passage, ask together, "Where do we see that in the text?"

rel.note: The LORD hears the prayer of the righteous, the hope behind Agur's plea not to be refused.
The prayer of the upright is the LORD's delight, and Agur's prayer is offered in that spirit.
The next verse names the two requests Agur introduces here.

units.notes:
• Where the NKJV has "Deprive me not," the KJV reads "deny me them not" and the NASB "refuse me." Each pictures Agur asking God not to turn him away.
• Bridges: "His prayers are short, but comprehensive." Two requests cover both the soul (truth) and the body (daily provision).
• Henry: "In praying, we should think of dying, and pray accordingly." Agur's "before I die" asks for gifts that will last to the end.
• Compare the short prayer of Jabez (1 Chronicles 4:10) and Solomon's request for an understanding heart (1 Kings 3:5–9).
units.summary: Agur's prayer list was short enough to carry for a lifetime: two requests, held until his last breath.
units.principle: Humility shows itself in prayer, and wise prayer asks first for what will keep us faithful to God for the whole of life.
units.insight: Most of our prayers reach only to next week: the meeting, the test result, the bill. Agur's two requests reach to his deathbed. Solomon, offered anything he wished, asked for an understanding heart, and the request pleased the Lord (1 Kings 3:9–10). Jacob wrestled through the night and said, "I will not let You go unless You bless me!" (Genesis 32:26). Agur prays with that kind of earnestness, but for things that guard his soul rather than enlarge his life. What would you ask for if you could ask for only two things until you die? The answer shows what you value. Jesus also gave His disciples a short prayer, and its request for daily bread and its plea to be delivered from evil echo Agur's two requests (Matthew 6:11–13).
units.application: This week, write down the two things you most want God to give you for the rest of your life, and pray them daily. Young people: before you list goals for career and money, ask God for a truthful heart. Older believers: pray Agur's "before I die" for faithfulness to the end. If you lead a prayer meeting, model a short, earnest prayer rather than a long one.

rel.note: A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble, the same contentment Agur seeks.
The warning not to wear oneself out for riches that fly away supports Agur's refusal to ask for wealth.
The "lies" Agur asks God to remove share a root with the "liar" who adds to God's words.
This verse names the two requests that 30:7 introduces.
The next verse explains why Agur fears both riches and poverty.

units.notes:
• The KJV reads "vanity" for "falsehood," bringing out the sense of emptiness: Agur fears not only spoken lies but a life built on hollow things.
• For "the food allotted to me," the NASB reads "my portion," and the KJV margin gives "allowance." The manna in the wilderness is the picture: each person gathered what he needed, "he who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack" (Exodus 16:18).
• Jesus taught the same request: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Paul wrote, "having food and clothing, with these we shall be content" (1 Timothy 6:8).
• Ironside: "it is most unusual to find one who dreads wealth and prays to be kept from riches." Everyone prays against poverty; Agur also prays against riches.
• Compare Psalm 119:29, 37 ("Turn away my eyes from looking at worthless things"); Philippians 4:11–12.
units.summary: Pray for a truthful heart and a daily portion: enough to live on, not enough to forget God.
units.principle: A truthful heart and enough to live on are better gifts than wealth, because they keep a person dependent on God and guarded from the snares at both extremes.
units.insight: Israel in the wilderness learned Agur's prayer by daily experience. God sent manna each morning, enough for the day, and those who hoarded it found it full of worms by morning (Exodus 16:18–20). God was teaching His people to trust Him one day at a time. Our hearts resist that lesson. We pray against poverty readily, but almost no one prays against riches, because we do not believe riches could hurt us. Agur did. He also knew that lies and emptiness do not only surround us; they grow within us. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread (Matthew 6:11) and lived that prayer Himself, with nowhere to lay His head (Matthew 8:20), yet in perfect trust in His Father. In Him we learn the secret Paul learned: to be content in plenty and in want (Philippians 4:11–13).
units.application: If you are building a career, decide now what "enough" looks like for your household, and give God the surplus instead of raising the bar. If money is tight this month, pray for today's needs by name and refuse any shortcut that would compromise your honesty. Parents: let your children hear you thank God for ordinary provision. And ask God to show you one hollow thing, a lie you have believed about money or worth, and to remove it.

rel.note: The rich man's wealth becomes a high wall in his own esteem, the self-sufficiency that says "Who is the LORD?"
Integrity matters more than whether a person is poor or rich, the concern behind Agur's prayer.
This verse gives the reasons for the request in 30:8 for neither poverty nor riches.
People do not despise a thief who steals because he is starving, yet he must still repay; that is the snare of poverty Agur fears.

units.notes:
• "Profane the name of my God": the KJV has "take the name of my God in vain," the language of the third commandment (Exodus 20:7). A theft by one of God's people would bring His name into disgrace.
• The KJV margin gives "belie thee" for "deny You": to live as though God were not there, a lie about Him told by the way one lives.
• Deuteronomy 32:15 shows the danger of fullness in one line: "But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked." Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "In sum, the glory of God, not his personal need, motivates Agur's requests."
• Henry sums up Agur's fear: "Lest I be rich and sin, or poor and sin." He dreads not the cares of wealth or the hardships of poverty but the sin each could lead him into.
• Compare Hosea 13:6; 1 Timothy 6:9–10, 17.
units.summary: Too much can make us forget God, and too little can tempt us to shame Him; Agur feared both.
units.principle: Both wealth and want carry temptations, and the wise person prays to be kept from the sins each invites, caring most for the honor of God's name.
units.insight: Scripture shows the danger of fullness in real lives. King Uzziah was marvelously helped by God, but "when he was strong his heart was lifted up, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:15–16). Solomon himself, with more than anyone, let his heart turn after other gods in old age (1 Kings 11:4). Scripture also shows how a believer's sin dishonors God's name: after David's sin with Bathsheba, Nathan told him that he had given "great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme" (2 Samuel 12:14). Agur's prayer searches us. Which way does my heart lean when the bank balance changes? Do I pray more when money is short and less when it is plenty? Jesus became poor for our sakes, that we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He frees us to honor God's name in either condition.
units.application: If your income has grown, check whether your prayer life and giving have grown with it or shrunk. Set a regular time to thank God by name for what you have. If you are under financial pressure, decide ahead of time where you will not cut corners: taxes, timesheets, expense reports, the extra change at the register. Church leaders: care for members in need so that desperation does not become temptation.

rel.note: The LORD pleads the cause of the poor and afflicted against those who exploit their weakness.
False witness against a neighbor wounds like a club, a sword and an arrow.
A curse without cause does not alight, so the servant's curse lands only because the slanderer is truly guilty.
Running down the weak with words opens a section that ends in devouring the poor.

units.notes:
• The word translated "malign" means to use the tongue against someone, that is, to slander. The KJV margin gives the literal sense, "Hurt not with thy tongue," and the ESV reads "slander."
• Bridges: "Let not this Proverb be a shelter for unfaithfulness." In plain words, the verse forbids malicious or needless accusation; it does not forbid reporting real wrongdoing in a fair and loving way (compare Matthew 18:15).
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Behind this injunction is a demand that one respect the person of the menial worker."
• Servants in Israel were often slaves with little power to answer an accuser. The law of Moses protected even a runaway slave from being handed back to his master (Deuteronomy 23:15–16).
• Compare Leviticus 19:16; Romans 14:4 ("Who are you to judge another's servant?"); Titus 3:2.
units.summary: The weak are not fair game; God hears the servant you run down to his master.
units.principle: Words used to bring down the defenseless bring guilt on the speaker, because God takes up the cause of the weak.
units.insight: David knew what it was to be maligned to his master. He asked King Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Indeed David seeks your harm'?" (1 Samuel 24:9). Later he prayed that if men had stirred Saul against him, "may they be cursed before the LORD" (1 Samuel 26:19). Ziba slandered Mephibosheth to King David and was rewarded with his master's land (2 Samuel 16:1–4; 19:24–29). The temptation is ordinary: mentioning a coworker's failure to the boss, reporting a server's mistake with relish, describing the new hire in the worst light. Behind it is a heart that wants to rise by pushing someone else down. Jesus never did this. He stood beside the woman others dragged before Him to accuse (John 8:3–11), and He now intercedes for those whom others accuse (Romans 8:33–34).
units.application: Employees and managers: before you report a coworker's mistake, ask whether it needs reporting and whether you have spoken to them first (Matthew 18:15). Customers: treat the server, cleaner or cashier with the respect you would want from your own boss. If you supervise people, be slow to believe a complaint about someone who is not present to answer it. Parents: teach children the difference between telling to hurt and telling to help.

rel.note: Whoever curses father or mother will have his lamp put out, the same sin this generation commits.
The command not to despise a mother when she is old is the blessing this generation withholds.
One who robs his parents and calls it no transgression shows the same contempt for father and mother.
Agur returns to contempt for parents and names its shameful end.

units.notes:
• The NASB renders "generation" as "a kind," and the ESV as "those," showing that the word describes a type of people rather than an age group or historical period.
• Exodus 21:17 shows how seriously God's law took this sin: "And he who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death."
• Jesus condemned a tradition that let a son withhold support from his parents, and He quoted the same law, "He who curses father or mother, let him be put to death" (Matthew 15:4–6). Withholding care from a parent breaks the same command as cursing one.
• Bridges: "The authority of parents, even in the lowest degradation, must be respected, when we dare not, must not, follow their examples." Honor is owed even to parents whose example a child must not follow.
• Compare 30:17; 20:20; Ephesians 6:1–3; 2 Timothy 3:2 ("disobedient to parents").
units.summary: A generation's corruption shows first at home, in how it speaks of father and mother.
units.principle: Contempt for parents, whether in open cursing or in cold neglect, is the first mark of a heart that has thrown off honor, and it rarely stays at home.
units.insight: Ham saw his father's shame and told his brothers instead of covering it (Genesis 9:22). Absalom stole the hearts of Israel and then drove his father from Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:6–14). Both show how contempt for a parent grows. Few of us curse our parents aloud, but many withhold blessing: the call not made, the thanks never spoken, the sarcasm about Mom over coffee with friends. This verse names that silence as part of the same sin. Some readers had parents who wounded them deeply. Honoring them does not mean pretending or following their example, and it may mean refusing to curse them while still protecting yourself. Jesus kept this command even on the cross. In His agony He made sure His mother would be cared for (John 19:26–27).
units.application: This week, bless your mother or father by name: a call, a note, a specific thank you for something they did. If they have died, thank God for them aloud in front of your children. Teenagers: notice how you talk about your parents to your friends. Parents: model honor by how you speak of your own parents. If your relationship with a parent is painful, ask a pastor how to honor them without enabling harm.

rel.note: A man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirits.
No one can say he has made his own heart clean, yet this generation is pure in its own eyes.
Confessing sin, rather than denying it, is the way to mercy and cleansing.
Agur confesses his lack before God, while this generation boasts of a purity it does not have.
The adulterous woman also insists she has done no wickedness, blind to her own sin as this generation is to its filth.

units.notes:
• The ESV reads "clean" for "pure" and "filth" for "filthiness."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, describes this generation as people "who may observe all outer ritual but pay no attention to inner cleansing."
• Bridges speaks of the self-deceived man, "little knowing the infinite distinction between being pure in his own eyes, and being pure in the sight of God."
• Jesus pictured this generation in the Pharisees: "you cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of extortion and self-indulgence" (Matthew 23:25).
• Compare 20:9 ("Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin'?"); Isaiah 65:5; Luke 18:9–14; 1 John 1:8–9.
units.summary: The dirtiest people are often the ones most sure they are clean.
units.principle: Self-righteousness is blind to its own stain, and no one seeks cleansing until he stops believing he is clean.
units.insight: In Jesus' parable, the Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men, while the tax collector would not even raise his eyes, but beat his breast and said, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" Jesus said it was the tax collector who went home justified (Luke 18:11–14). Naaman had to wash in a river he despised before he was clean (2 Kings 5:10–14). Self-righteousness thrives among church people, because we know the right words and do the right things. A simple test helps: when did I last confess a specific sin, not merely a general sinfulness? The good news is that the washing we need is offered freely. "The blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7), but only those who stop pretending come to be washed (1 John 1:8–9).
units.application: This week, ask a trusted friend or spouse, "Where do you see me excusing myself?" and listen without defending. Before you take Communion, name specific sins to God rather than offering a vague apology. Leaders and long-time believers: watch for the moment you start measuring yourself against newer or messier Christians. Parents: let your children hear you apologize, so they learn that grown-ups need washing too.

rel.note: The pride shown in lofty eyes goes before destruction.
A haughty look and a proud heart are named together as sin.
The arrogance of lofty eyes prepares the way for the cruelty of the next portrait.
A proud look heads the list of things the LORD hates.

units.notes:
• The NASB adds the words "in arrogance" in brackets to make the sense of raised eyelids explicit, and the NLT speaks of "disdainful" glances.
• Proverbs joins the eyes and the heart in 21:4: "A haughty look, a proud heart, And the plowing of the wicked are sin."
• Poole, quoted by Guzik, describes them as people "proud and insolent, advancing themselves, and despising all others in comparison of themselves."
• Scripture gives portraits of this look in Haman, who boasted of his riches and promotion (Esther 5:11), and in Herod, struck down when he accepted the crowd's praise as a god (Acts 12:21–23).
• Compare Psalm 101:5 ("The one who has a haughty look and a proud heart, Him I will not endure"); Psalm 131:1; Isaiah 2:11.
units.summary: Pride can be seen before it is heard: it lives in the way we look at people.
units.principle: Pride reveals itself in how we look at others, and a heart that looks down on people is already on the road to treating them cruelly.
units.insight: Nebuchadnezzar looked out over Babylon and said, "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built…?" While the words were still in his mouth, judgment fell. Only when he lifted his eyes to heaven did he learn that "those who walk in pride He is able to put down" (Daniel 4:30–37). Pride's lifted eyelids are visible to everyone except the proud. We see it in ourselves when we roll our eyes at a slow coworker, size up a visitor's clothes at church, or half-listen to someone we consider beneath us. Jesus, who had every right to look down, "humbled Himself" (Philippians 2:8). He lifted up His eyes to heaven to pray (John 17:1), and He looked on the crowds with compassion (Matthew 9:36).
units.application: Notice your eyes this week: the eye-roll in a meeting, the glance that dismisses a person before they speak. Leaders: look people in the eye and listen fully, especially those with the least status in the room. Teenagers: watch the contempt that can creep into how you look at parents and teachers. When you catch pride in your look, confess it and do one humble act of service for that person.

rel.note: Whoever oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker, the God who defends them.
The LORD pleads the cause of the poor and plunders those who plunder them.
A wicked ruler over poor people is pictured as a roaring lion and a charging bear.
The section that began with slandering a servant ends with devouring the poor.
The arrogance of lofty eyes grows into the cruelty of devouring teeth.
The leech's endless "Give and Give!" pictures the insatiable appetite of this devouring generation.

units.notes:
• The NASB, KJV and AMP read "jaw teeth" for "fangs." The ESV leaves out "like," giving a stronger picture in which the teeth are swords.
• The four portraits of 30:11–14 each begin "There is a generation," and they move from the home (parents) to the self (purity, pride) to society (the poor).
• Bridges, on the cowardice of such cruelty: "It is not the wolf with the wolf, but with the defenceless lamb."
• The psalms use the same picture: evildoers "eat up my people as they eat bread" (Psalm 14:4), and enemies have "teeth" that "are spears and arrows" (Psalm 57:4).
• Compare Amos 8:4; Micah 3:1–3; Mark 12:40 ("who devour widows' houses").
units.summary: When pride goes unchecked, people become predators, and the poor are the first to be eaten.
units.principle: Unchecked contempt and pride turn into cruelty toward the defenseless, and whoever preys on the poor sets himself against the God who made them.
units.insight: Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard. Jezebel arranged false witnesses, Naboth was stoned, and the king took his land (1 Kings 21:1–16). God sent Elijah to pronounce judgment on that very ground. The prophets thundered against rulers who stripped the skin from God's people and ate their flesh (Micah 3:2–3), and Jesus warned scribes who "devour widows' houses" behind long prayers (Mark 12:40). The teeth in this verse belong to respectable people, not only to criminals. They show in predatory lending, wage theft, exploiting a tenant or a worker who cannot complain, or an online pile-on against someone with no platform. Each of us should ask whether our gain comes from someone else's loss. Christ came the opposite way. The Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11) instead of feeding on them.
units.application: Business owners and managers: pay fairly and on time, and never use someone's desperation to drive down what they are owed. Landlords: treat tenants with the fairness you would want from God. If you see the poor being devoured in your town, church or workplace, speak up and use your influence for them. Check your spending too: do the bargains you enjoy depend on someone else's exploitation?

rel.note: The one who covets greedily all day long shows the leech's appetite, while the righteous gives freely.
Hell and Destruction are never full, and neither are the eyes of man, the same endless appetite.
The leech's cry pictures the never-satisfied hunger of the generation that devours the poor.
The next verse names the four things that never say "Enough!"
The same numerical pattern, one number and then the next, gathers examples for emphasis.

units.notes:
• The word for "leech" occurs only here in the Old Testament and comes from a root meaning to suck. The KJV reads "horseleach," and the NLT takes the two daughters as the leech's two "suckers."
• The pattern of one number followed by the next recurs through the chapter (30:15, 18, 21, 29), as it does in 6:16 and in Amos's oracles, "For three transgressions… and for four" (Amos 1:3).
• Caryl, quoted by Bridges, takes the two daughters as greed that hoards and wastefulness that spends: "The former cries—Give, to keep; the latter cries—Give, to spend."
• Compare 27:20 ("Hell and Destruction are never full; So the eyes of man are never satisfied"); Ecclesiastes 5:10; Habakkuk 2:5.
units.summary: Greed knows only one word, and it always says it twice: "Give! Give!"
units.principle: Appetite fed for its own sake only grows hungrier; greed is never cured by giving it more.
units.insight: Gehazi watched Naaman leave with his gifts refused and could not let it go. He ran after him, lied for silver and garments, and went away a leper (2 Kings 5:20–27). Judas kept the money bag and helped himself from it, and in the end he sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver (John 12:6; Matthew 26:15). The leech lives in us as well: one more purchase, one more compliment, the promotion that satisfies for a week. None of these ever says "Enough." Only God can fill a soul He made for Himself. Jesus offered the woman at the well water after which she would never thirst again (John 4:13–14). Paul, having Christ, could say, "I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11). What in your life keeps crying, "Give"?
units.application: Name the "Give! Give!" in your life this week: spending, food, screens, approval. Choose one practice of saying "Enough": a pause on spending, a day away from the phone, giving away something you like. Parents: teach children to say thank you before they ask for more. If you lead a business or ministry, ask whether growth has become an appetite instead of a calling.

rel.note: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, the ache behind the barren womb's unquieted longing.
The enticers speak of swallowing their victims alive like Sheol, the devouring grave pictured here.
Hell and Destruction are never full, the same picture of the grave that is never satisfied.
This verse names the four things the previous verse said never say "Enough!"

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB read "Sheol" for "The grave," the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.
• The NLT renders the third and fourth items as "the thirsty desert" and "the blazing fire," without repeating the phrase about never saying enough.
• Hannah's grief shows that the barren womb is a picture of sorrow, not sin: she prayed "in bitterness of soul" and wept before the LORD (1 Samuel 1:10).
• Ironside, on the fire: "were there more material to feed upon, it would go on destroying still."
• Augustine's prayer, quoted by Ironside, names the deepest hunger behind every restless appetite: "Thou hast made us for Thyself… and our hearts will never be at rest, until they rest in Thee."
• Compare Habakkuk 2:5; Ecclesiastes 1:8 ("The eye is not satisfied with seeing"); James 3:5–6.
units.summary: The grave, the dry ground and the fire never say "Enough!", and neither does a heart that lives for itself.
units.principle: Some hungers in this world are never filled by more of the same; only God can satisfy the deepest longing of the human heart.
units.insight: This verse holds a warning and a comfort. The warning is for the appetite that devours: Ahab had a kingdom and still lay sulking on his bed for one more vineyard (1 Kings 21:4). The comfort is for those who know the ache of the barren womb, or any longing God has not yet answered. Scripture does not shame that ache. It names it beside the grave as one of life's deepest hungers, and it records how God remembered Hannah and Rachel (1 Samuel 1:19–20; Genesis 30:22). Not every longing is answered as we ask, but every longing can be brought to Him. Jesus said, "I am the bread of life. He who comes to Me shall never hunger" (John 6:35). He alone meets the hunger that the grave, the fire and the dry ground can only picture.
units.application: If you are walking through infertility or another unanswered longing, bring it openly to God and let trusted friends carry it with you; your longing is not sin. Friends and church leaders: do not offer quick answers to the childless; sit with them and pray. For the rest of us, when you notice an appetite that keeps demanding more, stop feeding it for a week and turn that hunger into prayer.

rel.note: The son who mistreats his father and chases away his mother brings shame and reproach.
Heeding a father's instruction and a mother's teaching is a graceful ornament, the opposite of the mocking eye.
Whoever curses father or mother has his lamp put out, another picture of the shameful end of contempt for parents.
The earlier portrait describes the same contempt for father and mother; this verse names its end.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NLT read "vultures" for "young eagles." The Hebrew word covers large birds of prey, including both eagles and vultures, and vultures fit the picture of birds feeding on a corpse.
• For "the valley," the KJV margin offers "the brook," another rendering of the same Hebrew word.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "His eye reveals his inner cast of mind." The look on a face can show what the heart holds.
• To be left unburied was a mark of disgrace and judgment in Israel. Jeremiah said of King Jehoiakim, "He shall be buried with the burial of a donkey" (Jeremiah 22:19; compare 1 Kings 14:11).
• Compare 20:20; Deuteronomy 21:18–21; Ephesians 6:2–3, where honoring parents is "the first commandment with promise."
units.summary: A mocking look at a parent may seem small, but it points down a road with a shameful end.
units.principle: Contempt for parents, even a scornful look, sets a person on a road that ends in shame, because God upholds the honor He commands.
units.insight: Absalom shows this verse with terrible clarity. He despised his father, stole the people's loyalty and took up arms against David. He died hanging in a tree, and his body was thrown into a pit in the forest under a heap of stones (2 Samuel 18:9–17), far from the burial of a king's son. Yet David wept, "O my son Absalom… if only I had died in your place!" (2 Samuel 18:33). That cry points beyond David. God's own Son did die in the place of rebellious sons and daughters (Romans 5:8). The verse also turns to us. A mocking eye often begins in small ways: a sigh, a smirk, a look exchanged with a sibling. God sees those looks. He also welcomes every child who has despised a parent and comes home (Luke 15:18–24).
units.application: Teenagers and young adults: pay attention to your face when your parents speak, because contempt often shows before words. Ask God to change the look and the heart behind it. Parents: correct a mocking look early, calmly and consistently, never with rage. If you treated a parent with contempt in the past, it is not too late to ask their forgiveness, or, if they are gone, to confess it to God.

rel.note: It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, and Agur stands in wonder before such concealed things.
The next verse names the four ways too wonderful for Agur.
The man who confessed he could not grasp the Holy One now marvels at what he cannot explain.

units.notes:
• Compare David's wonder in Psalm 139:6: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; It is high, I cannot attain it."
• Bridges: "The kingdom of nature is full of wonder, and these wonders full of instruction."
• Henry, on the shape of the list: "The first three are natural things, and are only designed as comparisons for the illustration of the last." The fourth way carries the weight of the saying.
• Compare Job 42:3 ("Things too wonderful for me, which I did not know"); Romans 11:33.
units.summary: A wise man is not ashamed to say, "This is too wonderful for me."
units.principle: True wisdom keeps the capacity for wonder; admitting what we cannot explain is part of honoring the God who made it.
units.insight: Job demanded answers from God and received instead a tour of creation: the sea, the stars, the wild donkey, the eagle. He ended by saying, "I have uttered what I did not understand, Things too wonderful for me" (Job 42:3). His wonder healed what explanations could not. Our age prizes knowing and explaining, and we are uneasy with mystery. Yet a life without wonder becomes small and proud. When we stop being amazed at the sky, the sea or a marriage that lasts fifty years, we start thinking we understand everything. Agur stands with David, who said of God's knowledge of him, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me" (Psalm 139:6). At the center of the faith stands the greatest wonder of all: "great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh" (1 Timothy 3:16).
units.application: Take a walk this week without headphones, notice one thing in creation you cannot explain, and thank God for it. Parents: when your children ask hard questions, sometimes answer, "I don't know, but isn't God amazing?" Teachers and preachers: do not flatten every mystery with a neat explanation. Married couples: thank God aloud for the mystery that drew you together.

rel.note: Finding a wife is a good thing and a gift of the LORD's favor.
The previous verse introduces these four ways as too wonderful for Agur.
The adulterous woman's way also leaves no trace, but it is the counterfeit of the faithful love pictured here.
The book closes with the virtuous wife, whom the deeper reading also sees as the Bride of Christ.
The father celebrates the delight of a man in the wife of his youth, the same wonder of rightful love.

units.notes:
• The word translated "virgin," 'almah, describes a young woman of marriageable age. It is used of Rebekah ("the virgin," Genesis 24:43), of Miriam ("the maiden," Exodus 2:8) and in Isaiah 7:14. The ESV agrees with "virgin"; the NASB and KJV read "maid."
• "In the midst of the sea" is literally "in the heart of the sea," as the KJV margin notes, meaning far out in open water.
• Van Leeuwen, cited by Waltke and quoted by Guzik, says Agur's "small poem sings implicit praise to God for the glories of creation." The fourth way is a wonder to praise God for, not a sin to warn against.
• Some older commentators read the fourth way as a seducer's hidden arts. Its place among God's wonders and its contrast with the adulteress of 30:20 point instead to the wonder of rightful love.
• Compare Acts 1:9; John 3:8; John 14:30; 1 Corinthians 10:4; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:31–32.
units.summary: An eagle, a snake, a ship and young love: each moves in a way no one can fully trace.
units.principle: God's world is full of untraceable wonders, and the love that joins a man and a woman is among the greatest, a picture Scripture applies to Christ and His Church (Ephesians 5:32).
units.insight: The New Testament lets us see further than Agur did. As a spiritual reading, the eagle pictures the risen Christ, who "was taken up, and a cloud received Him out of their sight" (Acts 1:9), or the Spirit, who moves like wind no one can trace (John 3:8). The serpent on the rock pictures Satan's temptation of Jesus, which left no mark on the Rock; Jesus said, "the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in Me" (John 14:30). The ship pictures the Church carried through the waters of this world by the wind of the Spirit. The man with a virgin pictures the greatest mystery: "This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32). The question for each reader is personal: do you know Christ's love as His Bride, or only admire it from a distance?
units.application: Married couples: thank God together for the mystery of how He brought you to each other, and guard that love as something holy. Young people: treat attraction as a wonder from God, not a game, and let it move toward faithful commitment. Single believers: you belong fully to the Bride Christ loves. When temptation presses, remember that the serpent found no hold on Christ, and in Him you can stand.

rel.note: Whoever confesses and forsakes sin finds mercy, unlike the woman who says she has done no wickedness.
The generation pure in its own eyes shares her refusal to see her own filth.
The last of the four wonderful ways pictures the faithful love that the adulterous woman counterfeits.
Folly's "bread eaten in secret" uses the same picture of sin as a pleasant meal.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB render her last word as "wrong": "I have done no wrong."
• "She eats" pictures sin as an ordinary appetite, as in Folly's call: "Stolen water is sweet, And bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (9:17).
• Kidner, quoted by Guzik, calls her "the fifth, and unnatural, marvel": "a person utterly at ease and in her element in sin."
• Bridges: "Where shame ceases to accompany it, the ruin of the victim is accomplished." When sin no longer brings shame, the ruin is complete.
• A similar denial appears in 28:24, where one who robs his parents says, "It is no transgression."
• Compare Jeremiah 6:15 ("They were not at all ashamed; Nor did they know how to blush"); Hebrews 3:13; 1 John 1:8–10.
units.summary: Sin that leaves no trace on the outside can still leave a heart that no longer blushes.
units.principle: The most dangerous stage of sin is when it no longer feels like sin; denial closes the door that confession would open to mercy.
units.insight: David committed adultery with Bathsheba and covered it for months, even arranging her husband's death (2 Samuel 11). Like the woman of this verse, he wiped his mouth. Only when Nathan said, "You are the man!" did David confess, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:7, 13). The adulterous woman stands for a heart, in any man or woman, that has learned to sin without blushing. It happens slowly: the browser history cleared, the messages deleted, the explanation rehearsed. Each wipe of the mouth makes the next one easier. The way back is the way David took. At the deeper level, Christ's Bride is not the one who has never sinned but the one He has washed and made clean (Ephesians 5:25–27). He offers mercy to everyone who stops saying, "I have done no wickedness" (1 John 1:9).
units.application: If you are hiding sexual sin, tell one mature believer this week and ask for help; secrecy keeps sin alive. Husbands and wives: keep your phones and accounts open to each other. Parents: teach teenagers that the shame they feel after wrongdoing is a gift that leads to confession, not something to wipe away. Pastors: preach both the warning and the welcome, because people in the pews are wiping their mouths.

rel.note: Luxury for a fool and a servant ruling princes are named as things that do not fit.
When the wrong person rules, the people groan, the upheaval this saying describes.
The next verse names the first two reversals the earth cannot bear.
The last two reversals complete the list this verse introduces.

units.notes:
• The ESV reads "trembles" for "is perturbed," and the NASB "quakes."
• Bridges: "Next to things which were unsearchable, Agur now mentions some things that were intolerable."
• Henry describes the four as "four sorts of persons that are very troublesome to the places where they live." The weight falls on the people around them, who must live with the upheaval.
• The three-then-four pattern gathers examples for emphasis, as in 30:15, 18 and 29; no special meaning lies in the numbers themselves.
• Compare Ecclesiastes 10:5–7, where the Preacher laments that "Folly is set in great dignity" while servants ride and princes walk.
units.summary: A rise in position with no change of heart shakes everyone standing nearby.
units.principle: Position does not change character; when people rise faster than their hearts are formed, everyone around them feels the tremor.
units.insight: Saul looked the part of a king, taller than anyone in Israel, but power did not change his heart, and his reign sank into jealousy and fear (1 Samuel 10:23; 18:8–9). David, by contrast, was tested for years as a shepherd and a fugitive before he took the throne. Sudden reversals still shake homes, churches and workplaces: the untested leader, the overnight celebrity, the newly wealthy relative. The verse also searches us. Are we asking God for a larger position before He has formed a heart that can carry it? Jesus is the perfect reversal in the other direction. He took "the form of a bondservant," and God highly exalted Him, because His character never changed (Philippians 2:7–9). In Him, God lifts the lowly safely (Luke 1:52).
units.application: Church leaders: do not hand a platform to someone untested, however gifted; let character be proven in small things first (1 Timothy 3:6). Managers: support a newly promoted employee with mentoring, not just a title. If you have recently risen in pay, influence or position, ask a trusted friend to tell you if you are changing for the worse. Parents: build character in your children before you give them freedom.

rel.note: A wise servant can rule well, so the danger here lies in unready character, not in a servant's station.
Luxury for a fool and a servant ruling princes are named together as things that do not fit.
A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food, the harm done when the lowly gain power without wisdom.
The introductory verse frames these as reversals the earth cannot bear.

units.notes:
• The ESV and NASB read "slave" for "servant" and "becomes king" for "reigns."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "A servant who gains authority over others has neither the training nor disposition to rule well." The problem is the unprepared character, not the person's origin.
• Joseph shows the other side: a servant raised to rule who governed wisely because God had formed his character first (Genesis 41:38–44).
• Zimri shows the danger. A servant who commanded half the king's chariots, he murdered his master and reigned seven days amid civil war (1 Kings 16:9–20).
• Nabal pictures a fool filled with food: rich and holding "a feast in his house, like the feast of a king," he insulted David's men and endangered his household (1 Samuel 25:10–11, 36).
units.summary: Power does not make a servant a king, and a full stomach does not make a fool wise.
units.principle: Power and plenty magnify what is already in a person; without wisdom and grace, they make the unready and the foolish a burden to everyone.
units.insight: Nabal had flocks, servants and a feast fit for a king, and his plenty only made him more insulting. He answered David's request with contempt and nearly brought ruin on his household (1 Samuel 25:10–11, 36–38). Haman was lifted above all the princes and used his power to plot the destruction of a whole people (Esther 3:1–6). These verses show no contempt for servants. Joseph and Daniel ruled well because God had shaped their hearts before He raised them up. The question is personal: what would sudden power or plenty reveal in me? A promotion, an inheritance or a large following can expose a heart that was hidden. Jesus, the true King, "did not come to be served, but to serve" (Mark 10:45), and He makes faithful servants into rulers in His kingdom (Luke 19:17).
units.application: If you have just been promoted, ask God daily for wisdom before you use your new authority, and refuse to settle old scores. Boards and pastors: look for proven character, not only availability, when you fill leadership roles. If you have more money than before, watch for new carelessness or arrogance at the table, at work or online. Parents: do not give a teenager more freedom or money than their character can carry.

rel.note: An excellent wife is her husband's crown, the opposite of a bitter spirit carried into marriage.
Living with a contentious and angry woman is worse than the wilderness, the strife the first line describes.
A servant pampered from childhood will claim a son's place in the end, another household reversal.
The introductory verse frames these as reversals the earth cannot bear.

units.notes:
• The word behind "hateful" means hated or unloved. The ESV and NASB read "unloved," and the KJV "odious." The same word describes Leah: "the LORD saw that Leah was unloved" (Genesis 29:31).
• On the reading "unloved," the line describes a woman long rejected who suddenly gains a husband and a household. The saying names the upheaval of such a sudden change; it does not say that being unloved makes a woman bitter or unfit for marriage.
• The ESV reads "displaces" for "succeeds," and the KJV says the handmaid is "heir" to her mistress.
• Henry draws the lesson for anyone raised from humble beginnings: watch "against that sin which will most easily beset them, pride and haughtiness."
• Compare 21:9, 19; 27:15, on the misery of a home filled with strife.
units.summary: A wedding ring or a new title does not heal a bitter heart; it gives bitterness a bigger stage.
units.principle: A new position in a marriage or a household does not change a heart; without humility and grace, a sudden rise spreads strife through a home.
units.insight: Hagar's story is painful on every side. Sarai gave her to Abram; when Hagar conceived, she despised her mistress, and Sarai answered with harshness until Hagar fled into the desert (Genesis 16:1–6). Everyone in that home was wounded by a sudden change of place. Yet the God who saw the strife also saw Hagar, and she called Him "You-Are-the-God-Who-Sees" (Genesis 16:13). Leah, the unloved wife, found that "the LORD saw" her too (Genesis 29:31), and at the birth of Judah she said, "Now I will praise the LORD" (Genesis 29:35). This verse warns us against carrying bitterness into a new role and against grasping at another's place. It also comforts the unloved and the displaced: God sees. In Christ, the rejected are welcomed into His household not as slaves but as sons and daughters (Galatians 4:4–7).
units.application: If you are about to marry, deal with bitterness and resentment now; a wedding will not cure them. Newly married couples: ask an older couple to help you build peace at home. Blended families and households with new members: name the tensions openly and give everyone a fair place. If you have been unloved or pushed aside, take your hurt to the God who sees, and let Him heal it before it hardens.

rel.note: A wise man scales the city of the mighty, wisdom accomplishing what strength cannot.
The ant, the rock badger, the locust and the spider are the four little creatures this verse introduces.
The sluggard is sent to the ant to learn wisdom, as Agur learns from small creatures.

units.notes:
• "Exceedingly wise" is literally "wise, made wise," as the KJV margin notes. The doubled wording strengthens the description, and the second word is passive: it describes a wisdom the creatures have been given rather than one they achieved.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the verse "uniquely uses 'wise' for animals to denote their skill to cope." Their wisdom is a practical skill for surviving with the little strength they have.
• Henry draws out what "made wise" implies, that the wisdom is given: "All that are wise to salvation are made wise by the grace of God."
• Compare Job 12:7 ("But now ask the beasts, and they will teach you"); Matthew 6:26; 1 Corinthians 1:27.
units.summary: Size is no measure of wisdom; some of God's smallest creatures are among His wisest teachers.
units.principle: God has built lessons of wisdom into the smallest parts of creation, and weakness joined with wisdom accomplishes what strength alone cannot.
units.insight: God answered Job not with a lecture but with a tour of His creatures (Job 38–41). Jesus told anxious disciples to look at the birds and consider the lilies (Matthew 6:26–28). Agur does the same. Many of us feel small: too little education, too little money, too little influence to matter. These four creatures say that littleness is no barrier to wisdom. God has always delighted to work through the small. He chose Gideon, the least in his father's house in the weakest clan of Manasseh (Judges 6:15), and David, the youngest son out with the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11–13). Paul wrote that "God has chosen the weak things of the world to put to shame the things which are mighty" (1 Corinthians 1:27). The question is whether we are humble enough to learn from small teachers.
units.application: If you feel too small to matter in a big church, a large company or a crowded classroom, ask what skill for living God has given you, and use it faithfully. Parents: take your children outside this week to watch ants, birds or bees, and talk about what they teach. Leaders: do not overlook the quiet, little-noticed people on your team; they are often the wisest.

rel.note: He who gathers in summer is a wise son, as the ant gathers while food is plentiful.
The wise keep treasure in store, while the foolish squander it.
The ant is the first of the four little creatures that are exceedingly wise.
The ant provides her supplies in summer and gathers food in harvest, the same lesson of foresight.

units.notes:
• Scripture can call a group of creatures "a people" or "a nation"; Joel uses such language for a swarm of locusts (Joel 1:6; 2:2).
• Bridges, on the ant's weakness: "so weak, that thousands are crushed by one tread of the foot; yet wise in preparing their meat in the summer." In older English, "meat" means food of any kind.
• The ants of the land of Israel include grain-gathering kinds that store seed, a habit the first hearers could watch for themselves.
• Henry: "When the ravening lions lack, and suffer hunger, the laborious ants have plenty, and know no want."
• Compare 6:6–8; 10:5; Genesis 41:34–36, where Joseph stored grain in the years of plenty.
units.summary: The ant never waits for winter to start getting ready for it.
units.principle: Wisdom uses today's opportunity to prepare for tomorrow's need, and weakness is no excuse for failing to prepare.
units.insight: Joseph did what the ant does. In seven years of plenty he stored grain, and when famine came, Egypt and his own family lived (Genesis 41:47–57). Jesus told of a rich man who also stored up, but only for himself, and never prepared his soul; God called him a fool (Luke 12:16–21). The ant's lesson reaches both. Many of us live as if summer will never end: no savings, no habits of prayer, no Scripture stored in the heart for the day of trouble. Then the winter of illness, grief or temptation finds us empty. Today is summer for something in your life. Jesus said He must work "while it is day; the night is coming when no one can work" (John 9:4), and He calls us to use our days well.
units.application: Young adults: start saving something from every paycheck, however small. Families: plan this month for next year's known expenses. Students: study steadily now instead of cramming at the end. Spiritually, store up Scripture in good seasons: memorize one verse this week so that it is there when hard days come. Church leaders: train the next generation of leaders before you need them.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD His children have a place of refuge.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower where the righteous run and are safe, the refuge to which the badger's lesson points.
The prudent foresee danger and hide themselves, as the rock badger takes shelter in the crags.
The rock badger is one of the four little creatures that are exceedingly wise.

units.notes:
• The animal is the rock hyrax, a small, shy, furry animal. The NLT reads "hyraxes," the KJV "conies," and the NASB keeps the Hebrew name, shephanim.
• The hyrax has soft, padded feet that cannot dig burrows, so it lives in the clefts of rocks. It is timid and quick to retreat at the first sign of danger.
• Henry turns the lesson to people: "Sense of our own indigence and weakness should drive us to him that is a rock higher than we for shelter and support." "Indigence" means need.
• Compare 22:3 ("A prudent man foresees evil and hides himself"); 18:10; Psalm 61:2 ("Lead me to the rock that is higher than I").
units.summary: The rock badger's strength is not in itself but in knowing where to hide.
units.principle: Wisdom admits its weakness and makes its home in a place of real safety, rather than trusting strength it does not have.
units.insight: David spent years hiding among the rocks and caves of the wilderness, from the cave of Adullam to the Rocks of the Wild Goats near En Gedi (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:1–2). There he learned to sing, "The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer" (Psalm 18:2). Scripture uses the same picture of rocks and refuge for God Himself (Psalm 61:2). Our temptation is the opposite of the badger's wisdom. We stand in the open, trusting our own strength, plans and willpower, until we are overwhelmed. Wisdom begins by saying, "I am feeble." Jesus invites all who labor and are heavy laden to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28), and Paul learned that Christ's strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Where are you still trying to stand in the open?
units.application: Know your weak spots and stay out of the open: if late nights alone online are dangerous for you, set boundaries before temptation comes. In anxious seasons, run first to prayer and to God's people instead of trying to tough it out. Young believers: stay close to a church where you are known. Leaders: admit your limits and build accountability around yourself.

rel.note: Safety lies in many counselors working together, as strength lies in the locusts' unity.
The man who isolates himself rages against wise judgment, the opposite of the locusts' ranks.
The locust is one of the four little creatures that are exceedingly wise.
The ant also works without captain, overseer or ruler, yet does its work in order.

units.notes:
• The word behind "advance in ranks" means to divide; here it pictures the locusts dividing themselves into companies as they move. The KJV margin gives "gathered together," and the ESV and NLT speak of marching in rank or formation.
• Jerome, quoted by Bridges, described a swarm he had watched keep order "so as not to be an hair's-breadth out of their several ranks."
• Henry: "sense of weakness should engage us to keep together, that we may strengthen the hands of one another."
• Compare Joel 1:4–6; Exodus 10:12–15; Ephesians 4:3, 16.
units.summary: No king, no commander, and still in step: the locust shows the strength of disciplined unity.
units.principle: Disciplined unity multiplies the strength of the weak; those who keep their place together achieve what none could do alone.
units.insight: When Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, each family took its own section, and the work was finished in fifty-two days, though no one could have done it alone (Nehemiah 3; 6:15). In the early church the believers "continued steadfastly" together, and the Lord added to their number daily (Acts 2:42–47). Many believers today prefer to march alone: no church, no team, no one to answer to. The locust rebukes that independence. We also need to watch the opposite danger, division that breaks ranks over small things. Unlike the locusts, the Church does have a King. Christ is the Head, and from Him "the whole body, joined and knit together," grows as every part does its share (Ephesians 4:15–16). Am I keeping my place in the ranks?
units.application: Commit to a local church and serve on one team there this month instead of watching from the edge. Church members: do your part faithfully even when no leader is watching. Leaders: build clear roles so people can work together well without being driven. In your family or workplace, refuse to break ranks over minor disagreements; settle them and keep moving together.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent will rule, persistence carrying the weak upward.
The man who excels in his work will stand before kings, as the skillful spider is found in kings' palaces.
The spider is the last of the four little creatures that are exceedingly wise.

units.notes:
• The identity of this creature is uncertain. The NKJV and KJV read "spider," while the ESV, NASB and NLT read "lizard." The ESV and NASB also take the first line to mean that the creature can be caught in the hand, so the contrast is between how easily it is taken and where it is found.
• Either way the lesson is the same: a creature with no power to force its way in still finds its way into the king's house.
• Henry: "If one well-spun web be swept away, it is but making another." In other words, when its web is destroyed, the spider simply spins a new one.
• Compare 22:29 ("Do you see a man who excels in his work? He will stand before kings"); Genesis 41:46; Daniel 1:19–20.
units.summary: Small enough to catch in your hand, the spider still ends up in the king's palace.
units.principle: Skill and persistence can carry the weak further than force, though God, not effort alone, decides where they finally stand.
units.insight: Daniel arrived in Babylon a captive young man with no rights and no power. Through faithful skill, steady prayer and quiet integrity, he served in the courts of kings for decades (Daniel 1:19–21; 6:3). Nehemiah was a cupbearer, a servant, yet he stood before the king and won help for Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1–8). We easily think the doors are closed to us because we are small. The spider never asks permission. It holds on and keeps climbing, while many of us give up after one web is swept away. The gospel takes this further. We could never climb into the King's house by our own grip, but Christ has opened "a new and living way" into God's presence (Hebrews 10:19–22), and He has prepared a place for us in His Father's house (John 14:2).
units.application: If you feel stuck at the bottom of an organization, keep doing excellent work and building skill; faithfulness is noticed more often than you think. When a plan is swept away, start the next web instead of quitting. Parents: praise your children's persistence more than their talent. Employers: notice the quiet, skilled people who keep showing up, and open doors for them.

rel.note: The lion is the first of the four that are stately in walk.
The list rises to its climax in the king whose troops are with him.
The next saying warns against the self-exaltation that rightful dignity exposes.

units.notes:
• The ESV uses "stately" in both lines, with "tread" and "stride," and the KJV speaks of things that "go well" and are "comely in going." "Comely" is older English for graceful or attractive.
• This is the last of the chapter's four three-then-four sayings (30:15, 18, 21, 29); the pattern gathers examples for emphasis and builds to the final item.
• Bridges draws a lesson for believers: "Cultivate not only the integrity, but the comeliness of the Christian character." He means that a Christian life should be not only upright but also attractive in the way it carries itself.
• Compare 30:32; 28:1; Ecclesiastes 8:2–4.
units.summary: Agur ends his lists by watching how things walk; the way a creature carries itself shows the strength behind it.
units.principle: A dignified bearing is admirable when it rests on real strength and rightful standing; it becomes folly when it is only a pose.
units.insight: When David went out to meet Goliath, he refused Saul's armor and did not strut like a warrior. He walked out "in the name of the LORD of hosts," and his confidence rested on God (1 Samuel 17:38–47). Goliath had the swagger without any standing before God. Many of us carry ourselves either with false bravado or with constant apology. Scripture calls believers to a different bearing: not arrogance, but the steady walk of people who know whose they are. Paul urged believers to "walk worthy of the calling with which you were called, with all lowliness and gentleness" (Ephesians 4:1–2). Jesus "steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), the most stately walk in history, straight toward the cross.
units.application: Notice how you carry yourself at work and at church: are you shrinking back in fear or swaggering for attention? Ask God for a steady bearing rooted in Him. Leaders: walk into hard conversations calmly and courteously, without bluster. Parents: show children how to stand with quiet confidence instead of bullying or cowering. Young people: let your confidence rest on who you are in Christ, not on your image.

rel.note: The righteous are bold as a lion, the same fearless bearing this verse admires.
The introductory verse names the four that are stately in walk.
The list continues to its climax in a king with his troops.

units.notes:
• The ESV reads "turn back" and the NASB "retreat" for "turn away."
• Henry: "The lion turns not away, nor alters his pace, for fear of any pursuers, since he knows he is too hard for them." "Too hard for them" means too strong for them.
• The lion appears across Scripture as a picture of strength and courage. Jacob called Judah "a lion's whelp" (Genesis 49:9), and the Gadites who joined David had faces "like the faces of lions" (1 Chronicles 12:8).
• Compare 28:1; 19:12; 2 Samuel 17:10.
units.summary: The lion does not hurry and does not back down, because its confidence is real.
units.principle: Real courage comes from real strength; the person secure in what God has made him can stand firm without bluster.
units.insight: Nehemiah was urged to hide in the temple when enemies plotted to kill him. He refused: "Should such a man as I flee?" (Nehemiah 6:10–11). Like the lion, he did not turn away, because his confidence was in God, not in show. Our courage often depends on how strong we feel that day. The verse points us to a deeper security. The righteous are bold as a lion (28:1) because they have nothing to hide and Someone to trust. Scripture calls Jesus "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5). He did not turn away from the cross, and He gives His people a courage that does not depend on their own strength. Where are you tempted to back away from what is right?
units.application: When you must take an unpopular stand at work, in your family or in a church meeting, prepare in prayer and then do not retreat from what is right. Young believers: do not hide your faith to fit in. Leaders: stand firm on conviction while staying courteous; a lion does not need to roar to be strong. If fear is driving your choices, name the fear and bring it to God.

rel.note: A king's honor lies in a multitude of people, as this king is most stately with his troops around him.
Mercy and truth preserve the king, the inner strength that wins willing loyalty.
The king is the climax of the four that are stately in walk.
The lion is the first of the stately four whose list climbs to the king.
Rightful majesty stands against the folly of exalting oneself without standing.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew name of the second animal occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. It describes a creature "girt in the loins," that is, with a belt drawn tight around the waist, a way of picturing a lean, trim body. The KJV margin offers "horse," and the ESV, NASB and NLT read "strutting rooster."
• The last line is also difficult. The KJV reads it as a king against whom there is "no rising up," and the current NIV (2011) similarly speaks of a king secure against revolt, noting that the Hebrew is uncertain. The ESV and NASB speak of a king with his army.
• Poole, quoted by Bridges, thought the wisest interpreter of the uncertain animal is the one "who confesses he knows not what it is."
• Henry, on the male goat that leads the flock: "It is the comeliness of a Christian's going to go first in a good work and to lead others in the right way." "Comeliness" means beauty or fittingness.
• Compare 14:28; 20:28; 1 Kings 4:24–25.
units.summary: A king walks tallest when his people stand with him.
units.principle: Rightful authority carries itself with dignity, and its strength lies in the people who willingly stand with it.
units.insight: David's mighty men risked their lives to bring him water from the well of Bethlehem simply because he longed for it (2 Samuel 23:15–17). That is a king whose troops are with him. Absalom had an army too, but he had won it by flattery, and it was routed in a single day (2 Samuel 15:6; 18:6–8).
