Every leader, parent, pastor or manager carries some measure of this kind of authority. The question is whether people follow us because they trust us or only because they must. Jesus is the King whose people follow Him willingly: "Your people shall be volunteers In the day of Your power" (Psalm 110:3). Like the goat at the head of the flock, He goes before His sheep, and they follow Him (John 10:4).
units.application: Leaders at work or church: earn loyalty by going first in hard tasks, as the male goat leads the flock, rather than demanding it. Ask your team or family where your leadership feels distant. Parents: let your children see you do the things you ask of them. Followers: stand with leaders who lead well, and tell them so; a leader backed by willing people serves everyone better.

rel.note: Even a fool is counted wise when he holds his peace.
Whoever guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from troubles, the counsel of the hand over the mouth.
Agur began with humble confession; self-exaltation is its opposite.
The stately walk of the four rests on real strength, unlike foolish self-exaltation.
The king's rightful majesty exposes the folly of lifting oneself up without standing.
The next verse explains why: pressing anger only produces strife.

units.notes:
• The NLT takes "put your hand on your mouth" as covering the mouth in shame.
• Job's words show the gesture's meaning: "Behold, I am vile; What shall I answer You? I lay my hand over my mouth" (Job 40:4).
• Henry: "It is bad to think ill, but it is much worse to speak it, for that implies a consent to the evil thought and a willingness to infect others with it."
• Bridges: "Better to keep in the infirmity, than to give it vent." In plain words, it is better to hold a weakness inside and deal with it before God than to let it out in words.
• Compare 17:28; 21:23; Micah 7:16; James 1:19.
units.summary: When pride or a scheme rises in you, the wisest move is a hand over your mouth.
units.principle: Pride and evil plans grow by being spoken; the wise stop them at the mouth and humble themselves before God.
units.insight: Job had argued long and loudly with God. When the LORD finally spoke, Job said, "I lay my hand over my mouth. Once I have spoken, but I will not answer" (Job 40:4–5). Peter, by contrast, took Jesus aside and rebuked Him for speaking of the cross, and Jesus answered, "Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:22–23). Most of the damage done by pride and scheming passes through the mouth: the boast in the meeting, the plan shared with a friend, the angry reply drafted at midnight. The verse gives a simple, physical remedy: cover your mouth, then bring what you were about to say to God. Jesus, who could have defended Himself before His accusers, "opened not His mouth" (Isaiah 53:7). He bore our sins, including the words we did not stop in time.
units.application: This week, when you feel the urge to boast or to win an argument, pause and say nothing for ten seconds. Before sending an angry email or text, wait a day. If you have been plotting how to get back at someone, stop talking about it and confess it to God. Leaders and parents: when you realize you have spoken from pride, admit it quickly and stop defending yourself.

rel.note: A soft answer turns away wrath, the opposite of forcing it.
A wrathful man stirs up strife, but patience calms contention.
Stop contention before a quarrel starts, the counsel this verse illustrates.
A contentious man kindles strife as charcoal feeds a fire.
The hand over the mouth stops the pressure before it produces strife.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew uses the same noun three times, a word meaning squeezing or pressing. The NKJV varies it as "churning," "wringing" and "forcing," while the ESV keeps "pressing" throughout. The repetition makes the point plain: the same kind of pressure that brings butter from milk and blood from a nose brings strife out of anger.
• The verse also plays on words. The Hebrew word for "nose" is also the ordinary word for anger, which was pictured in flared nostrils and hard breathing, and "wrath" in the third line is a form of the same word. In Hebrew, pressing the nose and pressing anger sound almost alike.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "So the intent of this concluding advice is to strive for peace and harmony through humility and righteousness."
• Henry describes how forced wrath grows: "one angry word begets another, and that a third."
• Compare 15:1, 18; 17:14; 26:21; James 3:16.
units.summary: Squeeze milk and you get butter; squeeze a nose and you get blood; squeeze anger and you get a fight.
units.principle: Pressure applied to anger yields strife, so the wise stop pressing before a quarrel is born.
units.insight: Nabal pressed David's anger with insults, and David strapped on his sword. Abigail released the pressure with humble words and gifts, and bloodshed was avoided (1 Samuel 25:10–13, 23–35). Rehoboam pressed the people's grievance with harsh words and lost most of his kingdom (1 Kings 12:13–16). We all know how to press: the old grievance raised again, the tone that provokes, the last word we cannot resist. Then we act surprised when blood or strife comes out. The wise ask, "Am I squeezing?" Jesus, "when He was reviled, did not revile in return" (1 Peter 2:23), and He calls His followers to be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9). At the cross He bore the wrath our sins deserved rather than pressing it back on us, and so He made peace (Colossians 1:20).
units.application: In marriage, when a conversation heats up, stop pressing your point; lower your voice or take a break. Parents: do not poke at a child's sore spot to win an argument. Online, do not post the reply you know will provoke. Leaders: when tension rises in a meeting, call a pause instead of forcing a decision. In every setting this week, ask yourself, "Am I squeezing?"

rel.note: The book opens by charging a son not to forsake his mother's law; here a king preserves what his mother taught him.
Agur's heading uses the same word "utterance" for another collection from a wise voice beyond Solomon.
The mother's teaching named in the heading begins with her tender cry to her son.
Solomon recalls what his father taught him as a boy, just as Lemuel records his mother's words.
The father again tells his son to keep his mother's law, the kind of teaching Lemuel received and handed on.

units.notes:
• *Utterance* translates massa, the same word that heads Agur's words in 30:1. It is often rendered "oracle" or "burden," a weighty message; the ESV and NASB have "oracle," and the KJV "prophecy." Calling a mother's counsel by this word marks it as serious instruction, not passing advice.
• Some read massa as the name of a people, Massa, descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14). On that reading the heading means "Lemuel, king of Massa," a king from outside Israel.
• Jewish tradition identified Lemuel with Solomon, and some older Christian writers followed it, naming Bathsheba as his mother. The text does not support this: Solomon is named in the book's own headings (1:1; 10:1; 25:1), and Scripture never calls him Lemuel.
• The name Lemuel is usually explained as "belonging to God." Matthew Henry: "the name signifies one that is for God, or devoted to God."
• Compare 2 Timothy 1:5 and 3:15, where Timothy's faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and he knew the Scriptures from childhood.
units.summary: A king handed these words on, but his mother first put them in his heart.
units.principle: No one rises above the need to be taught; those who will lead others must first receive instruction themselves.
units.insight: Scripture records the names of the mothers of Judah's kings again and again, as if to say that a reign begins at home. Some taught well. Timothy's faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Others taught badly: King Ahaziah walked in the ways of Ahab's house, "for his mother advised him to do wickedly" (2 Chronicles 22:3). Lemuel's mother used her influence well, and her son was humble enough to keep her words and pass them on. That is the harder half of the lesson. It takes humility for a king to say, "This is what my mother taught me." Who taught you the ways of God, and do you still honor what they gave? Even Jesus, in His humanity, grew up under His mother's care and "increased in wisdom" (Luke 2:52).
units.application: Parents and grandparents: your words to your children are an "utterance," not small talk, so choose them with prayer. Mothers, do not underestimate the influence God has given you, even when your children are grown. Adult sons and daughters: write down one lesson a parent or mentor taught you, and thank them, or thank God for them if they are gone. If no one taught you this way, you can be that voice for someone younger.

rel.note: The mother who bore a son rejoices when he grows wise, the hope behind this mother's anxious cry.
The father also appeals to his son personally, asking first for his heart before giving his warnings.
The heading names this as the teaching Lemuel's mother gave him, and this verse opens her words.
Solomon remembers being "tender and the only one in the sight of my mother" when his father taught him.

units.notes:
• The Hebrew simply repeats "what" three times with no verb. The ESV fills it out as "What are you doing, my son?" while the NLT turns the verse into tender addresses beginning "O my son." Others hear in it a mother searching for words: "What shall I say to you?"
• *Son of my vows.* A vow was a solemn promise made to God, often with a prayer for a child. Hannah vowed that if the LORD gave her a son, she would give him to the LORD all the days of his life (1 Samuel 1:11).
• The word for "son" in this verse is bar, the Aramaic form, rather than the usual Hebrew ben. Aramaic was a sister language of Hebrew, spoken by Israel's neighbors. The Aramaic form may point to a setting outside Israel; Garrett, quoted by Guzik, notes that "several Aramaisms appear in the text," that is, Aramaic word forms.
• Compare 1 Samuel 1:27–28 ("For this child I prayed") and 2 Timothy 3:15.
units.summary: Before Lemuel's mother warns him, she reminds him whose he is: her son, her child, her prayer.
units.principle: Hard counsel carries the weight of the love behind it; the right to warn grows out of the love that has prayed.
units.insight: Hannah wept and prayed for a son, vowed him to the LORD, and later said, "For this child I prayed" (1 Samuel 1:27). Bridges asks, "If there were more Hannahs, would there not be more Samuels?" Lemuel's mother was such a woman, and her prayers gave her the right to speak hard words. Warnings land differently when we know the one warning us has loved and prayed for us. That is how God speaks to His people. "How can I give you up, Ephraim?" He cries, even while He warns (Hosea 11:8). Jesus grieved over Jerusalem and longed to gather her children "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings" (Matthew 23:37). When Scripture warns us, we are hearing the voice of that love. And if you are praying for a wandering child, your vows and tears are not wasted.
units.application: Parents: before you correct, remind your child whose they are and how much you love them; let the warning come wrapped in relationship. Pray for your children by name, and tell them you do. Youth workers and mentors: earn the right to speak hard truth by praying long before you speak it. Grown children: when a parent's warning comes with tears, listen for the love underneath before you argue with the words.

rel.note: The strength the king must not squander is the very quality, chayil, praised in the woman of valor.
His mother moves from the danger of women to the danger of wine, the second thing that ruins kings.
Sexual sin hands a man's honor, years and labor to others, as the king is warned not to give away his strength.
The immoral woman has brought down many, and "all who were slain by her were strong men."

units.notes:
• *Strength* translates chayil, the same word rendered "virtuous" in 31:10 and "done well" in 31:29. The king must not squander his chayil on women; the closing poem then praises a woman who has chayil herself. The echo shows the warning is about indulgence, not a low view of women.
• The ESV reads the second line as people rather than a thing: "those who destroy kings." Either way the danger is whatever brings rulers down.
• Nehemiah used Solomon as the warning: "Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? ... pagan women caused even him to sin" (Nehemiah 13:26).
• Compare Deuteronomy 17:17 and 1 Kings 11:1–4. Proverbs 5:9–10 gives the same picture of a man who hands his honor, his years and his labors to strangers.
units.summary: A king can lose a kingdom without a battle, simply by spending his strength in the wrong place.
units.principle: Strength given to indulgence is stolen from calling, and whatever we give ourselves to will in the end rule us.
units.insight: Samson is the Bible's sharpest picture of this verse. Set apart from birth, he spent his strength on women who used him, until he told Delilah all his heart and "his strength left him" (Judges 16:17–19). David fell another way. At the time when kings go out to battle he stayed home, saw Bathsheba, and set loose a sword that never left his house (2 Samuel 11:1; 12:10). Neither man set out to give away a kingdom. Each gave away one evening, then another. The same quiet drain can happen to any of us through pornography, an emotional affair, or an indulgence we tell ourselves is private. Jesus was tempted in every way yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). For those who have already given their strength away, David's prayer is still open: "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10).
units.application: Leaders, pastors and business owners: guard the places where power and loneliness meet, such as late-night messages, travel and private meetings, and build accountability before you need it. Young men: decide now what you will not give your strength to, before the moment comes. If something is already draining you, tell a trusted friend this week and take one concrete step away from it.

rel.note: A throne is established by righteousness, so anything that leads a king into wrongdoing undermines his rule.
Wine and strong drink mock and lead astray those who give themselves to them.
The portrait of the drunkard shows what wine does to judgment and self-control.
The warning against wine follows the warning against giving a king's strength to women.
The next verse gives the reason for this warning: the drunken king forgets the law and wrongs the afflicted.

units.notes:
• The ESV, NASB and KJV read "strong drink" for "intoxicating drink," and the NASB speaks of rulers who "desire" it, turning the warning toward the craving itself.
• Matthew Henry: "that which for the time unmans them does for the time unking them." In plain words, drink that robs a man of his self-control robs a king of his kingship for as long as it lasts.
• Scripture records drunken rulers. Elah was murdered while "drinking himself drunk" (1 Kings 16:9). Ben-Hadad and his allies "were getting drunk" when Israel attacked (1 Kings 20:16). Belshazzar feasted with wine the night his kingdom fell (Daniel 5:1–4, 30).
• Compare Ecclesiastes 10:17, "Blessed are you, O land, when ... your princes feast at the proper time— For strength and not for drunkenness!" The New Testament asks the same of church leaders: "not given to wine" (1 Timothy 3:3).
units.summary: A clear head is not a king's private property; it belongs to everyone who depends on his judgment.
units.principle: The greater our responsibility for others, the less freedom we have to cloud our own judgment.
units.insight: Ironside: "He who would rule well over a nation, must first be master of himself." Scripture shows what happens when rulers forget it. Noah, the head of a new world, became drunk and lay exposed in his tent (Genesis 9:20–21). King Ahasuerus, "merry with wine," summoned Queen Vashti to be put on display (Esther 1:10–11). Herod, at his birthday feast, made a rash oath that cost John the Baptist his head (Mark 6:21–28). In each case drink did not create the sin, but it loosened what should have held it back. Wine is not the only thing that clouds judgment; so do rage, exhaustion and the craving for approval. Scripture gives the better way: "do not be drunk with wine, in which is dissipation; but be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). Those who lead others need a mind governed by God, not by appetite.
units.application: If you lead a family, a team or a church, set your own limits higher than the rules require, because others pay for your lapses. Do not make decisions, send angry emails or discipline children when something is clouding your mind, whether alcohol, anger or exhaustion. Elders and pastors: take "not given to wine" (1 Timothy 3:3) as a protection for the flock, not a burden on you.

rel.note: Twisting a case so that the guilty go free or the innocent are condemned is an abomination to the LORD.
The king who judges the poor with truth has his throne established; the drunken king perverts their justice.
This verse completes the warning against kings drinking wine by giving its reason.
The king must not drink lest he forget the law; strong drink may be given to the dying, who have no more cases to judge.
The same word "forget" returns: the king must not forget the law, while the dying sufferer may forget his misery.
The clear-minded king opens his mouth for the very afflicted whose justice the drunken king perverts.

units.notes:
• *The law* here translates a word meaning what has been decreed, the statutes a king is bound to uphold; the ESV has "what has been decreed," and the NASB "what is decreed." Both read "rights" for "justice."
• *All the afflicted* is literally "all the sons of affliction," as the KJV margin shows: the whole class of people who live under hardship. *Pervert* means to change or twist; the KJV margin offers "alter."
• Bridges tells of a woman wrongly condemned by Philip of Macedon while he was drunk. She cried out, "I appeal to Philip, but it shall be when he is sober." Sober, he examined her case again and judged rightly.
• Compare Isaiah 28:7, where priest and prophet "have erred through intoxicating drink" and "stumble in judgment," and Hosea 4:11, "Harlotry, wine, and new wine enslave the heart."
units.summary: A drunk king forgets the law, and the poor are the ones who pay for it.
units.principle: Self-control in those who hold power is a form of justice, because the weak depend on a clear mind to defend them.
units.insight: Amos condemned Israel's leaders who drank "wine from bowls" and were "not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" (Amos 6:6). Their feasting was not harmless pleasure. While they lounged, the poor were sold "for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6). This is the hidden cost of self-indulgence: someone else always pays. A parent's numbed evenings are paid for by children who needed attention. An elder's distracted mind is paid for by the struggling member no one noticed. Everyone who carries responsibility for others has an "afflicted" who depends on them. Over against every failing ruler stands the King of whom Isaiah wrote, "with righteousness He shall judge the poor" (Isaiah 11:4). Jesus never forgot the law, never twisted a case and never looked past the afflicted. He is the standard, and He is the refuge for everyone earthly judges have failed.
units.application: Ask this week who depends on your clear judgment: children, employees, a congregation, an aging parent. Then ask what dulls you when they need you, whether drink, endless scrolling or exhaustion, and cut it back. If you judge or supervise others, review one decision you made while tired or distracted, and correct it if the weaker person was wronged. Make it easy for people without power to bring their case to you.

rel.note: The heart knows its own bitterness, the deep grief of those this verse calls "bitter of heart."
The book's portrait of the drunkard shows that this verse is no license for drinking to escape.
The king must refuse strong drink so he can judge; here it is given to the dying, who have no more judging to do.
The next verse completes the thought: the sufferer may drink and forget his misery for a time.

units.notes:
• *Him who is perishing*: the KJV has "him that is ready to perish," someone at the point of death. *Bitter of heart* is literally "bitter of soul," as the KJV margin notes; the ESV and NLT read "those in bitter distress."
• Matthew Henry: "wine is a cordial, and therefore to be used for want and not for wantonness." A cordial was a reviving medicine; Henry means wine is for real need, not for self-indulgence.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik, says the queen mother "does not recommend a free beer program for the poor or justify its use as an opiate for the masses."
• The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) cites this verse for a later Jewish custom of giving a man led out to execution wine mixed with frankincense to dull his senses. That later practice does not settle the verse's original setting. Mark records that Jesus was offered "wine mingled with myrrh to drink, but He did not take it" (Mark 15:23); the Gospel does not explain that drink by this custom.
units.summary: What a king must refuse for his own pleasure may be given in mercy to the dying.
units.principle: God's gifts are meant for real need, not indulgence; what would ruin a ruler's judgment may be a mercy to the suffering.
units.insight: These words come from a mother who cared about the dying. She did not want her son drinking for pleasure, but she did want the suffering eased. The Good Samaritan showed the same mercy, pouring "oil and wine" on a stranger's wounds (Luke 10:34). Paul, no friend of drunkenness, told Timothy to "use a little wine for your stomach's sake" (1 Timothy 5:23). God's gifts have their place when they serve real need. Yet the verse searches us too. It is easy to reach for something that dulls our own pain and call it mercy to ourselves. Jesus, hanging on the cross, was offered wine mingled with myrrh and "did not take it" (Mark 15:23). He chose to drink the Father's cup to the end with a clear mind (John 18:11), so that the perishing and the bitter of heart could have a comfort no wine can give.
units.application: If you care for the dying, as family, nurse or hospice volunteer, see easing pain as part of love, not a lack of faith. When someone is bitter of heart after a loss, sit with them and bring comfort before you bring correction. If you are tempted to numb your own grief with drink or anything else, pour out your heart to God (Psalm 62:8) and tell a trusted friend instead.

rel.note: The drunkard wakes only to seek another drink, showing that drink's forgetting never lasts.
The king who drinks forgets the law; the sufferer who drinks forgets his misery.
The previous verse names the perishing and the bitter of heart as the ones who may be given drink.
The true remedy for the poor follows: a king who opens his mouth and pleads their cause.

units.notes:
• *Forget* is the same word as in 31:5. The two verses mirror each other: the drinking king forgets the law and harms the afflicted; the dying sufferer forgets his misery for a time. The repeated word shows that the mother's point lies in the contrast.
• The NASB reads "trouble" for "misery." The ESV and NLT put 31:6–7 in the plural, applying the verses to all the afflicted of 31:6.
• Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "Those who fly to the bottle for consolation might as soon fly to hell to find a heaven."
• Compare 23:35, where the drunkard wakes only to say, "When shall I awake, that I may seek another drink?" The forgetting that drink brings never lasts.
• Compare Isaiah 61:1–3 ("the oil of joy for mourning") and Matthew 11:28.
units.summary: Wine can make a sufferer forget his misery for a night; only justice can change his morning.
units.principle: Relief can ease suffering for a moment, but only justice and the comfort of God can lift it.
units.insight: Hannah was "in bitterness of soul" (1 Samuel 1:10), the very condition this passage describes. Eli thought she was drunk. She answered, "I have drunk neither wine nor intoxicating drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15). She took her bitterness to God, and afterward "her face was no longer sad" (1 Samuel 1:18). That is the better way. Wine can blur misery for a night, but it cannot remove it. Jesus came "to heal the brokenhearted" (Luke 4:18), and He offers what no cup can: rest for the weary and heavy laden (Matthew 11:28). He also gives a forgetting deeper than this verse imagines. Through Him God says of our sins, "I will remember no more" (Hebrews 8:12). Where do you go to forget? The answer shows what you trust for comfort.
units.application: If you are carrying grief or money troubles, name where you go to forget, and bring that pain to God in prayer this week, as Hannah did. Friends and deacons: do more than offer comfort; help with the hardship itself, through a bill paid, a job lead or a meal. Leaders: remember that relief eases suffering for a while, but fair decisions and speaking up for the poor change their circumstances (31:8–9).

rel.note: Mercy and truth preserve the king, the qualities this charge asks him to show the weak.
The LORD Himself pleads the cause of the poor against those who rob and oppress them.
Deliver those drawn toward death, for God weighs the heart of anyone who claims not to have known.
The king who judges the poor with truth has his throne established forever.
The righteous considers the cause of the poor, as the king is charged to plead it.
The woman of valor opens her hands to the same "poor" and "needy" the king is charged to defend.
The king is told to open his mouth for justice; the woman of valor opens hers with wisdom and kindness.
The drunken king perverts the justice of the afflicted; the sober king opens his mouth for them.

units.notes:
• v8 *Speechless*: the ESV and NASB have "mute." Behind "appointed to die" is a Hebrew phrase meaning literally "the sons of destruction," which the KJV gives in its margin; the ESV reads "destitute," taking it of those perishing through want.
• v9 The words translated "plead the cause" (din) are legal language: to judge, defend or argue a case in court. The ESV and NASB have "defend the rights," bringing out the courtroom setting.
• v9 *Poor and needy* ('ani and 'ebyon) are the afflicted and the destitute, a pair Scripture often uses for the most vulnerable (Psalm 72:12–13). The same pair returns in 31:20, where the woman of valor opens her hands to them.
• These verses close the words of Lemuel (31:1–9). Whether the poem that follows continues his mother's words is debated.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "For her the king's throne is truly founded on righteousness."
• Compare Deuteronomy 16:18–20; Psalm 82:3–4; Jeremiah 22:15–16; Job 29:12–16.
units.summary: Power is given to be a voice for those who have none.
units.principle: Authority is a trust held for the weak, and it is measured by how it treats those who cannot repay or resist.
units.insight: God says of King Josiah, "He judged the cause of the poor and needy… Was not this knowing Me?" (Jeremiah 22:16). Defending the weak is not a side issue to knowing God; it is a mark of it. We see this in Esther, who opened her mouth for her doomed people at the risk of her life (Esther 7:3–4), and in Job, "a father to the poor" (Job 29:16). Bridges refuses to confine the charge to kings: "why should we restrict these wise injunctions within the narrow limits of royalty?" Above all, these verses point to Christ. When He stood condemned, no one opened a mouth for Him, and He was silent as a lamb (Isaiah 53:7). Now He pleads for those who were justly condemned (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1). Everyone He has defended is called to speak up for others.
units.application: Notice who has no voice where you have one: the employee who cannot challenge a manager, the family lost in a hospital or court system, the child no one is listening to, the elderly member being taken advantage of. Use your access for them. Make the call, go to the meeting, put in the word. If you lead at work, in church or at home, judge complaints fairly, especially when the less powerful person is the one bringing it.

rel.note: The same Hebrew phrase, "An excellent wife," is the crown of her husband.
Finding a wife is called a good gift and echoes the language of finding Wisdom in 8:35.
A prudent wife is a gift from the LORD, not merely an inheritance from parents.
Her husband's words, "you excel them all," answer the question this verse asks.
The king is warned not to give his strength, chayil, to women; the poem praises a woman who has chayil herself.
The fear of the LORD is the ground of her praise, closing the poem this verse opens.
Wisdom too is "more precious than rubies," so the woman of valor is wisdom lived out.
Whoever finds Wisdom finds life, and the poem now shows the son a woman worth finding.

units.notes:
• *Virtuous* (chayil) means strength, ability, wealth or valor. The phrase appears in 12:4 ("An excellent wife") and Ruth 3:11, where Boaz calls Ruth "a virtuous woman." The same word describes Gideon as a "mighty man of valor" (Judges 6:12) and the "able men" Jethro advised Moses to appoint (Exodus 18:21). It returns in 31:3 ("strength") and 31:29 ("done well").
• Allen Ross, quoted by Guzik, says the language "has the ring of an ode to a champion"; the "gain" of 31:11 is literally spoil taken in battle.
• *Rubies* (peninim) is a precious stone whose exact identity is uncertain; red coral and pearls are suggested, and the ESV has "jewels."
• The acrostic runs from the first letter (aleph) in 31:10 to the last (tav) in 31:31; compare Psalm 119 and Lamentations 1–4. Whether the poem continues Lemuel's mother's words is debated, since it has no heading of its own.
• Augustine (Sermon 37) is an early witness to reading the woman as the Church.
units.summary: Proverbs began by urging a son to find wisdom; it ends by showing him wisdom lived out in a woman worth finding.
units.principle: Godly character is worth more than any treasure, and its source is the fear of the LORD, not achievement.
units.insight: Because a mother speaks these words to her son, Enduring Word calls the poem "primarily a search-list for a man, and only secondarily a check-list for a woman." That matters, because many women have heard Proverbs 31 as a standard they can never meet. The poem is praise, not a scorecard, and its last word places her worth not in her output but in this: "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised" (31:30). For young men it reorders the search. Bridges laments, "Too often is the search made for accomplishments, not for virtues." At the deepest level the poem holds the gospel in miniature. Christ sought a Bride who had nothing to commend her, paid the highest price for her, "His own blood" (Acts 20:28), and will present her to Himself "a glorious church" (Ephesians 5:27). Her worth is first His gift.
units.application: Husbands and sons: praise the specific character you see in the women in your life, such as faithfulness, wisdom or courage, not only what they get done (31:28–29). Young men: let character and the fear of the LORD, not looks or status, lead your search. Women, including single women and widows: hear this poem as praise of what God grows in you, not as a test. Churches: honor such women openly, as the poem does "in the gates" (31:31).

rel.note: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, the source of his honor rather than his shame.
Many claim to be good, "But who can find a faithful man?" This wife is the faithful one the book searches for.
The next verse gives the lifelong record of goodness on which her husband's trust rests.
Her wise purchase of a field shows why her husband can leave the household's affairs in her hands.
The husband whose heart trusts her in silence later praises her aloud.
The immoral woman betrays her absent husband; this wife can be trusted completely when hers is away.

units.notes:
• *Gain* translates a word that usually means spoil or plunder taken in war, as the KJV's "no need of spoil" shows. It suits a poem about a woman of valor. Ross, quoted by Guzik, suggests "the gain will be as rich and bountiful as the spoils of war," though here it is the household's honest increase, not literal plunder.
• *Safely trusts* translates the ordinary verb for trusting, the same one used in "Trust in the LORD with all your heart" (3:5). It means to lean on someone with settled confidence; her husband can lean his full weight on her.
• Martin Luther, quoted by Bridges, described his own wife this way: "The greatest gift of God is a pious amiable spouse, who fears God, loves his house, and with whom one can live in perfect confidence."
• Contrast the immoral woman of 7:19–20, who uses her husband's long absence to betray him; this wife is most trustworthy when her husband is away.
• Compare Ruth 3:11 and 1 Corinthians 4:2, "it is required in stewards that one be found faithful."
units.summary: A husband who never has to wonder about his wife is a rich man, whatever his bank balance.
units.principle: Faithfulness proven over time creates a trust that frees others and enriches everything it touches.
units.insight: Potiphar trusted Joseph so completely that "he did not know what he had except for the bread which he ate" (Genesis 39:6). Joseph had earned that trust, and he kept it even when betraying it would have been easy. Trust like that is one of life's richest gifts, between husband and wife, between friends, or between a worker and an employer. Can the people closest to you rest their full weight on you, or do they have to check? At a deeper, layered level, this verse pictures something astonishing. Christ, the Bridegroom, has entrusted His Bride with His treasure: the gospel, the care of souls and the work of His household until He returns. Paul tells Timothy, "That good thing which was committed to you, keep by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us" (2 Timothy 1:14). The Bride keeps that trust by His Spirit, not by her own strength.
units.application: Husbands and wives: build trust in small things this week. Do what you said, be where you said, and tell the truth about money. If trust has been broken, rebuild it with patient openness rather than demanding to be trusted. Employees, volunteers and friends: be the person no one has to check up on. Husbands: tell your wife specifically where she has earned your confidence.

rel.note: The wise woman builds her house, as this wife builds her husband's welfare day by day.
A friend loves at all times, the same unchanging faithfulness this wife shows all her days.
The contentious wife makes a home so miserable that a corner of the roof is better; this wife brings only good.
Her lifelong goodness is the reason her husband's heart can safely trust her.

units.notes:
• *Evil* here means harm; the ESV and NLT read "harm," making clear that the line concerns the effect of her conduct on her husband.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "Her commitment to her husband's well being is true, not false; constant, not temperamental; reliable, not fickle."
• Her goodness can outlast her husband. Matthew Henry: "if she survive him, still she is doing him good in her care of his children, his estate, and good name." A widow's faithfulness to her late husband's family and name is part of this verse.
• Scripture also shows wives who did their husbands harm. Eve gave Adam the forbidden fruit (Genesis 3:6). Jezebel "stirred him up," urging her husband Ahab into wickedness (1 Kings 21:25). Job's wife urged him, "Curse God and die!" (Job 2:9).
• Compare 1 Corinthians 13:7–8, "Love ... endures all things. Love never fails."
units.summary: A faithful wife's love is not a mood; it is a lifetime of choosing her husband's good.
units.principle: Love is proved by steady goodness over a lifetime, not by intensity in a moment.
units.insight: Ruth showed this kind of goodness. A young widow, she bound herself to her mother-in-law: "wherever you go, I will go" (Ruth 1:16). She kept faith with Naomi through poverty and hard labor, and Boaz blessed her because "you have shown more kindness at the end than at the beginning" (Ruth 3:10). Goodness that grows over time is rarer than goodness that dazzles at first. Many marriages begin with intensity and drift into mere coexistence or quiet harm. This verse invites husbands and wives alike to ask whether their spouse is better off this year because of them. Faithfulness like this does not come from willpower alone. It flows from the God whose "compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:22–23). Those who receive His unfailing love each day are the ones who can keep giving it.
units.application: Husbands and wives: ask your spouse this week, "What is one way I could do you more good?" and act on the answer. Watch for small harms, such as sarcasm in front of others or complaints shared with friends, and stop them. Widows: the good you still do for your late husband's name and family counts. Anyone in a long commitment, as friend, caregiver or church member: be as faithful in year twenty as in year one.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent makes rich, as her willing hands bring increase to her household.
The lazy man craves and has nothing, while the diligent woman seeks and works and is supplied.
Her hands take up the distaff and spindle to turn these raw materials into thread.
The wool and flax she seeks become the linen garments and sashes she sells to merchants.

units.notes:
• *Willingly works with her hands* is literally "works with the delight of her palms": hands that are glad to work. The ESV has "works with willing hands," and the NASB "in delight." The wording pictures pleasure in the task, not grim duty.
• Flax was grown in Israel, and its stalks were dried before being worked into linen thread. Rahab hid the spies under "the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order on the roof" (Joshua 2:6).
• Matthew Henry describes her as one who "lays not only her hand, but her mind to it, and goes on in it without weariness in well-doing."
• Compare Colossians 3:23, "whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord and not to men," and 2 Corinthians 9:7.
units.summary: A wise woman does not wait for work to find her; she goes looking for it and does it gladly.
units.principle: Work prepared for carefully and done gladly honors God more than work done grudgingly, however much is accomplished.
units.insight: When Israel built the tabernacle, "All the women who were gifted artisans spun yarn with their hands" (Exodus 35:25), and their gifts came from willing hearts (Exodus 35:29). Later Dorcas was "full of good works and charitable deeds," and the widows wept as they showed the tunics and garments she had made (Acts 9:36, 39). Ironside: "It is only love that can render service like this sweet and delightful." The question is not only how much we do but what heart we bring to it. Grumbling can turn worthy work into drudgery, and love can make ordinary tasks an offering. Christ is the pattern: "I delight to do Your will, O my God" (Psalm 40:8). At a deeper, layered level, the Bride's one garment is woven from both threads, outward mercy and inward purity. Neither alone is enough.
units.application: Before your work this week, whether in an office, a kitchen, a classroom or a workshop, prepare well: gather what you need instead of scrambling. Then watch your attitude, and when you catch yourself grumbling, turn the task into an offering (Colossians 3:23). Parents: let your children see you work gladly, not just hard. Church volunteers: serve where you can serve willingly, and say so plainly when you cannot.

rel.note: Diligent care for one's flocks provides food for the household and the maidservants, as her trading does.
The food she brings from afar is what she sets before her household before dawn.
Her trade runs both ways: she brings food in and sends her goods out to the merchants.
The ant gathers her food in harvest, as this woman takes initiative to supply her house.

units.notes:
• *Merchant ships* is literally "ships of a trader." The NLT has "a merchant's ship," and the ESV speaks of "the ships of the merchant."
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The simile with the merchant ships suggests that she brings a continual supply of abundance." A simile is a comparison using "like," as this verse does.
• Matthew Henry: "No merchants' ships, no, not Solomon's navy, ever made a more advantageous return than her employments do."
• Compare 1 Kings 9:26–28 and 10:22, where Solomon's fleet sailed to Ophir and came back with gold.
units.summary: A wise provider's household eats well because she looks past the nearest market.
units.principle: Wise provision takes initiative, looking beyond the nearest and easiest to secure what others truly need.
units.insight: Ruth went out to glean in fields that were not her own, worked from morning until evening, and carried home enough barley for Naomi (Ruth 2:7, 17–18). Love made her go farther than comfort required. That is the spirit of this verse. Caring for people often means going out of our way: the longer trip, the extra planning, the harder search, so that those who depend on us are well supplied. Laziness settles for whatever is nearest; love looks farther. At a deeper, layered level, the merchant ships picture the Church gathering nourishment from among the nations. We see this in the church at Antioch, fed by prophets and teachers from many lands: Barnabas of Cyprus, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene and Saul of Tarsus (Acts 13:1; 4:36). The Church is richer for every nation she draws from, and Christ's household is fed from afar.
units.application: Whoever plans meals, budgets or supplies for a household, team or ministry: plan ahead this week instead of settling for the quickest, nearest option. Compare, research and buy wisely. Missions committees and church leaders: learn from believers in other countries and cultures, and invite their teaching as well as supporting their work. Single adults: provide wisely for yourself too; good stewardship is not only for families.

rel.note: Love of sleep leads to poverty, but open eyes bring enough bread.
Diligent stewardship supplies food for the household and nourishment for the maidservants.
The food she sets before her household is the food she brought from afar like the merchant ships.
Her lamp burning by night is the companion picture of her rising before day.
The sluggard keeps sleeping while poverty creeps up; she rises early to provide.

units.notes:
• *Portion* can mean an allotted share of food or an assigned task. The NLT takes it as planning "the day's work for her servant girls," while the ESV and NASB read "portions" for her maidens.
• *Food* translates a word that often means prey, as when young lions "roar after their prey" (Psalm 104:21). The poet's choice of this word keeps the poem's picture of a strong, valiant woman providing for her own.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "This implies first that she cares even for the serving girls and second that she is diligent about overseeing them."
• Compare Matthew 25:6, "at midnight a cry was heard: 'Behold, the bridegroom is coming,'" and Mark 1:35, where Jesus rose "a long while before daylight" to pray.
units.summary: Before the sun is up, a wise woman's care already reaches everyone under her roof.
units.principle: Wise care thinks of others before the day makes its demands, and it includes the people easiest to overlook.
units.insight: Early one morning the risen Jesus stood on the shore with a fire of coals already burning, fish laid on it and bread ready, and said to His tired disciples, "Come and eat breakfast" (John 21:4, 9, 12). Love often shows itself in what is done before anyone else is awake. That is the heart of this verse, not a rule about alarm clocks. Many mothers of young children, shift workers and caregivers already rise in the dark, and this verse honors them; it does not shame anyone whose season or health is different. Notice, too, who is included: the maidservants. Do the people at the bottom of your household or workplace receive your care, or only your instructions? At a deeper, layered level, the Bride rising in the night pictures the Church awake through this dark age, listening for the cry, "Behold, the bridegroom is coming" (Matthew 25:6).
units.application: Parents and caregivers: do one thing this week to prepare for your household's day before it begins, such as packing lunches or praying for each person by name. Managers and business owners: make sure the lowest-paid workers receive their "portion" first: fair pay, clear tasks and a word of thanks. If you are worn out from rising early for others, take heart that God sees it, and ask for help where you need it.

rel.note: Wealth gathered by labor increases, as her vineyard grows from her own earnings.
The plans of the diligent lead to plenty, while haste leads to poverty.
Prepare the field first and build afterward: the same ordered, thought-through work she shows.
Her careful dealings explain why her husband can safely trust her with the household.
The fruit of her hands that buys the vineyard is what the poem finally says she should be given.

units.notes:
• *From her profits* is literally "from the fruit of her palms," which the ESV and KJV render "with the fruit of her hands." The purchase is tied to her own work. A similar phrase returns in 31:31, "Give her of the fruit of her hands."
• For "buys," the KJV margin notes that the Hebrew verb is literally "taketh": she takes possession of the field.
• Matthew Henry: "Many have undone themselves by buying without considering; but those who would make advantageous purchases must consider, and then buy."
• Compare Luke 14:28, "which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost," and Matthew 25:14–30, the parable of the talents.
units.summary: A wise woman thinks before she buys and plants what will feed her family for years.
units.principle: Wisdom weighs a decision before acting, then invests the fruit of honest work in what will keep bearing fruit.
units.insight: Lydia of Thyatira was "a seller of purple," a businesswoman whose heart the Lord opened (Acts 16:14). Her home became a gathering place for the believers in Philippi (Acts 16:15, 40). Scripture never treats skill in business as worldly in itself; it asks how we use it. This woman thinks before she buys, and she puts her profit to work instead of spending it on show. Contrast the servant in Jesus' parable who buried his master's money because he was afraid (Matthew 25:25). Impulse and fear are opposite failures, and both waste what God gives. Some of us spend before we think; others never act at all. The faithful servant hears, "Well done, good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:21), not because he avoided every risk, but because he used what was entrusted to him for his master's good.
units.application: Before any major purchase this week, whether a car, a home or a business expense, sleep on it, ask a wise friend and count the cost (Luke 14:28). If you have savings or profit, consider what could keep producing for your family or for God's work instead of disappearing on show. Church finance teams: plan for long-term fruit, not only this year's budget. Women with gifts for business: this verse honors you.

rel.note: The hand of the diligent will rule, while the lazy are put to forced labor.
A wise man is strong, and knowledge increases strength, as her wisdom shows itself in vigor.
The strength she girds on for work becomes the clothing of her character.

units.notes:
• *Girds herself* is literally "girds her loins," the wording the KJV keeps; the ESV has "dresses herself with strength." The loins are the hips and waist, where a belt gathered up a long robe for action.
• Scripture uses the same picture for readiness. Israel ate the first Passover "with a belt on your waist," ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11), and Elijah "girded up his loins and ran ahead of Ahab" (1 Kings 18:46).
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik, says the phrase describes getting ready for some "kind of heroic or difficult action."
• Matthew Henry: she "will go through with work that requires all the strength she has, which she will use as one that knows it is the way to have more."
• Compare Luke 12:35, "Let your waist be girded and your lamps burning," and 1 Peter 1:13, "gird up the loins of your mind."
units.summary: The woman of valor dresses for hard work the way a soldier dresses for battle.
units.principle: Faithful work calls for readiness and strength, and strength grows as it is spent on the duties God gives.
units.insight: Rebekah met Abraham's servant at the well and said, "I will draw water for your camels also," then ran back and forth until ten thirsty camels had finished drinking (Genesis 24:10, 19–20). Her strength and willingness marked her as the woman God had appointed for Isaac. This verse honors that kind of vigor. But strength is more than muscle. Many faithful women live with illness, age or disability, and their readiness of heart is the same strength the verse praises. The fullest picture is Jesus, who on the night before the cross "took a towel and girded Himself" and washed His disciples' feet (John 13:4–5). The Lord of glory dressed for the lowliest work. When your strength feels small, remember the promise: "He gives power to the weak" (Isaiah 40:29). Gird yourself, then, not with pride in your own ability, but with His strength.
units.application: Face the hardest task on your list this week first, prepared and ready rather than dreading it. Care for your body through rest, food and exercise, so you have strength for those who depend on you. Young people: do not despise physical work; it builds character as well as muscle. If illness or age limits you, offer the strength you have, and let others carry what you cannot, without shame.

rel.note: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked goes out.
In all labor there is profit, the profit she tastes and finds good.
The lamp of the wicked will be put out, while hers keeps burning through the night.
Her rising while it is still night is the companion picture of her watchful care.

units.notes:
• *Perceives* is literally "tastes," as the KJV margin notes: she has tasted her trading and found it good. The same verb and the same "good" appear in Psalm 34:8, "Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good." Her confidence comes from firsthand testing.
• The NLT has "her lamp burns late into the night," and the ESV and NASB read "at night."
• Proverbs uses a lamp going out as a picture of a life or household ending in ruin (13:9; 20:20; 24:20). Her lamp burning through the night pictures the opposite: a house that is alive and provided for.
• Ironside: "she realizes the importance of being ever watchful as well as energetic."
• Compare Luke 12:35 and Matthew 25:1–13.
units.summary: The woman of valor keeps her lamp burning: a house well supplied and a heart still watching.
units.principle: Confidence in honest work and steady watchfulness keep a household supplied; the wise do not let the light go out.
units.insight: In the tabernacle the lamp was to "burn continually" (Exodus 27:20), and the boy Samuel heard God's voice "before the lamp of God went out" (1 Samuel 3:3). A lamp kept burning meant someone was tending it. This verse is not a call to stay up all night. Scripture warns, "It is vain for you to rise up early, To sit up late ... For so He gives His beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2). The point is a household where the oil does not run out, and a heart that keeps watching. Many believers are busy but not watchful; activity has replaced attention to God. At a deeper, layered level, the Bride's lamp burns through the night of this age. In Jesus' parable the foolish virgins had lamps but no oil, and the door was shut (Matthew 25:8–10). Is your lamp trimmed with oil, or only lit?
units.application: Take stock of your work this week: is what you produce good, honest and worth what people pay for it? Check your household's "oil," the supplies, savings and margin that keep things running. Then check your soul's oil: daily Scripture and prayer. If you are a weary mother or caregiver working late, hear Psalm 127:2 as God's permission to rest. Small-group leaders: ask one another how your lamps are burning.

rel.note: In all labor there is profit, including the patient, repeated labor of spinning.
The one who excels in his work will stand before kings; skill in ordinary work is honored.
The wool and flax she sought out are what her hands now spin into thread.
The same hands and the same verb turn from the spindle to the poor in the next verse.

units.notes:
• In Hebrew the words for her hands form a crossing pattern across 31:19–20: "hands" then "palms" in 31:19, "palm" then "hands" in 31:20. The same verb, translated "stretches out" here and "reaches out" in 31:20, appears in both verses. The hands that reach to the spindle are the hands that reach to the needy.
• Ironside describes spinning without a wheel: "They hold the distaff in one hand and twirl their long wool spindles with the other."
• The KJV reverses the two tools, putting her hands to the spindle and the distaff in her hands.
• Compare Exodus 35:25, where the skilled women of Israel "spun yarn with their hands" for the tabernacle.
units.summary: The hands that buy a field still reach for the spindle; for a wise woman no task is beneath her.
units.principle: True greatness does not outgrow humble work; faithfulness in small, repeated tasks is part of wisdom.
units.insight: Before He preached a sermon, Jesus worked with His hands, and His neighbors knew Him by it: "Is this not the carpenter?" (Mark 6:3). Paul, apostle to the nations, reminded the Ephesian elders, "these hands have provided for my necessities" (Acts 20:34). The Lord who made the world did not despise ordinary work, and neither should His people. Much of life is spindle work: diapers, dishes, data entry, the same repairs again and again. It is easy to think such work does not count, or to hand it off as soon as we can. This verse says it counts. Paul went on, "by laboring like this ... you must support the weak" (Acts 20:35). Hidden, patient work done for love is often what makes generosity possible.
units.application: This week, do one ordinary task you usually avoid or delegate, and do it carefully as service to God. Parents: teach a child a practical skill with your hands beside theirs. Leaders and professionals: honor the people who do repetitive work in your office or church, such as custodians and nursery workers, by name. Parents at home: your daily, unseen work is the kind this verse praises.

rel.note: Whoever has mercy on the needy honors his Maker.
He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD, and her open hand is that pity made a habit.
The generous person gives bread to the poor and is blessed.
The hands that held the spindle are the hands that now reach out to the needy.
The king is charged to plead for the poor and needy; she reaches out her hands to the same people.

units.notes:
• *Extends* translates a verb meaning to spread out, as the KJV margin's "She spreadeth" shows: the picture is an open hand. The ESV has "opens her hand." Compare Deuteronomy 15:8, "you shall open your hand wide to him."
• The hand words cross over from 31:19. The same hands, and the same verb ("stretches out," "reaches out"), now turn from the spindle to the needy, so her work and her giving are one motion.
• *The poor* and *the needy* are the same pair Lemuel's mother charged the king to defend (31:9). He was to plead their cause in court; this woman opens her hands to them herself.
• Matthew Henry: "She is as intent upon giving as she is upon getting."
• Compare Job 29:12–13 and Ephesians 4:28.
units.summary: A wise woman's hands work hard so they can open wide.
units.principle: Diligence finds its purpose in generosity; we work not only to have but to give.
units.insight: Cornelius was "a devout man and one who feared God with all his household, who gave alms generously to the people" (Acts 10:2). His fear of God showed in open hands, like this woman's. Paul wrote to people who had once stolen, "let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give him who has need" (Ephesians 4:28). Work is meant to end in open hands. It is possible to be hardworking and stingy at the same time, to labor hard and hold tight. That heart trusts its earnings more than God. The cure is to look at Christ: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). He opened His hands to us, and they were pierced. Those who have received grace like that cannot keep their hands closed.
units.application: Set aside part of what you earn this month for someone in need before you spend on yourself. Families: let your children help choose and deliver a gift to a neighbor in hardship. Business owners: build generosity into your plans, as Boaz did when he told his workers to leave extra grain for Ruth (Ruth 2:15–16). Church members: get to know one needy person by name, not only a program.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, and His children have a place of refuge.
The prudent foresee trouble and prepare, while the simple pass on and suffer.
Having clothed her household in scarlet, she then clothes herself in fine linen and purple.
Because she has prepared, she can rejoice at the time to come.
The ant provides in summer for the season ahead, as she clothes her household before winter.

units.notes:
• *Scarlet*: the KJV margin offers "double garments," a reading that understands the Hebrew word differently, and the NLT simply has "warm clothes." Kidner, quoted by Guzik, explains the doubt: "The word has a plural ending, which is abnormal for 'scarlet'; so that both form and sense arouse suspicion." In other words, both the grammar and the meaning lead some readers to prefer "double garments."
• Scarlet dye came from a crushed insect and was costly. Saul had clothed the daughters of Israel "in scarlet, with luxury" (2 Samuel 1:24), so scarlet clothing meant both warmth and honor.
• Matthew Henry pictures the household "clothed in scarlet, strong cloth and fit for winter, and yet rich and making a good appearance."
• Compare Exodus 12:13 and Joshua 2:18–19, where blood on the doorposts and a scarlet cord in the window marked households for protection.
units.summary: A wise woman does not fear the snow, because she prepared long before it fell.
units.principle: Preparation made in advance drives out fear; those who provide for others before the storm can face it calmly.
units.insight: On the plain level this verse is about coats and blankets, and it honors every parent who has thought ahead for a family's winter. Fear often grows where preparation has been put off. At a deeper, layered level, the scarlet reaches further. When judgment came on Jericho, Rahab tied a scarlet cord in her window, and her whole household was spared (Joshua 2:18–19; 6:25). On the first Passover, God said of the blood on Israel's doorposts, "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exodus 12:13). Peter says we were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Peter 1:19). A household covered by that blood need not fear what is coming. Are the people you love covered? Pray for them by name, and point them to Christ while there is time.
units.application: Parents and household managers: look ahead this week to the next season's needs, such as winter clothing, school costs or an emergency fund, and take one step now. Church benevolence teams: find out who in your congregation will face the cold without enough. Anxious believers: replace worry with preparation where you can, and with prayer where you cannot (Philippians 4:6). Pray by name for each person in your household to know Christ.

rel.note: A gracious woman retains honor, the honor her dress reflects.
She clothes her household in scarlet before she dresses herself in linen and purple.
The poem moves from her fine clothing to the strength and honor that clothe her character.
The immoral woman spreads her bed with tapestry to trap a young man; this woman's coverings adorn an honorable home.

units.notes:
• *Tapestry*: the ESV and NASB have "coverings," and the ESV ties them to her bed. The same word appears in 7:16, where the immoral woman says, "I have spread my bed with tapestry." There the coverings lure a young man to ruin; here they belong to an honorable home.
• *Fine linen*: the KJV has "silk," but most modern versions read "fine linen," the cloth often paired with purple as the dress of the wealthy (Luke 16:19).
• Purple dye came from shellfish of the eastern Mediterranean and was costly to produce. Lydia of Thyatira traded in it as "a seller of purple" (Acts 16:14).
• The New Testament places a woman's true adornment within, "the hidden person of the heart" (1 Peter 3:3–4; 1 Timothy 2:9–10), without forbidding dignity in dress.
units.summary: The woman of valor dresses with dignity, and her clothing matches the worth of her life.
units.principle: Dignity in appearance is fitting when it reflects a life of honorable work, but true worth is never in the cloth itself.
units.insight: The rich man in Jesus' parable was also "clothed in purple and fine linen," while Lazarus lay starving at his gate (Luke 16:19–20). The same cloth can cover a generous life or an empty one. God is not against beauty; He designed Aaron's garments "for glory and for beauty" (Exodus 28:2). What matters is whether the outside matches the inside. Some of us neglect ourselves out of false humility, and others dress to be admired. This woman did neither. She clothed her household first, and her own fine clothing simply fit who she was. At a deeper, layered level, Revelation shows the Bride arrayed in fine linen at the marriage of the Lamb. Notice that "it was granted" to her (Revelation 19:8). The Church's beauty is her Bridegroom's gift before it is ever her own work.
units.application: Dress with dignity this week, suited to your work and setting, without spending to impress. Parents: teach teenagers that clothing should express who they are, not buy them an identity. If you tend to neglect yourself while caring for everyone else, it is not selfish to make or buy something good for yourself. Each morning as you dress, ask God to clothe you with Christ's righteousness.

rel.note: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, the honor he wears in public.
The fool has nothing to say in the gate, while this husband takes his seat among the elders.
The husband who trusts her at home is honored in public because of her.
The gates where he sits honored are where her own works will finally praise her.

units.notes:
• *The gates*: the city gate served as the town's court, council chamber and public square. Boaz settled Ruth's redemption there, sitting down at the gate before ten of the elders of the city (Ruth 4:1–2, 11).
• The NLT has "city gates" and says her husband is "well known" there.
• Ironside: "His wife's thrift and good judgment reflect credit upon him, adding to the esteem in which he is held."
• Compare Job 29:7–11, where Job takes his seat at the gate and is honored by young and old, and Hebrews 1:3.
units.summary: A husband's honor in public is often built quietly by a wife's faithfulness at home.
units.principle: Faithfulness at home strengthens leadership in the community; public honor often rests on private loyalty.
units.insight: Paul says an overseer must be "one who rules his own house well ... (for if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the church of God?)" (1 Timothy 3:4–5). Public trust grows from private order. Behind many respected leaders stands someone whose faithfulness at home made their service possible. Priscilla and Aquila served side by side, risked their necks for Paul, and opened their home to the church (Romans 16:3–5). Husbands who are honored at work or in church should ask whose quiet labor stands behind that honor, and thank her. At a deeper, layered level, the husband in the gates pictures Christ, seated in honor at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). His place is secure. The Bride's joy is that her Husband is known, honored and reigning.
units.application: Husbands: tell your wife, and others in her hearing, how her faithfulness has strengthened your work and reputation. Leaders and pastors: before you accept public honor, thank those whose support made it possible. Wives and support staff whose work goes unseen: God sees it, and it reaches the gate. Churches choosing elders and deacons: look at how candidates lead at home before entrusting them with the church.

rel.note: Honest scales delight the LORD, the standard for every sale she makes.
The one who excels in his work will stand before kings, as her skill finds a place in the market.
The wool and flax she sought out have become the goods she now sells.
Her trade runs both ways: food comes in from afar and her goods go out to the merchants.

units.notes:
• *Merchants* translates the name "Canaanite." The peoples of the land before Israel, especially the coastal cities, were known for trade, so the name came to mean a trader. Hosea uses it the same way: "A cunning Canaanite! Deceitful scales are in his hand" (Hosea 12:7).
• *Sashes* are "belts" in the NASB and "girdles" in the KJV, a valued item of dress for both men and women.
• Ross, quoted by Guzik: "The poet did not think it strange or unworthy for a woman to engage in honest trade."
• Compare Acts 16:14 (Lydia, "a seller of purple") and Acts 18:3 (Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers).
units.summary: The woman of valor turns her home into a workshop whose goods reach every passing trader.
units.principle: Skilled, honest work that serves others beyond our own walls is a fitting part of a wise and godly life.
units.insight: When Paul came to Corinth he found Aquila and Priscilla, "and because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked; for by occupation they were tentmakers" (Acts 18:3). A married couple's workshop became a base for the gospel. God filled Bezalel "with the Spirit of God" for skilled work in gold, silver, bronze and wood (Exodus 31:2–5). Scripture does not divide life into sacred and secular compartments. Making and selling good products with honesty is one way of loving our neighbor. The question for each of us is not whether our work looks "spiritual" but whether it is skilled, honest and useful to others. Does what leaves your hands make other people's lives better? Do you sell what is worth the price? Faithfulness in the marketplace is part of the fear of the LORD.
units.application: Whatever you make or sell this week, whether reports, meals, repairs or products, do it well enough that you would gladly buy it yourself. Business owners: price fairly and keep your promises to suppliers and customers (11:1). Those who work from home: your work is real work, so give it set hours and real standards. Churches: honor members' craftsmanship and business skill as service to God, not only their volunteer hours.

rel.note: In the fear of the LORD there is strong confidence, the ground of her joy about the future.
Strength is the glory of the young and splendor belongs to the old; she is clothed with both.
The strength she girded on for her work now clothes her whole character.
Her calm before the winter snow is one example of her readiness for the time to come.
The poem moves from her linen and purple to the deeper clothing of strength and honor.

units.notes:
• *Honor*: the ESV, NASB and NLT have "dignity." *Rejoice*: the ESV and NLT have "laughs," and the NASB says she "smiles" at the future. The picture is of a woman who looks at the days ahead and is not afraid.
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "The praise of the woman can hardly be higher: it attributes to her the advantages of both youth and old age." He has 20:29 in mind, where strength is the glory of the young and splendor, the same word as "honor" here, belongs to the old.
• Scripture often pictures character as clothing. Job said, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me" (Job 29:14). Believers are told to "put on tender mercies, kindness, humility" (Colossians 3:12).
• Ironside: "Godliness and joyfulness are inseparable."
• Compare Psalm 112:7, "He will not be afraid of evil tidings; His heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD," and Isaiah 52:1, "Put on your strength, O Zion."
units.summary: A godly woman's finest clothing is her character, and dressed in it she can smile at tomorrow.
units.principle: Character is the clothing that lasts, and those who fear the LORD can face the future with joy instead of dread.
units.insight: Anna was a widow of about eighty-four "who did not depart from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day" (Luke 2:37). When she saw the infant Jesus, she "gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of Him to all those who looked for redemption" (Luke 2:38). Decades of widowhood had not made her bitter. Strength and honor were her clothing, and she rejoiced at what God was doing. Many of us dress carefully but go out wearing anxiety about the future. Joy in the time to come is not mere optimism; it is confidence in the God who holds the future. At a deeper, layered level, the Bride wears strength and honor because her Bridegroom has promised, "I will come again and receive you to Myself" (John 14:3). She can smile at the future because He is already there.
units.application: When you dress tomorrow morning, pray Colossians 3:12 and ask God to clothe you with strength, honor and kindness. If you are anxious about the future, whether retirement, health or your children, write down one fear and one promise of God that answers it. Older women and widows: your steady joy preaches to younger believers. Younger believers: seek out such women and learn from them.

rel.note: The tongue of the wise uses knowledge rightly, as hers does.
Sweetness of the lips increases learning, as her kind teaching helps others learn.
The son was told not to forsake his mother's law; this woman gives that kind of teaching.
The king is told to open his mouth for justice; she opens hers with wisdom and kindness.

units.notes:
• *Law* translates torah, which means instruction or teaching, not a legal code; the ESV and NASB have "teaching." Torah is the word behind "the law of your mother" (1:8) and "my law" in the father's speeches (3:1; 4:2).
• *Kindness* translates chesed, the word for God's steadfast love and covenant faithfulness, which the NKJV often renders "mercy," as in "For His mercy endures forever" (Psalm 136:1). "The law of kindness" means teaching given in kindness.
• *She opens her mouth* echoes the charge to the king, "Open your mouth" (31:8–9). He was to open his mouth for justice; she opens hers with wisdom and kindness.
• Matthew Henry: "The law of love and kindness is written in the heart, but it shows itself in the tongue."
• Compare Ephesians 4:15 ("speaking the truth in love") and Colossians 4:6 ("Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt").
units.summary: When a wise woman speaks, people grow wiser, and no one walks away wounded.
units.principle: Wise speech joined with steady kindness teaches without wounding and reflects the God whose love never fails.
units.insight: Abigail met an armed and angry David on the road and spoke with such wisdom and grace that he turned back from bloodshed: "blessed is your advice and blessed are you" (1 Samuel 25:33). Priscilla and Aquila heard the gifted preacher Apollos, "took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26). They corrected him privately and kindly, and he went on to greatly help the believers in Achaia (Acts 18:27). That is the law of kindness: truth given in a way that helps people receive it. Some of us have wisdom but deliver it with a sharp edge. Others are kind but say nothing useful. Jesus joined both perfectly; people "marveled at the gracious words which proceeded out of His mouth" (Luke 4:22). His Spirit can shape our tongues to be like His.
units.application: Before you correct a child, an employee or a friend this week, ask two questions: Is this wise? Is it kind? If either answer is no, wait. Mothers and grandmothers: your instruction carries the weight of 1:8, so give it gently and often. Teachers and small-group leaders: when someone gets something wrong, take them aside privately, as Priscilla and Aquila did. Notice one person whose words consistently build others up, and tell them so.

rel.note: The wise woman builds her house, and watching over it is part of that building.
Laziness brings deep sleep and the idle go hungry, the opposite of her watchful diligence.
Be diligent to know the state of your flocks, as she watches over the ways of her household.
The sluggard folds his hands to sleep while poverty comes; she never eats the bread of idleness.

units.notes:
• *Watches over* describes an ongoing habit: she is "one who keeps watch" over her household. The same verb is used of a watchman, as when God tells Ezekiel, "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 3:17). The ESV and NASB have "looks well to."
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "eating the 'bread of idleness' is idiomatic for indulging in laziness." An idiom is a figure of speech; she does not live off others while doing nothing.
• Ironside: "Without nagging and ill-temper, she yet exercises a firm but loving discipline over each one."
• Compare 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12, "If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat."
units.summary: Like a watchman on the wall, a wise woman watches her home, and idleness never eats at her table.
units.principle: Faithful stewardship pays close attention to what has been entrusted and refuses to live idly on the labor of others.
units.insight: Job watched over the ways of his household. After his children's feasts he rose early to offer sacrifices for each of them, saying, "It may be that my sons have sinned" (Job 1:5). Eli, by contrast, knew his sons were doing evil, "and he did not restrain them" (1 Samuel 3:13). Watching over a household is not spying or nagging. It is loving attention: noticing a child's new friends, a spouse's weariness, a room that has gone quiet. It is easy to be busy in a home without watching over it, present in body but absent in attention. Jesus is the model of watchful care. He said to His Father of His disciples, "those whom You gave Me I have kept" (John 17:12). The Good Shepherd calls His own sheep by name (John 10:3), and He never stops watching over them.
units.application: Parents: put the phone down for an evening this week and give full attention to each child's mood, friends and questions. Spouses: ask each other, "How are you really doing?" and listen to the answer. Anyone who manages a team or a ministry: walk through your area of responsibility and notice what needs care before it becomes a crisis. If you have been coasting on others' work, take up your share.

rel.note: The memory of the righteous is blessed, as her children call her blessed.
Parents rejoice in wise children; here the children rise to bless their mother in return.
The husband whose heart trusted her in silence now praises her aloud.
The next verse gives the husband's own words of praise.

units.notes:
• *Call her blessed*: the NASB and NLT have "bless her." The word means to pronounce someone happy or favored, from the same root as the opening word of Psalm 1, "Blessed is the man."
• Standing up was a sign of honor in Israel: "You shall rise before the gray headed and honor the presence of an old man" (Leviticus 19:32). Her children "rise up" for her in the same spirit.
• Matthew Henry calls the children's praise "a debt which they owe her, a part of that honour which the fifth commandment requires to be paid to father and mother."
• Compare Luke 1:48, where Mary says, "henceforth all generations will call me blessed," and Exodus 20:12.
units.summary: The people who see a godly mother on her hardest days are the first to call her blessed.
units.principle: The truest praise comes from those who know us best, and it is earned by faithfulness lived out day after day.
units.insight: In His dying hour Jesus looked down from the cross, saw His mother, and placed her in John's care: "Behold your mother!" (John 19:26–27). The Son of God honored the woman who had raised Him, even in agony. Many of us save our kindest words for colleagues and strangers and give our families what is left over. This verse reverses that. Praise belongs first at home, spoken to the people who carry us day after day. Not every faithful woman hears this praise. Some have children who are not yet grateful; some have no children or husband at all. Their worth is not diminished. The poem grounds a woman's praise in the fear of the LORD (31:30), and the Father who sees in secret will reward openly what no one else has thanked her for (Matthew 6:4).
units.application: Children of any age: tell your mother this week one specific thing she did that shaped you; if she has died, thank God for her aloud with your family. Husbands: praise your wife in front of your children. Churches: on Mother's Day and every day, remember women without children, widows and mothers whose children have wandered, and honor their faithfulness too. Parents: teach your children to say thank you at home first.

rel.note: An excellent wife, the same phrase as "virtuous wife," is the crown of her husband.
The husband's praise answers the opening question about who can find a woman of valor.
The previous verse introduces these words as the husband's praise.
A husband is told to rejoice with the wife of his youth, and here he does so aloud.

units.notes:
• *Done well* translates chayil, the same word as "virtuous" in 31:10. The KJV's "done virtuously" keeps the link, and the NASB has "nobly." The KJV margin offers "gotten riches," because the same word can also mean wealth.
• *Daughters* here means women in general, as often in Hebrew poetry: "Like a lily among thorns, So is my love among the daughters" (Song of Solomon 2:2).
• Ross, quoted by Guzik, calls "excel them all" "an expression that signifies victory," fitting a poem that praises her like a champion.
• Compare Ruth 3:11, where Boaz tells Ruth, a widow from Moab, "all the people of my town know that you are a virtuous woman," using the same word.
units.summary: A husband's best praise is personal: many women have done well, but to him she is the one.
units.principle: Love speaks its praise personally and directly, honoring the one it cherishes without belittling anyone else.
units.insight: Boaz said to Ruth, a widow and a foreigner, "all the people of my town know that you are a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:11). The lover in the Song of Solomon tells his bride, "You are all fair, my love" (Song of Solomon 4:7). Scripture is not embarrassed by a man praising a woman out loud. Many husbands feel this way and never say it. Others praise only by comparison, which wounds more than it blesses. This husband gives both other women and his wife their due. Paul tells husbands to love their wives "just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her" (Ephesians 5:25).
