The LORD does not love His people grudgingly or in silence; He "will rejoice over you with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17). Husbands, your words of delight are meant to echo His.
units.application: Husbands: this week tell your wife, in your own words, what she excels in, and say it to her, not only about her. Never praise her by putting other women down. Wives can do the same for their husbands. Engaged couples: practice specific, honest praise now. Single women and widows: Boaz's words to Ruth show that this praise is not tied to marriage; a life of strength and worth is honored wherever it is lived.

rel.note: Beauty without discretion is like a gold ring in a pig's snout; beauty is never enough on its own.
The book opens with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge and closes by honoring a woman who lives it.
The question that opened the poem is answered here: her worth lies in the fear of the LORD.
The son is warned not to lust after the immoral woman's beauty, a charm that deceives.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, the root of everything praised in her.

units.notes:
• *Passing* translates hevel, a breath or vapor, the word Ecclesiastes uses for "vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The ESV, NASB and KJV read "vain." Beauty is real, but it lasts about as long as a breath.
• *Charm*: the KJV has "Favour." The word means grace or attractiveness, the pleasing impression a person makes on others.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "Charm and beauty are not bad; they simply are inadequate reasons to marry a girl."
• Waltke, quoted by Guzik: "By definition, the fear of the Lord means in part living according to the wisdom revealed in this book."
• The fear of the LORD frames the whole book: "the beginning of knowledge" (1:7), "the beginning of wisdom" (9:10), and here the source of a woman's worth. Compare 1 Samuel 16:7, "man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart," and 1 Peter 3:3–5.
units.summary: The book that began with the fear of the LORD ends by praising a woman who lived it.
units.principle: Lasting worth rests not on appearance or achievement but on the fear of the LORD, and that honor is open to everyone who fears Him.
units.insight: In all Israel "there was no one who was praised as much as Absalom for his good looks" (2 Samuel 14:25), and by his charm he "stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6). His charm led a nation into rebellion and him to his death. Scripture says the opposite of the Messiah: "He has no form or comeliness ... There is no beauty that we should desire Him" (Isaiah 53:2). Yet in Him all worth is found. Our culture spends fortunes on what this verse calls a breath, and many women feel their value fading as it fades. This verse lifts that weight: the praise God gives does not depend on youth, beauty, marriage or productivity. It rests on fearing Him, and that is open to the woman in a hospital bed, the widow living alone and the single woman serving, as fully as to anyone.
units.application: Young men: let the fear of the LORD, not looks or charm, lead your search for a wife (31:10). Parents: praise your daughters for character more than appearance. Women facing aging or illness: rest your worth where God rests it. Single women and widows: this praise is yours as fully as any wife's. Churches: honor women for faithfulness and godliness, not only for visible achievements or family status.

rel.note: The recompense of a person's hands will be rendered to him, the justice this verse asks for her.
Wisdom first cried out at the city gates; the book ends with wisdom lived out and praised in the gates.
Whoever tends the fig tree eats its fruit, as she is to be given the fruit of her hands.
The fruit of her hands that planted the vineyard is the fruit she is now to be given.
The gates where her husband sits among the elders are where her own works now praise her.

units.notes:
• *Give her* is addressed to the community: those who have benefited from her are to honor her. The NLT reads "Reward her for all she has done," and takes the second line as her deeds publicly declaring her praise.
• The acrostic ends here with tav, the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The portrait of the woman of valor is complete from first letter to last.
• Garrett, quoted by Guzik: "She is no less than Woman Wisdom made real."
• Matthew Henry: "if her relations and neighbours altogether hold their peace, her good works will proclaim her praise."
• Compare Acts 9:39, where the widows showed the garments Dorcas had made, and Revelation 14:13, "their works follow them."
units.summary: A wise woman's works need no herald; they praise her in the gates where Wisdom first called.
units.principle: Faithful work deserves honor, and a life of wisdom grounded in the fear of the LORD bears its own public witness.
units.insight: When Mary of Bethany poured costly oil on Jesus, others criticized her (John 12:3–5). Jesus defended her: "wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told as a memorial to her" (Matthew 26:13). He gave her the fruit of her hands, and her deed still praises her wherever the gospel goes. Many women's labor goes unthanked: mothers, caregivers, quiet servants in the church. This verse tells the community to stop overlooking them. It also frees the woman herself from chasing applause. She does not need to announce her own worth; her life speaks. The final word belongs to the Lord, who sees every hidden faithfulness and will say, "Well done, good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:21). A life lived in the fear of the LORD will be honored when He comes.
units.application: Name one woman whose faithful work you have taken for granted, such as a mother, a ministry volunteer or a colleague, and honor her publicly this week: a note, a word in a meeting, thanks given in front of others. Church leaders: build regular, public recognition of quiet servants into church life. Women who serve unseen: you need not promote yourself; let your work speak, and leave the praise to God.
